articles.content:
*Continued from [Part 2](/blog/d80fc125-cardiovascular-system-examination-revised-2012-past-paper-part-2).*

## Topic 5: Percussion and Auscultation
Objectives

At the end of the lesson the learner will be able to: -
1) Percuss and palpate the preacordium in examination of the heart
2) Interpret the findings on physical examination

PERCUSSION

•   Is not routinely done because of the great accuracy of radiological examination.
•   Has some valve if patient is too ill to move by showing the increased area of
    dullness due to pericardial effusion.
•   It may demonstrate the basal dullness of right sternum in cases of aortic
    aneurysm.
•   Is done when there is a possibility of cardiomegally and cardiac tamponade.

AUSCULTATION

### 1.0 Introduction

•   Is an important examination method.
•   Use a suitable stethoscope with:-
    1) A flat diaphragm - filters out low pitched sounds and helps identifying high
        pitched sounds e.g. murmur of aortic regurgitation.
    2) A bell - that is used for auscultation of low-pitched sounds e.g. murmur of
        Mitral stenosis.
    3) The ear-pieces should fit comfortably.
    4) Tubing of about 25 cm long and thick enough to reduce external sounds
•   Auscultation is used to confirm the rate and rhythm of the heart compared to the
    pulse.
•   Will give information on the state of the myocardium/pericardium and the
    functioning of the heart valves.
•   On auscultation, examine for:-
    1) Heart sounds.
    2) Heart rate and rhythm
    3) Murmurs
    4) Other added sounds like the pericardial rub
    5) The different auscultatory areas are chosen due to variability of the heart
        sounds at these areas.

Table: The Auscultatory/Landmark
Area                     Surface marking/Landmark
Mitral/Apex              Apex beat 5th ICS midclavicular line
                         1st heart sound loudest
                         Mitral murmurs and aortic regurgitation murmur
                         3rd & 4th heart sounds
Tricuspid                4th ICS left of the sternum/left sternal edge
Pulmonary                2nd ICS 1 cm to the left of the sternum
Aortic                   2nd ICS 1 cm to the right of the sternum

Auscultation Areas

•   Auscultate over the whole praecordium listening to: the apex, upper and lower
    left edge, upper right sternal edge and over the carotids and into the axial

### 3.0 The procedure of examination

•   At each site:
    o Identify the 1st and 2nd heart sounds
    o Assess the character and intensity of the heart sounds.
    o Listen to the interval between heart and sounds for added sounds and
        murmurs.
    o Roll the patient onto the left side and listen at the apex using the bell lightly
        applied to the skin to detect the murmur of Mitral stenosis.
    o Sit the patient up, leaning forward and listen with the diaphragm for the
        murmur of aortic regurgitation and for the pericardial friction.
    o Note the features of any murmur heard.
    o If a murmur is present, palpate again for an accompanying thrill with the
        patient leaning forward and rolled onto the left side.

### 4.0 The Heart Sounds

•   Auscultate for the heart sounds (1st and 2nd ) and note the following:
    1) The rhythm
    2) Character
    3) Intensity
    4) Splitting of the heart sounds

The Rhythm

•   In a normal rhythm the 1st and 2nd heart sounds are quite close together with

internal following 2nd heart sound being relatively longer.
•   The sequence is lub-dup-pause, lub-dub-pause.

Intensity

•   The intensity can be normal, exaggerated or diminished
•   Exaggeration – the heart sounds become louder in conditions that increase the
    activity of the heart.

    1) Nervousness
    2) Exercise
    3) Hyperthyroidism
    4) Most obvious in the 1st heart sound

•   Diminution is more due to extracardiac than to cardiac causes like:- emphysema
    and fluid/air in pleural/pericardial cavities

Splitting of sounds

• In a normal heart the 1st and 2nd sounds are quite close but, the interval
  following the 2nd sounds is relatively long.
THE FIRST HEART SOUND (1ST HS)

•   Is due to the closure of mitral and tricuspid valves (mainly from the mitral
    element that is louder hence most easily heard)
•   Best heard at the apex region
•   Splitting ‘I-Lub’ -’Dup’ is due to asynchronous closure of Mitral and tricuspid
    valves (not pathological).
•   Abnormalities of intensity of the 1st heart sounds include:- quiet heart sounds,
    loud heart sounds or variable heart sounds

Quiet 1st HS

1) Low cardiac output e.g. pericardial effusion, air in pericardial cavity and mitral
   regurgitation
2) Poor left ventricular function
3) Low filling pressure
4) Emphysema
5) Pleural effusion
6) Air in the pleural cavity

Loud 1st HS

1) Increased cardiac output
2) Large stroke volume
3) Mitral stenosis
4) Atrial fibrillation

Variable 1st HS

1) Atrial fibrillation
2) Extra systoles

3) Complete heart block

THE SECOND HEART SOUNDS (2ND HS)

•   Due to the closure of pulmonary and aortic valves.
•   Best heard using the diaphragm of the stethoscope at the upper sternum at the
    level of 2nd intercostal space.
•   The aortic component is the loudest and is best heard at the aortic area and
    transmitted to the apex.
•   The pulmonary component is best heard at the pulmonary area.
•   Both may be heard (normal splitting) with the aortic component proceeding the
    pulmonary - ‘lub-d-dub’.
•   Intensity of the components varies with age in that the aortic component
    dominates in the older age group as does the pulmonary in the young
    individuals.
•   Splitting of the 2nd Hs persisting throughout the respiratory cycle is due to right
    bundle branch block.
•   Wide fixed splitting of the 2nd Hs is a feature of septal defects.

Abnormalities of the second heart sound.

Quiet
1) Low cardiac output
2) Calcific aortic stenosis
3) Extreme vasodilatation
4) Aortic stenosis
Loud
1) Systemic hypertension (aortic component)
2) Pulmonary hypertension
3) Mitral stenosis
4) Congenital Heart Disease (CHD)
5) Pulmonary disease
6) Corrected transposition of the great vessels

Splitting
1) Fixed splitting (unaffected by respiration)
        a. Aortic septal defect (ASD)
        b. Widens in inspiration (enhanced physiological splitting)
        c. Right bundle branch block
        d. Pulmonary stenosis
        e. Pulmonary hypertension
        f. Ventricular septal defects (VSD)
2) Widens in expiration (reverse splitting)
        a. Left ventricular outflow obstruction
        b. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
        c. Left bundle branch block

THE THIRD HEART SOUND (3RD HS)

•   Is a low-pitched sound (lub-dup-dum, lub-dup-dum) not heard in all subjects and
    comes after the 2nd Hs.
•   Best heard with the bell at the apex and left sternal boarder with patient in a

recumbent position.
•   It is associated with a large stroke volume
•   Physiologically heard in:- children, health young adults, athletes and during
    pregnancy
•   Heard pathologically in-patients with a large poorly contracting ventricle (e.g.
    dilated Cardiomyopathy) or when ventricular stroke volume is increased due to a
    leaking heart valve.

Causes of a third Hs

Physiological
1) Health young adults
2) Athletes
3) Pregnancy
4) Fever

Pathological
1) Large poorly contraction heart (Cardiomyopathy)
2) Mitral and aortic reflux - Large stroke volume
3) Constrictive pericarditis
4) Rheumatic Mitral stenosis
5) Mitral regurgitation
6) Aortic regurgitation
7) Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy

•   3rd Hs is associated with a fast heart beat and quiet 1st and 2nd Hs giving a triple
    rhythm - called a gallop rhythm (S3 gallop).
•   It is a sign of serious myocardial disease.
•   It is best-heard parasternally or in the epigastrium.

FOURTH HEART SOUND (4TH HS)

•   Is a soft low-pitched sound that occurs just before the 1st sound (da-lub-dup,
    da-lub-dup)
•   Caused by increased atrial activity.
•   Also called S4 gallop/presystolic gallop/triple rhythm
•   Heard at the apex

Causes

1) Left ventricular disease
2) Left ventricular hypertrophy
3) Dilated cavity/hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
4) Acute myocardial infarction/Ischaemic heart disease
5) Pulmonary stenosis
6) Pulmonary hypertension

### 5.0 The Heart Rate

•   Determine the heart rate and compare with the pulse rate.

THE RHYTHM

•   Determine whether the rhythm is:-
     o Regular
     o Irregular (regularly irregular or irregularly irregular)
•   Compare with the pulse rhythm.

### 6.0 Added Sounds

•   Examine for
    1) Murmurs
    2) Pericardial rub

MURMURS

Introduction

•   Are musical sounds made by the turbulent blood flow in the heart.
•   Murmurs can be innocent (insignificant) or organic (significant).
•   Are produced by normal volume of blood passing through an abnormal valve or
    increased volume of blood passing through a normal valve (flow murmurs).
•   Originate at the valves or great vessels.
•   Tend to be propagated in the same direction of flow of blood.
•   When examining murmurs consider the following features.
       1. Site
       2. Timing
       3. Character
       4. Intensity/Pitch
       5. Radiation
       6. Relationship to respiration, posture and exercise

Causes of Murmurs

•   Murmurs result from turbulence/velocity of blood flow and Eddy currents
    resulting from modification in size of valve opening, irregularities and
    deformities of the valve and/or its surrounding.
•   Murmurs can be innocent (insignificant) or organic (significant)

    1) Systolic murmurs

       a. Ejection (mid) systolic
              i. Aortic stenosis
             ii. Pulmonary stenosis
            iii. Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)
            iv. Left outflow obstruction e.g. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HOLM)
             v. Right outflow obstruction e.g. Fallot’s tetrology
            vi. Anaemia
           vii. Thyrotoxicosis
          viii. Pregnancy
            ix. Skeletal abnormalities e.g. Kyphoscoliosis and Funnel chest

       b. Pan-systolic
             i. Mitral regurgitation (blowing murmurs)
            ii. Tricuspid regurgitation (low pitched)
           iii. Ventricular septal defect (loud and rough)

       c. Late systolic
             i. Dynamic out flow obstruction (HOCM)
            ii. Mitral valve prolapse
           iii. Coarctication of the aorta

    2) Diastolic
       a. Mid diastolic
             i. Mitral stenosis (low frequency rumbling)
            ii. Tricuspid stenosis
           iii. Austin Flint Murmur
       b. Early diastolic
             i. Aortic regurgitation (Blowing with a variable pitch)
            ii. Graham Steel in pulmonary hypertension (due to Mitral stenosis)

    3) Combined systolic and diastolic
       a. PDA - Patent Ductus Arterious
       b. Aortic stenosis and regurgitation
       c. Mitral stenosis and regurgitation

Timing

•   A murmur can be:-
    1) Systolic - occurs during ventricular systole and accompany the pulse, .follows
       the 1st Hs immediately
    2) Diastolic - occurs during diastolic and follow the pulse, appears immediately
       after the 2nd heart sound.
•   Use the cardiac impulse or carotid pulse to time the murmur.

Systolic Murmurs

•   Can be ejection, pansystolic or late systolic murmur

Ejection Murmur
• Commences after 1st Hs
• They increase in amplitude to a peak about mid-systole becoming quiet towards
   the end of systole (crescendo-decrescendo cadence).
• Appear as a diamond shape on phonocardiogram.
• Are due to:-
    1.Ejection of a normal quantity of blood through a stenosed (normal) aortic or
      pulmonary valve. These are harsh and high-pitched murmurs.
    2.       Ejection of an increased volume of blood through a normal valve (flow
      murmurs)
• Characteristics of flow murmurs.
       o Are of an ejection pattern.
       o May have either a grunting or a musical component
       o Their timing is generally earlier in systole than murmurs due an organic
          obstruction of flow.
       o Arise from either left or right ventricular outflow tracts.
       o Are never associated with any abnormality of the thoracic wall e.g. a
          depressed sternum.
       o The intensity may be increased by physiological maneuvers that increase
          the cardiac output
• Flow murmurs are commonly seen in children, young adults and the elderly.
   They also occur when the stroke volume is increased as in:-
       - Anaemia
       - Thyrotoxicosis
       - Pregnancy
       - Hypertension
       - Chronic anxiety

Pansystolic Murmurs

•   Extend throughout systole right up to and beyond 2nd Hs
•   Have a “blowing” or tearing sound.
•   Show a constant amplitude on phonocardiogram (with a slight accentuation in
    mid systole)
•   Causes
    1) Leakage (regurgitation) - mitral and tricuspid valve
    2) Congenital/Acquired Ventricular Septal Defect
•   Late systolic murmurs are variants of Pansystolic murmurs (e.g. Mitral valve
    prolapse).

Diastolic Murmurs

•   Divided into:- early and mid-diastolic murmurs

Early Diastolic Murmurs

•   Usually due to aortic or pulmonary valve regurgitation.

•   Start immediately after the second heart sound and become quieter as diastole
    proceeds (‘decrescendo murmur’).
•   Sounds like a whispered letter ‘r’.
•   Aortic regurgitation murmur is:
       o Best heard along the left sternal boarder
       o High pitched hence best heard with the diaphragm
       o The patient sits up leaning forward and breathes out fully
       o Radiates in the direction of the regurgitant blood
•   Pulmonary regurgitation murmur.
       o Rare
       o Sometimes heard in-patients with pulmonary hypertension (“Graham
           Steell” murmur -Pulmonary regurgitation secondary to Mitral stenosis).

Mid Diastolic Murmurs

•   Best exemplified by the murmur of Mitral stenosis
•   Begins with the 2nd heart sound and are blowing (High pitched).
•   Mitral stenosis murmur
       o Starts just after the second heart sound.
       o Is proceeded by an opening snap.
       o Is a low-pitched rumbling murmur.
       o Best heard with bell of the stethoscope and with the patient rolled onto
           the left-hand side.

Continuous Murmur

•   Bridges systole and diastole.
•   Most important cause is PDA (Persistent Ductus Arterious duct).

INTENSITY OF MURMURS

•   Described in terms of ‘grades’.
•   Six grades are used to describe systolic while 4 grades for diastolic murmurs.
•   Changes in intensity are of prognostic significant.

Table: The grading of Murmur Intensity
Grade Intensity                      Diastolic
Grade Very soft                      Very soft, Heard only in good circumstances
1
Grade Soft                           soft
2
Grade Moderate, Easily heard, no Moderate
3        thrill                      Heard all over the precordium
         Heard     all   over    the
         precordium
Grade A loud murmur, with a Loud                  or         associated       with
4        thrill                      a palpable thrill
Grade Very loud with thrill,         often heard over wide area with thrill
5

Grade    Extremely   loud,       heard Associated with a palpable thrill
6        without
         stethoscope

CHARACTER/QUALITY

•   Vary from soft blowing to harsh rasping murmurs.
•   Loud and rough murmurs suggest organic valvular or congenital lesions.
•   Soft murmurs are usually innocent (although an aortic regurgitation murmur is
    soft).
•   There is no correlation between the loudness of a murmur and the
    haemodynamic severity of the lesions causing it.

DISTRIBUTION/SITE

• Murmurs are heard over the session causing them.
• Describe the position/site where the murmur is best-heard (area of greatest
  intensity of the murmur) and its place of origin (production).
RADIATION/SPREAD OF MURMURS

•   Murmurs radiate in the direction of the turbulent blood flow.
•   When the maximum intensity of a murmur has been noted, move the
    stethoscope radically from this point in different directions and determine
    whether the murmur is circumscribed/localized or widely transmitted/radiating.
•   The absence or presence of radiation is a characteristic of some murmurs

Table: Radiation of Murmurs
MURMUR                    RADIATION PATTERN
Aortic Stenosis           To upper right sternal edge and neck
Aortic Regurgitation      Down left sternal boarder and towards the apex
Mitral Stenosis           To apex (very localized)
Mitral Regurgitation      Apex to axilla and back
Pulmonary Stenosis        To upper left sternal boarder, beneath clavicle
                          and to back
Pulmonary                 Down left sternal boarder
Regurgitation
Tricuspid Stenosis        Lower left sternal boarder (Localized)
Tricuspid Regurgitation Lower left and right sternal boarder and
                          epigastrium
Ventricular        Septal Lower sternal boarder
Defect

RELATION TO RESPIRATION, POSTURE AND EXERCISE

•   Innocent murmurs are modified by respiration.
•   Aortic diastolic murmurs can best be heard on expiration while tricuspid
    murmurs on inspiration.
•   Aortic diastolic murmur is best heard when patient is sitting leaning forward.
•   Mitral diastolic murmur is best heard when patient is recumbent especially in left

lateral position.

ADDED SOUNDS

1) Valve opening sounds in thickened valves
2) Prosthetic heart valves
3) Pericardial rub
   • A feature of acute pericarditis
   • Best heard with the diaphragm
   • Most obvious in systole
   • Listen for it in both inspiration and expiration
4) Bruits
   • Non-cardiac sounds
   • Due to arterial stenosis
   • Are murmurs arising from a peripheral artery
   • Occur at the sites of arterial stenosis

## Topic 7: Investigations and Therapeutic Procedures
Objectives

At the end of the lesson the learner will be able to: -
1) Outline investigations in cardiovascular diseases and disorders
2) Interpret the common investigation findings in cardiovascular diseases and
    disorders

INTRODUCTION

1. IMAGING

 i) CHEST X-RAY

   •   Is taken in postero-anterior (PA) direction at maximum inspiration.
   •   The heart is close to the X-ray film to minimize magnification of the chest with
       respect to the thorax.
   •   Lateral view chest X-ray may give more information when PA is abnormal.
   •   Look at the heart size, calcification and lung fields

Heart Size

i) The cardio-thoracic Ratio (CTR)
    • The maximum transverse diameter of the heart is compared with the
        maximum

•   Transverse diameter of the chest measured from the inside of the ribs.
       •   Is usually less than 0.5 (50%) except in:-
           1) Neonates
           2) Infants
           3) Athletes
           4) Patients with skeletal deformities (Scoliosis, funnel chest)
       •   A transverse cardiac diameter of more than 15.5 cm is abnormal.
       •   Pericardial effusion or cardiac dilation increases the ratio.

ii) Patterns of specific chamber enlargement seen on the chest X-ray

       a. Left Atrial dilatation
           • Prominence of the left atrial appendage on the left heart boarder.
           • A double atrial shadow to the right of the sternum.

       b. Left ventricular enlargement
           • Increased CTR
           • Smooth elongation and increased convexity of the heart border.

       c. Right Atrial enlargement
           • Right boarder of the heart projects into right lower lung field.

       d. Right ventricular enlargement

           •   Increased CTR
           •   Upward displacement of the apex of the heart.

       e. Ascending aortic dilatation/enlargement
           • Prominence of the aortic shadow

       f. Dissecting of the ascending aorta
           • Widening of the mediastinum

  Calcification

  ✓ Occurs due to tissue degeneration
  ✓ Seen on the lateral or a penetrated PA view but best studied by CT scanning
  ✓ Calcification can be seen in:- Pericardial
  ✓ Valvular

  Lung Fields

  •    Increased in vascularity an in size of hilar vessels seen when there are left to
       right shunts.
  •    When there is pulmonary ligaemia there is a paucity of vascular markings and a
       reduction in diameter of arteries.
  •    Prominence of pulmonary arteries hili and pruned (reduced in size) at the
       peripheral Lung fields as seen in pulmonary arterial hypertension.

iii)   MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging)

  - Non-invasive imaging technique


- A powerful magnetic field is used

iv)


Nuclear Imaging

 •    Primarily used is Ischaemic Heart Disease
 •    Myocardial structure & function can be assessed by radio-nucleide imaging
      techniques
 •    Thallium (with behaves as potassium) is taken up by healthy myocardium
 •    Ischaemia or infarction produces unclear image with a “cold” spot.

v)    CT Scanning

 •    Useful showing the size and shape of the cardiac chambers as well as the
      thoracic abdominal aorta and Mediastinum.

 2.    ELECTROCARDIOGRAM (EGG)

     • Is a recording of the electrical activity of the heart
     • Is the only way of diagnosing rhythm and conduction problems
     • Is the vector sum of the depolarization and repolarization potential of the
       myocardial cells (Summation of action potentials of all myocardial cells)
     • The shape of the wave form of the EGG depends on the speed and direction of
       the depolarization process through the heart
     • Depolarization initiating each heart beat begins at Sino-Atrial node and spreads
       as an advancing wave through the atria which are depolarized simultaneously to
       the A-V Node
     • Depolarization spreads from the atria to ventricles via the Bundle of HIS that
       begins at A-V Node passing into the interventricular septum where it divides into
       right and left branches
     • Left branch divides into 2 smaller branches (fascicles) which supply anterior and
       posterior parts of left ventricle respectively
     • Bundle branches subdivide into the Purkinje fibres that form a network of cells
       to carry the depolarization wave to the myocardial cells
     • Return of ventricular muscle cells to their resting electrical state is called
       repolarization

 EGG Waveform


Terminology

•   P wave - 1st deflection corresponds to depolarization and the atria
•   QRS Complex - 3 deflections - 1st downwards (Q wave), 2nd upwards (R wave)
    and 3rd downwards (S wave) corresponds to depolarization of the ventricle.
•   T Wave        - repolarization of ventricular muscles.
•   Upward deflection is a depolarization wave is moving towards recording
    electrodes
•   Downward deflection repolarization wave is moving away from the recording
    electrodes.

Time intervals

•   All EGG recorders run a standard paper speed of 25 mm/s.
•   EGG paper is standardized so that 5 large squares pass under the recorder stylus
    each second.
•   One large square is equivalent to 0.2 sec.
•   Each large square is subdivided into five small squares each equivalent to 0.04s.
•   Heart rate can be calculated from the number of squares between QRS
    complexes.
•   Time taken by each part of the depolarization sequence in each cardiac cycle is
•   Calculated by the number of small squares it occupies.

PR interval
• Is the time taken for depolarisation to spread from SAN to Atria to AVN through
   the Bundle of HIS bundle to the ventricle
• Shown by number of small squares between beginning of P wave and the
   beginning of the ORS complex.
• Normal upper limit 0.20 seconds.
• Width of QRS complex indicates the time taken by the depolarisation wave to
   spread throughout the ventricles.

QT intervals
• Time taken for the whole depolarization sequence in ventricles.
• Obtained from the number of squares between beginning of QRS complex and of

T wave.

Abnormalities of Conduction

(a) AV Node/Bundle of HIS
• Prolonged PR interval
    1) 1st degree heart block - P Wave is followed by QRS complex.
    2) 2nd degree heart block - some P waves are followed by QRS complexes but
       others are not. There are 3 varieties of 2nd degree heart block
    3) 3rd degree (complex) – no P waves are conducted, ventricular escape rhythm
       controls the heart with a slow rate, QRS complexes are wide and abnormal.

(b) His bundle branches

•   Right bundle - Branch block, broadening of QRS complex
•   Left bundle branch block - wide QRS complex, inverted T wave

3. ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY

- Use echoes of ultrasound waves to map the heart and study its function.

4. PHONOCARDIOGRAPHY

•   Application of a sensitive microphone to the chest which allows heart sounds and
    murmurs to be recorded.

5. CARDIAC CATHETERIZATION

•   Is introduction of a thin radio-opaque tube (catheter) into the circulation
•   The pressure in the right heart chambers, left ventricle, Aorta and pulmonary
    artery can be measured.
•   During the procedure blood samples can be taken to measure the concentration
    of Ischaemic metabolites e.g. lactate oxygen content.
•   Radio opaque contrast material is injected.
•   Quality intra-cardiac shunts

6. Others

1) Full Haemogram + ESR
2) Blood Cultures
3) Urea/Electrolytes
4) Liver Function Tests
5) Urinalysis

# Cardiovascular System Examination — Complete Study Guide

Clinical Methods and Communication
                                  Carey Francis Okinda
                                   March/April 2012

          Examination of the Cardiovascular System – 10 hours

Unit Outline
1) Review of anatomy and physiology                      -      2 hours
2) History taking                                 -      1 hour
3) Introduction and general examination           -      2 hours
4) Inspection and Palpation                       -      2 hours
5) Percussion and Auscultation                    -      2 hours
6) Investigations and therapeutic procedures             -      1 hour

## Topic 1: Review of Anatomy and Physiology
Objectives
At the end of the lesson the learner will be able to: -
1) Describe the structure of the organs of the cardiovascular system
2) Describe the functions of the cardiovascular system
3) Explained the functional organization of the cardiovascular system

### 1.0 Introduction
The Circulatory system is a continuous circuit comprising of the cardiovascular system
(heart and blood vessels) and lymphatic system (lymph vessels, lymph nodes and
lymphoid-organs -spleen, thymus and tonsils). Blood serves numerous functions
including the transport of respiratory gases, nutritive molecules, metabolic wastes and
hormones. Blood is transported through the body in a system of vessels leading from
and returning to the heart.
Figure 1.1: The Cardiovascular system

Functions of the Circulatory System

1) Transportation
   • Respiratory - red blood cells (erythrocytes) transport oxygen to tissue cells and
      carbon dioxide is transported by blood to the lungs foe elimination
   • Nutritive - blood carries absorbed products of digestion through the liver to
      body cells
   • Excretory - metabolic wastes, excessive water and ions are filtered through the
      capillaries of the kidney and excreted in urine

2) Regulation
   • Blood carries hormones and other regulatory molecules from the site of origin
      to target tissues

3) Protection
   • Protects against injury and foreign microbes or toxins
   • Clotting mechanism prevents blood loss when vessels are damaged
   • Leucocytes (white blood cells) provide immunity

THE CARDIOVASCULAR SYSTEM

Is made up of the heart and blood vessels

The Heart

The heart is a four chambered; double pump that keeps blood flowing through the
circulation and a normal heart weighs 250 – 350 g in an adult. Its pumping action
creates the pressure needed to push blood in the vessels to the lungs and body cells.
The function of the heart is to pump sufficient oxygenated blood containing nutrients,
metabolites and hormones to meet the moment to moment metabolic needs and
preserve a constant milieu. The flow of blood through the circulatory system is made
possible by the pumping action of the ventricles and atria

Figure 2: The Heart

The Heart Pump

The heart has 2 main pumps that operate as connected in series i.e. the left pump
(for the peripheral organs) and the right pump (for the lungs). The right and left
pumps are separated by a muscular wall (septum) which prevents mixing of blood
from the two sides of the heart. Each pump has 2 chambers (the ventricle and the
atria). In detail the heart has 4 pumps of which 2 are primer pumps (the atria) and 2
power pumps (the ventricles). The atria receive blood from the venous system then
pump it into the ventricles which pump blood into the arterial system.

The Heart Valves

Normal functioning of the heart depends on the mechanical efficiency of the 4 valves
namely aortic valve, mitral valve, tricuspid valve and pulmonary valve. The
atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid valves) consist of 4 kinds of structures
namely an annulus ring, cusps, papillary muscles and chordae tendinae. Normal
functioning depends on the mechanical efficiency of the cusps, chordae tendinae,
papillary muscles, pliability and size of the fibrous ring or annulus and adequacy of left
ventricular contraction. The semi-lunar valves (aortic and pulmonary valves) each
consist of 2 kinds of structures namely an annulus and semi-lunar cusps

The Conducting System

The contraction and relaxation of the heart’s musculature is highly coordinated during
the cardiac cycle. The coordination is controlled by a system of highly specialized
myocardial cells (the conducting system). The conducting system provide a nodular
cluster of cells which initiate the conduction signal and supplies cellular tracts to
propagate this signal through the atria and ventricular musculature. The 3 parts of the
conducting system found in the walls of the right atrium are: - sino-atrial node (SAN),

the internodal tracts and atrio-ventricular node (AVN). The atrioventricular (AV)
bundle (bundle of his) is a tract of cells originating from the AV node and passing
through an opening in the fibrous annulus of tricuspid valve extending through the
membranous part of the inter-ventricular septum. At the boarder between
membranous and muscular parts of the inter-ventricular septum it divides into 2
major branches (left and right bundle branches). Purkinje fibres are the terminal
cells of the conducting system in both ventricles. They are very large diameter cells
whose terminal process ends in the sub-endocardial myocardium. Transmit the
contraction signal directly to the sub-endocardial myocardium of the ventricular walls

Functioning of the Heart

•   It has 2 essential characteristics of contractility and rhythmicity
•   Is a pumping organ whose physiological function is maintained by healthy muscles,
    efficient Heart valves, efficient conducting system and coordination of the
    chambers and normal peripheral resistance
•   Has 3 major types of cardiac muscle - atrial, ventricular and specialized excitatory
    and conductive muscles
•   The Atrial and ventricular muscle types contract as skeletal muscles but the
    duration of contraction is much longer
•   The specialized excitatory and conductive fibres contract feebly but have
    rhythmical properties and rapid conduction
•   The cardiac muscles as a syncytium
    o Comprises of many cells connected in series with intercalated discs(contain
       specialized structures) separating the cells
    o The special structures are: -
        ▪ Facia adherens that give the mechanical links
        ▪ Mucula adherens(desmosome) the site for cytoplasmic filaments and is the
           lattice structure for the cell
        ▪ Gap junction which makes adjacent cells close and allows low permeability of
           ions through the membrane prolonging the electrical signal
•   The heart is composed of 2 separate syncytium namely the atrial and ventricular
    which are separated by fibrous tissue

Energy for contraction
• The coronary blood flow is 0.8ml/min/g
• Arterial oxygen content is 180ml/L
• Coronary sinus oxygen content is 68ml/L(oxygen saturation of 37% and PCO2 =
   25mmHg)
• The heart weighs 300mg therefore oxygen consumption is 27ml/min for the whole
   heart or 0.09/ml/g

       68 x 37 = 27.16(27ml/min)               =      27/300 = 0.09/ml/g/min
         100

•   The oxygen utilized in the mitochondria to generate ATP which is transported
    across the mitochondria membrane

Calcium

•   When sufficient ATP is present, contraction of the cardiac muscle is brought about
    by changes in concentration of calcium within the cell

All or Nothing Principle

•   Due to syncytial and interconnecting, stimulation of any single atrial muscle fibre
    causes the action potential to travel over the entire muscle mass. The same holds
    for the ventricles
•   If the A-V bundle is intact the action potential spreads from the atria to the
    ventricles (All Or Nothing Principle)

Action Potentials in Cardiac muscle

•   The resting membrane potential of normal cardiac muscle is -85 t0 –95mV and for
    the specialized areas is –90 to –100mV
•   Action potential of ventricular mass of +105mV indicates a rise from the normal
    very negative( -85mV to –95Mv) value to slight positive value of +20mV( -85Mv +
    105Mv = +20mV).This change of potential from –ve to +ve , the positive portion is
    called overshoot potential
•   After the initial spike, the membranes remain depolarized (0.2 sec for the atria and
    3.0sec for ventricles) exhibiting a plateau
•   The plateau in the action potential causes contraction to last 20 to 50 times longer
    than the skeletal muscles
•   The action potential for cardiac muscle is long and has a plateau because:

    1. Skeletal muscles action potential is caused by sudden opening of sodium
       channels which remain open for a short time whereas in the cardiac muscle the
       action potential is caused by 2 types of channels
           ✓ Fast sodium channels
           ✓ Slow calcium sodium channels which are slow to open and remain open
              longer
    2. After the onset of actin potential the permeability of cardiac muscle membrane
       for K+ ions decreases fivefold decreasing the out flux of K+ ions hence
       preventing early recovery and prolonging the state of depolarization

Figure 3: Action potentials (2)

The Cardiac Cycle

Is the period from the end of one heart contraction to the end of the next consisting of
relaxation (diastole) period followed by the contraction (systole) period. Events of the
cardiac cycle include - phase I (atrial contraction), phase II (isovolumic
ventricular/Isometric) contraction, phase III (ventricular systole – period of ejection),
phase IV (isovolumic ventricular/Isometric) relaxation and phase V

Diagram 4: The Cardiac Cycle

Cardiac Output

The five basic mechanisms by which Cardiac output can be adjusted are -
1. Heart rate

2. Filling pressure
3. Ventricular dispensability
4. Systemic vascular resistance
5. Ventricular contractility

Cardiac output = Heart rate (HR) x Stroke volume of the left ventricle (SV)

               = Total oxygen absorbed per minute
                 Oxygen absorbed by each litre of blood

               = Oxygen absorbed per minute by the lungs (mls/min)
                 Artero-venous oxygen difference (mls/litre of blood)

Normal cardiac output for a young healthy male adult is 5.6 litres per minute (4 – 8
litres per minute). Females have 10% less

Stroke volume

Is the diastolic volume of the ventricle – the volume of blood in the ventricle at the end
of systole. Cardiac index is the cardiac output per square meter of the body surface
area (the normal for a young male adult is 3.0 litres/minute and changes with age)

Ohms Law

Blood flow = Input resistance – output resistance
                    Resistance

Venous return = Arterial pressure – right atrial pressure
                   Total peripheral resistance

              BUT right atrial pressure is 0

Therefore Venous return =          Arterial pressure
                                   Total peripheral resistance

BLOOD VOLUMES

1) End-diastolic volume: - during diastole, filling of ventricles increases volume of
   each ventricle to 120 – 130 mls (End-diastolic volume)
2) Stroke volume output - during systole (emptying) volume decreases by 70mls
   (Stroke volume output)
3) End-systolic volume - remaining volume of 50 – 60mls (End systolic volume)
4) Ejection fraction - stroke volume (70mls) X 100 = 58.3 %( 60%), End-diastolic
   volume

THE LAWS

1. Starling’s Law
   • Increase dilatation leads to increased filling, contraction and stroke volume.
   • During exertion, there is a greater venous return to the heart with subsequent
      increase in diastolic filling and the stretching of the muscle fibre. The response
      is a more vigorous contraction

2. Frank-Starling Law
   • Within physiological limits, the heart pumps all the blood that comes to it
      without allowing excessive damming of blood in the veins
   • The greater the heart is filled during diastole, the greater will the amount of
      blood pumped into the aorta

3. Laplaces Law
   • The circumferential force tending to stretch the muscle fibres in the vessel wall
      is proportional to the to diameter of the vessel multiplied by the pressure
      inside the vessel
   • F=DXP
   • Or the wall tension required to counteract a given pressure in a spherical cavity
      is proportional to the radius of the cavity

Regulation of Heart Function

4 essential factors are: -
   1) Venous return
   2) Outflow resistance
   3) Ionotropic state or contractility
   4) Heart rate

•   Venous return, Pre-load and Frank-Starling law depends on: - intrinsic state of the
    muscle, prevailing neuro-hormonal state
•   Outflow resistance and after-load
•   Myocardial contractility and ionotropic State
•   Heart rate

BLOOD VESSELS

•   Form a tubular network throughout the body that permits blood flow to flow from
    the heart to all the living cells of the body and back to the heart
•   The thick muscle layer of the arteries allows them to transmit blood ejected from
    the heart under high pressure and the elastic recoil of the larger arteries further
    contributes to blood flow
•   The thinner muscle layer of veins allows them to distend when an increased
    amount of blood enters them and their one-way valves ensure that blood flows
    back to the heart
•   Capillaries are composed of a single layer of endothelium which allows water and
    other molecules to move across the capillary walls permitting exchanges between

the blood and tissue fluid
•   The walls of arteries and veins have 3 coats(“tunics”) – tunica externa, media and
    intima
•   The arterial system branches extensively to deliver blood to over 40 billion
    capillaries in the body
•   Capillaries provide a total surface area of 1000 sq. Miles for exchanges between
    blood and tissue fluid
•   Pre-capillary sphincter muscles determine the amount of blood passing through a
    particular capillary bed
•   Blood flow through an organ is determined by the action of pre-capillary sphincters
    and the degree of resistance to blood flow due to constriction or dilatation of small
    arteries and arterioles in the organ
•   The walls of capillaries are composed of only one cell layer – a simple squamous
    epithelium or endothelium
•   Absence of smooth muscle and connective tissue layers allows rapid rate of
    transport of materials between the blood and tissues

Types of Capillaries

•   Different organs have different capillaries
•   Classified in terms of their endothelial lining
•   There are 3 types – continuous, discontinuous and fenestrated
•   Continuous capillaries found in muscles, lungs, adipose tissue and central nervous
    system (CNS) have their adjacent endothelial cells are closely joined together. In
    the CNS they lack intercellular channels a fact that contributes to the blood-brain
    barrier. In other organs they have narrow intercellular channels that allow passage
    of small molecules
•   Discontinuous capillaries found in bone marrow, liver and spleen appear as little
    cavities(sinusoids) and have the distance between endothelial cells is so great
•   Fenestrated capillaries found in endocrine glands, kidneys and intestines have wide
    intercellular pores covered by a layer serving as a diaphragm

Topic 2 – History Taking in Cardiovascular Disease
Objectives
At the end of the lesson the learner will be able to: -

1) Take a comprehensive history of a patient with cardiovascular disease

### 1.0 Approach to the Patient

•   We can use the (5) fingers of the hand to outline the relevant items for
    Cardiovascular System examination as represented below:
    1) Thumb                 -     Medical History
    2) Index finger          -     Physical Examination
    3) Middle finger         -     Chest X-ray (CXR)
    4) Ring finger           -     ECG
    5) Small finger          -     Special Diagnostic Procedures
•   A clenched fist will therefore imply that all the diagnostic techniques are used
    together and are correlated.
•   Examination of the CVs should be performed in 5 stages.
    1) General appearance
    2) Physical signs associated with arterial circulation
    3) Physical signs associated with venous circulation
    4) Physical signs in the lungs as part of the circulation
    5) Physical signs associated with the heart itself.

Making a Diagnosis
A complete diagnosis of cardiovascular disease can be: -
1) Etiological e.g. Rheumatic Heart Disease, Hypertension
2) Anatomical e.g. Mitral stenosis, Right Ventricular Hypertrophy, Left ventricular
   Hypertrophy
3) Physiological e.g. Congestive Cardiac Failure (CCF)
4) Physical Capacity - i) Functional and ii) Therapeutic
5) Functional - Based on Dyspnoea Assessment Cardiac Status Assessment

Table 1: Grading Of Dyspnoea
The New York Heart Association Functional and Therapeutic Classification
Grade     Features
Grade 1   No breathlessness
Grade 2   Breathlessness on severe
          exertion
Grade 3   Breathlessness      on    mild
          exertion
Grade 4   Breathlessness at rest

Table 2: Grading Of Cardiac status
Grade       Features
Grade 1     Uncompromised
Grade 2     Slightly compromised
Grade 3     Moderately compromised
Grade 4     Severely compromised
Diagnosis will therefore involve: -

1) History taking which should be thorough, informative and comprehensive
2) Physical examination should be thorough and systematic using the correct
   techniques of examination. This involves both general and systemic examination
3) Investigations will give clues to the causes and extend of the damage. They will be
   very useful in monitoring the progress of the patient during the period of
   management. This will include radiological and laboratory investigations

History Taking

•   Remember the words of Xenophanes - a Greek philosopher 500 BC who said “All of
    him sees, all of him listens and all of him thinks”
•   Therefore history taking will involve:- talking, listening, observing and thinking
•   When taking the history - many diagnostic clues are found, ascertain severity of the
    disease and asses the personality of the patient
•   Establish good Doctor/Patient relationship

### 2.0 Symptoms Of Cardiovascular Disease

1) Principal symptoms
      a. Dyspnoea
      b. Pain
      c. Oedema/ankle swelling
      d. Palpitations
      e. Dizziness/blackouts

2) Other symptoms include - easy fatiguability, haemoptysis, fatigue, cyanosis, poor
   vision, disturbed renal function, gastro-intestinal symptoms, cerebral symptoms
   and impairment of liver function

1. Dyspnoea

Dyspnoea is breathlessness, shortness of breath (“unhappy breathing”) or undue
awareness of the respiratory effort or need to increase the effort. The awareness of
respiratory effort is related to the increased force used to ventilate the lungs e.g. rigid
thoracic cage and abnormally rigid pleura

Causes
• What are the causes of dyspnoea?

Sensation of Dyspnoea

•   Is derived from receptors sensitive to stretch and deflation in thoracic cage and
    lungs, chemoreceptors in aorta, Carotid arteries and Reticular substance (medulla)
    sensitive to oxygen lack, excess carbon-dioxide and pH changes.

Mechanism of Cardiac Dyspnoea: -

Reflex vasoconstriction/                         Central Perception
Tachycardia                                of Dyspnoea

Raised Left atrial          pulmonary venous           altered muscle metabolism
Pressure                    distension

                            Stimulation of                             Muscle
                            Lung Receptors                            receptors

Increased Lung                     Pulmonary                                         Lactic
Stiffness                   interstitial                                  Acidosis
                            Oedema

                            HYPOXAEMIA
Grading of Dyspnoea

Grade I       Breathing feels as good as that of others of own age, sex and build at
              work, walking, climbing hills or stairs.

Grade II      Able to walk with others of own age, sex and build on levels but more to
              keep up on hills and stairs

Grade III     Unable to keep on level but bale to walk to about one mile or more at
              own speed

Grade IV      Unable to walk more than 100 yards on level without resting due to
              breathlessness

Grade V       Breathlessness on talking or undressing or inability to leave house
              because of breathlessness

Clinical aspects and causes of Dyspnoea

•   Dyspnoea at rest - acute pulmonary oedema, acute pulmonary embolism
•   Orthopnoea - cardiac failure
•   Dyspnoea on effort
•   Paroxysmal nocturnal Dyspnoea (PND)
    o Acute pulmonary oedema (Acute left ventricular failure LVF), Ischaemic Heart
        Disease, Aortic Valve Disease, Hypertension, Cardiomyopathy, Atrial Fibrillation,
        Rarely in Mitral Disease or Atrial Tumours
•   Differential diagnosis of dyspnoea
        - Asthma
        - Sleep apnoea Syndrome

Table 4: Timing of the onset of breathlessness
Time             Causes
Seconds/Minut Left Ventricular Failure (LVF), Pulmonary Embolism,
es               Pneumothorax, Asthma
   Hours/Days Left Ventricular Failure (LVF), Pneumonia, Asthma
                 Pleural Effusion, Allergic Alveolitis, Adult Respiratory Distress
                 Syndrome
   Weeks         Left Ventricular Failure (LVF), Anaemia, Asthma, Pleural Effusion
   Months/Yea Chronic Inflow Obstruction, Asthma, Pulmonary Fibrosis,
   rs            Anaemia

Table 5: The differences and similarities between Pulmonary Oedema and Asthma

Pulmonary Oedema                           Asthma
Severely breathless                        Severely breathless
Dry cough                                  Cough variable
Sputum – white froathy and may             Sputum – variable, not pink or blood
be pink or blood flecked                   flecked
Patient wants to sit up                    Patient restless, may want to sit up
Pale, cold, sweaty                         Sweaty (if severe)
Cyanosis if severe                         Cyanosis is severe
Shallow rapid breathing                    Expiration > inspiration
Widespread crepitations, wheezing          Wheezing (not invariable)
Past history of heart disease              History of asthma

Causes of Breathlessness

1) Cardiac:- heart failure, ischaemic heart disease, pulmonary embolism and
   pulmonary hypertension
2) Respiratory disease:- disease of the lungs, bronchi, pleura and thoracic Cage
3) Increased demand: - as a result of central receptors by hypoxia, high altitude and
   anaemia
4) Acidosis:- diabetes, uraemia
5) Increases metabolic demand:- fever, thyrotoxicosis
6) Psychogenic factors:- Anxiety and hyperventilation
7) Obesity
8) Lack of physical fitness

2. Pain

•   Chest pain is an important symptom of heart disease which is usually associated
    with Ischaemic Heart Disease.

Causes of Chest Pain

1) Cardiac - ischaemic heart disease/angina, pericarditis, dissecting aneurysm of the
   aorta and mitral valve prolapse
2) Respiratory - pneumothorax, pleuritic pain/pleurisy, pulmonary embolism and
   pulmonary hypertension
3) Oesophagitis and Oesophageal Rupture
4) Mediastinitis
5) Costocondritis
6) Musculo-skeletal pain - bone and muscle pain
7) Nervous - nerve root pain, anxiety and “precordial catch” - effort(Da Costas)
   syndrome

The characteristics of pain include: - SOCRATES

Types of cardiac pain
1) Angina
2) Myocardial infarct
3) Pericarditic pain
4) Dissecting aneurysm

Angina

•   Site - is retro-sternal
•   Radiates to arm, epigastrium, neck
•   Precipitated by: - physical exertion, emotional exertion, emotional excitement, cold,
    exercise, after meal
•   Relieving factors include:- rest, warm weather, nitrates

Table 6: Grading of Angina in Effort - The Canadian Cardiovascular Society Grading of
Angina in Effort

Grade Features
I     Ordinary physical activity does not cause Angina (strenuous physical
      activity provokes Angina)
II    Slight limitations of ordinary physical activity (climbing more than one
      flight of stairs or walking uphill provokes Angina)
III   Marked limitations of physical activity ( walking on the level or climbing
      one flight of stairs provokes Angina)
IV    Inability to carry on any physical activity ( Angina may be present at rest)

Myocardial Infarction

•   Site - as Angina
•   No obvious precipitation(s)
•   Not relieved by rest/nitrates
•   Usually severe (may be silent)
•   Anxiety is severe

•   Increased sympathetic activity

Pericarditic Pain

•   Site - Retro-sternal may radiate to left shoulder or back, felt in the center of the
    chest
•   Onset - No obvious initial precipitating factor, tends to fluctuate in intensity
•   Nature - May be stabbing or ‘raw-like sand paper’ usually described as sharp nd
    rarely described as tight or heavy
•   Made worse by changes in posture, respiration and movement
•   Relieved by analgesics
•   Accompanied by a pericardial rub
•   Is due to Pericarditis whose causes include:- bacterial and viral pericarditis,
    myocardial infarction, rheumatic fever, connective tissue disorder, trauma,
    uraemia

Dissecting Aortic Aneurysm/Enlarging Aortic Aneurysm

•   Site - often felt between the shoulder blades, may be felt retro-sternal, in neck or
    in abdomen, characteristically radiates to the back
•   Onset - usually sudden, may follow sudden twist or exertion
•   The pain is sudden and is usually described as ‘tearing’ in nature
•   The pain tends to persist and the patients are often restless
•   Is accompanied by:- asymmetrical pulses, unexpected bradycardia, early diastolic
    murmur, weakness in the legs

Pleuritic Chest Pain

1) Pleural disease e.g. infective e.g. pneumonia; pulmonary infarction/pulmonary
   emboli; neoplasm – primary, secondary; collagen diseases - S.L.E., rheumatoid
   arthritis; Asbestos related
2) Musculo-skeletal system e.g. fracture of the ribs, muscular strains and Herpes
   zooster (pre-rash stage)

3. Oedema

•   Ankle swelling/sacral swelling
•   Pulmonary oedema is a feature of acute left heart failure

Systemic Causes

1) Cardiac e.g. heart failure, venous stasis/venous insufficiency, constrictive
   Pericarditis
2) Renal e.g. nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis and renal failure
3) Liver disease - low plasma albumin, hepatic failure, hepatitis, cirrhosis
4) Malnutrition

Local Causes

1) Venous obstruction in pelvis/abdomen
2) Drugs, idiopathic oedema (mainly in women)
3) Immobility and lymphatic obstruction

4. Palpitations

•   This is the increased awareness of the normal heart beat or the sensation of slow
    or rapid heart rate or an irregular heart rhythm.
•   Causes
     o Normal heart beat is sensed when patient is:- anxious, excited, exercising, lying
           on the left side
     o Cardiac Arrhythmias e.g. premature ectopic beats and paroxysmal Tachycardia

5. Syncope

• Is the transient loss of consciousness due to an acute decrease in cerebral
   blood flow.,

Vasovagal syncope
• Both vagal slowing of the heart and decreased vasomotor tone
• Patient complains of dizziness before the faint
• Occurs in severe circulatory catastrophes e.g. - severe myocardial infarction,
   severe pulmonary embolism

Causes:

1) Cardiac
   • Arrhythmias e.g. ventricular tachycardia, rapid super-ventricular tachycardia,
      atrio-ventricular block, artificial pacemaker failure
   • Obstruction       -    aortic/pulmonary      stenosis,  hypertrophic/obstructive
      cardiomyopathy, Fallot’s tetralogy, pulmonary hypertension/embolism, atrial
      myoxoma, atrial thrombus, defective prosthetic valve
   • Situational - neurocardiogenic/reflexic/vasovagal
   • Haemorrhage
   • Fear/pain
   • Anoxia
   • Upright posture (postural hypotension)
   • Carotid sinus syndrome
2) Micturition syncope
3) Areflexia/paralytic postural hypotension e.g. Tabes dorsalis, diabetes, alcohol and
   drugs, traumatic quadriplegia and polyneuropathy

6. Easy Fatigability
   • The ordinary daily chores/tasks become a burden to the patient e.g. climbing
      stairs, fast walking
   • Patient complains of fatigue

7. Haemoptysis
   • Is blood stained sputum
   • Varies from small streaks of blood to massive haemoptysis
   • Massive haemoptysis (> 200 mls of blood in 24 hours) is usually due to
     bronchiectasis or tuberculosis.
   • Causes of haemoptysis

       Common
         1) Pulmonary thromboembolism
         2) Bronchial carcinoma
         3) Tuberculosis
         4) Chronic bronchitis
         5) Bronchiectasis
         6) Pulmonary Oedema
         7) Suppurative pneumonia
         8) Mitral stenosis/heart failure

Uncommon
         1) Chest trauma
         2) Arterio-venous malformations
         3) Benign tumours
         4) Foreign
         5) Clotting disorders
8.

Cyanosis

   •   Is the dusky blue discolouration of the skin particularly at the extremities and
       mucous membranes (Causes - See general examination)

9. Disturbed Vision

   •   Retinal haemorrhage in hypertension
   •   Embolism as in rheumatic heart disease and infective endocarditiss

10. Renal Function
    • Disturbed renal function is a feature in severe cardiac failure as it depends on
      the cardiac output.

11. Liver Function
   •   Liver function disturbances that occur in cardiac failure include jaundice and
       abdominal pain

12. Gastro-Intestinal Tract

   •   Gastro-intestinal symptoms can be encountered in compromised cardiac
       function states.

### 3.0 Family History

   •   Establish any family history of heart disease
   •   Take note of any associated heart disease like Marfan’s syndrome, hypertrophic
       cardiomyopathy, ischaemic heart disease and hypertension
   •   Family history of hypertension

### 4.0 Past Medical History

   •   Thorough history of disease conditions and the medication the patient is taking
       or Has been taking
   •   Past history of myocardial infarction and stroke
   •   Make a complete list of medications taken (prescribed and PTC drugs) as the
       patient’s complains could be related to (or as a result of) use of drugs
       1) Dyspnoea - Beta-blockers in Asthmatics, exacerbation of cardiac failure by: -
          beta-blockers, Calcium channel blockers and NSAIDS
       2) Pain - Oesophageal pain from medication (tetracycline)
       3) Oedema - fluid retention from corticosteroids, NSAID’S
       4) Palpitations - tachycardia/arrhythmia from:- sympathomimetics (ephedrine),
          salbutamol,       methylxanthines(Aminophylline),          digoxin    toxicity,
          hyperkalaemia from diuretics

### 5.0 Occupational History

•   May lead to causation of heart disease or exaggerate an existing heart lesion
   •   May influence the diagnosis and management of the patient
   •   Some occupations require high standards of cardiovascular fitness e.g. pilots,
       armed forces, police and public transport/heavy goods drivers
   •   Occupational exposure exacerbates pre-existing cardiac conditions (lesions)
   •   Cold – angina, Raynaud’s disease
   •   Deep sea diving - embolization through foramen ovale, organic solvents
   •   Arrthymias
   •   Cardiomyopathies
   •   Alcoholic cardiomyopathy

### 6.0 Social History

   •   Take note of the patient’s smoking habits, alcohol intake and amount of physical
       effort

### 7.0 General Systemic Review

   •   Enquire about history of fever, weight loss, appetite, sleep pattern, mood and
       appearance

### 8.0 Systemic Review

   •   Respiratory – wheezing, coughing up blood, difficulty in breathing
   •   Gastrointestinal - heartburn, vomiting, anorexia, weight loss, jaundice
   •   Nervous - headache - stroke, dizziness, blackouts
   •   Renal/urinary - cystitis, haematuria
   •   Musculoskeletal - arthritis, painful back, growing - pains’ in childhood


---

articles.content:
# Respiratory System Examination — Complete Study Guide

CLINICAL METHODS – RESPIRATORY SYSTEM

Carey F. Okinda
October/Nov 2011

## TOPIC 1: REVIEW OF ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF THE RESPIRATORY SYSTEM

OBJECTIVES

At the end of the session the learner should be able to

1. Take appropriate history of respiratory system disorders
2. Describe the key symptoms of respiratory disease

### 1.0 ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY

#### 1.1 Introduction

Living organisms require constant supply of energy which in most instances is
obtained from oxidation of high-energy carbon compounds which occurs through
several steps. This results in formation of carbon dioxide. Energy released at each
stage d harnessed in form of high energy compounds e.g. ATP. Respiration is the
process by which O2 is transported to and used by cells and CO2 is produced and
eliminated from the body. The primary function of the respiratory system is to
obtain oxygen for use by the body’s cells and eliminate carbon dioxide that the cells
produce. The term respiration includes two processes – external respiration and
internal respiration which refer to three separate but related functions namely: -
Ventilation (breathing), Gas exchange and Oxygen utilization. External
respiration is the absorption of O2 and removal of CO2 from the body as a whole and
internal respiration is the utilization of O2 and production of CO2 by the cells and the
gaseous exchanges between the cells and their fluid medium.

#### 1.2 Major Parts of the Respiratory System

The respiratory system consists of a gas exchange organ (the lungs) and a pump
that ventilates the lungs. The pump consists of the chest wall, respiratory muscles
which increase and decrease the size of the thoracic cavity, areas in the brain which
control the muscles and tract and nerves that connect the brain to the muscles.

#### 1.3 Divisions of Respiratory System

The respiratory system has functional and structural divisions. The respiratory system
is divided functionally into the conducting division and the respiratory division.
The conducting division includes all of the cavities and structures that transport gases
(nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, the bronchi, bronchioles) to the respiratory
division which has the structures involved in the gas exchange (alveoli) in the lungs
between the air and blood. Structurally it is divided into the upper respiratory tract (
and lower respiratory tract(


Diagram 1: Parts of the Respiratory System

#### 1.4 Organization of the Respiratory System

The respiratory system comprises of lungs and respiratory passages (airways),
which work in intimate collaboration with the thoracic cage, respiratory muscles and
the pulmonary circulation. It uses highly effective convective systems of ventilation
and circulation for long distance transport of O2 and CO2 and uses diffusion exclusively
for short distance movements of O2 and CO2. The main components of the respiratory
system are: - the air pump, mechanism for oxygen and carbon dioxide carrying, gas
exchange surface, circulatory system and regulatory mechanisms.

1. The air pump

This is made up of the lungs, airways, thoracic cavity and associated skeletal muscles
and the muscles of respiration. The pump is responsible for alveolar ventilation which
involves delivery of air to and removal of air from the alveoli spaces. This is achieved
via inspiration and expiration mechanisms (mechanics of respiration)


2. Mechanism for carrying O2 and CO2

This is made possible by the red blood cells which contain haemoglobin

3. Surface area for gas exchange

The gas exchange barrier consists of the alveoli and pulmonary capillaries. The alveoli
provide a large surface area for diffusion of gases.

4. Circulatory system

The circulatory system comprises of the systemic circulation and pulmonary
circulation which are responsible for transport of gases throughput the body. Blood
flow to the lungs is described as pulmonary perfusion.

5. Regulatory mechanisms

a. Local regulatory mechanisms

These are mechanisms responsible for local regulation of ventilation and perfusion of
the lung tissues. This is achieved via local chemoreceptors

b. Central regulatory mechanisms

1. The respiratory control centres in the CNS rhythmically stimulate the muscles of
   inspiration
2. Modify ventilation patterns during exercise, or changes in physical or mental
   activity
3. This is made possible by central chemoreceptors which sense changes in partial
   pressures of O2 and CO2 and the pH. These chemoreceptors are part of the
   feedback loops.

#### 1.5 Functions of the Respiratory System

1. Provide oxygen to the blood stream and remove carbon dioxide
2. Enables sound production or vocalization as expired air passes over the vocal cords
3. Assists in abdominal compression during micturation (urination), defecation and
     parturition (childbirth)
4.   Lung Defence mechanism - protective and reflexive non-breathing air movements
     e.g. coughing and sneezing to keep the air passageways clean.
5.   Temperature regulation – loss of heat during expiration
6.   Maintenance of water balance - small amounts of water are lost during expiration
7.   Regulation of acid-base balance
8. Anticoagulant function – lungs contain mast cells which secret heparin which
    prevents intravascular clotting
9. Metabolic functions – manufacture surfactant for local use, fibrinolytic system
10. Endocrine functions
    a. Endothelial cells of the pulmonary capillaries secrete angiotensin converting
       enzyme (ACE) which activates angiotensin I into angiotensin II

b. Lung tissues synthesize prostaglandins, acetylcholine, bradykinin and serotonin

## TOPIC 2 - HISTORY TAKING IN RESPIRATORY DISORDERS

Outline

a)   Symptoms of Respiratory Disease
b)   Chief complains
c)   History of presenting illness
d)   History of previous illness (past medical history)
e)   Family history
f)   Personal/Social history
g)   Occupational history
h)   Review Of Systems

### 1.0 Symptoms of Respiratory disease

#### 1.1 Principal complains

The main symptoms of respiratory disease include: -
1. Cough
2. Haemoptysis
3. Breathlessness
4. Chest pain
5. Wheeze
6. Sputum production

#### 1.2 The History of Presenting Illness or complain (HPI or HPC)

•    Approach differs according to the nature of illness – i.e. whether Acute, sub-acute or a
     chronic illness.
•    Take a narrative history and describe the symptoms.
•    Make specific inquiry about principal respiratory symptoms not mentioned in the narrative
     history.
•    Consider all conditions that might be responsible for the patient’s symptoms.
•    Ask supplementary questions designed to provide evidence for and against possible
     diagnosis.
•    In acute illness, it is important to inquire about the onset of the illness.
•    In chronic illness history taking is complex and time consuming.
•    Record the major incidents describe and assess interval or background symptoms.

Systemic Review

•    Diseases of the respiratory system can produce symptoms in other parts of the body

a) Constitutional symptoms on GIT e.g. loss of appetite, loss of weight, lassitude, sweat and
   dyspepsia e.g. in tuberculosis and carcinoma
b) Symptoms of hypoxia and carbon dioxide retention (hypercapnia) e.g. mental disturbance,
   headaches, sweats, tremors, convulsions and coma e.g. in bronchitis

c) Evidence of Pulmonary Heart Disease (Co Pulmonale) e.g. oedema, jugular venous
   engorgement, liver distension and ascites

d) Finger clubbing and painful swelling in the limbs.
e) Distal manifestations associated with malignancies          e.g.   endocrine   disorders,
   myoneuropathy and other organs involvement

History of Previous Illness

•   Diagnosis
•   Admissions
•   Treatment/Management
•   Attending clinics
•   Drugs
    ▪ Asprin, NSAID’S frequently worsen airflow obstruction
    ▪ Many drugs cause pulmonary oesinophilia
    ▪ Nitrofurantoin, Busulphan are associated with Pulmonary Fibrosis
•   Previous radiological examination (X-ray)
•   Chest injuries
•   Recent general anaesthetic or loss of consciousness

#### 1.3 Family History

•   Certain infections e.g. TB may be transmitted from one person to another, any contact
    with an infected person is important.
•   Allergic disorders e.g. B’asthma, eczema and hay fever
•   General living conditions may predispose to respiratory disorders.

#### 1.4 Social History

A full social history should be taken.
• Detailed sexual history since the possibility OF aids should be considered where there are
    unexplained respiratory symptoms or chest X-ray abnormalities evidence of opportunistic
    infections.
• Pets (Animals and Birds)
• Drinking and smoking habits
• Hobbies – Budgerigars and pigeous may cause extrinsic allergic alveolitis
• The other occupants in the home, rooms, sanitation.

#### 1.5 Occupational History

Full occupational history is important in respiratory medicine.
• Numerous chemicals, moulds, organics dusts and animals proteins can cause asthma and
    allergic alveolitis.
• Silica, coal dust and asbestos cause pneumoncoiosis and malignant disease.

### 2.0 SYMPTOMS OF RESPIRATORY DISEASE

#### 2.1 Upper Respiratory Tract Symptoms

2.1.1. Nose and Nasopharynx

Obstruction

•   Persistent obstruction of nasal airway e.g. adenoidal enlargement and polyp
•   Intermittent obstruction e.g. mucosal oedema and excessive secretions

Runny, Blocked Nose and Sneezing

•   Nasal symptoms are common
•   Nasal secretions are usually thin and runny in rhinitis but thicker and yellow.
•   Green in common cold.
•   Nasal bleeds and blood stained nasal discharge are common.
•   Blood stained nasal discharge associated with nasal obstruction and pain may suggest a
    nasal tumour.
•   Nasal polyps cause total nasal blockage.
•   Epistaxis.

2.1.2. Larynx

•   Hoarseness of voice – slight harshness
•   Complete loss (aphonia)
•   Stridor – High pitched crowing sound occurring in inspiration.
•   Caused by foreign body, laryngeal spasm and oedema. The sound is aggravated by cough.
•   Cough: - dry barking cough
•   Pain due to inflammation (Acute laryngitis), advanced TB laryngitis and laryngeal
    carcinoma.

2.1.3. Trachea

•   Pain – Is referred behind the sternal manubrium, intense on coughing but subsides as the
    cough becomes productive.
•   Stridor – due to obstruction of tracheal lumen e.g. malignant tumour. Lower in pitch

#### 2.2 Cough

Introduction

•   Cough is the commonest manifestation of lower respiratory tract disease. Cough is a
    defensive reflex designed to protect the lower respiratory tract.
•   Cough is not a disease itself, but rather a manifestation of underlying pathology. A
    cough is a protective action, and it can be initiated both voluntarily and via
    stimulation of cough receptors located throughout the respiratory tract (ear,
    sinuses, upper and lower airways to the level of the terminal bronchioles, pleura,
    pericardium, and diaphragm). A cough may serve to remove irritating substances
    or excessive or abnormal secretions, or it may be secondary to intrinsic or extrinsic
    airway compression.
•   A cough is divided into three distinct phases:
        1. A deep inspiration
        2. Closure of the glottis with contraction of expiratory muscles, and
        3. Glottis opening.
•   Classification should initially involve differentiating an acute from a chronic cough.
    A chronic cough is one that lasts longer than 3 weeks. Furthermore, the clinical
    description of the cough can often be helpful in suggesting an etiology: staccato
    (pertussis, chlamydia), barking (croup), grunting (asthma), or honking
    (psychogenic).

•   There are two main types of cough, dry and chesty. The cough is an involuntary
    action by the brain to clear a blockage or irritant from the body’s airways. A cough
    may also be due to a viral infection such as the flu or common cold.Thedry cough is
    often seen as the less productive of the two types. Whereas the chesty cough
    brings up phlegm or mucus from the lungs, a dry cough can just seem plain
    irritating.
•   The cough reflex can be initiated by the stimulation of irritant receptors in the larynx,
    trachea and major bronchi.         This receptors respond to mechanical irritation by
    intraluminal material e.g. mucus, dust, sputum and FB or chemical irritators by fumes and
    irritant gases.
•   Cough involves making a forced expiratory effort against a closed glottis which then
    suddenly opens resulting in explosive release of air carrying with it respiratory secretions.
•   Frequency severity and character of cough depends on:-
    a) Situation of lesion causing cough
    b) Nature of lesion causing cough
    c) Presence or absence of sputum
    d) Co-existing abnormalities e.g. Vocal cord paralysis
•   Clinical description of cough relies on – timing, sound and whether there is expectoration
    or not.

#### 2.3 Sputum Production

Introduction
• About 100 mls of mucous is produced daily in a healthy non-smoking individual, It flows at
   regular pace up the airways through the larynx and is swallowed.
• Excess mucous is expectorated as sputum.
• Cigarette smoking is the commonest cause of excessive mucous production.
• Characteristics of the sputum
      a. Amount
      b. Viscosity
      c. solid material
      d. Taste or odour
      e. Colour

Amount

•   Usually not accurately described by patient (ash how many tea or table spoonful)
•   Large amounts may be found in:
       a) Bronchiectasis – seen in regular coughing
       b) Pulmonary abscess – occasional sudden
       c) Rupture of an empyema into a bronchus
       d) Pulmonary oedema – with pink tinge
       e) Alveolar cell cancer – watery

Viscosity

•   Mucoid sputum is more viscous than purulent and hence difficult to cough up.
•   Serous sputum is watery with low viscosity

Solid material
• In asthma the sputum has viscid secretions that accumulate in the airway and when
    coughed up appear as casts (solid material)
• Other solid – necrotic tumours, inhaled FB e.g., food

Taste or Odour

•   Patient describes the taste.
•   Observer’s own sense of smell should be used to assess odour.
•   Foul or vile tasting or smelling sputum is caused by
        o Anaerobic bacterial infections
        o Bronchiectasis
        o Lung abscess
        o Empyema

Colour

•   Yellowish or green sputum is usually purulent.
•   Green sputum – pus
•   Yellow sputum – pus with high oesinophil content
•   Clear or white, grey mucoid sputum in industrial areas – bronchial mucous glands
    hypersecretion.
•   Rusty

Types of Sputum

•   Can be:

    a. Serous
    b. Mucoid
    c. Purulent/Mucopurulent
    d. Blood stained (Haemoptysis)
    e. Rusty

#### 2.4 Haemoptysis

•   Expectoration of blood (blood stained sputum)
•   Amount varies from steaks to several pints
•   May consist of pure blood or be mixed with sputum or salivary secretions.
•   Examine the mouth and throat to rule out local cases of blood which has been spat out.
