articles.content:
# General & Systemic Pathology SAQ Paper II — 15 July 2025 (MBPA 3500, MKU Year 3)

*Mount Kenya University, School of Medicine, Department of Pathology. Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery — Year 3. Unit Code: MBPA 3500 — Unit Title: General & Systemic Pathology SAQ, Paper II. Main Exam, 15th July 2025, 2:30 PM. Time: 3 Hours. This exam consists of two sections: Section A — 10 short answer questions (10 marks each, attempt all); Section B — three long essay questions (20 marks each, attempt all). Model answers below are written for revision; they are not an official marking scheme.*

# SECTION A — SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS
### Attempt all. Each question carries 10 marks.

---
Question 1

Give an outline of the various congenital neural tube defects, mentioning their distinguishing features. (10 Marks)

**Answer:**
- **Anencephaly** — failure of closure of the rostral (cranial) neuropore; absence of the cranial vault, scalp and most of the brain (only a rudimentary brainstem/area cerebrovasculosa remains); incompatible with life, frequently associated with polyhydramnios (absent fetal swallowing reflex).
- **Spina bifida occulta** — failure of fusion of the vertebral arches only, with an intact overlying skin and no herniation of neural tissue; often an incidental finding, sometimes marked by a skin dimple, hairy patch or lipoma over the lumbosacral spine.
- **Meningocele** — herniation of the meninges (dura and arachnoid) through a vertebral defect, forming a fluid-filled sac covered by skin; the spinal cord itself remains in its normal position, so neurological deficit is uncommon.
- **Myelomeningocele** — herniation of both meninges and neural tissue (spinal cord/nerve roots) through the vertebral defect; the most common and most severe open form, usually associated with significant motor/sensory deficit below the lesion and with hydrocephalus (Arnold-Chiari II malformation).
- **Encephalocele** — herniation of meninges (± brain tissue) through a cranial defect, most often occipital.
- All are caused by failure of neural tube closure between the 3rd and 4th week of gestation; folate deficiency is a major modifiable risk factor, hence periconceptional folic acid supplementation for prevention.

---
Question 2

Classify chemical carcinogenic agents giving examples of each class and the cancers they are associated with. (10 Marks)

**Answer:**
Chemical carcinogens are classified as **direct-acting** (require no metabolic conversion) and **indirect-acting/procarcinogens** (require metabolic activation, usually hepatic cytochrome P450, to become the active "ultimate carcinogen").

- **Direct-acting agents:** alkylating agents (e.g. cyclophosphamide, busulfan) — associated with treatment-related acute myeloid leukaemia.
- **Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons** (indirect-acting): benzo[a]pyrene and other products of tobacco smoke, smoked/charred food, and fossil fuel combustion — associated with lung, laryngeal and bladder cancer.
- **Aromatic amines/azo dyes** (indirect-acting): e.g. beta-naphthylamine, benzidine (rubber/dye industry exposure) — associated with transitional cell (urothelial) carcinoma of the bladder.
- **Nitrosamines:** formed endogenously from nitrites/nitrates in preserved and smoked foods — associated with gastric and oesophageal carcinoma.
- **Aflatoxin B1** (from *Aspergillus flavus* on stored grains/groundnuts): associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, especially synergistic with chronic Hepatitis B infection.
- **Asbestos:** associated with malignant mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma.
- **Vinyl chloride:** associated with hepatic angiosarcoma.
- **Arsenic:** associated with skin and lung cancer.
- **Benzene:** associated with acute myeloid leukaemia.

---
Question 3

Compare and contrast autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive disorders focusing on their mode of transmission and the manifestation of their clinical features. (10 Marks)

**Answer:**

| Feature | Autosomal Dominant | Autosomal Recessive |
|---|---|---|
| Gene dose required | One mutant allele (heterozygous) is sufficient | Two mutant alleles (homozygous, or compound heterozygous) required |
| Transmission pattern | Vertical — affects successive generations; affected individual has ~50% risk of transmitting to each child | Horizontal — typically skips generations; both parents are usually unaffected carriers; ~25% of offspring of two carriers affected |
| Sex ratio | Equal in males and females | Equal in males and females |
| Parental consanguinity | Not typically relevant | Increases risk, since it raises the chance both parents share the same rare recessive allele |
| Onset/severity | Often later onset; clinical expression can be milder because one normal allele is still present | Usually earlier and more uniform/severe onset, since no normal gene product is produced |
| Variability of expression | Marked — shows **variable expressivity** (severity differs between affected individuals) and **incomplete penetrance** (some gene carriers show no phenotype at all) | Expression tends to be more uniform/complete penetrance within a family, since the biochemical defect is total loss of function |
| Typical mechanism | Usually involves structural/regulatory proteins (e.g. receptors, structural proteins) — a 50% reduction in gene product (haploinsufficiency) or a dominant-negative effect is enough to cause disease | Usually involves enzyme deficiencies — 50% of normal enzyme activity (heterozygote) is typically still sufficient for normal function, so disease requires near-total loss |
| Examples | Huntington disease, Marfan syndrome, familial hypercholesterolaemia, neurofibromatosis | Cystic fibrosis, phenylketonuria, sickle cell disease, most inborn errors of metabolism |

---
Question 4

Discuss the different pathophysiological categories of oedema giving two examples for each. (10 Marks)

**Answer:**
Oedema results from a disturbance of the Starling forces or lymphatic drainage across the capillary wall.
- **Increased hydrostatic pressure** — e.g. congestive cardiac failure (venous congestion raises capillary hydrostatic pressure), and deep venous thrombosis/venous obstruction (localised).
- **Reduced plasma oncotic pressure** (hypoalbuminaemia) — e.g. nephrotic syndrome (urinary protein loss), and liver cirrhosis/chronic liver failure (reduced hepatic albumin synthesis) or protein-losing enteropathy/malnutrition.
- **Increased vascular permeability** — e.g. acute inflammation (histamine, bradykinin, and other mediators widen endothelial junctions), and burns/anaphylaxis.
- **Lymphatic obstruction (lymphoedema)** — e.g. filariasis, and post-surgical/post-radiotherapy lymph node dissection (e.g. after axillary clearance in breast cancer) or tumour infiltration of lymphatics.
- **Sodium and water retention** — e.g. renal failure (reduced GFR) and secondary hyperaldosteronism (as in heart failure/cirrhosis, compounding the hydrostatic/oncotic mechanisms above).

---
Question 5

Describe the immune mechanisms involved in glomerular injury. (10 Marks)

**Answer:**
Most glomerulonephritides are immunologically mediated, via two principal mechanisms:
- **In-situ immune complex formation** — circulating antibody binds directly to a fixed (intrinsic) glomerular antigen or to a "planted" antigen trapped within the glomerulus. Example: **anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease**, where autoantibodies target the NC1 domain of type IV collagen in the glomerular basement membrane, producing a characteristic linear pattern on immunofluorescence.
- **Circulating immune complex deposition** — antigen-antibody complexes form in the circulation (from an endogenous antigen, e.g. DNA in SLE, or an exogenous antigen, e.g. streptococcal antigen in post-streptococcal GN) and are subsequently trapped in the glomerular capillary wall or mesangium, producing a **granular ("lumpy-bumpy")** pattern on immunofluorescence.
- Deposited immune complexes activate the **complement cascade**, generating C5a (a chemotactic factor) which recruits neutrophils and monocytes; these release proteases, oxygen free radicals and other mediators that damage the basement membrane and podocytes.
- **Cell-mediated immunity** — T-cell-mediated injury, implicated particularly in minimal change disease and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, where a circulating permeability factor (of presumed T-cell origin) causes podocyte foot-process effacement without significant immune complex deposition.
- **Alternative complement pathway activation** — as in C3 glomerulopathy/dense deposit disease, where dysregulation of the alternative pathway (e.g. C3 nephritic factor) causes glomerular injury independent of classical immune complexes.
- Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (**ANCA**) — associated with pauci-immune (little/no immune complex deposition) crescentic glomerulonephritis, as seen in granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis.

---
Question 6

Give an outline of the major risk factors for atherosclerosis. (10 Marks)

**Answer:**
- **Non-modifiable:** increasing age, male sex (or post-menopausal female), and a positive family history/genetic predisposition (e.g. familial hypercholesterolaemia).
- **Modifiable — major:** hyperlipidaemia (particularly elevated LDL and reduced HDL cholesterol), hypertension, cigarette smoking, and diabetes mellitus.
- **Modifiable — additional/soft risk factors:** obesity (especially central), physical inactivity, a diet high in saturated fat, chronic stress, and hyperhomocysteinaemia.
- **Inflammatory markers:** elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), reflecting an inflammatory contribution to plaque formation and instability.
- **Other:** chronic kidney disease and lipoprotein(a) elevation are increasingly recognised independent risk factors.

---
Question 7

Discuss the aetiology, pathogenesis, and morphology of liver cirrhosis. (10 Marks)

**Answer:**
**Aetiology:** chronic viral hepatitis (Hepatitis B and C), chronic alcohol use, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease/metabolic-associated steatohepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, biliary disease (primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, biliary atresia), and inherited metabolic disorders (haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency).

**Pathogenesis:** repeated cycles of hepatocyte injury and death (from any of the causes above) activate hepatic stellate cells, which transform into myofibroblast-like cells and deposit collagen (fibrosis) in the space of Disse. Progressive fibrous septa link portal tracts to central veins, dividing the liver into structurally abnormal nodules of regenerating hepatocytes. This distorts the normal vascular architecture, causing sinusoidal compression, increased intrahepatic vascular resistance and portal hypertension, while also impairing hepatocyte-to-blood exchange, contributing to hepatocellular dysfunction.

**Morphology:**
- **Macroscopic:** the liver may be enlarged early but becomes small, firm and nodular in end-stage disease; nodules may be **micronodular** (<3 mm, typical of alcoholic cirrhosis) or **macronodular** (>3 mm, typical of post-viral hepatitis cirrhosis), or mixed.
- **Microscopic:** regenerative parenchymal nodules of hepatocytes are completely surrounded by bridging fibrous septa; loss of normal lobular architecture; variable inflammatory infiltrate depending on the underlying cause; ductular proliferation at the fibrous septal margins.
- **Complications** arising from this morphology: portal hypertension (leading to ascites, splenomegaly, oesophageal varices, caput medusae), hepatocellular failure (jaundice, coagulopathy, hypoalbuminaemia, hepatic encephalopathy), and increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

---
Question 8

Compare and contrast Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus under the following headings: Aetiology, Pathogenesis, Clinical features. (10 Marks)

**Answer:**

| | Type 1 DM | Type 2 DM |
|---|---|---|
| **Aetiology** | Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, in a genetically susceptible individual (HLA-DR3/DR4 association), often triggered by an environmental factor (e.g. viral infection) | Combination of genetic predisposition (stronger heritability than Type 1) and environmental/lifestyle factors — obesity, physical inactivity, ageing |
| **Pathogenesis** | T-cell-mediated autoimmune insulitis destroys beta cells, causing an **absolute** insulin deficiency; islet autoantibodies (anti-GAD, anti-insulin, anti-IA2) are usually present | **Peripheral insulin resistance** (in muscle, liver and fat) combined with a **relative** insulin deficiency from progressive beta-cell dysfunction/exhaustion; hyperinsulinaemia is often present early, before beta-cell failure supervenes |
| **Age of onset** | Typically children/young adults | Typically middle-aged/older adults, though increasingly seen in obese adolescents |
| **Body habitus** | Usually normal weight/lean | Usually overweight/obese |
| **Onset** | Acute/abrupt, often presenting with diabetic ketoacidosis | Gradual/insidious, often detected incidentally or after years of asymptomatic hyperglycaemia |
| **Ketosis** | Prone to ketoacidosis (absolute insulin lack permits unrestrained lipolysis/ketogenesis) | Rarely ketotic (residual insulin is usually sufficient to suppress ketogenesis), though hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state can occur |
| **Treatment dependence** | Exogenous insulin is mandatory for survival | Managed with lifestyle change, oral hypoglycaemics, and insulin only in later disease/failure of other measures |
| **Complications** | Both share the long-term microvascular (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular complications of chronic hyperglycaemia | Same as Type 1 — the severity relates to duration/control of hyperglycaemia, not the subtype |

---
Question 9

Describe the stages and biological processes involved in fracture healing, including the role of cells in the formation of callus. (10 Marks)

**Answer:**
1. **Haematoma formation (within hours):** bleeding from the fracture ends and disrupted periosteal/endosteal vessels forms a haematoma; this activates the coagulation cascade and releases cytokines/growth factors (e.g. PDGF, TGF-beta, BMPs) that initiate the healing/inflammatory response, and the ischaemic fracture margins undergo a small zone of necrosis.
2. **Inflammatory phase (days 1–7):** neutrophils and macrophages infiltrate to clear necrotic debris; mesenchymal stem cells and fibroblasts migrate into the haematoma, and angiogenesis begins, forming granulation tissue.
3. **Soft (procallus) callus formation (1–2 weeks):** fibroblasts and chondroblasts lay down a collagenous and fibrocartilaginous matrix bridging the fracture gap — a soft callus that provides limited mechanical stability but no rigidity.
4. **Hard (bony) callus formation (2–6 weeks):** osteoblasts (derived from periosteal and endosteal mesenchymal cells) progressively replace the fibrocartilaginous callus with woven (immature) bone via **endochondral ossification** (cartilage template calcified then replaced by bone) and **intramembranous ossification** (direct osteoblastic bone formation beneath the periosteum) occurring simultaneously; this bridges and stabilises the fracture.
5. **Remodelling (months to years):** coordinated **osteoclastic resorption** and **osteoblastic deposition** gradually convert the disorganised woven bone into mature lamellar bone, restoring the original cortical/medullary architecture and the bone's original shape and mechanical strength, guided by mechanical loading (Wolff's law).

---
Question 10

Give an outline of the aetiology, characteristics, and examples of the major categories of diarrhoeal illness. (10 Marks)

**Answer:**
- **Secretory diarrhoea** — caused by a toxin or hormone that stimulates active intestinal chloride/fluid secretion (e.g. cyclic AMP–mediated in cholera); characteristically large-volume, watery, persists even with fasting, and has a normal stool osmotic gap. Example: *Vibrio cholerae* toxin, enterotoxigenic *E. coli*, VIPoma.
- **Osmotic diarrhoea** — caused by non-absorbable solutes drawing water into the bowel lumen; characteristically improves/stops with fasting, and has an increased stool osmotic gap. Example: lactase deficiency (lactose intolerance), laxative abuse (e.g. magnesium salts), malabsorption syndromes (e.g. coeliac disease).
- **Exudative (inflammatory) diarrhoea** — caused by mucosal inflammation/ulceration with exudation of mucus, blood and protein; characteristically small-volume, frequent stools, often with blood/pus and tenesmus. Example: shigellosis, inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease), amoebic colitis.
- **Diarrhoea due to deranged motility** — caused by abnormally increased or decreased intestinal transit time affecting absorption. Example: irritable bowel syndrome, diabetic autonomic neuropathy, post-vagotomy/surgical states, hyperthyroidism.
- Mixed mechanisms are common in practice — e.g. many infective diarrhoeas combine a secretory toxin effect with an inflammatory/exudative component.

---

# SECTION B — LONG ESSAY QUESTIONS
### Attempt all. Each question carries 20 marks.

---
Question 1

Discuss the following aspects of acute inflammation:
a) Cellular events in acute inflammation
b) Cell-derived mediators of inflammation
c) Plasma-derived mediators of inflammation
d) Local and systemic effects of acute inflammation

**Answer:**

**a) Cellular events (7 marks)**
- **Vascular events precede the cellular events:** transient vasoconstriction, then vasodilatation (increasing blood flow — the cause of erythema/heat), then increased vascular permeability (endothelial cell contraction widening intercellular junctions), causing exudation of protein-rich fluid and slowing of flow (stasis).
- **Margination and rolling:** as flow slows, leukocytes move from the axial stream to marginate along the endothelium, then roll along it — mediated by selectins (P-selectin and E-selectin on endothelium, binding sialyl-Lewis X on leukocytes).
- **Adhesion:** firm adhesion of leukocytes to endothelium is mediated by integrins (e.g. LFA-1, Mac-1) on leukocytes binding to ICAM-1/VCAM-1 (immunoglobulin superfamily) on endothelium, upregulated by cytokines such as TNF and IL-1.
- **Transmigration (diapedesis):** leukocytes squeeze between endothelial cells (mediated by PECAM-1/CD31) into the interstitium, guided along a chemotactic gradient (chemokines, C5a, LTB4, bacterial products).
- **Phagocytosis:** recognition (via opsonins — IgG, C3b) and attachment, engulfment (forming a phagosome that fuses with lysosomes), and intracellular killing/degradation (via reactive oxygen species/the respiratory burst, and lysosomal enzymes).

**b) Cell-derived mediators (5 marks)**
- **Preformed, released from storage granules:** histamine (mast cells, basophils, platelets) — causes vasodilatation and increased vascular permeability; serotonin (platelets) — similar vascular effects.
- **Newly synthesised (on activation):**
  - **Arachidonic acid metabolites** — prostaglandins (via cyclo-oxygenase: vasodilatation, pain, fever), leukotrienes (via lipoxygenase: LTB4 is chemotactic, LTC4/D4/E4 cause bronchoconstriction and permeability).
  - **Cytokines** — TNF-alpha and IL-1 (endothelial activation, fever, acute phase response), IL-6 (acute phase proteins), chemokines (leukocyte chemotaxis, e.g. IL-8).
  - **Platelet-activating factor (PAF)** — platelet aggregation, vasodilatation/permeability, leukocyte activation.
  - **Nitric oxide** — vasodilatation, microbicidal activity.
  - **Lysosomal enzymes and reactive oxygen species** — tissue damage and microbial killing.

**c) Plasma-derived mediators (4 marks)**
- **Complement system** — activation generates C3a and C5a (anaphylatoxins: vasodilatation, increased permeability, mast cell degranulation), C5a (potent neutrophil chemoattractant), and the C5b-9 membrane attack complex (microbial lysis).
- **Kinin system** — activation of the Hageman factor (Factor XII) generates bradykinin via kallikrein, causing vasodilatation, increased permeability and pain.
- **Coagulation/fibrinolytic systems** — thrombin generated during clotting also has pro-inflammatory (protease-activated receptor) effects; fibrinopeptides increase vascular permeability and are chemotactic; plasmin generates further complement fragments.

**d) Local and systemic effects (4 marks)**
- **Local (cardinal signs):** rubor (redness, from vasodilatation), calor (heat), tumor (swelling, from oedema), dolor (pain, from bradykinin/PGE2 sensitising nociceptors), and loss of function.
- **Systemic — the acute phase response:** fever (IL-1/IL-6/TNF acting on the hypothalamus, raising the thermoregulatory set point via prostaglandins), leukocytosis (with a left shift), elevated acute phase proteins (CRP, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A — raising ESR), tachycardia, and in severe/systemic infection, features of sepsis (hypotension, disseminated intravascular coagulation, multi-organ dysfunction).

---
Question 2

Discuss the risk factors, aetiology, pathogenesis, morphological changes and clinical features of carcinoma of the uterine cervix. (20 Marks)

**Answer:**

**Risk factors/aetiology:** persistent infection with high-risk **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)** — chiefly types 16 and 18 — is the central causal factor. Cofactors that increase risk of persistent HPV infection/progression include early age of first intercourse, multiple sexual partners (or a partner with multiple partners), high parity, cigarette smoking, immunosuppression (e.g. HIV infection), long-term oral contraceptive use, and co-infection with other sexually transmitted infections.

**Pathogenesis:** HPV infects the metaplastic squamous epithelium of the transformation zone. The viral oncoproteins **E6** and **E7** drive malignant transformation: **E6** binds and promotes degradation of the tumour suppressor **p53**, disabling apoptosis and DNA-damage checkpoint control; **E7** binds and inactivates **retinoblastoma protein (Rb)**, releasing the transcription factor E2F and driving unchecked cell cycle progression. The combined loss of p53 and Rb function permits accumulation of genetic damage and progression through cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN I → II → III) to invasive carcinoma, typically over 10–20 years.

**Morphological changes:**
- **Pre-invasive (CIN/squamous intraepithelial lesion):** graded by the proportion of epithelial thickness replaced by atypical, disordered basaloid cells with loss of maturation, increased mitoses and nuclear atypia — CIN I (lower third), CIN II (two-thirds), CIN III/carcinoma-in-situ (full thickness), without breach of the basement membrane.
- **Invasive carcinoma:** once the basement membrane is breached, tumour cells infiltrate the underlying stroma. **Squamous cell carcinoma** (~80%) shows nests/sheets of malignant squamous cells (may show keratinisation, intercellular bridges); **adenocarcinoma** (~15–20%) arises from the endocervical glandular epithelium.
- Gross appearance ranges from an exophytic, fungating/polypoid mass to an ulcerative or infiltrative endophytic lesion causing a "barrel-shaped" cervix.

**Clinical features:** early disease is often asymptomatic (detected by cervical screening/Pap smear). Symptomatic disease presents with abnormal vaginal bleeding (post-coital, intermenstrual, or post-menopausal), watery or blood-stained vaginal discharge, and pelvic pain. Advanced disease may cause ureteric obstruction (hydronephrosis, renal failure), fistula formation (vesicovaginal or rectovaginal), and leg oedema from lymphatic/venous obstruction. Staging (FIGO) is largely clinical, based on the extent of local spread, parametrial/pelvic sidewall involvement, and distant metastasis.

---
Question 3

Discuss the three major pathways of breast cancer development and their resultant immunohistochemical staining patterns, including the clinical and prognostic significance of each pathway. (20 Marks)

**Answer:**
Breast cancer is now understood as a group of molecularly distinct diseases, classified by immunohistochemistry (IHC) for **Oestrogen Receptor (ER)**, **Progesterone Receptor (PR)**, and **HER2/neu**, broadly reflecting three major pathogenic pathways:

**1. Oestrogen-driven (ER/PR-positive, HER2-negative) pathway — "Luminal" tumours**
- **Pathogenesis:** driven by prolonged, unopposed oestrogenic stimulation of ductal epithelium (risk factors: early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity/late first pregnancy, obesity, exogenous hormone use), causing sustained proliferative drive and accumulation of genetic alterations, typically arising through a relatively low-grade, well-differentiated pathway (often via atypical ductal hyperplasia → ductal carcinoma in situ → invasive carcinoma, frequently of no special type or lobular type).
- **IHC pattern:** ER-positive, PR-positive (or positive/negative), HER2-negative. Subdivided into **Luminal A** (ER/PR strongly positive, low Ki-67 proliferation index — better prognosis) and **Luminal B** (lower hormone receptor positivity or higher Ki-67, ± HER2 positivity — intermediate/worse prognosis than Luminal A).
- **Clinical/prognostic significance:** the most common subtype; generally the best overall prognosis; responsive to endocrine therapy (tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors); tends to present in older women and to be slower-growing.

**2. HER2-driven (HER2-amplified) pathway**
- **Pathogenesis:** amplification of the **HER2/neu (ERBB2)** oncogene on chromosome 17, leading to overexpression of the HER2 tyrosine kinase receptor, which drives constitutive downstream proliferative signalling (RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT pathways) independent of hormonal stimulation.
- **IHC pattern:** HER2 positive (3+ on IHC, or amplified by FISH), ER/PR variable — may be hormone receptor-positive ("Luminal B, HER2-enriched") or hormone receptor-negative ("HER2-enriched" subtype).
- **Clinical/prognostic significance:** historically aggressive with poor prognosis, but the availability of targeted anti-HER2 therapy (trastuzumab, pertuzumab) has substantially improved outcomes; tends to be higher grade with a higher propensity for early nodal/visceral metastasis if untreated.

**3. Basal-like/triple-negative pathway**
- **Pathogenesis:** associated with loss of function of DNA-repair/tumour suppressor pathways, classically **BRCA1** mutation (germline or somatic), producing genomically unstable, high-grade tumours; lacks a clear hormone-receptor or HER2 driver.
- **IHC pattern:** ER-negative, PR-negative, HER2-negative ("triple-negative"); often positive for basal cytokeratins (CK5/6, CK14) and EGFR, reflecting a basal/myoepithelial-like differentiation.
- **Clinical/prognostic significance:** the most aggressive subtype, with high histological grade, high proliferation rate, and the highest early recurrence/visceral (including CNS) metastasis rate; no targeted hormonal or HER2-directed therapy is available, so treatment relies on cytotoxic chemotherapy (± emerging PARP inhibitors in BRCA-mutated disease and immunotherapy); more common in younger women and in women of African ancestry.

**Overall significance:** this molecular classification (rather than histological type alone) now determines both prognosis and treatment selection — endocrine therapy for luminal tumours, anti-HER2 targeted therapy for HER2-driven tumours, and chemotherapy (± novel agents) for triple-negative disease — making ER/PR/HER2 IHC a mandatory part of the diagnostic work-up of every invasive breast cancer.

---

*End of Paper. Source: Mount Kenya University, MBChB Year 3, General & Systemic Pathology (MBPA 3500) Paper II, Main Exam sat 15th July 2025. Model answers compiled for revision by Ompath Study; not an official university marking scheme.*

# Medical Physiology Assorted SAQs — With Answers (Past Paper Study Guide)

*Short-answer questions from various Medical Physiology past papers, University of Nairobi Level 1 (MBChB/BPharm), with model answers by Vincent Kipkorir and Fiona Nyaanga. A companion, questions-only version of a related set is published separately.*

---
**1.** With a diagram describe the different components of a negative feedback system


**2.** Briefly describe two different modes of fluid movements between body fluid
    compartments.
     In the body, water moves through semi-permeable membranes of cells and from one
     compartment of the body to another by osmosis. Osmosis is basically the diffusion of water
     from regions of higher concentration to regions of lower concentration, along an osmotic
     gradient across a semi-permeable membrane. As a result, water will move into and out of cells
     and tissues, depending on the relative concentrations of the water and solutes found there. An
     appropriate balance of solutes inside and outside of cells must be maintained to ensure normal
     function. Endosmosis is movement of water into the cell while exosmosis is movement of
     water out of the cells.

Cells can also take water into their intracellular compartment through pinocytosis. It's a mode
of endocytosis in which small water particles are brought into the cell, forming an invagination,
and then suspended within small vesicles. It's also called cell drinking.


**3.** State five functional differences between parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous
    systems

| SYMPATHETIC | PARASYMPATHETIC |
| --- | --- |
| Thoraco-lumbar outflow | Cranio-sacral outflow |
| Ganglia lie near the CNS and away from the effector | Ganglia lie near the effector and away from the CNS |
| Fight-or-flight: heart rate increases, respiratory rate increases, diverts blood to skeletal muscles, breaks down glycogen | Rest-and-digest: involved in activities that conserve and restore energy |
| Postganglionic fibres use norepinephrine as neurotransmitter | Postganglionic fibres use acetylcholine as neurotransmitter |
| Short cholinergic preganglionic and long adrenergic postganglionic fibres | Long cholinergic preganglionic and short cholinergic postganglionic fibres |
| Ratio of preganglionic to postganglionic fibres is 1:20 | Ratio of preganglionic to postganglionic fibres is 1:3 |
| Extensive divergence | Limited divergence |
| Activity involves mass discharge of the entire system | Activity is normally localized to discrete organs |


**4.** Describe how protein hormones stimulate protein synthesis
    Steroid hormones are lipid soluble and thus travel through blood with the help of a
    protein carrier. When they get to the target cell they detach from the carrier and

traverse the cell membrane and enter the cell by simple diffusion. Receptors for steroid
hormones are located inside target cells, in the cytoplasm or nucleus. The hormone will
either bind to a cytoplasmic receptor and then enter the nucleus as a hormone-receptor
complex or enter the nucleus to encounter its receptor. The receptors function as
ligand-dependent transcription factors. That is to say, the hormone-receptor complex
binds to promoter regions of responsive genes and stimulate or sometimes inhibit
transcription from those genes.

Thus, the mechanism of action of steroid hormones is to modulate gene expression in
target cells. By selectively affecting transcription from a battery of genes, the
concentration of those respective proteins are altered, which clearly can change the
phenotype of the cell. When hormone binds to receptor, a characteristic series of
events occurs:

•  Receptor activation is the term used to describe conformational changes in the

receptor induced by binding hormone. The major consequence of activation is that the

receptor becomes competent to bind DNA.

•  Activated receptors bind to "hormone response elements", which are short

specific sequences of DNA which are located in promoters of hormone-responsive

genes. In most cases, hormone-receptor complexes bind DNA in pairs, as shown in the

figure below.

•  Transcription from those genes to which the receptor is bound is affected. Most

commonly, receptor binding stimulates transcription. The hormone-receptor complex

thus functions as a transcription factor.


**5.** In relation to sensory physiology, describe adaptation, law of specific nerve energies
    and law of projection.

Adaptation- occurs when sensory receptors change their sensitivity to the particular
stimulus after being exposed to the same stimulus continuously for a long time.

Law of specific nerve energies- the nature of perception is defined by the pathway over
which sensory information is carried. Hence the origin of the sensation is not important
but instead different sensations are differentiated from each other by the different
nervous structures these stimuli excite.

Law of projection - no matter where along the nerve is stimulated, the sensation will
be felt at the site of the receptor.


**6.** Explain the difference between end plate potential, inhibitory post-synaptic potential
    and excitatory post-synaptic potential. For each give the neurotransmitter involved.

End plate potential- depolarizations of skeletal muscle fibres caused by
neurotransmitter acetylcholine binding to postsynaptic membrane receptors in
neuromuscular junction.

    Inhibitory post-synaptic potential- temporary hyperpolarization of postsynaptic
    membrane caused by flow of negatively charged ions into postsynaptic cells.
    Neurotransmitters are inhibitory such as GABA.
    Excitatory post-synaptic potential- temporary depolarization of post-synaptic
    membrane caused by flow of positively charged ions as a result of ligand-sensitive
    channels. Neurotransmitters are excitatory such as glutamate.

**7.** List the different types of transport across cell membrane and an example of each.
    Passive transport- transport of substances downhill along a concentration gradient.
    (a) Diffusion- simple diffusion of particles occurs across a lipid membrane or protein

         layer of the cell membrane. Passive diffusion occurs with the help of carrier proteins
         of the cell membrane
    (b) Osmosis- movement of water from there are of high solvent concentration to an
         area of low solvent concentration via a semi-permeable membrane.
    Active transport- transport of substances against a concentration gradient with the use
    of energy.
    (a) Primary active transport- an example is using the sodium-potassium pump where
         each individual ion is using energy to move against their gradient.
    (b) Secondary active transport- a type of active transport across a biological membrane
         in which a transport protein couples the movement of an ion (typically Na+ or H+)
         down its electrochemical gradient to the movement of another ion or molecule
         against a concentration or electrochemical gradient.

**8.** With a diagram show 5 cell organelles and the function of each.

| Cell organelle | Function(s) |
| --- | --- |
| Cell membrane | Limits and protects the contents of the cell from the external environment; controls movement of substances and molecules across it |
| Mitochondrion | Forms ATP for energy; induces apoptosis; supports cellular proliferation; heme and steroid synthesis |
| Nucleus | Storage of the genetic imprint; storage of coded messages for physiological processes; synthesis of DNA; directs protein synthesis and cell reproduction |
| Ribosomes | Site of protein synthesis |
| Rough endoplasmic reticulum | Assists in transport of synthesized proteins |
| Smooth endoplasmic reticulum | Synthesis of lipid substances; site of detoxification; site of steroid synthesis in steroid-synthesizing cells |
| Nucleolus | Synthesis of ribosomes |

   9. Define axoplasmic flow and the proteins involved in their transport

        Axoplasmic flow is the movement of organelles, synaptic vesicles and substances to and
        from the cell body of a neuron through the axoplasm. Anterograde movement is
        movement of organelles, nutrients, synaptic vesicles and substances from the cell body
        to the axon terminal. Motor protein involved is kinesin. Retrograde movement is
        movement of waste materials and other substances from the axon terminal to the cell
        body. Motor protein that facilitates this is dynein.

   10. Describe the role of voltage gated action potentials (sodium and potassium)

        They allow a rapid and coordinated depolarization in response to voltage change in
        excitable tissues like neurons. The opening and closing of the channels are triggered by
        changing the ion concentration and hence change in gradient between the sides of the
        cell membrane triggering an action potential.

   11. Describe the replicative stage of HIV-1

   HIV uses its genetic material (RNA) to reproduce by hijacking the genetic machine of the
   host cell. In doing so, it can churn out multiple copies of itself. The process, called viral
   uncoating, requires that the protective coating surrounding the RNA must be dissolved.
   Without this step, the conversion of RNA to DNA (the building blocks for a new virus)
   cannot take place. Transcription and Translation- Once in the cell, the single stranded RNA
   of HIV must be converted to the double stranded DNA. It accomplishes this with the help of
   the enzyme called reverse transcriptase. Reverse transcriptase uses building blocks from
   the T-cell to literally transcribe the genetic material in reverse: from RNA to DNA. Once
   converted DNA, the genetic machine has the coding needed to effect viral replication.
   Integration- In order for HIV to hijack the host cell's genetic machinery, it must integrate
   the newly formed DNA into the nucleus of the cell with the help of enzyme integrase.
   Assembly- Once integration has occurred, HIV must manufacture protein building blocks
   that it uses to assemble new virus. It does so with the protease enzyme, which chops
   protein into smaller bit and then assembles the pieces into new, fully formed HIV virions.


**12.** Explain how the normal range is calculated (95% interval)

Establish the values falling at the 2.5 and 95 percentiles at the populations the upper and
lower limits respectively. The first e=step is to sort the values in ascending order of magnitude.

The number of values are then multiplied by 0.025 and 0.975 to obtain the percentile ranks of
the upper and lower limits respectively. The normal range is the central 95% of the data


**13.** Describe the cyclic AMP signal pathway

    Hormone binds with the receptor in the cell membrane and forms the hormone-receptor
    complex. It activates the G protein. G protein releases GDP from  GDP unit. The  subunit
    now binds with a new molecule of GTP. This triggers the dissociation of  GTP unit and -
    dimmer from the receptor. The  GTP and  dimmer unit now activates the enzyme
    adenylyl cyclase. Activated adenylyl cyclase converts ATP of cytoplasm into cAMP


**14.** Describe 5 properties of cell membrane receptors.

They transmit signals via transmembrane signaling thus converting an extracellular signal into
an intracellular signal.

They are ligand binding receptors which have high affinity for binding sites for external ligand
molecules.

Produce conformational changes within transmembrane receptor proteins.

Their intracellular either becomes enzymatically active or protein

They undertake transmembrane transduction as same of the span across cell membrane even
seven times.


**15.** Explain how proton gradient across the mitochondrial membrane is created

Oxidative phosphorylation is made possible by the close association of the electron carriers
and the protein molecules. The proteins guide the electrons along the respiratory chain so that
the electrons move sequentially from one enzyme complex to the next with no short circuits.
The transfer of electrons is coupled to oriented hydrogen ions uptake and release across the
inner membrane from the matrix to the intermembrane space driven by energetically
favorable flow of electrons. This movement of hydrogen ions causes a proton gradient


**16.** Explain the inhibitory postsynaptic potentials and their ionic basis

Direct inhibition

Develops when an inhibitory neurotransmitter like GABA acts on postsynaptic membrane by
binding with receptor. Transmitter-receptor complex opens the ligand gated K+ channels
instead of Na+ channels. Simultaneously, Cl- channels open and chloride ions move into the
cell. This K+ efflux and Cl- influx cause more negativity inside leading to hyperpolarization.

Transcription: In the nucleus, there is a transcription unit. Each transcription unit has a
sequence above it called the upstream sequence. The upstream sequence is the promoter and
has a specific sequence of repetitions — the **TATA box**, consensus sequence `TATAAA`, base-paired with its complementary strand `ATATTT`.

in either of 2 directions, upstream (towards the 3end) or downstream (towards the 5' end).
RNA polymerase copies the DNA sequence downstream onto an mRNA from the point of the
TATA Box.The double helix of the DNA is unzipped by RNA polymerase from TATA box as it
reads the nitrogenous bases. RNA polymerase lets it re-zip behind it and lets mRNA peel away
until it reaches the termination signal that triggers it to pull away.

poly A tail is added to the 3' end. This is for ease for mRNA to leave nucleus, for protection and
ease of binding with other organelles later on. Before leaving nucleus, RNA splicing occurs
whereby the introns are spliced by spliceosomes and then axons fuse to form MRNA which can
now move out of nucleus.

codon. Therefore, a new don is exposed. The cycle is repeated to create the desires protein

**41.** Write an essay on erythropoiesis

Erythropoiesis is the process of origin, development and maturation of erythrocytes. Stem
cells are the primary cells that are capable of differentiating into specialized cells. The stem
cells that form blood cells are called hematopoietic cells. The hematopoietic stem cells are
called uncommitted pluripotent hematopoietic stems cells because they are not designed to
form a particular type of blood cells. When the cell is designed to form a particular type of
blood cell it is called committed pluripotent stem cell. Erythrocytes are formed from colony
forming blastocytes as their committed pluripotent stem cell. Colony forming blastocytes then
differentiate to colony forming -unit erythrocytes (CFU-E) which develop into erythrocytes.

Erythropoiesis occurs in several stages. The first stage is the proerythroblast or megaloblast. It
is derived from the CFU-E and has a diameter of 20u. It has a large nucleus with two or
more nucleoli and a reticular network. The cytoplasm is basophilic. Synthesis of hemoglobin
commences in this stage but its appearance is not visible.

The second stage is the early normoblast. It has a diameter of 15u. The nucleoli in the nucleus
disappear. The reticular network condenses and becomes dense. Cytoplasm is also basophilic
in nature.

The third stage is the intermediate normobalst. It has a diameter of about 10-12u. The nucleus
is still present but the reticular network shows further condensation. The hemoglobin starts
appearing. Cytoplasm is still basophilic but because the hemoglobin is acidophilic the cell is
polychromatic.

The fourth stage is the late normoblast. Its diameter is about 8 to 10u. The nucleus becomes
smaller with very much condensed chromatin network. Quantity of hemoglobin increases and
cytoplasm becomes almost acidophilic. The nucleus the disintegrates and disappears by the
process known as pyknosis. The final remnant is extruded from the cell.

The fifth stage is the reticulocyte. It is slightly larger than the mature RBC. The cytoplasm of
the reticulocyte contains the reticular network which is formed by remnants of disintegrated
organelles. The number of reticulocytes decreases during the first week after birth but
increases when there is need for RBC production. Cytoplasm is basophilic due to remnants of
disintegrated golgi apparatus, mitochondria and other organelles. During this stage, the cells
enter the blood capillaries through capillary membrane from site of production by diapedesis.
The final stage is the mature erythrocyte stage. The reticular network disappears and the cell

becomes a mature RBC and attains its biconcave shape. Its diameter is now 7.2u. The mature
RBC is hemoglobin but without nucleus.
It requires 7 days for the development and maturation of RBC from proerythroblast. It requires
5 days upto stage of reticulocyte and 2 more to mature RBC.
There are several factors necessary for the process of erythropoiesis. One of them is
erythropoietin which enhances rate of mitosis, MRNA formation and protein synthesis but
decreases maturation time in bone marrow.
Vitamin B12 is also a necessary factor whose role is in DNA synthesis and normoblastic
maturation. Therefore if deficient or malabsorbed , megaloblastic anaemia is likely to develop.
Folic acid is also a factor necessary and it facilitates DNA synthesis and normoblastic
maturation. It also causes megaloblastic anaemia if deficiency occurs.
Iron is also a factor necessary as it assists in formation of the heme part of hemoglobin. Iron
deficiency eg from menstruation may cause iron-deficiency anaemia.

     a. Activation gates of voltage gated sodium channels

     potential and the Na+ channels in their deactivated state blocked on the
     extracellular side by their activation gates. In response to the action potential, the
     activation gates open allowing positively charged Na+ to flow into the neuron
     through the channels causing an increase in membrane voltage. Therefore,
     depolarisation occurs.

                  b. Inactivation gates of voltage gated sodium channels

         At the peak of action potential, when enough Na+ has entered the neuron, the Na+
channels inactivate themselves by closing their inactivation gates. Closure of the
inactivation gates causes Na+ to flow through the channel to stop thereby the membrane
potential stops rising. With its inactivation gates closed, the channel is said to be inactivated
and the membrane potential eventually goes back to the resting membrane potential.

                  c. Voltage gated potassium channels

During action potential, depolarization causes a conformational change of K+ thereby
activating them by opening their gates. This causes K+ efflux which thereby leads to
repolarisation because the membrane potential becomes less positive and more negative.

**66.** Discuss the different types of anemia, their presentations and causes
Macrocytic normochromic - megaloblastic RBSs; caused by decreased amount of foliate,
decreased amount of vitamin b12, alcoholism, hypothyroidism and liver disease.
Macrocytic hypochromic - small and pale RBCs; caused by iron deficiency,
haemoglobinopathies like SCA and thalassemia and sideroblastic anaemia (defective heme

failure and infection

**67.** Write an essay on cell signalling

         Cell signalling is part of any communication process that governs basic activities of cells
and coordinates all cell actions. It can occur in the same cell or different cells. Cell signalling
helps in monitoring the environment, process gathering information, responds accordingly
modification of behaviour and countless intracellular and extracellular signals. Extracellular
and intracellular signals control growth and division.

         Components of the cell signalling system are extracellular chemical signal molecules
(first messengers), ligands, agonists (either hydrophilic or hydrophobic), cell membrane
receptors, regulatory proteins and intracellular chemical signals (second messengers)

         Extracellular signals molecules work in combinations to regulate behaviour of cells. An
individual cell requires multiple signals to survive, divide and differentiate. Deprivation of the
cell signals for survival causes the cell to go through programmed cell death or apoptosis.
Extracellular chemical signalling molecules can be amine acids, proteins, small peptides,
nucleotides, steroids, retinoids and fatty acid derivatives.

         Reception of chemical signals depends on cell membrane receptors, binding the signal
molecule, activation of the cell membrane receptors, intracellular signalling pathways and
intracellular signalling proteins. Effectors of signals are transcription, regulators, ion channels,
components of metabolic pathway and parts of cytoskeleton.

         Principles of cell signaling are communication and influence one another`s behavior,
complex signaling systems, collaboration, coordination and govern. There are five types of cell
signaling; contact dependent, paracrine, autocrine, synaptic and endocrine.

         Contact dependent signaling is whereby the signaling molecule remains bound to the
cell membrane and extends long thin processes between the signaling cell and the target cell.
Contact dependent signaling is present in immune responses.

         Paracrine signaling is between closely related cells. The signaling molecule is secreted
into the extracellular fluid. It is mediated by paracrine like acetylcholine, histamine, gastrin and
simvastatin. It is present in parietal cells.

         Autocrine signaling is in the same cell. The cell secretes the signaling molecule into the
extracellular fluid and by self-mediators on the cell membrane receptors emit their own
chemical signals. Autocrine signaling is present in cancer cells for survival and proliferation.

         Synaptic signaling occurs in chemical synapses. They extend long branching processes.
There is propagation of an action potential in a synaptic cell. Calcium then enters into synaptic
cell. There is release of neurotransmitters via exocytosis. The neurotransmitters then bind
onto cell membrane receptors on the postsynaptic cell.

         Endocrine signaling is over long distances via the blood stream. Different hormones are
transported to different target organs for different responses. Mediated via endocrines which
are either hydrophilic or hydrophobic. They bind to cell membrane receptors of distant target
cells either systolic or nuclear receptors. Endocrine signaling is found in the ovaries, testes,
pituitary, thyroid, thymus and other organs.


**68.** Discuss the renin-angiotensin system

         The renin-angiotensin system plays an important role in regulating blood volume and
systemic vascular resistance which in turn influence cardiac output and arterial pressure. A
reduction in afferent arteriole pressure in the renal glomerulus causes release of renin by the
juxtaglomerular cells. When renin is released into the bloodstream, it acts upon angiotensin in
the liver to form angiotensin I. Vascular endothelium, particularly in the lungs, has the
angiotensin converting enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II
then acts on the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone which in turn acts on the kidneys to
increase sodium and fluid retention.


**69.** Write an essay on the basis of Frank-Starling law of the heart

         The Frank-Starling law of the heart states that stroke volume increases with an increase
in the volume of blood in the ventricles before contraction (end diastolic volume) when all
other factors remain constant.

         Increasing afterload or decreasing inotropy (force of contraction) shifts the curve down
and to the right whereas decreasing afterload or increasing inotropy shifts the curve up and to
the left results in a higher stroke volume.

         Increased venous return increases the ventricular filling (end diastolic volume) and
therefore preload which is the initial stretching of the cardiac myocytes prior to contraction.
Myocyte stretching increase the sarcomere length, which increase in force generation and
enables the heart to eject the additional venous return, thereby increasing the stroke volume.

         This phenomenon can be described in mechanical terms by length-tension and force-
velocity relationships of cardiac muscle. Increasing preload increases the active tension
developed by the muscle fibre and increases velocity of fibre shortening at a given afterload
and ionotropic state.

         One mechanism to explain how preload influences contractile force is increasing the
sarcomere length increases troponin C calcium sensitivity which increases the rate of cross
bridge attachment and detachment and the amount of tension developed by the muscle fibre.
The effect is increased sarcomere length on the contractile proteins is termed length-
dependent activation.


**70.** Discuss the starling forces in oedema formation.

         Oedema occurs when and excessive volume of fluid accumulates in the tissues either
within cells (cellular edema) or in the interstitial spaces (interstitial oedema).Interstitial
oedema may occur as a result of imbalance between hydrostatic (which may be increased),

oncotic (which may be low) and interstitial pressure (which may be low).The hydrostatic,
oncotic and interstitial pressure are the starling`s forces. This causes increased capillary
basement membrane permeability and poor reabsorption.


**71.** Write an essay on control of cardiac output.

         Cardiac output is the amount of blood ejected by the ventricles per minute. It is the
product of stroke volume (the amount of blood ejected by the ventricles per beat) and the
heart rate. The cardiac output cannot exceed the rate of venous return to it and therefore
factors governing venous return are primarily responsible for cardiac output. Other factors
include afterload, contractility, stroke volume and heart rate.

         Preload or venous return is the force distending the ventricle. The greater the stretch,
the greater the force of contraction. This mechanism is known as Frank Starling mechanism. It
occurs before stretching the myofibrils results in more efficient creation of cross bridges
between the contractile proteins. Thus, an increase in the distension of the ventricle will result
in an increase in the force of contraction sufficient to pump the extra volume. An increase in
preload will result in an increase in cardiac output.

         Afterload or total peripheral resistance is the force against which the ventricles must
act in order to eject blood. This largely depends on vascular resistance; however; it also
contains a component of myocardial stiffening. Increasing afterload increases myocardial
oxygen consumption and may decrease stroke volume eventually decreasing cardiac output.

         Contractility is the strength of the force of myocardial contraction. The degree of
contractility is also known as ionotropic state. A positive ionoresponse is an increase in
contractility. When contractility is reduced, stroke volume will fall which eventually causes a
fall in cardiac output.

         Stroke volume which is the amount of blood ejected by the ventricles per beat has a
direct control on cardiac output. The ejection fraction is the proportion of the stroke volume
which s ejected. Stroke volume is determined by volume and pressure of the blood filling the
ventricles (preload), resistance to ejection (afterload) and myocell shortening (contractility).
volume overload by Valsalva manoeuvre or isotonic exercise learning eventually increases
cardiac output.

         Herat rate is controlled by balance of parasympathetic and sympathetic innervation. An
increase in heart rate is known as positive chronotropic state (tachycardia) while a decrease of
heart rate id known as negative chronotropic state (bradycardia). When the sympathetic
system acts on increasing the heart rate, this eventually increases the cardiac output and vice
versa for the parasympathetic system.


**72.** What is the function of cholesterol and lipids in cell membranes?

         Give the cell extra support. Cholesterol is more rigid than some of the other lipids in
the membrane. Cholesterol helps immobilize some of the lipid molecules around them. This
extra rigidity makes the cell membrane stronger and makes it harder for small molecules to
pass through the membrane.

         Keeps the cell membrane fluid. Cholesterol helps generate some extra space between
the lipids which keeps them from getting together into their `crystalline` state thus allowing
them to move freely throughout the membrane as needed.

         Construction of lipid rafts. Lipids rafts are made up of high amounts of cholesterol and
sphingolipids. They are used for exporting proteins out of the cell, anchors specific proteins in
the membrane and keep protein clusters together.

**73.** Describe the steps in extracellular signaling

         Synthesis of signaling molecule by the signaling cell
         Packing of signaling molecule
         Release of signaling molecule
         Binding of signaling molecule to receptors of target cells
         Response of receptor-signal complex
         Removal of signaling molecule

**74.** Define and give examples:
Monosynaptic reflex- has one synapse but no interneuron; direct synapse between sensory
and motor neuron; tastes e.g. stretch reflex
         Polysynaptic reflex- has many synapses; slower e.g. withdrawal reflex


**75.** Briefly describe the immune response after the inhalation of pollen
         The body usually identifies the allergen (pollen) as harmful as soon as they enter the

sinuses. The immune system responds by producing antibodies to fight off the allergen.
Although the immune system produces antibodies in relatively small amounts the first time, it
encounters an allergen subsequent exposure result in a greater immune response. The
immunoglobulin produced in allergic reactions is IgE.

    76. Differentiate between classical and alternate pathways of complimentary system?
    a. Classical pathway
    In this the C1 binds with the antibodies and triggers a series of events in which other
    enzymes are activated in sequence. These enzymes or the by-products formed during
    these events produce the following activities:
    i. Opsonization: Activation of neutrophils and macrophages to engulf the bacteria, which
    are bound with a protein in the plasma called opsonin.
    ii. Lysis: Destruction of bacteria by rupturing the cell membrane.

iii. Chemotaxis: Attraction of leukocytes to the site of antigen-antibody reaction.
iv. Agglutination: Clumping of foreign bodies like RBCs or bacteria.
v. Neutralization: Covering the toxic sites of antigenic products.
vi. Activation of mast cells and basophils, which liberate histamine: Histamine dilates the
blood vessels and increases capillary permeability.
So, plasma proteins from blood enter the tissues and inactivate the antigenic products
b. Alternate pathway
Complementary system is also activated by another way, which is called alternate
pathway. It is due to a protein in circulation called factor I. It binds with polysaccharides
present in the cell membrane of the invading organisms. This binding activates C3 and C5,
which ultimately attack the antigenic products of invading organism through the same
activities highlighted in classical pathway above. Immunoglobulins M and G activate this
pathway.

**77.** What is the role of vitamin K in hemostasis?

   Vitamin K, which is a necessary cofactor for the enzyme that catalyses the conversion of
   glutamic acid residues to -carboxyglutamic acid residues. Six of the proteins involved in
   clotting require conversion of a number of glutamic acid residues to -carboxyglutamic
   acid residues before being released into the circulation, and hence all six are vitamin K-
   dependent. These proteins are factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X, protein C, and
   protein S. Vitamin K is required by the liver for normal formation of prothrombin as well
   as for formation of a few other clotting factors.

**78.** Explain the role of folic acid in haematopoiesis

    Folic acid and vitamin B12 are important for the final maturation of the red blood cells.
    Both of these are essential for the synthesis of DNA, because each in a different way is
    required for the formation of thymidine triphosphate, one of the essential building
    blocks of DNA.
    Therefore, lack of either vitamin B12 or folic acid causes abnormal and diminished DNA
    and, consequently, failure of nuclear maturation and cell division.
    The erythroblastic cells of the bone marrow, in addition to failing to proliferate rapidly,
    produce mainly larger than normal red cells called macrocytes, and the cell itself has a
    flimsy membrane and is often irregular, large, and oval instead of the usual biconcave
    disc

79. .In an ECG what do the following signify in terms of cardiac function?

      • P wave - depolarization of atria
      • QRS complex -depolarization of ventricular muscle, repolarization of atria.
      • T wave -repolarization of ventricular muscle
      • `U' WAVE- `U' wave is not always seen. It is also an insignificant wave in ECG. It is

           supposed to be due to repolarization of papillary muscle.
      • `Q-T' INTERVAL- `Q-T' interval is the interval between the onset of `Q' wave and

           the end of `T' wave. It indicates the ventricular depolarization and ventricular
           repolarization, i.e. it signifies the electrical activity in ventricles.
      • `P-R' INTERVAL - `P-R' interval is the interval between the onset of `P' wave and
           onset of `Q' wave. `P-R' interval signifies the atrial depolarization and conduction
           of impulses through AV node. It shows the duration of conduction of the impulses
           from the SA node to ventricles through atrial muscle and AV node. `P' wave
           represents the atrial depolarization. Short isoelectric (zero voltage) period after
           the end of `P' wave represents the time taken for the passage of depolarization
           within AV node.
      • ST segment- It is present between the end of S wave and the beginning of T wave
           (Fig. 7.16). It is isoelectric in the recording. If the ST segment deviates above the
           isoelectric line, it indicates the presence of myocardial infarction. The deviation of
           the ST segment will occur in the lead where the exploring electrode is facing the
           infarction

**85.** The adrenal medulla may be considered as an autonomic ganglion, explain?
    The adrenal medulla is a special case of autonomic innervation.
    It is considered a modified sympathetic ganglion
    Cells in the adrenal medulla are innervated by sympathetic preganglionic neurons.
    Like postganglionic neurons of sympathetic ganglia, cells in the adrenal medulla release
    norepinephrine (also epinephrine) and released into the circulation.
    Which bind to adrenergic receptors thus having similar physiological effect as
    sympathetic neural stimulation.


**86.** Differentiate between ionotropic and metabotropic receptors giving examples of
    each one of them.

**Ionotropic receptors**
1. Change shape when bound by a ligand, creating a channel that allows ions to flow through, e.g. nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.
2. The binding site of endogenous ligands on LGIC protein complexes is normally located on a different portion of the protein (allosteric site) than the location of the ion conduction pore.
3. Open quickly but remain open for only a few milliseconds, hence have a short-lived effect.
4. Have an effect only in the immediate region of the receptor.

**Metabotropic receptors**
1. When activated, a series of intracellular events are triggered that can also result in ion channels opening, but must involve a range of second messenger chemicals, e.g. glutamate receptors (GPCRs).
2. Have seven hydrophobic transmembrane domains.
3. On the presynaptic membrane, can inhibit or (more rarely) facilitate neurotransmitter release from presynaptic neurons, e.g. GABA receptors.
4. Are open for a longer period, so have a much longer-lasting effect due to signal cascade rather than direct channel opening, e.g. serotonin receptors.
5. Effect is widespread throughout the cell, e.g. muscarinic metabotropic receptors.


**87.** Compare and contrast Band T lymphocytes.
    B Lymphocytes
    -Processed in the liver during fetal life and in the bone marrow after birth
    -After processing they are transformed into two types (plasma cells and memory cells)
    -B-cells can connect to antigens right on the surface of the invading virus or bacteria.
    --cells for humoral or antibody-mediated immune system (AMIS).
    -They defend against viruses and bacteria that enter the blood and lymph.
    -They are formed by the division plasma cells.
    -Plasma cells do not move to the site of infection.
    -Plasma cells do not react against transplants and cancer cells.

    -Plasma cells have no inhibitory effect on immune system.
    T Lymphocytes
    -Processed in the thymus
    -Transformed into 4 types during processing (Helper T cells/inducer T cells, cytotoxic T
    cells, suppresser T cells, memory T cells)
    -T-cells, which can only connect to virus antigens on the outside of infected cells.
    -T-cells form cell-mediated immune system (CSM).
    -They defend against pathogens including protists and fungi that enter the cells.
    -They are formed by the division of lymphoblasts of three types: killer, helper and
    suppressor cells.
    -Lymphoblasts move to the site of infection.
    -Killer cells react against transplants and cancer cell

**88.** Distinguish between blood grouping and cross-matching
    Blood grouping- Blood grouping is done based on the Antigens A, B, AB & O to
    determine a person's blood type whereas cross matching considers other blood
    proteins apart from the ones used in blood grouping. Cross matching considers if the
    other proteins found in blood match together and if the blood from two individuals is
    compatible for transfusion.


**89.** Describe the difference in nerve transmission between myelinated and unmyelinated
    nerve fibres.
    Myelinated nerve fibres- Conduction is fast due to salutatory conduction as the
    impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to another. Thus depolarization only occurs at
    nodes of Ranvier. The nodes of Ranvier are subsequent gaps in between bundles of
    myelin sheath.
    Unmyelinated nerve fibres- Conduction is slow as it is conducted along the whole
    nerve fibre. Depolarization occurs along the whole nerve fibre.

    1. Renal failure
    2. TB
    3. Rheumatoid arthritis
    4. Excessive bleeding

    5. Infection
    6. Hypothyroidism

    -Relax GIT sphincters
    -Contract GIT smooth muscles
    -Decrease heart rate
    -Saliva secretion
    -Sweat production in sympathetic stimulation
    It's used as a neurotransmitter in preganglionic neurons of both parasympathetic and
    sympathetic neurons, in postganglionic parasympathetic neurons and postganglionic
    neurons of sympathetic system in sweat glands and blood vessels.


**92.** Distinguish between type 1 and type 2 muscle fibres

| Type I muscle fibre | Type II muscle fibre |
| --- | --- |
| High myoglobin | Less myoglobin |
| Rich blood supply | Poor blood supply |
| Numerous mitochondria | Fewer mitochondria |
| Poorly developed sarcoplasmic reticulum | Extensive sarcoplasmic reticulum |
| Adapted for slow contractions | Adapted for fast, fine movements |
| More resistant to fatigue | Less resistant to fatigue |


**93.** Discuss the inflammatory process.

The inflammatory response (inflammation) occurs when tissues are injured by bacteria,
trauma, toxins, heat, or any other cause. The damaged cells release chemicals including
histamine, bradykinin, and prostaglandins. These chemicals cause blood vessels to leak
fluid into the tissues, causing swelling. This helps isolate the foreign substance from
further contact with body tissues. The chemicals also attract white blood cells called
phagocytes that "eat" germs and dead or damaged cells.

This process is called phagocytosis. Phagocytes eventually die. Pus is formed from a
collection of dead tissue, dead bacteria, and live and dead phagocytes.


**94.** Discus the mechanisms for receptor regulation and the need for both.

    Receptors can be up-regulated when the stimuli is lowly concentrated and down-
    regulated when the
    Stimuli is highly concentrated. Up-regulation involves;
    -Synthesis of receptors
    -Exocytosis of more receptors.
    Down-regulation involves;
    -Endocytosis of the receptors
    -Degradation of receptors

**95.** Describe the various heart sounds with regards to their source and timings
    There are 4 heart sounds produced during each cardiac cycle.
    1st the sound (lubb) produced during isometric contraction period and early part of
    ejection period; 0.1 -0.17. Source; closure atrio-ventricular valve.
    2nd heart sound (dub) - produced during isometric relaxation; 0.1-0.14. It's due to
    closure of semilunar valve.
    3rd heart sound - produced during rapid filling phase, it's a low pitched sound and is
    inaudible. O.07-0.10. due to rushing of blood into the ventricle (ventricular filling).
    4th ventricle - produced during arterial systole; duration of 0.02-0.04 caused by
    contraction of atrial musculature.

**96.** Distinguish between absolute and relative refractory periods.
    Absolute refractory period: The period immediately following the firing of a nerve fiber
    when it cannot be stimulated no matter how great a stimulus is applied.
    Relative refractory period: The period shortly after the firing of a nerve fiber when
    partial repolarization has occurred and a greater than normal stimulus can stimulate a
    second response.

**97.** Describe mechanisms of intracellular communication in the body
    Paracrine signalling- occurs between cells that are close to each other and uses long
    branching processes; example is in parietal cells.
    Endocrine signaling- occurs between cells that are distant from each other via the
    bloodstream. Hormones are used in communication. Examples is in testes and ovaries.
    Synaptic signaling- when an action potential arrives at the synapse there is calcium
    influx that leads to exocytosis of neurotransmitter. It then binds onto the postsynaptic
    membrane receptors to cause a response. Occurs in neurotransmitter junctions.

         Contact-dependent signaling- ligands of the signaling cell remain attached to the cell
         membrane and extends thin processes to the target cell. Occurs in immune response.

    98. Describe the four stages of sensory information gathering

         Accession- environmental energy travels to the receptor through sensory organs by
         selection of modalities and modification.
         Transduction- environmental energy is converted into a receptor potential by 2nd
         messengers, G-proteins, enzymes etc.

         Conduction- messages are separated fast and slow. Urgent ones are prioritized.

         Integration- decisions are made, storage of memory and reflexes discarded.

    99. Explain how glucose is absorbed by intestinal epithelial cells(enterocytes)

         Absorption of Glucose and other monosaccharides: Transport across the Intestinal
         Epithelium absorption of glucose entails transport from the intestinal lumen, across the
         epithelium and into blood. The transporter that carries glucose and galactose into the
         enterocyte is the sodium-dependent hexose transporter, known more formally as
         SGLUT-1. As the name indicates, this molecule transports both glucose and sodium ion
         into the cell and in fact, will not transport either alone. The essence of transport by the
         sodium-dependent hexose transporter involves a series of conformational changes
         induced by binding and release of sodium and glucose, and can be summarized as
         follows:

         1. The transporter is initially oriented facing into the lumen-at this point it is capable
             of binding sodium, but not glucose.

         2. Sodium binds, inducing a conformational change that opens the glucose-binding
         pocket

         3. Glucose binds and the transporter reorients in the membrane such that the pockets
         holding sodium and glucose are moved inside the cell

         4. Sodium dissociates into the cytoplasm, causing glucose binding to destabilize

         5. Glucose dissociates into the cytoplasm and the unloaded transporter reorients back
         to its original, outward-facing position.


**100.** Differentiate between summation, reverberation, divergence and convergence

Summation- this is the additive effect of several electrical impulses on a neurotransmitter
junction. Individually, the stimuli cannot evoke any response but collectively they can generate
a response.

Reverberation- this is the process whereby there is continuous discharge of impulses by closed
chains of neurons from collateral of their cells and to the repeated echoing of sound.

Convergence- the axons of multiple neurons all send information to a single target neuron.
Divergence- the axons of one neuron sends information to many other neurons in a network.
