# Biochemistry Mid-Semester Exam — 2019 (Past Paper)

*University of Nairobi Level 1 Biochemistry mid-semester exam, 2019. Full text transcription of the original scanned paper — questions only.*

---

Surname: **COSPETER** Other names **FAITH NAIPUTA**
Reg. No. **I29/1966/2018** Group. **B2**

UNIVERSITY OF NAIROBI
DEPARTMENT OF BIOCHEMISTRY
MID OF FIRST SEMESTER CONTINUOUS ASSESSMENT TEST FOR YEAR-I
MBCHB, BPHARM & BDS (2018/2019)

DATE: Tuesday, January 22, 2019 TIME: 0900AM - 1200 NOON

## SECTION A (30 Marks): Answer ALL questions in the spaces provided

1. (a) State:-
    - Beer's Law
    When a ray of monochromatic light passes through an absorbing medium, its absorbance is directly proportional to the concentration of the solution.
    - Lamberts Law
    When a ray of monochromatic light passes through an absorbing medium, its absorbance is directly proportional to the length of the medium light path.
(b) Write the formula/expression for Beer- Lamberts Law and show how
Absorbance and Transmittance are related
Transmittance = Absorbance x Extinction coefficient
Extinction coefficient

| Absorbance (A) = log(T) | Absorbance = I0/I |
| :---------------------- | :---------------- |
| - log I/I = kcl         |                   |

I0 - intensity of incident light
I - final intensity of light

(c) With illustration, explain the relationship between absorbance and
concentration of a given absorbing medium?
The higher the concentration of a given solution the higher the absorbance this is due to higher number of particles per unit volume hence more light is absorbed by the particles.
e.g. 1 mole of hydrochloric acid in 500ml of water
& 1 mole of hydrochloric acid in 1000ml of water
The solution A obtained has higher absorbance as compared to the solution B, this is because the number of hydrochloric particles per unit volume of water in solution A is higher than in solution B thus greater Absorbance of solution A, when a ray of monochromatic light is passed through it.

Page 1 of 14

(c) A solution Y of 29.3 g/litre has an absorbance of 0.25 at 260nm. If the light path
is 1 cm and the molecular weight is 586, calculate:-
    - The molar extinction coefficient
    E = Absorbance / length of light path
    = 0.25 / 1
    = 0.25
    - The transmittance of 10 µmole/litre of solution Y
    T = 0.25 x 10
    = 2.5
(d) What is the importance of Beer-Lambert Law in biochemistry/medicine?
    - used in pharmaceutical in the manufacture of drugs, in determination of the drug's concentration.
    - used in diagnosis and prognosis of a certain disease, by use of biochemistry knowledge.

Page 2 of 14

2. (a) Identify the three bonding theories
    (i) Lewis Bonding theory
    (ii) Valence Bonding theory
    (iii) Molecular orbital theory
(b) In reference to NO
    (i) How many electrons are in NO molecule? 15 electrons
    (ii) Draw a clearly labeled molecular orbital diagram of NO

(Molecular orbital diagram of NO with energy levels, atomic orbitals (2s, 2p) and molecular orbitals (sigma, pi) for Nitrogen and Oxygen, showing electron filling)

State
    (i) The magnetic properties Paramagnetic
    (ii) The Bond Order 2.5 and, comment on the existence of
the NO? It exists. Justify your answer
Its bond order is more than zero

Page 3 of 14

3. The compound, 2-methyl-pent-2-ene can undergo an acid catalyzed addition
reaction with hydrogen halides following Markovnikov addition reaction rule.
(a) Explain the meaning of Markovnikov's rule (1 mark)
When Hx (hydrogen halide) is added to an alkene compound the major product
is formed when the H is bonded to a carbon atom with most number of
hydrogen atoms while X is bonded to the carbon atom with number of hydrogen
atoms.

(b) Using curly arrows to show the movement of electron pairs, describe the stepwise
mechanism of an electrophilic addition reaction between 2-methyl-pent-2-ene and
hydrogen bromide (4 marks)

(Chemical structures showing the reaction mechanism of 2-methyl-pent-2-ene with HBr, forming a carbocation intermediate and then the final product)

When 2-methyl pent-2-ene and hydrogen bromide
undergo additional reaction we would have an electron
rich area hence reacts with hydrogen ion electron
deficiency at point of carbon atom. The carbon atom is electron
positively charged with less number of hydrogen bromide ion
likely carbocations formed in the reaction mechanism.

(c) Draw the structure of the two most likely carbocations formed in the reaction
above (1 mark)

(Chemical structures of two carbocations)

(d) Give the structural formula and the IUPAC names of the major and minor
products formed in the above addition reaction (4 marks)

(Chemical structures of major and minor products)

Major product
2-Bromo-2-methylpentane

Minor product
2-Bromo-3-methylpentane

## SECTION B (30 Marks) : Answer all questions in the spaces provided

1. Write the Lewis structures of the following molecule/ions and indicate dative bonds and
formal charges (on the respective atoms). Atomic number: C=6, N=7, O=8, H=1

Page 4 of 14

1. (i) N₂O

| | N₂O | HCO₃⁻ anion |
| :---------------- | :------------------------------ |

8. The following elements are paramagnetic except;
A. N, 7 1S² 2S² 2P³
B. O, 8
C. B, 5
D. Cl, 17
E. He, 2

9. Dative bond
A. is possible between a Lewis acid and a Lewis base
B. is possible between a molecule with complete octet and one with incomplete
octet
C. involves sharing a pair of electrons
D. all of the above
E. none of the above

10. The f orbital has
A. l=2
B. n=3
C. nine orbitals
D. sixteen orbitals
E. none of the above

11. In the Periodic Table atomic size;
A. Decreases down the Period
B. -Increases down the Group
C. -Decreases across the Period
D. Decreases down the Period
E. B & C above are true

12. If two electrons (i) and (ii) in an atom are described by the quantum numbers shown below
the following is true EXCEPT;
| | n | l | m₁ | mₛ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (i) | 2 | 1 | 1 | +½ |
| (ii) | 3 | 1 | -1 | +½ |
A. They have the same spin
B. They are located in p orbitals
C. Are in different sub-shells
D. They differ in their energy levels
E. All the above are true

13. On acids and bases: -
A. All Bronsted acids are Arrhenius acids
B. All Lewis acids are Bronsted acids
C. All Bronsted acids are Lewis acids
D. Strong acids form strong conjugate bases in water
E. Weak acids form weak conjugate bases in water

Page 9 of 14

14. The following is true about the S-atomic orbitals
A. are asymmetric
B. are symmetrical along xyz axes
C. never form sigma-molecular orbitals
D. they never hybridize with d-atomic orbitals
E. all the above are false

15. An element with high electron affinity
A. is likely in Group II
B. has high ionization energy
C. is likely to be in group I
D. readily form ionic compound with group IV elements
E. sodium is a good example

16. The following elements are paramagnetic except;
A. N, 7
B. O, 8
C. B, 5
D. Cl, 17
E. He, 2

17. In p orbital;
A. l=2
B. n=1
C. 4p is higher in energy than 3d orbital
D. 3d is higher in energy than 4p orbital
E. none of the above

18. The following are noble gases except;
A. Hydrogen
B. Helium
C. Neon
D. Argon
E. Radon

19. In the Periodic Table, the difference between Group IVA and Group VIA elements is that;
A. The latter are metals the former are non metals
B. The latter are non metals former are metals
C. The latter are very reactive while the former are relatively inert
D. The former are more reactive in comparison to the latter
E. All the above are incorrect

20. The following is true on d-orbitals;
A. accommodate a maximum of 14 electrons
B. First appear at principal quantum number (n) = 2
C. An electron occupying the orbital can have a magnetic quantum number of -½
D. Can have a principal quantum number (n) of 3
E. An electron in this orbital can have a magnetic quantum number of +½

Page 10 of 14

21. Between (CH₃)₃NH⁺ and (CH₃)₃NH₂, the H in
A. the former is a stronger Lewis acid
B. latter is a stronger Lewis acid
C. Both are of equal acidity
D. the former is a stronger Lewis acid due to a donating effect of CH₃ - group
E. the latter is a stronger Lewis acid due to withdrawing effect of CH₃ - groups.

22. In the molecule HSD, the acidic properties of the hydrogen (H);
A. Increases when D is more electronegative than S
B. Increases when D is electropositive than S
C. Remains unchanged when D is replaced by a more electronegative element
D. A, B & C are not true
E. A, B & C are all true

23. An electron occupying a given atomic orbital
A. always must remain in that orbital
B. may occupy a higher orbital after absorbing the necessary quantum energy
C. may occupy a lower orbital after absorbing the necessary quantum energy
D. may occupy a higher orbital after losing the necessary quantum energy
E. None of the above.

24. Molecular orbitals
A. Are due to atomic orbital hybridization
B. Are of the bonding and antibonding types
C. Exist only as bonding type
D. Exists only as antibonding type
E. None of the above is true

25. The most stable electronic configuration of copper is:
A. [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹
B. [Ar]3d⁹4s²
C. [Ar]3d⁸4s³
D. Both A & B
E. None of the above is true

26. Which one of the following compound is obtained by the oxidation of secondary
alcohols by [O]?
A. Ketone
B. Aldehyde
C. Ether
D. Amine
E. Ester.

Page 11 of 14

27. The boiling point of water is about 200°C higher than one would predict from the
boiling points of hydrogen sulfide and hydrogen selenide. One may explain this
apparent anomaly by which of the following?
A. Water has the lowest molecular weight.
B. The H-O covalent bond is much stronger than the H-S and H-Se bonds.
C. Water is less polar than hydrogen sulfide and hydrogen selenide.
D. The water molecule is lighter than the other two molecules.
E. The intermolecular attractive forces are much greater in water than in hydrogen
sulfide and hydrogen selenide.

28. Which of the following compounds has the highest boiling point?
A. Hexane
B. 2-methylpentane
C. 2,2-dimethylbutane
D. 3-methylpentane
E. Butane

29. What will be the major product obtained from the acid-catalysed hydration of pent-1-
ene?
A. Pentan-1-ol
B. Pentan-1,2-diol
C. Pentan-2-ol
D. Pentane
E. Pentanoic acid

30. How many aromatic isomers of dibromobenzene exist?
A. 2
B. 3
C. 4
D. 6
E. 8

31. The correct IUPAC name for CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ is
A. isopropyl alcohol.
B. 2-methyl ethanol.

Page 12 of 14

C. 2-propanol.
D. Hydroxypropane
E. 2-methylpropanol.

32. Alcohols have higher boiling points than alkanes of similar molecular mass because
A) alcohols are ionic compounds and alkanes are covalent compounds.
B) alkane molecules are polar and alcohol molecules are not.
C) H-bonding occurs between alcohol molecules but not between alkane molecules.
D) alcohols are acidic and alkanes are not.
E) Alcohols are usually larger molecules as compared to alkanes

33. Acid catalysed hydration of alkenes except ethene leads to the formation of
A) mixture of secondary and tertiary alcohols
B) mixture of primary and secondary alcohols
C) secondary or tertiary alcohol
D) primary alcohol
E) a tertiary alcohol

34. Among the alkenes which one produces tertiary butyl alcohol on acid hydration
A) CH3 – CH = CH CH2CH3
B) CH3 – CH = CH – CH3
C) (CH3)2C= CH2
D) CH3 – CH2 – CH = CH2
E) CH3 – CH = CH2

35. An ether is more volatile than an alcohol having the same molecular formula. This is due to
A) dipolar character of ethers
B) alcohols having resonance structures
C) Ethers have less covalent bonds than alcohols
D) inter-molecular hydrogen bonding in ethers
E) inter-molecular hydrogen bonding in alcohols

36. The name of the alkane isomer of cis-3-hexene is:
A) 2-methylpentane
B) 3-methylpentane
C) n-hexane
D) 2,3-dimethylbutane
E) cyclohexane

37. What is the relationship between the structures shown?

    H     H             H     Cl
    \   /               \   /
     C = C               C = C
    /   \               /   \
  H3C   Cl            H3C   H

A) structural isomers
B) geometric isomers
C) conformational structures
D) identical structures
E) optical isomers

38. Which is the best description of a carbonyl group?
A) a carbon atom joined to an oxygen atom by a double bond
B) a nitrogen and a hydrogen bonded to a carbon atom
C) a sulfur and a hydrogen bonded to a carbon atom
D) an oxygen double-bonded to a carbon and a hydroxyl group
E) a carbon bonded directly to oxygen by a single bond

39. Hexane and 3-methylpentane are examples of:
A) Enantiomers.
B) Stereoisomers.
C) Diastereomers.
D) Constitutional isomers.
E) Position isomers

40. Which of the following groups has the highest priority according to the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog sequence rules?
A) CH3
B) CH2Cl
C) CH2OH
D) CHO
E) COOH

# Biochemistry Mid-Semester Exam — 2016 (Past Paper)

*University of Nairobi Level 1 Biochemistry mid-semester exam, 2016. Full text transcription of the original scanned paper — questions only.*

---

" MARKING SCHEME "

Other names ___________________________________
Reg. No. ______________________ Group______

UNIVERSITY OF NAIROBI
DEPARTMENT OF BIOCHEMISTRY

MID OF SECOND SEMESTER CONTINUOUS ASSESSMENT TEST FOR LEVEL - I MBCHB, BPHARM & BDS (2016/2017)

DATE: Wednesday, May 4 2016
TIME: 2.00 – 5.00 PM

SECTION A (30Marks) : Answer ALL questions in the spaces provided

1. Write the two half reactions (i and ii) and the overall equation (iii) for:-

(a) Aerobic glycolysis

(i) Glucose $\longrightarrow$ 2 Pyruvate$^-$ + 2 H$^+$
(ii) 2 ADP + 2 Pi + 2 NAD$^+$ + 4 ADP $\longrightarrow$ 4 ATP + 2 H$_2$O + 2 NADH + 2 H$^+$ + 2 ADP

b) ATP acting on PDH activates PDH

d) The active form of PDH is the phosphorylated form
e) Inactivated fatty acids inactivates PDH

21. Enzyme driven metabolic pathways can be made more efficient by
a) Concentrating enzymes within specific cellular compartment
b) Grouping enzymes into free- floating multienzyme complexes
c) fixing enzyme into membranes so that they are adjacent to each other

e) None of the above

22. Which of the following about enzymes or their functions is true?
a) Enzymes do not alter the overall change in free energy for a reaction
b) Enzymes are proteins whose three-dimensional form is key for their functions.
c) Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering activation energy
d) All of the above
e) None of the above

23. In the enzyme-catalyzed reaction shown below, what will be the effects on substances A, B, C and D of inactivating the enzyme labeled E2?

A----(E1)---->B----(E2)---->C------(E3)---->D

a) A, B, C, and D will all still be produced
b) A, B and C will still be produced
c) A and B will still be produced but not C and D
d) A will still be produced, but not B, C and D

24. Enzymes having slightly different molecular structures but performing identical activity are
a) Holoenzymes
b) Apoenzymes
c) Isoenzymes
d) Coenzymes
e) None of the above

25. Which factor is responsible for inhibition of enzymatic process during feedback?
a) Enzymes
b) End product
c) Temperature
d) Substrate
e) pH

26. Vitamin K is required for
a) Change of prothrombin to thrombin
b) Synthesis of prothrombin
c) Change of fibrinogen to fibrin
d) Formation of thromboplastin
e) All of the above

27. Calcium deficiency in the body occurs in the absence of
a) Vitamin C
b) Vitamin D
c) Vitamin A
d) Vitamin E
e) None of the above

28. To which of the following families do folic acid and pantothenic acid belong?
a) Vitamin C
b) Vitamin K
c) Vitamin A
d) Vitamin B complex
e) All of the above

29. Which of the following is a fat-soluble vitamin and its related deficiency?
a) Vitamin B1 - retinal Xerophthamia
b) Cobalamine -Beri beri
c) Calciferol -Pellagra
d) Ascorbic acid - scurvy
e) None of the above

30. Which of the following is mismatched?
a) Vitamin A-xerophthalmia
b) Vitamin D-rickets
c) Vitamin K-beri beri
d) Vitamin C-scurvy
e) None of the above

# Biochemistry End of Year Exam — 2014 (Past Paper)

*University of Nairobi Level 1 Biochemistry end-of-year exam, 2014. Scanned original exam paper, reproduced as page images — questions only.*

---

SECTION A (30 MARKS): Attempt any THREE Questions.

1. The Henderson - Hasselbalch equation is important in the calculation of a pH of a buffer solution.

a) With a specific, physiological example, explain the term "buffer solution". (2 Marks)

b) Derive the Henderson Hasselbalch equation using a hypothetical weak acid HA. (3 Marks)

c) How many grams of acetic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$) and sodium acetate are needed to make up to one litre of a 50 mm acetate buffer with a pH of 5.0. $\text{ka} = 1.75 \times 10^{-5}$ (4 Marks)

2. (a) State 4 functions of carbohydrates. (4 Marks)

(b) Explain the basis of reduction tests as a means of identifying sugars in unknown solutions. (2 Marks)

SECTION A: Attempt any THREE Questions (30 Marks)

1. Hyperammonemia is lethal and can result in serious mental retardation. Describe the main pathway for removal of ammonia from the body.

2. With regards to glycolysis;
a) Describe in detail, the reactions catalysed by kinases
b) With relevant reaction(s), distinguish between aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis.
c) Which of the two types of glycolysis proceeds with a higher overall standard free energy ($\Delta G^{01}$)? Why?

3. (i) What are enzymes?
(ii) Describe the factors which affect the rate of enzymatic reactions.

4. (a) Briefly discuss fate of amino acid pool.
(b) Outline metabolic circumstances under which amino acids undergo oxidative deamination and list 4 human disorders associated with amino acids catabolism.

5. (a) Explain the term "Genetic code is degenerate".
(b) Explain 'Wobble Hypothesis' showing clearly all the permitted interactions.
(c) With regards to ribosomes:-
(i) Differentiate between prokaryotic and eukaryotic types
(ii) Explain the biological role in living organisms.

SECTION B: Answer ALL questions in the spaces provided (30 marks)

1. Synthesis of amino acids is mainly catalyzed by enzymes called ___________________ which catalyses the transfer of an amino group from an amino acid to a keto acid via a process called ___________________. Nevertheless, amino acids can also be catabolized by various pathways. For instance, the catabolism of branched amino acids namely isoleucine, leucine and ___________________ initially share the first, second and third reactions in their pathways. Deficiency in one of the common enzymes namely ___________________ leads to a disease called ___________________. Catabolism of branched amino acid ___________________ which is classified exclusively as ___________________ produce a ketone namely ___________________ whereas the catabolism of isoleucine result in both 2-carbon and 4-carbon citric acid cycle intermediates namely ___________________ and ___________________ respectively.

2. To enter the glycolytic pathway, ___________________, ___________________, ___________________ and ___________________ are firstly converted to ___________________, ___________________, ___________________ and ___________________ respectively. They all end up as a common product namely ___________________ and from which a high-energy compound known as ___________________ is formed.

3. The following graph represents a titration curve for the amino acid, lysine. answer the following questions (a-h) choosing answers I-VIII

![titration curve for lysine with pH vs Equivalents OH- showing points I through VII](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-biochem-eoy2014-p004-bce9cdfb.jpg)

(a) Identify all the $\text{pK}_\text{a}$ values on the lysine titration curve ______ [0.75 marks]

(b) At which points does lysine have maximum buffering capacity? ______ [0.95 marks]

(c) Would lysine have a good buffering capacity at pH 7.6? ______
Explain briefly...................................................................................
......................................................................................................... [1 mark]

(d) Which point corresponds to pI of lysine? ______ [0.5 marks]

(e) At which point has the carboxyl group been completely titrated? ______ [0.5 marks]

(f) At which pint is lysine completely titrated (i.e. all protons neutralized)?
____________________ [0.5 marks]

(g) At which point is the average net charge of lysine equal to -1? ______ [0.5 marks]

(h) At which pint is the average net charge of lysine equal to 0? ______ [0.5 marks]

4.

| Statement | Answer |
| :--- | :--- |
| (i) Name a 'stop' code for protein biosynthesis | UAG, UGA, UAA. |
| (ii) The enzyme that lays an RNA primer in DNA replication/ | |
| (iii) The enzyme that makes a double stranded DNA from a single strand RNA template in viral replication | |
| (iv) Translocase in protein biosynthesis is also referred to as | |
| (v) A compound that inhibits transcription | |

(vi) Name three post-transcriptional modifications in eukaryotes:

__________________________________________________

__________________________________________________

__________________________________________________


(viii) Name two types of post-translational modifications on OH containing amino acid proteins:

__________________________________________________

__________________________________________________


5. Urea cycle begin inside mitochondria where carbamoyl Phosphate donate its carbamoyl group to ornithine to form ________________. The reaction is catalyzed by ________________________________, and the product passes form the ________________ to the ________________. The second amino group then enters the cycle by a condensation reaction between the amino groups of ________________ and ureido group of citrulline, forming ________________ in a reaction catalyzed by ________________
the product is then cleaved by the enzyme ________________
to form fumarate and ________________. In the last reaction of the urea cycle, the cytosolic enzyme ________________ cleaves ________________ to yield urea and ornithine.

6. Using the active site concept and substrate binding concept, fill the missing words in the following paragraph.
The __________ dimensional structures which have been elucidated for some enzymes allow for a detailed description of their __________. Although an enzyme typically has more than 100 amino acids residues in its structure, only a small number of __________ comprise __________ dimensional site which directly contacts the __________. Such an __________ is often a cleft in molecule's exterior. In some cases, the crevice, containing the __________ and, if needed, __________ binding sites, may provide a largely hydrophobic environment. In the 1890s Fisher *et al* proposed the __________ model (hypothesis), which accounts for substrate binding by the matching of complementary substrate and active-site structures. Over the years Koshland proposed Fishers model by suggesting a __________ type of relationship between some enzymes and their substrates.

SECTION C: Multiple Choice Questions.
For each statement, choose the most suitable answer from the 5 choices and put an X on the correct box in the answer sheet provided. Marks will not be awarded where more than one box is filled.

1. A positive redox potential means a compound has;
a) Lower affinity for electron
b) Higher affinity for electron
c) Lower affinity for proton
d) Higher affinity for proton
e) No affinity for proton or electron

2. Oxidation of a molecule involves;
a) Gain of electron
b) Loss of electron
c) Gain of proton
d) Loss of proton
e) None of the above

3. How many molecules of ATP are synthesized per NADH oxidized?
a) 2
b) 3
c) 1
d) 4
e) 5

4. How many ATPS are produced by oxidation of 1 molecule of acetyl CoA?
a) 8
b) 10
c) 12
d) 14
e) 16

5. A kinase is an enzyme that;
a) Uses NADH to change the oxidation state of a substrate
b) Uses ATP to fix a carbon to a substrate
c) Removes water from a double bond
d) Removes phosphate groups of substrates
e) Uses ATP to add a phosphate group to a substrate

6. In the glycogen synthase reaction, the precursor to glycogen is;
a) G6P
b) G1P
c) UDP-glucose
d) UTP-glucose
e) CDP-glucose

7. Pyruvate is initially converted to which of the following in gluconeogenesis?
a) Glycerol
b) PEP
c) OAA
d) AcetylCoA
e) Lactate

8. The damage caused by UV light on DNA is:
a) Depuration
b) Thymine dimerization
c) Loss of pyrimidine bases
d) covalent linkage between adjacent purine nucleotides
e) None of the above

9. On a gene sequence, the correct amino acid start code is:
a) 5' ATG --- 3'
b) 3' ATG --- 5'
c) 5' AAG --- 3'
d) 3' AAG --- 5'
e) 5' AAT --- 3'

10. The Okazaki's fragments are:-
a) formed on the 'leading strand'
b) formed on the 'lagging stand'
c) formed on both the 'leading' and 'lagging' strands
d) removed by DNA ligase
e) removed by DNA topoisomerases

11. The following is NOT correctly matched to their role in DNA replication
a) Addition of nucleotides to 3' OH end - DNA polymerase III
b) Removal of RNA primers - DNA polymerase I
c) Formation of phosphodiester bond in DNA breaks - DNA ligase
d) Joining of Okazakis' fragments - DNA topoisomerases
e) Separation of DNA strands - DNA helicases

12. Which of the following catalyse the second step of the elongation cycle in protein biosynthesis?
a) Translocase
b) Amino acyl tRNA synthetase
c) Peptidyl transferase
d) Topoisomerase
e) None of the above

13. In a DNA-RNA hybrid duplex, respectively
a) U base pairs with T
b) T base pairs with U
c) C base pairs with U
d) A base pairs with U
e) None of the above

14. Inability of cells to repair bulk lessions on their DNA results in a condition/disorder known as:
a) Lesch-Nyhan syndrome
b) Xeroderma pigmentosum
c) Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)
d) Gout
e) Alkaptonuria

15. Hydroxylation of phenylalanine to tyrosine requires all of the following EXCEPT;
a) Phenylalanine hydroxylase
b) Tetrahydrobiopterin
c) $\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+$
d) Molecular oxygen
e) Biotin

16. Maple syrup urine disease is an inborn error of metabolism of:
a) Sulphur-containing amino acids
b) Aromatic amino acids
c) Branched chain amino acids
d) Dicarboxylic amino acids
e) Both methionine and threonine

17. The defective enzyme in histidinemia is:
a) Histidine carboxylase
b) Histidine decarboxylase
c) Histidase
d) Histine oxidase
e) None of the above

18. Most of the ammonia released from amino acids reflects the coupled action of transaminase and
a) Glutamate dehydrogenase
b) Amino acid oxidase
c) Histidase
d) Serine dehydratase
e) Histidine decarboxylase

19. All the following statements about albinism are correct EXCEPT:
a) Tyrosine hydroxylase (tyrosinase) is absent or deficient in melanocytes
b) Skin is hypopigmented
c) It results in mental retardation
d) Eyes are hypopigmented
e) It is an inherited disorder

20. Cysteine can be synthesized from:
a) Serine
b) Homeserine
c) Homocysteine
d) Threonine
e) Tryptophan

21. Genetics defect in phenylalanine hydroxylase leads to:
a) Alkaptonuria
b) Protenuria
c) Phenylketonuria
d) Phenylalalinuria
e) Tyrosinemia II

22. The carbon skeletons of the following two amino acids ultimately enter the citric acid cycle as oxaloacetate
a) Glutamate and glutamine
b) Tyrosine and phenylalanine
c) Lysine and isolencine
d) Asparagine and aspartate
e) Glycine and threonine

23. The following amino acids are both ketogenic and glucogenic EXCEPT:
a) Alanine
b) Glycine
c) Serine
d) Lysine
e) Threonine

24. The carbon skeletons of the following amino acids are degraded by pathways that yield succinyl-CoA EXCEPT:-
a) Leucine
b) Methionine
c) Isoleucine
d) Threonine
e) Valine

25. Oxidative deamination is catalized by
a) L-glutamine dehydrogenase
b) L-glutamate dehydrogenase
c) Glutamine synthetase
d) Glutaminase
e) Lactate dehydrogenase

26. The following enzymes are important in diagnosis of heart attack and liver damage EXCEPT:
a) Glutamate dehydrogenase
b) Creatine kinase
c) Alanine aminotransferase
d) Asparate aminotrasferase
e) Lactate dehydrogenase

27. During starvation, alanine transports amino group to the liver in a non-toxic form, via a pathway called:
a) Cori cycle
b) Citric acid cycle
c) Urea cycle
d) Glucose-alanine cycle
e) Glyoxylate cycle

28. The structural integrity of supramolecular complexes are bonded to each other by all of the following forces, EXCEPT:
a) covalent bonds
b) van der Waals forces
c) hydrogen bonds
d) hydrophobic interactions
e) ionic interactions

29. What is the nucleotide sequence of the DNA strand that is complementary to 5'-ATCGCAACTGTCACTA-3'?
a) 5'-TAGCGTTGACAGTGAT-3'
b) 5'-UAGUGACAGUUGCGAU-3'
c) 5'-TAGCGTTGACAGTGAT-3'
d) 5'-TAGTGACAGTTGCGAT-3'
e) 5'-ATCACTGTCAACGCTA-3'

articles.content:
*Continued from [Part 3](/blog/medical-biochemistry-ii-paper-a-mbmb-2200-part-3).*

# MEDICAL BIOCHEMISTRY EXAM ANSWERS
## BMB 2105: BIOCHEMISTRY OF SPECIALIZED TISSUES
### 
---

## SECTION A - MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS (30 MARKS)
### Question 1
**What cell protein binds Calcium ions after signal transduction?**


- a) Adenylate cyclase
- b) Guanylate cyclase
- c) Calmodulin
- d) Calsequestrin

**Answer: c) Calmodulin**


**Explanation:** Calmodulin is a calcium-binding messenger protein that binds calcium ions after signal transduction. It undergoes conformational changes upon binding calcium and then activates various target proteins including enzymes and ion channels.


---

### Question 2
**Muscles respond to insulin by:**


- a) Forming more glycogen
- b) Breaking down glycogen
- c) Breaking down lipids
- d) Breaking down amino acids

**Answer: a) Forming more glycogen**


**Explanation:** Insulin promotes anabolic processes in muscle tissue. It activates glycogen synthase and inhibits glycogen phosphorylase, leading to increased glycogen formation and storage in skeletal muscle.


---

### Question 3
**Which of the following processes would you expect to find in a normal person after a meal?**


- a) Enhanced glycogen synthase activity in the liver
- b) An increased ratio of phosphorylase A to phosphorylase B in the liver
- c) An increased rate of lactate formation by enterocytes
- d) Inhibition of glycogen synthase phosphatase activity in the liver

**Answer: a) Enhanced glycogen synthase activity in the liver**


**Explanation:** After a meal, insulin levels rise, promoting glycogen synthesis. Glycogen synthase activity is enhanced through dephosphorylation (activation) to store excess glucose as glycogen in the liver.


---

### Question 4
**A person has just had a nice meal. Which of the following enzymes would you not expect to find in their system?**


- a) Glycogen phosphorylase
- b) Glycogen synthase
- c) Lipoprotein lipase
- d) Acetyl-CoA carboxylase

**Answer: a) Glycogen phosphorylase**


**Explanation:** After a meal, the fed state promotes anabolic processes. Glycogen phosphorylase (which breaks down glycogen) would be inhibited, while glycogen synthase, lipoprotein lipase, and acetyl-CoA carboxylase would be active to promote storage.


---

### Question 5
**Glucagon has the following effect on lipid metabolism in the liver:**


- a) The net synthesis of triacylglycerides is increased
- b) Hormone-sensitive lipase is activated
- c) Both glycogen phosphorylase and glycogen synthase are activated but at markedly different rates
- d) Glycogen phosphorylase is inactivated while glycogen synthase is activated

**Answer: b) Hormone-sensitive lipase is activated**


**Explanation:** Glucagon activates hormone-sensitive lipase through cAMP-dependent protein kinase, promoting lipolysis and fatty acid mobilization during fasting states.


---

### Question 6
**In blood plasma fatty acids circulate:**


- a) In the content of nuclei of plasma lipoprotein particles
- b) In the content of an outer shell of plasma lipoprotein particles
- c) In the complex with serum albumin
- d) Freely without formation of any complexes

**Answer: c) In the complex with serum albumin**


**Explanation:** Free fatty acids in plasma are bound to albumin for transport due to their hydrophobic nature. This binding allows their solubility in the aqueous plasma environment.


---

### Question 7
**Histamine is made by:**


- a) Neutrophils
- b) Eosinophils
- c) Basophils
- d) Monocytes

**Answer: c) Basophils**


**Explanation:** Basophils and mast cells are the primary producers of histamine. They store histamine in granules and release it during allergic reactions and inflammatory responses.


---

### Question 8
**The oxidation of ethanol with acetaldehyde dehydrogenase results in the formation of:**


- a) Acetaldehyde
- b) NADH₂
- c) Acetate
- d) Pyruvate

**Answer: c) Acetate**


**Explanation:** Acetaldehyde dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidation of acetaldehyde to acetate, which is the second step in ethanol metabolism. This reaction also produces NADH.


---

### Question 9
**Which of the following reactions is marked as conjugation?**


- a) Attachment of a hydroxyl to a toxic substance
- b) Attachment of protons and electrons to a toxic substance
- c) Glucuronidation
- d) Any reactions of a synthesis

**Answer: c) Glucuronidation**


**Explanation:** Glucuronidation is a classic Phase II conjugation reaction where glucuronic acid is attached to substrates, making them more water-soluble for excretion.


---

### Question 10
**Troponin C is:**


- a) Responsible for the binding of calcium ions
- b) Responsible for the binding of G-actin
- c) Responsible for the inhibition of the actin and myosin interaction
- d) Phosphorylated by cAMP-dependent protein kinase

**Answer: a) Responsible for the binding of calcium ions**


**Explanation:** Troponin C is the calcium-binding subunit of the troponin complex in skeletal muscle. When calcium binds to troponin C, it initiates the conformational changes that allow muscle contraction.


---

### Question 11
**Exocytosis of acetylcholine-containing vesicles in the presynaptic cell is caused by influx of:**


- a) Sodium ions
- b) Potassium ions
- c) Chloride ions
- d) Calcium ions

**Answer: d) Calcium ions**


**Explanation:** Calcium influx through voltage-gated calcium channels triggers the fusion of acetylcholine-containing vesicles with the presynaptic membrane, leading to neurotransmitter release.


---

### Question 12
**A muscle is attached to the following molecule before contraction:**


- a) ATP
- b) AMP
- c) ADP
- d) Calcium

**Answer: a) ATP**


**Explanation:** ATP must bind to the myosin head before muscle contraction can occur. ATP binding causes the myosin head to detach from actin, and ATP hydrolysis provides energy for the power stroke.


---

### Question 13
**Mutations in the dystrophin gene can cause:**


- a) Duchenne muscular disease
- b) Tetany
- c) Hypertrophy
- d) Hyperplasia

**Answer: a) Duchenne muscular disease**


**Explanation:** Dystrophin gene mutations cause Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a severe X-linked genetic disorder characterized by progressive muscle degeneration and weakness.


---

### Question 14
**Which enzyme is attached to myosin head?**


- a) Adenylate cyclase
- b) GTP-ase
- c) Creatine kinase
- d) ATP-ase

**Answer: d) ATP-ase**


**Explanation:** Myosin head has intrinsic ATPase activity that hydrolyzes ATP to provide energy for muscle contraction and the conformational changes during the cross-bridge cycle.


---

### Question 15
**Which of the following is true about the sliding filament theory:**


- a) The cross size of a sarcomere increases during muscle contraction
- b) The cross size of a sarcomere decreases during muscle contraction
- c) The cross size of a sarcomere is not changed during muscle contraction
- d) The distance between z-membranes of a sarcomere decreases

**Answer: d) The distance between z-membranes of a sarcomere decreases**


**Explanation:** According to the sliding filament theory, actin and myosin filaments slide past each other without changing length, causing the sarcomere to shorten and the Z-lines to move closer together.


---

### Question 16
**Which is the major pathway for metabolizing carcinogens like aflatoxin?**


- a) Reduction
- b) Carboxylation
- c) Glutathione conjugation
- d) Hydroxylation

**Answer: c) Glutathione conjugation**


**Explanation:** Glutathione conjugation is a major Phase II detoxification pathway that conjugates glutathione to carcinogens like aflatoxin, making them more water-soluble for excretion.


---

### Question 17
**During fasting excessive lipolysis results in:**


- a) Ketogenesis
- b) Beta oxidation
- c) Glycogenesis
- d) Gluconeogenesis

**Answer: a) Ketogenesis**


**Explanation:** During prolonged fasting, excessive lipolysis produces large amounts of acetyl-CoA from fatty acid β-oxidation, which overwhelms the TCA cycle and leads to ketone body formation (ketogenesis).


---

### Question 18
**Which of the following processes would not occur during a well-fed state?**


- a) Glycogenesis
- b) Lipogenesis
- c) Gluconeogenesis
- d) Glycolysis

**Answer: c) Gluconeogenesis**


**Explanation:** In the well-fed state, glucose is abundant, so gluconeogenesis (glucose synthesis) is inhibited. Instead, anabolic processes like glycogenesis, lipogenesis, and glycolysis are promoted.


---

### Question 19
**The platelet plug is formed by the following except:**


- a) Exposed collagen
- b) Thromboxane
- c) Adenosine diphosphate
- d) Prostacyclin

**Answer: d) Prostacyclin**


**Explanation:** Prostacyclin (PGI₂) actually inhibits platelet aggregation and opposes platelet plug formation. The other factors promote platelet activation and aggregation.


---

### Question 20
**The first source of ATP in muscles is:**


- a) Anaerobic glycolysis (lactic acid system)
- b) Phosphagen system
- c) Aerobic system
- d) Aerobic glycolysis

**Answer: b) Phosphagen system**


**Explanation:** The phosphagen system (creatine phosphate system) provides immediate ATP for the first 10-15 seconds of high-intensity exercise through the creatine kinase reaction.


---

### Question 21
**The active muscle of a sprint runner would mostly use:**


- a) Phosphagen system - Creatine phosphate
- b) Glycolysis
- c) Fatty acid oxidation
- d) Protein catabolism

**Answer: a) Phosphagen system - Creatine phosphate**


**Explanation:** Sprint running requires immediate, high-intensity energy output. The phosphagen system provides ATP most rapidly for short-duration, high-intensity activities.


---

### Question 22
**As intensity of exercise in the active muscle increases:**


- a) Fat use increases
- b) Carbohydrate use increases
- c) Glycogen use decreases
- d) Protein synthesis increases

**Answer: b) Carbohydrate use increases**


**Explanation:** As exercise intensity increases, the body shifts from fat oxidation to carbohydrate utilization because carbohydrates can be metabolized more rapidly to meet the increased ATP demand.


---

### Question 23
**Fast-twitch muscles have the following except:**


- a) Less blood vessels
- b) Less mitochondria
- c) More mitochondria
- d) Greater tension

**Answer: c) More mitochondria**


**Explanation:** Fast-twitch (Type II) muscle fibers have fewer mitochondria compared to slow-twitch fibers because they rely more on anaerobic metabolism rather than aerobic oxidation.


---

### Question 24
**The short structural units of a myofibril are known as:**


- a) Sarcolemma
- b) Sarcomeres
- c) Myosins
- d) Actins

**Answer: b) Sarcomeres**


**Explanation:** Sarcomeres are the basic functional units of myofibrils, extending from one Z-line to the next Z-line, containing the contractile proteins actin and myosin.


---

### Question 25
**The hormone erythropoietin is made by:**


- a) Hypothalamus
- b) Pituitary gland
- c) Kidney
- d) Spleen

**Answer: c) Kidney**


**Explanation:** Erythropoietin is primarily produced by the kidneys in response to hypoxia. It stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow.


---

### Question 26
**What molecule do red blood cells use to defend themselves against oxidants?**


- a) Hemoglobin
- b) Glutathione
- c) Oxygen
- d) Carbon dioxide

**Answer: b) Glutathione**


**Explanation:** Glutathione is the major antioxidant in red blood cells, protecting them from oxidative damage through the glutathione peroxidase and reductase system.


---

### Question 27
**Which is the most abundant glucose carrier in the endothelial cell of the blood-brain barrier?**


- a) GLUT 1 45K
- b) GLUT 1 55K
- c) GLUT 2
- d) GLUT 3

**Answer: b) GLUT 1 55K**


**Explanation:** GLUT 1 55K is the predominant glucose transporter in brain endothelial cells, facilitating glucose transport across the blood-brain barrier to supply the brain's glucose needs.


---

### Question 28
**The increase in extracellular potassium and glutamate after synaptic activity triggers:**


- a) Glycolysis
- b) Gluconeogenesis
- c) Glycogen synthesis
- d) Lipid synthesis

**Answer: a) Glycolysis**


**Explanation:** Increased extracellular K⁺ and glutamate after synaptic activity stimulates astrocytes to increase glucose uptake and glycolysis to meet the increased energy demands of neural activity.


---

### Question 29
**Glutamate can be used as energetic fuel in the brain through transformation into:**


- a) α-ketoglutarate
- b) Glutamine
- c) Pyruvate
- d) Fatty acids

**Answer: a) α-ketoglutarate**


**Explanation:** Glutamate can be deaminated to α-ketoglutarate, which enters the TCA cycle as an energy substrate, serving as an alternative fuel source for brain metabolism.


---

### Question 30
**Immediately after exercise, people tend to suffer with afterburn where they need to take up a lot of oxygen. Which of the following is the reason for afterburn?**


- a) To replace oxygen that was withdrawn from hemoglobin and myoglobin during exercise
- b) To get extra O₂ required for metabolism of tissues warmed during exercise
- c) To get O₂ needed for metabolism of lactic acid produced during anaerobic respiration
- d) The oxygen is needed to refill the lungs and prevent pulmonary collapse

**Answer: c) To get O₂ needed for metabolism of lactic acid produced during anaerobic respiration**


**Explanation:** Post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) or "afterburn" is primarily needed to metabolize accumulated lactate through gluconeogenesis and to restore depleted oxygen stores in tissues.


---

## SECTION B - SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (30 MARKS)
### Question 1: Explain the astrocyte-neuron metabolic coupling in the brain (6 marks)
**Answer:** Astrocyte-neuron metabolic coupling, also known as the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle hypothesis, describes the metabolic partnership between these two cell types in the brain:


**Mechanism:**


- Astrocytes preferentially take up glucose from blood capillaries via GLUT1 transporters
- Glucose undergoes glycolysis in astrocytes, producing lactate even in the presence of adequate oxygen
- Lactate is released from astrocytes via monocarboxylate transporters (MCT1)
- Neurons take up lactate through MCT2 transporters
- Neurons convert lactate to pyruvate via lactate dehydrogenase
- Pyruvate enters neuronal mitochondria for oxidative metabolism via the TCA cycle

**Significance:**


- This coupling allows efficient energy supply to neurons during periods of high synaptic activity
- Astrocytes serve as glucose sensors and metabolic buffers
- The system provides rapid energy substrate delivery to active neurons
- It explains why brain glucose consumption exceeds what would be expected from direct neuronal uptake alone


---

### Question 2: How does insulin release affect metabolism in liver and skeletal muscle tissues? (8 marks)
**Answer:**


**Effects on Liver Metabolism:**


*Carbohydrate Metabolism:*


- Activates glycogen synthase (through dephosphorylation) promoting glycogen synthesis
- Inhibits glycogen phosphorylase, reducing glycogen breakdown
- Inhibits gluconeogenesis by suppressing key enzymes (PEPCK, G6Pase)
- Promotes glycolysis by activating key regulatory enzymes

*Lipid Metabolism:*


- Activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, promoting fatty acid synthesis
- Increases malonyl-CoA production, inhibiting fatty acid oxidation
- Promotes triglyceride synthesis and VLDL formation
- Inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase, reducing lipolysis

**Effects on Skeletal Muscle Metabolism:**


*Glucose Utilization:*


- Stimulates GLUT4 translocation to cell membrane, increasing glucose uptake
- Activates glycogen synthase, promoting muscle glycogen storage
- Enhances glycolysis for immediate energy needs
- Improves glucose tolerance and reduces blood glucose levels

*Protein Metabolism:*


- Stimulates amino acid uptake into muscle cells
- Promotes protein synthesis through mTOR pathway activation
- Inhibits protein degradation, creating positive nitrogen balance
- Enhances muscle growth and repair processes

**Overall Integration:**


- Shifts metabolism from catabolic (fasting) to anabolic (fed) state
- Coordinates substrate storage across tissues
- Maintains glucose homeostasis by promoting glucose utilization and storage


---

### Question 3: Elucidate the differences between how the body deals with moderate amounts of alcohol versus excess alcohol (8 marks)
**Answer:**


**Moderate Alcohol Consumption:**


*Primary Pathway - Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH):*


- Ethanol → Acetaldehyde (via ADH in liver cytoplasm)
- Acetaldehyde → Acetate (via aldehyde dehydrogenase in mitochondria)
- Rate-limited by NAD+ availability (zero-order kinetics)
- Typical elimination rate: 7-10g/hour
- Produces moderate amounts of NADH

*Metabolic Effects:*


- Mild inhibition of gluconeogenesis due to altered NAD+/NADH ratio
- Minimal impact on fatty acid oxidation
- No significant ketone body formation
- Normal lactate/pyruvate ratio maintained relatively well

**Excess Alcohol Consumption:**


*Secondary Pathway Activation - MEOS:*


- Microsomal Ethanol Oxidizing System (CYP2E1) is induced
- Located in liver endoplasmic reticulum
- Consumes NADPH and generates ROS (reactive oxygen species)
- Can handle higher alcohol concentrations

*Severe Metabolic Consequences:*


- Massive NADH production overwhelms NAD+ regeneration
- Severe inhibition of gluconeogenesis → hypoglycemia risk
- Blocked fatty acid oxidation → fatty acid accumulation
- Enhanced lipogenesis → fatty liver development
- Lactate accumulation → lactic acidosis
- Ketone body formation from impaired metabolism
- Acetaldehyde accumulation → toxic effects

*Pathological Effects:*


- Oxidative stress from ROS production
- Hepatocellular damage and inflammation
- Disrupted cellular energy charge
- Impaired protein synthesis
- Risk of alcoholic ketoacidosis


---

### Question 4: How does lipid metabolism contribute to ketoacidosis? (8 marks)
**Answer:**


**Initiation of Ketoacidosis:**


*Hormonal Triggers:*


- Insulin deficiency (diabetes) or glucagon excess
- Increased epinephrine and cortisol during stress
- Enhanced lipolysis in adipose tissue
- Massive free fatty acid release into circulation

**Hepatic Fatty Acid Metabolism:**


*Enhanced β-Oxidation:*


- Free fatty acids taken up by liver
- Converted to fatty acyl-CoA by acyl-CoA synthetase
- Transported into mitochondria via carnitine shuttle
- Undergoes rapid β-oxidation producing acetyl-CoA

*Overwhelming of TCA Cycle:*


- Acetyl-CoA production exceeds TCA cycle capacity
- Oxaloacetate depletion due to gluconeogenesis
- Unable to condense all acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate
- Excess acetyl-CoA diverted to ketogenesis

**Ketone Body Formation:**


*Biochemical Pathway:*


- Two acetyl-CoA → Acetoacetyl-CoA (via thiolase)
- Acetoacetyl-CoA + Acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA (via HMG-CoA synthase)
- HMG-CoA → Acetoacetate (via HMG-CoA lyase)
- Acetoacetate → β-hydroxybutyrate (via β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase)
- Spontaneous decarboxylation → Acetone

**Development of Acidosis:**


*Acid Production:*


- Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are strong organic acids
- Dissociate completely at physiological pH
- Release H+ ions into circulation
- Overwhelm blood buffering systems (bicarbonate, phosphate)

*Compensatory Mechanisms Overwhelmed:*


- Respiratory compensation (Kussmaul breathing) inadequate
- Renal H+ excretion capacity exceeded
- Progressive metabolic acidosis develops
- Can lead to coma and death if untreated

*Clinical Consequences:*


- Blood pH drops below 7.35
- Anion gap metabolic acidosis
- Dehydration from osmotic diuresis
- Electrolyte imbalances (K+, Na+, Cl-)


---

## SECTION C - LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS (40 MARKS)
### Question 1: Methanol Poisoning Case Study
**a) Explain the metabolism of methanol and the mechanism of its toxicity (15 marks)**


**Methanol Metabolism:**


*Phase 1 - Initial Oxidation:*


- Methanol (CH₃OH) enters hepatocytes
- Oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) to formaldehyde (HCHO)
- Same enzyme that metabolizes ethanol but with lower affinity for methanol
- Rate-limiting step in methanol toxicity

*Phase 2 - Toxic Metabolite Formation:*


- Formaldehyde rapidly oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenase
- Converted to formic acid (HCOOH) - the primary toxic metabolite
- Formic acid accumulates because its elimination is slow
- Half-life of formic acid is 20 hours vs. 2-3 hours for formaldehyde

*Phase 3 - Formic Acid Elimination:*


- Formic acid oxidized to CO₂ and H₂O via folate-dependent pathway
- Requires tetrahydrofolate and 10-formyltetrahydrofolate synthetase
- Process is easily saturated, leading to accumulation

**Mechanisms of Toxicity:**


*Metabolic Acidosis:*


- Formic acid is a strong organic acid (pKa = 3.8)
- Dissociates completely at physiological pH
- Produces severe anion gap metabolic acidosis
- Overwhelms blood buffering systems

*Cellular Toxicity:*


- Formic acid inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV)
- Blocks electron transport chain at final step
- Prevents oxygen utilization despite adequate oxygen delivery
- Creates "histotoxic hypoxia" condition

*Tissue-Specific Effects:*


- Retinal toxicity: Rod and cone cell death, optic nerve damage
- CNS toxicity: Basal ganglia necrosis, particularly putamen
- Systemic effects: Multi-organ dysfunction from cellular hypoxia

*Clinical Manifestations:*


- Initial CNS depression (similar to ethanol intoxication)
- Latent period (6-30 hours) as methanol is metabolized
- Severe acidosis with compensatory hyperventilation
- Visual disturbances progressing to blindness
- Altered mental status, seizures, coma

**b) Explain the rationale behind treatment of methanol poisoning with ethanol (5 marks)**


**Competitive Inhibition Mechanism:**


- Ethanol and methanol compete for the same enzyme (alcohol dehydrogenase)
- Ethanol has 10-20 times higher affinity for ADH than methanol
- Administration of ethanol preferentially occupies ADH active sites
- Prevents methanol conversion to toxic formaldehyde and formic acid

**Therapeutic Strategy:**


- Maintain blood ethanol levels at 100-150 mg/dL
- Allows time for methanol elimination through lungs and kidneys
- Methanol eliminated unchanged via these routes (20-25%)
- Prevents further toxic metabolite formation

**Clinical Implementation:**


- IV ethanol infusion or oral administration
- Monitor both ethanol and methanol blood levels
- Continue until methanol levels drop to safe range (<20 mg/dL)
- May require dialysis in severe cases to remove both methanol and metabolites

**Additional Benefits:**


- Buys time for supportive care measures
- Allows correction of acidosis with bicarbonate
- Prevents irreversible organ damage
- Modern alternative: fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole) - specific ADH inhibitor


---

### Question 2: Temperature regulation in infants with regard to adipose tissue (20 marks)
**Answer:**


**Introduction to Neonatal Thermoregulation:** Newborn infants face significant thermoregulatory challenges due to their high surface area-to-volume ratio, thin skin, limited subcutaneous fat, and immature nervous system. Unlike adults, infants cannot shiver effectively, making them dependent on specialized metabolic mechanisms for heat production.


**Brown Adipose Tissue (BAT) - The Primary Thermogenic Organ:**


*Anatomical Distribution:*


- Located primarily in interscapular, axillary, and perirenal regions
- Surrounds major blood vessels and organs (heart, kidneys, adrenals)
- Comprises 2-5% of total body weight in healthy newborns
- Rich vascularization with sympathetic innervation

*Cellular Characteristics:*


- Multilocular adipocytes (multiple small lipid droplets)
- High mitochondrial density (giving brown color)
- Abundant cytochrome c oxidase
- Expression of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1/thermogenin)

**Mechanism of Non-Shivering Thermogenesis:**


*Neural Activation:*


- Cold exposure detected by peripheral thermoreceptors
- Signal transmitted to hypothalamic thermoregulatory center
- Sympathetic nervous system activation
- Norepinephrine release at BAT sympathetic terminals

*Biochemical Cascade:*


- Norepinephrine binds β3-adrenergic receptors on brown adipocytes
- Activates adenylyl cyclase → increased cAMP levels
- Protein kinase A activation
- Phosphorylation and activation of hormone-sensitive lipase
- Lipolysis of stored triglycerides

*Mitochondrial Heat Production:*


- Free fatty acids activate UCP1 in inner mitochondrial membrane
- UCP1 allows protons to bypass ATP synthase
- Energy normally used for ATP synthesis is released as heat
- Process called "uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation"
- Can increase metabolic rate by 100-200%

**Metabolic Integration:**


*Substrate Utilization:*


- Primary reliance on stored triglycerides in BAT
- Glucose uptake increased to support thermogenesis
- Fatty acid oxidation provides both fuel and UCP1 activation
- Oxygen consumption dramatically increased

*Hormonal Regulation:*


- Thyroid hormones (T3, T4) essential for UCP1 expression
- Cortisol modulates thermogenic response
- Insulin affects glucose uptake in BAT
- Growth hormone influences BAT development

**Clinical Significance:**


*Risk Factors for Hypothermia:*


- Premature infants have less BAT
- Small for gestational age infants
- Hypoglycemia impairs thermogenesis
- Hypoxia reduces thermogenic capacity

*Assessment and Monitoring:*


- Core temperature maintenance (36.5-37.5°C)
- Monitoring for signs of cold stress
- Oxygen consumption as indicator of thermogenic stress
- Blood glucose monitoring during cold exposure

*Therapeutic Interventions:*


- Maintaining neutral thermal environment
- Appropriate clothing and swaddling
- Incubator temperature control
- Skin-to-skin contact (kangaroo care)
- Nutritional support to maintain energy stores

**Developmental Changes:**


- BAT activity highest in first weeks of life
- Gradual decrease as shivering capacity develops
- Transition to adult-type thermoregulation by 6 months
- Environmental temperature control remains critical during this period

**Pathological Conditions:**


- Hypothyroidism impairs BAT function
- Sepsis can overwhelm thermogenic capacity
- Malnutrition reduces substrate availability
- Drug effects (anesthetics) can impair thermoregulation


---

### Question 3: The three principles of fuel utilization during exercise (20 marks)
**Answer:**


## PRINCIPLE 1: EXERCISE INTENSITY DETERMINES FUEL SELECTION
**Low-Intensity Exercise (25-65% VO₂ max):**


*Fat as Primary Fuel:*


- Adequate oxygen availability for aerobic metabolism
- Fatty acids mobilized from adipose tissue via hormone-sensitive lipase
- Beta-oxidation produces acetyl-CoA for TCA cycle
- High ATP yield (129 ATP per palmitate molecule)
- Sustained energy supply for prolonged activities

*Metabolic Characteristics:*


- Low respiratory exchange ratio (RER = 0.70-0.85)
- Enhanced fat oxidation enzymes (CPT-1, HAD)
- Increased mitochondrial biogenesis with training
- Sparing of limited carbohydrate stores

**Moderate-Intensity Exercise (65-85% VO₂ max):**


*Mixed Fuel Utilization:*


- Combination of fat and carbohydrate oxidation
- Crossover point where carbohydrate becomes dominant
- Muscle glycogen and blood glucose contribute significantly
- Maintained aerobic metabolism with some anaerobic contribution

**High-Intensity Exercise (>85% VO₂ max):**


*Carbohydrate Dominance:*


- Rapid ATP demand exceeds fat oxidation capacity
- Muscle glycogen becomes primary fuel source
- Anaerobic glycolysis activated (lactate production)
- RER approaches 1.0 (pure carbohydrate metabolism)
- Limited duration due to substrate depletion and acidosis

## PRINCIPLE 2: EXERCISE DURATION AFFECTS SUBSTRATE DEPLETION AND UTILIZATION
**Immediate Energy (0-10 seconds):**


*Phosphocreatine System:*


- Creatine kinase rapidly regenerates ATP
- No oxygen requirement (alactic)
- Limited by phosphocreatine stores (~3-5 times ATP levels)
- Power output can exceed 1000 watts in trained athletes

**Short-Term Energy (10 seconds - 2 minutes):**


*Anaerobic Glycolysis:*


- Muscle glycogen breakdown without oxygen
- Rapid ATP production (3 ATP per glucose from glycogen)
- Lactate accumulation and pH decrease
- Performance limited by acidosis and enzyme inhibition

**Medium-Term Energy (2 minutes - 30 minutes):**


*Aerobic Glycolysis and Fat Oxidation:*


- Transition to oxidative metabolism
- Muscle glycogen remains primary carbohydrate source
- Increasing contribution from fat oxidation
- Blood glucose maintains brain function
- Liver glycogenolysis supports blood glucose

**Long-Term Energy (>30 minutes):**


*Progressive Substrate Shifts:*


- Muscle glycogen depletion after 60-90 minutes
- Increased reliance on blood glucose and fat
- Hepatic glucose production becomes critical
- Fat oxidation contribution increases progressively
- Potential for gluconeogenesis from amino acids

*"Hitting the Wall" Phenomenon:*


- Occurs when liver and muscle glycogen stores depleted
- Blood glucose falls, affecting brain and muscle function
- Performance dramatically decreases
- Can be delayed by carbohydrate feeding during exercise

## PRINCIPLE 3: TRAINING STATUS MODIFIES FUEL UTILIZATION PATTERNS
**Metabolic Adaptations in Trained Athletes:**


*Enhanced Fat Oxidation Capacity:*


- Increased mitochondrial density (mitochondrial biogenesis)
- Higher concentrations of oxidative enzymes
- Improved capillarization of muscle fibers
- Enhanced mobilization and transport of fatty acids
- Greater intramuscular triglyceride stores

*Improved Carbohydrate Utilization:*


- Increased muscle glycogen storage capacity
- Enhanced glucose transporters (GLUT4)
- Improved insulin sensitivity
- Better lactate clearance and buffering capacity
- Enhanced gluconeogenesis during prolonged exercise

**Fiber Type Influences:**


*Type I (Slow-Twitch) Fibers:*


- High oxidative capacity
- Abundant mitochondria and oxidative enzymes
- Preferential fat utilization
- Fatigue-resistant
- Dominant in endurance athletes

*Type IIa (Fast-Twitch Oxidative) Fibers:*


- Moderate oxidative and glycolytic capacity
- Adaptable to training stimulus
- Can utilize both fat and carbohydrate efficiently
- Important for sustained power output

*Type IIx (Fast-Twitch Glycolytic) Fibers:*


- High glycolytic capacity
- Limited oxidative capacity
- Preferential carbohydrate utilization
- Rapid fatigue
- Dominant in power/sprint athletes

**Training-Induced Adaptations:**


*Endurance Training Effects:*


- Shifts crossover point to higher exercise intensities
- Increases fat oxidation at submaximal intensities
- Spares carbohydrate stores
- Improves exercise economy and efficiency
- Enhances lactate threshold

*High-Intensity Training Effects:*


- Improves anaerobic power and capacity
- Enhances lactate buffering and clearance
- Increases muscle glycogen utilization
- Improves neuromuscular coordination
- Maintains high power output longer

**Nutritional Strategies Based on Fuel Utilization:**


*Pre-Exercise Nutrition:*


- Carbohydrate loading for events >90 minutes
- Fat adaptation strategies for ultra-endurance
- Timing of meals to optimize substrate availability
- Avoiding reactive hypoglycemia

*During Exercise Nutrition:*


- Carbohydrate feeding for events >60 minutes
- 30-60g carbohydrate per hour for moderate duration
- Up to 90g/hour for events >2.5 hours (multiple transporters)
- Maintaining blood glucose and sparing muscle glycogen

*Post-Exercise Nutrition:*


- Rapid glycogen resynthesis within 2-hour window
- Protein intake for muscle protein synthesis
- Replenishing intramuscular triglyceride stores
- Optimizing recovery for subsequent training

**Clinical Applications:**


*Metabolic Diseases:*


- Diabetes management during exercise
- Glycogen storage diseases
- Fatty acid oxidation disorders
- McArdle's disease (muscle phosphorylase deficiency)

*Performance Optimization:*


- Periodization of training and nutrition
- Altitude training adaptations
- Heat acclimatization effects on metabolism
- Age-related changes in fuel utilization

**Integration of the Three Principles:**


The three principles work synergistically to optimize energy production during exercise:


- **Intensity-Duration Interaction:** High-intensity exercise of short duration relies on stored phosphocreatine and anaerobic glycolysis, while low-intensity, long-duration exercise progressively shifts toward fat oxidation.
- **Training-Intensity Relationship:** Well-trained athletes can maintain higher intensities while still utilizing significant amounts of fat, effectively shifting their crossover point rightward.
- **Duration-Training Interaction:** Trained athletes have enhanced capacity for both carbohydrate storage and fat oxidation, allowing them to sustain exercise longer at any given intensity.

**Practical Applications:**


- Exercise prescription based on metabolic demands
- Nutrition periodization aligned with training phases
- Performance testing and monitoring
- Rehabilitation considerations for different populations
- Understanding individual metabolic responses

This comprehensive understanding of fuel utilization principles allows for evidence-based approaches to training, nutrition, and performance optimization across various exercise modalities and populations.


---

articles.content:
# Medical Physiology End of Semester 1 Exam — March 2019 (Past Paper)

*HMP 100/UPC 103/VMP 100 Medical Physiology, University of Nairobi First Year End of Semester Examinations, 2018/2019 academic year. Sat Wednesday, 13 March 2019, 9:00 a.m.–12:00 p.m. Full paper: Section A (40 MCQs), Section B (12 short answer questions), Section C (5 essay questions). Questions only — no answer key.*

---

**Instructions:**
- Section A consists of forty (40) multiple choice questions. Each question has a common stem giving rise to five choices — select only ONE correct or best choice.
- Section B consists of twelve (12) short answer questions — answer ALL.
- Section C consists of five (5) essay questions — answer only ONE.

---

## Section A: Multiple Choice Questions

**1.** The optimal condition that exists within the body is called:

a) The extra-cellular space
b) The intra-cellular space
c) Homeostasis
d) The internal environment
e) None of the above

**2.** In the theoretical physiological control model, the controlled variable:

a) Remains completely constant
b) Is a measurable entity
c) Is always measured
d) Is the input to the controlled system
e) Is the same as the forcing functions

**3.** In a positive feedback control system, the variable:

a) Rises continuously
b) Falls then rises
c) Rises until the system breaks down
d) Falls continuously
e) Rises until the system "cuts off"

**4.** In a negative feedback control system, the controlled variable:

a) Must have a set point
b) Need not have a set point
c) Is always anatomically direct from the controlled system
d) Is directly affected by external factors
e) Is located in the cervical nervous system

**5.** The controlled system changes its characteristics in response to demand of the controlled variable in which type of controlled system:

a) Open loop
b) Negative feedback
c) Positive feedback
d) Adaptive
e) Feed forward

**6.** The difference between intravascular volume and intravascular fluid quantity is approximately:

a) 5 L
b) 3.5 L
c) 1.5 L
d) 2.5 L
e) There is no differential

**7.** The main factor that allows entry of water into cells is:

a) Filtration
b) Osmosis
c) Diffusion
d) Active transport
e) Pinocytosis

**8.** Transcellular space measures about:

a) 42 L
b) 28 L
c) 10.5 L
d) 3.5 L
e) 1 L

**9.** An adult man loses this much water in 24 hours:

a) 0.5 L
b) 1.0 L
c) 1.5 L
d) 2.0 L
e) 3.0 L

**10.** Which of the following accounts for the largest amount of water that is lost daily from an adult male?

a) Urine
b) Sweating
c) Faeces
d) Respiratory losses
e) Insensible skin loss

**11.** Which one of the following statements is NOT CORRECT?

a) Vesicular transport is an active method of membrane transport
b) Most cells use fatty acids to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP)
c) Exocytosis enables selected carriers, channels, or receptors to be added to the cell membrane
d) Cells exchange Na⁺ and H⁺ by means of antiport
e) Pinocytosis refers to nonselective uptake of a sample of ECF

**12.** Select one of the following statements that is NOT CORRECT:

a) In the cell membrane, phospholipids are held together by strong chemical bonds
b) In the cell membrane, cholesterol molecules prevent fatty acid chains from packing together and crystallizing
c) Cell membrane integral proteins are embedded in the lipid bilayer
d) Peripheral proteins are found more commonly on the inner than on the outer surface of the cell membrane
e) Carbohydrates play an important role in "self-recognition" processes

**13.** Which one among the following statements is NOT CORRECT?

a) Ions move across the cell membrane along an electrical gradient passively
b) Aquaporins greatly increase membrane permeability to water
c) Carriers are never open to both the ECF and the ICF simultaneously
d) 5 million ions may pass through an open channel in 1 second
e) Histamine functions as an endocrine, a neurocrine, and as a paracrine

**14.** Select one of the following statements that is NOT CORRECT:

a) Microtubules are the smallest cytoplasmic cytoskeletal components
b) Fibronectin promotes cell adhesion and holds cells in position
c) Desmosomes are the strongest cell-to-cell connections
d) Ions and small molecules can be directly exchanged through gap junctions
e) Gap junctions are especially abundant in cardiac muscle and smooth muscle

**15.** Which one of the following statements is NOT CORRECT?

a) Cells of different types have different kinds of cell membrane carriers
b) The cell membrane of thyroid gland cells has carriers for iodine
c) Some membrane proteins are cell adhesion molecules (CAMs)
d) Cell membrane ion channels are highly nonselective
e) Integrins connect the inner membrane surface to the intracellular cytoskeletal scaffolding

**16.** The weights of a group of 105 subjects are displayed in Figure 1 (histogram) as: *(figure not reproduced in this transcription)*

a) A modal weight of 80 kilograms
b) Weight as a continuous variable
c) Bar charts of weight intervals
d) Normal distribution of weight
e) Mean weight of 10 kilograms

**17.** In the interpretation of weight measurements displayed in Figure 2 (percentile/summary statistics table): *(figure not reproduced in this transcription)*

a) Interquartile range is 38.5 kilograms
b) Standard error of the mean is 1.16
c) An outlier in the lower extreme weighs below 53.5 kilograms
d) A leptokurtic distribution curve should be observed
e) There is no skewing in these data

**18.** The following is a categorical variable:

a) Age interval
b) Fasting blood glucose (mM/L)
c) pH
d) Plasma sodium levels (mg/dL)
e) Body mass index (kg/m²)

**19.** The anatomy of the boxplot of weights displayed in Figure 3: *(figure not reproduced in this transcription)*

a) Q3 at 120 kilograms
b) Mean weight of 90 kilograms
c) Maximum value of 114 kilograms
d) 25th percentile at 60 kilograms
e) An outlier at 45 kilograms

**20.** The following are measurements of scale EXCEPT:

a) Diastolic blood pressure
b) Gender of cadres/health care workers
c) Pain severity score
d) Normal body temperature range
e) Waist to hip ratio

**21.** One of the following statements regarding cell membranes of normal cells is incorrect:

a) All cell membranes have continually changing polarity
b) The cell membranes of excitable tissues can be changed by appropriate stimuli
c) For a sensory nerve the normal stimulus may be a generator potential
d) Stimulation of receptors is not subject to the "all or nothing" law
e) The cell membrane can also be regarded as a fluid matrix

**22.** Non-propagated potentials:

a) Do not include end plate potentials
b) Are not seen in dendrites
c) Are not used in cellular communication
d) In the retina are always depolarizing
e) Have a duration which is proportional to their initial voltage

**23.** Pacemaker action potentials:

a) Are essential for the normal function of the heart
b) Are not associated with biological clock hypothalamic function
c) Do not play any part in the neural mechanisms of the regulation of breathing rhythm
d) Do not depend on voltage-gated calcium channels in the heart
e) In cardiac pacemaker cells, do not depend on, among other factors, the "funny current" produced by voltage-gated sodium channels

**24.** One of the following statements regarding sensory receptors is correct:

a) Not all of them are transducers
b) The ones that sense electromagnetic radiation are sensitive to the whole of the solar spectrum
c) Their communication with the central nervous system follows the labelled line principle
d) The ones termed vibration receptors are slowly adapting mechanoreceptors
e) Visceral receptors cannot sense pain and temperature

**25.** One of the following statements regarding hearing is correct:

a) Hearing (auditory sense) is a visceral sense
b) The receptors for hearing are in the middle ear
c) A young adult cannot detect audio signals in the frequency range of 30 Hertz to 15,000 Hertz
d) The mechanical vibrations of the tympanic membrane produce waves in the scala media of the cochlea which shake the tectorial membrane
e) The lower the frequency of sound the further the waves mentioned in (d) travel towards the apex of the cochlea

**26.** The vestibular apparatus:

a) Is located in the middle ear
b) Has four semicircular canals
c) Has the utricle which senses the position of the head in the vertical plane
d) Also has the saccule which senses the position of the head in the horizontal plane
e) Can sense deep loud bass musical tones

**27.** Axoplasmic transport:

a) Is either wholly orthograde or wholly anterograde in any one particular axon
b) Uses neurofilaments and cilia for transporting materials in the axoplasm
c) Uses neurofilaments and microtubules for transporting materials in the axoplasm
d) Uses the molecular motor dynein for anterograde transport
e) Uses kinesin for retrograde transport

**28.** Myelinated nerves:

a) Are on the whole thinner than unmyelinated nerves
b) Do not include group A-alpha motor nerves which supply voluntary muscles / conduct impulses faster than unmyelinated nerves
c) Do not include group A-delta fibres which carry cold sensation impulses
d) Do not include axons of Gamma motor neurons
e) *(option not fully captured in source scan)*

**29.** One of the following statements regarding unmyelinated nerves is incorrect:

a) Unmyelinated nerves are nonetheless electrically insulated
b) They are insulated by un-myelinating Schwann cells (the Remak cells)
c) Several of them may be insulated by one Remak cell in a bundle (Remak bundle)
d) The Remak cell insulates them with its own cytoplasm and cell membrane
e) The number of unmyelinated nerves in the Remak bundle is different for different anatomical regions of the same mixed spinal nerve, i.e. distal, intermediate or proximal zones

**30.** One of the following statements regarding the retina is wrong:

a) The photoreceptors (rods and cones) face backwards, i.e. towards the rear surface of the retina
b) The retina has neuroglia
c) The photoreceptors are protected from too much light by the melanin-containing choroid layer
d) The image from the lens is distorted by the various cells and nerve fibres found between the inner surface of the retina and the photoreceptors
e) The Müller cells act as fibre-optic light transmitters which conduct a clear image of the visual field from the anterior surface of the retina to the photoreceptors in all areas of the retina, including the fovea centralis

**31.** In paracrine signaling:

a) The messenger acts in a distant location
b) Local mediation occurs
c) Signal lingers in the extracellular matrix
d) Phosphorylation of ligand occurs
e) Contact is necessary

**32.** G-protein:

a) Is activated by conformational change of ligand
b) When activated, detaches from receptor
c) Is always stimulated by binding of receptor
d) Is a second messenger
e) Is activated by all ligands

**33.** Nitric oxide:

a) Binds specifically to target cell
b) Receptors are intracellular
c) Is synthesized from unique proteins
d) Binds guanylyl cyclase for action
e) Catalyzes GTP to cGMP

**34.** Enzymes that transfer a phosphate group to a protein are known as:

a) Protein phosphatases
b) Protein kinases
c) Receptor proteins
d) Ligands
e) Second messengers

**35.** What must a signaling molecule bind to in order to trigger transduction?

a) Transducer protein
b) Signaling protein
c) Relay protein
d) Response protein
e) Receptor protein

**36.** The human genome:

a) Comprises a total of 50 million genes
b) Is made up of 30,000 genes
c) Is composed of 3 × 10⁶ nucleic base pairs
d) Experiences only negative modification (mutation) when changes occur at meiosis
e) Has a capacity to transcript about 2 times its number in messenger RNAs

**37.** The spliceosomes that effect posttranscriptional modification of the mRNA are:

a) Protein kinases
b) Glycopeptides
c) RNA complexes
d) Triads of nucleic base pairs
e) Transcription factors

**38.** Cell membranes:

a) Have a protein to lipid ratio of 50:50 in reference to molecular composition
b) Contain many carbohydrate molecules
c) Are freely permeable to electrolytes but not to proteins
d) Have variable protein and lipid content depending on their location in the cell
e) Have a stable composition throughout the life of the cell

**39.** The NADPH produced during the Pentose Phosphate Pathway, rather than NADH, is useful for:

a) Increasing activity of free oxygen radicals in the mitochondria
b) Synthesizing essential amino acids
c) Synthesizing fatty acids
d) Direct generation of energy when oxidized in the cell
e) Catalyzing water formation in the matrix

**40.** Mitochondrial disease generally refers to deficiency of:

a) Porins on the inner mitochondrial membrane
b) Receptors for Acetyl-CoA
c) Muscle creatine phosphorylase
d) Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
e) β-Glycosidases

## Section B: Short Answer Questions

**1.** Explain what you understand by "signal transduction". (5 marks)

**2.** Explain how G-protein acts as a molecular switch. (5 marks)

**3.** Briefly describe the roles of sodium ions and potassium ions in the development and maintenance of the resting membrane potential.

**4.** (a) Define non-propagated potentials. (b) What are the characteristics of non-propagated potentials?

**5.** Describe the process of myelination of a myelinated peripheral nerve.

**6.** Identify the five-number summary for 105 subjects in Figure 4 (stem-and-leaf plot of weight). *(figure not reproduced in this transcription)*

**7.** Describe the structure of a cell membrane.

**8.** Define and explain feed-forward control with an example.

**9.** List and quantify the body fluid compartments.

**10.** Contrast the functional properties of the smooth and rough endoplasmic reticulum.

**11.** Describe the reasons why transfer RNA is often referred to as an adaptor molecule.

**12.** Describe the functions and properties of the inner mitochondrial membrane.

## Section C: Essays (answer only ONE)

**1.** Discuss cellular communication under the following sub-topics:
(a) Discuss the properties of membrane receptors. (15 marks)
(b) Discuss the various types of membrane receptors. (10 marks)
(c) Explain what a second messenger is and how it is formed. (5 marks)

**2.** Discuss the functions of the sodium-potassium ATPase pump under the following headings:
(a) The pump mechanism (5 marks)
(b) Effect on resting membrane potential (5 marks)
(c) The control of cell volume (5 marks)
(d) Cerebellar Purkinje cell function (5 marks)
(e) Absorption of glucose in the gut (5 marks)
(f) The movement of calcium in skeletal muscles (5 marks)

**3.** The weights of a group of subjects, displayed by gender, are as follows:

Male: 100, 82, 112, 120, 88, 120, 99, 94, 100, 45, 56, 45, 101, 93, 106, 62
Female: 88, 87, 112, 77, 88, 67, 143, 115, 88, 84, 101, 62, 112, 87, 100, 82

a) Draw a back-to-back stem and leaf plot. (2 marks)
b) List five-number summary statistics for: (i) all subjects, (ii) by gender. (5 + 8 marks)
c) Calculate the mean weight and variance for: (i) all subjects, (ii) by gender. (4 + 8 marks)
d) Calculate the standard error of the mean for: (i) all subjects, (ii) by gender. (1 mark + gender breakdown)

**4.** Write an essay under the following subheadings:
(a) Discuss how molecules move across cell membranes. (15 marks)
(b) Discuss the functions of membrane proteins. (15 marks)

**5.** Write an essay on Homeostasis under the following headings (10 marks each):
a) The internal environment
b) The theoretical control model types

---
