# HIT100: Information Technology — Course Syllabus

*Full course overview for HIT100 Information Technology, University of Nairobi, BDS Year 1. Covers the Windows environment, word processing, the internet and web browsing, search engines, medical informatics, and the ethics of IT in medicine.*

## Course Overview

HIT100: Information Technology is a foundation course offered to Bachelor of Dental Surgery (BDS) Year 1 students at the University of Nairobi. The course equips students with the practical computer skills they need to succeed in modern medical and dental practice — from managing files on a Windows computer, to searching the medical literature and accessing full-text e-books and journals online.

The course is organised around the following core themes:

## 1. Introduction to the Windows Environment

- **Folders and files** — how data is organised and stored on a computer; creating, renaming, moving, copying and deleting files and folders.
- **Windows navigation** — using the desktop, Start menu, Taskbar, File Explorer and dialog boxes to manage your work.
- Good file-management habits that keep your coursework and patient data organised.

## 2. Introduction to Word Processing

- Creating, editing, saving, printing and formatting documents using a word processor such as Microsoft Word.
- Formatting text (fonts, sizes, colours, alignment), formatting paragraphs and pages, and working with tables.
- Producing professional reports, assignments and letters.

## 3. Basic Elements of Web Browsing and Mailing Systems

- Using a web browser to navigate the World Wide Web: addresses (URLs), hyperlinks, tabs, bookmarks and browser settings.
- Using electronic mail: composing, sending, receiving and managing email messages and attachments.

## 4. Introduction to Search Engines and Directories

- How search engines and search directories work, and the difference between them.
- Building effective search strategies: keywords, operators, field searching and domain searching.
- Locating reliable, relevant information quickly.

## 5. Access to Medical Journals and Articles

- Accessing medical journals, journal articles, book information and full-text medical e-books online.
- **Medline via PubMed** — the biomedical literature database that is the backbone of evidence-based practice; how to search it and retrieve citations and abstracts.

## 6. Health Informatics

- The application of information technology to health care and biomedical research.
- **Ethical orientation in e-health** — the responsible use of electronic health information.
- Accessing medical information from the internet safely and ethically.

## 7. Introduction to Data Analysis Software

- An introduction to statistical software packages (e.g. SPSS and Excel) used for entering, summarising and analysing data.
- Running descriptive statistics, comparing groups, and producing charts and graphs.

## 8. Ethics of IT Utilisation in Medicine

- The professional, legal and ethical obligations that arise when information technology is used in health care.
- Issues of **confidentiality and patient privacy**, data security, informed consent, and the reliability of online health information.

## Why This Course Matters

Information technology is now central to the practice of medicine and dentistry — from electronic patient records and digital imaging, to online journals and telemedicine. By the end of HIT100, students should be able to manage computer files confidently, produce well-formatted documents, use the internet to find and evaluate medical information, and understand the ethical framework that governs the use of health information technology.

articles.title: Aponeurosis — Histology Question Bank
articles.content:
*A consolidated Year 1 Histology spot-question bank for the Aponeurosis collection, drawn from eight revision papers, organised by tissue type — cytology, epithelium, connective tissue, cartilage, bone, muscle, nervous tissue, and reproductive/endocrine histology. Tap any answer to reveal it.*
Cell Organelles & General Cytology
## Q1: Identify the organelle and its function, name cytoskeletal components, and state three ultrastructural features of hepatocytes![Rough endoplasmic reticulum on electron microscopy](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q32-24b5a9f6.jpg)**Answer:**
- Rough endoplasmic reticulum - synthesis and initial processing of secreted and membrane proteins
- Cytoskeleton: microtubules, microfilaments, and intermediate filaments
- Hepatocytes contain abundant rough ER, Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, smooth ER, glycogen, and peroxisomes
- 

---
## Q2: State two functions of the organelles labelled A and B (2+2 marks)![Electron micrograph of a mitochondrion (
A) beside rough endoplasmic reticulum (B)](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q21-c20823dc.jpg)**Answer:**
- A — mitochondrion. Two functions:
- ATP production via oxidative phosphorylation
- Site of the citric acid (Krebs) cycle
- B — rough endoplasmic reticulum. Two functions:
- Synthesis of proteins destined for secretion or membrane insertion
- Site of ribosome attachment and initial protein folding
- 

---
## Q3: Identify the type of chromatin labelled A and B; two features of a cell actively synthesizing protein (2+2 marks)![Electron micrograph of a nucleus with condensed chromatin (
A) and dispersed chromatin (B)](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q22-7e64c094.jpg)**Answer:**
- A — heterochromatin (condensed, transcriptionally inactive, seen at the nuclear periphery)
- B — euchromatin (dispersed, transcriptionally active)
- Two features of a cell actively synthesizing protein:
- A large, prominent nucleolus
- Abundant euchromatin (dispersed chromatin) and well-developed rough endoplasmic reticulum
- 

---
## Q4: Epithelial type displayed and one site; cell cycle phases (2+2 marks)![Photomicrograph of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (skin)](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q30-afbd2f83.jpg)**Answer:**
- Type: keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
- Distribution: epidermis of the skin (thick skin of the palms and soles)
- Cell cycle phase for preparation for DNA replication: G1 phase
- Cell cycle phase for cell division: M phase (mitosis)
- 

---
## Q5: State two sites where the tissue displayed is found![Q35 - mucoid connective tissue](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-pat3-2019-q35-d0ecfe59.jpg)**Answer:**
- Wharton's jelly of the umbilical cord
- Dental pulp of a developing tooth
- Nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc
- 

---
Epithelial Tissue
## Q6: Identify the organ, define metaplasia and its significance here, and name three gastric epithelial cell types with their products![Oesophagus](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q06-fcb241a7.jpg)**Answer:**
- Oesophagus - non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, submucosal glands, longitudinal folds, and proximity to the trachea
- Metaplasia is reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another; columnar metaplasia in Barrett oesophagus increases the risk of adenocarcinoma
- Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor; chief cells pepsinogen and gastric lipase; surface/neck mucous cells mucus and bicarbonate; enteroendocrine cells include G cells producing gastrin
- 

---
## Q7: Identify the alimentary segment, give two reasons, state three protective properties, and mention two adaptations for absorption![Duodenum](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q09-0cdc66ba.jpg)**Answer:**
- Duodenum - villi, crypts of Lieberkuhn, and submucosal Brunner glands
- Protection: bicarbonate-rich alkaline mucus, mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, and rapid epithelial regeneration
- Absorptive adaptations: great length/surface area, villi, microvilli, and muscularis mucosae movement
- 

---
## Q8: Identify the structure, name three associated receptor-cell types, state its innervation, and name its associated glands![Circumvallate papilla](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q11-268c29b9.jpg)**Answer:**
- Circumvallate papilla - mushroom-shaped papilla with grooves and parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium
- Taste buds contain gustatory receptor cells, sustentacular/supporting cells, and basal cells
- Taste innervation: glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
- Associated glands: serous glands of von Ebner
- 

---
## Q9: Identify the alimentary segment, give two reasons, name three regional cell types, and state three unique gross features![Colon](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q13-d8b32775.jpg)**Answer:**
- Colon - long straight glands, abundant goblet cells, absence of villi, and lymphoid aggregates
- Cell types include colonocytes/columnar absorptive cells, goblet cells, and enteroendocrine cells
- Gross features: appendices epiploicae, taeniae coli, and haustra
- 

---
## Q10: Identify the organ, give three reasons, and state ultrastructural features of most lining epithelial cells![Kidney histology](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q23-47356cfb.jpg)**Answer:**
- Kidney - renal corpuscles, medullary rays, numerous tubules, and a capsule
- Proximal tubular cells specialized for active ion transport have basal membrane infoldings, microvilli, tight junctions, and abundant basal mitochondria
- 

---
## Q11: Identify the organ, give two reasons, list two resident cells in zone D with functions, and state three functional-unit components![Lung histology with zone D](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q24-6fac1708.jpg)**Answer:**
- Lung - alveoli and airways with cartilage
- Type I pneumocytes form the thin gas-exchange lining; type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant and regenerate alveolar epithelium
- Functional unit (acinus): respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli
- 

---
## Q12: Identify the epithelium, give two reasons, state three sites, and name two parathyroid-gland cell types![Transitional epithelium](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q33-72660543.jpg)**Answer:**
- Transitional epithelium (urothelium) - umbrella-shaped surface cells and a variable number of layers
- Found in renal calyces/pelvis, ureters, urinary bladder, and proximal urethra
- Parathyroid gland cell types: principal (chief) cells and oxyphil cells
- 

---
## Q13: Identify the slide, name two cells responsible for myelination, and name two parts of the neurohypophysis![Ureter](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q38-944cd7d2.jpg)**Answer:**
- Ureter - urothelium, star-shaped lumen, and a muscular wall
- Myelinating cells: Schwann cells in the PNS and oligodendrocytes in the CNS
- Neurohypophysis: pars nervosa, infundibular stalk, and median eminence
- 

---
## Q14: Identify the artery, name two tunica-intima components, and list two capillary types with locations![Elastic conducting artery](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q40-2b473cb9.jpg)**Answer:**
- Elastic (conducting) artery - numerous elastic lamellae in the tunica media
- Tunica intima: vascular endothelium and subendothelial connective tissue; the internal elastic lamina is less distinct in elastic arteries
- Sinusoidal capillaries: liver and hematopoietic tissues
- Fenestrated capillaries: kidneys and endocrine organs
- 

---
## Q15: Identify the apical specialisation shown; state the filament found in it; state any 2 locations![Electron micrograph of tall stereocilia at a cell's apical surface](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-histology-embryology-spot-review-h-stereocilia-69d0be86.jpg)**Answer:**
- Apical specialisation: stereocilia
- Filament: actin
- Two locations: germinal epithelium of the epididymis and vas deferens; inner ear (cochlear hair cells)
- 

---
## Q16: Identify the slide; state the receptors for touch![Photomicrograph of skin showing a hair follicle with an attached sebaceous gland](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-histology-embryology-spot-review-h-pilosebaceous-f18d53be.jpg)**Answer:**
- Slide: pilosebaceous unit
- Receptors for touch: Meissner's corpuscle; Merkel discs
- 

---
## Q17: Identify the structures shown, giving 2 reasons; give two classes of these structures according to the mode of secretion![Photomicrograph of dilated glandular structures with a low cuboidal secretory epithelium](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-histology-embryology-spot-review-h-apocrine-afc2a29e.jpg)**Answer:**
- Structures shown: apocrine sweat glands — reasons: largely dilated lumen; low cuboidal secretory portion that secretes into the hair follicle
- Two classes of sweat gland by mode of secretion: apocrine; eccrine
- 

---
## Q18: State two sites where the epithelial specializations A and B are found (2+2 marks)![Electron micrograph of microvilli (
A) beside a coloured SEM image of stereocilia (B)](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q24-714f2fb4.jpg)**Answer:**
- Specialization A — microvilli. Sites: small intestine (brush border of enterocytes); proximal convoluted tubule of the kidney
- Specialization B — stereocilia. Sites: epididymis; vas deferens
- 

---
Connective Tissue
## Q19: Identify the fibre, give two reasons, state four locations, and give its main function![Reticular fibres](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q17-f56036c8.jpg)**Answer:**
- Reticular fibres (type III collagen) - highly branched, net-like fibres surrounding cells
- Found in liver, spleen, bone marrow, adipose tissue, lungs, basal lamina, and lymphoid tissue
- Function: delicate supporting framework/stroma
- 

---
## Q20: Identify the two cell types in this tissue; two hormones from this tissue![Photomicrograph of adipose tissue with signet-ring-shaped cells](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-anatomy-spot-revision-q24-29fcb345.jpg)**Answer:**
- Two cell types: unilocular adipocytes (white fat); multilocular adipocytes (brown fat)
- Two hormones from adipose tissue: adiponectin; leptin
- Also visible in this image (for revision): resistin is a third adipokine secreted by this tissue
- 

---
## Q21: Breast — identify A and B; two main lymph node groups draining the breast (2+2 marks)![Breast diagram with axillary tail (
A) and areolar region (
B) labelled](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q15-33949375.jpg)**Answer:**
- A — axillary tail of the breast
- B — areolar region
- Two main lymph node groups draining the breast: axillary lymph nodes; parasternal lymph nodes
- Also visible in this image (for revision): the breast is conventionally divided into four quadrants — upper outer, upper inner, lower outer, lower inner — the upper outer quadrant is where most breast tumours arise, due to the greater volume of glandular tissue there
- 

---
## Q22: Identify with a reason the connective tissue fibers displayed; two functions of adipose tissue (2+2 marks)![Silver-stained tissue showing reticular fibres around cell cords](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q25-753fe449.jpg)**Answer:**
- Fibres displayed: reticular fibres — reason: thin, branching fibres forming a delicate supportive meshwork, highlighted black by silver impregnation stain, typical of organs like the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes
- Two functions of adipose tissue: energy storage (as triglycerides); thermal insulation
- 

---
## Q23: Distribution of the connective tissue type displayed; two classes of cells in this connective tissue (2+2 marks)![Photomicrograph of dense regular connective tissue with parallel collagen fibres](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q26-38bab905.jpg)**Answer:**
- Distribution of dense regular connective tissue: tendons and ligaments
- Two classes of cells: fixed cells (fibroblasts/fibrocytes); wandering (transient) cells such as macrophages and mast cells
- 

---
## Q24: Giving reason, identify the epithelial type displayed![Q32 - ciliated epithelium over connective tissue](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-pat3-2019-q32-9f0dc6e8.jpg)**Answer:**
- Pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium
- Reason: cilia visible on the surface
- Reason: nuclei sit at varying levels
- All cells reach the basement membrane, not all reach the surface
- 

---
## Q25: State major collagen types in the tissue displayed![Q39 - connective tissue histology](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-pat3-2019-q39-fb37382a.jpg)**Answer:**
- Type I collagen
- Type II collagen
- 

---
## Q26: State two sites where the tissue displayed is found![Q35 - mucoid connective tissue around a small vessel](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-sdl-mock-marathon-q35-4a2d2ab8.jpg)**Answer:**
- Mucous (mucoid) connective tissue
- Wharton's jelly of the umbilical cord
- Dental pulp of a developing tooth
- Characteristic feature: stellate fibroblasts in an abundant gelatinous ground substance
- 

---
## Q27: State major collagen types in the tissue displayed![Q39 - dense regular connective tissue histology](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-sdl-mock-marathon-q39-7ff4c6d2.jpg)**Answer:**
- Tendon (dense regular connective tissue)
- Predominantly type I collagen
- Minor type III collagen in the surrounding endotenon
- Cells present: fibroblasts (tenocytes), arranged in parallel rows between collagen bundles
- 

---
## Q28: Scalp layers — identify A and B; what constitutes C and D (2+2 marks)![Coronal section through the scalp and meninges with X, A, B, C, D labelled](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-week-12-review-q12-a6bf4011.jpg)**Answer:**
- A — skull bone
- B — dura mater
- C — cerebral cortex — composed of grey matter
- D — superior sagittal sinus, containing venous blood and CSF reabsorbed from arachnoid granulations
- Also visible in this image (for revision): X marks the scalp layers overlying the skull (skin, connective tissue, aponeurosis, loose areolar tissue, pericranium)
- 

---
## Q29: Breast anatomy — identify A and C; functional variation of B; surface landmark of D (2+1+1 marks)![Sagittal section of the breast with A, B, C, D labelled](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-week-12-review-q13-2de7eff6.jpg)**Answer:**
- A — pectoralis major muscle
- C — loose areolar tissue surrounding the nipple (retromammary space)
- Functional variation of B (glandular/lobular tissue): in a lactating mammary gland it is well developed, while in a non-lactating gland it is not well developed
- Surface landmark of D (nipple): 4th intercostal space (in the midclavicular line)
- 

---
Cartilage
## Q30: Identify the connective tissue, state three distribution sites, and name the components of its outer layer![Elastic cartilage](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q07-ed959348.jpg)**Answer:**
- Elastic cartilage - chondrocytes in lacunae, elastic fibres in the matrix, and a perichondrium
- Found in the pinna, epiglottis, and small laryngeal cartilages
- Perichondrium has an outer fibrous layer and inner chondrogenic/cellular layer
- 

---
## Q31: Identify the tissue, give two reasons, state the connective-tissue fibre, and give its distribution and function![Fibrocartilage](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q20-774cf540.jpg)**Answer:**
- Fibrocartilage - chondroblasts/chondrocytes in lacunae among a dense fibrous matrix
- Predominant fibre: type I collagen
- Found in articular discs, symphyses, intervertebral discs, and tendon-to-bone attachments; resists compression and tensile stress
- 

---
## Q32: Identify the slide giving reasons![Photomicrograph of hyaline cartilage with chondrocytes in lacunae](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-histology-embryology-spot-review-h-hyaline-cartil-5dae18db.jpg)**Answer:**
- Slide: hyaline cartilage
- Reasons: cells in lacunae; cells in isogenous groups; homogeneous matrix
- 

---
## Q33: Identify two regions where this tissue is found; two congenital anomalies associated with it![Photomicrograph of elastic cartilage with elastic fibre network](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-anatomy-spot-revision-q26-d03a2a82.jpg)**Answer:**
- Two regions where elastic cartilage is found: pinna of the ear; eustachian tube
- Also visible in this image (for revision): epiglottis; external acoustic meatus are further sites of elastic cartilage
- Two congenital anomalies associated with elastic tissue: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome; Marfan syndrome
- 

---
## Q34: Two unique features of the cartilage type displayed; two cartilage types lacking a perichondrium (2+2 marks)![Photomicrograph of hyaline cartilage with chondrocytes in lacunae](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q27-1e5c76a9.jpg)**Answer:**
- Two unique features of hyaline cartilage: chondrocytes sit in lacunae, often arranged in isogenous groups; the matrix appears homogeneous/glassy since its type II collagen fibres are not visible on routine staining
- Two cartilage types that lack a perichondrium: fibrocartilage; articular (hyaline) cartilage
- 

---
## Q35: Give the salient features of the tissue displayed![Q37 - cartilage histology](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-pat3-2019-q37-2c216f1c.jpg)**Answer:**
- Elastic cartilage
- Abundant elastic fibres in the matrix
- Large lacunae housing chondrocytes
- Found at: epiglottis, external ear (pinna), auditory tube
- 

---
## Q36: Giving reason, identify the epithelial type displayed![Q32 - ciliated epithelium over cartilage](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-sdl-mock-marathon-q32-2b16d828.jpg)**Answer:**
- Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium (respiratory epithelium of the trachea)
- Reason: all cells rest on the basement membrane
- Reason: not all cells reach the free surface
- Nuclei sit at different levels, giving a falsely stratified look
- Cilia are visible on the luminal surface
- Also seen in this field: goblet cells within the epithelium, and hyaline cartilage of the tracheal ring beneath it
- 

---
## Q37: Give the salient features of the tissue displayed![Q37 - cartilage-type histology](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-sdl-mock-marathon-q37-35507f94.jpg)**Answer:**
- Hyaline cartilage
- Chondrocytes sit in lacunae, often as isogenous groups
- Matrix is basophilic/metachromatic (rich in chondroitin sulfate)
- Avascular
- Bounded by a perichondrium (absent at articular surfaces)
- Found at: articular surfaces, costal cartilages, trachea/bronchi, epiphyseal growth plate
- 

---
Bone Tissue
## Q38: Identify the structure and name its zones![Epiphyseal growth plate](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q14-74b46a2c.jpg)**Answer:**
- Epiphyseal growth plate - stacked chondrocytes lie parallel to the long axis of bone
- Zones: resting, proliferative, maturation/hypertrophy, calcified cartilage, and ossification
- 

---
## Q39: Identify the tissue, give three reasons, name its cells and their functions, name three outer-layer components, and state its mode of growth![Compact bone](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q27-23501f3d.jpg)**Answer:**
- Compact bone - Haversian canals, lamellar systems, and osteocytes in lacunae
- Osteoblasts synthesize bone; osteocytes maintain matrix; osteoclasts resorb bone
- Periosteum: outer fibrous layer and inner cellular/osteogenic layer, with Sharpey fibres anchoring it
- Bone grows appositionally; interstitial growth does not occur in mineralized bone
- 

---
## Q40: Identify the slide; state the role of the tissue shown; name one congenital anomaly affecting this structure![Photomicrograph of the epiphyseal growth plate showing columns of chondrocytes](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-histology-embryology-spot-review-h-epiphyseal-2425c120.jpg)**Answer:**
- Slide: epiphyseal growth plate
- Role: longitudinal bone growth
- Congenital anomaly: achondroplasia
- 

---
## Q41: List 2 main cell types in this tissue; name the various lamellae systems found in this tissue![Ground section of compact bone showing Haversian systems](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-histology-embryology-spot-review-h-bone-1fcf5a93.jpg)**Answer:**
- Two main cell types (any two): osteoblasts; osteocytes; osteoclasts
- Lamellae systems in bone: Haversian system; endosteal lamellae; periosteal lamellae; interstitial lamellae
- 

---
## Q42: Identify the tissue displayed, giving reasons![Ground section photomicrograph of compact (cortical) bone showing osteons](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-anatomy-spot-revision-q29-121d140d.jpg)**Answer:**
- Tissue: cortical (compact) bone
- Reasons: visible central (Haversian) canal; surrounding concentric lamellae; cells sitting in lacunae
- 

---
## Q43: Name four cell types in the tissue displayed and state the function of each (4 marks)![Ground section of compact bone showing Haversian systems](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q28-90373200.jpg)**Answer:**
- Osteoblasts — bone-forming cells; secrete osteoid (unmineralized bone matrix)
- Osteocytes — mature bone cells within lacunae; maintain bone matrix and sense mechanical strain
- Osteoclasts — large multinucleated cells; resorb bone
- Osteoprogenitor cells — stem cells that differentiate into osteoblasts
- 

---
## Q44: (a) Identify the region shown and a feature. (b) Name two other cell types found in the epidermis![Q24 - growth plate histology](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat8-2012-q24-6bd02248.jpg)**Answer:**
- Epiphyseal (growth) plate
- Feature: palisades/stacks of cells, multiple zones, lies adjacent to bone (any one)
- Merkel cells
- Langerhans cells
- 

---
## Q45: (a) Identify the tissue and its features. (b) Name the cells lining bone surfaces![Q31 - lactating mammary gland histology](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat8-2012-q31-6cc0bb7f.jpg)**Answer:**
- Lactating mammary gland
- Features: numerous alveoli, ducts, lobules, high vascularity, minimal stroma
- Bone-lining cells: bone-lining cells (flattened osteoblast-lineage cells covering quiescent bone surfaces)
- 

---
## Q46: Identify A and B![Q33 - bone histology with A and B labelled](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-pat3-2019-q33-9168ca26.jpg)**Answer:**
- A: Haversian canal
- B: osteocytes in lacunae
- Also visible in compact bone: concentric lamellae, canaliculi connecting lacunae
- 

---
## Q47: Name cell types found in region a![Q40 - bone marrow/ossification histology with region a marked](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-pat3-2019-q40-1a1f4442.jpg)**Answer:**
- Osteoclasts
- Osteocytes
- Osteoblasts
- Osteoprogenitor cells
- 

---
Muscle Tissue
## Q48: Identify the tissue, give three reasons, list three ultrastructural features, and state its functional unit![Skeletal muscle in longitudinal section](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q03-a4f46979.jpg)**Answer:**
- Skeletal muscle - long striated fibres with multiple peripheral nuclei
- Ultrastructure includes myofilaments, Z lines, M lines, H zones, I bands, T tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, and abundant mitochondria
- Functional unit: sarcomere
- 

---
## Q49: Identify the tissue, give two reasons, state two ultrastructural features, and name three cells with contractile properties![Cardiac muscle](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q19-5d1f9b2c.jpg)**Answer:**
- Cardiac muscle - branching, cross-striated fibres with one or two central nuclei and intercalated discs
- Ultrastructural features include diads and intercalated discs
- Other contractile cells: myofibroblasts, myoepithelial cells, and myoid cells
- 

---
## Q50: Identify the tissue; identify 2 ultrastructural features![Photomicrograph of cardiac muscle with branching fibres and intercalated discs](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-histology-embryology-spot-review-h-cardiac-muscle-08f8fc32.jpg)**Answer:**
- Tissue: cardiac muscle
- Two ultrastructural features: diads; intercalated discs containing gap junctions
- 

---
## Q51: Identify the slide; state any anomaly associated with it![Photomicrograph of skeletal muscle fibres in longitudinal section](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-histology-embryology-spot-review-h-skeletal-muscl-38450e72.jpg)**Answer:**
- Slide: skeletal muscle

Nervous & Ganglion Tissue
## Q55: Identify cell types A-C, give two reasons for each, and state where each is located![Pyramidal cell, Purkinje cell, and astrocytes](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q01-bddbb759.jpg)**Answer:**
- A: pyramidal neuron - pyramidal cell body and an apical dendrite; located in the cerebral cortex
- B: Purkinje neuron - flask-shaped cell body and extensive dendritic arborisation; located in the cerebellar cortex
- C: astrocytes - star-shaped cells with numerous branching processes; located throughout the central nervous system
-

## Q56: Identify the spinal-cord level, tracts 26 and 27, one structure traversing region 13, and organisms infecting regions 11 and 28![Thoracic spinal cord cross-section with numbered regions](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q10-4b53774a.jpg)**Answer:**
- Thoracic spinal cord - lateral horn is present and the anterior horn is relatively small
- 26: dorsal spinocerebellar tract
- 27: fasciculus cuneatus
- Anterior spinal artery traverses the anterior median fissure (region 13)
- Region 11: poliovirus
- Region 28: *Treponema pallidum* (tabes dorsalis)
-

## Q57: Identify the structure, name three cell types, and name two components of the membranous labyrinth![Organ of Corti in the cochlea](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q16-99447606.jpg)**Answer:**
- Organ of Corti - identified by the bony labyrinth, scalae, membranes, hair cells, spiral ganglion, and stria vascularis
- Cell types include outer and inner hair cells, outer and inner pillar cells, outer and inner phalangeal (Deiters') cells, and cells of Hensen and Claudius
- Membranous labyrinth: utricle and semicircular ducts; saccule and cochlear duct are also components
- 

---
## Q58: Identify the organ, name the layers of its outer zone, and name two fibre types entering it![Cerebellar folium](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q22-b00527fa.jpg)**Answer:**
- Cerebellum - folia, a cortical mantle, and central medulla are visible
- Cerebellar cortex layers: molecular, Purkinje-cell, and granular layers
- Afferent fibres: mossy fibres and climbing fibres
- 

---
## Q59: Identify the structure, categorize the cells in layer X, and name two other eye components![Retina with layer X marked](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q25-8bf047f9.jpg)**Answer:**
- Retina - recognized by its many neuronal layers and adjacent choroid
- Cell categories include association neurons, supporting cells, and first-order neurons
- Other eye components: iris and ciliary body
- 

---
## Q60: Identify the structure, name two cell types, one common infection, and its embryologic origin![Sensory ganglion](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q28-eb9d23c7.jpg)**Answer:**
- Sensory ganglion - large first-order neuronal cell bodies, surrounding satellite cells, open-faced euchromatic nuclei, and axonal bundles
- Cell types: sensory neurons and satellite (neurosatellite) cells
- Common infection: varicella-zoster virus
- Embryologic origin: neural crest
- 

---
## Q61: Identify the structure, two sensory modalities, and two dermal layers![Pacinian corpuscle](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q29-486f07d7.jpg)**Answer:**
- Pacinian corpuscle - onion-like lamellae, a capsule, and location in the hypodermis
- Detects vibration and deep pressure
- Dermal layers: papillary and reticular
- 

---
## Q62: Identify the epithelium, its location, and three cell types![Olfactory epithelium](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q34-903309ac.jpg)**Answer:**
- Olfactory epithelium
- Located in the roof of the nasal cavity, superior nasal concha, and upper nasal septum
- Basal cells, supporting (sustentacular) cells, and olfactory receptor cells
- 

---
## Q63: Identify the structure, name its components, and state the modalities transmitted by its neurons![Neuromuscular spindle](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q35-fb1feab8.jpg)**Answer:**
- Neuromuscular spindle - a capsule encloses intrafusal fibres among extrafusal muscle fibres
- Components: annulospiral and flower-spray sensory endings
- Conveys proprioception, including muscle length/stretch and vibration
- 

---
## Q64: Identify the slide, state the functional unit and its characteristics, and name two astrocyte types![Cerebral cortex](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q36-7251cbea.jpg)**Answer:**
- Cerebral cortex - highly cellular tissue with poorly defined zones
- Functional unit: cortical module/column, characterized by vertical arrangement and lateral inhibition
- Fibrous astrocytes and protoplasmic astrocytes
- 

---
## Q65: Identify A giving reasons![Photomicrograph of a Purkinje cell with extensive dendritic arborisation, labelled A](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-histology-embryology-spot-review-h-purkinje-2e90f8d9.jpg)**Answer:**
- A — Purkinje cell: large flask-shaped nucleus; dendritic arborisation
- Also visible in this image (for revision): Purkinje cells form the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex
- 

---
## Q66: Identify A giving reasons![Golgi-stained photomicrograph of a pyramidal-shaped neuron with multiple dendrites, labelled A](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-histology-embryology-spot-review-h-pyramidal-05cc2c1f.jpg)**Answer:**
- A — pyramidal cell: pyramidal-shaped cell body; multiple dendrites
- Also visible in this image (for revision): pyramidal cells are the principal projection neurons of the cerebral cortex, found chiefly in layers III and V
- 

---
## Q67: State two regions where this tissue is found![Photomicrograph of a sensory ganglion with clusters of large neuronal cell bodies](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-histology-embryology-spot-review-h-ganglion-b8c9842d.jpg)**Answer:**
- Dorsal root ganglion (DRG)
- Trigeminal ganglion
- 

---
## Q68: Identify A giving reasons; identify the tract associated with A![Photomicrograph of a multilamellated corpuscle with a central axon, labelled A](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-histology-embryology-spot-review-h-pacinian-679d13eb.jpg)**Answer:**
- A — Pacinian corpuscle: multilamellated; central axon
- Tract associated with A: dorsal column–medial lemniscal pathway
- 

---
## Q69: Identify the slide shown; two cell types![Photomicrograph of a peripheral (dorsal root) ganglion](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-anatomy-spot-revision-q21-479e17d8.jpg)**Answer:**
- Slide shown: peripheral ganglion
- Two cell types: neurons; satellite (neurosatellite) cells
- 

---
## Q70: (a) Identify the tissue and its features. (b) Name three cell types by functional class![Q23 - retina histology with a layer labelled Y](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat8-2012-q23-59745650.jpg)**Answer:**
- Retina
- Features: many distinct layers, lies adjacent to the choroid
- Association neurons: horizontal and amacrine cells
- 1st order neuron: bipolar neurons
- Supporting cell: Müller cell (any two of these three groups)
- 

---
## Q71: (a) Identify the structure tagged F. (b) State two cell types visible in this field![Q25 - dorsal root ganglion histology with F labelled](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat8-2012-q25-307ba0d8.jpg)**Answer:**
- Dorsal root (sensory) ganglion
- Identifying features: "open-faced" appearance, vesicular nuclei, cell bodies of sensory neurons, satellite (neurosatellite) cells, nerve fibres — any of these as reasoning
- Cell types: neurosatellite cells and sensory neurons (1st order neurons)
- 

---
## Q72: (a) Identify the cells and their location. (b) Name three supporting cell types in the organ of Corti![Q27 - cerebral cortex neuron histology](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat8-2012-q27-8a1b6a05.jpg)**Answer:**
- Pyramidal neurons, in the cerebral cortex
- Organ of Corti supporting cells: pillar cells
- Organ of Corti supporting cells: sustentacular (Deiters') cells
- Organ of Corti supporting cells: phalangeal cells
- 

---
## Q73: Neuroglia/cortex histology — two functions of cells in A; name and location of cells in B (2+2 marks)![Histology slides of astrocytes (
A) and pyramidal neurons (B)](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-week-12-review-q20-7bf73c82.jpg)**Answer:**
- Two functions of the cells in A (astrocytes):
- Form the blood–brain barrier
- Provide nourishment to brain tissue
- Cells in B: pyramidal cells, found in the cerebral cortex (layers III and V)
- 

---
Reproductive & Endocrine Histology
## Q74: Identify the gland, give two reasons, name two hormones acting on it, and state two cell types and their secretory products![Lactating mammary gland](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q02-fc12fd2a.jpg)**Answer:**
- Lactating mammary gland - lobulated, with a well-developed duct system and numerous alveoli
- Hormones: prolactin, oxytocin, and oestrogen
- Acinar/alveolar epithelial cells produce milk; myoepithelial cells contract to expel it
- 

---
## Q75: Identify the organ, give two reasons, and describe the cells in X and Y with their functions![Pancreas with exocrine acini and an islet](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q05-a5571de2.jpg)**Answer:**
- Pancreas - lobulated organ containing exocrine acini and endocrine islets
- X: acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes; centroacinar cells begin the duct system and contribute bicarbonate-rich fluid; pancreatic stellate cells support the stroma
- Y: alpha cells secrete glucagon, beta cells insulin, delta cells somatostatin, and PP cells pancreatic polypeptide
- 

---
## Q76: Identify the salivary gland, name its duct types, and list the components of a salivon![Submandibular salivary gland](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q08-c07a05ac.jpg)**Answer:**
- Submandibular gland - a mixed gland with serous and mucous portions, predominantly serous
- Ducts: intercalated, striated, and excretory ducts
- Salivon: terminal acinus plus intercalated, striated, and excretory duct components
- 

---
## Q77: Identify the gland, give two reasons, name its cell types and functions, and state one distinguishing feature![Thyroid gland](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q12-81f09ff0.jpg)**Answer:**
- Thyroid gland - follicles containing colloid, lined by follicular cells, with parafollicular cells between follicles
- Follicular cells produce T3 and T4; parafollicular (
C) cells produce calcitonin
- Distinguishing feature: thyroid hormone is stored extracellularly in colloid
- 

---
## Q78: Identify the organ, give two reasons, name three cell types with functions, and state its functional lobule![Liver histology](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q15-cc72301d.jpg)**Answer:**
- Liver - hepatocytes arranged in cords, central veins, portal triads, and sinusoids
- Hepatocytes are the main metabolic and synthetic cells; hepatic stellate cells store vitamin A and make extracellular matrix; Kupffer cells are phagocytes
- Functional lobule: hepatic acinus
- 

---
## Q79: Identify the gland, name two cell types in region Z, and categorize the secretory cells in region X![Pituitary gland with regions X, Y, and Z](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q18-50f62689.jpg)**Answer:**
- Pituitary gland - two lobes of differing cellularity separated by the pars intermedia/interglandular cleft
- Neurohypophysis (Z): pituicytes and axonal fibres/terminals
- Adenohypophysis (X): acidophils (somatotrophs and mammotrophs), basophils (thyrotrophs, corticotrophs, and gonadotrophs), and chromophobes
- 

---
## Q80: Identify the gland, give two reasons, outline control of its zones, and name two associated metabolic diseases![Adrenal gland](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q26-bfce5438.jpg)**Answer:**
- Adrenal gland - cortical and medullary regions, three cortical zones, and a central medullary vein
- Zona glomerulosa is regulated mainly by angiotensin II and potassium; zona fasciculata by ACTH; medulla by sympathetic preganglionic fibres
- Associated disorders include Cushing syndrome and secondary diabetes mellitus
- 

---
## Q81: Identify the slide, give three reasons, and name the cell types with their functions![Testis histology](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q37-253caaaf.jpg)**Answer:**
- Testis - seminiferous tubules, interstitial Leydig cells, and developing spermatozoa
- Sertoli cells support spermatogenesis; Leydig cells secrete testosterone; peritubular myoid cells contract; germ cells form spermatozoa
- 

---
## Q82: Identify the gland, name a tumour marker, list two components, and name two ovarian hormones with their sources![Prostate gland](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q39-5a0dea61.jpg)**Answer:**
- Prostate - compound tubuloalveolar glands in fibromuscular stroma, often with corpora amylacea
- Tumour marker: prostate-specific antigen (PS
A)
- Components include secretory glands and fibromuscular stroma/trabeculae
- Oestrogen is produced mainly by follicular (granulosa) cells with androgen substrate from theca interna; progesterone is produced mainly by the corpus luteum
- 

---
## Q83: Identify the parts labeled A and B; two functions of the follicular cells (2+2 marks)![Photomicrograph of an ovarian follicle with antrum (
A) and oocyte (
B) labelled](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q39-221d4fe1.jpg)**Answer:**
- A — antrum (fluid-filled follicular cavity)
- B — oocyte (within the cumulus oophorus)
- Two functions of the follicular (granulosa) cells: secrete oestrogen; nourish and support the developing oocyte
- 

---
Other / General
## Q84: Identify the slide, give two reasons, state two functions, and name the blood-air barrier components![Spleen](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q04-b926c79d.jpg)**Answer:**
- Spleen - capsule with incomplete trabeculae, red and white pulp, and central arterioles
- Functions include immune surveillance and removal/sequestration of aged red blood cells
- Blood-air barrier: type I alveolar epithelium, fused basal laminae, and capillary endothelium
- 

---
## Q85: Identify the structure, give three reasons, name two medullary components, and state two adaptive immune responses![Lymph node](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q21-a035ca53.jpg)**Answer:**
- Lymph node - capsule, lymphoid follicles, and germinal centres
- Medulla: medullary cords and medullary sinuses
- Adaptive immune responses: humoral and cell-mediated immunity
- 

---
## Q86: Identify the slide, give three reasons, name its four main cell types, and name four hormones it produces![Thymus](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q30-a7ce6eb2.jpg)**Answer:**
- Thymus - lobules with cortex and medulla, trabeculae, and Hassall corpuscles
- Main cells include thymocytes/T-cell precursors, epithelial reticular cells, macrophages, and hormone-producing epithelial cells
- Thymic hormones include thymosin, thymopoietin, thymulin, and thymic humoral factor
- 

---
## Q87: Identify the structures, give two reasons, name blood-thymus barrier components, and name two neural-crest cells in skin![Sweat glands in skin](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-review-of-histology-q31-d1bc19ae.jpg)**Answer:**
- Sweat glands - tubular profiles in cross-section within dermal/hypodermal connective tissue
- Blood-thymus barrier includes continuous capillary endothelium, thick basal lamina, perivascular connective tissue/macrophages, and epithelial reticular cells
- Neural-crest-derived skin cells: melanocytes and Merkel cells
- 

---
## Q88: Identify the slide; two organs where this tissue is found![Silver-stained photomicrograph showing a fine reticular fibre network](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-anatomy-spot-revision-q23-54e670cd.jpg)**Answer:**
- Slide: reticular fibres
- Two organs where found: liver; spleen
- Also visible in this image (for revision): reticular fibres also form the supporting framework of the kidney and lymph nodes
- 

---
## Q89: Identify the tissue; two adaptations of the tissue to its function![Photomicrograph of thick skin with a keratinized surface](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-anatomy-spot-revision-q25-42eb3273.jpg)**Answer:**
- Tissue: skin (keratinized stratified squamous epithelium)
- Two adaptations to function: keratinisation; stratification
- 

---
## Q90: Identify the tissue shown; three sites where it is found![Photomicrograph of fibrocartilage with scattered chondrocytes in dense fibrous tissue](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-anatomy-spot-revision-q28-a708db0d.jpg)**Answer:**
- Tissue shown: fibrocartilage — features: scattered cells, highly fibrous matrix, cells sit in lacunae
- Three sites where found: knee menisci; intervertebral discs; pubic symphysis
- 

---
## Q91: State three functions of the structure displayed![Electron micrograph of a mitochondrion](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-anatomy-spot-revision-q30-c16e1728.jpg)**Answer:**
- Structure: mitochondrion
- Three functions: oxidative phosphorylation (ATP production); heat production; calcium storage
- Also visible in this image (for revision): mitochondria also play a central role in initiating apoptosis
- 

---
## Q92: Two regions where the epithelium type displayed is found; two lateral epithelial adaptations (2+2 marks)![Photomicrograph of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q23-5dcf8668.jpg)**Answer:**
- Two regions where pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium is found: trachea; bronchi
- Two lateral epithelial adaptations: tight junctions (zonula occludens); desmosomes (macula adherens)
- 

---
## Q93: (a) Identify the tissue and two distinguishing features. (b) State three physiological properties of this tissue![Q28 - cardiac muscle histology](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat8-2012-q28-41185f4a.jpg)**Answer:**
- Cardiac muscle
- Distinguishing features: intercalated discs, branching fibres
- Properties: contractility
- Properties: excitability
- Properties: conductivity
- 

---
## Q94: (a) Identify the epithelium and three features. (b) Name a site with elastic laminae and a site with reticular fibres![Q30 - olfactory epithelium histology](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat8-2012-q30-4713a577.jpg)**Answer:**
- Olfactory epithelium (a pseudostratified epithelium)
- Features: multiple nuclear layers, Bowman's glands, cilia present, no goblet cells
- Interlaminar elastic fibres: found in large arteries (e.g. the aorta)
- Reticular fibres: found in the liver (supporting framework)

## Q95: (a) Identify the conditions shown in A and 
B. (b) Name two other cell types found in the epidermis apart from keratinocytes![Q32 - two skin condition photos, A and B](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat8-2012-q32-dde894c6.jpg)**Answer:**
- A: hypertrichosis (excessive hair growth)
- B: ichthyosis (dry, scaling skin)

- Other epidermal cells: melanocytes
- Other epidermal cells: Langerhans cells

## Q96: Name 1, 2, 3 and 4![Q36 - electron micrograph of a sarcomere](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-pat3-2019-q36-72a8c49b.jpg)**Answer:**
- 1: Z-disc

## Q97: Identify epithelium displayed and where it is found![Q38 - transitional epithelium histology](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-pat3-2019-q38-36a823d0.jpg)**Answer:**
- Transitional (urinary) epithelium
- Found in: renal calyces
- Found in: ureters
- Found in: urinary bladder
- Distinguishing feature: umbrella cells at the surface, able to stretch
- 

---
## Q98: Name a muscle that (a) originates and (b) inserts on the part probed, and state their innervation![Q9 - two fan-shaped muscles converging at a probed point](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-sdl-mock-marathon-q09-30bd59cd.jpg)**Answer:**
- (a) Pectoralis major
- Origin: clavicle, sternum, costal cartilages
- Innervation: medial and lateral pectoral nerves (C5–T1)
- (b) Pectoralis minor
- Inserts on the coracoid process
- Innervation: medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1)

## Q99: State the origin and innervation of the muscle probed![Q10 - probe on a fan-shaped chest wall muscle](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-sdl-mock-marathon-q10-e91c74d3.jpg)**Answer:**
- Pectoralis major
- Origin: medial half of clavicle
- Origin: sternum
- Origin: upper costal cartilages
- Innervation: medial and lateral pectoral nerves (C5–T1)
- Action: adducts and medially rotates the arm

## Q100: Name 1, 2, 3 and 4![Q36 - electron micrograph of a sarcomere](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-sdl-mock-marathon-q36-588b8fd7.jpg)**Answer:**
- 1: Z-line (Z-disc)
- 2: A-band

## Q101: Identify epithelium displayed and where it is found![Q38 - epithelium histology, source image is damaged/incomplete](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-sdl-mock-marathon-q38-d006ffa8.jpg)**Answer:**

articles.content:
*A consolidated Year 1 Anatomy spot-question bank for the Aponeurosis collection, drawn from eight revision papers and one lecture, organised by body region rather than by source paper — pelvis through hand for the lower and upper limbs, plus the vertebral column, skull, breast, and reference figures. Tap any answer to reveal it.*
Pelvis & Hip
## Q1: State the anatomical basis of a positive Trendelenburg sign![Normal and positive Trendelenburg stance](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-msaun-week-one-q01-534762e8.jpg)**Answer:**
- Weakness or paralysis of the hip abductors, principally gluteus medius and gluteus minimus, on the supporting side
- The pelvis drops on the unsupported side because the abductors cannot keep it level
- Common causes include superior gluteal nerve injury or hip disease
- 

---
## Q2: State two non-neural contents of the lesser sciatic foramen**Answer:**
- Internal pudendal vessels
- Tendon of obturator internus
- Neural contents for comparison are the pudendal nerve and nerve to obturator internus

## Q73: Bone A — two stability factors; two attachments on area X of bone B (2+2 marks)![Tibial plateau specimen A and femoral condyle specimen B with region X](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q04-5f707622.jpg)**Answer:**
- Two stability factors of bone A (tibial plateau/knee):
- Q angle
- Sweeping fibres of vastus medialis; the lateral tubercle of the femur also contributes
- Two structures attaching on area X of bone B:
- Anterior cruciate ligament
- Anterior edge of the menisci
- 

---
## Q74: Structures deep to A and B (1+3 marks)![Groin dissection with A and B labelled, ASIS marked](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q08-47c809d3.jpg)**Answer:**
- Structure deep to A: articularis genu muscle; suprapatellar bursa
- Structures deep to B (subsartorial/adductor canal): nerve to vastus medialis; saphenous nerve; femoral vessels
- 

---
## Q75: (a) Identify the fracture, its basis and a complication. (b) State the root values of the superficial peroneal and pudendal nerves![Q20 - knee X-ray, two views](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat8-2012-q20-00defd31.jpg)**Answer:**
- Supracondylar femoral fracture
- Basis: pull of gastrocnemius on the distal fragment
- Complication: injury to the popliteal artery
- Superficial peroneal nerve root value: L4, L5, S1
- Pudendal nerve root value: S2, S3, S4
- 

---
## Q76: Identify the muscle below and its innervation![Q29 - thenar eminence dissection](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-sdl-mock-marathon-q29-ce128871.jpg)**Answer:**
- Abductor pollicis brevis
- Innervation: recurrent (motor) branch of the median nerve
- Other thenar muscles in this group: flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis (all median nerve, except adductor pollicis which is ulnar)
- 

---
Leg, Ankle & Foot
## Q77: (a) Identify the tendon tagged. (b) Describe the stability factors of the ankle joint![Q10 - ankle dissection with a tendon tagged](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-marathon1-q10-b35a1650.jpg)**Answer:**
- Peroneus tertius
- Static stability: the mortise-and-tenon (talocrural) joint structure itself
- Static stability: deltoid ligament
- Static stability: anterior and posterior talofibular ligaments
- Static stability: distal tibiofibular ligament
- Static stability: calcaneonavicular ligament
- Dynamic stability: all tendons of the anterior and posterior leg compartments crossing the joint
- 

---
## Q78: (a) Identify the muscle tagged and its actions. (b) Describe the pattern of blood supply to N and its clinical relevance![Q11 - sole of the foot with N labelled](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-marathon1-q11-802e7ddb.jpg)**Answer:**
- Tibialis posterior
- Actions: inversion and plantarflexion of the foot
- N: the plantar "watershed" area
- Proximal part receives blood supply from the muscles forming it
- Distal part receives blood supply from the plantar aponeurosis
- Middle segment has poor blood supply
- Clinical relevance: slow healing after injury in this zone
- 

---
## Q79: (a) Identify and side the bone shown. (b) Name a muscle inserting on its body and the clinical relevance. (c) Name two joints where inversion/eversion occur![Q12 - isolated tarsal bone specimen](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-marathon1-q12-41f50b29.jpg)**Answer:**
- Left talus
- Sided by the "table-top test": with the rounded head pointing forward, the trochlear surface (convex front-to-back, concave side-to-side) faces upward
- No muscle inserts directly on the talus — this was left unanswered in the original source, but it's worth knowing that no tendon attaches to it at all
- Clinical relevance: with only ligamentous attachments and a retrograde blood supply, the talus is prone to avascular necrosis after a talar neck fracture
- Inversion/eversion occur at the subtalar joint
- Inversion/eversion also occur at the talocalcaneonavicular joint
- (the calcaneocuboid joint contributes too, as part of the transverse tarsal joint)
- 

---
## Q80: (a) Identify K and its terminal distribution. (b) Give two causes of injury to L![Q16 - right axilla and arm dissection with K and L labelled](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-marathon1-q16-99fad664.jpg)**Answer:**
- K: musculocutaneous nerve
- Terminal distribution: continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, supplying the lateral forearm
- L: median nerve
- Cause of injury: supracondylar humeral fractures
- Cause of injury: inflammation of tendons at the carpal tunnel
- 

---
## Q81: Identify the bone displayed; its pattern of blood supply![Illustration of the right talus](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-anatomy-spot-revision-q15-c95f6151.jpg)**Answer:**
- Bone displayed: right talus
- Pattern of blood supply: retrograde (blood enters distally and flows proximally — a reason the talus is prone to avascular necrosis after a fracture)
- 

---
## Q82: Foot — nerves supplying regions A and B; two structures behind the lateral malleolus (2+2 marks)![Dorsum of the foot with cutaneous regions A and B colour-coded](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q09-672bd9e8.jpg)**Answer:**
- A — superficial fibular (peroneal) nerve
- B — saphenous nerve
- Two structures behind the lateral malleolus: peroneus longus; peroneus brevis
- 

---
## Q83: Two arteries forming X; attachments of Y (2+2 marks)![Deep plantar dissection with X and Y labelled](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q10-0dbc15e4.jpg)**Answer:**
- X (plantar arterial arch) is formed by: the dorsalis pedis artery and the lateral plantar artery
- Y (peroneus longus tendon) attachments: base of the 1st metatarsal and the medial cuneiform
- 

---
## Q84: Forearm — identify muscle X and nerve Y; two causes of claw hand (2+2 marks)![Forearm dissection with muscle X and nerve Y labelled](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat3-2015-q20-536264fd.jpg)**Answer:**
- X — supinator muscle
- Y — median nerve
- Two causes of claw hand: damage to the ulnar and median nerves; damage to the blood supply of the lumbrical muscles
- 

---
## Q85: (a) State the clinical effect and basis of the nerve injury shown. (b) Name two other sources forming the arterial anastomosis around A![Q15 - humerus specimen with A and B labelled](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat8-2012-q15-0344ee22.jpg)**Answer:**
- Clinical effect: claw hand
- Basis: ulnar nerve injury
- Long head of biceps brachii contributes to the anastomosis
- Latissimus dorsi is also related to this region
- Ascending (anastomotic/articular) branch of profunda brachii artery — any two of these accepted
- 

---
## Q86: (a) Identify tendons A and 
B. (b) Name the bony landmark at this site and two ligaments attaching there![Q21 - ankle dissection with A, B, C labelled](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-pat8-2012-q21-86547d42.jpg)**Answer:**
- A: peroneus tertius
- B: extensor hallucis longus
- Landmark: lateral malleolus
- Ligaments: anterior talofibular ligament
- Ligaments: posterior talofibular ligament
- Ligaments: calcaneofibular ligament
- 

---
## Q87: State the communications of the space labelled X![Q23 - diagram of the palm with a fascial space labelled X](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-sdl-mock-marathon-q23-2e7d4981.jpg)**Answer:**
- Midpalmar space
- Proximally: continuous with the space of Parona in the forearm (via the carpal tunnel)
- Distally: communicates with the web spaces/dorsum of the fingers via the lumbrical canals
- Neighbouring space: the thenar space, separated from it by a fascial septum
- 

---
## Q88: State (a) the site of entrapment of the nerve below at the wrist, (b) its nerve roots![Q30 - nerve at the wrist crease](https://cdn.ompathstudy.com/uploads/2026/08/y1-anatomy-cropped-sdl-mock-marathon-q30-c4fc2e6a.jpg)**Answer:**
- Median nerve
- (a) Site: carpal tunnel, deep to the flexor retinaculum
- (b) Roots: C6, C7, C8, T1
- Clinical correlate: carpal tunnel syndrome — numbness of the lateral 3½ digits
- 

---

articles.title: Mastering Community Health: Diagnosis, Indicators & Care — Past Paper 2024
articles.content:
# MOUNT KENYA UNIVERSITY — UNIVERSITY EXAMINATION 2024/2025
**School of Public Health**
**Department of Community Health, Epidemiology and Biostatistics**
**Bachelor of Medicine and Surgery — Regular**
**Unit Code:** MBPH3700 **Unit Title:** Community Health
**Date:** Monday 21st July, 2025, 2.00PM **Main Exam** **Time:** 2 Hours
**Instructions:** Answer ALL questions in Section A and ANY TWO in Section B
*(Note: Questions 3–8 in Section A and Section B Qs 2–3 touch on lifecycle cohorts, home-based care, and outreach programs — content not present in your uploaded lecture materials. I've answered these from standard community health/public health principles so you have something to revise, but flag them to your lecturer/classmates to confirm they match the exact class framing.)*
---
## SECTION A (Answer ALL — 5 marks each)
### Q1. Describe the steps involved in conducting a community diagnosis. (5 marks)
1. **Community Entry** — Identify the community, its geographical location, rural/urban categorization, and social/economic/ethnic background; identify gatekeepers (key persons) to contact first.
2. **Setting Objectives** — Formulate SMART objectives (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-bound) to guide the diagnosis.
3. **Data Collection** — Use questionnaires, interviews, observation checklists, and FGDs to gather quantitative and qualitative data; determine sample size using the Community Health Unit (CHU = 100 households).
4. **Data Analysis** — Analyze quantitative data using statistical methods and qualitative data using thematic methods.
5. **Report Writing, Findings & Conclusion** — Compile results into a structured report (title, introduction, objectives, literature review, methodology) and draw conclusions to guide intervention planning.
---
### Q2. Identify four key indicators used to measure community health status. (5 marks)
1. **Demographic indicators** — e.g. Crude Birth Rate, Crude Death Rate, Infant Mortality Rate — measure population-level vital statistics.
2. **Health status indicators** — e.g. immunization coverage, ANC utilization — measure how much illness/service use is occurring.
3. **Healthcare access indicators** — e.g. doctor:patient ratio, doctor:nurse ratio (recommended 1:4) — measure system capacity to deliver care.
4. **Disease quantification indicators** — e.g. disease prevalence, incidence rate, relative risk — measure disease burden and spread.
*(Could also mention: socioeconomic, mental health, nutritional, or environmental indicators if asked for more than four.)*
---
### Q3. Explain how lifecycle cohorts (e.g., children, adolescents, elderly) influence community health planning. (5 marks)
1. **Different health needs per life stage** — Children need immunization/nutrition programs, adolescents need reproductive health/substance abuse education, and the elderly need chronic disease management — so a single generic program cannot serve everyone.
2. **Resource allocation** — Planners must distribute limited health resources (staff, budget, facilities) according to which cohorts are largest or most vulnerable in that specific community.
3. **Targeted service design** — Outreach messaging, service delivery times, and locations must be tailored to each cohort (e.g. school-based programs for children, workplace programs for adults).
4. **Risk factor variation** — Each cohort faces distinct risk factors (e.g. malnutrition in children, teenage pregnancy in adolescents, non-communicable diseases in the elderly), requiring cohort-specific prevention strategies.
5. **Improved program effectiveness** — Planning around lifecycle cohorts ensures interventions are relevant and acceptable to the target group, increasing uptake and impact.
---
### Q4. Write short notes on the importance of home-based care in chronic disease management. (5 marks)
1. **Reduces hospital burden** — Patients with chronic conditions (e.g. diabetes, hypertension) can be managed at home, freeing up hospital beds for acute cases.
2. **Cost-effective** — Reduces the financial burden on both the health system and the patient/family compared to prolonged hospital stays.
3. **Improves quality of life** — Patients remain in a familiar, comfortable environment surrounded by family, which supports psychological wellbeing.
4. **Continuity of care** — Enables regular monitoring of chronic conditions, medication adherence, and early detection of complications.
5. **Empowers caregivers** — Family members are trained to provide basic care, creating sustainable long-term management of the illness.
---
### Q5. List four services typically provided during community health outreach programs. (5 marks)
1. **Immunization services** — administering vaccines to children and at-risk groups within the community.
2. **Health education** — teaching on hygiene, nutrition, disease prevention, and healthy behaviors.
3. **Screening services** — early detection of diseases such as hypertension, diabetes, HIV, and malnutrition.
4. **Maternal and child health services** — antenatal care, growth monitoring, and family planning services.
*(Could also include: referral services, distribution of health commodities like mosquito nets/deworming tablets.)*
---
### Q6. Describe the role of community diagnosis in prioritizing health interventions. (5 marks)
1. **Identifies actual community needs** — Community diagnosis generates evidence-based data on the real health problems present, rather than relying on assumptions.
2. **Enables prioritization criteria** — Uses factors such as number of people affected, available resources, political feasibility, and democratic input to rank which needs should be addressed first.
3. **Establishes a baseline** — Creates an epidemiological baseline against which the success of interventions can later be measured and evaluated.
4. **Reflects community attitudes** — Determines the community's own perception and readiness toward specific health issues, ensuring interventions are accepted.
5. **Guides efficient resource use** — Since resources are limited, community diagnosis ensures they are directed to the most urgent and impactful problems first.
---
### Q7. Identify three health indicators commonly used in monitoring maternal and child health. (5 marks)
1. **Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR)** — (Maternal deaths ÷ Total live births) × 100,000 — measures deaths related to pregnancy/childbirth complications.
2. **Infant Mortality Rate** — (Dead infants ÷ Total live births) × 100,000 — measures survival of infants in their first year.
3. **Under-5 Mortality Rate** — (Deaths of children under 5 ÷ Total live births) × 100,000 — measures overall child survival and reflects broader health system quality (nutrition, sanitation, care access).
*(Additional indicator that could be mentioned: ANC attendance/coverage rate, or immunization coverage.)*
---
### Q8. Explain why targeting lifecycle cohorts is essential in delivering effective community health interventions. (5 marks)
1. **Ensures relevance** — Interventions matched to a cohort's specific health risks (e.g. vaccines for infants, NCD screening for the elderly) are more likely to be accepted and effective.
2. **Maximizes limited resources** — Focusing efforts on the cohort most affected by a specific problem avoids wasting resources on a broad, unfocused approach.
3. **Improves health outcomes across the life course** — Addressing health needs at each life stage (childhood, adolescence, adulthood, old age) creates cumulative long-term benefits, since poor health early in life often predicts poor health later.
4. **Supports early intervention** — Identifying and acting on risks specific to a cohort (e.g. teenage pregnancy in adolescents) allows prevention before problems escalate.
5. **Enhances community trust and participation** — Cohort-specific programs (e.g. youth-friendly clinics) make target groups feel understood, increasing engagement and program success.
---
## SECTION B (Answer ANY TWO — 15 marks each)
### Section B, Q1. You have been assigned to conduct a community diagnosis in a peri-urban settlement with high rates of malnutrition and poor sanitation. Describe the steps you would follow to gather data, engage the community, identify key health problems, and propose relevant interventions. (15 marks)
1. Community Entry (2–3 marks)
- Identify and enter the peri-urban settlement, establishing its geographical boundaries and categorization.
- Describe the community's social, economic, and ethnic background to understand context relevant to malnutrition/sanitation.
- Identify gatekeepers (local chiefs, community health volunteers, religious leaders) to gain trust and access.
2. Setting SMART Objectives (2 marks)
- Define clear, specific objectives, e.g. "To determine the prevalence and causes of malnutrition and poor sanitation practices in [settlement name] within 3 months."
3. Data Collection — Engaging the Community (3–4 marks)
- Use a mix of quantitative tools (household questionnaires on nutrition status, water/sanitation access) and qualitative tools (FGDs with mothers/caregivers, key informant interviews with health workers).
- Use observation checklists to physically assess sanitation infrastructure (latrines, waste disposal, water sources).
- Determine sample size using the Community Health Unit standard (100 households per unit); ensure representation across all sub-areas of the settlement.
4. Data Analysis (2 marks)
- Analyze quantitative data (e.g. prevalence rates of stunting/wasting, % households with improved sanitation) statistically.
- Analyze qualitative data thematically to identify root causes (e.g. poverty, lack of clean water, poor feeding practices).
5. Identifying Key Health Problems (2 marks)
- Prioritize identified problems using criteria: number of people affected (e.g. children under 5 with malnutrition), severity, available resources, and community input.
- Establish an epidemiological baseline (e.g. current malnutrition prevalence, sanitation coverage %) for future comparison.
6. Proposing Interventions (3 marks)
- **Malnutrition:** growth monitoring and promotion programs, supplementary feeding programs, nutrition education for caregivers, links to income-generating projects to improve food access.
- **Sanitation:** construction/improvement of latrines, provision of safe water sources, hygiene promotion campaigns (handwashing, safe waste disposal).
- Involve intersectoral collaboration (health, water/sanitation authorities, local administration) and ensure community participation for sustainability.
---
### Section B, Q2. As a public health officer, you are tasked with designing an outreach program to reduce teenage pregnancy in a rural district. Explain how you would target the appropriate lifecycle cohort, involve community stakeholders, and evaluate the effectiveness of your outreach strategy. (15 marks)
1. Targeting the Appropriate Lifecycle Cohort (4–5 marks)
- Identify the adolescent cohort (roughly ages 10–19) as the primary target, since they are at highest risk of teenage pregnancy.
- Conduct a needs assessment within schools and community youth groups to understand knowledge gaps, cultural beliefs, and access barriers to reproductive health services among adolescents.
- Design age-appropriate, youth-friendly messaging and services (e.g. peer educators, youth-friendly clinic hours) to increase comfort and uptake.
- Address root causes specific to this cohort — lack of sex education, poverty-driven transactional relationships, early marriage practices.
2. Involving Community Stakeholders (4–5 marks)
- Engage **parents/guardians** to support open communication about reproductive health at home.
- Involve **school administrators and teachers** to integrate reproductive health education into the curriculum.
- Partner with **religious and community leaders** to address cultural/traditional barriers and gain community buy-in.
- Collaborate with **local health facilities** to ensure adolescent-friendly contraceptive and counseling services are available.
- Involve **local government/administration** for policy support (e.g. enforcing laws against early marriage).
3. Evaluating Effectiveness of the Outreach Strategy (4–5 marks)
- Establish baseline data on teenage pregnancy rates before the program begins (epidemiological baseline).
- Monitor process indicators: number of adolescents reached, number of education sessions held, contraceptive uptake among adolescents.
- Monitor outcome indicators: change in teenage pregnancy rate, age-specific birth rate (ASBR) for the adolescent age band, school dropout rates due to pregnancy.
- Use pre- and post-program surveys/FGDs to assess changes in knowledge, attitudes, and practices among adolescents.
- Conduct periodic review meetings with stakeholders to adjust strategy based on findings (continuous monitoring principle).
---
### Section B, Q3. You are implementing a home-based care program for chronically ill patients in a low-resource setting. Discuss the elements you would consider in planning and delivering care, including caregiver training, monitoring patient outcomes, and ensuring sustainability of services. (15 marks)
1. Caregiver Training (4–5 marks)
- Identify and select family members or community volunteers willing to act as primary caregivers.
- Train caregivers on basic care skills: medication administration, wound care, hygiene practices, recognizing danger signs/complications.
- Provide training on psychological support techniques, since chronic illness affects both patient and caregiver mental health.
- Ensure caregivers understand when and how to escalate care (referral pathways to health facilities for emergencies).
2. Monitoring Patient Outcomes (4–5 marks)
- Establish a system for regular follow-up visits by community health workers to assess patient progress.
- Use simple monitoring tools/checklists to track vital signs, medication adherence, and symptom changes.
- Set clear outcome indicators (e.g. reduction in hospital readmissions, improved disease control markers like blood sugar/blood pressure levels).
- Maintain patient records for continuity of care and to identify when a case needs escalation to a higher level of care.
3. Ensuring Sustainability of Services (4–5 marks)
- Involve local community structures (community health units, volunteers) to reduce dependency on external/donor funding.
- Build capacity through continuous training and refresher courses for caregivers and community health workers.
- Advocate for intersectoral collaboration and local government support/funding to institutionalize the program.
- Incorporate community feedback mechanisms to adapt the program to actual needs and improve acceptability.
- Link the home-based care program with existing health facility services to ensure a smooth referral and support system, avoiding a parallel, unsustainable structure.
---
### Section B, Q4. A county government is developing a community health improvement plan. Describe how you would use community health indicators to assess needs, guide resource allocation, and monitor progress over time. (15 marks)
1. Assessing Needs (4–5 marks)
- Use **demographic indicators** (CBR, CDR, infant/under-5/maternal mortality rates) to identify the population's basic health burden and vulnerable groups.
- Use **disease quantification indicators** (prevalence, incidence rate, relative risk) to identify which diseases are most burdensome or spreading fastest in the county.
- Use **socioeconomic indicators** (poverty rate, median household income) to understand underlying drivers of poor health.
- Use **health status and access indicators** (immunization coverage, ANC utilization, doctor:patient ratio) to identify gaps between need and actual service delivery.
2. Guiding Resource Allocation (4–5 marks)
- Prioritize funding and staff deployment toward sub-counties/wards showing the poorest indicator values (e.g. highest under-5 mortality, lowest immunization coverage).
- Use healthcare access indicators (doctor:nurse ratio — recommended 1:4, facility numbers) to identify where infrastructure or workforce gaps need urgent investment.
- Apply prioritization criteria — numbers affected, resource availability, political feasibility, democratic input — to rank competing needs (e.g. malaria control vs. maternal health services) when the budget is limited.
- Allocate resources toward high-impact, cost-effective interventions identified through the indicator data (e.g. investing in ANC services if MMR is high).
3. Monitoring Progress Over Time (4–5 marks)
- Establish baseline values for key indicators (e.g. current MMR, immunization coverage %) at the start of the improvement plan.
- Conduct periodic re-measurement of the same indicators (continuous monitoring) to track whether interventions are producing the intended change.
- Use trend analysis to compare year-on-year progress (e.g. is CDR falling, is disease incidence declining).
- Use health services efficiency indicators (bed turnover, patient satisfaction) to assess whether service delivery quality is improving alongside access.
- Adjust the community health improvement plan based on findings — reallocating resources or redesigning interventions where indicators show insufficient progress, closing the loop back into the "evidence-based operation" principle of community health.
---
