43. Discuss in detail the Pathogenesis, morphologic features and Clinical presentation of Colorectal Carcinoma (20 Marks)
- *Pathogenesis:* Adenoma-carcinoma sequence (APC, KRAS, p53 mutations); APC mutation typically initiating; further mutations drive invasion; alternative pathway via microsatellite instability (Lynch syndrome)
- *Morphology:* Napkin ring/annular lesions (left colon); large polypoid masses (right colon); mucinous variant; haemorrhage in advanced lesions
- *Clinical presentation:* Change in bowel habits, occult/overt bleeding, iron deficiency anaemia, abdominal pain, weight loss, palpable mass, obstruction (left-sided)
44. Discuss in detail the Pathogenesis, morphologic features and Clinical presentation of Tuberculosis (20 Marks)
- *Pathogenesis:* Inhalation of M. tuberculosis; macrophage ingestion/survival; Ghon focus formation, spreads to hilar nodes (Ghon complex); cell-mediated hypersensitivity at ~3 weeks causes granuloma formation
- *Morphology:* Caseating granulomas; Ghon complex; secondary TB — apical cavitating lesions; Miliary TB — widespread small granulomas
- *Clinical presentation:* Chronic productive cough/haemoptysis, low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss, chest pain, possible extrapulmonary spread
45. Outline the morphologic changes of the heart in Dilated cardiomyopathy (5 Marks)
- Gross: Ventricular hypertrophy/dilatation (systolic dysfunction), flabby enlarged heart, all 4 chambers dilated
- Microscopic: Myocyte hypertrophy, variable necrosis, interstitial/perivascular fibrosis
- Mural thrombi may be present due to stasis
46. Briefly outline the classification of Vasculitis based on size of vessel afflicted (5 Marks)
- Large vessel — Giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis
- Medium vessel — Polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease
- Small vessel — Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, Churg-Strauss
47. Write short notes on Rheumatic Heart Disease (5 Marks)
- Follows Group A Strep pharyngitis; molecular mimicry (M protein cross-reacts with cardiac antigens)
- Acute: Aschoff bodies, pericardial effusion
- Chronic: valve thickening, fibrosis, commissural fusion, calcification
- Mitral valve most affected; leads to stenosis/regurgitation
48. Compare and contrast Acute and Sub Acute Infective endocarditis (5 Marks)
| Acute IE | Subacute IE |
|---|---|
| Highly virulent (e.g. Staph aureus) | Less virulent (e.g. Strep viridans) |
| Previously normal valves | Previously damaged valves |
| High mortality | Lower mortality with treatment |
| Rapid onset | Insidious onset |
| Large, friable vegetations | Smaller vegetations |
49. Write short notes on Uterine Endometriosis (5 Marks)
- Functional endometrial tissue outside uterine cavity
- Sites: ovary (most common), pelvic peritoneum, retrovaginal septum, uterine ligaments
- Theories: metaplastic, regurgitation, haematogenous/lymphatic spread
- Features: dyspareunia, dysmenorrhoea, infertility, chronic pelvic pain
- Morphology: "chocolate cysts"
50. Briefly Outline the Classification of Primary Malignant Ovarian neoplasms (5 Marks)
- Surface epithelial tumours — serous, mucinous, endometrioid (majority)
- Germ cell tumours — dysgerminoma, malignant teratoma, choriocarcinoma, yolk sac tumour
- Sex cord-stromal tumours — granulosa cell, Sertoli-Leydig cell
- Metastatic — e.g., Krukenberg tumour
51. Outline the morphologic features of Uterine leiomyoma (5 Marks)
- Well-circumscribed, round, firm, grey-white, whorled cut surface
- Smooth muscle bundles resembling myometrium
- Degenerative changes: hyaline, cystic, myxoid, fatty, calcification, red/haemorrhagic
- Located submucosally, intramurally, or subserosally
52. Write short notes on PAGET's disease of the Vulva (5 Marks)
- Intraepithelial neoplasia with malignant epithelial (Paget) cells in epidermis
- Erythematous, eczematous, pruritic vulvar lesion
- Usually in-situ carcinoma
- Diagnosis: biopsy showing large pale-staining Paget cells
53. Discuss the Pathogenesis and Morphologic features of Pulmonary Thromboemboli (10 Marks)
- *Pathogenesis:* Most arise from DVT of lower limbs; Virchow's triad (stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial injury); thrombus dislodges, travels to right heart, lodges in pulmonary circulation; large emboli cause saddle embolus/sudden death; smaller emboli cause infarction
- *Morphology:* Saddle embolus at bifurcation; peripheral wedge-shaped haemorrhagic infarcts; recurrent small emboli cause pulmonary hypertension; shower embolism
54. Discuss the morphologic events/stages in development of atherosclerosis (10 marks)
- Fatty streak — lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) in intima
- Intermediate lesion — foam cells, extracellular lipid, smooth muscle cells
- Atheroma — lipid core with fibrous cap
- Complicated lesion — rupture, calcification, ulceration, haemorrhage, thrombosis
- Complications: thrombosis, embolization, aneurysm, critical stenosis/ischaemia
55. Discuss Cervical Carcinoma Under the following subheadings: Risk Factors, Pathogenesis, Morphology, Grading and Staging (20 Marks)
- *Risk Factors:* Age (45+), HPV (16, 18), multiple sexual partners, smoking, immunosuppression
- *Pathogenesis:* HPV infects transformation zone; genome integrates; E6/E7 inactivate p53/Rb; progressive dysplasia (CIN I-III); progression to invasive carcinoma
- *Morphology:* Exophytic/ulcerating/infiltrative growth; squamous cell carcinoma (most common) — malignant squamous nests; adenocarcinoma — malignant glandular proliferation
- *Grading and Staging:* Grading assesses differentiation; Staging uses FIGO/TNM; Bethesda system distinguishes LSIL vs HSIL
---
# 📅 WEDNESDAY: Immunopathology
## MCQs
**1. Tumors evade the immune system through the following mechanisms EXCEPT:** *(options a and b not visible in scan)*
c. Localization in immune privileged sites
d. Stimulating T regulatory cells to produce immunosuppressive cytokines
e. None of the above
**Answer: not marked**
2. In tumorigenesis, a good prognosis indication is if the tumor agent is:
a. Embryonic antigen AFP
b. Oncogenic
c. Necrotize
d. Tumor Specific Antigen
e. Transplantation specific Tumor Antigens
**Answer: not marked**
## Short Answer Questions
1. Outline the pathogenesis of a Type IV HSR (15 Marks)
- Sensitization phase: antigen presented by APCs (e.g., Langerhans cells) to naïve CD4+ T cells, generating memory Th1 cells (takes 1-2 weeks on first exposure)
- Re-exposure activates sensitized memory T cells within 24-72 hours
- Activated Th1 cells release cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF, IL-2) that recruit and activate macrophages
- Activated macrophages release proteolytic enzymes and reactive oxygen species causing tissue damage
- May progress to granuloma formation if antigen persists (e.g., TB, sarcoidosis)
- Cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) may also directly kill antigen-bearing cells
2. List secondary causes of immunodeficiency and explain how they cause the same. (10 Marks)
- Malnutrition — protein-calorie deficiency impairs lymphocyte proliferation and antibody production
- HIV/AIDS — destroys CD4+ T helper cells, crippling cell-mediated and humoral immunity
- Malignancy (e.g., leukaemia, lymphoma) — replaces/suppresses normal marrow/lymphoid tissue
- Immunosuppressive drugs/chemotherapy — suppress lymphocyte proliferation
- Chronic diseases (diabetes, renal failure) — impair leukocyte function
- Splenectomy — loss of splenic macrophage filtering, increased risk of encapsulated organism infections
3. Define what is made by: Autograft, Allograft, Xenograft, Syngeneic graft (10 Marks)
- Autograft — tissue transplanted from one site to another within the same individual
- Allograft — tissue transplanted between genetically different individuals of the same species
- Xenograft — tissue transplanted between individuals of different species
- Syngeneic graft (isograft) — tissue transplanted between genetically identical individuals (e.g., identical twins)
4. Briefly describe how immune cells attack tumor cells (15 Marks)
- Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8+) — recognize tumour antigens via MHC I, induce apoptosis via perforin/granzyme
- Natural killer (NK) cells — kill tumour cells lacking MHC I (missing-self recognition), no prior sensitization needed
- Macrophages — phagocytose tumour cells, present antigens, release cytotoxic mediators (e.g., TNF)
- Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADC
C) — antibodies bind tumour antigens, recruit NK cells/macrophages via Fc receptors
- Cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF) — enhance antigen presentation, inhibit tumour proliferation/induce apoptosis
5. How is peripheral tolerance maintained? (10 Marks)
- Anergy — T cells recognizing self-antigen without co-stimulation become unresponsive
- Regulatory T cells (Tregs) — suppress autoreactive T cells via IL-10, TGF-β
- Activation-induced cell death — repeated stimulation of self-reactive lymphocytes triggers apoptosis
- Immune privilege — certain sites (eye, testis, brain) limit immune cell access
- Antigen sequestration — self-antigens hidden behind physical barriers
## Essay
**A young lady presented in difficulty in breathing, anxiety, and wheezing. She was diagnosed with acute asthmatic attack. Describe the pathogenesis of her condition and her management. (30 Marks)**
*Pathogenesis:*
- Allergen exposure triggers IgE-mediated Type I hypersensitivity in sensitized individuals
- Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells causes degranulation, releasing histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins
- Early phase (minutes): bronchoconstriction, mucosal oedema, increased mucus secretion causing acute airflow obstruction
- Late phase (4-8 hours later): eosinophil, Th2 lymphocyte, and neutrophil infiltration sustains airway inflammation
- Chronic inflammation leads to airway hyperresponsiveness, bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy, airway remodelling
- Clinical presentation reflects airway obstruction: wheezing, dyspnoea, chest tightness, anxiety due to hypoxia
*Management:*
- Immediate: high-flow oxygen, nebulized short-acting beta-2 agonist (e.g., salbutamol), nebulized ipratropium bromide
- Systemic corticosteroids (oral/IV) — reduce airway inflammation
- IV magnesium sulphate — for severe/life-threatening attacks
- Monitor peak expiratory flow, oxygen saturation, arterial blood gases
- Escalate to ICU/intubation if exhaustion, silent chest, or worsening hypoxia/hypercapnia
- Long-term: inhaled corticosteroids, beta-2 agonists, trigger avoidance education, inhaler technique
---

articles.title: Chemical Pathology Exam Paper: Acid-Base, Electrolytes, Diabetes & Renal — Notes
articles.content:
**Chemical Pathology** paper (BPA2103 – Human Pathology III, Tue 7th Dec 2021):
## SECTION A: MCQs
1. Which would be consistent with respiratory alkalosis?
a. pH increased; PCO2 normal; Bicarbonate increased
b. pH increased; PCO2 decreased; Bicarbonate normal
c. pH decreased; PCO2 normal; Bicarbonate decreased
d. pH decreased; PCO2 increased; Bicarbonate normal
**Answer: b**
2. Which of the following laboratory results is consistent with primary hypoparathyroidism?
a. Low calcium; high inorganic phosphorus (Pi)
b. Low calcium; low Pi
c. High calcium; high Pi
d. High calcium; low Pi
**Answer: a**
3. Which of the following conditions is associated with hypokalemia?
a. Addison's disease
b. Hemolytic anemia
c. Digoxin intoxication
d. Alkalosis
**Answer: d**
4. Which of the following results falls within the diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus?
a. Fasting plasma glucose of 6.7 mmol/L
b. Two-hour postprandial plasma glucose of 8.9 mmol/L
c. Two-hour plasma glucose of 10 mmol/L following a 75g oral glucose challenge
d. Random plasma glucose of 13.9 mmol/L and presence of symptoms
**Answer: d**
5. The modification of diet in renal disease (MDR
D) formula for calculating eGFR requires which four parameters?
a. Urine creatinine, serum creatinine, height, weight
b. Serum creatinine, age, gender, race
c. Serum creatinine, height, weight, age
d. Urine creatinine, gender, weight, age
**Answer: b** (not clearly marked in script; b is the standard correct MDRD parameter set)
6. The following conditions cause metabolic alkalosis:
a. Excessive antacid ingestion
b. Diabetes complications
c. Renal failure
d. Cardiac disease
**Answer: a**
7. The following are causes of metabolic acidosis EXCEPT:
a. Renal failure
b. Cardiac failure
c. Renal tubular acidosis type IV
d. Excessive vomiting
**Answer: b** (marked in script; note vomiting causes alkalosis not acidosis, so also arguably an exception)
8. The following are causes of respiratory alkalosis EXCEPT:
a. Salicylate poisoning
b. Hysterical over breathing
c. Chronic lung disease
d. Protracted vomiting
**Answer: d**
9. Fluoride is the anticoagulant used in testing blood for:
a. Blood sugar
b. Coagulation
c. Electrolyte
d. CBC
**Answer: a**
10. Regarding the regulation of water excretion, all the following statements are true EXCEPT:
a. In the presence of ADH, the collecting duct becomes permeable to water
b. In the absence of ADH, the distal nephron is almost impermeable to water
c. ADH binds to V2 receptors in the distal nephron to enhance the passive movement of water
d. In the thick ascending limb of loop of Henle, sodium and chloride are preferably absorbed without water and hence called the Diluting segment
**Answer: not marked in script**
---
## SECTION B: Short Answer Questions
1. A 5 month old bottle-fed infant with severe diarrhoea has the following serum biochemistry:
Sodium 153 mmol/l (135-145), Potassium 2.2 mmol/l (3.3-5.2), Chloride 116 mmol/l (99-113), Bicarbonate 13 mmol/l (19-29), Urea 7.8 mmol/l (<5.5), Creatinine 40 µmol/l (<45)
a. State the likely fluid status of this child? (2 marks)
- Hypertonic (hypernatremic) dehydration
b. State the laboratory values that confirm this state? (3 marks)
- Elevated serum sodium (153 mmol/l) — indicates water loss exceeding sodium loss
- Raised urea (7.8 mmol/l) — reflects pre-renal component from volume depletion
- Hypokalemia and low bicarbonate together with raised chloride — reflect diarrhoeal fluid/electrolyte loss and metabolic acidosis contributing to the dehydrated state
2. A 65 year old presented with visible jaundice, deepening in colour, weight loss, pale stools. Total bilirubin 250 µmol/l (<17), ALT 92 U/l (1-41), AST 87 U/l (1-38), ALP 850 U/l (39-117).
a. State 2 differential diagnoses (2 marks)
- Carcinoma of the head of pancreas (obstructive/malignant biliary obstruction)
- Cholangiocarcinoma / gallstone causing common bile duct obstruction
b. State 3 other investigations that would be helpful and expected result (3 marks)
- Abdominal ultrasound/CT scan — dilated bile ducts, mass lesion, or stone
- Serum GGT — markedly elevated (confirms cholestatic/obstructive pattern)
- Tumour markers (CA 19-9) — elevated in pancreatic/biliary malignancy
- ERCP/MRCP — may show site and cause of obstruction
3. State 3 endocrine diseases which can lead to secondary diabetes and explain the mechanism in each case.
- **Cushing's syndrome** — excess cortisol promotes gluconeogenesis and antagonizes insulin action, causing insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia
- **Acromegaly** — excess growth hormone induces insulin resistance in peripheral tissues, reducing glucose uptake
- **Phaeochromocytoma** — excess catecholamines inhibit insulin secretion and stimulate glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis, raising blood glucose
4. List with examples 5 factors that may cause intra-individual variation of laboratory values (5 marks)
- Diurnal/circadian variation (e.g., cortisol higher in morning, lower at night)
- Posture (e.g., protein and calcium levels higher standing vs supine)
- Exercise (e.g., raised creatine kinase after strenuous exercise)
- Diet/fasting status (e.g., glucose and triglycerides affected by recent meals)
- Stress (e.g., raised cortisol and glucose during acute stress)
- Menstrual cycle/pregnancy (e.g., hormone level fluctuations)
5. Briefly describe the laboratory tests important in the investigation of a 40 year old female with hypercalcemia (5 marks)
- Serum total and ionized calcium — confirms hypercalcemia
- Serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) — elevated in primary hyperparathyroidism, suppressed in malignancy-associated hypercalcemia
- Serum phosphate — low in hyperparathyroidism, variable in malignancy
- Serum ALP — elevated with bone involvement
- 24-hour urinary calcium — assesses renal calcium handling/differentiates familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia
- PTHrP, vitamin D levels, and imaging (chest X-ray/CT) — to screen for malignancy or granulomatous disease as underlying cause
6. State the tests that comprise the 'liver function tests' briefly explaining what each test indicates
- **ALT/AST** — hepatocellular injury/damage (ALT more liver-specific)
- **ALP** — cholestasis/biliary obstruction, also bone disease
- **GGT** — confirms hepatobiliary origin of raised ALP; sensitive to alcohol use
- **Bilirubin (total/conjugated)** — assesses jaundice and differentiates pre-hepatic, hepatic, post-hepatic causes
- **Serum albumin** — reflects synthetic liver function (chronic disease)
- **Prothrombin time (PT/INR)** — reflects synthetic function of clotting factors, sensitive marker of acute liver failure
---
## SECTION C: Essay
1. Describe the laboratory investigations and expected laboratory abnormalities in acute and chronic renal failure. (30 marks)
**
A. Acute Renal Failure (Acute Kidney Injury)**
*Renal function tests:*
- Serum creatinine — rapidly rising (within days)
- Serum urea — elevated, often disproportionately high with dehydration/catabolism (pre-renal)
- eGFR — acutely reduced
*Electrolytes:*
- Hyperkalemia — due to reduced renal excretion
- Hyponatremia or hypernatremia — depending on fluid status
- Hyperphosphatemia
- Hypocalcemia (reduced 1,25-vitamin D activation, phosphate retention)
*Acid-base:*
- Metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap — from accumulation of acid metabolites
*Urinalysis:*
- Pre-renal: concentrated urine, low urinary sodium (<20 mmol/l), high urine osmolality
- Intrinsic (ATN): muddy brown granular casts, urinary sodium >40 mmol/l, isosthenuria
- Post-renal: haematuria, evidence of obstruction on imaging
*Other:*
- Full blood count — may show anaemia if chronic component; normal in pure acute
- Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) — differentiates pre-renal vs intrinsic causes
**
B. Chronic Renal Failure (Chronic Kidney Disease)**
*Renal function:*
- Persistently elevated serum creatinine and urea (over >3 months)
- Progressively declining eGFR — used for staging (CKD stages 1–5)
*Electrolytes and acid-base:*
- Hyperkalemia (advanced stages)
- Metabolic acidosis (chronic, due to reduced acid excretion and bicarbonate regeneration)
- Hyperphosphatemia
- Hypocalcemia — due to reduced renal activation of vitamin D and phosphate retention
- Secondary hyperparathyroidism — elevated PTH in response to hypocalcaemia/hyperphosphataemia
*Haematological:*
- Normocytic normochromic anaemia — due to reduced erythropoietin production
*Bone profile:*
- Elevated ALP — renal osteodystrophy
- Low vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin
D)
*Urinalysis and imaging:*
- Proteinuria (often significant, e.g., in diabetic/glomerular disease)
- Reduced kidney size on ultrasound (except in some infiltrative/diabetic disease where kidneys may be enlarged)
- Broad, waxy casts on microscopy (long-standing damage)
*Other markers:*
- Lipid abnormalities — hypertriglyceridemia common
- Hypoalbuminemia — if nephrotic-range proteinuria present

articles.title: Pharmacology Cheat Code — Notes
articles.content:
Question 1
What impacts drug response by changing number of receptors?
a) Down regulation
b) Receptor affinity
c) Signal transduction
d) Cell membrane fluidity
**Answer:** a) Down regulation
**Explanation:** Chronic agonist exposure reduces receptor numbers (downregulation), lowering the cell's response over time.
---
Question 2
What type of medication is griseofulvin?
a) Antiretroviral
b) Antibacterial
c) Antifungal
d) Antiviral
**Answer:** c) Antifungal
**Explanation:** It disrupts fungal microtubule function, blocking mitosis; used for dermatophyte (ringworm) infections.
---
Question 3
What term refers to the amount of drug at the site of action?
a) Bioavailability
b) Half-life
c) Absorption
d) Biopharmaceutics
**Answer:** a) Bioavailability
**Explanation:** It's the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged and available to act.
---
Question 4
Rimantadine is used to treat or prevent:
a) Influenza A
b) Influenza B
c) Measles
d) Mumps
**Answer:** a) Influenza A
**Explanation:** It blocks the M2 ion channel, which only Influenza A possesses — Influenza B lacks this channel.
---
Question 5
Diphenhydramine is classified as which type of drug?
a) Antibiotic
b) ACE inhibitor
c) Antihistamine
d) Antifungal
**Answer:** c) Antihistamine
**Explanation:** A first-generation H1 receptor blocker; sedating, used for allergies and as a sleep aid.
---
Question 6
Dactinomycin is identified as which type of medication?
a) Antifungal agent
b) Alkylating agent
c) Antimetabolite
d) Antitumor antibiotic
**Answer:** d) Antitumor antibiotic
**Explanation:** It intercalates DNA and inhibits RNA polymerase; used in Wilms tumor and rhabdomyosarcoma.
---
Question 7
What impacts oral absorption but not injectable bioavailability?
a) Ionization
b) First-pass metabolism
c) P-glycoprotein transporters
d) Lipophilicity
**Answer:** b) First-pass metabolism
**Explanation:** Oral drugs pass through the gut wall and liver before reaching systemic circulation; injected drugs bypass this step.
---
Question 8
Fluconazole is used to treat which type of infections?
a) Viral
b) Protozoal
c) Fungal
d) Bacterial
**Answer:** c) Fungal
**Explanation:** A triazole antifungal that inhibits 14-α-demethylase, blocking ergosterol synthesis in fungal cell membranes.
---
Question 9
Enzymatic metabolism that introduces reactive groups is called:
a) First-pass effect
b) Phase I metabolism
c) Dealkylation
d) Glucuronidation
**Answer:** b) Phase I metabolism
**Explanation:** Phase I reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis via CYP450) add or expose reactive groups, preparing the drug for Phase II conjugation.
---
Question 10
Which medication is an antifungal in the polyene class?
a) Fluconazole
b) Amphotericin B
c) Itraconazole
d) Terbinafine
**Answer:** b) Amphotericin B
**Explanation:** Polyenes bind ergosterol in fungal membranes, forming pores that cause cell death; Amphotericin B is used for severe systemic mycoses.
---
Question 11
What statement best describes pharmacodynamics?
a) Drug transit in the body
b) Biologic response to a drug
c) Liver enzyme metabolism
d) Route of administration
**Answer:** b) Biologic response to a drug
**Explanation:** Pharmacodynamics (P
D) is "what the drug does to the body" — the mechanism and effect of a drug on its target.
---
Question 12
Mercaptopurine is used to treat:
a) Autoimmune disorders
b) Cancer
c) Tuberculosis
d) Bacterial infections
**Answer:** b) Cancer
**Explanation:** A purine antimetabolite that interferes with DNA/RNA synthesis; used mainly in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).
---
Question 13
Which receptor type uses cAMP as a second messenger?
a) GABA
b) Nicotinic
c) Glycine
d) Adrenergic
**Answer:** d) Adrenergic
**Explanation:** Adrenergic receptors are G-protein coupled; beta-adrenergic activation raises cAMP via adenylyl cyclase.
---
Question 14
Ganciclovir is used to treat infections caused by:
a) Human immunodeficiency virus
b) Hepatitis C virus
c) Cytomegalovirus
d) Hepatitis B virus
**Answer:** c) Cytomegalovirus
**Explanation:** A guanosine analog that inhibits viral DNA polymerase; the drug of choice for CMV, especially in immunocompromised patients.
---
Question 15
What is the study of time course of drug absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion?
a) Pharmacodynamics
b) Pharmacokinetics
c) Pharmacotherapeutics
d) Pharmacogenetics
**Answer:** b) Pharmacokinetics
**Explanation:** Pharmacokinetics (PK) is "what the body does to the drug" — ADM
E.
---
Question 16
Vincristine is classified as a (an):
a) Monoclonal antibody
b) Alkylating agent
c) Vinca alkaloid
d) Taxane
**Answer:** c) Vinca alkaloid
**Explanation:** Binds tubulin, inhibiting microtubule formation and arresting mitosis; notable for causing peripheral neuropathy.
---
Question 17
What antidiarrheal medication is an opioid agonist used to slow bowel movements?
a) Sucralfate
b) Polyethylene glycol
c) Magnesium hydroxide
d) Diphenoxylate
**Answer:** d) Diphenoxylate
**Explanation:** An opioid agonist acting on gut mu-receptors to slow peristalsis; combined with atropine (as in Lomotil) to deter abuse.
---
Question 18
Which process increases dissolution rate to aid oral absorption?
a) Ionization
b) First-pass metabolism
c) Micronization
d) Conjugation
**Answer:** c) Micronization
**Explanation:** Reducing particle size increases surface area, speeding drug dissolution and improving absorption.
---
Question 19
Methotrexate is which type of agent?
a) Antimetabolite
b) Alkylating agent
c) Antibiotic
d) Corticosteroid
**Answer:** a) Antimetabolite
**Explanation:** A folic acid antagonist that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking DNA synthesis; used in cancer and autoimmune disease.
---
Question 20
Miconazole is commonly administered via which route for fungal infections?
a) Oral
b) Intravenous
c) Topical
d) Intramuscular
**Answer:** c) Topical
**Explanation:** Primarily used topically for skin and mucosal fungal infections (e.g., candidiasis, athlete's foot).
---
Question 21
What term refers to duration of drug action?
a) Half-life
b) Onset of action
c) Bioavailability
d) Clearance
**Answer:** a) Half-life
**Explanation:** Half-life reflects how long a drug's effective concentration persists, determining dosing frequency and duration of action.
---
Question 22
Thioguanine is used in combination with other agents to treat:
a) Systemic mycoses
b) Hypertension
c) Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
d) Hypothyroidism
**Answer:** c) Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
**Explanation:** A purine antimetabolite that disrupts DNA synthesis; used in combination chemotherapy regimens for leukemia.
---
Question 23
Fluorouracil is classified as which type of antineoplastic?
a) Antitumor antibiotic
b) Plant alkaloid
c) Antimetabolite
d) Topoisomerase inhibitor
**Answer:** c) Antimetabolite
**Explanation:** A pyrimidine analog that inhibits thymidylate synthase, blocking DNA synthesis.
---
Question 24
Which factor does not impact oral drug bioavailability?
a) Drug solubility
b) Gastric residence time
c) Drug polarity
d) Volume of distribution
**Answer:** d) Volume of distribution
**Explanation:** Volume of distribution describes how a drug distributes into body tissues after absorption — it's a distribution parameter, not an absorption/bioavailability factor.
---
Question 25
First-pass metabolism occurs primarily in which organ?
a) Kidney
b) Gut
c) Liver
d) Lungs
**Answer:** c) Liver
**Explanation:** Orally absorbed drugs travel via the portal vein straight to the liver, where extensive metabolism can occur before reaching systemic circulation.
---
Question 26
What type of drug interaction results in reduced efficacy of a drug?
a) Synergistic
b) Additive
c) Antagonistic
d) Idiosyncratic
**Answer:** c) Antagonistic
**Explanation:** An antagonistic interaction means one drug reduces or blocks the effect of another, lowering overall efficacy.
---
Question 27
Acyclovir is specifically used to treat infections caused by:
a) Bacteria
b) Fungi
c) Viruses
d) Protozoa
**Answer:** c) Viruses
**Explanation:** A guanosine analog activated by viral thymidine kinase; inhibits viral DNA polymerase — effective mainly against herpesviruses (HSV, VZV).
---
Question 28
Sulfonamides act by inhibiting:
a) Cell wall synthesis
b) Protein synthesis
c) Folic acid synthesis
d) DNA replication
**Answer:** c) Folic acid synthesis
**Explanation:** They inhibit dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folate synthesis needed for bacterial nucleic acid production.
---
Question 29
Didanosine (ddI) is used together with other medications to treat:
a) HIV
b) Influenza
c) Herpes virus
d) Hepatitis B virus
**Answer:** a) HIV
**Explanation:** A nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) used in combination antiretroviral therapy.
---
Question 30
Nystatin is commonly used to treat:
a) Systemic mycoses
b) Cutaneous candidiasis
c) Aspergillosis
d) Cryptococcal meningitis
**Answer:** b) Cutaneous candidiasis
**Explanation:** A polyene antifungal too toxic for systemic use; applied topically/orally for local Candida infections (oral thrush, skin, GI tract).
---

Understood — let me go much deeper, especially for Section C since 20 marks needs comprehensive coverage (diagnosis, drug choice with doses, mechanism, monitoring, complications, prevention). Here's the expanded version.
---
## Section B: Short Answer Questions (4 marks each)
Question 1
Define pharmacokinetics (PK) and pharmacodynamics (PD), highlighting their respective roles in drug therapy. Discuss the interplay between PK and PD in determining drug efficacy and safety.
**Answer:**
- **Pharmacokinetics (PK)** — "what the body does to the drug"
  - **A**bsorption — how drug enters systemic circulation (route, bioavailability)
  - **D**istribution — movement into tissues (protein binding, volume of distribution)
  - **M**etabolism — biotransformation, mainly hepatic (Phase I/II)
  - **E**xcretion — removal, mainly renal (clearance, half-life)
- **Pharmacodynamics (PD)** — "what the drug does to the body"
  - Receptor binding, mechanism of action
  - Dose-response relationship (potency, efficacy)
  - Therapeutic and adverse effects
- **Role in drug therapy:**
  - PK determines the **concentration** of drug reaching the target site and how long it stays there
  - PD determines the **magnitude of effect** produced at that concentration
- **Interplay:**
  - A drug with good PD (strong receptor affinity) but poor PK (poor absorption, rapid clearance) will fail clinically
  - Conversely, excellent PK with weak PD produces a safe but ineffective drug
  - Together they define **therapeutic index** — the margin between effective and toxic doses
  - Individual variability in PK (renal/hepatic impairment, age, genetics — e.g., CYP450 polymorphisms) directly changes PD outcomes, explaining why dosing must be individualized
  - This interplay underlies concepts like **loading dose, maintenance dose, and therapeutic drug monitoring**
---
Question 2
Briefly evaluate the role of healthcare information technology in supporting rational prescribing. Discuss how electronic prescribing systems and decision support tools can enhance medication safety and adherence.
**Answer:**
- **Rational prescribing** means the right drug, right dose, right route, right patient, right time — HIT supports every one of these
- **Electronic Prescribing (e-Prescribing):**
  - Eliminates illegible handwriting and transcription errors
  - Directly transmits prescriptions to pharmacy, reducing miscommunication
- **Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS):**
  - Real-time alerts for **drug-drug interactions**
  - Allergy cross-checking
  - Renal/hepatic dose adjustment prompts
  - Duplicate therapy warnings
- **Automated dosing calculators:** reduce pediatric/geriatric dosing errors
- **Integrated Electronic Health Records (EHR):**
  - Full visibility of past medications, labs, and diagnoses across providers
  - Prevents polypharmacy conflicts
- **Barcode Medication Administration (BCMA):** verifies right patient/right drug at bedside
- **Adherence support:**
  - Automated refill reminders
  - SMS/app-based dosing reminders
  - Pharmacy synchronization programs
- **Limitations to note (for balance):** alert fatigue (clinicians ignoring frequent pop-ups), system downtime, cost of implementation, need for staff training
- **Overall impact:** reduces medication errors, adverse drug events, hospital readmissions, and improves long-term adherence and outcomes
---
Question 3
Briefly describe the role of diphenhydramine in managing allergic reactions, and discuss alternative treatment options available for allergic conditions.
**Answer:**
- **Diphenhydramine** — first-generation H1-receptor antagonist
- **Mechanism:** competitively blocks histamine at H1 receptors, preventing histamine-mediated vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, itching, and bronchoconstriction
- **Clinical uses:**
  - Allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus
  - Adjunct in anaphylaxis management (after epinephrine, never as monotherapy)
  - Mild allergic transfusion reactions
  - Also used off-label as a sedative/sleep aid due to CNS penetration
- **Limitations:** sedation, anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision), short duration requiring frequent dosing
- **Alternative treatment options:**
  - **Second-generation antihistamines** (loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine) — less sedating, longer acting, preferred for chronic allergic conditions
  - **Intranasal corticosteroids** (fluticasone) — first-line for allergic rhinitis
  - **Systemic corticosteroids** (prednisone) — for severe or persistent allergic reactions
  - **Epinephrine** — first-line, life-saving in anaphylaxis
  - **Leukotriene receptor antagonists** (montelukast) — useful in allergic rhinitis with asthma overlap
  - **Mast cell stabilizers** (cromolyn sodium) — prophylactic, prevents mediator release
  - **Immunotherapy (allergy shots)** — long-term desensitization for chronic allergic disease
---
Question 4
Define drug potency and drug efficacy. Explain the differences between these two concepts and how they are measured in pharmacology. Provide examples of drugs that are highly potent, highly efficacious, and those that exhibit both characteristics.
**Answer:**
- **Potency:**
  - The dose of a drug required to produce a given effect
  - Inversely related to **EC50** (concentration producing 50% of maximal effect) — lower EC50 = higher potency
  - Reflected on the **x-axis** of the dose-response curve (shifted left = more potent)
- **Efficacy:**
  - The **maximum effect (Emax)** a drug can produce, regardless of dose
  - Reflected on the **y-axis** (plateau/ceiling of the curve)
- **Key differences:**
  - Potency = "how little drug is needed"; Efficacy = "how much effect the drug can achieve at its best"
  - A drug can be very potent but have limited efficacy (partial agonist)
  - Clinically, efficacy is usually more clinically relevant than potency
- **Examples:**
  - **High potency, lower efficacy:** Buprenorphine — very potent opioid partial agonist, but has a **ceiling effect**, capping maximal analgesia
  - **High efficacy, lower potency:** Morphine — full agonist with high maximal analgesic effect, but requires relatively higher doses than fentanyl
  - **Both high potency and high efficacy:** Fentanyl — tiny doses (micrograms) achieve maximal analgesic effect, full agonist activity
- **Clinical relevance:** Choosing between drugs isn't just about potency — a highly potent but low-efficacy drug (e.g., a partial agonist) may be less useful in severe pain than a full agonist requiring higher doses
---
Question 5
Define drug potency and drug efficacy. Explain the differences between these two concepts and how they are measured in pharmacology.
**Answer:**
- **Potency:**
  - Amount of drug (dose) needed to produce a specific effect
  - Measured using **EC50** on a dose-response curve
  - Lower EC50 = more potent drug (less dose needed for same effect)
- **Efficacy:**
  - Maximum possible effect a drug can produce at its highest dose
  - Measured using **Emax**
  - Represents the plateau of the dose-response curve
- **Differences summarized:**
  - Potency compares **doses** needed between drugs for the same effect
  - Efficacy compares **maximum achievable effect**, independent of dose
  - Two drugs can have identical efficacy (same Emax) but very different potency (different doses to reach that Emax)
  - Conversely, two equally potent drugs (same EC50) can have very different maximal efficacy
- **Measurement tools:** dose-response curves plotting % response (y-axis) against log dose (x-axis); comparing curve position (potency) versus curve height (efficacy)
- **Clinical significance:** efficacy generally guides drug choice for treating severe conditions; potency mainly affects dosing convenience, not necessarily therapeutic superiority
---

## Section C: Patient Case Scenarios (choose ONE — 20 marks)
---
### Patient Case Scenario 1: Visceral Leishmaniasis
*Patient Profile:* 35-year-old male, prolonged fever, weight loss, splenomegaly, pancytopenia, positive rK39 antigen test.
*Exam Question:* Discuss the initial steps in management, choice of antileishmanial drugs and duration, challenges in managing VL, and strategies to address them.
**Answer:**
**
A. Initial Assessment/Steps**
- Confirm diagnosis: rK39 rapid diagnostic test (already positive here), supported by splenic/bone marrow aspirate microscopy showing amastigotes if confirmation needed
- Baseline investigations: full blood count (assess degree of pancytopenia), renal function tests, liver function tests, ECG (baseline QT interval before antimonials)
- HIV testing — mandatory in all VL patients (HIV-VL co-infection is common and changes prognosis/management)
- Nutritional assessment and correction of anemia if severe (transfusion if Hb critically low)
**
B. Drug Treatment — First-line (East Africa protocol)**
- **Sodium Stibogluconate (SSG) + Paromomycin combination therapy**
  - Duration: **17 days**
  - SSG: pentavalent antimonial, mechanism — inhibits parasite glycolysis and fatty acid oxidation
  - Paromomycin: aminoglycoside, inhibits protein synthesis in the parasite
  - Combination shortens treatment duration and reduces resistance development compared to monotherapy
**
C. Alternative Agents**
- **Liposomal Amphotericin B**
  - Preferred in: HIV co-infection, pregnancy, relapse cases, antimonial-resistant regions, cardiac disease patients
  - Mechanism: binds ergosterol in parasite membrane, forms pores, causes cell lysis
  - Given as short course or single high-dose regimen depending on protocol
- **Miltefosine**
  - Oral option — useful where parenteral therapy is impractical
  - Contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic)
**
D. Monitoring During Treatment**
- ECG monitoring for QT prolongation (SSG cardiotoxicity)
- Renal function monitoring (Amphotericin B nephrotoxicity)
- Serial FBC for bone marrow recovery
- Watch for pancreatitis (SSG-associated)
**
E. Challenges in Managing VL**
- Prolonged parenteral therapy requiring hospitalization
- Drug toxicity (cardiotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, pancreatitis)
- Emerging antimonial resistance in some regions
- Poor treatment adherence (painful daily injections)
- HIV-VL co-infection — higher relapse rates, poorer response
- Limited access/high cost of safer alternatives (Liposomal Amphotericin B, Miltefosine) in resource-limited settings
- Relapse and post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) as a reservoir for continued transmission
**F. Strategies to Address Challenges**
- Combination therapy to shorten duration and limit resistance
- Vector control — sandfly control programs (insecticide spraying, bed nets)
- Improve access to liposomal Amphotericin B through subsidized/donated drug programs (e.g., WHO-negotiated pricing)
- Universal HIV screening and integrated HIV-VL care
- Active case finding and surveillance in endemic areas
- Community health education on early symptom recognition
---
### Patient Case Scenario 2: Viral Conjunctivitis
*Patient Profile:* 30-year-old female, bilateral redness, tearing, gritty sensation, recent URTI, contact exposure, bilateral conjunctival injection without purulent discharge.
*Exam Question:* Discuss the role of antiviral therapy given the likely viral etiology; if considered, specify drug of choice, mechanism, and limitations.
**Answer:**
**
A. Clinical Diagnosis**
- Presentation strongly suggests **adenoviral conjunctivitis**:
  - Bilateral involvement
  - Watery (non-purulent) discharge
  - Recent URTI and household contact exposure
  - Gritty/foreign body sensation typical of follicular conjunctivitis
- Differentiate from bacterial conjunctivitis (purulent discharge, often unilateral initially) and allergic conjunctivitis (itching predominant, bilateral, seasonal history)
**
B. Role of Antiviral Therapy**
- For **adenoviral conjunctivitis** specifically: **no specific effective antiviral agent exists**; management is largely supportive
- Antivirals become relevant **only if HSV keratoconjunctivitis is suspected instead** — distinguishing features would be:
  - Usually **unilateral**
  - Dendritic corneal ulcers on fluorescein staining
  - Vesicular skin lesions around the eye
  - History of recurrent cold sores
**
C. If HSV Suspected — Drug of Choice**
- **Topical Acyclovir (3% ointment)** or **Trifluridine 1% drops**
- **Mechanism of action (Acyclovir):**
  - Guanosine analog
  - Phosphorylated by **viral thymidine kinase** (selective for infected cells)
  - Converted to acyclovir triphosphate, which inhibits **viral DNA polymerase** and causes chain termination
  - High selectivity for virus-infected cells minimizes toxicity to normal cells
- **Oral Acyclovir** may be added for HSV keratoconjunctivitis to reduce recurrence
**
D. Limitations of Antiviral Therapy**
- Completely ineffective against adenovirus (the actual likely cause here)
- Requires early initiation for maximum benefit in HSV cases
- Topical formulations can cause local irritation, punctate keratopathy
- Resistance can develop with prolonged/repeated use
- Does not shorten adenoviral conjunctivitis course, which is self-limiting regardless
**
E. Actual Management for This Patient (Adenoviral Conjunctivitis)**
- **Supportive care only:**
  - Cold compresses for comfort
  - Artificial tears/lubricants
  - Analgesics if needed
- **Avoid topical corticosteroids** unless prescribed by ophthalmologist — may prolong viral shedding and worsen course
- **Antibiotics not indicated** (no bacterial component)
- **Infection control counseling:**
  - Highly contagious — avoid touching eyes, frequent handwashing
  - Avoid sharing towels/pillows
  - Avoid work/school attendance during acute phase to prevent spread
- Course typically self-resolves within 1–3 weeks
---
### Patient Case Scenario 3: Uncomplicated Lower UTI (Cystitis)
*Patient Profile:* 28-year-old female, dysuria, frequency, urgency; urinalysis positive for leukocytes and nitrites.
*Exam Question:* Outline management approach, choice of antimicrobials, duration, factors influencing selection, potential complications, and prevention strategies for recurrent UTIs.
**Answer:**
**
A. Diagnosis Confirmation**
- Classic triad: dysuria, frequency, urgency
- Positive nitrites → suggests gram-negative organism (nitrate-reducing, e.g., *
E. coli* — most common cause, ~80–90% of cases)
- Positive leukocytes → confirms pyuria/inflammatory response
- Urine culture not always necessary for uncomplicated cystitis in young, otherwise healthy women, but useful if diagnosis unclear or recurrent
**
B. First-Line Antimicrobial Agents**
- **Nitrofurantoin** — 5-day course; good choice as first-line, low resistance rates, concentrates in urine
- **Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)** — 3-day course; effective if local resistance <20%
- **Fosfomycin** — single-dose sachet; convenient option, especially for adherence concerns
- **Second-line/Alternatives:** Beta-lactams (amoxicillin-clavulanate) or fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) — reserved due to higher resistance/side-effect profile, fluoroquinolones generally avoided as first-line now due to safety concerns
**
C. Factors Influencing Drug Selection**
- Local antimicrobial resistance patterns (critical in choosing between nitrofurantoin vs TMP-SMX)
- Pregnancy status:
  - Avoid TMP-SMX in first trimester (folate antagonism, neural tube defects) and near term (kernicterus risk)
  - Avoid nitrofurantoin near term (hemolytic anemia risk in newborn, G6PD deficiency)
- Renal function — avoid nitrofurantoin if eGFR <30 (inadequate urinary concentration, reduced efficacy, toxicity risk)
- Drug allergies (sulfa allergy excludes TMP-SMX)
- Cost and availability
- Patient adherence potential (single-dose fosfomycin useful for poor adherence)
**
D. Duration of Treatment**
- Uncomplicated cystitis: short courses preferred (3–7 days depending on agent)
- Shorter courses reduce risk of resistance development and side effects while maintaining efficacy
**
E. Potential Complications**
- **Ascending infection → pyelonephritis** (fever, flank pain, systemic symptoms)
- **Urosepsis** in severe, untreated, or immunocompromised cases
- **Recurrent UTIs** (≥2 in 6 months or ≥3 in 12 months)
- **Antimicrobial resistance** from repeated or inappropriate antibiotic use
- Renal scarring with recurrent pyelonephritis (more relevant in children/structural abnormalities)
**F. Strategies to Prevent Recurrent UTIs**
- **Behavioral measures:**
  - Adequate hydration
  - Post-coital voiding
  - Avoid delayed urination
  - Proper wiping technique (front to back)
  - Avoid spermicide-based contraceptives (alters vaginal flora)
- **Prophylactic strategies (for confirmed recurrent UTI):**
  - Low-dose continuous antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g., nightly nitrofurantoin)
  - Post-coital single-dose antibiotic prophylaxis if UTIs are coitally related
  - **Cranberry products** — some evidence for reducing recurrence (inhibits bacterial adhesion to uroepithelium)
  - **Vaginal estrogen** in postmenopausal women (restores protective vaginal flora)
  - Patient education on early symptom recognition and prompt treatment-seeking

articles.title: Medical Entomology & Parasitology CAT — MCQs, Essays & Answers
articles.content:
---

> ⚠️ **Answers added by AI**: some answers in this document were generated by AI from general medical knowledge, not the original exam paper. Verify against your course material before relying on them for the exam.
Question 1
Fish are second intermediate hosts of?

A. Echinostoma ilocaanum
B. Faciola hepatica
C. Fasciolopsis buski
D. Hymenolepis nana
E. Clorchis sinesis

**Answer:
E. Clonorchis sinensis**
Explanation: Fish serve as the second intermediate host for *Clonorchis sinensis* (Chinese liver fluke); the snail is the first intermediate host.

---
Question 2
Which of the following secretes defensive secretions to cause irritation on human skin?

A. Millipedes
B. Centipedes
C. Necator americanus
D. Enterobius vermicularis
E. All of the above

**Answer:
A. Millipedes**
Explanation: Millipedes release chemical defensive secretions causing skin irritation on contact; centipedes envenomate by biting instead.

---
Question 3
Holometabolous insects have?

A. 2 life stages
B. 3 life stages
C. 4 life stages
D. 5 life stages
E. 1 life stage

**Answer:
C. 4 life stages**
Explanation: Complete metamorphosis = egg, larva, pupa, adult.

---
Question 4
Which of the following transmits parasites for river blindness?

A. Culex species
B. Chrysops species
C. Simulium species
D. Toxorhynchintinae species
E. All of the above

**Answer:
C. Simulium species**
Explanation: *Simulium* (blackfly) transmits *Onchocerca volvulus*, causing river blindness.

---
Question 5
Which insecticide targets GABA in its action?

A. DDT
B. DEET
C. Permethrin
D. Bendiocarb
E. Malathion

**Answer: No listed option is correct.**
Explanation: DDT and permethrin act primarily on voltage-gated sodium channels. Cyclodiene insecticides such as aldrin/dieldrin and phenylpyrazoles such as fipronil are the classic GABA-gated chloride-channel antagonists. This source item is flawed.

---
Question 6
Presence of triatomine bugs could predispose the population to?

A. Sleeping sickness
B. Leishmaniasis
C. Malaria
D. Chagas disease
E. River blindness

**Answer:
D. Chagas disease**
Explanation: Triatomine (kissing/reduviid) bugs transmit *Trypanosoma cruzi*.

---
Question 7
People living in forested areas like Arabuko Sokoke are at risk of?

A. Sleeping sickness
B. Leishmaniasis
C. Malaria
D. Encephalitis
E. River blindness

**Answer:
A. Sleeping sickness**
Explanation: Arabuko Sokoke forest is a known tsetse fly habitat, putting residents at risk for African trypanosomiasis.

---
Question 8
Which of the following insects are commonly found in Latin America?

A. Glossina species
B. Triatomine bugs
C. Cimex species
D. Chrysops species
E. Steam bugs

**Answer:
B. Triatomine bugs**
Explanation: Triatomine bugs are native to Central/South America; *Glossina* (tsetse fly) is exclusively African.

---
Question 9
Pruritis can be best diagnosed for?

A. Sarcoptes scabiei
B. Leptotrombidium species
C. Blattella species
D. Pediculus species
E. Pthirus species

**Answer:
A. Sarcoptes scabiei**
Explanation: Intense itching (pruritis) is diagnostic for scabies, caused by this mite.

---
Question 10
If you found lice eggs (nits) in someone's clothing, what species would they most likely be from?

A. Crab lice
B. Pediculus humanus
C. Pediculus capitis
D. Pthirus species
E. All of the above / Hog lice

**Answer:
B. Pediculus humanus**
Explanation: The body louse lays its eggs in clothing seams, unlike head or crab lice.

---
Question 11
Which of the following is odd one out in terms of transmission?

A. Vibrio cholera
B. Entamoeba histolytica
C. Rotavirus
D. Thelazia species
E. None of the above

**Answer:
D. Thelazia species**
Explanation: The other three are faecal-oral; *Thelazia* (eyeworm) is transmitted by fruit flies feeding on eye secretions.

---
Question 12
Which one of the following is larviparous?

A. Phlebotomus species
B. Lutzomyia species
C. Triatomine bugs
D. Glossina gambiense
E. Dermacentos species

**Answer: D. Glossina gambiense**
Explanation: Tsetse flies (*Glossina*) are adenotrophically viviparous: the female nourishes one larva internally and deposits a mature larva. *Lutzomyia* sandflies lay eggs and are not larviparous.

---
Question 13
Argasid ticks have?

A. One host
B. Two hosts
C. Three hosts
D. Multiple hosts
E. Four hosts

**Answer:
D. Multiple hosts**
Explanation: Soft ticks feed briefly and repeatedly across multiple hosts.

---
Question 14
Ixodid ticks have ______ nymphal stages.

A. One
B. Two
C. Three
D. Four
E. Multiple

**Answer:
A. One**
Explanation: Hard ticks have only one nymphal stage in their 3-host life cycle.

---
Question 15
Traps for Aedes mosquitoes are composed of?

A. Black and white colors
B. Black and blue colors
C. White and blue colors
D. White only
E. Black only

**Answer:
B. Black and blue colors**

---
Question 16
Traps for Glossina species are composed of?

A. Black and white colors
B. Black and blue colors
C. White and blue colors
D. White only
E. Black only

**Answer:
B. Black and blue colors**
Explanation: Same trap coloring attracts both *Aedes* and tsetse flies.

---
Question 17
Black water disease is due to presence of ______ in the environment.

A. Simulium species
B. Anopheles species
C. Culicoides species
D. Lutzomyia species
E. Musca species

**Answer: B. Anopheles species**
Explanation: Blackwater fever is a severe haemolytic complication associated with *Plasmodium falciparum* malaria; *Anopheles* is the malaria vector. *Simulium* transmits *Onchocerca volvulus* and is unrelated to blackwater fever.

---
Question 18
Hepatitis B virus has been associated with?

A. Cimex species
B. Xenopsylla species
C. Pthirus species
D. Tabanids species
E. Steam bugs

**Answer:
A. Cimex species**
Explanation: Bedbugs have been epidemiologically linked to Hepatitis B, though transmission is not confirmed as truly biological.

---
Question 19
Which of the following insects are included in the order Blattaria?

A. Cockroaches
B. Lice
C. True flies
D. Beetles
E. All of the above

**Answer:
A. Cockroaches**

---
Question 20
Which of the following insects is included in the order Diptera?

A. Cockroaches
B. Lice
C. True flies
D. Fleas
E. None of the above

**Answer:
C. True flies**
Explanation: Lice belong to Anoplura/Phthiraptera, fleas to Siphonaptera.

---
Question 21
Which of the following insects transmits cholera pathogens?

A. True flies
B. Haematogogus
C. Sabathes
D. Fannia
E. Stomoxys (housefly)

**Answer:
E. Stomoxys/houseflies**
Explanation: Houseflies mechanically transmit *Vibrio cholerae* via contaminated body parts.

---
Question 22
Arboviruses are mainly transmitted by?

A. Aedes species
B. Culex species
C. Cimex species
D. Culicoides species
E. All of the above

**Answer:
A. Aedes species**

---
Question 23
Anthropophilic insects prefer?

A. Animal hosts
B. Human hosts
C. Bird hosts
D. Amphibian hosts
E. Any of the above

**Answer:
B. Human hosts**

---
Question 24
Exophagic insects prefer?

A. Resting indoors
B. Feeding indoors
C. Resting outdoors
D. Feeding outdoors
E. C and D

**Answer:
D. Feeding outdoors**
Explanation: "Exo-" = outside; "-phagic" refers to feeding, so exophagic = feeds outdoors specifically (not resting, which is the "-philic" suffix).

---
Question 25
Presence of chrysops in the environment predisposes the community to ______ infections?

A. River blindness
B. Pink eye disease
C. Trachoma
D. Lymphedema
E. Conjunctivitis

**Answer:
B. Pink eye disease**
Explanation: *Chrysops* (deer fly) transmits *Loa loa*, associated with Calabar swellings and eye migration causing "pink eye disease"/Loiasis.

---
Question 26
Which stage of filarial nematodes will you find in the chest muscles of their vectors?

A. Larval stage 1
B. Larval stage 2
C. Larval stage 3
D. Larval stage 4
E. Microfilariae

**Answer:
C. Larval stage 3 (L3)**
Explanation: L3 is the infective stage found in the vector's thoracic muscles, ready for transmission on the next bite.

---
Question 27
Pediculosis can be best treated with?

A. Antibiotics
B. A fine tooth-comb
C. Bed nets
D. Insecticides
E. Vaseline jelly

**Answer: B and D (fine tooth-comb + insecticides)**
Explanation: Antibiotics are a wrong-answer trap — lice are arthropods, not bacteria; combing plus insecticide treatment is standard.

---
Question 28
Which of the following arthropods is most likely to be monophagous?

A. Louse
B. Flea
C. Culex
D. Tick
E. Anopheles

**Answer:
A. Louse**
Explanation: Lice feed exclusively on humans; fleas, mosquitoes, and ticks feed on multiple host species.

---
Question 29
Aedes albopictus is mainly found in?

A. Asia
B. Africa
C. America
D. Europe
E. Canada

**Answer:
A. Asia**

---
Question 30
Mosquito life cycle has ______ larval instars.

A. One
B. Two
C. Three
D. Four
E. Five

**Answer:
D. Four**

---
Question 31
Which one of the following is a repellant?

A. DDT
B. DEET
C. Permethrin
D. Bendiocarb
E. All of the above

**Answer:
B. DEET**
Explanation: DEET repels but does not kill insects, unlike the other listed agents, which are insecticides.

---
Question 32
Which one has the GABA site as its target?

A. DDT
B. DEET
C. Permethrin
D. Bendiocarb
E. Malathion

**Answer: No listed option is correct.**
Explanation: DDT acts on voltage-gated sodium channels, not the GABA site. The source question lacks a valid GABA-targeting choice.

---
Question 33
Presence of anthills (ticks, in original context) could predispose the population to?

A. Sleeping sickness
B. Leishmaniasis
C. Malaria
D. Encephalitis
E. River blindness

**Answer:
B. Leishmaniasis** *(as marked in this specific paper — likely referring to sandfly-favorable habitat conditions rather than literal anthills; treat with caution and confirm with your lecturer)*

---
Question 34
Which of the following vectors transmit Trypanosome parasites in Latin America?

A. Glossina species
B. Triatomine bugs
C. Cimex species
D. Chrysops species
E. Simullium species

**Answer:
B. Triatomine bugs**

---
Question 35
Aedes albopictus is mainly found in? (repeat variant — see Question 29)

---
Answer: A. Asia (duplicate of Question 29)
Question 36
What kinds of roaches might you expect to encounter in a temperate city (e.g., Athens)?

A. German roaches
B. American roaches
C. Smokey brown roaches
D. All of the above
E. None of the above

**Answer:
D. All of the above**

---
Question 37
What is the main advantage of using larval control against mosquitoes?

A. Control will supplement natural control
B. Larvae are restricted to confined aquatic habitats that can be treated
C. Larval habitats do not support sensitive other organisms
D. All of the above
E. None of the above

**Answer: B**
Explanation: Unlike free-flying adults, larvae are stuck in identifiable water bodies, making them an easier, more targeted control point.

---
Question 38
What are effective non-pesticide ways to control problems from cockroaches?

A. Store food in plastic containers
B. Clean your kitchen counter tops nightly
C. Seal up cracks and seams around pipes and cabinets
D. All of the above
E. A and C

**Answer:
D. All of the above**

---
Question 39
The pupal stage is found in:

A. Incomplete metamorphosis
B. Complete metamorphosis
C. Both incomplete and complete metamorphosis
D. Neither incomplete nor complete metamorphosis
E. None of the above

**Answer:
B. Complete metamorphosis**

---
Question 40
What is simulotoxicosis?

A. A form of pesticide poisoning
B. A negative reaction to the saliva of black flies
C. A viral disease vectored by mosquitoes
D. An allergic reaction to cockroaches
E. B and C

**Answer: B**
Explanation: Simulotoxicosis is an allergic/toxic reaction specifically to *Simulium* (black fly) saliva during feeding, not a pesticide-related condition.

---
Question 41
How does insecticide resistance develop?

A. By using Integrated Pest Management practices
B. By using low doses of insecticides
C. By using high or prolonged doses of insecticide
D. B and C
E. None of the above

**Answer: C**
Explanation: Sustained selective pressure from high/prolonged insecticide use, not low doses, drives resistance development.

---
Question 42
What is the pathogen that causes river blindness?

A. Simulium damnosum
B. Borrelia recurrentis
C. Aedes aegypti
D. Difilaria immitis
E. None of the above

**Answer:
E. None of the above**
Explanation: *Simulium damnosum* is the vector, not the pathogen — the actual pathogen is *Onchocerca volvulus*, making all listed options technically incorrect for "pathogen."

---
Question 43
Ceratopogonidae larvae are found in:

A. Freshwater marshes
B. Salt marshes
C. Wet muddy areas around cattle watering tanks
D. All of the above
E. A and B

**Answer:
D. All of the above**

---
Question 44
Integrated Pest Management:

A. Relies solely on pesticides
B. Relies solely on biological and natural control
C. Considers the biology of the target pest
D. A and B
E. All of the above

**Answer: C**
Explanation: IPM's defining feature is that control methods are chosen based on understanding the target pest's biology and behavior, not relying on any single approach.

---
Question 45
The stage of Leishmania that develops in the sandfly and is transmitted to humans is the:

A. Gametocyte
B. Promastigote
C. Microfilaria
D. Amastigote
E. Any of the above

**Answer:
B. Promastigote**

---
Question 46
Which of these sub-families is not in the family Culicidae?

A. Culicinae
B. Anophelinae
C. Phlebotominae
D. Toxorhynchitinae
E. None of the above

**Answer:
C. Phlebotominae**
Explanation: Phlebotominae (sandflies) belong to a different family (Psychodidae); the other three are genuine Culicidae subfamilies.

---
Question 47
Epidemic typhus and Chagas disease can both be vectored via:

A. The saliva of a vector
B. Feces (frass) of a vector
C. Mosquitoes
D. Cockroaches
E. A and B

**Answer:
B. Feces (frass) of a vector**
Explanation: Both diseases are transmitted when a person scratches the bite site, rubbing infected vector faeces into the wound — not via the bite/saliva itself.

---
Question 48
Which of the following groups of Glossina species is insignificant in the transmission of Trypanosome brucei rhodesiense?

A. Palpalis group
B. Morsitans group
C. Fusca group
D. None of the above
E. All of the above

**Answer:
C. Fusca group**
Explanation: Only the Morsitans group is significant for *T. b. rhodesiense*; the Fusca group plays no meaningful role.

---
Question 49
Which of these habitats would be likely places for mosquito larvae to live?

A. Clogged drainage ditch
B. Fast flowing stream
C. Lake or reservoir
D. A and B
E. All of the above

**Answer:
A. Clogged drainage ditch**
Explanation: Mosquito larvae need still or slow-moving water; fast-flowing streams are unsuitable (contrast with *Simulium*, which specifically needs fast water).

---
Question 50
Which of the above does NOT attract host-seeking mosquitoes?

A. Carbon dioxide
B. Host odors
C. The color white
D. A and C
E. All of these attract mosquitoes

**Answer:
C. The color white**
Explanation: Dark colors, CO2, and host odors attract mosquitoes; white/light colors do not.

---
Question 51
Glossina species are easily controlled by traps impregnated with which colors?

A. Red and blue
B. Red and white
C. Blue and black
D. Black and white
E. Any of the above

**Answer:
C. Blue and black**

---
Question 52
Which of the following organisms have the characteristics to be an effective mechanical vector of human disease?

A. Simulium
B. Culicine
C. Blattela
D. All of the above
E. None of the above

**Answer:
C. Blattela (cockroach)**
Explanation: Cockroaches are classic mechanical vectors; *Simulium* and Culicine mosquitoes are biological vectors, where the pathogen develops inside them.

---
Question 53
Where might you look if you suspected bedbugs have infested your house?

A. Behind the headboard of the bed
B. Between the mattress and box spring
C. In cavities in the bed frame
D. A and B
E. All of the above

**Answer:
E. All of the above**

---
Question 54
Malaria-infected patients experience cycles of extreme fever followed by chills then a brief recovery period. These cycles occur because:

A. Merozoites are synchronously emerging from red blood cells, briefly stimulating a strong immune reaction before disappearing into new red cells
B. Merozoites alter expression of surface proteins, so parasite levels rise and fall as the immune system clears and selects for new variants
C. Merozoites emerge from the liver, stimulate an immune reaction, then re-invade liver cells
D. Sporozoites synchronously emerge from red blood cells, briefly stimulating a strong immune reaction before disappearing into new red cells
E. C and D

**Answer: A**
Explanation: The synchronized rupture of infected RBCs releasing merozoites triggers the cyclical fever; option B describes antigenic variation (explains chronicity, not the cycle itself), and sporozoites are not involved in this blood-stage cycle at all.

---
Question 55
Secondary metabolites of microbes are formed during the ______ phase of growth.

A. Exponential
B. Stationary
C. Trophophase
D. Idiophase
E. Lag

**Answer: D. Idiophase**
Explanation: Secondary metabolites are characteristically produced during the idiophase, which commonly overlaps the stationary phase. Because both are offered, idiophase is the more precise single-best answer.

---
Question 56
Which of the following structure is part of the bacterial cell envelope? *(cross-listed — appears in the same combined paper)*

A. Peptidoglycan
B. Lipopolysaccharide
C. Capsule
D. Gas vacuole
E. Flagella

**Answer: A, B, and C are all valid cell envelope components** *(the paper's marked single answer was peptidoglycan; treat gas vacuole and flagella as clearly wrong)*

---
Question 57
Microbial resistance to drugs is acquired through:

A. Conjugation
B. Transformation
C. Transduction
D. A and C
E. All of the above

**Answer:
E. All of the above**

---
Question 58
Which of the following microorganisms can be part of the normal vaginal flora and can cause meningitis in newborns?

A. Candida albicans
B. Corynebacterium species
C. Ureaplasma urealyticum
D. Staphylococcus epidermidis
E. Group B Streptococci

**Answer:
E. Group B Streptococci**
Explanation: *Streptococcus agalactiae* (Group B strep) is normal vaginal flora but the leading cause of neonatal meningitis, transmitted during delivery.

---
Question 59
Which of the following is not a symptom of septicemia?

A. Fever
B. Respiratory alkalosis
C. Shaking chills
D. High blood pressure
E. None of the above

**Answer: B and D are both atypical — paper marks Respiratory alkalosis as the "not a symptom" answer in one instance, and High Blood Pressure in another; septicemia classically causes hypotension, not hypertension, and often causes respiratory changes due to sepsis-related acidosis rather than alkalosis specifically**
Explanation: Be aware this question appeared with slightly different marked answers across paper versions — septicemia classically presents with fever, chills, and hypotension (not high blood pressure).

---
Question 60
Certain microorganisms can never be considered to be members of the normal flora. They are always considered to be pathogens. Which of the following is true?

A. Commensals
B. Opportunistic pathogens
C. True pathogens
D. Transient pathogens
E. C and D

**Answer:
C. True pathogens**

---
Question 61
This sporeformer contaminates meats as well as vegetables and is also the causative agent of gas gangrene:

A. Bacillus cereus
B. Clostridium perfringens
C. Shigella species
D. Salmonella species
E. Staphylococcus aureus

**Answer:
B. Clostridium perfringens**

---
Question 62
A/an ______ is a passive animal transporter of pathogens.

A. Zoonosis
B. Biological vector
C. Mechanical vector
D. Asymptomatic carrier
E. None of the above

**Answer:
C. Mechanical vector**

---
Question 63
Using examples, distinguish anautogenous development and autogenous development *(short-answer style, listed here as it recurs as a definitional MCQ-adjacent question)*

**Answer:**
- Anautogenous — requires a blood meal before the first batch of eggs can be laid (most mosquitoes)
- Autogenous — can lay the first batch of eggs without a blood meal, using stored larval nutrient reserves instead

---
Question 64
Outline biological control of mosquitoes — recurring short note; commonly tested organisms:

**Answer:**
- Tilapia (fish) — eat mosquito larvae
- Cat fish — larvivorous fish option
- Mosquito fish (*Gambusia*)
- Tadpoles — predatory on larvae
- Bti (*Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis*) — bacterial larvicide

---
Question 65
Discuss the medical importance of flea (20 marks — recurring essay; key point-form answer)

**Answer:**
- Discomfort/irritation from bites
- Vector of disease: endemic (murine) typhus (*Rickettsia typhi*), bubonic plague (via oriental rat flea, *Xenopsylla cheopis*)
- Primary pest of animals
- Intermediate host of dog tapeworm (*Dipylidium caninum*)
- Causes allergic skin reactions from flea bites

---

---

## Verification sources

- [WHO malaria entomology and vector control training module](https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2017-06/9789241505819_eng.pdf)
- [NCBI MeSH: Blackwater fever](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/mesh/68001742)
