articles.title: Streptococcus Classification, S. pyogenes, Rheumatic Fever, AGN — MCQ Bank
articles.content:
---
**STREPTOCOCCUS — CLASSIFICATION**
- Classified primarily by **haemolytic properties**: alpha (partial/green haemolysis), beta (complete haemolysis), non-haemolytic (gamma)
- This — not Lancefield grouping — is the single most important method for classifying/speciating streptococci (tested directly)
- *Streptococcus pneumoniae* (pneumococci) — alpha-hemolytic, can be serotyped based on their **polysaccharide capsule**
- Enterococci — group D streptococci, classified by ability to grow in **6.5% sodium chloride** and **45% bile**; most strains sensitive to penicillin, sulfonamides, cephalosporins, gentamicin, streptomycin (NOT resistant, as a distractor claims)
- Viridans streptococci — alpha-hemolytic; **NOT** identified by Lancefield grouping (that's the wrong statement in the "except" question) — Lancefield grouping is based on the C-carbohydrate in the cell wall and applies to other groupable streptococci
- Pneumococci vs viridans streptococci — both alpha-hemolytic but differentiated by **bile solubility test** and **susceptibility to optochin** (pneumococci are bile-soluble and optochin-sensitive; viridans strep are not)
- Group B Streptococcus (*S. agalactiae*) — part of normal vaginal flora, but can cause **neonatal meningitis** — a key exception to "normal flora doesn't cause disease"
**STREPTOCOCCUS PYOGENES — VIRULENCE FACTORS AND PATHOGENESIS (5–20 marks, appears repeatedly)**
- **Toxins:**
 - Streptolysin O and S (hemolysins) — responsible for hemolysis and leukocidal activity (kill white blood cells)
 - Pyrogenic/erythrogenic toxin (scarlet fever toxin) — a superantigen, causes the scarlet fever rash and anti-inflammatory/immune-inhibiting effects
- **Enzymes (spreading factors):**
 - Streptokinase — promotes lysis of fibrin by converting plasminogen to plasmin
 - DNase (streptodornase) — depolymerizes DNA, liquefying pus
 - Hyaluronidase — breaks down hyaluronic acid in connective tissue, aiding spread through tissue
 - Lipase — degrades lipids/phospholipids on host cell membranes
- **Cell wall components:**
 - Capsule — antiphagocytic (protects from being engulfed by phagocytes)
 - M protein — major virulence factor, gives rigidity, resists phagocytosis, and is the antigen basis for immune classification (also key in rheumatic fever pathogenesis via molecular mimicry)
 - Pili — mediate attachment to host cells
- **Clinical complications caused by *S. pyogenes*:** pharyngitis, scarlet fever, rheumatic fever — "all of the above" is the typical MCQ answer
- **Complication of streptococcal pharyngitis specifically:** rheumatic fever (not pseudomembrane formation, not meningococcemia — those belong to other organisms)
**RHEUMATIC FEVER vs ACUTE GLOMERULONEPHRITIS (post-streptococcal complications — 10 mark comparison, repeated)**
- Site of infection that precedes each:
 - Glomerulonephritis — can follow either **skin or throat** infection
 - Rheumatic fever — follows **throat** infection only
- Latent period before onset:
 - Glomerulonephritis — 1–3 weeks
 - Rheumatic fever — 2–5 weeks
- Prior sensitization needed:
 - Glomerulonephritis — not essential
 - Rheumatic fever — essential
- Repeated attacks:
 - Glomerulonephritis — absent; one heals completely, doesn't recur from the same episode pattern
 - Rheumatic fever — repeated attacks are common
- Serotypes responsible:
 - Glomerulonephritis — nephritogenic strains, associated with skin and throat serotypes
 - Rheumatic fever — associated with throat serotypes specifically
- Clinical manifestation:
 - Glomerulonephritis — hematuria, albuminuria, edema; pathology at the base of the glomerulus
 - Rheumatic fever — swelling of joints, inflammation of heart muscle (myocarditis, pericarditis, endocarditis)
- Pathogenesis:
 - Glomerulonephritis — antibody-antigen immune complex deposition at the glomerulus (type III hypersensitivity)
 - Rheumatic fever — antibody against the streptococcal antigen cross-reacts with heart tissue antigen (molecular mimicry, type II hypersensitivity)
---
**STAPHYLOCOCCUS**
- Coagulase test — differentiates *S. aureus* (coagulase-positive) from *S. epidermidis* (coagulase-negative)
- Nose is the most likely source of *S. aureus* in an outbreak of neonatal nursery sepsis (normal flora reservoir)
- Toxin-mediated diseases from *S. aureus*:
 - Scalded skin syndrome — caused by exfoliative toxin (exfoliatin)
 - Toxic shock syndrome — caused by TSST-1 (a superantigen); classic scenario: nasal tampon left in place post-surgery, fever, hypotension, diffuse erythematous rash including palms/soles, elevated liver enzymes, renal failure
 - Food poisoning (food intoxication, not infection) — caused by a preformed **enterotoxin** in food; rapid onset (~2 hours), vomiting-predominant
- Biofilm-related infection (e.g., long-term central venous catheter with *S. epidermidis*):
 - The complex molecular interactions within the biofilm make it difficult to provide effective antimicrobial therapy — catheter often needs removal to cure infection
 - Biofilm does NOT wash off easily, and bacteria in it are NOT more susceptible to antibiotics from slowed metabolism (both are wrong distractors)
- Associated with formation of a bacterial biofilm: classic example is airway colonization in a cystic fibrosis patient with a mucoid (alginate-producing) strain of ***Pseudomonas aeruginosa*** (this exact scenario is used to test biofilm concept generally, not just Staph)
---
**CLOSTRIDIUM SPECIES**
**Clostridium tetani (tetanus)**
- Spores germinate in dirty, neglected wounds with some tissue necrosis
- Produces **tetanospasmin** (tetanus toxin)
- Mechanism of action: toxin binds to gangliosides at the neuromuscular junction, is taken up and transported retrograde along the axon to the CNS, then travels via **cranial nerve/cranial pathway** transsynaptically to reach the spinal cord/brainstem
- In the CNS, the toxin **blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters** (glycine and GAB
A) from inhibitory interneurons
- Loss of inhibitory signals → unopposed, sustained muscle contraction → **spastic/rigid paralysis** (opposite mechanism to botulism, which causes flaccid paralysis)
- Clinical picture: trismus (lockjaw), facial muscle spasms, inability to open mouth, generalized rigidity
- Necrotic tissue significance: necrotic/anaerobic tissue provides the low-oxygen environment *
C. tetani* spores need to germinate and produce toxin
- How infection is acquired: through a contaminated wound (e.g., stepping on a nail, dirty cut) that creates an anaerobic pocket
- Treatment: tetanus antitoxin (passive immunization) plus antibiotics such as **erythromycin or tetracycline** (metronidazole/penicillin also acceptable), plus wound debridement
- Should treatment wait for lab confirmation? — **No**; treatment should be started immediately on clinical suspicion because tetanus is rapidly fatal and lab confirmation takes too long
- Prevention: **tetanus toxoid immunization** induces effective protection (note: antitoxin against tetanus does NOT cross-protect against botulism — they are different toxins with different antigenic sites, a common wrong-answer trap)
**Clostridium botulinum (botulism)**
- Toxin ingested (preformed in improperly canned/preserved food) — classic scenario involves home-canned goods
- Mechanism: toxin is absorbed from the gut, enters the bloodstream, and blocks **release of acetylcholine** at the neuromuscular junction (presynaptic)
- This causes **flaccid paralysis** (opposite of tetanus)
- Treatment for ingested botulism toxin: large doses of **antitoxin** must be administered (not antibiotics — the disease is toxin-mediated, not an ongoing bacterial infection at that stage)
- Type of exotoxin most commonly associated with human botulism disease: **Type A and Type C** (from the exam: "A and C" was the marked correct answer)
**Clostridium perfringens**
- Causes **gas gangrene** (myonecrosis) and food poisoning
- Produces an **enterotoxin**
- Produces a **double zone of beta-hemolysis** on blood agar (this is a classic identifying lab feature)
- Some strains are aerotolerant, though the organism is fundamentally anaerobic and **multiplies in foods only under anaerobic conditions**
- It is **NOT** the most common cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea (that's *
C. difficile* — this is the "EXCEPT" trap in that question)
- Classic clinical scenario: wound with gas felt in the tissue (crepitus), blackened/necrotic skin, severe pain, fever — gram-positive rod on gram stain of exudate
- Toxin mechanism: alpha-toxin is a **lecithinase** that degrades cell membranes, causing tissue necrosis and hemolysis; the lecithinase specifically does NOT cause diarrhea (that's a distractor — the enterotoxin, a separate protein, causes the diarrheal illness)
- This organism contaminates both meats AND vegetables and is the sporeformer responsible for gas gangrene specifically among the options given
**General Clostridium immunization fact**
- Antitoxin against tetanus does NOT also protect against botulism, even though both are clostridial toxins — they have different antigenic sites and require separate antitoxins
- Immunization with **tetanus toxoid** induces effective protection specifically against tetanus toxin
---
**CORYNEBACTERIUM DIPHTHERIAE (Diphtheria)**
- Causes a **pseudomembrane** (grayish exudate) over the tonsils/pharynx — classic presentation in an 8-year-old with severe sore throat
- Organism: **club-shaped, gram-positive bacillus**, sometimes described as showing metachromatic (Babes-Ernst) granules
- Diphtheria toxin mechanism:
 - The **A subunit** causes **ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2 (EF-2)**
 - This **inhibits protein synthesis** in host cells → cell death, and formation of the pseudomembrane
 - It does NOT form pores in RBCs, degrade lecithin, or increase cAMP (all wrong distractors used repeatedly)
- Elek's test — used to test for **toxin/antitoxin reaction** (confirms toxin production by the organism); a strip of filter paper impregnated with diphtheria antitoxin is placed on blood agar, the organism is streaked at right angles to it, and after incubation a line of precipitation forms where toxin meets antitoxin, confirming a toxigenic strain
- Diagnosis of diphtheria is confirmed by **demonstration of toxin production** by a suspicious isolate (i.e., Elek's test) — NOT simply by microscopy or culture alone
---
**MYCOBACTERIUM TUBERCULOSIS**
- Route of entry: inhalation of aerosols/droplets or dust particles containing tubercle bacilli
- Pathogenesis:
 - Bacilli lodge in the lungs, engulfed by alveolar macrophages
 - Replicate inside macrophages using virulence factors: **mycolic acid, mycosides, lipoarabinomannan, trehalose dimycolate (cord factor)**
 - This causes death of macrophages, forming an inflammatory lesion called the **Ghon focus**
 - Activated macrophages form a **granuloma** around the primary infection site to contain it
 - Bacilli also spread to adjacent lymph nodes; dendritic cells present the bacilli to T cells, causing T cell activation and cytokine release, which activates further immune cells
- Cell wall protective factors:
 - Bacterial inhibition of phagosome-lysosome fusion, and interference with endosomal acidification — this is how the bacterium **survives after being ingested by macrophages** (correct answer over complement inhibition, poor immunogenicity, or oxidative resistance)
- Types of disease caused: pulmonary TB, miliary TB, bone/joint TB, renal/urogenital TB, tuberculous meningitis, tuberculous lymphadenitis
- Diagnosis: sputum for **acid-fast staining** (Ziehl-Neelsen), viewed under microscope to demonstrate the organism
- Mantoux (tuberculin) test — used to identify **TB exposure** (not active disease); a positive result (induration) means the person was previously exposed to the organism, not necessarily that they have active disease
- *M. tuberculosis* is classified as a **true pathogen** — never considered part of normal flora, unlike *
E. coli* or *S. aureus*
- Why penicillin doesn't work against Mycobacterium: **the cell wall of these organisms is not affected by penicillin** (high mycolic acid content makes the cell wall impermeable to many antibiotics)
- Classic clinical vignette clue: plant nursery worker (soil exposure), chronic cough, weight loss, bilateral upper lobe cavitary infiltrates, acid-fast bacilli on sputum → acquired by **inhaling aerosolized droplets**, not from soil contact directly (the soil-exposure detail is a distractor pointing toward a different organism in some vignettes, but for classic TB the answer is always inhalation)
---
**NEISSERIA GONORRHOEAE**
- Gram-negative diplococci — classic finding in urethral discharge (kidney-bean shaped, seen within neutrophils)
- Classic vignette: young man with penile discharge, dysuria, gram-negative diplococci on Gram stain → gonorrhea
- Antibiotics used: **ceftriaxone/rifampin/azithromycin type regimens** (dual therapy is standard due to resistance concerns; exam answer key noted rifampin/azithromycin in one instance — go with current dual-therapy logic but know ceftriaxone is the backbone)
- Complications:
 - In men: can ascend to cause epididymitis
 - In women: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PI
D) → can lead to **infertility** (the classic sequela tested)
 - Salpingitis is associated with **gonorrhea** and can lead to **sterility**
 - Ophthalmia neonatorum is associated with **gonorrhea AND chlamydia** (two organisms, both must be known as the answer)
- Why partners must be treated even if asymptomatic: prevents reinfection and prevents complications like PID/infertility in the partner, even without symptoms
- Gonococcal conjunctivitis of newborns is now rare because of **silver nitrate or erythromycin prophylaxis** given at birth
- Definitive diagnosis is NOT by detecting antibodies in serum (this is the wrong/EXCEPT answer) — diagnosis is by culture (Thayer-Martin agar) or Gram stain/NAAT, not serology
---
**CHLAMYDIA TRACHOMATIS**
- Causes: PID, ophthalmia (with gonorrhea), trachoma (via mechanical vector *Musca sorbens* — see parasitology notes)
- Life cycle (asked as a 6-mark essay) — obligate intracellular organism with two forms:
 - **Elementary body (EB)** — the infectious, metabolically inactive form; enters the host cell by endocytosis
 - Inside the cell, EB converts into the **reticulate body (RB)** — the metabolically active, replicating form
 - RB divides repeatedly by binary fission inside a vacuole (inclusion body)
 - RBs eventually condense back into infectious EBs
 - The host cell ruptures, releasing new EBs to infect adjacent cells — cycle repeats
- Diagnosis of PID caused by Chlamydia: tissue culture inoculum is used because Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular organism and cannot be grown on standard bacterial media — it needs living host cells
- Staining shows **cell inclusions** — this is the classic clue pointing to Chlamydia in a PID case with a "single sexual partner and condom use" history (patient may not realize partner-transmitted infections can persist/recur)
---
**TREPONEMA PALLIDUM (Syphilis) vs HAEMOPHILUS DUCREYI (Chancroid) — comparison, repeated 5–10 marks**
- **Similarities:**
 - Both originate as pustules at the site of inoculation, progressing to ulcerated lesions
 - Both are caused by sexually transmitted organisms
 - Both typically appear on the genitals of infected individuals
 - Both can present with multiple sites/multiple lesions
- **Differences:**
| Feature | Syphilitic chancre | Chancroid |
|---|---|---|
| Organism | *Treponema pallidum* | *Haemophilus ducreyi* |
| Pain | Painless | Painful |
| Exudate | Non-exudative | Soft, green-yellow purulent exudate |
| Edge | Hard/indurated edge | Soft edge |
| Healing | Heals spontaneously in 3–6 weeks | Does NOT resolve spontaneously |
| Extragenital sites | Chancre can involve extragenital sites | Mostly confined to genitals |
- **Syphilis clinical stages (5 marks, repeated as its own short note):**
 - Primary stage — painless chancre at inoculation site, heals spontaneously
 - Secondary stage — characterized by widespread skin lesions, including involvement of palms and soles, with desquamation; lesions frequently ulcerate
 - Tertiary stage — widespread bone, joint, and soft tissue destruction; extensive destruction of bone/cartilage (e.g., gummas, saddle nose)
- Serology interpretation: non-treponemal test (RPR) non-reactive + treponemal test (TP-P
A) reactive in a pregnant woman previously treated for syphilis → indicates past treated infection, **but the baby is still considered at risk for congenital syphilis** and must be evaluated (this exact scenario has appeared)
---
**HELICOBACTER PYLORI**
- Survives the acidic stomach environment via multiple mechanisms (5-mark short note, repeated):
 - **Urease enzyme** — converts urea to ammonia and CO2, neutralizing acid locally around the organism
 - **Flagella** — allow motility to burrow through the mucus layer toward the less acidic gastric epithelium, escaping the most acidic luminal environment
 - **Adhesins** — allow attachment to gastric epithelial cells, resisting being washed away
 - Ability to sense the pH gradient and swim toward more neutral pH
 - Produces urease-generated ammonia which also helps neutralize local acid and can damage epithelium
- Urease specifically neutralizes stomach acid (HCl) — this is a direct fill-in-the-blank MCQ answer
---
**VIBRIO CHOLERAE**
- Causes profuse "rice water" watery diarrhea — classic vignette: 15-year-old girl, >1L diarrhea in 90 minutes, no fever
- Toxin mechanism: cholera toxin has A and B subunits; the toxin **increases intracellular cAMP** (yields increase in intracellular cAMP levels) — this drives massive chloride/water secretion into the gut lumen, NOT cleavage of AMP, NOT cleaving SNARE (that's botulinum's mechanism), NOT blocking EF-1
- Cholera toxin is **not** attached to the flagella (a wrong distractor) — it's a separately secreted AB toxin
- Most important treatment step: **fluid and electrolyte replacement** — this takes priority over antibiotics, antitoxin, or even confirming the exact organism first, because the mortality risk is from dehydration
- Classic outbreak vignette: airline passengers from Peru who ate crab salad, two developed severe watery diarrhea after landing — likely cause: **Vibrio cholerae O139** (crab/seafood-associated, lipopolysaccharide O antigen 139)
---
**ESCHERICHIA COLI**
- UTI pathogenesis: **P-fimbriae (P-pili)** are the virulence factor associated with ability to cause urinary tract infection, specifically in patients with the **P blood group antigen** (fimbriae bind to a receptor related to this blood group)
- *
E. coli* O157:H7 — associated with **lipopolysaccharide O antigen 157, flagellar antigen H7**; a cause of hemorrhagic colitis (Shiga-toxin producing strain), not typically the answer for classic cholera-like outbreaks (see Vibrio above, where O157:H7 was the wrong answer in favor of *V. cholerae* O139)
- LPS (lipopolysaccharide) — part of the cell wall of *
E. coli*; interacts with macrophages and monocytes, triggering **release of cytokines** — this is the toxic mechanism of endotoxin generally (correct statement across multiple repeated MCQs); LPS does NOT form pores in RBCs, does NOT cause hypothermia, does NOT cause paralysis (all wrong distractors)
- Verotoxin of *
E. coli* is similar to **Shiga toxin** (both inhibit protein synthesis by attacking the ribosome, structurally/functionally related toxins)
---
**LISTERIA MONOCYTOGENES**
- Pathogenesis:
 - Enters host cells by phagocytosis
 - Produces **listeriolysin O**, which damages the phagosomal membrane, allowing the bacterium to escape into the cytoplasm
 - Grows and multiplies **intracellularly** (in the cytoplasm)
 - Produces actin-based motility proteins that help it spread **cell-to-cell** without ever being exposed to the extracellular environment/antibodies (this is the correct mechanism — NOT simply "produces an enzyme that helps spread cell to cell" in a vague sense; it specifically hijacks host actin polymerization)
- Clinical relevance: can cross the placenta, causing miscarriage or neonatal meningitis; also causes meningitis in immunocompromised adults
---
**BACILLUS ANTHRACIS**
- First microorganism to satisfy Koch's postulates (late 19th century)
- Vaccination facts: current vaccine is well tolerated but not routinely given to the general public; recombinant vaccine trials undergoing evaluation
- Woolsorter's disease = **inhalational anthrax** (occupational exposure to contaminated wool/animal hair)
- Cutaneous anthrax — classic black eschar lesion
---
**GENERAL BACTERIOLOGY CONCEPTS (recurring across all papers)**
*Normal flora vs true pathogens*
- Organisms **never** considered normal flora, always pathogens when found: *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* (the repeated correct answer over *S. pneumoniae,
E. coli, S. aureus, N. meningitidis*, which CAN be part of normal/carrier flora in some contexts)
*Lipopolysaccharide (LPS/endotoxin)*
- Part of the cell wall of gram-negative bacteria like *
E. coli*
- Interacts with macrophages/monocytes → cytokine release (correct, repeated statement)
- Toxic component is **lipid A**, not the O side chain (the O side chain is the antigenic/serotyping portion, not the toxic part) — watch for this distinction if asked
*Type III secretion systems*
- Directly inject bacterial proteins into host cells across both bacterial and host cell membranes, promoting pathogenesis of infection — this is the correct mechanism (not simply "release into extracellular environment," which describes a different secretion type)
*Biofilms*
- Complex molecular interactions within a biofilm make it difficult to treat with antimicrobials effectively — often require device/catheter removal to cure
- Classic biofilm example: mucoid alginate-producing *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* in cystic fibrosis airway colonization
*Bacterial growth and resistance*
- Secondary metabolites (including some antibiotics produced by bacteria themselves) are formed during the **stationary phase** of bacterial growth
- Microbial resistance to drugs is acquired through **conjugation, transformation, and transduction** — "all of the above" is the typical correct answer
*Gastrointestinal/food safety organisms*
- *Bacillus cereus* — spore-forming, motile rod causing foodborne illness in diarrheal or emetic form (classic vignette: reheated fried rice)
- Whipple disease — caused by *Tropheryma whipplei*; diagnosis confirmed by **PCR amplification and sequencing** of an appropriate DNA segment (not culture, since it's difficult to culture)
*Miscellaneous clinical vignette organisms (each tested once, know the pairing)*
- Nocardia/Actinomyces — branching, partially acid-fast gram-positive rods; classic vignette is a breast cancer patient with pulmonary nodules and brain lesions → ***Nocardia*** (partially acid-fast distinguishes it from *Actinomyces*, which is NOT acid-fast); treated with **trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole**
- Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae — gram-positive rod causing violaceous nodular skin lesions after a fishhook injury (fish handling exposure), forms long filaments, causes greenish discoloration of agar
- Corynebacterium urealyticum — short, irregular gram-positive rod causing UTI with struvite/bladder stones in a catheterized patient
- Mycoplasma pneumoniae — treated with tetracycline or erythromycin (no cell wall, so beta-lactams don't work)
- Gardnerella vaginalis — bacterial vaginosis; thin gray-white discharge, pH >4.5, clue cells; the organism **decreased** in bacterial vaginosis is **Lactobacillus species** (normal flora that's lost)
- Whooping cough (*Bordetella pertussis*) — paroxysm (rapid-fire cough) is characteristic of pertussis; disease stages: catarrhal (mild, runny nose) → paroxysmal (severe cough, apnea/vomiting) → convalescent (recovery); pertussis toxin is an A-B toxin causing tissue damage/inflammation; adhesin (filamentous hemagglutinin) mediates attachment to upper respiratory epithelium
- Brain abscess 1 month after dental extraction — most likely organism: **anaerobic streptococci**
---

Full compilation of the remaining bacteriology gaps, same format.
---
**NEISSERIA MENINGITIDIS**
- Portal of entry: **inhalation** (droplet spread person-to-person)
- Attachment: organism attaches to nasopharyngeal epithelial cells with the help of **pili**
- Can exist as **part of normal flora** in the nasopharynx without causing symptoms (asymptomatic carriage is common)
- From the nasopharynx, the organism can invade the bloodstream, producing symptoms — this progression from upper respiratory tract colonization to bloodstream invasion is the key pathogenic step
- Once in blood → **meningococcemia**
- **Fulminant meningococcemia** — the severe form — presents with:
 - High fever
 - Hemorrhagic (petechial) rash
 - Intravascular coagulation (DI
C)
 - Circulatory collapse
- During meningococcemia, there is thrombosis of small blood vessels, perivascular infiltration, and petechial hemorrhage
- Major virulence factor: **capsular polysaccharide** — serogroups A, B, C, D, X, Y, Z, W135, 29E (these letters/numbers are the actual serogroup names, occasionally asked to identify)
- Epidemic waves specifically associated with **mass gatherings, religious pilgrims, sub-Saharan Africa** (the "meningitis belt")
- Once organism reaches the meninges: meninges become acutely inflamed, with thrombosis of blood vessels and exudation of polymorphonuclear leukocytes — so the surface of the brain becomes covered with thick purulent exudate
- Clinical onset: usually begins with intense headache, vomiting, stiff neck (classic meningeal signs), progressing to coma within a few hours in severe cases
- Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome — bilateral adrenal hemorrhage/failure specifically associated with fulminant meningococcemia (this is a distractor option in some questions asking about strep pharyngitis complications — it belongs to *N. meningitidis*, NOT *S. pyogenes*)
---
**CAUSES OF BACTERIAL MENINGITIS BY ORGANISM (20-mark essay — "discuss the major causes of bacterial meningitis")**
- **Neisseria meningitidis** — as detailed above; a major cause across all age groups, especially adolescents/young adults, epidemic potential
- **Streptococcus pneumoniae** — most important cause of acute bacterial meningitis in adults generally
- **Haemophilus influenzae** — historically a major cause in children before vaccination programs
- **Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus)** — the **most common cause of neonatal meningitis** in the developed world/West; part of normal vaginal flora, transmitted to the newborn during delivery
- **Listeria monocytogenes** — important cause in:
 - Neonates (can cross the placenta during pregnancy, causing miscarriage or premature delivery; newborns infected during delivery can develop acute meningitis)
 - Immunocompromised adults (adults with weakened immunity are also at risk)
- **Escherichia coli** — also a cause, particularly in neonates (has K1 capsular antigen associated with neonatal meningitis specifically)
- **Mycobacterium tuberculosis** — causes **tuberculous meningitis**; tubercle bacilli reach the meninges via the bloodstream; occurs frequently in **non-immune infants and young children**
---
**STREPTOCOCCUS PNEUMONIAE (expanding beyond classification)**
- Most common cause of **"typical" (classic, lobar) pneumonia** — correct answer over *H. influenzae, M. pneumoniae, L. pneumophila,
B. pertussis*
- Alpha-hemolytic
- Serotyped based on its **polysaccharide capsule** — the capsule is the major virulence factor, antiphagocytic
- Distinguished from viridans streptococci (also alpha-hemolytic) by:
 - **Bile solubility test** — pneumococci are bile-soluble, viridans strep are not
 - **Optochin sensitivity** — pneumococci are optochin-sensitive, viridans strep are resistant
- Important cause of bacterial meningitis in adults (see above)
- Complication of pneumococcal pharyngitis/URTI can include otitis media, sinusitis, and pneumonia itself as the progression
---
**SALMONELLA AND SHIGELLA**
**Infective dose (ID50) comparison — repeatedly tested**
- ***Shigella sonnei*** has the **lowest ID50** (as few as 10–100 organisms can cause disease) — this is the correct answer whenever compared against *Salmonella typhi, Vibrio cholerae, Campylobacter jejuni*
- *Salmonella typhi* — ID50 around 10^5 to 10^6 organisms (higher than Shigella)
- *Vibrio cholerae* — needs a much larger inoculum, around 10^6–10^11 organisms (large numbers needed because most are destroyed by stomach acid before reaching the intestine)
- Why this matters clinically: Shigella's very low infective dose explains why it spreads so easily person-to-person and in contaminated food/water even with minimal contamination
**Host defense against Salmonella-caused dysentery**
- Most important host defense preventing dysentery caused by *Salmonella*: **gastric juice** (stomach acid barrier) — this is the correct answer over salivary enzymes, normal mouth flora, or alpha interferon
- This is why conditions that reduce stomach acid (e.g., antacid use, achlorhydria) increase susceptibility to Salmonella infection
**Shigella virulence factors** (if asked as a short note)
- Shiga toxin — inhibits protein synthesis by acting on the ribosome (60S subunit), causing cell death; contributes to bloody dysentery and can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome in severe cases
- Very low infective dose (as above) is itself a virulence-related factor — allows efficient person-to-person spread
- Invasion of colonic epithelial cells causing local inflammation and ulceration
---
**ENTEROCOCCUS (expanding beyond Streptococcus classification)**
- Normal flora of the **lower intestinal tract and vagina**
- Can grow in **6.5% sodium chloride** and **45% bile** — this combination of tests is the classic identifying feature separating enterococci from other streptococci
- Can be **alpha-hemolytic or non-hemolytic** (not strictly one or the other)
- Most strains are **sensitive** to penicillin, sulfonamides, cephalosporins, gentamicin, and streptomycin — the wrong/EXCEPT-style distractor claims resistance, which is incorrect for typical strains (though clinically some enterococci do show acquired resistance, e.g., VRE — but for this exam's purposes, "sensitive" is the marked correct answer)
---
**PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA**
- Why Pseudomonas infections are difficult to treat and prevent: **the bacteria is highly resistant to detergents and antibiotics** — this is the specific marked correct answer over "metabolically versatile," "found everywhere," or "causes nosocomial infection" (those are true statements about Pseudomonas but not the reason infections are hard to treat)
- Associated with **biofilm formation** — classic example: airway colonization in a cystic fibrosis patient with a **mucoid, alginate-producing strain** of *P. aeruginosa*
- Toxin: **lecithinase** — degrades cell membranes, causes tissue damage (this is the answer for "which toxin accounts for tissue damage" when Pseudomonas is the organism in question — same enzyme class as *
C. perfringens'* alpha toxin, but a different organism context)
- Common cause of nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infections — particularly in burns, catheters, and immunocompromised patients
---
**TOXIC SHOCK SYNDROME vs SCALDED SKIN SYNDROME (5-mark comparison, both caused by *S. aureus* toxins)**
| Feature | Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) | Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) |
|---|---|---|
| Toxin | TSST-1 (a superantigen) | Exfoliative toxin (exfoliatin) |
| Mechanism | Superantigen causes massive, non-specific T-cell activation and cytokine release | Toxin cleaves desmoglein, causing separation within the epidermis |
| Key clinical features | High fever, hypotension (shock), diffuse erythematous rash resembling sunburn (including palms/soles), multiorgan involvement (elevated liver enzymes, renal failure) | Widespread blistering and peeling of the skin, resembling a burn/scald; usually in infants/young children; no hypotension or multiorgan failure typically |
| Classic scenario | Retained nasal tampon/foreign body, or menstruation-associated | Neonates/young children, localized staph infection triggering toxin release systemically |
| Systemic shock present? | Yes | No |
- Both are classified as **toxin-generated *S. aureus* diseases resulting from contact** — this grouping ("both B and C are correct," referring to scalded skin syndrome and toxic shock syndrome together) has been the marked answer when listed alongside purpuric fever and pseudomembranous colitis as distractors
---

articles.title: Female & Male Genital Pathology: Ulcers, HPV, Endometriosis, Pre-eclampsia — Notes
articles.content:
# FEMALE GENITAL SYSTEM — ADDITIONAL ESSAYS
Q23. State the aetiology of any 5 genital ulcer diseases.
- Syphilis — *Treponema pallidum* (painless, indurated ulcer/chancre)
- Chancroid — *Haemophilus ducreyi* (painful, ragged-edged ulcer)
- Genital herpes — Herpes simplex virus type 2 (multiple painful vesicles/ulcers)
- Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) — *Chlamydia trachomatis* serovars L1-L3 (small ulcer + painful inguinal lymphadenopathy)
- Granuloma inguinale (Donovanosis) — *Klebsiella granulomatis* (beefy-red, painless, progressive ulcer, Donovan bodies)
Q24. Explain the pathogenesis of cervical squamous cell carcinoma.
- Persistent infection with high-risk HPV (16, 18) is the essential cause
- Viral oncoproteins **E6** degrades **p53** (loses apoptosis/DNA repair control); **E7** degrades **RB** (loses G1/S checkpoint control)
- Result: unchecked proliferation of cervical squamous cells at the transformation zone
- Progression: normal epithelium → low-grade CIN I → high-grade CIN II/III (carcinoma in situ) → invasion through basement membrane → invasive SCC
- Cofactors that promote progression: smoking, multiple sexual partners, early coitarche, immunosuppression (HIV), multiparity, long-term OCP use
- Without HPV clearance/screening (Pap smear detects dysplasia early), progression to invasive cancer can take 10-20 years
Q25. State 5 theories in the pathogenesis of endometriosis.
- **Retrograde menstruation (Sampson's theory)** — menstrual endometrium flows backward through fallopian tubes and implants on pelvic peritoneum/ovaries
- **Coelomic metaplasia** — peritoneal mesothelium undergoes metaplastic transformation into endometrial-type tissue
- **Vascular/lymphatic dissemination** — endometrial cells spread via blood or lymphatics to distant sites (explains rare extrapelvic endometriosis, e.g. lung)
- **Direct implantation** — surgical transplantation of endometrial tissue (e.g. into a caesarean scar)
- **Induction theory** — hormonal/immune factors induce undifferentiated peritoneal cells to differentiate into endometrial tissue
- *(Bonus)* Stem cell theory — bone-marrow-derived stem cells differentiate into ectopic endometrial tissue
Q26. State 5 degenerative changes uterine leiomyomas can undergo.
- **Hyaline degeneration** — most common, homogenous pink hyaline change
- **Cystic degeneration** — liquefaction creating cystic spaces
- **Calcification** — especially in postmenopausal, poorly vascularized fibroids
- **Red (carneous) degeneration** — haemorrhagic infarction, classically in pregnancy
- **Myxoid degeneration** — gelatinous, mucoid change
- *(Bonus)* Fatty change and necrosis (in rapidly growing or twisted pedunculated fibroids)
Q27. Classify ovarian neoplasms with examples.
- **Surface epithelial tumours** (most common category overall)
 — Serous (cystadenoma, cystadenocarcinoma)
 — Mucinous (cystadenoma, cystadenocarcinoma)
 — Endometrioid carcinoma
 — Clear cell carcinoma
 — Brenner tumour
- **Germ cell tumours** (mostly in young women)
 — Mature cystic teratoma (benign, commonest germ cell tumour)
 — Dysgerminoma
 — Yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumour
 — Choriocarcinoma
 — Embryonal carcinoma
- **Sex cord-stromal tumours**
 — Granulosa cell tumour (oestrogen-secreting, Call-Exner bodies)
 — Thecoma / Fibroma
 — Sertoli-Leydig tumour (androgen-secreting, virilizing)
- **Metastatic tumours**
 — Krukenberg tumour (bilateral, signet-ring cells, usually from gastric primary)
Q28. Discuss the pathogenesis of toxaemia of pregnancy (pre-eclampsia/eclampsia).
- Root cause: **abnormal trophoblastic invasion** of maternal spiral arteries — cytotrophoblasts fail to remodel the spiral arteries into low-resistance vessels
- Result: persistently high-resistance, narrow spiral arteries → **placental hypoperfusion/ischemia**
- Ischemic placenta releases anti-angiogenic factors: increased **sFlt-1** (soluble Flt-1, a VEGF/PlGF antagonist) and decreased **PlGF** (placental growth factor)
- These circulate systemically → widespread **endothelial dysfunction**
- Endothelial dysfunction → vasospasm, increased vascular permeability, activation of coagulation
- Clinical result: maternal hypertension, proteinuria, oedema (pre-eclampsia); severe cases → seizures (eclampsia), HELLP syndrome (Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets)
Q29. Write short notes on Uterine Endometriosis.
- Definition: presence of endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine cavity, most commonly ovaries, uterosacral ligaments, and pelvic peritoneum
- Pathogenesis: see Q25 theories (retrograde menstruation most widely accepted)
- Morphology: blue-black "powder-burn" lesions; ovarian involvement forms "chocolate cysts" (endometriomas) from cyclic bleeding of trapped old blood
- Clinical features: chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, infertility
- Diagnosis: laparoscopy with biopsy showing endometrial glands + stroma + haemosiderin-laden macrophages
- Complications: infertility, adhesions, rarely malignant transformation (endometrioid or clear cell carcinoma)
Q30. Outline the classification of Primary Malignant Ovarian neoplasms.
- **Malignant epithelial tumours**
 — Serous cystadenocarcinoma (most common malignant ovarian tumour, often bilateral, psammoma bodies)
 — Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma
 — Endometrioid carcinoma (may coexist with endometriosis)
 — Clear cell carcinoma
 — Malignant Brenner tumour
- **Malignant germ cell tumours**
 — Dysgerminoma (most common malignant germ cell tumour)
 — Yolk sac tumour (AFP marker)
 — Embryonal carcinoma
 — Choriocarcinoma (β-hCG marker)
 — Immature teratoma
- **Malignant sex cord-stromal tumours**
 — Granulosa cell tumour (malignant potential, low-grade)
 — Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour (malignant forms)
Q31. Outline the morphologic features of Uterine Leiomyoma.
- Gross: well-circumscribed, round, firm, greyish-white mass with a characteristic **whorled cut surface**; often multiple, variable in size
- Location: intramural (within muscle wall, most common), submucosal (bulging into cavity — causes most bleeding symptoms), or subserosal (bulging outward, may become pedunculated)
- Microscopic: interlacing bundles/whorls of uniform, benign-appearing spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells with elongated, cigar-shaped nuclei
- Low mitotic activity, no significant nuclear atypia (distinguishes from leiomyosarcoma, which shows high mitotic rate + atypia + necrosis)
- Susceptible to degenerative changes (see Q26)
Q32. Write short notes on Paget's disease of the Vulva.
- Definition: intraepithelial adenocarcinoma of vulvar skin, arising from apocrine gland-bearing epithelium
- Clinical: erythematous, eczematous, scaly/crusted plaque, often pruritic, mimics dermatitis (delayed diagnosis common)
- Histology: large, pale "Paget cells" with abundant clear/pale cytoplasm scattered singly or in nests within the epidermis; PAS-positive, mucin-positive
- Key distinguishing point from breast Paget's disease: vulvar Paget's is usually a **primary intraepithelial adenocarcinoma confined to the epidermis** and is **less often** associated with an underlying invasive adenocarcinoma (though this should still be excluded), whereas breast Paget's is almost always associated with underlying DCIS or invasive ductal carcinoma
- Management: wide local excision; must exclude underlying invasive carcinoma or associated visceral malignancy

**Q33. Discuss Cervical Carcinoma: Risk Factors, Pathogenesis, Morphology, Grading & Staging** *(highest-yield essay — likely 20 marks)*

**Risk factors:**
- High-risk HPV infection (16, 18) — essential cause
- Multiple sexual partners / early coitarche
- Smoking
- Immunosuppression (HIV/AIDS, transplant patients)
- Multiparity
- Low socioeconomic status / lack of screening
- Long-term oral contraceptive use

**Pathogenesis:**
- HPV E6 protein degrades p53 → loss of apoptosis/DNA damage response
- HPV E7 protein degrades RB → loss of G1/S checkpoint control
- Combined effect: unregulated proliferation of infected basal squamous cells at the transformation zone
- Progresses through cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) stages before becoming invasive

**Morphology:**
- Precursor lesions (CIN) confined to epithelium, graded by depth of dysplastic cell involvement
- Invasive carcinoma: most commonly squamous cell carcinoma (~80%), arising at the squamocolumnar transformation zone; less commonly adenocarcinoma
- Gross: exophytic (fungating) or ulcerative/infiltrative mass; may be clinically inapparent (microinvasive)

**Grading (CIN system — based on depth of dysplastic epithelium):**
- CIN I — dysplasia confined to lower 1/3 of epithelium (mild dysplasia; often regresses)
- CIN II — dysplasia extends to lower 2/3 (moderate dysplasia)
- CIN III — full-thickness dysplasia without invasion (severe dysplasia/carcinoma in situ)
- Invasive carcinoma — dysplastic cells breach the basement membrane

**Staging (FIGO, simplified):**
- Stage 0 — carcinoma in situ (CIN III, no invasion)
- Stage I — confined to the cervix
- Stage II — extends beyond cervix but not to pelvic wall or lower 1/3 of vagina
- Stage III — extends to pelvic wall and/or lower 1/3 of vagina, and/or causes hydronephrosis
- Stage IV — extends beyond the true pelvis, or involves bladder/rectal mucosa, or distant metastasis

**Screening/prevention:** Pap smear, HPV DNA testing, HPV vaccination (Gardasil) targeting types 16, 18, 6, 11

---

# MALE REPRODUCTIVE & BREAST PATHOLOGY (standard curriculum — revise alongside textbook)

**5 causes of testicular infertility**
- Cryptorchidism (undescended testis)
- Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)
- Varicocele
- Testicular torsion (if untreated/delayed)
- Post-infectious (mumps orchitis)
- *(Bonus)* Chemotherapy/radiation-induced germ cell damage

**Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)**
- Arises in the **transition zone** of the prostate (surrounds urethra)
- Driven by **DHT** (dihydrotestosterone, via 5α-reductase conversion of testosterone)
- Causes nodular hyperplasia of glandular and stromal tissue → urethral compression → urinary symptoms (hesitancy, frequency, weak stream)
- Does **not** increase risk of prostate cancer (different zone, different pathogenesis)

**Prostate carcinoma**

- Arises in the **peripheral zone** (posterior lobe) — palpable on digital rectal exam
- Graded by the **Gleason grading system** (architectural pattern-based, most common + second most common pattern scored 1-5 each, summed for total score)
- **PSA** used for screening (not fully specific — also raised in BPH/prostatitis)
- Often multifocal; spreads to bone (osteoblastic metastases) characteristically

**Cryptorchidism**
- Failure of testicular descent into the scrotum
- Associated with **increased infertility risk** (impaired spermatogenesis from higher intra-abdominal temperature)
- Associated with **increased malignancy risk** (germ cell tumours) — risk persists even after surgical correction (orchiopexy), though correction reduces the risk somewhat and allows earlier tumour detection

**Testicular tumours**
- **Seminoma** — most common testicular germ cell tumour, **radiosensitive**, good prognosis, uniform cells resembling primordial germ cells (same lineage as ovarian dysgerminoma)
- **Non-seminomatous germ cell tumours** — more aggressive:
 — Embryonal carcinoma
 — Yolk sac tumour (AFP marker; most common testicular tumour in infants/children)
 — Choriocarcinoma (β-hCG marker, early haematogenous spread)
 — Teratoma

**Varicocele**
- Dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus
- Classically **left-sided** — due to the left testicular vein draining at a right angle into the left renal vein (higher pressure), versus the right testicular vein draining obliquely and directly into the IVC
- Causes a "bag of worms" scrotal swelling; associated with subfertility due to increased scrotal temperature

**Testicular torsion**
- Surgical emergency — twisting of the spermatic cord cuts off blood supply
- Sudden severe scrotal pain, **absent cremasteric reflex** is a key clinical sign
- Time-critical: irreversible ischemic damage within hours; requires emergency surgical detorsion

**Fibroadenoma**
- Most common **benign** breast tumour, typically in young women (teens-30s)
- Well-circumscribed, mobile, painless mass ("breast mouse")
- Biphasic proliferation of stromal and glandular epithelial elements

**Fibrocystic change**
- Most common benign breast condition overall (not a true neoplasm)
- Cystic dilation of ducts, apocrine metaplasia, fibrosis; fluctuates with menstrual cycle
- Some subtypes (e.g. with atypical hyperplasia) carry increased future cancer risk

**Invasive ductal vs invasive lobular carcinoma**

- **Invasive ductal carcinoma** — most common type of breast cancer overall; forms a firm, irregular mass
- **Invasive lobular carcinoma** — characteristically **bilateral**, grows in a **single-file ("Indian file") pattern**, associated with **loss of E-cadherin** expression (unlike ductal, which retains E-cadherin)

**Paget's disease of the breast**
- Eczematous, crusted change of the **nipple/areola**
- Almost always associated with an underlying **ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)** or invasive ductal carcinoma
- Paget cells (large, clear, malignant cells) infiltrate the epidermis of the nipple, spreading from the underlying carcinoma via the lactiferous ducts

**Breast cancer risk factors**
- BRCA1/2 mutations (impaired homologous recombination DNA repair)
- Early menarche / late menopause (prolonged oestrogen exposure)
- Nulliparity
- Family history
- Obesity (postmenopausal), alcohol use, prior chest radiation

**Receptor status and treatment implications**
- **ER/PR-positive** → responsive to hormonal therapy (e.g. tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors)
- **HER2-positive** → responsive to targeted anti-HER2 therapy (e.g. trastuzumab/Herceptin)
- **Triple-negative** (ER-, PR-, HER2-) → most aggressive subtype, no targeted hormonal/HER2 therapy available, relies on chemotherapy

Fair question — let me match it to the exact Q33 format/depth (that one was explicitly flagged as the 20-mark model), continuing the numbering, and be honest about what actually earns 20 marks.
Q34. Discuss Prostate Carcinoma: Risk Factors, Pathogenesis, Morphology, Grading & Staging
**Risk factors:**
- Age >50 (strongest factor)
- Black race — higher incidence and mortality
- Family history / genetics (BRCA2, HOXB13)
- Androgen dependence (testosterone/DHT drive growth)
- High animal fat diet
- Geographic factors (higher in Western countries)
**Pathogenesis:**
- Arises in the **peripheral zone** (vs BPH — transition zone)
- Precursor lesion: high-grade **Prostatic Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PIN)**
- **TMPRSS2-ERG gene fusion** in ~50% of cases → overexpression of ERG oncogene
- **PTEN loss** → activates PI3K/AKT pathway → uncontrolled proliferation/survival
- **MYC amplification**
- **Androgen receptor (AR) signalling** drives growth throughout the disease course, including castration-resistant stage
- Progression: PIN → localized carcinoma → local invasion (periprostatic fat, seminal vesicles) → metastasis
- Often multifocal
**Morphology:**
- Gross: firm, irregular, gritty yellow-white areas, poorly demarcated from normal parenchyma
- Micro: small, crowded glands, back-to-back pattern, **loss of basal cell layer** (key diagnostic feature), prominent nucleoli
**Grading:**
- **Gleason system** — primary and secondary architectural patterns each scored 1–5, summed for total (e.g. 3+4=7); newer Grade Groups 1–5 derived from this
**Staging:**
- TNM system — T (local extent: confined/capsule invasion/seminal vesicle invasion/adjacent structures), N (regional nodes), M (distant, especially bone)
**Spread:**
- Local: seminal vesicles, bladder base
- Distant: **osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone metastases** — spine, pelvis, femur — via Batson's venous plexus
**Screening/Diagnosis:**
- PSA (not fully specific — also raised in BPH/prostatitis), DRE, biopsy with Gleason scoring
---
Q35. Discuss Breast Carcinoma: Risk Factors, Pathogenesis, Morphology, Grading & Staging
**Risk factors:**
- BRCA1/2 mutations
- Early menarche / late menopause (prolonged oestrogen exposure)
- Nulliparity
- Family history
- Obesity (postmenopausal), alcohol use, prior chest irradiation
**Pathogenesis:**
- Progression model: normal epithelium → atypical ductal hyperplasia → **DCIS** (confined by intact basement membrane) → invasive ductal carcinoma
- Loss of **E-cadherin** underlies lobular carcinoma's discohesive, single-file growth (ductal carcinoma retains E-cadherin)
- Prolonged unopposed oestrogen exposure promotes proliferative drive
- HER2 gene amplification drives a distinct aggressive subtype
**Morphology:**
- **Invasive ductal carcinoma** (most common, ~70-80%) — firm, irregular, stellate/spiculated mass, gritty cut surface
- **Invasive lobular carcinoma** — bilateral, single-file ("Indian file") infiltration, less often forms a discrete mass
- **Paget's disease of the breast** — eczematous nipple/areola change; Paget cells (large, clear, malignant) infiltrating epidermis, almost always with underlying DCIS/invasive carcinoma
**Grading:**
- **Nottingham (modified Bloom-Richardson) grading** — tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, mitotic count, each scored 1-3, summed into Grade I-III
**Staging:**
- TNM — tumour size, nodal status (axillary), metastasis (bone, lung, liver, brain)
**Receptor status (guides treatment, often asked as part of this essay):**
- ER/PR+ → hormonal therapy (tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors)
- HER2+ → trastuzumab (Herceptin)
- Triple-negative → most aggressive, chemotherapy-only
---
Q36. Discuss Cervical Carcinoma: Risk Factors, Pathogenesis, Morphology, Grading & Staging
*(this is your original Q33 — repeating it here so all three sit together in the same sequence/format)*
**Risk factors:**
- High-risk HPV infection (16, 18) — essential cause
- Multiple sexual partners / early coitarche
- Smoking
- Immunosuppression (HIV/AIDS, transplant patients)
- Multiparity
- Low socioeconomic status / lack of screening
- Long-term oral contraceptive use
**Pathogenesis:**
- HPV **E6** protein degrades **p53** → loss of apoptosis/DNA damage response
- HPV **E7** protein degrades **RB** → loss of G1/S checkpoint control
- Combined effect: unregulated proliferation of infected basal squamous cells at the transformation zone
- Progresses through CIN stages before becoming invasive
**Morphology:**
- Precursor lesions (CIN) confined to epithelium, graded by depth of dysplastic cell involvement
- Invasive carcinoma: most commonly **squamous cell carcinoma (~80%)**, arising at the squamocolumnar transformation zone; less commonly adenocarcinoma
- Gross: exophytic (fungating) or ulcerative/infiltrative mass; may be clinically inapparent (microinvasive)
**Grading (CIN system — depth of dysplastic epithelium):**
- CIN I — lower 1/3 (mild dysplasia; often regresses)
- CIN II — lower 2/3 (moderate dysplasia)
- CIN III — full-thickness dysplasia, no invasion (severe dysplasia/CIS)
- Invasive carcinoma — breach of basement membrane
**Staging (FIGO, simplified):**
- Stage 0 — carcinoma in situ (CIN III, no invasion)
- Stage I — confined to cervix
- Stage II — beyond cervix, not pelvic wall or lower 1/3 vagina
- Stage III — pelvic wall and/or lower 1/3 vagina and/or hydronephrosis
- Stage IV — beyond true pelvis, or bladder/rectal mucosa, or distant metastasis
**Screening/Prevention:**
- Pap smear, HPV DNA testing, HPV vaccination (Gardasil — types 16, 18, 6, 11)
---

articles.content:
# 15 SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (5+ marks)
Q1. Describe the hallmarks of cancer.
- Self-sufficiency in growth signals — RAS locked GTP-active, HER2 overexpression
- Insensitivity to growth inhibitors — RB loss, TGF-β pathway loss
- Evasion of apoptosis — BCL-2↑ blocks cytochrome c; p53 loss removes damage trigger
- Limitless replicative potential — telomerase reactivation bypasses senescence
- Sustained angiogenesis — HIF-1α stabilized by hypoxia → VEGF
- Invasion/metastasis — E-cadherin loss, MMP-driven ECM degradation
- Immune evasion — PD-L1 upregulation inhibits cytotoxic T cells
- (Emerging) Reprogrammed metabolism — Warburg effect, MYC-driven glycolysis
- Conclusion: cumulative, stepwise acquisition of these — not one mutation
Q2. Compare oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes.
- Oncogenes: from proto-oncogenes, gain-of-function, only 1 allele needed (dominant), activating mutation — examples: RAS, HER2, BCR-ABL, MYC
- Tumour suppressors: loss-of-function, both alleles needed (Knudson two-hit), recessive at cell level — examples: RB, p53, APC, BRCA1/2
- Key line: oncogene mutations = activating; TSG mutations = inactivating
Q3. Explain Knudson's two-hit hypothesis using retinoblastoma.
- Both RB alleles must be inactivated for retinoblastoma
- Hereditary: 1st hit germline (present in every cell) → only 1 somatic hit needed → early + bilateral
- Sporadic: both hits must occur in same cell by chance → later + unilateral
- Explains classic clinical pattern; same logic applies to BRCA1/2, APC
Q4. Describe the intrinsic apoptosis pathway and how BCL-2 disrupts it.
- DNA damage/stress activates BAX/BAK
- BAX/BAK form pores in outer mitochondrial membrane
- Cytochrome c released into cytosol
- Cytochrome c + APAF-1 → apoptosome → caspase-9 → caspase-3 → apoptosis
- BCL-2 blocks BAX/BAK → prevents pore formation/cytochrome c release
- Clinical: follicular lymphoma t(14;18) → BCL-2 overexpression → apoptosis resistance
Q5. Outline the steps of tumour invasion and metastasis.
1. Detachment — loss of E-cadherin
2. ECM degradation — MMPs, cathepsins
3. Migration — altered integrins, cytoskeletal remodeling
4. Intravasation — entry into blood/lymphatics
5. Survival in circulation — evade anoikis, immune surveillance (PD-L1)
6. Extravasation — exit vessel at distant site
7. Colonization — proliferation + new angiogenesis (VEGF)
Q6. Differentiate the major patterns of inheritance with examples.
- AD: 1 allele sufficient, vertical transmission, every generation, 50% risk — Huntington, Marfan
- AR: both alleles needed, carrier parents unaffected, skips generations, 25% recurrence — CF, PKU
- X-linked recessive: mostly males affected, carrier mothers, no male-to-male transmission — DMD, Fragile X
- Mitochondrial: maternal transmission to ALL children, fathers transmit none, variable severity (heteroplasmy) — LHON
Q7. Explain genomic imprinting and contrast Prader-Willi with Angelman syndrome.
- Imprinting = gene expressed from only one parental allele, other silenced by methylation
- Same locus: 15q11–13
- Paternal deletion → Prader-Willi — hypotonia, hyperphagia/obesity, intellectual disability, hypogonadism
- Maternal deletion → Angelman — severe intellectual disability, ataxia, seizures, inappropriate laughter
- Teaching point: same region, opposite parent-of-origin, opposite disease
Q8. Describe the karyotype and clinical features of Turner, Klinefelter, Down, and Edwards syndromes.
- Turner (45,X): short stature, webbed neck, streak ovaries, coarctation of aorta, primary amenorrhea
- Klinefelter (47,XXY): tall, gynecomastia, small testes, infertile, ↓testosterone ↑LH/FSH
- Down (Trisomy 21): simian crease, AV septal defect, ↑leukemia risk, hypotonia, early Alzheimer's
- Edwards (Trisomy 18): micrognathia, clenched fists, CHD, rocker-bottom feet, poor prognosis
- (Patau, Trisomy 13, if asked): cleft lip/palate, holoprosencephaly, polydactyly, CHD, poor prognosis
Q9. Differentiate endometriosis from adenomyosis.
- Endometriosis: glands/stroma OUTSIDE uterus (ovary, peritoneum) → chocolate cysts, cyclic pelvic pain, infertility, "powder-burn" lesions on laparoscopy
- Adenomyosis: glands/stroma WITHIN the myometrium → diffusely enlarged boggy uterus, dysmenorrhea + menorrhagia, typically multiparous women 40s
- Key distinguishing point: location of ectopic tissue determines the different clinical pattern
Q10. Outline the grades of endometrial hyperplasia and their malignant potential.
- Cause: unopposed oestrogen (no balancing progesterone) — risk factors: obesity, PCOS, nulliparity, early menarche/late menopause, oestrogen-only HRT
- Simple hyperplasia without atypia — mild crowding, low risk
- Complex hyperplasia without atypia — glandular crowding/complexity, still low-moderate risk
- Hyperplasia WITH atypia — nuclear atypia, highest risk, direct precursor to endometrial carcinoma
- Progression: unopposed oestrogen → hyperplasia → atypia → carcinoma
Q11. Match the major causes of vaginal discharge/STI to their organism and key features.
- Cottage cheese discharge, itchy, pseudohyphae — Candida albicans
- Frothy green discharge, strawberry cervix — Trichomonas vaginalis
- Thin grey discharge, fishy odour (BV) — Gardnerella vaginalis
- Mucopurulent discharge, intracellular gram-negative diplococci — Neisseria gonorrhoeae
- No cell wall, obligate intracellular, NAAT-detected — Chlamydia trachomatis
- Painless genital ulcer, spirochetes on dark-field — Treponema pallidum
Q12. Compare chronic bronchitis and emphysema.
- Chronic bronchitis: productive cough ≥3 months for 2 consecutive years; goblet cell/mucus gland hyperplasia; clinical picture = "blue bloater"
- Emphysema: destruction of alveolar walls, loss of elastic recoil, no significant fibrosis; clinical picture = "pink puffer"
- Shared cause: smoking; shared result: airflow obstruction (COP
D)
Q13. Describe the pathological phases of ARDS.
- Exudative phase: hyaline membranes, interstitial/intra-alveolar oedema and haemorrhage, neutrophil collections, alveolar epithelial necrosis
- Proliferative/organizing phase: fibrin exudate organization, type II pneumocyte proliferation
- Fibrotic phase: interstitial fibrosis in prolonged/severe cases
- Common triggers: sepsis, aspiration, pancreatitis, trauma, fat embolism
Q14. Outline the major lung carcinoma types, location, histology, and associations.
- Squamous cell carcinoma: central, keratin pearls + intercellular bridges, strongly smoking-linked
- Adenocarcinoma: peripheral, gland formation/mucin, EGFR mutation common in non-smokers, associated with clubbing
- Small cell carcinoma: central, neuroendocrine markers, aggressive, paraneoplastic SIADH/Cushing/Lambert-Eaton
- Large cell carcinoma: peripheral, undifferentiated
Q15. Describe the pathogenesis of cirrhosis and its major causes.
- Causes: viral hepatitis B/C (most common worldwide), alcohol (most common cause in the West), NAFLD/steatosis, autoimmune hepatitis, biliary disease, Wilson disease, haemochromatosis
- Sequence: chronic hepatocyte injury → stellate cell activation → fibrosis (bridging) → regenerative nodules → architectural distortion → portal hypertension
- Complications: portal hypertension, varices, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatocellular carcinoma risk

---

# 5 MUST-KNOW ESSAYS (point form)

**E1. Discuss the molecular pathogenesis of cancer.**
- Oncogene activation: RAS, HER2, MYC — 1 hit, gain of function
- Tumour suppressor loss: p53, RB, APC, BRCA1/2 — 2 hits, loss of function
- Evasion of apoptosis: BCL-2↑ blocking cytochrome c release
- Immortalization: telomerase reactivation
- Angiogenesis: VEGF/HIF-1α
- Immune evasion: PD-L1↑
- Conclusion: cancer = multi-step accumulation across all these pathways

**E2. Discuss the classification of genetic disorders.**
- Chromosomal — numerical (Down, Turner, Klinefelter) or structural deletions (Cri-du-chat)
- Single-gene/Mendelian — AD (Marfan, Huntington), AR (CF, PKU), X-linked (DMD, Fragile X)
- Mitochondrial — LHON, maternal inheritance, heteroplasmy
- Multifactorial/polygenic — T2DM, hypertension, cleft lip; gene + environment; recurrence risk ∝ relatedness
- Close with: role of genetic counselling and predictive testing

**E3. Discuss the pathogenesis of COPD (chronic bronchitis and emphysema).**
- Smoking → protease-antiprotease imbalance (neutrophil elastase > α1-antitrypsin) → alveolar wall destruction → emphysema
- Smoking → chronic irritation → goblet cell/mucus gland hyperplasia → chronic bronchitis
- Both → airflow obstruction, hyperinflation, V/Q mismatch → hypoxia → cor pulmonale
- Complications: infections, pneumothorax, respiratory failure, cor pulmonale

**E4. Discuss the pathogenesis of colorectal carcinoma.**
- Adenoma-carcinoma sequence: APC loss → small adenoma → KRAS mutation → large adenoma → p53 loss → carcinoma (chromosomal instability pathway, ~80%)
- Microsatellite instability pathway: MLH1/MSH2 defects → Lynch syndrome, right-sided, less polyp-dependent
- FAP: germline APC mutation → thousands of polyps → ~100% cancer risk without colectomy
- Risk factors: age, diet, IBD, family history

**E5. Discuss the aetiology and complications of pelvic inflammatory disease.**
- Main organisms: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis (most common overall)
- Ascending infection: cervix → endometrium → fallopian tubes → peritoneum
- Complications: infertility (tubal scarring/hydrosalpinx), ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, tubo-ovarian abscess, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis)
- Risk factors: multiple partners, young age, no barrier contraception

articles.title: Essential Cardiovascular Pathology: Atherosclerosis to Endoc — Notes
articles.content:
# Year 3 Pathology — Cardiovascular, Respiratory & GI/Hepatobiliary
## SECTION A: CARDIOVASCULAR PATHOLOGY
### A1. Atherosclerosis
- Stages: fatty streak → fibrous plaque → complicated plaque (calcification, ulceration, haemorrhage, thrombosis)
- Complicated plaque causes clinical events: MI, stroke, peripheral vascular disease, aneurysm
- Risk factors: hyperlipidaemia, hypertension, smoking, diabetes, age, male sex, family history
- Pathogenesis (response-to-injury hypothesis): endothelial injury → lipid insudation → macrophage foam cell formation → smooth muscle proliferation → fibrous cap formation
### A2. Myocardial Infarction
| Time after MI | Gross/microscopic change |
|---|---|
| <24 hours | Coagulative necrosis (earliest change) — may look normal grossly |
| 1–3 days | Neutrophil infiltration, yellow pallor |
| 3–7 days | Macrophages clear debris, yellow-tan, soft (weakest point, highest rupture risk) |
| 1–3 weeks | Granulation tissue formation, red-grey border |
| Weeks–months | Collagen scar formation, grey-white, firm |
**Complications by timing:** arrhythmia (first hours, #1 cause of death) → cardiogenic shock → papillary muscle rupture (day 3–5) → free wall rupture (day 4–7, coincides with softest phase above) → ventricular aneurysm (weeks–months, in the scarred phase)
### A3. Dilated Cardiomyopathy
- Cardiomegaly, all four chambers dilated; dilation predominates over hypertrophy
- Mural thrombi common in dilated chambers (embolism risk)
- Microscopic: non-specific myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis
- Functional consequence: systolic (contractile) dysfunction → congestive heart failure
- Causes: idiopathic (most common), viral myocarditis (esp. Coxsackie B), alcohol, peripartum, genetic, doxorubicin toxicity
**Compare with:**
- *Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy* — diastolic dysfunction, asymmetric septal hypertrophy, myocyte disarray, cause of sudden death in young athletes
- *Restrictive cardiomyopathy* — diastolic dysfunction from myocardial infiltration (amyloid, sarcoidosis)
### A4. Vasculitis — Classified by Vessel Size
| Vessel size | Examples |
|---|---|
| Large | Takayasu arteritis (young Asian women, aortic arch); Giant cell/temporal arteritis (elderly, headache, jaw claudication, blindness risk) |
| Medium | Polyarteritis nodosa (necrotising, Hep B-associated); Kawasaki disease (children, coronary artery aneurysms) |
| Small | Granulomatosis with polyangiitis/Wegener's (c-ANCA, upper/lower respiratory + renal); Microscopic polyangiitis (p-ANC
A) |
### A5. Rheumatic Heart Disease
**Pathogenesis:** follows untreated Group A streptococcal pharyngitis; molecular mimicry — antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac tissue; acute rheumatic fever → chronic RHD with repeated episodes
**Morphology:**
- Aschoff bodies — pathognomonic granulomatous lesions containing Anitschkow cells, found in myocardium
- Mitral valve most commonly affected → mitral stenosis (fish-mouth/buttonhole deformity)
- Valve changes: leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, chordae tendineae shortening
**Diagnosis (Jones criteria):** Major — carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules. Minor — fever, arthralgia, raised ESR/CRP
### A6. Infective Endocarditis — Acute vs Sub-acute
| Feature | Acute IE | Sub-acute IE |
|---|---|---|
| Organism | Staphylococcus aureus (virulent) | Streptococcus viridans (less virulent) |
| Valve affected | Often previously normal | Usually previously damaged |
| Onset | Rapid, days | Slow, weeks–months |
| Vegetations | Large, destructive | Smaller |
| Course | Severe, rapidly fatal if untreated | Indolent |
**Related non-infective forms:** Non-bacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis — sterile vegetations, associated with malignancy/hypercoagulable states. Libman-Sacks endocarditis — associated with SL
E.
### A7. Pulmonary Thromboembolism
**Pathogenesis:** most emboli arise from DVT of the lower limbs (femoral, iliac veins); Virchow's triad predisposes — venous stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial injury; thrombus dislodges → right heart → pulmonary arteries
**Consequences by size:**
- Small — often asymptomatic/silent
- Large — sudden death via saddle embolus occluding the pulmonary artery bifurcation
- Medium — pulmonary infarction (wedge-shaped, haemorrhagic) if collateral circulation inadequate
- Chronic recurrent — pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale
---
## SECTION B: RESPIRATORY PATHOLOGY
### B1. Emphysema vs Chronic Bronchitis
| Feature | Emphysema (pink puffer) | Chronic bronchitis (blue bloater) |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Permanent airspace enlargement distal to terminal bronchiole, wall destruction | Chronic productive cough ≥3 months, 2 consecutive years |
| Main mechanism | Protease-antiprotease imbalance (↓alpha-1 antitrypsin), elastin destruction | Chronic irritation (smoking) → mucous gland hyperplasia (↑Reid index) |
| Appearance | Thin, breathless, pink complexion | Overweight, cyanotic, oedematous |
| Hypoxia/CO2 retention | Mild, compensates by hyperventilating | Marked hypoxia and CO2 retention |
| Cor pulmonale | Late | Early and more severe |
**Pathogenesis of emphysema:** cigarette smoke recruits neutrophils/macrophages → release proteases (elastase); normally alpha-1 antitrypsin inhibits elastase, but smoking also inactivates it; net effect — unopposed elastase destroys alveolar walls → permanent airspace enlargement. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (genetic) causes early-onset panacinar emphysema, especially lower lobes.
**Types by distribution:** centriacinar/centrilobular (smoking-related, upper lobes) vs panacinar (α1-AT deficiency, lower lobes) vs paraseptal (adjacent to pleura, risk of spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults)
### B2. Asthma — Bronchiole Changes (5 features)
- Bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy
- Mucous gland hyperplasia with mucus plugging
- Basement membrane thickening
- Eosinophilic infiltration of the airway wall
- Curschmann spirals (mucus casts) and Charcot-Leyden crystals (eosinophil breakdown products) in sputum
**Pathogenesis (Type I hypersensitivity):** allergen exposure → IgE sensitisation of mast cells → re-exposure → mast cell degranulation → early phase (bronchospasm, minutes) and late phase (inflammatory cell recruitment, hours later — drives the chronic airway remodelling above)
### B3. Diffuse Alveolar Damage / ARDS (5 histomorphological features)
- Hyaline membrane formation lining alveolar walls (protein-rich exudate)
- Alveolar septal oedema and congestion
- Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia (regenerative response)
- Interstitial and intra-alveolar inflammatory infiltrate
- Progression to interstitial fibrosis in the organising phase
**Causes:** sepsis, aspiration, severe trauma, pneumonia, pancreatitis
**Phases:** exudative (hyaline membranes, oedema; days 1–7) → proliferative (type II pneumocyte hyperplasia, organising; week 1–3) → fibrotic (if unresolved; weeks+)
### B4. Pneumoconioses — Classification
- Coal worker's pneumoconiosis — carbon dust, upper lobes, "black lung"
- Silicosis — silica dust (mining, quarrying), upper lobes, egg-shell calcification of hilar nodes, increased TB risk
- Asbestosis — asbestos fibres, **lower lobes**, ferruginous bodies, risk of mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma
- Berylliosis — beryllium exposure, non-caseating granulomas (mimics sarcoidosis)
*Note: asbestos is the odd one out — lower lobes, and the only one strongly linked to mesothelioma (a pleural tumour, not a lung tumour). Common exam trap.*
### B5. Nasal Polyps (5 histomorphological features)
- Oedematous stroma
- Eosinophilic inflammatory infiltrate
- Thickened basement membrane
- Covered by respiratory (ciliated columnar) epithelium
- Absence of malignant features (benign lesion)
Associated with allergic rhinitis, chronic sinusitis, asthma, aspirin sensitivity — **Samter's triad**: asthma + nasal polyps + aspirin sensitivity
### B6. Lung Carcinoma
| Type | Location | Key features |
|---|---|---|
| Squamous cell carcinoma | Central | Strongly smoking-associated, keratin pearls, may cavitate |
| Adenocarcinoma | Peripheral | Most common overall (incl. non-smokers), glandular pattern |
| Small cell carcinoma | Central | Neuroendocrine, worst prognosis, strongly paraneoplastic |
| Large cell carcinoma | Peripheral | Undifferentiated, poor prognosis |
**5 paraneoplastic syndromes:**
1. SIADH (small cell) — hyponatraemia
2. Ectopic ACTH secretion (small cell) — Cushing's syndrome
3. Hypercalcaemia via PTHrP (squamous cell)
4. Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (small cell) — autoantibodies against presynaptic calcium channels
5. Clubbing / hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (adenocarcinoma)
### B7. Tuberculosis
**Pathogenesis:** inhalation of M. tuberculosis droplets → alveolar macrophages phagocytose but fail to kill initially → cell-mediated (Type IV) hypersensitivity develops over 2–4 weeks → granuloma formation walls off the organism — Ghon focus (primary lesion, subpleural, mid/lower zone); Ghon focus + hilar lymph node = Ghon complex → outcome: contained (latent T
B) or, if immunocompromised, progresses to active/miliary TB
**Morphology:** caseating granulomas — central caseous necrosis surrounded by epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells, lymphocytes. Secondary/reactivation TB typically apical, due to higher oxygen tension favouring the organism.
**Clinical presentation:** chronic cough >2 weeks, haemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, low-grade fever
**Diagnosis:** Ziehl-Neelsen stain (gold standard for acid-fast bacilli), sputum culture, GeneXpert
---
## SECTION C: GI / HEPATOBILIARY PATHOLOGY
### C1. Alcoholic Liver Disease — Progressive Spectrum
- Hepatic steatosis (fatty liver) — reversible, macrovesicular fat accumulation
- Alcoholic hepatitis — hepatocyte swelling/ballooning, Mallory-Denk bodies (eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions), neutrophilic infiltrate, perivenular fibrosis
- Cirrhosis — irreversible, diffuse fibrosis with regenerative nodules, typically micronodular
### C2. Pancreatitis — Aetiology
Gallstones (commonest, obstruct ampulla of Vater); alcohol (second commonest); hypertriglyceridaemia; hypercalcaemia; drugs (thiazides, azathioprine); trauma/post-ERCP; idiopathic
**Mnemonic — I GET SMASHED:** Idiopathic, Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion sting, Hyperlipidaemia/Hypercalcaemia, ERCP, Drugs
**Key complication:** hypocalcaemia = poor prognostic sign (fat saponification consumes calcium)
### C3. Barrett's Oesophagus — Pathogenesis
- Chronic GERD exposes lower oesophageal squamous epithelium to acid
- Chronic injury triggers metaplasia — squamous epithelium replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal-type metaplasia)
- Protective adaptation to acid, but premalignant
- Progresses through dysplasia (low-grade → high-grade) → risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma
### C4. Gallstones — Types Compared
| Type | Composition | Risk factors |
|---|---|---|
| Cholesterol (most common, developed countries) | Cholesterol | "5 F's": Female, Fat, Forty, Fertile, Family history |
| Pigment (black) | Unconjugated bilirubin | Haemolytic conditions (sickle cell, spherocytosis) |
| Pigment (brown) | Calcium bilirubinate | Biliary infection/infestation (e.g. Clonorchis) |
| Mixed | Cholesterol + pigment | Most common overall |
### C5. Colorectal Carcinoma
**Pathogenesis — adenoma-carcinoma (Vogelstein) sequence:**
Normal epithelium → APC gene mutation → adenoma formation → KRAS mutation → adenoma growth/progression → p53 mutation → invasive carcinoma
**Alternative pathway:** Lynch syndrome/HNPCC follows the microsatellite instability pathway (mismatch repair gene mutations — MLH1, MSH2), distinct from the APC/chromosomal instability pathway above
**Morphology:** most arise in the rectosigmoid region; annular "napkin-ring" lesions in the left colon (obstructive); polypoid fungating masses in the right colon (bleeding, anaemia)
**Clinical presentation:**
- Left-sided — change in bowel habit, obstruction, blood-streaked stool
- Right-sided — iron deficiency anaemia, occult bleeding, vague abdominal pain (presents later, wider lumen)
**Risk factors:** familial adenomatous polyposis (APC gene), Lynch syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, low-fibre/high-fat diet, age
### C6. H. pylori Gastritis — Pathogenesis
- Colonises the gastric antrum, produces urease (neutralises acid locally) and cytotoxins (CagA, Vac
A)
- Triggers chronic inflammation — initially neutrophilic (active), then chronic lymphocytic/plasma cell infiltrate
- Damages mucosal barrier → predisposes to peptic ulcer disease
- Chronic infection → intestinal metaplasia → risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma
### C7. Crohn's Disease vs Ulcerative Colitis
| Feature | Crohn's disease | Ulcerative colitis |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Anywhere mouth to anus (commonly terminal ileum) | Colon only, starts at rectum |
| Distribution | Skip lesions | Continuous |
| Depth | Transmural | Mucosal only |
| Gross appearance | Cobblestone mucosa, strictures | Continuous ulceration, pseudopolyps |
| Granulomas | Present (non-caseating) | Absent |
| Complications | Fistulas, strictures, malabsorption | Toxic megacolon, ↑colorectal cancer risk (higher than Crohn's) |
### C8. Bilirubin Metabolism Disorders
- Crigler-Najjar type II — reduced UGT activity
- Dubin-Johnson syndrome — conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, black liver pigmentation on gross examination
- Gilbert syndrome — mild UGT deficiency, unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, benign, very common
- Rotor syndrome — conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, **no** black liver pigmentation (key differentiator from Dubin-Johnson)
---
## PAST PAPER QUESTIONS — QUICK INDEX
**Cardiovascular:** Q1 Dilated cardiomyopathy morphology (A3) · Q2 Vasculitis classification (A4) · Q3 Rheumatic heart disease (A5) · Q4 Acute vs sub-acute IE (A6) · Q5 Pulmonary thromboemboli (A7) · Q6 Atherosclerosis stages (A1)
**Respiratory:** Q7 Paraneoplastic syndromes (B6) · Q8 Asthma bronchiole changes (B2) · Q9 DAD features (B3) · Q10 Emphysema pathogenesis (B1) · Q11 Pneumoconioses classification (B4) · Q12 Nasal polyps features (B5) · Q13 Emphysema vs bronchitis (B1) · Q14 ARDS morphology (B3) · Q15 Lung carcinoma classification (B6) · Q16 TB pathogenesis/morphology/presentation (B7)
**GI/Hepatobiliary:** Q17 Alcoholic liver disease (C1) · Q18 Pancreatitis aetiology (C2) · Q19 Barrett's oesophagus (C3) · Q20 Gallstone types (C4) · Q21 Colorectal carcinoma (C5) · Q22 H. pylori gastritis (C6)
