articles.title: Bone & Soft Tissue Tumour Pathology: Must-Know Diagnoses — CAT
articles.content:
Bone & Soft Tissue Pathology — Must-Knows
---
## Soft Tissue Tumours — Fat, Fibrous, Muscle**Lipoma vs liposarcoma**
- Lipoma: mature fat cells, thin capsule, benign — the most common soft tissue tumour overall
- Well-differentiated liposarcoma: looks almost identical to lipoma under the microscope, but is malignant — the only way to tell them apart is a genetic test showing MDM2/CDK4 gene amplification (region 12q13-15)
- Myxoid liposarcoma: has a jelly-like (myxoid) background plus immature fat cells called lipoblasts; caused by a specific gene fusion, t(12;16) FUS-DDIT3
- Pleomorphic liposarcoma: the most aggressive type, cells look wildly different from each other (pleomorphic)

**Nodular fasciitis — the great impersonator**

- Grows fast, has lots of dividing cells (mitoses) — looks alarming, like cancer
- But it's actually benign and self-limiting (goes away on its own)
- Caused by a gene fusion: t(17;22) MYH9-USP6
- Exam trap: don't call this a sarcoma just because it grows fast and has mitoses

**Desmoid tumour (deep fibromatosis)**

- Grows into surrounding tissue (locally invasive) but never spreads to distant organs (no metastasis)
- Linked to a faulty APC gene — same gene that's faulty in familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), a condition causing hundreds of colon polyps
- On biopsy: bland-looking fibroblasts, but with abnormal build-up of a protein called beta-catenin inside the nucleus (because APC normally breaks beta-catenin down, and when APC is broken, beta-catenin piles up)

**Rhabdomyosarcoma (skeletal muscle cancer)**

- Embryonal type — most common type in children; the "botryoid" (grape-like) variant grows as clusters in the vagina or bladder of young children
- Look for cross-striations on histology — proof the cells are trying to become muscle

**Leiomyoma vs leiomyosarcoma**

- Leiomyoma: benign smooth muscle tumour, very common in the uterus (fibroids); cells have blunt-ended nuclei and minimal atypia
- Leiomyosarcoma: malignant version, seen in deep sites like the retroperitoneum; markers SMA and desmin (both smooth muscle markers) are positive, but the cells look atypical and hyperchromatic

**Synovial sarcoma**

- Confusing name — it does NOT come from the joint synovium
- Occurs near joints in young adults, grows slowly over years
- Defining feature: a translocation, t(X;18) SS18-SSX

**Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS)**

- This is a "leftover" diagnosis — given only when a high-grade sarcoma doesn't show any specific line of differentiation on special stains (not fat, not muscle, not anything specific)

---

## Nerve Sheath Tumours**Schwannoma**
- Comes from Schwann cells (which make the myelin sheath around peripheral nerves)
- Encapsulated (has a clear boundary), painless
- Classic histology: Antoni A areas (densely packed cells) and Antoni B areas (loose, myxoid) — plus Verocay bodies (rows of nuclei lined up around a pale zone)
- Positive for S100 stain

**Neurofibroma types — and how they link to NF1 vs NF2**

- Localised cutaneous neurofibroma: a single small nodule in the skin
- Diffuse neurofibroma: spreads more broadly through the dermis
- Plexiform neurofibroma: grows along the length of a nerve, looks like a "bag of worms" — this type is specifically linked to NF1, and carries a 15-20% lifetime risk of turning into a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST)
- NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) → neurofibromas are the hallmark
- NF2 (neurofibromatosis type 2) → bilateral schwannomas (especially in the internal auditory canal, causing hearing loss) are the hallmark instead — don't mix these two up

---

## Bone Tumours**Osteosarcoma**
- Most common in teenagers, at the distal femur (metaphysis, near the knee)
- Look for: a Codman triangle on X-ray (a triangular shadow where the tumour lifts the periosteum off the bone) and a mixed lytic (bone-destroying) and sclerotic (bone-forming) pattern

**Osteoid osteoma vs osteoblastoma — same family, different size**

- Osteoid osteoma: small (under 2cm), causes severe night pain that is dramatically relieved by aspirin (because the tumour produces prostaglandins, which aspirin blocks) — commonly in the proximal tibia
- Osteoblastoma: essentially a bigger version (over 2cm), often in the posterior elements of the spine, but does NOT respond dramatically to aspirin the way osteoid osteoma does

**Osteochondroma**

- A painless bony bump that grows outward from the metaphysis
- Key finding: the medullary cavity (the hollow center of the bone) is continuous with the tumour's own cavity — proving it's really just an outgrowth of normal bone with a cartilage cap on top

**Chondrosarcoma**

- A malignant tumour made of cartilage-producing cells
- Classic site: pelvis or axial skeleton (unlike osteosarcoma, which favours long bone metaphyses)

**Ewing sarcoma**

- Occurs in adolescents, made of small round blue cells (very immature-looking cells with little cytoplasm)
- Defining translocation: t(11;22) EWS-FLI1
- Positive for CD99 marker

**Fibrous dysplasia**

- Caused by a GNAS gene mutation
- On X-ray/histology, the bone trabeculae look like "Chinese letters" — an odd, curved shape

---

## Bone Infection and Death**Osteomyelitis**
- Bacterial infection of bone, most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus
- In children, it typically starts in the metaphysis (because blood flow there is sluggish, letting bacteria settle)
- Chronic osteomyelitis can form a sinus tract (a channel to the skin surface) containing a piece of dead bone
- Sequestrum = the dead piece of bone
- Involucrum = new bone that grows around the sequestrum to try to wall it off
- Easy to confuse these two — sequestrum is dead, involucrum is the new living shell around it

**Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis)**

- Death of bone due to loss of blood supply
- Classic cause: prolonged high-dose corticosteroid use
- Classic site: femoral head, seen on MRI as subchondral collapse (the bone surface just under the joint caves in)

---

## Joint Disease**Osteoarthritis**
- "Wear and tear" — pain worsens with activity, improves with rest
- X-ray triad: joint space narrowing (cartilage loss) + osteophytes (bone spurs) + subchondral sclerosis (dense bone just under the joint surface)

**Rheumatoid arthritis**

- Autoimmune, affects small joints symmetrically (both hands, MCP and PIP joints)
- Blood test: positive anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPA), raised ESR

**Ankylosing spondylitis**

- Affects the spine, causes stiffness and reduced mobility
- Strongly linked to the HLA-B27 gene

**Gout vs pseudogout — the crystal difference is everything**

- Gout: caused by monosodium urate crystals, which look needle-shaped and are negatively birefringent under polarized light; classic site is the big toe (first MTP joint), often in obese men
- Pseudogout: caused by calcium pyrophosphate (CPP
D) crystals, which look rhomboid-shaped and are positively birefringent — easy to mix up with gout if you don't remember the crystal shape/birefringence difference

---
## Nerve and Muscle Disease**Guillain-Barré syndrome**
- Ascending weakness (starts in the legs, moves upward) and loss of reflexes
- Often follows a Campylobacter jejuni gut infection
- CSF shows raised protein but a normal cell count — this specific combo is called albuminocytologic dissociation

**Axonal vs demyelinating neuropathy — read the nerve conduction study**

- Axonal damage → reduced amplitude (fewer working axons), but conduction velocity stays roughly normal
- Demyelinating damage → reduced velocity (signal travels slower without myelin), amplitude may be preserved
- Diabetic neuropathy is a classic example of axonal damage

**Myasthenia gravis vs Lambert-Eaton — opposite mechanisms**

- Myasthenia gravis: antibodies attack acetylcholine receptors AFTER the nerve-muscle junction (postsynaptic); weakness gets WORSE with repeated muscle use
- Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome: antibodies attack calcium channels BEFORE the junction (presynaptic), often as a paraneoplastic syndrome from small cell lung cancer; weakness actually IMPROVES briefly with repeated use, because each contraction pushes a bit more calcium into the nerve terminal
- Learn them as mirror opposites — that's exactly how they're tested

**Dermatomyositis vs polymyositis vs inclusion body myositis**

- Dermatomyositis: inflammation clusters around blood vessels and at the edges of muscle bundles (perifascicular atrophy) — thought to be an antibody-driven, vessel-based process; often paraneoplastic (linked to an underlying cancer) in adults
- Inclusion body myositis: seen in older patients (over 50), affects the quadriceps and wrist flexors, shows rimmed vacuoles on biopsy
- Polymyositis: inflammation is inside the muscle fascicle (endomysial), driven directly by T-cells

**Botulinum toxin**

- Blocks the release of acetylcholine from the nerve terminal (presynaptic) — this is why it paralyzes muscle

**Leprosy**

- Mycobacterium leprae specifically invades Schwann cells, causing segmental demyelination — this is why leprosy causes nerve damage and sensory loss in the skin

---

## Histopathology Technique (comes up almost every CAT)**Tissue processing order — memorize this sequence exactly**
- Fixation (10% formalin — stops decay, preserves structure)
- Dehydration (increasing strengths of alcohol, removes water)
- Clearing (xylene — replaces alcohol with something wax-compatible)
- Embedding (paraffin wax — gives the tissue a firm block to cut)
- Sectioning (microtome, usually 4-5 μm thick)
- Staining
- Mounting

**Why fixation matters**

- Stops autolysis (the tissue's own enzymes digesting itself) — this is different from putrefaction, which is bacterial decomposition, not the tissue's own enzymes

**Special stains — match the stain to what it shows**

- H&E: routine stain — nuclei blue-purple, cytoplasm pink
- PAS (Periodic Acid-Schiff): basement membranes, glycogen — bright magenta
- Masson's trichrome: collagen/fibrosis — shows up blue/green against red muscle
- Congo red: amyloid — shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light (this is the gold-standard test for amyloidosis)
- Ziehl-Neelsen: acid-fast bacilli (T
B)

---
## Oral Pathology- Oral squamous cell carcinoma (HPV-negative type, linked to smoking/alcohol): classic site is the ventral tongue and floor of mouth, where carcinogens pool in saliva
- Erythroplakia (red patch) carries a much higher cancer risk than leukoplakia (white patch) — red lesions are more likely to already show severe dysplasia
- Pyogenic granuloma: a fast-growing, bleeding gum mass in pregnant women (nicknamed "pregnancy tumour") — hormone-driven
- Aphthous ulcers: shallow, painful, self-healing within about 10 days
- Oral candidiasis: white plaques that scrape off to reveal red, raw mucosa underneath — common in chemotherapy patients
- Keratocystic odontogenic tumour: a jaw cyst with a corrugated keratin lining, tends to recur after removal

articles.title: Master Bone & Soft Tissue Pathology: CAT 2 MCQs & Answers — CAT 2025
articles.content:
## PAPER INTRODUCTION

**Mount Kenya University — School of Medicine**
- Programme: Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery, Year 3
- Unit: Bone and Soft Tissue Pathology
- Assessment: Continuous Assessment Test (CAT 2), End of Semester 3
- Two versions here: **June 2025 CAT** (30 MCQs — soft tissue/nerve/muscle) and **June 2026 CAT** (30 MCQs + 2 SAQs — bone/joint/histotech/oral pathology)
- Format: 30 MCQs, choose most correct answer, 22 minutes

---

## SET 1 — JUNE 2025 CAT

**Q1.** A 45-year-old woman presents with a 5 cm, soft, mobile, painless subcutaneous mass on her thigh. Histology shows mature adipocytes with a thin fibrous capsule. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Lipoma
B) Hibernoma
C) Conventional liposarcoma
D) Epidermal inclusion cyst
E) Dermatofibroma

**Answer: A — Lipoma**
Explanation: Classic benign fatty tumour — mature adipocytes, thin capsule, no atypia. Commonest soft tissue tumour overall.

---

**Q2.** A 64-year-old man has a deep-seated thigh mass; biopsy reveals atypical adipocytes and amplification of the 12q13–q15 region including MDM2. Which subtype of liposarcoma is most likely?
A) Myxoid liposarcoma
B) Well-differentiated liposarcoma
C) Pleomorphic liposarcoma
D) Round-cell liposarcoma
E) Dedifferentiated liposarcoma

**Answer: B — Well-differentiated liposarcoma**
Explanation: MDM2/CDK4 amplification at 12q13-15 is the molecular hallmark distinguishing this from benign lipoma — same-looking cells, but genetically malignant.

---

**Q3.** A 25-year-old man develops a rapidly growing 3 cm forearm mass with a history of minor trauma. Histology shows plump fibroblasts, frequent mitoses, and a t(17;22) MYH9–USP6 fusion. What is the diagnosis?
A) Nodular fasciitis
B) Desmoid (deep fibromatosis)
C) Fibrosarcoma
D) Myositis ossificans
E) Schwannoma

**Answer: A — Nodular fasciitis**
Explanation: Rapid growth + high mitotic activity mimics sarcoma, but it's a benign, self-limiting reactive proliferation. MYH9-USP6 fusion is diagnostic.

---

**Q4.** A 30-year-old woman with familial adenomatous polyposis develops an infiltrative abdominal wall mass. Histology shows bland fibroblasts with nuclear β-catenin accumulation. What is the most likely lesion?
A) Dermatofibroma
B) Nodular fasciitis
C) Desmoid tumour (deep fibromatosis)
D) Solitary fibrous tumour
E) Neurofibroma

**Answer: C — Desmoid tumour (deep fibromatosis)**
Explanation: APC mutation (FAP) → unopposed β-catenin accumulation in nucleus → fibroblast proliferation. Locally aggressive, doesn't metastasize.

---

**Q5.** A 6-year-old child presents with a grape-like mass protruding from her vagina. Tumour cells are small, round, and show cross-striations on special stain. Which variant of rhabdomyosarcoma is this?
A) Alveolar
B) Embryonal (sarcoma botryoides)
C) Pleomorphic
D) Spindle cell/sclerosing
E) Botryoid liposarcoma

**Answer: B — Embryonal (sarcoma botryoides)**
Explanation: Botryoid ("grape-like") variant of embryonal RMS occurs in vagina/bladder of young children. Cross-striations = skeletal muscle differentiation (desmin+, myogenin+).

---

**Q6.** An adult presents with a deep retroperitoneal mass composed of interweaving fascicles of hyperchromatic spindle cells, positive for smooth muscle actin and desmin. What is the diagnosis?
A) Rhabdomyosarcoma
B) Leiomyoma
C) Fibrosarcoma
D) Leiomyosarcoma
E) Angiosarcoma

**Answer: D — Leiomyosarcoma**
Explanation: SMA+/desmin+ spindle cells with atypia in a deep/retroperitoneal site = malignant smooth muscle tumour (leiomyomas are rarely retroperitoneal or this atypical).

---

**Q7.** A 28-year-old man has a deep-seated knee mass present for several years. Histology shows uniform spindle cells in short fascicles and a t(X;18) SS18–SSX fusion. Which tumour is this?
A) Synovial sarcoma
B) Nodular fasciitis
C) Liposarcoma
D) Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
E) Desmoid tumour

**Answer: A — Synovial sarcoma**
Explanation: Despite the name, does NOT arise from synovium. t(X;18) SS18-SSX is pathognomonic. Occurs near joints in young adults.

---

**Q8.** A 55-year-old patient has a large, high-grade pleomorphic spindle-cell sarcoma in the thigh with no identifiable line of differentiation. What is the most appropriate classification?
A) Fibrosarcoma
B) Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma
C) Leiomyosarcoma
D) Liposarcoma
E) Rhabdomyosarcoma

**Answer: B — Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma**
Explanation: Diagnosis of exclusion — once IHC rules out muscle, fat, and other specific lineage markers, "no identifiable differentiation" = UPS (formerly called MFH).

---

**Q9.** A patient with neurofibromatosis type 2 develops bilateral cerebellopontine-angle masses causing hearing loss. The lesions are encapsulated, S100-positive, and show Antoni A and B areas. What are these?
A) Neurofibromas
B) Schwannomas
C) Meningiomas
D) Ependymomas
E) Metastatic carcinoma

**Answer: B — Schwannomas**
Explanation: Bilateral vestibular (CP
A) schwannomas = hallmark of NF2 (distinct from NF1, which features neurofibromas). Antoni A (compact) and Antoni B (loose/myxoid) areas are classic.

---

**Q10.** In patients with NF1, what is the approximate lifetime risk of malignant transformation of a plexiform neurofibroma into a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST)?
A) 1–2%
B) 5–10%
C) 15–20%
D) 25–30%
E) >50%

**Answer: C — 15–20%**
Explanation: Key exam number — plexiform (not localized) neurofibromas carry this transformation risk in NF1 patients, unlike the near-zero risk of solitary cutaneous neurofibromas.

---

**Q11.** A 60-year-old man presents with rapidly progressive ascending weakness and areflexia 2 weeks after a Campylobacter jejuni infection. CSF shows elevated protein without pleocytosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
B) Guillain-Barré syndrome
C) Poliomyelitis
D) Botulism
E) Myasthenia gravis

**Answer: B — Guillain-Barré syndrome**
Explanation: Post-infectious (classically Campylobacter) ascending paralysis + albuminocytologic dissociation (↑protein, normal cell count) is the classic GBS triad.

---

**Q12.** A long-standing diabetic patient develops numbness in a stocking-and-glove distribution. Nerve conduction studies show reduced amplitudes with relatively preserved velocities. Which pathological process is most likely?
A) Segmental demyelination
B) Axonal neuropathy
C) Neuronopathy
D) Compression neuropathy
E) Neuromuscular junction blockade

**Answer: B — Axonal neuropathy**
Explanation: Reduced amplitude = axon loss (fewer functioning axons); preserved velocity = myelin still intact. Opposite pattern (↓velocity, preserved amplitude) suggests demyelination.

---

**Q13.** A 35-year-old woman has numbness and tingling of the palmar aspect of her thumb, index, and middle fingers, worse at night. Tinel's and Phalen's signs are positive. Which nerve is compressed?
A) Ulnar nerve at the elbow
B) Radial nerve in the spiral groove
C) Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
D) Saphenous nerve at the ankle
E) Sciatic nerve in the gluteal region

**Answer: C — Median nerve at the carpal tunnel**
Explanation: Classic median nerve sensory distribution (thumb, index, middle, half of ring finger) + positive provocative tests = carpal tunnel syndrome.

---

**Q14.** A 30-year-old woman complains of fluctuating ptosis and diplopia that worsen with exertion. Autoantibodies to the acetylcholine receptor are detected. What is the diagnosis?
A) Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
B) Myasthenia gravis
C) Polymyositis
D) Guillain-Barré syndrome
E) Botulism

**Answer: B — Myasthenia gravis**
Explanation: Anti-AChR antibodies (postsynaptic) → fatigable weakness that worsens with repeated use — opposite pattern to Lambert-Eaton.

---

**Q15.** A 55-year-old man with small cell lung cancer develops proximal muscle weakness that improves transiently after brief exercise. Electrophysiology shows incremental response on rapid repetitive stimulation. What is the cause?
A) Anti-ACh receptor antibodies
B) Anti-presynaptic voltage-gated calcium-channel antibodies
C) Anti-muscle-specific kinase antibodies
D) Sarcolemmal membrane autoantibodies
E) Botulinum toxin poisoning

**Answer: B — Anti-presynaptic voltage-gated calcium-channel antibodies**
Explanation: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome — paraneoplastic (small cell lung Ca), presynaptic defect, improves with exercise (incremental response), unlike MG.

---

**Q16.** A muscle biopsy shows perivascular and perifascicular inflammatory infiltrates with atrophy of fibres at the edges of fascicles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Polymyositis
B) Inclusion body myositis
C) Dermatomyositis

**Answer: C — Dermatomyositis**
Explanation: Perifascicular atrophy pattern + perivascular (not endomysial) inflammation is the defining histologic signature of dermatomyositis (humoral/complement-mediated microangiopathy) vs polymyositis (endomysial, T-cell mediated).

---

**Q17.** A 65-year-old presents with slowly progressive quadriceps and wrist-flexor weakness. Biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles and cytoplasmic inclusions. Which condition is most consistent with these findings?
A) Polymyositis
B) Dermatomyositis
C) Inclusion body myositis
D) Mitochondrial myopathy
E) Lambert-Eaton syndrome

**Answer: C — Inclusion body myositis**
Explanation: Rimmed vacuoles + characteristic distal/quadriceps weakness pattern in an elderly patient = IBM, the most common inflammatory myopathy in patients over 50.

---

**Q18.** A muscle biopsy reveals subsarcolemmal aggregates of mitochondria ("ragged red fibres"). Which mitochondrial disorder is characterised by myoclonus and ragged red fibres?
A) MELAS
B) MERRF
C) Leigh syndrome
D) Kearns-Sayre syndrome
E) Leber hereditary optic neuropathy

**Answer: B — MERRF**
Explanation: Mnemonic match — Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged Red Fibres. MELAS instead features stroke-like episodes + lactic acidosis.

---

**Q19.** A patient with small cell lung carcinoma develops an asymmetric, painful sensory neuropathy affecting dorsal root ganglia with anti-Hu antibodies. What is this presentation?
A) Mononeuropathy multiplex
B) Paraneoplastic sensory neuronopathy
C) Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
D) Guillain-Barré syndrome
E) Idiopathic small-fiber neuropathy

**Answer: B — Paraneoplastic sensory neuronopathy**
Explanation: Anti-Hu antibodies specifically target dorsal root ganglion neurons — classic paraneoplastic syndrome of small cell lung cancer.

---

**Q20.** A patient with HIV develops a distal, symmetric, painful sensory neuropathy unresponsive to antiretroviral therapy. Which mechanism is most likely involved?
A) Direct HIV-mediated cytotoxicity
B) Microvascular ischemia
C) Immune dysregulation and cytokine-mediated damage
D) Opportunistic bacterial infection
E) Vitamin B12 deficiency

**Answer: C — Immune dysregulation and cytokine-mediated damage**
Explanation: HIV-associated sensory neuropathy is driven by immune/cytokine mechanisms (not direct viral invasion of neurons), which is why it persists despite ART.

---

**Q21.** Vincristine is known to cause peripheral neuropathy in cancer patients. What is its primary mechanism of neurotoxicity?
A) Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase
B) Microtubule disruption impairing axonal transport
C) Destruction of Schwann cells via complement fixation
D) Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels
E) Direct axonal membrane lysis

**Answer: B — Microtubule disruption impairing axonal transport**
Explanation: Vincristine binds tubulin, disrupting microtubules needed for axonal transport — a dose-limiting toxicity of vinca alkaloids.

---

**Q22.** In lepromatous leprosy, which organism invades and proliferates within Schwann cells, causing segmental demyelination?
A) Mycobacterium leprae
B) Mycobacterium tuberculosis
C) Borrelia burgdorferi
D) Corynebacterium diphtheriae
E) Varicella-zoster virus

**Answer: A — Mycobacterium leprae**
Explanation: M. leprae has tropism for Schwann cells (and cooler body areas — skin, peripheral nerves), causing segmental demyelination.

---

**Q23.** A 42-year-old woman has multiple uterine masses composed of intersecting fascicles of smooth muscle cells with blunt-ended nuclei and minimal atypia. What is the diagnosis?
A) Leiomyoma
B) Leiomyosarcoma
C) Rhabdomyoma
D) Fibrosarcoma
E) Endometrial stromal sarcoma

**Answer: A — Leiomyoma**
Explanation: Blunt-ended nuclei, minimal atypia, well-circumscribed = benign fibroid, the most common uterine tumour.

---

**Q24.** A bone tumour in an adolescent shows sheets of small round blue cells with a t(11;22) EWS-FLI1 fusion. What is the diagnosis?
A) Ewing sarcoma
B) Osteosarcoma
C) Chondrosarcoma
D) Osteoblastoma
E) Chordoma

**Answer: A — Ewing sarcoma**
Explanation: t(11;22) EWS-FLI1 is pathognomonic. Small round blue cell tumour, CD99+, occurs in diaphysis of long bones in children/adolescents.

---

**Q25.** Which of the following neoplasms is strongly associated with germline APC mutations in familial adenomatous polyposis?
A) Lipoma
B) Schwannoma
C) Desmoid tumour
D) Rhabdomyosarcoma
E) Leiomyosarcoma

**Answer: C — Desmoid tumour**
Explanation: Part of Gardner syndrome (FAP variant) — APC mutation → β-catenin accumulation → desmoid fibromatosis.

---

**Q26.** A patient has a well-circumscribed, encapsulated nerve sheath tumour showing Verocay bodies on histology. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Neurofibroma
B) Schwannoma
C) Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
D) Synovial sarcoma
E) Granular cell tumour

**Answer: B — Schwannoma**
Explanation: Verocay bodies (nuclear palisading around acellular zones) + encapsulation are classic schwannoma features (neurofibromas are unencapsulated).

---

**Q27.** A 35-year-old woman presents with a large, plaque-like cutaneous tumour diffusely infiltrating the dermis, composed of bland Schwann cells, mast cells, and fibroblasts. What is this lesion?
A) Localised cutaneous neurofibroma
B) Diffuse neurofibroma
C) Plexiform neurofibroma
D) Schwannoma
E) Dermatofibroma

**Answer: B — Diffuse neurofibroma**
Explanation: Diffuse infiltrative growth pattern in skin, distinct from the discrete localized cutaneous type and the "bag of worms" plexiform type.

---

**Q28.** Which neurofibroma subtype is uniquely associated with NF1 and has a "bag of worms" appearance grossly?
A) Localised cutaneous neurofibroma
B) Diffuse neurofibroma
C) Plexiform neurofibroma
D) Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
E) Schwannoma

**Answer: C — Plexiform neurofibroma**
Explanation: Pathognomonic for NF1; "bag of worms" gross appearance from tortuous, expanded nerve fascicles. Carries the 15-20% MPNST transformation risk.

---

**Q29.** Botulinum toxin (Botox) causes flaccid paralysis by which mechanism?
A) Blockade of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors
B) Inhibition of acetylcholine release from presynaptic terminals
C) Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase
D) Direct myofibre necrosis
E) Destruction of Schwann cells

**Answer: B — Inhibition of acetylcholine release from presynaptic terminals**
Explanation: Cleaves SNARE proteins needed for ACh vesicle release — presynaptic blockade, unlike MG (postsynaptic receptor loss).

---

**Q30.** In adults, dermatomyositis often presents as a paraneoplastic syndrome. Which of the following is the most common associated finding?
A) Underlying malignancy
B) Viral hepatitis
C) Diabetes mellitus
D) HIV infection
E) Hypothyroidism

**Answer: A — Underlying malignancy**
Explanation: Adult-onset dermatomyositis has a well-documented malignancy association (ovarian, lung, GI, lymphoma) — warrants cancer screening at diagnosis.

---

## SET 2 — JUNE 2026 CAT
**Bone and Soft Tissue CAT II, Semester III 2026**
**Q1.** A 17-year-old boy presents with progressive pain and swelling around the distal femur. Radiography demonstrates a destructive mixed lytic and sclerotic lesion with a Codman triangle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osteochondroma
B) Osteoid osteoma
C) Osteosarcoma
D) Chondroma
E) Giant cell tumour
**Answer: C — Osteosarcoma**
Explanation: Codman triangle (periosteal reaction where tumour lifts periosteum) + mixed lytic/sclerotic pattern in adolescent distal femur = classic osteosarcoma presentation.
---
**Q2.** A 15-year-old boy complains of severe nocturnal pain in the proximal tibia. The pain is dramatically relieved by aspirin. Radiography reveals a small radiolucent nidus surrounded by dense reactive bone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osteoblastoma
B) Osteoid osteoma
C) Osteosarcoma
D) Enchondroma
E) Ewing sarcoma
**Answer: B — Osteoid osteoma**
Explanation: Small nidus (<2cm), dramatic aspirin/NSAID relief (due to prostaglandin production by nidus), and dense surrounding reactive bone are pathognomonic.
---
**Q3.** A 20-year-old man presents with persistent back pain. Imaging demonstrates a 3-cm tumour arising from the posterior elements of a vertebra. The pain is not relieved by aspirin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osteoblastoma
B) Osteoid osteoma
C) Osteochondroma
D) Chondrosarcoma
E) Osteomyelitis
**Answer: A — Osteoblastoma**
Explanation: "Big brother" of osteoid osteoma — larger (>2cm), posterior vertebral elements, lacks the dramatic aspirin response that defines osteoid osteoma.
---
**Q4.** A 65-year-old man develops severe hip pain six months after prolonged high-dose corticosteroid therapy. MRI demonstrates subchondral collapse of the femoral head. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osteoarthritis
B) Osteomyelitis
C) Osteonecrosis
D) Chondrosarcoma
E) Osteoporosis
**Answer: C — Osteonecrosis**
Explanation: Corticosteroids are a classic cause of avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) — subchondral collapse of femoral head is the hallmark finding.
---
**Q5.** A 10-year-old child presents with fever and severe pain in the metaphysis of the tibia. Blood culture grows Staphylococcus aureus. Which diagnosis is most likely?
A) Osteosarcoma
B) Osteoid osteoma
C) Pyogenic osteomyelitis
D) Ewing sarcoma
E) Chondroma
**Answer: C — Pyogenic osteomyelitis**
Explanation: Metaphysis is the classic site for haematogenous osteomyelitis in children (rich vascular supply, sluggish flow); S. aureus is the most common causative organism.
---
**Q6.** A patient with chronic osteomyelitis develops a fragment of devitalised bone within a draining sinus tract. What is the term for this dead fragment of bone?
A) Involucrum
B) Pannus
C) Sequestrum
D) Osteophyte
E) Tophus
**Answer: C — Sequestrum**
Explanation: Sequestrum = dead bone fragment; involucrum = new reactive bone that forms around it (easy to confuse — sequestrum is the dead piece).
---
**Q7.** A 45-year-old man presents with a painful enlarging pelvic mass. Biopsy demonstrates malignant cartilage-producing cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osteochondroma
B) Chondroma
C) Chondrosarcoma
D) Osteosarcoma
E) Ewing sarcoma
**Answer: C — Chondrosarcoma**
Explanation: Malignant cartilage-forming tumour; pelvis/axial skeleton is the classic site (unlike osteosarcoma, which favours the appendicular skeleton/metaphysis of long bones).
---
**Q8.** A 19-year-old man has a painless bony outgrowth arising from the metaphysis of the distal femur. Radiography shows continuity of the medullary cavity with the host bone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osteochondroma
B) Enchondroma
C) Osteoblastoma
D) Osteosarcoma
E) Fibrous dysplasia
**Answer: A — Osteochondroma**
Explanation: Continuity of medullary cavity with host bone is the defining radiographic feature — the tumour is essentially an outgrowth of normal bone with a cartilage cap.
---
**Q9.** A 68-year-old woman reports chronic knee pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest. Radiographs demonstrate joint-space narrowing, osteophyte formation, and subchondral sclerosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Rheumatoid arthritis
B) Septic arthritis
C) Osteoarthritis
D) Gout
E) Ankylosing spondylitis
**Answer: C — Osteoarthritis**
Explanation: Classic triad — joint space narrowing (cartilage loss), osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis; pain with activity/relief with rest = mechanical/degenerative pattern.
---
**Q10.** A 40-year-old woman presents with symmetrical swelling of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints. Laboratory findings: positive anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPA), elevated ESR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Osteoarthritis
B) Rheumatoid arthritis
C) Gout
D) Reactive arthritis
E) Septic arthritis
**Answer: B — Rheumatoid arthritis**
Explanation: Symmetric small joint (MCP/PIP) involvement + ACPA positivity is highly specific for R
A.
---
**Q11.** A 28-year-old man presents with chronic lower back pain and reduced spinal mobility. Testing reveals positivity for HLA-B27. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Rheumatoid arthritis
B) Osteoarthritis
C) Ankylosing spondylitis
D) Gout
E) Septic arthritis
**Answer: C — Ankylosing spondylitis**
Explanation: HLA-B27 association + young male + axial (spinal) involvement with reduced mobility is classic for AS (a seronegative spondyloarthropathy).
---
**Q12.** A 55-year-old obese man develops sudden onset of severe pain, redness and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Synovial fluid examination reveals needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Septic arthritis
B) Rheumatoid arthritis
C) Osteoarthritis
D) Gout
E) Pseudogout
**Answer: D — Gout**
Explanation: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals = monosodium urate. First MTP joint ("podagra") is the classic site. (Pseudogout = rhomboid, positively birefringent CPPD crystals — a common exam trap.)
---
**Q13.** A 52-year-old woman undergoes a breast biopsy. The tissue specimen is immediately placed in 10% formalin before processing. What is the primary purpose of tissue fixation?
A) To remove calcium salts from tissue
B) To preserve tissue architecture and prevent autolysis
C) To increase tissue transparency
D) To facilitate paraffin embedding only
E) To enhance nuclear staining exclusively
**Answer: B — To preserve tissue architecture and prevent autolysis**
Explanation: Fixation cross-links proteins, halting autolytic/bacterial degradation and preserving structure for accurate histological examination.
---
**Q14.** A pathology laboratory receives a delayed liver biopsy specimen that was left at room temperature for 24 hours before fixation. Which process is most likely responsible for self-digestion of the tissue?
A) Putrefaction
B) Calcification
C) Autolysis
D) Decalcification
E) Keratinisation
**Answer: C — Autolysis**
Explanation: Autolysis = self-digestion by the tissue's own enzymes in the absence of fixation (sterile process); putrefaction requires bacterial action.
---
**Q15.** A forensic pathologist examines a decomposing body with foul-smelling gases and extensive bacterial tissue breakdown. Which process best explains these findings?
A) Apoptosis
B) Autolysis
C) Necrosis
D) Putrefaction
E) Fixation
**Answer: D — Putrefaction**
Explanation: Bacterial decomposition producing gas and foul odour = putrefaction, distinct from sterile autolysis.
---
**Q16.** A histotechnologist is preparing a femoral bone biopsy for microscopic examination. Which procedure must be performed before sectioning?
A) Clearing
B) Embedding
C) Decalcification
D) Staining
E) Mounting
**Answer: C — Decalcification**
Explanation: Bone must have calcium removed before it can be sectioned on a microtome (calcified tissue would damage the blade and can't be cut thinly).
---
**Q17.** A histology laboratory is processing tissue for routine light microscopy. Which sequence correctly follows fixation?
A) Embedding → Dehydration → Clearing
B) Clearing → Embedding → Dehydration
C) Dehydration → Clearing → Embedding
D) Staining → Clearing → Embedding
E) Sectioning → Clearing → Embedding
**Answer: C — Dehydration → Clearing → Embedding**
Explanation: Standard tissue processing order: fixation → dehydration (increasing ethanol grades) → clearing (xylene, removes alcohol) → embedding (paraffin wax) → sectioning → staining.
---
**Q18.** A pathology trainee is asked to identify the tissue-processing step that replaces alcohol with a solvent compatible with paraffin wax. Which step is being described?
A) Fixation
B) Dehydration
C) Clearing
**Answer: C — Clearing**
Explanation: Clearing agents (xylene, chloroform) are miscible with both alcohol and paraffin wax, acting as the bridge between dehydration and wax infiltration.
---
**Q19.** A tissue block is sectioned at 4 μm thickness for routine histological examination. Which instrument is primarily used?
A) Centrifuge
B) Cryostat
C) Spectrophotometer
D) Microtome
E) Cytospin
**Answer: D — Microtome**
Explanation: Standard instrument for cutting thin paraffin sections (routine thickness ~4-5 μm). Cryostat is used specifically for frozen sections.
---
**Q20.** A pathologist examines a routine tissue section stained blue-purple in the nuclei and pink in the cytoplasm. Which stain has been used?
A) PAS stain
B) Congo red stain
C) H&E stain
D) Giemsa stain
E) Alcian blue stain
**Answer: C — H&E stain**
Explanation: Haematoxylin stains nuclei blue-purple (basic dye, binds acidic DNA/RNA); eosin stains cytoplasm pink (acidic dye, binds basic proteins). The routine standard stain.
---
**Q21.** A renal biopsy demonstrates thickened basement membranes highlighted by a bright magenta colour. Which stain was most likely used?
A) Congo red
B) Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS)
C) Giemsa
D) Oil Red O
E) Toluidine blue
**Answer: B — Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS)**
Explanation: PAS highlights basement membranes, glycogen, and mucin in bright magenta/pink — essential for renal pathology (e.g. diabetic nephropathy, glomerular basement membrane assessment).
---
**Q22.** A liver biopsy is examined to assess the extent of fibrosis. Which stain is most appropriate for demonstrating collagen deposition?
A) Giemsa stain
B) Oil Red O stain
C) PAS stain
D) Masson's trichrome stain
E) Congo red stain
**Answer: D — Masson's trichrome stain**
Explanation: Trichrome stains collagen (fibrosis) blue/green against red muscle fibres — the standard stain for assessing hepatic fibrosis staging.
---
**Q23.** A patient is suspected of having systemic amyloidosis. Which stain would demonstrate characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarised light?
A) PAS
B) Alcian blue
C) Congo red
D) Giemsa
E) Van Gieson
**Answer: C — Congo red**
Explanation: Apple-green birefringence under polarized light after Congo red staining is the gold-standard diagnostic test for amyloid.
---
**Q24.** A 67-year-old smoker presents with haemoptysis and a suspicious lung mass. Which cytopathological specimen would be most useful for detecting malignant exfoliated respiratory epithelial cells?
A) Urine cytology
B) Sputum cytology
C) CSF cytology
D) Synovial fluid cytology
E) Peritoneal fluid cytology
**Answer: B — Sputum cytology**
Explanation: Non-invasive method to detect exfoliated malignant respiratory epithelial cells from central airway lesions.
---
**Q25.** A 58-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history presents with a persistent non-healing ulcer on the floor of the mouth. Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Which site is most associated with classic HPV-negative keratinising SCC of the oral cavity?
A) Hard palate only
B) Dorsal tongue only
C) Ventral tongue and floor of mouth
D) Buccal mucosa exclusively
E) Upper lip only
**Answer: C — Ventral tongue and floor of mouth**
Explanation: This is the classic "high-risk zone" for tobacco/alcohol-related HPV-negative oral SCC, where carcinogens pool in saliva.
---
**Q26.** A 45-year-old man is noted to have a red velvety lesion on the lateral border of the tongue. Histological examination reveals severe epithelial dysplasia. Which lesion has the highest risk of malignant transformation?
A) Oral candidiasis
B) Leukoplakia
C) Traumatic ulcer
D) Erythroplakia
E) Lichen planus
**Answer: D — Erythroplakia**
Explanation: Erythroplakia (red velvety patch) carries a much higher malignant transformation risk than leukoplakia (white patch) — often already shows severe dysplasia/carcinoma in situ at diagnosis.
---
**Q27.** A 23-year-old pregnant woman develops a rapidly enlarging, red, ulcerated gingival mass that bleeds easily. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Fibroma
B) Ameloblastoma
C) Peripheral giant cell granuloma
D) Pyogenic granuloma
E) Leukoplakia
**Answer: D — Pyogenic granuloma**
Explanation: "Pregnancy tumour" / granuloma gravidarum — hormonally-driven vascular proliferation, classic in pregnant women, bleeds easily due to rich vascularity.
---
**Q28.** A 32-year-old man presents with recurrent painful oral ulcers. The lesions are shallow, surrounded by erythema, and heal spontaneously within 10 days. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Herpetic ulcer
B) Aphthous ulcer
C) Squamous papilloma
D) Oral candidiasis
E) Syphilitic ulcer
**Answer: B — Aphthous ulcer**
Explanation: Recurrent, shallow, self-healing (~7-10 days) painful ulcers with erythematous halo = classic aphthous stomatitis ("canker sores").
---
**Q29.** A patient receiving chemotherapy develops white plaques on the oral mucosa that can be easily scraped away, revealing an erythematous base. Which organism is most likely responsible?
A) Aspergillus fumigatus
B) Candida albicans
C) Histoplasma capsulatum
D) Cryptococcus neoformans
E) Mucor species
**Answer: B — Candida albicans**
Explanation: Scrapable white plaques on erythematous base = pseudomembranous candidiasis ("thrush"), common in immunosuppressed/chemotherapy patients.
---
**Q30.** A 35-year-old man has a multilocular radiolucent lesion in the posterior mandible. Histology demonstrates a keratinised stratified squamous epithelial lining with a corrugated surface. Which diagnosis is most likely?
A) Dentigerous cyst
B) Radicular cyst
C) Keratocystic odontogenic tumour
D) Odontoma
E) Ameloblastoma
**Answer: C — Keratocystic odontogenic tumour**
Explanation: Corrugated parakeratinised epithelial lining + multilocular radiolucency in posterior mandible + high recurrence rate are defining features (formerly called odontogenic keratocyst).
---
## SAQs (Short Answer Questions)
Q1. List five eye malignant neoplasms. (5 marks)
1. Retinoblastoma (childhood, RB1 gene mutation)
2. Uveal/choroidal melanoma (most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults)
3. Squamous cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva
4. Basal cell carcinoma of the eyelid (most common eyelid malignancy)
5. Sebaceous gland carcinoma of the eyelid
6. (Extra) Lymphoma of the orbit/conjunctiva
Q2. List five defining histomorphology findings of papillary thyroid carcinoma. (5 marks)
1. Papillary architecture (fibrovascular cores lined by tumour cells)
2. Nuclear features — "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei (optically clear, ground-glass nuclei)
3. Nuclear grooves
4. Nuclear pseudoinclusions (cytoplasmic invaginations into the nucleus)
5. Psammoma bodies (concentric calcified structures)
6. (Extra) Overlapping nuclei with irregular contours

articles.content:
.
## CARDIOVASCULAR PATHOLOGY
**Atherosclerosis**
Pathogenesis (response-to-injury):
- Chronic endothelial injury (HTN, smoking, hyperlipidaemia, hyperglycaemia, turbulent flow at branch points)
- Injured endothelium → permeable to LDL → LDL enters intima, oxidizes
- Oxidized LDL attracts monocytes → become macrophages → engulf lipid → foam cells
- Foam cell accumulation = fatty streak (earliest lesion)
- Growth factors → smooth muscle migrates from media to intima, proliferates, lays collagen → fibrous cap over lipid core = fibrous plaque
- Plaque calcifies, ulcerates, haemorrhages, or ruptures = complicated plaque → thrombus → acute occlusion
Morphology by stage: fatty streak (flat, yellow, macrophages only) → fibrous plaque (raised, fibrous cap + necrotic core) → complicated plaque (calcification, haemorrhage, ulceration, superimposed thrombus)
Risk factors: hyperlipidaemia, hypertension, smoking, diabetes, age, male sex, genetics
---
**Rheumatic Heart Disease**
- Follows group A β-haemolytic strep pharyngitis (not skin infection)
- Mechanism: molecular mimicry — antibodies to strep M protein cross-react with cardiac tissue (Type II hypersensitivity)
- Acute RHD: pancarditis — fibrinous pericarditis, myocarditis with **Aschoff bodies** (pathognomonic — fibrinoid necrosis + lymphocytes + Anitschkow/"caterpillar" cells), verrucous endocarditis along valve closure lines
- Chronic RHD: valve leaflet fibrosis/fusion, chordae shortening, "fish-mouth"/"buttonhole" mitral stenosis
- Mitral valve most affected > aortic
- Clinical (Jones criteria): fever, migratory polyarthritis, carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea
---
**Infective Endocarditis**
| | Acute | Subacute |
|---|---|---|
| Organism | *S. aureus* (virulent) | *Strep viridans* (low virulence) |
| Valve | Previously normal | Previously damaged |
| Course | Rapid, fulminant | Indolent, weeks-months |
| Destruction | Extensive | Minimal |
Shared features: vegetations (fibrin+platelets+organisms+inflammatory cells), septic emboli, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, immune-complex glomerulonephritis
---
**Dilated Cardiomyopathy**
- Morphology: all 4 chambers dilated, walls thin/normal, mural thrombi common, nonspecific fibrosis on microscopy
- Mechanism: loss of contractility → systolic dysfunction → dilation → increased wall stress → worsening (vicious cycle)
- Causes: idiopathic/genetic, viral myocarditis (Coxsackie B), alcohol, peripartum, doxorubicin
**Other cardiomyopathies (likely add-on)**
- Hypertrophic: asymmetric septal hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, myocyte disarray, cause of sudden death in young athletes, genetic (sarcomere protein mutations)
- Restrictive: normal chamber size, stiff walls, diastolic dysfunction — amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, endomyocardial fibrosis
---
**Vasculitis by vessel size**
- Large: Takayasu (young Asian women, aortic arch), Giant Cell/Temporal Arteritis (elderly, headache, jaw claudication, blindness risk)
- Medium: PAN (Hep B association, spares lungs), Kawasaki (children, coronary aneurysms)
- Small: GPA/Wegener's (c-ANCA, resp tract + kidney), Microscopic Polyangiitis (p-ANCA, no granulomas), Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA-mediated)
---
**Pulmonary Thromboembolism**
- Source: >95% from DVT (femoral/iliac/popliteal) — Virchow's triad
- Saddle embolus → sudden death (acute cor pulmonale)
- Medium embolus → haemorrhagic wedge infarct
- Small/recurrent → chronic pulmonary hypertension
**Ischaemic Heart Disease / MI (add-on — high-yield, not in your list but commonly examined)**
- Coagulative necrosis at 4-24h (earliest microscopic change ~12-24h)
- Neutrophil infiltrate 1-3 days
- Macrophages/granulation tissue 3-7 days
- Scar formation by 6 weeks
- Complications: arrhythmia (early, commonest cause of death), cardiogenic shock, free wall rupture (day 3-7, weakest point), papillary muscle rupture, mural thrombus, Dressler syndrome (autoimmune pericarditis weeks later)
**Cor Pulmonale (add-on)**
- Right heart failure secondary to pulmonary hypertension from lung disease
- Commonest cause: COPD
- Right ventricular hypertrophy ± dilation
---
## RESPIRATORY PATHOLOGY
**Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease — Emphysema vs Chronic Bronchitis**
Emphysema pathogenesis:
- Protease-antiprotease imbalance
- Smoking recruits neutrophils/macrophages → release elastase
- Smoking also oxidizes/inactivates α1-antitrypsin; genetic deficiency worsens this
- Unchecked elastase destroys alveolar septae → permanent airspace enlargement distal to terminal bronchiole
- Loss of elastic recoil → air trapping
- "Pink puffer": thin, dyspnoeic, compensatory hyperventilation
Chronic bronchitis:
- Clinical definition: productive cough >3 months/year, 2 consecutive years
- Mucus gland hyperplasia — measured by Reid index (increased)
- "Blue bloater": cyanotic, obese, hypoxic/hypercapnic, less compensation
| | Emphysema | Chronic Bronchitis |
|---|---|---|
| Site | Alveoli/acinus | Bronchi |
| Mechanism | Protease-antiprotease imbalance | Gland hyperplasia |
| Marker | ↓Elastic recoil | ↑Reid index |
| Cor pulmonale | Late | Early |
**Bronchiectasis (add-on — often paired with COPD topics)**
- Permanent dilation of bronchi due to destruction of muscle/elastic tissue
- Causes: recurrent infection, cystic fibrosis, obstruction, immune deficiency
- Copious purulent sputum, clubbing, risk of abscess/amyloidosis
---
**Asthma**
Pathogenesis (Type I hypersensitivity):
- Sensitization: allergen → Th2 response → IgE → binds mast cells
- Re-exposure: allergen cross-links IgE → mast cell degranulation
- Early phase (mins): histamine, leukotrienes → bronchospasm, mucus, permeability
- Late phase (hrs): eosinophils, Th2 cytokines (IL-4,5,13) → sustained inflammation, remodeling
Microscopic bronchiole changes:
1. Smooth muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia
2. Mucus gland hyperplasia/plugging
3. Curschmann spirals
4. Charcot-Leyden crystals
5. Basement membrane thickening
6. Eosinophilic infiltration
---
**Diffuse Alveolar Damage / ARDS**
- Alveolar-capillary injury (sepsis, trauma, aspiration) → increased permeability → protein-rich exudate
- Morphology: hyaline membranes, alveolar/interstitial oedema, Type I pneumocyte necrosis + Type II hyperplasia, fibrin microthrombi, progression to fibrosis
---
**Pneumoconioses**
- Coal worker's: upper lobes, anthracotic pigment, progressive massive fibrosis
- Silicosis: upper lobes, silicotic nodules, ↑TB risk
- Asbestosis: lower lobes, ferruginous bodies, ↑mesothelioma + bronchogenic Ca risk
- Berylliosis: non-caseating granulomas (mimics sarcoid)
---
**Lung Carcinoma**
Classification:
- Squamous: central, smoking, keratin pearls, cavitates, PTHrP→hypercalcaemia
- Adenocarcinoma: peripheral, commonest overall (incl. non-smokers), glandular/mucin
- Large cell: undifferentiated, poor prognosis
- Small cell: central, neuroendocrine, aggressive, strongest paraneoplastic link, worst prognosis
Paraneoplastic syndromes: SIADH, ectopic ACTH/Cushing, Lambert-Eaton, PTHrP/hypercalcaemia, clubbing/hypertrophic osteoarthropathy
---
**Tuberculosis**
- Inhaled *M. tuberculosis* → macrophage engulfment, blocks phagolysosome fusion → Type IV hypersensitivity (2-4wks) → granuloma
- Ghon focus (subpleural, mid/lower lobe) + hilar node = Ghon complex = primary TB
- Granuloma: caseous necrosis + epithelioid cells + Langhans giant cells + lymphocyte cuff
- Secondary/reactivation: apical, cavitating, can disseminate (miliary)
- Diagnosis: Ziehl-Neelsen (AF
B)
---
**Nasal Polyps**
- Oedematous stroma, eosinophil-rich chronic inflammation, goblet cell hyperplasia, thickened basement membrane, squamous metaplasia (variable), respiratory epithelium lining
**Sarcoidosis (add-on)**
- Non-caseating granulomas, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
- ↑ACE levels, restrictive lung pattern
- Unknown aetiology, exaggerated T-cell response
**Restrictive vs Obstructive lung disease (add-on — common short-answer trap)**
- Obstructive: ↓FEV1/FVC ratio (asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis)
- Restrictive: normal/↑FEV1/FVC, ↓lung volumes (fibrosis, sarcoidosis, ARDS-related fibrosis)

# MOUNT KENYA UNIVERSITY
## UNIVERSITY EXAMINATION 2025/2026
**Medical School | Department of Pathology**
**Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBChB)**
**End of Year Examination — Year Three**

---

## UNIT CODE: MBPA 3500 | UNIT TITLE: GENERAL & SYSTEMIC PATHOLOGY
## PAPER TWO

**Time: 3 Hours | Total Marks: 100**

**Instructions:**
- Section A: Answer ANY 10 questions (10 marks each)
- Section B: Answer ANY 3 questions (20 marks each)
- Write clearly and legibly
- Begin each answer on a new page
- Indicate your registration number only — do not write your name

---

# SECTION A — SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS
### Answer ANY 10 questions. Each question carries 10 marks.

---
Question 1
Discuss the pathogenesis of cervical squamous cell carcinoma, including the mechanism of action of HPV E6 and E7 oncoproteins.

---
Question 2
Give an outline of the classification of ovarian neoplasms with examples of each category.

---
Question 3
Compare and contrast Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus under the following headings:
- Aetiology
- Pathogenesis
- Clinical features

---
Question 4
Discuss the pathophysiological categories of oedema, giving an example of each.

---
Question 5
Describe the immune mechanisms involved in glomerular injury.

---
Question 6
Outline the major risk factors for atherosclerosis, distinguishing between modifiable and non-modifiable factors.

---
Question 7
Discuss the aetiology, pathogenesis, and morphology of liver cirrhosis.

---
Question 8
Classify chemical carcinogenic agents, giving examples of each class and the cancers they are associated with.

---
Question 9
Compare and contrast autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance patterns, giving two examples of disorders for each.

---
Question 10
Describe the stages and biological processes involved in fracture healing, including the role of callus formation.

---
Question 11
Give an outline of the aetiology, characteristics, and examples of the major categories of diarrhoeal illness.

---
Question 12
Write short notes on Rheumatic Heart Disease under the following headings:
- Aetiology and pathogenesis
- Morphological changes
- Complications

---
Question 13
Outline the classification of vasculitis based on vessel size, giving one example and its key features for each category.

---
Question 14
Discuss the pathogenesis of pre-eclampsia/toxaemia of pregnancy, including its effects on maternal organ systems.

---

# SECTION B — LONG ESSAY QUESTIONS
### Answer ANY 3 questions. Each question carries 20 marks.

---
Question 1
Discuss cervical carcinoma under the following headings:
a) Risk factors
b) Aetiology
c) Pathogenesis
d) Morphological changes
e) Clinical features and staging

*(20 Marks)*

---
Question 2
Discuss the three major pathways of breast cancer development and their resultant immunohistochemical staining patterns, including the clinical and prognostic significance of each pathway.

*(20 Marks)*

---
Question 3
Discuss the following aspects of acute inflammation:
a) Cellular events in acute inflammation
b) Cell-derived mediators of inflammation
c) Plasma-derived mediators of inflammation
d) Local and systemic effects of acute inflammation

*(20 Marks)*

---
Question 4
Discuss Tuberculosis under the following headings:
a) Pathogenesis
b) Morphological events (primary and secondary)
c) Clinical presentation and complications

*(20 Marks)*

---
Question 5
Discuss the pathogenesis and morphological events in the development of atherosclerosis, including its major complications — myocardial infarction, stroke, and peripheral arterial disease.

*(20 Marks)*

---
Question 6
Compare wound healing by primary and secondary intention under the following headings:
a) Mechanism and stages of each
b) Factors affecting wound healing
c) Complications of wound healing

*(20 Marks)*

---
---

# MOUNT KENYA UNIVERSITY
## UNIVERSITY EXAMINATION 2025/2026
**Medical School | Department of Haematology**
**Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBChB)**
**End of Year Examination — Year Three**

---

## UNIT CODE: MBML 3200 | UNIT TITLE: HAEMATOLOGY

**Time: 3 Hours | Total Marks: 100**

**Instructions:**
- Section A: MCQs — Answer ALL (40 marks)
- Section B: Short Answer Questions — Answer ANY 7 (42 marks)
- Section C: Long Essay — Answer ANY 1 (18 marks)
- Write clearly and legibly
- Indicate your registration number only — do not write your name

---

# SECTION B — SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (Clinical Vignette Style)
### Answer ANY 7 questions.

---
Question 1
A 45-year-old male presents with fatigue, early satiety, and massive splenomegaly. Full blood count shows WBC 120×10⁹/L with neutrophilia, left shift, and prominent basophilia.
a) What is the most likely diagnosis? (1 mark)
b) Outline the laboratory investigations you would request to confirm this diagnosis, stating the expected findings for each. (9 marks)

---
Question 2
A 32-year-old woman with a history of heavy menstrual bleeding presents with progressive fatigue, pallor, and pica.
a) What is the most likely diagnosis? (1 mark)
b) State three clinical signs you would expect to find on examination. (3 marks)
c) List four confirmatory laboratory tests and state the expected result for each. (6 marks)

---
Question 3
A 10-year-old child presents with a rapidly growing jaw mass, fever, and night sweats. Biopsy reveals a starry sky pattern on histology.
a) What is the most likely diagnosis? (1 mark)
b) Describe the laboratory investigations needed to confirm this diagnosis, including histological, immunophenotypic, and molecular findings. (9 marks)

---
Question 4
A 50-year-old man with known liver cirrhosis and splenomegaly is found to have a platelet count of 60×10⁹/L on routine bloods.
a) Interpret this platelet count in the context of his clinical condition. (2 marks)
b) State two causes of thrombocytopenia in this patient. (2 marks)
c) Outline the laboratory tests you would perform to reach a definitive diagnosis, stating the expected findings. (6 marks)

---
Question 5
A 6-year-old boy presents with recurrent haemarthroses and easy bruising following minor trauma. Coagulation screen shows prolonged APTT with a normal PT and normal platelet count.
a) Interpret these coagulation results. (2 marks)
b) What is the most likely diagnosis? (1 mark)
c) List four additional confirmatory laboratory tests and the expected finding for each. (7 marks)

---
Question 6
A 28-year-old woman who is HIV-positive and on zidovudine-based antiretroviral therapy develops progressive fatigue. Full blood count reveals MCV of 110 fL with a haemoglobin of 8.2 g/dL.
a) Explain the mechanism by which zidovudine causes this type of anaemia. (3 marks)
b) List three confirmatory laboratory tests with expected results. (3 marks)
c) State three other causes of macrocytic anaemia. (4 marks)

---
Question 7
Describe five laboratory features of haemolytic anaemia, explaining the pathophysiological basis and diagnostic significance of each finding.

*(10 marks)*

---
Question 8
Outline the immunophenotypic markers used to differentiate acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) from acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), explaining the significance of each marker.

*(10 marks)*

---
Question 9
A 68-year-old man presents with persistent bone pain, fatigue, and recurrent infections. Serum electrophoresis reveals a monoclonal spike in the gamma region.
a) What is the most likely diagnosis? (1 mark)
b) Describe the full diagnostic workup for this condition, including biochemical, haematological, radiological, and bone marrow findings. (9 marks)

---

# SECTION C — LONG ESSAY QUESTION
### Answer ANY 1 question. (18 marks)

---
Question 1
Discuss the components of blood and blood products under the following headings:
a) Types of blood products and their preparation
b) Indications for transfusion of each product
c) Complications of blood transfusion, including transfusion reactions and their management

*(18 Marks)*

---
Question 2
Describe the full blood count components and explain the diagnostic significance of an abnormality in each parameter, giving a clinical example for each.

*(18 Marks)*

---
Question 3
Discuss Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia (CML) under the following headings:
a) Pathogenesis, including the role of the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL fusion gene
b) Clinical features and laboratory findings at presentation
c) Diagnosis and monitoring of treatment response

*(18 Marks)*

---

*End of Paper*
