articles.title: Oncopathology MCQs: Test Your Knowledge on Cancer Pathology — MCQ Bank
articles.content:
**Oncopathology MCQs**
---
**Q1.** Neoplasia
a. Is the process of formation of new normal growths in the body
b. Is any new abnormal and unregulated growth in the body – also called tumour
c. Is a process of formation of tumours that stops after removal of inciting stimulus
d. Is the process of formation of clonal tumours
e. Includes growths from infections such as solid granulomas and cystic abscesses
**Answer: b**
*This is the standard pathology definition. c is wrong because neoplastic growth persists even after the inciting stimulus is removed (unlike hyperplasia); e is wrong because granulomas/abscesses are inflammatory, not neoplastic.*
---
**Q2.** True of tumours
a. Supportive stroma represents the proliferative component of tumours
b. The parenchyma provides connective tissue framework for the tumour
c. The stromal and parenchymal components of tumour do not influence each other
d. The behaviour and pathologic consequences of a tumour depend on its parenchymal component
e. The growth and evolution of a tumour depend on its parenchymal component
**Answer: d**
*Parenchyma = the neoplastic cells themselves, which determine biologic behavior (benign/malignant, differentiation). Stroma (connective tissue + vessels) provides support and blood supply, which actually governs a tumor's growth/survival — not the parenchyma (making e false), and stroma/parenchyma interact closely (making c false).*
---
**Q3.** Which of the following is true regarding the nomenclature of tumours?
a. Papillomas and papillary cystadenomas are synonyms for benign tumours with identical morphology
b. Adenomas include benign glandular neoplasms and malignant polyps in general
c. Some benign tumours are composed of undifferentiated cells and are termed poorly differentiated tumours
d. Mature teratomas are benign teratogenous tumours derived from totipotential cells
e. Immature teratomas are malignant mixed tumours derived from one germ cell layer
**Answer: d**
*Mature (benign) teratomas arise from totipotential germ cells and differentiate into mature tissue from all three germ layers. "Poorly differentiated" is a malignant, not benign, descriptor; immature teratomas are malignant but still derive from all germ layers, not just one.*
---
**Q4.** Anaplasia is marked by the following morphological changes except?
a. Pleomorphism
b. Abnormal nuclear morphology
c. High mitotic rate in supportive stroma
d. Loss of polarity
e. Formation of tumour giant cells
**Answer: c**
*Anaplasia describes changes in the neoplastic (parenchymal) cells themselves — increased mitoses occur in tumor cells, not the stroma.*
---
**Q5.** In dysplasia
a. There is uniformity of individual cells
b. There is architectural orientation
c. There is disordered growth
d. There is increase in the number of cells in the tissue
e. There is increase in the size of normal cells
**Answer: c**
*Dysplasia = disordered, atypical epithelial growth with loss of normal architectural orientation and cellular uniformity — the opposite of a, b, and e (which describe normal/hyperplastic tissue).*
---
**Q6.** The following statements are false except?
a. Haematogenous spread is exclusively seen in sarcomas
b. Lymphatic spread is the least common pathway for dissemination of carcinomas
c. Direct seeding of body cavities is the most common pathway of spread for sarcomas
d. Nodal enlargement in proximity to a cancer is always due to metastasis
e. Liver and lungs are most frequently involved in haematogenous spread of cancers
**Answer: e**
*Liver and lungs receive the largest blood flow/filtration load and are classic sites of blood-borne metastasis. a/c/d are overgeneralized absolutes that are false (carcinomas also spread hematogenously; sarcomas spread mainly hematogenously not by seeding; reactive nodal enlargement can be non-metastatic).*
---
**Q7.** Which of the following is benign?
a. Seminoma
b. Meningioma
c. Mesothelioma
d. Melanoma
e. None of the above
**Answer: b**
*Meningioma is typically a benign tumor of meningeal (arachnoid cap) cells. The other four are all malignant.*
---
**Q8.** Which of the following is true of benign tumours?
a. Most papillary cystadenomas are solid masses with finger-like projections on the surface
b. Papillomas are projecting structures of fibro-vascular tissue supporting benign epithelial surface
c. Benign tumours are less common than malignant tumours
d. Benign tumours typically regress spontaneously
e. When a benign tumour causes death via pressure effects it counted as a malignancy
**Answer: b**
*This correctly describes papilloma histology. Cystadenomas are cystic, not solid (a false); benign tumors are actually more common than malignant ones overall; benign tumors don't typically regress; and a benign tumor causing death (e.g., a benign brain tumor causing herniation) remains histologically benign, not reclassified as malignant.*
---
**Q9.** Which of the following is not true of malignant tumours?
a. Malignant change may occur secondary to an infection
b. Malignant mesenchymal tumours are always anaplastic
c. Most cells within cancerous tumours are typically in the G0 and G1 cell cycle phase
d. Hormonal stimulation may affect growth of some types of cancers
e. Different cancers have different growth rate
**Answer: b**
*Not all sarcomas (malignant mesenchymal tumors) are anaplastic — many are well-differentiated. The rest are accurate (e.g., HPV/EBV-driven cancers for a; hormone-sensitive cancers like breast/prostate for d).*
---
**Q10.** Benign tumours
a. Have a capacity to infiltrate but not invade adjacent tissues
b. Have capsules that restrict their growth
c. Are considered pre-invasive and sometimes termed carcinoma in situ
d. May relocate to a different body organ by sliding
e. Are usually candidates for surgical enucleation
**Answer: e**
*Because they're well-circumscribed/encapsulated and don't invade, benign tumors can typically be "shelled out" (enucleated) surgically. They don't infiltrate, don't metastasize by "sliding," and carcinoma in situ is a pre-invasive malignant (not benign) lesion.*
---
**Q11.** In Kenya,
a. Breast cancer has the highest mortality rate among all cancers
b. Cancer is the leading cause of death
c. The risk of developing cancer before the age of 75 years is 14.3% among men and 18% among women
d. The risk of death from cancer before the age of 75 years is 20.6%
e. The incidence of cervical, prostate and ovarian cancer is below the global average
**Answer: c**
*Reflects Kenya-specific cancer statistics (GLOBOCAN-type data used in local curricula). Cervical cancer, not breast, has the highest cancer mortality in Kenya; cardiovascular disease/infections still outrank cancer as overall leading cause of death; cervical/prostate incidence in Kenya is actually above global averages.*
---
**Q12.** The five commonest cancers in Kenya are
a. Breast, cervical, prostate, oesophageal and retinoblastoma
b. Breast, cervical, prostate, pancreatic and colorectal
c. Breast, cervical, prostate, oesophageal and leukaemia
d. Breast, cervical, prostate, colorectal and lung
e. Breast, cervical, prostate, oesophageal and colorectal
**Answer: e**
*Matches Kenya National Cancer Registry top-5 rankings.*
---
**Q13.** Which of the following statements is not false?
a. Cancers are most common at the two extremes of age
b. Cancer causes majority of all deaths among children younger than 15 years
c. The major lethal cancers in children are oral and renal carcinomas
d. The incidence of cancer varies with age but not race and genetic background
e. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, chronic myeloid leukaemia, Kaposi sarcoma and malignant ovarian teratomas account for about 50% of all cancer cases globally
**Answer: a**
*Cancer incidence does show a bimodal age distribution (childhood cancers + rising incidence with age). Cancer is not the leading cause of childhood death (infections/trauma outrank it); pediatric lethal cancers are mainly leukemias/CNS tumors, not oral/renal; cancer incidence strongly varies with race/genetics; and the disease list in e is not accurate as ~50% of global cases.*
---
**Q14.** The following cancers can be prevented by vaccination except one. Which one?
a. Cervical cancer
b. Vaginal cancer
c. Vulvar cancer
d. Liver cancer
e. Thyroid cancer
**Answer: e**
*Thyroid cancer has no available preventive vaccine. The others are prevented via HPV vaccination (a–c) and Hepatitis B vaccination (d, preventing HBV-related HCC).*
---
**Q15.** Which of the following statements is false?
a. Most cancers are sporadic
b. Hereditary predisposition accounts for more cancers than sporadic cases
c. Autosomal dominant predisposition is usually linked to inheritance of a germ line mutation of cancer suppressor genes
d. Autosomal recessive predisposition is typically associated with inherited defects in DNA repair
e. Preneoplastic disorders are known to be associated with an increased risk for development of cancer
**Answer: b**
*The overwhelming majority of cancers are sporadic, not hereditary — this is the false/reversed statement.*
---
**Q16.** One of the following is not true regarding precursor lesions
a. Removal of precursor lesions does not prevent the development of a cancer
b. Squamous dysplasia of the bronchial mucosa seen in habitual smokers is a risk factor for lung cancer
c. Squamous metaplasia of the bronchial mucosa seen in habitual smokers is not a risk factor for lung cancer
d. Endometrial hyperplasia and dysplasia seen in women with unopposed estrogenic stimulation is a risk factor for endometrial carcinoma
e. Leukoplakia of the oral cavity, vulva, or penis may progress to squamous cell carcinoma
**Answer: a**
*Removing a precursor lesion (e.g., colon polyp, cervical dysplasia) is precisely how screening programs prevent progression to invasive cancer — so this statement is false as written.*
---
**Q17.** Villous adenomas of the colon
a. Are associated with a high risk of transformation to colorectal carcinoma
b. Are associated with HPV 16 and 18
c. Develop cancerous change as they increase in size in about 5% of cases
d. Rarely increase in size and never undergo cancerous change
e. Are only seen in animals and offer good study models for human cancers
**Answer: a**
*Villous adenomas carry the highest malignant transformation risk (up to ~40%) among colonic polyps — far higher than the ~5% quoted in c. They're unrelated to HPV and are a human, not animal, entity.*
---
**Q18.** Screening of cancers
a. Is the process whereby doctors offer health talks to a healthy population to avoid exposure to risk factors in order to avoid cancer
b. Is the process whereby symptomatic patients with lumps and masses get biopsied during a medical camp and thereafter diagnosis and staging of cancer is done
c. Only requires laboratory tests without the need of radiological investigations
d. Is the application of simple tests across a healthy population before they develop any symptoms of cancer to identify those with cancer
e. Includes all the above
**Answer: d**
*This is the textbook definition of screening: applying tests to an asymptomatic population to catch disease early. a describes health education (primary prevention); b describes diagnostic workup of symptomatic patients, not screening.*
---
**Q19.** Early detection of cancers
a. Is a futuristic approach to make diagnosis of cancers at early stage a possibility
b. Is a concept of timely diagnosis of cancer that includes early diagnosis and screening
c. Is generally not cost effective as it is more expensive than treating cancer
d. Is currently only possible for pancreatic and ovarian cancers
e. Applies only to cancers of infancy and early childhood
**Answer: b**
*Early detection is an umbrella term encompassing both screening (asymptomatic population testing) and early diagnosis (prompt recognition once symptoms occur) — it's already a current, cost-effective strategy applicable across many cancer types and all ages.*
---
**Q20.** Which of the following is not true regarding global cancer statistics?
a. About 33% of cancer cases are linked to exposure to tobacco smoke
b. The four most common cancers are breast, lung, bowel and prostate cancers
c. The four mentioned in (b) above account for more than 40% of all cancers diagnosed
d. About 10 million deaths in the year 2020 were attributed to cancer
e. The incidence of cancer cases is in sharp decline and expected to continue up to 2040
**Answer: e**
*Global cancer incidence is actually projected to rise (not decline) through 2040 due to aging/growing populations and lifestyle risk factors.*
---
**Q21.** The following statements on molecular properties of cancers are not true except one. Which one?
a. All mutations that lead to carcinogenesis are either due to exogenous agents or endogenous products of cell metabolism
b. A lethal genetic mutation is required for carcinogenesis to occur
c. Stochastic non-lethal mutations are responsible for the formation of some cancers
d. Mixed tumours arise from two subsequent mutations (two hits) in chromosomes of two cells from two different cell lines
e. Phenotypic attributes of malignant neoplasms such as excessive growth and ability to metastasize are all acquired in a single step process
**Answer: c**
*Cancer arises from an accumulation of random (stochastic), non-lethal mutations that confer survival/growth advantage — a lethal mutation would kill the cell, not transform it; malignant traits accumulate stepwise (multistep carcinogenesis), not in one single step; and tumors are clonal (from one cell line), not "mixed" from two different lineages.*
---
**Q22.** One of the following statements is false. Which one?
a. Oncogenes induce a transformed phenotype when expressed in cells
b. Oncogenes are mutated or over expressed versions of proto-oncogenes
c. Oncogenes encode transcription factors and growth regulating proteins
d. Oncogene encode proteins involved in cell survival and cell to cell interactions
e. Oncogenes are considered recessive because mutation of both alleles is required for cellular transformation
**Answer: e**
*Oncogenes act in a dominant fashion — a single mutated/activated allele is sufficient to drive transformation (unlike tumour suppressor genes, which typically need both alleles inactivated).*
---
**Q23.** Which statement is not true regarding tumour suppressor genes?
a. They are genes that prevent uncontrolled growth
b. When over expressed lead to transformation of cells
c. Their mutation or loss from a cell allows the transformed phenotype
d. Usually both normal alleles of tumour must be damaged for transformation to occur
e. Loss of a single allele can promote transformation (haploinsufficiency)
**Answer: b**
*Tumour suppressor genes cause transformation when they are LOST or inactivated — not when overexpressed (overexpression would enhance, not impair, growth control).*
---
**Q24.** Regarding retinoblastoma, the following statements are true except which one?
a. Majority of cases are familial
b. The predisposition to develop the tumour is transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait
c. In hereditary cases one genetic change (first hit) is present in all somatic cells
d. In sporadic cases two mutations (first and second hit) occur in one retinal cell only
e. The RB gene is located on chromosome 13
**Answer: a**
*The majority of retinoblastoma cases are actually sporadic (~60%), not familial — this reflects Knudson's classic two-hit hypothesis (b–d correctly describe hereditary vs. sporadic mechanisms).*
---
**Q25.** Tumour suppressor genes
a. Are responsible for sensing genomic damage
b. Are involved in directly recognizing and suppressing small tumours before they metastasize
c. When mutated lead to direct malignant transformation of cells
d. When mutated are not associated with increased mutations in other genes
e. Include TP53 and BCL2
**Answer: a**
*Many tumour suppressors (e.g., TP53, ATM) function as DNA-damage sensors/checkpoint regulators. They don't act as an "immune-like" surveillance system against existing tumours (b); their loss alone is usually insufficient for full transformation without further hits (c); loss of DNA-repair suppressors actually increases downstream mutation rates (d is false); and BCL2 is an oncogene (anti-apoptotic), not a tumour suppressor (e is false).*
---
**Q26.** Genetic lesions in cancer include the following except
a. Balanced translocations
b. Additions
c. Deletions
d. Gene amplifications
e. Aneuploidy
**Answer: b**
*"Additions" is not a recognized standard category of cancer-associated genetic lesion; the others (translocations, deletions, amplifications, aneuploidy) are all classic mechanisms.*
---
**Q27.** MicroRNAs (miRNAs)
a. Do not contribute to carcinogenesis when overexpressed
b. When overexpressed lead to increased expression of tumour suppressors
c. Are a subcategory of tumour suppressor genes
d. When deleted or lost can lead to overexpression of proto-oncogenes
e. Have no role in carcinogenesis
**Answer: d**
*miRNAs normally silence target mRNAs (including oncogene transcripts); losing a tumour-suppressive miRNA removes this brake, causing oncogene overexpression. They can act as either oncogenes or tumour suppressors depending on context, not purely one category.*
---
**Q28.** The following genes function as tumour suppressors except
a. INK4a/ARF
b. PTEN
c. VHL
d. The TGF-β Pathway
e. Xq27.3
**Answer: e**
*Xq27.3 is the Fragile X syndrome locus (FMR1 gene), unrelated to tumour suppression. The others are all well-established tumour suppressor genes/pathways.*
---
**Q29.** The following statements are true about tumour progression except one. Which one?
a. It is typified by progression from a highly malignant tumour to a benign smaller tumour after administration of chemotherapeutic agents
b. It is associated with heterogeneity resulting from multiple mutations that accumulate independently in different cells within the tumour
c. It involves generation of subclones with different characteristics
d. It relies on characteristics such as ability to invade, metastatic ability, hormonal responsiveness, and susceptibility to antineoplastic drugs
e. It relies on subclones that are adept at survival, growth, invasion, and metastasis
**Answer: a**
*Tumour progression describes cancers becoming MORE aggressive/malignant over time through accumulating mutations and clonal selection — not regression to a benign state with treatment.*
---
**Q30.** Which of the following does not help tumours to invade local tissues
a. Loosening of cell–cell contacts
b. Degradation of extracellular matrix
c. Attachment to novel extracellular components
d. Cohesive tumour clusters
e. Migration of tumour cells
**Answer: d**
*Invasion requires cells to detach and move individually; staying cohesively clustered would actually hinder infiltration into surrounding tissue.*
---
**Q31.** A 22-year-old female has a palpable nodule in her thyroid. FNA and cytopathology revealed cells consistent with thyroid carcinoma. Which of the following would you consider relevant in her past medical history?
a. Exposure to arsenic compounds
b. Blunt trauma from a fall
c. Radiation in childhood
d. Ataxia telangiectasia
e. Chronic alcoholism
**Answer: c**
*Childhood head/neck radiation exposure is a well-established, strong risk factor for papillary thyroid carcinoma.*
---
**Q32.** Which of the following tumours may be preceded by actinic keratosis
a. Basal cell carcinoma
b. Squamous cell carcinoma
c. Kaposi sarcoma
d. Melanoma
e. Mycosis fungoides
**Answer: b**
*Actinic (solar) keratosis is the classic UV-induced precursor lesion for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.*
---
**Q33.** A 35-year old male living with HIV develops hyperpigmented skin lesions. Which of the following infectious agents is likely to have played a role in the pathogenesis of the lesions?
a. Adenovirus
b. Hepatitis B virus
c. Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
d. Ebstein-Barr virus (EBV)
e. Human Herpes Virus 8
**Answer: e**
*This describes Kaposi sarcoma, an AIDS-defining illness strongly linked to HHV-8 (KSHV) infection.*
---
**Q34.** One of the following lymphoproliferative disorders is found commonly and particularly in children in Kenya
a. Burkitt Lymphoma
b. Immunoblastic Lymphoma
c. EBV-induced Hodgkin Lymphoma
d. Non-EBV induced Hodgkin Lymphoma
e. HIV-associated non-Hodgkin Lymphoma
**Answer: a**
*Endemic Burkitt lymphoma (EBV-associated) is classically prevalent in equatorial African children, including Kenya, linked to malaria co-endemicity.*
---
**Q35.** Which tumour marker would be most useful in a patient with ovarian cancer?
a. CA 125
b. CA 15.3
c. CA 19.9
d. CEA
e. CA 72.2
**Answer: a**
*CA 125 is the standard tumour marker used for monitoring epithelial ovarian cancer (though not specific enough for screening).*
---
**Q36.** Regarding grading of tumours
a. It is a system of classifying tumours based on the degree of differentiation
b. It is far superior than staging of tumours in terms of relevance in prognostication
c. Small tumours are always low grade and large tumours always high grade
d. Grading uses the TNM criteria in order of increasing abnormality
e. All the above are true
**Answer: a**
*Grade reflects cellular differentiation/aggressiveness at the microscopic level. Staging (extent of spread, using TNM — not grading) is generally the stronger prognostic factor; tumour size doesn't dictate grade.*
---
**Q37.** Which of the following statements regarding staging of cancers is false?
a. It is based on the size of the primary tumour
b. It is based on the extent of local invasion
c. It is based on evidence of metastasis of the tumour
d. It can only be done by radiologists who image the entire body
e. The major system currently used is the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC)
**Answer: d**
*Staging is a multidisciplinary process combining clinical exam, surgery/pathology findings, and imaging — it isn't performed solely by radiologists.*
---
**Q38.** Paraneoplastic syndromes
a. Are symptoms occurring late in cancer and are confirmatory of a cancer diagnosis
b. Are tumour-associated syndromes not directly related to the spread of the tumour
c. Are groups of symptoms that mimic cancer in the absence of an actual tumour
d. Include cancer-associated hypercalcemia due to osteolysis induced by metastases
e. Are usually typical endocrinopathies and not those occurring due to ectopic hormone production
**Answer: b**
*Paraneoplastic syndromes arise from indirect tumour effects (e.g., ectopic hormone/cytokine secretion), not from direct tumour bulk or metastatic invasion. They can occur early and don't require an existing detectable tumour to be excluded; hypercalcemia in paraneoplastic syndrome is due to PTHrP secretion, not osteolytic metastasis (that's a separate mechanism, making d misleading here); and paraneoplastic endocrinopathies are typically atypical/ectopic, not "usual" hormone patterns.*
---
**Q39.** Cancer cachexia
a. Is demonstrated by increased anabolism of muscle and adipose tissues
b. Is a state of reduced synthesis of fat and increased storage of the same
c. Is largely driven by TNF and other cytokines
d. Is caused specifically by the great energy requirements of tumour cells
e. Is usually seen as loss of body fat with maintenance of lean body mass and normal energy levels
**Answer: c**
*Cachexia is a catabolic, cytokine-driven (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) systemic wasting syndrome — not simply due to the tumour's own metabolic demands, and it wastes BOTH fat and lean muscle mass, with increased (not normal) resting energy expenditure.*
---
**Q40.** Both benign and malignant tumours can cause problems due to
a. Spread to distant sites
b. Invasion of adjacent structures
c. Hormone production
d. Both (b) and (c)
e. Both (a) and (c)
**Answer: c**
*Hormone-secreting tumours (e.g., benign pituitary/adrenal adenomas as well as malignant endocrine tumours) can cause problems purely from hormone excess regardless of malignant potential. Distant spread (a) and true invasion (b) are essentially malignant-specific behaviors.*
---
**Q41.** The following are inherited predispositions to cancer due to autosomal recessive syndromes of defective DNA repair except one. Which one?
a. Xeroderma pigmentosum
b. Ataxia-telangiectasia
c. Bloom syndrome
d. Fanconi anemia
e. BRCA1/2 associated breast cancer
**Answer: e**
*BRCA1/2-associated breast/ovarian cancer syndrome is autosomal dominant, unlike the other classic autosomal recessive DNA-repair-defect syndromes listed.*
---
**Q42.** The following are inherited predispositions to cancer due to autosomal dominant syndromes except one. Which one?
a. Retinoblastoma
b. Li-Fraumeni syndrome
c. Cervical squamous cell carcinoma
d. Familial adenomatous polyposis/colon cancer
e. Neurofibromatosis 1 and 2
**Answer: c**
*Cervical SCC is driven by HPV infection, not an inherited autosomal dominant cancer syndrome, unlike the other four classic examples.*
---
**Q43.** The following occupational cancers are correctly matched to their causative agents except which one?
a. Benzene – Leukemia
b. Cadmium – Prostate cancer
c. Asbestos – Mesothelioma
d. Radon – Bone cancer
e. Ethylene oxide – Leukemia
**Answer: d**
*Radon exposure is classically linked to lung cancer, not bone cancer (radium, not radon, is linked to bone cancer/sarcoma).*
---
**Q44.** The following are risk factors for HPV associated cancers except one. Which one?
a. Intramuscular Gardasil 9 and Cervarix
b. Early sexual debut
c. Having multiple sexual partners
d. Having a sexual partner with multiple sexual partners
e. Immunosuppression
**Answer: a**
*Gardasil 9 and Cervarix are prophylactic HPV vaccines — they reduce risk rather than being a risk factor themselves.*
---
**Q45.** The WHO estimates about 5% of all cancer cases worldwide are associated with HPV. The following include examples of HPV associated cancers except which one?
a. Cervical and oropharyngeal cancers
b. Vulval and vaginal cancers
c. Seminoma
d. Penile cancer
e. Anal cancer
**Answer: c**
*Seminoma is a testicular germ cell tumour with no established HPV association, unlike the other listed HPV-related anogenital/oropharyngeal cancers.*
---
**Q46.** The following are currently preventable through vaccination except?
a. Hepatocellular carcinoma
b. Meningioma
c. Cervical squamous cell carcinoma
d. Anal warts
e. Oropharyngeal cancer
**Answer: b**
*Meningioma has no infectious/viral etiology and thus no vaccine-preventable pathway, unlike HBV-related HCC and HPV-related cervical/anal/oropharyngeal disease.*
---
**Q47.** Grading of malignant tumours is based on the following features except?
a. Pleomorphism
b. Mitotic rate
c. Local invasion
d. Nuclear size
e. Dysplasia
**Answer: c**
*Local invasion is a staging concept (extent of spread), not a grading criterion (which focuses on cytologic/architectural differentiation features like a, b, d, e).*
---
**Q48.** Natural ultraviolet radiation from the sun
a. Causes chromosome breakage, translocations and point mutations
b. Damages DNA by forming pyrimidine dimers
c. Poses greater risk to lighter skinned people than darker skinned people in causing skin cancers
d. Is associated with melanomas that are with intense intermittent exposure—as occurs with sunbathing
e. Is only known to cause melanomas
**Answer: e**
*UV radiation causes basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma as well as melanoma — it's not limited to melanoma alone, making this the false statement.*
---
**Q49.** Which statement is not true of *Helicobacter pylori* infection?
a. It is associated with an increased risk for the development of gastric lymphomas of B cell origin
b. Eradication of *H. pylori* "cures" the lymphoma by removing antigenic stimulus for T cells
c. It is implicated in the genesis of both gastric adenocarcinomas and gastric lymphomas
d. The sequence of histopathological changes after infection consists of initial development of chronic inflammation/gastritis, followed by gastric atrophy, intestinal metaplasia of the lining cells, dysplasia, and cancer
e. Adenocarcinoma or lymphoma results in up to 97% of infected persons
**Answer: e**
*Only a small minority of infected individuals ever develop gastric cancer or MALT lymphoma — 97% is a vast overstatement.*
---
**Q50.** Which statement is not true of Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections
a. About 70% to 85% of hepatocellular carcinomas worldwide are due to infection with HBV or HCV
b. HBV carries multiple genomes that encode viral oncoproteins
c. Carcinogenesis by the two is immunologically mediated through chronic inflammation with hepatocyte death leading to regeneration and genomic damage
d. Vaccination against HBV confers a reduced risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in the population
e. Chronic infection by either virus predisposes to hepatocellular carcinoma
**Answer: b**
*HBV has a single small circular partially double-stranded DNA genome (not "multiple genomes") that encodes the HBx oncoprotein among others.*
---
**Q51.** Which of the following is a physiologic antitumour effector mechanism?
a. Cytotoxic T lymphocytes
b. Neutrophils
c. Eosinophils
d. Basophils
e. IgA antibodies
**Answer: a**
*Cytotoxic (CD8+) T lymphocytes are the principal cell-mediated antitumour immune effectors; the other cell types/antibody class listed have no primary antitumour surveillance role.*
---
**Q52.** Which statement is true regarding antitumour effector mechanisms?
a. Cell-mediated immunity is the least dominant antitumour mechanism in vivo
b. Antibodies against tumours are more effective than cell mediated immunity
c. Tumours that fail to express MHC class I antigens are not recognized by NK cells
d. Cytotoxic T-lymphocytes offer no protective role against virus associated neoplasms
e. A monoclonal antibody against CD20, a B cell surface antigen, is used for treatment of certain non-Hodgkin lymphomas
**Answer: e**
*This describes rituximab, an established anti-CD20 therapy for B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas. Cell-mediated immunity is actually the DOMINANT antitumour mechanism (making a and b false); NK cells specifically target cells with LOW/absent MHC-I (the opposite of c); and CTLs are important against virus-driven cancers (making d false).*
---
**Q53.** The following are immune evasion mechanisms by tumours except one. Which one?
a. Selective outgrowth of antigen negative variants
b. Loss or reduced expression of histocompatibility molecules
c. Antigen masking
d. Immune surveillance
e. Downregulation of co-stimulatory molecules
**Answer: d**
*Immune surveillance is the host's protective anticancer mechanism, not a tumour strategy to evade the immune system — the opposite of the others listed.*
---
**Q54.** The following laboratory tests are tumour morphology-based except
a. Routine haematoxylin and eosin staining of histology sections
b. Frozen section
c. Fine needle aspiration cytology
d. Tumour markers
e. Immunohistochemistry
**Answer: d**
*Tumour markers are biochemical/serologic assays (e.g., blood tests), not tests that assess tissue morphology under the microscope like the others.*
---
**Q55.** The following are utilities of molecular techniques in oncopathology except one. Which one?
a. Diagnosis of malignancy
b. Establishing the prognosis and behaviour of a cancer
c. Detection of minimal residual disease
d. Determining the pleomorphism of the tumour
e. Therapeutic decision-making
**Answer: d**
*Pleomorphism (variation in cell/nuclear size and shape) is a morphological/histological assessment made by light microscopy, not something molecular techniques are used to determine.*
---
**Q56.** True of molecular profiling of tumours except one. Which one?
a. It is currently carried out routinely in all histopathology laboratories
b. It is done by cDNA arrays and sequencing
c. Involves determining expression of large segments of the genome
d. Is useful in molecular cataloguing of all the mutations in a tumour genome
e. Involves stratification of otherwise histologically identical tumours, or those of distinct histogenesis that share a mutation, for treatment and prognostication purposes
**Answer: a**
*Molecular profiling remains a specialized, resource-intensive technique available mainly in reference/research labs — it is not yet routine practice in all histopathology laboratories, especially in resource-limited settings.*
---
**Q57.** Which of the following is false regarding chemical carcinogenic agents?
a. Aflatoxin B1 is a naturally occurring agent produced by some strains of *Aspergillus*
b. Promoters such as phorbol esters are directly carcinogenic and do not require prior exposure to an initiating agent
c. Vinyl chloride, arsenic, nickel, chromium, insecticides, and polychlorinated biphenyls are carcinogens of occupational health concern
d. Nitrites used as food preservatives cause concern since they form nitrosamines suspected to be carcinogenic
e. Aflatoxin B1 produces characteristic "signature mutations" in the TP53 gene whose detection establishes it as the causative agent
**Answer: b**
*Tumour promoters like phorbol esters are NOT carcinogenic on their own — they only enhance tumour formation in cells previously exposed to an initiating (mutagenic) agent. This is the false statement.*
---
**Q58.** Direct-acting carcinogenic agents
a. Require metabolic conversion to become carcinogenic
b. Are in general the most potent carcinogens known to man
c. Include some anticancer medications used in chemotherapy regimens, e.g. alkylating agents, that may cause a subsequent, second form of cancer
d. Include certain viruses with a risk of causing a subsequent, second form of cancer
e. Typically act on benign tumours to convert them to malignant ones
**Answer: c**
*By definition, direct-acting carcinogens act without needing metabolic activation (unlike "indirect-acting"/procarcinogens, making a false). A key clinical example is alkylating chemotherapy agents (e.g., cyclophosphamide), which are themselves direct-acting carcinogens and can cause secondary malignancies (like leukemia) years after treatment.*
---
**Q59.** The following are benign tumours except
a. Schwannoma
b. Psammoma bodies
c. Leiomyoma
d. Papilloma
e. Condyloma acuminatum
**Answer: b**
*Psammoma bodies are concentric calcified structures seen microscopically within certain tumours (e.g., papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous ovarian tumours, meningioma) — they are a histological finding, not a tumour type themselves.*
---
**Q60.** The following are malignant tumours except
a. Melanoma
b. Immature teratoma
c. Ductal carcinoma
d. Mature teratoma
e. Lymphoma
**Answer: d**
*A mature teratoma is benign (well-differentiated adult-type tissues); an immature teratoma, by contrast, is malignant.*
---

articles.title: General Pathology MCQs: Fixatives, FNA, Endocrine & ARDS — MCQ Bank
articles.content:
G**eneral Pathology (Paper One)**

**11.** The preferred fixative for tissue specimen collected for electron microscopy is
a. 10% neutral buffered formalin
b. Glutaraldehyde
c. Nitric acid
d. Methanol
e. Ethanol
**Answer: b** *Glutaraldehyde preserves ultrastructural detail needed for EM; formalin lacks the resolution/cross-linking speed required.*
---
**Q12.** Pap smears are fixed using
a. Ethanol
b. 10% neutral buffered formalin
c. Glutaraldehyde
d. Nitric acid
e. Air-drying
**Answer: a** *Wet fixation in 95% ethanol immediately after smearing preserves nuclear/cytoplasmic detail for cytology.*
---
**Q13.** Which is true of fine needle aspiration?
a. It is an exfoliative technique
b. Ideal for bony tissue
c. Ideal for wounds and ulcers
d. Ideal for superficial masses
e. Expensive and time consuming
**Answer: d** *FNA is a minimally invasive, quick, cheap technique best suited to palpable/superficial lumps.*
---
**Q14.** The most common side effect of fine needle aspiration is
a. Minor pain/discomfort
b. Haematoma formation
c. Fainting
d. Infection
e. Psychological trauma
**Answer: a** *FNA is very low-risk; mild discomfort at the needle site is by far the commonest complaint.*
---
**Q15.** Fluid cytopathology specimens include the following except
a. Urine
b. Pleural fluid
c. Peritoneal fluid
d. Cystic masses
e. Lump aspirate
**Answer: e** *A lump aspirate is a solid-mass FNA sample, not a fluid specimen.*
---
**Q16.** Graves disease
a. Is the most common cause of hypothyroidism
b. Occurs after upper respiratory tract viral infection
c. Manifests with characteristic exophthalmos
d. Demonstrates decreased uptake of radioactive iodine
e. Is demonstrated by raised TSH levels
**Answer: c** *Exophthalmos from retro-orbital lymphocytic infiltration/glycosaminoglycan deposition is a hallmark; Graves causes hyperthyroidism with increased iodine uptake and suppressed TSH.*
---
**Q17.** Which statement regarding diabetes insipidus is false?
a. It is caused by similar mutations as diabetes mellitus
b. It can occur after neurosurgical intervention
c. It is characterized by inability of kidneys to concentrate urine
d. Polyuria is the universal presentation
e. It is characterized by urine with low specific gravity
**Answer: a** *DI (ADH deficiency/resistance) and DM (insulin/glucose disorder) are pathophysiologically unrelated.*
---
**Q18.** Features of diabetic nephropathy include the following except?
a. Nodular glomerulosclerosis
b. Diffuse mesangial sclerosis
c. Necrotizing papillitis
d. Necrotizing fasciitis
e. Capillary basement thickening
**Answer: d** *Necrotizing fasciitis is a soft-tissue infection, unrelated to renal pathology.*
---
**Q19.** Clinical features of hyperaldosteronism include
a. Systolic BP 80–100mmHg
b. Lower than normal diastolic BP
c. Tetany
d. Hyperkalemia
e. Hypertension with refractory response to spironolactone
**Answer: e** *Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalemia (not hyperkalemia/hypotension); its diagnostic hallmark is BP responsiveness to the aldosterone antagonist spironolactone.*
---
**Q20.** Distinguishing histological feature of pituitary adenoma from normal tissue is
a. Local invasion
b. Cellular monomorphism and lack of a reticulin network
c. Marked cellular pleomorphism
d. Marked cellular polymorphism
e. Hypocellularity
**Answer: b** *Loss of the normal acinar reticulin framework with a monomorphic cell population is the key diagnostic clue on histology.*
---
**Q21.** Responsible for alveolar damage in ARDS except one. Which one?
a. Leukotrienes
b. Oxidants
c. Proteases
d. Platelet-activating factor (PAF)
e. Interleukin-10 (IL-10)
**Answer: e** *IL-10 is anti-inflammatory; the others are damaging mediators released by activated neutrophils/macrophages.*
---
**Q22.** Which is NOT a diffuse obstructive pulmonary disease?
a. Paraseptal emphysema
b. Chronic bronchitis
c. Relaxation atelectasis
d. Occupational asthma
e. Bronchiectasis due to cystic fibrosis
**Answer: c** *Atelectasis is lung collapse from external compression/pneumothorax, not an obstructive airway disease.*
---
**Q23.** NOT a typical finding in COPD?
a. Normal or slightly decreased FVC
b. Decreased expiratory flow rate
c. Decreased FEV1
d. Increased FEV/FVC ratio
e. Increase in airflow resistance
**Answer: d** *COPD's hallmark is a DECREASED FEV1/FVC ratio (airflow obstruction), not increased.*
---
**Q24.** Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
a. Has a weak epidemiologic link to Epstein-Barr virus
b. Tends to be radiosensitive
c. Metastasizes to the lungs at stage 2
d. Tends to be accompanied by atypical lymphocytosis
e. Has one histologic variant only
**Answer: b** *NPC (especially the non-keratinizing/undifferentiated type) is notably radiosensitive; it has a strong (not weak) EBV link and multiple histologic subtypes.*
---
**Q25.** Tumour suppressor gene abnormality most common in both Small Cell and Non-Small Cell Lung Carcinoma?
a. 3p deletions
b. Rb mutations
c. p16/CDKN2A mutations
d. P53 mutations
e. KRAS mutations
**Answer: d** *TP53 mutation is the single most common genetic alteration shared across both major lung cancer types.*
---
**Q26.** Gastric biopsies predominantly demonstrate *H. pylori* organisms
a. Within giant multinucleated macrophages
b. Within cytoplasm of glandular epithelial cells
c. Within superficial mucus overlying epithelial cells
d. Within the interstitium
e. Within blood vessels
**Answer: c** *H. pylori is a non-invasive, surface organism residing in the mucus layer above the gastric epithelium.*
---
**Q27.** Defects in celiac disease include
a. Intraluminal digestion
b. Terminal digestion
c. Blood flow
d. Lymphatic transport
e. All the above
**Answer: b** *Celiac disease primarily damages the villous brush border, impairing terminal (mucosal) digestion/absorption; it doesn't primarily involve pancreatic secretion, blood flow, or lymphatics.*
---
**Q28.** Features of *Vibrio cholerae* infection include
a. Predominantly invasive infection
b. Increased absorption of sodium
c. Increased absorption of bicarbonate
d. Release of chloride ions into the lumen after opening of CFTR
e. Massive inflammatory diarrhoea
**Answer: d** *Cholera toxin activates adenylate cyclase, opening the CFTR chloride channel and driving secretory (non-invasive, non-inflammatory) diarrhoea.*
---
**Q29.** NOT a feature of Crohn disease?
a. Affects ileum and colon
b. Skip lesions are found
c. Bowel wall appearance is thick
d. Perianal fistulas
e. Toxic megacolon
**Answer: e** *Toxic megacolon is classically a complication of ulcerative colitis, not Crohn disease.*
---
**Q30.** Features of *Clostridium difficile* infection except?
a. Formation of pseudomembranes
b. Hyperplasia of surface epithelium
c. Dense infiltrate of neutrophils
d. Occasional fibrin thrombi within capillaries
e. Damaged crypts distended by mucopurulent exudate that "erupts" to the surface
**Answer: b** *C. diff colitis causes epithelial injury/necrosis, not hyperplasia.*
---
**Q31.** Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia
a. Peaks in incidence at about age 20 years
b. Is a slow but inevitable/irreversible progression to cervical cancer
c. Is always treated by surgical intervention to prevent progression
d. Cannot be prevented/reduced by vaccination
e. Is always manifested by cytological atypia and by dysplasia
**Answer: e** *By definition CIN requires atypia/dysplasia on cytology/histology; progression is neither inevitable nor always requiring surgery, and HPV vaccination does reduce risk.*
---
**Q32.** Aetiological theories for endometriosis except one. Which one?
a. Metaplastic theory
b. Vascular dissemination theory
c. Neoplastic theory
d. Lymphatic dissemination theory
e. Regurgitation theory
**Answer: c** *"Neoplastic theory" is not a recognized mechanism of endometriosis; the accepted theories are retrograde menstruation (regurgitation), metaplasia, and vascular/lymphatic dissemination.*
---
**Q33.** True of serous endometrial cancer?
a. It is the most common type
b. Exposure to unopposed oestrogen is a risk factor
c. PTEN mutations occur early
d. TP53 mutations occur in nearly all cases
e. Women with Cowden syndrome are at higher risk
**Answer: d** *Serous (Type II) endometrial cancer is p53-driven and occurs in atrophic, not estrogen-stimulated, endometrium — unlike endometrioid (Type I) cancer, which relates to b, c, e.*
---
**Q34.** Leiomyomata
a. Occur most frequently in the cervix uteri
b. Have a 50-50 chance of malignant transformation
c. Often occur in postmenopausal women
d. Are often asymptomatic and multiple
e. Vary histologically from resembling leiomyoma to wildly anaplastic neoplasms
**Answer: d** *Uterine fibroids are typically multiple and often asymptomatic; they mostly occur in the corpus (not cervix), regress after menopause, and essentially never turn malignant.*
---
**Q35.** The most frequent tumours of the ovary are
a. Sex cord stromal tumours
b. Germ cell tumours
c. Surface epithelial-stromal cell tumours
d. Immature teratomas
e. Tubo-ovarian abscesses
**Answer: c** *Epithelial tumours account for the majority of ovarian neoplasms, especially in adults.*
---
**Q36.** NOT true regarding juvenile idiopathic arthritis?
a. Oligoarthritis is common
b. Systemic disease frequently occurs
c. Small joints are affected more than large joints
d. Rheumatoid nodules and rheumatoid factor are usually absent
e. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) seropositivity is common
**Answer: c** *In JIA, large joints (knees, ankles) are more commonly affected, especially in the oligoarticular subtype — unlike adult RA which favors small joints.*
---
**Q37.** Most common causative agent of pyogenic osteomyelitis is
a. *Salmonella typhi*
b. *Salmonella paratyphi*
c. *Streptococcus pyogenes*
d. *Staphylococcus aureus*
e. *Treponema pallidum*
**Answer: d** *S. aureus causes the vast majority of pyogenic bone infections (Salmonella is notable in sickle cell patients specifically).*
---
**Q38.** Which is true of osteosarcoma?
a. It is a rare primary bone tumour
b. Benign forms account for 20% of cases
c. Women are affected more than men
d. 75% of cases occur before the age of 20 years
e. All the above are true
**Answer: d** *Osteosarcoma is actually the most common primary malignant bone tumor, has no benign form, and slightly favors males — but it does show a strong predilection for adolescents/young adults.*
---
**Q39.** Benign soft tissue tumours include the following except?
a. Haematoma
b. Haemangioma
c. Lipoma
d. Schwannoma
e. Neurofibroma
**Answer: a** *A haematoma is a blood collection, not a neoplasm.*
---
**Q40.** A malignant tumour of smooth muscle cells is known as?
a. Leiomyomata
b. Fibrosarcoma
c. Leiomyoma
d. Rhabdomyosarcoma
e. Leiomyosarcoma
**Answer: e** *Leiomyosarcoma is the malignant counterpart of leiomyoma (smooth muscle); rhabdomyosarcoma arises from striated/skeletal muscle instead.*
---
**Q41.** True of testicular tumours except one. Which one?
a. Germ cell tumours are the most common testicular neoplasms
b. Cryptorchidism and infertility are risk factors
c. Seminomas are insensitive to radiotherapy
d. Nonseminomatous tumors tend to spread early via lymphatic and hematogenous routes
e. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common testicular tumor in men older than 60
**Answer: c** *Seminomas are actually classically exquisitely radiosensitive — this is the false statement.*
---
**Q42.** NOT a characteristic of nephritic syndrome?
a. Haematuria
b. Oliguria
c. Azotemia
d. Proteinuria
e. Hypotension
**Answer: e** *Nephritic syndrome causes fluid retention and HYPERtension, not hypotension.*
---
**Q43.** The most common cause of pyelonephritis is
a. *Escherichia coli*
b. *Proteus mirabilis*
c. *Klebsiella sp.*
d. *Enterobacter sp.*
e. *Streptococcus faecalis*
**Answer: a**
---
**Q44.** The most common type of renal stones is
a. Struvite
b. Uric acid
c. Calcium oxalate
d. Cysteine
e. Unknown
**Answer: c**
---
**Q45.** The most common subtype of malignant renal neoplasms is
a. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma
b. Papillary renal cell carcinoma
c. Squamous cell carcinoma
d. Sarcoma
e. Angiomyolipoma
**Answer: a**
---
**Q46.** Molluscum contagiosum
a. Is caused by a poxvirus
b. Is typically sexually transmitted
c. Is a common type of plantar wart
d. Is caused by low risk HPV strains
e. Is caused by high risk HPV strains
**Answer: a** *Poxvirus infection, spread by direct contact (not exclusively sexual); unrelated to HPV.*
---
**Q47.** NOT a sign that a patch could be melanoma?
a. Asymmetry
b. Irregular borders
c. Variegated colour
d. Increasing diameter
e. Persistence from birth
**Answer: e** *The ABCDE rule covers Asymmetry, Border, Colour, Diameter, Evolving — a lesion unchanged since birth is not itself a red flag.*
---
**Q48.** NOT true of benign epithelial breast lesions?
a. Usually do not cause symptoms
b. The majority are precursors of cancer
c. Nonproliferative breast changes include duct ectasia and apocrine metaplasia
d. Fibroadenoma is a type of proliferative disease without atypia
e. They are frequently detected as mammographic calcifications
**Answer: b** *Most benign breast lesions (fibrocystic change, fibroadenoma) do NOT progress to cancer.*
---
**Q49.** NOT a risk factor for developing breast cancer?
a. Female gender
b. Increasing age
c. Late menarche
d. Strong family history
e. High breast density
**Answer: c** *Late menarche is protective (shorter lifetime estrogen exposure); early menarche is the actual risk factor.*
---
**Q50.** Mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2
a. Are responsible for 80–90% of single gene familial breast cancers
b. Are responsible for 3–6% of all breast cancers
c. Increase the risk of ovarian carcinoma
d. Increase the risk for other epithelial cancers, such as prostatic and pancreatic carcinoma
e. All the above are true
**Answer: e**
---
**Q51.** The hallmark of acute inflammation is:
a. Increased blood flow
b. Rubor, calor, dolor, increased permeability of microcirculation
c. Increased vascular permeability of microcirculation
d. Vascular stasis
e. Ischaemia
**Answer: c** *Increased microvascular permeability (leading to exudation) is the defining vascular hallmark of acute inflammation.*
---
**Q52.** The hallmark of chronic inflammation is:
a. Increased permeability of microcirculation
b. Migration of macrophages at site of injury
c. Tissue destruction
d. Tissue remodelling
e. Mononuclear cell infiltration
**Answer: e** *Chronic inflammation is defined by lymphocyte/macrophage/plasma cell (mononuclear) infiltration.*
---
**Q53.** "Heart failure cells" found in the lungs in chronic passive congestion are actually
a. T-lymphocytes
b. B-lymphocytes
c. Neutrophils
d. Macrophages
e. Eosinophils
**Answer: d** *Hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages, from phagocytosed extravasated RBCs due to pulmonary venous congestion.*
---
**Q54.** Which disorder is most likely to be associated with an exudate rather than a transudate?
a. Congestive heart failure
b. Suppurative inflammation
c. Glomerulonephritis
d. Peritonitis
e. Nephrotic syndrome
**Answer: b** *Suppurative (pus-forming) inflammation is protein/cell-rich exudate by definition; CHF and nephrotic syndrome classically produce transudates from hydrostatic/oncotic imbalance.*
---
**Q55.** Classic astrocytoma has which microscopic features?
a. Widespread concentric calcifications
b. Fibrillary astrocytes in the background of loosely structured microcysts
c. Cells with rounded vesicular nuclei, small distinct nucleoli, perinuclear halos, chicken wire vessels
d. Microvascular proliferation and geographic necrosis
e. Granulation tissue
**Answer: b** *(c describes oligodendroglioma's "fried egg" appearance; d describes glioblastoma.)*
---
**Q56.** NOT a good prognostic marker of glioblastoma multiforme?
a. Age <50 years
b. Secondary glioblastoma
c. MGMT promoter methylation
d. Presence of necrosis
e. Absence of necrosis
**Answer: d** *Necrosis is a hallmark of aggressive, poor-prognosis GBM.*
---
**Q57.** NOT true about pilomyxoid astrocytoma?
a. Has a monophasic architecture
b. Has a predominant myxoid background
c. Angiocentric pattern is very rare
d. Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic bodies are very rare
e. Optic chiasma is always affected
**Answer: e** *An absolute "always" overstates the typical (hypothalamic/chiasmatic-predominant, not universal) location.*
---
**Q58.** True regarding small cell glioblastoma?
a. Tumour cells show severe nuclear atypia
b. Often associated with EGFR amplification
c. Most of the tumours are IDH-mutated
d. All of the above
e. None of the above
**Answer: b** *Small cell GBM is typically IDH-wildtype with frequent EGFR amplification, despite deceptively bland/monotonous nuclei.*
---
**Q59.** 48-year-old woman, 3-week headaches, grand mal seizure, low-grade fever, papilledema, 3cm ring-enhancing right parietal lesion on CT. Most likely diagnosis?
a. Astrocytoma multiforme
b. Herpes simplex encephalitis
c. Arteriovenous malformation
d. Cerebral abscess
e. Multiple sclerosis plaque
**Answer: d** *Fever plus a ring-enhancing lesion favors an infectious abscess over a tumor.*
---
**Q60.** 42-year-old man, progressive choreiform movements, behavioral change, intact memory, affected brother. Most likely diagnosis?
a. Huntington disease
b. Parkinson's disease
c. Alzheimer's disease
d. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
e. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
**Answer: a**
---
**Q61.** In a state of shock there is:
a. Decreased hydrostatic pressure and increased osmotic pressure
b. Cardiovascular collapse
c. An active process leading to increased volume of blood
d. Decreased pulse rate
e. Fever
**Answer: b**
---
**Q62.** The most frequent sites of venous thrombosis are
a. Veins of lower extremity
b. Pelvic veins
c. Portal veins
d. Hepatic veins
e. Pulmonary veins
**Answer: a**
---
**Q63.** NOT a malignant tumour?
a. Glioma
b. Lymphoma
c. Melanoma
d. Leiomyoma
e. Medulloblastoma
**Answer: d** *Leiomyoma is benign.*
---
**Q64.** Aflatoxin B1, derived from a fungus contaminating grain foods, most commonly induces:
a. Transitional cell carcinoma of the lung
b. Adenocarcinoma of the rectum
c. Squamous cell carcinoma of skin
d. Hepatocellular carcinoma
e. Renal cell carcinoma
**Answer: d**
---
**Q65.** Grading of cancer is based on which of the following?
a. Size of the primary tumor
b. Spread of cancer cells to regional lymph nodes
c. Presence of bloodborne metastasis
d. Degree of differentiation of tumor cells and the number of mitosis and anaplasia
e. Presence of capsular invasion by tumor cells
**Answer: d** *a, b, c describe staging (TNM); grading assesses differentiation/mitotic activity/anaplasia.*
---
**Q66.** A malignant tumour of mesenchymal origin is termed:
a. Carcinoma
b. Hepatoma
c. Hematoma
d. Sarcoma
e. Teratoma
**Answer: d**
---
**Q67.** Which pair does NOT correctly match the tumour with its causative agent?
a. Anogenital carcinoma – HPV (16 and 18)
b. Burkitt lymphoma – EBV
c. Hepatocellular carcinoma – hepatitis A virus
d. Carcinoma of the stomach – *Helicobacter pylori*
e. Squamous cell carcinoma skin – ultraviolet radiation
**Answer: c** *HCC is linked to hepatitis B/C, not hepatitis A.*
---
**Q68.** 39-year-old man, testicular mass removed and examined. Most compelling evidence the lesion is malignant:
a. Cells infiltrate a narrow band of tunica albuginea
b. Two mitoses found in every high power field
c. Nuclei are viable in size and tend to stain
d. X-ray shows two round nodules in the left lung and one in the right, not present two years ago
e. The patient is found to be infertile
**Answer: d** *New metastatic lesions are the most definitive proof of malignant behavior.*
---
**Q69.** 6-month-old baby, blue eyes, decreased pigmentation of hair/skin, mousy odor, severe mental retardation. Enzyme deficiency?
a. Homogentisate oxidase
b. Phenylalanine oxidase
c. P-hydroxyphenyl pyruvate hydroxylase
d. Tyrosinase
e. Alpha glucocerebrosidase
**Answer: b** *Describes classic phenylketonuria (PKU) — deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase.*
---
**Q70.** Rare early-onset disorder, males and females equally affected, only homozygous persons affected. Mode of inheritance?
a. Autosomal dominant
b. Autosomal recessive
c. X-linked dominant
d. X-linked recessive
e. Mitochondrial inheritance
**Answer: b**
---
**Q71.** Caseation necrosis is most characteristic of:
a. Acute myocardial infarction
b. Tuberculosis
c. Acute pancreatitis
d. Cerebral infarct
e. Pulmonary pneumoconiosis
**Answer: b**
---
**Q72.** The most characteristic feature of granulation tissue is the:
a. Growth of fibroblasts and new capillaries
b. Resemblance to a granuloma
c. Character of the exudate
d. Granular scale that results
e. Presence of monocytes and fibroblasts
**Answer: a**
---
**Q73.** Growth factor elaborated by macrophages, recruiting macrophages/fibroblasts to the wound site and inducing all steps in angiogenesis:
a. Vascular endothelial growth factor
b. Fibroblast growth factor
c. Epithelial growth factor
d. Platelet derived growth factor
e. Endostatin
**Answer: a**
---
**Q74.** 20-year-old man, lacerated arm wound stitched, healed but disfigured by a prominent raised irregular nodular scar over the next 2 months. Best describes:
a. Organization
b. Dehiscence
c. Resolution
d. Keloid formation
e. Secondary union
**Answer: d**
---
**Q75.** Morphological changes seen in chronic nonspecific inflammation include an increase in:
a. Neutrophils
b. Neutrophils, lymphocytes and liquefaction necrosis
c. Lymphocytes, macrophages and fibrosis
d. Neutrophils, macrophages and coagulative necrosis
e. Neutrophils, giant cells and caseous necrosis
**Answer: c**
---
**Q76.** Granuloma formation is most frequently associated with:
a. The healing process
b. Acute inflammation
c. Wound contraction
d. Fibroblasts and neovascularization
e. A persistent irritant
**Answer: e**
---
**Q77 (*2 – repeats the "hallmark of acute inflammation" theme from Q51, with different choices).**
Which of the following is the hallmark of acute inflammation:
a. Neutrophils
b. Connective tissue
c. Granulation tissue
d. Macrophages
e. A persistent irritant
**Answer: a** *At the cellular level, neutrophil recruitment is the defining early hallmark, complementing Q51's vascular-permeability framing of the same concept.*
---
**Q78.** Which molecules are thought to mediate many of the systemic effects of inflammation, and are chemotactic and stimulate adhesion?
a. Interleukin 1 (IL-1) and tumor necrosis factor
b. C5a and leukotriene B4
c. C3b
d. Leukotriene C4, D4, E4
e. Bradykinin
**Answer: a** *IL-1/TNF drive systemic effects (fever, acute phase response, endothelial adhesion molecule expression); C5a/LTB4 are chemotactic but act mainly locally.*
---
**Q79.** Which of the following is a reversible change:
a. Karyorrhexis
b. Pyknosis
c. Karyolysis
d. Swelling of endoplasmic reticulum
e. Gangrenous necrosis
**Answer: d** *The others are nuclear/necrotic changes marking irreversible injury; ER swelling is a classic early reversible finding.*
---
**Q80.** Metaplasia is most closely associated with:
a. Diminished blood supply
b. Increased workload
c. Necrosis
d. Chronic irritation
e. Hypercalcemia
**Answer: d**
---
**Q81.** A localized area of ischemic necrosis is mostly associated with:
a. Ascites
b. Petechiae
c. Infarction
d. Emboli formation
e. Hematoma
**Answer: c**
---
**Q82.** Dystrophic calcification is most closely associated with:
a. Hypercalcemia
b. Necrosis
c. Chronic irritation
d. Diminished blood flow
e. Increased workload
**Answer: b** *Dystrophic calcification occurs in dead/damaged tissue with normal serum calcium (vs. metastatic calcification, linked to hypercalcemia).*
---
**Q83.** Which type of necrosis is most commonly associated with chemical injury?
a. Coagulative necrosis
b. Liquefactive necrosis
c. Caseous necrosis
d. Fat necrosis
e. Gangrenous necrosis
**Answer: b** *Corrosive chemical injuries (strong acids/alkalis) digest tissue enzymatically, producing liquefactive necrosis.*
---
**Q84.** Which type of necrosis is grossly opaque and chalky white:
a. Coagulation necrosis
b. Liquefactive necrosis
c. Caseous necrosis
d. Fat necrosis
e. Gangrenous necrosis
**Answer: d** *Saponification (calcium soap formation) gives fat necrosis its chalky white gross appearance.*
---
**Q85.** 35-year-old man struck on the leg by a falling pallet rack; skin intact; purple bruise develops, and 16 days later there's a yellow-brown color at the site. Substance responsible:
a. Lipofuscin
b. Bilirubin
c. Melanin
d. Hemosiderin
e. Glycogen
**Answer: d** *Hemoglobin breakdown within a resolving bruise progresses to hemosiderin, giving the late golden-brown discoloration.*
---
**Q86.** 43-year-old man, chronic burning substernal pain, biopsy of lower esophageal mucosa shows columnar epithelium with goblet cells, no mass/ulceration/hemorrhage. Represents:
a. Dysplasia
b. Hyperplasia
c. Carcinoma
d. Ischemia
e. Metaplasia
**Answer: e** *Classic Barrett's esophagus — squamous-to-intestinal (columnar with goblet cells) metaplasia from chronic reflux.*
---
**Q87.** 71-year-old woman, loss of consciousness >1 hour, MCA occlusion on angiogram; 3 months later CT shows a 5cm cystic area in the left parietal cortex. This is the consequence of resolution from which pathologic cellular event?
a. Liquefactive necrosis
b. Atrophy
c. Coagulative necrosis
d. Caseous necrosis
e. Apoptosis
**Answer: a** *Cerebral infarcts undergo liquefactive necrosis, ultimately leaving a cystic cavity.*
---
**Q88.** 19-year-old woman breastfeeds successfully for nearly a year with no difficulty. Which cellular process, begun during pregnancy, allowed this?
a. Stromal hypertrophy
b. Epithelial dysplasia
c. Steatocyte atrophy
d. Ductal epithelial metaplasia
e. Lobular hyperplasia
**Answer: e** *Pregnancy-driven lobular/glandular hyperplasia expands milk-producing tissue.*
---
**Q89.** An IHC stain identifies intermediate filaments within cells. This cytokeratin stain is most useful for which diagnostic purpose?
a. Cytoskeletal alterations indicate impending cell death
b. A neoplasm is determined to be a carcinoma
c. Contractile properties of the cells can be assessed
d. A history of chronic alcoholism can be confirmed
e. The degree of metaplasia or dysplasia can be assessed
**Answer: b** *Cytokeratin is the classic epithelial-lineage marker used to confirm a tumor is a carcinoma.*
---
**Q90.** 20-year-old woman, Goodpasture syndrome progressing to chronic kidney disease, hypertensive, on chronic dialysis, enlarged heart on chest X-ray. The cardiac enlargement is most likely from which myocardial fiber process?
a. Hypertrophy
b. Fatty infiltration
c. Hyperplasia
d. Fatty degeneration
e. Edema
**Answer: a** *Cardiac myocytes cannot meaningfully proliferate (hyperplasia); chronic pressure/volume overload from hypertension and renal failure causes hypertrophy.*
---
**Q91.** A study identifies predisposing risks for epithelial metaplasia. In which situation is metaplasia most likely to occur?
a. Tanning of the skin following sunlight exposure
b. Lactation following pregnancy
c. Vitamin A deficiency
d. Acute myocardial infarction
e. Urinary obstruction from an enlarged prostate
**Answer: c** *Vitamin A deficiency classically causes squamous metaplasia of respiratory and urinary epithelium.*
---
**Q92.** 60-year-old woman, dark red-black great toe and second/third toes for a month, cold and no sensation, absent dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial pulses, transmetatarsal amputation performed. Most typical for which condition?
a. Diabetes mellitus
b. Gout
c. Blunt force trauma
d. AIDS
e. Rheumatoid arthritis
**Answer: a** *Peripheral vascular disease with dry gangrene is classic in longstanding diabetes.*
---
**Q93.** 18-year-old primigravida, 18 weeks' gestation, uniformly enlarged uterus on ultrasound. Which cellular change leads to this increase in uterine size?
a. Myometrial hypertrophy
b. Endothelial hyperplasia
c. Fatty infiltration
d. Endometrial metaplasia
e. Inflammatory cell infiltration
**Answer: a**
---
**Q94.** 79-year-old man, large MI involving much of the LV free wall, CHF with decreased cardiac output; a year later, worsening CHF with a bulging akinetic LV aneurysm on echo. Which lab test would best indicate poor peripheral tissue perfusion?
a. Elevated troponin I
b. Increased sodium
c. Elevated lactate
d. Increased hematocrit
e. Increased sedimentation rate
**Answer: c** *Lactate rises from anaerobic metabolism when tissue perfusion/oxygen delivery is inadequate.*
---
**Q95.** 40-year-old woman, sudden severe abdominal pain, diffuse tenderness/guarding/rigidity; AST 43, ALT 30, LDH 630, lipase 415; CT shows peritoneal fluid collections and pancreatic enlargement with decreased attenuation. Which cellular change most likely accompanies these findings?
a. Coagulative necrosis
b. Dry gangrene
c. Fat necrosis
d. Apoptosis
e. Liquefactive necrosis
**Answer: c** *Acute pancreatitis: released lipase causes enzymatic fat necrosis of peripancreatic/omental fat.*
---
**Q96.** 26-year-old man, 2 days of high fever, heart murmur, echocardiography shows destruction of the aortic valve by large irregular vegetations, *S. aureus* bacteremia; develops LUQ pain, and abdominal CT shows a wedge-shaped 1.5x3cm splenic lesion with base on the capsule. The splenic lesion most likely results from which cellular abnormality?
a. Coagulative necrosis
b. Abscess formation
c. Metaplasia
d. Caseous necrosis
e. Liquefactive necrosis
**Answer: a** *A wedge-shaped splenic infarct from a septic embolus undergoes coagulative necrosis, characteristic of solid-organ infarcts.*
---
**Q97.** 71-year-old man, urinary retention with frequent trips to the restroom, diffusely enlarged prostate on DRE. Which represents the pathologic change leading to this problem?
a. Dysplasia
b. Hypertrophy
c. Hyperplasia
d. Metaplasia
e. Neoplasia
**Answer: c** *Benign prostatic hyperplasia = increase in glandular/stromal cell number.*
---
**Q98.** 55-year-old man, 30-year history of poorly controlled diabetes, extensive black discoloration of the right foot with yellowish exudate for 2 months, *S. aureus* cultured, below-knee amputation performed. The amputation specimen most likely demonstrates:
a. Neoplasia
b. Gangrene
c. Vasculitis
d. Hemosiderosis
e. Caseation
**Answer: b** *Wet gangrene, given the co-existing bacterial infection and exudate.*
---
**Q99.** Lifestyle study of healthy 20-30-year-olds; a subset consumes a lot of pizza with very little exercise. Which tissue change is most likely to develop as a consequence?
a. Fatty metamorphosis of liver
b. Pancreatic fat necrosis
c. Fatty degeneration of myocardium
d. Hypertrophy of steatocytes
e. Metaplasia of muscle to adipose tissue
**Answer: a** *Excess dietary fat/calories with sedentary lifestyle classically causes hepatic steatosis (fatty liver).*
---
**Q100.** 38-year-old man, traumatic blow to the upper left arm; pain/tenderness persist after 3 months. Plain film shows a 4cm circumscribed soft tissue mass adjacent to the humerus with peripheral areas of brightness on X-ray; the mass gradually resolves over the next year. Which term best describes these changes?
a. Dysplasia
b. Hyperplasia
c. Hypertrophy
d. Metaplasia
e. Neoplasia
**Answer: d** *This describes myositis ossificans — reactive heterotopic bone formation after trauma, where fibroblasts undergo osteoblastic metaplasia; it's benign and self-limited/resolving, unlike neoplasia (note: this is the best-fit answer among imperfect options).*
---
