articles.title: Clinical Genetics: Master Mendelian Disorders & Molecular Basis — Notes
articles.content:
# GENETIC DISORDERS: A FOUNDATIONAL GUIDE
**Mount Kenya University — School of Medicine**
**Human Pathology / Medical Genetics — Year 3 MBChB**

---

## Why Genetics Is Clinically Important

**The scale of the problem**
- Approximately 5% of individuals under 25 years develop a serious disease with a significant genetic component — this is not a rare, footnote topic
- Genetic diagnosis and screening are generally **neither easy nor cheap**
- Only around 50% of early pregnancy miscarriages show demonstrable chromosomal abnormalities — not 100%, a common exam trap

**The three master categories**
Every genetic disorder falls into one of three buckets. Identify the bucket first, and the rest of the logic follows:
1. **Mendelian (single-gene) disorders** — one gene, one major effect, predictable inheritance pattern
2. **Chromosomal disorders** — whole chromosomes or large segments missing, extra, or rearranged
3. **Complex/multigenic disorders** — many genes interacting with environment (e.g., diabetes, hypertension, most common adult diseases)

---

## Mendelian Inheritance — The Underlying Logic

Understand *why* each pattern behaves the way it does — the disease lists become obvious afterward.

**Autosomal Dominant (AD)**
- One abnormal copy of the gene (from either parent) is sufficient to cause disease, because the gene sits on a non-sex chromosome
- **Pattern on a family tree:** disease appears in every generation, no skipping; affected parent has 50% chance of passing it to each child; both sexes equally affected
- **Molecular theme:** typically involves **structural proteins** (collagen, cytoskeletal proteins) or receptors — one bad copy disrupts structure even with a normal copy present
- **Onset:** often adulthood
- **Disorders to know as a set:** Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1), Huntington disease (trinucleotide repeat), familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor defect), polycystic kidney disease, hereditary spherocytosis (~75% of cases)

**Autosomal Recessive (AR)**
- Need TWO abnormal copies (one from each parent) to manifest disease; single copy = silent carrier
- **Pattern:** skips generations; both sexes equally affected; parents typically unaffected carriers; often only one sibling affected
- **Molecular theme:** typically involves **enzyme deficiencies** — one working copy usually produces enough enzyme to avoid disease
- **Onset:** often childhood
- **Disorders to know as a set:** phenylketonuria, galactosemia, glycogen storage diseases, mucopolysaccharidoses, sickle cell anaemia (structural protein exception — one normal beta-globin gene still makes enough normal haemoglobin), most lysosomal storage diseases

**X-linked Recessive**
- Gene is on the X chromosome. Males have only one X, so a single abnormal copy causes disease. Females have two X's, so need two abnormal copies to be affected — usually just carriers
- **Pattern:** almost exclusively affects males; affected males cannot pass it to sons; carrier mothers pass it to 50% of sons (affected) and 50% of daughters (carriers)
- **Key example:** Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) — the most tested X-linked recessive disorder in this course
- **Why carrier females are usually protected:** random X-inactivation (lyonization) means roughly half their cells express the normal X

**The trap option**
"All sex-linked disorders are X-linked recessive" is FALSE: Y-linked disorders exist (rare), and **X-linked dominant** disorders exist too (e.g., vitamin D–resistant rickets).

---

## The Molecular Basis — Mutations

**Types of mutation**
- **Missense:** one amino acid swapped for another; protein still made but altered. Sickle cell anaemia is the textbook example — Glu→Val substitution at codon 6 of beta-globin
- **Nonsense:** a codon becomes a "stop" signal, truncating the protein — usually far more damaging than missense
- **Silent:** DNA changes, but the resulting amino acid is the same (codon redundancy) — no effect on protein

**SNPs (Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms)**
- The most common form of human genetic variation
- Almost always **biallelic**
- Millions exist across the genome (not "less than 100")
- Majority lie **outside coding regions** (not "99% in coding regions")
- Used clinically for disease-risk stratification

**CNVs (Copy Number Variations)**
- Large contiguous stretches of DNA that vary in copy number between individuals
- Responsible for millions of base pairs of difference between any two people
- **DO involve coding sequences/genes** — a common false-statement trap says otherwise
- Immune system and nervous system genes disproportionately affected
- Can be biallelic or complex (multiple alleles)

**Epigenetics**
- Modulation of gene or protein expression **without any change to the underlying DNA sequence** — via DNA methylation, histone modification
- Not the same as a silent mutation (that's DNA-sequence-level)
- Becomes critical later in genomic imprinting (Prader-Willi, Angelman)

---

## Lysosomal Storage Diseases — A High-Yield Cluster

| Disease | Enzyme deficiency | Substance accumulated |
|---|---|---|
| **Tay-Sachs disease** | Hexosaminidase A | GM2 ganglioside |
| **Niemann-Pick A/B** | Sphingomyelinase | Sphingomyelin |
| **Niemann-Pick C** | Defect in intracellular cholesterol transport | Cholesterol and other lipids |
| **Gaucher disease** | Glucocerebrosidase | Glucocerebroside (NOT mucopolysaccharides) |
| **Mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS)** | Various lysosomal enzymes | Mucopolysaccharides (glycosaminoglycans) |

All lysosomal storage diseases are **autosomal recessive**. The single most common trap: confusing Gaucher disease's storage product with mucopolysaccharides — Gaucher = glucocerebroside, MPS = mucopolysaccharides.

---

## Complex (Multigenic) Disorders

- Caused by interaction of **multiple variant genes AND environment** together — neither alone is sufficient
- Environment **strongly** modifies phenotype expression
- Occur when many polymorphisms are co-inherited
- Some disease polymorphisms are shared across diseases; others are disease-specific
- Even **normal** phenotypic traits (height, skin colour, intelligence) are multigenic

---

## Single-Gene Disorders of Large Effect — General Properties

- Individually rare, but collectively account for roughly **1% of adult hospital admissions**
- Follow Mendelian inheritance patterns
- A single mutated gene can cause **multiple phenotypic effects** (pleiotropy)
- Different protein classes produce different severities when defective:
 - Enzyme defects → often mild if partial function remains (AR pattern)
 - Receptor defects → moderate, dose-dependent effects
 - Structural protein defects → often the most dramatic phenotypes (AD pattern)
 - These do **NOT** all present with similar magnitude of dysfunction

---

## Chromosomal Disorders — The Basics

**What counts as a chromosomal disorder**
- May result from **numerical** alterations (too many/too few chromosomes) or **structural** alterations (rearranged, deleted, duplicated segments)
- May affect **autosomes or sex chromosomes**
- Usually **NOT** inherited in a family pattern — most arise **de novo** during gametogenesis

**General rules**
- Loss of chromosomal material is generally **worse** than gain
- Sex chromosome imbalances are tolerated far **better** than autosomal imbalances
- Sex chromosome disorders often produce subtle abnormalities, sometimes undetected at birth
- Virtually all chromosomal syndromes have some congenital malformation component

**Numerical terminology**
- **Euploid** = any exact multiple of the haploid number (n)
- **Polyploid** = 3n, 4n, etc. — generally results in spontaneous abortion
- **Aneuploid** = any number NOT an exact multiple of n (trisomy = 2n+1, monosomy = 2n−1)

---

## Karyotyping and Cytogenetic Notation

**Karyotyping**
- Photographic representation of a stained metaphase spread, arranged by decreasing length
- G-banding produces alternating light/dark bands, allowing mapping of loci and identification of **large** structural abnormalities
- **Critical limitation:** resolution is in the megabase range — **cannot** detect point mutations

**Reading ISCN shorthand**
Example: **46,XX,t(2;5)(q31;p14)**
- 46,XX = total chromosome number and sex chromosomes
- t(2;5) = reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 2 and 5
- (q31;p14) = breakpoints listed in the **same order** as chromosomes named: chr2 breaks at **q31** (long arm), chr5 breaks at **p14** (short arm)
- Memory rule: **p = petit = short arm; q = the other one = long arm**

---

## The Autosomal Trisomies

| Syndrome | Chromosome | Key point |
|---|---|---|
| **Patau syndrome** | Trisomy 13 | Severe malformations, life expectancy usually <1 year |
| **Edward syndrome** | Trisomy 18 | Severe malformations, life expectancy usually <1 year |
| **Down syndrome** | Trisomy 21 | Milder phenotype, life expectancy often 50–60 years |

**Comparing Patau and Down syndrome**
- Similar: both trisomies, both cytogenetic disorders, both associated with increased maternal age, both associated with congenital malformations
- **Different: life expectancy** — Patau/Edward are drastically shorter-lived than Down syndrome. Any option claiming similar life expectancy (~40 years) in both is false.

**Robertsonian translocation trap (21q21q)**
If a mother carries a 21q21q Robertsonian translocation, every viable pregnancy results in Down syndrome — **100%**. Her gametes carry either both copies of 21 (→ trisomy 21) or neither (→ monosomy 21, non-viable). No "normal" outcome is possible.

---

## Structural Chromosomal Deletions

**Cri du chat syndrome**
- Partial deletion of the **short arm (p arm) of chromosome 5** (5p−)
- NOT a Robertsonian translocation, NOT a trisomy or monosomy

**22q11.2 deletion syndrome**
- Small interstitial deletion of the **long arm** of chromosome 22
- Includes **DiGeorge syndrome** and **velocardiofacial syndrome**
- Features: congenital heart disease, facial dysmorphism, thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia
- Diagnosed by FISH
- **Confers an INCREASED risk** of schizophrenia/bipolar disorder — one of the strongest known genetic risk factors for schizophrenia

---

## Trinucleotide Repeat Disorders

- **Fragile X syndrome** — CGG repeat expansion in FMR1. Clinical picture: large everted ears, long face, large mandible, macroorchidism, intellectual disability
- **Huntington's disease** — CAG repeat expansion
- **Myotonic dystrophy** — CTG repeat expansion
- **Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease)** — CAG repeat expansion

Fraccaro syndrome (achondrogenesis type 1A) is **NOT** a trinucleotide repeat disorder — a common distractor placed among this list.

---

## Sex Chromosome Disorders

**Klinefelter syndrome**
- Karyotypes: 47,XXY (classic), 46,XY/47,XXY (mosaic), 47,XXY/48,XXXY (mosaic variant)
- 46,XY alone is simply a normal male karyotype
- Features: **tall stature** (not short), eunuchoid body habitus, gynecomastia, reduced facial/body/pubic hair, hypogonadism
- A coexisting normal 46,XY cell line in mosaic Klinefelter produces a **milder**, not more severe, phenotype

**Turner syndrome**
- Karyotype: 45,X (monosomy X)
- Features: short stature (below 3rd percentile), webbed neck, shield-like chest with widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus, streak ovaries (not testicular atrophy — Turner affects females), primary amenorrhea, decreased estrogen, increased FSH/LH

**Extreme sex chromosome deviations**
- 49,XXXXY is compatible with life — sex chromosome aneuploidies are tolerated far better than autosomal ones
- 47,XYY individuals have essentially normal life expectancy
- **X-inactivation (lyonization)** explains tolerance of extra X's: only one X is active per cell. Lyonization occurs only on X, never autosomes.

**Disorders of sex development**
- **Androgen insensitivity syndrome:** 46,XY karyotype, tissues cannot respond to androgens → phenotypically female external appearance, primary amenorrhea, presents in adolescence. Classic vignette: "17-year-old phenotypic female, primary amenorrhea, XY karyotype."

---

## Genomic Imprinting

**The concept**
- Transcriptional silencing of one parent's copy of a gene (paternal or maternal, depending on the gene), established during gametogenesis
- Result: only ONE functional copy exists, even though two were inherited
- **Critical point:** loss of the one functional allele is NOT compensated — the imprinted (silenced) copy cannot rescue the loss

**The two classic imprinting diseases — same region, opposite parent of origin**

| Syndrome | Genetic defect | Clinical picture |
|---|---|---|
| **Prader-Willi syndrome** | Deletion of **paternal** 15q11-13 | Hyperphagia, obesity, hypotonia, intellectual disability |
| **Angelman syndrome** | Deletion of **maternal** 15q11-13 | Severe intellectual disability, seizures, ataxic/jerky gait, inappropriate laughter, fair complexion |

Memory anchor: fair complexion + severe mental retardation + seizures + ataxic gait + inappropriate laughter = **Angelman syndrome** (maternal deletion).

---

## Mitochondrial Inheritance

- Mitochondrial DNA is inherited **exclusively from the mother**
- **Fathers never transmit mitochondrial mutations to any child** — sons or daughters
- Only daughters of an affected woman can transmit the mutation onward
- Rare diseases; affect tissues with high energy demand: skeletal muscle, heart, brain
- **Leber hereditary optic neuropathy** is the prototypical mitochondrial disease

---

## Dysmorphology — Malformation, Deformation, Disruption, Sequence

Separate these four terms by **mechanism**:
- **Malformation** — primary error of morphogenesis; developmental process **intrinsically** abnormal from the start
- **Deformation** — a normally-formed structure physically distorted by **extrinsic mechanical forces** (e.g., oligohydramnios compression)
- **Disruption** — secondary destruction of a previously **normal** organ/region by an external event (e.g., amniotic bands). Disruptions are **not heritable**, no recurrence risk
- **Sequence** — a cascade of anomalies triggered by a single **primary defect**. Example: bilateral renal agenesis → oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia and limb deformities (Potter sequence)

Not all malformations are evident at birth; the majority overall have **unknown causes**.

---

## Teratogens and Congenital Anomaly Prevention

- Teratogen-sensitive window: roughly **weeks 3–9**, peaking at **weeks 4–5** (organogenesis)
- **Thalidomide** → classic cause of severe limb malformations
- **Maternal smoking** → linked to placental abnormalities and SIDS
- **Maternal alcohol** → prenatal and postnatal growth retardation (fetal alcohol syndrome)
- **Vitamin A:** both deficiency AND excess in early pregnancy are teratogenic — a U-shaped risk
- **Vaccination against viral teratogens** (e.g., rubella) is protective
- "Lack of morning sickness" is not a validated marker of teratogenesis — treat as a false/distractor statement

---

## Diagnostic Techniques

**What enabled the molecular diagnostics era**
Human genome sequencing plus public reference databases, tailor-made PCR kits, high-resolution DNA/RNA microarrays, and automated next-generation sequencing — together.

**FISH (Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization)**
- Fluorescent DNA probes specific to particular chromosomal regions
- Probes hybridize to metaphase spreads or interphase nuclei
- Requires a fluorescence microscope — **not** a cheap, ordinary-light-microscopy technique
- Resolution ~100 kilobases; requires knowing in advance what region to probe
- Uses: rapid diagnosis, detecting numeric chromosomal abnormalities, subtle microdeletions/complex translocations, gene amplification analysis
- Purely **diagnostic** — no role in genetic therapy

**Array-based Comparative Genomic Hybridization (array-CGH)**
- Test and reference DNA labelled with two different fluorescent dyes
- Amplifications → increased signal; deletions → decreased signal, relative to normal DNA
- **Key advantage over FISH:** detects abnormalities genome-wide **without needing prior knowledge** of what to look for

**PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)**
- Direct molecular detection method; exponential amplification of a target DNA sequence
- RNA starting material must first be reverse-transcribed into cDNA (RT-PCR)
- Requires the normal gene sequence known beforehand, to design primers
- **Does not involve microscopy** of any kind

**Indications for postnatal genetic testing**
Diagnosing a genetic disorder in a symptomatic child, recurrent miscarriage workup (ruling out parental balanced translocation), assessing genetic/mental illness risk in a child born to affected parents, resolving disputed paternity when a child's diagnosis is otherwise hard to pin down.

articles.title: Haematology Exam 2025: MCQs on Anaemia, Leukaemia & Clotting — Past Paper
articles.content:
# HAEMATOLOGY END OF YEAR EXAMINATION 2024/2025
**Institution:** Mount Kenya University
**School:** School of Medicine
**Department:** Department of Pathology
**Programme:** Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery — Year 3
**Unit Code:** MBML 3200
**Unit Title:** Haematology
**Date:** 14th July, 2025
**Time:** 2:00 PM
**Duration:** 2 Hours 30 Minutes
**Paper:** Paper One
**Structure:** Section A — 60 MCQs (60 marks) | Section B — 7 Short Answer Questions (60 marks) | Section C — 1 Long Answer Question (20 marks)
---
# SECTION A: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS
**Q1.** A 28-year-old woman presents with fatigue and pallor. Complete blood count shows low haemoglobin level and peripheral blood film shows microcytic hypochromic red blood cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Vitamin B12 deficiency
B) Iron deficiency anaemia
C) Aplastic anaemia
D) Haemolytic anaemia
E) Sickle cell anaemia
**Answer:** B) Iron deficiency anaemia
**Explanation:** Microcytic hypochromic red cells are the classic morphological pattern of iron deficiency anaemia, reflecting impaired haemoglobin synthesis.
---
**Q2.** The primary site of haematopoiesis in adults is:
A) Liver
B) Spleen
C) Bone marrow
D) Lymph nodes
E) Thymus
**Answer:** C) Bone marrow
**Explanation:** After birth, the bone marrow (particularly axial skeleton) becomes the main site of blood cell production, replacing the fetal liver and spleen.
---
**Q3.** Which blood cell type is primarily responsible for defence against parasitic infections?
A) Neutrophils
B) Basophils
C) Eosinophils
D) Monocytes
E) Lymphocytes
**Answer:** C) Eosinophils
**Explanation:** Eosinophils release cytotoxic granule proteins effective against helminths and other parasites, and are typically elevated in parasitic infection.
---
**Q4.** Which clotting factor is deficient in Haemophilia A?
A) Factor V
B) Factor VII
C) Factor VIII
D) Factor IX
E) Factor X
**Answer:** C) Factor VIII
**Explanation:** Haemophilia A is an X-linked deficiency of Factor VIII, causing prolonged APTT with normal PT.
---
**Q5.** A patient presents with recurrent infections, petechiae, and anaemia. A bone marrow biopsy shows reduced cellularity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Iron deficiency anaemia
B) Sickle cell disease
C) Polycythaemia vera
D) Aplastic anaemia
E) Thalassaemia
**Answer:** D) Aplastic anaemia
**Explanation:** Pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow reflects failure of haematopoietic stem cells, defining aplastic anaemia.
---
**Q6.** Haemopoiesis is the process of:
A) Blood clot formation
B) White blood cell destruction
C) Blood cell production
D) Plasma protein synthesis
E) Iron transport
**Answer:** C) Blood cell production
**Explanation:** Haemopoiesis refers to the formation of all cellular blood components from haematopoietic stem cells.
---
**Q7.** A 62-year-old man presents with fatigue, fever and bruising. His full blood count shows WCC 40 × 10⁹/L with 25% circulating blasts, Hb 90 g/L and platelets 50 × 10⁹/L. Which investigation is required to definitively diagnose acute myeloid leukaemia?
A) Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
B) Peripheral blood smear
C) Flow cytometry of peripheral blood
D) Computed tomography scan
E) Serum lactate dehydrogenase
**Answer:** A) Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
**Explanation:** Marrow examination with immunophenotyping and cytogenetics is required for definitive diagnosis and classification of AML.

**Q8.** Which cytochemical stain is most useful to confirm lymphoblasts in suspected ALL?
A) Myeloperoxidase (MPO)
B) Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT)
C) Sudan Black B
D) Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP)
E) Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)
**Answer:** B) Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT)
**Explanation:** TdT is a nuclear enzyme expressed in immature lymphoid precursors, positive in the vast majority of ALL cases.

**Q9.** A patient receiving chemotherapy shows a drop in neutrophil count. This condition is termed:
A) Anaemia
B) Leukocytosis
C) Neutropenia
D) Thrombocytopenia
E) Erythrocytosis
**Answer:** C) Neutropenia
**Explanation:** Neutropenia is defined as an abnormally low absolute neutrophil count, a common chemotherapy toxicity.

**Q10.** Which chromosomal translocation is pathognomonic of chronic myeloid leukaemia?
A) t(8;21)
B) t(15;17)
C) t(9;22)(q34;q11)
D) t(4;11)

**Q11.** Thrombopoietin primarily regulates the production of:
A) Red blood cells
B) Plasma cells
C) Platelets
D) Monocytes
E) Eosinophils
**Answer:** C) Platelets
**Explanation:** Thrombopoietin stimulates megakaryocyte proliferation and maturation, driving platelet production.

**Q12.** Which of the following is a stem cell marker used to identify haematopoietic stem cells?
A) CD3
B) CD4
C) CD19
D) CD34

**Q13.** In a bone marrow biopsy of a patient with aplastic anaemia, you would expect to find:
A) Hypercellular marrow with many erythroblasts
B) Increased megakaryocytes
C) Fatty replacement and hypocellularity

**Q14.** Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) is used clinically to:
A) Increase platelet production
B) Stimulate lymphocyte activation
C) Promote neutrophil recovery after chemotherapy

**Answer:** C) Promote neutrophil recovery after chemotherapy

**Q15.** A patient with Chronic Lymphoid Leukaemia develops a warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Which test is essential to confirm this complication?

B) Indirect antiglobulin test

**Answer:** A) Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test

**Q16.** A 25-year-old woman presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and night sweats. Excisional lymph node biopsy shows large binucleated cells expressing CD15 and CD30. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Classical Hodgkin lymphoma
B) Follicular lymphoma

**Q17.** A 60-year-old man on warfarin therapy for atrial fibrillation attends clinic for monitoring. His prothrombin time is 30 seconds (normal 11–15s) and his APTT is within normal limits. Which test is used to standardise his anticoagulant dose?

**Answer:** B) Prothrombin time / international normalised ratio (PT/INR)

**Q18.** Which of the following laboratory findings is typically associated with haemolytic anaemia?
A) Decreased reticulocyte count
B) Increased haptoglobin
C) Increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
D) Decreased unconjugated bilirubin

**Q19.** A patient with HIV has an absolute neutrophil count of 0.4 × 10⁹/L. Which pathogen poses the greatest risk with this degree of neutropenia?

**Q20.** A 25-year-old man of Mediterranean descent presents with mild anaemia and target cells on a blood film. What is the most likely diagnosis?

**Q21.** A patient with chronic atrophic gastritis is at risk of which type of anaemia?

**Q22.** In thalassaemia major, anaemia is primarily caused by:

**Q23.** The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) in normal pregnancy is typically:

**Q24.** What is the universal donor blood group for red blood cell transfusion?

**Q26.** Which of the following is used to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease in immunocompromised patients?

**Q27.** Which of the following blood components is indicated in a patient with thrombocytopenia and active bleeding?

**Q28.** Which infection is most commonly screened for in donated blood?

**Q29.** A peripheral blood film from a patient with suspected AML shows numerous blasts. Which cytochemical stain is most specific for confirming a myeloid lineage?

**Q30.** Which of the following transfusion reactions is associated with hypotension and respiratory distress due to donor antibodies against recipient leukocytes?

**Q31.** Why is group O blood not suitable for plasma transfusion in emergencies?

**Q39.** Which immunophenotypic marker is typically positive in follicular lymphoma?

**Q49.** A 55-year-old man presents with fatigue, weight loss and splenomegaly. His full blood count shows WCC 140 × 10⁹/L with marked neutrophilia, left shift and basophilia. Which investigation is required to confirm the diagnosis of chronic myeloid leukaemia?

**Q52.** Which of the following is a hallmark feature of polycythaemia vera?

**Q55.** In the context of the reticuloendothelial system, what is a key histological feature of reactive lymphadenopathy?
A) Sheets of plasma cells
B) Starry-sky appearance

**Q56.** Mycosis fungoides, a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, characteristically expresses:

**Q57.** A 20-year-old man presents with recurrent joint bleeds. His prothrombin time is normal, activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) is prolonged, thrombin time (TT) is normal. Which coagulation factor abnormality is most likely?

**Q60.** In acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL), which coagulation abnormality is most characteristic of disseminated intravascular coagulation?

# SECTION B: SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS
---
**Question 1.** A 45-year-old presents with fatigue, early satiety and splenomegaly. The full blood count shows white blood cells -120 × 10⁹/L, (reference levels 4-12 X 10⁹/l) neutrophilia with a left shift and basophilia.
**a) What is the diagnosis? (1 Mark)**
- Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML)
**b) Outline the laboratory investigations to confirm the diagnosis? (9 Marks)**
- Full blood count and peripheral blood film — shows marked leucocytosis with a full spectrum of granulocyte maturation (myeloblasts to mature neutrophils), basophilia, eosinophilia
- Bone marrow aspirate — hypercellular marrow with granulocytic hyperplasia
- Bone marrow trephine biopsy — assesses cellularity and degree of marrow fibrosis
- Cytogenetic analysis (karyotyping) — detects the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22)(q34;q11)
- Fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) — rapid detection of BCR-ABL1 fusion in interphase cells
- Quantitative RT-PCR for BCR-ABL1 transcript — confirms diagnosis and provides a baseline for monitoring treatment response
- Leucocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score — typically low in CML (helps differentiate from leukemoid reaction)
- Serum uric acid — often elevated due to high cell turnover
- Serum vitamin B12/B12 binding capacity — often elevated in CML due to increased transcobalamin production
---
**Question 2.** A 32-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding presents with fatigue, pallor and pica.
**a) Name the diagnosis. (1 Mark)**
- Iron deficiency anaemia
**b) Name three clinical signs of the diagnosis. (3 Marks)**
- Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails)
- Angular stomatitis / cheilosis
- Glossitis (smooth, sore tongue)
- Pallor of mucous membranes and conjunctiva
- Brittle hair/nails
**c) Discuss the four laboratory tests and expected results. (4 Marks)**
- Full blood count — low haemoglobin, low MCV (microcytic), low MCH (hypochromic)
- Peripheral blood film — microcytic, hypochromic red cells, anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, occasional pencil cells
- Serum ferritin — low (most sensitive and specific marker of depleted iron stores)
- Serum iron and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) — low serum iron, raised TIBC, low transferrin saturation
**d) Name two confirmatory laboratory tests. (2 Marks)**
- Serum ferritin
- Bone marrow iron stain (Perls' stain) — absent stainable iron confirms deficiency
---
**Question 3.** 10-year-old child presents with a rapidly growing jaw mass. Describe laboratory investigations needed to diagnose Burkitt lymphoma. (10 Marks)
- Full blood count and peripheral blood film — may show anaemia, or circulating lymphoma cells if marrow involved
- Excisional lymph node/tissue biopsy — gold standard, shows sheets of medium-sized lymphoid cells with a "starry-sky" appearance (tingible body macrophages among tumour cells)
- Immunohistochemistry/immunophenotyping — positive for CD10, CD19, CD20, CD79a; surface IgM positive; Ki-67 proliferation index near 100%
- Cytogenetic analysis — detects t(8;14) translocation (MYC-IGH fusion), or variants t(2;8) and t(8;22)
- Fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) — confirms MYC gene rearrangement
- Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy — assesses marrow infiltration/staging
- Lumbar puncture with CSF cytology — evaluates for CNS involvement
- Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) — elevated, reflects high tumour burden/turnover, used for prognosis
- Serum uric acid and electrolytes (potassium, phosphate, calcium) — baseline before treatment, screening for tumour lysis syndrome risk given rapid cell turnover
- Renal function tests — baseline assessment before chemotherapy, and for tumour lysis monitoring
- Imaging (CT/MRI/PET scan) — for staging and extent of disease
---
**Question 4.** A 50-year-old man with cirrhosis and splenomegaly has a platelet count of 60 × 10⁹/L. (Reference levels are 150-450 x 10⁹/L)
**a) Interpret the result. (1 Mark)**
- Thrombocytopenia (moderately reduced platelet count)
**b) Name two causes. (2 Marks)**
- Hypersplenism (splenic sequestration of platelets secondary to portal hypertension)
- Reduced hepatic thrombopoietin production due to cirrhosis
**c) Discuss the laboratory tests to make a diagnosis and expected results. (7 Marks)**
- Full blood count — confirms thrombocytopenia, may show accompanying anaemia/leucopenia if hypersplenism is causing pancytopenia
- Peripheral blood film — excludes platelet clumping (pseudothrombocytopenia) and assesses platelet morphology/size
- Liver function tests — deranged (raised bilirubin, low albumin, deranged AST/ALT) confirming underlying liver disease
- Prothrombin time/INR — prolonged due to reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factors
- Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler — confirms splenomegaly and evidence of portal hypertension
- Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy — if diagnosis unclear, shows normal or increased megakaryocytes (indicating peripheral destruction/sequestration rather than production failure)
- Viral hepatitis serology — to identify underlying aetiology of cirrhosis
---
**Question 5.** A 6-year-old boy presents with recurrent haemarthroses and easy bruising.
| Test | Result | Reference Level |
|---|---|---|
| APTT | 55 seconds | 28–42 seconds |
| PT | 13 seconds | 12.3–15.1 seconds |
**a) Interpret and comment on the results. (2 Marks)**
- Prolonged APTT with normal PT
- Pattern indicates an isolated defect in the intrinsic coagulation pathway (Factor VIII, IX, XI, or XII)
**b) What is the diagnosis? (1 Mark)**
- Haemophilia (most likely Haemophilia A — Factor VIII deficiency; Haemophilia B/Factor IX deficiency is a differential)
**c) Discuss four additional tests and expected findings. (8 Marks)**
- Factor VIII assay — reduced/low activity confirms Haemophilia A
- Factor IX assay — performed to differentiate from Haemophilia B; normal in Haemophilia A
- Mixing studies (APTT with normal plasma, 50:50 mix) — correction of prolonged APTT confirms a factor deficiency rather than an inhibitor
- Von Willebrand factor antigen and activity — to exclude Von Willebrand disease as a differential cause of bleeding
- Thrombin time — expected normal, helps exclude fibrinogen abnormalities
- Genetic/molecular testing — identifies specific factor VIII or IX gene mutation, useful for family counselling and carrier detection
---
**Question 6.** A 28-year-old woman on a zidovudine-based ART regimen develops symptomatic macrocytic anaemia (MCV 110 fL).
**a) Describe the mechanisms of zidovudine-induced anaemia. (4 Marks)**
- Zidovudine directly inhibits DNA polymerase (including mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma), impairing erythroid precursor DNA synthesis
- Causes ineffective erythropoiesis with maturation arrest at the erythroblast stage
- Results in macrocytosis due to asynchronous nuclear-cytoplasmic maturation
- Can progress to bone marrow suppression/myelotoxicity with prolonged use, reducing red cell production
- Dose-dependent and generally reversible on dose reduction or discontinuation
**b) Name three additional tests and describe the expected laboratory findings. (3 Marks)**
- Full blood count and reticulocyte count — low reticulocyte count (reflecting impaired marrow production rather than haemolysis)
- Peripheral blood film — macrocytic red cells without megaloblastic features (no hypersegmented neutrophils, unlike true B12/folate deficiency)
- Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels — typically normal, helps exclude true megaloblastic anaemia as the cause
- Bone marrow aspirate (if performed) — shows erythroid hypoplasia with vacuolation of erythroid and myeloid precursors, a characteristic drug-toxicity picture
**c) List three other causes of macrocytic anaemia. (3 Marks)**
- Vitamin B12 deficiency
- Folate deficiency
- Chronic alcohol use/liver disease
- Hypothyroidism
- Myelodysplastic syndrome
---
# SECTION C: LONG ANSWER QUESTION
**Question 1.** Discuss the components of blood and blood products stating the indications of each. (20 Marks)
**Whole Blood**
- Contains red cells, plasma, and clotting factors (largely inactive after storage)
- Indication: rarely used now; considered in massive acute haemorrhage with combined need for volume and oxygen-carrying capacity, where component therapy is unavailable
**Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBCs)**
- Red cells with most plasma removed
- Indication: symptomatic anaemia, acute blood loss, chronic anaemia requiring transfusion (e.g., in renal failure, thalassaemia), to restore oxygen-carrying capacity
**Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP)**
- Contains all clotting factors, including labile factors V and VIII
- Indication: coagulopathy with active bleeding (e.g., liver disease, DIC), warfarin reversal, massive transfusion protocols, replacement of multiple clotting factor deficiencies
**Cryoprecipitate**
- Rich in fibrinogen, Factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, and Factor XIII
- Indication: hypofibrinogenaemia (e.g., DIC, massive transfusion), von Willebrand disease, haemophilia A (when specific factor concentrate unavailable), fibrinogen replacement
**Platelet Concentrate**
- Concentrated platelets from whole blood donation or apheresis
- Indication: thrombocytopenia with active bleeding, prophylaxis before invasive procedures in severely thrombocytopenic patients, platelet function disorders with bleeding
**Granulocyte Concentrate**
- Concentrated neutrophils
- Indication: severe neutropenia with life-threatening bacterial/fungal infection unresponsive to antimicrobial therapy (rarely used)
**Albumin (Human Albumin Solution)**
- Plasma protein fraction, available in 4-5% and 20-25% concentrations
- Indication: volume expansion in hypoalbuminaemia, large-volume paracentesis, burns, plasma exchange procedures
**Clotting Factor Concentrates (e.g., Factor VIII, Factor IX concentrates)**
- Purified/recombinant specific clotting factors
- Indication: specific factor deficiencies (Haemophilia A — Factor VIII; Haemophilia B — Factor IX), preferred over cryoprecipitate/FFP due to reduced infection transmission risk and precise dosing
**Immunoglobulin Preparations**
- Pooled antibodies from donor plasma
- Indication: immunodeficiency states, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, autoimmune conditions (e.g., Guillain-Barré syndrome), passive immunisation
**General principles guiding component selection:**
- Choice of product depends on the specific deficiency being corrected (oxygen-carrying capacity vs clotting factors vs platelets vs volume)
- Component therapy is preferred over whole blood to reduce unnecessary exposure to blood products and allow targeted replacement
- All transfusions require proper cross-matching/compatibility testing to avoid transfusion reactions
