articles.title: Medical Virology: Hepatitis, Viral Carcinogenesis & Oncogenic Viruses — Notes
articles.content:
# MEDICAL VIROLOGY — SECTION 2 (Comprehensive Notes)
*Covers: Hepatitis Viruses → Oncogenic Viruses → Arboviruses → HIV (everything after the Mid-Term CAT)*

## 1. Hepatitis Viruses

**General concept**: "Hepatitis" = liver inflammation. Several unrelated viruses cause it — they differ completely in genome, transmission, and chronicity potential. This comparison table is one of the most commonly tested areas.

| Virus | Genome/Family | Transmission | Incubation | Chronicity? | Key exam points |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Hep A** | (+)ssRNA, Picornavirus | Faecal-oral (contaminated food/water) | 2–6 weeks | **No** chronic state | Self-limiting; vaccine available; common in poor sanitation areas |
| **Hep B** | dsDNA-RT (Baltimore class VII), Hepadnavirus | Blood, sexual contact, vertical (mother-to-child) | 1–6 months | **Yes** — can become chronic, especially if acquired at birth | Has surface antigen (HBsAg) used for screening; vaccine available; risk of cirrhosis & hepatocellular carcinoma |
| **Hep C** | (+)ssRNA, Flavivirus | Blood (transfusion, needles, IV drug use) | 2 weeks–6 months | **Yes** — majority (~75-85%) become chronic | NO vaccine available; treated with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) now, very high cure rates; major cause of liver cirrhosis/HCC globally |
| **Hep D (Delta)** | ssRNA, defective/satellite virus | Blood, sexual | Variable | Yes, worsens disease | **Requires Hep B co-infection to replicate** (uses HBsAg as its own coat) — cannot infect alone |
| **Hep E** | (+)ssRNA, Hepevirus | Faecal-oral (contaminated water) | 2–8 weeks | No (except in immunocompromised) | Similar to Hep A clinically, BUT **high mortality in pregnant women** (can exceed 20% in 3rd trimester) — important exam point |
| **Non-A Non-B** | Historical term | — | — | — | Used before Hep C/E were identified as distinct agents; now mostly replaced by these specific diagnoses |

**Clinical course pattern to remember for essays**: Acute hepatitis (any cause) → fever, malaise, nausea, jaundice, dark urine, pale stool, raised liver enzymes (ALT/AST) → either resolves (Hep A, E) or can progress to chronic carrier state/cirrhosis/hepatocellular carcinoma (Hep B, C, D).

**Serological markers — Hep B (commonly examined)**:
- **HBsAg** – surface antigen; marker of current infection (acute or chronic)
- **Anti-HBs** – antibody to surface antigen; marker of immunity (from vaccine OR past cleared infection)
- **HBeAg** – marker of active viral replication/high infectivity
- **Anti-HBc IgM** – marker of recent/acute infection
- **Anti-HBc IgG** – marker of past infection (with or without clearance)

---

## 2. Oncogenic Viruses (Viral Carcinogenesis)

**Key terms — distinguish clearly for exam**:

- **Carcinogenesis** – the overall multi-step process by which normal cells become cancerous
- **Oncogenesis** – specifically the development of a tumor through activation of oncogenes/inactivation of tumor suppressor genes
- **Tumorigenesis** – the formation and progression of a tumor mass

**How viruses cause cancer (general mechanisms — important for essay answers)**:
1. **Insertional mutagenesis** – viral genome integrates near a host proto-oncogene, disrupting normal control and activating it
2. **Viral oncogenes** – virus carries its own cancer-causing genes (e.g. HPV's E6 and E7 proteins)
3. **Inactivation of tumor suppressor genes** – e.g. HPV E6 degrades p53; E7 inactivates Rb (retinoblastoma protein) — both are critical "brakes" on cell division
4. **Chronic inflammation** – persistent infection/inflammation (e.g. chronic Hep B/C) damages tissue and promotes cell turnover, increasing mutation risk
5. **Immunosuppression** – some oncogenic viruses act mainly by suppressing host immunity, allowing other oncogenic processes to proceed unchecked (e.g. EBV in immunocompromised patients)

**Major human oncogenic viruses — table form**:

| Virus | Associated Cancer(s) | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **HPV (Human Papillomavirus)** types 16, 18 | Cervical cancer, also anal/oropharyngeal cancers | E6 degrades p53; E7 inactivates Rb |
| **HSV / VZV** (mentioned in outline re: latent infection) | Not strongly oncogenic themselves, but their latency mechanism is the model studied alongside oncogenic herpesviruses | Establish lifelong latency in neurons; reactivate under stress/immunosuppression |
| **CMV** | Implicated in some cancers (e.g. glioblastoma) — less definitive than others; well known for congenital infection | Possible oncomodulation (alters tumor microenvironment) rather than direct transformation |
| **EBV (Epstein-Barr Virus)** | Burkitt lymphoma, Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma | Infects B cells; drives them to proliferate continuously (immortalization); associated with c-myc translocation in Burkitt lymphoma |
| **Hepatitis B & C** | Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) | Chronic inflammation + (for HBV) insertional mutagenesis into host genome |
| **HHV-8** | Kaposi's sarcoma | Drives proliferation of endothelial cells, especially in immunosuppressed (HIV/AIDS) patients |
| **HTLV-1** (retrovirus, often grouped here) | Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma | Tax protein interferes with cell cycle control |

**Exam tip**: If asked "discuss oncogenic viruses," structure your answer as: (1) define carcinogenesis/oncogenesis/tumorigenesis, (2) explain general mechanisms, (3) go through 3–4 specific viruses with their mechanism + cancer, (4) mention prevention (HPV vaccine, HBV vaccine = cancer prevention vaccines).

---

## 3. Arboviruses (Arthropod-Borne Viruses)

**Definition**: Viruses transmitted to humans by arthropod vectors (mosquitoes, ticks). Not a taxonomic group — a transmission-based grouping. Most are zoonotic (animal reservoir, humans often incidental/"dead-end" hosts).

| Virus | Vector | Family | Key clinical features |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chikungunya** | *Aedes* mosquito | Togavirus | Severe joint pain (arthralgia) that can persist for months; fever, rash |
| **Dengue** | *Aedes* mosquito | Flavivirus | Fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, rash; **Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever/Shock Syndrome** on repeat infection with different serotype (antibody-dependent enhancement) |
| **Eastern Equine Encephalitis (EEE)** | Mosquito | Togavirus (Alphavirus) | Severe encephalitis, high mortality, mainly in horses & humans in the Americas |
| **St. Louis Encephalitis** | *Culex* mosquito | Flavivirus | Encephalitis, especially in older adults; USA |
| **West Nile Virus** | *Culex* mosquito | Flavivirus | Most infections mild/asymptomatic; can cause encephalitis/meningitis especially in elderly/immunocompromised; birds are reservoir |
| **Yellow Fever** | *Aedes* mosquito | Flavivirus | Jaundice (hence "yellow"), hemorrhagic fever, can be severe with liver failure; vaccine available (live attenuated) |
| **Zika** | *Aedes* mosquito | Flavivirus | Usually mild in adults; **major concern is congenital Zika syndrome** — microcephaly when mother infected during pregnancy |

**Exam tip**: Group by vector and by family — many arboviruses are Flaviviruses (Dengue, Zika, West Nile, Yellow Fever, St. Louis encephalitis), so know what they share: (+)ssRNA, enveloped, mosquito-borne, can cause hemorrhagic fever or encephalitis depending on the specific virus and host factors.

---

## 4. HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) — High-Yield Section

**Classification**: Retrovirus → genus **Lentivirus** ("slow virus" — long incubation before AIDS develops). Baltimore Class VI (ssRNA-RT). Enveloped, icosahedral capsid containing two copies of (+)ssRNA genome plus reverse transcriptase enzyme.

**History (brief, for context in essays)**:
- First clinically recognized in 1981 (USA) — clusters of unusual *Pneumocystis* pneumonia and Kaposi's sarcoma in young men
- HIV identified as the causative agent by 1983-84 (Montagnier, Gallo)
- Believed to have originated from zoonotic transmission of SIV (Simian Immunodeficiency Virus) from primates in Africa

**HIV Structure**:
- Two glycoproteins on envelope: **gp120** (binds CD4 receptor) and **gp41** (mediates membrane fusion)
- Core enzymes carried in virion: **Reverse transcriptase**, **Integrase**, **Protease**

**HIV Replication Cycle (Life Cycle) — special/distinguishing features**:
1. **Attachment** – gp120 binds CD4 receptor on host cell (T-helper cells, macrophages, dendritic cells) PLUS a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4)
2. **Fusion/Penetration** – gp41 mediates fusion of viral envelope with host membrane
3. **Reverse transcription** – viral RNA genome converted into dsDNA by reverse transcriptase (error-prone → high mutation rate, drives drug resistance and immune evasion)
4. **Integration** – viral DNA integrates permanently into host genome via integrase, forming a **provirus** — this is why HIV can never be fully eradicated from an infected person, only suppressed
5. **Transcription & translation** – host machinery transcribes provirus, viral proteins synthesized
6. **Assembly** – immature virions bud from cell surface
7. **Maturation** – viral protease cleaves precursor proteins into functional ones, creating an infectious mature virion (this step is OUTSIDE the cell, after budding — key fact, distinguishes maturation from assembly)

**Natural history of untreated HIV infection (clinical course — common essay)**:
- **Acute/seroconversion phase** – flu-like illness 2–4 weeks post-infection, high viral load, CD4 count dips transiently
- **Clinical latency (chronic phase)** – can last years; virus still replicating but immune system keeps pace; CD4 count slowly declines
- **AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome)** – CD4 count drops below 200 cells/µL (or development of AIDS-defining opportunistic infections/cancers, e.g. *Pneumocystis* pneumonia, Kaposi's sarcoma, candidiasis, TB, CMV retinitis)

**Epidemiology** (general points to mention): Sub-Saharan Africa carries the highest global burden; transmission via sexual contact, blood/blood products, mother-to-child (vertical), needle-sharing; prevention via ART for prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), condom use, PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis), male circumcision (reduces female-to-male transmission risk).

**Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) — drug classes and mechanism**:

| Drug Class | Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **NRTIs** (Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors) | Chain-terminate viral DNA synthesis during reverse transcription | Zidovudine (AZT), Lamivudine, Tenofovir |
| **NNRTIs** (Non-Nucleoside RT Inhibitors) | Bind directly to reverse transcriptase enzyme, block its activity (different binding site from NRTIs) | Efavirenz, Nevirapine |
| **Protease Inhibitors (PIs)** | Block viral protease → prevents cleavage of precursor proteins → produces immature, non-infectious virions | Ritonavir, Lopinavir, Atazanavir |
| **Integrase Inhibitors** | Block integrase → prevents viral DNA from integrating into host genome | Raltegravir, Dolutegravir |
| **Entry/Fusion Inhibitors** | Block gp41-mediated fusion, or block CCR5 co-receptor | Enfuvirtide (fusion), Maraviroc (CCR5 antagonist) |

**Why combination therapy (HAART/cART) is used**: HIV mutates extremely fast (error-prone reverse transcriptase, no proofreading) — using a single drug rapidly selects for resistant mutants. Combining 3+ drugs from different classes makes it statistically very unlikely the virus develops resistance to all simultaneously.

**Challenges for HIV vaccine production** (classic essay question — know this well):
1. **Extremely high mutation/antigenic variability** — reverse transcriptase has no proofreading, so the virus constantly changes its surface proteins, making it a "moving target" for antibodies
2. **Integration into host genome** — once integrated as a provirus, it becomes part of the host's own DNA and hides from immune surveillance (latent reservoir)
3. **Destroys the very cells needed to fight it** — HIV infects and kills CD4+ helper T cells, which are essential for coordinating an effective immune/vaccine response
4. **Lack of a clear correlate of protection** — unlike other diseases, no natural human has ever fully cleared HIV infection, so scientists don't have a known "successful immune response" blueprint to replicate with a vaccine
5. **Glycan shield** — gp120 is heavily coated in sugar molecules that physically hide it from antibodies
6. **Latent reservoirs in resting cells** — virus can remain dormant in long-lived memory T cells, invisible to both immune system and most antivirals, for the patient's lifetime
7. **Genetic diversity across global subtypes (clades)** — different HIV subtypes dominate in different regions, complicating a single universal vaccine

---

articles.title: Essential Medical Virology: Structure, Classification & Replication — Notes
articles.content:
# MEDICAL VIROLOGY — SECTION 1 (Comprehensive Notes)
## Introduction to Virology
- A **virus** is an obligate intracellular parasite — it has no ribosomes, no independent metabolism, and cannot reproduce outside a living host cell. It hijacks host machinery to replicate.
- This is why antivirals target specific *steps* in replication rather than killing the organism outright (unlike antibiotics on bacteria).
- **Structure of a virion**:
 - **Genome**: DNA or RNA (never both), single-stranded (ss) or double-stranded (ds), linear or circular
 - **Capsid**: protein shell made of capsomeres; protects genome, mediates attachment in non-enveloped viruses
 - **Envelope**: lipid bilayer derived from host membrane, studded with viral glycoproteins (only some viruses have this)
- **Enveloped vs Non-enveloped — clinical relevance**:
 - Enveloped = fragile (destroyed by heat, drying, alcohol, detergents) → spreads by direct contact, droplets, blood (e.g. HIV, influenza, herpesviruses)
 - Non-enveloped = tough, survives acid/drying → spreads faecal-oral, on surfaces (e.g. poliovirus, rotavirus, adenovirus)
- **Capsid symmetry** (3 types):
 - Helical – coiled rod shape (influenza, rabies)
 - Icosahedral – 20-sided, most efficient packing (poliovirus, adenovirus, herpesvirus)
 - Complex – irregular, doesn't fit either (poxvirus, bacteriophages)
---
## 1. Classification — ICTV and Baltimore System
**ICTV (International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses)**
- Function: gives every virus one internationally standardized name; sets the rules for viral taxonomy
- Hierarchy used: Order → Family → Subfamily → Genus → Species
- Naming based on genome type, structure, replication strategy, host range — NOT on disease caused
**Baltimore Classification** — groups viruses by genome type + how they make mRNA. This determines their whole replication strategy.
| Class | Genome | mRNA synthesis | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | dsDNA | Direct transcription by host RNA pol (or own pol) | Herpesvirus, Adenovirus, Poxvirus |
| II | ssDNA (+) | Converted to dsDNA first, then transcribed | Parvovirus |
| III | dsRNA | Viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) transcribes mRNA directly from genome | Rotavirus (Reovirus) |
| IV | (+)ssRNA | Genome **IS** the mRNA — translated directly | Poliovirus, Rubella, Hep A, Coronaviruses |
| V | (–)ssRNA | Must first be transcribed into (+)RNA by viral RdRp before translation | Influenza, Rabies, Measles |
| VI | ssRNA-RT (Retrovirus) | Reverse transcriptase converts RNA → DNA → integrates into host genome → transcribed | HIV |
| VII | dsDNA-RT | dsDNA → transcribed to RNA → reverse transcribed back to DNA | Hepatitis B |
**Why this matters for exams**: (+)ssRNA viruses can act as their own mRNA immediately (fast replication); (–)ssRNA viruses must carry their own RdRp packaged in the virion (because the cell has no enzyme to read negative-sense RNA); retroviruses are unique in permanently integrating into host DNA, which is why HIV can never be fully cleared.
**Atypical infectious agents** (don't fit normal virus definition):
- **Prions**: infectious misfolded proteins, NO nucleic acid at all; cause spongiform encephalopathies (CJD, Kuru, BSE/mad cow); resistant to normal heat sterilization and disinfectants — need special protocols
- **Slow viruses / slow infections**: conventional viruses but with very long incubation and progressive course (e.g. measles virus causing SSPE years later)
---
## 2. Viral Replication Cycle (general steps, all viruses)
1. **Attachment** – viral surface protein binds specific host receptor (explains tissue tropism, e.g. HIV needs CD4+CCR5)
2. **Penetration** – entry by fusion (enveloped) or endocytosis
3. **Uncoating** – capsid removed, genome released into cytoplasm/nucleus
4. **Biosynthesis** – transcription, genome replication, protein translation (mechanism depends on Baltimore class — see table above)
5. **Assembly** – new capsids package new genomes
6. **Maturation** – proteins cleaved/folded into infectious form
7. **Release** – by cell lysis (non-enveloped, kills cell) or budding (enveloped, cell may survive)
**One-step growth curve** (used to study phage/virus replication kinetics):
- **Adsorption** – attachment to host
- **Latent period** – no free infectious virus detectable (replication happening inside, hidden)
- **Rise period (burst)** – progeny virus released rapidly
- **Burst size** – number of new virions released per infected cell
**Lytic vs Lysogenic cycle** (classically taught with bacteriophages, but concept applies to latent viruses generally):
| Feature | Lytic | Lysogenic |
|---|---|---|
| Outcome | Host cell destroyed immediately | Phage DNA integrates as **prophage**; host survives |
| Timing | Immediate replication | Dormant, can persist for many generations |
| Reactivation | N/A | Induction (e.g. UV light, stress) → switches to lytic |
| Example | T4 phage | Lambda phage |
**Effects of lysogeny on the host cell**:
- **Immunity to superinfection** — lysogenized cell resists infection by the same/similar phage
- **Lysogenic (phage) conversion** — host bacterium gains new genetic traits from prophage genes (classic exam example: *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* only produces diphtheria toxin when carrying the tox gene from a lysogenic phage; same principle with cholera toxin in *Vibrio cholerae*)
- Prophage can excise later and re-enter lytic cycle, killing the cell
---
## 3. Pathogenesis and Immunopathogenesis
**Stages of pathogenesis**: Entry at portal → Primary replication at entry site → Spread (local spread along nerves/mucosa, or systemic spread via blood = **viremia**) → Tropism (virus reaches specific target organ based on receptor distribution) → Cell injury/disease manifests → Shedding (virus exits to infect new host)
**Immunopathogenesis** — disease/damage caused by the *host's own immune response*, not direct viral killing:
- Example: Hepatitis B liver damage is largely caused by cytotoxic T cells attacking infected hepatocytes, not the virus itself
- Example: Immune complex deposition (Type III hypersensitivity) in chronic Hep B/C → glomerulonephritis, vasculitis
**Persistent viral infections — 3 types** (important distinction):
- **Chronic infection** – virus continuously produced at low levels, may eventually clear or progress (Hep B, Hep C)
- **Latent infection** – viral genome present but transcriptionally silent; reactivates under stress/immunosuppression (HSV, VZV, EBV, CMV — all herpesviruses do this)
- **Slow infection** – long silent incubation then progressive fatal disease (prion diseases, SSPE from measles)
**Host defenses**:
- *Non-specific (innate)* — first line:
 - Physical: skin, mucus, cilia
 - Interferons (α, β) — secreted by infected cells, warn neighboring cells, induce an antiviral state
 - NK cells — kill virus-infected cells without prior sensitization
 - Complement, fever, phagocytes
- *Specific (adaptive)* — slower but targeted:
 - Humoral: B cells → antibodies. IgM = current/acute infection marker; IgG = past infection/long-term immunity; IgA = mucosal protection (respiratory/GI)
 - Cell-mediated: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells directly; CD4+ helper T cells coordinate the whole response and help B cells mature
**Laboratory diagnosis of viral infections**:
- **Cell culture** – grow virus in susceptible cell line, observe **cytopathic effect (CPE)**: cell rounding, syncytia (cell fusion, e.g. RSV, measles), inclusion bodies (e.g. Negri bodies in rabies, Cowdry type A in herpes, owl's eye in CMV)
- **Microscopy** – electron microscopy visualizes the actual virion; light microscopy detects inclusion bodies
- **Serology** – ELISA, complement fixation, hemagglutination inhibition; detects antibody response (IgM = acute) or viral antigen directly
- **Molecular** – PCR/RT-PCR; detects viral nucleic acid directly; most sensitive, fastest, now gold standard for many viruses (e.g. HIV viral load, COVID testing)
---
## 4. Antiviral Agents — by Stage of Action
| Stage Blocked | Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Attachment/Penetration** | Block receptor binding or membrane fusion | Enfuvirtide, Maraviroc, Docosanol, Palivizumab |
| **Uncoating** | Prevent capsid from releasing genome | Amantadine, Rimantadine, Pleconaril, Arbidol |
| **Replication (genome synthesis)** | Nucleoside/nucleotide analogues inhibit viral polymerase → chain termination | Acyclovir, Zidovudine (AZT), Lamivudine, Ribavirin |
| **Release** | Neuraminidase inhibitors block budding/release of new virions | Oseltamivir, Zanamivir, Peramivir, Laninamivir |
*(Bonus, often tested with HIV): Protease inhibitors (Ritonavir, Lopinavir) block viral maturation; Integrase inhibitors (Raltegravir) block integration into host genome.)*
---
## 5. Vaccines
| Type | How it works | Advantage | Disadvantage | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Live attenuated | Weakened live virus replicates mildly | Strong, long-lasting immunity (cellular + humoral) | Risk of reversion to virulence; unsafe in immunocompromised/pregnancy | MMR, OPV, Yellow fever, Varicella |
| Inactivated (killed) | Whole virus killed (heat/chemical) | Safe, no reversion risk | Weaker, shorter immunity; often needs boosters | IPV, Hep A, Flu shot (injectable) |
| Subunit/recombinant | Only antigenic protein piece used | Very safe | May need adjuvant + boosters for strong response | Hepatitis B vaccine |
| Toxoid | Inactivated bacterial toxin (not the organism) | Targets toxin-mediated disease | Not applicable to all infections | Tetanus, Diphtheria (bacterial, included for contrast) |
| mRNA | mRNA delivered, host cells produce the antigen themselves | Fast to develop, strong immune response | Cold-chain storage requirements | COVID-19 (Pfizer, Moderna) |
| Viral vector | Harmless carrier virus delivers antigen gene | Strong cellular immunity | Pre-existing immunity to vector can reduce efficacy | Some COVID vaccines, Ebola vaccine |
---
## 6. DNA vs RNA Viruses — Differences and Clinical Implications
| Feature | DNA Viruses | RNA Viruses |
|---|---|---|
| Replication site | Mostly nucleus (exception: Poxvirus replicates in cytoplasm) | Mostly cytoplasm (exception: Influenza replicates in nucleus) |
| Mutation rate | Low — host DNA polymerase proofreads | High — RNA polymerase has no proofreading |
| Clinical implication of mutation rate | More stable → vaccines work long-term, latency common | Rapid evolution → antigenic drift/shift, frequent vaccine updates needed (e.g. annual flu shot), faster drug resistance |
| Stability outside host | Generally more stable | Generally less stable |
| Examples | Herpesviruses, Adenovirus, Poxvirus, Papillomavirus, Parvovirus, Hep B | Influenza, HIV, Measles, Poliovirus, Hep A/C/E, Rabies |
---
## 7. DNA Enveloped Viruses
**Herpesviruses** (all dsDNA, enveloped, ALL establish lifelong latency):
| Virus | Disease(s) | Site of latency | Key exam point |
|---|---|---|---|
| HSV-1 | Oral herpes/cold sores, gingivostomatitis, herpes encephalitis | Trigeminal ganglion | Spread by direct contact/saliva |
| HSV-2 | Genital herpes | Sacral ganglion | STI; risk of neonatal transmission during vaginal delivery |
| VZV | Chickenpox (primary infection), Shingles (reactivation) | Dorsal root ganglia | Spread airborne + direct contact |
| EBV | Infectious mononucleosis; linked to Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma | B lymphocytes | Diagnosed with heterophile antibody (Monospot) test; "kissing disease" |
| CMV | Mononucleosis-like illness; severe congenital infection in newborns; retinitis in immunocompromised (HIV/AIDS) | Monocytes, lymphocytes | "Owl's eye" intranuclear inclusion bodies on histology |
| HHV-8 | Kaposi's sarcoma | B cells, endothelial cells | Strongly associated with AIDS patients |
**Poxvirus**
- **Smallpox (Variola)**: largest known virus, complex symmetry, brick-shaped, unusually replicates in the **cytoplasm** (not nucleus, unlike other DNA viruses)
- Produces **Guarnieri bodies** (cytoplasmic inclusion bodies) — key histology answer
- Eradicated globally in 1980 through vaccination (vaccinia virus vaccine) — a key public health success story to mention in essays
---
## 8. DNA Non-Enveloped Viruses
| Virus | Genome | Disease |
|---|---|---|
| Adenovirus | dsDNA | Conjunctivitis, pharyngitis, respiratory infection, gastroenteritis |
| Papillomavirus (HPV) | dsDNA | Common warts; high-risk types 16 & 18 → cervical cancer |
| Parvovirus B19 | ssDNA (smallest known DNA virus) | Erythema infectiosum ("Fifth disease"/slapped-cheek rash in children); aplastic crisis in sickle cell patients; fetal hydrops if infected in pregnancy |
---
## 9. RNA Enveloped Viruses
| Family | Virus | Genome | Key disease/feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Orthomyxovirus | Influenza A/B/C | (–)ssRNA, **segmented** | Segmented genome allows **antigenic shift** (reassortment, causes pandemics) vs **antigenic drift** (point mutation, causes seasonal epidemics); hemagglutinin (attachment) & neuraminidase (release) spikes |
| Paramyxovirus | Measles | (–)ssRNA | Koplik spots, rash; can cause SSPE years later (slow infection) |
| | Mumps | (–)ssRNA | Parotitis, orchitis |
| | RSV | (–)ssRNA | Bronchiolitis, major cause of infant hospitalization |
| | Parainfluenza | (–)ssRNA | Croup (barking cough) in children |
| Togavirus | Rubella | (+)ssRNA | Mild rash in kids; **Congenital Rubella Syndrome** (deafness, cataracts, heart defects) if mother infected in first trimester |
| Rhabdovirus | Rabies | (–)ssRNA, bullet-shaped | Transmitted via animal bite/saliva; **Negri bodies** (cytoplasmic inclusions in neurons); ~100% fatal once symptoms appear |
---
## 10. RNA Non-Enveloped Viruses
| Family | Virus | Disease |
|---|---|---|
| Picornavirus | Poliovirus | Paralytic poliomyelitis (destroys anterior horn motor neurons) |
| | Coxsackievirus | Hand-foot-mouth disease, viral myocarditis, aseptic meningitis |
| | Rhinovirus | Common cold (most frequent cause) |
| Reovirus | Rotavirus | Severe gastroenteritis/diarrhea in infants — leading global cause of child mortality from diarrhea |
---

articles.title: Haematology & Blood Transfusion Pathology: MDS, Stem Cell Transplant — Notes
articles.content:
## SEMESTER THREE — REMAINING TOPICS (7–11)**7. Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS)**- Clonal disorder of haemopoietic stem cells → **dysplastic (abnormally formed), ineffective** blood cell production, despite a normal or hypercellular marrow.
- Key concept (must-know, often tested as a contrast question): "ineffective haemopoiesis" — marrow is busy, but cells die before release or don't function properly → peripheral cytopenias **despite** a cellular marrow. This is the opposite picture from aplastic anaemia (hypocellular marrow), a classic exam contrast.
- Cause: mostly idiopathic (de novo), or secondary/therapy-related (prior chemotherapy or radiotherapy — "t-MDS").
- More common in older adults.
- **Clinical features**: result from cytopenias — fatigue/pallor (anaemia), infections (neutropenia), bleeding (thrombocytopenia). No major organomegaly typically.
- **Blood film/marrow clues (must-know dysplastic features):**

Red cells — macrocytosis, ring sideroblasts (iron-loaded mitochondria around the nucleus)

- Neutrophils — hypogranular cytoplasm, hypo-segmented nuclei (**pseudo-Pelger-Huët cells**)
- Megakaryocytes — micromegakaryocytes, abnormal nuclear lobulation
- Diagnosis: cytopenias + dysplasia on marrow morphology + cytogenetics (e.g. del(5q) — a favourable-prognosis subtype, also must-know).
- **Important progression fact**: MDS can transform into **AML** — a key link question connecting this topic back to WBC malignancies.
- Management: supportive (transfusions, growth factors), hypomethylating agents (azacitidine), allogeneic stem cell transplant (only curative option, for eligible/fit patients).

**8. Stem Cell Transplantation**

- Replacing diseased/failed marrow with healthy haemopoietic stem cells. Two broad types — must-know distinction:

**Autologous** — patient's own stem cells, harvested before treatment, re-infused after high-dose therapy (used in myeloma, some lymphomas). No risk of GVHD or rejection but no "graft-versus-tumour" effect either.

- **Allogeneic** — stem cells from a donor (sibling, unrelated matched donor, or cord blood). Curative potential is higher (graft-versus-leukaemia effect) but carries GVHD risk.
- **Process sequence (essay skeleton):**

Stem cell collection — peripheral blood (after mobilisation with G-CSF) or bone marrow harvest

- Conditioning — chemotherapy ± radiotherapy to destroy the patient's own marrow/immune system, creating "space" and eliminating disease
- Infusion of stem cells — engraftment follows over 2–4 weeks
- Supportive care during the pancytopenic window (infection prophylaxis, transfusion support)
- **Complications (must-know list):**

Graft failure/rejection

- Infections (bacterial, fungal, viral reactivation — e.g. CMV) during the immunosuppressed period
- **Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD)** — donor T cells attack recipient tissues; acute (skin, gut, liver) vs chronic forms — only a risk in allogeneic transplant
- Veno-occlusive disease of the liver (from conditioning toxicity)
- Long-term: infertility, secondary malignancy, organ toxicity from conditioning regimens
- Indications: leukaemias (esp. high-risk/relapsed), aplastic anaemia, myeloma, lymphoma, some inherited disorders (thalassaemia major, sickle cell disease).

**9. Haematological Changes in Systemic Disease**

- Blood often reflects disease happening elsewhere in the body — a classic "clinicopathological correlation" essay theme.
- **Anaemia of chronic disease (must-know mechanism)**: chronic inflammation → hepcidin release from the liver → traps iron in macrophages/reduces gut iron absorption → functional iron deficiency despite normal/high body iron stores. Seen in chronic infection, autoimmune disease (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis), malignancy, chronic kidney disease.
- **Renal disease** — reduced erythropoietin production → normocytic anaemia; uraemia can also impair platelet function (bleeding tendency despite normal platelet count).
- **Liver disease** — reduced clotting factor synthesis (all factors except VIII) → raised PT/aPTT; macrocytosis; thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism (portal hypertension).
- **Connective tissue/autoimmune disease** (e.g. SLE) — can cause autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia (cytopenias are part of diagnostic criteria for SLE).
- **Malignancy (non-haematological)** — anaemia of chronic disease, marrow infiltration by metastases, paraneoplastic effects (e.g. polycythaemia from renal cell carcinoma producing ectopic EPO).
- **Must-know exam link**: anaemia of chronic disease vs iron deficiency anaemia is a frequently tested differentiation — both can be microcytic, but ferritin is low in true iron deficiency and normal/high in anaemia of chronic disease (since ferritin is also an acute-phase protein).

**10. Pregnancy and Neonatal Haematology**

- **Normal physiological changes in pregnancy (must-know — easily mistaken for pathology):**

Plasma volume increases more than red cell mass → **dilutional/physiological anaemia** — Hb falls but this is expected and not always pathological

- Mild thrombocytopenia can occur (gestational thrombocytopenia) — usually benign
- Procoagulant state — pregnancy is prothrombotic (raised clotting factors, reduced protein S) → increased VTE risk, a key obstetric safety point
- **Iron and folate deficiency** are common and clinically important in pregnancy — increased demand from the fetus and expanded maternal red cell mass; folate deficiency specifically linked to neural tube defects, hence folate supplementation pre-conception/early pregnancy.
- **Haemolytic Disease of the Newborn (HDN) — top must-know topic here:**

Caused by maternal alloantibodies (most classically anti-D) crossing the placenta and destroying fetal/neonatal RBCs

- Mechanism: Rh-negative mother becomes sensitised (prior pregnancy, transfusion, or sensitising event) to Rh-positive fetal blood → produces anti-D IgG → crosses placenta in a subsequent pregnancy → haemolyses Rh-positive fetal RBCs
- Clinical features: fetal anaemia, hydrops fetalis (severe cases), neonatal jaundice (often severe and early-onset — risk of **kernicterus**, bilirubin deposition in the brain, if untreated), hepatosplenomegaly
- **Prevention (must-know for clinical/essay relevance)**: anti-D immunoglobulin given to Rh-negative mothers at sensitising events and routinely in pregnancy (prophylaxis) — prevents maternal sensitisation in the first place
- Management: phototherapy or exchange transfusion for neonatal jaundice depending on severity; intrauterine transfusion in severe antenatal cases
- ABO incompatibility can also cause a milder form of HDN (mother type O, baby type A or B) — generally less severe than Rh disease.

**11. Haematology in HIV**

- HIV causes haematological abnormalities through multiple mechanisms — a good essay structure is "direct viral effects vs drug effects vs opportunistic disease":
- **Direct effects of HIV:**

Anaemia — most common haematological abnormality in HIV; multifactorial (chronic disease, marrow suppression by the virus itself, opportunistic infection)

- Neutropenia and thrombocytopenia — from direct marrow effects and immune-mediated destruction (HIV-associated immune thrombocytopenia resembles ITP)
- Lymphopenia — progressive **CD4+ T-cell depletion** is the hallmark of HIV progression and the basis for staging/monitoring disease
- **Drug-related effects (must-know — frequently tested):**

Zidovudine (AZT) — classically causes marrow suppression → anaemia and neutropenia

- Other antiretrovirals can cause varying cytopenias; co-trimoxazole prophylaxis can also suppress marrow
- **Opportunistic disease effects:**

Marrow infiltration by opportunistic infections (e.g. disseminated TB, fungal infection) or HIV-associated lymphomas (Non-Hodgkin lymphoma — AIDS-defining illness)

- Increased risk of haematological malignancies overall with advancing immunosuppression
- **Must-know clinical link**: CD4 count is both a marker of immune status and a haematological parameter directly used to guide opportunistic infection prophylaxis decisions — a strong cross-topic exam link (pathology + clinical medicine).

articles.content:
**MOUNT KENYA UNIVERSITY** **SCHOOL OF MEDICINE — DEPARTMENT OF PATHOLOGY** **Course: Human Pathology — Year Three** **Unit: Haematology and Blood Transfusion Pathology** **Crash Revision Notes — Semester Two (Sem 1) | Compiled for exam prep, June 2026**
## SEMESTER TWO — COMPLETE NOTES**1. Introduction to Haematology**
- Study of blood, blood-forming organs (marrow, lymphoid tissue, spleen), and their diseases.
- Blood = plasma (~55%) + cells (~45%): RBCs, WBCs, platelets.
- **Sites of haemopoiesis across life (must-know sequence):**
Mesoblastic stage — yolk sac (weeks 2–10 gestation)
- Hepatic stage — liver/spleen (6 weeks–7 months gestation)
- Medullary stage — bone marrow (from ~5 months gestation; sole site by birth)
- Adult red (active) marrow confined to: vertebrae, sternum, ribs, skull, pelvis, proximal femur/humerus.
- Yellow marrow (fatty, inactive) can revert to red marrow under stress (e.g. severe chronic anaemia).
- **Essay angle**: "Describe the sites of haemopoiesis from foetal life to adulthood" is a classic short essay — use the 3-stage sequence as your skeleton.
**2. Haemopoiesis**
- Process forming/maturing all blood cells from one ancestor: **pluripotent haemopoietic stem cell (HSC)**, capable of self-renewal and differentiation.
- Splits into two lineages:
**Myeloid** → erythrocytes, granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils), monocytes, megakaryocytes/platelets
- **Lymphoid** → T cells, B cells, NK cells
- **Growth factors (must-know matching for MCQs):**
Erythropoietin (EPO) → RBCs (renal origin, hypoxia-triggered)
- Thrombopoietin → platelets (mainly hepatic origin)
- G-CSF / GM-CSF → granulocytes
- Interleukins (IL-3, IL-7…) → early progenitors
- Bone marrow stroma (stromal cells, fat, sinusoids) physically/chemically supports developing cells — "the soil the seed grows in."
**3. Erythrocytes**
- Biconcave, anucleate discs, ~7–8 µm diameter, lifespan **~120 days**.
- Function: O2/CO2 transport via haemoglobin; biconcave shape maximises surface area and flexibility for capillary passage.
- **Maturation sequence (must-know, often asked to list in order):** Proerythroblast → Basophilic erythroblast → Polychromatic erythroblast → Orthochromatic erythroblast → Reticulocyte → Mature erythrocyte
Nucleus extruded at the orthochromatic stage — why mature RBCs are anucleate.
- Reticulocytes retain residual RNA (bluish/polychromatic tint on stain), circulate ~1–2 days before full maturity — reticulocyte count is a marker of marrow erythropoietic activity.
- Production driven by EPO; destruction mainly extravascular in the spleen — Hb broken down to globin (recycled to amino acids) and heme (→ iron recycled, protoporphyrin → bilirubin → excreted, hence jaundice if haemolysis is excessive).
- **Red cell indices (must-know definitions — common MCQ stem):**
MCV — mean cell volume (average size)
- MCH — mean cell haemoglobin (average Hb mass per cell)
- MCHC — mean cell Hb concentration (Hb relative to cell volume)
- Haematocrit/PCV — % of blood volume occupied by RBCs
**4. Haemoglobin**
- Tetramer of 4 globin chains (adult: 2 alpha + 2 beta), each carrying one heme group with central Fe²⁺ that binds O2 reversibly.
- Loads O2 in lungs (high pO2), unloads in tissues (lower pO2, higher CO2/H⁺ — **Bohr effect** shifts the O2-Hb dissociation curve right, favouring unloading).
- **Haemoglobin types (must-know chain composition — classic matching question):**
HbA (α2β2) — major adult Hb (~97%)
- HbA2 (α2δ2) — minor adult component (~2%)
- HbF (α2γ2) — dominant foetal Hb, falls sharply after birth (residual <1% in adults)
- Synthesis requires: adequate iron supply, normal globin genes (alpha cluster — chromosome 16; beta cluster — chromosome 11), and protoporphyrin (heme synthesis pathway).
- **Abnormal haemoglobins (high-yield for both MCQ and essay):**
**HbS (sickle cell disease)** — single point mutation, beta chain: glutamic acid → valine at position 6; causes Hb polymerisation under deoxygenation → sickling, vaso-occlusion, haemolysis
- **Thalassaemias** — reduced/absent globin chain synthesis (alpha-thalassaemia = alpha gene defect; beta-thalassaemia = beta gene defect) → chain imbalance → ineffective erythropoiesis + haemolysis
**5. Anaemia**
- Definition: Hb/red cell mass below normal reference range for age and sex → reduced O2-carrying capacity.
- **Classify by mechanism (essay skeleton #1):**
Decreased production — iron deficiency, megaloblastic anaemia (B12/folate deficiency), aplastic anaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, marrow infiltration (leukaemia, metastases)
- Increased destruction (haemolytic) — hereditary (sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency) or acquired (autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, malaria, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia/DIC)
- Blood loss — acute (trauma/haemorrhage) or chronic (GI bleed, menorrhagia)
- **Classify by morphology using MCV (essay skeleton #2 — the one examiners love most):**
Microcytic (MCV <80fl) — iron deficiency, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic anaemia
- Normocytic (MCV 80–100fl) — acute blood loss, anaemia of chronic disease, early haemolytic anaemia, aplastic anaemia, renal disease
- Macrocytic (MCV >100fl) — B12/folate deficiency, liver disease, hypothyroidism, raised reticulocytes
- Clinical features: fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea, tachycardia, dizziness + specific clues — koilonychia/spoon nails (iron deficiency), jaundice (haemolytic), glossitis (B12/folate deficiency).
- Key investigations: FBC, peripheral blood film, reticulocyte count, iron studies (ferritin, TIBC, serum iron), B12/folate, Hb electrophoresis, marrow exam when indicated.
- **Must-know exam pattern**: vignette gives symptoms + film appearance + MCV → you must name BOTH the anaemia type AND its mechanism. This is the single most-tested clinical reasoning skill in this whole unit.
**6. Leukocytes**
- **Granulocytes**: neutrophils (most abundant, first responders to bacterial infection/acute inflammation), eosinophils (allergic reactions, parasitic infections), basophils (allergic/hypersensitivity reactions, contain histamine/heparin)
- **Mononuclear cells**: lymphocytes (B cells, T cells, NK cells — adaptive immunity) and monocytes (phagocytic; become tissue macrophages)
- Normal differential count (approx): neutrophils 40–75%, lymphocytes 20–45%, monocytes 2–10%, eosinophils 1–6%, basophils 0–1%.
- Origin: granulocytes/monocytes from myeloid lineage; lymphocytes from lymphoid lineage (T cells mature in thymus, B cells mature in bone marrow).
- **Must-know clinical pairings (favourite MCQ format):**
Neutrophilia — bacterial infection, stress, steroid use
- Eosinophilia — allergy, parasitic infection
- Lymphocytosis — viral infection
- Neutropenia — viral infection, certain drugs, marrow failure
**7. White Blood Cell Malignancies 1 — Acute Leukaemias**
- Malignant clonal proliferation of immature blasts in the marrow, suppressing normal haemopoiesis.
- **AML (Acute Myeloid Leukaemia)** — myeloid blasts; more common in adults; **Auer rods** on blood film = must-know diagnostic clue.
- **ALL (Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia)** — lymphoid blasts; the most common leukaemia of childhood.
- Pathogenesis: chromosomal translocation/mutation arrests differentiation at the blast stage → blasts accumulate and crowd out normal marrow elements → pancytopenia.
- Clinical features: anaemia (fatigue, pallor), neutropenia (recurrent infections), thrombocytopenia (bruising, bleeding) + infiltrative features — hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bone pain, gum hypertrophy (especially AML-M5), CNS involvement (especially ALL).
- Diagnosis: marrow blast count ≥20% (WHO criteria); immunophenotyping/flow cytometry distinguishes AML from ALL; cytogenetics guide prognosis.
- **Must-know cytogenetics**: t(15;17) — AML-M3 (acute promyelocytic leukaemia), strongly associated with DIC at presentation, treated with ATRA (all-trans retinoic acid).
**8. White Blood Cell Malignancies 2 — Chronic Leukaemias & Lymphomas**
- **CML (Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia):**
Clonal proliferation of mature/maturing myeloid cells
- Hallmark: **Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) → BCR-ABL fusion gene** (constitutive tyrosine kinase activity) — the single most important fact in this topic
- Phases: chronic → accelerated → blast crisis
- Film: marked leukocytosis with the full spectrum of granulocyte maturation, splenomegaly common
- Treatment: tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib) — a classic "mechanism of drug action" essay link
- **CLL (Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia):**
Clonal proliferation of mature but functionally incompetent B lymphocytes
- Commonest leukaemia in older adults, often picked up incidentally
- Film: small mature lymphocytes + **smear/smudge cells** — classic must-know film finding
- Lymphadenopathy/hepatosplenomegaly if advanced
- **Lymphomas (brief overview — detailed coverage usually a separate topic):**
Hodgkin lymphoma — **Reed-Sternberg cells** (binucleate, "owl-eye" nuclei) — must-know diagnostic cell
- Non-Hodgkin lymphoma — heterogeneous group, no Reed-Sternberg cells
**9–10. Platelet Structure and Morphology**
- Anucleate cytoplasmic fragments budded off **megakaryocytes** in the marrow; lifespan ~7–10 days; normal count 150,000–400,000/µL.
- **Granule contents (must-know for mechanism questions):**
Alpha granules — von Willebrand factor (vWF), fibrinogen, PDGF
- Dense granules — ADP, ATP, serotonin, calcium
- **Primary haemostasis — 3-step sequence (essay skeleton):**
Adhesion — platelet GpIb receptor binds subendothelial collagen via a vWF bridge
- Activation — shape change; releases ADP and thromboxane A2, recruiting further platelets
- Aggregation — GpIIb/IIIa receptors link platelets to each other via fibrinogen bridges
- Regulated by thrombopoietin (mainly hepatic).
- **Disorders (must-know classification):**
Thrombocytopenia — decreased production (marrow failure, aplastic anaemia, leukaemic infiltration) vs increased destruction (ITP, DIC, hypersplenism)
- Thrombocytosis — reactive (infection, inflammation, iron deficiency, post-splenectomy) vs primary/clonal (essential thrombocythaemia)
- Qualitative defects — Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GpIIb/IIIa deficiency), Bernard-Soulier syndrome (GpIb deficiency), von Willebrand disease (commonest inherited bleeding disorder overall)
- **Key clinical differentiator**: platelet/vascular bleeding is mucocutaneous — petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding — contrast this directly against coagulation factor bleeding below.
**11. Coagulation System**
- Secondary haemostasis — stabilises the platelet plug into a durable fibrin clot.
- **Classic cascade (most exam-relevant model, even though physiologically the cell-based model is now preferred):**
Intrinsic pathway — XII → XI → IX → VIII; measured by **aPTT**
- Extrinsic pathway — tissue factor + factor VII; measured by **PT**
- Common pathway — factor X → prothrombin (II) → thrombin → fibrinogen (I) → fibrin
- Factor numbering I–XIII; know especially I = fibrinogen, II = prothrombin.
- **Vitamin K-dependent factors (must-know list)**: II, VII, IX, X
- Natural anticoagulants (limit clot extension): antithrombin III, protein C, protein S.
- Fibrinolysis: plasmin degrades fibrin → **D-dimer**, a clinical marker of clot turnover (e.g. DVT/PE workup).
- **Must-know disorder/lab-pattern table — high-yield for MCQs:**
Haemophilia A — Factor VIII deficiency, X-linked, ↑aPTT, normal PT
- Haemophilia B — Factor IX deficiency, X-linked, same lab pattern as A
- Von Willebrand disease — ↓/dysfunctional vWF, ↑aPTT + abnormal platelet function tests
- Vitamin K deficiency / warfarin / liver disease — ↑PT (± ↑aPTT in severe cases)
- DIC — ↑PT AND ↑aPTT, ↓platelets, ↓fibrinogen, ↑D-dimer (consumption of everything at once — the giveaway pattern)
- Clinical bleeding pattern: factor deficiencies cause deep bleeding — haemarthroses (joint bleeds), muscle haematomas — directly contrast with the mucocutaneous bleeding of platelet disorders. This contrast is a near-guaranteed essay or MCQ differentiator.

articles.title: Exam Prep: Skin Infections, Psoriasis & Pemphigus — Notes
articles.content:
# SECTION 1: SKIN PATHOLOGY (DERMATOPATHOLOGY)
**Intro:** This section covers the major disease categories of the skin — infections, chronic inflammatory dermatoses, blistering disorders, disorders of epidermal appendages, and disorders of pigmentation/melanocytes (including melanoma). Focus areas for exams: pathogenesis mechanisms, key morphological buzzwords, and distinguishing features between similar-looking conditions (e.g., pemphigus vs. pemphigoid).
---
## 1. INFECTIOUS DERMATOSES
### A. Bacterial Infections (Impetigo)
- Range: superficial (impetigo) → deep dermal abscesses (e.g., Pseudomonas, puncture wounds)
- **Organism:** *S. aureus* (most common) or *S. pyogenes*
- **Morphology:** neutrophils beneath stratum corneum → **subcorneal pustule**; Gram stain shows cocci
- **Clinical:** mainly children; starts as small macule (face/extremities) → **honey-colored crust**
- Bullous variant of childhood impetigo can mimic autoimmune blistering disease
### B. Fungal Infections
- Spectrum: superficial (Tinea, Candida) → deep/systemic (Aspergillus in immunosuppressed)
- **Morphology:** superficial → neutrophilic epidermal infiltrate; Candida → psoriasiform hyperplasia; deep → granulomatous response; Aspergillus = angioinvasive
- **Stains:** PAS and Gomori methenamine silver (GMS)
- **Clinical:** superficial = pruritic erythematous scaly macules (can mimic psoriasis — always exclude fungal cause before diagnosing new psoriasis)
### C. Viral – Verrucae (Warts)
- Caused by **HPV**; self-limited (resolve in 6 mo–2 yrs)
- Low-risk HPV → warts (no transforming potential); high-risk HPV → anogenital cancers (via E6/E7 oncoproteins)
- **Types:** Verruca vulgaris (hands, most common), Verruca plana (flat, face), Verruca plantaris/palmaris (soles/palms), Condyloma acuminatum (genital)
- **Morphology:** verrucous epidermal hyperplasia + **koilocytosis** (perinuclear vacuolization/halo)
---
## 2. CHRONIC INFLAMMATORY DERMATOSES
### A. Psoriasis
- Affects 1–2%; linked to ↑ CV risk, arthritis (10%)
- **Pathogenesis:** multifactorial immune disease — CD4+ TH17/TH1 and CD8+ T cells → keratinocyte hyperproliferation; **Koebner phenomenon** (trauma-induced lesions); HLA association
- **Morphology:** well-demarcated salmon plaque with silvery scale; **acanthosis** with "test-tube in rack" rete ridges; loss of stratum granulosum; **parakeratosis**; thin suprapapillary plates with dilated vessels → **Auspitz sign** (pinpoint bleeding); neutrophil microabscesses (Munro)
- **Clinical:** elbows, knees, scalp, lumbosacral, glans penis; nail pitting (30%)
- **Treatment:** NSAIDs, cyclosporine, TNF antagonists
### B. Lichen Planus
- Mnemonic: **"Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar Papules and Plaques"**
- **Pathogenesis:** CD8+ T cell cytotoxic response vs. basal layer antigens (post-viral/drug)
- **Morphology:** **Wickham striae** (white lines on papules); interface dermatitis; **sawtooth** rete ridges; **Civatte/colloid bodies** (necrotic basal cells); squamatization
- **Clinical:** middle-aged adults; wrists, elbows, glans penis; 70% oral mucosa (reticulate white pattern); skin lesions resolve in 1–2 yrs, oral lesions persist
### C. Lichen Simplex Chronicus
- Response to chronic rubbing/scratching; nodular form = **prurigo nodularis**
- **Morphology:** acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, dermal fibrosis (resembles thickened volar skin)
- **Clinical:** can mask underlying pruritic dermatosis — rule out cause
---
## 3. BLISTERING (BULLOUS) DISORDERS
### A. Inflammatory — Pemphigus Group
- **Common mechanism:** IgG autoantibodies vs. **desmogleins** → **acantholysis** (loss of cell-cell adhesion)
| Type | Level of blister | Key feature |
|---|---|---|
| Pemphigus vulgaris (>80%) | Suprabasal | "Row of tombstones"; oral ulcers first |
| Pemphigus vegetans | Suprabasal | Verrucous plaques, no true blisters |
| Pemphigus foliaceus | Subcorneal (superficial) | Fogo selvagem (Brazil); mucosa spared |
| Pemphigus erythematosus | Superficial | Localized, malar/lupus-like |
| Paraneoplastic pemphigus | — | Associated with NHL |
- IF: net-like intercellular IgG deposits
### B. Bullous Pemphigoid
- Elderly patients; thighs, forearms, axillae, groin
- **Pathogenesis:** autoantibodies vs. **BPAG2** (hemidesmosome component) → complement activation → eosinophil/neutrophil recruitment
- **Morphology:** **tense bullae** (don't rupture easily, unlike pemphigus); **subepidermal, nonacantholytic** blister; eosinophils beneath basal layer
### C. Dermatitis Herpetiformis
- Associated with **celiac disease**; males, 3rd–4th decade; intensely pruritic
- **Pathogenesis:** IgA anti-gliadin cross-reacts with reticulin → subepidermal blister
- **Morphology:** **microabscesses at dermal papillary tips** (fibrin + neutrophils); IF = **granular IgA** at papillary tips
- Responds to gluten-free diet
### D. Noninflammatory Blistering Disorders
- **Epidermolysis Bullosa** (defects in structural proteins; blisters at trauma sites from birth):
  - Simplex — keratin 5/14 mutation (AD, most common)
  - Junctional — laminin or BPAG2 mutation (AR), lamina lucida split
  - Dystrophic — COL7A1 mutation, beneath lamina densa
  - Mixed — multiple levels
- **Porphyria:** disturbed porphyrin metabolism; 5 types (congenital erythropoietic, erythrohepatic protoporphyria, acute intermittent, porphyria cutanea tarda, mixed); photosensitive subepidermal vesicles with vessel wall thickening
---
## 4. DISORDERS OF EPIDERMAL APPENDAGES
### A. Acne Vulgaris
- Universal in teens; worse in males; exacerbated by androgens, drugs, occlusive cosmetics
- **4 pathogenic factors:** (1) follicular keratin plug, (2) sebaceous hypertrophy (androgen-driven), (3) *Propionibacterium acnes* colonization → proinflammatory fatty acids, (4) secondary inflammation
- **Morphology:** open comedones (black, oxidized melanin) vs. closed comedones (trapped plug); severe form = acne conglobata (scarring)
- **Treatment:** antibiotics (anti-*P. acnes*), isotretinoin (antisebaceous)
### B. Rosacea
- Middle-aged females
- **4 stages:** flushing → persistent erythema/telangiectasia → papules/pustules → **rhinophyma**
- **Pathogenesis:** abnormal cathelicidin processing (via kallikrein 5, TLR2 activation)
- **Morphology:** perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate, telangiectasia; rhinophyma = sebaceous hypertrophy + keratotic plugging
---
## 5. DISORDERS OF PIGMENTATION & MELANOCYTES
### A. Freckle (Ephelis)
- Childhood; ↑ melanin in basal keratinocytes (not ↑ melanocyte number); darkens with sun, fades in winter
### B. Lentigo
- Benign melanocyte hyperplasia (linear, non-nested) just above basement membrane; does **not** darken with sun (unlike freckle)
### C. Melanocytic Nevus (Mole)
- Acquired **RAS/BRAF** activating mutations → limited by **oncogene-induced senescence** (p16/INK4a)
- **Progression:** Junctional nevus (DEJ) → Compound nevus (epidermis + dermis) → Intradermal nevus (dermis only)
- Deep cells show **neurotization** (loss of pigment, neural-like morphology) — helps distinguish from melanoma
### D. Dysplastic Nevi
- Precursor/marker of melanoma risk; **dysplastic nevus syndrome** (AD, germline **CDKN2A**/p16 or CDK4 mutation) → >50% lifetime melanoma risk
- **Morphology:** >5mm, pebbly/target lesions; **lentiginous hyperplasia**, architectural + cytologic atypia, melanin incontinence, lamellar fibrosis around rete ridges
### E. Melanoma
- Most lethal skin cancer; UV-induced (~85–90% sporadic), 10–15% familial (CDKN2A, telomerase genes)
- **Growth phases:**
  - **Radial** — horizontal spread, no metastatic potential (subtypes: lentigo maligna, superficial spreading [most common], acral/mucosal lentiginous [UV-independent])
  - **Vertical** — downward invasion, metastatic potential, heralded by a nodule
- **Morphology:** irregular borders, color variation, large nuclei with peripheral clumped chromatin, prominent nucleoli; no neurotization (unlike nevi)
- **Clinical — ABCDEs:** **A**symmetry, **B**order irregularity, **C**olor variegation, **D**iameter increase, **E**volution/change

## 6. PANNICULITIS
- Inflammation of subcutaneous fat (lobular and/or septal); often lower legs
| Feature | Erythema Nodosum | Erythema Induratum |
|---|---|---|
| Population | Any age | Adolescents/menopausal women |
| Cause | Hypersensitivity (strep, TB, sarcoid, IBD, drugs, malignancy) | Primary vasculitis of deep dermal vessels (TB-related historically) |
| Lesion | Tender plaques/nodules, no ulceration | Nodule that **ulcerates** |
| Histology | **Septal** panniculitis, **no vasculitis** | **Granulomatous + caseous necrosis**, **vasculitis present** |
- **Other types:** Weber-Christian disease (relapsing febrile nodular panniculitis), factitial panniculitis (self-inflicted), lymphoma-related, lupus panniculitis

# SECTION 2: BREAST PATHOLOGY
**Intro:** This section covers benign and malignant breast disease — benign epithelial lesions (and their cancer-risk stratification), inflammatory/infective breast disorders, stromal tumors, and breast carcinoma (the most clinically important topic — focus heavily here for exams).
---
## 1. BENIGN EPITHELIAL LESIONS OF THE BREAST
Classified into **3 risk groups**:
### A. Nonproliferative Changes ("Fibrocystic Changes") — *no ↑ cancer risk*
- **Cysts** — dilated lobules; lined by flattened or apocrine metaplastic epithelium; calcifications common; resolves on FNA
- **Fibrosis** — from cyst rupture → chronic inflammation
- **Adenosis** — ↑ acini/lobule; normal in pregnancy
- **Lactational adenoma** — palpable mass in pregnancy/lactation; regresses after weaning
- **Flat epithelial atypia** — earliest clonal lesion (16q deletion); mild atypia; risk only when combined with atypical hyperplasia
### B. Proliferative Disease WITHOUT Atypia — *small ↑ risk (1.5–2×)*
- **Epithelial hyperplasia** — filled ducts/lobules, both luminal + myoepithelial cells, irregular lumens
- **Sclerosing adenosis** — compressed acini in fibrotic stroma; can mimic invasive carcinoma
- **Complex sclerosing lesion / Radial scar** — central hyalinized nidus + radiating projections; mimics carcinoma radiologically/grossly/histologically (NOT from trauma, despite name)
- **Papilloma** — branching fibrovascular cores in dilated duct; large duct type (solitary, nipple discharge) vs small duct type (multiple, deeper)
### C. Proliferative Disease WITH Atypia — *moderate ↑ risk (4–5×)*
- **Atypical Ductal Hyperplasia (ADH)** — resembles DCIS but only partially fills duct
- **Atypical Lobular Hyperplasia (ALH)** — identical to LCIS cells, but fills <50% of acini in a lobule
- Both: ER-positive, low proliferation; ALH shows **loss of E-cadherin** (shared with LCIS)
### D. Gynecomastia
- Only common benign male breast lesion; subareolar button-like enlargement
- **Cause:** estrogen/androgen imbalance — cirrhosis (↓ estrogen metabolism), aging (↓ androgens), drugs (alcohol, marijuana, anabolic steroids), Klinefelter syndrome, Leydig/Sertoli cell tumors
- Histology: ↑ collagenous stroma + ductal epithelial hyperplasia; **no lobule formation**
### Clinical Significance
- Risk reduction: prophylactic mastectomy, tamoxifen (ER antagonist)
- <20% of atypical hyperplasia patients ever develop cancer → many opt for surveillance over intervention
---
## 2. INFLAMMATORY DISORDERS OF THE BREAST
| Condition | Key Features |
|---|---|
| **Acute Mastitis** | 1st month of breastfeeding; *S. aureus* (abscess) or strep (cellulitis); via nipple cracks; treat with antibiotics |
| **Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts** (Periductal mastitis / Zuska disease / recurrent subareolar abscess) | **>90% smokers**; keratin plug → duct dilation/rupture → granulomatous inflammation; nipple inversion; treat = duct excision |
| **Duct Ectasia** | 5th–6th decade, multiparous women; thick nipple discharge; **not** smoking-related; dilated ducts + periductal chronic inflammation + lipid-laden macrophages → fibrosis/retraction; mimics carcinoma |
| **Fat Necrosis** | History of trauma/surgery (~50%); mimics cancer; liquefactive necrosis → giant cells/calcification → scarring |
| **Lymphocytic Mastopathy** (Sclerosing Lymphocytic Lobulitis) | Type 1 DM or autoimmune thyroid disease; dense collagenized stroma + lymphocytic infiltrate around atrophic ducts |
| **Granulomatous Mastitis** | Systemic granulomatous disease (TB, sarcoid, GPA) or localized; granulomas around lobules with lipid vacuoles; cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis (Corynebacteria) |
---
## 3. STROMAL TUMORS
- Breast stroma = **intralobular** (gives biphasic tumors) vs **interlobular** (gives connective-tissue tumors as elsewhere in the body)
- Fibroadenoma & phyllodes tumor are both driven by **MED12 mutations**
### A. Fibroadenoma
- **Most common benign tumor of the female breast**; women in 20s–30s; hormonally responsive (grows in pregnancy, regresses post-menopause)
- Well-circumscribed, rubbery; pericanalicular or intracanalicular epithelial pattern
- Cyclosporin A (post-transplant) → multiple bilateral fibroadenomas (reversible)
### B. Phyllodes Tumor
- Less common; **6th decade** (later than fibroadenoma); leaf-like ("phyllodes") protrusions
- Distinguished from fibroadenoma by: ↑ cellularity, ↑ mitoses, stromal overgrowth, infiltrative border
- Malignant variants have additional **TERT** mutations; only stromal component metastasizes; axillary node dissection NOT indicated
### C. Interlobular Stroma Lesions
- **Myofibroblastoma** — equally common in males
- **Lipoma**
- **Fibromatosis** — locally aggressive, no metastasis; associated with FAP/Gardner syndrome
- **Angiosarcoma** (malignant) — rare; sporadic (young women) or post-radiation (older women, 5–10 yrs latency)
---
## 4. CARCINOMA OF THE BREAST
*(High-yield — most heavily tested topic)*
### Epidemiology & Risk Factors
- Most common cancer-related cause of death in women globally
- **Risk ↑:** age, female sex (99%), lifetime estrogen exposure, genetic mutations, obesity, alcohol, delayed childbearing/fewer pregnancies/reduced breastfeeding
- **Risk ↓:** early pregnancy (<20 yrs), prolonged breastfeeding, prophylactic mastectomy (~90% ↓), ER-antagonist chemoprevention
### Molecular Classification (by ER/HER2)
| Group | ER | HER2 |
|---|---|---|
| Luminal | + | − |
| HER2 | +/− | + |
| Triple-negative (TNBC) | − | − (also PR−) |
- 3 main pathogenic pathways: Luminal (precursor = flat epithelial atypia/atypical hyperplasia) → TNBC (precursor = p53-overexpressing normal cells) → HER2 (no defined precursor)
- **Hereditary genes** (germline): **BRCA1, BRCA2** (most important), TP53, PTEN, CDH1, STK11, ATM, CHEK2, PALB2
### Carcinoma In Situ (confined by basement membrane — cannot metastasize)
**DCIS:**
- Patterns: comedo, cribriform, micropapillary, papillary
- Untreated low-grade DCIS → invasive cancer ~1%/year; mastectomy curative >95%
**LCIS:**
- Dyscohesive cells, **loss of E-cadherin (CDH1)**; signet-ring cells; **pagetoid spread** within ducts (≠ Paget disease of nipple)
- Bilateral in 20–40% (vs DCIS 10–20%); always ER/PR+, HER2−
**Paget Disease of the Nipple:**
- Malignant (Paget) cells from DCIS spread via lactiferous sinuses into nipple skin (without crossing BM) → eczema-like eruption
- Palpable mass present → usually invasive (ER−, HER2+ overexpressing); no mass → usually just DCIS
### Invasive Carcinoma
- **Invasive Carcinoma of No Special Type (NST)** = majority; hard, gritty, desmoplastic mass → skin/nipple retraction
- **Grading (Nottingham):** tubule formation + nuclear pleomorphism + mitotic rate → Grade 1–3
- **Special types:**
  - **Lobular carcinoma** — biallelic CDH1 loss; single-file infiltration; metastasizes to peritoneum, leptomeninges, GI tract, ovary/uterus; germline CDH1 → also ↑ gastric signet-ring risk
  - **Medullary pattern** — associated with BRCA1 (germline or promoter hypermethylation); paradoxically better prognosis; heavy lymphocytic infiltrate
### Prognostic & Predictive Factors
- **Most important:** axillary lymph node status
- Others: distant metastases, tumor size, locally advanced disease (skin/muscle invasion), lymphovascular invasion, **inflammatory carcinoma** (dermal lymphatic invasion, 3-yr survival only 3–10%), gene expression profiling, response to neoadjuvant chemo
### Male Breast Cancer
- Rare (1% of female incidence); strongest hereditary factor = **germline BRCA2** (~6% of carriers affected)
- >90% luminal type; presents as subareolar mass/nipple discharge; similar prognosis to women when matched for stage

# SECTION 3: RENAL, URINARY TRACT & MALE REPRODUCTIVE PATHOLOGY

**Intro:** This is the largest section — kidney parenchymal disease (glomerular, tubulointerstitial, vascular), urinary tract obstruction/stones, renal tumors, lower urinary tract disease (ureter, bladder, urethra), and male reproductive pathology (penis, testis, prostate). Glomerular diseases and prostate/testis tumors are the highest-yield exam topics here.

---

## 1. CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS OF RENAL DISEASE

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Azotemia** | ↑BUN/creatinine from ↓GFR. **Prerenal** = hypoperfusion (shock, CHF, cirrhosis); **Postrenal** = obstruction distal to kidney (reversible on relief) |
| **Uremia** | Azotemia + clinical/biochemical syndrome (GI, neuro, cardiac — e.g., **fibrinous pericarditis**) |
| **Nephritic syndrome** | Hematuria (dysmorphic RBCs/RBC casts), ↓GFR, mild-mod proteinuria, HTN. Classic = post-strep GN |
| **Nephrotic syndrome** | Proteinuria >3.5g/day, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia, lipiduria |
| **AKI** | Rapid ↓GFR (hrs-days); glomerular/interstitial/vascular/tubular causes |
| **CKD** | GFR persistently <60 mL/min/1.73m² for ≥3 months and/or albuminuria; **most common causes = diabetes & hypertension** |
| **ESRD** | GFR <5% of normal |
| **Renal tubular defects** | Polyuria, nocturia, electrolyte disorders (e.g., metabolic acidosis) |
| **UTI** | Bacteriuria + pyuria; pyelonephritis (kidney) or cystitis (bladder) |
| **Nephrolithiasis** | Renal colic + hematuria |

---

## 2. GLOMERULAR DISEASES
*(Highest-yield topic — know mechanisms + IF/EM patterns cold)*

### Classification terms
- **Diffuse** (all glomeruli) vs **Focal** (some glomeruli); **Global** (whole glomerulus) vs **Segmental** (part of glomerulus)

### Basic Tissue Reactions to Injury
1. **Hypercellularity** — mesangial/endothelial proliferation, leukocyte infiltration, **crescents** (epithelial cell proliferation + leukocytes, from fibrin deposition after capillary wall injury)
2. **GBM thickening** — immune complex deposition / ↑ matrix synthesis (diabetes) / new BM layers (MPGN)
3. **Hyalinosis** — insudated plasma proteins, occludes capillary lumens
4. **Sclerosis** — collagenous matrix deposition

### Pathogenesis (Immune Mechanisms)
- **In situ immune complex formation** → **granular** IF pattern (e.g., membranous nephropathy)
- **Anti-GBM antibody disease** → **linear** IF pattern (Goodpasture-type; <5% of GN but causes severe crescentic RPGN)
- **Circulating immune complex deposition** → granular IF; antigens may be endogenous (SLE, IgA nephropathy) or exogenous (post-infectious — strep, Hep B/C, malaria)
- **Alternative complement pathway activation** → Dense Deposit Disease (MPGN type II) / C3 glomerulopathies
- Mediators: neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, T cells, platelets, mesangial cells

### A. NEPHRITIC SYNDROME DISEASES
| Disease | Key Features |
|---|---|
| **Acute Postinfectious (Post-strep) GN** | Subepithelial immune complexes, neutrophils, ↑glomerular cellularity; children mostly recover, worse in adults |
| **Crescentic (Rapidly Progressive) GN — RPGN** | Severe injury + GBM breaks + crescents; antibody-mediated (anti-GBM) or immune-complex or **ANCA-associated** (pauci-immune) |

### B. NEPHROTIC SYNDROME DISEASES
| Disease | Mechanism | EM/IF | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Membranous Nephropathy** | Autoimmune anti-**PLA2R** (or THSD7A) on podocytes | Subepithelial granular IgG4 deposits, GBM "spikes" | 75% primary; secondary = drugs, malignancy, SLE, Hep B/C; 1/3 remit, 1/3 stable, 1/3 →ESRD |
| **Minimal Change Disease (MCD)** | Podocyte foot process effacement (EM only); normal LM | No deposits | **Most common pediatric nephrotic syndrome** (peak 2–6yrs); dramatic steroid response; adults → think Hodgkin lymphoma |
| **Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)** | Podocytopathy | Focal/segmental sclerosis + hyalinosis | **Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults**; genetic forms (podocin, α-actinin-4, TRPC6); collapsing variant = worst prognosis, linked to **HIV** |
| **HIV-Associated Nephropathy** | Collapsing FSGS variant; APOL1 risk alleles | Tubuloreticular inclusions (also in SLE) | Microcystic tubular dilation |
| **Membranoproliferative GN (MPGN)** | Type I = immune complex (IgG+complement); Type II = **Dense Deposit Disease** (alternative complement activation, ↓C3, normal C1/C4) | — | A "pattern" not single disease |
| **Fibrillary GN** | Fibrillary deposits, Congo red **negative** (unlike amyloid) | IgG4, DNAJB9 marker | Recurs in transplant |

### C. OTHER PRIMARY GLOMERULOPATHIES
- **IgA Nephropathy** — **most common GN worldwide**; mesangial IgA deposits; children/young adults; recurrent hematuria
- **Alport Syndrome** — hereditary; **COL4A** (type IV collagen) mutation; hematuria + progressive renal failure + (deafness, ocular defects — classic triad)
- **Thin Basement Membrane Nephropathy** — also COL4 mutation; benign course

### D. SYSTEMIC DISEASE-ASSOCIATED GLOMERULAR LESIONS
- **Lupus Nephritis** — wide spectrum (hematuria → nephrotic → RPGN)
- **Henoch-Schönlein Purpura** — children 3–8yrs; purpura (extensor surfaces) + abdominal pain + arthralgia + hematuria; **mesangial IgA** (same spectrum as IgA nephropathy)
- **Diabetic Nephropathy** — leading cause of CKD; up to 40% of diabetics affected
- **Goodpasture / Microscopic Polyangiitis / GPA (Wegener)** — necrotizing + crescentic GN, often pauci-immune (ANCA)
- **Essential Mixed Cryoglobulinemia** — IgG-IgM complexes; associated with **Hepatitis C**; → MPGN pattern

---

## 3. TUBULAR AND INTERSTITIAL DISEASES

### A. Acute Tubular Injury (ATI) — *most common cause of AKI (~50% hospitalized)*
- **Causes:** Ischemic (shock, hypovolemia) vs **Nephrotoxic** (aminoglycosides, contrast, heavy metals)
- **Pathogenesis:** loss of cell polarity → ↑Na delivery distally → tubuloglomerular feedback vasoconstriction → cell detachment → luminal obstruction → backleak of filtrate
- **Morphology:** patchy necrosis with skip areas; straight proximal tubule + thick ascending limb most vulnerable; **tubulorrhexis**
- **3 Clinical Phases:** Initiation (~36h, ↓UOP) → Maintenance (oliguria, hyperkalemia, acidosis) → Recovery (polyuria, hypokalemia, infection risk)
- Prognosis: ~95% recover with supportive care (toxic); sepsis/multiorgan failure → >50% mortality

### B. Tubulointerstitial Nephritis (TIN)

- **Distinguishing feature vs glomerular disease:** NO nephritic/nephrotic syndrome; tubular dysfunction instead (polyuria, salt wasting, acidosis)

**Pyelonephritis** (most common cause of TIN):
| | Acute Pyelonephritis | Chronic Pyelonephritis |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | Ascending infection (E. coli most common) ± hematogenous | Recurrent infection + VUR or obstruction |
| Morphology | Patchy suppuration, neutrophils in tubules, **glomeruli spared early** | **Coarse, asymmetric corticomedullary scars** over blunted calyces; "thyroidization" of tubules |
| Complications | Papillary necrosis (diabetics, sickle cell, obstruction), pyonephrosis, perinephric abscess | Xanthogranulomatous variant (Proteus, foamy macrophages — mimics RCC); secondary FSGS → proteinuria (poor prognosis) |
| Clinical | Costovertebral pain, fever, dysuria, **WBC casts** | Often silent until HTN/renal insufficiency found |

**Drug/Toxin-Induced TIN:**
- **Acute drug-induced interstitial nephritis** — hypersensitivity (Type I/IV); methicillin classic cause; fever + eosinophilia + rash + ↑creatinine; interstitial edema + eosinophils + lymphocytes; reversible on drug withdrawal
- **NSAID nephropathy** — AKI (↓prostaglandin → ischemia), acute interstitial nephritis, MCD + nephrotic syndrome, membranous nephropathy
- Other: Analgesic nephropathy (phenacetin, historical), Urate nephropathy, Light-chain cast nephropathy ("myeloma kidney")

---

## 4. RENAL VASCULAR DISEASES

| Disease | Key Points |
|---|---|
| **Nephrosclerosis** | Associated with HTN/aging/diabetes; hyaline arteriolosclerosis + fibroelastic hyperplasia → ischemic glomerulosclerosis; grossly "granular, leather-like" cortex; ↑risk in Black patients, severe HTN, diabetics; **malignant nephrosclerosis** = with malignant HTN (BP >200/120, retinal hemorrhage, papilledema) |
| **Renal Artery Stenosis** | 2–5% of HTN, surgically curable; **70% atheroma** (older men) vs **fibromuscular dysplasia** (younger women); ↑renin → angiotensin II → HTN |
| **Thrombotic Microangiopathies (TMA)** | **Typical HUS** = Shiga toxin (E. coli O157:H7); **Atypical HUS** = complement dysregulation; **TTP** = ADAMTS13 deficiency → large vWF multimers. 2 triggers: endothelial injury (HUS) vs platelet activation (TTP) |

---

## 5. URINARY TRACT OBSTRUCTION & UROLITHIASIS

### Obstructive Uropathy
- Causes: congenital anomalies, calculi, BPH, tumors, inflammation, pregnancy, neurogenic
- **Hydronephrosis** = pelvicalyceal dilation + progressive renal atrophy; initial defect = tubular (↓concentrating ability) → later ↓GFR
- Post-relief of complete obstruction → **post-obstructive diuresis**

### Urolithiasis (Renal Stones)
- 5–10% lifetime prevalence; men > women; peak 20–30yrs
- **4 types:** Calcium oxalate/phosphate (~70%) > Struvite/Mg-ammonium-phosphate (15%, infection stones) > Uric acid (5–10%) > Cystine (1–2%)
- Key mechanism: **supersaturation** of urine + deficiency of stone inhibitors (citrate, pyrophosphate, nephrocalcin)

---

## 6. NEOPLASMS OF THE KIDNEY

**Benign:** Papillary adenoma; **Angiomyolipoma** (associated with **tuberous sclerosis**, TSC1/TSC2); **Oncocytoma** (eosinophilic cells from collecting duct intercalated cells)

**Malignant — Renal Cell Carcinoma (85% of adult renal cancers):**
- Risk factors: **smoking** (most significant), obesity, HTN, ESRD/acquired cystic disease, tuberous sclerosis
- Hereditary syndromes (4%): **Von Hippel-Lindau**, hereditary leiomyomatosis, hereditary papillary carcinoma, Birt-Hogg-Dubé
- **Subtypes:** Clear cell (70–80%) > Papillary (10–15%) > Chromophobe (5%) > Xp11 translocation > Collecting duct/Bellini (1%)

**Urothelial Carcinoma of Renal Pelvis:** 5–10% of primary renal tumors; poor prognosis

---

## 7. DISORDERS OF THE LOWER URINARY TRACT

### URETERS
- **UPJ obstruction** — most common cause of hydronephrosis in infants/children
- **Obstruction causes:** Intrinsic (calculi, strictures, tumors, clots) vs Extrinsic (pregnancy, periureteral inflammation, endometriosis, tumors)
- **Sclerosing Retroperitoneal Fibrosis (Ormond disease)** — idiopathic or **IgG4-related disease**; encases ureters → hydronephrosis; treat with steroids ± stents

### URINARY BLADDER
- **Congenital:** Vesicoureteral reflux (most important — predisposes to pyelonephritis); diverticula; **exstrophy** (↑adenocarcinoma risk); **urachal anomalies** (urachal cysts → 20–40% of bladder adenocarcinomas despite being rare overall)

**Cystitis:**
- Most common organism: **E. coli**; women > men (short urethra)
- **Schistosoma haematobium** → squamous metaplasia → **squamous cell carcinoma** (endemic regions)
- Special forms: **Interstitial cystitis** (chronic pelvic pain, Hunner ulcers, mast cells); **Malakoplakia** (defective phagocytosis, **Michaelis-Gutmann bodies**); Polypoid cystitis (catheter-related, mimics carcinoma)
- **Metaplastic lesions:** Cystitis glandularis/cystica (von Brunn nests) — intestinal metaplasia → adenocarcinoma risk; Squamous metaplasia → SCC risk (esp. schistosomiasis); **Nephrogenic adenoma** (implanted renal tubular cells, mimics cancer)

**Bladder Neoplasms** (~90% urothelial):
- Two precursor pathways: **Papillary tumors** (FGFR3, RAS, PI3K mutations; recur but only ~20% progress to muscle-invasive) vs **Flat CIS** (p53/RB mutations; 50–75% progress if untreated)
- **Key prognostic factor:** invasion of **muscularis propria (detrusor)** — 30% 5-yr mortality once invaded
- Risk factors: smoking (3–7× risk), aryl amines (2-naphthylamine), Schistosoma (→ SCC), cyclophosphamide, analgesics
- Clinical: **painless hematuria** (most common symptom)
- Other types: Squamous cell carcinoma (schistosomiasis), Adenocarcinoma (urachal/intestinal metaplasia), Small-cell carcinoma (TP53/RB mutations), Leiomyoma (most common benign mesenchymal), Rhabdomyosarcoma (children, "sarcoma botryoides"), Leiomyosarcoma (adults)

**Bladder Outlet Obstruction:** Males → BPH (most common); Females → cystocele; morphology = trabeculation → diverticula → massive dilation

### URETHRA
- **Urethritis:** Gonococcal vs Nongonococcal (Chlamydia, Mycoplasma); reactive arthritis (Reiter) triad = arthritis + conjunctivitis + urethritis
- **Urethral caruncle** — small painful mass at meatus, older females
- Proximal urethral cancer → urothelial type; Distal → squamous (HPV-related)

---

## 8. MALE REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM

### PENIS
- **Hypospadias** (ventral urethral opening, more common) vs **Epispadias** (dorsal)
- **Balanitis/Balanoposthitis** — poor hygiene, smegma irritant; **Phimosis** — prepuce can't retract
- **Squamous Cell Carcinoma** — HPV 16/18, smegma, smoking; **Bowen disease** = SCC in situ (→invasive in ~10%); **Verrucous carcinoma** = locally invasive, doesn't metastasize

### TESTIS
- **Cryptorchidism** — undescended testis; 3–5× ↑ testicular cancer risk (via intratubular germ cell neoplasia); orchiopexy reduces risk
- **Torsion** — venous obstruction first (arteries patent longer); Neonatal (no anatomic defect) vs Adult ("**bell-clapper**" deformity); surgical emergency, viable if untwisted within ~6h

**Testicular Germ Cell Tumors** (95% of postpubertal testis tumors; all malignant; isochromosome **i(12p)** in virtually all):
| Tumor | Peak Age | Marker |
|---|---|---|
| Seminoma | 40–50 | ~10% ↑hCG |
| Embryonal carcinoma | 20–30 | Negative (pure) |
| Yolk sac tumor | 3 (children) | 90% ↑**AFP** |
| Choriocarcinoma | 20–30 | 100% ↑**hCG** |
| Teratoma | All ages | Negative (pure) |
| Mixed tumor | 15–30 | ↑hCG + AFP |
- Seminoma → lymphatic spread (iliac/para-aortic nodes) late hematogenous; Nonseminomatous → early lymphatic + hematogenous (liver, lung)

### PROSTATE
- **Prostatitis:** Acute bacterial (2–5%), Chronic bacterial (2–5%), Chronic pelvic pain/nonbacterial (**90–95%**, most common), Asymptomatic inflammatory
- **BPH:** Androgen-dependent (DHT via **5α-reductase type 2**); inner **transitional zone**; nodules compress urethra; symptoms: hesitancy, weak stream, urgency/frequency/nocturia; Tx = finasteride (5α-reductase inhibitor) or alpha-blockers (tamsulosin)
- **Prostate Carcinoma:** Most common male cancer; outer **peripheral zone**; **TMPRSS2-ETS fusion**, PI3K/AKT mutations; graded by **Gleason system**; bone metastases typically **osteoblastic**; screened by **PSA** (imperfect — false +/−)
