articles.title: High-Yield Clinical Exam Notes: Cranial Nerves, Respiratory, Cardio — Past Paper
articles.content:
MBIM 3100 — Clinical Techniques: Past Paper Notes
**Source:** MKU past papers (CATs + Main Exams, 2016–2022)
**Compiled topics:** Cranial nerves, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Abdominal, CNS/Cerebellar, Neurology
---
## CRANIAL NERVES — HIGH-YIELD FACTS| Nerve | Key Function | Clinical Clue |
|---|---|---|
| CN V — Trigeminal | Sensation: forehead, cheeks, lower jaw; Motor: mastication | Most-tested CN in these papers |
| CN VII — Facial | Motor: face muscles; Sensory: anterior 2/3 tongue (taste) | UMN vs LMN palsy distinction |
| CN IX — Glossopharyngeal | Taste + sensation: posterior 1/3 tongue | "Cannot taste posterior tongue" |
| CN III — Oculomotor | Most eye movements, pupil constriction, levator palpebrae | Ptosis + poor light reflex = CN III |
| CN VI — Abducens | Lateral rectus (SO4 LR6) | Lateral rectus weakness = CN VI |
| CN IV — Trochlear | Superior oblique | NOT lateral rectus |
| CN XII — Hypoglossal | Tongue movement (motor only) | Not taste |
**Meninges (superficial → deep):** Dura mater → Arachnoid → Pia mater. Dura is most superficial.
**Pupillary reflexes:**
- Direct reflex = pupil constricts when light shone into it
- Consensual = contralateral pupil constricts
- Accommodation = pupils constrict + converge bilaterally
- Snellen chart = visual acuity, NOT color blindness

**UMN vs LMN Facial Palsy:**

| Feature | UMN | LMN |
|---|---|---|
| Forehead sparing | Yes (bilateral cortical supply) | No — whole face affected |
| Causes | Stroke, brain tumor | Bell's palsy, parotid tumor, infection |
| Tone | Spastic | Flaccid |
---
## RESPIRATORY EXAMINATION — HIGH-YIELD FACTS**Breath sounds:**
- Vesicular = normal; soft, low-pitched, over most of both lungs
- Bronchial = loud, harsh, pause between I and E; over consolidation
- Egophony = over consolidation / above pleural effusion level

**Percussion notes and their conditions:**

| Note | Condition |
|---|---|
| Tympany | Pneumothorax |
| Hyperresonance | COPD, emphysema, pneumothorax |
| Dullness | Consolidation, lobar collapse |
| Stony dullness | Pleural effusion |
| Resonance | Normal air-filled lungs |
**Adventitious sounds:**
- Stridor = partial obstruction of larynx/trachea — requires urgent attention
- Monophonic wheeze = focal bronchiole obstruction
- Rhonchi = widespread airway narrowing (asthma)
- Pleural friction rub = rubbing/grating; like two pieces of leather; pleuritis
- Crepitations/crackles = fluid in alveoli

**Stethoscope:** Diaphragm = high-pitched sounds. Bell = low-pitched (heart murmurs, etc.)

**Consolidation vs Pleural Effusion:**
| Feature | Consolidation | Pleural Effusion |
|---|---|---|
| Vocal resonance | Increased | Reduced/absent |
| Tactile fremitus | Increased | Reduced |
| Percussion | Dull | Stony dull |
| Breath sounds | Bronchial | Reduced/absent |
**Pneumothorax findings:** Decreased breath sounds, hyperresonance, decreased tactile fremitus, tracheal deviation away from affected side.
**Respiratory causes of finger clubbing:** Lung cancer (including mesothelioma), pulmonary fibrosis, suppurative lung disease (bronchiectasis, abscess), cystic fibrosis.
**Bilateral reduced chest expansion causes:** Bilateral pleural effusions, end-stage IPF, COPD, bilateral pneumothorax.
**Common causes of wheeze:** Asthma, COPD, cardiac failure, foreign body, tumour.
**Kyphosis** = exaggerated posterior thoracic curvature (hunchback).
**Lordosis** = exaggerated lumbar curvature (swayback).
**Scoliosis** = lateral spinal curvature.
**Cheyne-Stokes** = slow→rapid→slow→apnea cycle; caused by heart failure, opioid OD, renal failure, meningitis.
---
## CARDIOVASCULAR EXAMINATION — HIGH-YIELD FACTS**Heart sounds:**
- S1 = closure of AV valves = start of systole; heard best at apex
- S2 = closure of semilunar valves = end of systole
- Lubb (S1) = AV closure; Dubb (S2) = semilunar closure

**Apex beat:** Normal = 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line. Displaced laterally = cardiomegaly.

**JVP (Jugular Venous Pulse) vs Carotid:**
- Arterial = wagging ear lobe, no variation with posture, not pulsatile hepatojugular reflux
- JVP = fills from above, varies with posture, positive hepatojugular reflux
- Patient lies at 45°; neck muscles relaxed; good lighting; timing with radial pulse NOT necessary

**Hepatojugular reflux** — elevated in: constrictive pericarditis, right heart failure, restrictive cardiomyopathy. Associated with LEFT ventricular failure = FALSE.

**High output heart failure causes:** Anaemia, sepsis, hyperthyroidism, thiamine deficiency (beriberi), Paget's disease, systemic AV fistula. Iron overload is NOT a classic cause.
**Narrow pulse pressure:** Aortic stenosis, cardiac tamponade.
**Wide pulse pressure:** Aortic regurgitation (collapsing pulse, dancing carotid).
**Left parasternal heave** = right ventricular hypertrophy.
**Virchow's node** = left supraclavicular lymph node; associated with GIT malignancies (especially gastric).
**Spider naevi:** Can be normal in pregnancy; >5 suggest chronic liver disease.
**Bruit** = swishing sound over artery; abnormal narrowing (atherosclerosis).
**Thrill** = vibrating sensation on palpation of artery; abnormal finding.
**Capillary refill:** Normal = less than 2 seconds.
**Claudication** = cramp-like lower limb pain on walking; due to arterial insufficiency.
**Ischemia** = decreased oxygenated blood supply due to arterial narrowing.
---
## ABDOMINAL EXAMINATION — HIGH-YIELD FACTS**Order of examination of abdomen:** Inspection → Auscultation → Percussion → Palpation (unique because auscultation before palpation prevents stimulating bowel sounds).
**Abdominal signs:**
- Rovsing's sign = palpate LLQ → pain in RLQ = appendicitis
- Psoas sign = hip extension pain = retrocecal appendix / iliopsoas irritation
- Obturator sign = hip flexion/rotation pain = appendix in contact with obturator internus
- Murphy's sign = catch of breath on deep palpation RUQ = cholecystitis (inflamed gallbladder)
- Cullen's sign = periumbilical bruising = haemorrhagic pancreatitis
- Grey Turner's sign = flank bruising = retroperitoneal haemorrhage

**5 F's of abdominal distension:** Fat, Faeces, Foetus, Flatus, Fluid (ascites).

**Ascites elicitation:**
- Inspection: bulging flanks, distended abdomen
- Percussion: flank dullness → shifting dullness (roll patient to side, dullness shifts)
- Fluid thrill: flick one flank, feel impulse on other; assistant's hand midline to block fat transmission

**Jaundice:** Best assessed at the sclera. Itching = obstructive jaundice.

**Koplik spots** = on mucous membrane of mouth = measles.
**Caput medusae** = dilated abdominal veins around umbilicus = portal hypertension / liver cirrhosis.
**Groin mass causes:** Inguinal hernia, femoral hernia, femoral aneurysm, enlarged lymph node.
**Spleen vs Kidney on examination:**
| Feature | Spleen | Kidney |
|---|---|---|
| Enlargement direction | Diagonally toward RLQ | Inferiorly, ipsilateral pelvis |
| Notch | Present | Absent |
| Percussion | Dull | Tympanic (overlying gas) |
| Moves with respiration | Yes | No |
| Ballotable | No | Yes |
**Charcot's triad** = jaundice + fever (with rigors) + RUQ pain = ascending cholangitis.
**Signs of chronic liver disease (general examination):**
- Palmar erythema, spider naevi, leukonychia, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy
- Dupuytren's contracture, finger clubbing, caput medusae, jaundice, bruising, parotid enlargement, hair loss, peripheral oedema (hypoalbuminaemia)

**Murphy's sign** (definition): Catch of breath/pain elicited by pressing RUQ while asking patient to take a deep breath. Positive = sign of inflamed gallbladder.

---
## CNS / CEREBELLAR EXAMINATION — HIGH-YIELD FACTS**Cerebellar dysfunction signs (DANISH mnemonic):**
- Dysdiadochokinesia (inability to perform rapid alternating hand movements)
- Ataxia (limb, truncal)
- Nystagmus
- Intention tremor
- Slurred/staccato speech (dysarthria)
- Heel-shin test positive
- Tandem gait abnormal

**Festinant gait** = Parkinson's disease, NOT cerebellar.

**Cerebellar tests:**
- Tandem gait = tests gait/cerebellar function
- Finger-nose test = upper limb coordination
- Dysdiadochokinesia = rapid alternating movements
- Heel-shin test = lower limb coordination
- Romberg's test = proprioception/vestibular, NOT cerebellar

**Romberg's sign:** Patient stands feet together, arms at sides, closes eyes. Positive = falls without correction = proprioception or vestibular dysfunction. Swaying with correction = cerebellar (truncal ataxia).

**Cerebellar region receiving proprioceptive input from spinal cord:** Vermis.
**Cerebellum does NOT process:** Visual information.
**Causes of cerebellar degeneration:** Chronic alcohol abuse, paraneoplastic disorders, nutritional deficiency, inherited gene mutations.
**UMN vs LMN Lesion:**
| Feature | UMN | LMN |
|---|---|---|
| Tone | Spastic/rigid, clonus | Hypotonic, no clonus |
| Reflexes | Hyperreflexia | Hyporeflexia/absent |
| Plantar | Extensor (Babinski +ve) | Flexor |
| Wasting | Disuse (long-standing) | Prominent, early |
| Fasciculations | Absent | Present (especially tongue) |
| Weakness pattern | Extensors in arms, flexors in legs | Distribution of nerve/root |
**Muscle power grading (MRC scale):**
| Grade | Description |
|---|---|
| 0 | No contraction |
| 1 | Flicker/trace |
| 2 | Movement with gravity eliminated |
| 3 | Movement against gravity |
| 4 | Movement against gravity + resistance |
| 5 | Normal power |
**Reflex grading:** 0 = absent, 1 = diminished, 2 = normal, 3 = hyperactive (no clonus), 4 = hyperactive with clonus.
**GCS scoring components:** Eyes (1–4) + Verbal (1–5) + Motor (1–6). Patient in vignette: eyes open to pain (2) + groaning/sounds (2) + abnormal flexion (3) = **GCS 7**.
**GCS classification:** Mild = 13–15; Moderate = 9–12; Severe = 3–8.
**Allodynia** = pain from normally non-painful stimulus (e.g., light touch).
**Dysaesthesia** = unpleasant sensation from ordinary stimuli; due to sensory pathway lesions.
**Cremasteric reflex:** Stroking inner thigh → ipsilateral testicular retraction. Absence = acute scrotum (e.g., torsion).
---
## GENERAL EXAMINATION — HIGH-YIELD QUICK FACTS- **Best site for jaundice:** Sclera
- **Best site for anaemia:** Conjunctiva/mucous membranes
- **BMI formula:** Weight (kg) ÷ Height² (m²)

 - Underweight <18.5 / Normal 18.5–24.9 / Overweight 25–29.9 / Obese ≥30

- **Capillary refill:** Press nail for 5 seconds; refill <2 seconds = normal
- **Cyanosis:** Central = tongue/mucous membranes; Peripheral = fingertips
- **Edema assessment:** Press for 5 seconds 5cm above medial malleolus; pitting = fluid
- **PERRLA** = Pupils Equal, Round, Reactive to Light and Accommodation
- **Glasgow Coma Scale** = standardized objective measurement of consciousness level
- **Proprioception exam** = body position sense, cerebellar and dorsal column function
- **Posture** = indicative of acute/chronic respiratory distress
- **Preferred position for rectal exam** = left lateral position with knees flexed

---

ESSAY SECTION — QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS
---
**Q1. List 5 signs of chronic liver disease observable on general examination.**
- Palmar erythema
- Spider naevi (>5 are significant)
- Leukonychia (white nails)
- Gynaecomastia
- Testicular atrophy
- Dupuytren's contracture
- Jaundice (scleral icterus)
- Finger clubbing
- Caput medusae (dilated periumbilical veins)
- Bruising / excoriations
- Peripheral oedema (from hypoalbuminaemia)
- Hair loss

*(Give any 5 for full marks)*

---
**Q2. Describe how to assess a patient's hydration status clinically.**
- Skin turgor — pinch skin; slow return = dehydration
- Mucous membranes — dry mouth/tongue
- Intraocular tension — reduced in dehydration
- Blood pressure — postural hypotension in dehydration
- Jugular venous pressure — reduced in hypovolaemia
- Pulse — tachycardia in dehydration
- Urine output — oliguria
- Haemoconcentration on bloods (raised haematocrit, raised urea)

---

**Q3. How is BMI calculated and classified?**
- BMI = Weight (kg) ÷ Height² (m²)
- Underweight: < 18.5
- Normal: 18.5–24.9
- Overweight: 25.0–29.9
- Obese Class I: 30–34.9
- Obese Class II: 35–39.9
- Obese Class III: ≥ 40

---

**Q4. How do you differentiate UMN from LMN facial nerve palsy?**
| Feature | UMN | LMN |
|---|---|---|
| Forehead | Spared (bilateral cortical representation) | Involved (whole face) |
| Weakness | Lower face only | Upper + lower face |
| Causes | Stroke, brain tumour, subdural haematoma | Bell's palsy, parotid tumour, infection |
---
**Q5a. GCS score for: abnormal flexor response + groaning + eyes open to pain**
- Eyes open to pain = 2
- Verbal = groaning/incomprehensible sounds = 2
- Motor = abnormal flexion = 3
- **Total GCS = 7**

**Q5b. Classify head injury by GCS:**

- Mild: 13–15
- Moderate: 9–12
- Severe: 3–8

---

**Q6. List 3 respiratory causes of finger clubbing.**
- Lung cancer (including mesothelioma)
- Pulmonary fibrosis
- Suppurative lung disease (bronchiectasis, lung abscess)
- Cystic fibrosis *(give any 3)*

---

**Q7. How do you differentiate consolidation from pleural effusion clinically?**
| Feature | Consolidation | Pleural Effusion |
|---|---|---|
| Vocal resonance | Increased | Reduced/absent |
| Breath sounds | Bronchial | Reduced/absent |
| Percussion | Dull | Stony dull |
| Tactile fremitus | Increased | Reduced |
---
**Q8. List 2 causes of dullness to percussion on respiratory examination.**
- Consolidation (pneumonia)
- Pleural effusion
- Lobar collapse *(any 2)*

---

**Q9. List 2 common causes of wheezing.**
- Asthma
- COPD
- Cardiac failure (cardiac asthma)
- Foreign body *(any 2)*

---

**Q10. List 10 symptoms/signs of renal failure. Describe features pointing to cardiac rather than renal disease.**
**Renal failure symptoms/signs:**
- Decreased urine output
- Fluid retention → ankle/leg swelling
- Shortness of breath
- Fatigue
- Chest pain
- Confusion
- Nausea
- Weakness
- Bloody urine (haematuria)
- Frothy urine (proteinuria)
- High blood pressure
- Dry, itchy skin
- Seizures/coma (severe)

**Features favouring cardiac over renal:**

- Finger clubbing
- Palpitations
- Dizziness and syncope
- Angina
- Splinter haemorrhages
- Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea
- Easy fatigability
- Displaced apex beat

---

**Q11. Outline history and examination for a patient with 5-month abdominal distension. Describe how to elicit ascites.**
**History:**
- Onset, duration, progression
- Associated symptoms: SOB (diaphragmatic impingement), abdominal heaviness, pain
- Alcohol and smoking history
- Drug history
- Past medical: cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, malignancy
- Sexual history; IV drug use
- Family history: Wilson's disease, haemochromatosis
- Socioeconomic history; living in hepatitis-endemic area
- Systemic review

**Examination:**

- General: jaundice, spider naevi, leukonychia, palmar erythema, clubbing
- Vitals
- Abdominal inspection: distension, caput medusae, visible veins, scars
- Auscultation → Percussion → Palpation (standard order)

**How to elicit ascites:**

- Inspection: bulging flanks, distended abdomen
- Percussion: percuss from umbilicus outward to flanks; note transition from tympanic to dull
- Shifting dullness: keep finger at dull zone; ask patient to roll to side; wait; re-percuss — dullness shifts if ascites present
- Fluid thrill: place assistant's hand on midline abdomen; flick one flank; feel impulse on opposite side — confirms large ascites

---

**Q12. Describe CNS examination to exclude cerebellar and vermian lesions.**
**For cerebellar lesions:**
- Gait: tandem gait (heel-toe walking); ataxic broad-based gait
- Romberg's test: to exclude proprioceptive/vestibular cause (cerebellar = sways with correction)
- Dysdiadochokinesia: rapid alternating hand movements
- Finger-nose test: intention tremor, past-pointing
- Heel-shin test: lower limb coordination
- Eye movements: nystagmus (horizontal = cerebellar)
- Speech: dysarthria (ataxic/staccato)

**Vermian lesions specifically cause:**

- Truncal ataxia
- Gait ataxia (tandem gait abnormal)
- Vermis receives proprioceptive input from spinal cord

---

**Q13. List cranial nerves 6–12. Describe CN VII palsy; differentiate UMN and LMN; give 2 causes each.**
**Cranial nerves 6–12:**
- CN VI — Abducens (lateral rectus)
- CN VII — Facial
- CN VIII — Vestibulocochlear
- CN IX — Glossopharyngeal
- CN X — Vagus
- CN XI — Accessory
- CN XII — Hypoglossal

**CN VII palsy presentation:**

- Motor: facial muscle weakness
- Sensory: loss of taste anterior 2/3 tongue

**UMN facial palsy:**

- Lower face weakness only (forehead spared)
- Causes: stroke, brain tumour

**LMN facial palsy:**

- Whole face involved (including forehead)
- Causes: Bell's palsy, parotid tumour, infection (e.g., HSV)

---

**Q14. Describe clinical examination findings in right-sided pleural effusion.**
- Tracheal deviation away from affected side (if large)
- Reduced chest expansion on right
- Stony dullness to percussion on right
- Reduced/absent breath sounds on right
- Reduced/absent vocal resonance on right
- Reduced/absent tactile fremitus on right
- Egophony above the effusion level
- Reduced vocal fremitus

---

**Q15. Describe clinical examination findings of aortic regurgitation.**
- Collapsing (waterhammer) pulse
- Wide pulse pressure
- Dancing carotids (Corrigan's sign)
- Displaced apex beat (volume overload → LV dilation)
- Early diastolic murmur (best heard at left sternal edge, sitting forward, expiration)
- De Musset's sign (head nodding)
- Quincke's sign (nail pulsations)

---

**Q16. Describe clinical examination findings in ascites.**
- Distended, symmetrically distended abdomen
- Bulging flanks on inspection
- Shifting dullness on percussion
- Fluid thrill (large ascites)
- Eversion of umbilicus
- Associated signs of underlying cause: jaundice, spider naevi (liver), peripheral oedema

---

**Q17. Describe history and examination for a patient presenting with heart failure. (56-year-old lady)**
**History:**
- Symptoms: SOB (exertional, orthopnoea, PND), ankle swelling, fatigue, palpitations, chest pain, syncope, dizziness
- Past medical: hypertension, IHD, valve disease, diabetes
- Drug history (cardiotoxic drugs e.g. anthracyclines)
- Alcohol/smoking history
- Family history of cardiac disease
- Social history

**Examination findings supporting heart failure:**

- General: raised JVP, peripheral oedema, tachycardia, tachypnoea
- Hands: cold peripheries, cyanosis, clubbing (if chronic)
- Pulse: may be irregular (AF), tachycardia
- BP: may be elevated or low
- Apex beat: displaced laterally
- Auscultation: S3 gallop, murmurs (valve disease), bilateral basal crepitations
- Abdomen: hepatomegaly (right heart failure), ascites

---

**Q18. A 34-year-old presents with headache, neck stiffness and confusion. Describe relevant history and examination to arrive at a diagnosis (meningitis).**
**History:**
- Fever, headache (onset, severity, character)
- Photophobia, phonophobia
- Neck stiffness
- Rash (non-blanching = meningococcaemia)
- Confusion, seizures
- Recent URTI, ear infection, sinusitis
- Immunocompromised status, HIV history
- Travel history, contacts

**Examination:**

- Vitals: fever, tachycardia, hypotension (septic)
- Neck stiffness: passive flexion of neck resisted
- Kernig's sign: flex hip 90°, attempt knee extension → pain/resistance = positive
- Brudzinski's sign: flex neck → involuntary hip + knee flexion = positive
- Fundoscopy: papilloedema (raised ICP — do before LP)
- Rash: petechiae / purpura (non-blanching) = meningococcal
- GCS assessment
- Cranial nerve examination

---
## MISSING MCQ TOPICS — HIGH-YIELD ADDITIONS---
**OCULAR EXAMINATION**
- Ptosis causes: congenital, acquired, myasthenia gravis, Horner's syndrome, CN III palsy, apical lung tumour (Pancoast)
- Ptosis IS associated with myasthenia gravis — the exam statement saying it's not is **false**
- CN III lesion → ptosis + poor direct AND consensual light reflex + poor accommodation + diplopia
- Lateral rectus weakness → CN VI (Abducens)
- Superior oblique → CN IV (Trochlear): SO4 LR6
- Nystagmus = repeated involuntary eye movement; can be idiopathic or cerebellar

---

**ORAL/MOUTH EXAMINATION**
| Finding | Association |
|---|---|
| Angular stomatitis | Iron/B2 deficiency, NOT liver disease |
| Oral candidiasis | HIV, immunosuppression, steroids (not exclusive to HIV) |
| Aphthous ulcers | Trauma, vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency |
| Koplik spots | Measles (on buccal mucosa) |
| Smooth tongue | Iron deficiency anaemia |
| Bleeding gums | Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) |
| Pharyngitis | Inflammation of the pharynx (throat), NOT tongue |
---
**BLOOD PRESSURE**
- Narrow pulse pressure = aortic stenosis, cardiac tamponade
- Wide pulse pressure = aortic regurgitation
- Malignant hypertension: BP > 200mmHg systolic / >120mmHg diastolic
- Pallor checked via capillary refill, conjunctiva, palmar creases

---

**APEX BEAT**
- Normal position: 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
- Displaced laterally + inferiorly = dilated cardiomyopathy, volume overload
- Displaced to right = dextrocardia
- Tapping apex beat = mitral stenosis
- Heaving apex beat = pressure overload (hypertension, aortic stenosis)

---

**ABDOMINAL EXAMINATION — EXTRA**
- Preferred order: **Inspection → Auscultation → Percussion → Palpation**
- Visible peristalsis = intestinal obstruction (NOT peritonitis)
- Symmetrically distended abdomen = fluid, fat, flatus, foetus, faeces
- Cullens sign = periumbilical bruising = haemorrhagic pancreatitis / ectopic pregnancy
- Right hypochondrium enlarged organ = liver (NOT spleen — spleen is left)
- Caput medusae = cirrhosis/portal hypertension

---

**FEMALE REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM**
- Vagina = approximately **8–9 cm** long (the exam question says 5cm — that is **false**, making it the correct answer)
- Vulva = labia majora + labia minora + clitoris + vestibule
- Uterus = muscular, pear-shaped, midline structure — **true**
- Abnormal vaginal bleeding: in longstanding cases → bounding pulse (hyperdynamic circulation from anaemia); associated with iron deficiency anaemia; oligomenorrhoea IS a feature of PCOS

---

**MENTAL STATE EXAMINATION**
Components:
- Appearance and behaviour
- Speech and language
- Mood and affect
- Thought content
- Perception
- Cognition: recent AND distant memory, orientation
- Insight

**Walking/abnormal gait is NOT part of mental state exam** — that is a neurological examination finding. This was the false statement tested.

---
**DRUG HISTORY — IMPORTANCE**
- Determine drugs the patient is already taking
- Identify drug allergies
- Assess drug interactions
- Check compliance
- Identify drugs causing the current illness (e.g., drug-induced hepatitis)
- Know which drugs to avoid in the context of the illness

---

**GYNAECOLOGICAL HISTORY in a patient with PV bleeding**
- LMP, cycle regularity, duration of bleeding
- Amount (number of pads)
- Associated pain, discharge, odour
- Sexual history, contraception use
- Obstetric history (G/P)
- Smear history
- Menopausal status
- Drug history (anticoagulants, OCPs)
- Family history of gynaecological malignancy

---

**GENERAL EXAMINATION — VITAL SIGNS**
Include: Temperature, BP, Oxygen saturation, Respiratory rate, Pulse rate, Weight/BMI. Any shift from normal in any parameter may indicate underlying disease.
**General examination positives to note before systemic review:**
- Pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, clubbing, oedema, lymphadenopathy, dehydration signs, nutritional status, level of consciousness, any obvious distress

---

# MBIM 3100 — Clinical Techniques: Gap-Fill Additions
**Mount Kenya University — School of Medicine, Department of Internal Medicine**
| | |
|---|---|
| **Unit Code** | MBIM 3100 |
| **Unit Title** | Clinical Techniques |
| **Source Exam** | University Examination 2021/2022, Main Exam, Section B |
| **Date** | Friday 28th, 8:00 AM |
| **Duration** | 2 Hours |
This addition covers the remaining Section B items from the 2021/2022 main exam: COPD-related cardiac signs, chest expansion technique, combined causes of reduced expansion, and the abdominal distension case question.
---
## Q1a. Signs of Chronic Cardiac Disease Due to COPD (5 marks)
*List 5 signs of chronic cardiac disease due to COPD observable during general examination.*
These are features of **cor pulmonale** — right heart strain from chronic pulmonary hypertension.
- Raised jugular venous pressure (JVP)
- Peripheral oedema (ankle/sacral)
- Parasternal heave (right ventricular hypertrophy)
- Loud or palpable P2 (pulmonary hypertension)
- Central cyanosis
- Pulsatile, congested hepatomegaly
- Tricuspid regurgitation murmur (pansystolic, left sternal edge)
*(Any 5 for full marks)*
---
## Q1b. Assessing Symmetrical Chest Expansion (2 marks)
*Briefly describe how to assess clinically for symmetrical chest expansion.*
- Stand behind (posterior) or in front (anterior) of the patient
- Place both hands flat on the chest wall, thumbs meeting in the midline, fingers spread laterally — do not grip the ribcage
- Ask the patient to take a deep breath in
- Compare how far each thumb moves from the midline
- **Normal:** both thumbs move apart equally
- **Abnormal:** one side lags or fails to rise — thumbs separate unevenly, indicating reduced expansion on that side
---
## Q1c. Causes of Reduced Chest Expansion (3 marks)
*List 3 causes of unilateral and bilateral reduced chest wall expansion.*
**Unilateral**
- Pneumothorax
- Pleural effusion
- Lobar collapse / consolidation
**Bilateral**
- COPD / emphysema
- End-stage idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
- Bilateral pleural effusions
*(Any 3 total, from either list)*
---
## Q4. Case — 25-Year-Old with Abdominal Distension (10 marks)
*A 25-year-old presents to OPD with abdominal distension. Outline your history taking and physical examination towards an impression/diagnosis.*
**History**
- Onset, duration, progression
- Associated symptoms: pain, SOB, early satiety, weight change, vomiting, bowel habit change
- Menstrual/obstetric history (pregnancy as a cause in a young patient)
- Past medical history: liver disease, cardiac disease, malignancy, TB
- Drug, alcohol, sexual history
- Family history of liver or GI disease
**Examination**
- General: jaundice, pallor, lymphadenopathy, signs of chronic liver disease
- Vitals
- Abdominal inspection: symmetry, visible veins, scars, masses
- Auscultation → Percussion → Palpation
- Assess for ascites: shifting dullness, fluid thrill
- Check for organomegaly, masses, hernial orifices

articles.title: MBChB Clinical Exam: Cranial Nerves, Resp & Abdominal Skills — CAT
articles.content:
**MOUNT KENYA UNIVERSITY**
**MEDICAL SCHOOL — DEPARTMENT OF INTERNAL MEDICINE**
**BACHELOR OF MEDICINE AND BACHELOR OF SURGERY (MBChB)**
**UNIT CODE: MBIM 3100 | UNIT TITLE: CLINICAL TECHNIQUES**
**MAIN EXAMINATION — 2021/2022 | DATE: FRIDAY 28TH, 2022 | TIME: 2 HOURS**
---
**Compiled Past Papers — MBIM 3100: Clinical Techniques**
This compilation draws together Clinical Techniques exams and continuous assessment tests from Mount Kenya University's School of Medicine spanning the 2018/2019 through 2021/2022 academic years, including the 2021/2022 main exam, CAT I, CAT II, and a dedicated respiratory system assignment. Together they cover cranial nerve examination, respiratory and cardiovascular signs, abdominal and cerebellar/CNS assessment, and general examination findings — the full breadth of bedside clinical skills tested across Year 3.

**SECTION 1 — MAIN EXAM 2021/2022**
**Topic: General Examination, Cranial Nerves, Respiratory & Abdominal Examination**
*Choose the single best answer*
---
**1.** Which of the following statements is true regarding oral findings?
a) Angular stomatitis is associated with liver disease
b) Oral candidiasis is only seen in HIV/AIDS patients
c) Trauma, vitamin B12 deficiency and folate deficiency are associated with aphthous ulceration
d) All of the above
**ANSWER: C**
Trauma, vitamin B12 deficiency and folate deficiency are associated with aphthous ulceration
---
**2.** Which of the following is FALSE regarding essentials of a mental state exam?
a) Recent and distant memory
b) Walking/abnormal gait
c) Poor dressing, dirty person
d) Appropriate language and speech
**ANSWER: B**
Mental state examination assesses cognition, appearance, behaviour, speech, and memory — not gait. Gait is part of a neurological/physical exam.
---
**3.** Which cranial nerve conducts sensory touch from the forehead, cheeks and lower jaw AND motor signals to the muscles of mastication?
a) Facial nerve
b) Trigeminal
c) Hypoglossal
d) Abducens
**ANSWER: B**
CN V (Trigeminal) has three sensory divisions (ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular) covering the face, plus a motor branch to the muscles of mastication.
---
**4.** A middle-aged man cannot taste anything on the POSTERIOR portion of his tongue. Which nerve innervates this area?
a) Glossopharyngeal
b) Hypoglossal
c) Facial
d) Trigeminal
**ANSWER: A**
CN IX (Glossopharyngeal) carries taste from the posterior 1/3 of the tongue. CN VII (Facial) carries taste from the anterior 2/3.
---
**5.** A patient has diplopia, poor accommodation, absent direct and consensual light reflexes, and ptosis. Which statement is true?
a) Oculomotor supplies the superior levator palpebrae
b) Horner's syndrome should be considered
c) A cerebellar lesion is most likely
d) Trigeminal nerve supplies motor fibres to the frontalis
**ANSWER: A**
CN III (Oculomotor) supplies the superior levator palpebrae (raising the eyelid), the pupillary constrictor, and most extraocular muscles. Lesion causes ptosis, mydriasis, and loss of light reflexes.
---
**6.** Which of the following indicates a PARTIAL obstruction of a focal bronchiole/bronchus?
a) Diffuse rhonchi
b) Stridor
c) Pleural rub
d) Monophonic wheeze
**ANSWER: D**
A monophonic (single-pitched) wheeze indicates partial obstruction of a single airway. Stridor indicates laryngeal/tracheal obstruction. Diffuse rhonchi suggest widespread airway disease.
---
**7.** On drooping of the eyelid (ptosis), which statement is FALSE?
a) It can be congenital or acquired
b) It can be due to injury or stretching of the eye muscles
c) Has been associated with apical lung tumors
d) It is not associated with Myasthenia gravis
**ANSWER: D**
Ptosis IS associated with Myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular junction disorder). Apical lung tumors cause Horner's syndrome which also features ptosis.
---
**8.** The BEST place to check for jaundice is:
a) Conjunctiva
b) Sclera
c) Nail beds
d) Frenulum
**ANSWER: B**
The sclera is the best site — bilirubin deposits in the scleral elastin earliest and is most visible there, especially in dark-skinned individuals where conjunctival pallor may be easier to detect for anaemia.
---
**9.** The following percussion notes are matched to conditions — which is TRUE?
a) Resonance — pneumothorax
b) Stony dullness — pneumonia
c) Stony dullness — intestinal obstruction
d) Fluid thrill — gross ascites
**ANSWER: D**
Fluid thrill is elicited in gross ascites. Stony dullness = pleural effusion. Resonance = normal lung. Hyperresonance = pneumothorax. Dullness = consolidation.
---
**10.** Which of the following statements on abdominal examination is TRUE?
a) Symmetrically distended abdomen may be due to fluid
b) Visible peristalsis may be due to peritonitis
c) Cullens sign is associated with ectopic pregnancy
d) Visible right hypochondrial scar may be due to appendicectomy
**ANSWER: A**
Symmetrical distension can result from ascites, obesity, gas, or organomegaly. Cullen sign (periumbilical bruising) is associated with haemoperitoneum, including ruptured ectopic pregnancy and acute pancreatitis — so C is partially true, but A is the most straightforwardly correct statement.
---
**11.** Which of the following statements is TRUE?
a) Bleeding of gums is due to lack of vitamin B12
b) Koplik spots are found on mucous membrane of the mouth
c) Pharyngitis is inflammation of the tongue
d) Smooth tongue is usually due to angular stomatitis
**ANSWER: B**
Koplik spots are pathognomonic of measles and appear on the buccal mucosa. Gum bleeding relates to vitamin C deficiency or platelet disorders. Pharyngitis is inflammation of the pharynx (throat), not tongue.
---
**12.** All the following are associated with HIGH OUTPUT heart failure EXCEPT:
a) Iron overload
b) Hyperthyroidism
c) Systemic arteriovenous fistula
d) Paget disease
**ANSWER: A**
Iron overload (haemochromatosis) causes a restrictive/dilated cardiomyopathy — a LOW output failure. High output failure causes include hyperthyroidism, AV fistula, Paget disease, severe anaemia, beriberi, and pregnancy.
---
**13.** What is the preferred order for abdominal examination?
a) Inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation
b) Percussion, auscultation, palpation, inspection
c) Auscultation, inspection, palpation, percussion
d) Inspection, auscultation, palpation, percussion
**ANSWER: A**
Unlike other systems, auscultation comes BEFORE percussion and palpation in the abdomen — to avoid artificially altering bowel sounds by manual stimulation.
---
**14.** A 15-year-old with RLQ pain: palpating the LEFT lower quadrant causes pain in the RIGHT lower quadrant. What is this sign?
a) Psoas sign
b) Obturator sign
c) Rovsing's sign
d) Cutaneous hyperesthesia
**ANSWER: C**
Rovsing's sign — pressure on the LLQ transmits pain to the RLQ, suggesting peritoneal irritation around an inflamed appendix.
---
**15.** Which is TRUE regarding Virchow's node?
a) It is a right supraclavicular lymph node
b) Associated with lung malignancies
c) The right Virchow's node is associated with lung malignancies
d) GIT malignancies have been linked to it
**ANSWER: D**
Virchow's node is the LEFT supraclavicular lymph node. It signals metastasis from abdominal/GIT malignancies (gastric cancer most classically) via the thoracic duct.
---
**16.** A patient with SOB and productive cough — consolidation is present if you find:
a) Dullness to percussion over the affected base
b) Bronchial breath sounds throughout
c) Increased tactile fremitus throughout
d) Inspiratory and expiratory wheezes
**ANSWER: A**
Consolidation produces dullness to percussion, increased vocal resonance/fremitus, and bronchial breath sounds over the AFFECTED area only — not throughout. Dullness is the most reliable single indicator.
---
**17.** On ocular movement, which statement is NOT TRUE?
a) Nystagmus is repeated involuntary eye movement
b) Nystagmus can be idiopathic
c) Oculomotor serves all extraocular muscles except superior oblique and lateral rectus
d) The lateral rectus muscle is supplied by cranial nerve IV
**ANSWER: D**
The lateral rectus is supplied by CN VI (Abducens), not CN IV. CN IV (Trochlear) supplies the superior oblique muscle. Mnemonic: SO4, LR6.
---
**18.** Teenage boy: sharp pain, SOB, cyanosis, tachypnea, tracheal deviation to RIGHT, decreased TF on LEFT, hyperresonance LEFT, decreased breath sounds LEFT. Diagnosis?
a) Acute GERD
b) Asthmatic attack
c) Acute tension pneumothorax
d) Spontaneous pneumothorax
**ANSWER: C**
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side strongly suggests a tension pneumothorax, where air accumulates under pressure and pushes the mediastinum to the opposite side.
---
**19.** Of the female reproductive system, which statement is FALSE?
a) The vagina is 5 cm long
b) Labia majora are fat pads covered with hair
c) The vulva consists of the labia majora and minora
d) The uterus is a muscular pear-shaped midline structure
**ANSWER: A**
The vagina is approximately 7–10 cm long (anterior wall ~7 cm, posterior wall ~9 cm). 5 cm is incorrect.
---
**20.** On abnormal vaginal bleeding, which statement is TRUE?
a) Anaemia is always a finding
b) It is not usually associated with iron deficiency anaemia
c) In longstanding cases the patient may present with a bounding pulse
d) Oligomenorrhoea is not a feature of polycystic ovarian disease
**ANSWER: C**
Chronic blood loss leads to iron deficiency anaemia; severe anaemia causes a hyperdynamic circulation with a bounding pulse. Oligomenorrhoea IS a feature of PCOS.
---
**21.** Causes of BILATERAL reduction in chest wall expansion include all EXCEPT:
a) Bilateral symmetrical pleural effusions
b) End-stage idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
c) COPD
d) Pneumothorax
**ANSWER: D**
A pneumothorax is typically UNILATERAL, causing reduced expansion on one side only. Bilateral causes include bilateral effusions, severe COPD, and bilateral fibrosis.
---
**22.** On pupillary light reflexes, all are true EXCEPT:
a) Direct pupillary reflex is constriction of the pupil light is shown into
b) Constriction of the contralateral pupil is known as the consensual light reflex
c) Snellen charts are used to assess for colour blindness
d) On accommodation, pupils constrict and converge bilaterally
**ANSWER: C**
Snellen charts assess visual acuity (distance), NOT colour blindness. Colour vision is tested with Ishihara plates.
---
**23.** In bronchial breathing, which statement is FALSE?
a) Associated with a clear distinct pause between inspiratory and expiratory phases
b) Louder than vesicular sounds
c) Quiet low-pitched rustling
d) Can be likened to auscultation of the trachea
**ANSWER: C**
Bronchial breathing is LOUD and HIGH-PITCHED, not quiet or low-pitched. Quiet, low-pitched rustling describes vesicular breath sounds.
---
**24.** Which is FALSE on vocal resonance?
a) Pleural effusion is associated with reduced or absent vocal resonance
b) Consolidation is associated with increased vocal resonance
c) Increased vocal fremitus is seen in consolidation
d) In vocal fremitus, decreased vibration suggests presence of fluid or air
**ANSWER: D/all..— this is actually TRUE**, making it the odd one out in this "false" question format. All of a, b, c are true. The question likely intends C as it states "increased vocal fremitus" — which is correct in consolidation. Review with your lecturer as the stem wording is ambiguous.
---
**25.** On examination of the hands, which is TRUE?
a) Leuconychia — most common cause is trauma to the hands
b) Liver disease is the most common cause of leuconychia
c) Uraemia is associated with flapping tremors (asterixis)
d) Finger clubbing is only seen in chronic respiratory and cardiovascular conditions
**ANSWER: C**
Asterixis (flapping tremor) is classically associated with hepatic encephalopathy AND uraemia. Leuconychia is most commonly due to hypoalbuminaemia (liver disease). Clubbing also occurs in GIT disease (IBD, cirrhosis).
---
**26.** On spider naevi, which statement is TRUE?
a) Can be a normal finding in pregnancy
b) Finger clubbing can be a sign of chronic cardiovascular, respiratory and GIT disease
c) Janeway lesions are found on the face
d) Aortic dissection is associated with radio-femoral delay
**ANSWER: A**
Spider naevi can be normal in pregnancy and in OCP use due to raised oestrogen. Janeway lesions (painless, palms/soles) are seen in infective endocarditis. Radio-femoral delay is associated with coarctation of the aorta.
---
**27.** On blood pressure reading, which statement is TRUE?
a) Narrow pulse pressure is considered normal
b) Aortic stenosis and cardiac tamponade have been associated with narrow pulse pressure
c) Wide pulse pressure is associated with aortic stenosis
d) All of the above are true
**ANSWER: B**
Narrow pulse pressure (<25 mmHg) occurs in aortic stenosis, cardiac tamponade, and severe heart failure. Wide pulse pressure is seen in aortic regurgitation, thyrotoxicosis, and anaemia.
---
**28.** On hepatojugular reflux, which statement is FALSE?
a) Can be elevated in constrictive pericarditis
b) Is associated with LEFT ventricular failure
c) Rise should not last more than 5 cycles
d) Restrictive cardiomyopathy is a known cause
**ANSWER: B**
Hepatojugular reflux is a sign of RIGHT heart failure (or raised right-sided filling pressures). It is NOT a feature of isolated left ventricular failure.
---
**29.** Which statement is TRUE on the apex beat?
a) Lateral and inferior apex beat is diagnostic of constrictive cardiomyopathy
b) If displaced to the right, suggests possible dextrocardia
c) The apex beat is at the mid-axillary 6th intercostal space
d) Normal position is the 6th intercostal space mid-clavicular line
**ANSWER: B**
Normal apex beat: 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line. Rightward displacement suggests dextrocardia or mediastinal shift. Leftward/downward displacement suggests cardiomegaly.
---
**30.** Left supraclavicular lymph node — which is the FALSE statement?
a) Also called Virchow's node
b) Is associated with CNS malignancies
c) Can be associated with gastric tumors
d) The right supraclavicular node points more towards a GIT malignancy
**ANSWER: B**
Virchow's node (left supraclavicular) is associated with GIT/abdominal malignancies, NOT CNS malignancies. The right supraclavicular node is more associated with lung and oesophageal cancer.
---

articles.content:
# COMPREHENSIVE REVISION NOTES
## BATCH 3 | Topics 15 – 18 (Final)

---

## TOPIC 15: BLOOD GROUPS & TRANSFUSION COMPATIBILITY

**Definition:**
- Blood typing based on antigens (A, B, Rh/D) present on RBC surface
- Compatibility testing prevents haemolytic transfusion reactions

**ABO System — Basics:** (★)

| Blood Group | RBC Antigen | Plasma Antibody |
|---|---|---|
| A | A | Anti-B |
| B | B | Anti-A |
| AB | A and B | None |
| O | None | Anti-A and Anti-B |

**Universal Donor / Recipient Rules:** (★)
- **Universal donor for RBCs: O negative** (★) — no A, B, or Rh(D) antigens to trigger reaction
- **Universal recipient for RBCs: AB positive** — no antibodies against A, B, or D
- **Universal donor for PLASMA: AB** (opposite logic) — plasma contains no anti-A/anti-B antibodies
- **Group O is NOT suitable for plasma transfusion** because O plasma **contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies** (★) — would attack recipient's A/B antigens if recipient is not group O

---

## TOPIC 16: TRANSFUSION REACTIONS

**Classification by Onset and Mechanism:** (★)

| Reaction | Onset | Mechanism | Key Features |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction** | Within 30 min – 24h | ABO incompatibility — recipient antibodies destroy donor RBCs | Fever, chills, **hypotension**, back pain, haemoglobinuria, DIC risk (★) |
| Febrile non-haemolytic reaction | During/shortly after transfusion | Cytokines from donor leucocytes | Fever, chills — NO hypotension/haemolysis |
| Allergic reaction | During transfusion | IgE-mediated to donor plasma proteins | Urticaria, itching ± mild fever |
| **TRALI** | Within 6 hours | Donor anti-leucocyte antibodies react with recipient WBCs → pulmonary capillary damage | **Hypotension + respiratory distress** (non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema) (★) |
| TACO | During/after transfusion | Volume overload | Dyspnoea, hypertension (not hypotension), signs of fluid overload |
| Delayed haemolytic reaction | Days to weeks | Anamnestic antibody response to minor antigens | Mild jaundice, falling Hb |
| Iron overload | Long-term (multiple transfusions) | Cumulative iron deposition | Organ damage (liver, heart, endocrine) |

**Distinguishing the two "look-alike" reactions:** (★)
- Fever + chills + **hypotension within 30 min** = acute haemolytic transfusion reaction (ABO mismatch)
- Fever + chills WITHOUT hypotension/haemolysis = febrile non-haemolytic reaction (most common reaction overall)
- Hypotension + **respiratory distress**, donor antibodies against recipient leucocytes = **TRALI** (★)

---

## TOPIC 17: BLOOD COMPONENTS, PRODUCTS & SAFETY MEASURES

**Major Blood Components and Their Indications:** (★ — core long-answer topic)

| Component | Contains | Key Indications |
|---|---|---|
| **Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBC)** | RBCs, minimal plasma | Symptomatic anaemia, acute blood loss |
| **Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP)** | All clotting factors | Coagulopathy with active bleeding, **liver failure with bleeding** (★), warfarin reversal, DIC |
| **Platelet concentrate** | Platelets | **Thrombocytopenia with active bleeding** (★), prophylaxis pre-procedure if very low count |
| **Cryoprecipitate** | Fibrinogen, Factor VIII, vWF, Factor XIII | Hypofibrinogenaemia, DIC, von Willebrand disease (if specific concentrate unavailable) |
| **Albumin** | Plasma protein | Volume expansion, hypoalbuminaemia, large-volume paracentesis |
| Granulocyte concentrate | Neutrophils | Severe neutropenia with infection unresponsive to antibiotics (rare) |

**Storage of PRBCs:** (★)
- Citrate-Phosphate-Dextrose-Adenine-1 (CPDA-1) anticoagulant-preservative
- Standard shelf life: **35 days** (★) at 2–6°C

**Safety Measures in Transfusion:** (★)

| Measure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Irradiation of blood products** | Prevents **transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GVHD)** in immunocompromised recipients (★) — inactivates donor lymphocytes |
| Leucodepletion (leucoreduction) | Reduces febrile non-haemolytic reactions, CMV transmission, HLA alloimmunisation |
| Washing of RBCs | Removes plasma proteins — used in IgA deficiency, severe allergic reactions |
| ABO cross-matching | Prevents ABO-incompatible haemolytic reactions (not GVHD) |
| Pathogen reduction technology | Reduces transfusion-transmitted infections |

- Key distinction: **irradiation prevents TA-GVHD**; leucodepletion prevents febrile reactions and CMV — these are commonly confused on exams (★)

**Infectious Screening of Donated Blood:** (★)
- Mandatory screens universally include: **HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, syphilis** (★)
- **Hepatitis B** is the most classically cited and highest-yield answer for "most commonly screened infection" in donated blood (★)
- Other infections (malaria, HTLV) screened regionally based on endemicity

---

## TOPIC 18: CLINICAL SCENARIO INTEGRATION (SAQ-STYLE REASONING)

This section consolidates the clinical-reasoning patterns the SAQs test — useful as a "thinking template" for similarly-framed questions.

**A. Splenomegaly + Very High WCC + Neutrophilia + Left Shift + Basophilia** → **CML** (★)
- Work-up: FBC/PBF → bone marrow aspirate + trephine with cytogenetics → BCR-ABL by RT-PCR or FISH → karyotyping for t(9;22)

**B. Heavy Menstrual Bleeding + Fatigue + Pallor + Pica** → **Iron deficiency anaemia** (★)

- Clinical signs: koilonychia, angular cheilitis, glossitis
- Lab tests: FBC (↓Hb, ↓MCV), serum ferritin (↓), serum iron/TIBC, peripheral film
- Confirmatory: serum ferritin + serum iron studies (± bone marrow iron stores in unclear cases)

**C. Rapidly Growing Jaw Mass in a Child** → **Burkitt lymphoma** (★)
- Work-up: excisional biopsy ("starry-sky" histology) → immunophenotyping (CD10+, CD20+) → cytogenetics for t(8;14) → bone marrow aspirate (staging) → LDH → CSF cytology (CNS involvement) → imaging for staging

**D. Cirrhosis + Splenomegaly + Low Platelet Count** → **Thrombocytopenia secondary to hypersplenism/portal hypertension** (★)
- Causes: hypersplenism (sequestration), reduced thrombopoietin production (liver synthesises TPO), splenic pooling
- Work-up: FBC + film (rule out pseudothrombocytopenia/clumping), liver function tests, coagulation screen (PT/APTT — often deranged in cirrhosis too), bone marrow biopsy if diagnosis unclear, abdominal ultrasound/spleen size

**E. Recurrent Haemarthroses + Easy Bruising in a Child** → **Haemophilia (Factor VIII or IX deficiency)** (★)
- Pattern: Normal PT, prolonged APTT, normal TT → intrinsic pathway defect
- Additional tests: Factor VIII and IX assay levels, von Willebrand factor antigen/activity (to exclude vWD), mixing studies (correct with normal plasma confirms factor deficiency vs inhibitor)

**F. Zidovudine + Macrocytic Anaemia** → **Drug-induced bone marrow suppression** (★)
- Mechanism: mitochondrial toxicity + impaired DNA synthesis in erythroid precursors
- Additional tests: B12, folate (exclude as competing causes), reticulocyte count (low — marrow suppression, not compensatory response), peripheral film
- Other macrocytic anaemia causes: B12/folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, liver disease/alcohol, myelodysplastic syndrome

---

articles.title: Acute Leukaemia (AML/ALL) & WBC Disorders: Haematology Guide — Notes
articles.content:
# COMPREHENSIVE REVISION NOTES
## BATCH 2 | Topics 7 – 14

---

## TOPIC 7: WHITE BLOOD CELLS — FUNCTION & DISORDERS

**Definition:**
- Leucocytes — nucleated blood cells of the immune system
- *Leukos* (Greek) = white | *kytos* = cell

**Classification by Function:** (★)

| Cell | % of WBC | Primary Role |
|---|---|---|
| Neutrophils | 60–70% | Bacterial/fungal phagocytosis — first responders |
| **Eosinophils** | 1–4% | **Parasitic infections** (★), allergic/IgE reactions |
| Basophils | <1% | Allergic reactions, release histamine and heparin |
| Monocytes | 2–8% | Phagocytosis; differentiate into tissue macrophages |
| Lymphocytes | 20–40% | Adaptive immunity (T-cells, B-cells, NK cells) |

- Eosinophils release **major basic protein (MBP)** and eosinophil cationic protein, recruited by **IL-5**, to kill helminths and parasites (★)

**Key Terminology:** (★)

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Leucocytosis | ↑ WBC count |
| Leucopenia | ↓ WBC count |
| Neutrophilia | ↑ neutrophils (bacterial infection, stress) |
| **Neutropenia** | ↓ neutrophils, ANC <1.5 × 10⁹/L |
| Lymphocytosis | ↑ lymphocytes (viral infection, CLL) |
| Lymphopenia | ↓ lymphocytes (HIV, steroids) |
| Eosinophilia | ↑ eosinophils (parasites, allergy, drugs) |
| Erythrocytosis | ↑ RBCs |
| Thrombocytopenia | ↓ platelets |
| Thrombocytosis | ↑ platelets |

**Neutropenia:**
- Mild: 1.0–1.5 ×10⁹/L | Moderate: 0.5–1.0 ×10⁹/L | **Severe: <0.5 ×10⁹/L** — high infection risk (★)
- Most common cause in clinical practice: **chemotherapy** (★)
- Other causes: aplastic anaemia, viral infections, drugs (clozapine, carbimazole), autoimmune, severe sepsis
- Management: G-CSF, isolate from infection sources, prompt antibiotics if febrile (febrile neutropenia = medical emergency)

---

## TOPIC 8: ACUTE LEUKAEMIA (AML & ALL)

**Etymology:** *Leukos* = white | *haima* = blood

**Definition:**
- Malignant clonal proliferation of immature haematopoietic blasts
- WHO criterion: **≥20% blasts in bone marrow or peripheral blood** confirms acute leukaemia (★)

**Acute vs Chronic:**
- Acute: blasts dominate, rapid onset, pancytopenia + circulating blasts
- Chronic: mature cells dominate, indolent course

---

**ACUTE MYELOID LEUKAEMIA (AML)**

**Definition:** Clonal proliferation of myeloid blasts (myeloblasts, monoblasts, etc.)

**Clinical Presentation:** (★)
- Anaemia → fatigue, pallor
- Neutropenia (despite high WCC — non-functional blasts) → fever, infections
- Thrombocytopenia → bruising, bleeding, petechiae
- Gum hypertrophy, skin infiltration (especially monocytic subtypes)

**Diagnosis:** (★)
- Gold standard: **bone marrow aspirate + trephine biopsy** with cytogenetics and immunophenotyping
- **Auer rods** — pathognomonic pink needle-like cytoplasmic inclusions in myeloblasts (★)
- Flow cytometry for immunophenotyping
- Peripheral smear alone is insufficient for definitive diagnosis

**Cytochemical Stains — Confirming Lineage:** (★)

| Stain | Lineage |
|---|---|
| **Myeloperoxidase (MPO)** | Myeloid — most specific (★) |
| Sudan Black B | Myeloid (less specific than MPO) |
| Non-specific esterase (NSE) | Monocytic (M4/M5 subtypes) |
| **Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)** | Lymphoid (ALL) and erythroid |
| **TdT (Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase)** | Lymphoblasts — confirms ALL (★) |
| TRAP | Hairy cell leukaemia |

**FAB Classification of AML:** (★)

| Subtype | Name | Key Feature |
|---|---|---|
| M0 | Undifferentiated | — |
| M1 | Without maturation | — |
| M2 | With maturation | t(8;21) |
| **M3** | **Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL)** | t(15;17) — PML-RARA fusion; **DIC risk**; treated with ATRA (★) |
| M4 | Myelomonocytic | inv(16) |
| **M5** | **Monocytic** | **Gingival hypertrophy and skin infiltration** (★) |
| M6 | Erythroleukaemia | — |
| M7 | Megakaryoblastic | — |

---

**ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKAEMIA (ALL)**

**Definition:** Clonal proliferation of lymphoid blasts (B- or T-lineage); most common childhood leukaemia

**Diagnosis:**
- TdT positive — confirms lymphoblast origin (★)
- PAS positive
- Cytogenetics/molecular: best sample = **bone marrow aspirate** (preferred over peripheral blood for cytogenetic/molecular analysis) (★)

**Immunophenotyping markers:** (★)

| Marker | Lineage |
|---|---|
| CD19, CD10, CD20 | B-cell ALL |
| **CD3** | **T-cell ALL** (★) |
| CD33, CD13 | Myeloid (AML) |

---

## TOPIC 9: CHRONIC LEUKAEMIAS

**CHRONIC MYELOID LEUKAEMIA (CML)**

**Definition:** Clonal myeloproliferative disorder of granulocyte precursors

**Pathognomonic finding:** (★)
- **t(9;22)(q34;q11)** — the **Philadelphia chromosome**
- Forms **BCR-ABL fusion gene** → constitutive tyrosine kinase activity → uncontrolled proliferation

**Clinical Presentation:** (★)
- Fatigue, weight loss, splenomegaly (massive)
- Very high WCC (often >100 ×10⁹/L)
- **Neutrophilia with left shift and basophilia** — classic triad (★)

**Investigations to confirm diagnosis:** (★)
- FBC + PBF: leucocytosis with full spectrum of granulocyte maturation, basophilia
- **Bone marrow aspirate + trephine biopsy with cytogenetic analysis**
- **Quantitative RT-PCR for BCR-ABL transcripts** — used for diagnosis confirmation AND monitoring treatment response (★)
- FISH — detects Philadelphia chromosome in interphase cells (doesn't require dividing cells, faster than conventional cytogenetics) (★)
- Conventional cytogenetics (karyotyping) — detects t(9;22) directly but requires metaphase cells

**Treatment:**
- **Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs)**: imatinib (first-line), dasatinib, nilotinib — target BCR-ABL (★)

**Distinguishing CML from Polycythaemia Vera:** (★)
- CML: BCR-ABL fusion transcript positive, JAK2 negative
- PV: **JAK2 V617F mutation** positive (>95% of cases), BCR-ABL negative

---

**CHRONIC LYMPHOCYTIC LEUKAEMIA (CLL)**

**Definition:** Clonal proliferation of mature but dysfunctional B-lymphocytes; most common leukaemia in adults in the West

**Key Complication — Warm Autoimmune Haemolytic Anaemia (AIHA):** (★)
- CLL patients can develop autoantibody-mediated RBC destruction
- Confirmatory test: **Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test** — detects antibody/complement on RBC surface (★)
- Distinguish from indirect Coombs (detects antibodies in serum, used in pre-transfusion testing, not for diagnosing AIHA)

**CNS Involvement in CLL:**
- Presents with headache, blurred vision in established disease
- Investigation of choice: **lumbar puncture with CSF cytology** (★) — direct assessment for malignant cell infiltration of CNS

**PBF finding:** smudge cells (fragile lymphocytes that rupture during slide preparation) — characteristic but not asked directly here

---

## TOPIC 10: MYELOPROLIFERATIVE NEOPLASMS

**Definition:** Clonal proliferation of one or more myeloid lineages (RBC, WBC, platelet, fibroblast) in the bone marrow

**Overview Table:** (★)

| Disease | Primary Cell Affected | Key Mutation |
|---|---|---|
| Polycythaemia vera (PV) | Erythroid | JAK2 V617F (>95%) |
| Essential thrombocythaemia (ET) | Megakaryocytic | **JAK2** (most common), CALR, MPL (★) |
| Myelofibrosis | Fibroblastic reaction (reactive) | JAK2, CALR, MPL |
| CML | Granulocytic | BCR-ABL |

---

**POLYCYTHAEMIA VERA (PV)**

**Hallmark feature:** (★)
- **Elevated haematocrit/red cell mass with LOW erythropoietin** (★) — distinguishes primary (PV) from secondary polycythaemia (where EPO is high due to hypoxia, e.g. COPD, high altitude)
- JAK2 V617F mutation present in >95% of cases

---

**ESSENTIAL THROMBOCYTHAEMIA (ET)**

- Marked thrombocytosis (platelets often >450–600 ×10⁹/L)
- Most commonly associated mutation: **JAK2** (~50–60%), followed by CALR (~25%), MPL (~5%) (★)
- Risk of both thrombosis and paradoxical bleeding

---

**MYELOFIBROSIS**

**Definition:** Clonal myeloproliferative disorder with reactive bone marrow fibrosis

**Key findings:** (★)
- **Fibrotic bone marrow with tear-drop red blood cells (dacrocytes)** on peripheral smear (★)
- Massive splenomegaly (extramedullary haematopoiesis)
- Leukoerythroblastic blood picture (immature RBCs and WBCs in circulation)
- Increased reticulin/collagen deposition in marrow (not decreased)

---

## TOPIC 11: LYMPHOMA

**Definition:** Malignant proliferation of lymphocytes, primarily affecting lymph nodes and lymphoid tissue

**Classification:** Hodgkin lymphoma vs Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL)

---

**CLASSICAL HODGKIN LYMPHOMA**

**Key features:** (★)
- Painless lymphadenopathy (often cervical), night sweats, fever, weight loss (B symptoms)
- Diagnostic cell: **Reed-Sternberg cells** — large binucleated cells
- Immunophenotype: **CD15+ and CD30+** (★)
- Excisional lymph node biopsy = gold standard for diagnosis (★) — preserves architecture, needed over FNA/core biopsy

---

**NON-HODGKIN LYMPHOMA — Key Subtypes and Markers** (★)

| Lymphoma | Marker(s) | Translocation | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Follicular lymphoma | **CD10**, CD20, BCL2 | t(14;18) | Indolent |
| Mantle cell lymphoma | CD5, CD20 | t(11;14) | Cyclin D1 |
| **Burkitt lymphoma** | CD10, CD20 | **t(8;14)** (★) | "Starry-sky" histology; MYC gene; rapidly growing jaw mass in children (endemic form) |
| Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma | CD20 | Variable | Most common aggressive NHL |
| **Mycosis fungoides** (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma) | **CD3** (★) | — | T-cell marker since it's a T-cell lymphoma |

**Burkitt Lymphoma — Diagnostic Work-up:** (★)
- Excisional biopsy of mass — histology shows "starry-sky" appearance (sheets of lymphoid cells with scattered macrophages)
- Cytogenetics: **t(8;14)** — MYC-IGH translocation (also less commonly t(2;8) or t(8;22))
- Immunohistochemistry: CD10+, CD20+, BCL6+, Ki-67 (very high proliferation index)
- Bone marrow aspirate — assess marrow involvement/staging
- LDH — prognostic marker, often very elevated (rapid cell turnover)
- Imaging (CT/PET) for staging
- LP with CSF cytology — assess CNS involvement (common in Burkitt)

**Tumour Markers in Lymphoma — Prognosis:** (★)
- **Beta-2 microglobulin** — most widely used prognostic tumour marker in lymphoma (★)
- LDH — reflects tumour burden/turnover, part of International Prognostic Index (IPI)

**Reactive Lymphadenopathy (Benign):**

- Histology: **follicular hyperplasia with preserved lymph node architecture** (★) — distinguishes from malignant infiltration, which shows architecture effacement

---

## TOPIC 12: PLASMA CELL DISORDERS

**MULTIPLE MYELOMA**

**Definition:** Malignant proliferation of plasma cells producing monoclonal immunoglobulin (paraprotein/M protein)

**Classic Presentation — "CRAB":** (★)
- **C**alcium elevated (hypercalcaemia — bone resorption)
- **R**enal impairment (light chain deposition)
- **A**naemia (marrow infiltration)
- **B**one lesions — **lytic lesions** (★, most common clinical finding), bone pain, pathological fractures

**Key Investigations:** (★)
- Serum protein electrophoresis — **monoclonal spike (M-spike/paraprotein)** (★)
- Bence Jones proteins in urine = free monoclonal **kappa or lambda light chains** (★)
- Bone marrow: increased plasma cells (>10%)
- Skeletal survey/CT: punched-out lytic lesions, especially skull
- Serum free light chain assay

**Distinguishing MGUS from Multiple Myeloma:** (★)
- MGUS = **elevated M protein WITHOUT end-organ damage** (no CRAB features) (★)
- Myeloma = M protein WITH end-organ damage
- MGUS can progress to myeloma (~1% per year risk) — requires monitoring

---

## TOPIC 13: COAGULATION DISORDERS & HAEMOSTASIS

**Overview of Coagulation Cascade:** (★)

| Pathway | Factors | Screening Test |
|---|---|---|
| Intrinsic | XII, XI, IX, VIII | **APTT** |
| Extrinsic | VII, Tissue factor | **PT** |
| Common | X, V, II (prothrombin), I (fibrinogen) | Both |

---

**HAEMOPHILIAS**

| Disease | Deficient Factor | Inheritance |
|---|---|---|
| **Haemophilia A** | **Factor VIII** (★) | X-linked recessive |
| Haemophilia B | Factor IX | X-linked recessive |

**Clinical clue (★):** Recurrent haemarthroses (joint bleeds) + easy bruising in a male child/young man, with:

- **Normal PT** + **Prolonged APTT** + **Normal TT** → points to an **intrinsic pathway factor deficiency** (Factor VIII or IX) (★)
- This pattern = Factor VIII deficiency (Haemophilia A) most commonly tested

**Von Willebrand Disease:**
- Most common inherited bleeding disorder
- Deficiency/dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (carries Factor VIII, mediates platelet adhesion)
- Causes both mucocutaneous bleeding AND prolonged APTT (due to ↓ Factor VIII)

---

**MONITORING ANTICOAGULANTS** (★)

| Drug | Monitoring Test | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **Warfarin** | **PT/INR** (★) | Inhibits vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X) |
| **Unfractionated heparin** | **APTT** (★) | Potentiates antithrombin III, inhibits thrombin and Xa |
| Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) | Anti-factor Xa (routine monitoring not usually needed) | Inhibits factor Xa |

- Warfarin therapy monitoring: PT alone is not standardised across labs → **INR (International Normalised Ratio)** is used to standardise results between labs (★)
- Unfractionated heparin infusion: monitored via **APTT** (★)

---

**DISSEMINATED INTRAVASCULAR COAGULATION (DIC)**

**Definition:** Widespread activation of coagulation → consumption of clotting factors and platelets → simultaneous thrombosis and bleeding

**Classic cause in haematology:** Acute Promyelocytic Leukaemia (APL/M3) — release of procoagulant material from promyelocytic granules

**Lab findings in DIC:** (★)
- **Decreased fibrinogen** (consumed) (★)
- Decreased platelets (thrombocytopenia, not thrombocytosis)
- **Increased D-dimer** (not decreased) — reflects fibrinolysis
- Prolonged PT and APTT (not shortened)

---

## TOPIC 14: HAEMOSTASIS IN PREGNANCY & HIV-RELATED HAEMATOLOGY

**PREGNANCY — PHYSIOLOGICAL CHANGES** (★)

| Parameter | Change in Pregnancy |
|---|---|
| ESR | **Markedly elevated** — due to ↑ fibrinogen (★) |
| Fibrinogen | **↑ markedly** — most increased coagulation factor (★) |
| Factor VIII, von Willebrand factor | ↑ |
| **Protein S** | **↓** — physiologically reduced, contributes to hypercoagulable state of pregnancy (★) |
| Protein C, Antithrombin III | Relatively unchanged or mildly altered |
| Platelet count | Mild gestational thrombocytopenia possible |

- Pregnancy = physiological **hypercoagulable state** — protective against haemorrhage at delivery, but increases VTE risk (★)

---

**HIV-ASSOCIATED HAEMATOLOGICAL CHANGES**

**Early HIV infection (before CD4 decline):** (★)
- Characteristic change: **lymphopenia** (★) — even before major CD4 fall, generalized lymphocyte changes occur

**Neutropenia in HIV — infection risk:**
- Severe neutropenia (ANC <0.5 ×10⁹/L) — greatest risk pathogen: **Pneumocystis jirovecii** (★) (note: PJP risk is classically tied to low CD4 count rather than neutropenil count specifically, but is the answer expected for opportunistic infection risk in this severely immunocompromised context)

**HIV-Associated Thrombocytopenia:**
- Autoantibodies typically directed against **Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa** (★) on platelet surface — similar mechanism to ITP

**Zidovudine (AZT)-Induced Macrocytic Anaemia:**
- Mechanism: zidovudine inhibits **mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma** and interferes with **DNA synthesis** in erythroid precursors → ineffective erythropoiesis → macrocytosis (★)
- It is a direct **bone marrow toxic/myelosuppressive effect**, independent of B12/folate
- Additional tests to confirm cause: serum B12 and folate (to exclude as competing cause — typically normal in pure AZT toxicity), reticulocyte count (low, reflecting marrow suppression rather than compensation)
- Other causes of macrocytic anaemia to differentiate: **B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, liver disease, alcohol excess, myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)** (★)

---

articles.content:
MOUNT KENYA UNIVERSITY
### School of Medicine | Department of Pathology### Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery — Year 3**Unit Code:** MBML 3200 | **Unit Title:** HAEMATOLOGY
**Examination:** University Examination 2024/2025 — Main Exam
**Date:** 14th July, 2025 | **Time:** 2 Hours 30 Minutes
**Sections:** A — 60 MCQs | B — 7 SAQs | C — 1 LAQ
---
COMPREHENSIVE REVISION NOTES
## BATCH 1 | Topics 1 – 5---
## TOPIC 1: HAEMATOPOIESIS**Etymology:** *Haema* (Greek) = blood | *Poiesis* = making/production
**Definition:**
- Continuous process of **blood cell production** from pluripotent stem cells (★)
- Replaces cells lost through senescence, destruction, or haemorrhage
- Produces ~200 billion RBCs and ~100 billion WBCs daily

---
**SITES OF HAEMATOPOIESIS — BY DEVELOPMENTAL STAGE** (★)
| Phase | Site | Period |
|---|---|---|
| Mesoblastic | Yolk sac | 0–2 months fetal |
| Hepatic | Liver (primary), spleen, lymph nodes | 2–7 months fetal |
| Myeloid | Bone marrow | 5 months → adult life |
- In healthy adults: **bone marrow is the sole site** (★)
- Active marrow in adults: sternum, vertebrae, pelvis, ribs, skull, proximal femur and humerus
- **Extramedullary haematopoiesis** = reactivation of liver/spleen in disease states (e.g. myelofibrosis, thalassaemia major) (★)

---
**THE HAEMATOPOIETIC STEM CELL (HSC)**
- Pluripotent and self-renewing
- Surface marker: **CD34+** (★) — also CD38−, CD117+, HLA-DR+
- Differentiates into two main progenitors:

 - **Common Myeloid Progenitor (CMP)** → RBCs, platelets, neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes

- **Common Lymphoid Progenitor (CLP)** → T-cells, B-cells, NK cells
**Common CD markers — know the difference:** (★)
- CD34 = HSC marker
- CD3 = T-cell marker
- CD4 = T-helper cell
- CD19, CD20 = B-cell markers
- CD33 = myeloid marker

---
**GROWTH FACTORS & CYTOKINES** (★)
| Factor | Primary Target | Clinical Use |
|---|---|---|
| Erythropoietin (EPO) | RBC production (erythroid line) | Anaemia of CKD |
| Thrombopoietin (TPO) | **Platelet** production via megakaryocytes (★) | — |
| G-CSF (Filgrastim) | **Neutrophil** production and recovery (★) | Post-chemotherapy neutropenia |
| GM-CSF | Neutrophils + monocytes | Stem cell mobilisation |
| IL-3 | Multi-lineage stimulation | — |
| SCF (Stem cell factor) | HSC survival and proliferation | — |
- G-CSF = Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor → promotes **neutrophil recovery after chemotherapy** (★)
- Thrombopoietin → acts on megakaryocytes → **platelets** (★)

---
## TOPIC 2: ANAEMIA — GENERAL + IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA (IDA)**Etymology:** *An-* = without | *haima* = blood
**Definition of Anaemia:**
- Reduction in haemoglobin concentration below normal for age and sex
- WHO thresholds: Hb <13 g/dL (adult male) | <12 g/dL (adult non-pregnant female) | <11 g/dL (pregnant)

---
**CLASSIFICATION OF ANAEMIA BY MCV** (★)
| Type | MCV | Causes |
|---|---|---|
| Microcytic (<80 fL) | ↓ | IDA, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic |
| Normocytic (80–100 fL) | Normal | Aplastic anaemia, haemolytic anaemia, acute blood loss, CKD |
| Macrocytic (>100 fL) | ↑ | B12/folate deficiency, liver disease, hypothyroidism, drugs (zidovudine, hydroxyurea, methotrexate) |
---
**IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA (IDA)** (★)
**Definition:** Most common anaemia worldwide — due to negative iron balance leading to insufficient haem synthesis
**Iron Metabolism — The Pathway:**
- Dietary iron: haem iron (meat) absorbed 20–30% | non-haem iron (plant) absorbed 5–10%
- Absorbed in **duodenum and proximal jejunum** as Fe²⁺ (ferrous form)
- Carried in blood bound to **transferrin**
- Stored as **ferritin** (soluble, reflects body stores — best early marker) and **haemosiderin** (insoluble)
- Regulated by **hepcidin** — liver hormone that blocks ferroportin → ↓ iron absorption and release

**Stages of IDA:** (★)
- Stage 1: ↓ ferritin (depleted stores) — no anaemia yet
- Stage 2: ↓ serum iron, ↑ TIBC, ↓ transferrin saturation — iron-deficient erythropoiesis
- Stage 3: ↓ Hb, microcytic hypochromic anaemia — overt IDA

**Causes:**
- ↑ Loss: heavy menstrual bleeding (commonest in premenopausal women), GI bleeding (peptic ulcer, colorectal Ca, hookworm)
- ↓ Intake: poor diet, malnutrition
- ↓ Absorption: coeliac disease, gastrectomy, achlorhydria, H. pylori
- ↑ Demand: pregnancy, infancy, adolescent growth spurt

**Clinical Features:**
- General anaemia: fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations, headache, dizziness
- IDA-specific signs: (★)

 - **Koilonychia** — spoon-shaped nails

- **Angular cheilitis** — cracking at corners of mouth
- **Glossitis** — smooth, beefy-red, painful tongue
- **Pica** — craving non-food substances (ice, soil, clay, paper)
- **Plummer-Vinson syndrome** — IDA + dysphagia + post-cricoid oesophageal web (★)
**Laboratory Findings:** (★)
| Test | IDA Result |
|---|---|
| Hb | ↓ |
| MCV | ↓ (<80 fL) — microcytic |
| MCH | ↓ — hypochromic |
| Serum ferritin | ↓ ← earliest and most sensitive indicator |
| Serum iron | ↓ |
| TIBC (transferrin capacity) | ↑ |
| Transferrin saturation | ↓ (<15%) |
| Reticulocyte count | ↓ or normal |
| PBF | Microcytes, hypochromia, pencil/cigar cells, anisocytosis, poikilocytosis |
| Serum soluble transferrin receptor | ↑ (useful in pregnancy) |
**Confirmatory Tests:**
- Serum ferritin — most sensitive and specific
- Serum iron + TIBC
- Bone marrow aspirate with Prussian blue stain — absent iron stores (gold standard, rarely done)

**Treatment:**
- Oral ferrous sulphate (FeSO₄) — first line
- Parenteral iron — if oral not tolerated or malabsorption
- Blood transfusion — only if severely symptomatic or haemodynamically unstable
- Address underlying cause

---
## TOPIC 3: APLASTIC ANAEMIA**Etymology:** *A-* = without | *plastic* = forming — failure to form blood cells
**Definition:**
- Pancytopenia resulting from **bone marrow failure** — destruction or suppression of HSCs
- Results in ↓ RBCs + ↓ WBCs + ↓ platelets

**Causes:** (★)
- Idiopathic (~70%) — autoimmune T-cell mediated destruction of HSCs
- **Drugs:** chloramphenicol (★), NSAIDs, anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin), chemotherapy, gold
- **Infections:** Hepatitis (non-A, non-B, non-C — most common viral cause), EBV, CMV, **Parvovirus B19** (causes pure red cell aplasia — affects erythroid precursors only) (★)
- Radiation exposure
- Chemicals: benzene
- Inherited: Fanconi anaemia (autosomal recessive, chromosome fragility)

**Clinical Features:**
- Anaemia → fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea
- **Neutropenia → recurrent/severe infections** (★)
- **Thrombocytopenia → petechiae, purpura, mucosal bleeding, easy bruising** (★)
- No splenomegaly (distinguishes from other causes of pancytopenia)

**Bone Marrow Findings:** (★)
- **Fatty replacement** of haematopoietic tissue
- **Hypocellularity** (<25% cellularity)
- Reduced all cell lines
- Remaining cells are morphologically normal

**Investigations:**
- FBC: pancytopenia
- Reticulocyte count: ↓ (hypoproliferative)
- Bone marrow aspirate + trephine biopsy: confirms fatty replacement and hypocellularity (★)
- Cytogenetics: rule out MDS and Fanconi anaemia

**Treatment:**
- Mild-moderate: supportive (transfusions, antibiotics, G-CSF)
- Severe: **allogenic bone marrow transplant (BMT)** — curative (★)
- If no donor: **anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) + ciclosporin** (immunosuppression)

---
## TOPIC 4: HAEMOLYTIC ANAEMIA**Definition:**
- Premature destruction of RBCs — normal RBC lifespan 120 days; in haemolysis significantly shorter
- Compensatory ↑ erythropoiesis (reticulocytosis)

**Classification:** (★)
| Type | Examples |
|---|---|
| Intravascular haemolysis | ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency, PNH, mechanical valves |
| Extravascular haemolysis | Hereditary spherocytosis, AIHA, sickle cell, thalassaemia |
| Intrinsic (intracorpuscular) | Hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, sickle cell, thalassaemia |
| Extrinsic (extracorpuscular) | AIHA, transfusion reactions, microangiopathic HA (TTP, HUS) |
**Laboratory Findings:** (★)
| Test | Result | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Hb | ↓ | RBC destruction |
| Reticulocyte count | **↑** | Compensatory erythropoiesis |
| Serum LDH | **↑** (★) | Released from lysed RBCs |
| Unconjugated bilirubin | ↑ | Hb breakdown → bilirubin |
| Haptoglobin | ↓ | Binds free Hb → consumed |
| Urobilinogen in urine | ↑ | — |
| Haemoglobinuria | Present (intravascular) | Free Hb in urine |
| PBF | Spherocytes / schistocytes / sickle cells depending on cause | — |
- Key: **↑ LDH + ↑ reticulocytes + ↓ haptoglobin + ↑ unconjugated bilirubin** = haemolytic picture (★)

---
## TOPIC 5: THALASSAEMIA**Etymology:** *Thalassa* (Greek) = sea | *Haima* = blood — first described in Mediterranean populations
**Definition:**
- Inherited disorders of **globin chain synthesis** leading to ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis
- Result: unstable or insufficient haemoglobin

**Normal Haemoglobin:**
- HbA (adult, major) = α₂β₂ — 95–97% of adult Hb
- HbA₂ = α₂δ₂ — 2–3%
- HbF (fetal) = α₂γ₂ — <1% in adults

**Types:** (★)
| Type | Defect | Genetics |
|---|---|---|
| α-thalassaemia | Deletion of α-globin genes | Chromosome 16 (HBA1/HBA2) |
| β-thalassaemia | Point mutations in β-globin gene | Chromosome 11 (HBB) |
**β-Thalassaemia Spectrum:** (★)
| Genotype | Disease | Features |
|---|---|---|
| β/β (normal) | — | Normal |
| β/β+ or β/β° | Thalassaemia trait (minor) | Mild microcytic anaemia, target cells, asymptomatic |
| β+/β° or β°/β° | Thalassaemia major (Cooley's anaemia) | Severe transfusion-dependent anaemia |
| Intermediate forms | Thalassaemia intermedia | Between minor and major |
**Thalassaemia Trait — Features:** (★)
- Mild microcytic hypochromic anaemia
- **Target cells (codocytes)** on PBF (★)
- ↑ HbA₂ (>3.5%) on Hb electrophoresis — diagnostic
- Common in Mediterranean, Middle East, SE Asia, sub-Saharan Africa
- Patients often asymptomatic; detected incidentally

**Thalassaemia Major — Features:** (★)
- Presents at 6 months (when HbF → HbA switch occurs and no functioning β-chains)
- Severe anaemia — transfusion dependent
- **Primary mechanism: defective globin chain synthesis** (★)
- Excess unpaired α-chains → precipitate → damage RBC membrane → ineffective erythropoiesis + haemolysis
- Hepatosplenomegaly (extramedullary haematopoiesis)
- Bone deformities: **frontal bossing, chipmunk facies** (marrow expansion)
- Iron overload from repeated transfusions → heart failure, liver cirrhosis, endocrinopathies
- PBF: severe microcytosis, hypochromia, target cells, nucleated RBCs, tear-drop cells

**Diagnosis:**
- Hb electrophoresis / HPLC (★)
- ↑ HbF, absent or ↓ HbA, ↑ HbA₂ (β-thal trait)
- DNA analysis for specific mutations
- Serum ferritin (iron overload monitoring)

**Treatment:**
- Trait: no treatment; genetic counselling
- Major: regular transfusions + **iron chelation** (desferrioxamine or deferasirox) + **allogenic BMT** (curative) (★)

---
## TOPIC 6: VITAMIN B12 DEFICIENCY & PERNICIOUS ANAEMIA**Definition:**
- B12 (cobalamin) deficiency → impaired DNA synthesis → megaloblastic anaemia + neurological damage
- **Pernicious anaemia** = autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells → loss of intrinsic factor (IF) → B12 malabsorption (★)

**B12 Absorption Pathway:** (★)
- Dietary B12 (meat, dairy, eggs) binds R-protein in stomach
- Gastric **parietal cells** secrete **intrinsic factor (IF)**
- B12–IF complex absorbed in **terminal ileum**
- Chronic atrophic gastritis → no parietal cells → no IF → no B12 absorption → pernicious anaemia

**Causes of B12 Deficiency:**
- Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune — most common in developed world) (★)
- Strict veganism / vegetarianism
- Gastrectomy (loss of parietal cells)
- Crohn's disease / ileal resection (loss of absorption site)
- Bacterial overgrowth (fish tapeworm — Diphyllobothrium latum)

**Clinical Features:**
- Macrocytic anaemia: fatigue, pallor, glossitis
- **Subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord (SACD)** — B12 needed for myelin synthesis (★)

 - Dorsal column loss: vibration, proprioception

- Lateral column loss: spastic weakness
- Peripheral neuropathy
- Psychiatric: depression, memory loss ("megaloblastic madness")

**Lab Findings:** (★)
| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Hb | ↓ |
| MCV | ↑ (macrocytic >100 fL) |
| PBF | Macro-ovalocytes, **hypersegmented neutrophils** (★) (>5 lobes) |
| Serum B12 | ↓ |
| Homocysteine | ↑ |
| Methylmalonic acid (MMA) | ↑ (specific for B12 deficiency, not folate) |
| Intrinsic factor antibodies | Positive in pernicious anaemia |
| Parietal cell antibodies | Positive (less specific) |
| Bone marrow | Hypercellular, megaloblasts, giant metamyelocytes |
**Treatment:**
- IM hydroxocobalamin injections (lifelong if pernicious anaemia) (★)
- Oral B12 if dietary deficiency

---
