---

# Part 1: Hepatitis Viruses

## 1. Introduction

Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver. Viral hepatitis is caused by a group of viruses that primarily target hepatocytes — liver cells. Despite being caused by completely unrelated viruses from different families, they all share the common clinical feature of hepatitis. Understanding their differences in transmission, natural history, chronicity, and prevention is essential for clinical practice. At MKU, hepatitis viruses appear consistently in MCQs testing transmission routes, diagnostic methods, and specific clinical features.

---

## 2. Overview — The Five Hepatitis Viruses

| Feature | HAV | HBV | HCV | HDV | HEV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Family | Picornaviridae | Hepadnaviridae | Flaviviridae | Deltaviridae | Hepeviridae |
| Genome | ssRNA | dsDNA (partial) | ssRNA | ssRNA | ssRNA |
| Envelope | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Transmission | Fecal-oral | Parenteral, sexual, vertical | Parenteral | Parenteral (needs HBV) | Fecal-oral |
| Chronicity | Never | Yes (5–10% adults) | Yes (75–85%) | Yes | Never (except immunocompromised) |
| Vaccine | Yes | Yes | No | HBV vaccine prevents | No licensed vaccine |
| Oncogenic | No | Yes — HCC | Yes — HCC | Yes | No |

---

## 3. Hepatitis A Virus (HAV)

### Classification
- **Family:** Picornaviridae
- **Genome:** Single-stranded positive-sense RNA
- **Non-enveloped** — survives in water, acidic environments, and on surfaces
- **Transmission:** Fecal-oral — contaminated food and water, poor sanitation

### Pathogenesis
- Ingested virus survives stomach acid
- Infects intestinal epithelial cells → enters portal circulation → reaches liver
- Infects hepatocytes — virus replicates in hepatocytes and is shed into bile → excreted in faeces
- Liver damage is primarily immune-mediated — cytotoxic T cells destroy infected hepatocytes

### Clinical Features
- **Incubation period:** 2–6 weeks
- Prodrome — fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, right upper quadrant pain
- Jaundice — appears after prodrome; tea-coloured urine, pale stools, pruritis
- Hepatomegaly and tenderness
- Self-limiting — complete recovery in most cases
- No chronic infection — ever
- Fulminant hepatitis — rare but life-threatening

### High-Risk Groups
- Children in developing countries — most infections subclinical
- Travellers to endemic areas
- Men who have sex with men
- Injection drug users

### Diagnosis — High Yield
- **IgM anti-HAV** — gold standard for acute infection; appears early, lasts 3–6 months
- **IgG anti-HAV** — indicates past infection or vaccination; persists lifelong
- **Detection of faecal HAV by immunoelectron microscopy** — research setting
- **Raised ALT and AST** — liver enzymes elevated; ALT more specific for hepatocyte damage

### Treatment
- No specific antiviral
- Supportive — rest, adequate nutrition, avoid hepatotoxic drugs and alcohol
- Hospitalization for severe cases

### Prevention
- **Improved sanitation and clean water** — most important
- **Handwashing** — especially food handlers
- **HAV vaccine** — inactivated; two doses; highly effective; recommended for travellers and high-risk groups
- **Passive immunization** — normal human immunoglobulin (HNIG) for post-exposure prophylaxis within 2 weeks

---

## 4. Hepatitis B Virus (HBV)

### Classification
- **Family:** Hepadnaviridae
- **Genome:** Partially double-stranded circular DNA — unique among human hepatitis viruses
- **Enveloped virus**
- **Replication:** Uses reverse transcriptase — unique for a DNA virus; HBV replicates through an RNA intermediate

### Transmission — High Yield
HBV is present in blood, semen, vaginal secretions, saliva, breast milk, and other body fluids.

- **Parenteral** — blood transfusion, sharing needles, needlestick injuries
- **Sexual contact** — highly efficient sexually transmitted infection
- **Vertical transmission** — mother to child during delivery (most important route globally)
- **Horizontal transmission** — child-to-child in endemic areas via minor skin breaks

### Virology — Key Antigens and Antibodies

| Marker | Meaning |
|---|---|
| HBsAg (surface antigen) | Present in active infection — acute or chronic; first marker to appear |
| Anti-HBs | Antibody to surface antigen; indicates immunity — from vaccination or recovery |
| HBeAg (e antigen) | Marker of active viral replication; high infectivity |
| Anti-HBe | Seroconversion from HBeAg; lower replication, lower infectivity |
| HBcAg (core antigen) | Not detectable in serum — only in liver tissue |
| Anti-HBc IgM | Acute HBV infection |
| Anti-HBc IgG | Past or chronic infection |
| HBV DNA | Viral load — measures active replication |

**Window period:**
- HBsAg disappears but anti-HBs not yet detectable
- Only anti-HBc IgM positive — the only marker of infection during window period

### Natural History

**Acute HBV infection:**
- Incubation: 1–6 months
- 70% subclinical or mild
- 30% symptomatic hepatitis — jaundice, malaise, anorexia
- Less than 1% fulminant hepatitis

**Outcomes after acute infection:**
- 95% of immunocompetent adults — complete recovery, virus cleared, anti-HBs develops
- 5% of adults — progress to chronic infection
- 90% of neonates infected at birth — chronic infection (immature immune system)
- 30–50% of children infected aged 1–5 — chronic infection

**Chronic HBV infection:**
- HBsAg positive for more than 6 months
- Phases: immune tolerant → immune active → inactive carrier → reactivation
- Complications: liver cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)
- HBV causes HCC through: chromosomal integration, HBx protein activating oncogenes, chronic inflammation

### Diagnosis
- **HBsAg** — first marker; confirms infection
- **Anti-HBc IgM** — acute infection
- **HBeAg and HBV DNA** — active replication, infectivity
- **Liver function tests** — ALT/AST elevated
- **Liver biopsy** — assess fibrosis and inflammation in chronic disease

### Treatment
- **Acute HBV** — supportive; no antivirals unless fulminant
- **Chronic HBV:**
  - **Tenofovir** — first-line nucleotide analogue; inhibits HBV reverse transcriptase
  - **Entecavir** — first-line nucleoside analogue
  - **Pegylated IFN-α** — 48-week course; induces immune response; HBeAg seroconversion
  - Lamivudine, adefovir — older agents, high resistance rates

### Prevention
- **HBV vaccine** — recombinant HBsAg; 3 doses (0, 1, 6 months); highly effective; part of national immunisation schedules
- **Neonatal vaccination** — within 24 hours of birth + HBIG for babies of HBsAg-positive mothers
- **HBIG (Hepatitis B Immunoglobulin)** — passive immunization for post-exposure prophylaxis
- **Safe injection practices** — needle exchange programmes
- **Blood screening** — all donated blood screened for HBsAg
- **Safe sex** — condom use

---

## 5. Hepatitis C Virus (HCV)

### Classification
- **Family:** Flaviviridae
- **Genome:** Single-stranded positive-sense RNA
- **Enveloped virus**
- **Highly variable** — 7 genotypes; high mutation rate due to error-prone RNA polymerase

### Transmission
- **Parenteral** — sharing needles (most common in developed world), blood transfusion (before screening), needlestick injuries
- **Sexual transmission** — less efficient than HBV; increases with HIV co-infection
- **Vertical transmission** — less common than HBV
- **NOT transmitted** by fecal-oral route

### Natural History
- Incubation: 2–12 weeks
- Acute infection often asymptomatic — 80% no symptoms
- **75–85% progress to chronic infection** — highest chronicity rate of all hepatitis viruses
- Chronic HCV → cirrhosis (20–30% over 20 years) → hepatocellular carcinoma
- HCV is a leading indication for liver transplantation globally

### Diagnosis
- **Anti-HCV antibody** — screening test; ELISA; appears 8–12 weeks after infection
- **HCV RNA by PCR** — confirms active infection; used in window period and to monitor treatment
- **HCV genotype** — guides treatment duration and drug choice
- No antigen test widely used clinically

### Treatment
- **Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs)** — revolutionary; cure rates over 95%
  - Sofosbuvir (NS5B polymerase inhibitor)
  - Ledipasvir, Daclatasvir (NS5A inhibitors)
  - Simeprevir (NS3/4A protease inhibitor)
  - Combinations: Sofosbuvir/Ledipasvir, Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir
- **Pegylated IFN-α + Ribavirin** — older regimen; largely replaced by DAAs

### Prevention
- **No vaccine available** — high mutation rate makes vaccine development difficult
- Needle exchange programmes
- Blood screening
- Safe sex practices
- Testing and treatment of infected individuals — reduces transmission

---

## 6. Hepatitis E Virus (HEV)

### Classification
- **Family:** Hepeviridae
- **Genome:** Single-stranded positive-sense RNA
- **Non-enveloped**
- **Transmission:** Fecal-oral — contaminated water; zoonotic (pigs, deer)

### Clinical Features
- Self-limiting acute hepatitis — similar to HAV
- No chronic infection in immunocompetent
- **Special feature:** Very high mortality in pregnant women — up to 20–25% in third trimester
- Causes fulminant hepatic failure in pregnancy — most important clinical fact

### Diagnosis
- Anti-HEV IgM — acute infection
- HEV RNA by PCR — most sensitive

### Prevention
- Clean water and sanitation
- HEV vaccine — licensed in China; not widely available

---

---

# Part 2: Oncogenic Viruses

## 1. Introduction

Oncogenic viruses are viruses capable of causing cancer in humans. They account for approximately 15–20% of all human cancers worldwide. Understanding viral oncogenesis is important both clinically and scientifically — it explains the geographic distribution of certain cancers, provides targets for cancer prevention through vaccines, and illuminates the molecular mechanisms of cancer in general. At MKU, oncogenic viruses appear in MCQs and one essay question — comparing normal cells with cancer cells.

---

## 2. Mechanisms of Viral Carcinogenesis

Viruses cause cancer through several distinct mechanisms:

### Direct Mechanisms

**1. Integration of viral DNA into host genome:**
- Viral DNA integrates near or within host proto-oncogenes or tumour suppressor genes
- Disrupts normal gene regulation
- Example: HBV integration near oncogenes → HCC

**2. Viral oncoproteins:**
- Viral proteins directly inactivate tumour suppressor proteins
- **HPV E6 protein** — binds and degrades p53 tumour suppressor
- **HPV E7 protein** — binds and inactivates Rb (retinoblastoma) protein
- p53 and Rb are the two most important tumour suppressor proteins in human cells
- Loss of both → uncontrolled cell proliferation

**3. Insertional mutagenesis:**
- Viral genome inserts next to a cellular proto-oncogene
- Viral promoter drives overexpression of the proto-oncogene → oncogene
- Example: HTLV-1 Tax protein activates NF-κB → promotes T cell proliferation

**4. B cell immortalization:**
- EBV immortalizes B lymphocytes — they proliferate indefinitely
- Combined with chromosomal translocation → malignant lymphoma

### Indirect Mechanisms

**5. Chronic inflammation:**
- Chronic viral infection → persistent inflammation → mutagenic environment
- Reactive oxygen and nitrogen species damage DNA
- Example: HBV and HCV → chronic hepatitis → cirrhosis → HCC

**6. Immunosuppression:**
- HIV destroys CD4+ T cells → severe immunosuppression
- Impaired immune surveillance → other oncogenic viruses cause cancer unopposed
- Example: HIV → KS (HHV-8), lymphoma (EBV), cervical cancer (HPV)

---

## 3. Normal Cell vs Cancer Cell — High Yield Essay Topic

| Feature | Normal Cell | Cancer Cell |
|---|---|---|
| Growth control | Controlled by growth factors and cell cycle checkpoints | Uncontrolled — ignores growth signals |
| Cell cycle | Regulated by cyclins, CDKs, p53, Rb | Cell cycle checkpoints bypassed |
| Contact inhibition | Stops dividing when touching other cells | Loses contact inhibition — piles up |
| Apoptosis | Undergoes programmed death when damaged | Resists apoptosis — p53 inactivated |
| Differentiation | Fully differentiated — performs specific function | Poorly differentiated — loses normal function |
| Telomeres | Shorten with each division — limits lifespan | Telomerase activated — immortal |
| Angiogenesis | Normal vascular supply | Induces new blood vessel formation (angiogenesis) via VEGF |
| Invasion | Stays within tissue boundaries | Invades surrounding tissues |
| Metastasis | Does not spread to distant sites | Spreads via blood and lymphatics |
| Antigenic profile | Normal surface antigens | Expresses tumour-associated antigens |
| Energy metabolism | Oxidative phosphorylation | Warburg effect — aerobic glycolysis |

---

## 4. Key Oncogenic Viruses and Their Associated Cancers

### Human Papillomavirus (HPV)

- **Family:** Papillomaviridae
- **Genome:** dsDNA, non-enveloped
- **Oncogenic types:** HPV 16 and HPV 18 — cause 70% of cervical cancers
- **Low-risk types:** HPV 6 and 11 — cause genital warts (condylomata acuminata)

**Mechanism of oncogenesis:**
- HPV infects basal epithelial cells of cervical transformation zone
- E6 protein → degrades p53
- E7 protein → inactivates Rb protein
- Loss of p53 and Rb → cells cannot arrest or undergo apoptosis → uncontrolled proliferation
- Accumulation of further mutations → invasive carcinoma

**Associated cancers:**
- Cervical carcinoma — most important
- Vulvar, vaginal, penile carcinoma
- Anal carcinoma
- Oropharyngeal carcinoma (base of tongue, tonsil) — increasing incidence

**Prevention:**
- **HPV vaccine** — Gardasil (types 6, 11, 16, 18) or Cervarix (types 16, 18)
- Most effective when given before sexual debut
- **Cervical screening** — Pap smear detects precancerous CIN lesions
- Condom use — reduces but does not eliminate transmission

### Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) — HHV-4

- **Associated cancers:**
  - **Burkitt's lymphoma** — most common childhood cancer in equatorial Africa; jaw mass; t(8;14) translocation activating c-myc oncogene; EBV in 95% of endemic cases
  - **Nasopharyngeal carcinoma** — especially in Southern China; EBV in virtually all cases
  - **Hodgkin's lymphoma** — EBV in 40–50% of cases
  - **Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD)**
  - **Primary CNS lymphoma** — in AIDS

### Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) and Hepatitis C Virus (HCV)

- Both cause **hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)**
- HBV — direct oncogenesis via integration and HBx protein; also chronic inflammation
- HCV — primarily through chronic inflammation and cirrhosis
- HCC is the third most common cause of cancer death worldwide
- Prevention: HBV vaccine, DAAs for HCV

### Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) — Kaposi's Sarcoma Herpesvirus (KSHV)

- Causes **Kaposi's sarcoma** — vascular tumour; purple/red skin lesions
- Three forms:
  - Classic KS — elderly Mediterranean men
  - Endemic KS — Sub-Saharan Africa
  - AIDS-related KS — most common AIDS-defining malignancy; aggressive
- Also causes: primary effusion lymphoma, multicentric Castleman disease
- Treatment: ART for AIDS-related KS (restores immune control), chemotherapy for disseminated disease

### HTLV-1 (Human T-cell Lymphotropic Virus Type 1)

- **Family:** Retroviridae
- **Associated cancer:** Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATL)
- Transmitted by: sexual contact, blood, breast milk
- Endemic in: Japan, Caribbean, Sub-Saharan Africa
- Tax protein activates NF-κB → T cell proliferation → lymphoma
- Also causes: HTLV-1-associated myelopathy (tropical spastic paraparesis)

### Merkel Cell Polyomavirus (MCPyV)

- Causes **Merkel cell carcinoma** — rare aggressive skin cancer in elderly and immunocompromised

---

---

# Part 3: Paramyxoviruses — Measles, Mumps, RSV, Parainfluenza, and Rubella

## 1. Introduction

Paramyxoviruses are a family of enveloped RNA viruses that cause some of the most important childhood infections in history — measles, mumps, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Rubella, though technically a togavirus, is traditionally grouped with these in clinical teaching because of its similar epidemiology and the MMR vaccine. These viruses caused massive childhood morbidity and mortality before vaccination, and remain important in unvaccinated populations. At MKU they appear primarily in MCQs testing clinical features, vaccines, and distinguishing features of each virus.

---

## 2. General Features of Paramyxoviruses

- **Family:** Paramyxoviridae
- **Genome:** Single-stranded negative-sense RNA — non-segmented
- **Enveloped virus**
- **Two key surface glycoproteins:**
  - **Haemagglutinin-neuraminidase (HN)** — attachment and neuraminidase activity
  - **Fusion protein (F)** — mediates cell-to-cell fusion → multinucleated giant cells (syncytia) formation — characteristic cytopathic effect
- Transmitted primarily by respiratory droplets

---

## 3. Measles Virus

### Key Facts
- **Genus:** Morbillivirus
- **Only one serotype** — effective lifelong immunity after infection or vaccination
- **Receptor:** CD46 and SLAM (signalling lymphocyte activation molecule) on immune cells
- **Most contagious human virus known** — R0 of 12–18

### Pathogenesis
- Inhaled droplets → infects respiratory epithelium and regional lymph nodes
- Primary viremia → spreads to lymphoid tissue throughout body
- Secondary viremia → skin, respiratory tract, CNS, eyes
- Giant cell (syncytia) formation in respiratory epithelium — Warthin-Finkeldey giant cells in lymphoid tissue
- Rash caused by immune-mediated damage to skin blood vessels — not direct viral effect

### Clinical Features
- **Incubation:** 10–14 days
- **Prodrome (3 Cs):** Cough, Coryza, Conjunctivitis — plus high fever
- **Koplik's spots** — pathognomonic; white spots on bright red buccal mucosa opposite lower molars; appear 1–2 days before rash
- **Rash** — maculopapular; starts behind ears and hairline → spreads downward to face, trunk, limbs; lasts 4–7 days
- **Fever** — high; may reach 40°C

### Complications
- **Otitis media** — most common complication
- **Pneumonia** — most common cause of death; primary viral or secondary bacterial
- **Encephalitis** — 1 in 1000 cases; acute post-infectious demyelinating encephalitis
- **Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE)** — rare, fatal; occurs years after measles; progressive CNS degeneration; caused by persistent measles virus in brain
- **Measles inclusion body encephalitis** — in immunocompromised
- **Vitamin A deficiency** worsens measles severity — supplement routinely in developing countries
- **Immunosuppression** — measles causes lymphopenia and immune suppression lasting weeks → window for secondary infections

### Diagnosis
- Clinical — characteristic prodrome and rash
- IgM serology — acute infection
- PCR — from throat, urine, blood
- Viral culture

### Treatment
- Supportive
- **Vitamin A supplementation** — reduces mortality in developing countries
- Ribavirin — for severe measles in immunocompromised

### Vaccine
- **MMR vaccine** — live attenuated; given at 12–15 months and 4–6 years
- Highly effective — one dose 93% protective, two doses 97% protective
- Contraindicated in immunocompromised and pregnancy

---

## 4. Mumps Virus

### Key Facts
- **Genus:** Rubulavirus
- **Receptor:** Sialic acid on ductal epithelial cells — explains tropism for glands
- Transmitted by respiratory droplets and saliva

### Clinical Features
- **Incubation:** 14–25 days
- **Parotitis** — painful swelling of parotid glands; bilateral in 70%; pathognomonic of mumps
- Fever, malaise, headache
- Submandibular and sublingual gland swelling possible

### Complications
- **Orchitis** — most important; occurs in 20–30% of post-pubertal males; usually unilateral; can cause testicular atrophy; rarely causes sterility
- **Oophoritis** — in post-pubertal females
- **Aseptic meningitis** — most common CNS complication; usually benign
- **Encephalitis** — rare but serious
- **Pancreatitis** — elevated amylase
- **Sensorineural hearing loss** — rare but important

### Diagnosis
- Clinical — bilateral parotitis
- Serology — IgM anti-mumps
- PCR — from saliva, urine, CSF

### Treatment
- Supportive only
- Scrotal support and analgesics for orchitis

### Vaccine
- MMR — live attenuated; same schedule as measles

---

## 5. Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)

### Key Facts
- **Genus:** Pneumovirus
- **Most important cause of lower respiratory tract infection in infants and young children worldwide**
- Two subtypes — A and B; both circulate simultaneously
- No haemagglutinin or neuraminidase — distinguished from other paramyxoviruses
- **Fusion protein (F)** — mediates syncytia formation; major target of immune response and therapeutics
- Transmitted by respiratory droplets and direct contact with secretions

### Pathogenesis
- Infects upper respiratory epithelium first
- Spreads to lower respiratory tract — bronchioles
- F protein causes cell fusion → syncytia formation → airway obstruction
- Immune response contributes to inflammation and bronchospasm
- Narrow bronchioles of infants → severe disease with obstruction

### Clinical Features

**In infants and young children (most severe):**
- **Bronchiolitis** — most characteristic; wheeze, tachypnoea, hyperinflation, feeding difficulty
- **Pneumonia** — fever, cough, respiratory distress
- Peak age: 2–6 months
- Most common cause of hospitalisation in infants in winter

**In older children and adults:**
- Common cold-like illness — mild upper respiratory tract infection
- More severe in elderly and immunocompromised

### High-Risk Groups for Severe RSV

- Premature infants
- Infants with congenital heart disease
- Infants with chronic lung disease
- Immunocompromised
- Elderly

### Diagnosis
- **Rapid antigen detection** — nasopharyngeal swab; quick; used in clinical setting
- **PCR** — most sensitive
- **Viral culture** — shows syncytia formation — characteristic
- **Direct immunofluorescence** — from nasopharyngeal aspirate

### Treatment
- **Supportive** — oxygen, hydration, feeding support
- **Ribavirin** — inhaled; limited evidence; used in severe cases in immunocompromised
- **Bronchodilators** — limited benefit in bronchiolitis

### Prevention
- **Palivizumab** — monoclonal antibody against RSV F protein; given monthly during RSV season to high-risk infants; passive immunization
- **Nirsevimab** — newer long-acting monoclonal antibody; single dose; now recommended for all infants
- RSV vaccines — now available for adults (Abrysvo, mRESVIA); approved 2023
- Handwashing and contact precautions in hospitals

---

## 6. Rubella Virus

### Classification
- **Family:** Togaviridae — not a paramyxovirus; grouped here clinically
- **Genus:** Rubivirus
- **Genome:** Single-stranded positive-sense RNA
- **Enveloped**
- Transmitted by respiratory droplets

### Clinical Features — Postnatal Rubella
- **Incubation:** 14–21 days
- Mild illness in children — low-grade fever, lymphadenopathy (especially suboccipital and postauricular), mild rash
- **Rash** — pink maculopapular; starts on face → spreads downward; fades within 3 days
- Arthralgia — common in adult women
- Forchheimer spots — petechiae on soft palate — rare but characteristic

### Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) — Most Important Feature

Rubella infection in pregnancy, especially first trimester, causes severe fetal damage.

**Mechanism:** Rubella infects placental endothelium → crosses to fetus → infects fetal cells → disrupts organogenesis

**Risk of CRS by trimester:**
- First trimester — 85% risk of fetal abnormality
- Second trimester — 25% risk
- After 20 weeks — risk very low

**Classic triad of CRS:**
- **Cataracts** — most characteristic eye finding
- **Cardiac defects** — patent ductus arteriosus (most common), pulmonary artery stenosis, VSD
- **Sensorineural deafness** — most common single defect

**Other features of CRS:**
- Microcephaly
- Mental retardation
- Retinopathy (salt and pepper retinopathy)
- Hepatosplenomegaly
- Thrombocytopenic purpura — blueberry muffin rash
- Glaucoma
- Bone lesions

### Diagnosis
- **IgM serology** — acute rubella infection
- **PCR** — from throat, urine, blood
- **Prenatal diagnosis** — PCR on amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling

### Treatment
- No specific antiviral
- Supportive

### Prevention
- **MMR vaccine** — most important prevention strategy
- Vaccination of all children and seronegative women of childbearing age
- Contraindicated in pregnancy — live vaccine
- Screen all pregnant women for rubella immunity in first antenatal visit

---

---

# Part 4: Arboviruses

## 1. Introduction

Arboviruses (Arthropod-Borne Viruses) are a diverse group of viruses transmitted to humans through the bites of arthropod vectors — primarily mosquitoes and ticks. They belong to multiple unrelated viral families but share the common feature of transmission by arthropod vectors. They cause a wide spectrum of diseases — from mild febrile illness to haemorrhagic fever, encephalitis, and severe congenital defects. Arboviruses are particularly relevant in tropical and subtropical regions including sub-Saharan Africa and Kenya. At MKU they appear primarily in MCQs.

---

## 2. Key Arboviruses — Overview

| Virus | Family | Vector | Geographic Distribution | Key Disease |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dengue | Flaviviridae | Aedes aegypti | Tropics and subtropics globally | Dengue fever, DHF, DSS |
| Yellow Fever | Flaviviridae | Aedes aegypti | Africa, South America | Yellow fever |
| Zika | Flaviviridae | Aedes aegypti | Americas, Africa, Pacific | Zika fever, microcephaly |
| West Nile | Flaviviridae | Culex mosquitoes | Africa, Middle East, Europe, Americas | West Nile fever, encephalitis |
| Chikungunya | Togaviridae | Aedes aegypti, Aedes albopictus | Africa, Asia, Americas | Chikungunya fever |
| Rift Valley Fever | Phenuiviridae | Aedes, Culex mosquitoes | Sub-Saharan Africa | Fever, hepatitis, haemorrhage |
| Japanese Encephalitis | Flaviviridae | Culex mosquitoes | Asia | Encephalitis |

---

## 3. Dengue Virus

### Classification
- **Family:** Flaviviridae
- **Genome:** ssRNA positive-sense
- **Enveloped**
- **Four serotypes** — DENV-1, 2, 3, 4; infection with one confers lifelong immunity to that serotype but not others
- **Vector:** Aedes aegypti mosquito — bites during daytime

### Pathogenesis
- Mosquito bite → virus deposited in skin → infects dendritic cells
- Spreads to regional lymph nodes → viremia → disseminates to liver, spleen, bone marrow, endothelium
- **Antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE)** — critical concept:
  - After first infection, antibodies form against that serotype
  - If infected by a different serotype, cross-reactive antibodies bind virus but cannot neutralize it
  - Instead facilitate viral entry into Fc receptor-bearing monocytes → higher viral loads → more severe disease
  - This explains why second dengue infection with a different serotype causes DHF/DSS

### Clinical Syndromes

**Classic Dengue Fever (Break-bone fever):**
- Incubation: 4–10 days
- Sudden high fever — biphasic (saddle-back) pattern
- Severe headache, retro-orbital pain
- Severe myalgia and arthralgia — break-bone fever
- Maculopapular rash — appears 3–4 days after fever onset
- Lymphadenopathy
- Leukopenia and thrombocytopenia on blood count
- Self-limiting — recovery in 7–10 days

**Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever (DHF):**
- Occurs with second infection (different serotype) — ADE mechanism
- Thrombocytopenia — below 100,000/mm³
- Evidence of plasma leakage — rising haematocrit, pleural effusion, ascites
- Haemorrhagic manifestations — petechiae, purpura, mucosal bleeding

**Dengue Shock Syndrome (DSS):**
- Severe plasma leakage → hypovolaemic shock
- Life-threatening
- Rapid deterioration — circulatory failure

### Diagnosis
- **NS1 antigen** — detectable in first 5 days; rapid test
- **IgM serology** — appears after day 5
- **RT-PCR** — most sensitive in first 5 days; detects viral RNA
- **FBC** — leukopenia, thrombocytopenia

### Treatment
- No specific antiviral
- Supportive — IV fluids, careful fluid management
- Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs — worsen bleeding
- Platelet transfusion — only for severe bleeding

### Prevention
- **Dengvaxia vaccine** — only for seropositive individuals aged 9–45; risk of severe disease in seronegative recipients
- **Mosquito control** — eliminate breeding sites (stagnant water), insecticides
- **Personal protection** — repellents, long sleeves, bed nets

---

## 4. Yellow Fever Virus

### Classification
- **Family:** Flaviviridae
- **Vector:** Aedes aegypti (urban) and forest mosquitoes (sylvatic)
- **Three transmission cycles:**
  - Sylvatic (jungle) — forest monkeys to humans via forest mosquitoes
  - Intermediate (savannah) — semi-domestic mosquitoes in Africa
  - Urban — Aedes aegypti human-to-human

### Clinical Features
- **Incubation:** 3–6 days
- **Phase 1 (Infection):** Fever, headache, myalgia, nausea — 3–4 days
- **Phase 2 (Remission):** Symptoms improve — 24–48 hours
- **Phase 3 (Intoxication)** — occurs in 15% of patients:
  - **Jaundice** — liver failure; the yellow in yellow fever
  - **Haemorrhage** — black vomit (haematemesis), bleeding gums, epistaxis
  - **Renal failure**
  - **Bradycardia despite high fever** — Faget's sign; characteristic
  - **Case fatality rate:** 20–50% in this phase

### Diagnosis
- **Serology** — IgM anti-yellow fever
- **RT-PCR** — acute phase
- **Liver histology** — Councilman bodies (eosinophilic degeneration of hepatocytes); midzonal necrosis

### Treatment
- Supportive only
- No specific antiviral

### Prevention
- **Yellow fever vaccine** — live attenuated (17D strain); single dose; highly effective; lifelong protection
- Required for entry to many countries — international certificate of vaccination
- Mosquito control

---

## 5. Zika Virus

### Classification
- **Family:** Flaviviridae
- **Vector:** Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus
- **Also transmitted by:** Sexual contact (unique among arboviruses — persists in semen), blood transfusion, vertical transmission

### Clinical Features
- Most infections (80%) asymptomatic
- Mild fever, rash, arthralgia, conjunctivitis — self-limiting

### Most Important Clinical Associations — High Yield

**Congenital Zika Syndrome:**
- Zika in pregnancy → crosses placenta → infects fetal neurons
- **Microcephaly** — most characteristic; severe brain underdevelopment
- Cortical malformations
- Eye defects
- Joint contractures
- Most severe with first trimester infection

**Guillain-Barré Syndrome:**
- Post-infectious immune-mediated polyneuropathy
- Ascending flaccid paralysis
- Follows Zika infection by 2–4 weeks

### Diagnosis
- **RT-PCR** — from blood, urine (urine positive longer than blood), saliva
- **IgM serology** — cross-reacts with other flaviviruses (dengue, yellow fever)

### Treatment
- No specific antiviral
- Supportive

### Prevention
- Mosquito control
- Condom use — prevents sexual transmission
- Pregnant women advised to avoid travel to Zika-endemic areas
- No vaccine available

---

## 6. Chikungunya Virus

### Classification
- **Family:** Togaviridae (same family as rubella — but an arbovirus)
- **Genus:** Alphavirus
- **Vector:** Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus

### Clinical Features
- **Incubation:** 2–12 days
- High fever — sudden onset
- **Severe arthralgia and arthritis** — most characteristic feature; affects multiple joints; can persist for months to years
- Maculopapular rash
- Headache, myalgia
- Name means "that which bends up" in Makonde language — describes the stooped posture from joint pain

### Diagnosis
- RT-PCR — acute phase (first 5 days)
- IgM serology — after day 5

### Treatment
- Supportive
- NSAIDs for arthralgia
- No specific antiviral

### Prevention
- Mosquito control
- Personal protection
- No licensed vaccine

---

## 7. West Nile Virus

### Classification
- **Family:** Flaviviridae
- **Vector:** Culex mosquitoes (unlike dengue and Zika which use Aedes)
- **Reservoir:** Birds — mosquitoes transmit from birds to humans; humans are dead-end hosts

### Clinical Features
- 80% asymptomatic
- 20% — West Nile fever: mild febrile illness, rash, lymphadenopathy
- Less than 1% — **neuroinvasive disease:**
  - West Nile meningitis
  - West Nile encephalitis
  - Acute flaccid paralysis — polio-like; due to anterior horn cell infection

### High-Risk for Neuroinvasive Disease

- Elderly
- Immunocompromised
- Organ transplant recipients

### Diagnosis
- IgM in CSF — confirms neuroinvasive disease
- RT-PCR — blood or CSF

### Treatment
- Supportive
- No specific antiviral or vaccine for humans

---

# Vaccines & Antivirals, Rabies, CMV & EBV, Adenovirus & Enteroviruses
## High-Yield Revision Notes

**Institution:** Mount Kenya University — School of Medicine & Surgery

**Unit:** MBMM 3300 — Medical Virology and Mycology

**Level:** MBChB Year 3

---

### Papers & Examinations Covered

| Exam | Date | Paper |
|---|---|---|
| Main Exam | January 2022 | MBMM 3300 Paper 1 |
| Main Exam | February 2021 | MBMM 3300 Paper 2 |
| Main Exam | July 2019 | MBMM 3300 Paper 2 |
| Main Exam | January 2023 | MBMM 3300 Paper 2 |
| End of Term CAT | December 2020 | MBMM 3333 Medical Virology |
| CAT II | 2018/2019 | MBMM 3233 Medical Virology |

---

### Topics Covered

- Vaccines and Antivirals — types, mechanisms, OPV vs IPV, selective toxicity, stages of antiviral action
- Rabies Virus — structure, pathogenesis, clinical features, post-exposure prophylaxis
- CMV and EBV — structure, pathogenesis, congenital infection, oncogenesis, treatment
- Adenovirus and Enteroviruses — structure, diseases, transmission, prevention, encephalitis

---

---

# Part 1: Vaccines and Antivirals

## 1. Introduction

Vaccines and antiviral drugs are the two primary strategies for controlling viral infections. Vaccines work by preparing the immune system before infection occurs — they are preventive. Antiviral drugs work by interfering with specific steps in the viral replication cycle — they are therapeutic. Both strategies depend on understanding viral structure, replication, and the host immune response. These topics are among the most consistently examined at MKU, appearing in essays across virtually every past paper, particularly questions on OPV vs IPV, active vs passive immunization, and the mechanism of selective toxicity of antivirals.

---

## 2. Vaccines

### What is a Vaccine

A vaccine is a biological preparation that induces active immunity against a specific pathogen by stimulating the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells without causing the disease itself.

### Mechanism of Protection

1. Vaccine antigen is administered
2. Antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages) process the antigen
3. Presented to CD4+ T-helper cells via MHC class II
4. T-helper cells activate B cells → differentiate into plasma cells
5. Plasma cells produce specific antibodies against the viral antigen
6. CD8+ cytotoxic T cells also activated — important for live vaccines
7. Long-lived memory B and T cells formed
8. On exposure to real virus — rapid, amplified secondary immune response
9. Virus neutralized before disease can develop

### Types of Vaccines

**1. Live Attenuated Vaccines**
- Contain weakened but living virus — reduced virulence, retained antigenicity
- Produced by: repeated passage of virus in non-human cells until it loses ability to cause disease in humans
- Advantages:
  - Strongest and most durable immunity — mimics natural infection
  - Both humoral and cell-mediated immunity induced
  - Single dose often sufficient
  - Mucosal immunity produced (especially important for gut/respiratory viruses)
- Disadvantages:
  - Risk of reversion to virulence — attenuated virus can mutate back
  - Cannot be given to immunocompromised patients — can cause disease
  - Requires cold chain — heat sensitive
  - Cannot be given in pregnancy
- Examples: OPV (oral polio), MMR (measles, mumps, rubella), Yellow fever vaccine, Varicella vaccine, LAIV (live attenuated influenza)

**2. Inactivated (Killed) Vaccines**
- Contain killed virus — treated with heat, formalin, or beta-propiolactone
- Virus cannot replicate but antigens are preserved
- Advantages:
  - Cannot cause disease — safer
  - Can be given to immunocompromised patients
  - Stable — does not revert to virulence
- Disadvantages:
  - Weaker immunity — mainly humoral, less cell-mediated
  - Multiple doses required (boosters needed)
  - Adjuvant often needed to boost response
  - No mucosal immunity
- Examples: IPV (injected polio), inactivated influenza vaccine, Hepatitis A vaccine, Rabies vaccine

**3. Subunit Vaccines**
- Contain only specific viral proteins — not whole virus
- Examples: Hepatitis B vaccine (HBsAg), HPV vaccine (L1 capsid protein)
- Very safe — no viral genetic material
- Requires adjuvant and boosters

**4. Toxoid Vaccines**
- Not strictly viral — used for bacterial toxins
- Inactivated toxin — cannot cause disease but induces antitoxin antibodies

**5. mRNA Vaccines**
- Deliver mRNA encoding viral antigen into host cells
- Host cells produce the antigen → immune response
- Examples: COVID-19 vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna)
- Advantages: rapid production, no live virus needed

---

### OPV vs IPV — The Most Examined Vaccine Comparison

This comparison has appeared in essay form multiple times at MKU.

| Feature | OPV (Oral Polio Vaccine) | IPV (Inactivated Polio Vaccine) |
|---|---|---|
| Type | Live attenuated | Killed/inactivated |
| Route | Oral (swallowed) | Injected (intramuscular) |
| Developed by | Albert Sabin | Jonas Salk |
| Immunity type | Humoral + cell-mediated + mucosal (gut IgA) | Humoral only |
| Herd immunity | Yes — vaccine virus shed in stool, spreads to contacts | No — does not spread |
| Dose | Single dose effective | Multiple doses required |
| Cost | Cheaper | More expensive |
| Risk | Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) — rare but real | No risk of VAPP |
| Use in immunocompromised | Contraindicated — can cause disease | Safe |
| Cold chain | Required | Required |
| Why some countries prefer IPV | Eliminate risk of VAPP, especially in countries with low polio burden | Safer for immunocompromised populations |

**Why OPV produces better gut immunity:**
- OPV is swallowed → replicates in gut epithelium → stimulates local mucosal IgA production
- Gut IgA blocks poliovirus entry at the primary site of infection
- IPV injected → only systemic IgG produced → no gut mucosal immunity
- This is why OPV is better at preventing transmission — it blocks infection at the gut

**Why some countries prefer IPV:**
- Risk of VAPP — approximately 1 in 2.4 million doses causes vaccine-associated paralysis
- Countries that have already eliminated wild poliovirus use IPV to avoid the risk of introducing vaccine-derived poliovirus into a susceptible population

---

### Active vs Passive Immunization — High Yield

| Feature | Active Immunization | Passive Immunization |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Stimulating the host immune system to produce its own antibodies | Administering pre-formed antibodies directly |
| Onset | Slow — days to weeks | Immediate — within hours |
| Duration | Long-lasting — months to years (memory cells) | Short-lived — weeks (antibodies degraded) |
| Source | Vaccine or natural infection | Human or animal serum, immunoglobulins |
| Memory | Yes — immunological memory formed | No memory cells produced |
| Use | Prevention before exposure | Treatment after exposure, or in immunocompromised |
| Examples | All standard vaccines | Rabies immunoglobulin, tetanus immunoglobulin, HNIG, anti-D |

**How an attenuated vaccine protects a child:**
1. Attenuated virus administered — cannot cause disease in immunocompetent child
2. Virus replicates minimally — enough to stimulate immune response
3. B cells produce antibodies against viral antigens
4. Memory B and T cells formed
5. On exposure to wild virus — memory cells activated rapidly
6. Large amounts of antibody produced within days — neutralize virus before disease develops
7. Child is protected

---

## 3. Antiviral Drugs

### Introduction

Antiviral drugs work by targeting specific steps in the viral replication cycle. Unlike antibiotics, antivirals must be selectively toxic — they must inhibit viral replication without significantly harming host cells. This selectivity is achieved by targeting viral enzymes or processes that are unique to the virus or significantly different from host cell equivalents.

### The Viral Replication Cycle and Drug Target Sites

Antiviral drugs can target any of the following stages:

**Stage 1: Attachment/Adsorption**
- Target: viral spike — host receptor interaction
- Drugs: Maraviroc (blocks CCR5 co-receptor — HIV), Monoclonal antibodies against viral spikes

**Stage 2: Penetration and Fusion**
- Target: membrane fusion
- Drugs: Enfuvirtide/Fuzeon (blocks HIV gp41 fusion), Amantadine (blocks influenza M2 ion channel — prevents uncoating)

**Stage 3: Uncoating**
- Target: release of viral genome inside the cell
- Drugs: Amantadine, Rimantadine (influenza M2 channel blockers)

**Stage 4: Replication of Viral Genome**
- Target: viral polymerases — most important drug target stage
- Drugs:
  - NRTIs — Zidovudine, Tenofovir, Lamivudine (HIV reverse transcriptase)
  - NNRTIs — Nevirapine, Efavirenz (HIV reverse transcriptase)
  - Acyclovir triphosphate (HSV DNA polymerase)
  - Ganciclovir (CMV DNA polymerase)
  - Sofosbuvir (HCV RNA polymerase)
  - Oseltamivir — technically targets release but also reduces replication efficiency

**Stage 5: Transcription and Translation**
- Less commonly targeted
- Drugs: Fomivirsen (antisense oligonucleotide — CMV)

**Stage 6: Assembly**
- Target: viral protease — processing of polyproteins into functional proteins
- Drugs: Protease inhibitors — Lopinavir, Ritonavir, Atazanavir (HIV)

**Stage 7: Release/Budding**
- Target: neuraminidase — release of influenza virions
- Drugs: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu), Zanamivir — neuraminidase inhibitors

---

### Selective Toxicity — How Antivirals Spare Host Cells

Selective toxicity means a drug is toxic to the virus or virus-infected cells but not to normal host cells. This is achieved through:

**1. Targeting virus-specific enzymes not present in host cells:**
- HIV reverse transcriptase — host cells do not reverse transcribe RNA into DNA
- HIV integrase — host cells do not integrate foreign DNA via viral integrase
- Influenza neuraminidase — host cells do not express neuraminidase

**2. Targeting viral enzymes that differ sufficiently from host equivalents:**
- Viral DNA polymerases (HSV, CMV) differ from human DNA polymerase in structure
- Acyclovir triphosphate has much higher affinity for HSV DNA polymerase than human DNA polymerase

**3. Requiring virus-specific activation:**
- Acyclovir requires viral thymidine kinase for first phosphorylation
- Only HSV-infected cells contain viral TK → only infected cells activate acyclovir
- Uninfected cells cannot activate acyclovir → spared

---

### Key Antiviral Drugs Summary

| Drug | Virus Target | Mechanism | Stage Blocked |
|---|---|---|---|
| Acyclovir | HSV, VZV | Inhibits viral DNA polymerase after activation by viral TK | Replication |
| Ganciclovir | CMV | Inhibits CMV DNA polymerase | Replication |
| Zidovudine (AZT) | HIV | NRTI — inhibits reverse transcriptase | Replication |
| Nevirapine | HIV | NNRTI — inhibits reverse transcriptase | Replication |
| Raltegravir | HIV | Integrase inhibitor | Integration |
| Lopinavir/Ritonavir | HIV | Protease inhibitor | Assembly |
| Enfuvirtide (Fuzeon) | HIV | Fusion inhibitor — blocks gp41 | Penetration/Fusion |
| Maraviroc | HIV | CCR5 antagonist | Attachment |
| Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) | Influenza A and B | Neuraminidase inhibitor | Release |
| Amantadine | Influenza A only | M2 channel blocker | Uncoating |
| Sofosbuvir | HCV | NS5B RNA polymerase inhibitor | Replication |
| Ribavirin | Broad spectrum | Multiple mechanisms | Replication |

---

---

# Part 2: Rabies Virus

## 1. Introduction

Rabies is an acute, progressive, invariably fatal viral encephalitis caused by the Rabies virus. It is one of the oldest known infectious diseases and remains a significant public health problem in Africa and Asia. Despite being almost universally fatal once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is completely preventable through vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis. This stark contrast — preventable yet fatal — makes it one of the most clinically important viruses to understand. At MKU, rabies has appeared in essay questions asking students to describe its pathogenesis and the management of an exposed patient.

---

## 2. Classification and Structure

- **Family:** Rhabdoviridae
- **Genus:** Lyssavirus
- **Genome:** Single-stranded, negative-sense RNA
- **Enveloped virus**
- **Shape:** Bullet-shaped — distinctive, unique among human viruses
- **Key surface protein:** Glycoprotein G — mediates attachment to host receptors; target of neutralizing antibodies; basis of rabies vaccine

**Internal proteins:**
- **N protein (nucleoprotein)** — encapsidates RNA genome; used in diagnosis
- **L protein** — RNA-dependent RNA polymerase
- **P protein** — polymerase cofactor
- **M protein** — matrix protein; links envelope to nucleocapsid

---

## 3. Transmission

- **Animal bite** — primary route; infected saliva introduced into wound
- **Scratch** — if contaminated with infected saliva
- **Licking of broken skin or mucous membranes** — by infected animal
- **Aerosol transmission** — very rare; reported in bat caves with high bat density
- **Transplantation** — extremely rare; infected cornea or organ transplant

**Reservoir animals:**
- Dogs — most common source of human rabies globally, especially in Africa and Asia
- Bats — main reservoir in Americas
- Foxes, raccoons, skunks — in specific geographic regions
- Wild animals — jackals, mongooses, wolves

**Important:** Virus is present in saliva of infected animals. Animals are infectious before showing symptoms — in the prodromal phase.

---

## 4. Pathogenesis — High Yield

The pathogenesis of rabies is one of the most distinctive in virology and explains all the clinical features.

### Step 1: Inoculation
- Infected animal bites → virus deposited in wound
- Virus remains at the wound site, replicating in local muscle cells
- **Incubation at wound site:** days to weeks — this is the window for post-exposure prophylaxis

### Step 2: Peripheral Nerve Entry
- Virus binds to **nicotinic acetylcholine receptors** at neuromuscular junctions
- Also binds NCAM (neural cell adhesion molecule) and p75 neurotrophin receptor
- Virus enters peripheral nerve endings at the wound site

### Step 3: Retrograde Axonal Transport

- Virus travels **retrograde** (from nerve ending toward cell body) along peripheral sensory and motor nerves
- Travels inside axons — protected from immune system
- Rate of travel: approximately 50–100 mm per day
- This is why wounds closer to the CNS (face, neck) cause faster disease — shorter journey
- Wounds on feet or hands cause slower disease — longer journey to CNS

### Step 4: CNS Entry and Spread
- Virus reaches the spinal cord and brain
- Spreads rapidly throughout CNS — infects neurons extensively
- Primarily infects the **limbic system, brainstem, and cerebellum**
- No inflammatory destruction of neurons — virus causes functional disruption rather than cell death
- This explains why there is little structural damage on pathology despite severe clinical disease

### Step 5: Centrifugal Spread

- Virus spreads **centrifugally** (outward from CNS) along peripheral nerves to many organs
- Reaches salivary glands → virus present in saliva — this is how transmission occurs
- Also reaches cornea, skin, heart, adrenal glands, kidneys

### Step 6: Death
- Death from respiratory failure, cardiovascular collapse, or brainstem dysfunction
- Almost 100% fatal once clinical symptoms appear

---

## 5. Clinical Features

**Incubation period:**
- Average: 1–3 months
- Range: 4 days to several years (rare)
- Shorter with: head/neck bites, severe wounds, large inoculum

### Phase 1: Prodromal Phase (2–10 days)
- Non-specific symptoms — fever, malaise, headache, fatigue
- Paraesthesia or pain at the wound site — highly specific early sign
- Anxiety, agitation, irritability

### Phase 2: Acute Neurological Phase (2–7 days)

**Furious (Encephalitic) Rabies — 80% of cases:**
- Hydrophobia — fear of water; attempts to swallow trigger violent pharyngeal spasms — pathognomonic of rabies
- Aerophobia — fear of air/drafts; similar spasms triggered by air on skin
- Hypersalivation — virus in salivary glands; swallowing painful
- Hyperexcitability, agitation, aggression
- Hallucinations, confusion
- Autonomic dysfunction — tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia
- Periods of calm between episodes of spasm

**Paralytic (Dumb) Rabies — 20% of cases:**
- Ascending flaccid paralysis — resembles Guillain-Barré syndrome
- Less dramatic — often misdiagnosed
- Eventually progresses to coma

### Phase 3: Coma and Death (days)
- Progressive coma
- Respiratory failure
- Death — virtually 100% once symptomatic

---

## 6. Diagnosis

- **Clinical diagnosis** — in endemic areas, classic presentation is sufficient
- **Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test** — gold standard; detects rabies antigen in brain tissue (post-mortem) or skin biopsy (corneal epithelium)
- **Negri bodies** — eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies in neurons (especially Purkinje cells of cerebellum and hippocampal neurons); pathognomonic on histology
- **RT-PCR** — detects viral RNA in saliva, CSF, skin
- **Serology** — antibody detection; useful in vaccinated individuals

---

## 7. Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) — High Yield

PEP is effective because of the long incubation period before virus reaches the CNS. Once the virus enters peripheral nerves and travels to the brain, PEP is no longer effective.

### Wound Management — First and Most Critical Step

- Immediate and thorough washing of wound with soap and water for at least 15 minutes
- Apply antiseptic — povidone iodine or alcohol
- Do not suture wound primarily if possible — suturing can push virus deeper
- This simple step significantly reduces viral inoculum

### Passive Immunization — Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG)
- Administered once — at the time of first presentation
- Infiltrated directly into and around the wound — neutralizes virus locally
- Remaining dose given intramuscularly at a distant site
- Human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG) — preferred; 20 IU/kg
- Equine rabies immunoglobulin (ERIG) — cheaper alternative; test for allergy first
- Purpose — provides immediate protection while active immunity develops

### Active Immunization — Rabies Vaccine
- Modern cell-culture rabies vaccines — HDCV (Human Diploid Cell Vaccine), PCECV (Purified Chick Embryo Cell Vaccine)
- Schedule for unvaccinated person: days 0, 3, 7, 14 (and sometimes day 28)
- Schedule for previously vaccinated person: days 0 and 3 only — no RIG needed
- Vaccine induces active immunity — antibodies against glycoprotein G
- Takes 7–14 days to produce protective antibody levels

### Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP)
- For high-risk groups — veterinarians, wildlife workers, laboratory workers, travellers to endemic areas
- Three doses — days 0, 7, 21 or 28
- Simplifies PEP if exposed — only 2 booster doses needed, no RIG

---

---

# Part 3: CMV and EBV

## 1. Introduction

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) are both members of the Herpesviridae family and share the fundamental herpesvirus property of establishing lifelong latent infection. However, they differ significantly in their target cells, clinical manifestations, and oncogenic potential. CMV is the most important cause of congenital viral infection worldwide and is a major pathogen in immunocompromised patients. EBV is the cause of infectious mononucleosis and is strongly associated with several malignancies including Burkitt's lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Both are high-yield topics at MKU, appearing in MCQs and essays.

---

## 2. Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

### Classification
- **Family:** Herpesviridae
- **Subfamily:** Betaherpesvirinae
- **Genome:** Double-stranded DNA — largest herpesvirus genome
- **Enveloped virus**
- Characteristic **owl-eye inclusion bodies** in infected cells — large intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo

### Epidemiology
- Ubiquitous — infects 50–90% of adults worldwide
- Transmitted through: saliva, urine, breast milk, sexual contact, blood transfusion, organ transplantation, transplacental
- Primary infection usually asymptomatic in immunocompetent individuals
- Establishes latency in monocytes, macrophages, and endothelial cells

### Target Cells
- Virtually all nucleated cells — explains why CMV causes disseminated disease
- Latency in: monocytes and their precursors in bone marrow
- Reactivation when cell-mediated immunity falls

### CMV in Immunocompetent Patients
- Usually asymptomatic
- Can cause a mononucleosis-like syndrome — fever, fatigue, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis
- Distinguished from EBV mononucleosis by negative monospot test (heterophile antibody negative)

### Congenital CMV — Highest Yield

Congenital CMV is the most common congenital viral infection worldwide.

**Transmission:**
- Transplacental — primary maternal infection during pregnancy most dangerous
- Risk of transmission: 30–40% if primary infection in pregnancy
- Secondary infection (reactivation) can also transmit but causes less severe disease

**Clinical features — the congenitally infected neonate:**
- 90% asymptomatic at birth — but 10–15% develop late sequelae
- 10% symptomatic at birth:
  - **Microcephaly** — small head; most serious sequela
  - **Periventricular calcifications** — on CT scan; pathognomonic
  - Hepatosplenomegaly
  - Jaundice
  - Petechiae and purpura — blueberry muffin appearance
  - Chorioretinitis — can cause blindness
  - Sensorineural hearing loss — most common long-term sequel
  - Mental retardation
  - Seizures

**Diagnosis of congenital CMV:**
- **Urine culture or PCR** — within first 3 weeks of life; virus shed in urine
- Blood PCR — detects CMV DNA
- Serology — IgM in neonate (IgM does not cross placenta — presence confirms active neonatal infection)

**Treatment:**
- Ganciclovir (IV) or Valganciclovir (oral prodrug)
- Given to symptomatic neonates — reduces hearing loss progression
- Mechanism: Ganciclovir inhibits CMV DNA polymerase

### CMV in Immunocompromised Patients

In transplant recipients and HIV/AIDS patients, CMV causes severe disease:
- **CMV retinitis** — most common in AIDS; causes progressive blindness; treated with ganciclovir
- **CMV pneumonitis** — severe, life-threatening pneumonia in bone marrow transplant patients
- **CMV colitis** — bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain
- **CMV encephalitis** — in advanced AIDS
- **CMV hepatitis**

**Treatment of CMV disease:**
- **Ganciclovir** (IV) — first-line
- **Valganciclovir** (oral) — prodrug; used for maintenance
- **Foscarnet** — used when resistance to ganciclovir
- **Cidofovir** — second-line

### Diagnosis
- **Owl-eye inclusions** — histology of infected tissue
- **PCR** — most sensitive; detects CMV DNA in blood, urine, CSF
- **Shell vial culture** — rapid culture method
- **pp65 antigenemia** — detects CMV antigen in leukocytes; used to monitor transplant patients

---

## 3. Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)

### Classification
- **Family:** Herpesviridae
- **Subfamily:** Gammaherpesvirinae
- **Genome:** Double-stranded DNA
- **Enveloped virus**

### Transmission
- Saliva — primary route; kissing disease
- Blood transfusion — rare
- Organ transplantation

### Target Cells
- **B lymphocytes** — primary target; EBV binds CD21 (complement receptor 2)
- Epithelial cells of oropharynx and nasopharynx
- Latency in B lymphocytes — lifelong

### Infectious Mononucleosis (Glandular Fever)

**Pathogenesis:**
- EBV infects oropharyngeal epithelial cells → spreads to B lymphocytes in tonsillar tissue
- B cells become immortalized and proliferate massively
- CD8+ cytotoxic T cells respond aggressively to destroy infected B cells
- The reactive T cells are the atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells) seen on blood film
- Clinical disease is largely immune-mediated — the T cell response causes symptoms

**Clinical features:**
- Affects adolescents and young adults predominantly
- **Triad:** fever, pharyngitis (exudative tonsillitis), lymphadenopathy (especially posterior cervical)
- Splenomegaly — in 50%; risk of splenic rupture — avoid contact sports
- Hepatomegaly and mild hepatitis
- Periorbital oedema
- Maculopapular rash — especially if ampicillin/amoxicillin given — characteristic drug reaction
- Fatigue — can persist for weeks to months

**Diagnosis:**
- **Monospot test (Paul-Bunnell test)** — detects heterophile antibodies; positive in 85–90% of cases
- **Blood film** — atypical lymphocytes (large, activated CD8+ T cells)
- **EBV-specific serology** — VCA IgM (acute infection), VCA IgG (past infection), EA antibodies (active replication), EBNA antibodies (appear late, confirm past infection)
- **PCR** — detects EBV DNA; used in immunocompromised
- **FBC** — lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes

**Treatment:**
- Supportive — rest, analgesia, adequate hydration
- Avoid ampicillin/amoxicillin — causes rash in EBV infection
- Avoid contact sports until splenomegaly resolves — risk of splenic rupture
- Steroids — for severe airway obstruction from tonsillar enlargement
- No specific antiviral — acyclovir has limited benefit

### EBV and Oncogenesis — High Yield

EBV is one of the most important oncogenic viruses. It causes malignancy through:
- B cell immortalization via latent gene expression
- Integration of viral DNA near oncogenes
- Immunosuppression in host allows uncontrolled B cell proliferation

**EBV-associated malignancies:**

| Malignancy | Key Facts |
|---|---|
| Burkitt's lymphoma | B cell lymphoma; jaw mass in African children; t(8;14) translocation — c-myc oncogene activation; endemic in malaria belt of Africa |
| Nasopharyngeal carcinoma | Common in Southern China and Southeast Asia; EBV in virtually all cases |
| Hodgkin's lymphoma | EBV in 40–50% of cases; Reed-Sternberg cells contain EBV |
| Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) | Uncontrolled EBV-driven B cell proliferation in immunosuppressed transplant recipients |
| Primary CNS lymphoma | In AIDS patients with very low CD4 counts |

---

---

# Part 4: Adenovirus and Enteroviruses

## 1. Introduction

Adenoviruses and enteroviruses are both non-enveloped viruses that cause a wide range of clinical diseases. Adenoviruses are DNA viruses causing respiratory, ocular, and gastrointestinal infections. Enteroviruses are RNA viruses that enter through the gut but cause systemic disease including meningitis, encephalitis, myocarditis, and paralysis. Both groups have appeared in MKU essay questions — adenovirus as a full essay on transmission, diseases, and prevention, and enteroviruses as essay questions on portal of entry, diseases caused, and viral encephalitis.

---

## 2. Adenovirus

### Classification and Structure
- **Family:** Adenoviridae
- **Genome:** Double-stranded DNA
- **Non-enveloped** — this is clinically important
- **Shape:** Icosahedral capsid with characteristic **fiber proteins** projecting from each vertex — these are the attachment proteins (bind host cell receptors)
- **Stable in environment** — non-enveloped viruses resist drying, heat, detergents, and disinfectants — this explains their ability to spread via fomites and water

### Transmission — High Yield

Adenoviruses are transmitted by multiple routes:

- **Respiratory droplets** — sneezing, coughing; causes respiratory infections
- **Fecal-oral route** — contaminated food and water; causes gastroenteritis
- **Direct contact** — hand-to-eye; causes conjunctivitis
- **Swimming pools (waterborne)** — epidemic keratoconjunctivitis from contaminated pool water
- **Fomites** — virus survives on surfaces for extended periods due to non-enveloped structure
- **Blood transfusion and organ transplantation** — in immunocompromised patients

### Diseases Caused — High Yield

| Disease | Notes |
|---|---|
| Acute febrile pharyngitis | Most common; fever, sore throat, cervical lymphadenopathy; types 1–5, 7 |
| Pharyngoconjunctival fever | Fever, pharyngitis, follicular conjunctivitis; associated with swimming pools; types 3, 7 |
| Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis | Severe eye infection; corneal infiltrates; highly contagious; types 8, 19, 37 |
| Acute respiratory disease (ARD) | Pneumonia, bronchitis; types 4, 7; especially in military recruits |
| Gastroenteritis | Diarrhea in children; types 40, 41 (enteric adenoviruses) |
| Haemorrhagic cystitis | Bloody urine; types 11, 21; especially in immunocompromised |
| Disseminated infection | Hepatitis, pneumonia, encephalitis; in immunocompromised and neonates |

### Prevention

- **Handwashing** — most important general measure
- **Proper chlorination of swimming pools** — prevents waterborne spread
- **Avoid sharing towels, eye drops** — prevents conjunctivitis spread
- **Live oral adenovirus vaccine** — types 4 and 7; used in military recruits in some countries; not widely available
- **Isolation of infected patients** — in healthcare settings
- **Adequate water treatment and sanitation** — prevents fecal-oral transmission

### Diagnosis
- **PCR** — most sensitive; detects adenovirus DNA in respiratory secretions, stool, blood, urine
- **Viral culture** — from respiratory secretions, conjunctival swab, stool
- **Antigen detection** — rapid tests for stool adenovirus (types 40/41)
- **Serology** — four-fold rise in antibody titre

### Treatment

- No specific antiviral approved for adenovirus
- Supportive treatment
- **Cidofovir** — used in severe adenovirus disease in immunocompromised patients

---

## 3. Enteroviruses

### Classification and Structure
- **Family:** Picornaviridae
- **Genus:** Enterovirus
- **Genome:** Single-stranded, positive-sense RNA
- **Non-enveloped** — stable in acidic environment of stomach; survives GIT passage
- Small icosahedral viruses

### Members of the Enterovirus Genus — High Yield

| Virus | Serotypes | Key Disease |
|---|---|---|
| Poliovirus | Types 1, 2, 3 | Poliomyelitis — flaccid paralysis |
| Coxsackievirus A | 23 serotypes | Herpangina, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, aseptic meningitis |
| Coxsackievirus B | 6 serotypes | Myocarditis, pericarditis, Bornholm disease (pleurodynia), aseptic meningitis |
| Echovirus | 28 serotypes | Aseptic meningitis, rash, respiratory illness |
| Enterovirus 71 (EV71) | — | Hand-foot-and-mouth disease, encephalitis |
| Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) | — | Acute flaccid myelitis, respiratory illness |

### Portal of Entry — High Yield

The portal of entry for all enteroviruses is the **gastrointestinal tract** — specifically the oropharynx and small intestine.

**Route:**
1. Virus ingested in contaminated food or water (fecal-oral transmission)
2. Survives stomach acid — non-enveloped capsid is acid-resistant
3. Infects epithelial cells and lymphoid tissue (Peyer's patches) of small intestine
4. Primary replication in gut
5. Spreads to regional lymph nodes
6. Viremia → target organs (CNS, heart, skin, muscle)

### Transmission
- **Fecal-oral route** — primary route; contaminated water and food
- **Respiratory droplets** — for some serotypes causing pharyngitis
- **Direct contact** — hand-to-mouth

### Diseases Caused — High Yield

**Poliovirus:**
- **Subclinical infection** — 95% of infections
- **Abortive poliomyelitis** — 4–8%; non-specific febrile illness; no neurological involvement
- **Non-paralytic poliomyelitis (aseptic meningitis)** — 1–2%; meningeal irritation without paralysis
- **Paralytic poliomyelitis** — less than 1%; destruction of anterior horn motor neurons → flaccid paralysis
  - Bulbar poliomyelitis — involves brainstem; respiratory paralysis; most fatal form

**Coxsackievirus A:**
- **Herpangina** — vesicular lesions on soft palate and uvula; high fever in children
- **Hand-foot-and-mouth disease** — vesicular lesions on hands, feet, and oral mucosa; caused by CA16 and EV71
- Aseptic meningitis

**Coxsackievirus B:**
- **Myocarditis** — inflammation of heart muscle; can cause dilated cardiomyopathy
- **Pericarditis** — inflammation of pericardium
- **Bornholm disease (epidemic pleurodynia)** — severe pleuritic chest pain and myalgia; devil's grip
- Aseptic meningitis, neonatal sepsis

**Echoviruses:**
- Aseptic meningitis — most common cause of viral meningitis
- Febrile rash illness
- Respiratory illness

### Viral Encephalitis — High Yield

**Definition:** Inflammation of the brain parenchyma caused by viral infection, as distinct from meningitis (inflammation of meninges only).

**Enteroviruses that cause encephalitis:**
- Enterovirus 71 (EV71) — most important; causes brainstem encephalitis in children
- Coxsackievirus A and B
- Echoviruses
- Poliovirus — encephalitis rare; paralysis more common

**Other important causes of viral encephalitis (non-enterovirus):**
- **HSV-1** — most common cause of fatal sporadic encephalitis
- **Rabies virus**
- **Japanese encephalitis virus** (arbovirus)
- **West Nile virus** (arbovirus)
- **CMV** — in immunocompromised
- **Measles** — post-infectious encephalitis
- **VZV** — in elderly and immunocompromised

**Clinical features of viral encephalitis:**
- Fever
- Headache
- Altered consciousness — confusion, disorientation
- Seizures
- Focal neurological deficits
- Behavioural changes

**Diagnosis:**
- **MRI brain** — gold standard imaging; shows temporal lobe involvement in HSV
- **CSF analysis** (lumbar puncture):
  - Lymphocytic pleocytosis
  - Normal or mildly elevated protein
  - Normal glucose
- **CSF PCR** — gold standard for diagnosis; identifies specific virus
- **EEG** — temporal lobe changes in HSV encephalitis

**Treatment:**
- **IV Acyclovir** — started empirically for all encephalitis until HSV excluded
- Supportive — anticonvulsants, management of raised ICP, ICU care
- No specific treatment for most enterovirus encephalitis — supportive only

### Diagnosis of Enteroviruses
- **PCR** — gold standard; detects enterovirus RNA in CSF, stool, throat swab, blood
- **Viral culture** — from stool, throat, CSF
- **Serology** — less useful due to many serotypes

### Treatment
- No specific antiviral for most enteroviruses
- Supportive treatment
- **Pleconaril** — an experimental capsid inhibitor; has been used for severe enterovirus disease in some settings
- **IVIG** — intravenous immunoglobulin for severe neonatal enterovirus sepsis and enterovirus in immunocompromised

### Prevention
- **Handwashing** — most important
- **Clean water and sanitation** — prevents fecal-oral spread
- **Poliovirus vaccines** — OPV and IPV (as detailed in Part 1)
- No vaccine available for other enteroviruses except EV71 vaccine (licensed in China)
