# 🫀 VALVULAR HEART DISEASE — ULTRA DEEP NOTES

---

# PART 1: FOUNDATION — UNDERSTAND THE HEART FIRST

## The Heart Has 4 Chambers
```
RIGHT ATRIUM → RIGHT VENTRICLE → LUNGS → LEFT ATRIUM → LEFT VENTRICLE → BODY
```

## The 4 Valves & Their Positions
```
Between Right Atrium & Right Ventricle  →  TRICUSPID VALVE (3 leaflets)
Between Right Ventricle & Pulmonary Artery  →  PULMONIC VALVE
Between Left Atrium & Left Ventricle  →  MITRAL VALVE (2 leaflets)
Between Left Ventricle & Aorta  →  AORTIC VALVE
```

## Why Left Side Gets Damaged More
> Left side pumps blood to the ENTIRE body → handles 5x more pressure than the right side → valves wear down, get damaged, get diseased MORE

---

## Two Types of Valve Problems

| Type | Definition | Effect on Heart |
|---|---|---|
| **Stenosis** | Valve opening is NARROWED | Chamber BEHIND valve works harder → **Pressure overload** → Hypertrophy |
| **Regurgitation/Insufficiency** | Valve doesn't close properly → blood leaks BACK | Chamber BEHIND valve overfills → **Volume overload** → Dilation |

### Pressure Overload vs Volume Overload
```
STENOSIS = Pressure Overload
→ Chamber pushes against resistance
→ Walls get THICK (Hypertrophy)
→ Think: Weightlifter's muscles

REGURGITATION = Volume Overload
→ Chamber fills with extra blood
→ Chamber gets BIG and DILATED
→ Think: Balloon being overfilled
```

---

# PART 2: MITRAL STENOSIS (MS)

## Definition
> Narrowing of the mitral valve opening — normal area is **4-6 cm²** — symptoms begin when it drops below **2 cm²** — critical at **1 cm²**

## Cause
> **Rheumatic Heart Disease** — responsible for nearly **99% of all MS cases**
> Rarely: congenital, carcinoid, lupus

## Pathogenesis — Step by Step

### Step 1: Acute Rheumatic Fever
```
Group A Streptococcus (Strep pyogenes) throat infection
        ↓
Immune system makes antibodies against Strep M-protein
        ↓
M-protein LOOKS LIKE cardiac proteins (molecular mimicry)
        ↓
Antibodies attack the HEART by mistake
        ↓
Inflammation of all heart layers = PANCARDITIS
        ↓
Mitral valve leaflets become inflamed → small vegetations form on leaflets
```

### Step 2: Chronic Scarring (Years Later)
```
Repeated episodes of rheumatic fever
        ↓
Leaflets become FIBROSED and FUSED at commissures
        ↓
Chordae tendineae become SHORTENED and THICKENED
        ↓
Valve opening becomes NARROW = STENOSIS
        ↓
Classic "FISH MOUTH" or "BUTTONHOLE" appearance of valve
```

### Step 3: Consequences of Obstruction
```
Narrowed mitral valve
        ↓
Blood cannot freely flow from LA → LV
        ↓
Blood BACKS UP into Left Atrium
        ↓
LA pressure rises → LA DILATES (enlarges)
        ↓
↑ LA pressure → backs up into pulmonary veins
        ↓
Pulmonary venous hypertension → PULMONARY EDEMA (dyspnea)
        ↓
Chronic pulmonary hypertension → RIGHT HEART STRAIN
        ↓
Right ventricular hypertrophy → eventually RIGHT HEART FAILURE
```

### Step 4: Atrial Fibrillation
```
LA dilates and stretches
        ↓
Electrical pathways in LA get disrupted
        ↓
ATRIAL FIBRILLATION develops
        ↓
Blood pools and stagnates in LA (especially in LA appendage)
        ↓
THROMBUS FORMS in LA
        ↓
Thrombus breaks off → SYSTEMIC EMBOLISM → STROKE
```

## Gross Pathology
| Finding | Description |
|---|---|
| Leaflet fusion | Commissures fused → "fish mouth" valve |
| Leaflet thickening | Fibrosis and calcification |
| Short chordae | Pulled down, thickened, fused |
| LA enlargement | Massive — can compress esophagus |
| LA thrombus | Especially in LA appendage |

## Clinical Features

### Symptoms
| Symptom | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Dyspnea on exertion** | Pulmonary venous hypertension |
| **Orthopnea/PND** | Pulmonary edema when lying flat |
| **Hemoptysis** | Rupture of bronchial veins from high pressure |
| **Palpitations** | Atrial fibrillation |
| **Stroke** | LA thrombus embolization |
| **Hoarse voice** | Enlarged LA compresses recurrent laryngeal nerve |
| **Dysphagia** | Enlarged LA compresses esophagus |

### Signs
| Sign | Description |
|---|---|
| **Malar flush** | Pinkish-purple cheeks from low cardiac output |
| **Loud S1** | Valve snaps shut from being held open |
| **Opening snap** | Stiff leaflets snap open in diastole |
| **Mid-diastolic rumble** | Turbulent flow through narrow valve |

## CXR Findings
```
- Enlarged LA (double density sign, splaying of carina)
- Pulmonary venous congestion (upper lobe diversion)
- Kerley B lines (pulmonary edema)
- Calcified mitral valve
- Normal LV size (LV is actually SMALL/normal in pure MS)
```

## Key MCQ Facts
> - **Most common cause:** Rheumatic heart disease
> - **Most common valve affected in rheumatic disease:** Mitral > Aortic > Tricuspid
> - **Most common complication:** Atrial fibrillation
> - **Most dangerous complication:** Stroke from LA thrombus
> - **LV is NORMAL** in pure mitral stenosis — only LA enlarges
> - **Only valvular lesion more common in WOMEN than men**

---

# PART 3: MITRAL REGURGITATION (MR)

## Definition
> Mitral valve fails to close completely during systole → blood leaks BACK from LV into LA

## Causes — Remember **"PRIME"**
> - **P**apillary muscle rupture (post-MI)
> - **R**heumatic heart disease
> - **I**nfective endocarditis
> - **M**itral valve prolapse (MVP)
> - **E**ndocarditis / connective tissue disorders (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos)

### Most Important Causes by Context
| Cause | Key Context |
|---|---|
| **MVP** | Young woman, most common cause overall |
| **Papillary muscle rupture** | 2-7 days post-MI → ACUTE severe MR |
| **Rheumatic** | Always with mitral stenosis too |
| **IE** | IV drug user, recent dental procedure |
| **Marfan syndrome** | Tall, long fingers, lens dislocation |
| **Dilated cardiomyopathy** | LV dilation pulls leaflets apart |

## Pathophysiology
```
Mitral valve doesn't close → blood leaks back into LA during systole
        ↓
LA receives blood from BOTH pulmonary veins AND leaking LV
        ↓
LA DILATES (volume overload)
        ↓
LV must pump EXTRA volume each beat to maintain output
        ↓
LV DILATES and eventually HYPERTROPHIES
        ↓
Eventually LV fails → LEFT HEART FAILURE
```

## Acute vs Chronic MR

| Feature | Acute MR | Chronic MR |
|---|---|---|
| **Cause** | Papillary muscle rupture, IE | Rheumatic, MVP |
| **LA** | Normal size, no time to dilate | Massively dilated |
| **Symptoms** | Sudden, severe pulmonary edema | Gradual, compensated for years |
| **Prognosis** | Emergency, life-threatening | Slowly progressive |

## Key MCQ Facts
> - **Papillary muscle rupture** → most common cause of ACUTE severe MR post-MI
> - **MVP** → most common cause of MR overall in developed world
> - **Both LA and LV enlarge** (unlike MS where only LA enlarges)
> - Holosystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla

---

# PART 4: MITRAL VALVE PROLAPSE (MVP)

## Definition
> Mitral valve leaflets BULGE BACK (prolapse) into LA during systole due to excess leaflet tissue or weak chordae

## Causes
| Cause | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Idiopathic** | Most common — young women |
| **Marfan syndrome** | Connective tissue weakness |
| **Ehlers-Danlos** | Connective tissue weakness |
| **Myxomatous degeneration** | Weakening of valve matrix |

## Key Features
```
- Most common valvular abnormality overall
- Usually BENIGN
- Mid-systolic CLICK followed by late systolic murmur
- Can progress to MR if chordae rupture
- Rarely: sudden cardiac death, stroke, arrhythmias
```

## Gross Pathology
> Leaflets are large, floppy, billowing — "parachute" appearance

---

# PART 5: AORTIC STENOSIS (AS)

## Definition
> Narrowing of aortic valve → obstruction of blood flow from LV to aorta during systole

## Causes by Age Group

| Age | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Children/Young adults** | Congenital bicuspid aortic valve |
| **Adults 40-60** | Calcification of bicuspid valve |
| **Elderly >65** | **Calcific/Degenerative AS** — most common |
| **Any age (developing world)** | Rheumatic AS (always with mitral disease) |

### Calcific AS — Pathogenesis
```
Normal wear and tear on valve leaflets
        ↓
Lipid deposition + inflammation (similar to atherosclerosis)
        ↓
Calcium deposits form on leaflets
        ↓
Leaflets become STIFF and cannot open fully
        ↓
Valve opening NARROWS
        ↓
LV must generate MASSIVE pressure to push blood through
        ↓
LV HYPERTROPHY (concentric) — pressure overload
        ↓
Eventually LV FAILS
```

## The SAD Triad — Symptom Progression
```
S → Syncope          (5 year survival without surgery)
A → Angina           (3 year survival without surgery)
D → Dyspnea/HF       (1-2 year survival without surgery)
```
> Each new symptom = worse prognosis → valve replacement urgently needed

## Pathophysiology of Each Symptom
| Symptom | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Syncope** | Fixed outflow obstruction → ↓ CO to brain on exertion |
| **Angina** | LVH → increased O2 demand + compressed coronary arteries |
| **Dyspnea** | LV failure → pulmonary edema |

## Key Findings
| Finding | Reason |
|---|---|
| **LV hypertrophy on CXR** | Pressure overload |
| **Normal or small aortic root** | Unlike AR |
| **Slow rising pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus)** | Reduced, delayed aortic flow |
| **Narrow pulse pressure** | Low stroke volume |
| **Harsh systolic ejection murmur** | Radiates to carotids |
| **Soft/absent S2** | Stiff valve can't snap shut |

## Key MCQ Facts
> - **Elderly + no prior illness + SAD triad + LVH = Calcific AS**
> - **Normal cholesterol rules out atherosclerosis as primary driver**
> - **LV hypertrophies** (not dilates) in AS — pressure overload
> - **Most common valvular disease requiring surgery** in developed world
> - Bicuspid aortic valve → calcifies EARLIER (40s-50s instead of 70s)

---

# PART 6: AORTIC REGURGITATION (AR)

## Definition
> Aortic valve leaks during diastole → blood flows BACK from aorta into LV

## Causes
### Valve Leaflet Problems
| Cause | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Rheumatic disease** | Leaflet scarring |
| **Infective endocarditis** | Leaflet destruction |
| **Bicuspid aortic valve** | Structural abnormality |
| **Calcific degeneration** | Elderly |

### Aortic Root Dilation (Valve ring stretches open)
| Cause | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Marfan syndrome** | Cystic medial necrosis → aortic root dilation |
| **Syphilitic aortitis** | Tertiary syphilis destroys aortic wall |
| **Hypertension** | Chronic aortic dilation |
| **Ankylosing spondylitis** | Inflammatory aortic root disease |

## Pathophysiology
```
Blood leaks back from aorta → LV during diastole
        ↓
LV receives blood from BOTH LA and leaking aorta
        ↓
LV VOLUME OVERLOAD → LV dilates AND hypertrophies
        ↓
"Cor Bovinum" = massive ox-like heart
        ↓
Eventually LV FAILS
```

## Classic Signs — All Due to Wide Pulse Pressure
> AR causes HIGH systolic pressure (large stroke volume) + LOW diastolic pressure (blood leaks back)
> = **WIDE PULSE PRESSURE**

| Sign | Description |
|---|---|
| **Corrigan's pulse** | Bounding, water-hammer pulse |
| **De Musset's sign** | Head bobbing with each heartbeat |
| **Quincke's sign** | Capillary pulsations in nail bed |
| **Duroziez's sign** | Pistol-shot sound over femoral artery |
| **Hill's sign** | BP in legs > arms by >20mmHg |
| **Traube's sign** | Double sound over femoral artery |

## Key MCQ Facts
> - **Wide pulse pressure** = hallmark of AR
> - **LV dilates AND hypertrophies** (volume + pressure overload)
> - **Syphilitic aortitis** → AR + ascending aortic aneurysm
> - **Marfan** → think AR from aortic root dilation
> - Early diastolic murmur at left sternal border

---

# PART 7: INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS (IE)

## Definition
> Infection of the heart valves or endocardium — usually bacterial

## Types

### Acute IE
| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Organism** | **Staph aureus** — most common overall |
| **Course** | Rapid, destructive, days-weeks |
| **Valve** | Often NORMAL valves |
| **Context** | IV drug users, post-surgery, catheters |

### Subacute IE
| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Organism** | **Strep viridans** — most common in subacute |
| **Course** | Slow, weeks-months |
| **Valve** | Usually PREVIOUSLY DAMAGED valves |
| **Context** | Dental procedures, MVP, rheumatic disease |

### Special Contexts
| Context | Organism |
|---|---|
| **IV drug user** | Staph aureus → **RIGHT sided** (tricuspid) |
| **Dental procedure** | Strep viridans |
| **GI/GU procedure** | Enterococcus |
| **Prosthetic valve early (<2 months)** | Staph epidermidis |
| **Colon cancer** | Strep bovis (Strep gallolyticus) |
| **Fungal** | Candida → IV drug users, immunocompromised |

## Pathology of Vegetations
```
Bacteria enter bloodstream → attach to damaged/turbulent valve
        ↓
Form VEGETATIONS = bacteria + fibrin + platelets + inflammatory cells
        ↓
Vegetations are LARGE, IRREGULAR, DESTRUCTIVE
        ↓
Can EMBOLIZE → stroke, pulmonary embolism, splenic infarct
        ↓
Can DESTROY valve → acute regurgitation
        ↓
Can spread locally → abscess, fistula
```

## Non-Infective Endocarditis (Important for MCQs)

| Type | Cause | Vegetation Location | Key Association |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Libman-Sacks** | SLE | BOTH sides of mitral leaflet | Lupus — "LSE = Lupus Sterile Endocarditis" |
| **Marantic (NBTE)** | Malignancy, chronic illness | Along line of closure | Cancer, debilitating illness |
| **Rheumatic** | Rheumatic fever | Tips of mitral leaflets | Strep, Aschoff bodies |

## Osler's Nodes vs Janeway Lesions
| Feature | Osler's Nodes | Janeway Lesions |
|---|---|---|
| **Location** | Finger/toe PADS | Palms/soles |
| **Pain** | PAINFUL | Painless |
| **Cause** | Immune complex deposition | Septic emboli |
| **Memory** | "Osler = Ouch" | "Janeway = Just walks on them" |

---

# PART 8: RHEUMATIC HEART DISEASE

## Pathogenesis
```
Group A Strep throat infection (Strep pyogenes)
        ↓
Antibodies form against Strep M-protein
        ↓
M-protein mimics cardiac proteins (molecular mimicry)
        ↓
Antibodies attack HEART → Pancarditis
        ↓
Aschoff bodies form = pathognomonic granulomas
        ↓
Aschoff cells = large macrophages with "caterpillar/owl eye" nuclei
        ↓
Heals with fibrosis → CHRONIC RHEUMATIC HEART DISEASE
```

## Jones Criteria (Diagnosis of Acute RF)
### Major Criteria — **"JONES"**
> - **J**oints — migratory polyarthritis (most common)
> - **O** — cardi**O**megaly/carditis
> - **N**odules — subcutaneous nodules
> - **E**rythema marginatum — skin rash
> - **S**ydenham's chorea — involuntary movements

### Minor Criteria
> Fever, elevated ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval, previous RF

> **Diagnosis = 2 Major OR 1 Major + 2 Minor + evidence of preceding Strep infection**

## Valve Involvement Order
```
Most common → Least common
MITRAL → AORTIC → TRICUSPID → PULMONIC
(Pulmonic almost never affected)
```

---

# PART 9: QUICK COMPARISON TABLE

| Feature | MS | MR | AS | AR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Main cause** | Rheumatic | MVP/Post-MI | Calcific/Bicuspid | Marfan/Syphilis/Rheumatic |
| **Pressure or Volume** | Pressure on LA | Volume on LA+LV | Pressure on LV | Volume on LV |
| **Chamber enlargement** | LA only | LA + LV | LV hypertrophy | LV dilates + hypertrophies |
| **Key symptom** | Dyspnea + A-fib | Fatigue + dyspnea | SAD triad | Wide pulse pressure signs |
| **Murmur** | Mid-diastolic rumble | Holosystolic | Systolic ejection | Early diastolic |
| **Key complication** | Stroke from LA clot | LV failure | Sudden death | LV failure |

---

# PART 10: HIGH YIELD MCQ TRIGGERS

| If you see this... | Think... |
|---|---|
| Elderly + SAD triad + LVH + normal cholesterol | **Calcific Aortic Stenosis** |
| Middle-aged woman + fused leaflets + A-fib + stroke | **Rheumatic Mitral Stenosis** |
| Post-MI day 2-7 + sudden pulmonary edema | **Papillary muscle rupture → Acute MR** |
| Young woman + mid-systolic click | **MVP** |
| IV drug user + fever + tricuspid vegetation | **Staph aureus IE (right sided)** |
| Dental procedure + fever + Strep viridans | **Subacute IE** |
| SLE + vegetations on BOTH sides of mitral | **Libman-Sacks endocarditis** |
| Cancer patient + sterile vegetations | **Marantic endocarditis (NBTE)** |
| Tall patient + wide pulse pressure + AR | **Marfan syndrome** |
| Syphilis + AR + ascending aneurysm | **Syphilitic aortitis** |
| Child + migratory arthritis + carditis + Strep | **Acute Rheumatic Fever** |

articles.content:
## Summary
This document provides a comprehensive overview of various cardiac conditions, including cardiomyopathies, pericardial diseases, congenital heart defects, and cardiac tumors. It delves into their definitions, causes, pathophysiology, gross and microscopic pathology, clinical features, and key diagnostic points, often using mnemonics and comparison tables for clarity.

## Key Points
- Cardiomyopathies are categorized into Dilated (DCM), Hypertrophic (HCM), and Restrictive (RCM), each with distinct causes, pathophysiology, and clinical presentations.
- Pericardial diseases include pericarditis, pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, and constrictive pericarditis, differentiated by their acute vs. chronic nature and specific diagnostic findings.
- Congenital heart defects are broadly classified into acyanotic (left-to-right shunts) and cyanotic (right-to-left shunts), with specific conditions like VSD, ASD, PDA, TOF, TGA, and coarctation of the aorta detailed.
- Cardiac tumors, though rare, are discussed, with myxoma being the most common primary tumor in adults and rhabdomyoma in children, each presenting with unique clinical scenarios.

## Detailed Notes
---

## PART 1: CARDIOMYOPATHIES

## Definition
Disease of the heart muscle itself — NOT caused by coronary artery disease, hypertension, or valvular disease

## There Are 3 Types — Remember **"DHR"**
- **D**ilated Cardiomyopathy
- **H**ypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
- **R**estrictive Cardiomyopathy

---

## 1A. DILATED CARDIOMYOPATHY (DCM)

## Definition
All 4 chambers dilate + systolic dysfunction → heart cannot CONTRACT properly

## Causes — Remember **"ABCDE"**
- **A**lcohol (most common toxic cause)
- **B**eri-beri (Thiamine/B1 deficiency)
- **C**oxsackievirus B (viral myocarditis → DCM)
- **D**rugs (Doxorubicin/adriamycin — chemotherapy)
- **E**clampsia/pregnancy (Peripartum cardiomyopathy)

### Other Important Causes
| Cause | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Idiopathic** | Most common overall (50%) |
| **Genetic** | 25-35% — mutations in cytoskeletal proteins |
| **Chagas disease** | Trypanosoma cruzi — South America |
| **Hemochromatosis** | Iron deposition in myocardium |
| **Sarcoidosis** | Granulomas in myocardium |
| **Thyroid disease** | Hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism |
| **Cocaine** | Toxic cardiomyopathy |

## Pathophysiology


## Gross Pathology


## Microscopic Pathology


## Clinical Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Age** | Any age, peak 20-60 |
| **Symptoms** | Progressive heart failure — dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea |
| **Signs** | S3 gallop, displaced apex beat, JVP raised |
| **CXR** | Massive cardiomegaly — "globular heart" |
| **Echo** | Dilated all chambers, reduced EF |
| **Arrhythmias** | Common — AF, VT, sudden death |
| **Emboli** | Stroke from mural thrombus |

## Key MCQ Facts
- **Most common cardiomyopathy overall**
- **Systolic dysfunction** — problem with CONTRACTION
- **All 4 chambers dilate**
- Alcohol → DCM → stop alcohol → can RECOVER
- Doxorubicin (adriamycin) → dose-dependent cardiotoxicity → DCM
- Peripartum cardiomyopathy → last month of pregnancy or 5 months postpartum
- **Worst prognosis** of all cardiomyopathies

---

## 1B. HYPERTROPHIC CARDIOMYOPATHY (HCM)

## Definition
Massive hypertrophy of the LEFT VENTRICLE (especially septum) WITHOUT dilation → diastolic dysfunction

## Key Feature
**Asymmetric Septal Hypertrophy (ASH)** — interventricular septum thicker than LV free wall

## Cause
**Autosomal dominant** genetic mutation — mutations in sarcomere proteins
Most common: **Beta-myosin heavy chain** or **myosin binding protein C** mutations

## Pathophysiology


## Systolic Anterior Motion (SAM)


## Gross Pathology


## Microscopic Pathology — PATHOGNOMONIC

> **Myofiber disarray = diagnostic of HCM**

## Clinical Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Age** | Young adults, athletes |
| **Symptoms** | Dyspnea, angina, syncope on exertion |
| **Murmur** | Harsh systolic murmur — INCREASES with Valsalva/standing, DECREASES with squatting |
| **Pulse** | Jerky, bifid pulse |
| **Sudden death** | Exercise-triggered VF |

## The Murmur Trick — High Yield


## Key MCQ Facts
- **Most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes**
- **Autosomal dominant** — always ask about family history
- **Diastolic dysfunction** — problem with RELAXATION not contraction
- **EF is NORMAL or HIGH** (squeezes well, can't relax)
- **Small LV cavity** (opposite of DCM)
- **Myofiber disarray** = pathognomonic on microscopy
- Treatment: **Beta-blockers** (slow heart, improve filling)
- Avoid: nitrates, digoxin, diuretics (reduce preload → worsen obstruction)

---

## 1C. RESTRICTIVE CARDIOMYOPATHY (RCM)

## Definition
Heart muscle becomes STIFF and cannot relax → diastolic dysfunction → impaired filling
Walls are NOT thickened, NOT dilated — but rigid and non-compliant

## Causes — Remember **"HASSI"**
- **H**emochromatosis (iron deposition)
- **A**myloidosis (most common cause overall)
- **S**arcoidosis (granulomas)
- **S**cleroderma (fibrosis)
- **I**diopathic / Endomyocardial fibrosis (Loeffler)

### Most Important Causes
| Cause | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Amyloidosis** | Most common — amyloid deposits stiffen heart |
| **Hemochromatosis** | Iron overload — deposits in myocardium |
| **Sarcoidosis** | Non-caseating granulomas |
| **Loeffler endocarditis** | Hypereosinophilia → endomyocardial fibrosis |
| **Radiation** | Post-radiation fibrosis |
| **Glycogen storage diseases** | Pompe disease |

## Pathophysiology


## Key Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Systolic function** | NORMAL (EF preserved) |
| **Diastolic function** | SEVERELY impaired |
| **Ventricular size** | Normal (not dilated) |
| **Wall thickness** | Normal or slightly increased |
| **Atria** | Massively dilated (blood backs up) |
| **Symptoms** | Right heart failure predominates |

## Amyloidosis — Special Focus


## Key MCQ Facts
- **Least common** cardiomyopathy
- **Diastolic dysfunction** with NORMAL systolic function
- **Amyloidosis** = most common cause
- **Congo red stain** → apple-green birefringence = amyloid
- **Massive atrial dilation** — diagnostic clue
- Hardest to treat — no specific therapy for most causes

---

## CARDIOMYOPATHY COMPARISON TABLE

| Feature | DCM | HCM | RCM |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chamber size** | All dilated | LV small, thick | Normal |
| **Wall thickness** | Thin | Massively thick | Normal/slightly thick |
| **Dysfunction** | Systolic | Diastolic | Diastolic |
| **EF** | Reduced (<40%) | Normal/High | Normal |
| **Main cause** | Idiopathic/alcohol | Genetic (AD) | Amyloidosis |
| **Key microscopy** | Fibrosis, hypertrophy | **Myofiber disarray** | Amyloid deposits |
| **Sudden death** | Can occur | **Most common cause in athletes** | Rare |
| **Treatment** | Diuretics, ACEi, ICD | Beta-blockers | Treat underlying cause |

---

## PART 2: PERICARDIAL DISEASE

## The Pericardium


---

## 2A. PERICARDITIS

## Definition
Inflammation of the pericardium

## Causes — Remember **"VITAL"**
- **V**iral (most common) — Coxsackievirus B, echovirus
- **I**diopathic
- **T**uberculosis (most common cause of constrictive pericarditis worldwide)
- **A**utoimmune — SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, Dressler syndrome
- **L**ocal/other — MI (days 2-3), uremia (renal failure), malignancy, radiation

### Causes by Type
| Type | Causes |
|---|---|
| **Fibrinous** | MI (days 2-3), uremia, rheumatic fever, SLE |
| **Serous** | Viral, SLE, rheumatic fever |
| **Purulent** | Bacterial infection (Staph, Strep) |
| **Hemorrhagic** | TB, malignancy, trauma |
| **Caseous** | TB (pathognomonic) |

## Fibrinous Pericarditis — Most Important Type


## Clinical Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Chest pain** | Sharp, pleuritic — WORSE lying down, BETTER sitting forward |
| **Friction rub** | Scratchy sound — pathognomonic |
| **ECG** | Diffuse ST elevation (saddle-shaped) in ALL leads |
| **Fever** | Common in viral/bacterial |

## Dressler Syndrome


---

## 2B. PERICARDIAL EFFUSION

## Definition
Abnormal accumulation of fluid in pericardial space (>50mL)

## Types of Fluid
| Type | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Transudate** | Heart failure, hypoalbuminemia |
| **Exudate** | Infection, malignancy, autoimmune |
| **Hemorrhagic** | Trauma, aortic dissection, malignancy |
| **Chylous** | Lymphatic obstruction |

## Key Point
The RATE of accumulation matters MORE than the volume


---

## 2C. CARDIAC TAMPONADE

## Definition
Life-threatening compression of the heart by pericardial fluid → impaired cardiac filling → reduced cardiac output

## Causes
Trauma, aortic dissection, MI rupture, malignancy, TB, post-cardiac surgery

## Pathophysiology


## Beck's Triad — MUST KNOW
1. HYPOTENSION — reduced cardiac output
2. RAISED JVP (distended neck veins) — backed up venous blood
3. MUFFLED HEART SOUNDS — fluid dampens sounds

## Pulsus Paradoxus
Normal: BP drops slightly (<10mmHg) during inspiration
Tamponade: BP drops >10mmHg during inspiration

Why?
During inspiration → right ventricle expands
→ Pushes septum LEFT (constrained by tamponade)
→ LV fills less → BP drops significantly

> **Pulsus paradoxus >10mmHg = hallmark of cardiac tamponade**

## ECG Findings
- Low voltage complexes (fluid insulates)
- Electrical alternans — QRS complex alternates in height
  (Heart swinging back and forth in fluid)
- Sinus tachycardia

## Treatment
**PERICARDIOCENTESIS** — emergency needle drainage of pericardial fluid
Needle inserted at left xiphocostal angle

---

## 2D. CONSTRICTIVE PERICARDITIS

## Definition
Chronic fibrosis and calcification of pericardium → forms rigid shell around heart → impairs filling

## Causes
| Cause | Notes |
|---|---|
| **TB** | Most common worldwide |
| **Viral pericarditis** | After healing |
| **Radiation** | Post-radiotherapy |
| **Cardiac surgery** | Post-operative |
| **Purulent pericarditis** | After bacterial infection |

## Pathophysiology


## Key Features
- Kussmaul's sign: JVP RISES on inspiration (opposite of normal)
- Pericardial knock: early diastolic sound
- CXR: pericardial calcification
- Features of RIGHT heart failure: JVP raised, hepatomegaly, ascites, edema
- Quiet, non-displaced apex beat

## Tamponade vs Constrictive Pericarditis

| Feature | Tamponade | Constrictive Pericarditis |
|---|---|---|
| **Cause** | Fluid accumulation | Fibrosis/calcification |
| **Onset** | Acute | Chronic |
| **Pulsus paradoxus** | **YES — prominent** | Mild or absent |
| **Kussmaul's sign** | Absent | **YES** |
| **CXR** | Enlarged cardiac silhouette | Pericardial calcification |
| **Treatment** | Pericardiocentesis | Pericardiectomy (surgery) |

---

## PART 3: CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE (CHD)

## Overview
Structural abnormalities of the heart present from birth

## Two Main Groups

### Acyanotic (Left-to-Right Shunts) — "Pink Babies"


### Cyanotic (Right-to-Left Shunts) — "Blue Babies"


---

## 3A. VENTRICULAR SEPTAL DEFECT (VSD)

## Definition
Hole in the interventricular septum — most commonly in membranous septum

## Key Facts
**Most common congenital heart defect overall**

## Pathophysiology


## Clinical Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Small VSD** | Loud harsh pansystolic murmur (Maladie de Roger) — may close spontaneously |
| **Large VSD** | Heart failure in infancy, failure to thrive |
| **CXR** | Cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary markings |
| **Complications** | Pulmonary hypertension, IE, Eisenmenger |

---

## 3B. ATRIAL SEPTAL DEFECT (ASD)

## Definition
Hole in the interatrial septum

## Types
| Type | Location | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Ostium secundum** | Fossa ovalis region | Most common (70%) |
| **Ostium primum** | Near AV valves | Associated with Down syndrome |
| **Sinus venosus** | Near SVC/IVC | Less common |

## Pathophysiology


## Key Features
- **Fixed wide split S2** — pathognomonic
- Soft systolic murmur (pulmonary flow murmur)
- Often asymptomatic until adulthood
- **Most common CHD presenting in adults**
- Associated with **Down syndrome** (ostium primum type)

---

## 3C. PATENT DUCTUS ARTERIOSUS (PDA)

## Definition
Failure of ductus arteriosus to close after birth
Ductus arteriosus = connects pulmonary artery to aorta in fetal circulation

## Normal Fetal Circulation


## Why It Stays Open
- **Prematurity** — most common cause
- **Rubella infection** (congenital rubella syndrome)
- High altitude

## Pathophysiology

(The rest of the Pathophysiology for PDA was cut off in the original prompt. Assuming it would detail the left-to-right shunt leading to pulmonary overcirculation and potential Eisenmenger.)

---

## 3D. TETRALOGY OF FALLOT (TOF)

## Definition
Four congenital heart defects present together:
1. Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)
2. Pulmonary Stenosis (RV outflow tract obstruction)
3. Overriding Aorta (aorta receives blood from both RV and LV)
4. Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (due to RV outflow obstruction)

## Pathophysiology


## Key Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Cyanosis** | Present from birth |
| **CXR** | **"Boot-shaped" heart** (due to RV hypertrophy and upturned apex) |
| **Murmur** | Harsh systolic murmur at LUSB (pulmonary stenosis) |
| **"Tet spells"** | Episodes of severe cyanosis, treated by squatting |

## Key MCQ Facts
- **Most common cyanotic CHD presenting after infancy** (after TGA at birth)
- **Squatting** is characteristic
- **VSD + Pulm Stenosis + Overriding Aorta + RVH** = Tetralogy of Fallot

---

## 3E. TRANSPOSITION OF THE GREAT ARTERIES (TGA)

## Definition
Aorta and pulmonary artery are transposed — aorta arises from RV, pulmonary artery arises from LV

## Pathophysiology


## Key Facts
- **Most common cyanotic CHD presenting at BIRTH** (before TOF)
- Associated with maternal **diabetes**
- **"Egg on a string"** CXR appearance — narrow mediastinum
- Treatment: **Prostaglandin E1** (keep PDA open) → **Arterial switch operation** (surgery)

---

## 3F. COARCTATION OF THE AORTA

## Definition
Narrowing of the aorta — most commonly just DISTAL to left subclavian artery (juxtaductal)

## Associations
- **Turner syndrome** (45, X) — most important association
- Bicuspid aortic valve (50% of cases)
- Berry aneurysms

## Pathophysiology


## Key Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **BP difference** | HIGH in arms, LOW in legs |
| **Pulses** | Weak/absent femoral pulses |
| **Collaterals** | Intercostal artery enlargement → **"Rib notching"** on CXR |
| **CXR** | **"Figure 3 sign"** — indentation of aorta |
| **Murmur** | Systolic murmur over back/scapula |

## Key MCQ Facts
- **Turner syndrome** → coarctation of aorta
- **Rib notching** on CXR = classic
- **Figure 3 sign** on CXR
- **Radio-femoral delay** — pulse in groin delayed vs wrist

---

## 3G. EISENMENGER SYNDROME

## Definition
Reversal of left-to-right shunt to right-to-left shunt due to pulmonary hypertension

## Pathophysiology


## Key MCQ Facts
- **Irreversible** — surgical repair contraindicated once Eisenmenger develops
- Complication of ANY large left-to-right shunt
- Patient was pink → now becomes CYANOTIC (late presentation)
- **Clubbing + polycythemia + cyanosis** in adult with known CHD = Eisenmenger

---

## CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE SUMMARY TABLE

| Condition | Shunt | Cyanosis | Key Finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| **VSD** | L→R | No (unless Eisenmenger) | Most common CHD, pansystolic murmur |
| **ASD** | L→R | No (unless Eisenmenger) | Fixed split S2, common in adults |
| **PDA** | L→R | No (unless Eisenmenger) | Continuous machinery murmur, rubella |
| **TOF** | R→L | YES from birth | Boot-shaped heart, tet spells, squatting |
| **TGA** | None (parallel) | YES from birth | Egg on string CXR, maternal diabetes |
| **Coarctation** | None | No | Rib notching, Turner syndrome, BP difference |
| **Eisenmenger** | R→L (reversed) | YES (late) | Irreversible, cyanosis in adult with CHD |

---

## PART 4: CARDIAC TUMORS

## Overview
Cardiac tumors are RARE — metastatic tumors to heart are more common than primary

---

## 4A. CARDIAC MYXOMA

## Definition
Most common **PRIMARY** cardiac tumor in adults

## Location
**LEFT ATRIUM** in 75% of cases — attached to interatrial septum near fossa ovalis

## Gross Pathology


## Microscopic Pathology


## Pathophysiology


## Clinical Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Positional symptoms** | Syncope/dyspnea changes with position (classic) |
| **"Tumor plop"** | Early diastolic sound as tumor hits mitral valve |
| **Emboli** | Stroke, peripheral embolism |
| **Constitutional** | Fever, weight loss, elevated ESR, anemia |
| **Mimics** | Mitral stenosis, IE, autoimmune disease |

## Key MCQ Triggers
- Left atrium + pedunculated mass + positional syncope = **Myxoma**
- Fever + emboli + elevated ESR but cultures negative = **Myxoma** (not IE)
- "Tumor plop" on auscultation = **Myxoma**
- Treatment: **Surgical excision** — curative

---

## 4B. RHABDOMYOMA

## Definition
Most common **PRIMARY** cardiac tumor in **CHILDREN/INFANTS**

## Key Association
**Tuberous sclerosis** — hamartomatous condition
- Always think: child + cardiac tumor + tuberous sclerosis

## Location
Ventricular myocardium — often multiple

## Gross Pathology
Gray-white nodules in ventricular wall — often multiple

## Microscopic Pathology
**"Spider cells"** — large cells with central nucleus connected to cell membrane by cytoplasmic processes (glycogen-filled)

## Key Facts
- Most common cardiac tumor in CHILDREN
- Associated with **tuberous sclerosis**
- Often REGRESS spontaneously
- Can cause arrhythmias, outflow obstruction
- Treatment: often observation — may resolve on own

---

## 4C. OTHER CARDIAC TUMORS

| Tumor | Key Facts |
|---|---|
| **Metastatic tumors** | Most common overall — lung, breast, melanoma, lymphoma |
| **Lipoma** | Benign, in epicardium — usually incidental |
| **Fibroma** | Children — ventricular wall — associated with Gorlin syndrome |
| **Angiosarcoma** | Most common PRIMARY malignant cardiac tumor — right atrium |
| **Papillary fibroelastoma** | On valve surfaces — risk of embolism |

---

## CARDIAC TUMORS SUMMARY TABLE

| Tumor | Age | Location | Key Feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Myxoma** | Adults | Left atrium | Positional syncope, tumor plop, emboli |
| **Rhabdomyoma** | Children | Ventricles | Tuberous sclerosis, spider cells, regresses |
| **Angiosarcoma** | Adults | Right atrium | Most common malignant primary tumor |
| **Metastatic** | Any | Any | Most common cardiac tumor overall |
| **Fibroma** | Children | Ventricles | Gorlin syndrome |

---

## 🔑 FINAL MEGA MCQ TRIGGER TABLE

| If you see this... | Think... |
|---|---|
| Young athlete + sudden death + myofiber disarray | **HCM** |
| All 4 chambers dilated + reduced EF + alcoholic | **DCM** |
| Stiff heart + normal EF + amyloid Congo red stain | **RCM** |
| Murmur louder with Valsalva | **HCM** |
| Doxorubicin chemotherapy + heart failure | **DCM** |
| Peripartum woman + heart failure | **Peripartum cardiomyopathy (DCM)** |
| Beck's triad (hypotension + raised JVP + muffled sounds) | **Cardiac tamponade** |
| Pulsus paradoxus >10mmHg | **Cardiac tamponade** |
| Electrical alternans on ECG | **Cardiac tamponade** |
| Kussmaul's sign + pericardial calcification | **Constrictive pericarditis** |
| Pleuritic chest pain better sitting forward + friction rub | **Pericarditis** |
| 2-10 weeks post-MI + fever + pericarditis | **Dressler syndrome** |
| Most common CHD overall | **VSD** |
| Fixed split S2 | **ASD** |
| Continuous machinery murmur | **PDA** |
| Boot-shaped heart + squatting child | **Tetralogy of Fallot** |
| Egg on string CXR + cyanosis at birth + maternal diabetes | **TGA** |
| Turner syndrome + upper limb hypertension + rib notching | **Coarctation of aorta** |
| Adult with known CHD now cyanotic | **Eisenmenger syndrome** |
| LA mass + positional syncope + tumor plop | **Cardiac myxoma** |
| Child + cardiac tumor + tuberous sclerosis | **Rhabdomyoma** |
| Most common malignant primary cardiac tumor | **Angiosarcoma** |
| Most common cardiac tumor overall | **Metastatic tumor** |

---

## Practice Questions
1. A 55-year-old man presents with fatigue, shortness of breath, and a history of heavy alcohol use. Echocardiogram shows dilation of all four cardiac chambers with a reduced ejection fraction. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM)
2. A young athlete collapses during a competition and is found to have a markedly thickened left ventricular wall on echocardiogram, particularly the interventricular septum. There is no chamber dilation and the ejection fraction is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM)
3. A patient presents with symptoms of right-sided heart failure, including leg edema and ascites. Echocardiogram reveals normal ventricular size and function but markedly thickened, non-compliant ventricular walls. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Restrictive Cardiomyopathy (RCM)
4. A patient presents with acute onset of sharp, pleuritic chest pain that is worse when lying down and relieved by sitting forward. A friction rub is heard on auscultation. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation in all leads. What is the likely diagnosis? → Pericarditis
5. During a physical examination, you note hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds in a patient with a rapid atrial fibrillation. What is the immediate life-threatening condition to consider? → Cardiac Tamponade
6. A 3-month-old infant presents with poor feeding, tachypnea, and a loud, harsh pansystolic murmur heard best at the left lower sternal border. Echocardiogram confirms a defect in the interventricular septum. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)
7. A 40-year-old woman is found to have a continuous "machinery-like" murmur on cardiac auscultation. She has a history of prematurity and rubella infection in childhood. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)
8. A child presents with cyanosis present from birth, a harsh systolic murmur, and squatting behavior during episodes of increased cyanosis. Chest X-ray shows a "boot-shaped" heart. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

# 🫀 MISSING TOPICS — ULTRA DEEP NOTES

---

# PART 1: CARDIOMYOPATHIES

## Definition
> Disease of the heart muscle itself — NOT caused by coronary artery disease, hypertension, or valvular disease

## There Are 3 Types — Remember **"DHR"**
> - **D**ilated Cardiomyopathy
> - **H**ypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
> - **R**estrictive Cardiomyopathy

---

# 1A. DILATED CARDIOMYOPATHY (DCM)

## Definition
> All 4 chambers dilate + systolic dysfunction → heart cannot CONTRACT properly

## Causes — Remember **"ABCDE"**
> - **A**lcohol (most common toxic cause)
> - **B**eri-beri (Thiamine/B1 deficiency)
> - **C**oxsackievirus B (viral myocarditis → DCM)
> - **D**rugs (Doxorubicin/adriamycin — chemotherapy)
> - **E**clampsia/pregnancy (Peripartum cardiomyopathy)

### Other Important Causes
| Cause | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Idiopathic** | Most common overall (50%) |
| **Genetic** | 25-35% — mutations in cytoskeletal proteins |
| **Chagas disease** | Trypanosoma cruzi — South America |
| **Hemochromatosis** | Iron deposition in myocardium |
| **Sarcoidosis** | Granulomas in myocardium |
| **Thyroid disease** | Hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism |
| **Cocaine** | Toxic cardiomyopathy |

## Pathophysiology
```
Myocardial damage from any cause above
        ↓
Cardiomyocytes injured → lose contractile function
        ↓
Heart compensates → dilates to maintain stroke volume
        ↓
ALL 4 chambers dilate (biventricular dilation)
        ↓
Systolic dysfunction → EF drops (<40%)
        ↓
Heart failure symptoms develop
        ↓
Dilated chambers → stagnant blood → MURAL THROMBUS
        ↓
Thrombus embolizes → stroke
```

## Gross Pathology
```
- Massive enlargement of all 4 chambers
- Flabby, pale myocardium
- Thin walls despite dilation
- Mural thrombi in ventricles (especially apex)
- "Globular" heart shape on CXR
```

## Microscopic Pathology
```
- Hypertrophied cardiomyocytes with large nuclei
- Interstitial fibrosis
- Myocyte degeneration and dropout
- No specific diagnostic finding
```

## Clinical Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Age** | Any age, peak 20-60 |
| **Symptoms** | Progressive heart failure — dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea |
| **Signs** | S3 gallop, displaced apex beat, JVP raised |
| **CXR** | Massive cardiomegaly — "globular heart" |
| **Echo** | Dilated all chambers, reduced EF |
| **Arrhythmias** | Common — AF, VT, sudden death |
| **Emboli** | Stroke from mural thrombus |

## Key MCQ Facts
> - **Most common cardiomyopathy overall**
> - **Systolic dysfunction** — problem with CONTRACTION
> - **All 4 chambers dilate**
> - Alcohol → DCM → stop alcohol → can RECOVER
> - Doxorubicin (adriamycin) → dose-dependent cardiotoxicity → DCM
> - Peripartum cardiomyopathy → last month of pregnancy or 5 months postpartum
> - **Worst prognosis** of all cardiomyopathies

---

# 1B. HYPERTROPHIC CARDIOMYOPATHY (HCM)

## Definition
> Massive hypertrophy of the LEFT VENTRICLE (especially septum) WITHOUT dilation → diastolic dysfunction

## Key Feature
> **Asymmetric Septal Hypertrophy (ASH)** — interventricular septum thicker than LV free wall

## Cause
> **Autosomal dominant** genetic mutation — mutations in sarcomere proteins
> Most common: **Beta-myosin heavy chain** or **myosin binding protein C** mutations

## Pathophysiology
```
Genetic mutation → abnormal sarcomere proteins
        ↓
Massive LV hypertrophy (especially septum)
        ↓
TWO problems:

PROBLEM 1 — DIASTOLIC DYSFUNCTION
Stiff, non-compliant LV → cannot RELAX and fill properly
        ↓
Reduced cardiac output
        ↓
Dyspnea, fatigue

PROBLEM 2 — OUTFLOW TRACT OBSTRUCTION
Hypertrophied septum + abnormal mitral valve
        ↓
Blocks LV outflow tract during systole
        ↓
Called: Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM)
        ↓
Syncope, angina, sudden death
```

## Systolic Anterior Motion (SAM)
```
During systole, blood rushes through narrow outflow tract
        ↓
Creates Venturi effect → sucks mitral valve leaflet FORWARD
        ↓
Mitral valve obstructs outflow tract further
        ↓
AND causes mitral regurgitation
```

## Gross Pathology
```
- Massively hypertrophied LV
- Septum disproportionately thick (ratio >1.3:1)
- Small LV cavity (opposite of DCM)
- Banana-shaped LV cavity
- Thickened, abnormal mitral valve
```

## Microscopic Pathology — PATHOGNOMONIC
```
MYOFIBER DISARRAY — most important finding
- Cardiomyocytes arranged in chaotic, whirled pattern
- Instead of normal parallel arrangement
- Hypertrophied myocytes with bizarre nuclei
- Interstitial fibrosis
```
> **Myofiber disarray = diagnostic of HCM**

## Clinical Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Age** | Young adults, athletes |
| **Symptoms** | Dyspnea, angina, syncope on exertion |
| **Murmur** | Harsh systolic murmur — INCREASES with Valsalva/standing, DECREASES with squatting |
| **Pulse** | Jerky, bifid pulse |
| **Sudden death** | Exercise-triggered VF |

## The Murmur Trick — High Yield
```
INCREASES obstruction (louder murmur):
→ Valsalva maneuver
→ Standing up
→ Dehydration
→ Nitrates
(Less blood in LV → septum closer to outflow → more obstruction)

DECREASES obstruction (softer murmur):
→ Squatting
→ Lying down
→ IV fluids
→ Beta-blockers
(More blood in LV → pushes septum away → less obstruction)
```

## Key MCQ Facts
> - **Most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes**
> - **Autosomal dominant** — always ask about family history
> - **Diastolic dysfunction** — problem with RELAXATION not contraction
> - **EF is NORMAL or HIGH** (squeezes well, can't relax)
> - **Small LV cavity** (opposite of DCM)
> - **Myofiber disarray** = pathognomonic on microscopy
> - Treatment: **Beta-blockers** (slow heart, improve filling)
> - Avoid: nitrates, digoxin, diuretics (reduce preload → worsen obstruction)

---

# 1C. RESTRICTIVE CARDIOMYOPATHY (RCM)

## Definition
> Heart muscle becomes STIFF and cannot relax → diastolic dysfunction → impaired filling
> Walls are NOT thickened, NOT dilated — but rigid and non-compliant

## Causes — Remember **"HASSI"**
> - **H**emochromatosis (iron deposition)
> - **A**myloidosis (most common cause overall)
> - **S**arcoidosis (granulomas)
> - **S**cleroderma (fibrosis)
> - **I**diopathic / Endomyocardial fibrosis (Loeffler)

### Most Important Causes
| Cause | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Amyloidosis** | Most common — amyloid deposits stiffen heart |
| **Hemochromatosis** | Iron overload — deposits in myocardium |
| **Sarcoidosis** | Non-caseating granulomas |
| **Loeffler endocarditis** | Hypereosinophilia → endomyocardial fibrosis |
| **Radiation** | Post-radiation fibrosis |
| **Glycogen storage diseases** | Pompe disease |

## Pathophysiology
```
Infiltration/deposition of abnormal material in myocardium
        ↓
Myocardium becomes STIFF and non-compliant
        ↓
Ventricles CANNOT relax and fill properly
        ↓
Diastolic dysfunction → reduced filling
        ↓
Reduced cardiac output
        ↓
Elevated filling pressures → heart failure symptoms
        ↓
RIGHT heart failure signs predominate
(JVP raised, hepatomegaly, ascites, edema)
```

## Key Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Systolic function** | NORMAL (EF preserved) |
| **Diastolic function** | SEVERELY impaired |
| **Ventricular size** | Normal (not dilated) |
| **Wall thickness** | Normal or slightly increased |
| **Atria** | Massively dilated (blood backs up) |
| **Symptoms** | Right heart failure predominates |

## Amyloidosis — Special Focus
```
Amyloid protein deposits between cardiomyocytes
        ↓
"Sparkling" or "granular" appearance on Echo
        ↓
Heart feels rubbery and firm
        ↓
Classic: elderly + heart failure + thick walls + normal EF
        ↓
Congo red stain → apple-green birefringence under polarized light
```

## Key MCQ Facts
> - **Least common** cardiomyopathy
> - **Diastolic dysfunction** with NORMAL systolic function
> - **Amyloidosis** = most common cause
> - **Congo red stain** → apple-green birefringence = amyloid
> - **Massive atrial dilation** — diagnostic clue
> - Hardest to treat — no specific therapy for most causes

---

## CARDIOMYOPATHY COMPARISON TABLE

| Feature | DCM | HCM | RCM |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chamber size** | All dilated | LV small, thick | Normal |
| **Wall thickness** | Thin | Massively thick | Normal/slightly thick |
| **Dysfunction** | Systolic | Diastolic | Diastolic |
| **EF** | Reduced (<40%) | Normal/High | Normal |
| **Main cause** | Idiopathic/alcohol | Genetic (AD) | Amyloidosis |
| **Key microscopy** | Fibrosis, hypertrophy | **Myofiber disarray** | Amyloid deposits |
| **Sudden death** | Can occur | **Most common cause in athletes** | Rare |
| **Treatment** | Diuretics, ACEi, ICD | Beta-blockers | Treat underlying cause |

---

# PART 2: PERICARDIAL DISEASE

## The Pericardium
```
Two layers:
- Visceral pericardium (epicardium) — inner layer, on heart surface
- Parietal pericardium — outer fibrous layer

Between them: 15-50 mL of lubricating fluid normally
```

---

# 2A. PERICARDITIS

## Definition
> Inflammation of the pericardium

## Causes — Remember **"VITAL"**
> - **V**iral (most common) — Coxsackievirus B, echovirus
> - **I**diopathic
> - **T**uberculosis (most common cause of constrictive pericarditis worldwide)
> - **A**utoimmune — SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, Dressler syndrome
> - **L**ocal/other — MI (days 2-3), uremia (renal failure), malignancy, radiation

### Causes by Type
| Type | Causes |
|---|---|
| **Fibrinous** | MI (days 2-3), uremia, rheumatic fever, SLE |
| **Serous** | Viral, SLE, rheumatic fever |
| **Purulent** | Bacterial infection (Staph, Strep) |
| **Hemorrhagic** | TB, malignancy, trauma |
| **Caseous** | TB (pathognomonic) |

## Fibrinous Pericarditis — Most Important Type
```
Inflammatory exudate (fibrin) deposited on pericardial surfaces
        ↓
Pericardial surfaces become rough and shaggy
        ↓
Called "BREAD AND BUTTER" pericarditis
(Looks like two pieces of buttered bread pulled apart)
        ↓
Friction rub heard on auscultation
        ↓
Heals with resolution OR progresses to constrictive pericarditis
```

## Clinical Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Chest pain** | Sharp, pleuritic — WORSE lying down, BETTER sitting forward |
| **Friction rub** | Scratchy sound — pathognomonic |
| **ECG** | Diffuse ST elevation (saddle-shaped) in ALL leads |
| **Fever** | Common in viral/bacterial |

## Dressler Syndrome
```
2-10 weeks after MI or cardiac surgery
        ↓
Autoimmune reaction against cardiac antigens
        ↓
Fibrinous pericarditis + pleuritis + fever
        ↓
Elevated ESR, anti-heart antibodies
        ↓
Treatment: NSAIDs, colchicine
```

---

# 2B. PERICARDIAL EFFUSION

## Definition
> Abnormal accumulation of fluid in pericardial space (>50mL)

## Types of Fluid
| Type | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Transudate** | Heart failure, hypoalbuminemia |
| **Exudate** | Infection, malignancy, autoimmune |
| **Hemorrhagic** | Trauma, aortic dissection, malignancy |
| **Chylous** | Lymphatic obstruction |

## Key Point
> The RATE of accumulation matters MORE than the volume
```
SLOW accumulation (e.g. 1000mL over months):
→ Pericardium stretches to accommodate
→ May be asymptomatic

RAPID accumulation (e.g. 200mL over minutes):
→ Pericardium cannot stretch
→ Compresses heart → CARDIAC TAMPONADE
```

---

# 2C. CARDIAC TAMPONADE

## Definition
> Life-threatening compression of the heart by pericardial fluid → impaired cardiac filling → reduced cardiac output

## Causes
> Trauma, aortic dissection, MI rupture, malignancy, TB, post-cardiac surgery

## Pathophysiology
```
Rapid fluid accumulation in pericardial space
        ↓
Pressure in pericardial sac RISES
        ↓
Compresses all 4 chambers from outside
        ↓
Chambers cannot fill properly during diastole
        ↓
Reduced stroke volume → reduced cardiac output
        ↓
Compensatory tachycardia + vasoconstriction
        ↓
If untreated → cardiogenic shock → death
```

## Beck's Triad — MUST KNOW
```
1. HYPOTENSION — reduced cardiac output
2. RAISED JVP (distended neck veins) — backed up venous blood
3. MUFFLED HEART SOUNDS — fluid dampens sounds
```

## Pulsus Paradoxus
```
Normal: BP drops slightly (<10mmHg) during inspiration
Tamponade: BP drops >10mmHg during inspiration

Why?
During inspiration → right ventricle expands
→ Pushes septum LEFT (constrained by tamponade)
→ LV fills less → BP drops significantly
```
> **Pulsus paradoxus >10mmHg = hallmark of cardiac tamponade**

## ECG Findings
```
- Low voltage complexes (fluid insulates)
- Electrical alternans — QRS complex alternates in height
  (Heart swinging back and forth in fluid)
- Sinus tachycardia
```

## Treatment
> **PERICARDIOCENTESIS** — emergency needle drainage of pericardial fluid
> Needle inserted at left xiphocostal angle

---

# 2D. CONSTRICTIVE PERICARDITIS

## Definition
> Chronic fibrosis and calcification of pericardium → forms rigid shell around heart → impairs filling

## Causes
| Cause | Notes |
|---|---|
| **TB** | Most common worldwide |
| **Viral pericarditis** | After healing |
| **Radiation** | Post-radiotherapy |
| **Cardiac surgery** | Post-operative |
| **Purulent pericarditis** | After bacterial infection |

## Pathophysiology
```
Chronic pericarditis → fibrin deposition → fibrosis
        ↓
Pericardium thickens, calcifies → rigid shell
        ↓
Heart encased in hard "concrete-like" shell
        ↓
ALL chambers impaired from filling
        ↓
Fixed, low cardiac output
        ↓
Raised filling pressures → venous congestion
```

## Key Features
```
- Kussmaul's sign: JVP RISES on inspiration (opposite of normal)
- Pericardial knock: early diastolic sound
- CXR: pericardial calcification
- Features of RIGHT heart failure: JVP raised, hepatomegaly, ascites, edema
- Quiet, non-displaced apex beat
```

## Tamponade vs Constrictive Pericarditis

| Feature | Tamponade | Constrictive Pericarditis |
|---|---|---|
| **Cause** | Fluid accumulation | Fibrosis/calcification |
| **Onset** | Acute | Chronic |
| **Pulsus paradoxus** | **YES — prominent** | Mild or absent |
| **Kussmaul's sign** | Absent | **YES** |
| **CXR** | Enlarged cardiac silhouette | Pericardial calcification |
| **Treatment** | Pericardiocentesis | Pericardiectomy (surgery) |

---

# PART 3: CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE (CHD)

## Overview
> Structural abnormalities of the heart present from birth

## Two Main Groups

### Acyanotic (Left-to-Right Shunts) — "Pink Babies"
```
Oxygenated blood (left side) shunts to deoxygenated side (right)
→ Extra blood goes to lungs → pulmonary hypertension
→ Baby is PINK (blood reaching body is still oxygenated)
→ BUT if untreated → Eisenmenger syndrome → becomes CYANOTIC
```

### Cyanotic (Right-to-Left Shunts) — "Blue Babies"
```
Deoxygenated blood (right side) bypasses lungs → goes directly to body
→ Baby is BLUE/CYANOTIC from birth
→ "Blue baby"
```

---

# 3A. VENTRICULAR SEPTAL DEFECT (VSD)

## Definition
> Hole in the interventricular septum — most commonly in membranous septum

## Key Facts
> **Most common congenital heart defect overall**

## Pathophysiology
```
Hole in septum → blood flows LEFT → RIGHT (LV pressure > RV pressure)
        ↓
Extra blood flows into RV → to lungs
        ↓
Pulmonary overcirculation → pulmonary hypertension
        ↓
If large, untreated → Eisenmenger syndrome
        ↓
RV pressure eventually EXCEEDS LV pressure
        ↓
Shunt REVERSES → Right to Left → CYANOSIS develops late
```

## Clinical Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Small VSD** | Loud harsh pansystolic murmur (Maladie de Roger) — may close spontaneously |
| **Large VSD** | Heart failure in infancy, failure to thrive |
| **CXR** | Cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary markings |
| **Complications** | Pulmonary hypertension, IE, Eisenmenger |

---

# 3B. ATRIAL SEPTAL DEFECT (ASD)

## Definition
> Hole in the interatrial septum

## Types
| Type | Location | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Ostium secundum** | Fossa ovalis region | Most common (70%) |
| **Ostium primum** | Near AV valves | Associated with Down syndrome |
| **Sinus venosus** | Near SVC/IVC | Less common |

## Pathophysiology
```
Hole in atrial septum → blood flows LEFT → RIGHT (LA pressure > RA pressure)
        ↓
Extra blood in RA → RV → lungs
        ↓
Volume overload on right side
        ↓
RA and RV enlarge
        ↓
Fixed split S2 (hallmark)
        ↓
Eventually pulmonary hypertension → Eisenmenger
```

## Key Features
> - **Fixed wide split S2** — pathognomonic
> - Soft systolic murmur (pulmonary flow murmur)
> - Often asymptomatic until adulthood
> - **Most common CHD presenting in adults**
> - Associated with **Down syndrome** (ostium primum type)

---

# 3C. PATENT DUCTUS ARTERIOSUS (PDA)

## Definition
> Failure of ductus arteriosus to close after birth
> Ductus arteriosus = connects pulmonary artery to aorta in fetal circulation

## Normal Fetal Circulation
```
Fetal lungs not working → blood bypasses lungs via ductus arteriosus
At birth → lungs expand → O2 rises → prostaglandins drop → ductus CLOSES
        ↓
Normally closes within 48-72 hours
```

## Why It Stays Open
> - **Prematurity** — most common cause
> - **Rubella infection** (congenital rubella syndrome)
> - High altitude

## Pathophysiology
```
PDA → blood flows from AORTA → PULMONARY ARTERY (Aorta pressure > PA)
        ↓
Continuous left-to-right shunt (throughout cardiac cycle)
        ↓
Lungs overloaded → pulmonary hypertension
        ↓
Eventually → Eisenmenger → right-to-left shunt
        ↓
DIFFERENTIAL CYANOSIS — lower body cyanotic, upper body pink
```

## Key Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Murmur** | **Continuous "machinery" murmur** — best heard at left infraclavicular area |
| **Pulse** | Wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses |
| **CXR** | Cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary markings |
| **Differential cyanosis** | Lower limbs blue, upper limbs pink (if Eisenmenger) |

## Treatment
> - **Indomethacin** (NSAID) — closes PDA by inhibiting prostaglandins — works in premature infants
> - **Surgical ligation** — if indomethacin fails
> - **Keep PDA OPEN** with prostaglandin E1 — in ductus-dependent lesions (e.g. Tetralogy of Fallot)

---

# 3D. TETRALOGY OF FALLOT (TOF)

## Definition
> Most common **CYANOTIC** congenital heart disease

## The 4 Components — Remember **"PROVE"**
> - **P**ulmonary stenosis (most important — causes cyanosis)
> - **R**ight ventricular hypertrophy
> - **O**veriding aorta (aorta sits over both ventricles)
> - **V**entricular septal defect
> - **E** — Extra reminder: All caused by anterosuperior displacement of infundibular septum

```
All 4 defects caused by ONE embryological error:
Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum
```

## Pathophysiology
```
Pulmonary stenosis → obstruction of RV outflow
        ↓
RV pressure RISES → RV hypertrophies
        ↓
RV pressure exceeds LV pressure
        ↓
Blood shunts RIGHT → LEFT through VSD
        ↓
Deoxygenated blood enters aorta (overriding aorta makes this worse)
        ↓
CYANOSIS from birth
```

## Clinical Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Cyanosis** | From birth or early infancy |
| **"Tet spells"** | Episodic severe cyanosis on crying/feeding — child squats to relieve |
| **Squatting** | Increases systemic resistance → forces more blood to lungs |
| **Clubbing** | Chronic hypoxia → finger clubbing |
| **Polycythemia** | Chronic hypoxia → ↑ RBC production |
| **CXR** | **"Boot-shaped heart"** (Coeur en sabot) — RVH lifts apex |
| **ECG** | Right axis deviation, RVH |

## Why Squatting Helps
```
Squatting → compresses femoral arteries
        ↓
Increases systemic vascular resistance
        ↓
Forces more blood through pulmonary stenosis into lungs
        ↓
More oxygenated blood returns → cyanosis improves
```

## Key MCQ Facts
> - **Most common cyanotic CHD**
> - **Boot-shaped heart** on CXR
> - **"Tet spells"** relieved by squatting
> - **Right-to-left shunt** from birth
> - Pulmonary stenosis is the KEY defect — determines severity
> - Treatment: **Surgical repair** — Blalock-Taussig shunt (palliative) or total correction

---

# 3E. TRANSPOSITION OF THE GREAT ARTERIES (TGA)

## Definition
> Aorta arises from RIGHT ventricle + Pulmonary artery arises from LEFT ventricle

## Why It's Deadly
```
Two SEPARATE, PARALLEL circuits — no mixing:
Circuit 1: Body → RV → Aorta → Body (deoxygenated blood circulating systemically)
Circuit 2: Lungs → LV → Pulmonary artery → Lungs (oxygenated blood never reaches body)
        ↓
Incompatible with life unless there's a mixing defect (ASD, VSD, PDA)
```

## Key Facts
> - **Most common cyanotic CHD presenting at BIRTH** (before TOF)
> - Associated with maternal **diabetes**
> - **"Egg on a string"** CXR appearance — narrow mediastinum
> - Treatment: **Prostaglandin E1** (keep PDA open) → **Arterial switch operation** (surgery)

---

# 3F. COARCTATION OF THE AORTA

## Definition
> Narrowing of the aorta — most commonly just DISTAL to left subclavian artery (juxtaductal)

## Associations
> - **Turner syndrome** (45, X) — most important association
> - Bicuspid aortic valve (50% of cases)
> - Berry aneurysms

## Pathophysiology
```
Narrowing of aorta → obstruction
        ↓
PROXIMAL to narrowing: HIGH pressure
→ Hypertension in upper body (arms)
→ Headaches, epistaxis

DISTAL to narrowing: LOW pressure
→ Hypotension in lower body (legs)
→ Weak femoral pulses, claudication, cold legs
```

## Key Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **BP difference** | HIGH in arms, LOW in legs |
| **Pulses** | Weak/absent femoral pulses |
| **Collaterals** | Intercostal artery enlargement → **"Rib notching"** on CXR |
| **CXR** | **"Figure 3 sign"** — indentation of aorta |
| **Murmur** | Systolic murmur over back/scapula |

## Key MCQ Facts
> - **Turner syndrome** → coarctation of aorta
> - **Rib notching** on CXR = classic
> - **Figure 3 sign** on CXR
> - **Radio-femoral delay** — pulse in groin delayed vs wrist

---

# 3G. EISENMENGER SYNDROME

## Definition
> Reversal of left-to-right shunt to right-to-left shunt due to pulmonary hypertension

## Pathophysiology
```
Large left-to-right shunt (VSD/ASD/PDA) — untreated
        ↓
Chronic excess blood flow to lungs
        ↓
Pulmonary vascular remodeling → pulmonary hypertension
        ↓
RV pressure rises to equal then EXCEED LV pressure
        ↓
Shunt REVERSES → Right to Left
        ↓
Deoxygenated blood enters systemic circulation
        ↓
CYANOSIS develops (late complication)
        ↓
Irreversible — cannot surgically repair at this stage
```

## Key MCQ Facts
> - **Irreversible** — surgical repair contraindicated once Eisenmenger develops
> - Complication of ANY large left-to-right shunt
> - Patient was pink → now becomes CYANOTIC (late presentation)
> - **Clubbing + polycythemia + cyanosis** in adult with known CHD = Eisenmenger

---

## CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE SUMMARY TABLE

| Condition | Shunt | Cyanosis | Key Finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| **VSD** | L→R | No (unless Eisenmenger) | Most common CHD, pansystolic murmur |
| **ASD** | L→R | No (unless Eisenmenger) | Fixed split S2, common in adults |
| **PDA** | L→R | No (unless Eisenmenger) | Continuous machinery murmur, rubella |
| **TOF** | R→L | YES from birth | Boot-shaped heart, tet spells, squatting |
| **TGA** | None (parallel) | YES from birth | Egg on string CXR, maternal diabetes |
| **Coarctation** | None | No | Rib notching, Turner syndrome, BP difference |
| **Eisenmenger** | R→L (reversed) | YES (late) | Irreversible, cyanosis in adult with CHD |

---

# PART 4: CARDIAC TUMORS

## Overview
> Cardiac tumors are RARE — metastatic tumors to heart are more common than primary

---

# 4A. CARDIAC MYXOMA

## Definition
> Most common **PRIMARY** cardiac tumor in adults

## Location
> **LEFT ATRIUM** in 75% of cases — attached to interatrial septum near fossa ovalis

## Gross Pathology
```
- Gelatinous, mucoid, polypoid mass
- Attached by stalk (pedunculated)
- Lobulated surface
- Can be smooth or villous (friable — more embolic risk)
```

## Microscopic Pathology
```
- Myxoma cells (stellate/spider cells) embedded in myxoid stroma
- Abundant mucopolysaccharide ground substance
- Blood vessels scattered throughout
```

## Pathophysiology
```
Pedunculated tumor in LA
        ↓
Moves back and forth with heartbeat
        ↓
THREE problems:

1. OBSTRUCTION
Tumor prolapses into mitral valve → mimics mitral stenosis
→ Dyspnea, syncope (especially when changing position)

2. EMBOLISM
Friable tumor fragments break off
→ Systemic emboli → stroke, peripheral emboli

3. CONSTITUTIONAL SYMPTOMS
Tumor produces IL-6
→ Fever, weight loss, fatigue, elevated ESR
→ Mimics infective endocarditis or autoimmune disease
```

## Clinical Features
| Feature | Details |
|---|---|
| **Positional symptoms** | Syncope/dyspnea changes with position (classic) |
| **"Tumor plop"** | Early diastolic sound as tumor hits mitral valve |
| **Emboli** | Stroke, peripheral embolism |
| **Constitutional** | Fever, weight loss, elevated ESR, anemia |
| **Mimics** | Mitral stenosis, IE, autoimmune disease |

## Key MCQ Triggers
> - Left atrium + pedunculated mass + positional syncope = **Myxoma**
> - Fever + emboli + elevated ESR but cultures negative = **Myxoma** (not IE)
> - "Tumor plop" on auscultation = **Myxoma**
> - Treatment: **Surgical excision** — curative

---

# 4B. RHABDOMYOMA

## Definition
> Most common **PRIMARY** cardiac tumor in **CHILDREN/INFANTS**

## Key Association
> **Tuberous sclerosis** — hamartomatous condition
> - Always think: child + cardiac tumor + tuberous sclerosis

## Location
> Ventricular myocardium — often multiple

## Gross Pathology
> Gray-white nodules in ventricular wall — often multiple

## Microscopic Pathology
> **"Spider cells"** — large cells with central nucleus connected to cell membrane by cytoplasmic processes (glycogen-filled)

## Key Facts
> - Most common cardiac tumor in CHILDREN
> - Associated with **tuberous sclerosis**
> - Often REGRESS spontaneously
> - Can cause arrhythmias, outflow obstruction
> - Treatment: often observation — may resolve on own

---

# 4C. OTHER CARDIAC TUMORS

| Tumor | Key Facts |
|---|---|
| **Metastatic tumors** | Most common overall — lung, breast, melanoma, lymphoma |
| **Lipoma** | Benign, in epicardium — usually incidental |
| **Fibroma** | Children — ventricular wall — associated with Gorlin syndrome |
| **Angiosarcoma** | Most common PRIMARY malignant cardiac tumor — right atrium |
| **Papillary fibroelastoma** | On valve surfaces — risk of embolism |

---

## CARDIAC TUMORS SUMMARY TABLE

| Tumor | Age | Location | Key Feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Myxoma** | Adults | Left atrium | Positional syncope, tumor plop, emboli |
| **Rhabdomyoma** | Children | Ventricles | Tuberous sclerosis, spider cells, regresses |
| **Angiosarcoma** | Adults | Right atrium | Most common malignant primary tumor |
| **Metastatic** | Any | Any | Most common cardiac tumor overall |
| **Fibroma** | Children | Ventricles | Gorlin syndrome |

---

# 🔑 FINAL MEGA MCQ TRIGGER TABLE

| If you see this... | Think... |
|---|---|
| Young athlete + sudden death + myofiber disarray | **HCM** |
| All 4 chambers dilated + reduced EF + alcoholic | **DCM** |
| Stiff heart + normal EF + amyloid Congo red stain | **RCM** |
| Murmur louder with Valsalva | **HCM** |
| Doxorubicin chemotherapy + heart failure | **DCM** |
| Peripartum woman + heart failure | **Peripartum cardiomyopathy (DCM)** |
| Beck's triad (hypotension + raised JVP + muffled sounds) | **Cardiac tamponade** |
| Pulsus paradoxus >10mmHg | **Cardiac tamponade** |
| Electrical alternans on ECG | **Cardiac tamponade** |
| Kussmaul's sign + pericardial calcification | **Constrictive pericarditis** |
| Pleuritic chest pain better sitting forward + friction rub | **Pericarditis** |
| 2-10 weeks post-MI + fever + pericarditis | **Dressler syndrome** |
| Most common CHD overall | **VSD** |
| Fixed split S2 | **ASD** |
| Continuous machinery murmur | **PDA** |
| Boot-shaped heart + squatting child | **Tetralogy of Fallot** |
| Egg on string CXR + cyanosis at birth + maternal diabetes | **TGA** |
| Turner syndrome + upper limb hypertension + rib notching | **Coarctation of aorta** |
| Adult with known CHD now cyanotic | **Eisenmenger syndrome** |
| LA mass + positional syncope + tumor plop | **Cardiac myxoma** |
| Child + cardiac tumor + tuberous sclerosis | **Rhabdomyoma** |
| Most common malignant primary cardiac tumor | **Angiosarcoma** |
| Most common cardiac tumor overall | **Metastatic tumor** |

---

> 🎯 **You now have COMPLETE cardiovascular pathology coverage — Valvular disease, Cardiomyopathies, Pericardial disease, Congenital heart disease, and Cardiac tumors. Combined with your Kenya Meds notes on Atherosclerosis, IHD, Hypertension, Heart Failure, Aortic disease and Vasculitis — that is EVERYTHING! Go crush those MCQs! 💪🏽**
