articles.title: ENDOCRINE PATHOLOGY — Notes
articles.content:
## Summary
This document provides comprehensive MBChB-level revision notes on endocrine pathology, covering disorders of the pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal glands, and pancreas, as well as multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes. It includes detailed explanations of anatomy, pathophysiology, clinical features, diagnosis, and treatment for a wide range of endocrine conditions.

## Key Points
- Pituitary disorders include hyperpituitarism (e.g., adenomas causing hormone excess or mass effects) and hypopituitarism (deficiency of pituitary hormones).
- Thyroid disorders encompass goiters, hypothyroidism (e.g., Hashimoto's), hyperthyroidism (e.g., Graves' disease), and various types of thyroiditis and tumors.
- Parathyroid disorders involve hyperparathyroidism (primary, secondary, tertiary) leading to hypercalcemia and hypoparathyroidism causing hypocalcemia.
- Adrenal disorders cover hyperfunction (Cushing syndrome, hyperaldosteronism, adrenogenital syndromes) and hypofunction (Addison's disease).
- Pancreatic endocrine disorders primarily focus on diabetes mellitus (T1DM, T2DM, MODY, gestational DM) and its acute and chronic complications, as well as pancreatic tumors.
- Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) syndromes are inherited disorders characterized by tumors in multiple endocrine glands, with MEN1, MEN2A, and MEN2B being key examples.

## Detailed Notes
### TOPIC 1: PITUITARY DISORDERS

#### Anatomy & Overview
The pituitary gland (hypophysis) is located in the **sella turcica** and has two main lobes: the **anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis)**, responsible for producing GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, and Prolactin, and the **posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis)**, which stores and releases ADH (vasopressin) and Oxytocin.

---

### A. HYPERPITUITARISM

This condition is most commonly caused by a **functioning pituitary adenoma**.

#### Pituitary Adenomas
These are benign tumors of anterior pituitary cells, classified by size (<1 cm = **microadenoma**; >1 cm = **macroadenoma**) and the hormone they secrete.

| Adenoma Type | Hormone | Clinical Syndrome |
|---|---|---|
| Somatotroph | GH | Gigantism (children) / Acromegaly (adults) |
| Lactotroph (most common) | Prolactin | Hyperprolactinemia |
| Corticotroph | ACTH | Cushing disease |
| Thyrotroph | TSH | Hyperthyroidism |
| Gonadotroph | FSH/LH | Usually non-functioning |
| Null cell | None | Mass effects only |

#### Mass Effects of Pituitary Adenoma
Compression by a pituitary adenoma can lead to **bitemporal hemianopia** (due to compression of the optic chiasm), headache, hypopituitarism, and **cranial nerve palsies** (III, IV, VI) if the cavernous sinus is invaded.

---

#### 1. Hyperprolactinemia
The most common functioning pituitary adenoma is the prolactinoma.
- **Causes:** Prolactinoma, drugs (dopamine antagonists, opioids), hypothyroidism, stalk compression, and physiological states (pregnancy, breastfeeding).
- **Effects:** In women, it causes **galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility**. In men, it can lead to impotence, decreased libido, infertility, and gynecomastia.
- **Treatment:** Dopamine agonists like bromocriptine and cabergoline.

#### 2. Growth Hormone Excess
- **Gigantism** results from excess GH before epiphyseal closure, leading to excessive linear growth.
- **Acromegaly** occurs when excess GH is present after epiphyseal closure. Features include enlarged hands and feet, coarse facial features, prognathism, macroglossia, and increased hat/shoe/ring size. Organomegaly (cardiomegaly, hepatomegaly), **carpal tunnel syndrome**, arthritis, **diabetes mellitus** (due to GH's anti-insulin effects), hypertension, and increased cancer risk are also associated.
- **Diagnosis:** Elevated IGF-1 levels and lack of GH suppression by an oral glucose tolerance test.

#### 3. ACTH Excess (Cushing Disease)
A pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma causes bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and excess cortisol, leading to Cushing disease. This is discussed further under Adrenal section.

---

### B. HYPOPITUITARISM

#### Definition
This is the deficiency of one or more anterior pituitary hormones.

#### Causes
The most common cause is a **pituitary adenoma** compressing normal tissue. Other causes include **Sheehan syndrome** (postpartum pituitary necrosis), craniopharyngioma, traumatic brain injury, radiation, empty sella syndrome, granulomas, and hemochromatosis.

#### Clinical Effects (order of loss — GH lost first)
The hormones are typically lost in a specific order:
1. **GH deficiency**: Growth failure in children; fatigue and reduced muscle mass in adults.
2. **FSH/LH deficiency**: Hypogonadism, infertility, amenorrhea, and decreased libido.
3. **TSH deficiency**: Secondary hypothyroidism.
4. **ACTH deficiency**: Secondary adrenal insufficiency (without hyperpigmentation).
5. **Prolactin deficiency**: Failure to lactate postpartum.

#### Panhypopituitarism
This is the deficiency of all anterior pituitary hormones and can be a medical emergency if acute.

---

### C. POSTERIOR PITUITARY DISORDERS

#### Diabetes Insipidus (DI)
This condition is characterized by the **deficiency of ADH action**, leading to an inability to concentrate urine and resulting in **polyuria (large volumes of dilute urine) and polydipsia**.
- **Types:**
  - **Central DI**: Decreased ADH production (causes: head trauma, surgery, tumors, Sheehan syndrome, idiopathic). Treatment: **desmopressin (DDAVP)**.
  - **Nephrogenic DI**: Kidneys do not respond to ADH (causes: lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, genetic factors). Treatment: thiazides, low-salt diet.
- **Diagnosis:** Water deprivation test followed by a response to desmopressin.
- **Lab findings:** Low urine osmolality, high serum osmolality, and hypernatremia.

#### Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH (SIADH)
This involves **excess ADH**, leading to excessive water retention and **dilutional hyponatremia**.
- **Causes:** CNS disorders (meningitis, stroke, head trauma), pulmonary conditions (pneumonia, TB), **malignancy (Small cell carcinoma of the lung)**, drugs (carbamazepine, SSRIs), hypothyroidism, and Addison disease.
- **Lab findings:** Low serum sodium, low serum osmolality, **inappropriately concentrated urine** (urine osmolality > serum osmolality), and high urine sodium.
- **Symptoms:** Nausea, confusion, seizures, and coma due to cerebral edema.
- **Treatment:** Fluid restriction; hypertonic saline for severe cases; demeclocycline or tolvaptan.

---

## TOPIC 2: THYROID DISORDERS

### Normal Thyroid Function
The thyroid gland produces T3 (active) and T4 (prohormone), regulated by TSH from the pituitary, which is in turn regulated by TRH from the hypothalamus. T3 and T4 increase metabolic rate, protein synthesis, cardiac output, and gut motility.

---

### A. GOITER

#### Definition
A **goiter** is an **enlargement of the thyroid gland**, regardless of its cause.

#### Types
**1. Diffuse Non-toxic Goiter (Simple/Colloid Goiter)**
This is a generalized, smooth thyroid enlargement in euthyroid individuals.
- **Causes:** **Iodine deficiency** (most common worldwide) and goitrogens (e.g., cabbage, cassava).
- **Mechanism:** Low T3/T4 leads to increased TSH, causing thyroid hyperplasia and goiter.
- **Histology:** Follicles are distended with colloid, and the follicular epithelium is flattened.

**2. Multinodular Goiter**
This results from long-standing simple goiter with uneven hyperplasia leading to nodules. It can be toxic (causing hyperthyroidism) or non-toxic and may cause tracheal or esophageal compression. **Plummer syndrome** refers to toxic multinodular goiter, where autonomous nodules produce excess T3/T4.

---

### B. HYPOTHYROIDISM

#### Definition
A deficiency of thyroid hormone, leading to a **decreased metabolic rate**.

#### Primary vs Secondary
- **Primary hypothyroidism** originates in the thyroid gland (high TSH, low T4).
- **Secondary hypothyroidism** originates in the pituitary (low TSH, low T4).

#### Causes of Primary Hypothyroidism
The most common cause in iodine-sufficient areas is **Hashimoto thyroiditis**. Other causes include iodine deficiency, post-radioiodine therapy or thyroidectomy, certain drugs, and congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism).

#### Clinical Features
Hypothyroidism causes a slowing of all metabolic processes, including cold intolerance, weight gain, fatigue, constipation, bradycardia, and hypertension (diastolic). **Myxedema**—non-pitting edema due to glycosaminoglycan accumulation—is characterized by periorbital puffiness, a puffy face, and macroglossia. Other features include dry, coarse skin; coarse, brittle hair with hair loss (outer third of eyebrows); delayed reflexes; menorrhagia; infertility; hyperlipidemia; and cognitive slowing.
- **Cretinism** is hypothyroidism in infancy or childhood, leading to **irreversible intellectual disability**, short stature, coarse features, an umbilical hernia, and a protruding tongue.

#### Myxedema Coma
This is a severe, life-threatening form of hypothyroidism characterized by hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, and altered consciousness, often precipitated by infection, cold exposure, or surgery. Treatment includes IV T3/T4 and hydrocortisone.

---

### C. HYPERTHYROIDISM (THYROTOXICOSIS)

#### Definition
This condition involves excess thyroid hormone, leading to an **increased metabolic rate**.

#### Causes
The most common cause is **Graves disease** (60–80%). Other causes include toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis (subacute, postpartum), excess iodine, TSH-secreting pituitary adenomas, and struma ovarii.

#### Clinical Features
Symptoms reflect an acceleration of metabolic processes, including heat intolerance, weight loss despite increased appetite, tachycardia, palpitations, atrial fibrillation, tremor, anxiety, diarrhea, warm moist skin, fine hair, hair loss, oligomenorrhea, infertility, and proximal muscle weakness. **Lid lag and lid retraction** are common due to sympathetic stimulation.

#### Thyroid Storm (Thyrotoxic Crisis)
This is a life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism, presenting with high fever, extreme tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, delirium, and coma. Treatment involves antithyroid drugs, beta-blockers, iodine, hydrocortisone, and supportive care.

---

### D. GRAVES DISEASE

#### Definition
Graves disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroidism caused by **TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies (TRAb/TSI)**.

#### Pathogenesis
IgG autoantibodies (TSI) bind to the TSH receptor, mimicking TSH and causing continuous stimulation of the thyroid gland, leading to hyperplasia and excess T3/T4 production.

#### Classic Triad (Unique to Graves)
1. **Hyperthyroidism with diffuse goiter**.
2. **Exophthalmos (proptosis)**: Eyeball protrusion due to retroorbital tissue inflammation and glycosaminoglycan deposition, which is not reversed by treating hyperthyroidism.
3. **Pretibial myxedema (dermopathy)**: Localized, non-pitting skin thickening over the shins.

#### Additional Features
**Thyroid acropachy** (clubbing and periosteal new bone formation) is a rare feature. A diffuse smooth goiter and a bruit over the thyroid (due to increased vascularity) are also common.

#### Histology
Characterized by tall columnar follicular epithelium, scalloping of colloid, lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centers, and increased vascularity.

#### Lab
Low TSH, high T3/T4, positive TRAb/TSI, and diffuse uptake on radioiodine scan.

#### Treatment
Options include anti-thyroid drugs (carbimazole, propylthiouracil), **radioactive iodine (¹³¹I)** (most common definitive treatment), beta-blockers for symptom control, and surgery (thyroidectomy).

---

### E. THYROIDITIS

#### 1. Hashimoto Thyroiditis (Chronic Autoimmune Thyroiditis)
This is the **most common cause of hypothyroidism** in iodine-sufficient countries and the **most common thyroid disease overall**. It involves autoimmune destruction of the thyroid, with associated antibodies being anti-thyroid peroxidase (Anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin (Anti-Tg).
- **Pathogenesis:** Primarily mediated by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, with autoantibodies also playing a role.
- **Histology:** Dense lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centers, **Hürthle cell change** (large pink cells), follicular atrophy, and fibrosis.
- **Clinical course:** Can present with transient hyperthyroidism ("Hashitoxicosis") followed by hypothyroidism. The thyroid is typically firm and rubbery.
- **Complications:** Increased risk of thyroid lymphoma and papillary thyroid carcinoma.
- **Lab:** High TSH, low T4, positive anti-TPO antibodies.
- **Treatment:** Levothyroxine (T4 replacement).

#### 2. Subacute (De Quervain) Granulomatous Thyroiditis
This is the **most common cause of painful thyroid** and typically follows a viral infection. It is self-limiting and progresses through transient hyperthyroid, euthyroid, and hypothyroid phases before recovery.
- **Histology:** Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells.
- **Lab:** Elevated ESR and low radioiodine uptake.
- **Treatment:** NSAIDs, steroids for severe cases, and beta-blockers for hyperthyroid symptoms.

#### 3. Riedel Thyroiditis
A rare condition characterized by dense fibrous replacement of the thyroid, extending into surrounding structures, making the thyroid feel **"woody" or "iron"**. It can cause dysphagia, stridor, and hoarseness.

#### 4. Postpartum Thyroiditis
An autoimmune condition occurring within a year of delivery, similar to Hashimoto's, typically presenting with transient hyperthyroidism followed by hypothyroidism.

---

### F. THYROID TUMORS

#### Benign: Follicular Adenoma
This is the most common benign thyroid tumor. It is solitary, encapsulated, and well-defined, with no capsular or vascular invasion. It is usually non-functioning ("cold" nodule) and does not progress to carcinoma. Treatment is typically a lobectomy to exclude carcinoma.

---

#### Malignant Thyroid Tumors

**Overview:**

| Type | Frequency | Origin | Prognosis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Papillary | ~80% | Follicular cells | Excellent |
| Follicular | ~10% | Follicular cells | Good |
| Medullary | ~5% | Parafollicular C cells | Moderate |
| Anaplastic | ~1–2% | Follicular cells | Very poor |

---

**1. Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma — Most Common Thyroid Cancer**
This accounts for 80% of thyroid malignancies and has an excellent prognosis (>95% 10-year survival). It is associated with **radiation exposure** and RET/PTC rearrangements. Spread is primarily via **lymphatics** to cervical lymph nodes.
- **Histology:** Characterized by **Orphan Annie eye nuclei** (clear nuclei with dispersed chromatin), **nuclear grooves**, **psammoma bodies**, and a papillary architecture.

**2. Follicular Carcinoma**
This accounts for about 10% of thyroid cancers. Diagnosis requires evidence of **capsular or vascular invasion**. It spreads hematogenously, often to bone and lungs.

**3. Medullary Carcinoma**
Derived from parafollicular C cells, it secretes **calcitonin**. It is part of the MEN 2 syndromes and is characterized by amyloid deposition in the tumor stroma.

**4. Anaplastic Carcinoma**
This is a highly aggressive tumor with a very poor prognosis, typically affecting the elderly. It grows rapidly and invades locally, often presenting as a large, fixed mass with compressive symptoms.

---

### G. THYROID FUNCTION TESTS (TFTs)

- **Euthyroid Sick Syndrome:** Low TSH, low T3, low T4 in the context of severe systemic illness (e.g., sepsis, starvation). This is a physiological adaptation, not a true thyroid disorder.

## TOPIC 3: PARATHYROID DISORDERS

### Normal Parathyroid Function
The parathyroid glands secrete **parathyroid hormone (PTH)**, which is the primary regulator of **calcium and phosphate homeostasis**. PTH increases serum calcium by:
1. **Increasing bone resorption** (osteoclast activation).
2. **Increasing renal calcium reabsorption** (distal tubules).
3. **Increasing renal phosphate excretion**.
4. **Increasing 1α-hydroxylase activity** in the kidney, which converts calcidiol to calcitriol (active Vitamin D), thereby increasing intestinal calcium absorption.

---

### A. HYPERPARATHYROIDISM

#### Definition
Excess PTH production, leading to **hypercalcemia**.

#### Primary Hyperparathyroidism
This is due to **autonomous overproduction of PTH** by one or more parathyroid glands.
- **Causes:**
  - **Solitary adenoma** (80%) — most common
  - **Hyperplasia** of all four glands (15%)
  - Multiple adenomas (5%)
  - Parathyroid carcinoma (rare)
- **Associated conditions:** MEN1, MEN2A, radiation exposure to the neck.
- **Clinical Features:** "Stones, bones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans."
  - **Stones:** Renal calculi (calcium stones)
  - **Bones:** Osteitis fibrosa cystica (brown tumors), subperiosteal resorption (pathognomonic on X-ray), osteoporosis
  - **Abdominal groans:** Constipation, nausea, pancreatitis, peptic ulcers
  - **Psychic moans:** Depression, fatigue, confusion, memory loss
  - Hypertension, hyperuricemia, gout
- **Lab:** **Hypercalcemia**, **low/normal phosphate**, **high PTH**, high urine calcium, **elevated alkaline phosphatase** (bone formation)
- **Diagnosis:** Measuring serum calcium and PTH; imaging if needed (ultrasound, sestamibi scan).
- **Treatment:** Surgical removal of affected glands (parathyroidectomy). Indications include symptomatic hypercalcemia, serum calcium >1 mg/dL above normal, reduced bone mineral density (T-score < -2.5), or reduced renal function.

#### Secondary Hyperparathyroidism
This is **reactive PTH excess** in response to **chronic hypocalcemia**.
- Most common cause: **Chronic renal failure (CRF)**.
  - CRF leads to phosphate retention (hyperphosphatemia), which binds calcium, causing hypocalcemia.
  - CRF also reduces 1α-hydroxylase activity, impairing Vitamin D activation and thus calcium absorption.
  - Both factors stimulate PTH secretion, leading to hyperplasia of all four glands.
- Other causes: Vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption.
- **Lab:** **Low/normal calcium, high phosphate, high PTH**.
- **Treatment:** Correcting the underlying cause, Vitamin D supplements, phosphate binders, and calcimimetics.

#### Tertiary Hyperparathyroidism
This occurs when glands become **autonomous** after long-standing secondary hyperparathyroidism, leading to hypercalcemia even after the initial cause is corrected (e.g., post-kidney transplant). Parathyroidectomy may be required.

---

### B. HYPOPARATHYROIDISM

#### Causes
The most common cause is **post-surgical** removal or damage during thyroid or neck surgery. Other causes include autoimmune destruction, DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion), hypomagnesemia, and infiltration by conditions like hemochromatosis.

#### Clinical Features of Hypocalcemia
These include **neuromuscular excitability** such as tetany, **Chvostek sign** (facial nerve tapping), **Trousseau sign** (carpal spasm), perioral numbness, tingling, and seizures. Cardiac arrhythmias due to a prolonged QT interval, dry skin, brittle nails, hair loss, and papilledema can also occur.

#### Pseudohypoparathyroidism
This is a condition of **end-organ resistance to PTH**, characterized by high PTH levels but low calcium. It is often associated with **Albright hereditary osteodystrophy**, which includes short stature, round face, short metacarpals/metatarsals, and subcutaneous calcifications.

## TOPIC 4: ADRENAL DISORDERS

### Anatomy & Zones
The adrenal cortex has three zones: **Zona Glomerulosa** (mineralocorticoids - Aldosterone), **Zona Fasciculata** (glucocorticoids - Cortisol), and **Zona Reticularis** (sex steroids - Androgens). The inner **Adrenal Medulla** produces catecholamines (Epinephrine, Norepinephrine).

---

### A. ADRENOCORTICAL HYPERFUNCTION

#### 1. Cushing Syndrome — Excess Cortisol

**Causes:**
- **Cushing Disease** (pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma) — most common endogenous cause.
- **Ectopic ACTH** production by tumors (e.g., small cell lung cancer).
- **Primary adrenal tumor** (adenoma or carcinoma).
- **Iatrogenic** (exogenous corticosteroid therapy) — most common overall cause.

**Clinical Features:**
These include central obesity (buffalo hump, moon face), **purple striae**, proximal muscle weakness, skin thinning, easy bruising, osteoporosis, hypertension, hyperglycemia/diabetes, immunosuppression, hypokalemia (in ectopic ACTH), **hyperpigmentation** (in ACTH-dependent causes), acne, hirsutism, menstrual irregularities, and psychological changes.

**Lab:**
Elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol, loss of diurnal cortisol rhythm, and abnormal responses to dexamethasone suppression tests (low-dose for screening, high-dose to differentiate pituitary from ectopic/adrenal causes).

#### 2. Hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome)

**Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome):** Autonomous overproduction of aldosterone, usually from an adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia.
- **Lab:** Hypokalemia, hypernatremia, metabolic alkalosis, **hypertension**, low renin, and high aldosterone.
- **Diagnosis:** Elevated aldosterone:renin ratio.
- **Treatment:** Surgical removal for adenoma, spironolactone for hyperplasia.

**Secondary Hyperaldosteronism:** Aldosterone excess due to high renin levels (e.g., renal artery stenosis, heart failure).

#### 3. Adrenogenital Syndromes (Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia — CAH)
These are autosomal recessive enzyme deficiencies in cortisol synthesis, leading to low cortisol and high ACTH. This results in bilateral adrenal hyperplasia and shunting of precursors into androgen synthesis.

---

### B. ADRENOCORTICAL HYPOFUNCTION (Adrenal Insufficiency)

#### Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison Disease)
This is a deficiency of both cortisol and aldosterone due to **adrenal gland destruction**.
- **Causes:**
  - **Autoimmune destruction** (most common in developed countries) — associated with other autoimmune diseases (e.g., Type 1 DM, Hashimoto's, hypoparathyroidism — APS Type 2).
  - **Infections** (TB, fungal infections, viral) — TB was historically common.
  - **Metastases**, hemorrhage (waterhouse-friderichsen syndrome in meningococcemia), drugs.
- **Clinical Features:**
  - **Cortisol deficiency:** Fatigue, weakness, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, hypoglycemia.
  - **Aldosterone deficiency:** Salt craving, postural hypotension, dehydration.
  - **Hyperpigmentation** of skin and mucous membranes (due to high ACTH and MSH).
- **Lab:** **Low cortisol**, **high ACTH** (primary deficiency), **hyponatremia**, **hyperkalemia**, **hypotension**.
- **Diagnosis:** **ACTH stimulation test** (low baseline cortisol, no rise after ACTH administration).
- **Treatment:** **Hydrocortisone** (cortisol replacement) and **fludrocortisone** (aldosterone replacement). **Adrenal crisis** is a life-threatening emergency requiring IV fluids, IV hydrocortisone, and electrolyte correction.

#### Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency
This is deficiency of **cortisol** due to **pituitary ACTH deficiency**. Aldosterone production is usually preserved as it is primarily regulated by the renin-angiotensin system.
- **Causes:** Pituitary tumors, Sheehan syndrome, cranial irradiation, head trauma.
- **Clinical Features:** Similar to primary but **NO hyperpigmentation** and usually **NO hyperkalemia/hyponatremia**.
- **Lab:** **Low cortisol**, **low/normal ACTH**.
- **Diagnosis:** ACTH stimulation test shows no cortisol rise.
- **Treatment:** Hydrocortisone replacement.

---

### C. ADRENAL MEDULLA DISORDERS

#### Pheochromocytoma
A catecholamine-secreting tumor of chromaffin cells (medulla).
- **Clinical Features:** **Paroxysmal hypertension** (episodic severe headaches, palpitations, sweating), anxiety, tremor. Can also be sustained hypertension.
- **Lab:** Elevated urinary or plasma **free metanephrines** (metabolites of epinephrine and norepinephrine) — most sensitive test.
- **Diagnosis:** Imaging (CT/MRI).
- **Treatment:** **Alpha-blockade first** (e.g., phenoxybenzamine) to control blood pressure, followed by beta-blockade if needed for tachycardia, then surgical removal.

---

## TOPIC 5: DIABETES MELLITUS

### Definition
A group of metabolic disorders characterized by **hyperglycemia** resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both.

---

### Types of Diabetes Mellitus

#### Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)
- Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic **β-cells** → absolute insulin deficiency.
- Typically presents in childhood or adolescence but can occur at any age.
- **Insulitis** (inflammation of islets) and β-cell loss are characteristic histological findings.
- Associated with HLA-DR3, DR4.
- **Ketoacidosis** is common at diagnosis.
- Requires **insulin therapy** lifelong.

#### Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM)
- Heterogeneous disorder characterized by **insulin resistance** and **relative insulin deficiency**.
- Strong genetic predisposition, associated with obesity and physical inactivity.
- Histology shows **amyloid deposition** in islets.
- **Ketoacidosis** is rare at diagnosis but can occur with severe stress (e.g., infection).
- Treated with diet, exercise, oral hypoglycemic agents, and often insulin.

#### Other Specific Types of DM
- **MODY (Maturity Onset Diabetes of the Young)**: Monogenic, autosomal dominant forms with various mutations.
- **Gestational DM**: Occurs during pregnancy due to insulin resistance; increases risk of macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia, and future T2DM.
- **Secondary DM**: Caused by other conditions (pancreatitis, hemochromatosis, Cushing syndrome, acromegaly) or drugs (steroids).

---

### COMPLICATIONS OF DIABETES MELLITUS

#### Acute Complications

**1. Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) — mainly T1DM**
Caused by severe insulin deficiency leading to hyperglycemia, metabolic acidosis, and ketonemia.
- **Features:** Hyperglycemia (>11 mmol/L), low pH (<7.3), ketonemia/ketonuria.
- **Symptoms:** Polyuria, polydipsia, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, **Kussmaul breathing**, **fruity breath**.
- **Treatment:** IV fluids, IV insulin infusion, potassium replacement.

**2. Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS/HONK) — mainly T2DM**
Extreme hyperglycemia (>33 mmol/L) with severe dehydration and high serum osmolality, but without significant ketoacidosis.
- **Features:** Extreme dehydration, confusion, seizures, coma.
- **Treatment:** Gradual rehydration, low-dose insulin.

**3. Hypoglycemia**
Low blood glucose (<3.9 mmol/L), often caused by excess insulin or oral agents. Symptoms are adrenergic (sweating, tremor) and neuroglycopenic (confusion, seizures).

---

#### Chronic Complications

These arise from hyperglycemia leading to vascular and nerve damage.

**A. Microvascular Complications**

**1. Diabetic Nephropathy**
Damage to the glomerulus, characterized by diffuse or nodular glomerulosclerosis (**Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesion**), thickened GBM, and hyaline arteriolosclerosis in afferent and efferent arterioles. The earliest sign is **microalbuminuria**. Treatment involves ACE inhibitors/ARBs, glucose control, and BP control.

**2. Diabetic Retinopathy**
- **Non-proliferative:** Microaneurysms, hemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots.
- **Proliferative:** **Neovascularization**, leading to vitreous hemorrhage and retinal detachment. Requires laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF therapy.

**3. Diabetic Neuropathy**
- **Peripheral symmetric polyneuropathy:** Loss of sensation in extremities ("stocking and glove"), leading to **diabetic foot** ulcers.
- **Autonomic neuropathy:** Affecting gut motility (gastroparesis), blood pressure regulation (orthostatic hypotension), and sexual function.
- **Mononeuropathy:** Affecting individual nerves (e.g., cranial nerve III palsy).

**B. Macrovascular Complications**
Accelerated atherosclerosis leading to **ischemic heart disease**, stroke, and peripheral arterial disease.

**C. Other Complications**
Including diabetic foot ulcers, recurrent infections, cataracts, and glaucoma.

## TOPIC 6: MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA (MEN)

### Definition
Rare **autosomal dominant** inherited syndromes characterized by tumors in two or more endocrine glands.

---

### MEN 1 (Wermer Syndrome)
Caused by mutation in the **MEN1 gene**. Characterized by the "3 Ps":
- **Parathyroid hyperplasia/adenoma** (most common, hypercalcemia).
- **Pituitary adenoma** (most commonly prolactinoma).
- **Pancreatic islet cell tumors** (e.g., gastrinoma causing Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, insulinoma).

---

### MEN 2A (Sipple Syndrome)
Caused by mutations in the **RET proto-oncogene**. Characterized by:
- **Medullary thyroid carcinoma** (virtually always present; calcitonin marker).
- **Pheochromocytoma** (often bilateral).
- **Parathyroid hyperplasia** (less common).
**Prophylactic thyroidectomy** is recommended.

---

### MEN 2B (MEN 3)
Also caused by **RET proto-oncogene** mutations. It is more aggressive and presents in childhood. Features include:
- **Medullary thyroid carcinoma** (most aggressive, earliest onset).
- **Pheochromocytoma**.
- **Mucosal neuromas** (lips, tongue).
- **Marfanoid habitus**.
- **NO parathyroid disease**.

---

### Summary Table — MEN Syndromes

| Feature | MEN 1 | MEN 2A | MEN 2B |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gene | MEN1 (11q13) | RET (10q11) | RET (10q11) |
| Parathyroid | Yes (90%) | Yes (20–30%) | No |
| Pituitary | Yes (30–40%) | No | No |
| Pancreas | Yes (60–70%) | No | No |
| MTC | No | Yes (90–100%) | Yes (most aggressive) |
| Pheo | No | Yes (50%) | Yes (50%) |
| Mucosal neuromas | No | No | Yes |
| Marfanoid habitus | No | No | Yes |

---

### Additional High-Yield Points for Exam

**Carcinoid Tumors (Neuroendocrine Tumors — NETs)**
These arise from enterochromaffin cells and most commonly occur in the appendix, ileum, and rectum. They secrete serotonin, and **carcinoid syndrome** occurs when liver metastases lead to systemic release of serotonin. Features include flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm, and right-sided valvular heart disease. Diagnosis is via elevated urinary 5-HIAA.

## Practice Questions
1. What is the most common cause of hyperpituitarism? → A functioning pituitary adenoma.
2. What is the classic visual field defect associated with a pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm? → Bitemporal hemianopia.
3. What is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas? → Hashimoto thyroiditis.
4. What are the three classic features unique to Graves disease? → Hyperthyroidism with diffuse goiter, exophthalmos, and pretibial myxedema.
5. What is the characteristic histological finding in diabetic nephropathy known as Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions? → Nodular glomerulosclerosis.
6. Which MEN syndrome is characterized by parathyroid hyperplasia, pituitary adenomas, and pancreatic islet cell tumors? → MEN 1.
7. A patient presents with episodic headaches, palpitations, and sweating, along with paroxysmal hypertension. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Pheochromocytoma.
8. What is the primary difference in presentation between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus regarding ketoacidosis? → Ketoacidosis is common at diagnosis in T1DM, but rare in T2DM.

# ENDOCRINE PATHOLOGY
### MBChB Level | Comprehensive Exam Revision Notes

---

## TOPIC 1: PITUITARY DISORDERS

### Anatomy & Overview
- Pituitary gland (hypophysis) sits in **sella turcica**
- Two lobes:
  - **Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis)** — produces GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, Prolactin
  - **Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis)** — stores and releases ADH (vasopressin) and Oxytocin

---

### A. HYPERPITUITARISM

Most commonly caused by a **functioning pituitary adenoma**.

#### Pituitary Adenomas
- Most common pituitary lesion
- Benign tumors of anterior pituitary cells
- **<1 cm = microadenoma; >1 cm = macroadenoma**
- Classified by hormone secreted:

| Adenoma Type | Hormone | Clinical Syndrome |
|---|---|---|
| Somatotroph | GH | Gigantism (children) / Acromegaly (adults) |
| Lactotroph (most common) | Prolactin | Hyperprolactinemia |
| Corticotroph | ACTH | Cushing disease |
| Thyrotroph | TSH | Hyperthyroidism |
| Gonadotroph | FSH/LH | Usually non-functioning |
| Null cell | None | Mass effects only |

#### Mass Effects of Pituitary Adenoma
- **Bitemporal hemianopia** — compression of optic chiasm
- Headache
- Hypopituitarism (compression of normal gland)
- **Cranial nerve palsies** (III, IV, VI) if cavernous sinus invaded

---

#### 1. Hyperprolactinemia
- Most common functioning pituitary adenoma
- **Causes:**
  - Prolactinoma (most common)
  - Drugs: dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide, antipsychotics), opioids
  - Hypothyroidism (TRH stimulates prolactin)
  - Stalk compression (any pituitary mass)
  - Pregnancy, breastfeeding (physiological)
- **Effects:**
  - Women: **galactorrhea, amenorrhea, infertility** (inhibits GnRH → low FSH/LH)
  - Men: impotence, decreased libido, infertility, gynecomastia
- **Treatment:** Dopamine agonists (bromocriptine, cabergoline)

#### 2. Growth Hormone Excess
- **Gigantism** — excess GH before epiphyseal closure → excessive linear growth
- **Acromegaly** — excess GH after epiphyseal closure → cannot grow taller
  - Features: enlarged hands/feet, coarse facial features, prognathism (jaw protrusion), macroglossia, widely spaced teeth, increased hat/shoe/ring size
  - Organomegaly: cardiomegaly, hepatomegaly
  - **Carpal tunnel syndrome**, arthritis
  - **Diabetes mellitus** (GH is anti-insulin)
  - Hypertension
  - **Diagnosis:** elevated IGF-1; GH not suppressed by oral glucose tolerance test
  - Complications: cardiovascular disease, sleep apnea, diabetes, increased cancer risk

#### 3. ACTH Excess (Cushing Disease)
- Pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma → bilateral adrenal hyperplasia → excess cortisol
- See Cushing syndrome under Adrenal section

---

### B. HYPOPITUITARISM

#### Definition
Deficiency of one or more anterior pituitary hormones.

#### Causes
- **Pituitary adenoma** (compression of normal tissue) — most common
- **Sheehan syndrome** — postpartum pituitary necrosis due to hemorrhagic shock during delivery; ischemic infarction of enlarged pituitary; presents as failure to lactate, amenorrhea
- Craniopharyngioma (most common suprasellar tumor in children)
- Traumatic brain injury
- Radiation
- Empty sella syndrome
- Granulomas (sarcoidosis, TB)
- Hemochromatosis

#### Clinical Effects (order of loss — GH lost first)
1. **GH deficiency** — growth failure in children; fatigue, reduced muscle mass in adults
2. **FSH/LH deficiency** — hypogonadism, infertility, amenorrhea, decreased libido
3. **TSH deficiency** — secondary hypothyroidism
4. **ACTH deficiency** — secondary adrenal insufficiency (no hyperpigmentation unlike primary)
5. **Prolactin deficiency** — failure to lactate (postpartum)

#### Panhypopituitarism
- Deficiency of ALL anterior pituitary hormones
- Medical emergency if acute

---

### C. POSTERIOR PITUITARY DISORDERS

#### Diabetes Insipidus (DI)
- **Deficiency of ADH action** → inability to concentrate urine → **polyuria (large volumes of dilute urine) + polydipsia**
- Types:
  - **Central DI** — decreased ADH production; causes: head trauma, surgery, tumors, Sheehan, idiopathic; Treatment: **desmopressin (DDAVP)**
  - **Nephrogenic DI** — kidneys don't respond to ADH; causes: lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, genetic; Treatment: thiazides, low-salt diet
- Diagnosis: water deprivation test + response to desmopressin
- Lab: low urine osmolality, high serum osmolality, hypernatremia

#### Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH (SIADH)
- **Excess ADH** → excessive water retention → **dilutional hyponatremia**
- **Causes:**
  - CNS disorders: meningitis, stroke, head trauma
  - Pulmonary: pneumonia, TB, mechanical ventilation
  - **Malignancy: Small cell carcinoma of lung** (most common ectopic ADH)
  - Drugs: carbamazepine, SSRIs, cyclophosphamide
  - Hypothyroidism, Addison disease
- **Lab:** Low serum sodium, low serum osmolality, **inappropriately concentrated urine** (urine osmolality > serum osmolality), high urine sodium
- **Symptoms:** nausea, confusion, seizures, coma (cerebral edema)
- **Treatment:** fluid restriction; hypertonic saline if severe; demeclocycline/tolvaptan

---

## TOPIC 2: THYROID DISORDERS

### Normal Thyroid Function
- Thyroid produces T3 (active) and T4 (prohormone)
- Regulated by TSH from pituitary (which is regulated by TRH from hypothalamus)
- **T3/T4 increase metabolic rate**, protein synthesis, cardiac output, gut motility

---

### A. GOITER

#### Definition
**Enlargement of the thyroid gland**, regardless of cause.

#### Types
**1. Diffuse Non-toxic Goiter (Simple/Colloid Goiter)**
- Generalized smooth thyroid enlargement
- Euthyroid (normal thyroid function)
- Causes: **iodine deficiency** (most common worldwide), goitrogens (cabbage, cassava)
- Mechanism: low T3/T4 → increased TSH → thyroid hyperplasia → goiter
- Histology: follicles distended with colloid; follicular epithelium flattened

**2. Multinodular Goiter**
- Long-standing simple goiter → uneven hyperplasia → nodules
- Mix of hyperplastic and colloid-filled follicles
- May be toxic (hyperthyroid) or non-toxic
- Can cause tracheal/esophageal compression → dysphagia, dyspnea, stridor
- **Plummer syndrome** — toxic multinodular goiter (autonomous nodules producing excess T3/T4)

---

### B. HYPOTHYROIDISM

#### Definition
Deficiency of thyroid hormone → **decreased metabolic rate**

#### Primary vs Secondary
- **Primary:** problem in thyroid itself (high TSH, low T4)
- **Secondary:** problem in pituitary (low TSH, low T4)

#### Causes of Primary Hypothyroidism
- **Hashimoto thyroiditis** (most common in iodine-sufficient areas)
- Iodine deficiency (most common worldwide)
- Post-radioiodine therapy / thyroidectomy
- Drugs: amiodarone, lithium, carbimazole
- Congenital (cretinism)

#### Clinical Features
**Slowing of all metabolic processes:**
- **Cold intolerance**, weight gain, fatigue, constipation
- Bradycardia, hypertension (diastolic)
- **Myxedema** — non-pitting edema due to glycosaminoglycan accumulation in tissues; periorbital puffiness, puffy face, macroglossia
- Dry, coarse skin; coarse brittle hair; hair loss (outer third of eyebrows)
- Delayed reflexes ("hung-up reflexes")
- Menorrhagia, infertility
- Hyperlipidemia
- Depression, cognitive slowing
- **Cretinism** — hypothyroidism in infancy/childhood → **irreversible intellectual disability**, short stature, coarse features, umbilical hernia, protruding tongue

#### Myxedema Coma
- Severe life-threatening hypothyroidism
- Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, altered consciousness
- Precipitated by: infection, cold exposure, surgery, drugs
- Treatment: IV T3/T4 + hydrocortisone (in case of associated adrenal insufficiency)

---

### C. HYPERTHYROIDISM (THYROTOXICOSIS)

#### Definition
Excess thyroid hormone → **increased metabolic rate**

#### Causes
1. **Graves disease** (most common) — 60–80%
2. Toxic multinodular goiter (Plummer syndrome)
3. Toxic adenoma (single hyperfunctioning nodule)
4. Thyroiditis (subacute, postpartum) — transient
5. Excess iodine (Jod-Basedow effect)
6. TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma
7. Struma ovarii (ectopic thyroid in ovary)

#### Clinical Features
**Acceleration of all metabolic processes:**
- **Heat intolerance**, weight loss despite increased appetite
- **Tachycardia, palpitations, atrial fibrillation**
- Tremor, anxiety, irritability, insomnia
- Diarrhea, increased gut motility
- Warm, moist, smooth skin
- Fine hair, hair loss
- Oligomenorrhea, infertility
- Proximal muscle weakness (thyroid myopathy)
- Osteoporosis (long-term)
- **Lid lag, lid retraction** (sympathetic stimulation — in all causes)

#### Thyroid Storm (Thyrotoxic Crisis)
- Life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism
- Precipitants: infection, surgery, trauma, stopping antithyroid drugs
- Features: high fever, extreme tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, delirium, coma
- Treatment: **antithyroid drugs (PTU/carbimazole) + beta-blockers + iodine (Lugol's solution) + hydrocortisone + supportive care**

---

### D. GRAVES DISEASE

#### Definition
Autoimmune hyperthyroidism caused by **TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies (TRAb/TSI)**

#### Pathogenesis
- **IgG autoantibodies** (anti-TSH receptor antibodies = TSI = Thyroid Stimulating Immunoglobulins) bind TSH receptor → mimic TSH → continuous stimulation → diffuse thyroid hyperplasia + excess T3/T4

#### Classic Triad (Unique to Graves)
1. **Hyperthyroidism with diffuse goiter**
2. **Exophthalmos (proptosis)** — protrusion of eyeballs; due to glycosaminoglycan deposition and inflammation in retroorbital tissue; NOT reversed by treating hyperthyroidism
3. **Pretibial myxedema (dermopathy)** — localized non-pitting skin thickening over shins; due to glycosaminoglycan deposition

#### Additional Features
- **Thyroid acropachy** — clubbing + periosteal new bone formation (rare)
- Diffuse smooth goiter
- Bruit over thyroid (increased vascularity)

#### Histology
- Tall columnar follicular epithelium (hyperplastic)
- Scalloping of colloid
- Lymphocytic infiltration with germinal center formation
- Increased vascularity

#### Lab
- Low TSH, High T3/T4
- Positive TRAb/TSI
- Diffuse uptake on radioiodine scan

#### Treatment
- Anti-thyroid drugs: **carbimazole, propylthiouracil (PTU)**
- **Radioactive iodine (¹³¹I)** — most common definitive treatment
- **Beta-blockers** (propranolol) — symptom control
- **Surgery** (thyroidectomy) — large goiter, failed medical therapy

---

### E. THYROIDITIS

#### 1. Hashimoto Thyroiditis (Chronic Autoimmune Thyroiditis)
- **Most common cause of hypothyroidism** in iodine-sufficient countries
- **Most common thyroid disease overall**
- Autoimmune destruction of thyroid
- **Autoantibodies:** Anti-thyroid peroxidase (Anti-TPO) — most sensitive; Anti-thyroglobulin (Anti-Tg)
- More common in women; associated with HLA-DR3, DR5
- **Pathogenesis:** CD8+ cytotoxic T cells destroy follicular cells; autoantibodies block TSH receptor or activate complement
- **Histology:** Dense lymphocytic infiltration with germinal center formation; **Hürthle cell (oxyphilic) change** of follicular epithelium (large pink cells); follicular atrophy; fibrosis
- **Clinical course:**
  - May have transient hyperthyroidism early ("Hashitoxicosis") → then euthyroid → then **hypothyroidism**
  - Firm, rubbery, diffuse goiter
  - Eventually thyroid atrophies
- **Complications:** **Increased risk of thyroid lymphoma** (primary B-cell NHL); increased risk of papillary thyroid carcinoma
- **Lab:** High TSH, low T4, positive anti-TPO antibodies
- **Treatment:** Levothyroxine (T4 replacement)

#### 2. Subacute (De Quervain) Granulomatous Thyroiditis
- **Most common cause of painful thyroid**
- Follows **viral infection** (mumps, influenza, Coxsackievirus)
- Self-limiting; lasts weeks to months
- **Clinical course:** Painful tender thyroid + fever → transient hyperthyroid → euthyroid → transient hypothyroid → **recovery** (most cases)
- **Histology:** Granulomatous inflammation; giant cells around disrupted follicles; neutrophils early
- **Lab:** Elevated ESR, low radioiodine uptake (destroyed follicles release preformed hormone but can't take up new iodine)
- **Treatment:** NSAIDs; steroids for severe cases; beta-blockers for hyperthyroid symptoms

#### 3. Riedel Thyroiditis
- Rare; dense fibrous replacement of thyroid + extension into surrounding structures
- Thyroid becomes **hard as wood ("woody" or "iron" thyroid)**
- Can cause: dysphagia, stridor, hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve compression)
- Associated with other fibrosing conditions (retroperitoneal fibrosis, IgG4-related disease)
- Must distinguish from anaplastic carcinoma

#### 4. Postpartum Thyroiditis
- Autoimmune; occurs within 1 year of delivery
- Similar to Hashimoto; positive anti-TPO
- Transient hyperthyroid → hypothyroid → recovery in most
- May become permanent hypothyroidism

---

### F. THYROID TUMORS

#### Benign: Follicular Adenoma
- Most common thyroid tumor
- Solitary, encapsulated, well-defined
- Surrounded by fibrous capsule — NO capsular or vascular invasion
- Usually non-functioning ("cold" nodule on scan)
- Histology: follicular pattern, uniform cells, intact capsule
- Does NOT progress to carcinoma
- Treatment: lobectomy (to exclude carcinoma)

---

#### Malignant Thyroid Tumors

**Overview:**

| Type | Frequency | Origin | Prognosis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Papillary | ~80% | Follicular cells | Excellent |
| Follicular | ~10% | Follicular cells | Good |
| Medullary | ~5% | Parafollicular C cells | Moderate |
| Anaplastic | ~1–2% | Follicular cells | Very poor |

---

**1. Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma — Most Common Thyroid Cancer**
- Most common thyroid malignancy (80%)
- Excellent prognosis (>95% 10-year survival)
- Associated with: **radiation exposure** (childhood), RET/PTC rearrangements, BRAF mutations
- Spreads via **lymphatics** → cervical lymph nodes (but this does NOT worsen prognosis significantly)
- **Histology — MUST KNOW:**
  - **Papillary architecture** (finger-like projections with fibrovascular cores)
  - **"Orphan Annie eye" nuclei** — optically clear, empty-looking nuclei ("ground glass nuclei")
  - **Nuclear grooves** and **intranuclear pseudoinclusions**
  - **Psammoma bodies** — concentric calcified spherules (pathognomonic)
  - Fibrous stroma
- **Variants:** Classic, follicular variant, tall cell variant (aggressive)
- **Treatment:** Total thyroidectomy + radioactive iodine + TSH suppression (levothyroxine)

**2. Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma**
- Second most common (~10%)
- Associated with **iodine deficiency**
- RAS mutations, PAX8-PPARγ rearrangements
- **CANNOT distinguish from follicular adenoma on FNA** — requires histological evidence of capsular or vascular invasion
- Spreads **hematogenously** → lungs, bone (lytic lesions), liver ("distant metastases")
- Histology: follicular pattern; **capsular and/or vascular invasion** — key distinguishing feature from adenoma
- Treatment: Total thyroidectomy + radioactive iodine

**3. Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma**
- Arises from **parafollicular C cells** (not follicular cells)
- Secretes **calcitonin** — tumor marker
- Associated with **MEN 2A and MEN 2B** (RET proto-oncogene mutation)
- 25% familial; associated with RET mutations
- **Histology:** sheets of polygonal cells; **amyloid stroma** (from calcitonin deposits, Congo red positive)
- Spreads: lymphatics and blood
- **Screening:** RET mutation testing in family members; calcitonin levels
- Treatment: Total thyroidectomy (radioiodine does NOT work — C cells don't take up iodine)

**4. Anaplastic (Undifferentiated) Thyroid Carcinoma**
- Most aggressive thyroid cancer; **almost universally fatal**
- Elderly patients (>60 years)
- Rapid growth; invades local structures → dysphagia, stridor, hoarseness
- May arise from dedifferentiation of papillary or follicular carcinoma
- **Histology:** Pleomorphic giant cells, spindle cells, marked atypia, necrosis
- **TP53 mutations** common
- No effective treatment; median survival **<6 months**
- Radioiodine does NOT work

---

## TOPIC 3: PARATHYROID DISORDERS

### Normal Function
- Parathyroid glands (4 glands) produce **PTH (parathyroid hormone)**
- PTH effects:
  - **↑ Bone resorption** (releases Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻)
  - **↑ Renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption** (distal tubule)
  - **↓ Renal PO₄³⁻ reabsorption** → phosphaturia
  - **↑ Renal 1α-hydroxylase** → activates Vitamin D → ↑ intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption
- Net effect: **↑ serum calcium, ↓ serum phosphate**

---

### A. HYPERPARATHYROIDISM

#### Primary Hyperparathyroidism
- **Autonomous overproduction of PTH** by parathyroid gland itself
- Most common cause of **hypercalcemia in outpatients**
- **Causes:**
  - **Parathyroid adenoma** (80–85%) — most common; solitary; benign
  - **Primary hyperplasia** (15%) — all 4 glands enlarged; associated with MEN 1 and MEN 2A
  - **Parathyroid carcinoma** (<1%) — rare
- **Lab:** High PTH, **high calcium, low phosphate**, high urinary calcium, elevated alkaline phosphatase

**Clinical Features — "Bones, Stones, Groans, Psychic Moans":**
- **Bones:** Bone pain, **osteitis fibrosa cystica** (severe); brown tumors; pathological fractures; subperiosteal bone resorption (radial side of middle phalanx on X-ray)
- **Stones:** Renal calculi (calcium oxalate/phosphate); nephrocalcinosis; polyuria, polydipsia (nephrogenic DI)
- **Groans:** Nausea, vomiting, constipation, anorexia, peptic ulcer disease (Ca²⁺ stimulates gastrin)
- **Psychic Moans:** Depression, anxiety, cognitive impairment, confusion

**Osteitis Fibrosa Cystica (von Recklinghausen disease of bone):**
- Severe prolonged hyperparathyroidism
- Bone resorption → fibrous replacement
- **Brown tumors** — hemorrhagic tumors in bone (reactive giant cell lesions, not true tumors)
- Cyst formation
- Pathological fractures
- **"Salt and pepper" skull on X-ray**

#### Secondary Hyperparathyroidism
- **Reactive PTH excess** in response to **chronic hypocalcemia**
- Most common cause: **Chronic renal failure (CRF)**
  - CRF → decreased phosphate excretion → hyperphosphatemia → binds Ca²⁺ → hypocalcemia
  - CRF → decreased 1α-hydroxylase → decreased Vitamin D → decreased Ca²⁺ absorption
  - Both → stimulate PTH secretion → all 4 glands hyperplastic
- Other causes: Vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption
- Lab: **Low/normal calcium, high phosphate, high PTH**
- Treatment: correct underlying cause; Vitamin D supplements; phosphate binders; calcimimetics

#### Tertiary Hyperparathyroidism
- Long-standing secondary hyperparathyroidism → parathyroid glands become **autonomous** (no longer responsive to calcium)
- Hypercalcemia develops even after correction of renal failure (e.g., post-transplant)
- Requires parathyroidectomy

---

### B. HYPOPARATHYROIDISM

#### Causes
- **Post-surgical** (thyroidectomy, neck dissection) — most common
- **Autoimmune** — isolated or part of **APS type 1** (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy)
- **DiGeorge syndrome** — 22q11 deletion; parathyroid aplasia
- Hypomagnesemia (Mg needed for PTH secretion)
- Infiltration: hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, sarcoidosis

#### Clinical Features of Hypocalcemia
- **Neuromuscular excitability:**
  - **Tetany** — carpopedal spasm (main paw position)
  - **Chvostek sign** — tapping facial nerve → ipsilateral facial muscle contraction
  - **Trousseau sign** — inflating BP cuff → carpal spasm (most specific)
  - Perioral numbness, tingling in extremities
  - Seizures
  - Laryngospasm → stridor
- **Prolonged QT interval** on ECG → cardiac arrhythmias
- Cataracts (chronic)
- Dry skin, brittle nails, hair loss
- Papilledema (raised intracranial pressure)

#### Pseudohypoparathyroidism
- **End-organ resistance to PTH** (PTH levels are HIGH but calcium is LOW)
- Caused by mutation in Gsα protein (GNAS1 gene)
- **Albright hereditary osteodystrophy:**
  - Short stature, obesity, round face, short metacarpals/metatarsals (shortened 4th and 5th)
  - Subcutaneous calcifications
  - Intellectual disability

---

## TOPIC 4: ADRENAL DISORDERS

### Anatomy & Zones
**Adrenal Cortex** (outer, 90%) — 3 zones:
- **Zona Glomerulosa** (outermost) — **Mineralocorticoids** (Aldosterone)
- **Zona Fasciculata** (middle) — **Glucocorticoids** (Cortisol)
- **Zona Reticularis** (inner) — **Sex steroids** (Androgens)

**Mnemonic: GFR → Salt (mineralocorticoids), Sugar (glucocorticoids), Sex (androgens)**

**Adrenal Medulla** (inner, 10%) — **Catecholamines** (Epinephrine 80%, Norepinephrine 20%)

---

### A. ADRENOCORTICAL HYPERFUNCTION

#### 1. Cushing Syndrome — Excess Cortisol

**Causes (MUST KNOW):**

| Cause | Mechanism | ACTH level |
|---|---|---|
| **Cushing Disease** (most common endogenous) | Pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma → bilateral adrenal hyperplasia | High |
| **Ectopic ACTH** | ACTH from non-pituitary tumor (small cell lung ca, carcinoid) | Very High |
| **Primary adrenal tumor** (adenoma/carcinoma) | Autonomous cortisol production | Low (suppressed) |
| **Iatrogenic** (most common overall) | Exogenous corticosteroid therapy | Low (suppressed) |

**Clinical Features:**
- **Central (truncal) obesity** — buffalo hump (dorsocervical fat pad), moon face, supraclavicular fat pads
- **Purple striae** — wide, purple stretch marks on abdomen/thighs (weakened collagen)
- **Proximal muscle weakness** (steroid myopathy)
- **Skin thinning** and easy bruising
- **Osteoporosis** → pathological fractures
- **Hypertension** (cortisol has mineralocorticoid effect)
- **Hyperglycemia/diabetes** (cortisol is anti-insulin, gluconeogenic)
- **Immunosuppression** → recurrent infections
- **Hypokalemia** (in ectopic ACTH — excessive mineralocorticoid activity)
- **Hyperpigmentation** — only in ACTH-dependent causes (ACTH has melanotropic effect via POMC)
- Acne, hirsutism (from androgens)
- Menstrual irregularities
- Depression, psychosis
- Growth retardation in children

**Lab:**
- Elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol
- Loss of diurnal variation of cortisol
- **Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (DST):**
  - Normal: cortisol suppressed by low-dose dexamethasone
  - Cushing syndrome: cortisol NOT suppressed
- **High-dose DST:**
  - Cushing Disease (pituitary): cortisol IS suppressed (pituitary responds to higher dose)
  - Ectopic ACTH / adrenal tumor: cortisol NOT suppressed

#### 2. Hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome)

**Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome):**
- Excess aldosterone production independent of renin-angiotensin system
- Causes:
  - **Aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn adenoma)** — most common (65%)
  - Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (35%)
  - Adrenal carcinoma (rare)
- **Lab:** Hypokalemia, hypernatremia, metabolic alkalosis, **hypertension**, **low renin** (suppressed), high aldosterone
- Clinical: hypertension (often resistant), muscle weakness (hypokalemia), polyuria/polydipsia (hypokalemia → nephrogenic DI), headache
- **Diagnosis:** Elevated aldosterone:renin ratio → CT adrenal → adrenal vein sampling
- **Treatment:** adenoma → surgical removal; hyperplasia → spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist)

**Secondary Hyperaldosteronism:**
- High aldosterone due to **high renin** (activation of RAAS)
- Causes: renal artery stenosis, heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, dehydration
- **High renin + high aldosterone**

#### 3. Adrenogenital Syndromes (Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia — CAH)

- Autosomal recessive enzyme deficiencies in cortisol synthesis pathway
- Low cortisol → high ACTH (no negative feedback) → adrenal hyperplasia → shunting to sex steroids

**Most Common: 21-hydroxylase deficiency (>90% of CAH)**
- Cannot make cortisol or aldosterone
- Builds up precursors → shunted to androgens
- Features:
  - **Salt-wasting crisis** in neonates (no aldosterone) — hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, shock
  - **Virilization of females** — ambiguous genitalia at birth; clitoromegaly; fused labia
  - **Precocious puberty** in males
  - Tall children but short adults (early epiphyseal closure)
- Lab: Low sodium, high potassium, low cortisol, high 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) — key marker
- Treatment: glucocorticoid replacement (reduces ACTH drive) + mineralocorticoid replacement

**11β-hydroxylase deficiency (second most common):**
- Cannot make cortisol → excess androgens (virilization)
- 11-deoxycorticosterone accumulates → **hypertension + hypokalemia** (mineralocorticoid effect)

---

### B. ADRENOCORTICAL HYPOFUNCTION

#### Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison Disease)

**Definition:** Destruction of the adrenal cortex → deficiency of ALL adrenal cortical hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, androgens)

**Causes:**
- **Autoimmune adrenalitis** — most common in developed world (70–80%); associated with APS type 1 and 2; anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies
- **TB** — most common cause worldwide (historically); granulomatous destruction
- **Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome** — bilateral adrenal hemorrhage due to **meningococcal septicemia** (Neisseria meningitidis); also Pseudomonas
- Metastatic cancer (lung, breast, melanoma)
- Fungal infections (histoplasmosis)
- HIV/AIDS
- Drugs: ketoconazole, rifampicin (enzyme inducers)

**Clinical Features:**
- **Cortisol deficiency:** fatigue, weakness, weight loss, hypoglycemia, hypotension, poor stress response
- **Aldosterone deficiency:** hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, salt craving, dehydration
- **Androgen deficiency:** loss of pubic/axillary hair in women; decreased libido
- **Hyperpigmentation** — PATHOGNOMONIC of primary adrenal insufficiency; due to elevated ACTH and MSH (from POMC cleavage); affects skin creases, buccal mucosa, scars, sun-exposed areas, nipples
- Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
- Depression, irritability

**Lab:**
- Low cortisol, **high ACTH** (primary)
- Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia
- **Short Synacthen (ACTH stimulation) test** — gold standard diagnosis; adrenal fails to respond
- Eosinophilia, lymphocytosis

**Addisonian Crisis (Acute Adrenal Insufficiency)**
- Life-threatening emergency
- Precipitated by: infection, surgery, trauma, stopping steroid therapy
- Features: severe hypotension/shock, fever, confusion, severe hyponatremia/hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, vomiting
- Treatment: **IV hydrocortisone + IV saline + IV dextrose** (immediate)

#### Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency
- Due to **pituitary ACTH deficiency** or **exogenous steroid use** (suppresses HPA axis)
- Cortisol and androgens deficient; **aldosterone preserved** (regulated by RAAS, not ACTH)
- **NO hyperpigmentation** (ACTH is low)
- **NO hyperkalemia** (aldosterone preserved)
- **Hyponatremia** can occur (from ADH excess due to cortisol deficiency)

---

### C. ADRENAL MEDULLA TUMORS

#### Pheochromocytoma
- Tumor of **adrenal medulla chromaffin cells** → secretes catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine)
- **"Rule of 10s":**
  - 10% malignant
  - 10% bilateral
  - 10% extra-adrenal (paraganglioma)
  - 10% in children
  - 10% familial (MEN 2A, MEN 2B, VHL syndrome, NF1, SDH mutations)
- Modern estimates: actually higher than 10% in each category

**Clinical Features:**
- **Paroxysmal (episodic)** or sustained **hypertension** — most important feature
- **Classic triad:** Headache + Palpitations + Profuse sweating (episodic)
- Pallor (not flushing — catecholamines cause vasoconstriction)
- Anxiety, tremor
- Hyperglycemia (catecholamines are anti-insulin)
- Hypertensive crisis triggered by: stress, surgery, anesthesia, certain drugs (beta-blockers alone, opioids, contrast media)

**Diagnosis:**
- 24-hour urine **metanephrines and catecholamines** (most sensitive and specific)
- Plasma free metanephrines
- CT/MRI adrenal for localization
- **MIBG scan** — for extra-adrenal/metastatic disease

**Treatment:**
- **Alpha-blockade FIRST** (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) → then beta-blockade (to control tachycardia)
- **NEVER give beta-blocker alone** (would leave alpha receptors unopposed → hypertensive crisis)
- Surgery (adrenalectomy) after adequate alpha blockade

**Histology:**
- "Zellballen" (ball-like nests) of chromaffin cells
- Cannot distinguish benign from malignant on histology — only by **presence of metastases**

#### Neuroblastoma
- Most common **extracranial solid tumor in children** (<5 years)
- Tumor of neural crest origin; arises from adrenal medulla or sympathetic ganglia
- Secretes catecholamines → **elevated urinary HVA and VMA**
- Clinical: abdominal mass crossing midline, fever, weight loss, bone pain (metastases)
- Staging: localized (good prognosis) vs disseminated
- **N-MYC amplification** — poor prognosis
- **Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome** (dancing eyes, dancing feet) — paraneoplastic
- Treatment: surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, bone marrow transplant

---

## TOPIC 5: PANCREATIC ENDOCRINE DISORDERS — DIABETES MELLITUS

### Normal Pancreatic Endocrine Function
Islets of Langerhans contain:
- **β cells (70%)** — Insulin
- **α cells (20%)** — Glucagon
- **δ cells (10%)** — Somatostatin
- **PP cells** — Pancreatic polypeptide

### Insulin Actions
- Promotes glucose uptake (muscle, fat — GLUT4)
- Promotes glycogen synthesis (liver, muscle)
- Promotes lipogenesis (fat)
- Inhibits gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, ketogenesis
- Anabolic effects: promotes protein synthesis

---

### DIABETES MELLITUS (DM)

#### Definition
A group of metabolic diseases characterized by **hyperglycemia** resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both.

#### Diagnostic Criteria (WHO/ADA)
- Fasting plasma glucose ≥**7.0 mmol/L** (126 mg/dL) — on two occasions
- Random plasma glucose ≥**11.1 mmol/L** (200 mg/dL) + symptoms
- 2-hour OGTT ≥**11.1 mmol/L** (200 mg/dL)
- **HbA1c ≥6.5%** (48 mmol/mol)

---

### TYPE 1 DIABETES MELLITUS (T1DM)

#### Characteristics
- **Absolute insulin deficiency** — autoimmune destruction of β cells
- Formerly "juvenile-onset" or "insulin-dependent"
- Onset usually in childhood/adolescence but can occur at any age
- Thin patients
- Prone to **diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)**
- Requires **insulin therapy**

#### Pathogenesis
- **Autoimmune destruction of β cells** in genetically susceptible individuals
- HLA associations: **HLA-DR3, HLA-DR4** (HLA-DQ8)
- Triggered by environmental factors: viral infections (Coxsackievirus B, rubella), dietary factors
- **Insulitis** — lymphocytic infiltration of islets (CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells, macrophages)
- Autoantibodies (not primary pathogenic but markers):
  - **Islet cell antibodies (ICA)**
  - **Anti-GAD65** (glutamic acid decarboxylase) — most sensitive marker
  - **Anti-insulin antibodies (IAA)**
  - **Anti-IA2 antibodies**
- Progressive β cell destruction → eventually >80–90% destroyed → clinical DM

#### Morphology (Histology)
- **Insulitis** — lymphocytic infiltration of islets (early stages)
- Reduction in size and number of islets
- β cell loss; preservation of α cells (relative)
- Islet fibrosis (late)

---

### TYPE 2 DIABETES MELLITUS (T2DM)

#### Characteristics
- **Relative insulin deficiency** — combination of insulin resistance + progressive β cell dysfunction
- Formerly "adult-onset" or "non-insulin-dependent"
- Most common type (90–95% of all DM)
- Strongly associated with **obesity, physical inactivity**
- Usually in adults >45 years (but increasingly in younger people/children due to obesity epidemic)
- Insidious onset; often diagnosed incidentally
- NOT prone to DKA (some residual insulin); can develop HONK/HHS

#### Pathogenesis
**Two major defects:**
1. **Insulin resistance** — target tissues (liver, muscle, fat) fail to respond normally to insulin
   - Central obesity → adipose tissue releases free fatty acids and adipokines → reduce insulin signaling
   - Glucose transporter downregulation
   - Compensatory hyperinsulinemia initially maintains glucose

2. **Progressive β cell dysfunction** — initial compensatory hyperinsulinemia → β cells exhaust → reduced insulin secretion → hyperglycemia

#### Genetic factors
- Polygenic
- Strong family history
- NOT HLA-associated
- Concordance in identical twins: 50–80%

#### Morphology
- **Amyloid (islet amyloid polypeptide — IAPP/amylin) deposition** in islets — characteristic
- Congo red positive; β-pleated sheet structure
- Reduction in β cell mass (less than T1DM)
- No insulitis

#### Risk Factors for T2DM
- Obesity (especially central/abdominal)
- Physical inactivity
- Family history (first-degree relative)
- Age >45
- Gestational diabetes (history)
- Prediabetes (IFG or IGT)
- Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
- Hypertension, dyslipidemia
- Ethnic groups: African, Asian, Hispanic

---

### Comparison: T1DM vs T2DM

| Feature | Type 1 | Type 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Age of onset | Usually <30 | Usually >40 (but rising in young) |
| Body habitus | Thin | Obese |
| Onset | Acute | Insidious |
| Insulin levels | Very low/absent | Normal/high initially, then low |
| Insulin resistance | No | Yes (central) |
| Autoimmune | Yes | No |
| HLA association | Yes (DR3, DR4) | No |
| Ketoacidosis | Common | Rare |
| Islet histology | Insulitis, β cell loss | Amyloid deposition |
| Treatment | Insulin always | Diet, exercise, oral agents, ± insulin |

---

### Other Specific Types of DM
- **MODY (Maturity Onset Diabetes of the Young)** — monogenic, autosomal dominant; young lean patients; various glucokinase/transcription factor mutations
- **Gestational DM** — during pregnancy; insulin resistance of pregnancy; risk of macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia; increased risk T2DM later
- **Secondary DM:** Pancreatitis/pancreatectomy, hemochromatosis ("bronze diabetes"), Cushing syndrome, acromegaly, drugs (steroids, thiazides)

---

### COMPLICATIONS OF DIABETES MELLITUS

#### Acute Complications

**1. Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) — mainly T1DM**
- Insulin deficiency → hyperglycemia + unrestrained lipolysis → free fatty acids → **ketone body formation** (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, acetone)
- Features: hyperglycemia (>11 mmol/L), metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3), ketonemia/ketonuria, dehydration
- Symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, **Kussmaul breathing** (deep rapid breathing to compensate for acidosis), **fruity/acetone breath**
- Precipitants: infection, missed insulin, new diagnosis T1DM, surgery
- Treatment: IV fluids + IV insulin infusion + potassium replacement + treat precipitant

**2. Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS/HONK) — mainly T2DM**
- Extreme hyperglycemia (>33 mmol/L) + severe dehydration + high serum osmolality (>320 mOsm/kg)
- **NO significant ketoacidosis** (residual insulin prevents unrestrained lipolysis)
- Elderly T2DM patients; precipitated by: infection, poor fluid intake
- Features: extreme dehydration, confusion, seizures, coma
- Higher mortality than DKA
- Treatment: gradual rehydration + low-dose insulin

**3. Hypoglycemia**
- Most common acute complication
- BG <3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL)
- Causes: excess insulin/sulfonylureas, missed meals, exercise
- Symptoms: sweating, tremor, palpitations (adrenergic) → confusion, seizures, coma (neuroglycopenic)
- Treatment: oral glucose (conscious) or IV dextrose/IM glucagon (unconscious)

---

#### Chronic Complications — MUST KNOW

Caused by: **hyperglycemia → advanced glycation end products (AGEs), sorbitol pathway activation, oxidative stress, PKC activation** → vascular and nerve damage

**A. Microvascular Complications (Specific to Diabetes)**

**1. Diabetic Nephropathy — Leading cause of end-stage renal disease**
- Glomerular changes:
  - **Diffuse glomerulosclerosis** — most common; diffuse increase in mesangial matrix
  - **Nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesion)** — PATHOGNOMONIC; nodular deposits in mesangium; periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) positive
  - Thickening of glomerular basement membrane (GBM)
  - **Hyaline arteriolosclerosis** — affects both afferent AND efferent arterioles (unique to diabetic nephropathy)
- Progression: microalbuminuria → macroalbuminuria → declining GFR → ESRD
- Early marker: **microalbuminuria** (30–300 mg/day)
- Treatment: ACE inhibitors/ARBs (slow progression), glucose control, blood pressure control

**2. Diabetic Retinopathy — Most common cause of blindness in working-age adults**

Non-proliferative (background) retinopathy:
- Microaneurysms (earliest sign)
- Dot and blot hemorrhages
- Hard exudates (lipid deposits)
- Soft exudates/cotton wool spots (ischemic infarcts of nerve fiber layer)
- Venous dilation

Proliferative retinopathy (more severe):
- **Neovascularization** — new fragile vessels on retina/vitreous → risk of vitreous hemorrhage, traction retinal detachment → blindness
- Requires urgent laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF therapy

**3. Diabetic Neuropathy — Most common chronic complication**
Types:
- **Peripheral symmetric polyneuropathy** — most common; "stocking and glove" distribution; loss of pain, temperature, vibration sense → painless injuries → **diabetic foot**
- **Autonomic neuropathy** — gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension, impotence, neurogenic bladder, diarrhea/constipation
- **Mononeuropathy** — single nerve affected; common: cranial nerve III palsy (diplopia, ptosis with spared pupil)
- **Amyotrophy** (diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexopathy) — painful proximal muscle weakness

**B. Macrovascular Complications (Accelerated Atherosclerosis)**

- **Ischemic heart disease** — MI (2–4x increased risk; often silent MI due to neuropathy)
- **Stroke** — 2–3x increased risk
- **Peripheral arterial disease** — limb ischemia, gangrene, amputation
- DM accelerates atherosclerosis through: dyslipidemia, hypertension, endothelial dysfunction, hypercoagulability

**C. Other Complications**
- **Diabetic foot** — combination of neuropathy + ischemia + infection → ulceration → gangrene → amputation
- **Recurrent infections** — impaired neutrophil function, poor circulation; common: UTI, skin (Candida, Staphylococcus), mucormycosis (in DKA)
- **Cataracts** — sorbitol accumulation in lens
- **Glaucoma** — neovascular glaucoma from retinal ischemia

---

## TOPIC 6: MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA (MEN)

### Definition
Rare **autosomal dominant** inherited syndromes characterized by **tumors in two or more endocrine glands**.

---

### MEN 1 (Wermer Syndrome)
- **Gene:** MEN1 gene (chromosome 11q13) — tumor suppressor gene
- **"3 Ps":**
  - **P**arathyroid hyperplasia/adenoma (90–100%) — most common; hypercalcemia; usually first manifestation
  - **P**ituitary adenoma (30–40%) — most commonly **prolactinoma**; also GH, ACTH
  - **P**ancreatic islet cell tumors (60–70%) — **Gastrinoma** (most common functional; Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), insulinoma, glucagonoma, VIPoma

**Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome:**
- Gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma) → massively elevated gastrin → massive gastric acid secretion → multiple, recurrent, intractable peptic ulcers + diarrhea
- Gastrinomas most commonly in **duodenum/pancreas**
- Most in MEN1 are multiple and malignant

---

### MEN 2A (Sipple Syndrome)
- **Gene:** RET proto-oncogene mutation (chromosome 10q11)
- **"2 Ms + 1 P":**
  - **M**edullary thyroid carcinoma (90–100%) — virtually always present; CALCITONIN marker
  - **P**heochromocytoma (50%) — bilateral, benign usually; screen before thyroid surgery
  - **P**arathyroid hyperplasia (20–30%) — hypercalcemia

**Important:** Medullary thyroid carcinoma in MEN2A is the most life-threatening component. **Prophylactic thyroidectomy** recommended in RET mutation carriers.

---

### MEN 2B (MEN 3)
- **Gene:** RET proto-oncogene (different codon from MEN 2A)
- Most aggressive; presents in childhood
- **Components:**
  - **M**edullary thyroid carcinoma — most aggressive, earliest onset
  - **P**heochromocytoma (50%)
  - **Mucosal neuromas** — lips, tongue, GI tract (distinguishes from MEN 2A)
  - **Marfanoid habitus** — tall, thin, long limbs (but NO lens dislocation or aortic aneurysm)
  - Ganglioneuromatosis of GI tract
  - **NO parathyroid disease** (distinguishes from MEN 2A)

---

### Summary Table — MEN Syndromes

| Feature | MEN 1 | MEN 2A | MEN 2B |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gene | MEN1 (11q13) | RET (10q11) | RET (10q11) |
| Parathyroid | Yes (90%) | Yes (20–30%) | No |
| Pituitary | Yes (30–40%) | No | No |
| Pancreas | Yes (60–70%) | No | No |
| MTC | No | Yes (90–100%) | Yes (most aggressive) |
| Pheo | No | Yes (50%) | Yes (50%) |
| Mucosal neuromas | No | No | Yes |
| Marfanoid habitus | No | No | Yes |

---

### Additional High-Yield Points for Exam

**Carcinoid Tumors (Neuroendocrine Tumors — NETs)**
- Arise from **enterochromaffin cells** (Kulchitsky cells) in GI tract, lungs, pancreas
- Most common site: **appendix** (usually benign), then ileum, then rectum
- Secrete: **serotonin** (5-HT), substance P, histamine, bradykinin
- **Carcinoid syndrome** — only occurs when liver metastases present (liver normally inactivates serotonin)
- Features of carcinoid syndrome: **FLUSHING** (episodic), **diarrhea**, **bronchospasm**, **right-sided valvular heart disease** (tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonary stenosis — left side protected by lungs inactivating serotonin)
- **Diagnosis:** elevated 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid)
- **Treatment:** somatostatin analogues (octreotide) for symptom control; surgery

---

*These notes cover all major endocrine pathology topics at MBChB level — everything likely to appear in your exam. Good luck! ✅*
