1. Normal Lung Structure
Key concepts: Airway anatomy · Acinus · Alveolar wall components · Cell types

Respiratory system develops as outgrowth from ventral wall of foregut
Right lung → 3 lobes (3 main bronchi); Left lung → 2 lobes (2 main bronchi)
Bronchi → Bronchioles (no cartilage, no submucosal glands) → Terminal bronchioles → Acinus
Acinus — part of lung distal to terminal bronchiole; composed of respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs → alveoli (site of gas exchange)

Alveolar wall components (blood to air):

Capillary endothelium + basement membrane
Pulmonary interstitium — elastic fibres, collagen, fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, mast cells, mononuclear cells
Alveolar epithelium:

Type I pneumocytes — flat, plate-like; cover 95% of alveolar surface
Type II pneumocytes — rounded; synthesise surfactant; main cell involved in repair after type I injury


Alveolar macrophages — lie free in alveolar space; contain carbon particles in urban dwellers


2. Atelectasis (Collapse)
Conditions covered: Resorption · Compression · Contraction atelectasis

Loss of lung volume caused by inadequate expansion of air spaces
Results in ventilation-perfusion imbalance → hypoxia
Except contraction type, atelectasis is potentially reversible

Three forms:
Resorption Atelectasis

Obstruction prevents air from reaching distal airways → air gradually absorbed → alveolar collapse
Most common cause: obstruction of bronchus
Causes: postoperative mucous plugs, foreign body aspiration (especially children), bronchial asthma, bronchiectasis, chronic bronchitis, intrabronchial tumour (may be first sign of malignancy)

Compression Atelectasis

Accumulation of fluid, blood, or air in pleural cavity compresses lung
Causes: pleural effusion (congestive heart failure), pneumothorax (air leakage into pleural cavity)
Basal atelectasis — failure to breathe deeply; occurs in bedridden patients, ascites, post-surgery

Contraction Atelectasis (Cicatrization)

Local or diffuse fibrosis of lung or pleura → hampers lung expansion
Irreversible


3. Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
Key concepts: DAD · Neutrophil-mediated injury · Hyaline membranes · Clinical course

Defined as respiratory failure within 1 week of a known clinical insult with bilateral opacities on chest imaging, not fully explained by effusions, atelectasis, cardiac failure, or fluid overload
Graded based on severity of arterial blood oxygenation changes
Most frequent triggers: Pneumonia (35–45%) and Sepsis (30–35%); also aspiration, trauma, pancreatitis, transfusion reactions
NOT the same as respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn — neonatal RDS is caused by surfactant deficiency due to prematurity

Pathogenesis

Integrity of alveolar-capillary membrane compromised by endothelial and epithelial injury
Within 30 minutes of acute insult → pulmonary macrophages synthesise IL-8 (potent neutrophil chemotactic agent)
IL-8 + IL-1 + TNF → endothelial activation → neutrophil sequestration and activation in pulmonary capillaries
Activated neutrophils release reactive oxygen species and proteases → damage alveolar epithelium and endothelium
Result: vascular leakiness + loss of surfactant → alveolar unit unable to expand
Outcome determined by balance between destructive forces and endogenous anti-proteases and anti-oxidants

Morphology — Acute Phase

Lungs: dark red, firm, airless, heavy
Capillary congestion, necrosis of alveolar epithelial cells, interstitial and intraalveolar oedema and haemorrhage
Hyaline membranes — most characteristic finding; line distended alveolar ducts; composed of fibrin-rich oedema fluid + remnants of necrotic epithelial cells
Collections of neutrophils in capillaries (especially with sepsis)

Morphology — Organising Stage

Type II pneumocytes proliferate vigorously → attempt to regenerate alveolar lining
Fibrin-rich exudates organise into intraalveolar fibrosis
Marked thickening of alveolar septa due to interstitial cell proliferation and collagen deposition

Clinical Features

Affects ~190,000 patients per year in the USA
85% of cases develop within 72 hours of initial insult
Overall hospital mortality 38.5% (27% mild, 32% moderate, 45% severe)
Poor prognosis: advanced age, bacteraemia, multiorgan failure
Survivors: most recover normal respiratory function within 6–12 months; rest develop diffuse interstitial fibrosis


4. Obstructive vs Restrictive Lung Disease
Key distinction — Pulmonary Function Tests:
FeatureObstructiveRestrictiveFVCNormal or slightly decreasedReducedFEV1Significantly decreasedNormal or reduced proportionatelyFEV1/FVC ratioDecreasedNear normalMechanismIncreased resistance to airflowReduced lung expansion
Obstructive diseases: Emphysema, Chronic bronchitis, Asthma, Bronchiectasis
Restrictive diseases: ARDS (acute), Pneumoconioses, IPF, Sarcoidosis (chronic); also chest wall disorders (obesity, pleural disease, neuromuscular disorders)

5. Obstructive Lung Diseases
Conditions covered: Emphysema · Chronic Bronchitis · Asthma · Bronchiectasis

Emphysema

Permanent enlargement of air spaces distal to terminal bronchioles with destruction of their walls WITHOUT significant fibrosis
Classified according to anatomic distribution within the acinus

Four Types:
TypeLocation AffectedAssociationCentriacinar (centrilobular)Central/proximal acinus — respiratory bronchioles; distal alveoli sparedCigarette smoking; upper lobes; most commonPanacinar (panlobular)Entire acinus uniformly enlarged — from respiratory bronchiole to terminal alveoliα1-antitrypsin deficiency; lower lobesDistal acinar (paraseptal)Proximal acinus normal; distal part involved; adjacent to pleura and septaYoung adults; spontaneous pneumothorax; may form bullaeIrregularAcinus irregularly involved; associated with scarringHealed inflammatory disease; clinically asymptomatic; possibly most common form

Only centriacinar and panacinar cause significant airway obstruction
Centriacinar is ~20 times more common than panacinar

Pathogenesis — Key Mechanisms:

Smoking and noxious particles → lung damage and inflammation → parenchymal destruction
Protease-antiprotease imbalance — proteases (elastase) from neutrophils and macrophages destroy connective tissue; anti-protease deficiency worsens destruction
α1-antitrypsin deficiency — encoded on chromosome 14 (Pi locus); homozygous Z allele → markedly decreased serum levels; >80% develop symptomatic panacinar emphysema; worsened by smoking; ~1% of all emphysema cases
Oxidative stress — reactive oxygen species from cigarette smoke and activated macrophages/neutrophils cause additional tissue damage
Inflammatory mediators — leukotriene B4, IL-8, TNF → recruit neutrophils, macrophages, CD4+/CD8+ T cells
Airway infection — not initiating, but causes acute exacerbations
Loss of elastic tissue in alveolar walls → reduced radial traction on small airways → airways collapse during expiration → functional airflow obstruction

Morphology:

Panacinar: pale, voluminous lungs often obscuring the heart at autopsy
Centriacinar: deeper pink, less voluminous, upper two-thirds more severely affected
Histology: destruction of alveolar walls without fibrosis → enlarged air spaces; diminished alveolar capillaries; terminal and respiratory bronchioles deformed
Bullous emphysema — large subpleural blebs/bullae >1 cm; may rupture → pneumothorax

Clinical Features:

Dyspnoea — first and most prominent symptom; insidious onset, steadily progressive
Reduced FEV1, normal/near-normal FVC → reduced FEV1/FVC ratio
"Pink puffers" — pure emphysema; barrel-chested, dyspnoeic, prolonged expiration, hunched forward; adequate oxygenation until late; prominent hyperventilation
"Blue bloaters" — emphysema + chronic bronchitis; less dyspnoea, CO2 retention, hypoxic, cyanotic, often obese; recurrent infections
Secondary pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure) in 20–30%
Death from respiratory failure or right-sided heart failure

Conditions Related to Emphysema:

Compensatory emphysema — dilation of residual alveoli after surgical removal of diseased lung/lobe
Obstructive overinflation — expansion due to air trapping from subtotal obstruction; can be life-threatening
Mediastinal (interstitial) emphysema — air enters lung interstitium → tracks to mediastinum and subcutaneous tissue; may follow sudden increase in intraalveolar pressure (vomiting, violent coughing), whooping cough, respirator use; subcutaneous emphysema = patient "blows up like a balloon" with crackling crepitation


Chronic Bronchitis

Defined clinically: Persistent productive cough for at least 3 consecutive months in at least 2 consecutive years
Common in cigarette smokers and urban dwellers; affects 20–25% of men aged 40–65

Pathogenesis:

Distinctive feature: hypersecretion of mucus beginning in large airways
Cigarette smoking most important cause; also sulfur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide
Irritants → hypertrophy of mucous glands in trachea/bronchi + increase in goblet cells in smaller bronchi/bronchioles
Inflammation: macrophages, neutrophils, lymphocytes — no eosinophils (unlike asthma)
Airflow obstruction results from:

Small airway disease (chronic bronchiolitis) — mucous plugging, inflammation, bronchiolar wall fibrosis
Coexistent emphysema


IL-13 from T cells and innate lymphoid cells mediates many effects; transcription of mucin gene and neutrophil elastase production increased by tobacco smoke
Microbial infection has a secondary role — maintains inflammation, exacerbates symptoms

Morphology:

Mucosal lining of larger airways hyperaemic, swollen, covered by mucinous/mucopurulent secretions
Enlargement of mucus-secreting glands — diagnostic feature; assessed by Reid index (ratio of submucosal gland thickness to bronchial wall thickness; normally ≤0.4; increased in chronic bronchitis)
Chronic bronchiolitis — goblet cell metaplasia, mucous plugging, inflammation, fibrosis
Severe cases: complete obliteration of lumen — bronchiolitis obliterans
Emphysematous changes often coexist

Clinical Features:

Cough and sputum production may persist without ventilatory dysfunction in some patients
Others develop COPD with hypercapnia, hypoxaemia, cyanosis
Frequent exacerbations, more rapid progression, poorer outcomes than emphysema alone
Progressive disease → pulmonary hypertension → cardiac failure; recurrent infections; respiratory failure


Asthma

Chronic inflammatory disorder of airways causing recurrent episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and cough (particularly at night/early morning)
Hallmarks: Intermittent reversible airway obstruction · Chronic bronchial inflammation with eosinophils · Bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy and hyperreactivity · Increased mucus secretion
Incidence has increased significantly in Western world over past 4 decades
Hygiene hypothesis — lack of exposure to infectious organisms in early childhood → defects in immune tolerance → hyperreactivity later in life

Types of Asthma:
1. Atopic Asthma (most common)

Classic type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction
Usually begins in childhood; positive family history of atopy
Triggered by allergens (dust, pollen, animal dander, food) or infections
Skin test with offending antigen → immediate wheal-and-flare reaction
Driven by TH2 cells — key cytokines:

IL-4 and IL-13 → stimulate IgE production
IL-5 → activates eosinophils
IL-13 → stimulates mucus production


IgE coats submucosal mast cells → allergen exposure → mast cell degranulation → two waves of reaction:

Early (immediate) phase — bronchoconstriction, increased mucus, vasodilation; mediated by histamine, PGD2, leukotrienes LTC4/D4/E4, reflex neural pathways
Late phase — inflammatory; chemokines (including eotaxin) recruit TH2 cells, eosinophils, leukocytes → amplify inflammatory reaction



2. Non-Atopic Asthma

No evidence of allergen sensitisation; skin tests negative
Triggered by viral infections (rhinovirus, parainfluenza) and inhaled pollutants (SO2, ozone, NO2)
Virus-induced inflammation lowers threshold of subepithelial vagal receptors to irritants
Same ultimate mediators as atopic asthma → treated similarly

3. Drug-Induced Asthma

Aspirin most striking example — inhibits cyclo-oxygenase → abnormality in prostaglandin metabolism
Presents with rhinitis, nasal polyps, urticaria, bronchospasm

4. Occupational Asthma

Triggered by fumes (epoxy resins, plastics), organic/chemical dusts (wood, cotton, platinum), gases (toluene)
Attacks develop after repeated exposure to inciting antigen

Airway Remodelling — structural changes from repeated bouts of inflammation:

Hypertrophy of bronchial smooth muscle and mucous glands
Increased vascularity
Subepithelial collagen deposition
May occur years before symptoms begin

Morphology (fatal/biopsy cases):

Lungs distended due to air trapping; small areas of atelectasis
Curschmann spirals — mucous plugs containing whorls of shed epithelium occluding bronchi/bronchioles
Charcot-Leyden crystals — crystalloids made of eosinophil protein galectin-10
Airway remodelling changes:

Thickening of airway wall
Sub-basement membrane fibrosis — characteristic
Increased submucosal vascularity
Enlarged submucosal glands + goblet cell metaplasia
Hypertrophy/hyperplasia of bronchial muscle



Clinical Features:

Severe dyspnoea and wheezing from bronchoconstriction and mucus plugging → air trapping → progressive hyperinflation
Attacks last 1 to several hours; subside spontaneously or with therapy
Intervals between attacks free from overt respiratory difficulties
Status asthmaticus — severe paroxysm not responding to therapy, persisting days to weeks; associated hypercapnia, acidosis, severe hypoxia → potentially fatal
Treatment: glucocorticoids (anti-inflammatory), bronchodilators (beta-adrenergic drugs, leukotriene inhibitors), agents blocking IL-4/IL-5
Bronchial thermoplasty — controlled thermal energy delivery during bronchoscopy to reduce smooth muscle mass


Bronchiectasis

Permanent dilation of bronchi and bronchioles caused by destruction of smooth muscle and elastic tissue; typically results from or is associated with chronic necrotising infections
NOT a primary disorder — always secondary to persistent infection or obstruction

Predisposing Conditions:

Bronchial obstruction — tumours, foreign bodies, mucus impaction; also complicates asthma and chronic bronchitis
Cystic fibrosis — widespread severe bronchiectasis from obstruction by viscid mucus + secondary infections
Immunodeficiency states (especially immunoglobulin deficiencies) — recurrent bacterial infections
Primary ciliary dyskinesia (immotile cilia syndrome) — rare autosomal recessive; inherited abnormalities of cilia → impaired mucociliary clearance → persistent infections; associated with sterility in males
Necrotising/suppurative pneumonia — S. aureus, Klebsiella spp.; post-tuberculosis bronchiectasis significant in endemic areas

Pathogenesis:

Two intertwined processes: obstruction + chronic infection — either may be the initiator
Obstruction → impaired secretion clearance → infection → inflammatory damage → airway dilation → irreversible
Persistent necrotising infection → poor clearance → obstruction → peribronchial fibrosis + traction on bronchi → bronchiectasis

Morphology:

Usually affects lower lobes bilaterally (most vertical air passages)
Tumour/aspiration causes: sharply localised to single segment
Airways dilated up to four times usual diameter — visible almost to pleural surface (normal bronchioles not visible beyond 2–3 cm from pleura)
Histology varies with activity and chronicity:

Active cases: intense acute and chronic inflammatory exudate → desquamation of lining epithelium, ulceration
Organisms: staphylococci, streptococci, pneumococci, Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Healing: epithelium may regenerate but dilation and scarring persist; fibrosis of bronchial/bronchiolar walls; may form abscess cavity



Clinical Features:

Severe persistent cough + expectoration of mucopurulent sometimes fetid sputum
Dyspnoea, rhinosinusitis, haemoptysis
Episodes precipitated by upper respiratory tract infections or new pathogens
Severe widespread disease → obstructive ventilatory defects → hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale
Complications (now less frequent): brain abscess, amyloidosis, cor pulmonale


6. Chronic Interstitial (Restrictive, Infiltrative) Lung Diseases
Key shared features:

Bilateral, often patchy, pulmonary fibrosis mainly affecting alveolar walls
Reduced compliance (stiff lungs) → increased effort to breathe (dyspnoea)
Damage to alveolar epithelium and interstitial vasculature → abnormal ventilation-perfusion ratio → hypoxia
Chest radiograph: small nodules, irregular lines, ground-glass shadows
Advanced disease: respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale → end-stage "honeycomb lung"
FVC reduced; FEV1/FVC ratio near normal (restrictive pattern)


Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF)

Pulmonary disorder of unknown aetiology characterised by patchy, progressive bilateral interstitial fibrosis
Also known as cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis
Males > females; disease of aging — virtually never before age 50 (rarely before 55)
Histologic/radiologic pattern = Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP) — required for diagnosis
Diagnosis of exclusion — similar changes seen in asbestosis, collagen vascular diseases

Pathogenesis:

Repeated injury and defective repair of alveolar epithelium in genetically predisposed individual
Genetic associations:

Germline mutations in telomerase genes → cellular senescence → profibrotic phenotype
MUC5B gene variant (in ~35% of affected individuals) — alters mucin production
Germline mutations in surfactant genes
All these genes expressed only in lung epithelial cells → epithelial cell abnormality is primary initiator


Abnormal epithelial repair → exuberant fibroblastic/myofibroblastic proliferation → fibroblastic foci
Excessive activation of TGF-β (profibrotic factor) drives fibrosis

Morphology:

Pleural surfaces cobblestoned — retraction of scars along interlobular septa
Cut surface: firm, rubbery white areas of fibrosis — preferentially in lower lobe, subpleural regions, along interlobular septa
Histology: patchy interstitial fibrosis varying in intensity — hallmark
Earliest lesions: fibroblastic foci (exuberant fibroblastic proliferation)
Over time: areas become more collagenous and less cellular
Honeycomb fibrosis — dense fibrosis → collapse of alveolar walls → cystic spaces lined by hyperplastic type II pneumocytes or bronchiolar epithelium
Interstitial inflammation: patchy; mostly lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, mast cells, eosinophils
Secondary pulmonary hypertensive changes often present

Clinical Features:

Gradual onset of non-productive cough and progressive dyspnoea
Physical exam: "dry" or "Velcro-like" crackles during inspiration — characteristic
Late stages: cyanosis, cor pulmonale, peripheral oedema
Anti-inflammatory therapies: little use (inflammation is secondary)
Anti-fibrotic therapies:

Nintedanib — tyrosine kinase inhibitor
Pirfenidone — inhibitor of TGF-β
Both approved for IPF with positive clinical trial outcomes


Overall prognosis poor — survival 3–5 years; lung transplantation only definitive treatment

Other Fibrosing Diseases:

NSIP (Non-specific Interstitial Pneumonia) — chronic bilateral interstitial lung disease; frequently associated with collagen vascular disorders (rheumatoid arthritis); much better prognosis than IPF; mild to moderate interstitial chronic inflammation/fibrosis that is patchy but uniform
Cryptogenic organising pneumonia — cough, dyspnoea; subpleural/peribronchial patchy airspace consolidation from intraalveolar plugs of loose organising connective tissue; some recover spontaneously; most treated with oral steroids


Pneumoconioses

Lung disorders caused by inhalation of mineral dusts (broadened to include organic/inorganic particulates and chemical fumes)
Three most common: coal dust, silica, asbestos
Tobacco smoking worsens all inhaled mineral dust effects — more so with asbestos

Key pathogenic principle:

Particles 1–5 µm in diameter are most dangerous — lodge at bifurcation of distal airways
Particles >5–10 µm: unlikely to reach distal airways
Particles <0.5 µm: move in and out of alveoli without substantial deposition
Pulmonary alveolar macrophages are key — phagocytose particles → activate inflammasome → produce IL-1 → initiate inflammatory response → fibroblast proliferation + collagen deposition


Coal Worker's Pneumoconiosis (CWP)
Spectrum of disease:

Anthracosis — most innocuous; carbon pigment engulfed by macrophages; accumulates in connective tissue along pulmonary/pleural lymphatics and draining lymph nodes; seen in coal miners, urban dwellers, tobacco smokers; no cellular reaction
Simple CWP — coal macules (dust-laden macrophages + small amounts of collagen in delicate network) and larger coal nodules; upper lobes and upper zones of lower lobes more heavily involved; centrilobular emphysema may occur
Complicated CWP (PMF — Progressive Massive Fibrosis) — coalescence of coal nodules over many years; multiple dark black scars >2 cm (sometimes up to 10 cm); dense collagen and pigment; less than 10% of simple CWP cases progress to PMF

Key points:

CWP usually benign with little lung function decrement
PMF → increasing pulmonary dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale
No increased frequency of lung carcinoma in coal miners (distinguishes CWP from silica and asbestos)
PMF tends to progress even without further exposure


Silicosis

Most prevalent chronic occupational disease in the world
Caused by inhalation of crystalline silica — sandblasting and hard-rock mining highest risk
Most toxic forms: crystalline silica (quartz, cristobalite, tridymite); quartz most commonly implicated
Silica particles → activate inflammasome → macrophages release IL-1, TNF, fibronectin, oxygen free radicals, fibrogenic cytokines
When mixed with other minerals (e.g. hematite), fibrogenic effect of quartz is reduced

Morphology:

Early: tiny, barely palpable, discrete pale-to-black nodules in upper zones
Silicotic nodule — concentrically arranged hyalinised collagen fibres surrounding amorphous centre; "whorled" appearance of collagen — distinctive
Polarised microscopy: weakly birefringent silica particles in centre of nodules
As disease progresses: nodules coalesce → hard collagenous scars → PMF; honeycomb pattern may develop
Fibrotic lesions also in hilar lymph nodes and pleura

Clinical Features:

Usually detected in asymptomatic workers on routine chest radiograph — fine nodularity in upper zones
Shortness of breath only late in course after PMF present
PMF → pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale
Increased susceptibility to tuberculosis — silicosis depresses cell-mediated immunity; crystalline silica inhibits macrophage killing of phagocytosed mycobacteria; nodules of silicotuberculosis often have central caseation
Relationship between silica and lung cancer: unsettled but most studies suggest some increased risk


Asbestosis and Asbestos-Related Diseases

Asbestos = family of crystalline hydrated silicates with fibrous geometry
Six disease processes linked to asbestos exposure:

Parenchymal interstitial fibrosis (asbestosis)
Localised fibrous pleural plaques or diffuse pleural fibrosis
Pleural effusions
Lung carcinoma
Malignant pleural and peritoneal mesothelioma
Laryngeal carcinoma


Risk extends to family members of asbestos workers and individuals exposed outside workplace

Pathogenesis:

Asbestos fibres phagocytosed by macrophages → activate inflammasome → damage phagolysosomal membranes → release proinflammatory and fibrogenic mediators
Asbestos functions as both tumour initiator and promoter
Reactive free radicals generated preferentially in distal lung close to mesothelial layer → oncogenic effects on mesothelium
Tobacco smoking + asbestos → remarkable synergy for lung carcinoma (carcinogens in smoke adsorbed onto asbestos fibres)

Morphology:

Asbestos bodies — golden brown, fusiform or beaded rods with translucent centre; asbestos fibres coated with iron-containing proteinaceous material (ferritin from macrophages) — hallmark of exposure
Asbestosis begins in lower lobes and subpleurally (contrast with CWP and silicosis which affect upper lobes); spreads to middle and upper lobes
Honeycombing in advanced cases; visceral pleural fibrosis → adhesions between lungs and chest wall
Pleural plaques — most common manifestation of asbestos exposure; well-circumscribed plaques of dense collagen, often containing calcium; on anterior and posterolateral parietal pleura and over diaphragm; usually asymptomatic

Clinical Features:

Progressively worsening dyspnoea 10–20 years after exposure + cough + sputum production
May remain static or progress to congestive heart failure, cor pulmonale, death
Lung carcinoma risk: 5-fold increased for asbestos workers
Mesothelioma risk: >1000 times greater than normal (normally 2–17 cases per million)
Concomitant cigarette smoking greatly increases lung carcinoma risk but NOT mesothelioma risk


Sarcoidosis

Multisystem disease of unknown aetiology characterised by noncaseating granulomatous inflammation in many tissues and organs
Diagnosis of exclusion — other diseases causing noncaseating granulomas (mycobacterial/fungal infections, berylliosis) must be excluded
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy or lung involvement — major finding at presentation in most cases

Epidemiology:

Predilection for adults younger than 40 years
High incidence in Danish, Swedish populations; in USA — African Americans (10x higher than whites)
Higher prevalence among non-smokers — virtually unique to sarcoidosis among pulmonary diseases

Pathogenesis — Immunologic Abnormalities:

Cell-mediated response to unidentified antigen; driven by CD4+ TH1 cells
Intraalveolar and interstitial accumulation of CD4+ TH1 cells with peripheral T cell cytopenia
Increased TH1 cytokines: IL-2 and IFN-γ → T cell proliferation + macrophage activation
Increases in IL-8, TNF, macrophage inflammatory protein-1α → recruit T cells and monocytes → granuloma formation
Anergy to common skin test antigens (Candida, PPD)
Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia
Sarcoidosis recurs in new lungs in at least one-third of patients after lung transplantation

Morphology:

Cardinal feature: nonnecrotising epithelioid granuloma — discrete compact collection of epithelioid cells rimmed by outer zone of CD4+ T cells; intermixed multinucleate giant cells
Over time: fibroblasts proliferate → lay down collagen → hyalinised scar
Two microscopic features sometimes seen (not required for diagnosis):

Schaumann bodies — laminated concretions of calcium and proteins
Asteroid bodies — stellate inclusions within giant cells


Rarely, foci of central necrosis in nodular form
Lungs involved in 90% of patients; granulomas in interstitium with tendency to localise around bronchioles and pulmonary venules ("lymphangitic" distribution); BAL contains abundant CD4+ T cells; 5–15% develop honeycomb lung
Hilar and paratracheal lymph nodes enlarged in 75–90%; characteristically painless, firm, rubbery, non-matted (non-adherent) — unlike tuberculosis
Skin (~25%): Erythema nodosum — hallmark of acute sarcoidosis; raised, red, tender nodules on anterior legs; discrete painless subcutaneous nodules also occur
Eye and lacrimal glands (20–50%): iritis or iridocyclitis → corneal opacities, glaucoma, vision loss; posterior uveal tract → choroiditis, retinitis; lacrimal involvement → sicca syndrome (dry eyes)
Parotid glands (<10%): painful enlargement; xerostomia (dry mouth)
Mikulicz syndrome — combined uveoparotid involvement
Spleen: granulomas in ~75%; clinically enlarged in ~10%
Liver: granulomas usually in portal triads in ~75%; hepatomegaly in ~33%
Hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria — increased calcium absorption secondary to active vitamin D production by granuloma macrophages (NOT bone destruction)

Clinical Features:

Many asymptomatic — discovered on routine chest films (bilateral hilar adenopathy) or incidental at autopsy
Symptomatic cases (~2/3): gradual respiratory symptoms (dyspnoea, dry cough, substernal discomfort) or constitutional symptoms (fever, fatigue, weight loss, night sweats)
No definitive diagnostic test — requires compatible clinical/radiologic findings + exclusion of other disorders + noncaseating granulomas in tissue + tuberculosis must be excluded
Course unpredictable: progressive chronicity or periods of activity with remissions
65–70% recover with minimal/no residual manifestations
20% develop permanent lung dysfunction or visual impairment
10–15% succumb to progressive pulmonary fibrosis and cor pulmonale


Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis

Immunologically mediated inflammatory lung disease primarily affecting alveoli — also called allergic alveolitis
Usually occupational — heightened sensitivity to inhaled antigens (moldy hay, contaminated water, bird feathers, isocyanates)
Unlike asthma (bronchi affected), damage occurs at the alveolar level → manifests as restrictive lung disease with decreased diffusion capacity, compliance, and total lung volume

Evidence of immunologic mediation:

BAL: increased CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes
Most patients have specific antibodies against offending antigen in serum
Complement and immunoglobulins demonstrated in vessel walls by immunofluorescence
Noncaseating granulomas in lungs of two-thirds of patients

Morphology:

Patchy mononuclear cell infiltrates in pulmonary interstitium with peribronchiolar accentuation
Lymphocytes predominate; also plasma cells, epithelioid macrophages; neutrophils in acute form
Loose, poorly formed granulomas without necrosis in >2/3 of cases — peribronchiolar location
Advanced chronic cases: bilateral upper-lobe dominant interstitial fibrosis (UIP pattern)

Clinical Features:

Acute form: fever, cough, dyspnoea, constitutional symptoms arising 4–8 hours after exposure; diagnosis obvious due to temporal relationship with antigen
Chronic form: insidious onset of cough, dyspnoea, malaise, weight loss
Termination of antigen exposure after acute attacks → complete resolution within days
Failure to remove inciting agent → irreversible chronic interstitial pulmonary disease


Pulmonary Eosinophilia

Disorders characterised by pulmonary infiltrates rich in eosinophils — generally immunologic origin

Categories:

Acute eosinophilic pneumonia — rapid onset fever, dyspnoea, hypoxia, diffuse infiltrates; BAL >25% eosinophils; prompt response to corticosteroids
Simple pulmonary eosinophilia (Loeffler syndrome) — transient pulmonary lesions, blood eosinophilia, benign clinical course; alveolar septa thickened by eosinophils and occasional giant cells
Tropical eosinophilia — caused by microfilariae and helminthic parasites
Secondary eosinophilia — associated with asthma, drug allergies, certain vasculitides
Idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonia — aggregates of lymphocytes and eosinophils in septal walls and alveolar spaces, typically at lung periphery; high fever, night sweats, dyspnoea; diagnosis of exclusion


Smoking-Related Interstitial Diseases
Desquamative Interstitial Pneumonia (DIP)

Most striking feature: accumulation of large numbers of macrophages containing dusty-brown pigment (smoker's macrophages) in air spaces
Alveolar septa thickened by sparse inflammatory infiltrate (usually lymphocytes); mild interstitial fibrosis
Pulmonary function: mild restrictive abnormality
Good prognosis and excellent response to steroids and smoking cessation
Some patients progress despite therapy

Respiratory Bronchiolitis

Common lesion in smokers
Pigmented intraluminal macrophages in bronchiocentric distribution (first and second order respiratory bronchioles)
Mild peribronchiolar fibrosis
Symptoms: gradual onset dyspnoea and dry cough; recede with smoking cessation

articles.title: Outline of Female Reproductive Pathology — Notes
articles.content:
## Summary
This document provides a comprehensive outline of female reproductive pathology, covering diseases affecting the vulva, cervix, uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and conditions related to pregnancy. It details various inflammatory processes, benign and malignant neoplasms, and specific disease entities within each anatomical region. The outline also touches upon the pathogenesis of certain conditions, diagnostic approaches, and relevant clinical correlations.

## Key Points
- **Vulva Pathology:** Includes inflammation (vulvitis), chronic inflammatory conditions (Lichen Sclerosus, Lichen Simplex Chronicus), infectious lesions (Condylomas), and malignancies (Carcinoma of the Vulva, Extramammary Paget Disease).
- **Cervical Pathology:** Encompasses cervicitis, neoplastic changes (CIN) with a focus on HPV pathogenesis and grading, invasive carcinoma, and benign polyps.
- **Uterine (Body) Pathology:** Covers endometritis, adenomyosis, endometriosis, abnormal uterine bleeding, endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma, endometrial polyps, and uterine smooth muscle tumors (Leiomyoma, Leiomyosarcoma).
- **Fallopian Tube & Ovarian Pathology:** Addresses salpingitis, fallopian tube carcinoma, ovarian cysts, Polycystic Ovarian Disease (PCOS), and various ovarian tumors including surface epithelial and germ cell types.
- **Diseases of Pregnancy:** Discusses placental infections, ectopic pregnancy, gestational trophoblastic diseases, and hypertensive disorders like preeclampsia/eclampsia and HELLP syndrome.

## Detailed Notes
## OUTLINE — Female Reproductive Pathology

**1. Vulva**
- Vulvitis (causes, Bartholin gland complication)
- Lichen Sclerosus
- Lichen Simplex Chronicus
- Condylomas (Condyloma Lata vs Condylomata Acuminata)
- Carcinoma of the Vulva (HPV-related vs Non-HPV)
- Extramammary Paget Disease

**2. Cervix**
- Cervicitis (acute vs chronic, causative agents)
- Neoplasia of the Cervix — Pathogenesis (HPV, transformation zone, E6/E7, LKB1)
- CIN — Grading (CIN I, II, III → LSIL/HSIL), Pap smear, colposcopy, vaccine
- Invasive Carcinoma of the Cervix
- Endocervical Polyp

**3. Uterus (Body)**
- Endometritis (acute vs chronic, causes)
- Adenomyosis
- Endometriosis (theories, morphology, clinical features)
- Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (dysfunctional types)
- Endometrial Hyperplasia (classification, risk of carcinoma, PTEN)
- Endometrial Carcinoma (Endometrioid vs Serous type)
- Endometrial Polyps
- Leiomyoma
- Leiomyosarcoma

**4. Fallopian Tubes & Ovaries**
- Salpingitis (PID, complications)
- Fallopian Tube Carcinoma (BRCA)
- Follicle & Luteal Cysts
- Polycystic Ovarian Disease (PCOS)
- Ovarian Tumours — Surface Epithelial (Serous, Mucinous, Endometrioid, Brenner)
- Germ Cell Tumours — Teratomas (Mature, Immature, Specialized)
- Clinical Correlations (CA-125, symptoms)

**5. Diseases of Pregnancy**
- Placental Inflammations & Infections (ascending vs haematogenous, TORCH)
- Ectopic Pregnancy
- Gestational Trophoblastic Disease:
  - Hydatidiform Mole (Complete vs Partial)
  - Invasive Mole
  - Gestational Choriocarcinoma
  - Placental Site Trophoblastic Tumour
- Preeclampsia / Eclampsia (HELLP syndrome)

## Practice Questions
1. What are the two main categories of carcinoma of the vulva based on their etiology? → HPV-related and Non-HPV related.
2. Which grading system is used for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), and what do these grades correspond to in terms of squamous intraepithelial lesions? → CIN I, II, III correspond to LSIL (CIN I) and HSIL (CIN II and III).
3. What are the two main histological types of endometrial carcinoma? → Endometrioid and Serous types.
4. Which genetic mutation is associated with an increased risk of fallopian tube carcinoma? → BRCA mutations.
5. What are the two main types of hydatidiform mole? → Complete and Partial.
6. What is the primary difference in the pathogenesis of ascending versus haematogenous placental infections? → Ascending infections begin in the lower genital tract and move upwards, while haematogenous infections spread through the bloodstream.
7. What does the acronym HELLP syndrome stand for in the context of preeclampsia/eclampsia? → Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelet count.
8. Besides vulvitis, name two chronic inflammatory conditions affecting the vulva. → Lichen Sclerosus and Lichen Simplex Chronicus.

articles.title: Disorders of the Vagina and Breast — Notes
articles.content:
## SummaryThis content details various disorders affecting the vagina and the breast, including both benign and malignant conditions. For the vagina, common issues like vaginitis caused by infections (Trichomonas, Candida, bacterial vaginosis, STIs) and atrophic changes are discussed, alongside rare but significant malignancies such as squamous cell carcinoma, clear cell adenocarcinoma (linked to DES exposure), and sarcoma botryoides (a pediatric tumor). The breast section covers fibrocystic changes with varying risks of carcinoma, inflammatory processes like mastitis and fat necrosis, and a range of breast tumors including fibroadenomas, phyllodes tumors, intraductal papillomas, and various forms of carcinoma (in situ and invasive). Special attention is given to the molecular subtypes of breast cancer, inflammatory breast cancer, prognostic factors, and common lesions in the male breast, such as gynecomastia and carcinoma.
## Key Points- **Vaginitis:** Common condition characterized by discharge, itching, or burning, with key infectious causes including *Trichomonas vaginalis*, *Candida albicans*, and *Gardnerella vaginalis* (bacterial vaginosis).
- **Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma of the Vagina:** Strongly associated with in utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES).
- **Sarcoma Botryoides:** The most common malignant vaginal tumor in infants and young girls under 5 years.
- **Fibrocystic Changes:** A spectrum of benign breast changes driven by hormonal fluctuations, categorized into nonproliferative, proliferative, and atypical hyperplasia, with increasing risk of carcinoma correlating with atypia.
- **Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (IDC) - NST:** The most common type of invasive breast cancer, characterized by a firm, gritty mass and desmoplastic stromal reaction.
- **Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (ILC):** Characterized by loss of E-cadherin, leading to single-file infiltration and often bilateral/multicentric presentation.
- **Molecular Subtypes of Breast Cancer:** Categorized by ER/PR and HER2 status (Luminal A, Luminal B, HER2-enriched, Triple-negative), impacting prognosis and treatment.
- **Gynecomastia:** Enlargement of the male breast due to an imbalance between estrogen and androgen activity.
- **Male Breast Carcinoma:** Rare, but almost always ER and PR positive, with a prognosis similar to female breast cancer at the same stage.

## Detailed Notes## 6. Disorders of the Vagina**Conditions covered:** Vaginitis · Squamous Cell Carcinoma · Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma · Sarcoma Botryoides
### Vaginitis**Key causes:** Infections · Atrophic changes · Chemical irritation
Vaginitis is extremely common and often presents with vaginal discharge, itching, and burning.
**Important infectious causes:**
- **Trichomonas vaginalis:** A flagellated protozoan, sexually transmitted. Characterized by frothy, yellow-green discharge and a "strawberry cervix" on examination.
- **Candida albicans:** Causes thick, white, cottage-cheese-like discharge with intense pruritus. Common in diabetics, pregnant women, antibiotic users, and the immunocompromised.
- **Gardnerella vaginalis (Bacterial vaginosis):** Results in a thin, grey-white, fishy-smelling discharge. It's not strictly an STI but an overgrowth of anaerobes replacing normal lactobacilli. Clue cells (epithelial cells studded with bacteria) are seen on microscopy.
- **N. gonorrhoeae / C. trachomatis:** Can cause ascending infections involving the upper genital tract.
- **HSV-2:** Presents with painful vesicular ulcers.

**Atrophic vaginitis:** Occurs postmenopausally due to loss of estrogen, leading to a thin, dry epithelium that is prone to inflammation and bleeding.
**Key point:** The normal vaginal flora is dominated by lactobacilli, which maintain an acidic pH. Disruption of this balance predisposes to infection.
---
### Malignant Neoplasms of the Vagina**Conditions covered:** Squamous Cell Carcinoma · Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma · Sarcoma Botryoides
#### Squamous Cell Carcinoma
Primary vaginal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is **rare**; most vaginal malignancies are secondary metastases. It occurs mostly in women over 60 years. **HPV** (types 16 and 18) plays a role, similar to cervical SCC. It is preceded by **vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia (VAIN)**.
- **Location:** Most commonly in the upper posterior vaginal wall.
- **Presentation:** Vaginal bleeding, discharge, dyspareunia.
- **Spread:** Direct extension to the bladder, rectum, and pelvic sidewall; lymph node metastasis.
- **Prognosis:** Generally poor due to late presentation.

#### Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma
This is **strongly associated with in utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES)**. It develops in young women (teens to early 20s) whose mothers took DES during pregnancy. DES exposure causes **vaginal adenosis**, which is the persistence of glandular epithelium in the vagina.
- **Histology:** Characterized by clear cells with hobnail nuclei protruding into glandular lumina.
- **Location:** Usually the anterior wall of the upper vagina.
- **Key point:** This tumor is now historically rare but important for examination purposes.

#### Sarcoma Botryoides (Embryonal Rhabdomyosarcoma)
This is the **most common malignant vaginal tumor in infants and young girls under 5 years**. It arises from embryonal rhabdomyoblasts beneath the vaginal epithelium.
- **Gross appearance:** Soft, grape-like polypoid masses protruding from the vagina.
- **Histology:** Small primitive cells with occasional large strap cells (rhabdomyoblasts) showing cross-striations; a characteristic **cambium layer** (dense subepithelial condensation of tumor cells) is present.
- **Presentation:** Vaginal mass or bleeding in a young child.
- **Behaviour:** Highly aggressive, invading locally and metastasizing widely.
- **Treatment:** Combined surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation.

---
## 7. Disorders of the Breast**Conditions covered:** Fibrocystic Changes · Inflammatory Processes · Tumours (Fibroadenoma · Phyllodes Tumour · Intraductal Papilloma · Carcinoma) · Lesions of the Male Breast
---
### Fibrocystic Changes**Conditions covered:** Nonproliferative Changes · Proliferative Changes · Relationship to Carcinoma
Fibrocystic changes are the most common breast disorder, affecting women of reproductive age. It's a broad term encompassing morphologic changes driven by hormonal fluctuations. Presentation is often as breast lumps, tenderness, or nodularity that fluctuates with the menstrual cycle.
#### Nonproliferative Changes
These changes carry **no increased risk of carcinoma**.
- **Cyst formation:** Fluid-filled cysts lined by flattened or apocrine metaplastic epithelium. Appear as "blue-dome cysts" on gross examination.
- **Apocrine metaplasia:** Benign lining cells resembling apocrine sweat gland cells.
- **Mild epithelial hyperplasia:** A slight increase in cell layers lining ducts, without atypia.
- **Stromal fibrosis:** Increase in fibrous stroma, giving the breast a firm, rubbery texture.

#### Proliferative Changes
These carry a slightly to significantly increased risk of carcinoma.
- **Moderate to florid epithelial hyperplasia (without atypia):** Slightly increased risk (~1.5–2x) of carcinoma.
- **Sclerosing adenosis:** Increased acini per lobule with stromal fibrosis; can mimic carcinoma but is benign.
- **Atypical hyperplasia (ductal or lobular):** Significant increased risk (~4–5x) of carcinoma.
 - **Atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH):** Partial involvement of ducts by cells resembling DCIS.

- **Atypical lobular hyperplasia (ALH):** Partial involvement of lobules by cells resembling LCIS.
#### Relationship of Fibrocystic Changes to Breast Carcinoma
| Type | Relative Risk of Carcinoma |
| :------------------------------------- | :------------------------- |
| Nonproliferative changes | No increased risk |
| Proliferative changes without atypia | 1.5–2x increased risk |
| Atypical hyperplasia (ADH or ALH) | 4–5x increased risk |
| Atypical hyperplasia + family history of breast cancer | 10x increased risk |
**Key point:** The risk is bilateral, applying to both breasts.
---
### Inflammatory Processes of the Breast**Conditions covered:** Acute Mastitis · Fat Necrosis · Mammary Duct Ectasia
#### Acute Mastitis
Almost exclusively occurs during **lactation**. Most commonly caused by **S. aureus**, entering via nipple fissures. Presents as a painful, red, swollen breast with fever, and may progress to abscess. Treatment includes antibiotics and, if necessary, surgical drainage. Breastfeeding should continue if possible.
#### Fat Necrosis
Follows **trauma or surgery** to the breast. It presents as a firm, sometimes calcified mass that can **mimic carcinoma**. Histologically, it shows necrotic fat cells surrounded by inflammatory cells and fibrosis. It is **benign**.
#### Mammary Duct Ectasia
Dilation of major ducts with thickened secretions and inflammation, occurring in **perimenopausal and postmenopausal women**. Presents with thick, white/greenish nipple discharge, a subareolar mass, and skin retraction, mimicking carcinoma. Histologically, dilated ducts are seen with inflammatory changes. It is **benign** but clinically important.
---
### Tumours of the Breast**Conditions covered:** Fibroadenoma · Phyllodes Tumour · Intraductal Papilloma · Carcinoma
#### Fibroadenoma
The **most common benign tumour of the breast**, most frequent in women under 30. It is a biphasic tumor of stroma and epithelium. Grossly, it is a well-circumscribed, firm, rubbery, mobile mass ("breast mouse"). Histologically, it shows a loose stroma surrounding duct-like spaces. It is estrogen-sensitive and has **no significant malignant potential**.
#### Phyllodes Tumour
Similar to fibroadenoma but with **more cellular stroma and a leaf-like architecture**. Occurs in older women (40s–50s). It has a **spectrum from benign to malignant**. Malignant phyllodes tumours can metastasize hematogenously. Treatment is wide local excision.
#### Intraductal Papilloma
A benign papillary growth within a **lactiferous duct**, usually near the nipple. Most common in women **35–55 years**. The classic presentation is **unilateral bloody or serous nipple discharge**. Solitary papillomas have low malignant risk, while multiple peripheral papillomas have a higher risk. Histologically, they have fibrovascular cores lined by epithelial and myoepithelial cells (presence of myoepithelial cells confirms benignity). Treatment is surgical excision.
#### Carcinoma of the Breast
The most common malignancy in women. **Risk factors** include female sex, increasing age, family history, BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations, hormonal factors, and prior breast biopsy with atypical hyperplasia.
##### BRCA1 and BRCA2
Tumor suppressor genes involved in DNA repair. BRCA1 carriers have a ~60-80% lifetime risk of breast cancer; BRCA2 carriers have a ~40-70% risk. Both also increase ovarian cancer risk. BRCA1-associated cancers are often ER-negative, high-grade, and triple-negative.
##### In Situ Carcinomas
- **Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS):** Malignant cells confined within ducts. Detected by mammography (microcalcifications). The **comedo type** is high-grade and most aggressive. If untreated, it has a significant risk of progressing to invasive carcinoma. Treatment is surgical excision ± radiation ± tamoxifen.
- **Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS):** Malignant cells filling lobular acini. Often an incidental finding, it is a **marker of increased risk** for invasive carcinoma in **both breasts**. Associated with loss of **E-cadherin** expression. Treatment is observation with surveillance or bilateral prophylactic mastectomy in high-risk cases.

##### Invasive (Infiltrating) Carcinomas
- **Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (IDC) — No Special Type (NST):** Most common type (~70–80%). Presents as a firm, gritty, stellate mass. Spreads to **axillary lymph nodes**, which are the most important prognostic factor. Graded I–III.
- **Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (ILC):** ~10–15% of invasive cancers. Characterized by loss of **E-cadherin**, leading to infiltration in single file ("Indian file pattern"). Often **bilateral and multicentric**, and can be difficult to detect. Tends to metastasize to unusual sites.
- **Special Types (better prognosis):** Tubular carcinoma, mucinous (colloid) carcinoma, medullary carcinoma.

##### Molecular Subtypes of Breast Cancer
| Subtype | ER/PR | HER2 | Features |
| :--------------- | :-------- | :------ | :------------------------------------------- |
| Luminal A | Positive | Negative | Best prognosis; hormone therapy |
| Luminal B | Positive | Positive or negative | Intermediate prognosis |
| HER2-enriched | Negative | Positive | Aggressive; targeted therapy (trastuzumab) |
| Triple-negative | Negative | Negative | Worst prognosis; associated with BRCA1 |
##### Inflammatory Breast Carcinoma
An aggressive clinical presentation mimicking acute mastitis, caused by **tumour emboli blocking dermal lymphatics**. Characterized by peau d'orange appearance. Very poor prognosis.
##### Clinical Features and Spread
Presents as a painless lump, nipple discharge, or skin changes. Spreads to **axillary lymph nodes**, then internal mammary and supraclavicular nodes. Distant metastases commonly occur in bone, lung, liver, brain, and adrenal glands. **Sentinel lymph node biopsy** is used for staging.
##### Prognostic Factors
The most important prognostic factor is **lymph node status**. Other factors include tumor size, histologic grade, hormone receptor status, HER2 status, and molecular subtype.
---
### Lesions of the Male Breast**Conditions covered:** Gynecomastia · Carcinoma
#### Gynecomastia
**Enlargement of the male breast** due to an **imbalance between oestrogen and androgen activity**. Causes include physiological changes (neonates, puberty, elderly), liver disease, Klinefelter syndrome, estrogen-secreting tumors, and certain drugs (e.g., spironolactone, digoxin). Histologically, it shows ductal epithelial hyperplasia with periductal oedematous stroma. It is **not premalignant**.
#### Male Breast Carcinoma
Rare, accounting for ~1% of all breast cancers. **Risk factors** include Klinefelter syndrome, BRCA2 mutations, exogenous estrogens, and liver disease. Most are **invasive ductal carcinoma** and almost always **ER and PR positive**. Presents as a subareolar mass. Prognosis is stage-for-stage similar to female breast cancer, but often diagnosed later. Treatment includes mastectomy and hormone therapy.
---
## Practice Questions- A 25-year-old woman presents with a complaint of vaginal discharge that is described as thin, grey-white, and fishy-smelling. Microscopic examination reveals clue cells. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Bacterial vaginosis (caused by *Gardnerella vaginalis*)
- A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with vaginal bleeding and a palpable mass in the upper posterior vaginal wall. Biopsy reveals squamous cell carcinoma. What is the most likely risk factor associated with this type of malignancy? → HPV infection
- A 4-year-old girl presents with a rapidly growing, grape-like mass protruding from her vagina. Biopsy shows small primitive cells with a characteristic subepithelial condensation of tumor cells. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Sarcoma botryoides (Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma)
- A 45-year-old woman undergoes a breast biopsy for a palpable lump. Histology reveals moderate to florid epithelial hyperplasia without atypia. What is the increased risk of developing breast carcinoma associated with this finding? → 1.5–2 times the baseline risk
- A 50-year-old woman presents with bloody nipple discharge from her right breast. Mammography and biopsy reveal a benign papillary growth within a lactiferous duct. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Intraductal papilloma
- A 60-year-old man presents with a palpable, painless lump in the subareolar region of his left breast. Mammography and biopsy confirm invasive ductal carcinoma. Given the typical characteristics of male breast cancer, what hormone receptor status is most likely to be positive? → Estrogen Receptor (ER) and Progesterone Receptor (PR) positive
- A 30-year-old woman is found to have a breast mass on self-examination. It is well-circumscribed, firm, rubbery, and mobile. Histological examination reveals proliferating stromal and epithelial elements. What is the most common benign breast tumor presenting in this demographic? → Fibroadenoma
- A patient is diagnosed with HER2-enriched breast cancer. Based on the molecular subtype, what is the expected prognosis and common treatment approach? → Aggressive prognosis, treated with targeted therapy such as trastuzumab.

**Conditions covered:** Vaginitis · Squamous Cell Carcinoma · Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma · Sarcoma Botryoides

---

### Vaginitis
**Key causes:** Infections · Atrophic changes · Chemical irritation

- Extremely common; often presents with vaginal discharge, itching, burning
- **Important infectious causes:**
  - **Trichomonas vaginalis** — flagellated protozoan; sexually transmitted; frothy, yellow-green discharge; "strawberry cervix" on examination

  - **N. gonorrhoeae / C. trachomatis** — ascending infections; may involve upper genital tract
  - **HSV-2** — painful vesicular ulcers
- **Atrophic vaginitis** — postmenopausal; loss of oestrogen → thin, dry epithelium → prone to inflammation and bleeding
- **Key point:** Vaginal flora is normally dominated by lactobacilli which maintain an acidic pH — disruption of this balance predisposes to infection

---

### Malignant Neoplasms of the Vagina

**Conditions covered:** Squamous Cell Carcinoma · Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma · Sarcoma Botryoides

#### Squamous Cell Carcinoma
- Primary vaginal SCC is **rare** — most vaginal malignancies are secondary (metastatic from cervix, endometrium, or vulva)
- Occurs mostly in women **over 60 years**
- **HPV** (types 16 and 18) plays a role — similar pathogenesis to cervical SCC
- Preceded by **vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia (VAIN)** — analogous to CIN
- **Location:** Most commonly in the upper posterior vaginal wall
- **Presentation:** Vaginal bleeding, discharge, dyspareunia
- **Spread:** Direct extension to bladder, rectum, and pelvic sidewall; lymph node metastasis
- **Prognosis:** Depends on stage; generally poor because most present late

#### Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma
- **Strongly associated with in utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES)** — a synthetic oestrogen given to pregnant women in the 1950s–1970s to prevent miscarriage
- Develops in young women (teens to early 20s) whose mothers took DES during pregnancy
- DES exposure causes **vaginal adenosis** — persistence of glandular (Müllerian) epithelium in the vagina where it is normally replaced by squamous epithelium — this is the precursor lesion
- **Histology:** Clear cells with hobnail nuclei protruding into glandular lumina — characteristic appearance
- **Location:** Usually anterior wall of upper vagina
- **Key point:** DES is no longer used, so this tumour is now historically rare but exam-important

#### Sarcoma Botryoides (Embryonal Rhabdomyosarcoma)
- **Most common malignant vaginal tumour in infants and young girls under 5 years**
- Arises from embryonal rhabdomyoblasts (primitive skeletal muscle cells) beneath the vaginal epithelium
- **Gross appearance:** Soft, grape-like polypoid masses protruding from the vagina — hence the name "botryoides" (Greek for grape-like)
- **Histology:** Small primitive cells with occasional large strap cells (rhabdomyoblasts) showing cross-striations; characteristic **cambium layer** — dense subepithelial condensation of tumour cells just beneath the surface epithelium
- **Presentation:** Vaginal mass or bleeding in a young child
- **Behaviour:** Highly aggressive; invades locally and metastasizes widely
- **Treatment:** Combined surgery + chemotherapy + radiation; outcomes have improved significantly with multimodal therapy

---

## 7. Disorders of the Breast

**Conditions covered:** Fibrocystic Changes · Inflammatory Processes · Tumours (Fibroadenoma · Phyllodes Tumour · Intraductal Papilloma · Carcinoma) · Lesions of the Male Breast

---

### Fibrocystic Changes

**Conditions covered:** Nonproliferative Changes · Proliferative Changes · Relationship to Carcinoma

- Most common breast disorder; affects women of reproductive age (20s–50s)
- Broad term encompassing a spectrum of morphologic changes — not a single disease
- Driven by hormonal fluctuations (oestrogen/progesterone imbalance)
- Presents as breast lumps, tenderness, or nodularity — often fluctuates with menstrual cycle

#### Nonproliferative Changes
- **No increased risk of carcinoma**
- **Cyst formation** — most characteristic; fluid-filled cysts lined by flattened or apocrine metaplastic epithelium; cysts appear blue-domed on gross examination ("blue-dome cysts")
- **Apocrine metaplasia** — lining cells take on features of apocrine sweat gland cells; large eosinophilic cytoplasm; benign
- **Mild epithelial hyperplasia** — slight increase in cell layers lining ducts; no atypia
- **Stromal fibrosis** — increase in fibrous stroma giving breast a firm, rubbery texture

#### Proliferative Changes
- **Moderate to florid epithelial hyperplasia (without atypia)** — slightly increased risk (~1.5–2x) of carcinoma
- **Sclerosing adenosis** — increased number of acini per lobule with stromal fibrosis; may mimic carcinoma on mammography and grossly; but benign
- **Atypical hyperplasia (ductal or lobular)** — significant increased risk (~4–5x) of carcinoma; cells show features approaching carcinoma in situ but do not fully qualify
  - **Atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH)** — partial involvement of ducts by cells resembling DCIS
  - **Atypical lobular hyperplasia (ALH)** — partial involvement of lobules by cells resembling LCIS

#### Relationship of Fibrocystic Changes to Breast Carcinoma
| Type | Relative Risk of Carcinoma |
|---|---|
| Nonproliferative changes | No increased risk |
| Proliferative changes without atypia | 1.5–2x increased risk |
| Atypical hyperplasia (ADH or ALH) | 4–5x increased risk |
| Atypical hyperplasia + family history of breast cancer | 10x increased risk |

- **Key point:** The risk is bilateral — increased risk applies to BOTH breasts, not just the affected side

---

### Inflammatory Processes of the Breast

**Conditions covered:** Acute Mastitis · Fat Necrosis · Mammary Duct Ectasia

#### Acute Mastitis
- Almost exclusively occurs during **lactation** (first few weeks postpartum)
- Organisms: **S. aureus** most common; occasionally streptococci
- Entry via cracks/fissures in the nipple
- Presents as painful, red, swollen breast with fever
- May progress to abscess formation
- Treatment: antibiotics; surgical drainage if abscess forms; breastfeeding should continue if possible

#### Fat Necrosis
- Follows **trauma or surgery** to the breast (often patient does not recall the injury)
- Results in a firm, sometimes calcified mass that can **mimic carcinoma** clinically and on mammography — important diagnostic trap
- Histology: necrotic fat cells surrounded by lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells), giant cells, and fibrosis
- **Benign** — no malignant potential; biopsy needed to exclude carcinoma

#### Mammary Duct Ectasia
- Dilation of major ducts with inspissated (thickened) secretions and periductal inflammation
- Occurs in **perimenopausal and postmenopausal women**
- Presents as: thick, white/greenish nipple discharge + subareolar mass + skin retraction (can mimic carcinoma)
- Histology: dilated ducts filled with granular debris, foamy macrophages; periductal chronic inflammation and fibrosis
- **Benign** — but clinically important because it mimics cancer

---

### Tumours of the Breast

**Conditions covered:** Fibroadenoma · Phyllodes Tumour · Intraductal Papilloma · Carcinoma

#### Fibroadenoma
- **Most common benign tumour of the breast**; most frequent in women under 30 years
- Composed of both proliferating stromal and epithelial elements (biphasic tumour)
- **Gross:** Well-circumscribed, firm, rubbery, mobile mass ("breast mouse") — moves freely under the examining hand; grey-white with slit-like spaces on cut section
- **Histology:** Loose fibromyxoid stroma surrounding compressed, elongated duct-like spaces (intracanalicular pattern) or open rounded glands (pericanalicular pattern)
- Oestrogen-sensitive → may enlarge during pregnancy; tends to shrink postmenopausally
- **No significant malignant potential**
- Treatment: excision if symptomatic or enlarging; observation acceptable for small lesions

#### Phyllodes Tumour
- Similar to fibroadenoma but with **more cellular stroma and leaf-like architecture** — hence "phyllodes" (Greek for leaf)
- Occurs in older women (40s–50s) compared to fibroadenoma
- **Spectrum from benign to malignant** — classified as benign, borderline, or malignant based on stromal cellularity, mitotic activity, and margin characteristics
- **Gross:** Large, bulky mass with leaf-like clefts on cut section
- Malignant phyllodes tumours can metastasize — typically via **haematogenous route** (not lymphatics)
- Treatment: wide local excision with clear margins; lymph node dissection generally not required

#### Intraductal Papilloma
- Benign papillary growth within a **lactiferous duct**, usually near the nipple
- Most common in women **35–55 years**
- **Classic presentation: unilateral bloody or serous nipple discharge** — most important clinical feature
- Solitary papillomas (central, near nipple) — low malignant risk
- Multiple peripheral papillomas — higher risk of associated carcinoma
- Histology: fibrovascular cores lined by both epithelial and myoepithelial cells (presence of myoepithelial cells confirms benignity)
- Treatment: surgical excision of the involved duct

#### Carcinoma of the Breast
- Most common malignancy in women; second most common cause of cancer death in women (after lung cancer)
- **Risk factors:** Female sex, increasing age, family history, BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations, early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, late first pregnancy, obesity (postmenopausal), exogenous oestrogen/HRT, prior breast biopsy with atypical hyperplasia, radiation exposure

##### BRCA1 and BRCA2
- **BRCA1** — chromosome 17q; tumour suppressor; DNA repair; BRCA1 cancers tend to be ER-negative, high grade, triple-negative
- **BRCA2** — chromosome 13q; DNA repair; associated with male breast cancer also
- BRCA1 carriers: ~60–80% lifetime risk of breast cancer; BRCA2 carriers: ~40–70%
- Both also increase risk of ovarian cancer

##### In Situ Carcinomas
**Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS)**
- Malignant epithelial cells confined within ducts — basement membrane intact, no stromal invasion
- Detected mainly by mammography (microcalcifications)
- **Comedo type** — high-grade DCIS with central necrosis; calcifications form in necrotic centre; most aggressive in situ type
- If left untreated, significant proportion progress to invasive carcinoma
- Treatment: surgical excision ± radiation ± tamoxifen

**Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS)**
- Malignant cells fill and distend lobular acini — no invasion
- Often **incidental finding** on biopsy; does not form a palpable mass; not typically detected by mammography
- **Marker of increased risk** rather than direct precursor — increases risk of invasive carcinoma in **both breasts**
- Associated with loss of **E-cadherin** expression — hallmark finding
- Treatment: observation with close surveillance; bilateral prophylactic mastectomy in high-risk cases

##### Invasive (Infiltrating) Carcinomas
**Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (IDC) — No Special Type (NST)**
- Most common type — ~70–80% of all invasive breast cancers
- Firm, gritty, stellate mass with irregular borders; grates when cut (like cutting an unripe pear)
- Elicits prominent **desmoplastic stromal reaction** (dense fibrous stroma)
- Spreads to axillary lymph nodes — most important prognostic factor
- Graded I–III (Nottingham grading system) based on tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, mitotic count

**Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (ILC)**
- ~10–15% of invasive cancers
- Loss of **E-cadherin** → cells lose cohesion → infiltrate in single file ("Indian file pattern") through stroma
- Often **bilateral and multicentric**
- May be difficult to detect clinically and mammographically — does not form a discrete mass
- Tends to metastasize to unusual sites — peritoneum, retroperitoneum, meninges, GI tract, ovary

**Special Types (better prognosis):**
- **Tubular carcinoma** — well-differentiated, open tubules; excellent prognosis
- **Mucinous (colloid) carcinoma** — tumour cells floating in lakes of mucin; elderly women; good prognosis
- **Medullary carcinoma** — syncytial sheets of large cells with prominent lymphocytic infiltrate; despite high grade, relatively good prognosis; associated with BRCA1 mutations

##### Molecular Subtypes of Breast Cancer
| Subtype | ER/PR | HER2 | Features |
|---|---|---|---|
| Luminal A | Positive | Negative | Best prognosis; hormone therapy |
| Luminal B | Positive | Positive or negative | Intermediate prognosis |
| HER2-enriched | Negative | Positive | Aggressive; targeted therapy (trastuzumab) |
| Triple-negative | Negative | Negative | Worst prognosis; no targeted therapy; associated with BRCA1 |

##### Inflammatory Breast Carcinoma
- Aggressive clinical presentation — breast appears red, warm, oedematous, resembling acute mastitis
- NOT caused by inflammation — caused by **tumour emboli blocking dermal lymphatics**
- Peau d'orange (orange-peel skin) appearance due to lymphatic obstruction
- Very poor prognosis

##### Clinical Features and Spread
- Presents as painless breast lump (most common); nipple discharge; skin changes; nipple retraction
- Spreads to: **axillary lymph nodes** (most important); also internal mammary nodes, supraclavicular nodes
- Distant metastases: bone (most common distant site), lung, liver, brain, adrenal glands
- **Sentinel lymph node biopsy** — first lymph node draining the tumour; if negative, axillary dissection may be avoided

##### Prognostic Factors
- **Lymph node status** — most important prognostic factor
- Tumour size
- Histologic grade
- Hormone receptor status (ER/PR positive = better prognosis)
- HER2 status
- Molecular subtype

---

### Lesions of the Male Breast

**Conditions covered:** Gynecomastia · Carcinoma

#### Gynecomastia
- **Enlargement of the male breast** — most common male breast disorder
- Due to **imbalance between oestrogen and androgen activity** — relative oestrogen excess
- **Causes:**
  - Physiologic — neonates (maternal oestrogens), puberty (transient), elderly (declining testosterone)
  - Liver disease (cirrhosis) — impaired oestrogen metabolism
  - Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) — decreased testosterone
  - Oestrogen-secreting tumours (testicular, adrenal)
  - Drugs — **spironolactone, digoxin, cimetidine, marijuana, anabolic steroids, chemotherapy agents**
- **Histology:** Ductal epithelial hyperplasia + periductal oedematous stroma; lobule formation is absent (unlike female breast)
- **Not premalignant** — but important to identify and treat underlying cause

#### Male Breast Carcinoma
- Rare — accounts for ~1% of all breast cancers
- **Risk factors:** Klinefelter syndrome, BRCA2 mutations (more than BRCA1), exogenous oestrogens, liver disease, radiation exposure, family history
- Most are **invasive ductal carcinoma**; almost always **ER and PR positive** (higher rate than female breast cancer)
- Presents as subareolar mass ± nipple discharge ± skin/nipple involvement
- **Prognosis:** Stage for stage, similar to female breast cancer; but often diagnosed later → worse overall outcomes
- Treatment: mastectomy + hormone therapy (tamoxifen); chemotherapy if needed

---

Those are the two complete sections. Your notes now cover the full scope of the lecture series from Vagina through to Male Breast. Everything is in the same must-know format as the rest of your published article.
