Here are your **Respiratory System Pathology MUST-KNOWS** — exam-ready, topic by topic, covering MCQs, SAQs, and essays:

---

# RESPIRATORY SYSTEM PATHOLOGY — COMPLETE MUST-KNOWS

## EXAM BLUEPRINT OVERVIEW
**MCQs test:** Definitions, specific numbers/percentages, eponyms, "most common," pathogens, mechanisms.
**SAQs test:** Pathogenesis steps, morphology, clinical features.
**Essays test:** Compare/contrast (e.g., obstructive vs restrictive), full disease discussions with epidemiology → pathogenesis → morphology → clinical features.

---

## 1. UPPER RESPIRATORY TRACT

### ACUTE INFECTIONS — MUST KNOWS

**Common Cold:**
- Most common pathogen: **Rhinovirus**
- Others: coronavirus, RSV, parainfluenza, influenza, adenovirus, enteroviruses, Group A β-hemolytic streptococci
- ~40% of cases have no identifiable cause
- Self-limiting, usually <1 week
- Complications: bacterial **otitis media** or **sinusitis**

**Acute Pharyngitis:**
- Most common form = mild, accompanies common cold
- Severe form with exudate = **β-hemolytic streptococci** or adenovirus
- ⚠️ Streptococcal tonsillitis → risk of **peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)**, **poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis**, **acute rheumatic fever**
- Coxsackievirus A → **herpangina** (pharyngeal vesicles/ulcers)
- EBV → **infectious mononucleosis** ("kissing disease") — important cause of pharyngitis

**Acute Epiglottitis:**
- Agent: **H. influenzae** (mainly in children)
- Features: **abrupt onset**, pain, **airway obstruction** → can be fatal
- Prevented by **H. influenzae vaccination**

**Laryngitis:**
- Common cold agents + inhalants + allergens
- Uncommon but important: **tuberculous laryngitis** (from infected sputum) and **diphtheritic laryngitis**
- Diphtheria: **Corynebacterium diphtheriae** → necrosis + fibrinopurulent exudate → **dirty-gray pseudomembrane**
- Hazards of diphtheria: pseudomembrane aspiration (airway obstruction) + toxin absorption (myocarditis, peripheral neuropathy)

**Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis):**
- Most common cause: **parainfluenza virus** (children)
- Also: RSV
- Features: **inspiratory stridor**, harsh persistent cough
- Self-limited but can cause respiratory failure

---

### NASOPHARYNGEAL CARCINOMA — MUST KNOWS

- Strongly linked to **EBV** (genome found in virtually ALL cases)
- High incidence in **Chinese populations** → viral oncogenesis + genetic susceptibility
- EBV: first replicates in nasopharyngeal epithelium → infects tonsillar B lymphocytes → epithelial transformation
- **3 histologic variants:**
  1. Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma
  2. Non-keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma
  3. **Undifferentiated carcinoma** — most common, most closely linked to EBV
- Undifferentiated type: large epithelial cells, indistinct borders ("syncytial" growth), prominent **eosinophilic nucleoli**
- Background of **reactive lymphocytes** → can mimic non-Hodgkin lymphoma → need **immunohistochemical stains** to confirm epithelial origin
- Behavior: locally invasive → cervical lymph nodes → distant metastasis
- **Radiosensitive** — 5-year survival ~50% even in advanced disease

---

### LARYNGEAL TUMORS — MUST KNOWS

**Most common presenting symptom of ALL laryngeal lesions:** HOARSENESS

**Vocal Cord Nodules ("Polyps" / Singer's Nodes):**
- <0.5 cm, smooth, hemispherical, on true vocal cords
- Fibrous tissue + stratified squamous mucosa
- Associated with **heavy smokers** and **singers** (chronic irritation)

**Laryngeal Papilloma:**
- Benign, on true vocal cords, raspberry-like, <1 cm
- Histology: finger-like projections with fibrovascular cores + squamous epithelium
- Caused by **HPV types 6 and 11**
- In **children** → **Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis (RRP)** — multiple, recur after excision
- Transmission in children: **vertical transmission during delivery**
- Do NOT become malignant, often regress at puberty
- **HPV vaccine** (types 6 & 11) can prevent RRP

**Carcinoma of the Larynx:**
- Only **2% of all cancers**
- More common after age 40, **M:F ratio = 7:1**
- Risk factors: **cigarette smoking** (almost all cases), alcohol, asbestos exposure
- HPV sequences in ~15% → **better prognosis**
- **95% are squamous cell carcinomas**
- Location breakdown:
  - **Glottic (vocal cord): 60–75%** — best prognosis (early symptoms + sparse lymphatics)
  - Supraglottic: 25–40% — ~1/3 metastasize to cervical lymph nodes
  - Subglottic: <5% — clinically silent until advanced
- Begins as in situ lesion → pearly gray wrinkled plaques → ulceration → fungation
- Adjacent mucosa may show squamous dysplasia or carcinoma in situ (field effect from carcinogen exposure)
- **Glottic tumors: ~90% confined to larynx at diagnosis** (early hoarseness saves lives)
- Death: infection of distal respiratory passages OR widespread metastases + cachexia

---

## 2. ATELECTASIS (COLLAPSE)

### MUST KNOWS

- Definition: loss of lung volume from inadequate expansion → **ventilation-perfusion imbalance** → **hypoxia**
- Blood shunting: inadequately oxygenated blood from pulmonary arteries → veins

**3 Types:**

| Type | Mechanism | Key Cause |
|------|-----------|-----------|
| **Resorption** | Obstruction → air absorbed distally | Mucous plug, foreign body, tumor, asthma |
| **Compression** | Fluid/blood/air in pleural space compresses lung | Pleural effusion, pneumothorax (CHF common) |
| **Contraction** | Fibrosis prevents expansion + increases elastic recoil | Local or generalized lung/pleural fibrosis |

- Resorption atelectasis — most common cause = **mucous/mucopurulent plug**
- Basal atelectasis: bedridden patients, ascites, post-surgery (elevated diaphragm)
- **Contraction atelectasis is irreversible**; the other two are potentially reversible
- Treat promptly → prevent hypoxemia and superimposed infection

---

## 3. ACUTE LUNG INJURY (ALI) & ARDS

### MUST KNOWS

**ALI Clinical Triad (no primary left-sided heart failure):**
1. Acute onset of dyspnea
2. Decreased arterial oxygen pressure (hypoxemia)
3. Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiograph

- Infiltrates = **noncardiogenic pulmonary edema** (damage to alveolar capillary membrane, NOT cardiac failure)
- ALI can progress → **ARDS**

**ARDS:**
- Diffuse alveolar capillary AND epithelial damage
- Features: rapid onset respiratory insufficiency, **cyanosis**, severe **arterial hypoxemia refractory to oxygen therapy**, can → multisystem organ failure
- Histologic manifestation = **Diffuse Alveolar Damage (DAD)**
- Distinct from neonatal RDS (which is primary surfactant deficiency)

**Pathogenesis — KEY STEPS:**
1. Insult → pulmonary macrophages release **IL-8** (within 30 minutes) → neutrophil chemotaxis
2. Also IL-1, TNF → endothelial activation + neutrophil sequestration
3. Activated neutrophils release oxidants, proteases, PAF, leukotrienes → damage epithelium + endothelium
4. → Increased vascular permeability, alveolar flooding, loss of diffusion capacity, surfactant loss (type II pneumocyte damage)
5. Balance between destructive forces vs. antiproteases, antioxidants, IL-10 determines severity

**Morphology:**
- Acute phase: dark red, firm, airless, heavy lungs
- Microscopy: capillary congestion, alveolar epithelial necrosis, interstitial + intra-alveolar edema/hemorrhage, neutrophils in capillaries (sepsis)
- **HALLMARK:** **Hyaline membranes** lining distended alveolar ducts (fibrin-rich edema + necrotic epithelial cells)
- Organizing stage: type II pneumocyte proliferation + intra-alveolar fibrosis + alveolar septal thickening

**Clinical:**
- 85% develop within **72 hours** of insult
- Mortality: decreased from 60% → **40%** with improved supportive therapy
- Poor prognosis: advanced age, bacteremia (sepsis), multisystem (cardiac, renal, hepatic) failure
- Survivors may develop **diffuse interstitial fibrosis**

---

## 4. OBSTRUCTIVE vs. RESTRICTIVE DISEASE

### MUST KNOWS — HIGH YIELD TABLE

| Feature | Obstructive | Restrictive |
|---------|-------------|-------------|
| Problem | Airflow limitation | Reduced expansion |
| FVC | Normal or slightly ↓ | ↓ |
| FEV1 | Significantly ↓ | Normal or proportionately ↓ |
| FEV1/FVC ratio | **↓ (characteristic)** | Near normal |
| Diseases | Emphysema, chronic bronchitis, asthma, bronchiectasis | ARDS (acute), pneumoconioses, IPF, NSIP, sarcoidosis |

**Restrictive conditions:**
1. Chest wall disorders with normal lungs (severe obesity, pleural disease, Guillain-Barré)
2. Acute or chronic interstitial lung diseases

---

## 5. EMPHYSEMA

### MUST KNOWS

- **Definition:** Abnormal **permanent** enlargement of air spaces **distal to terminal bronchioles** + destruction of walls **without significant fibrosis**

**4 Types:**

| Type | Location | Association |
|------|----------|-------------|
| **Centriacinar (Centrilobular)** | Central/proximal acinus (respiratory bronchioles) — distal alveoli spared | Cigarette smoking; upper lobes |
| **Panacinar (Panlobular)** | Entire acinus uniformly enlarged | **α1-antitrypsin deficiency**; lower lobes |
| **Distal Acinar (Paraseptal)** | Distal acinus; adjacent to pleura/septa | Unknown cause; **spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults**; bullae |
| **Irregular** | Irregular acinar involvement, with scarring | Healed inflammatory disease; most common but **asymptomatic** |

- Clinically significant obstruction: only **centriacinar** and **panacinar**
- Centriacinar is **20x more common** than panacinar

**Pathogenesis — PROTEASE-ANTIPROTEASE IMBALANCE:**
- Tobacco/pollutants → inflammation (neutrophils, macrophages, lymphocytes) → release elastases, IL-8, oxidants
- Elastin degradation → more inflammation (positive feedback)
- Normally checked by **α1-antitrypsin** (antielastase) and antioxidants
- **>80% of α1-antitrypsin deficiency** patients develop symptomatic **panacinar emphysema**
- MMPs (especially **MMP-9 and MMP-12**) have pathogenic roles
- TGFB gene polymorphisms → reduced mesenchymal repair → inadequate elastin repair
- Key concept: emphysema = **insufficient wound repair** (loss of epithelial, endothelial, AND mesenchymal cells → no ECM scaffold)

**Morphology:**
- Panacinar: pale, voluminous lungs; may obscure heart at autopsy
- Centriacinar: deeper pink, less voluminous; upper 2/3 more affected
- Histology: alveolar wall destruction without fibrosis; reduced alveolar capillaries; airway collapse on expiration (loss of elastic tethering)

**Clinical:**
- Dyspnea — first symptom, insidious, progressive
- Reduced FEV1 with normal/near-normal FVC; ↓ FEV1/FVC ratio
- **"Pink Puffer"** — pure emphysema: barrel chest, dyspnea, prolonged expiration, hunched forward, low diffusing capacity; adequate oxygenation until late
- **"Blue Bloater"** — emphysema + chronic bronchitis: diminished respiratory drive, CO2 retention, hypoxia, cyanosis, often obese, cor pulmonale + edema
- Secondary pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale
- Death: pulmonary failure (respiratory acidosis, hypoxia, coma) OR right heart failure (cor pulmonale)

**Related Conditions (NOT true emphysema but called such):**
- **Compensatory emphysema** — alveolar dilation after surgical lung removal (no wall destruction)
- **Obstructive over-inflation** — air trapping by subtotal obstruction (tumor/foreign body) — medical emergency
- **Bullous emphysema** — subpleural blebs/bullae (>1 cm); can rupture → pneumothorax
- **Mediastinal (interstitial) emphysema** — air in connective tissue stroma/mediastinum/subcutaneous tissue; from sudden ↑ intra-alveolar pressure (vomiting, coughing)

---

## 6. CHRONIC BRONCHITIS

### MUST KNOWS

- **Clinical definition:** Persistent productive cough for **≥3 consecutive months in ≥2 consecutive years**
- Prevalence: 20–25% of men aged 40–65 years
- Major cause: **cigarette smoking**; also SO2, NO2 air pollutants

**Pathogenesis:**
- Hallmark: **mucus hypersecretion** beginning in large airways
- Irritants → **hypertrophy of mucous glands** (trachea/main bronchi) + **goblet cell metaplasia** in smaller airways
- Also: CD8+ lymphocytes, macrophages, neutrophils infiltrate (NO eosinophils — unlike asthma)
- **Airflow obstruction** (peripheral/small airways) due to:
  1. Small airway disease (goblet cell metaplasia + mucus plugging + bronchiolar wall fibrosis)
  2. Coexistent emphysema

- **IL-13** mediates many respiratory epithelial effects
- **MUC5AC** mucin gene transcription increased by tobacco smoke
- Neutrophil elastase production increased by tobacco smoke
- Microbial infection = secondary role (maintains inflammation)

**Reid Index:**
- Ratio of submucosal gland thickness to bronchial wall thickness
- Normal: **≤0.4**
- Chronic bronchitis: **>0.4** (gland enlargement)

**Morphology:**
- Large airways: hyperemic, edematous mucosa covered by mucinous/mucopurulent secretions
- Histology: enlarged mucus-secreting glands; inflammatory cells (mononuclear ± neutrophils)
- **Chronic bronchiolitis** = goblet cell metaplasia + mucous plugging + inflammation + fibrosis
- Severe: **bronchiolitis obliterans** (complete fibrotic obliteration of lumen)

**Clinical:**
- "Blue Bloater" — hypercapnia, hypoxemia, cyanosis
- Progression → pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure
- Recurrent infections + respiratory failure are constant threats

---

## 7. ASTHMA

### MUST KNOWS

- **Definition:** Chronic inflammatory disorder → **reversible** episodic airway obstruction + wheezing + breathlessness + chest tightness + cough (especially nocturnal/early morning)
- **Hallmarks:** Reversible airway obstruction + chronic eosinophilic bronchial inflammation + bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy + hyperreactivity + increased mucus secretion

**Pathogenesis (Atopic Asthma):**
- **TH2 cells** are central
- IL-4 → **IgE production**
- IL-5 → **eosinophil activation**
- IL-13 → **mucus production** + IgE production by B cells
- IgE coats mast cells → allergen exposure → **two-wave reaction:**

**Phase 1 (Early/Immediate):**
- Bronchoconstriction (vagal receptor stimulation) + increased mucus + vasodilation

**Phase 2 (Late):**
- Inflammation: eosinophils, neutrophils, T cells activated
- Epithelial cells release chemokines (including **eotaxin** — potent eosinophil chemoattractant)
- Amplifies TH2 cell and eosinophil recruitment

**Airway Remodeling (repeated bouts):**
- Smooth muscle hypertrophy + mucus gland enlargement
- ↑ vascularity + subepithelial collagen deposition

**Genetics:** Multiple susceptibility genes
- Chromosome **5q**: IL13, CD14, HLA class II, β2-adrenergic receptor gene, IL-4 receptor gene
- Chromosome **20q**: **ADAM-33** (regulates bronchial smooth muscle/fibroblast proliferation → airway remodeling)
- **YKL-40** (chitinase family) serum levels correlate with severity

**"Hygiene Hypothesis":** Eradication of infections → altered immune homeostasis → ↑ allergic responses (explains ↑ asthma incidence in Western world)

**4 Types of Asthma:**

| Type | Key Feature |
|------|-------------|
| **Atopic** | Most common; IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity; positive family history + skin test; triggered by environmental antigens |
| **Non-Atopic** | No allergen sensitization; skin test negative; triggered by viral infections + air pollutants |
| **Drug-Induced** | Aspirin most common — blocks COX → shifts to lipoxygenase → leukotrienes → bronchospasm; also nasal polyps + urticaria |
| **Occupational** | Fumes, organic/chemical dusts, gases; repeated exposure required |

**Morphology (Status Asthmaticus/Fatal Cases):**
- Overdistended lungs; small areas of atelectasis
- **Bronchi/bronchioles occluded by thick mucous plugs**
- Histology: **Curschmann spirals** (whorls of shed epithelium in mucus)
- **Charcot-Leyden crystals** (eosinophil protein crystalloids)
- **Airway remodeling:** thickened airway wall, sub-basement membrane fibrosis, ↑ vascularity, enlarged submucosal glands, goblet cell metaplasia, smooth muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia
- **Bronchial thermoplasty:** controlled thermal energy via bronchoscopy → reduces smooth muscle mass → reduces airway hyperresponsiveness

**Clinical:**
- Chief difficulty in **expiration** (bronchi constricted + filled with mucus)
- Progressive hyperinflation with trapped air
- **Status asthmaticus:** prolonged attack unresponsive to therapy (days/weeks) → hypercapnia + acidosis + severe hypoxia → can be fatal

## 8. BRONCHIECTASIS

### MUST KNOWS

- **Definition:** Permanent dilation of bronchi/bronchioles from destruction of muscle and elastic tissue due to chronic necrotizing infections
- NOT a primary disease — always secondary

**Predisposing Conditions:**
1. Bronchial obstruction (tumor, foreign body, mucus impaction, atopic asthma, chronic bronchitis)
2. Congenital/hereditary:
   - **Cystic fibrosis** — most important (viscid mucus → obstruction → infection)
   - Immunodeficiency states (especially **immunoglobulin deficiency**)
   - **Kartagener syndrome** — rare autosomal recessive; structural ciliary abnormalities → impaired mucociliary clearance + infections + male sterility (immotile spermatozoa)
3. Necrotizing pneumonia (S. aureus, Klebsiella) — post-TB bronchiectasis significant in endemic areas

**Pathogenesis — Two Intertwined Processes:**
- **Obstruction** + **chronic persistent infection** (either can come first)
- Obstruction → impaired clearance → secondary infection → inflammatory damage → airway dilation (irreversible)
- Chronic necrotizing inflammation → obstructive secretions → peribronchial fibrosis + traction → dilation

**Morphology:**
- Usually **lower lobes bilaterally** (most vertical airways)
- Localized = tumor/foreign body
- Airways dilated up to **4x normal diameter** — can be traced almost to pleural surface (normal bronchioles not visible within 2–3 cm of pleura)
- Histology (active): intense acute + chronic inflammatory exudate in bronchial/bronchiolar walls + epithelial desquamation/ulceration
- Mixed flora: staphylococci, streptococci, pneumococci, enteric organisms, anaerobes, H. influenzae, **Pseudomonas aeruginosa** (especially in children)
- Chronic: fibrosis of bronchial/bronchiolar walls; peribronchiolar fibrosis; abscess cavities

**Clinical:**
- Severe persistent cough + copious mucopurulent (sometimes fetid) sputum
- Hemoptysis (flecks or frank)
- Episodic, precipitated by URTI or new pathogens
- **Digital clubbing**
- Severe/widespread: obstructive ventilatory defects + hypoxemia + hypercapnia + pulmonary hypertension + cor pulmonale
- Complications: **metastatic brain abscesses** + **reactive amyloidosis**

## 9. CHRONIC INTERSTITIAL (RESTRICTIVE) LUNG DISEASES

### OVERVIEW MUST KNOWS

- Heterogeneous group; bilateral, often patchy, chronic involvement of pulmonary connective tissue (alveolar walls)
- Hallmark: **reduced compliance** (stiff lungs → more pressure needed to expand → dyspnea)
- Alveolar epithelial + interstitial vascular damage → V/Q mismatch → hypoxia
- CXR: diffuse infiltration — small nodules, irregular lines, "ground-glass shadows"
- End-stage: **"honeycomb lung"** (fibrosis + gross destruction)

---

### IDIOPATHIC PULMONARY FIBROSIS (IPF) — MUST KNOWS

- Also called: **Cryptogenic Fibrosing Alveolitis**
- Males > females; **~2/3 patients >60 years** at presentation
- Patchy progressive bilateral interstitial fibrosis → severe hypoxemia + cyanosis
- Histologic/radiologic pattern = **Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP)** — required for IPF diagnosis
- Must exclude known causes (asbestosis, collagen vascular diseases) before calling it "idiopathic"

**Pathogenesis:**
- Repeated cycles of epithelial injury (unknown agent)
- TH2 response with eosinophils, mast cells, IL-4, IL-13
- "Alternatively activated macrophages" important
- Abnormal repair → exuberant fibroblastic/myofibroblastic proliferation → **fibroblastic foci** (hallmark early lesion)
- **TGF-β1** (from injured type I pneumocytes) → fibroblast → myofibroblast transformation → excess collagen + ECM
- TGF-β1 also downregulates **caveolin-1** (endogenous inhibitor of fibrosis)
- Familial IPF: mutations shortening **telomeres** → rapid pneumocyte senescence/apoptosis

**Morphology:**
- Gross: cobblestone pleural surface (retraction along interlobular septa)
- Lower lobe predominance + subpleural/interlobular septal distribution
- Histologic hallmark: **patchy interstitial fibrosis with temporal heterogeneity** (early fibroblastic foci + late collagenous scars in same biopsy)
- **Honeycomb fibrosis:** cystic spaces lined by hyperplastic type II pneumocytes or bronchiolar epithelium
- Secondary pulmonary hypertensive changes

**Clinical:**
- Insidious onset: nonproductive cough + progressive dyspnea
- Characteristic: **"Velcro" crackles** on inspiration
- Late: cyanosis, cor pulmonale, peripheral edema
- Prognosis: **mean survival 3 years or less** — relentless progression despite therapy
- Only definitive therapy: **lung transplantation**

---

### NONSPECIFIC INTERSTITIAL PNEUMONIA (NSIP) — MUST KNOWS

- Chronic bilateral ILD; unknown etiology
- Important: **much better prognosis than IPF**
- Two patterns:
  - **Cellular pattern:** mild-moderate chronic interstitial inflammation (lymphocytes + few plasma cells); uniform/patchy; better outcome
  - **Fibrosing pattern:** diffuse/patchy interstitial fibrosis; NO temporal heterogeneity (unlike UIP); fibroblastic foci and honeycombing absent
- Presentation: dyspnea + cough over months

---

### CRYPTOGENIC ORGANIZING PNEUMONIA (COP) — MUST KNOWS

- Previously called: **BOOP** (Bronchiolitis Obliterans Organizing Pneumonia) — now COP preferred
- CXR: subpleural or peribronchial patchy areas of air-space consolidation
- Histology: **polypoid plugs of loose organizing connective tissue** within alveolar ducts, alveoli, and bronchioles; same age (no temporal heterogeneity); normal underlying lung architecture
- Treatment: oral steroids for 6+ months; some resolve spontaneously
- Note: organizing pneumonia can also occur secondary to infection, collagen vascular disease, transplant injury (then NOT cryptogenic)

---

### PNEUMOCONIOSES — MUST KNOWS

**Pathogenesis principles:**
- Particles 1–5 µm diameter = most dangerous (lodge at distal airway bifurcations)
- >5–10 µm = don't reach distal airways; <0.5 µm = move in/out without deposition
- Alveolar macrophage = key cell (inflammasome activation → IL-1 production → inflammation → fibrosis)
- Tobacco smoking worsens ALL inhaled mineral dusts (most so with **asbestos**)

**Coal Worker's Pneumoconiosis (CWP):**
- Spectrum: asymptomatic anthracosis → simple CWP → complicated CWP (**Progressive Massive Fibrosis/PMF**)
- <10% of simple CWP progresses to PMF
- Simple CWP: coal macules (dust-laden macrophages + delicate collagen) + coal nodules; upper lobes
- PMF: multiple intensely black scars **>2 cm** (up to 10 cm); dense collagen + pigment
- CWP: benign disease; PMF → pulmonary dysfunction + pulmonary hypertension + cor pulmonale
- **No increased lung carcinoma risk** in coal miners (unlike silica + asbestos)

**Silicosis:**
- Most prevalent **chronic occupational disease in the world**
- Crystalline silica (quartz most common); sandblasting + hard-rock mining highest risk
- Crystalline forms (quartz, cristobalite, tridymite) most toxic; amorphous forms less so
- Mechanism: macrophage activation → IL-1, TNF, fibronectin, oxygen free radicals, fibrogenic cytokines
- TNF key: anti-TNF antibodies block silica-induced fibrosis in mice
- Morphology: silicotic nodules — **concentrically arranged hyalinized collagen** with amorphous center; **"whorled" collagen** (distinctive); weakly birefringent silica particles by polarized microscopy
- Advanced: nodule coalescence → PMF; hilar lymph node "**eggshell calcification**"
- Clinical: detected on CXR (upper zone fine nodularity) before symptoms; PMF → pulmonary hypertension + cor pulmonale
- Key associations: **↑ susceptibility to tuberculosis** (silicosis depresses cell-mediated immunity + macrophages can't kill mycobacteria); **silicotuberculosis** nodules have central caseation
- Relationship with lung cancer: contentious/unresolved

**Asbestosis & Asbestos-Related Diseases:**

Asbestos exposure linked to:
1. **Asbestosis** (parenchymal interstitial fibrosis)
2. Pleural plaques / diffuse pleural fibrosis
3. Pleural effusions
4. **Lung carcinoma** (5x increased risk)
5. **Malignant mesothelioma** (>1000x increased risk — normally 2–17/million)
6. Laryngeal carcinoma

**2 forms of asbestos:**
- **Serpentine (chrysotile):** curly, flexible; most used in industry; impacted in upper respiratory tract; gradually leached from tissues; less pathogenic
- **Amphibole:** straight, stiff, brittle; less prevalent but **more pathogenic**; align in airstream → deeper lung penetration → stay longer (less soluble)
- Both forms cause asbestosis + lung cancer + mesothelioma

**Asbestos bodies:** golden-brown, fusiform/beaded rods with translucent center; asbestos fibers coated with iron-containing proteinaceous material (from phagocyte **ferritin**)

**Morphology of asbestosis:**
- Diffuse pulmonary interstitial fibrosis indistinguishable from UIP — except for **asbestos bodies**
- Starts **lower lobes + subpleural** (opposite of CWP/silicosis which are upper lobe)
- Progresses → honeycombing + pulmonary hypertension + cor pulmonale
- **Pleural plaques:** most common manifestation of asbestos exposure; well-circumscribed dense collagen, often calcified; anterior/posterolateral parietal pleura + diaphragm; NO asbestos bodies in plaques; usually asymptomatic

**Smoking + asbestos = remarkable synergy for lung carcinoma** (smoking does NOT increase mesothelioma risk)

---

### SARCOIDOSIS — MUST KNOWS

- Multisystem disease of **unknown etiology**; noncaseating granulomas in many tissues
- Diagnosis of **exclusion** (must rule out mycobacterial/fungal infections, berylliosis)
- Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy = major presenting manifestation
- Eye and skin involvement: ~25% each

**Epidemiology:**
- All races, ages, both genders; adults <40 years predominate
- High incidence: Danish/Swedish populations + **African-Americans** (10x higher than whites)
- Higher prevalence in **non-smokers** (rare among lung diseases)

**Pathogenesis:**
- Disordered immune regulation; genetically predisposed + environmental agents
- **CD4+ TH1 cell-driven** response
- Key abnormalities:
  - ↑ CD4+ TH1 cells in alveoli and interstitium
  - ↑ IL-2 and IFN-γ (T cell expansion + macrophage activation)
  - ↑ IL-8, TNF, MIP-1α (granuloma formation)
  - **Anergy** to skin test antigens (PPD, Candida) — CD4+ T cells recruited to lung
  - Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia
- Genetic: HLA class I (HLA-A1, HLA-B8) association
- Sarcoidosis **recurs in transplanted lungs in 75% of patients**

**Morphology:**
- **Noncaseating epithelioid granuloma** = diagnostic hallmark (any organ)
- Compact collection of epithelioid cells (abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei) rimmed by CD4+ T cells
- Multinucleate giant cells common (macrophage fusion)
- Peripheral fibroblastic layer → eventual hyalinized scar
- Special inclusions (NOT required for diagnosis):
  - **Schaumann bodies:** laminated calcium + protein concretions
  - **Asteroid bodies:** stellate inclusions in giant cells
- **Rarely:** central foci of necrosis (NOT caseation — no caseating necrosis)
- Lungs: 90% involved; granulomas in interstitium with "lymphangitic" distribution (around bronchioles, pulmonary venules, pleura)
- 5–15% → **diffuse interstitial fibrosis** ("honeycomb lung")
- Hilar + paratracheal lymph nodes enlarged in **75–90%** of patients; lymph nodes are "**nonmatted**" (nonadherent, don't ulcerate) — unlike TB
- Skin: **Erythema nodosum** = hallmark of acute sarcoidosis (raised, red, tender nodules on anterior legs); sarcoidal granulomas uncommon in these
- Eye: iritis/iridocyclitis → corneal opacities, glaucoma, vision loss; lacrimal gland involvement → **sicca syndrome**
- **Mikulicz syndrome:** combined uveoparotid involvement
- **Hypercalcemia + hypercalciuria:** not from bone destruction — from **active vitamin D production by mononuclear phagocytes** in granulomas (increased calcium absorption)

**Clinical:**
- Many asymptomatic (found on CXR or autopsy)
- Symptomatic: respiratory symptoms (dyspnea, dry cough, substernal discomfort) OR constitutional (fever, fatigue, weight loss, night sweats)
- Diagnosis: noncaseating granuloma on biopsy (after exclusion of other causes)
- Course: unpredictable; spontaneous remissions common; steroid therapy
- **65–70% recover** with minimal/no residual disease
- 20% → permanent lung dysfunction/visual impairment
- 10–15% → progressive pulmonary fibrosis + cor pulmonale (die)

## 10. PULMONARY VASCULAR DISEASES

### PULMONARY EMBOLISM — MUST KNOWS

- **>95% of pulmonary emboli** arise from thrombi in **deep veins of lower legs** (popliteal + larger veins above)
- Among hospitalized patients: <1/3 diagnosed before death

**Risk factors:**
1. Prolonged bed rest (immobilized legs)
2. Orthopedic surgery (knee/hip)
3. Severe trauma (burns, multiple fractures)
4. Congestive heart failure
5. Peri-parturition / oral contraceptives (high-estrogen)
6. Disseminated cancer (Virchow's triad)

**Consequences depend on:** size of embolus + cardiopulmonary status

**Two key consequences of pulmonary arterial occlusion:**
1. ↑ pulmonary artery pressure (blockage + vasospasm from thromboxane A2, serotonin)
2. Ischemia of downstream parenchyma

**Pulmonary infarction:** only in **10% of patients** (because of dual blood supply: pulmonary arteries + bronchial arteries + direct from alveolar air)
- Occurs when: compromised cardiac function OR compromised bronchial circulation OR underlying pulmonary disease

**Morphology:**
- Large embolus → saddle embolus at bifurcation → instant death (acute cor pulmonale/hypoxia)
- Smaller emboli → medium/small pulmonary arteries
- Infarcts: **wedge-shaped** (base at pleura, apex toward hilum); **hemorrhagic**; raised, red-blue early → pales → red-brown (hemosiderin) → fibrotic scar
- **~3/4 infarcts affect lower lobes**; >half are **multiple**
- Fibrinous exudate on adjacent pleura

**Clinical outcomes (4 patterns):**
1. **60–80%** clinically silent (small, removed by fibrinolysis)
2. **5%** sudden death/acute cor pulmonale/shock (>60% vasculature obstructed)
3. **10–15%** pulmonary infarction (medium vessel + cardiac insufficiency present) → dyspnea
4. **<3%** recurrent multiple emboli → pulmonary hypertension + chronic cor pulmonale + pulmonary vascular sclerosis

- Patients with one PE have **30% chance of developing a second**
- Treatment: anticoagulation; massive PE → **thrombolytic therapy**

**Nonthrombotic emboli:** air, fat, amniotic fluid; IV drug abuse → **talc granulomatosis** → interstitial fibrosis + pulmonary hypertension

---

### PULMONARY HYPERTENSION — MUST KNOWS

- Normal pulmonary pressure = ~1/8 of systemic
- Pulmonary hypertension: mean pulmonary pressure ≥1/4 of systemic

**Secondary PH causes:**
1. COPD/interstitial lung disease → loss of alveolar capillaries → ↑ vascular resistance
2. Recurrent pulmonary emboli → reduced functional cross-sectional area
3. Antecedent heart disease (mitral stenosis → ↑ left atrial pressure → PH); left-to-right shunts

**Primary (Idiopathic) Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension:**
- All known causes excluded
- **Majority sporadic; 6% familial** (autosomal dominant)

**Pathogenesis:**
- Endothelial/smooth muscle dysfunction → ↓ vasodilators (NO, prostacyclin) + ↑ vasoconstrictors (endothelin) + growth factors → smooth muscle proliferation
- Familial: **BMPR-2** (bone morphogenetic protein receptor type 2) germline mutations in **50% of familial cases**; BMPR-2 normally inhibits proliferation; loss-of-function → abnormal endothelial + smooth muscle proliferation
- Sporadic: **serotonin transporter gene (5HTT)** polymorphisms → enhanced vascular smooth muscle proliferation

**Morphology — affects entire arterial tree:**
1. Atheromas in main elastic arteries
2. Intimal + medial thickening → narrowed lumina (medium arteries)
3. Medial hypertrophy + elastic membrane reduplication in small arteries/arterioles
4. **Plexiform lesions** (idiopathic PAH): endothelial proliferation forming multiple lumina in small arteries

**Clinical:**
- Primary PAH: young adults, **women > men**; fatigue, syncope on exercise, dyspnea on exertion, chest pain
- Death from **right heart failure (decompensated cor pulmonale)** within **2–5 years**
- Treatment: vasodilators, antithrombotics, prostacyclin infusions; definitive = lung transplant

---

### GOODPASTURE SYNDROME — MUST KNOWS

- Prototype diffuse alveolar hemorrhage syndrome
- Triad: **hemoptysis + anemia + diffuse pulmonary infiltrates**
- Also: rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
- Pathogenesis: antibodies against **noncollagenous domain of α3 chain of collagen IV** (affects lung + kidney basement membranes)
- Anti-GBM antibodies detectable in serum of **>90% of cases**
- Morphology: diffuse alveolar hemorrhage; hemosiderin (intra- and extracellular); **linear IgG deposition along alveolar septa** (also along glomerular BM — hallmark on renal biopsy)
- Treatment: **plasmapheresis** (removes antibodies) + **immunosuppressive drugs** (inhibit antibody production)
- Severe renal disease → renal transplantation

## 11. PNEUMONIA

### CLASSIFICATION MUST KNOWS

| Setting | Key Pathogens |
|---------|--------------|
| Community-acquired acute | S. pneumoniae (most common, >90% of lobar), H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, S. aureus, L. pneumophila, Klebsiella |
| Community-acquired atypical | M. pneumoniae, Chlamydia spp., Coxiella burnetii (Q fever), RSV, metapneumovirus, parainfluenza (children), influenza A/B (adults), adenovirus |
| Nosocomial (hospital-acquired) | Gram-negative rods (Klebsiella, Serratia, E. coli), Pseudomonas, **MRSA** |
| Aspiration | Anaerobic oral flora (Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus) ± aerobes |
| Immunocompromised | CMV, Pneumocystis jiroveci, MAC, Aspergillus, Candida, plus usual organisms |
| Chronic | Nocardia, Actinomyces, Mycobacteria, Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Blastomyces |

**Special associations:**
- **K. pneumoniae** → chronic alcoholics
- **P. aeruginosa** → cystic fibrosis, burn victims, neutropenia
- **L. pneumophila** → organ transplant recipients
- **S. aureus pneumonia** → usually secondary to viral respiratory infections

### LOBAR vs. BRONCHOPNEUMONIA

| Feature | Lobar | Bronchopneumonia |
|---------|-------|-----------------|
| Distribution | Contiguous air spaces of part/all of a lobe | Patchy, multiple lobes |
| Organism | S. pneumoniae >90% | Various organisms |
| Age | Any | More common at extremes of age |

**4 Stages of Lobar Pneumonia (pre-antibiotic era):**
1. **Congestion:** heavy, red, boggy lung; vascular congestion + protein-rich fluid + neutrophils + many bacteria in alveoli
2. **Red hepatization:** liver-like consistency; alveoli packed with neutrophils + RBCs + fibrin
3. **Gray hepatization:** dry, gray, firm; RBCs lysed; fibrinosuppurative exudate persists
4. **Resolution:** enzymatic digestion of exudate → granular semifluid debris → resorption/macrophage ingestion/coughed up/organized by fibroblasts; pleural reaction may → fibrous thickening/adhesions

**Complications of pneumococcal pneumonia** (especially serotype 3):
1. Abscess formation (tissue necrosis)
2. **Empyema** (suppurative pleural accumulation)
3. Organization → solid fibrous tissue
4. Bacteremic dissemination → meningitis, arthritis, infective endocarditis

**Atypical Pneumonia:**
- Respiratory distress **out of proportion** to clinical/radiologic signs
- Inflammation predominantly confined to **alveolar septa** (interstitial); alveolar spaces generally clear
- Septa widened + edematous; mononuclear infiltrate (lymphocytes, histiocytes, plasma cells)
- Severe cases → diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes
- Macroscopically: red-blue, congested, subcrepitant areas

## 12. TUBERCULOSIS

### MUST KNOWS

- Caused by **Mycobacterium tuberculosis**; M. tuberculosis complex includes M. africanum, M. canettii, M. bovis, others
- MDR strains exist
- Globally: ~10 million new TB cases/year; 1.4 million deaths; **India accounts for 26%** of global cases

**Pathogenesis:**
1. Inhalation → alveolar macrophages encounter bacteria
2. If not eliminated → invasion of lung interstitium (direct or via infected macrophages)
3. Dendritic cells transport MTB to lymph nodes → T cell priming → granuloma formation
4. Granuloma may contain infection (**latent TB**)
5. If granuloma fails → dissemination → bloodstream → other organs → re-entry into respiratory tract → **active TB**

**Primary TB:** first infection in uninfected host
**Secondary (reactivation) TB:** reactivation of latent TB
**Miliary TB:** hematogenous dissemination to lungs + other organs

**Morphology:**
- **Ghon focus:** subpleural nodule, often upper lobe
- **Ghon complex:** Ghon focus + lymphatic/hilar lymph node involvement
- **Ranke complex:** calcified Ghon complex (calcified Ghon lesion + calcified mediastinal lymph nodes) — represents old/healed primary TB
- **Caseous necrosis:** cheese-like, tan-to-white grumous material — pathognomonic
- Histologic hallmark: **necrotizing granulomatous inflammation** — central necrotic zone surrounded by epithelioid histiocytes + **Langhans giant cells** (nuclei in horseshoe pattern at cell periphery) + lymphocytes
- Langhans giant cells are NOT specific for TB (also seen in other granulomas)
- Organisms in central necrosis zone — seen on **special stains** (Ziehl-Neelsen/acid-fast)
- Complications: empyema, bronchiectasis, cavitary disease, tuberculomas

**Clinical features:**
- Chronic productive cough, weight loss, fever, **night sweats**, hemoptysis
- History of latent TB or exposure

## 13. LUNG CANCER

### MUST KNOWS — VERY HIGH YIELD

**4 Major Histologic Subtypes:**

| Type | Key Features |
|------|-------------|
| **Adenocarcinoma** | Most common overall; most common in **women + nonsmokers**; EGFR mutations + ALK mutations targetable |
| **Squamous Cell Carcinoma** | Strongly linked to smoking; central location; precursor = squamous dysplasia |
| **Large Cell Carcinoma** | Diagnosis of exclusion; aggressive |
| **Small Cell Carcinoma (SCLC)** | Neuroendocrine; almost always metastatic at presentation; **treat with chemotherapy**; NOT surgically resectable; very sensitive to chemo but invariably recurs; median survival **1 year** even with treatment |

- **Smoking = most important risk factor**
- NSCLCs (non-small cell) — may be curable by surgery if localized; combination chemo + targeted therapy (anti-EGFR for EGFR-mutant adenocarcinoma; ALK inhibitors for ALK-mutant)

**Precursor lesions:**
- **Squamous dysplasia** → squamous cell carcinoma
- **Atypical adenomatous hyperplasia** → some adenocarcinomas
- **Adenocarcinoma in situ** (formerly bronchioloalveolar carcinoma) → some adenocarcinomas; pure lepidic growth ≤3 cm without stromal invasion

**Symptoms:**
- Chronic cough, expectoration, hoarseness, chest pain
- Superior vena cava syndrome
- Pericardial/pleural effusion
- Persistent segmental atelectasis, pneumonitis
- Metastatic: brain (mental/neurologic changes), liver (hepatomegaly), bones (pain)
- SCLCs especially cause **paraneoplastic syndromes**

**Paraneoplastic Syndromes (3–10% of lung cancer patients):**

| Syndrome | Association |
|---------|-------------|
| Hypercalcemia (PTHrP secretion) | **Squamous cell carcinoma** most common |
| Cushing syndrome (ACTH) | SCLC most common |
| SIADH | SCLC most common |
| Neuromuscular (myasthenic syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, polymyositis) | SCLC |
| Clubbing + hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy | SCLC |
| Coagulation abnormalities (migratory thrombophlebitis, nonbacterial endocarditis, DIC) | Adenocarcinoma (hematologic syndromes) |

- Hypercalcemia from PTHrP = paraneoplastic (osteolytic metastases causing hypercalcemia = NOT paraneoplastic)
- Overall: **NSCLCs better prognosis than SCLCs**

## 14. PLEURAL LESIONS

### MUST KNOWS

**Pleural Effusion (≥15 cc fluid):**
- Causes: ↑ hydrostatic pressure (CHF), ↑ vascular permeability (pneumonia), ↓ oncotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome), ↑ intrapleural negative pressure (atelectasis), ↓ lymphatic drainage (carcinomatosis)
- Malignant effusions: usually **>500 mL**; often first evidence of malignancy
- For lung, breast, ovarian metastases: **92% ipsilateral** to primary lesion

**Types:**
- **Inflammatory:** serous/serofibrinous/fibrinous — from TB, pneumonia, infarct, abscess, bronchiectasis, collagen vascular disease, radiation
- **Empyema:** pus in pleural cavity; bacterial/fungal; usually from lung infection; organizes into dense adhesions (doesn't disappear)
- **Hydrothorax:** clear/straw-colored; CHF; not loculated, collects basally
- **Hemothorax:** aneurysm rupture/vascular trauma; large clots
- **Chylothorax:** milky white fluid (lymph + fat); usually **left-sided**; thoracic duct trauma/obstruction by malignancy

**Pneumothorax:**
- All types → compression atelectasis + respiratory distress
- **Spontaneous idiopathic** (young people): rupture of small peripheral apical subpleural blebs; usually resolves but may recur
- **Tension pneumothorax:** one-way valve → traps air during inhalation → compresses contralateral lung + mediastinal structures → emergency

**Malignant Mesothelioma:**
- Primary pleural malignancy
- Linked to **asbestos exposure** (>1000x increased risk vs. general population)
- Grim prognosis

articles.title: Heart Disease: Must Knows — Notes
articles.content:
## Summary
Heart disease encompasses various conditions that impair the heart's ability to effectively pump blood. Heart failure can arise from six primary mechanisms, including pump failure (systolic or diastolic), obstruction to flow, regurgitant flow, shunted flow, conduction disorders, or rupture. Congestive Heart Failure (CHF) is defined by the heart's inability to meet metabolic demands, often due to systolic or diastolic dysfunction, and triggers compensatory mechanisms like the Frank-Starling law, neurohumoral activation, and hypertrophy. While these initially maintain output, chronic hypertrophy can be pathological and lead to increased oxygen demand and sudden cardiac death. Left-sided heart failure typically presents with pulmonary congestion (dyspnea, orthopnea) and is often caused by ischemic heart disease (IHD) or hypertension, leading to "heart failure cells" in the lungs. Right-sided heart failure, frequently secondary to left-sided failure or pulmonary hypertension (cor pulmonale), manifests as systemic venous congestion, including peripheral edema and "nutmeg liver."

Ischemic Heart Disease (IHD), primarily caused by coronary atherosclerosis, represents an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand and is a leading cause of death worldwide. Its pathogenesis involves plaque formation, thrombosis following plaque disruption (often in plaques previously deemed non-critical), and vasospasm. "Vulnerable plaques" with large lipid cores and thin fibrous caps are prone to rupture, leading to acute coronary syndromes like unstable angina, acute myocardial infarction (MI), and sudden cardiac death. Stable angina, Prinzmetal angina, and chronic IHD are other clinical manifestations. Understanding these mechanisms, clinical presentations, and morphological changes is crucial for managing heart disease, which often progresses to biventricular CHF in its advanced stages.

## Key Points
-   **Pump failure**: Impaired cardiac output due to weak contraction (systolic) or impaired relaxation (diastolic).
-   **Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)**: Heart cannot generate sufficient output for metabolic needs, or only at elevated filling pressures.
-   **Forward failure**: Decreased cardiac output, almost always accompanied by backward failure (venous congestion).
-   **Concentric hypertrophy**: Sarcomeres added in parallel, caused by pressure overload (e.g., hypertension, valve stenosis).
-   **Eccentric/dilated hypertrophy**: Sarcomeres added in series, caused by volume overload (e.g., regurgitation, shunts).
-   **Heart failure cells**: Hemosiderin-laden macrophages found in the lungs, indicative of chronic left-sided CHF and pulmonary edema.
-   **Nutmeg liver**: Gross appearance of the liver in right-sided CHF, characterized by centrilobular congestion.
-   **Cor pulmonale**: Right ventricular hypertrophy and dilation due to pulmonary hypertension, an isolated right-sided pathology.
-   **Ischemic Heart Disease (IHD)**: Imbalance between coronary blood supply and myocardial oxygen demand, primarily due to coronary atherosclerosis.
-   **Critical stenosis**: >70% occlusion of a coronary artery, typically causing symptoms with exertion (stable angina).
-   **Vulnerable plaque**: Atherosclerotic plaque with a large lipid core, thin fibrous cap, and high macrophage load, prone to rupture.
-   **Acute coronary syndrome**: A spectrum of conditions including unstable angina, acute myocardial infarction, and sudden cardiac death, often initiated by plaque disruption and thrombosis.

## Detailed Notes

### OVERVIEW: 6 MECHANISMS OF HEART FAILURE
1.  **Pump failure** — systolic (weak contraction) or diastolic (impaired relaxation)
2.  **Obstruction to flow** — valve stenosis, hypertension, coarctation
3.  **Regurgitant flow** — backward flow → volume overload
4.  **Shunted flow** — abnormal chamber-to-chamber communication
5.  **Conduction disorders** — arrhythmias → reduced output
6.  **Rupture** — loss of circulatory continuity → exsanguination

### CONGESTIVE HEART FAILURE (CHF)
**Definition:** Heart cannot generate sufficient output to meet metabolic demands — OR can only do so at elevated filling pressures

**Epidemiology:** ~5 million affected in USA; >1 million hospitalizations/year; 300,000 deaths/year

**Causes:**
-   Systolic dysfunction (most common) — ischemic heart disease, hypertension
-   Diastolic dysfunction — LV hypertrophy, fibrosis, amyloid, constrictive pericarditis; more common in elderly, diabetics, women; accounts for **40–60% of CHF**
-   High-output failure — hyperthyroidism, anemia

**Key concept:** Forward failure (↓ output) is almost always accompanied by backward failure (venous congestion)

#### Compensatory Mechanisms

| Mechanism | Details |
| :---------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Frank-Starling | ↑ end-diastolic volume → ↑ stretch → ↑ contraction force |
| Neurohumoral | Norepinephrine (↑ HR, contractility); RAAS (salt/water retention); ANP (counters RAAS) |
| Hypertrophy | Pressure overload → concentric hypertrophy (sarcomeres added in parallel); Volume overload → eccentric/dilated (sarcomeres in series) |

**Compensated vs Decompensated:** When the dilated ventricle maintains output = compensated; when it can no longer meet body needs = decompensated

**Cost of hypertrophy:**
-   ↑ O₂ demand without proportional capillary expansion → ischemia risk
-   Fetal gene re-expression (myosin heavy chain changes)
-   Myocyte apoptosis, cytoskeletal changes, ↑ ECM deposition
-   Pathologic hypertrophy = independent risk factor for sudden cardiac death
-   Physiologic hypertrophy (aerobic exercise) = ↑ capillary density, ↓ resting HR/BP → protective

#### Left-Sided Heart Failure
**Causes:** IHD, hypertension, mitral/aortic valve disease, cardiomyopathy

**Clinical features:**
-   Dyspnea on exertion (earliest symptom)
-   Orthopnea → paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
-   Cardiomegaly, tachycardia, S3 heart sound
-   Fine basal rales
-   Mitral regurgitation (papillary muscle displacement) → systolic murmur
-   Atrial fibrillation → "irregularly irregular" pulse + thrombus risk → stroke
-   Prerenal azotemia, hypoxic encephalopathy in severe cases

**Morphology:**
-   Heart: LV hypertrophy ± dilation; interstitial fibrosis
-   Lungs: Heavy, boggy; alveolar edema; **heart failure cells** (hemosiderin-laden macrophages from extravasated RBCs)
-   Pleural effusion from ↑ hydrostatic pressure

#### Right-Sided Heart Failure
**Causes:** Most commonly secondary to left heart failure; also cor pulmonale (severe pulmonary hypertension), primary pulmonic/tricuspid disease

**Cor pulmonale:** RV hypertrophy + dilation due to pulmonary hypertension; isolated right-sided pathology

**Clinical features:** Peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites, pleural effusion — minimal respiratory symptoms in pure right-sided failure

**Morphology:**
-   Liver: Congestive hepatomegaly; **nutmeg liver** (centrilobular congestion); cardiac cirrhosis in chronic severe cases
-   Portal hypertension → congestive splenomegaly; bowel wall edema (impairs drug/nutrient absorption)
-   Peripheral edema (pedal/pretibial); anasarca in severe cases
-   Pleural/pericardial/peritoneal transudates — low protein, no inflammatory cells

Most patients present with **biventricular CHF** in chronic disease

### ISCHEMIC HEART DISEASE (IHD)
**Definition:** Imbalance between coronary blood supply and myocardial O₂/nutritional demand

**Cause:** >90% due to coronary atherosclerosis (CAD)

**Epidemiology:** Leading cause of death in USA + developed nations; 7 million deaths/year worldwide; mortality has declined ~50% since 1963 peak

#### Pathogenesis
**Critical stenosis:** >70% occlusion → symptoms with exertion (stable angina); ≥90% → symptoms at rest

**Key point:** Two-thirds of ruptured plaques had <50% stenosis pre-rupture; 85% had <70% stenosis → most MI-causing plaques were not previously symptomatic

**Three contributing mechanisms:**
1.  **Atherosclerosis** — inflammation-driven; macrophage metalloproteinases destabilize plaque
2.  **Thrombosis** — plaque disruption exposes thrombogenic core → acute occlusion
3.  **Vasospasm** — adrenergic stimulation, platelet products, endothelial dysfunction (↓ NO, ↑ endothelin)

**Vulnerable plaque features:**
-   Large atheromatous core
-   Thin fibrous cap
-   Fissures at cap-normal vessel junction (highest mechanical stress)
-   High macrophage load, few smooth muscle cells

**Statins:** Benefit beyond cholesterol lowering — reduce plaque inflammation, ↑ plaque stability

**Circadian pattern:** MI incidence highest 6 AM–12 noon (adrenergic surge on awakening)

**Collateral circulation:** Slowly progressive stenosis → collateral remodeling → protection from MI even with complete occlusion; acute blockage → no time for collaterals → infarction

#### Clinical Syndromes of IHD

| Syndrome | Key Features |
| :------------------ | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Stable angina | >70% fixed stenosis; predictable with exertion; relieved by rest/nitroglycerin |
| Prinzmetal angina | Coronary spasm at rest; responds to vasodilators + calcium channel blockers |
| Unstable angina | Plaque disruption + thrombus; increasing frequency/less exertion; harbinger of MI |
| Acute MI | Sufficient ischemia to cause cardiomyocyte death |
| Chronic IHD/CHF | Cumulative ischemic insults → pump failure |
| Sudden cardiac death | Most commonly lethal arrhythmia without myocyte necrosis |

**Acute coronary syndrome** = unstable angina + acute MI + sudden cardiac death

**Pain mechanism:** Ischemia → adenosine + bradykinin release → autonomic afferent stimulation → crushing/squeezing substernal pain radiating to left arm/jaw

### HIGH-YIELD ASSOCIATIONS SUMMARY

| Finding | Association |
| :-------------------------- | :------------------------------------------- |
| Heart failure cells | Left-sided CHF → pulmonary edema |
| Nutmeg liver | Right-sided CHF |
| Cardiac cirrhosis | Chronic severe right-sided CHF |
| Concentric hypertrophy | Pressure overload (HTN, stenosis) |
| Eccentric/dilated hypertrophy | Volume overload (regurgitation, shunts) |
| Physiologic hypertrophy | Aerobic exercise — protective |
| Pathologic hypertrophy | ↑ risk sudden cardiac death |
| S3 heart sound | Volume overload/CHF |
| Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea | Left-sided CHF |
| Anasarca | Severe right-sided CHF |

## Practice Questions
1.  A patient presents with progressively worsening dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. On examination, you hear fine basal rales. What type of heart failure is most likely? → Left-sided heart failure
2.  What is the significance of "heart failure cells" found in the lungs of a patient with chronic heart failure? → They are hemosiderin-laden macrophages indicating extravasated red blood cells due to chronic pulmonary congestion from left-sided heart failure.
3.  A patient with long-standing pulmonary hypertension develops right ventricular hypertrophy and dilation. What is this specific condition called? → Cor pulmonale
4.  Describe the morphological appearance of the liver in a patient with chronic severe right-sided heart failure. → Congestive hepatomegaly with a "nutmeg liver" appearance (centrilobular congestion), potentially progressing to cardiac cirrhosis.
5.  What is the primary difference in ventricular remodeling (hypertrophy) between a heart responding to chronic hypertension versus one responding to chronic mitral regurgitation? → Hypertension (pressure overload) leads to concentric hypertrophy (sarcomeres in parallel), while mitral regurgitation (volume overload) leads to eccentric/dilated hypertrophy (sarcomeres in series).
6.  A 55-year-old male experiences crushing substernal chest pain at rest that is relieved by sublingual nitroglycerin. Angiography shows no significant fixed coronary artery stenosis. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Prinzmetal angina (coronary vasospasm)
7.  What features characterize a "vulnerable plaque" that is prone to rupture and could lead to an acute coronary syndrome? → A large atheromatous core, a thin fibrous cap, fissures at the cap-normal vessel junction, and a high macrophage load with few smooth muscle cells.
8.  Which clinical syndromes are collectively referred to as "acute coronary syndrome"? → Unstable angina, acute myocardial infarction (MI), and sudden cardiac death.

articles.content:
## Congenital Heart Disease (CHD)
*Anatomy · March 3, 2026*
---
### Summary
Congenital Heart Disease (CHD) encompasses structural or functional abnormalities of the heart present at birth, typically classified as **acyanotic** or **cyanotic**. These defects arise from altered embryonic development, affecting approximately **0.8% of live births**. Etiology is frequently unknown, but genetic and environmental factors contribute to conditions like Tetralogy of Fallot, VSD, ASD, and TGA.
---
### Key Points
| Topic | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Definition** | Abnormality in cardio-circulatory structure or function present at birth |
| **Epidemiology** | ~0.8% of live births; extracardiac anomalies are common |
| **Etiology** | Unknown in ~90%; associated with maternal rubella, thalidomide, alcohol, and genetic factors (Trisomies, Turner syndrome) |
| **Classification** | Acyanotic (Left-to-Right shunt) vs. Cyanotic (Right-to-Left shunt) |
| **ASD Types** | Ostium secundum (most common), Ostium primum (Down syndrome), Sinus venosus, Coronary sinus |
| **PFO** | Present in ~25% of adults; linked to paradoxical embolism |
| **VSD** | Most common CHD (25%); haemodynamic effects depend on size |
| **PDA** | Persistence of ductus arteriosus; associated with prematurity; causes a **machinery murmur** |
| **Eisenmenger Syndrome** | Irreversible reversal of L→R shunt to R→L due to pulmonary hypertension |
| **TOF** | Most common cyanotic CHD; VSD + pulmonary stenosis + overriding aorta + RVH |
| **TGA** | Aorta from RV, PA from LV; incompatible with life without mixing (ASD/VSD/PDA) |
| **Ebstein's Anomaly** | Apical displacement of tricuspid leaflet; associated with maternal lithium use |
| **Coarctation of Aorta** | Narrowing of aorta → hypertension in upper limbs, hypotension in lower limbs |
---
### Detailed Notes
#### Introduction and Classification
CHD refers to structural or functional abnormalities of the heart and circulatory system present at birth, arising from altered embryonic development. It affects ~0.8% of live births and can be associated with extracardiac anomalies.
Broadly classified as:
- **Acyanotic** (left-to-right shunts): ASD, VSD, PDA, Coarctation of Aorta
- **Cyanotic** (right-to-left shunts): TOF, TGA, Ebstein's anomaly, Truncus arteriosus, Eisenmenger syndrome
Etiology is often unknown but involves environmental factors (maternal infections, substance use) and genetic factors (chromosomal abnormalities).
---
#### Embryonic Development
**Month 1 — Cardiac Tube Formation:**
Sinuatrium → Primitive ventricle → Bulbus cordis → Truncus arteriosus
**Month 2 — Septation and Folding:**
- **Atrial Septum:** Septum primum grows → ostium primum → perforates → ostium secundum. Septum secundum forms the fossa ovalis.
- **Ventricular Septum:** Cephalic growth of main ventricular septum fuses with endocardial cushions.
- **Great Arteries:** Truncus arteriosus divides and rotates to create the spiral relationship between the aorta and pulmonary artery.
---
#### Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)
| Type | Frequency | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Ostium secundum | 75% | Midseptal; associated with mitral valve prolapse |
| Ostium primum | 15% | Lower septal; associated with Down syndrome and AV valve clefts |
| Sinus venosus | 10% | Upper septal; associated with anomalous pulmonary venous return |
---
#### Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)
Most common CHD overall.
- **Types:** Muscular, Membranous (most common), Doubly committed subarterial
- **Pathophysiology:** Large defects → LV volume overload → may progress to Eisenmenger syndrome
---
#### Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)
Persistent connection between the proximal left pulmonary artery and the descending aorta.
- **Clinical:** Continuous **machinery murmur**
- **Treatment:** Indomethacin to close; Prostaglandins to keep open (e.g., in TGA where mixing is essential)
---
#### Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)
Most common **cyanotic** CHD. Four components:
1. VSD
2. Pulmonary Stenosis
3. Overriding Aorta
4. RVH (Right Ventricular Hypertrophy)
- **"Tet spells":** Episodes of cyanosis, often relieved by squatting (↑ systemic vascular resistance → improves oxygenation)
- **CXR:** "Boot-shaped heart"
---
#### Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA)
Aorta arises from RV; pulmonary artery arises from LV → two parallel circulations. Incompatible with life without a shunt (ASD, VSD, or PDA) to allow mixing.
---
#### Ebstein's Anomaly
Apical displacement of tricuspid leaflets → "atrialization" of part of the RV.
- Associated with **Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome**
- Linked to **maternal lithium use**
---
#### Coarctation of the Aorta
Narrowing of the aorta, typically in the juxtaductal region.
| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Radiofemoral delay** | Delayed/weak femoral pulses vs. radial pulses |
| **Rib notching** | Due to collateral vessel development (on CXR) |
| **"Figure 3 sign"** | On imaging |
| **Associations** | Turner syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve |
---
### Practice Questions
| Presentation | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| Cyanosis at birth, aorta from RV, PA from LV | **TGA** |
| Boot-shaped heart + Tet spells | **TOF** |
| Stroke in young adult with PFO | **Paradoxical embolism** |
| Continuous machinery-like murmur | **PDA** |
| Down syndrome + ASD near AV valves | **Ostium primum ASD** |
| HTN in upper limbs, weak lower pulses, rib notching | **Coarctation of the Aorta** |
| Maternal lithium + tricuspid displacement | **Ebstein's anomaly** |
| Irreversible reversal of L→R shunt due to pulmonary HTN | **Eisenmenger Syndrome** |

# CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE (CHD) — MUST KNOWS

---

## DEFINITION
- **Abnormality in cardio-circulatory structure or function present at birth** (even if discovered later)
- Results from **altered embryonic development** OR **failure to progress beyond an early developmental stage**

---

## EPIDEMIOLOGY
- Affects **~0.8% of live births**
- **Extracardiac anomalies** in ~25% of infants with significant cardiac disease → ↑ mortality

**Sex predilection:**

| More Common in Females | More Common in Males |
|---|---|
| PDA | Aortic valve stenosis |
| Ebstein anomaly | Coarctation of aorta |
| ASD | Hypoplastic left heart |
| | Pulmonary + tricuspid atresia |
| | Transposition of great arteries (TGA) |

---

## ETIOLOGY
- **Unknown in ~90% of cases**
- **Environmental factors:**
  - Maternal **rubella**
  - **Thalidomide** and **isotretinoin** ingestion early in gestation
  - Chronic maternal **alcohol abuse**
- **Genetic factors:**
  - Trisomies **13, 15, 18, 21** (Down syndrome)
  - **Turner syndrome**

---

## CLASSIFICATION

### By Cyanosis

| Acyanotic (L→R Shunt) | Cyanotic (R→L Shunt) |
|---|---|
| ASD | Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) |
| VSD | Transposition of Great Arteries (TGA) |
| PDA | Ebstein's anomaly |
| Aortic stenosis | Truncus arteriosus |
| Pulmonary stenosis | Tricuspid atresia |
| Coarctation of aorta | Total anomalous pulmonary venous return |
| | Eisenmenger's syndrome |

> 💡 **Cyanotic mnemonic: "5 Ts and 2 Es"** — TOF, TGA, Truncus arteriosus, Tricuspid atresia, Total anomalous pulmonary venous return + Ebstein's anomaly + Eisenmenger's syndrome

### By Complexity
- **Simple:** ASD, VSD, singular valvular abnormalities (Ebstein's)
- **Complex:** Multiple defects, AV canal defects, single ventricle physiology

---

## NORMAL EMBRYOLOGICAL DEVELOPMENT — KEY CONCEPTS

### Month 1 — Straight Cardiac Tube (Cephalad → Caudad)
1. Sinuatrium (most cephalad)
2. Primitive ventricle
3. Bulbus cordis
4. Truncus arteriosus (most caudad)

### Month 2 — Tube Doubles Over → Two parallel pumping systems
- **Two atria** ← from sinuatrium
- **AV canal** divided by endocardial cushions → tricuspid + mitral orifices
- **Right + left ventricles** ← from primitive ventricle + bulbus cordis
- Differential myocardial growth → tube bears RIGHT → bulboventricular portion doubles over → ventricles side by side
- AV canal migrates RIGHT; ventricular septum migrates LEFT → each ventricle aligns with its AV valve
- **Subpulmonary conus elongates; subaortic conus resorbs** → aorta moves posteriorly → connects with left ventricle

### Atrial Septum Formation
- **Septum primum** grows down from roof → creates **ostium primum** (inferior opening)
- Perforations in septum primum coalesce → **ostium secundum**
- **Septum secundum** develops to the right of septum primum
- Central opening in septum secundum = **fossa ovalis** covered by septum primum tissue = **valve of foramen ovale**
- **Endocardial cushions** form: inferior atrial septum, superior ventricular septum, septal leaflets of tricuspid + mitral valves

### Ventricular Septum Formation
- Cephalic growth of main ventricular septum → fuses with endocardial cushions + infundibular/conus septum

### Great Arteries Formation
- Truncus arteriosus connected to dorsal aorta by **6 pairs of aortic arches**
- Truncus divides into 2 great arteries via fusion of truncus septum
- **Rotation** of truncus → normal spiral relationship between aorta and pulmonary artery
- Semilunar valves formed by absorption/hollowing of truncus ridge tissue

---

## ABNORMAL DEVELOPMENT → SPECIFIC DEFECTS

| Developmental Failure | Resulting Defect |
|---|---|
| Septum primum + endocardial cushion fail to fuse | Ostium primum ASD |
| Septum secundum doesn't cover ostium secundum | Ostium secundum ASD |
| Deficiency/malalignment of ventricular septal components | VSD |
| Truncus fails to divide | Persistent truncus arteriosus |
| Subpulmonary conus resorbs instead of subaortic | TGA |
| Tricuspid orifice doesn't align over right ventricle | Double-inlet left ventricle |
| Partial partitioning failure of truncus | Aortopulmonary septal defect |

---

# ACYANOTIC CHD (L→R SHUNTS)

---

## ATRIAL SEPTAL DEFECT (ASD)

### Four Types

| Type | % of ASDs | Location | Key Associations |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ostium secundum** | **75%** | Fossa ovalis, midseptal | Mitral valve prolapse |
| **Ostium primum** | **15%** | Lower atrial septum, near AV valves | **Down syndrome**; cleft anterior mitral valve leaflet; tricuspid valve abnormalities |
| **Sinus venosus** | **10%** | Upper atrial septum, near SVC entry | Anomalous pulmonary venous connection (right lung → SVC or RA) |
| **Coronary sinus** | Rare | Around coronary sinus | — |

### Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO)
- Foramen ovale = tunnel between septum secundum and septum primum
- Closes in **75%** at birth by fusion
- **In utero:** oxygenated placental blood → IVC → crosses foramen ovale → systemic circulation
- **Persists in ~25%** of adults
- Associated with **paradoxical embolism** and cryptogenic stroke

---

## VENTRICULAR SEPTAL DEFECT (VSD)
- **Most common CHD — 25% of all CHD**
- Abnormal opening in ventricular septum → free communication between RV and LV

### Ventricular Septum Components
- **Inlet** septum
- **Trabecular** septum
- **Outlet** septum
- Small **membranous** septum (just under aortic valve)

### Types of VSD

| Type | Borders | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Muscular VSD** | Entirely myocardium | Can be trabecular, inlet, or outlet |
| **Membranous VSD** | Partly fibrous (AV valve + arterial valve continuity) | Most common; inlet/outlet/trabecular extension |
| **Doubly committed subarterial** | Fibrous continuity of aortic + pulmonary valves | More common in **Asian patients**; outlet septum |

### Haemodynamic Effects by Size

| Size | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Restrictive** | No significant haemodynamic derangement; may close spontaneously in childhood |
| **Moderately restrictive** | LV volume overload → LA + LV dilation + dysfunction; variable ↑ pulmonary vascular resistance |
| **Large/Non-restrictive** | LV volume overload early → progressive ↑ PA pressure → ↓ L→R shunting → ↑ pulmonary vascular resistance → **Eisenmenger syndrome** |

---

## PATENT DUCTUS ARTERIOSUS (PDA)
- Ductus arteriosus = derived from **left 6th primitive aortic arch**
- Connects **proximal left pulmonary artery** to **descending aorta** (just distal to left subclavian artery)
- **In utero:** carries deoxygenated blood from RV → descending aorta → placenta
- **Functional closure** (vasoconstriction) = shortly after term birth
- **Anatomical closure** (intimal proliferation + fibrosis) = several weeks after birth
- Persistence = **true congenital malformation**
- More common in **females** and **premature infants**
- **Machinery murmur** (continuous)
- **Treatment:** Indomethacin (inhibits prostaglandins → promotes closure); surgical ligation

---

## EISENMENGER SYNDROME
- Occurs when any **large L→R shunt** (VSD, ASD, PDA) causes progressive ↑ pulmonary vascular resistance
- Eventually pulmonary pressure **exceeds systemic pressure** → **shunt reverses to R→L**
- Results in **cyanosis, clubbing, polycythaemia**
- **Irreversible** — heart-lung transplant is only option at this stage
- Prevention = early correction of the underlying defect

---

# CYANOTIC CHD (R→L SHUNTS)

---

## TETRALOGY OF FALLOT (TOF)
- **Most common cyanotic CHD**

### 4 Components (all from ONE fundamental defect)
1. **Outlet VSD**
2. **Obstruction to right ventricular outflow** (pulmonary stenosis — usually subvalvular)
3. **Overriding aorta** (<50% override)
4. **Right ventricular hypertrophy** (RVH)

> 💡 **Fundamental defect:** Anterior + cephalad deviation of the outlet septum → malalignment with trabecular septum

- Dominant obstruction = **subvalvular (sub-pulmonic) level**
- Progressive hypoxaemia in first years of life
- **"Tet spells"** — hypercyanotic episodes; child squats to relieve (↑ SVR → ↑ L→R flow)
- Survival to adult life rare **without palliation or correction**
- **Boot-shaped heart** on CXR (coeur en sabot)
- **Treatment:** surgical correction

---

## TRANSPOSITION OF THE GREAT ARTERIES (TGA)
- **Common, potentially lethal** in newborns
- **Aorta arises from morphological RV; PA arises from morphological LV**
- Circulations run **in parallel** (not in series as normal)
- Circuit 1: Systemic venous blood → RA → RV → **Aorta** (deoxygenated blood to body)
- Circuit 2: Pulmonary venous blood → LA → LV → **Pulmonary artery** (oxygenated blood loops back to lungs)
- **Incompatible with life** unless mixing occurs (via PFO, ASD, VSD, or PDA)
- **Treatment:** Prostaglandin E1 to keep PDA open; **arterial switch operation** (definitive)
- Results from **resorption of subaortic instead of subpulmonary conus**

---

## EBSTEIN'S ANOMALY
- **Apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet** + leaflet dysplasia
- Anterior leaflet never displaced but may adhere to RV free wall → **RVOTO**
- Displacement → **"Atrialization" of RV inflow tract** → functionally small RV
- Associated with **PFO or ASD in ~50%** of patients
- More common in **females**
- Associated with **maternal lithium use** during pregnancy
- Features: tricuspid regurgitation, right heart failure, arrhythmias (WPW syndrome common)
- **"Sail-like" anterior tricuspid leaflet** on echo

---

## COARCTATION OF THE AORTA
- **Narrowing of the aorta**, usually at the **ductus arteriosus insertion** (juxtaductal)
- More common in **males**
- Associated with **Turner syndrome** and **bicuspid aortic valve** (most common association)
- Features:
  - **Hypertension in upper limbs**; hypotension in lower limbs
  - **Radiofemoral delay**
  - **Rib notching** on CXR (from collateral vessels)
  - Headaches, epistaxis, cold legs
- **"Figure 3 sign"** on CXR
- Treatment: surgical resection or balloon angioplasty ± stenting

---

## TRUNCUS ARTERIOSUS
- **Failure of truncus arteriosus to divide** into aorta and pulmonary artery
- Single great vessel overrides both ventricles
- Always associated with **VSD**
- Results in mixing of oxygenated + deoxygenated blood → cyanosis
- **Treatment:** surgical repair (Rastelli procedure)

---

# QUICK COMPARISON TABLE

| Defect | Type | Key Feature | Murmur | Key Association |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ASD (ostium secundum) | Acyanotic | Most common ASD (75%) | Ejection systolic + fixed split S2 | MVP |
| ASD (ostium primum) | Acyanotic | Near AV valves | As above | **Down syndrome** |
| VSD | Acyanotic | Most common CHD (25%) | Harsh pansystolic | Can → Eisenmenger |
| PDA | Acyanotic | Continuous machinery murmur | Machinery murmur | Prematurity; rubella |
| TOF | Cyanotic | Most common cyanotic CHD | Ejection systolic (pulmonary) | Boot-shaped heart; Tet spells |
| TGA | Cyanotic | Parallel circulations | Variable | Incompatible with life without mixing |
| Ebstein's | Cyanotic | Atrialized RV; apical displacement of tricuspid | TR murmur | WPW; lithium; ASD in 50% |
| Coarctation | Acyanotic | Juxtaductal narrowing | Ejection systolic; collaterals | Turner syndrome; bicuspid aortic valve |
| Eisenmenger | Cyanotic | Reversed shunt | Pulmonary regurgitation | Irreversible; late complication of L→R shunts |
| Truncus arteriosus | Cyanotic | Single great vessel | Variable | Always with VSD |

---

> ⚡ **EXAM TRIGGERS**
> - Down syndrome + ASD → **Ostium primum ASD** (+ mitral valve cleft)
> - Most common CHD overall → **VSD**
> - Most common cyanotic CHD → **TOF**
> - Boot-shaped heart on CXR → **TOF**
> - Machinery murmur → **PDA**
> - Fixed split S2 → **ASD**
> - Radiofemoral delay + rib notching → **Coarctation of aorta**
> - Turner syndrome + coarctation → high-yield combination
> - Atrialized RV → **Ebstein's anomaly**
> - Maternal lithium → **Ebstein's anomaly**
> - Parallel circulations incompatible with life → **TGA**
> - Large VSD/ASD/PDA left untreated → **Eisenmenger syndrome** (irreversible)
> - 25% of adults have persistent PFO → risk of **paradoxical embolism + cryptogenic stroke**
> - Subpulmonary conus resorbs instead of subaortic conus → **TGA**
> - Single great vessel + VSD → **Truncus arteriosus**
