articles.content:
## Lymphoma
---
### Definition and Introduction
Lymphoma is a neoplastic (clonal) lymphoproliferative disorder primarily involving solid lymphoid organs such as lymph nodes. Lymphoid cells can transform at any stage of maturation, leading to malignancies specific to that stage. These may present as leukaemia (bone marrow and blood involvement), lymphoma (solid organ involvement), or both (e.g., CLL/SLL).
---
### Major Categories
| Feature | Hodgkin Lymphoma (HL) | Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL) |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency | ~30% | ~70% |
| Spread | Orderly, contiguous | Irregular, unpredictable |
| Extranodal | Uncommon | Common |
| Diagnostic Cells | Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells | Absent |
| Origin | B-cell (Classical HL) | 85–90% B-cell; 10–15% T/NK-cell |
| Curability | Highly curable | Varies by subtype |
---
### Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL)
#### Classification (WHO System)
Modern classification integrates lineage, differentiation stage, morphology, immunophenotype, genetics, and clinical features.
**1. B-cell Neoplasms (85–90%)**
- *Precursor B-cell:* B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma (B-ALL/LBL).
- *Mature B-cell:* CLL/SLL, Follicular lymphoma, Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), Mantle cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, MALT lymphoma, Hairy cell leukaemia, Plasma cell myeloma.
**2. T/NK-cell Neoplasms (10–15%)**
- *Precursor T-cell:* T-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma.
- *Mature T/NK-cell:* Mycosis fungoides, Adult T-cell leukaemia (HTLV-1), Anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), Peripheral T-cell lymphoma.
#### Grading
**Low-Grade (Indolent):** Slow-growing, good chemo response but difficult to cure (e.g., Follicular, SLL, MALT).
**High-Grade (Aggressive):** Rapidly fatal if untreated, but more often curable with intensive therapy (e.g., DLBCL, Burkitt, Lymphoblastic).
---
### Pathogenesis and Aetiology
#### Infectious Associations
- **EBV:** Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, CNS lymphoma.
- **HTLV-1:** Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.
- **HIV-1:** DLBCL, Burkitt lymphoma.
- **H. pylori:** Gastric MALT lymphoma.
- **Hepatitis C:** Marginal zone lymphoma, CLL.
#### Genetic Alterations
Chromosomal translocations involving Immunoglobulin (Ig) genes often lead to oncogene overexpression:
- **Follicular Lymphoma:** t(14;18) → BCL-2 overexpression (inhibits apoptosis).
- **Mantle Cell Lymphoma:** t(11;14) → Cyclin D1 overexpression.
- **Burkitt Lymphoma:** t(8;14) → MYC overexpression.
- **ALCL:** t(2;5) → ALK overexpression.
---
### Clinical Features
**Lymphadenopathy:** Asymmetric, painless, superficial nodes.
**Constitutional (B) Symptoms:** Fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss (>10% in 6 months).
**Extranodal Disease:** GI tract (most common), skin, brain, testis, oropharynx (Waldeyer's ring).
**Cytopenias:** Due to bone marrow infiltration or hypersplenism.
---
### Investigations
**Biopsy (Gold Standard):** Excisional or Tru-cut biopsy. Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) is insufficient for primary diagnosis as tissue architecture is required.
**Laboratory:** FBC, ESR, LDH (prognostic marker), uric acid, LFTs, HIV screening.
**Imaging:** PET/CT scan for staging and assessing treatment response.
**Bone Marrow:** Aspirate and trephine biopsy for staging.
---
### Staging: Ann Arbor System
- **Stage I:** Single lymph node region or single extralymphatic site.
- **Stage II:** Two or more regions on the same side of the diaphragm.
- **Stage III:** Regions on both sides of the diaphragm; may include the spleen.
- **Stage IV:** Disseminated involvement of extralymphatic organs (e.g., bone marrow, liver).
- **Suffixes:** A (asymptomatic), B (B-symptoms present), E (extranodal extension).
---
### Treatment Principles
**Chemotherapy:** R-CHOP (Rituximab, Cyclophosphamide, Doxorubicin, Vincristine, Prednisolone) is the standard regimen for DLBCL.
**Immunotherapy:** Rituximab (Anti-CD20) targets B-cells via antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) and complement-mediated lysis.
**Targeted Therapy:** Ibrutinib (BTK inhibitor), Venetoclax (BCL-2 inhibitor), BRAF inhibitors for Hairy Cell Leukaemia.
**Stem Cell Transplant:** Used in relapsed or high-risk cases.
articles.original_notes:
# LYMPHOMA — COMPLETE MUST KNOWS

---

## DEFINITION & INTRODUCTION
- **Neoplastic (clonal) lymphoproliferative disorder** primarily involving solid lymphoid organs (lymph nodes)
- Lymphoid cells can transform at **any stage of maturation** → malignancy specific to that stage
- May present as **leukaemia** (bone marrow + blood), **lymphoma** (solid organs), or **both**
- This is why current classification includes both e.g. CLL/SLL

---

## TWO MAJOR CATEGORIES

| | Hodgkin Lymphoma (HL) | Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL) |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency | ~30% | ~70% |
| Spread | Orderly, contiguous | Irregular, unpredictable |
| Extranodal | Uncommon | Common |
| RS cells | Present | Absent |
| B-cell origin | Yes (classical HL) | 85–90% |
| Curability | Highly curable | Varies by subtype |

---

# PART 1: NON-HODGKIN LYMPHOMA (NHL)

---

## EPIDEMIOLOGY
- **85–90% B-cell origin**, 10–15% T/NK-cell origin
- Incidence: ~**17/100,000** — **5th most common malignancy** in developed countries
- Incidence markedly increased over last 50 years
- More variable presentation than HL; irregular spread; significant extranodal disease

---

## CLASSIFICATION (WHO — REAL/WHO)
Based on: **lineage + differentiation stage + morphology + immunophenotype + genetics + clinical features**

### Historical Classification Evolution
- **Rappaport (1966)** — morphology only (nodular vs diffuse)
- **Lukes & Collins (1974)** — T-cell vs B-cell
- **Kiel** — low and high grade
- **Working Formulation (1979)** — low/intermediate/high grade (still used in some settings)
- **REAL/WHO (1994/2001/2008)** — current gold standard; combines morphology + immunophenotype + genetics + clinical features

### B-cell Neoplasms (85–90%)

**Precursor B-cell:**
- Precursor B lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma (B-ALL/LBL)

**Mature B-cell:**
- CLL/SLL
- Follicular lymphoma
- Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) — multiple subtypes
- Mantle cell lymphoma
- Burkitt lymphoma
- MALT lymphoma (extranodal marginal zone)
- Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma
- Hairy cell leukaemia
- Splenic marginal zone lymphoma
- Plasma cell myeloma / Plasmacytoma

### T/NK-cell Neoplasms (10–15%)

**Precursor T-cell:**
- Precursor T lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma
- Blastic NK cell lymphoma

**Mature T/NK-cell:**
- Mycosis fungoides / Sézary syndrome
- Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (HTLV-1)
- Anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALK+)
- Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma
- Peripheral T-cell lymphoma (unspecified)
- Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma
- Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type
- Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma
- Subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma

---

## CELL OF ORIGIN
- B-cell lymphomas **mimic normal B cells at different developmental stages**
- **Unmutated Ig genes** → Mantle cell lymphoma, some B-CLL
- **Mutated Ig genes** → Marginal zone, DLBCL, Follicular, Lymphoplasmacytic, some B-CLL
- T-cell lymphomas mimic precursor T cells (bone marrow/thymus) or peripheral mature T cells
- In all lymphoid neoplasms: **antigen receptor gene rearrangement precedes transformation** → daughter cells synthesize identical antigen receptor proteins (basis of clonality)

---

## LOW-GRADE vs HIGH-GRADE

| Feature | Low-Grade | High-Grade |
|---|---|---|
| Course | Indolent, slow-growing | Aggressive, rapidly fatal |
| Chemo response | Good | Good |
| Curability | **Difficult to cure** | **More often curable** |
| Urgency | Watch and wait acceptable | Urgent treatment needed |
| Examples | Follicular, MALT, SLL | DLBCL, Burkitt, Lymphoblastic |

---

## PATHOGENESIS & ETIOLOGY

### Infectious Agents

| Agent | Associated Lymphoma |
|---|---|
| **EBV** | Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, Post-transplant lymphoma, Primary CNS DLBCL, Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma |
| **HTLV-1** | Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma |
| **HIV-1** | DLBCL, Burkitt, plasma cell myeloma, CNS lymphoma |
| **HHV-8** | Primary effusion lymphoma, Castleman's disease |
| **Hepatitis C** | Marginal zone lymphoma, CLL, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma |
| **H. pylori** | Gastric MALT lymphoma |
| **Borrelia spp** | MALT lymphoma of skin |
| **Chlamydia psittaci** | MALT lymphoma of eye |
| **Campylobacter jejuni** | MALT lymphoma of intestine |
| **Malaria** | Endemic Burkitt lymphoma |

### Other Etiological Factors
- Inherited and acquired **immunodeficiencies**
- **Autoimmune diseases** (e.g. Sjögren's → salivary gland MALT; Hashimoto's → thyroid MALT)
- Chemicals and radiation
- Chromosomal translocations involving **Ig genes on chromosomes 2, 14, 22** → oncogene overexpression → altered cell cycle / failed apoptosis
- Up to **80 somatic mutations** may be present at diagnosis

---

## CLINICAL FEATURES
1. **Superficial lymphadenopathy** — asymmetric, **painless** — most common
2. **Constitutional (B) symptoms** — fever, night sweats, weight loss — less common than HL; indicate disseminated disease
3. **Oropharyngeal** (5–10%) — Waldeyer's ring + mesenteric nodes commonly involved → sore throat, obstructed breathing
4. **Cytopenias** — anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia — bone marrow involvement OR autoimmune OR splenic sequestration
5. **Abdominal disease** — hepatosplenomegaly; GI tract = **most common extranodal site after bone marrow**
6. **Other organs** — skin, brain, testis, thyroid, salivary glands, stomach, lungs
7. Spread is **non-contiguous** (unlike HL)

---

## INVESTIGATIONS

### Gold Standard
- **Trucut / whole lymph node biopsy** — definitive
- ⚠️ **FNA is NOT sufficient** — biopsy must be obtained
- **κ or λ light chain** expression on immunophenotyping confirms clonality

### Lab Tests
- **FBC + ESR**
- **Serum LDH** — key prognostic marker; raised in aggressive/extensive disease
- **Beta-2 microglobulin** — prognostic in NHL
- Serum uric acid, renal function, uric acid, ALP, calcium, albumin, glucose
- Immunoglobulin electrophoresis — paraprotein
- HIV status
- **Bone marrow aspirate + trephine biopsy**
- Flow cytometry (B/T lymphocyte markers)
- Cytology: FNA, CSF, pleural fluid

### Imaging
- **PET/CT scan** — staging + monitoring treatment response
- CT scan abdomen/pelvis, MRI, Gallium-67 scan
- Chest X-ray
- Lymphangiography, abdominal/pelvic ultrasound

---

## KEY CYTOGENETICS & MUTATIONS

| Lymphoma | Translocation | Effect / Mutation |
|---|---|---|
| Follicular lymphoma | **t(14;18)** | BCL-2 overexpression → ↓ apoptosis |
| Mantle cell lymphoma | **t(11;14)** | Cyclin D1 overexpression → cell cycle dysregulation |
| Burkitt lymphoma | **t(8;14)**, t(2;8), t(8;22) | MYC overexpression |
| DLBCL (GCB) | t(14;18) | CREBBP, EZH2, MYC mutations |
| DLBCL (ABC) | t(3;14) | NFκB pathway activation |
| MALT lymphoma | t(11;18), t(1;14) | NFκB pathway activation — **no response to antibiotics** |
| ALCL | **t(2;5)** | ALK overexpression |
| Lymphoplasmacytic | Non-specific | **MYD88 mutation >90%** |
| Hairy cell leukaemia | Non-specific | **BRAF V600E >99%** |
| CLL/SLL | 13p, 11q, 17p deletions; trisomy 12 | TP53, ATM, NOTCH, SF3B1 |
| Precursor B-ALL/LBL | t(12;21), t(9;22), t(4;11) | Philadelphia chromosome (t(9;22) = worst prognosis) |

---

## IMMUNOPHENOTYPE SUMMARY

| Lymphoma | SIg | CD20 | CD5 | CD10 | CD23 | BCL2 | BCL6 | MUM1 | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SLL/CLL | weak | + | **+** | – | **+** | – | – | – | CD19+ |
| Hairy cell | + | + | – | – | – | – | – | – | CD25+, CD11c+ |
| Lymphoplasmacytic | + | + | – | – | – | – | – | + | MYD88 mut |
| MALT | + | + | – | – | +/– | – | – | +/– | — |
| **Follicular** | + | + | – | **+** | +/– | **+** | **+** | – | — |
| **Mantle cell** | + | + | **+** | – | **–** | + | – | – | **CyclinD1+** |
| DLBCL GCB | +/– | + | – | – | + | – | – | – | — |
| DLBCL ABC | +/– | + | – | – | – | – | – | + | — |
| Burkitt | + | + | – | **+** | – | **–** | + | – | BCL2− important |
| Precursor B-ALL | – | – | – | + | – | – | – | – | **TdT+**, CD19+, CD22+ |
| ALCL | – | – | – | – | – | – | – | – | **CD30+**, ALK+ |

> 💡 **MCL vs CLL:** Both CD5+/CD19+ but MCL is **CD23−/CyclinD1+** while CLL is **CD23+**
> 💡 **Burkitt vs Follicular:** Both CD10+ but Burkitt is **BCL2−** while Follicular is **BCL2+**

---

## STAGING — ANN ARBOR SYSTEM (Used for Both HL and NHL)

| Stage | Description |
|---|---|
| **I** | Single lymph node region OR single extralymphatic site (IE) |
| **II** | ≥2 lymph node regions on **same side** of diaphragm ± limited extralymphatic site (IIE) |
| **III** | Lymph node regions on **both sides** of diaphragm ± spleen (IIIS) ± extralymphatic site (IIIE) |
| **IV** | **Disseminated** involvement of ≥1 extralymphatic organs ± lymphatic involvement |

**Suffixes:**
- **A** = No B symptoms
- **B** = Fever, night sweats, weight loss >10% of normal
- **E** = Localized extralymphatic involvement
- **S** = Splenic involvement

> ⚠️ **Stage IV** = bone marrow involvement → bilateral iliac crest biopsies important in staging

---

## NCCN-IPI (High-Grade NHL Prognostic Score)

| Factor | Score |
|---|---|
| Age 40–60 | 1 |
| Age 60–75 | 2 |
| Age >75 | 3 |
| LDH 1–3× normal | 1 |
| LDH >3× normal | 2 |
| Stage III–IV | 1 |
| Extranodal disease (BM, CNS, liver/GI, lung) | 1 |
| Performance status ≥2 | 1 |

---

## TREATMENT PRINCIPLES
- **Combination chemotherapy + monoclonal antibody** is standard
- **Anti-CD20** (Rituximab, Ofatumumab, Obinutuzumab) — 85% of B-cell NHL
- **Anti-CD30** (Brentuximab) — ALCL + Hodgkin lymphoma
- **Anti-CD25** (Alemtuzumab) — CLL (more immunocompromising)

### How Rituximab Works
1. Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC)
2. Complement-mediated lysis
3. Direct apoptosis of target cell

### Targeted Agents

| Drug | Target | Used In |
|---|---|---|
| Ibrutinib | BTK inhibitor | B-CLL, MCL, LPL |
| Idelalisib | PI3K inhibitor | Follicular, CLL |
| Venetoclax | BCL-2 inhibitor | CLL, some NHL |
| Crizotinib | ALK inhibitor | ALCL |
| Bortezomib | Proteasome inhibitor | MCL, LPL |
| Vemurafenib | BRAF inhibitor | Hairy cell leukaemia |

### Key Chemotherapy Regimens

| Regimen | Components | Used In |
|---|---|---|
| **R-CHOP** | Rituximab + Cyclophosphamide + Hydroxydaunorubicin + Vincristine + Prednisolone | DLBCL, MCL |
| **R-CVP** | Rituximab + Cyclophosphamide + Vincristine + Prednisolone | Follicular lymphoma |
| **CODOX-M/IVAC** | Methotrexate + Cytosine arabinoside + Cyclophosphamide + Doxorubicin + Ifosfamide + Etoposide | Burkitt lymphoma |
| **R-ICE** | Rituximab + Ifosfamide + Carboplatin + Etoposide | Relapsed DLBCL |
| **Hyper C-VAD** | Cyclophosphamide + Vincristine + Doxorubicin + Dexamethasone | MCL, ALL |
| **CVP/CHOP** | Cyclophosphamide + Vincristine + Prednisolone ± Doxorubicin | CLL, follicular |

---

# SPECIFIC SUBTYPES — COMPLETE MUST KNOWS

---

## 🔵 PRECURSOR LYMPHOID NEOPLASMS

### Precursor B-cell ALL/Lymphoblastic Lymphoma
- Predominantly **children**
- Presents with: **pancytopenia** (marrow involvement), hepatosplenomegaly, CNS involvement, testicular/cutaneous lesions
- Aggressive
- **Histology:** lymphoblasts with condensed chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, scant agranular cytoplasm
- **Markers:** TdT+, CD19+, CD22+, CD10+
- **Translocations:** t(12;21) [best prognosis], t(9;22) Philadelphia [worst prognosis], t(4;11)
- **Treatment:** remission induction → consolidation (high-dose + CNS treatment) → maintenance
- **Prognosis:** children ~90% cure rate; adults ~50% long-term disease-free

### Precursor T-cell ALL/Lymphoblastic Lymphoma
- Predominantly **adolescent males**
- Presents with **thymic masses** (mediastinal), variable splenic/hepatic/BM involvement
- Aggressive
- **Markers:** CD1+, CD2+, CD5+, CD7+; late pre-T: CD3+, CD4+, CD8+; **TdT+**
- **Treatment:** aggressive chemo + CNS prophylaxis → >90% complete remission
- **Poor prognostic factors:** Age <2 or adolescent/adult; blasts >100,000; Philadelphia chromosome

---

## 🔵 LOW-GRADE B-CELL NHL

### CLL / Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL)
- **Older adults**; involves bone marrow, spleen, lymph nodes, liver
- **CLL** = peripheral blood lymphocytes **>5×10⁹/L**; **SLL** = lymph node distribution, <5×10⁹/L, no cytopenias
- Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia in minority
- **Morphology:** diffusely effaced lymph node architecture; small lymphocytes with round/irregular nuclei + condensed chromatin; **proliferation centres** (loose aggregates of prolymphocytes = pathognomonic)
- **Markers:** CD19+, CD20+, **CD5+, CD23+**; weak SIg
- **Genetics:** Trisomy 12; deletions 11q, 13q, 17p; **17p deletion = worst prognosis**

**Staging:**

*Rai System:*
- 0 = lymphocytosis only
- I = lymphocytosis + lymphadenopathy
- II = + splenomegaly/hepatomegaly
- III = + anaemia
- IV = + thrombocytopenia

*Binet System:*
- A = <3 lymphoid areas
- B = ≥3 lymphoid areas
- C = Hb <10g/dL or platelets <100×10⁹

**Treatment:**
- Rai 0 / Binet A → **follow up, no treatment** (10-year survival)
- Rai III–IV / Binet C → treatment required
- Glucocorticoids for autoimmune cytopenias
- Chlorambucil or fludarabine; **Rituximab + Fludarabine + Cyclophosphamide (RFC)** → 69% complete remission
- CVP or CHOP; **fludarabine regimens preferred**
- Alemtuzumab (anti-CD25) — more immunocompromising
- Allogeneic BMT — potentially curative

---

### Lymphoplasmacytic Lymphoma / Waldenström's Macroglobulinaemia
- **Men >50 years**; monoclonal **IgM paraprotein**
- Called Waldenström's when IgM paraprotein present
- Origin: post-GC B cell; **MYD88 mutation >90%** (near-diagnostic)
- **Key Complications:**
  - **Hyperviscosity syndrome** — IgM mainly intravascular → more viscous than IgG/IgA → visual disturbances (engorged retinal veins, haemorrhages, blurred disc), neurological symptoms, dyspnoea, heart failure
  - **Anaemia** — significant
  - **Bleeding tendency** — IgM interferes with coagulation factors + platelets
  - **Raynaud's phenomenon** — if IgM is a cryoglobulin
  - Raised ESR; peripheral blood lymphocytosis

**Treatment:**
- Asymptomatic → **no treatment**
- Symptomatic → Rituximab + chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide / fludarabine / bendamustine / bortezomib)
- Refractory → **Ibrutinib**
- Acute hyperviscosity → **Plasmapheresis** (effective because IgM is intravascular)
- Chronic anaemia → Erythropoietin or transfusions

---

### Marginal Zone Lymphomas
- Arise from **marginal zone B cells of germinal follicles**
- Mechanism: chronic antigen/inflammation → lymphoid hyperplasia → secondary genetic damage
- Occur at sites of chronic immune reactions: **Sjögren's** (salivary glands), **Hashimoto's** (thyroid), **H. pylori** (stomach)
- NFκB pathway mutations

**MALT Lymphoma:**
- Sites: **stomach** (most common), respiratory tract, skin, salivary glands, eyes, intestines
- Gastric MALT → **H. pylori**; early stage → **antibiotics curative**
- ⚠️ t(11;18) or t(1;14) → **does NOT respond to antibiotics** → chemotherapy needed
- Advanced → chlorambucil or follicular lymphoma regimens

**Splenic Marginal Zone:**
- Splenomegaly ± circulating **'villous' lymphocytes**
- Stage Ia → **local radiotherapy**
- Symptomatic → **splenectomy**

---

### Follicular Lymphoma
- **~25–29% of all NHL** — most common low-grade NHL
- **Older adults**; median age 60 years
- **t(14;18)** → constitutive **BCL-2 expression** → reduced apoptosis
- **Markers:** CD10+, CD19+, CD20+, CD79a+, CD79b+, **BCL-2+, BCL-6+**
- Derived from **germinal centres**; 2 cell types: **centrocytes** (small, cleaved nuclei) + **centroblasts** (large, open chromatin, multiple nucleoli)

**Histological Grading:**
- G1: 0–5 centroblasts/hpf
- G2: 6–15 centroblasts/hpf
- G3A: >15, mixed centrocytes + centroblasts
- G3B: >15, **pure centroblasts** → **treat as DLBCL**

**Prognostic Factors (FLIPI):** Age >60, Stage III–IV, Hb <12g/dL, nodal areas >4, high LDH

**Clinical:**
- Indolent; median survival **~10 years**
- Usually Stage III–IV at presentation
- Bone marrow involvement frequent
- **Histologic transformation: 30–50%** (3% per year to aggressive lymphoma)
- 25% undergo **spontaneous regression**

**Treatment:**
- Stage I → **radiotherapy** (potentially curative, ~10% of patients)
- Stage II–IV, asymptomatic → **"Watch and Wait"**
- Stage II–IV, symptomatic → **R-CVP** or R-bendamustine or R-chlorambucil (up to 90% response)
- Maintenance → Rituximab every 2–3 months
- Relapse → Rituximab + chemo → Autologous SCT
- **Only cure = Allogeneic SCT**
- New agents: Idelalisib (PI3K), Ibrutinib (BTK)

---

## 🔴 HIGH-GRADE B-CELL NHL

### Mantle Cell Lymphoma
- **Older males**; ~70% present at **Stage IV**
- Origin: **pre-GC naïve B cells** in mantle zone
- Can involve **small bowel and colon** → **lymphomatoid polyposis**
- **t(11;14)** → Cyclin D1 overexpression → **required for diagnosis**
- **Markers:** CD19+, CD20+, **CD5+, CD23−**, **CyclinD1+**, BCL2+, BCL6−
- **Histology:** homogenous small-medium lymphocytes with angular/irregular nuclei; intrasinusoidal infiltration prominent on trephine
- ATM, TP53, chromatin modification mutations also common
- **PBF:** cytopenias, pleomorphic cells, leukaemic phase

**Treatment:**
- R-CHOP / bendamustine / bortezomib / lenalidomide
- **Hyper C-VAD + Rituximab** → better response
- **Ibrutinib** — very effective in relapsed/early disease
- Aggressive chemo → **Allogeneic BMT** in young patients
- **Poor prognosis**; 15% have indolent CLL-like course

---

### Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL)
- **Most common NHL subtype (37%)**
- Predominantly **adults**; common in HIV
- Appears as **single rapidly growing mass**; 30% extranodal; aggressive
- **Large cells (4–5× normal lymphocyte)** with prominent nucleoli; diffuse pattern
- **Markers:** CD19+, CD20+, CD79a+, CD79b+; variable CD10 and BCL-6

**Subtypes:**
- **Mediastinal DLBCL** → superior vena cava syndrome
- **Plasmablastic type** → immunodeficiency, body cavity effusions
- **T-cell/histiocyte-rich** → spleen and marrow disease
- **ALK-positive DLBCL**
- **Intravascular DLBCL**
- **Primary effusion DLBCL** → HIV-related

**Two Main Molecular Subtypes:**
- **GCB (germinal centre B-cell)** — BCL-6+; **better prognosis**
- **ABC (activated B-cell)** — MUM1+; NFκB activation; **worse prognosis**

**Poor Prognostic Factors (IPI/NCCN-IPI):** Age, performance status, Stage III/IV, >1 extranodal site, high LDH, bulky disease >5cm, HIV+, ABC subtype, prior low-grade lymphoma

**Treatment:**
- **R-CHOP × 6–8 cycles** (3-weekly) + G-CSF support
- Localized → 3× R-CHOP + radiotherapy
- CNS prophylaxis: intrathecal or high-dose methotrexate (high-risk)
- Monitor: PET/CT mid-treatment + post-treatment
- Relapse → **R-ICE** → Autologous SCT
- **Overall long-term survival: ~65%** (>50% cured)

---

### Burkitt Lymphoma
- **Highest incidence in Eastern Africa**; first described as jaw sarcoma
- **Most common lymphoma in HIV patients (25%)**
- One of the **most highly proliferative tumours** — mitotic index **>95%**
- **Poorly responsive to CHOP**
- **MYC oncogene** overexpressed: **t(8;14)** [most common], t(2;8), t(8;22) → MYC expressed when it should be OFF

**Three Types:**

| | Endemic (African) | Sporadic | HIV-associated |
|---|---|---|---|
| EBV | **~100%** | ~20% | Variable |
| Co-factor | **Chronic malaria** | — | HIV |
| Presentation | **Jaw mass**, child | Abdominal mass | Aggressive |
| Geography | Sub-Saharan Africa | Worldwide | Worldwide |

- **CNS involvement in 20%** of cases
- **PBF:** lymphocytosis, cytopenias in marrow failure, large lymphoblasts with **basophilic cytoplasm containing vacuoles**
- **Markers:** SIgM+, CD19+, CD10+, CD20+, CD22+, BCL6+; **BCL2−** (important distinction from follicular)
- **Histology:** sheets of lymphoblasts + **'starry sky' tingible-body macrophages**

**Treatment:**
- **CODOX-M/IVAC** (methotrexate, cytosine arabinoside, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, ifosfamide, etoposide)
- Intrathecal chemotherapy
- Initially very responsive; excellent prognosis with aggressive regimens

---

### Primary CNS Lymphoma
- Rare; more common in **elderly + HIV+**
- Usually DLBCL type
- Treatment: **high-dose methotrexate + cytosine arabinoside** ± whole brain radiotherapy
- ⚠️ **Long-term cognitive dysfunction** is a major concern

---

### Lymphoblastic Lymphoma
- B or T-cell; mainly **children and young adults**
- Clinically + morphologically overlaps with **ALL**
- **TdT positive** — negative in ALL other NHL types
- Treated with **ALL-type protocols**

---

## 🟣 T-CELL LYMPHOMAS

### Peripheral T-cell Lymphoma (Unspecified)
- Heterogeneous; usually **CD4+**; T cells at various differentiation stages
- Treatment: CHOP; **poor prognosis**
- Autografting for chemo-sensitive disease

### Angioimmunoblastic T-cell Lymphoma
- **Elderly patients**
- Features: lymphadenopathy + hepatosplenomegaly + **skin rashes** + **polyclonal ↑ IgG**
- Treatment: chemotherapy or **histone deacetylase inhibitors**

### Mycosis Fungoides
- Chronic **cutaneous** T-cell lymphoma
- Progression: **inflammatory/mycotic phase → plaque phase → tumour phase**
- **Histology:** epidermis + upper dermis infiltrated with T-cells with **cerebriform nuclei**; **Pautrier microabscesses**
- Late stage: lymph nodes, spleen, liver, bone marrow
- Treatment: **phototherapy** or chemotherapy

### Sézary Syndrome
- Variant of mycosis fungoides
- Features: **erythroderma** + dermatitis + lymphadenopathy + circulating **Sézary cells**
- **Sézary cells:** CD4+ T-cells with **cerebriform (folded) nuclear chromatin** — pathognomonic
- Treatment: local irradiation, topical chemo, **PUVA** (psoralen + UV light); CHOP rarely effective long-term

### Adult T-cell Leukaemia/Lymphoma
- Associated with **HTLV-1** infection
- Common in **Japan, West Africa, Caribbean**
- Presents: **cutaneous lesions** + marrow involvement + **hypercalcaemia**
- **Tumour cells:** multilobated nuclei — **"clover leaf" or "flower cells"**
- Markers: **CD25+ (IL-2 receptor)**

### Enteropathy-Associated T-cell Lymphoma (EATL)
- Associated with **coeliac disease**
- **Very poor response** to treatment

### Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL)
- Common in **children and young adults**; nodal + soft tissue disease
- Usually T-cell phenotype
- **Histology:** large anaplastic cells with **horseshoe-shaped/embryo-like nuclei** + voluminous cytoplasm → **"hallmark cells"**; clusters around venules; infiltrate sinuses (can mimic metastasis)
- **Markers: CD30+**; **t(2;5)** → **ALK overexpression**
- **ALK+ = better prognosis; ALK− = worse prognosis**
- Treatment: **Crizotinib** (ALK inhibitor) + chemotherapy

### Extranodal NK/T-cell Lymphoma, Nasal Type
- Previously called **lethal midline granuloma**
- Adults with **destructive extranodal masses** — commonly **sinonasal**; sometimes testis
- Tumour cells **surround and invade small vessels** → extensive **ischaemic necrosis**
- Markers: NK markers **CD16+, CD56+**; lacks T-cell markers
- Associated with **EBV**

### Hepatosplenic T-cell Lymphoma
- Presents with hepatosplenomegaly
- Sinusoidal infiltration pattern
- Poor prognosis

---

# PART 2: HODGKIN LYMPHOMA (HL)

---

## INTRODUCTION
- First described by **Thomas Hodgkin in 1832**
- Distinct from NHL in: biology, morphology, immunophenotype, clinical features, treatment
- **B-cell origin** in virtually all cases
- ~**30% of all lymphomas**

---

## EPIDEMIOLOGY & ETIOLOGY
- **Unknown etiology** — infectious agents suspected
- **EBV genome** found in 20–40% of cases (LMP-1 upregulates NFκB)
- **Bimodal age distribution:** 15–34 years and >55 years
- Gender: **Males > Females** (×1.3–1.4)
- Race: Whites > Asians > Africans
- **Family history** in ~1%; siblings have 3–7× increased risk
- Immunodeficiency (congenital and acquired)
- **LMP-1** (EBV latent membrane protein I) → upregulates **NFκB** → lymphocyte activation → RS cell survival
- RS cells secrete cytokines (IL-5, IL-6, IL-13, TNF, GM-CSF) → recruit reactive cells → reactive infiltrate supports tumour growth

---

## WHO CLASSIFICATION OF HODGKIN LYMPHOMA

| Type | Frequency |
|---|---|
| **Classical HL (CHL)** | **95%** |
| — Nodular sclerosis | 60–80% |
| — Mixed cellularity | 20–25% |
| — Lymphocyte rich | 5% |
| — Lymphocyte depleted | <1% |
| **Nodular lymphocyte predominant HL (NLPHL)** | **5%** |

---

## REED-STERNBERG (RS) CELLS — ESSENTIAL FOR DIAGNOSIS

- **Diagnostic RS cell:** large (15–45μm); **multiple nuclei OR single nucleus with multiple lobes**; each lobe has **large inclusion-like nucleolus** (~size of a small lymphocyte, 5–7μm); abundant cytoplasm
- Must be present in **appropriate background** of non-neoplastic cells (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils)

### RS Cell Variants

| Variant | Description | Seen In |
|---|---|---|
| **Mononuclear (Hodgkin cell)** | Single round/oblong nucleus + large nucleolus | All classical HL |
| **Lacunar cell** | Delicate folded/multilobate nucleus; abundant pale cytoplasm; sits in artificial space ("lacuna") | **Nodular sclerosis** |
| **L&H cell (Popcorn cell)** | Polyloboid nucleus resembling **popcorn kernel**; inconspicuous nucleoli; moderate cytoplasm | **NLPHL** |

---

## CLINICAL FEATURES OF HL
- Localized to **single axial group of nodes** (cervical, mediastinal, para-aortic) at presentation
- **Orderly, contiguous spread:** nodal → splenic → hepatic → marrow → extranodal
- **Mesenteric nodes and Waldeyer's ring rarely involved** (opposite to NHL)
- **Extranodal involvement uncommon** (unlike NHL)
- May present: cough, chest pain, back pain, **pruritus**, **alcohol-induced pain** at nodal sites (classic HL symptom), hepatosplenomegaly, CNS symptoms
- Patients predisposed to **secondary malignancies** after therapy

---

## HL SUBTYPES — MUST KNOWS

### Nodular Lymphocyte Predominant HL (NLPHL)
- **5% of HL**; male predominant; age **30–50 years**
- Localized: cervical or axillary lymph nodes
- **B-cell neoplasm** — L&H (popcorn) cells are: **CD19+, CD20+, BCL6+, CD15−, CD30−, EBV−**
- Nodular proliferation with scattered **L&H cells** in background of small non-neoplastic lymphocytes
- **3–5% transform** to large B-cell lymphoma
- **Frequent relapses** but **good prognosis, rarely fatal**

---

### Nodular Sclerosis HL
- **Most common: 60–80% of HL**
- **Adolescents and young adults**; Stage I & II common
- **Mediastinal** involvement prominent
- **Lacunar variant** RS cells; **prominent bands of collagen/fibrosis**
- **Markers: CD15+, CD30+**, fascin, vimentin; **CD45−, EBV−**
- **Good prognosis**

---

### Mixed Cellularity HL
- **20–25% of HL**; **biphasic** age distribution: young + >55 years
- Common in **HIV-infected** and males
- Nodal effacement; **diffuse mixed infiltrate**; classical RS cells + mononuclear variants
- Involves abdominal nodes, spleen
- **Markers: CD15+, CD30+, EBV+ in 70%**
- >50% present at **Stage III or IV**
- **Poor prognosis**

---

### Lymphocyte Depleted HL
- **Rare: <1%**; common in **older males and HIV-infected**
- **Most advanced disease** at presentation
- Two variants: reticular (frequent RS cells) + diffuse fibrosis (hypocellular fibrillary background)
- **Markers: CD15+, CD30+, EBV+**
- **Worst prognosis**

---

### Lymphocyte Rich HL
- **5% of HL**; older adults; some cases nodular
- Frequent mononuclear + diagnostic RS cells in **T lymphocyte-rich background**
- **Markers: CD15+, CD30+, EBV+ in 40%; CD45−, CD20−**
- **Excellent prognosis**

---

## HL vs NHL — KEY DIFFERENCES

| Feature | Hodgkin Lymphoma | Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma |
|---|---|---|
| RS cells | **Present** | Absent |
| Spread | **Orderly, contiguous** | Irregular |
| Waldeyer's ring | Rarely involved | Commonly involved |
| Mesenteric nodes | Rarely involved | Commonly involved |
| Extranodal | Uncommon | **Common** |
| B symptoms | Common | Less common |
| Age | Bimodal (15–34, >55) | Older adults mainly |
| EBV association | 20–40% | Specific subtypes |
| Curability | **Highly curable** | Varies |

---

## STAGING (ANN ARBOR — BOTH HL AND NHL)

| Stage | Description |
|---|---|
| I | Single LN region or single extralymphatic site (IE) |
| II | ≥2 LN regions, same side of diaphragm ± extralymphatic (IIE) |
| III | Both sides of diaphragm ± spleen (IIIS) ± extralymphatic (IIIE) |
| IV | Disseminated extralymphatic involvement ± lymphatic |

- **A** = No B symptoms; **B** = Fever + night sweats + weight loss >10%
- **Stage IV** = bone marrow involvement → bilateral iliac crest biopsies essential

---

## QUICK COMPARISON — ALL SUBTYPES

| Subtype | Grade | Key Markers | Translocation | Hallmark | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Precursor B-ALL | High | TdT+, CD10+, CD19+ | t(12;21), t(9;22) | Children; pancytopenia | ALL protocols |
| SLL/CLL | Low | CD5+, CD23+, CD19+ | 13q del | Proliferation centres | Fludarabine ± Rituximab |
| Follicular | Low | BCL-2+, CD10+, BCL-6+ | **t(14;18)** | Watch & wait; 3%/yr transform | R-CVP; allo-SCT only cure |
| MALT | Low | CD20+ | t(11;18) | H. pylori → antibiotics | Antibiotics → chemo |
| LPL/Waldenström's | Low | IgM, MYD88 | — | Hyperviscosity | Rituximab + chemo; plasmapheresis |
| Mantle cell | Intermediate | CD5+, CyclinD1+, CD23− | **t(11;14)** | Angular nuclei; lymphomatoid polyposis | R-CHOP + Ibrutinib |
| DLBCL | High | BCL-6(GCB)/MUM1(ABC) | t(14;18)/t(3;14) | Most common NHL (37%) | **R-CHOP ×6–8** |
| Burkitt | High | CD10+, BCL2−, MYC | **t(8;14)** | Starry sky; >95% mitotic index | CODOX-M/IVAC |
| ALCL | High | CD30+, ALK+ | **t(2;5)** | Hallmark cells; children | Crizotinib |
| Mycosis fungoides | Low-Int | CD4+ | — | Skin plaques + pruritus; Pautrier abscesses | Phototherapy |
| Sézary syndrome | — | CD4+, cerebriform cells | — | Erythroderma + Sézary cells | PUVA |
| NLPHL | Low | CD20+, CD15−, CD30− | — | Popcorn cells; B-cell HL | Radiotherapy |
| NS-HL | — | CD15+, CD30+, EBV− | — | Lacunar cells; fibrosis; most common HL | ABVD |
| MC-HL | — | CD15+, CD30+, EBV+ 70% | — | Classical RS; HIV association | ABVD |

---

> ⚡ **EXAM TRIGGERS**
> - Jaw mass + African child + EBV + malaria → **Endemic Burkitt**
> - Watch and wait → **Follicular lymphoma (Stage II–IV, asymptomatic)**
> - H. pylori → antibiotics first → **Gastric MALT** (unless t(11;18) or t(1;14))
> - Skin plaques + pruritus → **Mycosis fungoides**
> - Erythroderma + cerebriform cells → **Sézary syndrome**
> - IgM + hyperviscosity → **Waldenström's** → plasmapheresis
> - CD5+ but CD23− + CyclinD1+ → **Mantle cell** (not CLL)
> - TdT+ lymphoma → **Lymphoblastic lymphoma / ALL**
> - Popcorn cells + CD15−/CD30− → **NLPHL**
> - Lacunar cells + fibrosis + mediastinum → **Nodular Sclerosis HL**
> - Alcohol-induced pain at lymph node sites → **Hodgkin Lymphoma**
> - Orderly spread + RS cells → **Hodgkin Lymphoma**
> - Flower/clover-leaf cells + hypercalcaemia + HTLV-1 → **Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma**
> - Horseshoe nuclei (hallmark cells) + CD30+ + child → **ALCL**
> - t(14;18) = Follicular | t(11;14) = Mantle cell | t(8;14) = Burkitt | t(2;5) = ALCL | t(9;22) = worst prognosis ALL

articles.content:
## Overview & Epidemiology
Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL) is a diverse group of clonal lymphoid tumors. Approximately 85% are of B-cell origin, while 15% arise from T or NK cells. It is the fifth most common malignancy in developed countries, with a rising incidence over the last 50 years. Unlike Hodgkin lymphoma, NHL is characterized by irregular spread, variable natural history, and significant extranodal involvement.

## WHO Classification
Classification is based on histology, immunophenotype, genotype, age, and site of origin.

### B-cell Subtypes (85%)
- Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL): 37%
- Follicular lymphoma: 29%
- CLL/SLL: 12%
- MALT lymphoma: 9%
- Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL): 7%
- Burkitt lymphoma, Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, Hairy cell leukaemia.

### T/NK-cell Subtypes (15%)
- Adult T-cell lymphoma/leukaemia (HTLV-1 associated)
- Mycosis fungoides / Sézary syndrome
- Anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALK+)
- Peripheral T-cell lymphoma

## Grading: Low-Grade vs. High-Grade
| Feature | Low-Grade (Indolent) | High-Grade (Aggressive) |
|---|---|---|
| Course | Slow-growing | Rapidly progressive |
| Examples | Follicular, MALT, SLL | DLBCL, Burkitt, Lymphoblastic |
| Curability | Difficult to cure | More often curable |
| Urgency | Watch and wait often acceptable | Urgent treatment required |

## Pathogenesis & Etiology
- **Chromosomal Translocations**: Often involve Immunoglobulin (Ig) genes on chromosomes 2, 14, or 22, leading to oncogene overexpression (e.g., BCL-2, MYC).
- **Infectious Associations**:
  - EBV: Burkitt lymphoma, PTLD.
  - HTLV-1: Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.
  - HHV-8: Primary effusion lymphoma.
  - H. pylori: Gastric MALT lymphoma.
  - Hepatitis C: Marginal zone lymphoma.
  - HIV-1: High-grade B-cell and CNS lymphomas.

## Clinical Features
1. **Lymphadenopathy**: Asymmetric, painless, superficial nodes (most common).
2. **B Symptoms**: Fever, night sweats, weight loss (indicates disseminated disease).
3. **Extranodal Disease**: GI tract (most common site after bone marrow), Waldeyer’s ring (oropharyngeal), skin, brain, and testis.
4. **Cytopenias**: Due to bone marrow involvement or splenic sequestration.

## Investigations
- **Biopsy (Gold Standard)**: Trucut or whole lymph node biopsy. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) is insufficient for architecture.
- **Immunophenotyping**: Confirms clonality via light chain restriction (kappa/lambda).
- **Laboratory**: FBC, LDH (prognostic marker for tumor burden), Uric acid, HIV status.
- **Imaging**: PET/CT for staging (Ann Arbor System) and monitoring response.

## Key Cytogenetics
- **Follicular**: t(14;18); BCL-2 overexpression.
- **Mantle Cell**: t(11;14); Cyclin D1 overexpression.
- **Burkitt**: t(8;14); MYC overexpression.
- **Anaplastic Large Cell (ALCL)**: t(2;5); ALK overexpression.

## Treatment Principles
- **Chemotherapy**: R-CHOP is the standard for DLBCL.
- **Monoclonal Antibodies**: Anti-CD20 (Rituximab) for B-cell NHL; Anti-CD30 (Brentuximab) for ALCL.
- **Targeted Therapy**: Ibrutinib (BTK inhibitor), Venetoclax (BCL-2 inhibitor), Idelalisib (PI3K inhibitor).
- **Specific Management**:
  - **Gastric MALT**: H. pylori eradication (antibiotics).
  - **Burkitt**: Intensive regimens (e.g., CODOX-M/IVAC) + CNS prophylaxis.
  - **Waldenström’s**: Plasmapheresis for acute hyperviscosity.
articles.original_notes:
# NON-HODGKIN LYMPHOMA (NHL) — MUST KNOWS

---

## OVERVIEW & EPIDEMIOLOGY
- Large group of **clonal lymphoid tumours** — **85% B-cell, 15% T/NK-cell** origin
- Incidence: ~**17/100,000** — 5th most common malignancy in developed countries
- Incidence has **markedly increased** over the last 50 years
- More **variable** presentation and natural history than Hodgkin lymphoma
- Characterized by **irregular spread** + significant **extranodal disease**
- Small numbers of malignant cells can circulate in blood in many NHL forms

---

## CLASSIFICATION (WHO)
Classified by: **histology + immunophenotype + genotype + age + site**

**B-cell (85%)** | **T/NK-cell (15%)**
---|---
CLL/SLL | Adult T-cell lymphoma/leukaemia (HTLV-1)
Follicular lymphoma | Mycosis fungoides
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) | Sézary syndrome
Mantle cell lymphoma | Anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALK+)
Burkitt lymphoma | Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma
MALT lymphoma | Peripheral T-cell lymphoma
Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma | Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma
Hairy cell leukaemia | Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type

> **Frequency of B-cell subtypes:** DLBCL 37% > Follicular 29% > CLL/SLL 12% > MALT 9% > MCL 7%

---

## CELL OF ORIGIN — KEY CONCEPT
- B-cell lymphomas **mimic normal B cells at different developmental stages**
- Divided into: precursor B-cell tumours (bone marrow) vs germinal centre/post-GC tumours (lymph nodes)
- **Unmutated Ig genes** → Mantle cell lymphoma, some B-CLL
- **Mutated Ig genes** → Marginal zone, DLBCL, Follicular, Lymphoplasmacytic, some B-CLL
- T-cell lymphomas mimic precursor T cells (bone marrow/thymus) or peripheral mature T cells

---

## LOW-GRADE vs HIGH-GRADE

| Feature | Low-Grade | High-Grade |
|---|---|---|
| Course | Indolent, slow-growing | Aggressive, rapidly fatal |
| Chemo response | Good | Good |
| Curability | **Difficult to cure** | **More often curable** |
| Urgency | Watch and wait acceptable | **Urgent treatment needed** |
| Examples | Follicular, MALT, SLL | DLBCL, Burkitt, Lymphoblastic |

---

## PATHOGENESIS
- Cause **unknown** in majority — infectious agents important in specific subtypes
- Chromosomal translocations involving **Ig genes on chromosomes 2, 14, 22** → oncogene overexpression → altered cell cycle / failed apoptosis
- Up to **80 somatic mutations** may be present at diagnosis

### Infections Associated with NHL

| Infectious Agent | Associated Lymphoma |
|---|---|
| **HTLV-1** | Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma |
| **EBV** | Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, PTLD |
| **HHV-8** | Primary effusion lymphoma, Castleman's disease |
| **HIV-1** | High-grade B-cell lymphoma, CNS lymphoma, Hodgkin |
| **Hepatitis C** | Marginal zone lymphoma |
| **H. pylori** | Gastric MALT lymphoma |
| **Malaria** (protozoa) | Burkitt lymphoma (endemic) |

---

## CLINICAL FEATURES
1. **Superficial lymphadenopathy** — asymmetric, **painless** — most common presentation
2. **Constitutional (B) symptoms** — fever, night sweats, weight loss — less common than Hodgkin; indicate disseminated disease
3. **Oropharyngeal** (5–10%) — Waldeyer's ring → sore throat, noisy/obstructed breathing
4. **Cytopenias** — anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia — from bone marrow involvement OR autoimmune OR splenic sequestration
5. **Abdominal disease** — hepatosplenomegaly; GI tract = **most common extranodal site after bone marrow** → acute abdomen possible
6. **Other organs** — skin, brain, testis, thyroid

---

## INVESTIGATIONS

### Gold Standard
- **Trucut / whole lymph node biopsy** — definitive
- ⚠️ Fine needle aspiration is **NOT sufficient** — biopsy must be obtained
- Immunophenotyping: **κ or λ light chain expression** confirms clonality (distinguishes from reactive node)

### Lab Tests
- FBC — anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia in advanced disease
- **Serum LDH** — raised in aggressive/extensive disease → key **prognostic marker**
- Serum uric acid — may be elevated
- Immunoglobulin electrophoresis — paraprotein
- **HIV status** — always test as indicated
- Bone marrow aspirate + **trephine biopsy**

### Imaging
- **PET/CT scan** — staging + monitoring treatment response
- Chest X-ray

### Key Cytogenetics & Mutations

| Lymphoma | Translocation | Effect / Mutation |
|---|---|---|
| Follicular lymphoma | **t(14;18)** | BCL-2 overexpression → ↓ apoptosis |
| Mantle cell lymphoma | **t(11;14)** | Cyclin D1 overexpression → cell cycle dysregulation |
| Burkitt lymphoma | **t(8;14)**, t(2;8), t(8;22) | MYC overexpression |
| DLBCL (GCB) | t(14;18) | CREBBP, EZH2, MYC mutations |
| DLBCL (ABC) | t(3;14) | NFκB pathway activation |
| MALT lymphoma | t(11;18), t(1;14) | NFκB pathway activation |
| ALCL | **t(2;5)** | ALK overexpression |
| Lymphoplasmacytic | Non-specific | **MYD88 mutation >90%** |
| Hairy cell leukaemia | Non-specific | **BRAF mutation >99%** |
| CLL | 13p, 11q, 17p deletions; trisomy 12 | TP53, ATM, NOTCH, SF3B1 |

### Immunophenotype Summary

| Lymphoma | SIg | CD20 | CD5 | CD10 | CD23 | BCL6 | MUM1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SLL/CLL | weak | + | **+** | – | **+** | – | – |
| Hairy cell leukaemia | + | + | – | – | – | – | – |
| Lymphoplasmacytic | + | + | – | – | – | – | + |
| MALT | + | + | – | – | +/– | – | +/– |
| **Follicular** | + | + | – | **+** | +/– | **+** | – |
| **Mantle cell** | + | + | **+** | – | – | – | – |
| DLBCL GCB | +/– | + | – | – | + | – | – |
| DLBCL ABC | +/– | + | – | – | – | – | + |
| Burkitt | + | + | – | **+** | – | + | – |

> 💡 **MCL vs CLL memory trick:** Both CD5+/CD19+ but MCL is CD22+/**CD23−** while CLL is CD23+

---

## STAGING
- Uses **Ann Arbor system** (same as Hodgkin — Stages I–IV)
- Less clearly related to prognosis than **histological subtype** in NHL
- Procedures: PET/CT, chest X-ray, bone marrow aspirate + trephine

### NCCN-IPI (for High-Grade NHL)
| Factor | Score |
|---|---|
| Age 40–60 | 1 |
| Age 60–75 | 2 |
| Age >75 | 3 |
| LDH 1–3× normal | 1 |
| LDH >3× normal | 2 |
| Stage III–IV | 1 |
| Extranodal disease (BM, CNS, liver/GI, lung) | 1 |
| Performance status ≥2 | 1 |

---

## TREATMENT PRINCIPLES
- **Combination chemotherapy + monoclonal antibody** is standard
- **Anti-CD20** (Rituximab, Ofatumumab, Obinutuzumab) — used in 85% of cases (B-cell NHL)
- **Anti-CD30** (Brentuximab) — Anaplastic large cell lymphoma + Hodgkin

### How Rituximab Works (3 mechanisms)
1. Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC)
2. Complement-mediated lysis
3. Direct apoptosis of target cell

### Targeted Agents
| Drug | Target | Used In |
|---|---|---|
| Ibrutinib | BTK inhibitor | B-CLL, MCL, LPL |
| Idelalisib | PI3K inhibitor | Follicular, CLL |
| Venetoclax | BCL-2 inhibitor | CLL, some NHL |
| Crizotinib | ALK inhibitor | ALCL |
| Bortezomib | Proteasome inhibitor | MCL, LPL |

---

## SPECIFIC SUBTYPES — MUST KNOWS

---

### 🔵 LOW-GRADE NHL

#### Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL)
- Identical to B-CLL but **<5×10⁹/L** peripheral B-cells and **no cytopenias**
- Difference is distribution: SLL = lymph node; CLL = bone marrow/blood
- Treat same as B-CLL

---

#### Lymphoplasmacytic Lymphoma / Waldenström's Macroglobulinaemia
- Mainly **men >50 years**
- Monoclonal **IgM paraprotein** → called Waldenström's when IgM present
- Origin: post-GC B cell with IgM-bearing memory B cell characteristics
- **MYD88 mutation in >90%** of cases — near-diagnostic

**Key Complications:**
- **Hyperviscosity syndrome** — IgM raises viscosity more than IgG/IgA (IgM mainly intravascular)
  - Visual disturbances (engorged retinal veins, haemorrhages, blurred disc)
  - Neurological symptoms, dyspnoea, heart failure
- **Anaemia** — usually significant
- **Bleeding tendency** — macroglobulin interferes with coagulation factors + platelets
- **Raynaud's phenomenon** — if IgM is a cryoglobulin

**Diagnosis:** Monoclonal serum IgM + BM/lymph node infiltration with lymphoplasmacytoid cells + MYD88 mutation + raised ESR

**Treatment:**
- Asymptomatic → **no treatment**
- Symptomatic → Rituximab + chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide / fludarabine / bendamustine / bortezomib)
- Refractory → **Ibrutinib**
- Acute hyperviscosity → **Plasmapheresis** (effective because IgM is intravascular)
- Chronic anaemia → Erythropoietin or transfusions

---

#### Marginal Zone Lymphomas
- Arise from **marginal zone B cells of germinal follicles**
- Mechanism: antigen/inflammation → lymphoid hyperplasia → secondary genetic damage → lymphoma
- Types: **Splenic, Nodal, MALT** (mucosa-associated)
- NFκB pathway mutations

**MALT Lymphoma:**
- Most common sites: **stomach** (most common), respiratory tract, skin, salivary glands
- Gastric MALT preceded by **H. pylori infection**
- Early stage → **antibiotics to eradicate H. pylori** can be curative
- Advanced → chemotherapy regimens as for follicular lymphoma

**Splenic Marginal Zone:**
- Presents as **splenomegaly** ± circulating 'villous' lymphocytes
- Stage Ia → **local radiotherapy** (potentially curative)
- Symptomatic → **splenectomy** useful

---

#### Follicular Lymphoma
- **~25% of all NHL** — most common low-grade NHL
- Median age: **60 years**
- **t(14;18)** → constitutive **BCL-2 expression** → reduced apoptosis
- Markers: CD10+, CD19+, CD20+, **BCL-2+, BCL-6+**
- Grading: I–III (by centrocyte:centroblast ratio) — **Grade IIIb = treat as DLBCL**

**Clinical:**
- Indolent; median survival **~10 years**
- Usually presents Stage III–IV (widespread painless lymphadenopathy)
- Bone marrow involvement frequent
- **Transformation rate: ~3% per year** to aggressive diffuse lymphoma
- Prognostic score: age + anaemia + LDH + disease burden

**Treatment:**
- Stage I → **radiotherapy** (potentially curative, ~10% of patients)
- Stage II–IV, asymptomatic → **"Watch and Wait"**
- Stage II–IV, symptomatic → **R-CVP** or R-bendamustine or R-chlorambucil (up to 90% response)
- Maintenance → Rituximab every 2–3 months
- Relapse → Rituximab + chemo → Autologous SCT
- Only cure = **Allogeneic SCT**
- New agents: Idelalisib (PI3K), Ibrutinib (BTK)

---

### 🔴 HIGH-GRADE NHL

#### Mantle Cell Lymphoma
- Origin: **pre-GC cells** in primary follicles / mantle zone of secondary follicles
- **t(11;14)** → Cyclin D1 overexpression → cell cycle dysregulation — **required for diagnosis**
- Phenotype: CD19+, **CD5+** (like CLL), but **CD22+, CD23−** (unlike CLL)
- Cells have **angular nuclei ('centrocytes')** on histology; often circulate in blood
- ATM, TP53, chromatin modification mutations also common
- Presents: lymphadenopathy + frequent bone marrow infiltration

**Treatment:**
- R-CHOP / bendamustine combinations / bortezomib / lenalidomide
- **Ibrutinib** — very effective in relapsed/early disease
- Autologous or allogeneic SCT
- Prognosis generally poor; 15% have indolent CLL-like course

---

#### Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL)
- **Most common NHL subtype (37%)**
- Classic high-grade lymphoma — large cells with **prominent nucleoli** on biopsy
- Two subtypes:
  - **GCB (germinal centre B-cell)** — BCL-6+, better prognosis
  - **ABC (activated B-cell)** — MUM1+, **worse prognosis**
- Common cytogenetics: IGH locus (chr 14), BCL-6 (chr 3q27), BCL-2 translocation in 20%

**Poor prognostic factors (IPI):** Age, performance status, Stage III/IV, extranodal sites >1, high LDH, bulky disease >5cm, HIV+, ABC subtype, prior low-grade lymphoma

**Treatment:**
- **R-CHOP** (Rituximab + Cyclophosphamide + Hydroxydaunorubicin + Vincristine/Oncovin + Prednisolone)
- 3-weekly cycles × **6–8 courses** + G-CSF support
- Localized → **3× R-CHOP + radiotherapy**
- CNS prophylaxis: intrathecal or high-dose methotrexate (high-risk patients)
- Monitor: repeat PET/CT mid-treatment + post-treatment
- Relapse → **R-ICE** (Rituximab + Ifosfamide + Carboplatin + Etoposide) → Autologous SCT
- **Overall long-term survival: ~65%** (>50% cured)

---

#### Burkitt Lymphoma
- One of the **most highly proliferative tumours** — mitotic index **>95%**
- MYC oncogene overexpressed: **t(8;14)** [most common], t(2;8), t(8;22)
- MYC translocated to Ig heavy-chain gene → expressed during phases it should be OFF

**Two Forms:**
| | Endemic (African) | Sporadic |
|---|---|---|
| Geography | Sub-Saharan Africa | Worldwide |
| EBV association | **Nearly 100%** | ~20% |
| Co-factor | **Chronic malaria** | — |
| Presentation | **Jaw mass** (mandible), child | Abdominal mass |
| HIV association | No | Increased incidence |

**Histology:** Sheets of lymphoblasts + **'starry sky' tingible-body macrophages**

**Treatment:**
- Aggressive chemo: **CODOX-M/IVAC** (methotrexate, cytosine arabinoside, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, ifosfamide, etoposide)
- Intrathecal chemotherapy also given
- Initially very responsive to chemo; **prognosis excellent** with aggressive regimens

---

#### Primary CNS Lymphoma
- Rare; more common in **elderly + HIV+ patients**
- Treatment: **high-dose methotrexate + cytosine arabinoside** ± whole brain radiotherapy
- ⚠️ Long-term **cognitive dysfunction** is a major concern

---

#### Lymphoblastic Lymphoma
- B or T-cell; mainly **children and young adults**
- Clinically and morphologically overlaps with **ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukaemia)**
- Unique feature: cells are **terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) positive** — negative in all other NHL
- Treated with **ALL-type protocols**

---

### 🟣 T-CELL LYMPHOMAS

#### Peripheral T-cell Lymphoma (unspecified)
- Heterogeneous group; usually **CD4+** phenotype
- Treatment: CHOP chemotherapy
- Poor prognosis; autografting for chemo-sensitive disease

#### Angioimmunoblastic Lymphadenopathy
- Elderly patients
- Features: lymphadenopathy + hepatosplenomegaly + **skin rashes** + **polyclonal ↑ IgG**
- Treatment: chemotherapy or **histone deacetylase inhibitors**

#### Mycosis Fungoides
- Chronic **cutaneous** T-cell lymphoma
- Presents: severe **pruritus + psoriasis-like skin lesions**
- Late stage: lymph nodes, spleen, liver, bone marrow affected
- Treatment: **phototherapy** or chemotherapy

#### Sézary Syndrome
- Features: dermatitis + **erythroderma** + lymphadenopathy + circulating T-lymphoma cells
- Cells: **CD4+** with **cerebriform (folded) nuclear chromatin** — pathognomonic
- Treatment: local irradiation, topical chemotherapy, **PUVA** (psoralen + UV light)
- CHOP rarely effective long-term

#### Adult T-cell Leukaemia/Lymphoma
- Associated with **HTLV-1** virus infection

#### Enteropathy-Associated T-cell Lymphoma (EATL)
- Associated with **coeliac disease**
- Very poor response to treatment

#### Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL)
- Common in **children**; usually T-cell phenotype
- Markers: **CD30+**; **t(2;5)** → **ALK overexpression**
- ALK-positive = better prognosis; **ALK-negative = worse prognosis**
- Aggressive course: systemic symptoms + extranodal involvement
- Treatment: **Crizotinib** (specific ALK inhibitor) + chemotherapy

---

## QUICK COMPARISON TABLE — HIGH-YIELD

| Subtype | Grade | Key Marker | Translocation | Hallmark | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SLL | Low | CD5+, CD23+ | — | = CLL but nodal | As CLL |
| Follicular | Low | BCL-2+, CD10+ | **t(14;18)** | Watch & wait; transforms 3%/yr | R-CVP; allo-SCT only cure |
| MALT | Low | CD20+ | t(11;18) | H. pylori → antibiotics | Antibiotics → chemo |
| Mantle cell | Intermediate | CD5+, CyclinD1+ | **t(11;14)** | Angular nuclei; CD23− | R-CHOP + Ibrutinib |
| DLBCL | High | BCL-6 (GCB) / MUM1 (ABC) | t(14;18)/t(3;14) | Most common NHL | **R-CHOP ×6–8** |
| Burkitt | High | CD10+, MYC | **t(8;14)** | >95% proliferative index; starry sky | CODOX-M/IVAC |
| ALCL | High | CD30+, ALK+ | **t(2;5)** | Children; extranodal | Crizotinib |
| Mycosis fungoides | Low-Int | CD4+ | — | Skin pruritus + plaques | Phototherapy |
| Sézary syndrome | — | CD4+, cerebriform cells | — | Erythroderma | PUVA |
| Lymphoblastic | High | TdT+ | — | Overlaps with ALL | ALL protocols |
| LPL/Waldenström's | Low | IgM paraprotein, MYD88 | — | Hyperviscosity | Rituximab + chemo; plasmapheresis |

---

> ⚡ **Exam Triggers to Remember:**
> - Jaw mass in African child + EBV + malaria area → **Burkitt lymphoma**
> - Watch and wait strategy → **Follicular lymphoma (Stage II–IV, asymptomatic)**
> - H. pylori → antibiotics first → **Gastric MALT**
> - Skin plaques + pruritus → **Mycosis fungoides**
> - Erythroderma + cerebriform cells → **Sézary syndrome**
> - IgM paraprotein + hyperviscosity → **Waldenström's**
> - CD5+ but CD23− → **Mantle cell** (not CLL)
> - TdT positive lymphoma → **Lymphoblastic lymphoma**
> - t(14;18) = Follicular | t(11;14) = Mantle cell | t(8;14) = Burkitt | t(2;5) = ALCL

articles.content:
## Summary
This article provides an exam-focused overview of common and high-yield gastrointestinal tumours, covering the oesophagus, stomach, and colon/appendix. It emphasizes key clinical features, risk factors, pathogenesis, histological differentiators, and genetic pathways crucial for understanding disease progression and diagnosis. Special attention is given to distinguishing features, common precursors, and prognostic indicators to aid in effective study for medical examinations.

## Key Points
- **Oesophageal Adenocarcinoma**: Arises in the distal 1/3 of the oesophagus, strongly linked to Barrett oesophagus (columnar metaplasia due to chronic GERD) and TP53 mutations. Predominant in white males in Western countries.
- **Oesophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)**: Typically affects the middle 1/3 of the oesophagus. Key risk factors are synergistic alcohol and tobacco use. Associated with squamous dysplasia and potentially HPV in high-risk regions.
- **Gastric Adenocarcinoma**: Classified as intestinal or diffuse type. The diffuse type is characterized by signet ring cells and linitis plastica ("leather bottle stomach"). *H. pylori* infection is a major risk factor for both types.
- **Gastric MALT Lymphoma**: A primary gastric lymphoma developing in response to chronic *H. pylori* gastritis. Early-stage disease often regresses with *H. pylori* eradication.
- **Carcinoid Tumours**: Neuroendocrine tumours most common in the GIT, especially the small intestine (most aggressive) and appendix (almost always benign). Carcinoid syndrome occurs with liver metastases.
- **Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumour (GIST)**: The most common mesenchymal tumour of the abdomen, primarily in the stomach. Arises from Interstitial Cells of Cajal with activating mutations in *c-KIT* or *PDGFRA*, responsive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors like Imatinib.
- **Colorectal Adenomas**: Premalignant neoplastic polyps characterized by cytologic dysplasia. Sessile serrated adenomas lack dysplasia but are also premalignant.
- **Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)**: Autosomal dominant condition due to an *APC* gene mutation, leading to >100 adenomatous polyps and near-certain colorectal cancer by age 30 if untreated. Represents the chromosomal instability pathway.
- **Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC/Lynch Syndrome)**: Caused by defects in DNA mismatch repair genes (*MLH1*, *MSH2*). Characterized by fewer polyps than FAP but an increased risk of colorectal and extracolonic cancers via the microsatellite instability pathway.
- **Colorectal Cancer Prognosis**: Primarily determined by the depth of invasion (T stage) and the presence or absence of lymph node metastases (N stage).
- **Pseudomyxoma Peritonei**: A severe complication of mucin-producing appendiceal tumours, leading to the abdomen filling with tenacious mucin, managed by debulking but ultimately fatal.

## Detailed Notes

### I. OESOPHAGUS

**1. Oesophageal Adenocarcinoma**
This rapidly increasing cancer primarily affects white males in Western countries. Its development is a classic example of metaplasia-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence:
*   **Pathogenesis**: Chronic GERD leads to **Barrett oesophagus** (intestinal metaplasia of squamous epithelium). Accumulation of genetic (e.g., *TP53* mutation) and epigenetic changes drives progression through low-grade and high-grade dysplasia to invasive adenocarcinoma.
*   **Morphology**: Typically located in the **distal 1/3** of the oesophagus, often invading the gastric cardia. Microscopically, it's a mucin-producing, gland-forming tumour, frequently with adjacent Barrett oesophagus.

**2. Oesophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)**
More common in adults >45, especially African Americans and in specific high-incidence regions globally.
*   **Risk Factors**: Alcohol and tobacco use are **synergistic**. Other risks include poverty, nutritional deficiencies, caustic injury, achalasia, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, very hot beverages, and, in high-risk regions, HPV.
*   **Pathogenesis**: Progression from normal squamous epithelium through squamous dysplasia (an in situ lesion) to invasive SCC.
*   **Morphology**: Most often found in the **middle 1/3** of the oesophagus. Early lesions are plaque-like; later stages can be polypoid, ulcerated, or diffusely infiltrative. Microscopic features include squamous differentiation.
*   **Spread**: Rich submucosal lymphatics allow for widespread local and longitudinal spread, including "skip lesions." Lymph node metastasis patterns vary by location: upper 1/3 to cervical nodes, middle 1/3 to mediastinal nodes, lower 1/3 to gastric/coeliac nodes. Local invasion can lead to tracheoesophageal fistulas (aspiration pneumonia) or aortic haemorrhage.

**Clinical Features (Both Oesophageal Tumours)**
Symptoms like progressive dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, and haemorrhage usually indicate advanced disease. Tracheoesophageal fistulas can present with aspiration.

**High-Yield Differentiators: Adenocarcinoma vs SCC**
| Feature        | Adenocarcinoma       | SCC                   |
|----------------|----------------------|-----------------------|
| Location       | Distal 1/3           | Middle 1/3            |
| Precursor      | Barrett oesophagus   | Squamous dysplasia    |
| Key Risk       | GERD, obesity, tobacco | Alcohol, tobacco, poverty |
| Demographics   | White males, Western | African Americans, rural/developing |
| Microscopy     | Glands, mucin        | Squamous differentiation |

### II. STOMACH

**3. Gastric Polyps**
*   **Inflammatory & Hyperplastic Polyps**: Reactive lesions associated with chronic gastritis. Malignant risk increases with size but is generally low.
*   **Gastric Adenomas**: True premalignant lesions arising in chronic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia. Require complete excision and surveillance.

**4. Gastric Adenocarcinoma**
Incidence varies geographically and is higher in lower socioeconomic groups.
*   **Aetiology**: *H. pylori* infection is the most common cause, along with chronic atrophic gastritis and EBV.
*   **Histologic Types**:
    *   **Intestinal Type**: Bulky, discrete, gland-forming masses, often ulcerated.
    *   **Diffuse Type**: Poorly cohesive, infiltrative growth of **signet ring cells** (mucin-filled cells with peripherally displaced nuclei). This leads to marked thickening of the gastric wall without a discrete mass, a condition known as **linitis plastica** ("leather bottle stomach").

**5. Gastric MALT Lymphoma**
*   This primary gastric lymphoma originates from MALT, which is typically absent in the stomach but develops in response to **chronic *H. pylori* gastritis**.
*   Crucially, eradication of *H. pylori* can lead to tumour regression in early-stage disease.

**6. Carcinoid Tumours**
*   Arise from neuroendocrine cells throughout the GIT.
*   **Prognosis by Location**: Small intestine carcinoids are generally the most aggressive, while appendix carcinoids are almost always benign, often discovered incidentally.
*   **Carcinoid Syndrome**: A paraneoplastic syndrome occurring when vasoactive substances produced by the tumour bypass hepatic metabolism, typically due to **liver metastases**. Symptoms include cutaneous flushing, sweating, bronchospasm, colicky abdominal pain, diarrhea, and right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis.

**7. Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumour (GIST)**
*   The most common mesenchymal tumour of the abdomen, predominantly found in the stomach.
*   Arises from the **Interstitial Cells of Cajal** (GIT pacemaker cells).
*   Driven by activating mutations in receptor tyrosine kinases, primarily **c-KIT** or **PDGFRA**.
*   **Treatment**: Responds well to **tyrosine kinase inhibitors** like Imatinib.

### III. COLON

**8. Colorectal Polyps**
*   **Non-Neoplastic**:
    *   **Hyperplastic Polyps**: Benign epithelial proliferations, usually in the left colon/rectum. **No malignant potential**; important to differentiate from sessile serrated adenomas.
    *   Inflammatory, Hamartomatous (e.g., Peutz-Jeghers).
*   **Neoplastic (Adenomas)**: Precursors to colorectal adenocarcinoma. Hallmark is **cytologic dysplasia**. **Sessile serrated adenomas**, despite lacking overt cytologic dysplasia, are also considered premalignant.

**9. Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)**
*   An autosomal dominant syndrome caused by a germline mutation in the **APC gene** (tumour suppressor, chromosome 5).
*   Defined by the presence of **>100 adenomatous polyps** in the colon.
*   Colorectal cancer is almost certain by age 30 if untreated. This represents the **chromosomal instability (CIN) pathway**.

**10. Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC / Lynch Syndrome)**
*   Autosomal dominant condition resulting from mutations in **DNA mismatch repair genes** (e.g., *MLH1, MSH2*).
*   Characterized by fewer polyps than FAP. Cancer develops earlier than sporadic CRC but typically later than FAP.
*   This condition exemplifies the **microsatellite instability (MSI) pathway**.

**High-Yield Differentiators: FAP vs HNPCC**
| Feature           | FAP                                | HNPCC (Lynch Syndrome)              |
|-------------------|------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Gene Mutation     | APC                                | Mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2)  |
| Polyp Number      | >100 adenomatous polyps            | Few adenomas, but increased CRC risk |
| Cancer Age        | Near 100% CRC by age 30 (if untreated) | Earlier than sporadic, later than FAP |
| Pathway           | Chromosomal Instability (CIN)      | Microsatellite Instability (MSI)    |

**11. Colorectal Adenocarcinoma**
*   The vast majority of colonic cancers are adenocarcinomas, with both CIN and MSI pathways contributing to sporadic cases.
*   **Most Important Prognostic Factors**: **Depth of invasion** (T stage) and **presence/absence of lymph node metastases** (N stage).

### IV. APPENDIX

**12. Appendix Tumours**
*   **Carcinoid Tumour**: The **most common appendix tumour**. Usually an incidental, benign finding at the distal tip of the appendix. Rarely metastasizes.
*   **Adenocarcinoma of the Appendix**: Less common but can invade through the wall, leading to **intraperitoneal seeding**. In women, these implants may **mimic mucinous ovarian tumours**.
*   **Pseudomyxoma Peritonei**: The most advanced complication of mucin-producing appendiceal tumours. The abdomen fills with tenacious, semisolid mucin, requiring repeated debulking. Although it can be managed for years, it is **ultimately fatal** in most cases.

## Practice Questions
1.  A 55-year-old white male presents with progressive dysphagia for solids. Endoscopy reveals an ulcerated mass in the distal oesophagus and biopsies show columnar metaplasia adjacent to adenocarcinoma. What is the most likely precursor condition? → Barrett oesophagus.
2.  Which oesophageal cancer is strongly associated with synergistic alcohol and tobacco use and typically affects the middle 1/3 of the oesophagus? → Oesophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
3.  A gastric biopsy from a patient with chronic *H. pylori* gastritis shows a lymphoid infiltrate suggesting lymphoma. What type of gastric lymphoma is most likely, and what is its initial management strategy? → Gastric MALT Lymphoma; *H. pylori* eradication.
4.  A patient with diffuse thickening of the gastric wall, described as "linitis plastica," is diagnosed with gastric adenocarcinoma. Which histological subtype is most likely responsible for this gross appearance? → Diffuse type with signet ring cells.
5.  A patient develops episodic flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm. Imaging reveals liver metastases from a primary small bowel tumour. What is the most likely diagnosis for the primary tumour? → Carcinoid tumour.
6.  A 60-year-old presents with abdominal pain. Imaging reveals a large gastric mass. Biopsy confirms a mesenchymal tumour. Genetic testing shows an activating mutation in *c-KIT*. What is the most effective targeted therapy for this tumour? → Imatinib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor).
7.  A 25-year-old is diagnosed with hundreds of adenomatous polyps in the colon. His family history includes early-onset colorectal cancer. Which genetic mutation is most likely present? → *APC* gene mutation.
8.  Which two factors are the most important for determining the prognosis of colorectal adenocarcinoma? → Depth of invasion (T stage) and presence/absence of lymph node metastases (N stage).
9.  A woman undergoes appendectomy for suspected appendicitis. Pathology reveals an incidental carcinoid tumour at the distal tip. What is the typical malignant potential of such a tumour? → Almost always benign.
10. A patient presents with a massively distended abdomen filled with gelatinous material, confirmed to be mucin. This is a complication of a resected appendiceal tumour. What is this condition called? → Pseudomyxoma Peritonei.
articles.original_notes:
# TUMOURS OF THE GIT — Comprehensive Study Notes

---

## TUMOURS COVERED:
1. Oesophageal Adenocarcinoma
2. Oesophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)
3. Gastric Polyps (Inflammatory, Hyperplastic, Adenomas)
4. Gastric Adenocarcinoma
5. Gastric MALT Lymphoma
6. Carcinoid Tumours
7. Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumour (GIST)
8. Colorectal Polyps (Non-neoplastic & Neoplastic)
9. Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)
10. Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC)
11. Colorectal Adenocarcinoma
12. Appendix Tumours (Carcinoid, Adenocarcinoma, Pseudomyxoma Peritonei)

---

## I. OESOPHAGUS

---

### 1. Oesophageal Adenocarcinoma

**Who:** White males; 7× more common in men; highest in developed Western countries; one of the fastest-rising cancers in incidence

**Risk Factors:** Barrett oesophagus, chronic GERD, documented dysplasia, tobacco, obesity, radiation | **Protective:** fruits & vegetables

**Pathogenesis:**
```
Chronic GERD
     ↓
Barrett Metaplasia (intestinal metaplasia replaces squamous epithelium)
     ↓ (TP53 mutation + chromosomal abnormalities appear here)
Low-grade Dysplasia
     ↓
High-grade Dysplasia
     ↓
Invasive Adenocarcinoma
```
> Each step = accumulation of **genetic + epigenetic changes**. Epithelial clones from non-dysplastic Barrett persist and accumulate mutations over time.

**Morphology:**
- **Location:** Distal 1/3 of oesophagus; may invade gastric cardia
- **Gross:** Early = flat/raised patches → Late = exophytic mass OR ulcerated OR diffusely infiltrating
- **Microscopy:** Mucin-producing, gland-forming tumour; Barrett oesophagus present adjacent to tumour

---

### 2. Oesophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)

**Who:** Adults >45 yrs; males 4× more; 6× more in African Americans than whites (NOT fully explained by alcohol/tobacco); incidence varies >100-fold between countries

**High-incidence countries:** Iran, central China, Hong Kong, Argentina, Brazil, South Africa

**Risk Factors:** Alcohol + tobacco (**synergistic**), poverty, nutritional deficiencies, caustic oesophageal injury, achalasia, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, very hot beverages, mediastinal radiation, polycyclic hydrocarbons, nitrosamines, fungus-contaminated foods, HPV (high-risk regions only)

**Pathogenesis:**
```
Normal squamous epithelium
     ↓ (carcinogens, alcohol, tobacco, HPV)
Squamous Dysplasia (in situ lesion)
     ↓
Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma
```

**Morphology:**
- **Location:** Middle 1/3 of oesophagus (contrast: adenocarcinoma = distal 1/3)
- **Gross:** Early = small grey-white plaque-like thickenings → Later = polypoid/obstructing OR ulcerated OR diffusely infiltrative (wall thickening + luminal narrowing)
- **Microscopy:** Moderately to well differentiated; variants = verrucous, spindle cell, basaloid SCC
- **Invasion of surrounding structures:**
  - Respiratory tree → pneumonia
  - Aorta → catastrophic haemorrhage
  - Mediastinum + pericardium
- **Spread:** Rich submucosal lymphatics → circumferential + longitudinal spread; skip lesions (intramural nodules several cm from main mass)

**Lymph Node Metastases by Location:**
| Location | LN Spread |
|---|---|
| Upper 1/3 | Cervical nodes |
| Middle 1/3 | Mediastinal, paratracheal, tracheobronchial |
| Lower 1/3 | Gastric + coeliac nodes |

---

### Clinical Features — Both Oesophageal Tumours
- Dysphagia → Odynophagia → Obstruction → Weight loss → Haemorrhage → Sepsis
- First symptom may be aspiration of food via **tracheoesophageal fistula**
- Symptomatic tumours are generally **very large** at diagnosis

---

### Adenocarcinoma vs SCC ⭐
| Feature | Adenocarcinoma | SCC |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Distal 1/3 | Middle 1/3 |
| Precursor | Barrett oesophagus | Squamous dysplasia |
| Key mutation | TP53, chromosomal | Alcohol + tobacco |
| Demographics | White males, Western | African Americans, rural/developing |
| HPV | No | Yes (high-risk regions) |
| Microscopy | Glands + mucin | Squamous differentiation |

---

## II. STOMACH

---

### 3. Gastric Polyps

**Inflammatory & Hyperplastic Polyps:**
- Reactive lesions associated with **chronic gastritis**
- Risk of dysplasia increases with polyp **size**
- No significant malignant potential on their own

**Gastric Adenomas:**
- Arise in background of chronic gastritis + **intestinal metaplasia** + glandular (mucosal) atrophy
- **Premalignant** — adenocarcinoma frequently arises within them
- Require **complete excision + surveillance** for recurrence

---

### 4. Gastric Adenocarcinoma

**Who:** More common in lower socioeconomic groups; marked geographic variation

**Aetiology:** **H. pylori** (most common), chronic atrophic gastritis, EBV infection → multiple pathways of neoplastic transformation

**Two Major Histologic Types:**
| Feature | Intestinal Type | Diffuse Type |
|---|---|---|
| Growth | Bulky, discrete, may be ulcerated | Diffuse infiltration |
| Cells | Gland-forming | **Signet ring cells** |
| Wall | Discrete mass | Thickened → **Linitis Plastica** |

> **Linitis Plastica** = "leather bottle stomach" — diffuse signet ring cell infiltration thickens entire gastric wall without forming a discrete mass

**Classification:** Based on location + gross + histologic morphology

---

### 5. Gastric MALT Lymphoma

- Derived from **mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)**
- MALT is **not normally present** in the stomach — develops in response to **chronic H. pylori gastritis**
- H. pylori eradication → tumour regression in early-stage disease
- Most common **primary gastric lymphoma**

---

### 6. Carcinoid Tumours

- Arise from **diffuse neuroendocrine system** (enterochromaffin/APUD cells)
- Most common in the **GIT**, particularly the **small intestine**

**Prognosis by location:**
| Location | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Small intestine | Most **aggressive** |
| Appendix | Almost always **benign** |

**Carcinoid Syndrome** (occurs when liver mets are present — vasoactive substances bypass liver):
- Cutaneous flushing
- Sweating
- Bronchospasm
- Colicky abdominal pain
- Diarrhoea
- Right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis

---

### 7. Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumour (GIST)

- **Most common mesenchymal tumour** of the abdomen
- Most often located in the **stomach**
- Arises from **Interstitial Cells of Cajal** (pacemaker cells of the GIT)
- **Mutations:** Activating mutations in **c-KIT** or **PDGFRA** tyrosine kinases
- **Treatment:** Responds to **tyrosine kinase inhibitors** (e.g. Imatinib/Gleevec)

**Clinical Features (Stomach tumours generally):**
- Abdominal swelling + pain
- Vomiting
- Gastric outlet obstruction

---

## III. COLON

---

### 8. Colorectal Polyps

**Non-Neoplastic Polyps:**
| Type | Origin | Malignant Potential |
|---|---|---|
| Inflammatory | Chronic cycles of injury + healing | None |
| Hamartomatous | Sporadic or genetic (e.g. Peutz-Jeghers) | Some (when part of genetic syndrome) |
| Hyperplastic | Benign epithelial proliferation; left colon + rectum | **None** — must be distinguished from sessile serrated adenomas |

**Neoplastic Polyps (Adenomas):**
- Hallmark = **cytologic dysplasia**
- Precursors of colonic adenocarcinoma
- **Sessile serrated adenomas** = lack cytologic dysplasia but share morphology with hyperplastic polyps; still carry malignant potential

---

### 9. Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)

- **Gene:** **APC mutation** (tumour suppressor gene, chromosome 5)
- **Features:** >100 adenomatous polyps; colorectal cancer almost certain by age **30** if untreated
- **Pathway:** APC loss → uncontrolled cell proliferation → massive polyposis → carcinoma
- Represents the **chromosomal instability (CIN) pathway**

---

### 10. HNPCC — Lynch Syndrome

- **Gene:** **DNA mismatch repair genes** (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2)
- **Features:** Fewer polyps than FAP; cancer develops earlier than sporadic CRC but later than FAP
- **Pathway:** Defective mismatch repair → **microsatellite instability (MSI)** → carcinoma
- Represents the **microsatellite instability pathway**

**FAP vs HNPCC ⭐**
| Feature | FAP | HNPCC |
|---|---|---|
| Gene | APC | Mismatch repair genes |
| Polyp number | >100 | Few |
| Cancer age | <30 yrs | Older than FAP, younger than sporadic |
| Pathway | Chromosomal instability | Microsatellite instability |

---

### 11. Colorectal Adenocarcinoma

- Vast majority of colonic cancers are **adenocarcinomas**
- Both FAP and HNPCC pathways also contribute to **sporadic** colon cancer

**Two Most Important Prognostic Factors:**
1. **Depth of invasion** (T stage)
2. **Presence or absence of lymph node metastases** (N stage)

### 12. Appendix Tumours

**Carcinoid (Most Common Appendix Tumour):**
- Usually an **incidental** finding at surgery or on resected appendix
- Located at **distal tip** of appendix
- Forms solid bulbous swelling up to **2–3 cm**
- Intramural + transmural extension may occur but nodal mets very rare; distant spread exceptional
- **Almost always benign**

**Adenocarcinoma of the Appendix:**
- Invasion through appendiceal wall → **intraperitoneal seeding**
- In women, peritoneal implants may mimic **mucinous ovarian tumours**

**Pseudomyxoma Peritonei:**
- Most advanced complication of mucin-producing appendiceal tumours
- Abdomen fills with tenacious, semisolid **mucin**
- Managed by repeated **debulking**
- Disease may be held in check for years but is **ultimately fatal** in most cases

|---|---|---|

| Oesophageal SCC | Middle 1/3 | Alcohol + tobacco synergy; HPV in high-risk areas |

| Gastric MALT Lymphoma | Stomach | H. pylori induced; regresses with eradication |

| Carcinoid | Small intestine/Appendix | Carcinoid syndrome; appendix = benign |
| FAP | Colon | APC mutation; >100 polyps; cancer <30 yrs |
| HNPCC | Colon | Mismatch repair defect; microsatellite instability |
| Colorectal Adenocarcinoma | Colon | Depth + LN mets = prognosis |

| Pseudomyxoma Peritonei | Peritoneum | Mucin-filled abdomen; ultimately fatal |

- Linitis plastica = **signet ring cell diffuse infiltration** of gastric wall
- MALT lymphoma = **H. pylori** induced; eradication can cause regression
- GIST = **Interstitial cells of Cajal** + **c-KIT/PDGFRA** mutations + **Imatinib** treatment
- Carcinoid syndrome = **liver metastases** required (vasoactive substances bypass liver)
- Carcinoid: small intestine = **aggressive**; appendix = **benign**

- Sessile serrated adenomas = **no dysplasia** but still **premalignant**

- Pseudomyxoma peritonei = mucin-filled abdomen; **ultimately fatal**
