## Hodgkin Lymphoma

**Key concepts:** Reed-Sternberg cells · Subtypes · Pathogenesis · Staging · Clinical features · Prognosis

Hodgkin lymphoma is characterised by the presence of **Reed-Sternberg (RS) giant cells** — the neoplastic cell — which are typically vastly outnumbered by non-neoplastic inflammatory cells. Unlike most NHLs, it arises in a **single lymph node or chain** and spreads in a **stepwise, contiguous fashion** to anatomically adjacent nodes.

**Reed-Sternberg cell morphology** — very large cells (15–45 µm) with an enormous multilobate nucleus, exceptionally prominent nucleoli, and abundant slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm. The classic form has two mirror-image nuclear lobes each containing a large acidophilic nucleolus surrounded by a clear zone — the **"owl-eye" appearance.** RS cells express **CD15 and CD30** and fail to express CD45, B cell antigens, and T cell antigens.

**Origin of RS cells** — long mysterious, but molecular studies on single microdissected RS cells showed every RS cell in a given case carries identical immunoglobulin gene rearrangements that have undergone somatic hypermutation → Hodgkin lymphoma is a **neoplasm of germinal centre B cells** that has lost normal B cell gene expression programmes.

**EBV and pathogenesis** — EBV is present in RS cells in up to **70% of mixed-cellularity cases** and a smaller fraction of other classical subtypes. EBV genome integration is identical in all RS cells within a case, indicating infection precedes transformation. RS cells secrete several cytokines generating the characteristic inflammatory background: **IL-5** (attracts eosinophils), **TGF-β** (fibrogenic), and **IL-13** (may stimulate RS cells via autocrine loop). In turn, responding inflammatory cells produce CD30 ligand which aids RS cell growth and survival.

---

### Subtypes

**Nodular Sclerosis** — most common subtype; equally frequent in men and women; strong predilection for lower cervical, supraclavicular, and mediastinal lymph nodes; most patients are adolescents or young adults; overall prognosis excellent.
- Characteristic RS cell variant: **lacunar cell** — large cell with single multilobate nucleus, multiple small nucleoli, and abundant pale cytoplasm; in formalin-fixed tissue, cytoplasm retracts leaving nucleus in an empty space (lacune)
- Collagen bands divide involved lymphoid tissue into circumscribed nodules; fibrosis may be scant or abundant; cellular infiltrate contains lymphocytes, eosinophils, histiocytes, and lacunar cells

**Mixed Cellularity** — most common subtype in patients >50 years; comprises ~25% of all cases; male predominance. Classic RS cells are plentiful within a heterogeneous inflammatory infiltrate of small lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells, and macrophages. More likely to be disseminated and associated with systemic manifestations than nodular sclerosis.

**Lymphocyte-Rich** — abundant lymphocytes; rare RS cells; best prognosis among classical subtypes.

**Lymphocyte Depletion** — few lymphocytes; many RS cells or fibrosis; worst prognosis; often advanced stage at presentation.

**Lymphocyte Predominance** — accounts for ~5% of Hodgkin lymphoma; set apart as a distinct entity. Characteristic RS cell variant: **lymphohistiocytic (L&H) "popcorn cell"** — delicate multilobed puffy nucleus. L&H variants are found within large nodules of mainly small resting B cells with variable macrophages; eosinophils, neutrophils, and plasma cells are scanty or absent. Unlike classical RS cells, **L&H variants express CD20** and usually fail to express CD15 and CD30. Most patients present with isolated cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy; prognosis typically excellent.

⚠️ Histologic diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma **rests on definitive identification of RS cells or variants in the appropriate reactive background.** Immunophenotyping plays an important adjunct role — some forms closely mimic inflammatory reactive processes.

---

### Clinical Features and Staging

| Feature | Hodgkin Lymphoma | Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma |
|---------|-----------------|---------------------|
| Node involvement | Single axial group (cervical, mediastinal, para-aortic) | Multiple peripheral nodes |
| Spread | Orderly, contiguous | Noncontiguous |
| Mesenteric nodes / Waldeyer ring | Rarely involved | Commonly involved |
| Extranodal involvement | Uncommon | Common |

**Ann Arbor Staging:**

| Stage | Distribution |
|-------|-------------|
| I | Single lymph node region (I) or single extralymphatic organ (IE) |
| II | Two or more lymph node regions on same side of diaphragm (II) ± limited contiguous extralymphatic organ (IIE) |
| III | Lymph node regions on both sides of diaphragm (III) ± spleen (IIIS) ± extralymphatic organ (IIIE) |
| IV | Multiple or disseminated extralymphatic organ involvement ± lymphatic involvement |

All stages further divided: **A** (no systemic symptoms) vs **B** (fever, night sweats, unexplained >10% weight loss).

Younger patients with favourable subtypes tend to present at stage I or II without systemic symptoms. Advanced disease (stages III and IV) more likely to present with systemic complaints, fever, weight loss, pruritus, and anaemia.

**Treatment** — even stage I disease is now treated with systemic chemotherapy due to long-term complications of radiotherapy. Advanced disease is treated with chemotherapy ± involved-field radiotherapy at sites of bulky disease. **Anti-CD30 antibodies** have produced excellent responses in disease failing conventional therapy.

**Prognosis** — outcomes are very good even with advanced disease:
- Stage I-A or II-A → **~100% 5-year survival**
- Stage IV-A or IV-B → **~50% 5-year disease-free survival**

⚠️ Long-term survivors treated with radiotherapy have significantly higher risk of secondary malignancies including **lung cancer, melanoma, and breast cancer** — this has driven development of less toxic treatment regimens.

---

## Miscellaneous Lymphoid Neoplasms

**Conditions covered:** Extranodal Marginal Zone Lymphoma · Hairy Cell Leukaemia · Mycosis Fungoides & Sézary Syndrome · Adult T Cell Leukaemia/Lymphoma · Peripheral T Cell Lymphomas

---

### Extranodal Marginal Zone Lymphoma

Indolent B cell tumour arising most commonly in epithelial tissues — stomach, salivary glands, small and large bowel, lungs, orbit, and breast. Develops in the setting of **autoimmune disorders** (Sjögren syndrome, Hashimoto thyroiditis) or **chronic infection** (H. pylori gastritis) — sustained antigenic stimulation contributes to development.

In **H. pylori-associated gastric marginal zone lymphoma**, eradication of the organism with antibiotic therapy often leads to tumour regression — tumour cells depend on cytokines secreted by H. pylori-specific T cells for growth and survival. When arising at other sites, often cured by local excision or radiotherapy.

Most common recurrent genetic abnormality: **(11;18) translocation** involving MALT1 and IAP2 genes. Presence of t(11;18) is highly predictive of **failure to respond to antibiotic treatment** in gastric tumours — an important clinical point.

---

### Hairy Cell Leukaemia

Uncommon, indolent B cell neoplasm. Tumour cells have **fine hairlike cytoplasmic projections** and express pan-B cell markers (CD19, CD20), surface immunoglobulin, **CD11c and CD103** — the latter two antigens are diagnostically useful as they are absent from most other B cell tumours. Virtually all cases are associated with **activating mutations in BRAF** serine/threonine kinase (same mutation found in diverse other cancers including melanoma).

Occurs mainly in **older males**. Manifestations result from bone marrow and spleen infiltration. **Massive splenomegaly** is the most common and sometimes only physical finding. Pancytopenia occurs in >50% of cases from marrow infiltration and splenic sequestration. Lymphadenopathy is rare. Leukaemia is present in only 15–20% but scattered hairy cells can be identified on peripheral blood smear in most cases.

Indolent but progressive if untreated. Unlike most other indolent lymphoid neoplasms, this tumour is **extremely sensitive to purine nucleoside chemotherapy** → complete durable responses are the rule; overall prognosis is excellent.

---

### Mycosis Fungoides and Sézary Syndrome

Tumours of neoplastic **CD4+ T cells** that home to the skin — collectively called **cutaneous T cell lymphoma.**

**Mycosis fungoides** — usually manifests as a nonspecific erythrodermic rash → progresses to a **plaque phase** → then a **tumour phase.** Histologically, neoplastic T cells with **cerebriform nuclei** (produced by marked nuclear membrane infolding) infiltrate the epidermis and upper dermis (**Pautrier microabscesses**). With disease progression, nodal and visceral dissemination appears.

**Sézary syndrome** — clinical variant characterised by (1) generalised **exfoliative erythroderma** and (2) circulating tumour cells (**Sézary cells**) in the peripheral blood. Circulating tumour cells are also present in up to 25% of plaque- or tumour-phase mycosis fungoides.

**Prognosis** — patients with early-phase mycosis fungoides often survive many years; tumour-phase disease, visceral disease, or Sézary syndrome → average survival 1–3 years.

---

### Adult T Cell Leukaemia/Lymphoma

Neoplasm of **CD4+ T cells** caused by **HTLV-1** (human T cell leukaemia virus type 1), a retrovirus. HTLV-1 infection is endemic in southern Japan, the Caribbean basin, and West Africa; occurs sporadically elsewhere including southeastern United States. In addition to lymphoid malignancies, HTLV-1 can cause **transverse myelitis** — a progressive demyelinating disease of the CNS and spinal cord.

**Clinical features** — skin lesions, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, hypercalcaemia, and variable numbers of malignant lymphocytes in peripheral blood. Leukaemic cells express CD4 and high levels of **CD25** (IL-2 receptor α chain).

**Prognosis** — most cases are very aggressive and respond poorly to treatment; median survival ~8 months. In 15–20% of patients, disease follows a chronic course resembling mycosis fungoides.

---

### Peripheral T Cell Lymphomas

Heterogeneous group comprising **10–15% of adult NHLs.** Most tumours are unclassifiable. Generally aggressive and respond poorly to therapy. Because these are tumours of functional T cells, patients often suffer symptoms from **tumour-derived inflammatory products** even at low tumour burden.

---

## Myeloid Neoplasms

**Conditions covered:** Acute Myeloid Leukaemia · Myelodysplastic Syndromes · Chronic Myeloproliferative Disorders (CML · Polycythaemia Vera · Primary Myelofibrosis)

Three broad categories:
- **Acute myeloid leukaemias (AML)** — neoplastic cells blocked at an early stage of myeloid development; immature blasts accumulate in marrow and peripheral blood
- **Myeloproliferative disorders** — neoplastic clone retains terminal differentiation capacity; increased production of formed elements; commonly associated with activating tyrosine kinase mutations
- **Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS)** — terminal differentiation occurs but is disordered and ineffective; dysplastic marrow precursors + peripheral blood cytopenias

All myeloid neoplasms arise from early multipotent progenitors; myelodysplastic syndromes and myeloproliferative disorders both can transform to AML.

---

### Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML)

Primarily affects older adults; **median age 50 years.** Clinical signs and symptoms closely resemble ALL — fatigue, pallor, abnormal bleeding, and infections — usually presenting within weeks of symptom onset. Splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy are generally less prominent than in ALL. On rare occasions AML mimics a lymphoma by manifesting as a discrete tissue mass (**granulocytic sarcoma**).

**Pathogenesis** — most AMLs harbour mutations in genes encoding transcription factors required for normal myeloid cell differentiation → maturation arrest → accumulation of myeloid precursors (blasts). These mutations are not sufficient alone; complementary mutations that enhance proliferation and survival are also required. Examples include **FLT3** (receptor tyrosine kinase) activating mutations and RAS mutations.

**Morphology** — by definition, myeloid blasts or promyelocytes compose **>20% of bone marrow cellularity.** Myeloblasts have delicate nuclear chromatin, 3–5 nucleoli, and fine azurophilic cytoplasmic granules. **Auer rods** — distinctive red-staining rodlike structures — are specific for neoplastic myeloblasts and are a helpful diagnostic clue when present; particularly numerous in acute promyelocytic leukaemia.

**Acute Promyelocytic Leukaemia — a key subtype:**
- **(15;17) translocation** → fusion of RARA (chromosome 17) with PML (chromosome 15) → PML/RARα fusion protein → blocks myeloid differentiation at promyelocytic stage
- Pharmacologic doses of **all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA)** overcome the differentiation block → neoplastic promyelocytes rapidly differentiate into neutrophils → which die within 6 hours → tumour rapidly cleared
- Combination of **ATRA + arsenic trioxide** (which degrades the PML/RARα fusion protein) is even more effective → **cures >80% of patients**
- This is an important example of highly effective targeted therapy directed at a tumour-specific molecular defect
- AMLs without RARA translocations do NOT respond to ATRA

**WHO Classification of AML:**

| Class | Examples | Prognosis |
|-------|---------|-----------|
| AML with recurrent chromosomal translocations | t(8;21), inv(16) — favourable; t(15;17) — favourable; t(11q23) MLL fusions — poor | Varies |
| AML with multilineage dysplasia | With or without prior MDS | Very poor to poor |
| AML, therapy-related | Alkylating agent–related; epipodophyllotoxin-related | Very poor |
| AML, not otherwise classified | Subclassed by predominant differentiation | Intermediate |

**Immunophenotype** — most tumours express myeloid-associated antigens: CD13, CD14, CD15, CD64, CD117 (cKIT), and CD33. Useful in distinguishing AML from ALL.

**Prognosis** — devastating overall. Tumours with good-risk karyotypes [t(8;21), inv(16)] → ~50% long-term disease-free survival. Overall survival with conventional chemotherapy is only **15–30%.** Increasing use of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for eligible patients.

---

### Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS)

Bone marrow partly or wholly replaced by the clonal progeny of a transformed multipotent stem cell that retains capacity to differentiate into red cells, granulocytes, and platelets but in a **disordered and ineffective** manner. Marrow is usually **hypercellular or normocellular** but peripheral blood shows one or more **cytopenias** — a hallmark paradox. The abnormal clone is genetically unstable → prone to additional mutations → eventual transformation to AML.

Most cases are **idiopathic**; some develop after chemotherapy with alkylating agents or exposure to ionising radiation.

**Pathogenesis** — poorly understood. Clonal cytogenetic abnormalities in up to 70% of cases. Translocations are generally lacking; losses or gains of whole chromosomes or parts thereof are frequent. Common abnormalities: monosomy 5 or 7; deletions of 5q, 7q, and 20q; trisomy 8. The **5q− syndrome** — deletion of 5q containing genes encoding a ribosomal protein and several microRNAs — occurs more often in women, is associated with severe anaemia and preserved/elevated platelet counts, and often responds to thalidomide analogues.

**Morphology** — abnormal-appearing haematopoietic precursors including:
- Megaloblastoid erythroid precursors
- **Ringed sideroblasts** — erythroid forms with iron deposits within mitochondria
- Granulocyte precursors with abnormal granules or nuclear maturation
- Small megakaryocytes with single small nuclei or multiple separate nuclei

**Clinical features** — MDS is about as common as AML, affecting up to **15,000 patients per year** in the United States. Most patients are between 50 and 70 years. Cytopenias lead to infections, anaemia symptoms, and haemorrhage. Response to conventional chemotherapy is usually poor. Transformation to AML occurs in **10–40%.** Median survival ranges from 9–29 months; worse with increased marrow blasts or cytogenetic abnormalities at diagnosis.

---

### Chronic Myelogenous Leukaemia (CML)

Principally affects adults between **25 and 60 years**; peak incidence in the fourth and fifth decades. ~4,500 new cases per year in the United States.

**Pathogenesis** — CML is **always** associated with a **BCR-ABL fusion gene.** In ~95% of cases, this results from a balanced **(9;22) translocation** — the **Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome** — moving ABL from chromosome 9 to chromosome 22 adjacent to BCR. In remaining 5%, cytogenetically cryptic or complex rearrangements are responsible. The BCR-ABL fusion gene is present in granulocytic, erythroid, megakaryocytic, B cell, and sometimes T cell precursors → tumour arises from a transformed **haematopoietic stem cell.** Ph chromosome is also present in 25% of adult B cell ALLs and a small subset of AMLs.

BCR-ABL encodes a fusion tyrosine kinase that **constitutively activates growth factor signalling pathways** → greatly decreased growth factor dependence of CML progenitors. Importantly, BCR-ABL does **not** inhibit differentiation → early disease course marked by excessive haematopoiesis rather than blast accumulation.

**Morphology:**
- Peripheral blood: leukocyte count elevated, often exceeding **100,000 cells/µL;** predominantly neutrophils, metamyelocytes, and myelocytes; basophils and eosinophils prominent; platelets usually increased; myeloblasts usually <5%
- Bone marrow: hypercellular with increased granulocytic and megakaryocytic precursors
- Spleen: markedly enlarged from extensive **extramedullary haematopoiesis** resembling bone marrow in the red pulp; proliferation may compromise local blood supply → splenic infarcts

**Clinical features** — onset is often insidious with nonspecific symptoms (fatigue, weakness, weight loss) or a dragging sensation in the abdomen from splenomegaly. Distinguished from leukemoid reaction by testing for the **BCR-ABL fusion gene** (by karyotyping, FISH, or PCR).

**Natural history:**
- Initially slow progression; even without treatment, median survival is 3 years
- After a variable period, ~50% enter an **accelerated phase** → increasing anaemia, new thrombocytopenia, additional cytogenetic abnormalities → **blast crisis**
- In remaining 50%, blast crisis occurs abruptly without accelerated phase
- In 30% of blast crises, the picture resembles **precursor-B cell ALL** (attesting to stem cell origin); in 70%, it resembles AML
- Less commonly, CML progresses to extensive bone marrow fibrosis resembling primary myelofibrosis

**Treatment** — the natural history has been dramatically altered by **BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitors** (imatinib, nilotinib) → complete remission in a high fraction of patients with little toxicity. Treatment may prevent blast crisis by suppressing the proliferative drive that leads to acquisition of further mutations. Relapse is often due to **acquired mutations in the BCR-ABL kinase domain** that prevent drug binding — these mutations are present in small numbers of cells at diagnosis and are selected out by therapy. For resistant disease, **allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation** is curative in 70% but carries substantial risks, particularly in older patients.

---

### Polycythaemia Vera

Characterised by excessive proliferation of erythroid, granulocytic, and megakaryocytic elements (**panmyelosis**), but most clinical signs and symptoms are related to an **absolute increase in red cell mass.** Must be distinguished from relative polycythaemia (haemoconcentration). Associated with **low serum erythropoietin** — a reflection of growth factor-independent growth of the neoplastic clone.

**Pathogenesis** — caused by **activating mutations in JAK2** (a tyrosine kinase in signalling pathways downstream of the erythropoietin receptor and other growth factor receptors). The most common JAK2 mutation — **valine-to-phenylalanine substitution at residue 617 (V617F)** — sharply lowers dependence of haematopoietic cells on growth factors.

**Morphology:**
- Plethoric congestion of many tissues
- Liver enlarged with foci of extramedullary haematopoiesis
- Spleen slightly enlarged (~250–300 g) from vascular congestion
- Thromboses and infarctions common (especially heart, spleen, kidneys) from increased blood viscosity and vascular stasis
- Haemorrhages in ~one third of patients from excessive vessel distension and abnormal platelet function
- Bone marrow hypercellular with increased erythroid, myeloid, and megakaryocytic forms; marrow fibrosis in 10% at diagnosis

**Clinical course** — appears insidiously in **late middle age.** Patients are plethoric and often cyanotic. Histamine released from neoplastic basophils → **pruritus** and increased peptic ulceration. Headache, dizziness, GI symptoms, haematemesis, and melena are common. Thrombotic complications in ~30% (usually brain or heart); Budd-Chiari syndrome is uncommon but grave. Symptomatic **gout** in 5–10% from high cell turnover; hyperuricaemia more common.

**Lab findings** — red cell count 6–10 million/µL; haematocrit often **≥60%;** granulocyte count up to 50,000 cells/µL; platelet count often >400,000/µL; basophilia common; giant platelets and megakaryocyte fragments on blood smear.

**Prognosis** — without treatment, death from vascular complications within months. Median survival increased to **~10 years** by repeated phlebotomy to lower red cell count. After average of 10 years, **15–20%** undergo transformation to a "spent phase" resembling primary myelofibrosis with massive splenomegaly. Transformation to AML blast crisis is much less frequent than in CML. JAK2 inhibitors are currently in clinical trials.

---

### Primary Myelofibrosis

A "spent phase" of marrow fibrosis supervenes **early** in the disease course, often after a brief period of granulocytosis and thrombocytosis. As haematopoiesis shifts from the fibrotic marrow to the spleen, liver, and lymph nodes, **extreme splenomegaly and hepatomegaly** develop. Extramedullary haematopoiesis at these sites is disordered and inefficient → anaemia and thrombocytopenia.

**Pathogenesis** — the fibroblasts laying down collagen in the marrow are **not neoplastic.** Marrow fibrosis is secondary — stimulated by **platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) and TGF-β** released from neoplastic megakaryocytes. The same **JAK2 V617F mutation** found in polycythaemia vera is present in ~50% of cases (as it is in ~50% of essential thrombocythaemia cases) — emphasising the overlap between these entities. It is not yet understood why tumours with the same mutation produce such varied clinical pictures.

**Morphology:**
- Peripheral blood markedly abnormal — **leukoerythroblastosis:** bizarre-shaped red cells (poikilocytes, **teardrop cells/dacryocytes**), nucleated erythroid precursors, and immature white cells (myelocytes, metamyelocytes); abnormally large platelets
- Spleen markedly enlarged (sometimes up to 4,000 g) from extensive extramedullary haematopoiesis; subcapsular splenic infarcts common; megakaryocytes numerous and dysplastic
- Moderate hepatomegaly from extramedullary haematopoiesis
- Lymph nodes involved by extramedullary haematopoiesis but not to degree causing enlargement
- Bone marrow: hypocellular and diffusely fibrotic in advanced cases; hypercellular with only focal fibrosis early in the course; megakaryocytes consistently increased and dysplastic throughout

**Clinical course** — most patients present in the phase of marrow fibrosis. Early-stage disease may resemble CML, but the **Ph chromosome is absent.** Most have moderate to severe anaemia at diagnosis; WBC may be normal, reduced, or markedly elevated; platelets eventually decrease. Hyperuricaemia and gout may complicate the picture from high cell turnover.

**Prognosis** — variable; **median survival 4–5 years.** Constant threat of thrombotic and haemorrhagic episodes from platelet abnormalities. Splenic infarctions are common. **5–15%** develop a blast crisis resembling AML.

---

## Histiocytic Neoplasms — Langerhans Cell Histiocytoses

**Key concepts:** Pathogenesis · Three clinical forms · BRAF mutation

"Histiocytosis" encompasses a variety of proliferative disorders of dendritic cells or macrophages. The Langerhans cell histiocytoses are a group of relatively rare tumours composed of **Langerhans cells** — immature dendritic cells normally found in the epidermis that capture antigens and display them to T cells.

The proliferating Langerhans cells express **MHC class II antigens, CD1a, and langerin.** Langerin is found in **Birbeck granules** — cytoplasmic pentalaminar rodlike tubular structures with a characteristic periodicity and sometimes a dilated terminal end giving a **"tennis racket" appearance** on electron microscopy. Under light microscopy, proliferating Langerhans cells have abundant vacuolated cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei resembling tissue macrophages rather than their normal dendritic counterparts.

**BRAF mutation** — different clinical forms are frequently associated with an acquired **BRAF V600E mutation** (valine to glutamate at residue 600) → kinase hyperactivity → drives cellular proliferation and survival. The same mutation is found in hairy cell leukaemia, benign nevi, malignant melanoma, papillary thyroid carcinoma, and some colon cancers.

---

### Three Clinical Forms

**1. Multisystem Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (Letterer-Siwe Disease)**
Usually occurs in children **<2 years of age.** Manifests with multifocal cutaneous lesions resembling seborrheic skin eruptions composed of Langerhans cells. Most affected patients have hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, pulmonary lesions, and destructive osteolytic bone lesions. Extensive marrow infiltration → pancytopenia → recurrent infections (otitis media, mastoiditis). **Rapidly fatal if untreated;** with intensive chemotherapy, 50% survive 5 years.

**2. Unisystem Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (Eosinophilic Granuloma)**
May be unifocal or multifocal. Characterised by expanding, erosive accumulations of Langerhans cells within medullary cavities of bones (most commonly calvaria, ribs, and femur) or less commonly skin, lungs, or stomach. Langerhans cells are admixed with lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, and usually prominent eosinophils.

- **Unifocal disease** — most often skeletal; may be asymptomatic or cause pain, tenderness, and pathologic fractures; indolent and may heal spontaneously or be cured by local excision or irradiation
- **Multifocal unisystem disease** — usually affects children; multiple erosive bony masses sometimes extending into soft tissues; in ~50% of cases, involvement of the posterior pituitary stalk leads to **diabetes insipidus;** the combination of **calvarial bone defects + diabetes insipidus + exophthalmos = Hand-Schüller-Christian triad;** many experience spontaneous regression; others treated effectively with chemotherapy

---

## Bleeding Disorders — Overview

**Conditions covered:** Vascular fragility disorders · Platelet disorders (thrombocytopenia, qualitative defects) · Coagulation factor deficiencies · DIC

Normal clotting involves the vessel wall, platelets, and clotting factors. Abnormalities in any of these components can lead to clinically significant bleeding.

**Key laboratory tests:**

**Prothrombin time (PT)** — assesses the **extrinsic and common** coagulation pathways. Measures time (in seconds) for plasma to clot after addition of tissue thromboplastin and Ca²⁺. Prolonged PT → deficiency of factor V, VII, or X, prothrombin, or fibrinogen, or an acquired inhibitor of the extrinsic pathway.

**Partial thromboplastin time (PTT)** — assesses the **intrinsic and common** coagulation pathways. Prolonged PTT → deficiency of factor V, VIII, IX, X, XI, or XII, prothrombin, or fibrinogen, or an acquired inhibitor of the intrinsic pathway.

**Platelet count** — reference range 150,000–450,000/µL. Counts outside this range must be confirmed by visual inspection of a peripheral blood smear.

**Tests of platelet function** — platelet aggregation tests; qualitative and quantitative tests of von Willebrand factor. The older bleeding time test has some value but is difficult to standardise and rarely performed.

---

### Categories of Bleeding Disorders

**1. Vascular fragility** — petechiae and ecchymoses appear "spontaneously" in skin and mucous membranes. Coagulation tests are usually normal. Causes include vitamin C deficiency (scurvy), systemic amyloidosis, chronic glucocorticoid use, inherited connective tissue disorders, and infectious/hypersensitivity vasculitides (meningococcaemia, infective endocarditis, rickettsial diseases, typhoid, Henoch-Schönlein purpura).

**2. Thrombocytopenia and qualitative platelet defects** — easy bruising, nosebleeds, excessive bleeding from minor trauma, menorrhagia. Qualitative defects may be acquired (uraemia, myeloproliferative disorders, aspirin ingestion) or inherited (von Willebrand disease and other rare congenital disorders).

**3. Coagulation factor deficiencies** — PT, PTT, or both are prolonged. Petechiae and mucosal bleeding are usually absent. Instead, haemorrhages tend to occur at trauma-prone sites such as lower extremity joints. Massive haemorrhage may occur after surgery, dental procedures, or severe trauma. Includes the **haemophilias.**

**4. Mixed defects** — bleeding from a combination of mechanisms; examples include DIC (thrombocytopenia + coagulation factor deficiency) and von Willebrand disease (both platelet function and coagulation factor function impaired).

---

## Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)

**Key concepts:** Pathogenesis · Consequences · Clinical features · Associations

DIC occurs as a complication of a wide variety of disorders. It is caused by **systemic activation of coagulation** throughout the microcirculation → formation of widespread microthrombi → consumption of platelets and coagulation factors → secondary activation of fibrinolysis. DIC therefore produces **two opposing consequences simultaneously:** tissue hypoxia/microinfarcts from microthrombi AND bleeding from depletion of haemostatic elements (**consumptive coagulopathy**). DIC probably causes bleeding more commonly than all congenital coagulation disorders combined.

**Pathogenesis — two main triggers:**

**1. Release of tissue factor / thromboplastic substances into the circulation:**
- Obstetric complications — tissue factor from placenta, retained dead fetus, or amniotic fluid
- Certain cancers — particularly acute promyelocytic leukaemia and adenocarcinomas; tumour cells release thromboplastic substances, proteolytic enzymes, and express tissue factor
- Gram-negative and gram-positive sepsis — endotoxins/exotoxins stimulate tissue factor release from monocytes; activated monocytes release IL-1 and TNF → stimulate tissue factor expression on endothelial cells and simultaneously decrease thrombomodulin expression → net result is enhanced thrombin generation and blunted inhibitory pathways

**2. Widespread endothelial cell damage:**
- Releases tissue factor and exposes subendothelial collagen and von Willebrand factor
- Even subtle endothelial damage can increase tissue factor expression on cell surfaces
- Causes include antigen-antibody complex deposition (e.g. SLE), temperature extremes (heat stroke, burns), infections (meningococci, rickettsiae), and endotoxaemia

**Most common clinical associations:** Sepsis, obstetric complications, malignancy, and **major trauma** (especially brain trauma — releases fat and phospholipids which activate the intrinsic coagulation cascade).

**Two main consequences:**

**1. Widespread fibrin deposition in microcirculation:**
- Obstruction → **ischaemia** in severely affected organs
- Red cells traumatised passing through fibrin-narrowed vessels → **microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia**

**2. Bleeding diathesis:**
- Depletion of platelets and clotting factors
- Secondary release of plasminogen activators → **plasmin** cleaves fibrin (fibrinolysis) AND factors V and VIII → further reduces their concentration
- Fibrin degradation products inhibit platelet aggregation, have antithrombin activity, and impair fibrin polymerisation → all contribute to haemostatic failure

---

*These notes are intended as a high-yield revision resource. Always correlate with clinical teaching and full textbook reading.*

articles.title: White Cell Disorders — Must-Know Notes — Notes
articles.content:
## Summary
This document provides a comprehensive overview of white blood cell disorders, encompassing both non-neoplastic conditions like leukopenias and reactive proliferations, and a range of neoplastic conditions. It details the pathogenesis, morphology, clinical features, and prognosis of various lymphoid and myeloid malignancies, alongside plasma cell tumors. Key emphasis is placed on molecular mechanisms, classification, and diagnostic distinctions for each entity.

## Key Points
*   Neutropenia, particularly when severe (agranulocytosis) with counts below 500 cells/µL, significantly elevates the risk of fatal bacterial and fungal infections.
*   Reactive leukocytosis, an increase in circulating white cells in response to stimuli, must be carefully distinguished from true leukemias, especially in **leukemoid reactions**.
*   Infectious mononucleosis, caused by **Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)**, is characterized by lymphocytosis of activated CD8+ T cells (atypical lymphocytes) and can lead to complications such as splenic rupture.
*   Chronic nonspecific lymphadenitis manifests in patterns like follicular hyperplasia (B cell), paracortical hyperplasia (T cell), or sinus histiocytosis (macrophages), requiring differentiation from lymphoma.
*   Lymphoid neoplasms are clonal proliferations often arising from **germinal center or post-germinal center B cells**, with classification based on morphology, immunophenotype, genotype, and clinical features.
*   Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is the most common childhood leukemia, primarily of pre-B cell origin, with a high cure rate in children, though prognosis varies with age and specific genetic abnormalities.
*   Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) and Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL) are indolent B cell tumours characterized by increased tumour cell survival due to **BCL2** and are the most common adult leukemias in the Western world, prone to immune dysregulation and transformation.
*   Follicular Lymphoma is a prevalent adult non-Hodgkin lymphoma defined by the **t(14;18) translocation** leading to **BCL2 overexpression** and a nodular proliferation of neoplastic germinal center B cells.
*   Multiple Myeloma, the most common plasma cell neoplasm, involves the bone marrow, causing **lytic lesions** throughout the skeleton and producing monoclonal immunoglobulins (**M proteins**) which lead to bone pain, hypercalcaemia, and renal dysfunction.
*   Hodgkin Lymphoma is distinct from non-Hodgkin lymphomas due to the presence of **Reed-Sternberg (RS) giant cells** and its predictable contiguous spread pattern, which allows for local therapy in early stages.

## Detailed Notes

### Non-Neoplastic Disorders of White Cells

**Conditions covered:** Leukopenia · Neutropenia · Reactive Leukocytosis · Infectious Mononucleosis · Reactive Lymphadenitis

### Leukopenia & Neutropenia

**Key concepts:** Mechanisms · Morphology · Clinical features · Treatment

**Leukopenia** results most commonly from a decrease in granulocytes. Lymphopenia is less common and is associated with congenital immunodeficiency, advanced HIV infection, and high-dose corticosteroid therapy.

**Neutropenia / Agranulocytosis** — a reduction in granulocyte count. When severe, it is called agranulocytosis. The risk of fatal bacterial and fungal infection rises sharply once the neutrophil count falls below **500 cells/µL.**

**Two mechanisms of neutropenia:**

**Decreased production** — caused by marrow failure (aplastic anaemia), extensive marrow replacement by tumour (e.g. leukaemia), cancer chemotherapy, or drugs that selectively impair differentiation of committed granulocytic precursors. Isolated neutropenias of this type are also caused by neoplastic proliferations of cytotoxic T cells and NK cells.

**Increased destruction** — caused by immune-mediated injury (sometimes drug-triggered), overwhelming bacterial, fungal, or rickettsial infections (increased peripheral utilisation), or splenomegaly (sequestration and accelerated removal of neutrophils).

**Morphology** — depends on the underlying cause. Marrow is hypercellular when there is excessive destruction or ineffective granulopoiesis (as in megaloblastic anaemia). Marrow is hypocellular when drugs suppress granulopoiesis. Most myelotoxic drugs reduce elements from all marrow lineages, not just granulocytes.

**Clinical features** — ulcerating, necrotizing lesions of the gingiva, floor of mouth, buccal mucosa, and pharynx (**agranulocytic angina**). Lesions contain large masses of organisms because of the absence of leukocytes.

**Treatment** — remove the offending drug, control infection, and administer **G-CSF** (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) to stimulate neutrophil production by the bone marrow.

### Reactive Leukocytosis

**Key concept:** Types and their distinguishing causes

An increase in circulating white cells in response to microbial or non-microbial stimuli. Classified according to the white cell series affected. In some cases, reactive leukocytosis may mimic leukaemia — these **leukemoid reactions** must be distinguished from true malignancy.

| Type | Common Causes |
|------|--------------|
| Neutrophilic leukocytosis | Acute bacterial infections (pyogenic organisms); sterile inflammation (MI, burns) |
| Eosinophilia | Allergic disorders (asthma, hay fever, pemphigus); parasitic infestations; drug reactions; Hodgkin lymphoma; collagen-vascular disorders; atheroembolic disease |
| Basophilia | Rare; often indicates myeloproliferative disease (e.g. CML) |
| Monocytosis | Chronic infections (TB, endocarditis, rickettsiosis, malaria); SLE; inflammatory bowel disease |
| Lymphocytosis | Chronic immunologic stimulation (TB, brucellosis); viral infections (hepatitis A, CMV, EBV); Bordetella pertussis |

### Infectious Mononucleosis

**Key concepts:** EBV pathogenesis · Morphology · Clinical features · Complications · EBV and malignancy

Infectious mononucleosis is an acute, self-limited disease of adolescents and young adults caused by **Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)**, a herpesvirus. It is characterised by fever, sore throat, generalised lymphadenitis, and a lymphocytosis of activated CD8+ T cells. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) can produce an identical syndrome distinguishable only by serology.

**Epidemiology** — EBV is ubiquitous. In the developing world, primary infection occurs in early childhood and is nearly universal but mostly asymptomatic. In developed countries with better hygiene, infection is delayed to adolescence or young adulthood. Only ~20% of healthy seropositive individuals in developed countries shed virus, and only ~50% of those exposed acquire infection.

**Transmission** — direct oral contact (**"kissing disease"**). The virus initially infects oropharyngeal epithelial cells, then spreads to B cells in underlying lymphoid tissue.

**B cell infection takes two forms:**
- **Lytic infection** (minority of cells) — viral replication → cell lysis → release of virions
- **Latent infection** (majority of cells) — virus persists as an extrachromosomal episome; drives polyclonal B cell activation and proliferation via several EBV-encoded proteins

Latently infected B cells secrete antibodies including **heterophil anti-sheep red cell antibodies** — the basis of the Monospot diagnostic test.

**Immune response** — early IgM antibodies against viral capsid antigens, later shifting to persistent IgG. More important are **cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and NK cells**, which control EBV-positive B cell proliferation. These virus-specific CD8+ T cells appear in the circulation as **atypical lymphocytes** — the hallmark of mononucleosis. A small number of latently infected B cells escape immune control and persist for life.

**Morphology:**
- Peripheral blood leukocytosis with WBC typically 12,000–18,000 cells/µL; >50% are large **atypical lymphocytes** (12–16 µm) with oval, indented, or folded nuclei and abundant cytoplasm — mainly CD8+ T cells
- Lymphadenopathy most prominent in posterior cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions; nodes flooded by atypical lymphocytes occupying paracortical (T cell) areas; occasional Reed-Sternberg-like cells may cause confusion with Hodgkin lymphoma
- Spleen enlarged (300–500 g); infiltration of trabeculae and capsule makes it fragile and prone to rupture
- Liver: atypical lymphocytes infiltrate portal areas and sinusoids; scattered apoptotic cells and foci of necrosis — may resemble viral hepatitis

**Clinical features** — fever, sore throat, malaise, marked fatigability, generalised lymphadenopathy. Atypical presentations include fever of unknown origin, hepatitis, or febrile rash resembling rubella.

**Diagnosis** (in increasing order of specificity):
1. Lymphocytosis with characteristic atypical lymphocytes
2. Positive **heterophil reaction** (Monospot test)
3. Rising titres of antibodies specific for EBV antigens (viral capsid antigens, early antigens, EBNA)

Most patients recover within **4–6 weeks**, though fatigue may persist longer.

**Complications:**
- Hepatic dysfunction — jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, rarely liver failure
- **Splenic rupture** (potentially fatal)
- Neurologic, renal, cardiac, pulmonary, haematologic involvement
- In immunocompromised hosts (transplant recipients, HIV): unimpeded EBV-driven polyclonal B cell proliferation → transforms to monoclonal B cell lymphoma over time; reconstitution of immunity can cause regression

**X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome** — rare inherited immunodeficiency; mutations in SH2D1A (encodes a signalling protein needed for T cell and NK cell activation). >50% of affected boys develop overwhelming fatal EBV infection; others develop lymphoma or hypogammaglobulinaemia.

### Reactive Lymphadenitis

**Key concepts:** Acute · Chronic (follicular hyperplasia, paracortical hyperplasia, sinus histiocytosis) · Cat-scratch disease

Infections and non-microbial stimuli activate immune cells in lymph nodes, causing lymphadenopathy. Histologic patterns are usually nonspecific.

**Acute Nonspecific Lymphadenitis** — may be localised (draining a local infection) or generalised (systemic infection). Nodes are swollen, grey-red, and engorged with large germinal centres and numerous mitotic figures. Pyogenic organisms cause a neutrophilic infiltrate; severe infections → follicle necrosis → abscess formation. With infection control, nodes may return to normal or undergo scarring.

**Chronic Nonspecific Lymphadenitis** — takes one of three patterns:

**Follicular hyperplasia** — B cell activation; reactive follicles contain activated B cells, scattered T cells, **tingible body macrophages** (containing nuclear debris), and follicular dendritic cells. Causes include rheumatoid arthritis, toxoplasmosis, and early HIV infection. Must be distinguished from follicular lymphoma — features favouring hyperplasia are: preserved nodal architecture, variation in germinal centre size and shape, mixed lymphocyte population, and prominent mitotic and phagocytic activity.

**Paracortical hyperplasia** — T cell zone reaction; parafollicular T cells transform into large proliferating immunoblasts that can efface B cell follicles. Seen in viral infections (especially EBV), after certain vaccinations (e.g. smallpox), and with certain drug reactions (especially phenytoin).

**Sinus histiocytosis** — distension of lymphatic sinusoids by hypertrophied endothelial cells and infiltrating macrophages (histiocytes). Often seen in nodes draining cancers; may represent an immune response to tumour products.

**Cat-Scratch Disease** — self-limited lymphadenitis caused by **Bartonella henselae**. Primarily affects children (<18 years in 90% of cases). Regional lymphadenopathy (most often axilla and neck) appears ~2 weeks after a cat scratch. Morphology: sarcoid-like granulomas that undergo central neutrophilic necrosis → **stellate necrotizing granulomas** — similar to those in lymphogranuloma venereum. The organism is extracellular and visible with silver stains. Diagnosis based on cat exposure history, serology for Bartonella antibodies, and characteristic morphology. Rarely complicated by encephalitis, osteomyelitis, or thrombocytopenia.

### Neoplastic Proliferations of White Cells

**Conditions covered:** Lymphoid neoplasms · Myeloid neoplasms · Histiocytic neoplasms

Tumours are the most important disorders of white cells. They fall into three broad categories:

*   **Lymphoid neoplasms** — non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs), Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocytic leukaemias, plasma cell neoplasms
*   **Myeloid neoplasms** — acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), myeloproliferative disorders, myelodysplastic syndromes
*   **Histiocytic neoplasms** — proliferations of macrophages and dendritic cells, including Langerhans cell histiocytoses

**Key principles of lymphoid neoplasm classification:**

B and T cell tumours are often composed of cells arrested at a specific stage of normal differentiation. Classification relies on immunohistochemistry or flow cytometry detecting lineage-specific antigens identified by their **CD (cluster of differentiation) number.**

The most common lymphomas are derived from **germinal centre or post-germinal centre B cells.** Germinal centre B cells undergo somatic hypermutation and immunoglobulin class switching — both are error-prone processes that place these cells at high risk for transforming mutations. Most recurrent chromosomal translocations in mature B cell malignancies involve immunoglobulin loci.

All lymphoid neoplasms are **clonal** — derived from a single transformed cell. Antigen receptor gene rearrangement precedes transformation, so all daughter cells share the same receptor gene configuration. This allows molecular distinction of clonal neoplasms from polyclonal reactive processes.

Lymphoid neoplasms often **disrupt normal immune function** — both immunodeficiency and autoimmunity may occur in the same patient. Patients with inherited or acquired immunodeficiency are themselves at high risk for EBV-associated lymphoid neoplasms.

NHLs are usually **widely disseminated at diagnosis** on sensitive molecular assays, even when clinically localised — systemic therapy is required. By contrast, **Hodgkin lymphoma** often arises at a single site and spreads predictably to contiguous lymph node groups — early-stage disease is sometimes treated with local therapy alone.

Classification is by the **WHO scheme**, incorporating morphology, immunophenotype, genotype, and clinical features. Three major categories: (1) B cell tumours, (2) T cell and NK cell tumours, (3) Hodgkin lymphoma.

### Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia / Lymphoblastic Lymphoma

**Key concepts:** Pathogenesis · Morphology · Genetics · Prognosis

ALL and lymphoblastic lymphoma are aggressive tumours of immature lymphocytes (lymphoblasts), occurring predominantly in children and young adults. They are morphologically and clinically indistinguishable and are treated similarly. ALL constitutes **80% of childhood leukaemia**, peaking at age 4, mostly of pre-B cell origin. Pre-T cell tumours are most common in males aged 15–20.

**Pathogenesis** — the principal defect is a **block in differentiation** caused by acquired mutations in lineage-specific transcription factors:
- B-ALL: TEL1, AML1, E2A, PAX5, EBF mutations
- T-ALL: TAL1 and NOTCH1 mutations

Complementary mutations allow **growth factor-independent proliferation.** In B-ALL, the most important is the **BCR-ABL fusion gene** created by the **(9;22) translocation** (Philadelphia chromosome).

**Clinical features** — symptoms relate to bone marrow suppression and tumour infiltration of other organs.
- Abrupt onset of symptom onset
- Fatigue (anaemia), fever (neutropenia-related infections), bleeding — petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, gum bleeding (thrombocytopenia)
- Bone pain and tenderness from marrow expansion and subperiosteal infiltration
- Generalised lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly — more pronounced in ALL than AML
- CNS manifestations (headache, vomiting, nerve palsies from meningeal spread) — more common in children and in ALL

**Laboratory findings** — WBC variable (may exceed 100,000/µL but is <10,000/µL in ~50%); anaemia almost always present; platelets usually <100,000/µL; neutropenia common. Diagnosis requires identification of blasts — peripheral blood may show none (aleukemic leukaemia), in which case marrow examination is essential.

**Morphology** — in ALL, blasts compose >25% of marrow cellularity. Lymphoblasts have coarse clumped chromatin, one or two nucleoli, and scant agranular cytoplasm. Cytoplasmic glycogen granules are PAS-positive. Distinguish from myeloblasts (finer chromatin, more cytoplasm, azurophilic granules, peroxidase-positive).

**Immunophenotype** — **TdT (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase)** is present in >95% of ALL cases and is specific for pre-B and pre-T cells. Further subtyping uses CD19 (B cell) and CD3 (T cell).

**Genetic features** — ~90% of ALLs have non-random karyotypic abnormalities:
- Childhood pre-B ALL: hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes) and t(12;21) involving TEL1/AML1 — good prognosis
- Adult pre-B ALL: ~25% have **t(9;22) BCR-ABL** — poor prognosis
- Pre-T ALL: diverse chromosomal aberrations including T cell receptor locus translocations

**Prognosis** — treatment of childhood ALL is one of oncology's great success stories. Children aged 2–10 have the best outcomes; up to **80% are cured** with intensive chemotherapy. Poor prognostic variables: male gender, age <2 or >10, high WBC at diagnosis, molecular evidence of persistent disease at day 28 of treatment, MLL rearrangement, or BCR-ABL fusion.

### Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia / Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma

**Key concepts:** Pathogenesis · Morphology · Immunophenotype · Clinical features · Transformation

CLL and SLL are essentially identical, differing only in degree of peripheral blood involvement. If peripheral blood lymphocyte count exceeds **4,000 cells/µL** → CLL; if not → SLL. **CLL is the most common leukaemia of adults in the Western world.** Both are much less common in Asian populations.

**Pathogenesis** — an indolent, slowly growing tumour where **increased tumour cell survival** (not proliferation) is the key mechanism. Tumour cells contain high levels of **BCL2** (anti-apoptotic protein) — not due to gene rearrangement (as in follicular lymphoma) but likely from loss of regulatory micro-RNAs encoded on chromosome 13.

Immune dysregulation is prominent: tumour cell accumulation suppresses normal B cell function → **hypogammaglobulinaemia** in >50% of patients. Paradoxically, ~15% of patients develop **autoantibodies** against their own red cells or platelets (made by non-malignant bystander B cells). Over time, tumour cells displace normal marrow elements → anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia.

**Morphology** — sheets of small lymphocytes with scattered ill-defined foci of larger, actively dividing cells (**proliferation centres**) diffusely efface lymph nodes. **Proliferation centres are pathognomonic for CLL/SLL.** Circulating tumour cells are fragile and produce characteristic **smudge cells** on blood smears.

**Immunophenotype and genetics** — mature B cells expressing CD19, CD20, CD23, surface immunoglobulin, and **CD5** (a helpful clue — among B cell lymphomas, only CLL/SLL and mantle cell lymphoma commonly express CD5). ~50% have karyotypic abnormalities: trisomy 12 and deletions of chromosomes 11, 13, and 17. Activating NOTCH1 mutations predict worse outcome. Chromosomal translocations are rare (unlike other B cell neoplasms).

**Clinical features** — often asymptomatic at first detection. Common signs: easy fatigability, weight loss, anorexia, generalised lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly (50–60% of patients). Hypogammaglobulinaemia → increased susceptibility to bacterial infections. Less commonly, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia occur.

**Prognosis** — extremely variable. Many patients live >10 years and die of unrelated causes; median survival 4–6 years. Over time, CLL/SLL tends to transform to more aggressive tumours resembling prolymphocytic leukaemia or **diffuse large B cell lymphoma (Richter transformation)** → median survival <1 year after transformation.

### Follicular Lymphoma

**Key concepts:** Pathogenesis · Morphology · Clinical features · Prognosis · Transformation

Follicular lymphoma constitutes **40% of adult NHLs** in the United States and is much less common in Asian populations.

**Pathogenesis** — neoplastic cells express **BCL2**, which is absent from normal germinal centre B cells. >85% of tumours have a **(14;18) translocation** fusing the BCL2 gene (chromosome 18) to the IgH locus (chromosome 14) → inappropriate BCL2 overexpression → tumour cell survival. ~One third of cases also have loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding **histone acetyl transferases** → epigenetic dysregulation contributes to tumourigenesis.

**Morphology** — lymph nodes show a **distinctly nodular (follicular) proliferation.** Neoplastic cells resemble germinal centre B cells — predominantly small **"cleaved" cells (centrocytes)** with angular nuclei and linear infoldings, mixed with variable numbers of larger cells (centroblasts) with vesicular chromatin and prominent nucleoli.

### Burkitt Lymphoma

Burkitt lymphoma is among the **fastest-growing human neoplasms**, yet with very aggressive chemotherapy, the majority of patients can be cured. It primarily affects children and young adults. Accounts for ~30% of childhood NHLs in the United States. Disease usually arises at extranodal sites:
- **Endemic (African) form** — commonly presents as maxillary or mandibular jaw masses; strongly EBV-associated
- **Sporadic form** — abdominal tumours involving bowel, retroperitoneum, and ovaries; EBV association weaker
- Leukaemic presentation occurs but must be distinguished from ALL (treated with different drug regimens)

### Multiple Myeloma & Related Plasma Cell Tumours

**Key concepts:** Multiple myeloma · Pathogenesis · Morphology · Clinical features · MGUS · Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma

Plasma cell neoplasms produce a single complete or partial immunoglobulin detectable in the serum — hence termed **monoclonal gammopathies** (**M proteins**). They account for **~15% of deaths from white blood cell tumours** and are most common in middle-aged and elderly persons.

**Six major variants:** (1) Multiple myeloma, (2) Solitary plasmacytoma, (3) Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, (4) Heavy-chain disease, (5) Primary amyloidosis, (6) MGUS.

### Multiple Myeloma

The most common variant. Approximately **20,000 new cases per year** in the United States. Median age at diagnosis is 70 years; more common in males and in people of African origin. Principally involves bone marrow with **lytic lesions** throughout the skeleton.

**M proteins produced:**
- IgG — 60% of cases
- IgA — 20–25%
- IgM, IgD, IgE — rare
- Free light chains only (κ or λ) — 15–20%; excreted in urine as **Bence Jones proteins**
- Most malignant plasma cells secrete both complete immunoglobulins and free light chains → both M proteins and Bence Jones proteins

**Pathogenesis:**
- Chromosomal translocations involving the IgH locus (chromosome 14) and various partners including cyclin D1, FGFR3, and cyclin D3 → **dysregulation of D cyclins is common**
- Late in course, MYC translocations may also occur
- Tumour cell proliferation is supported by **IL-6** produced by bone marrow stromal fibroblasts and macrophages
- Bone resorption results from myeloma cell secretion of IL-1β, TNF, and IL-6 → stimulate RANK-ligand production → osteoclast differentiation and activity
- Myeloma cells interfere with normal plasma cell function → **immunosuppression and defective antibody production** despite high total immunoglobulin (from M protein)

**Renal dysfunction** is a common, serious complication:
- Obstructive proteinaceous casts in distal tubules and collecting ducts (**Bence Jones proteins** + Tamm-Horsfall protein + albumin) → **myeloma nephrosis**
- Multinucleate giant cells from macrophages surround casts; adjacent epithelium becomes necrotic from toxic effects of Bence Jones proteins
- Light chain deposition in glomeruli or interstitium (as amyloid or linear deposits)
- Hypercalcaemia → dehydration and renal stones
- Recurrent bacterial pyelonephritis

**Morphology:**
- Multifocal destructive skeletal lesions most commonly in vertebral column, ribs, skull, pelvis, femur, clavicle, and scapula
- Lesions arise in medullary cavity → erode cancellous and cortical bone → pathologic fractures (most often vertebral column or femur)
- Bone lesions appear as **punched-out defects 1–4 cm** on X-ray or diffuse demineralisation
- Marrow shows >30% plasma cells, often with abnormal features: prominent nucleoli, abnormal cytoplasmic inclusions containing immunoglobulin
- Disease progression: plasma cells infiltrate spleen, liver, kidneys, lungs, lymph nodes, soft tissues; terminal stages may show leukaemic picture

**Clinical features:**
- **Bone pain** from pathologic fractures; vertebral fractures may cause spinal cord impingement — an oncologic emergency
- **Hypercalcaemia** → confusion, lethargy, renal dysfunction
- **Anaemia** from marrow replacement and suppressed haematopoiesis
- **Recurrent bacterial infections** (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, E. coli) from suppressed humoral immunity
- **Renal insufficiency** in up to 50% of patients
- **AL-type amyloidosis** in 5–10%
- Hyperviscosity symptoms (less characteristic than in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma)

**Diagnosis:** Characteristic punched-out skeletal defects on imaging + electrophoresis of serum and urine showing monoclonal complete immunoglobulin or free light chain in 99% of cases + bone marrow examination confirming plasma cell proliferation.

### Solitary Plasmacytoma

Plasma tumours manifesting as isolated lesions. **Skeletal plasmacytomas** occur in similar locations to myeloma and usually progress to full-blown multiple myeloma over **5–10 years.** **Soft tissue plasmacytomas** (most often upper respiratory tract) spread infrequently and are often cured by local resection.

### Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance (MGUS)

M proteins are found in the serum of **1–3% of otherwise healthy persons >50 years** — the most common plasma cell proliferation. Despite its name, MGUS is increasingly recognised as a **precursor lesion** — symptomatic plasma cell tumour (most commonly myeloma) develops at a rate of **1% per year.** Clonal plasma cells in MGUS contain the same chromosomal translocations as full-blown myeloma. Diagnosis requires <3 g/dL monoclonal protein in serum and no Bence Jones proteinuria.

### Lymphoplasmacytic Lymphoma / Waldenström Macroglobulinaemia

Composed of a mixture of small lymphocytes, plasmacytic lymphocytes, and plasma cells. Behaves like an indolent B cell lymphoma; involves lymph nodes, bone marrow, and spleen. Secretes **IgM (macroglobulin)** → blood viscosity increases → **Waldenström macroglobulinaemia:**
- Visual impairment from tortuous dilated retinal veins, retinal haemorrhages and exudates
- Neurological symptoms
- Bleeding from interference with platelet and coagulation factor function
- Raynaud phenomenon and cold urticaria (if IgM is a cryoglobulin)

Heavy and light chain synthesis is balanced → no free light chains → no Bence Jones proteinuria. **Unlike myeloma:** no lytic bone lesions; only rarely associated with amyloidosis.

**Other variants:**
- **Heavy-chain disease** — proliferations producing only heavy chains; IgA heavy-chain disease has predilection for GI/respiratory lymphoid tissue; may be a variant of extranodal marginal zone lymphoma
- **Primary amyloidosis** — monoclonal plasma cells secrete free light chains → AL-type amyloid deposits

### Hodgkin Lymphoma

**Key concepts:** Distinction from NHL · Reed-Sternberg cells · WHO classification · Spread pattern

Hodgkin lymphoma is set apart from NHLs by the presence of distinctive **Reed-Sternberg (RS) giant cells** — the neoplastic cell. RS cells are typically vastly outnumbered by non-neoplastic inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells, macrophages). The biologic behaviour and treatment of Hodgkin lymphoma differ importantly from NHLs.

**Key clinical distinction from NHL:** Hodgkin lymphoma often arises at a **single site** and spreads in a predictable, contiguous fashion to adjacent lymph node groups → early-stage disease is sometimes treated with **local radiotherapy alone.** NHLs are usually widely disseminated at diagnosis and require systemic therapy.

**WHO classification of Hodgkin lymphoma:**

| Subtype | Key Features |
|---------|-------------|
| Nodular sclerosis | Most common; collagen bands divide lymph node into nodules; lacunar RS cell variant; young adults; mediastinal involvement common |
| Mixed cellularity | Classic RS cells with mixed inflammatory background; intermediate prognosis |
| Lymphocyte-rich | Abundant lymphocytes; rare RS cells; best prognosis |
| Lymphocyte depletion | Few lymphocytes; many RS cells or fibrosis; worst prognosis; often advanced stage |
| Nodular lymphocyte predominance | Distinct entity; "popcorn" (L&H) RS cell variant; CD20+; indolent |

**Reed-Sternberg cells** — large cells with abundant cytoplasm and bilobed or multilobed nuclei each containing a huge inclusion-like nucleolus (**"owl-eye" appearance**). RS cells derive from germinal centre B cells — they have rearranged immunoglobulin genes but have lost normal B cell gene expression programmes.

## Practice Questions
1. What is the critical neutrophil count below which the risk of fatal bacterial and fungal infection rises sharply? → Below 500 cells/µL.
2. What are the three diagnostic criteria for infectious mononucleosis, in increasing order of specificity? → Lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, positive heterophil reaction (Monospot test), rising titres of antibodies specific for EBV antigens.
3. What is a key histologic feature pathognomonic for CLL/SLL? → The presence of proliferation centres.
4. Which chromosomal translocation is highly characteristic of Follicular Lymphoma and what gene is overexpressed as a result? → The t(14;18) translocation, leading to BCL2 overexpression.
5. In Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia, what gene fusion, created by the (9;22) translocation, indicates a poor prognosis in adult pre-B ALL? → The BCR-ABL fusion gene.
6. What are the major clinical complications of Multiple Myeloma related to bone involvement? → Bone pain from pathologic fractures and hypercalcaemia.
7. What is the most common plasma cell proliferation found in otherwise healthy individuals over 50 years old, and what is its clinical significance? → Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance (MGUS), recognized as a precursor lesion that progresses to symptomatic plasma cell tumour at a rate of 1% per year.
8. What is the key histological feature that distinguishes Hodgkin Lymphoma from non-Hodgkin Lymphoma? → The presence of distinctive Reed-Sternberg (RS) giant cells.
