# White Cell Disorders — Must-Know Notes
*March 12, 2026 · General Pathology*

---

This document covers disorders of white blood cells, including leukopenias, reactive proliferations, and neoplastic proliferations. It explores the pathogenesis, morphology, clinical features, and prognosis of conditions ranging from neutropenia and infectious mononucleosis to the major lymphoid malignancies, multiple myeloma, and acute leukemias. Emphasis is placed on molecular mechanisms, classification principles, and distinguishing features of each entity.

---

## Contents

- Non-Neoplastic Disorders of White Cells
- Leukopenia & Neutropenia
- Reactive Leukocytosis
- Infectious Mononucleosis
- Reactive Lymphadenitis
- Neoplastic Proliferations of White Cells
- Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia / Lymphoblastic Lymphoma
- Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia / Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma
- Follicular Lymphoma
- Mantle Cell Lymphoma
- Diffuse Large B Cell Lymphoma
- Burkitt Lymphoma
- Multiple Myeloma & Related Plasma Cell Tumours
- Hodgkin Lymphoma

---

## Non-Neoplastic Disorders of White Cells

**Conditions covered:** Leukopenia · Neutropenia · Reactive Leukocytosis · Infectious Mononucleosis · Reactive Lymphadenitis

---

## Leukopenia & Neutropenia

**Key concepts:** Mechanisms · Morphology · Clinical features · Treatment

Leukopenia results most commonly from a decrease in granulocytes. Lymphopenia is less common and is associated with congenital immunodeficiency, advanced HIV infection, and high-dose corticosteroid therapy.

**Neutropenia / Agranulocytosis** — a reduction in granulocyte count. When severe, it is called agranulocytosis. The risk of fatal bacterial and fungal infection rises sharply once the neutrophil count falls below **500 cells/µL.**

**Two mechanisms of neutropenia:**

**Decreased production** — caused by marrow failure (aplastic anaemia), extensive marrow replacement by tumour (e.g. leukaemia), cancer chemotherapy, or drugs that selectively impair differentiation of committed granulocytic precursors. Isolated neutropenias of this type are also caused by neoplastic proliferations of cytotoxic T cells and NK cells.

**Increased destruction** — caused by immune-mediated injury (sometimes drug-triggered), overwhelming bacterial, fungal, or rickettsial infections (increased peripheral utilisation), or splenomegaly (sequestration and accelerated removal of neutrophils).

**Morphology** — depends on the underlying cause. Marrow is hypercellular when there is excessive destruction or ineffective granulopoiesis (as in megaloblastic anaemia). Marrow is hypocellular when drugs suppress granulopoiesis. Most myelotoxic drugs reduce elements from all marrow lineages, not just granulocytes.

**Clinical features** — ulcerating, necrotizing lesions of the gingiva, floor of mouth, buccal mucosa, and pharynx (agranulocytic angina). Lesions contain large masses of organisms because of the absence of leukocytes.

**Treatment** — remove the offending drug, control infection, and administer G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) to stimulate neutrophil production by the bone marrow.

---

## Reactive Leukocytosis

**Key concept:** Types and their distinguishing causes

An increase in circulating white cells in response to microbial or non-microbial stimuli. Classified according to the white cell series affected. In some cases, reactive leukocytosis may mimic leukaemia — these **leukemoid reactions** must be distinguished from true malignancy.

| Type | Common Causes |
|------|--------------|
| Neutrophilic leukocytosis | Acute bacterial infections (pyogenic organisms); sterile inflammation (MI, burns) |
| Eosinophilia | Allergic disorders (asthma, hay fever, pemphigus); parasitic infestations; drug reactions; Hodgkin lymphoma; collagen-vascular disorders; atheroembolic disease |
| Basophilia | Rare; often indicates myeloproliferative disease (e.g. CML) |
| Monocytosis | Chronic infections (TB, endocarditis, rickettsiosis, malaria); SLE; inflammatory bowel disease |
| Lymphocytosis | Chronic immunologic stimulation (TB, brucellosis); viral infections (hepatitis A, CMV, EBV); Bordetella pertussis |

---

## Infectious Mononucleosis

**Key concepts:** EBV pathogenesis · Morphology · Clinical features · Complications · EBV and malignancy

Infectious mononucleosis is an acute, self-limited disease of adolescents and young adults caused by **Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)**, a herpesvirus. It is characterised by fever, sore throat, generalised lymphadenitis, and a lymphocytosis of activated CD8+ T cells. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) can produce an identical syndrome distinguishable only by serology.

**Epidemiology** — EBV is ubiquitous. In the developing world, primary infection occurs in early childhood and is nearly universal but mostly asymptomatic. In developed countries with better hygiene, infection is delayed to adolescence or young adulthood. Only ~20% of healthy seropositive individuals in developed countries shed virus, and only ~50% of those exposed acquire infection.

**Transmission** — direct oral contact ("kissing disease"). The virus initially infects oropharyngeal epithelial cells, then spreads to B cells in underlying lymphoid tissue.

**B cell infection takes two forms:**
- **Lytic infection** (minority of cells) — viral replication → cell lysis → release of virions
- **Latent infection** (majority of cells) — virus persists as an extrachromosomal episome; drives polyclonal B cell activation and proliferation via several EBV-encoded proteins

Latently infected B cells secrete antibodies including **heterophil anti-sheep red cell antibodies** — the basis of the Monospot diagnostic test.

**Immune response** — early IgM antibodies against viral capsid antigens, later shifting to persistent IgG. More important are **cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and NK cells**, which control EBV-positive B cell proliferation. These virus-specific CD8+ T cells appear in the circulation as **atypical lymphocytes** — the hallmark of mononucleosis. A small number of latently infected B cells escape immune control and persist for life.

**Morphology:**
- Peripheral blood leukocytosis with WBC typically 12,000–18,000 cells/µL; >50% are large atypical lymphocytes (12–16 µm) with oval, indented, or folded nuclei and abundant cytoplasm — mainly CD8+ T cells
- Lymphadenopathy most prominent in posterior cervical, axillary, and inguinal regions; nodes flooded by atypical lymphocytes occupying paracortical (T cell) areas; occasional Reed-Sternberg-like cells may cause confusion with Hodgkin lymphoma
- Spleen enlarged (300–500 g); infiltration of trabeculae and capsule makes it fragile and prone to rupture
- Liver: atypical lymphocytes infiltrate portal areas and sinusoids; scattered apoptotic cells and foci of necrosis — may resemble viral hepatitis

**Clinical features** — fever, sore throat, malaise, marked fatigability, generalised lymphadenopathy. Atypical presentations include fever of unknown origin, hepatitis, or febrile rash resembling rubella.

**Diagnosis** (in increasing order of specificity):
1. Lymphocytosis with characteristic atypical lymphocytes
2. Positive heterophil reaction (Monospot test)
3. Rising titres of antibodies specific for EBV antigens (viral capsid antigens, early antigens, EBNA)

Most patients recover within **4–6 weeks**, though fatigue may persist longer.

**Complications:**
- Hepatic dysfunction — jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, rarely liver failure
- Splenic rupture (potentially fatal)
- Neurologic, renal, cardiac, pulmonary, haematologic involvement
- In immunocompromised hosts (transplant recipients, HIV): unimpeded EBV-driven polyclonal B cell proliferation → transforms to monoclonal B cell lymphoma over time; reconstitution of immunity can cause regression

**X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome** — rare inherited immunodeficiency; mutations in SH2D1A (encodes a signalling protein needed for T cell and NK cell activation). >50% of affected boys develop overwhelming fatal EBV infection; others develop lymphoma or hypogammaglobulinaemia.

---

## Reactive Lymphadenitis

**Key concepts:** Acute · Chronic (follicular hyperplasia, paracortical hyperplasia, sinus histiocytosis) · Cat-scratch disease

Infections and non-microbial stimuli activate immune cells in lymph nodes, causing lymphadenopathy. Histologic patterns are usually nonspecific.

**Acute Nonspecific Lymphadenitis** — may be localised (draining a local infection) or generalised (systemic infection). Nodes are swollen, grey-red, and engorged with large germinal centres and numerous mitotic figures. Pyogenic organisms cause a neutrophilic infiltrate; severe infections → follicle necrosis → abscess formation. With infection control, nodes may return to normal or undergo scarring.

**Chronic Nonspecific Lymphadenitis** — takes one of three patterns:

**Follicular hyperplasia** — B cell activation; reactive follicles contain activated B cells, scattered T cells, tingible body macrophages (containing nuclear debris), and follicular dendritic cells. Causes include rheumatoid arthritis, toxoplasmosis, and early HIV infection. Must be distinguished from follicular lymphoma — features favouring hyperplasia are: preserved nodal architecture, variation in germinal centre size and shape, mixed lymphocyte population, and prominent mitotic and phagocytic activity.

**Paracortical hyperplasia** — T cell zone reaction; parafollicular T cells transform into large proliferating immunoblasts that can efface B cell follicles. Seen in viral infections (especially EBV), after certain vaccinations (e.g. smallpox), and with certain drug reactions (especially phenytoin).

**Sinus histiocytosis** — distension of lymphatic sinusoids by hypertrophied endothelial cells and infiltrating macrophages (histiocytes). Often seen in nodes draining cancers; may represent an immune response to tumour products.

**Cat-Scratch Disease** — self-limited lymphadenitis caused by **Bartonella henselae**. Primarily affects children (<18 years in 90% of cases). Regional lymphadenopathy (most often axilla and neck) appears ~2 weeks after a cat scratch. Morphology: sarcoid-like granulomas that undergo central neutrophilic necrosis → **stellate necrotizing granulomas** — similar to those in lymphogranuloma venereum. The organism is extracellular and visible with silver stains. Diagnosis based on cat exposure history, serology for Bartonella antibodies, and characteristic morphology. Rarely complicated by encephalitis, osteomyelitis, or thrombocytopenia.

---

## Neoplastic Proliferations of White Cells

**Conditions covered:** Lymphoid neoplasms · Myeloid neoplasms · Histiocytic neoplasms

Tumours are the most important disorders of white cells. They fall into three broad categories:

- **Lymphoid neoplasms** — non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs), Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocytic leukaemias, plasma cell neoplasms
- **Myeloid neoplasms** — acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), myeloproliferative disorders, myelodysplastic syndromes
- **Histiocytic neoplasms** — proliferations of macrophages and dendritic cells, including Langerhans cell histiocytoses

**Key principles of lymphoid neoplasm classification:**

B and T cell tumours are often composed of cells arrested at a specific stage of normal differentiation. Classification relies on immunohistochemistry or flow cytometry detecting lineage-specific antigens identified by their **CD (cluster of differentiation) number.**

The most common lymphomas are derived from **germinal centre or post-germinal centre B cells.** Germinal centre B cells undergo somatic hypermutation and immunoglobulin class switching — both are error-prone processes that place these cells at high risk for transforming mutations. Most recurrent chromosomal translocations in mature B cell malignancies involve immunoglobulin loci.

All lymphoid neoplasms are **clonal** — derived from a single transformed cell. Antigen receptor gene rearrangement precedes transformation, so all daughter cells share the same receptor gene configuration. This allows molecular distinction of clonal neoplasms from polyclonal reactive processes.

Lymphoid neoplasms often **disrupt normal immune function** — both immunodeficiency and autoimmunity may occur in the same patient. Patients with inherited or acquired immunodeficiency are themselves at high risk for EBV-associated lymphoid neoplasms.

NHLs are usually **widely disseminated at diagnosis** on sensitive molecular assays, even when clinically localised — systemic therapy is required. By contrast, **Hodgkin lymphoma** often arises at a single site and spreads predictably to contiguous lymph node groups — early-stage disease is sometimes treated with local therapy alone.

Classification is by the **WHO scheme**, incorporating morphology, immunophenotype, genotype, and clinical features. Three major categories: (1) B cell tumours, (2) T cell and NK cell tumours, (3) Hodgkin lymphoma.

---

## Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia / Lymphoblastic Lymphoma

**Key concepts:** Pathogenesis · Morphology · Genetics · Prognosis

ALL and lymphoblastic lymphoma are aggressive tumours of immature lymphocytes (lymphoblasts), occurring predominantly in children and young adults. They are morphologically and clinically indistinguishable and are treated similarly. ALL constitutes **80% of childhood leukaemia**, peaking at age 4, mostly of pre-B cell origin. Pre-T cell tumours are most common in males aged 15–20.

**Pathogenesis** — the principal defect is a **block in differentiation** caused by acquired mutations in lineage-specific transcription factors:
- B-ALL: TEL1, AML1, E2A, PAX5, EBF mutations
- T-ALL: TAL1 and NOTCH1 mutations

Complementary mutations allow **growth factor-independent proliferation.** In B-ALL, the most important is the **BCR-ABL fusion gene** created by the **(9;22) translocation** (Philadelphia chromosome) — the same translocation found in CML. BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase constitutively activates growth factor pathways. Some T-ALLs have NUP214-ABL with similar effects.

Blasts accumulating in the marrow suppress normal haematopoiesis by physical displacement and poorly understood mechanisms → **bone marrow failure** → the major clinical manifestations.

**Clinical features of acute leukaemia:**
- Abrupt, stormy onset — most present within 3 months of symptom onset
- Fatigue (anaemia), fever (neutropenia-related infections), bleeding — petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, gum bleeding (thrombocytopenia)
- Bone pain and tenderness from marrow expansion and subperiosteal infiltration
- Generalised lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly — more pronounced in ALL than AML
- CNS manifestations (headache, vomiting, nerve palsies from meningeal spread) — more common in children and in ALL

**Laboratory findings** — WBC variable (may exceed 100,000/µL but is <10,000/µL in ~50%); anaemia almost always present; platelets usually <100,000/µL; neutropenia common. Diagnosis requires identification of blasts — peripheral blood may show none (aleukemic leukaemia), in which case marrow examination is essential.

**Morphology** — in ALL, blasts compose >25% of marrow cellularity. Lymphoblasts have coarse clumped chromatin, one or two nucleoli, and scant agranular cytoplasm. Cytoplasmic glycogen granules are PAS-positive. Distinguish from myeloblasts (finer chromatin, more cytoplasm, azurophilic granules, peroxidase-positive).

**Immunophenotype** — TdT (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase) is present in >95% of ALL cases and is specific for pre-B and pre-T cells. Further subtyping uses CD19 (B cell) and CD3 (T cell).

**Genetic features** — ~90% of ALLs have non-random karyotypic abnormalities:
- Childhood pre-B ALL: hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes) and t(12;21) involving TEL1/AML1 — good prognosis
- Adult pre-B ALL: ~25% have t(9;22) BCR-ABL — poor prognosis
- Pre-T ALL: diverse chromosomal aberrations including T cell receptor locus translocations

**Prognosis** — treatment of childhood ALL is one of oncology's great success stories. Children aged 2–10 have the best outcomes; up to **80% are cured** with intensive chemotherapy. Poor prognostic variables: male gender, age <2 or >10, high WBC at diagnosis, molecular evidence of persistent disease at day 28 of treatment, MLL rearrangement, or BCR-ABL fusion.

---

## Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia / Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma

**Key concepts:** Pathogenesis · Morphology · Immunophenotype · Clinical features · Transformation

CLL and SLL are essentially identical, differing only in degree of peripheral blood involvement. If peripheral blood lymphocyte count exceeds **4,000 cells/µL** → CLL; if not → SLL. **CLL is the most common leukaemia of adults in the Western world.** Both are much less common in Asian populations.

**Pathogenesis** — an indolent, slowly growing tumour where **increased tumour cell survival** (not proliferation) is the key mechanism. Tumour cells contain high levels of **BCL2** (anti-apoptotic protein) — not due to gene rearrangement (as in follicular lymphoma) but likely from loss of regulatory micro-RNAs encoded on chromosome 13.

Immune dysregulation is prominent: tumour cell accumulation suppresses normal B cell function → **hypogammaglobulinaemia** in >50% of patients. Paradoxically, ~15% of patients develop **autoantibodies** against their own red cells or platelets (made by non-malignant bystander B cells). Over time, tumour cells displace normal marrow elements → anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia.

**Morphology** — sheets of small lymphocytes with scattered ill-defined foci of larger, actively dividing cells (proliferation centres) diffusely efface lymph nodes. **Proliferation centres are pathognomonic for CLL/SLL.** Circulating tumour cells are fragile and produce characteristic **smudge cells** on blood smears.

**Immunophenotype and genetics** — mature B cells expressing CD19, CD20, CD23, surface immunoglobulin, and **CD5** (a helpful clue — among B cell lymphomas, only CLL/SLL and mantle cell lymphoma commonly express CD5). ~50% have karyotypic abnormalities: trisomy 12 and deletions of chromosomes 11, 13, and 17. Activating NOTCH1 mutations predict worse outcome. Chromosomal translocations are rare (unlike other B cell neoplasms).

**Clinical features** — often asymptomatic at first detection. Common signs: easy fatigability, weight loss, anorexia, generalised lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly (50–60% of patients). Hypogammaglobulinaemia → increased susceptibility to bacterial infections. Less commonly, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia occur.

**Prognosis** — extremely variable. Many patients live >10 years and die of unrelated causes; median survival 4–6 years. Over time, CLL/SLL tends to transform to more aggressive tumours resembling prolymphocytic leukaemia or **diffuse large B cell lymphoma (Richter transformation)** → median survival <1 year after transformation.

---

## Follicular Lymphoma

**Key concepts:** Pathogenesis · Morphology · Clinical features · Prognosis · Transformation

Follicular lymphoma constitutes **40% of adult NHLs** in the United States and is much less common in Asian populations.

**Pathogenesis** — neoplastic cells express **BCL2**, which is absent from normal germinal centre B cells. >85% of tumours have a **(14;18) translocation** fusing the BCL2 gene (chromosome 18) to the IgH locus (chromosome 14) → inappropriate BCL2 overexpression → tumour cell survival. ~One third of cases also have loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding **histone acetyl transferases** → epigenetic dysregulation contributes to tumourigenesis.

**Morphology** — lymph nodes show a **distinctly nodular (follicular) proliferation.** Neoplastic cells resemble germinal centre B cells — predominantly small "cleaved" cells (centrocytes) with angular nuclei and linear infoldings, mixed with variable numbers of larger cells (centroblasts) with vesicular chromatin and nucleoli. Mitoses and apoptosis are inconspicuous (unlike follicular hyperplasia where both are prominent). Predominance of large cells correlates with more aggressive behaviour.

**Immunophenotype** — express pan-B cell markers (CD19, CD20), CD10, and BCL6. BCL2 positivity is particularly useful as it is absent from reactive germinal centres.

**Clinical features** — mainly affects adults >50 years; affects males and females equally. Usually presents with **painless, generalised lymphadenopathy.** Bone marrow is almost always involved at diagnosis; visceral disease is uncommon. Median survival 7–9 years but the disease is **not curable** with standard therapy. Treatment with cytotoxic drugs and rituximab (anti-CD20) is reserved for bulky or symptomatic disease.

**Transformation** — in ~40% of patients, follicular lymphoma transforms to **diffuse large B cell lymphoma** — an ominous event, as transformed tumours are much less curable than de novo DLBCL.

---

## Mantle Cell Lymphoma

**Key concepts:** Pathogenesis · Morphology · Immunophenotype · Clinical features

Mantle cell lymphoma is composed of cells resembling naive B cells of normal lymphoid follicle mantle zones. It constitutes **~4% of all NHLs** and occurs mainly in men >50 years.

**Pathogenesis and genetics** — almost all tumours have a **(11;14) translocation** fusing the **cyclin D1** gene to the IgH locus → dysregulation of cyclin D1 expression → uncontrolled cell cycle progression. Tumour cells coexpress surface IgM and IgD, pan-B cell antigens (CD19, CD20), and **CD5.** Distinguished from CLL/SLL by absence of proliferation centres and presence of **cyclin D1 protein.**

**Morphology** — diffuse or vaguely nodular growth pattern. Cells are slightly larger than normal lymphocytes with irregular nuclei, inconspicuous nucleoli, and scant cytoplasm. Bone marrow is involved in most cases; peripheral blood in ~20%. May arise in the GI tract as **lymphomatoid polyposis** — multifocal submucosal nodules resembling polyps.

**Clinical features** — most patients present with fatigue and lymphadenopathy and are found to have generalised disease involving bone marrow, spleen, liver, and GI tract. **Moderately aggressive and incurable.** Median survival 3–5 years.

---

## Diffuse Large B Cell Lymphoma

**Key concepts:** Pathogenesis · Morphology · Subtypes · Clinical features · Prognosis

DLBCL is the **most common type of lymphoma in adults**, accounting for ~50% of adult NHLs. It includes several subtypes sharing an aggressive natural history.

**Pathogenesis:**
- ~One third of tumours have rearrangements of the **BCL6 gene** (3q27); an even higher fraction have activating point mutations in the BCL6 promoter → increased BCL6 protein (a key transcriptional regulator in germinal centre B cells)
- ~30% have a **(14;18) translocation** involving BCL2 — some may represent transformed follicular lymphomas
- ~One third have loss-of-function mutations in histone acetyl transferase genes — similar to follicular lymphoma, suggesting epigenetic dysregulation is important

**Morphology** — large neoplastic B cells (at least 3–4× size of resting lymphocytes) with variable appearances. Most have round or oval nuclei with dispersed chromatin, several distinct nucleoli, and modest pale cytoplasm. Occasional tumours contain highly anaplastic cells resembling Reed-Sternberg cells.

**Immunophenotype** — express pan-B cell antigens (CD19, CD20); many also express surface IgM and/or IgG; CD10 and BCL2 are variably expressed.

**Subtypes:**
- **EBV-associated DLBCL** — arises in AIDS, iatrogenic immunosuppression (transplant recipients), and the elderly; in transplant setting, may begin as polyclonal EBV-driven proliferation and regress with restored immunity
- **Primary effusion lymphoma** — associated with KSHV (HHV-8); arises in pleural, pericardial, or peritoneal cavities; confined to immunosuppressed hosts; KSHV encodes cyclin D1 homologue
- **Mediastinal large B cell lymphoma** — most common in young women; predilection for spread to abdominal viscera and CNS

**Clinical features** — median age ~60 years but can occur at any age; constitutes ~15% of childhood lymphomas. Patients present with rapidly enlarging symptomatic mass at one or several sites. Extranodal presentations common (GI tract and brain among the most frequent sites). Liver, spleen, and bone marrow involvement is not common at diagnosis (unlike indolent lymphomas).

**Prognosis** — aggressive and rapidly fatal without treatment. With intensive combination chemotherapy and rituximab (anti-CD20), complete remissions in **60–80%**; approximately 50% of these appear cured. Molecular profiling predicts response to therapy.

---

## Burkitt Lymphoma

**Key concepts:** Pathogenesis · Morphology · Clinical features · Endemic vs sporadic

Burkitt lymphoma is endemic in parts of Africa and occurs sporadically elsewhere including the United States. The African and nonendemic forms are histologically identical but differ clinically and virologically.

**Pathogenesis** — highly associated with translocations involving the **MYC gene (chromosome 8).** Most common is **t(8;14)** fusing MYC with the IgH gene; variant translocations involve κ (chromosome 2) and λ (chromosome 22) light chain loci. The net result is **dysregulation and overexpression of MYC protein** — a master regulator of cell proliferation. In most endemic cases and ~20% of sporadic cases, tumour cells are latently infected with **EBV**, though its precise role in pathogenesis remains uncertain.

**Morphology** — intermediate-sized cells with round or oval nuclei, 2–5 distinct nucleoli, and moderate amounts of basophilic cytoplasm with lipid-filled vacuoles (seen on smears). Very high rates of both **proliferation and apoptosis** — the abundant apoptotic debris is ingested by macrophages surrounded by clear spaces, creating the classic **"starry sky" pattern.** Tumour cells express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL6.

**Clinical features** — affects mainly children and young adults. Accounts for ~30% of childhood NHLs in the United States. Disease usually arises at extranodal sites:
- **Endemic (African) form** — commonly presents as maxillary or mandibular jaw masses; strongly EBV-associated
- **Sporadic form** — abdominal tumours involving bowel, retroperitoneum, and ovaries; EBV association weaker
- Leukaemic presentation occurs but must be distinguished from ALL (treated with different drug regimens)

Burkitt lymphoma is among the **fastest-growing human neoplasms**, yet with very aggressive chemotherapy, the majority of patients can be cured.

---

## Multiple Myeloma & Related Plasma Cell Tumours

**Key concepts:** Multiple myeloma · Pathogenesis · Morphology · Clinical features · MGUS · Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma

Plasma cell neoplasms produce a single complete or partial immunoglobulin detectable in the serum — hence termed **monoclonal gammopathies** (M proteins). They account for **~15% of deaths from white blood cell tumours** and are most common in middle-aged and elderly persons.

**Six major variants:** (1) Multiple myeloma, (2) Solitary plasmacytoma, (3) Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, (4) Heavy-chain disease, (5) Primary amyloidosis, (6) MGUS.

---

### Multiple Myeloma

The most common variant. Approximately **20,000 new cases per year** in the United States. Median age at diagnosis is 70 years; more common in males and in people of African origin. Principally involves bone marrow with lytic lesions throughout the skeleton.

**M proteins produced:**
- IgG — 60% of cases
- IgA — 20–25%
- IgM, IgD, IgE — rare
- Free light chains only (κ or λ) — 15–20%; excreted in urine as **Bence Jones proteins**
- Most malignant plasma cells secrete both complete immunoglobulins and free light chains → both M proteins and Bence Jones proteins

**Pathogenesis:**
- Chromosomal translocations involving the IgH locus (chromosome 14) and various partners including cyclin D1, FGFR3, and cyclin D3 → **dysregulation of D cyclins is common**
- Late in course, MYC translocations may also occur
- Tumour cell proliferation is supported by **IL-6** produced by bone marrow stromal fibroblasts and macrophages
- Bone resorption results from myeloma cell secretion of IL-1β, TNF, and IL-6 → stimulate RANK-ligand production → osteoclast differentiation and activity
- Myeloma cells interfere with normal plasma cell function → **immunosuppression and defective antibody production** despite high total immunoglobulin (from M protein)

**Renal dysfunction** is a common, serious complication:
- Obstructive proteinaceous casts in distal tubules and collecting ducts (Bence Jones proteins + Tamm-Horsfall protein + albumin) → myeloma nephrosis
- Multinucleate giant cells from macrophages surround casts; adjacent epithelium becomes necrotic from toxic effects of Bence Jones proteins
- Light chain deposition in glomeruli or interstitium (as amyloid or linear deposits)
- Hypercalcaemia → dehydration and renal stones
- Recurrent bacterial pyelonephritis

**Morphology:**
- Multifocal destructive skeletal lesions most commonly in vertebral column, ribs, skull, pelvis, femur, clavicle, and scapula
- Lesions arise in medullary cavity → erode cancellous and cortical bone → pathologic fractures (most often vertebral column or femur)
- Bone lesions appear as **punched-out defects 1–4 cm** on X-ray or diffuse demineralisation
- Marrow shows >30% plasma cells, often with abnormal features: prominent nucleoli, abnormal cytoplasmic inclusions containing immunoglobulin
- Disease progression: plasma cells infiltrate spleen, liver, kidneys, lungs, lymph nodes, soft tissues; terminal stages may show leukaemic picture

**Clinical features:**
- **Bone pain** from pathologic fractures; vertebral fractures may cause spinal cord impingement — an oncologic emergency
- **Hypercalcaemia** → confusion, lethargy, renal dysfunction
- **Anaemia** from marrow replacement and suppressed haematopoiesis
- **Recurrent bacterial infections** (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, E. coli) from suppressed humoral immunity
- **Renal insufficiency** in up to 50% of patients
- **AL-type amyloidosis** in 5–10%
- Hyperviscosity symptoms (less characteristic than in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma)

**Diagnosis:** Characteristic punched-out skeletal defects on imaging + electrophoresis of serum and urine showing monoclonal complete immunoglobulin or free light chain in 99% of cases + bone marrow examination confirming plasma cell proliferation.

---

### Solitary Plasmacytoma

Plasma tumours manifesting as isolated lesions. **Skeletal plasmacytomas** occur in similar locations to myeloma and usually progress to full-blown multiple myeloma over **5–10 years.** **Soft tissue plasmacytomas** (most often upper respiratory tract) spread infrequently and are often cured by local resection.

---

### Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance (MGUS)

M proteins are found in the serum of **1–3% of otherwise healthy persons >50 years** — the most common plasma cell proliferation. Despite its name, MGUS is increasingly recognised as a **precursor lesion** — symptomatic plasma cell tumour (most commonly myeloma) develops at a rate of **1% per year.** Clonal plasma cells in MGUS contain the same chromosomal translocations as full-blown myeloma. Diagnosis requires <3 g/dL monoclonal protein in serum and no Bence Jones proteinuria.

---

### Lymphoplasmacytic Lymphoma / Waldenström Macroglobulinaemia

Composed of a mixture of small lymphocytes, plasmacytic lymphocytes, and plasma cells. Behaves like an indolent B cell lymphoma; involves lymph nodes, bone marrow, and spleen. Secretes **IgM (macroglobulin)** → blood viscosity increases → **Waldenström macroglobulinaemia:**
- Visual impairment from tortuous dilated retinal veins, retinal haemorrhages and exudates
- Neurological symptoms
- Bleeding from interference with platelet and coagulation factor function
- Raynaud phenomenon and cold urticaria (if IgM is a cryoglobulin)

Heavy and light chain synthesis is balanced → no free light chains → no Bence Jones proteinuria. **Unlike myeloma:** no lytic bone lesions; only rarely associated with amyloidosis.

**Other variants:**
- **Heavy-chain disease** — proliferations producing only heavy chains; IgA heavy-chain disease has predilection for GI/respiratory lymphoid tissue; may be a variant of extranodal marginal zone lymphoma
- **Primary amyloidosis** — monoclonal plasma cells secrete free light chains → AL-type amyloid deposits

---

## Hodgkin Lymphoma

**Key concepts:** Distinction from NHL · Reed-Sternberg cells · WHO classification · Spread pattern

Hodgkin lymphoma is set apart from NHLs by the presence of distinctive **Reed-Sternberg (RS) giant cells** — the neoplastic cell. RS cells are typically vastly outnumbered by non-neoplastic inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells, macrophages). The biologic behaviour and treatment of Hodgkin lymphoma differ importantly from NHLs.

**Key clinical distinction from NHL:** Hodgkin lymphoma often arises at a **single site** and spreads in a predictable, contiguous fashion to adjacent lymph node groups → early-stage disease is sometimes treated with **local radiotherapy alone.** NHLs are usually widely disseminated at diagnosis and require systemic therapy.

**WHO classification of Hodgkin lymphoma:**

| Subtype | Key Features |
|---------|-------------|
| Nodular sclerosis | Most common; collagen bands divide lymph node into nodules; lacunar RS cell variant; young adults; mediastinal involvement common |
| Mixed cellularity | Classic RS cells with mixed inflammatory background; intermediate prognosis |
| Lymphocyte-rich | Abundant lymphocytes; rare RS cells; best prognosis |
| Lymphocyte depletion | Few lymphocytes; many RS cells or fibrosis; worst prognosis; often advanced stage |
| Nodular lymphocyte predominance | Distinct entity; "popcorn" (L&H) RS cell variant; CD20+; indolent |

**Reed-Sternberg cells** — large cells with abundant cytoplasm and bilobed or multilobed nuclei each containing a huge inclusion-like nucleolus ("owl-eye" appearance). RS cells derive from germinal centre B cells — they have rearranged immunoglobulin genes but have lost normal B cell gene expression programmes.

---

articles.title: Adrenal Neoplasms and MEN Syndromes — Notes
articles.content:
## Summary
This document outlines key distinctions between adrenal adenoma and carcinoma, details various Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndromes, and differentiates parathyroid cell types. It further explains the various types of Renal Tubular Acidosis, emphasizing their unique characteristics, and provides a comprehensive overview of the pathogenesis, morphology, and clinical progression of Diabetic Nephropathy. The content highlights critical diagnostic features and clinical implications across these endocrine and renal disorders.

## Key Points
- Cytology alone cannot diagnose adrenal carcinoma; only **vascular invasion, capsular invasion, or metastasis** confirms malignancy.
- **MEN1 mutation** is found in 30–35% of sporadic parathyroid adenomas.
- **RET mutation** in MEN2 requires screening of family members and prophylactic thyroidectomy in carriers.
- **Phaeochromocytoma** patients should always be screened for MEN2.
- **Chief cells** predominate and are the functional cells of the parathyroid gland.
- **Oxyphil cells** increase with age and typically appear after puberty.
- Stromal fat in the parathyroid gland increases up to age 25, then plateaus at approximately 30% of the gland.
- **Adenomas** are mostly composed of **chief cells**, while **oxyphil adenomas** are rare.
- **Water-clear cell hyperplasia** involves glycogen-rich clear cells and is seen in some hyperplasia cases.
- **Type 4 Renal Tubular Acidosis** is the only RTA with **hyperkalaemia**, while all other types present with hypokalaemia.
- **Type 4 Renal Tubular Acidosis** is the most common RTA in clinical practice, often associated with **diabetic nephropathy**.
- **Microalbuminuria** is the earliest detectable sign of **diabetic nephropathy**.
- **ACEi/ARBs** slow the progression of **diabetic nephropathy** by reducing intraglomerular pressure through efferent arteriole dilation.
- Both afferent and efferent arteriolar **hyalinosis** are unique to **diabetic nephropathy**, distinguishing it from hypertensive nephropathy which typically affects only the afferent arteriole.

## Detailed Notes
### ADRENAL NEOPLASMS — Adenoma vs Carcinoma

| Feature | Adenoma | Carcinoma |
|---|---|---|
| Size | Small, <50g | Large, often >100g |
| Gross | Yellow, well-circumscribed, smooth | Grey-white, irregular, necrotic |
| Histology | Uniform clear cells, thin capsule, no invasion | Pleomorphic cells, mitoses, necrosis, **vascular invasion** |
| Capsule | Intact | Breached — **invasion** is diagnostic |
| Metastasis | No | Yes — only reliable criterion of malignancy alongside invasion |
| CDC73/parafibromin | Intact | Mutated in ~70% |
| ACTH | Suppressed (autonomous cortisol) | Suppressed |
| Prognosis | Excellent after adrenalectomy | Poor — local recurrence in 1/3, distant metastasis in 1/3 |

### MEN SYNDROMES (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia)

| Feature | MEN1 | MEN2A | MEN2B |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gene | **MEN1** (chromosome 11q13, tumour suppressor) | **RET proto-oncogene** | **RET proto-oncogene** |
| Parathyroid | Hyperplasia/adenoma ✅ | Hyperplasia ✅ | No |
| Pancreas | Islet cell tumours (**gastrinoma, insulinoma**) ✅ | No | No |
| Pituitary | Adenoma (**prolactinoma** most common) ✅ | No | No |
| Adrenal | No | **Phaeochromocytoma** ✅ | **Phaeochromocytoma** ✅ |
| Thyroid | No | **Medullary thyroid carcinoma** ✅ | **Medullary thyroid carcinoma** ✅ |
| Other | — | — | **Marfanoid habitus**, **mucosal neuromas** |

**Mnemonic:**
- **MEN1 = 3 Ps** — **Parathyroid** + **Pancreas** + **Pituitary**
- **MEN2A = 2 Ps** — **Parathyroid** + **Phaeochromocytoma** + **medullary thyroid**
- **MEN2B = Phaeochromocytoma** + **medullary thyroid** + **marfanoid/neuromas** (no parathyroid)

### PARATHYROID CELL TYPES

| Cell Type | Size | Cytoplasm | Function | Granules |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Chief cells** | 12–20 μm, predominant | Light to dark pink, polygonal | **PTH synthesis and secretion** | PTH secretory granules present |
| **Oxyphil cells** | Larger than chief cells | Deeply eosinophilic, packed with mitochondria | Unknown (transitional/inactive) | Sparse/absent secretory granules |

### RENAL TUBULAR ACIDOSIS (RTA)

**Definition:** Defect in renal acid-base handling, leading to normal anion gap metabolic acidosis despite normal or near-normal GFR.

| Feature | Type 1 (Distal) | Type 2 (Proximal) | Type 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Defect | Impaired **H⁺ excretion** in collecting duct | Impaired **HCO₃⁻ reabsorption** in proximal tubule | **Hypoaldosteronism** → impaired H⁺ and K⁺ excretion |
| Urine pH | Always >5.5 (cannot acidify) | <5.5 (can acidify when plasma HCO₃⁻ low) | >5.5 |
| Serum K⁺ | ↓ **Hypokalaemia** | ↓ **Hypokalaemia** | ↑ **Hyperkalaemia** |
| Serum HCO₃⁻ | Very low | Moderately low | Mildly low |
| Causes | Sjögren's, SLE, amphotericin B, medullary sponge kidney | Fanconi syndrome, multiple myeloma, Wilson's disease | **Diabetic nephropathy**, **ACEi/ARBs**, Addison's disease |
| Complications | **Nephrocalcinosis**, **nephrolithiasis**, **osteomalacia** | Rickets/osteomalacia | Arrhythmias from **hyperkalaemia** |
| Treatment | Oral bicarbonate (small doses) | Large oral bicarbonate + treat cause | **Fludrocortisone**, dietary K⁺ restriction |

### DIABETIC NEPHROPATHY — Pathogenesis & Morphology

**Pathogenesis (stepwise):**
The pathogenesis of **diabetic nephropathy** is a stepwise process initiated by **chronic hyperglycaemia**. This leads to the glycation of proteins, forming **advanced glycation end products (AGEs)**, which contribute to **mesangial expansion**. Hyperglycaemia also increases intraglomerular pressure due to afferent arteriole dilation exceeding efferent, resulting in **hyperfiltration** and subsequent **glomerular hypertension**. This hypertension, in turn, causes **glomerular basement membrane (GBM) thickening**, marking the onset of proteinuria, specifically **microalbuminuria**. As mesangial expansion progresses, it culminates in **nodular glomerulosclerosis**, characterized by **Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules**. Ultimately, diffuse glomerulosclerosis leads to a decrease in **GFR**, progressing to **chronic kidney disease (CKD)** and eventually **end-stage renal disease (ESRD)**.

**Morphology:**
The characteristic morphology of **diabetic nephropathy** includes several key features. **Diffuse glomerulosclerosis**, marked by uniform mesangial matrix expansion, is the most common finding. Another pathognomonic feature is **nodular glomerulosclerosis**, specifically **Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules**, which appear as ovoid or spherical nodules of acellular matrix located in the periphery of the glomerulus. Other morphological changes include **GBM thickening** and **hyaline arteriolosclerosis**. Notably, **hyaline arteriolosclerosis** in diabetic nephropathy affects both the afferent and efferent arterioles, with efferent involvement being unique and distinguishing it from hypertensive nephropathy. Additionally, **exudative lesions**, such as hyaline caps and capsular drops, may be observed.

**Clinical progression:**
The clinical progression of **diabetic nephropathy** typically unfolds in five stages. **Stage 1** is characterized by **hyperfiltration**, where an increased **GFR** is observed without proteinuria. **Stage 2** is a **silent** phase, marked by **GBM thickening** and other microstructural changes that occur without overt symptoms. The earliest clinical sign appears in **Stage 3** as **microalbuminuria** (30–300 mg/day). This progresses to **Stage 4**, where **macroalbuminuria** (>300 mg/day) is present, accompanied by a decreased **GFR** and **hypertension**. Finally, **Stage 5** represents **end-stage renal disease (ESRD)**, necessitating interventions such as dialysis or kidney transplant.

## Practice Questions
1.  What are the only reliable criteria for confirming the malignancy of an adrenal neoplasm? → **Vascular invasion, capsular invasion, or metastasis**.
2.  Which organs are typically affected in MEN1 syndrome, according to the mnemonic? → **Parathyroid, Pancreas, Pituitary** (3 Ps).
3.  What is the key distinguishing feature between MEN2A and MEN2B regarding parathyroid involvement? → MEN2A involves **parathyroid hyperplasia**, while MEN2B does not.
4.  Which cell type predominates and is responsible for PTH synthesis and secretion in the parathyroid gland? → **Chief cells**.
5.  What is the unique serum potassium abnormality observed in Type 4 Renal Tubular Acidosis compared to other RTA types? → **Hyperkalaemia**.
6.  What specific morphological finding is pathognomonic for diabetic nephropathy? → **Nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules)**.
7.  What is the earliest detectable clinical sign of diabetic nephropathy? → **Microalbuminuria** (30–300 mg/day).
8.  Which type of arteriolar hyalinosis is unique to diabetic nephropathy and helps distinguish it from hypertensive nephropathy? → Hyaline arteriolosclerosis affecting both **afferent AND efferent arterioles**.

articles.title: General Pathology Review Questions: Set 1 — MCQ Bank
articles.content:
Question 1
Vasoactive amines responsible for vasodilatation during inflammation are released from which cell type?

A. Plasma cells
B. Lymphocytes
C. Monocytes
D. Mast cells

Answer: D. Mast cells
Explanation: ** Mast cells contain preformed vasoactive mediators including histamine, which causes immediate vasodilation and increased vascular permeability during the early phase of acute inflammation.

---

Question 2
Bradykinin causes all the following during inflammation EXCEPT

A. Smooth muscle contraction
B. Pain
C. Dilatation of blood vessels
D. Opsonisation and Chemotaxis

Answer: D. Opsonisation and Chemotaxis
Explanation: ** Bradykinin is a vasoactive peptide that causes vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, smooth muscle contraction, and pain. It does not directly cause opsonization or chemotaxis.

---

Question 3
Granulomas are characterised by all of the following EXCEPT

A. Features of chronic inflammation
B. Accumulation of modified macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells
C. Initiation by both infectious and non-infectious agents
D. Acute inflammatory reaction

Answer: D. Acute inflammatory reaction
Explanation: ** Granulomas are a form of chronic inflammation characterized by collections of epithelioid cells, lymphocytes, and sometimes giant cells.

---

Question 4
During acute inflammation, tissue oedema occurs due to

A. Increased capillary permeability
B. Decreased capillary permeability
C. Decreased interstitial fluid
D. Decreased blood flow

Answer: A. Increased capillary permeability
Explanation: ** Tissue edema results from increased vascular permeability, allowing plasma proteins and fluid to leak into the interstitial space.

---

Question 5
The process by which white blood cells migrate from blood vessels through widened inter-endothelial junctions is referred to as

A. Pavementing
B. Diapedesis
C. Rouleaux formation
D. Chemotaxis migration

Answer: B. Diapedesis
Explanation: ** Diapedesis (transmigration) is the process by which leukocytes migrate between endothelial cells to exit the vascular compartment.

---

Question 6
During acute inflammation, Interleukin-1 (IL-1) helps in

A. Stimulation of T-lymphocytes
B. Inhibiting B-lymphocytes
C. Inhibiting chemotaxis of neutrophils and macrophages
D. Decreasing fibroblast and bone resorption activity

Answer: A. Stimulation of T-lymphocytes
Explanation: ** IL-1 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine that stimulates T-lymphocyte activation and proliferation.

---

Question 7
The following are mediators of inflammation EXCEPT

A. Interferons
B. Prostaglandins
C. Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF)
D. Myeloperoxidase enzyme

Answer: D. Myeloperoxidase enzyme
Explanation: ** Myeloperoxidase is an enzyme in neutrophil granules used for antimicrobial activity, not a primary mediator of inflammation.

---

Question 8
Caseating type granulomas are usually seen in

A. Viral infections
B. Tuberculosis
C. Pyogenic bacterial infections
D. Meningitis

Answer: B. Tuberculosis
Explanation: ** Caseating granulomas with central necrosis are characteristic of mycobacterial infections, particularly tuberculosis.

---

Question 9
In granulomas, epithelioid and giant cells are derived from

A. T-lymphocytes
B. B-lymphocytes
C. Plasma cells
D. Circulating monocytes

Answer: D. Circulating monocytes
Explanation: ** Epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells are derived from activated macrophages, which originate from circulating monocytes.

---

Question 10
The characteristic cells of chronic inflammation are all EXCEPT

A. Plasma cells
B. Macrophages
C. Lymphocytes
D. Polymorphonuclear cells (PMNs)

Answer: D. Polymorphonuclear cells (PMNs)
Explanation: ** PMNs (neutrophils) are the hallmark of acute inflammation; chronic inflammation involves mononuclear cells.

---

Question 11
The following vascular changes are observed in acute inflammation EXCEPT

A. Vasodilation
B. Stasis of blood
C. Increased vascular permeability
D. Decreased blood flow

Answer: D. Decreased blood flow
Explanation: ** Acute inflammation initially causes increased blood flow due to vasodilation.

---

Question 12
The most common fixative used to preserve tissue in histopathology is

A. 10% Formalin
B. Ethylene glycol
C. Haematoxylin
D. 95% Ethanol

Answer: A. 10% Formalin
Explanation: ** 10% neutral buffered formalin is the standard fixative used to cross-link proteins and preserve morphology.

---

Question 13
Cells which have the capacity to multiply throughout their lifespan are referred to as

A. Stable cells
B. Permanent cells
C. Labile cells
D. None of the above

Answer: C. Labile cells
Explanation: ** Labile cells (e.g., skin, GI epithelium) continuously divide to replace lost cells.

---

Question 14
The following cells have LEAST capacity for regeneration

A. Cardiac muscle
B. Skeletal muscle
C. Neuronal cells
D. Liver cells

Answer: C. Neuronal cells
Explanation: ** Neurons are permanent cells with minimal to no regenerative capacity in the adult CNS.

---

Question 15
The FIRST event in primary wound healing is

A. Epithelial changes
B. Organization
C. Formation of blood clot
D. Acute inflammatory response

Answer: C. Formation of blood clot
Explanation: ** Hemostasis and clot formation occur immediately to stop bleeding and provide a scaffold.

---

Question 16
Clean, uninfected, surgically incised wounds whose edges are approximated by surgical sutures heal by

A. Primary intention
B. Secondary intention
C. Cauterisation
D. Regeneration

Answer: A. Primary intention

---

Question 17
Large open wounds characterised by tissue loss and repaired by granulation tissue in the floor heal by

A. Secondary intention
B. Primary intention
C. Cauterisation
D. Regeneration

Answer: A. Secondary intention

---

Question 18
The following events are common to primary and secondary wound healing EXCEPT

A. Formation of blood clot
B. Inflammatory response
C. Epithelial changes
D. Wound contraction

Answer: D. Wound contraction
Explanation: ** Wound contraction is primarily a feature of secondary intention healing.

---

Question 19
The following factors inhibit wound healing EXCEPT

A. Infection
B. Cortisol
C. Foreign bodies
D. Proteins

Answer: D. Proteins
Explanation: ** Proteins are essential building blocks for repair and collagen synthesis.

---

Question 20
Granulation tissue consists of the following EXCEPT

A. Fibroblasts
B. Macrophages
C. Polymorphonuclear cells
D. Budding young blood vessels

Answer: C. Polymorphonuclear cells

---

Question 21
The correct sequence of the cell cycle is

A. G0 – G1 – S – G2 – M
B. G0 – G1 – G2 – S – M
C. G0 – M – G2 – S – G1
D. G0 – G1 – S – M – G2

Answer: A. G0 – G1 – S – G2 – M

---

Question 22
The following local factors influence wound healing EXCEPT

A. Nutrition
B. Adequate blood supply
C. Size and location of wound
D. Presence of infection

Answer: A. Nutrition
Explanation: ** Nutrition is a systemic factor, not a local factor.

---

Question 23
The term Metaplasia refers to

A. Irregular, atypical proliferative changes
B. Loss of cell substance producing shrinkage
C. Replacement of one type of adult cell by another
D. None of the above

Answer: C. Replacement of one type of adult cell by another

---

Question 24
Malignant neoplasms show all the following features EXCEPT

A. Disorganized cell structure
B. Capsulation
C. Invasion of local and distant tissues
D. Rapid, erratic growth

Answer: B. Capsulation
Explanation: ** Malignant tumors typically lack a capsule and are invasive.

---

Question 25
The increase in size of individual cells within an organ is referred to as

A. Hypertrophy
B. Hyperplasia
C. Atrophy
D. Differentiation

Answer: A. Hypertrophy

---

Question 26
The following is classified as a tumor suppressor gene

A. C-Myc
B. p53
C. RAS
D. BCR

Answer: B. p53

---

Question 27
Burkitt's lymphoma is associated with proliferation of

A. T-lymphocyte cells
B. B-lymphocyte cells
C. Lymph vessels
D. Lymph nodes

Answer: B. B-lymphocyte cells

---

Question 28
The following are oncogenic viruses in humans EXCEPT

A. Human Papilloma Virus (HPV)
B. Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)
C. Hepatitis B virus
D. Polio virus

Answer: D. Polio virus

---

Question 29
Which of the following is TRUE regarding pathologic assessment of tumours?

A. Grading is the degree of microscopic differentiation
B. Staging is the extent of spread
C. TNM and AJCC systems are used for staging
D. All of the above

Answer: D. All of the above

---

Question 30
Immune response and defense to tumours is mediated by the following cell types EXCEPT: ## SECTION B: SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS

A. Cytotoxic T-lymphocytes
B. Natural killer cells
C. Neutrophils
D. Macrophages

Answer: C. Neutrophils

articles.title: Lower Urinary Tract & Ureter Pathology: Obstruction & Tumors — Notes
articles.content:
---
DISORDERS OF THE LOWER URINARY TRACT — PART 1
---
CLINICAL ANATOMY
**Definition:** The renal pelves, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra (except the terminal portion) are lined by a special transitional epithelium called **urothelium**.
**Structure:**
- Composed of 5–6 cell layers with oval nuclei and linear nuclear grooves
- Surface layer = large, flattened **"umbrella cells"** with abundant cytoplasm

**Bladder Wall Layers — ⚠️ Know This:**

- **Muscularis mucosa** — wisps of smooth muscle in the lamina propria; discontinuous
- **Detrusor muscle (muscularis propria)** — deeper, well-defined, larger bundles
- Bladder cancers are **staged based on invasion of the detrusor muscle** — the two must not be confused
- Obstructed urine flow → ↑ intravesical pressure → bladder musculature **hypertrophy**

**Clinical Relationships:**

- Ureters are entirely **retroperitoneal** → retroperitoneal tumours or fibrosis can entrap and obstruct them
- Women (middle-aged/older): pelvic support relaxation → uterine prolapse → bladder floor descends → **cystocele** (bladder protrudes into vagina; fails to empty properly during micturition)
- Men: prostate lies posterior/inferior to bladder neck → **prostatic enlargement = major cause of urinary tract obstruction**

---

- URETERS

---

A. CONGENITAL ANOMALIES
**Incidence:** Found in ~2–3% of all autopsies; most clinically insignificant.
**UPJ (Ureteropelvic Junction) Obstruction:**
- Most common cause of **hydronephrosis in infants and children**
- In children: preferentially affects **males**; bilateral in **20%** of cases; often associated with other anomalies; minority have agenesis of the contralateral kidney
- In adults: more common in **women**; most often **unilateral**
- Cause: abnormal smooth muscle bundle organisation OR excess collagen deposition at UPJ OR (rarely) extrinsic compression by abnormal renal vessels

---

B. TUMOURS AND TUMOUR-LIKE LESIONS
**Benign Tumours:**
- Rare; generally of **mesenchymal origin**
- **Fibroepithelial polyp** — tumour-like lesion; common in children; composed of loose, vascularised connective tissue overlaid by urothelium

**Malignant Tumours:**

- Primary malignant ureteral tumours resemble those of the renal pelvis, calyces, and bladder
- Majority are **urothelial carcinomas**
- Peak incidence: **6th–7th decade** of life → cause obstruction of the ureteral lumen
- Commonly occur **concurrently** with urothelial carcinomas of the bladder or renal pelvis

---

C. OBSTRUCTIVE LESIONS
**Overview:**
- Intrinsic and extrinsic lesions may obstruct ureters → **hydroureter, hydronephrosis, pyelonephritis**
- Unilateral obstruction → proximal intrinsic or extrinsic causes (e.g., stones, neoplasms)
- Bilateral obstruction → distal causes (e.g., nodular hyperplasia of the prostate)

**Intrinsic Causes:**

- **Calculi** — typically of renal origin; usually ≤5 mm; impact at narrowings (UPJ, iliac vessel crossing, bladder entry) → excruciating **renal colic**
- **Strictures** — congenital or acquired
- **Tumours** — urothelial carcinomas; rarely benign tumours/fibroepithelial polyps
- **Blood clots** — from massive haematuria due to renal calculi, tumours, or papillary necrosis
- **Neurogenic** — interruption of neural pathways to the bladder

**Extrinsic Causes:**

- **Pregnancy** — physiologic smooth muscle relaxation OR uterine fundus pressure on ureters at the pelvic brim
- **Periureteral inflammation** — salpingitis, diverticulitis, peritonitis, sclerosing retroperitoneal fibrosis
- **Endometriosis** — pelvic lesions with scarring
- **Tumours** — cancers of rectum, bladder, prostate, ovaries, uterus, cervix; lymphomas; sarcomas

---

D. SCLEROSING RETROPERITONEAL FIBROSIS
**Definition:** Rare fibrotic proliferative inflammatory process that encases retroperitoneal structures → causes **hydronephrosis**.
**Epidemiology:**
- Middle to late age; more common in **males**

**Aetiology:**

- Subset linked to **IgG4-related disease** → elevated serum IgG4; fibroinflammatory lesions rich in IgG4-secreting plasma cells; affects multiple organs
- Other causes: drug exposures (ergot derivatives, β-adrenergic blockers), inflammatory conditions (vasculitis, diverticulitis, Crohn disease), malignancies (lymphomas, urinary tract carcinomas)
- Most cases: **no obvious cause → idiopathic (Ormond disease)**

**Morphology (Histology):**

- Fibrous tissue with prominent infiltrate of lymphocytes (often with germinal centres), plasma cells (frequently IgG4+), and eosinophils

**Treatment:**

- Initially: **corticosteroids**
- If resistant → ureteral stents or surgical ureterolysis (freeing ureters from surrounding fibrosis)

---

- URINARY BLADDER

---

A. CONGENITAL ANOMALIES
**Vesicoureteral Reflux:**
- Most common and serious congenital bladder anomaly
- Predisposes to **ascending pyelonephritis** and loss of renal function
- Abnormal connections between bladder and vagina/rectum/uterus → congenital **vesicouterine fistulae**

**Diverticula:**

- Pouch-like invaginations of the bladder wall; <1 cm to 10 cm in diameter
- **Congenital** — focal failure of musculature development OR obstruction during foetal development
- **Acquired** — most often from prostatic hyperplasia → ↑ intravesical pressure → outpouching of wall
- Most are small and asymptomatic
- Complications: urinary stasis → infection + bladder calculi
- Rarely: carcinoma may arise within diverticula — more advanced at diagnosis due to thin/absent muscularis propria

**Exstrophy of the Bladder:**

- Developmental failure of anterior abdominal and bladder wall → bladder communicates directly with abdominal surface
- Exposed bladder mucosa → undergoes **colonic glandular metaplasia** → chronic infection → often spreads to upper urinary tract
- Associated with increased risk of **adenocarcinoma** in the bladder remnant

**Urachal Anomalies:**

- Urachal canal connects foetal bladder to the allantois → normally obliterated at birth
- If fully patent → **fistulous connection between bladder and umbilicus**
- If partially patent (central region) → **urachal cyst** lined by urothelial or metaplastic glandular epithelium
- Urachal cysts at increased risk of neoplastic transformation
- Account for only 0.1–0.3% of all bladder cancers BUT constitute **20–40% of bladder adenocarcinomas**

---

B. INFLAMMATION — CYSTITIS
**Acute and Chronic Cystitis**
**Predisposing Factors:** bladder calculi, urinary obstruction, diabetes mellitus, instrumentation, immune deficiency
**Common Aetiologic Agents:**
- Coliforms: **E. coli** (most common) → Proteus → Klebsiella → Enterobacter
- Women more susceptible → shorter urethra
- **Tuberculous cystitis** — almost always a sequel to renal tuberculosis
- **Candida albicans** (and rarely Cryptococcus) — in immunosuppressed or long-term antibiotic users
- **Schistosoma haematobium** — important cause in Africa and Middle East
- Viruses: adenovirus, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma
- **Adenovirus + BK virus** → haemorrhagic cystitis
- **Clostridium perfringens** (gas-forming) → **emphysematous cystitis** (gas-filled vesicles in bladder wall)

**Morphology (Histology):**

- Acute cystitis: mucosal hyperaemia + neutrophilic infiltrate ± exudate
- Chronic cystitis: mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate
- **Iatrogenic cystitis** — from systemic chemotherapy or pelvic irradiation

 - Cyclophosphamide → **haemorrhagic cystitis**

- Radiation → acute or chronic radiation cystitis
- **Follicular cystitis** — lymphoid follicles in bladder mucosa and wall
- **Eosinophilic cystitis** — eosinophilic infiltrate in submucosa; nonspecific subacute inflammation OR manifestation of systemic allergic disorder

**Clinical Features:**

- Classic triad:

 - **Frequency** — may require urination every 15–20 minutes in acute cases

- **Lower abdominal/suprapubic pain**
- **Dysuria** — pain or burning on urination
- May precede **pyelonephritis** (more serious)
- Often secondary to underlying urinary stasis (BPH, cystocele, calculi, neoplasms) → treat the primary cause first

---

**Special Forms of Cystitis**
**Interstitial Cystitis (Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome):**
**Definition:** Disorder of unknown aetiology; most common in **women**; defined as unpleasant sensation (pain, pressure, discomfort) related to the urinary bladder with urinary symptoms lasting **>6 weeks** in the absence of infection or other identifiable cause.
**Features:**
- Intermittent, often severe suprapubic pain; urinary frequency; urgency; haematuria; dysuria
- Cystoscopy: **mucosal fissures + punctate haemorrhages (glomerulations)**
- Histology: nonspecific; mast cells often increased in submucosa (significance uncertain)
- ⚠️ Main role of biopsy = **rule out CIS**, which clinically mimics interstitial cystitis
- Some cases: chronic mucosal ulcers → **Hunner ulcers** (late/classic/ulcerative phase)
- Late course: transmural fibrosis → **contracted bladder**
- Treatment: largely empiric

**Malakoplakia:**

**Definition:** Distinctive chronic inflammatory reaction from **acquired defects in phagocyte function**; arises in setting of chronic bacterial infection (mostly E. coli, occasionally Proteus); increased frequency in immunosuppressed (e.g., renal transplant recipients).
**Morphology:**
- Cystoscopy: soft yellow, slightly raised mucosal plaques (~3–4 cm)
- Histology: aggregates of large **foamy macrophages** + occasional multinucleate giant cells + lymphocytes
- Macrophage cytoplasm: granular due to phagosomes stuffed with bacterial debris (defective phagolysosome function)
- Pathognomonic finding: **Michaelis-Gutmann bodies** — laminated mineralized concretions from calcium deposition in enlarged lysosomes within macrophages
- Similar lesions described in: colon, GI tract, brain, lungs, bones, endometrium, kidneys, prostate, epididymis

**Polypoid Cystitis:**

- Inflammatory lesion from irritation of bladder mucosa — most commonly from **instrumentation/indwelling catheters**
- Urothelium thrown into broad bulbous polypoid projections due to marked submucosal oedema
- ⚠️ May be **mistaken for papillary urothelial carcinoma** — both clinically and histologically

---

C. METAPLASTIC LESIONS
**Cystitis Glandularis and Cystitis Cystica:**
- Common lesions in which nests of urothelium (**von Brunn nests**) grow downward into the lamina propria
- Central cells undergo metaplasia:

 - **Cystitis glandularis** → cuboidal/columnar appearance

- **Cystitis cystica** → retract to form cystic spaces lined by flattened urothelium
- Often coexist → referred to as **cystitis cystica et glandularis**
- Variant: goblet cells present → epithelium resembles intestinal mucosa (**intestinal/colonic metaplasia**)
- ⚠️ Extensive, multifocal intestinal metaplasia = **precursor to adenocarcinoma**

**Squamous Metaplasia:**

- Response to chronic injury → urothelium replaced by nonkeratinizing or keratinizing squamous epithelium
- Distinguish from: glycogenated squamous epithelium normally found at the **trigone** in women (this is normal)
- ⚠️ Extensive multifocal **keratinizing** squamous metaplasia = precursor to squamous dysplasia, CIS, and invasive squamous cell carcinoma
- Classic example: **bladder schistosomiasis** → squamous metaplasia → squamous cell carcinoma in endemic areas

**Nephrogenic Adenoma:**

- Unusual lesion; may not be true metaplasia
- Evidence from renal transplant recipients: caused by implantation and growth of **renal tubular cells** at sites of bladder mucosal erosion
- Overlying urothelium focally replaced by cuboidal epithelium → may assume papillary growth
- Usually <1 cm; larger lesions can mimic cancer clinically
- Tubular proliferation can infiltrate lamina propria and superficial detrusor → **microscopically mimics malignancy**

---
