articles.title: Renal, Liver, Cardiac & Adrenal Function Tests for Year 3 — Notes
articles.content:
# MONDAY 14TH JULY — FULL REVISION PACK
## Chemical Pathology (8–11 AM) + Haematology & Blood Transfusion (2–5 PM)
---
# PART A: CHEMICAL PATHOLOGY (MBPA 3600)
---
## A1. RENAL FUNCTION
**Tests used:** Urea, creatinine, eGFR, electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺, HCO3⁻), urinalysis (protein, blood, casts)
**Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) — classify by cause:**
- Pre-renal — reduced perfusion (dehydration, hypotension, haemorrhage, heart failure)
- Renal/intrinsic — direct damage (acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, nephrotoxins)
- Post-renal — obstruction (stones, BPH, tumour)
**AKI lab pattern:**
- ↑Urea, ↑creatinine (rapid rise over hours–days)
- ↑K⁺ — risk of arrhythmia
- Oliguria
- Urea:creatinine ratio >20:1 → pre-renal cause
**Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) lab pattern:**
- Persistently ↑urea/creatinine (weeks–months)
- Anaemia — from ↓erythropoietin production
- Hypocalcaemia + hyperphosphataemia — from ↓active vitamin D
- ↓eGFR (calculated from creatinine + age + gender + race)
**Nephritic vs Nephrotic syndrome (commonly confused — know cold):**
| Feature | Nephritic | Nephrotic |
|---|---|---|
| Proteinuria | Mild | Heavy (>3.5g/day) |
| Haematuria | Prominent | Minimal |
| Blood pressure | ↑ | Normal/↑ |
| Oedema | Mild | Marked |
| Albumin | Normal | ↓ |
| Lipids | Normal | ↑ |
| Casts | RBC casts | Fatty/oval fat bodies |
**Other renal points:**
- ADH acts on V2 receptors in the collecting duct
- Thick ascending limb = "diluting segment"
- ATN = commonest cause of intrinsic AKI
---
## A2. LIVER FUNCTION TESTS (LFTs)
**Components and what each shows:**
- ALT, AST → hepatocellular injury
- ALP, GGT → cholestasis (bile flow obstruction)
- Albumin, PT/INR → synthetic function
- Bilirubin (total, conjugated/unconjugated) → excretory function
**Pattern recognition:**
- ALT/AST >> ALP → hepatocellular (viral hepatitis, alcohol, drugs)
- ALP/GGT >> ALT/AST → obstructive/cholestatic (gallstones, pancreatic head Ca)
- AST:ALT ratio >2 → suggests alcoholic liver disease
**Jaundice work-up:**
- Ultrasound — dilated ducts = obstructive; normal ducts = hepatocellular
- Viral serology (HBsAg, anti-HCV)
- PT/INR — doesn't correct with vitamin K in hepatocellular disease; corrects in obstructive disease
- Split bilirubin — conjugated fraction dominant in obstruction
**Bilirubin metabolism disorders:**
- Gilbert syndrome — mild ↓UGT activity, unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, benign
- Crigler-Najjar type II — reduced (not absent) UGT
- Crigler-Najjar type I — absent UGT, severe, fatal if untreated
- Dubin-Johnson syndrome — conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, black liver pigmentation
- Rotor syndrome — conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, no pigmentation
---
## A3. CARDIAC MARKERS
**Markers used to assess cardiac injury, in order of rise/fall:**
| Marker | Rises | Peaks | Returns to normal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Myoglobin | 1–2h | 6–12h | 24h |
| CK-MB | 3–6h | 12–24h | 48–72h |
| Troponin I/T | 3–6h | 12–24h | 7–14 days |
| LDH | 6–12h | 24–48h | 7–10 days |
- Troponin — most sensitive and specific for MI, gold standard
- CK-MB — useful for detecting re-infarction, since troponin stays elevated too long
- Myoglobin — earliest to rise, but not cardiac-specific (also from skeletal muscle)
- LDH — historically used; LDH1 > LDH2 ("flipped pattern") in MI, rarely used now
- Total CK also rises in skeletal muscle damage — CK-MB is the cardiac-specific fraction
---
## A4. ADRENAL DISORDERS
**Cushing's syndrome (↑cortisol):**
- Causes: pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease), adrenal adenoma, ectopic ACTH (small cell lung Ca), exogenous steroids
- Cortisol synthesis occurs in the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex
- Diagnostic tests: 24h urinary free cortisol, low-dose dexamethasone suppression test, late-night salivary cortisol
- Causes secondary diabetes via ↑gluconeogenesis + insulin resistance
**Addison's disease (adrenal insufficiency):**
- ↓Cortisol, ↓aldosterone
- Hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypotension
- ACTH stimulation (Synacthen) test — cortisol fails to rise
**Phaeochromocytoma:**
- Tumour of adrenal medulla chromaffin cells, secretes catecholamines
- **Key enzyme: Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT)** — converts noradrenaline to adrenaline, only found in the adrenal medulla
- Diagnostic test: 24h urinary metanephrines/catecholamines, plasma free metanephrines
- Causes secondary diabetes via glycogenolysis + inhibited insulin release
- Classic triad: episodic headache, sweating, palpitations (with hypertension)
**Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia:**
- Most common cause: 21-hydroxylase deficiency
- Leads to ↓cortisol, ↓aldosterone, ↑androgens (virilisation)
- Salt-wasting crisis in neonates (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia)
---
## A5. THYROID FUNCTION TESTS
- Primary hyperthyroidism — ↑T3/T4, ↓TSH (e.g. Graves' disease)
- Primary hypothyroidism — ↓T3/T4, ↑TSH (e.g. Hashimoto's thyroiditis)
- Secondary hypothyroidism — ↓T3/T4, ↓TSH (pituitary cause)
- Subclinical hypothyroidism — normal T3/T4, ↑TSH
- Graves' disease — TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) stimulate the gland
- Hashimoto's — anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies
---
## A6. CALCIUM, PHOSPHATE & BONE
**Hypercalcaemia work-up:**
- Serum calcium (ionised + total)
- PTH — ↑ in primary hyperparathyroidism, suppressed in malignancy
- Phosphate — ↓ in hyperparathyroidism
- PTHrP — ↑ in humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy
- Vitamin D — ↑ in toxicity/sarcoidosis
- 24h urinary calcium — distinguishes primary hyperparathyroidism from familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
**Hypoparathyroidism:** ↓calcium + ↑phosphate
**Vitamin D and bone markers:**
- ALP rises in bone disease (Paget's, osteomalacia, fractures) as well as liver disease — use GGT to distinguish source
- Rickets/osteomalacia — ↓vitamin D, ↓calcium, ↑ALP, ↑PTH (secondary)
---
## A7. DIABETES MELLITUS
**Diagnostic cutoffs:**
- Fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L
- 2-hour OGTT ≥11.1 mmol/L
- Random glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L + symptoms
- HbA1c ≥6.5%
**Secondary diabetes — causes and mechanism:**
- Cushing's syndrome — cortisol → gluconeogenesis + insulin resistance
- Acromegaly — GH → insulin resistance + ↑hepatic glucose output
- Phaeochromocytoma — catecholamines → glycogenolysis + ↓insulin release
- Glucagonoma — glucagon → gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis
- Chronic pancreatitis/haemochromatosis — destroys islet cells
**Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA):**
- ↑Glucose, ↑ketones, metabolic acidosis (↓HCO3⁻, ↓pH), ↑anion gap
- K⁺ may be normal/high initially but total body K⁺ is depleted
**DKA vs HHS:**
| Feature | DKA | HHS |
|---|---|---|
| Typical type | Type 1 | Type 2 |
| Glucose | Very high | Extremely high (>33) |
| Ketones | Present | Absent/minimal |
| pH | Low (acidotic) | Normal |
| Onset | Rapid (hours) | Slow (days) |
| Dehydration | Moderate | Severe |
**Diabetic Nephropathy:**
- Earliest sign: microalbuminuria (30–300mg/day)
- Progresses to overt proteinuria → nephrotic-range proteinuria → CKD
- Histology: **Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules** (nodular glomerulosclerosis)
- Mechanism: chronic hyperglycaemia glycates basement membrane proteins → thickening → mesangial expansion → glomerulosclerosis
- Efferent arteriolar hyalinosis initially raises GFR (hyperfiltration), later declines
**Diabetic Retinopathy:**
- Non-proliferative — microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates
- Proliferative — neovascularisation, risk of vitreous haemorrhage/retinal detachment
**Diabetic Neuropathy:**
- Peripheral — glove-and-stocking sensory loss (commonest)
- Autonomic — gastroparesis, postural hypotension, erectile dysfunction
- Mechanism: polyol pathway — glucose → sorbitol via aldose reductase → osmotic nerve damage
**Diabetic Macrovascular disease:** accelerated atherosclerosis → MI, stroke, PVD — leading cause of death in diabetics
**Monitoring:** HbA1c (8–12 week control), urine ACR (nephropathy screen), fasting lipid profile
---
## A8. ACID-BASE (memorise this grid cold)
| Disorder | pH | pCO2 | HCO3⁻ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Respiratory acidosis | ↓ | ↑ | N/↑ |
| Respiratory alkalosis | ↑ | ↓ | N |
| Metabolic acidosis | ↓ | N/↓ | ↓ |
| Metabolic alkalosis | ↑ | N | ↑ |
- Vomiting → metabolic alkalosis (loss of H⁺/HCl)
- Diarrhoea → metabolic acidosis (loss of HCO3⁻)
- Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO3⁻); normal 8–16
- High anion gap metabolic acidosis causes ("MUDPILES"): DKA, lactic acidosis, renal failure, toxins (methanol, ethylene glycol)
---
## A9. LIPID PROFILE
- Total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides
- LDL — "bad" cholesterol, atherogenic
- HDL — "good" cholesterol, protective
- Familial hypercholesterolaemia — LDL receptor defect, very high LDL, premature atherosclerosis
---
## A10. PANCREATIC FUNCTION
- Amylase — rises early in acute pancreatitis, normalises within days
- Lipase — more specific for pancreatitis, stays elevated longer
- Acute pancreatitis: **hypocalcaemia = poor prognostic sign** (fat saponification consumes calcium)
---
## A11. TUMOUR MARKERS
- AFP — hepatocellular carcinoma, yolk sac tumour, non-seminomatous germ cell tumours
- CEA — colorectal carcinoma (also raised in smokers)
- CA-125 — ovarian carcinoma
- CA 19-9 — pancreatic carcinoma
- PSA — prostate carcinoma (also raised in BPH, prostatitis)
- β-hCG — choriocarcinoma, hydatidiform mole, germ cell tumours
---
## A12. ISOLATED ELECTROLYTE DISORDERS
- Hyperkalaemia — causes: renal failure, ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics, acidosis, tissue breakdown (rhabdomyolysis, burns). ECG: peaked T waves, widened QRS.
- Hypokalaemia — causes: diuretics (loop/thiazide), vomiting, diarrhoea, alkalosis, insulin excess. ECG: flattened T waves, U waves.
- Hypernatraemia — causes: water loss (diabetes insipidus, inadequate intake), excess sodium intake
- Hyponatraemia — causes: SIADH, diuretics, heart failure, excessive water intake
---
## A13. INTRA-INDIVIDUAL VARIATION IN LAB VALUES
- Time of day (diurnal variation — cortisol highest in the morning)
- Posture (standing vs lying down — affects plasma volume, protein-bound analytes)
- Recent food intake (glucose, triglycerides)
- Exercise before sampling (↑CK, ↑lactate)
- Menstrual cycle phase (hormones)
- Stress/anxiety (↑cortisol, ↑glucose)
---
## A14. SAMPLE HANDLING
- Fluoride tube — glucose only (inhibits glycolysis)
- EDTA tube — FBC/haematology
- Citrate tube — coagulation studies
- Heparin tube — biochemistry when plasma needed fast
---
## A15. PAST PAPER QUESTIONS — FULL ANSWERS
**Question 1.** A 5-month-old infant presents with severe diarrhoea. You are given the child's sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate and urea levels.
(a) State the fluid status. *(2 marks)*
- Na⁺ <130 → hyponatraemic (hypotonic) dehydration
- Na⁺ 130–150 → isonatraemic (isotonic) dehydration — commonest in diarrhoea
- Na⁺ >150 → hypernatraemic (hypertonic) dehydration
(b) State the confirming lab values. *(3 marks)*
- ↑Urea/creatinine — pre-renal azotaemia from volume depletion
- ↓HCO3⁻ — lost in stool, causing metabolic acidosis
- K⁺ normal/↑ despite total-body deficit — acidosis shifts K⁺ extracellularly
- Urea:creatinine ratio >20:1 — confirms pre-renal cause
**Question 2.** A 65-year-old presents with jaundice. You are given bilirubin, ALT, AST and ALP levels.
(a) Give 2 differential diagnoses. *(2 marks)*
- Hepatocellular jaundice (ALT/AST dominant)
- Obstructive jaundice (ALP/GGT dominant, conjugated bilirubin high)
(b) State 3 further investigations and expected results. *(3 marks)*
- Ultrasound — duct dilation vs normal
- Viral serology — positive in viral hepatocellular cause
- PT/INR — correction with vitamin K in obstructive, not in hepatocellular
**Question 3.** State 3 endocrine diseases causing secondary diabetes, with mechanism.
- Cushing's syndrome, acromegaly, phaeochromocytoma (mechanisms above in A7). Glucagonoma as backup option.
**Question 4.** List 5 factors causing intra-individual variation in lab values.
- See A13 (6 listed, pick any 5).
**Question 5.** Lab tests for investigating hypercalcaemia in a 40-year-old female.
- See A6.
**Question 6.** Tests comprising "liver function tests" and what each indicates.
- See A2.
**Question 7 — Essay (30 marks).** Lab investigations and expected abnormalities in acute and chronic renal failure.
- Full answer in A1 (AKI classification + labs, CKD labs).
---
# PART B: HAEMATOLOGY & BLOOD TRANSFUSION (MBML 3200/3223)
---
## B1. ANAEMIA CLASSIFICATION
Classified by MCV (cell size) and MCHC (colour/haemoglobin content):
| Type | MCV | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Microcytic hypochromic | ↓ | Iron deficiency, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease (late) |
| Normocytic normochromic | Normal | Acute blood loss, haemolysis, anaemia of chronic disease (early), aplastic anaemia |
| Macrocytic | ↑ | B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis |
---
## B2. IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA
**Lab investigations:**
- ↓Serum ferritin (most specific — reflects iron stores)
- ↓Serum iron
- ↑Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)
- ↓Transferrin saturation
- Blood film: microcytic, hypochromic, anisopoikilocytosis, pencil cells
**Causes:** chronic blood loss (GI bleed, menorrhagia), poor dietary intake, malabsorption, increased demand (pregnancy)
---
## B3. MACROCYTIC ANAEMIA (B12/folate deficiency)
- Hypersegmented neutrophils on film (key diagnostic clue)
- ↓Serum B12 or folate
- Pernicious anaemia — autoimmune, anti-intrinsic factor antibodies, anti-parietal cell antibodies
**Case (past paper):** Elderly woman, Hb 8.0, MCV 130fL, MCHC 32pg.
(a) Diagnosis: macrocytic (megaloblastic) anaemia
(b) Confirmatory tests: serum B12/folate, blood film for hypersegmented neutrophils, intrinsic factor antibodies
---
## B4. HAEMOLYTIC ANAEMIA
**5 lab features:**
- ↑Reticulocyte count
- ↓Haptoglobin
- ↑Unconjugated bilirubin
- Haemoglobinuria/haemosiderinuria (intravascular haemolysis)
- Normocytic picture, spherocytes or schistocytes depending on cause
**Classify by mechanism:**
- Immune-mediated — AIHA, confirmed by positive Coombs/DAT test
- Microangiopathic — schistocytes (DIC, TTP, HUS, malignant hypertension)
- Membrane defect — hereditary spherocytosis
- Enzyme defect — G6PD deficiency
- Haemoglobinopathy — sickle cell disease, thalassaemia
---
## B5. HEREDITARY HAEMOLYTIC ANAEMIAS — MEMBRANE & ENZYME DEFECTS
**Hereditary Spherocytosis**
- Defect in membrane proteins — spectrin, ankyrin
- Spherical cells, trapped and destroyed in spleen
- Film: spherocytes (no central pallor)
- Confirmatory test: increased osmotic fragility test, or EMA binding test
- Treatment: splenectomy in severe cases
**G6PD Deficiency**
- X-linked, pentose phosphate pathway enzyme deficiency → vulnerable to oxidative stress
- Triggers: fava beans, antimalarials (primaquine), sulfonamides, infection
- Film: Heinz bodies, bite cells
- Acute haemolytic episodes after trigger exposure, otherwise asymptomatic
**Pyruvate Kinase Deficiency**
- Autosomal recessive, glycolysis defect → ATP depletion → red cell rigidity → destruction
- Chronic haemolytic anaemia, less trigger-dependent than G6PD
---
## B6. HAEMOGLOBINOPATHIES
**Sickle cell disease:**
- Point mutation: valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of the β-globin chain
- HbS polymerises under hypoxia → sickling → vaso-occlusion
- Film: sickle cells, target cells, Howell-Jolly bodies (autosplenectomy)
- Complications: vaso-occlusive crisis, sequestration crisis, aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19), autosplenectomy, stroke, avascular necrosis
**Thalassaemia:**
- α-thalassaemia — gene deletions; HbH disease = deletion of 3 of 4 alpha genes; Hb Barts (4-gene deletion) = hydrops fetalis, incompatible with life
- β-thalassaemia — point mutations reducing β-chain synthesis; major = transfusion-dependent, minor = mild/asymptomatic carrier
- Film: microcytic, hypochromic, target cells
---
## B7. WHITE CELL DISORDERS
**Reactive neutrophilia — film features confirming this:**
- Toxic granulation
- Left shift (increased band forms)
- Döhle bodies
**Neutropenia:**
- ANC <1.5×10⁹/L
- Predisposes to infection — does not result from bacterial infection (common trap)
- Causes: drugs (chemotherapy, clozapine), viral infection, autoimmune, marrow failure
**Lymphocytosis:** acute viral infection is the classic cause (EBV, CMV)
---
## B8. ACUTE LEUKAEMIA
**5 clinical features:**
- Anaemia symptoms — fatigue, pallor
- Bleeding/bruising — thrombocytopenia
- Recurrent infections — functional neutropenia despite high WBC
- Bone pain — marrow expansion
- Hepatosplenomegaly/lymphadenopathy (more in ALL)
**Lab pattern:** normocytic normochromic anaemia, cytopenias from marrow replacement, blasts on film
**Key facts:**
- ALL — peaks age 2–5 years, commonest childhood leukaemia
- AML — more common in adults, Auer rods on film
- CML — Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL translocation)
- CLL — smudge cells on film, commonest leukaemia in elderly
---
## B9. FULL BLOOD COUNT (FBC) COMPONENTS
| Component | Diagnostic significance if abnormal |
|---|---|
| Hb | ↓ = anaemia; ↑ = polycythaemia |
| MCV | Classifies anaemia (micro/normo/macrocytic) |
| WBC | ↑ = infection/leukaemia/inflammation; ↓ = marrow failure/viral/drugs |
| Neutrophils | ↑ = bacterial infection; ↓ = neutropenia, sepsis risk |
| Lymphocytes | ↑ = viral infection, CLL; ↓ = immunodeficiency |
| Platelets | ↑ = reactive/myeloproliferative; ↓ = bleeding risk, ITP, DIC, marrow failure |
| Reticulocytes | ↑ = marrow responding (haemolysis/blood loss); ↓ = marrow failure |
**For a full 20-mark essay, also state:**
- Normal reference ranges briefly for each parameter
- Correlate parameters together — e.g. ↓Hb + ↑reticulocytes = compensated haemolysis/blood loss; ↓Hb + ↓reticulocytes = marrow failure or deficiency state
- Pancytopenia (all three lines down) points to marrow failure/aplastic anaemia/marrow infiltration
- FBC numbers are incomplete without blood film correlation (blasts, schistocytes, spherocytes)
---
## B10. PLATELET DISORDERS
**Classify by mechanism:**
**(a) Decreased production**
- Bone marrow failure — aplastic anaemia, marrow infiltration (leukaemia, myeloma, metastases)
- B12/folate deficiency (affects all cell lines)
- Drugs — chemotherapy, chloramphenicol
**(b) Increased destruction**
*Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP)*
- Autoantibodies (IgG) against platelet glycoproteins (GPIIb/IIIa)
- Antibody-coated platelets destroyed by splenic macrophages
- Petechiae, purpura, mucosal bleeding, normal spleen size
- Diagnosis: isolated thrombocytopenia, normal/increased marrow megakaryocytes, diagnosis of exclusion
- Management: corticosteroids first-line, IVIG for acute severe bleeding, splenectomy for chronic refractory cases
*Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)*
- Deficiency of ADAMTS13 (cleaves vWF multimers)
- Large vWF multimers → platelet microthrombi
- Pentad: thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes), fever, renal impairment, neurological symptoms
- Management: urgent plasma exchange
*Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)*
- Antibodies against platelet factor 4-heparin complex
- Paradoxically causes thrombosis despite low platelets
- Onset 5–10 days after starting heparin
*DIC* — consumes platelets and clotting factors simultaneously (see B11)
**(c) Increased sequestration**
- Splenomegaly — pools platelets (hypersplenism)
**Platelet function tests:**
- Platelet count — normal 150–400 ×10⁹/L
- Bleeding time — historically used, largely replaced
- PFA-100 — modern test of platelet function under shear stress
- Platelet aggregation studies — response to ADP, collagen, ristocetin; ristocetin-induced aggregation abnormal in von Willebrand disease and Bernard-Soulier syndrome
**Inherited platelet disorders:**
- Von Willebrand Disease — commonest inherited bleeding disorder; deficient/defective vWF → impaired platelet adhesion AND low factor VIII; prolonged bleeding time, normal platelet count
- Bernard-Soulier syndrome — defective GPIb receptor → impaired adhesion; giant platelets on film
- Glanzmann thrombasthenia — defective GPIIb/IIIa receptor → impaired aggregation
---
## B11. COAGULATION DISORDERS
- Vitamin K needed for carboxylation (activation) of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X
- Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase → ↓these factors
- **PT/INR** — tests extrinsic + common pathway (factor VII, X, V, prothrombin, fibrinogen) — monitors warfarin
- **APTT** — tests intrinsic + common pathway (factors VIII, IX, XI, XII) — monitors heparin
**DIC (Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation)**
- Widespread coagulation activation → consumes platelets and clotting factors → paradoxical bleeding and clotting
- Causes: sepsis, obstetric emergencies (placental abruption, amniotic fluid embolism), malignancy, major trauma
- Labs: ↓platelets, ↓fibrinogen, ↑PT/APTT, ↑D-dimer, schistocytes on film
- Management: treat underlying cause, replace with FFP/cryoprecipitate/platelets as needed
**Haemophilia A vs B**
- Haemophilia A — factor VIII deficiency (commoner)
- Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) — factor IX deficiency
- Both X-linked recessive, prolonged APTT, normal PT, normal platelet count
---
## B12. BONE MARROW BIOPSY
- Adults — iliac crest
- Children under 2 years — tibial tuberosity
---
## B13. BLOOD PRODUCTS
**Whole blood** — rarely used now; massive haemorrhage only
**Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBCs)**
- Used for: symptomatic anaemia, acute blood loss
- 1 unit raises Hb by roughly 1g/dL
- Stored 2–6°C, shelf life ~35–42 days
**Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP)**
- Contains all clotting factors (including labile V and VIII)
- Used for: warfarin reversal, DIC, massive transfusion, liver disease with coagulopathy, multiple factor deficiencies
- Must be ABO compatible
- Stored frozen, thawed before use, used within hours of thawing
**Platelet concentrate**
- Used for: thrombocytopenia with bleeding, prophylaxis before procedures if very low, massive transfusion
- Not usually given in immune destruction (e.g. ITP) unless life-threatening bleeding
- Stored at room temperature with agitation, shelf life ~5 days (highest infection risk of all products)
**Cryoprecipitate**
- Rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, factor XIII
- Used for: hypofibrinogenaemia, DIC, von Willebrand disease, massive transfusion protocols
**Storage summary:**
| Product | Storage | Shelf life |
|---|---|---|
| Whole blood/PRBCs | 2–6°C (fridge) | 35–42 days |
| FFP | Frozen (-18°C or colder) | Up to 1 year; use within hours once thawed |
| Platelets | 20–24°C with continuous agitation | 5 days |
| Cryoprecipitate | Frozen | Up to 1 year |
---
## B14. ACUTE TRANSFUSION REACTIONS
For each: onset, mechanism, features, management.
**(a) Acute Haemolytic Transfusion Reaction**
- Onset: minutes to hours
- Mechanism: ABO incompatibility — pre-formed recipient antibodies bind donor RBC antigens → complement activation → intravascular haemolysis
- Features: fever, chills, loin/back pain, hypotension, haemoglobinuria, chest tightness, DIC in severe cases
- Management: stop transfusion immediately, IV fluids to protect kidneys, recheck crossmatch, monitor for DIC/renal failure
**(b) Febrile Non-Haemolytic Transfusion Reaction (FNHTR)**
- Onset: 1–6 hours
- Mechanism: recipient antibodies against donor WBCs, or cytokines accumulated in stored blood
- Features: fever, chills, rigors — without haemolysis (key distinguishing point)
- Management: slow/stop transfusion, antipyretics, rule out haemolysis/infection; commonest and most benign reaction
**(c) Allergic/Anaphylactic Reaction**
- Onset: minutes
- Mechanism: recipient IgE reacts against donor plasma proteins
- Features: mild — urticaria, itching; severe — bronchospasm, laryngeal oedema, hypotension, shock
- Management: mild — antihistamines, can continue slowly; severe — stop transfusion, adrenaline, IV fluids, steroids
**(d) Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury (TRALI)**
- Onset: within 6 hours
- Mechanism: donor anti-leukocyte antibodies react with recipient WBCs → pulmonary capillary leak
- Features: acute dyspnoea, hypoxaemia, bilateral infiltrates (ARDS-like), fever, hypotension
- Management: stop transfusion, supportive respiratory care — leading cause of transfusion-related death
**(e) Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload (TACO)**
- Onset: within 6 hours, especially elderly/cardiac/renal patients
- Mechanism: volume overload exceeding cardiac/renal capacity
- Features: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, hypertension (unlike TRALI), raised JVP, pulmonary oedema
- Management: stop/slow transfusion, sit upright, diuretics, oxygen
**(f) Bacterial Contamination/Sepsis**
- Onset: during or shortly after transfusion
- Mechanism: contaminated product (more common with platelets)
- Features: high fever, rigors, hypotension, septic shock
- Management: stop transfusion, cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics
**TRALI vs TACO:**
| Feature | TRALI | TACO |
|---|---|---|
| Blood pressure | ↓ | ↑ |
| Mechanism | Immune-mediated lung injury | Fluid overload |
| Response to diuretics | No improvement | Improves |
| JVP | Normal | Raised |
---
## B15. DELAYED/CHRONIC TRANSFUSION REACTIONS
**(a) Delayed Haemolytic Transfusion Reaction**
- Onset: days to weeks after transfusion
- Mechanism: anamnestic response to a minor RBC antigen from prior sensitisation (transfusion/pregnancy)
- Features: unexplained falling Hb, mild jaundice, low-grade fever, often subclinical
- Management: supportive; confirm with repeat crossmatch/antibody screen
**(b) Iron Overload (Transfusion Haemosiderosis)**
- Occurs with chronic transfusions (thalassaemia major, sickle cell on chronic transfusion)
- Iron deposits in heart, liver, endocrine organs → cardiomyopathy, cirrhosis, "bronze diabetes"
- Managed with iron chelation (desferrioxamine, deferasirox)
**(c) Transfusion-Associated Graft-versus-Host Disease (TA-GVHD)**
- Viable donor lymphocytes attack recipient tissues (mainly immunocompromised recipients)
- Features: fever, rash, liver dysfunction, diarrhoea, marrow failure — often fatal
- Prevention: irradiation of blood products in high-risk recipients
**(d) Post-Transfusion Purpura**
- Recipient develops antibodies against platelet antigens (anti-HPA-1a), destroying transfused and own platelets
- Severe thrombocytopenia 5–10 days post-transfusion
- Management: IVIG
**(e) Alloimmunisation**
- Repeated transfusions cause antibodies against minor RBC/HLA antigens
- Complicates future crossmatching, increases delayed haemolytic reaction risk
**Model essay structure for "discuss acute transfusion reactions":**
1. Definition — reaction occurring during or within 24 hours of transfusion
2. Classify: immune-mediated (haemolytic, febrile, allergic, TRALI) vs non-immune (TACO, sepsis, air embolism)
3. For each — mechanism, features, management
4. Conclude: immediate action is always to stop the transfusion, keep line open with saline, notify blood bank
---
## B16. PAST PAPER QUESTIONS — FULL ANSWERS
**Question 1.** Reactive neutrophilia — film features confirming this. See B7.
**Question 2.** Elderly woman, Hb 8.0, MCV 130fL, MCHC 32pg — diagnosis and confirmatory tests. See B3.
**Question 3.** 5 lab features of haemolytic anaemia. See B4.
**Question 4.** 5 clinical features of acute leukaemia. See B8.
**Question 5.** Lab investigations characterising iron deficiency anaemia. See B2.
**Question 6 — Essay (20 marks).** FBC components and diagnostic significance. See B9 in full, including the correlation/pancytopenia points.
**Question 7.** 5 acute transfusion reactions and mechanisms. See B14.
---

articles.title: Clinical Endocrinology Cases: Pituitary Tumour, PCOS, Type 1 Diabetes — Notes
articles.content:
![Clinical Endocrinology Cases: Pituitary Tumour, PCOS, Type 1 Diabetes, and HHS](https://ompathstudy.com/content-images/articles/clinical-endocrinology-cases-pituitary-tumour-pcos-type-1-diabetes-and-hhs/content/1-50535912.png)

## Summary
This document presents four detailed clinical endocrinology cases, each accompanied by questions and answers designed to test understanding of diagnosis, investigation interpretation, and management. The cases cover a pituitary macroadenoma causing acromegaly and hypogonadism, Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) with its characteristic hormonal and physical findings, a Type 1 Diabetes patient with poor self-monitoring leading to a discrepancy in glycaemic control indicators, and a Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) presenting as a diabetic emergency. Each case includes patient history, relevant investigations, and specific clinical questions with expert answers.

## Key Points
- **Acromegaly:** Characterized by elevated Growth Hormone (GH) that does not suppress with glucose, leading to somatic overgrowth and potential mass effects from pituitary tumors.
- **Pituitary Tumour Extension:** Suprasellar extension can cause visual field defects like bitemporal hemianopia due to optic chiasm compression.
- **Hyperprolactinemia:** Can suppress GnRH pulsatility, leading to secondary hypogonadism, manifesting as low LH, FSH, and testosterone.
- **Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS):** Diagnosed by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, often associated with an elevated LH:FSH ratio.
- **Hirsutism in PCOS:** Directly caused by elevated testosterone levels due to hyperandrogenism.
- **Type 1 Diabetes Monitoring:** HbA1c provides a 2-3 month average of blood glucose, while single glucose readings reflect immediate control, creating potential discrepancies.
- **Poor Glucose Monitoring Risks:** Can lead to undetected long-term complications from hyperglycemia or acute dangers from hypoglycemia.
- **Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS):** A diabetic emergency characterized by severe hyperglycemia, marked hyperosmolality, profound dehydration, and absence of significant ketosis, often seen in Type 2 diabetes.
- **HHS Pathophysiology:** Sufficient residual insulin inhibits lipolysis and ketogenesis, distinguishing it from DKA.
- **HHS Management:** Prioritizes careful IV fluid resuscitation and gradual insulin infusion to correct dehydration and hyperglycemia, while monitoring electrolytes and avoiding rapid osmolality shifts.

## Detailed Notes

### Case 1 — Pituitary Tumour / Acromegaly

**Q: A 40-year-old man consults his family doctor complaining of impotence. His wife has noticed excessive sweating at rest and coarsening of his facial features. He recently needed larger shoes as his old ones became uncomfortable. The GP found mild hypotension and glycosuria, and referred him to the endocrine clinic. Visual fields showed bitemporal hemianopia. Pituitary MRI showed a tumour with suprasellar extension. Investigations:**

| Investigation                 | Result               |
|-------------------------------|----------------------|
| Plasma Na                     | 8.5 mmol/L → 2 hrs later: 11.5 mmol/L |
| Serum Growth Hormone          | 20 mU/L → minimum 20 mU/L |
| 9 am Serum Prolactin          | 800 mU/L             |
| Testosterone                  | 11 mmol/L            |
| LH                            | 2.0 mU/L             |
| FSH                           | 1.5 mU/L             |
| Free T4                       | 16 pmol/L            |
| TSH                           | 0.8 mU/L             |
| Cortisol                      | 400 nmol/L           |
| Cortisol 30 min after tetracosactide | 700 nmol/L           |

**What is the most likely diagnosis?**
Acromegaly due to a GH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma with suprasellar extension.

**What is the significance of the growth hormone levels?**
A GH level that fails to suppress below 1 µg/L (or remains elevated at ≥20 mU/L) after glucose load confirms acromegaly — normal GH should suppress with rising glucose.

**How do you explain the low LH and FSH despite the elevated prolactin?**
The tumour causes hyperprolactinaemia, which suppresses GnRH pulsatility, leading to secondary hypogonadism (low LH, FSH, and testosterone) — explaining the impotence.

**What does the visual field defect indicate?**
Bitemporal hemianopia indicates compression of the optic chiasm by the suprasellar extension of the pituitary tumour.

**Is there adrenal insufficiency in this patient?**
No. Cortisol of 400 nmol/L rising to 700 nmol/L after tetracosactide (short Synacthen test) indicates intact HPA axis — a rise >550 nmol/L (or >200 nmol/L above baseline) is normal.

### Case 2 — Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)

**Q: A young woman consults her doctor because she is embarrassed by excess hair on her upper lip, lower abdomen, and thighs. She is mildly obese and has irregular periods. Investigations:**

- Serum Testosterone: 3.5 nmol/L
- Early morning LH: 14 units/L
- FSH: 3 units/L
- Ultrasound of ovaries: multiple cysts present bilaterally

**What is the most likely diagnosis?**
Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS).

**What is the significance of the LH:FSH ratio?**
An LH:FSH ratio >2:1 (here ~4.7:1) is characteristic of PCOS, reflecting dysregulated GnRH pulsatility favouring LH secretion.

**What is causing the hirsutism and irregular periods?**
Elevated testosterone (hyperandrogenism) causes hirsutism. Chronic anovulation due to disordered gonadotrophin secretion causes irregular periods.

**What would be your first-line management?**
Lifestyle modification (weight loss) is first-line. Combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) addresses irregular cycles and hirsutism. Metformin may be added if insulin resistance is present.

### Case 3 & 4 — Type 1 Diabetes / Poor Self-Monitoring

**Q: A young man with Type 1 Diabetes attends the outpatient department for his regular follow-up. He has been symptom-free since his last clinic visit. He was taught how to monitor his own blood glucose but has not been doing so because he dislikes pricking his fingers for capillary blood. Investigations:**

- Blood glucose 2 hrs after breakfast: 18 mmol/L
- HbA1c: 6.5%

**Is there a discrepancy between these two results? How do you explain it?**
Yes. A post-prandial glucose of 18 mmol/L suggests poor glycaemic control at that moment, yet an HbA1c of 6.5% implies good average control over the preceding 2–3 months. This discrepancy may mean the patient has post-meal spikes but overall reasonable control — or that the HbA1c is falsely low (e.g. due to haemolysis or haemoglobin variant). Clinical review and continuous monitoring are warranted.

**Why is HbA1c used to monitor diabetes long-term?**
HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over the preceding 2–3 months (lifespan of red blood cells), making it a reliable indicator of long-term glycaemic control, unlike a single glucose reading which only reflects that moment.

**What are the risks of poor glucose monitoring in Type 1 DM?**
Undetected hyperglycaemia leads to long-term complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, cardiovascular disease). Undetected hypoglycaemia can cause seizures, loss of consciousness, or death.

### Case 5 — Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) / Diabetic Emergency

**Q: A middle-aged widow living alone is admitted to hospital after her son found her semi-conscious at home. He had not seen her for a week but she appeared well at their last meeting. On examination she was extremely dehydrated but not ketotic. Breathing was normal.**

**Investigations:**
| Investigation      | Result      |
|--------------------|-------------|
| Serum Na           | 149 mmol/L  |
| K                  | 4.7 mmol/L  |
| HCO₃               | 18 mmol/L   |
| Urea               | 35 mmol/L   |
| Creatinine         | 150 µmol/L  |
| eGFR               | 27 mL/min   |
| Total Protein      | 90 g/L      |
| Serum Osmolality   | 370 mmol/L  |
| Blood Glucose      | 54 mmol/L   |

**What is the diagnosis?**
Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS), previously called HONK (Hyperosmolar Non-Ketotic coma). Characterised by severe hyperglycaemia (>30 mmol/L), markedly raised osmolality (>320 mmol/L), profound dehydration, and absence of significant ketosis.

**Why is there no ketosis?**
In HHS, sufficient residual insulin exists to inhibit lipolysis and ketogenesis, unlike DKA. This is typical of Type 2 diabetes.

**What do the renal results indicate?**
Urea of 35 mmol/L, creatinine 150 µmol/L, and eGFR of 27 mL/min indicate acute kidney injury (AKI) on top of possible chronic kidney disease — driven by severe dehydration and hypoperfusion.

**What is the immediate management priority?**
Careful IV fluid resuscitation with 0.9% normal saline (not hypotonic fluid) to correct dehydration slowly over 24–48 hrs, avoiding rapid osmolality shifts that can cause cerebral oedema. Low-dose insulin infusion once fluid resuscitation is underway. Monitor electrolytes closely — especially potassium.

## Practice Questions
1. A 45-year-old man presents with increased shoe size, coarsened facial features, and excessive sweating. His insulin resistance is high, and his growth hormone levels do not suppress appropriately with a glucose load. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Acromegaly.
2. A patient with a pituitary macroadenoma with suprasellar extension develops a bitemporal hemianopia. Which cranial nerve structure is most likely being compressed? → The optic chiasm.
3. A young woman has irregular periods, hirsutism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, with an LH:FSH ratio of 4:1. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS).
4. In a patient with PCOS, hirsutism is primarily caused by which hormonal abnormality? → Hyperandrogenism (elevated testosterone).
5. A Type 1 diabetic patient has an HbA1c of 7.0% but a random blood glucose of 25 mmol/L. What is the likely explanation for this discrepancy? → Poor day-to-day glucose monitoring leading to post-prandial spikes not fully reflected in the average HbA1c.
6. What are the primary long-term risks associated with poorly controlled Type 1 Diabetes? → Retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, and cardiovascular disease.
7. A patient presents with severe dehydration, a blood glucose of 45 mmol/L, serum osmolality of 350 mmol/L, and minimal ketosis. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS).
8. In HHS, why is there typically an absence of significant ketosis compared to Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)? → Sufficient residual insulin is present to inhibit lipolysis and ketogenesis.

articles.title: General Pathology I — MCQs, Short Answers & Explanations
articles.content:
Question 1
Name the response that best categorizes cells

A. Labile cells
B. Stable cells
C. Permanent cells
D. Semi permeable cells
E. A, B, and C

Answer: E. A, B, and C
Explanation: Cells are categorized into three types based on their proliferative capacity: labile cells (continuously dividing), stable cells (divide when stimulated), and permanent cells (non-dividing post-mitotic cells). ---

---

Question 2
All the granulomatous diseases EXCEPT

A. Tuberculosis
B. Sarcoidosis
C. Schistosomiasis
D. Syphilis
E. Asthma

Answer: E. Asthma
Explanation: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by eosinophilia and smooth muscle hypertrophy, not granulomatous inflammation. The others all cause granulomatous reactions. ---

---

Question 3
The following are chemical mediators of chronic inflammation EXCEPT

A. Leukotrienes
B. Complement proteins
C. Interleukins
D. Cytokines
E. Hormones

Answer: E. Hormones
Explanation: While hormones can modulate inflammatory responses, they are not considered primary chemical mediators of chronic inflammation. Leukotrienes, complement, interleukins, and cytokines are key inflammatory mediators. ---

---

Question 4
The most important cell in chronic inflammation is

A. Macrophages
B. Monocyte
C. Lymphocyte
D. Fibroblast
E. Smooth Muscle Cell

Answer: A. Macrophages
Explanation: Macrophages are the hallmark cells of chronic inflammation, responsible for phagocytosis, antigen presentation, and secretion of inflammatory mediators and growth factors. ---

---

Question 5
The following are causes of pathological atrophy EXCEPT

A. Reduced nervous supply
B. Ischaemia
C. Malnutrition
D. Muscle disease
E. None of the above

Answer: E. None of the above
Explanation: All listed options (denervation, ischemia, malnutrition, and muscle disease) are valid causes of pathological atrophy - reduction in cell size and organ mass. ---

---

Question 6
The following are functions of cellular adaptations EXCEPT

A. Phagocytosis
B. Antigen processing
C. Secretion of inflammatory substances
D. Lysis
E. None of the above

Answer: E. None of the above
Explanation: All listed functions can be part of cellular adaptations. Cells can adapt to perform various functions including phagocytosis, antigen processing, secretion, and lysis in response to environmental changes. ---

---

Question 7
Mechanisms of cell injury include all EXCEPT

A. Damaged mitochondrial functions
B. Leaky cell membrane
C. Normal protein synthesis
D. Deranged calcium homeostasis
E. Leakage of lysosomal enzymes

Answer: C. Normal protein synthesis
Explanation: Normal protein synthesis is a sign of cellular health, not injury. Cell injury involves mitochondrial dysfunction, membrane damage, calcium dysregulation, and lysosomal enzyme leakage. ---

---

Question 8
A tuberculous granuloma is comprised of

A. Fibroblasts and capillaries
B. Capillaries and giant cells
C. Endothelial cells and neutrophils
D. Young capillaries
E. Central necrotic area, epithelioid cells and lymphocytes

Answer: E. Central necrotic area, epithelioid cells and lymphocytes
Explanation: Tuberculous granulomas are characterized by central caseating necrosis surrounded by epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and a peripheral layer of lymphocytes and plasma cells. ---

---

Question 9
Events surrounding chronic inflammation include all EXCEPT

A. Infiltration with macrophages
B. Angiogenesis
C. Attempts at repair
D. Tissue destruction
E. Infiltration with neutrophils

Answer: E. Infiltration with neutrophils
Explanation: Neutrophil infiltration is characteristic of acute inflammation. Chronic inflammation is characterized by macrophage infiltration, angiogenesis, repair attempts, and tissue destruction. ---

---

Question 10
The heart and kidneys are prone to this type of cellular adaptation

A. Dysplasia
B. Hyperplasia
C. Hypertrophy
D. Atrophy
E. Anaplasia

Answer: C. Hypertrophy
Explanation: Heart and kidney cells are primarily post-mitotic, so they respond to increased workload by increasing cell size (hypertrophy) rather than cell number (hyperplasia). ---

---

Question 11
Low albumin results in

A. Increased interstitial hydrostatic pressure
B. Decreased colloid osmotic pressure
C. Decrease in capillary hydrostatic pressure
D. Decrease in interstitial pressure
E. None of the above

Answer: B. Decreased colloid osmotic pressure
Explanation: Albumin is the major contributor to plasma oncotic pressure. Low albumin (hypoalbuminemia) decreases colloid osmotic pressure, leading to fluid extravasation and edema. ---

---

Question 12
White blood cells attach to endothelial cells in the inflammatory process using their surface receptors called

A. Integrins
B. E-Selection
C. P-Selection
D. XCAMS
E. CD35

Answer: A. Integrins
Explanation: Integrins on leukocytes bind to adhesion molecules (like ICAM-1) on endothelial cells, allowing firm adhesion before transmigration. Selectins mediate rolling, not firm adhesion. ---

---

Question 13
A white blood cell that is involved in the acute inflammatory response is

A. Neutrophil
B. T-lymphocyte
C. B-lymphocyte
D. Fibroblast
E. Platelet

Answer: A. Neutrophil
Explanation: Neutrophils are the first and most numerous leukocytes recruited during acute inflammation, arriving within hours to perform phagocytosis and antimicrobial functions. ---

---

Question 14
In the process of phagocytosis, the oxidative arm produces the following EXCEPT

A. Collagenases
B. Elastases
C. O2
D. NO3
E. Iodine

Answer: A. Collagenases
Explanation: Collagenases are non-oxidative enzymes. The oxidative arm of phagocytosis produces reactive oxygen species like superoxide (O2-), nitrates, and hypohalites (including iodine compounds). ---

---

Question 15
Wound healing involves all the processes outlined below EXCEPT

A. Induction of an acute inflammatory response
B. Parenchymal cell regeneration
C. Migration and proliferation
D. Synthesis of intracellular proteins (ICM)
E. Remodeling of parenchymal elements to restore function and strength

Answer: D. Synthesis of intracellular proteins (ICM)
Explanation: Wound healing involves extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis, not intracellular proteins. The process includes inflammation, cell regeneration, migration/proliferation, and tissue remodeling. ---

---

Question 16
Which of the following is the correct response to describe how secondary healing differs from primary healing

A. Large tissue defects in secondary healing
B. Inflammatory response is more intense
C. Larger amounts of granulation tissues are observed
D. Wound contraction is a distinguishing feature
E. All of the above

Answer: E. All of the above
Explanation: Secondary healing (healing by second intention) involves all these features compared to primary healing: larger defects, more intense inflammation, extensive granulation tissue, and significant wound contraction. ---

---

Question 17
Wound healing is affected by all of the following EXCEPT

A. Infection
B. Malnutrition
C. Poor blood vessel supply
D. Absence of glucocorticoids
E. Type and location of tissue

Answer: D. Absence of glucocorticoids
Explanation: The absence of glucocorticoids would actually improve wound healing, as glucocorticoids impair healing by suppressing inflammation and collagen synthesis. The other factors all negatively affect healing. ---

---

Question 18
Haemorrhage can result in one of the following

A. Cardiogenic Shock
B. Septic Shock
C. Neurogenic Shock
D. Anaphylactic Shock
E. Hypovolaemic Shock

Answer: E. Hypovolaemic Shock
Explanation: Hemorrhage leads to blood volume loss, resulting in hypovolemic shock. The other shock types have different etiologies: cardiac dysfunction, infection, neurological injury, and allergic reactions respectively. ---

---

Question 19
The most common cause of oedema in the developing world secondary to reduced plasma colloid oncotic pressure is

A. Protein losing renal syndrome
B. Liver cirrhosis
C. Excessive protein loss from the gut
D. Malnutrition
E. Acute and chronic inflammatory

Answer: D. Malnutrition
Explanation: In developing countries, protein-energy malnutrition (kwashiorkor) is the most common cause of hypoproteinemic edema due to inadequate protein intake leading to low albumin synthesis. ---

---

Question 20
One of the following is not associated with the pathophysiology of oedema

A. Increased Hydrostatic Pressure
B. Reduced Plasma Oncotic Pressure
C. Lymphatic obstruction
D. Potassium retention
E. Inflammation

Answer: D. Potassium retention
Explanation: Potassium retention doesn't directly cause edema. Edema results from increased hydrostatic pressure, decreased oncotic pressure, lymphatic obstruction, increased vascular permeability (inflammation), and sodium retention. --- ## SECTION B: SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (5 MARKS EACH)

---

Question 21
Define the following terms. (5 marks)

a) Hypoxia
b) Necrosis
c) Apoptosis
d) Anoxia

Answer:

**a) Hypoxia:** Reduced oxygen availability to tissues. Causes include respiratory disease, anaemia, carbon-monoxide exposure, high altitude, and impaired perfusion. Persistent hypoxia reduces oxidative phosphorylation, depletes ATP, and promotes anaerobic glycolysis with lactate production.

**b) Necrosis:** Uncontrolled pathological cell death after severe injury, characterized by cell swelling, loss of membrane integrity, leakage of cellular contents, and an inflammatory response. Nuclear changes include pyknosis, karyorrhexis, and karyolysis.

**c) Apoptosis:** Regulated, energy-dependent cell death characterized by cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, fragmentation into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies, and phagocytosis without significant inflammation.

**d) Anoxia:** Complete absence of oxygen delivery to tissue. It is more severe than hypoxia and rapidly causes irreversible cellular injury if not corrected.
