The deep branch of the common peroneal nerve
questions.question: Following an injury to the leg, a patient is unable to dorsiflex their foot. Which nerve is most likely to be damaged?
questions.explanation: The deep peroneal nerve supplies the anterior compartment muscles (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus) which are responsible for dorsiflexion.
questions.correct_answer_text: The deep branch of the common peroneal nerve

options: It arises from the upper two thirds of the tibia
It is supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve
It has a broad tendon that lies between the lateral malleolus and the tendon of peroneus brevis
It inserts into the base of the 5th metatarsal
It is mainly supplied by L4 and L5 segments
questions.question: With respect to peroneus longus
questions.explanation: Peroneus longus is supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve (L5, S1). It inserts into the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform (not 5th metatarsal - that's peroneus brevis). It arises from the fibula.
questions.correct_answer_text: It inserts into the base of the 5th metatarsal

options: Arcuate popliteal ligament and anterior cruciate ligament
questions.question: The stability of the weightbearing flexed knee is maintained by
questions.explanation: The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) is the primary stabilizer of the flexed, weight-bearing knee. It prevents posterior displacement of the tibia on the femur when the knee is flexed.

options: Rectus femoris makes up part of the floor
It is bisected by the femoral nerve
The lateral border of sartorius muscle makes up its lateral boundary
The long saphenous vein joins the femoral vein within the triangle
The lateral border of the adductor longus makes up its medial boundary
questions.question: Regarding the femoral triangle
questions.explanation: The great (long) saphenous vein pierces the cribriform fascia and joins the femoral vein within the femoral triangle at the saphenous opening.
questions.correct_answer_text: The lateral border of the adductor longus makes up its medial boundary

questions.question: Inversion of the foot is performed by which pair of muscles?
questions.explanation: Inversion is performed by tibialis anterior (dorsiflexion + inversion) and tibialis posterior (plantarflexion + inversion). Peroneus muscles cause eversion.

options: Lies lateral to the deep peroneal nerve
Supplies the lateral compartment of the leg
Gives the nutrient artery to the tibia
questions.question: The anterior tibial artery
questions.explanation: The anterior tibial artery lies lateral to tibialis anterior in the anterior compartment. It pierces the interosseous membrane to enter the anterior compartment from the posterior, and lies medial to the deep peroneal nerve.

options: Does not communicate with the knee joint
Lies in front of the vastus intermedius muscle
Extends 5cm or more above the patella
Lies deep to the patellar retinacula
questions.question: The suprapatellar bursa
questions.explanation: The suprapatellar bursa extends approximately 5cm (two finger breadths) above the patella, lying between the femur and quadriceps tendon. It communicates freely with the knee joint cavity.
questions.correct_answer_text: Does not communicate with the knee joint

options: It acts to extend the knee joint
It is innervated by the tibial nerve
It inserts into the lateral meniscus of the knee joint
It inserts into the lateral condyle of the femur
It acts to laterally rotate the femur on the fixed tibia
questions.question: Which of the following does NOT apply to the popliteus muscle?
questions.explanation: Popliteus FLEXES the knee and "unlocks" it by laterally rotating the femur on the fixed tibia (or medially rotating the tibia on the femur). It does NOT extend the knee.
questions.correct_answer_text: It inserts into the lateral meniscus of the knee joint

options: The skin of the right lower limb
questions.question: A 30 year old man presents with adenopathy of the medial group of superficial inguinal lymph nodes on the right side. Which of the following is the primary site resulting in this finding?
questions.explanation: Medial superficial inguinal nodes drain the perineum, including the lower anal canal, external genitalia (except testes), and lower vagina/urethra. Testes drain to para-aortic nodes.

options: The small saphenous vein joins the popliteal vein before its entry into the fossa
It has a roof pierced by the tibial nerve
The popliteal artery lies superficial to the popliteal vein throughout the fossa
The common peroneal nerve passes through the lateral part of the fossa
questions.question: Regarding the popliteal fossa
questions.explanation: The common peroneal nerve runs along the lateral border of the popliteal fossa (following biceps femoris tendon). The fossa contains lymph nodes, and the popliteal artery is the deepest structure.
questions.correct_answer_text: The common peroneal nerve passes through the lateral part of the fossa

options: Popliteus 'unlocks' the extended knee by producing medial rotation of the femur
There is no active rotation of the extended knee
Passive extension of the knee does not result in 'locking' of the joint
The posterior cruciate ligament prevents backward displacement of the femur on the tibial plateau
The major role of the menisci is in flexion/extension of the knee
questions.question: Regarding the movements at the knee joint
questions.explanation: In full extension, the knee is "locked" and no active rotation is possible. Rotation only occurs when the knee is flexed. Popliteus unlocks the knee by laterally rotating the femur (or medially rotating the tibia).
questions.correct_answer_text: Popliteus 'unlocks' the extended knee by producing medial rotation of the femur

options: Lies lateral to the digital branch of the deep peroneal nerve
Lies medial to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus
Crosses superficial to the tendon of extensor hallucis brevis
Joins the lateral plantar artery to form the plantar arch
questions.question: The dorsalis pedis artery
questions.explanation: Dorsalis pedis passes into the sole through the first intermetatarsal space to join the lateral plantar artery, forming the deep plantar arch. It lies lateral to extensor hallucis longus and medial to the deep peroneal nerve.
questions.correct_answer_text: Lies medial to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus

questions.question: A 25 year old man is unable to plantar flex his foot. The most likely cause is damage to
questions.explanation: The tibial nerve supplies all the plantarflexors (gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus). Damage to this nerve would cause loss of plantarflexion.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of the second layer of the sole of the foot?
questions.explanation: The second layer consists of: flexor digitorum longus tendons, flexor hallucis longus tendon, quadratus plantae (flexor accessorius), and lumbricals. Abductor hallucis is in the first (superficial) layer.

options: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh
The inferior gluteal nerve and vessels
questions.question: Which of the following structures does NOT pass through the greater sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: The nerve to obturator externus is a branch of the obturator nerve and passes through the obturator foramen, NOT the greater sciatic foramen. All others pass through the greater sciatic foramen.

options: Passes across the front of the capsule of the hip joint
Is a powerful lateral rotator of the femur
Is supplied by L4 and L5 nerve roots
Arises from the iliac crest and sacroiliac joint
questions.question: The psoas muscle
questions.explanation: Psoas major passes anterior to the hip joint capsule (separated by a bursa). It inserts into the lesser trochanter, is a hip flexor and weak lateral rotator, and is supplied by L1-3 nerve roots directly from the lumbar plexus.
questions.correct_answer_text: Passes across the front of the capsule of the hip joint

options: Is formed from the same spinal segments as the obturator nerve
Divides after passing through the femoral triangle
Is formed from the anterior divisions of the anterior primary rami of L2-4
questions.question: The femoral nerve
questions.correct_answer_text: Is formed from the anterior divisions of the anterior primary rami of L2-4

mcq_sets.meta_title: Lower Limb Anatomy MCQ Compilation | OmpathStudy
mcq_sets.meta_description: Practise 48 Lower Limb Anatomy MCQ Compilation MCQs with answers and explanations for focused revision in Human Anatomy I.

mcq_sets.title: Weekly Year 2: Cellular Immunology Exam - March 27, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

questions.question: Which of the following cell types is primarily responsible for mediating the specific, adaptive immune response by producing antibodies?
questions.explanation: B lymphocytes (B cells) differentiate into plasma cells, which are the primary producers of antibodies, mediating humoral immunity, a key component of the adaptive immune response.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key characteristic that distinguishes innate immunity from adaptive immunity?
questions.explanation: Innate immunity provides an immediate, non-specific defense against pathogens, lacking memory and specific antigen recognition, which are hallmarks of adaptive immunity.

questions.question: The primary lymphoid organ where T lymphocytes mature and undergo selection processes is the:
questions.explanation: T lymphocytes originate in the bone marrow but migrate to the thymus for maturation, where they undergo positive and negative selection to ensure self-tolerance and MHC restriction.

questions.question: Which cell surface marker is characteristic of cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) and helps them recognize MHC Class I molecules?
questions.explanation: CD8 is a co-receptor found on cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) that binds to MHC Class I molecules, which present intracellular antigens to CD8+ T cells.

options: Fc region of the heavy chain
Variable region of both heavy and light chains
Constant region of the light chain
questions.question: Which component of an antibody molecule is responsible for its antigen-binding specificity?
questions.explanation: The variable regions (V regions) of both the heavy and light chains form the antigen-binding site (Fab region) and determine the antibody's specificity for a particular epitope.
questions.correct_answer_text: Variable region of both heavy and light chains

questions.question: Somatic recombination, a critical process for generating antibody diversity, involves the rearrangement of gene segments. Which segments are involved in generating the light chain variable region?
questions.explanation: The light chain variable region is formed by the rearrangement of Variable (V) and Joining (J) gene segments. The heavy chain also includes Diversity (D) segments.

questions.question: Which immunoglobulin class is typically found as a pentamer in serum and is the first antibody produced in a primary immune response?
questions.explanation: IgM exists as a pentamer in its secreted form and is the predominant antibody produced early in a primary immune response. It also functions as a monomer on the surface of B cells.

questions.question: MHC Class II molecules primarily present antigens that are derived from:
questions.explanation: MHC Class II molecules present antigens derived from extracellular pathogens and proteins, which are internalized by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) and processed in endosomal/lysosomal compartments.

options: Presenting antigens to naive T cells
questions.question: What is the main function of dendritic cells in the immune system?
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells are the most potent antigen-presenting cells (APCs) and are crucial for initiating primary T cell responses by presenting processed antigens to naive T cells in lymphoid organs.
questions.correct_answer_text: Presenting antigens to naive T cells

questions.question: Which of the following cytokines is critical for the proliferation and differentiation of T cells, often referred to as T cell growth factor?
questions.explanation: Interleukin-2 (IL-2) is a potent T cell growth factor, promoting the proliferation and differentiation of activated T cells, including cytotoxic T cells and regulatory T cells.

questions.question: The process by which B cells change the class of antibody they produce (e.g., from IgM to IgG) while maintaining the same antigen specificity is called:
questions.explanation: Class switch recombination (or isotype switching) allows B cells to change the constant region of their heavy chain, thereby changing the antibody class (e.g., from IgM to IgG, IgA, or IgE) without altering antigen specificity.

options: Virally infected cells and tumor cells
questions.question: Natural Killer (NK) cells are part of the innate immune system and primarily target:
questions.explanation: NK cells are lymphocytes of the innate immune system that recognize and kill virally infected cells and tumor cells, typically by detecting changes in MHC Class I expression on their surface.
questions.correct_answer_text: Virally infected cells and tumor cells

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an immunological technique that uses an enzyme (e.g., horseradish peroxidase) conjugated to an antibody for detection, often resulting in a colorimetric readout?
questions.explanation: ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) commonly uses enzyme-conjugated antibodies (like HRP) to detect antigens or antibodies, with the enzyme converting a substrate into a detectable product, often a color change.

options: Both MHC Class I and II
questions.question: The CD4 co-receptor on T helper cells binds to a non-polymorphic region of which MHC molecule?
questions.explanation: CD4 is a co-receptor on T helper cells that binds to the beta-2 domain of MHC Class II molecules, stabilizing the T cell receptor-MHC interaction.

questions.question: Which of the following terms describes the ability of a single B cell clone to express both IgM and IgD simultaneously on its surface, with identical antigen specificity?
questions.explanation: Mature naive B cells co-express IgM and IgD on their surface with the same antigen specificity. This is achieved by alternative RNA splicing of a single primary RNA transcript, not class switching.

questions.question: The complement system is a crucial part of innate immunity. Which pathway is activated by antigen-antibody complexes?
questions.explanation: The classical pathway of complement activation is primarily triggered by the binding of C1q to antibody-antigen complexes (typically IgM or IgG) or directly to pathogen surfaces.

questions.question: Which type of immunoglobulin is primarily found in external secretions like mucus, tears, saliva, and breast milk, providing mucosal immunity?
questions.explanation: Secretory IgA (sIgA), often found as a dimer, is the predominant antibody in mucosal secretions, playing a crucial role in protecting mucosal surfaces from pathogens.

options: They are positively selected and become helper T cells.
questions.question: Negative selection in the thymus ensures that developing T cells do not react strongly against self-antigens. What happens to T cells that bind too strongly to self-MHC/self-peptide complexes?
questions.explanation: During negative selection, T cells that bind too strongly to self-MHC/self-peptide complexes expressed by medullary thymic epithelial cells or dendritic cells undergo apoptosis to prevent autoimmunity.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the CD3 complex associated with the T cell receptor (TCR)?
questions.explanation: The CD3 complex (composed of CD3γ, CD3δ, CD3ε, and ζ chains) is non-covalently associated with the TCR and is essential for transmitting the signal from the antigen-bound TCR into the cell.

options: Junctional diversity at segment joining sites
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a mechanism contributing to antibody diversity?
questions.explanation: Class switch recombination changes the constant region (isotype) of the antibody but does not alter the antigen-binding specificity or diversity of the variable region. Somatic recombination, junctional diversity, and somatic hypermutation all contribute to creating diverse antigen-binding sites.

questions.question: A patient presents with a severe bacterial infection. Which type of leukocyte would you expect to be significantly elevated in their blood count?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are the most abundant type of white blood cell and are typically the first responders to bacterial infections, making their count elevated during such conditions (neutrophilia).

questions.question: Which cytokine is known for its potent antiviral effects and is produced by virally infected cells, leading to an 'antiviral state' in neighboring cells?
questions.explanation: Type I interferons, primarily IFN-α and IFN-β, are produced by virally infected cells and induce an antiviral state in uninfected cells, inhibiting viral replication and enhancing immune responses.

questions.question: The process of opsonization, which enhances phagocytosis, can be mediated by which of the following immune components?
questions.explanation: Opsonization is the process by which pathogens are marked for ingestion and destruction by phagocytes. Antibodies (IgG) and complement proteins (especially C3b) are major opsonins.

questions.question: Which professional antigen-presenting cell (APC) is highly efficient at cross-presentation, allowing it to present exogenous antigens on MHC Class I molecules?
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells are uniquely capable of cross-presentation, where they can take up extracellular antigens and present them on MHC Class I molecules to activate naive CD8+ T cells, important for antiviral and anti-tumor immunity.

options: Natural Killer cells and mast cells
questions.question: An individual with a defect in the RAG (Recombination Activating Gene) enzymes would most likely suffer from a severe deficiency in which cell types?
questions.explanation: RAG enzymes are essential for V(D)J recombination, the process that rearranges gene segments to form functional T cell receptors (TCRs) and B cell receptors (BCRs). A defect would severely impair the development of both T and B cells, leading to Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID).

options: To directly kill virally infected cells
To suppress immune responses and maintain self-tolerance
questions.question: What is the primary function of regulatory T cells (Tregs)?
questions.explanation: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) play a critical role in maintaining immunological self-tolerance and preventing excessive immune responses by suppressing the activity of other immune cells.
questions.correct_answer_text: To suppress immune responses and maintain self-tolerance

questions.question: Which of the following describes the immunological term for the small part of an antigen that is recognized by an antibody or T cell receptor?
questions.explanation: An epitope (or antigenic determinant) is the specific molecular structure on an antigen that is recognized and bound by an antibody or T cell receptor.

questions.question: The constant region of the heavy chain of an antibody determines its:
questions.explanation: The constant region (Fc region) of the heavy chain determines the antibody's class (e.g., IgG, IgM, IgA) and its biological effector functions, such as complement activation, opsonization, and placental transfer.

questions.question: Which immunological technique is commonly used to identify and quantify different cell populations in a heterogeneous sample based on their surface markers, using fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies and a laser?
questions.explanation: Flow cytometry uses fluorescently labeled antibodies to detect specific cell surface or intracellular markers, allowing for the rapid identification and quantification of different cell types in a mixed population.

questions.question: The process by which B cells increase the binding strength (affinity) of their antibodies to a specific antigen over time is called:
questions.explanation: Somatic hypermutation introduces point mutations in the variable regions of immunoglobulin genes, followed by affinity maturation, where B cells producing higher-affinity antibodies are preferentially selected and proliferate.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a primary function of the complement system?
questions.explanation: While complement components can enhance antigen presentation by B cells, the complement system itself does not directly present antigens to T cells. Its primary functions include lysis, opsonization, and promoting inflammation/chemotaxis.

questions.question: A patient with a defect in phagolysosome formation in macrophages would likely have impaired clearance of which type of pathogens?
questions.explanation: Phagolysosomes are formed by the fusion of phagosomes (containing internalized pathogens) with lysosomes. This is crucial for killing and degrading extracellular bacteria and fungi that are internalized by phagocytosis.

questions.question: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is mediated by IgE antibodies and involves mast cell degranulation and histamine release?
questions.explanation: Type I hypersensitivity (immediate hypersensitivity) is mediated by IgE antibodies binding to mast cells and basophils, leading to rapid degranulation upon re-exposure to the allergen and release of inflammatory mediators like histamine.

questions.question: The process by which immune cells are attracted to a site of infection or inflammation by chemical signals is known as:
questions.explanation: Chemotaxis is the movement of a cell or organism in response to a chemical stimulus. In immunology, it refers to the directed migration of immune cells (e.g., neutrophils, macrophages) towards chemoattractants at sites of infection or injury.

options: To induce apoptosis in target cells
To produce cytokines that promote inflammation
questions.question: What is the primary role of perforin and granzymes, secreted by cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs)?
questions.explanation: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) use perforin to create pores in the target cell membrane and granzymes (serine proteases) to enter the cell and initiate apoptotic pathways, leading to the destruction of infected or cancerous cells.
questions.correct_answer_text: To induce apoptosis in target cells

questions.question: Which of the following cell types is primarily involved in host defense against parasitic infections and allergic reactions?
questions.explanation: Eosinophils are granulocytes that play a key role in defense against parasitic helminths (worms) and are also heavily involved in allergic and asthmatic responses.

options: They are highly conserved among individuals.
They can switch their gene segments during development.
They have multiple alleles within the population.
They encode enzymes involved in antigen processing.
questions.question: The Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) genes are highly polymorphic. What does 'polymorphic' mean in this context?
questions.explanation: Polymorphism refers to the existence of multiple different alleles (variants) for a gene within a population. The high polymorphism of MHC genes ensures that a wide variety of peptides can be presented, contributing to population-level immunity.
questions.correct_answer_text: They have multiple alleles within the population.

questions.question: Which co-stimulatory molecule, found on antigen-presenting cells (APCs), is crucial for full activation of naive T cells by binding to CD28 on the T cell?
questions.explanation: B7 molecules (CD80 and CD86) on APCs provide the crucial co-stimulatory signal by binding to CD28 on naive T cells, which is necessary for complete T cell activation and proliferation, preventing anergy.

questions.question: Central tolerance for T cells occurs in the thymus, while peripheral tolerance mechanisms typically occur in:
questions.explanation: Central tolerance eliminates self-reactive lymphocytes during their development in primary lymphoid organs (thymus for T cells, bone marrow for B cells). Peripheral tolerance mechanisms function in secondary lymphoid organs and peripheral tissues to control self-reactive lymphocytes that escape central tolerance.

questions.question: Which immunoglobulin is associated with immediate hypersensitivity reactions and defense against parasitic infections, primarily by binding to Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils?
questions.explanation: IgE antibodies are strongly associated with allergic reactions (Type I hypersensitivity) and play a role in immunity against parasites. They bind with high affinity to Fc receptors (FcεRI) on mast cells and basophils.

options: Variable regions of alpha and beta chains
Constant regions of alpha and beta chains
questions.question: The specific region on the T cell receptor (TCR) that binds to an antigen-MHC complex is formed by:
questions.explanation: Similar to antibodies, the antigen-binding site of the TCR is formed by the variable regions of its alpha and beta (or gamma and delta) chains, allowing it to specifically recognize a processed peptide presented by an MHC molecule.
questions.correct_answer_text: Variable regions of alpha and beta chains

options: Lower activation threshold and increased numbers
Shorter lifespan compared to naive cells
questions.question: Which of the following is a key feature of memory T and B cells, crucial for a more rapid and robust secondary immune response?
questions.explanation: Memory lymphocytes (T and B cells) are more numerous than naive cells specific for the same antigen, have a lower activation threshold, and respond more quickly and effectively upon re-exposure to the antigen, leading to a faster and stronger secondary immune response.
questions.correct_answer_text: Lower activation threshold and increased numbers

options: To transport MHC Class I to the cell surface
To facilitate peptide loading onto MHC Class I
To prevent endogenous peptides from binding to MHC Class II in the ER
questions.question: What is the role of the invariant chain (Ii) in MHC Class II antigen presentation?
questions.explanation: The invariant chain (Ii) binds to the peptide-binding groove of MHC Class II molecules in the ER, preventing premature binding of endogenous peptides. It also directs MHC Class II to endosomal compartments where it eventually dissociates, allowing exogenous peptides to bind.
questions.correct_answer_text: To prevent endogenous peptides from binding to MHC Class II in the ER

questions.question: Which type of cytokine typically acts locally to induce inflammation and recruit immune cells to a site of infection?
questions.explanation: Chemokines are a family of small cytokines that act as chemoattractants, guiding the migration of various immune cells to sites of inflammation or to specific lymphoid organs.

questions.question: A defect in which complement protein would primarily impair the ability to form the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC)?
questions.explanation: C9 is the terminal component of the complement cascade. Multiple C9 molecules polymerize to form the pore-like structure of the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC), which causes osmotic lysis of target cells.

questions.question: The phenomenon where only one allele of an immunoglobulin heavy chain and one allele of an immunoglobulin light chain are expressed in a B cell is known as:
questions.explanation: Allelic exclusion ensures that each B cell expresses only one functional heavy chain allele and one functional light chain allele, leading to the production of antibodies with a single antigen specificity.

questions.question: Which cell type is crucial for activating naive CD8+ T cells against intracellular pathogens via cross-presentation?
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells are the most efficient APCs for initiating primary T cell responses, including the cross-presentation of exogenous antigens on MHC Class I molecules to activate naive CD8+ T cells.

options: To mediate somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination
To produce cytokines for B cell proliferation
To present antigens to T cells
questions.question: What is the function of AID (Activation-Induced Cytidine Deaminase) enzyme in B cells?
questions.explanation: AID is a critical enzyme in activated B cells that initiates somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination by deaminating cytosine to uracil in immunoglobulin genes, leading to DNA damage and subsequent repair pathways that introduce mutations or promote recombination.
questions.correct_answer_text: To mediate somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination

questions.question: Which type of T helper cell is primarily involved in host defense against intracellular bacteria and viruses by activating macrophages and promoting cytotoxic T cell responses?
questions.explanation: Th1 cells produce cytokines like IFN-gamma, which activate macrophages to kill phagocytosed microbes and promote the differentiation of cytotoxic T cells, crucial for cell-mediated immunity against intracellular pathogens.

questions.question: A lack of MHC Class I molecules on the surface of a host cell would make it a primary target for which immune cell?
questions.explanation: Natural Killer (NK) cells recognize and kill cells that have downregulated their MHC Class I expression, a common strategy used by viruses to evade cytotoxic T cell detection.

questions.question: Which of the following is a transmembrane glycoprotein that serves as a co-receptor for the T cell receptor (TCR), and is also known as a cytotoxic T cell (CTL)?
questions.explanation: CD8 is a transmembrane glycoprotein that functions as a co-receptor for the TCR on cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs). CTLs are also known as CD8+ T cells and recognize antigens presented by MHC Class I molecules.

questions.question: Which of the following would be used as preliminary screening for the presence of antibodies to HIV proteins in a patient's blood sample?
questions.explanation: ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) is a common and cost-effective method for preliminary screening of antibodies (e.g., anti-HIV antibodies) in a patient's serum due to its high throughput and sensitivity. Western blot can be used for confirmation.

questions.question: What color light is emitted when antigens are exposed to UV light after being treated with fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) in an immunofluorescence assay?
questions.explanation: Fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) is a common fluorochrome that emits green light when excited by ultraviolet (UV) or blue light, making it suitable for fluorescent microscopy and other immunoassays.

questions.question: Which of the following uses protein antigens separated by molecular weight using sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE)?
questions.explanation: Western blotting involves separating proteins by molecular weight using SDS-PAGE, transferring them to a membrane, and then detecting specific proteins using antibodies, often with an enzyme-linked secondary antibody.

questions.question: Each polypeptide chain (heavy and light) on an immunoglobulin molecule has a variable (V) and a constant (C) region. The C region determines the:
questions.explanation: The constant (C) regions of the heavy chains determine the immunoglobulin isotype (e.g., IgG, IgM, IgA) and dictate the antibody's effector functions, such as complement activation or binding to Fc receptors on immune cells.

questions.question: In somatic recombination for antibody diversity, the ____ rearranges first in the heavy chain. The ____ region of the antibody molecule is generated via somatic recombination as it binds to the antigen and contains both a constant region and a variable region.
questions.explanation: In heavy chain V(D)J recombination, the Diversity (D) and Joining (J) segments rearrange first, followed by the Variable (V) segment joining the DJ complex. The variable region of the antibody, containing VDJ (heavy chain) or VJ (light chain), is responsible for antigen binding.

questions.question: The two types of light chains found in human immunoglobulins are:
questions.explanation: In humans, there are two types of light chains, kappa (κ) and lambda (λ), which can associate with any heavy chain type. A single antibody molecule will have either two kappa or two lambda light chains, but never one of each.

questions.question: ____ is frequently found on the surface of B cells co-expressed with ____. These two classes are co-expressed not by class switching but by alternative processing of a primary RNA transcript. Both molecules expressed on the single mature B cell have the same binding specificity for antigen.
questions.explanation: Mature naive B cells co-express IgM and IgD on their surface. This co-expression of antibodies with identical antigen specificity is achieved by alternative splicing of the primary RNA transcript encoding the heavy chain, not by class switch recombination.

questions.question: If alternative processing of the heavy chain RNA transcript uses the first polyadenylation site, then what type of heavy chain mRNA is predominantly derived, resulting in secreted antibody?
questions.explanation: Alternative polyadenylation sites control whether the heavy chain mRNA includes transmembrane domains or ends prematurely. Using the first polyadenylation site typically leads to the exclusion of transmembrane exons, resulting in mRNA for the secreted form of the antibody.

questions.question: Phagocytic white cells (leukocytes, e.g., macrophages) congregate within _______ when foreign organisms get through a cut in the skin.
questions.explanation: Macrophages and other phagocytes act as antigen-presenting cells (APCs) in peripheral tissues. They migrate to secondary lymphoid organs, particularly lymph nodes, to present antigens to lymphocytes after encountering foreign organisms in the periphery.

questions.question: Which of the following mediates an early response to viral infections by the innate immune system?
questions.explanation: Interferons (Type I, like IFN-alpha and IFN-beta) are cytokines produced by cells in response to viral infection. They induce an antiviral state in neighboring cells and activate NK cells, representing an early innate immune response.

questions.question: Which of the following is a messenger that mediates the connection between the innate and adaptive immune systems?
questions.explanation: Antigen-presenting cells (APCs), particularly dendritic cells, bridge the innate and adaptive immune systems. They recognize pathogens via innate receptors, process antigens, and then present them to naive T cells in lymphoid organs, initiating adaptive responses.

options: All of the above recognize epitopes.
questions.question: Which of the following immune system components would NOT recognize a macromolecule epitope (binding site)?
questions.explanation: While B cell receptors and free antibodies can recognize intact macromolecule epitopes (e.g., on bacterial surfaces), T cell receptors only recognize processed peptide fragments presented within MHC molecules, not intact macromolecules.

questions.question: Which of the following is a large genomic region or gene family found in most vertebrates, playing an important role in immunity and tissue compatibility?
questions.explanation: The Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) is a gene family encoding MHC proteins crucial for antigen presentation to T cells, and it plays a central role in immune recognition and determining tissue compatibility.

questions.question: T cells are made in the _______ and complete their differentiation in the _______. Options
questions.explanation: T cells (T lymphocytes) originate as hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow, then migrate to the thymus to undergo maturation and selection processes, completing their differentiation.

questions.question: Which of the following produce large amounts of antibodies (Igs) and differentiate upon stimulation from CD4+ cells?
questions.explanation: Plasma cells are fully differentiated B cells that are specialized for the mass production and secretion of antibodies. Their differentiation often requires T cell help (from CD4+ T helper cells).

questions.question: Which of the following is a glycoprotein expressed on the surface of T helper cells, regulatory T cells, monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells?
questions.explanation: CD4 is a glycoprotein found on the surface of T helper cells (CD4+ T cells) and regulatory T cells, as well as on monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells, where it plays a role in MHC Class II recognition.

questions.question: Which of the following types of antigen presenting cells (APCs) is critical in uptake and presentation of antigen to T cells?
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells are considered the most potent professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) because they are highly efficient at capturing, processing, and presenting antigens to naive T cells, initiating primary immune responses.

questions.question: Which of the following types of antigen presenting cells (APCs) has immunoglobulin that functions as a receptor, then the antigen is internalized, degraded, and presented to T cells?
questions.explanation: B cells use their surface immunoglobulin (BCR) to bind specific antigens. Upon binding, the antigen is internalized, processed, and presented on MHC Class II molecules to T helper cells, providing T cell help for B cell activation.

questions.question: Which of the following types of antigen presenting cells (APCs) is specialized for degradation and presentation of particulate antigens to T cells?
questions.explanation: Macrophages are highly phagocytic cells that are specialized in engulfing and degrading particulate antigens (like bacteria or cellular debris). They then present processed antigens on MHC Class II molecules to T helper cells.

mcq_sets.title: Respiratory Pathology MCQs

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy had meconium ileus at birth, elevated sweat chloride, and recurrent Pseudomonas pneumonias. He is at greatest risk for which pulmonary abnormality?
questions.explanation: CF causes chronic airway inflammation and obstruction leading to bronchiectasis. Progressive loss of pulmonary vasculature leads to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

questions.question: A 70-year-old nursing home woman with Alzheimer's develops fever and coughs up yellowish sputum. CXR shows left lower lobe infiltrate. Sputum shows neutrophils and gram-positive diplococci. Most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Gram-positive diplococci + lobar pneumonia in a community/nursing home setting = Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia.

questions.question: An 11-year-old girl has 2 weeks of dyspnea. CXR shows hilar lymphadenopathy and a 1 cm peripheral right middle lobe nodule. No infiltrates. Sputum shows normal flora. Most likely condition?
questions.explanation: Peripheral nodule + hilar lymphadenopathy in a child = Ghon complex of primary TB. Enlarged nodes may compress airways causing dyspnea. Most primary infections are asymptomatic.

questions.question: On postoperative day 11 after a radical prostatectomy, a 70-year-old man suddenly becomes extremely dyspneic, diaphoretic with chest pain after walking to the bathroom. Most likely pulmonary complication?
questions.explanation: Prolonged immobilization after surgery → DVT → pulmonary thromboembolism upon ambulation. Classic sudden-onset presentation.

questions.question: A 50-year-old Swedish non-smoking seamstress has dyspnea, fever, hilar lymphadenopathy, reticulonodular infiltrates, anergy on skin testing, and non-caseating interstitial granulomas on biopsy. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Non-caseating granulomas + hilar lymphadenopathy + anergy = sarcoidosis. Corticosteroids are the treatment but infection must be excluded first.

questions.question: A 43-year-old woman has 8 years of worsening dyspnea, hyperresonance on percussion, increased lung volumes on CXR, and decreased attenuation in lower lobes on CT. Most likely lab finding?
questions.explanation: Emphysema in a non-smoker affecting lower lobes = alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency. Loss of anti-protease activity leads to panlobular emphysema by the 5th decade.

questions.question: A 55-year-old 50-pack-year smoker has hemoptysis. Sputum cytology shows atypical cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and orange-pink cytoplasm. Serum calcium is 11.3 mg/dL. Most likely CXR finding?
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma is central in location, arising in large bronchi, causing a hilar mass. Hypercalcemia is a paraneoplastic feature of squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.question: A 58-year-old non-smoker aspirates gastric contents during intubation. Over 10 days he develops a cough, fever, and a 4 cm right lung mass with an air-fluid level. Sputum shows mixed flora. Most likely condition?
questions.explanation: Aspiration + air-fluid level in the right lung = lung abscess. The right mainstem bronchus is straighter, conducting aspirated material more readily. Mixed flora is typical.

questions.question: A 66-year-old woman has a week of non-productive cough, mild fever, and bilateral interstitial infiltrates on CXR. Sputum shows normal flora and few neutrophils. She recovers fully in 2 weeks. Most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Bilateral interstitial infiltrates + non-productive cough + few neutrophils + full recovery = viral pneumonia. Influenza A is the most common cause. T lymphocytes dominate the interstitial inflammation.

questions.question: A 58-year-old smoker has 2 months of non-productive cough and blood-streaked sputum. CXR shows a 5 cm left hilar mass. Sputum cytology shows small hyperchromatic cells with scant cytoplasm. Most likely predisposing factor?
questions.explanation: Small cell anaplastic carcinoma is virtually always seen in smokers. It arises centrally and spreads aggressively. Smoking remains the most frequent cause of lung cancer overall.

questions.question: A 41-year-old man with weight loss, low CD4 count of 79, and Cryptosporidium in stool has bilateral patchy infiltrates. BAL yields pink foamy exudate with little inflammation. Most likely additional finding on GMS stain?
questions.explanation: Pink foamy exudate + severely low CD4 = Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. GMS stain reveals the characteristic cysts. PCP is the most common AIDS-defining opportunistic lung infection.

questions.question: A 64-year-old 90-pack-year smoker has had productive cough with copious mucoid sputum for more than 3 months per year for 5 years. He dies of septicemia and brain abscess. Autopsy shows mucus gland hypertrophy. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic bronchitis is defined as productive cough for at least 3 months in at least 2 consecutive years. Mucus gland hypertrophy is the pathologic hallmark. Smoking and air pollution are the key causes.

questions.question: A 66-year-old retired construction worker has dyspnea, bilateral diaphragmatic pleural plaques with calcification on CXR, diffuse interstitial disease, and ferruginous bodies on sputum cytology. Low FVC with normal FEV1/FVC. Most likely exposure?
questions.explanation: Pleural plaques with calcification + ferruginous bodies (iron-encrusted asbestos fibers) + restrictive pattern = asbestosis. Building construction is a classic occupational exposure.

questions.question: A 58-year-old smoker with obesity, BP 165/110, HgbA1C of 10%, and worsening orthopnea has bilateral lower lobe rales and infiltrates on CXR with a prominent left heart border. Most likely pulmonary problem?
questions.explanation: Hypertension + diabetes + obesity + smoking = multiple risk factors for left heart failure. Pulmonary edema results from elevated left-sided filling pressures causing fluid in the alveoli.

options: Pleomorphic cells with dark angular nuclei
questions.question: A 47-year-old man has lost 6 kg, has hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, and bilateral upper lobe infiltrates with cavitation. Sputum shows epithelioid cells with necrotic debris. Most likely additional histologic finding?
questions.explanation: Cavitating upper lobe infiltrates + epithelioid granulomas with caseous necrosis + constitutional symptoms = tuberculosis. Acid fast bacilli (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) are the expected finding.

questions.question: A 20-year-old man collapses while jogging with a minor hand abrasion. He rapidly develops dyspnea, absent right breath sounds, and mediastinal shift to the left. Thoracentesis yields a rush of air. Most likely condition?
questions.explanation: Spontaneous pneumothorax in a young man with no trauma = distal acinar (paraseptal) emphysema with subpleural bullae. Pulmonary function tests are normal between episodes.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man is intubated after severe hypotension from a vehicular accident. Despite increasing PEEP and 100% FiO2, saturations worsen. He dies. Autopsy shows hyaline membranes, thickened interstitium, and macrophages. Most likely pulmonary complication?
questions.explanation: Hyaline membranes + thickened interstitium after severe hypotension = diffuse alveolar damage (ARDS). It is the final common pathway following severe lung injury from shock, sepsis, or oxygen toxicity.

questions.question: A 51-year-old non-smoker has a slight cough for a week. Lung fields are clear. CXR shows a subpleural 2 cm coin lesion in the right upper lobe. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Solitary peripheral coin lesion in a non-smoker = most likely a granuloma from prior subclinical TB or fungal infection. Differential also includes adenocarcinoma and hamartoma.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man has a cough and right lower lobe consolidation. Antibiotic therapy over a month fails to resolve it. BAL yields atypical cells and alveolar macrophages. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Consolidation that does not respond to antibiotics + atypical cells on BAL = adenocarcinoma-in-situ (formerly bronchioloalveolar carcinoma). It can spread in a pneumonia-like pattern and occurs in non-smokers.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man receives a stem cell transplant for AML. Three weeks later he develops dyspnea, fever, and interstitial infiltrates. BAL cytology shows enlarged cells with prominent intranuclear inclusions. Most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Enlarged cells with prominent intranuclear inclusions = CMV cytopathic effect. CMV pneumonitis is a classic complication in immunocompromised transplant patients before engraftment.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman has a month of fever, dyspnea, and weight loss. CXR shows reticulonodular pattern and hilar lymphadenopathy. Transbronchial biopsy shows no organisms, no viral inclusions, no atypical cells. Most likely disease?
questions.explanation: Non-caseating granulomas with no identifiable organism + hilar lymphadenopathy = sarcoidosis. The absence of organisms on thorough workup is key before starting corticosteroids.

options: Plasma cortisol of 5 microgm/dL at 8 am
questions.question: A 59-year-old 42-year smoker has blood-streaked sputum, back pain, a right hilar mass, peripheral lung nodules, and vertebral bone scan uptake. Sputum shows small hyperchromatic cells with scant cytoplasm. Most likely lab finding?
questions.explanation: Small cell carcinoma produces ADH (SIADH), causing severe hyponatremia. Small cell is the lung cancer most associated with paraneoplastic syndromes due to its neuroendocrine origin.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman has a week of high fever, productive yellowish cough, diffuse rales, patchy infiltrates in all lung fields, and a 4 cm rounded consolidation with an air-fluid level in the left upper lobe. Most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Bronchopneumonia complicated by an abscess with air-fluid level = Staphylococcus aureus. More virulent bacteria cause liquefactive necrosis resulting in abscess formation.

questions.question: At autopsy, a 60-year-old man has a peripheral 7 cm golden-yellow consolidated area distal to a 3 cm hilar mass. Microscopically, alveoli are filled with foamy macrophages. Most likely underlying condition?
questions.explanation: Central hilar mass obstructing a large bronchus → distal lipid (endogenous) pneumonia with foamy macrophages = squamous cell carcinoma. Most squamous cell carcinomas are centrally located.

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl has acute dyspnea and wheezing, coughs up a thick mucus plug, and has 11% eosinophils on CBC and eosinophils in sputum. Similar episodes have occurred for 4 years. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Recurrent episodic wheezing + mucus plugs + peripheral and sputum eosinophilia in a child = bronchial asthma. Atopic asthma is initiated by type I hypersensitivity to allergens.

questions.question: A 41-year-old non-smoking woman has recurrent fever, non-productive cough, and dyspnea that resolved on vacation but returned when she came home to care for her canaries. Fine nodular infiltrates on CXR. Most likely inflammatory mechanism?
questions.explanation: Bird feather dust inhalation → extrinsic allergic alveolitis (hypersensitivity pneumonitis) via type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity. Can progress to type IV if chronic.

questions.question: A 63-year-old woman has 5 years of worsening dyspnea, hyperresonance, expiratory wheezes, increased lung volumes, and FEV1/FVC less than 70%. Which inhaled substance increases neutrophil elastase and most likely caused her disease?
questions.explanation: Nicotine is chemotactic for neutrophils and activates the alternative complement pathway. Cumulative neutrophil elastase activity over years destroys lung parenchyma, causing smoking-related emphysema.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman develops fever, dyspnea, non-productive cough, loss of smell, and ground-glass opacities on CXR. A single-stranded RNA virus is recovered. Three months later she still has myalgias, dyspnea, fatigue, and memory loss. Most likely virus?
questions.explanation: Loss of smell + ground-glass opacities + single-stranded RNA virus + persistent symptoms beyond 3 months = COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2). "Long COVID" affects at least a third of infected persons.

questions.question: A 44-year-old non-smoking woman has fever and cough. CXR shows a 6 cm right upper lobe infiltrate. Antibiotics fail to clear it; one month later a 3 cm peripheral mass is seen. Most likely neoplasm?
questions.explanation: Peripheral lung mass in a non-smoker that presented as a persistent "pneumonia" = adenocarcinoma. Peripheral lung cancers (adenocarcinoma, large cell) are less strongly associated with smoking than central ones.

questions.question: A 70-year-old bedridden woman (post-CVA, 5 weeks) has sudden dyspnea then 2 days later develops left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Imaging shows a wedge-shaped hemorrhagic area at the left lower lobe pleura. Most likely finding in her pulmonary arteries?
questions.explanation: Immobility → DVT → pulmonary thromboembolism → wedge-shaped hemorrhagic infarct at the pleural base. Pleuritic chest pain indicates pleural involvement by the infarct.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman has a non-productive cough for 4 days, low-grade fever, patchy interstitial infiltrates, mixed flora on gram stain, and an elevated cold agglutinin titer. She responds to erythromycin. Most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Elevated cold agglutinin titer + interstitial infiltrates + response to erythromycin = Mycoplasma pneumoniae (primary atypical pneumonia). Not cultured by routine bacterial methods.

questions.question: A 23-year-old primigravida with elevated HgbA1C delivers at 33 weeks. The infant is in severe respiratory distress requiring intubation within an hour. What pharmacologic therapy given to the mother could have helped prevent this?
questions.explanation: Maternal diabetes impedes fetal lung maturation and surfactant production. Antenatal corticosteroids (hydrocortisone/betamethasone) accelerate type II pneumocyte maturation and surfactant production in the fetus.

questions.question: A 51-year-old woman has 5 months of progressive lower leg swelling. CXR shows bilateral pleural effusions and prominent right heart border. AST, ALT, and LDH are elevated; CK is normal. Most likely underlying disease?
questions.explanation: Recurrent pulmonary emboli → pulmonary hypertension → right heart failure → hepatic passive congestion → elevated transaminases and LDH but normal CK (no myocardial ischemia).

questions.question: A cardiac transplant patient one month post-op develops fever, cough, and left lower lobe abscess on CT. Sputum shows normal flora. He fails antibiotics for 6 months and develops multiple brain abscesses. Most likely organism?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary abscess + brain dissemination in an immunocompromised patient not responding to standard antibiotics = Nocardia braziliensis. Brain involvement is a characteristic feature of disseminated nocardiosis.

questions.question: A previously healthy 5-year-old girl has fever, expiratory wheezes, and suddenly worsening dyspnea. WBC is 14,480. Emergency bronchoscopy reveals bronchi plugged by exudates. Most likely organism?
questions.explanation: High WBC + bronchi plugged by fibrin-rich neutrophilic exudates in a child after descending laryngotracheobronchitis = Haemophilus influenzae. Can cause bronchopneumonia with airway obstruction.

questions.question: A study reviews adults with sudden severe dyspnea, absent breath sounds over an entire lung, and complete pulmonary atelectasis on CXR. They are afebrile. Most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Penetrating chest trauma → pneumothorax → complete lung collapse (atelectasis). Absent breath sounds over the entire lung with sudden onset in an afebrile patient points to pneumothorax from trauma.

questions.question: A newborn male at 36 weeks gestation develops severe respiratory distress within an hour, requiring mechanical ventilation. He dies within 2 days. Autopsy shows extensive pink hyaline membranes. Most likely maternal condition that increased this risk?
questions.explanation: Gestational diabetes → fetal hyperinsulinism → impaired type II pneumocyte development → insufficient surfactant → hyaline membrane disease. Diabetes impedes fetal lung maturation even at 36 weeks.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy develops neck pain and halitosis 4 days after acute pharyngitis. CT shows a peritonsillar abscess growing anaerobic flora. Most likely aerobic organism also cultured?
questions.explanation: Peritonsillar abscess is a classic complication of streptococcal (Group A Strep) pharyngitis in children. The abscess contains mixed flora including anaerobes and the original streptococcal pathogen.

questions.question: A 65-year-old non-smoker has an 8 kg weight loss, malaise, non-tender supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, and multiple solid nodules 1–3 cm throughout all lung fields on CXR. No fever or cough. Hgb 11.6. Most likely pathologic process?
questions.explanation: Multiple bilateral solid pulmonary nodules + weight loss + supraclavicular lymphadenopathy in a non-smoker = metastatic carcinoma. Multiple nodules favor metastases over a primary lung tumor.

questions.question: A 43-year-old non-smoking woman has 8 years of progressive dyspnea, hyperresonance, decreased breath sounds, and increased lucency on CXR. Serum alpha-1-antitrypsin is 18 mg/dL. Which portion of the lung is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: AAT deficiency causes panacinar emphysema, destroying the distal acinus beyond the respiratory bronchiole, including the alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs. Lower lobes are more severely affected.

questions.question: A baby is delivered at 28 weeks after sudden placental abruption. The infant requires intubation and ventilation. CXR shows bilateral opacification the next day and the baby does not improve. Most likely histopathologic finding?
questions.explanation: Extreme prematurity (28 weeks) → lungs lack sufficient alveolar development and surfactant production → hyaline membrane disease. The primary finding is minimal alveolar saccular development.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman has episodic dyspnea with expiratory wheezes, elevated serum IgE, peripheral eosinophilia, sputum eosinophils, perihilar bronchiectasis on CXR, and detectable serum galactomannan. Most likely pathologic finding in her bronchi?
questions.explanation: Elevated IgE + eosinophilia + galactomannan (Aspergillus cell wall component) + bronchiectasis + asthma exacerbations = allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). The fungus colonizes bronchi non-invasively.

questions.question: A male infant born at 30 weeks requires intubation immediately after birth. Two months later he is taken off the ventilator but still oxygenates poorly. Most likely disease developed?
questions.explanation: Prematurity + prolonged mechanical ventilation with high FiO2 → bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Positive pressure ventilation, oxygen toxicity, and prolonged intubation all contribute to this chronic lung injury.

questions.question: A 6-year-old has sudden dyspnea, absent right breath sounds, and is afebrile. ABG shows pO2 95, pCO2 25, pH 7.55. After 100% FiO2, the ABG is unchanged. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Complete bronchial obstruction from a foreign body → V/Q mismatch shunt defect → 100% oxygen does not improve pO2 because no ventilation reaches the perfused lung. Respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman develops multi-organ failure after septic pneumonia. Cultures are now clear, but she requires increasing ventilatory pressures and her CXR shows progressive opacification of all lung fields. Most likely pathologic process?
questions.explanation: Progressive respiratory failure despite cleared infection + increasing opacification = diffuse alveolar damage (ARDS). It is the final common pathway for severe lung injury from sepsis, producing hyaline membranes and restrictive physiology.

mcq_sets.title: Weekly Pharmacology Exam - April 21, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

questions.question: A patient receives a drug dose of 500 mg daily. To express this dose normalized to body weight for a 70 kg patient, what unit would be most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Normalizing a dose to body weight is standardly expressed as mg of drug per kg of body weight (mg/kg).

questions.question: The LD50 of a new compound is determined to be 200 mg/kg, while its ED50 is 20 mg/kg. What is the Therapeutic Index (TI) of this drug?
questions.explanation: Therapeutic Index (TI) = LD50 / ED50. In this case, 200 / 20 = 10.

options: The lowest dose at which a measurable effect is first observed
The maximum dose that can be safely administered
The dose that kills 50% of the population
The dose required to achieve 100% efficacy
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the 'threshold dose' in a dose-response relationship?
questions.explanation: The threshold dose is the point on a dose-response curve where a response first begins to occur.
questions.correct_answer_text: The lowest dose at which a measurable effect is first observed

questions.question: A drug has an LD01 of 100 mg/kg and an ED99 of 80 mg/kg. What is the Margin of Safety (MOS)?
questions.explanation: The Margin of Safety is often calculated as LD01 / ED99. Here, 100 / 80 = 1.25.

questions.question: According to toxicity scales, a substance with an LD50 of 400 mg/kg would be classified as:
questions.explanation: Substances with LD50 between 50-500 mg/kg are generally classified as moderately toxic.

options: The concentration or dose of a drug required to produce a specific effect
The maximum effect a drug can produce
The safety profile of the drug
questions.question: In dose-response curves, 'potency' refers to:
questions.explanation: Potency is a measure of the amount of drug needed to produce an effect of a given intensity (often measured by EC50).
questions.correct_answer_text: The concentration or dose of a drug required to produce a specific effect

questions.question: NOAEL stands for:
questions.explanation: NOAEL (No Observed Adverse Effect Level) is the highest dose at which no statistically significant adverse effect is found.

questions.question: A drug with TD50 of 150 mg and ED50 of 50 mg would have what Therapeutic Index?
questions.explanation: TI = TD50 (Toxic Dose) / ED50 (Effective Dose). 150 / 50 = 3.

options: Drug A is more toxic than Drug B
Drug A is more efficacious than Drug B
Drug B is more potent than Drug A
Drug A is more potent than Drug B
questions.question: When comparing two drugs on a dose-response curve, if Drug A's curve is shifted to the left of Drug B's curve, this indicates:
questions.explanation: A leftward shift on the x-axis (dose) indicates that a lower dose is required to achieve the same effect, meaning higher potency.
questions.correct_answer_text: Drug A is more potent than Drug B

options: Displacing stored norepinephrine from synaptic vesicles
questions.question: Tyramine produces its sympathomimetic effects primarily by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Tyramine is an indirect-acting sympathomimetic that causes the release of stored catecholamines.
questions.correct_answer_text: Displacing stored norepinephrine from synaptic vesicles

options: It is not absorbed from the gut
It is rapidly metabolized by MAO-A in the gut wall and liver
It is inactivated by gastric acid
It has a very high volume of distribution
questions.question: Why is tyramine normally inactive when consumed orally in food?
questions.explanation: Dietary tyramine is normally broken down by Monoamine Oxidase (primarily MAO-A) in the GI tract before reaching systemic circulation.
questions.correct_answer_text: It is rapidly metabolized by MAO-A in the gut wall and liver

questions.question: A patient taking a nonselective MAO inhibitor consumes aged cheese containing high tyramine levels. What is the most likely consequence?
questions.explanation: MAO inhibitors prevent the breakdown of tyramine, leading to massive release of endogenous norepinephrine, causing a hypertensive crisis.

options: Biochemical and physiological effects of drugs and their mechanisms of action
The genetic basis of drug response
questions.question: Pharmacodynamics includes the study of:
questions.explanation: Pharmacodynamics deals with what the drug does to the body (mechanisms and effects), while pharmacokinetics deals with what the body does to the drug.
questions.correct_answer_text: Biochemical and physiological effects of drugs and their mechanisms of action

questions.question: Which of the following physiological changes in the elderly may lead to the need to reduce the dose of a prescribed medication?
questions.explanation: Reduced renal function (GFR) in the elderly reduces the clearance of many drugs, necessitating dose reduction to avoid toxicity.

options: The ability of a drug to produce a biological response
The strength of the bond between a drug and its receptor
The safety margin of a drug
questions.question: What does the term 'affinity' mean in pharmacology?
questions.explanation: Affinity refers to the tendency of a drug to bind to a specific receptor.
questions.correct_answer_text: The strength of the bond between a drug and its receptor

options: Binds to a receptor without activating it and prevents agonist binding
Binds to a receptor and activates it
Binds to a different site to enhance the agonist effect
Increases the degradation of the agonist
questions.question: A pharmacological antagonist is a drug that:
questions.explanation: Antagonists have affinity but zero intrinsic activity; they block the receptor from being activated by agonists.
questions.correct_answer_text: Binds to a receptor without activating it and prevents agonist binding

questions.question: Irreversible inhibition of a receptor or enzyme is typically due to:
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds are strong and stable, often resulting in permanent (irreversible) inhibition until new proteins are synthesized.

options: In the cytoplasm or nucleus only
Both the cell surface and intracellularly
questions.question: Drug receptors are found on:
questions.explanation: Receptors can be transmembrane G-protein coupled receptors, ion channels, or intracellular (nuclear) receptors like those for steroid hormones.
questions.correct_answer_text: Both the cell surface and intracellularly

questions.question: Which of the following is the neurotransmitter agent normally released in the sinoatrial node (SAN) of the heart in response to an increase in blood pressure?
questions.explanation: Increased BP triggers the baroreceptor reflex, leading to parasympathetic (vagal) release of Acetylcholine to slow the heart rate.

questions.question: Which of the following drugs facilitates catecholamine transmitter release from adrenergic nerve endings?
questions.explanation: Amphetamines act by increasing the release of norepinephrine and dopamine from presynaptic terminals.

questions.question: Full activation of the sympathetic nervous system (fight-or-flight) during maximal exercise will most likely result in:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic activation causes bronchodilation via beta-2 receptors to improve air flow during exercise.

questions.question: Probable signs of atropine overdose in toddlers include which one of the following?
questions.explanation: Atropine poisoning is characterized by 'Red as a beet, Dry as a bone, Blind as a bat, Mad as a hatter, and Hot as a hare'.

questions.question: Which is the treatment of choice in a child with signs of anaphylaxis after being stung by bees?
questions.explanation: Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis due to its ability to cause vasoconstriction, bronchodilation, and decreased mediator release.

questions.question: In the cardiovascular system, Epinephrine causes a decrease in:
questions.explanation: At low doses, epinephrine's beta-2 effect (vasodilation) predominates over alpha-1, leading to a decrease in peripheral resistance.

questions.question: The LD50 of a compound is 1000 mg/kg and the ED50 is 10 mg/kg. The Therapeutic Index is:
A drug that provides a maximal response while occupying only a small fraction of available receptors is said to have:
questions.explanation: Spare receptors exist when the maximal response is achieved with less than total receptor occupancy.

questions.question: Pharmacokinetics includes the study of:
questions.explanation: ADME is the foundation of pharmacokinetics.

options: To the right, without changing the maximum response
questions.question: Competitive antagonists shift the agonist dose-response curve in which direction?
questions.explanation: Competitive antagonists can be overcome by increasing the agonist concentration, resulting in a rightward shift of the ED50.
questions.correct_answer_text: To the right, without changing the maximum response

questions.question: Non-competitive antagonists change the dose-response curve of an agonist by:
questions.explanation: Non-competitive antagonists bind irreversibly or to an allosteric site, meaning no amount of agonist can restore the full Emax.

options: High affinity but lower maximal effect compared to a full agonist
Inability to bind to the receptor
questions.question: A partial agonist is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Partial agonists have intrinsic activity less than 1, meaning they cannot produce the same Emax as a full agonist even at saturation.
questions.correct_answer_text: High affinity but lower maximal effect compared to a full agonist

questions.question: Which route of administration has the highest bioavailability typically?
questions.explanation: Intravenous (IV) administration bypasses absorption barriers and first-pass metabolism, offering 100% bioavailability by definition.

questions.question: The primary site of drug metabolism is the:
questions.explanation: The liver contains the highest concentration of metabolic enzymes like Cytochrome P450.

questions.question: Biotransformation Phase I reactions include:
questions.explanation: Phase I reactions convert parent drugs into more polar metabolites via oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis.

questions.question: Biotransformation Phase II reactions typically involve:
questions.explanation: Phase II reactions are conjugation reactions (e.g., glucuronidation, acetylation) that make drugs more water-soluble for excretion.

options: Metabolism of a drug before it reaches systemic circulation
Binding of drug to plasma albumin
Selection of the drug for clinical trials
questions.question: The 'First-Pass Effect' refers to:
questions.explanation: Orally administered drugs go through the portal vein to the liver, where they may be extensively metabolized before reaching the heart and rest of the body.
questions.correct_answer_text: Metabolism of a drug before it reaches systemic circulation

options: The time it takes for 100% of the drug to be excreted
The time taken to reach the liver
The duration of the drug's effect
The time required for the plasma concentration to decrease by 50%
questions.question: What is the half-life (t1/2) of a drug?
questions.explanation: Half-life is the time required for the concentration of a drug in the plasma to fall to half of its initial value.
questions.correct_answer_text: The time required for the plasma concentration to decrease by 50%

options: Frequent dose adjustments and plasma level monitoring
questions.question: A drug with a narrow therapeutic index requires:
questions.explanation: Narrow TI drugs (e.g., lithium, digoxin, warfarin) have toxic doses very close to effective doses, requiring Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM).
questions.correct_answer_text: Frequent dose adjustments and plasma level monitoring

options: Increased plasma levels of co-administered drugs
Decreased plasma levels of co-administered drugs
questions.question: Induction of Cytochrome P450 enzymes usually results in:
questions.explanation: Enzyme induction speeds up the metabolism of drugs, thereby lowering their therapeutic concentrations.
questions.correct_answer_text: Decreased plasma levels of co-administered drugs

options: Increased risk of toxicity for co-administered drugs
questions.question: Inhibiting Cytochrome P450 enzymes can lead to:
questions.explanation: Inhibition slows metabolism, causing the drug to accumulate and potentially reach toxic levels.
questions.correct_answer_text: Increased risk of toxicity for co-administered drugs

questions.question: The main neurotransmitter of the parasympathetic nervous system is:
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine (ACh) is the neurotransmitter for both preganglionic and postganglionic parasympathetic neurons.

options: Effector organs of the parasympathetic system
questions.question: Muscarinic receptors are primarily located on:
questions.explanation: Muscarinic receptors mediate the effects of ACh on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands.
questions.correct_answer_text: Effector organs of the parasympathetic system

questions.question: Nicotinic receptors are found in:
questions.explanation: Nicotinic receptors are ionotropic receptors found at NMJs (Nm) and autonomic ganglia/adrenal medulla (Nn).

questions.question: Which of the following is a clinical use for Atropine?
questions.explanation: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors in the heart, increasing the heart rate by blocking vagal tone.

questions.question: Pilocarpine is used clinically to treat:

questions.question: Neostigmine acts by:
questions.explanation: Neostigmine is an anticholinesterase agent that increases the concentration of ACh at the synapse.

questions.explanation: Pralidoxime acts to 'regenerate' the inhibited acetylcholinesterase enzyme if given before 'aging' occurs.

questions.question: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors predominantly cause:
questions.explanation: Alpha-1 receptors are located on vascular smooth muscle and cause contraction (vasoconstriction) when stimulated.

questions.question: Beta-1 adrenergic receptors are located primarily in the:
questions.explanation: Beta-1 receptors increase heart rate (chronotropy) and contractility (inotropy).

questions.question: Beta-2 adrenergic receptor stimulation leads to:
questions.explanation: Beta-2 receptors cause relaxation of smooth muscles in the bronchioles and blood vessels of skeletal muscle.

questions.question: A patient with asthma should avoid which type of medication?
questions.explanation: Non-selective beta-blockers (like Propranolol) can block beta-2 receptors in the lungs, leading to life-threatening bronchospasm.

questions.question: Propranolol is a:
questions.explanation: Propranolol blocks both Beta-1 and Beta-2 receptors.

questions.question: Albuterol is a selective:
questions.explanation: Albuterol is used to induce bronchodilation in asthma and COPD patients by stimulating Beta-2 receptors.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the mechanism of Cocaine?
questions.explanation: Cocaine blocks the reuptake of catecholamines, leading to increased sympathetic activity.

questions.question: Prazosin is used to treat hypertension because it is an:
questions.explanation: By blocking alpha-1 receptors on blood vessels, Prazosin causes vasodilation and lowers blood pressure.

questions.question: Clonidine acts as an:
questions.explanation: Clonidine stimulates central alpha-2 receptors, which decreases sympathetic outflow from the brain.

questions.question: The primary second messenger for Beta-receptor signaling is:
questions.explanation: Beta receptors are coupled to Gs proteins, which activate adenylyl cyclase to increase cAMP.

questions.question: Which enzyme converts ATP to cAMP?
questions.explanation: Adenylyl cyclase is the effector enzyme for Gs-coupled receptors.

questions.question: Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM) is usually NOT required for:
questions.explanation: Penicillin has a very high therapeutic index and wide safety margin.

questions.question: What happens to the heart rate when a person receives a high dose of pure Alpha-1 agonist like Phenylephrine intravenously?
questions.explanation: Phenylephrine causes intense vasoconstriction (inc BP), which triggers the baroreceptor reflex to slow the heart rate.

questions.question: Atropine causes 'mydriasis,' which means:
questions.explanation: Blocking muscarinic receptors on the pupillary sphincter muscle allows the radial muscle to dilate the pupil.

Indications: Hypertension, Heart Failure, Diabetic Nephropathy. Adverse effects: Dry cough (due to bradykinin accumulation), hyperkalemia, angioedema, hypotension.","marks":5},{"question":"Explain the pharmacological basis for using low-dose Aspirin in the prophylaxis of myocardial infarction.","answer":"Irreversible inhibition of Cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) via acetylation. This inhibits the synthesis of Thromboxane A2 in platelets, which is a potent platelet aggregator. Since platelets are anucleated, they cannot synthesize new enzymes, leading to an anti-thrombotic effect for the lifespan of the platelet (7-10 days).","marks":5},{"question":"Compare and contrast the mechanism of action of Heparin and Warfarin.","answer":"Heparin: Indirect thrombin inhibitor; activates Antithrombin III to neutralize factors IIa and Xa; rapid onset; administered parenterally. Warfarin: Vitamin K antagonist; prevents gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, and X; slow onset (requires clearance of existing factors); administered orally.","marks":5},{"question":"Outline the mechanism of action and primary clinical use of Loop Diuretics.","answer":"Mechanism: Inhibit the Na+/K+/2Cl- symporter in the thick ascending limb of the Henle's loop. This results in significant excretion of sodium, water, potassium, and calcium. Clinical use: Pulmonary edema, refractory congestive heart failure, and hypercalcemia.","marks":5},{"question":"Define 'Volume of Distribution' (Vd) and list three factors that influence it.","answer":"Definition: The theoretical volume that would be necessary to contain the total amount of an administered drug at the same concentration that it is observed in the blood plasma. Extent of tissue binding/permeability.","marks":5},{"question":"Describe the mechanism of action and two characteristic side effects of Statins (HMG-CoA Reductase Inhibitors).","answer":"Mechanism: Competitive inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol synthesis, leading to increased expression of LDL receptors on hepatocytes and enhanced clearance of LDL from blood. Non-selective (Propranolol, Timolol), 2. Cardioselective/Beta-1 (Atenolol, Metoprolol), 3. Vasodilatory (Carvedilol, Labetalol). Mechanism: Competitive blockade of Beta-1 and/or Beta-2 receptors, reducing cAMP. Effects: Negative inotropy/chronotropy, decreased renin release. Clinical uses (Cardiovascular): Hypertension, Angina Pectoris, Post-MI, Heart Failure (stable), Cardiac Arrhythmias. Clinical uses (Non-cardiovascular): Glaucoma (Timolol), Essential Tremor, Prophylaxis of Migraine, Hyperthyroidism symptoms.
