mcq_sets.title: Cardiovascular Pathology MCQs

questions.question: A 63-year-old woman has sudden 'knife-like' chest pain radiating to the back, poorly controlled hypertension, and a widened mediastinum on CXR. CK is normal. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tearing back pain + widened mediastinum + hypertension = classic aortic dissection. Normal CK rules out MI.

questions.question: A man is examined 4 days after a large transmural anterolateral MI with cardiogenic shock. Most likely microscopic finding?
questions.explanation: At 3–4 days, necrosis persists with dominant neutrophils. Macrophages are just arriving. Peak risk for myocardial rupture.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman has orthopnea, dysphagia, and a prior stroke. CXR shows near-normal LV but prominent left atrial border. Most likely condition?
questions.explanation: Left atrial enlargement causing dysphagia and stroke from mural thrombus, with small LV = mitral stenosis from prior rheumatic fever.

questions.question: A 16-year-old is stabbed in the left chest. BP barely obtainable, lungs clear, heart sounds barely audible. Most useful treatment?
questions.explanation: Muffled heart sounds + hypotension + clear lungs after penetrating chest trauma = cardiac tamponade. Pericardiocentesis is immediately lifesaving.

questions.question: A 19-year-old with mid-systolic click, mitral insufficiency, aortic root dilation, and a dislocated lens dies suddenly. Ruptured chordae found at autopsy. Most likely gene mutation?
questions.explanation: Floppy mitral valve + aortic dilation + ectopia lentis = Marfan syndrome, caused by FBN1 mutations encoding fibrillin-1.

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman with no prior illness has three syncopal episodes then pulmonary edema. CXR shows LV prominence only. Cholesterol normal. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Elderly + no prior illness + syncope + LVH + pulmonary edema without systemic risk factors = senile calcific aortic stenosis.

options: Shortening and thickening of mitral chordae
Lack of development of the spiral septum
Supravalvular narrowing in the aortic root
Narrowing of the aorta past the ductus arteriosus
questions.question: A 17-year-old short girl with absent puberty, webbed neck, upper extremity hypertension, diminished lower extremity pulses, and rib notching on CXR. Most likely cardiovascular abnormality?
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome + rib notching + upper/lower BP discrepancy = postductal coarctation of the aorta.
questions.correct_answer_text: Narrowing of the aorta past the ductus arteriosus

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with 20 years of uncontrolled diabetes has sudden severe abdominal pain, diminished lower-extremity pulses, and a pulsatile abdominal mass. CK normal. Most likely condition?
questions.explanation: Pulsatile abdominal mass + lower extremity hypoperfusion + long-standing diabetes = infrarenal atherosclerotic aortic aneurysm.

questions.question: A 49-year-old woman with poorly controlled atrial fibrillation dies after a stroke. Autopsy shows fused mitral leaflets, shortened chordae, and thrombus-filled enlarged left atrium. Most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Fused mitral leaflets + shortened chordae + enlarged left atrium with mural thrombus = classic rheumatic mitral stenosis.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman with a malar rash has a friction rub, a faint systolic murmur, small mitral vegetations on echo, and a very high anti-Smith antibody titer. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Anti-Smith is highly specific for SLE. Libman-Sacks endocarditis (sterile vegetations) and fibrinous pericarditis (friction rub) are classic cardiac findings.

questions.question: A fetus at 18 weeks has a VSD, overriding aorta, and marked pulmonic atresia. If liveborn, what physical finding would most likely result?
questions.explanation: VSD + overriding aorta + pulmonic atresia = tetralogy of Fallot variant with right-to-left shunt, causing cyanosis from mixing of deoxygenated blood.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man has 3 hours of substernal chest pain, ST elevation in V1–V6, and pulmonary edema. Which lab finding is most likely?
questions.explanation: Anterior STEMI causes myocyte necrosis releasing troponin within 3–4 hours. It remains elevated 10–14 days, making it the best early and sustained marker.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman dies of a basal ganglia hemorrhage. She has LVH (550g heart), small scarred kidneys, and arterioles with concentric intimal thickening. Most likely condition?
questions.explanation: LVH + CNS hemorrhage + small kidneys + hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis = malignant hypertension with multi-organ end-organ damage.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman with rheumatic heart disease receives a porcine bioprosthesis. After 10 years it needs replacement. Most likely pathologic finding?
questions.explanation: Bioprosthetic valves avoid anticoagulation but undergo progressive calcification over 5–10 years, causing stenosis and requiring replacement.

questions.question: A healthy 25-year-old woman collapses suddenly. Echo shows global hypokinesis and reduced EF. Biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltrates with focal myocyte necrosis. Most likely infectious agent?
questions.explanation: Lymphocytic myocarditis in a young person = viral etiology. Coxsackie B virus is the most common cause and can result in sudden cardiac death.

options: Positive blood culture for Pseudomonas aeruginosa
questions.question: A 22-year-old IV drug user has fever, hypotension, a loud systolic murmur, pulmonary edema, splinter hemorrhages, and Osler nodes. Most likely lab finding?
questions.explanation: IV drug use is the key risk factor for infective endocarditis. Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staph aureus are the most common organisms in this setting.
questions.correct_answer_text: Positive blood culture for Pseudomonas aeruginosa

questions.question: A 2-year-old with failure to thrive has a large membranous VSD. What complication is she most likely to develop as an adult if untreated?
questions.explanation: Large left-to-right VSD causes chronic pulmonary overcirculation → pulmonary hypertension → eventual shunt reversal (Eisenmenger complex).

questions.question: A 53-year-old woman has progressive dyspnea, irregular pulse, enlarged right heart on CXR, thinned right ventricular wall, and reduced EF. Most likely etiology?
questions.explanation: Right ventricular thinning with fatty replacement in an autosomal dominant pattern = arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC), caused by desmosomal gene mutations.

options: Blood culture positive for S. viridans
questions.question: A 26-year-old woman recovers fully from 2 weeks of fever, palpitations, dyspnea, elevated troponin, and mild cardiomegaly. No valvular vegetations. What lab finding best explains the etiology?
questions.explanation: Self-limited myocarditis with full recovery in a young woman = viral myocarditis. Enteroviruses (echovirus, coxsackie) are the most common cause.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with 5 years of polyarthritis develops biventricular heart failure. Glucose is 167 mg/dL. What additional lab finding is most likely?
questions.explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy + diabetes + arthritis in a middle-aged man = hereditary hemochromatosis. Elevated ferritin reflects massive iron overload deposited in heart, pancreas, and joints.

questions.question: A 37-year-old man has a 10 cm right ventricular mass with hemorrhage and necrosis on CT, nearly filling the chest. Most likely neoplasm?
questions.explanation: A large hemorrhagic cardiac mass = malignancy. Angiosarcoma is the most common primary malignant cardiac tumor, typically arising in the right ventricle.

questions.question: A term baby girl is fine at birth but at 5 weeks develops pallor and a pansystolic murmur. Most likely congenital cardiac anomaly?
questions.explanation: VSD is the most common congenital cardiac defect. Symptoms emerge weeks after birth when pulmonary resistance drops and left-to-right shunting increases.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man with no prior illness has progressive pulmonary congestion, a systolic ejection click, prominent left heart border, normal glucose and cholesterol, no CK elevation. Most likely underlying disease?
questions.explanation: A bicuspid aortic valve is present from birth but calcifies and causes stenosis in older adults. Ejection click + LVH + pulmonary edema without systemic risk factors is characteristic.

questions.question: A 35-year-old delirious man with fever 39.3°C, BP 70/palpable, a heart murmur, palpable spleen, and splinter hemorrhages is brought to the ED. Most likely lab finding?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture is acute infective endocarditis. IV drug use is the major risk factor; positive opiate urine screen would confirm this predisposing condition.

questions.question: A 69-year-old woman has weight loss, painless jaundice, a pancreatic head mass, and liver/lung nodules. What cardiac abnormality is she most likely to develop?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic cancer causes Trousseau syndrome — a paraneoplastic hypercoagulable state leading to marantic (non-bacterial thrombotic) endocarditis with sterile valvular vegetations.

questions.question: A 51-year-old woman has recurrent syncope, a 1.5 cm cystic parietal cortex lesion on brain MRI, no cardiac enlargement, and normal cholesterol. Most likely cardiac lesion?
questions.explanation: Syncope + cerebral embolic infarct + no structural heart disease on CXR = left atrial myxoma, which can obstruct the mitral valve and embolize thrombus or tumor fragments.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man develops DVT postoperatively then has a left MCA stroke. CXR shows pulmonary hypertension. Troponin normal. Most likely lesion on echo?
questions.explanation: DVT → paradoxical embolism through an ASD → systemic arterial stroke. Pulmonary hypertension supports a long-standing shunt that has reversed (Eisenmenger complex).

questions.question: A 25-year-old man dies suddenly at a nightclub. Toxicology shows high cocaine levels. No gross cardiac pathology. Most likely histopathologic finding?
questions.explanation: Cocaine causes catecholamine surge via reuptake blockade, producing intense vasospasm and ischemia, resulting in contraction band necrosis — the earliest visible histopathologic change.

questions.question: A 49-year-old man has confirmed anterior LAD thrombosis with elevated troponin. During the next 24 hours, what is the most likely complication?
questions.explanation: The most common early complication of acute MI within the first 24–48 hours is arrhythmia, due to electrical instability of ischemic myocardium.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man had chest pain and 75% LAD stenosis. On day 4 he becomes hypotensive; pericardiocentesis yields 150 cc of bloody fluid. Most likely microscopic finding in his LV myocardium?
questions.explanation: At day 4, the infarct has both persistent neutrophils and arriving macrophages. This is the peak window for myocardial rupture, causing hemopericardium and tamponade.

questions.question: A 27-year-old man develops septic shock 3 days after tooth extraction. He has a split S2, a diastolic murmur, splinter hemorrhages, and splenomegaly. What cardiac condition predisposed him?
questions.explanation: A pre-existing ASD creates a structural abnormality that dental bacteremia can seed, causing infective endocarditis. The diastolic murmur and split S2 suggest this underlying defect.

questions.question: An epidemiologic study finds the 'bacon group' has more cardiovascular disease than the 'oat bran group.' What condition are they most likely to have?
questions.explanation: High-fat diet → atherosclerosis → MI. A ventricular aneurysm is a classic complication of transmural MI, forming when necrotic wall is replaced by thin, fibrotic, bulging scar.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man has 2 months of right-sided headaches, a palpable tender cord-like temporal lesion, and improves dramatically with corticosteroids. Most likely lab finding?
questions.explanation: Temporal headache + tender temporal artery + giant cell granulomatous arteritis + corticosteroid response = temporal arteritis. ESR is dramatically elevated, far out of proportion to the localized inflammation.

questions.question: A 17-year-old girl has exercise-induced syncope, LVH and broad Q waves on EKG, and a 'ground glass' septum on echo. Most likely microscopic feature?
questions.explanation: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy + exercise syncope + ground glass appearance = hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The hallmark microscopic finding is myofiber disarray with bizarre, whorled arrangements.

questions.question: A 78-year-old obese woman has 5 years of dyspnea, elevated CRP, LDL, and BNP, pulmonary edema, and segmental wall motion abnormalities on echo. Most likely cardiomyopathy?
questions.explanation: Obesity + elevated CRP and LDL + segmental (not global) wall motion abnormalities = ischemic cardiomyopathy from coronary artery disease causing patchy infarction and dysfunction.

questions.question: A 51-year-old man has 3 hours of substernal chest pain with diaphoresis. EKG shows ST elevation. Elevated troponin confirmed. Most prominent histopathologic feature at this early time point?
questions.explanation: Within the first few hours of MI, intracellular calcium overload causes hypercontraction of myofibers, producing contraction band necrosis — the earliest visible histopathologic change.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man has ascites, a cirrhotic liver on CT, and a globally enlarged heart on CXR. BP and HR are normal. Most likely cardiovascular condition?
questions.explanation: Cirrhosis + globally dilated heart without hypertension or ischemic features = alcoholic dilated cardiomyopathy. Alcohol is a direct myocardial toxin causing diffuse dilation.

questions.question: A 77-year-old man has progressive dyspnea, a diastolic murmur, a dilated thoracic aorta, and inflamed vasa vasora with medial elastic fiber disruption on histology. Most likely underlying condition?
questions.explanation: Vasa vasora inflammation → medial destruction → thoracic aortic aneurysm + aortic regurgitation = tertiary (cardiovascular) syphilis, occurring decades after initial infection.

questions.question: A term baby girl develops respiratory distress and 80% O2 saturation at 12 hours of life. Pulses are weak. Most likely cardiac finding?
questions.explanation: Severe cyanosis and cardiovascular collapse shortly after birth = hypoplastic left heart syndrome. The underdeveloped left heart cannot generate adequate systemic output once the ductus closes.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man has a friction rub on chest auscultation, BUN of 100 mg/dL, and creatinine of 9.8 mg/dL. Most likely form of pericarditis?
questions.explanation: Severe uremia from renal failure triggers fibrin exudation onto pericardial surfaces, producing fibrinous pericarditis with a classic friction rub on auscultation.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man with proliferative glomerulonephritis has elevated ANA and anti-ds-DNA. Most likely cardiac abnormality?
questions.explanation: Elevated ANA + anti-ds-DNA + glomerulonephritis = SLE. Libman-Sacks endocarditis — sterile small vegetations on the mitral and tricuspid valves — is the classic cardiac manifestation.

questions.question: A 53-year-old man has 3 months of malaise, distant heart sounds, a friction rub, and pericardiocentesis yields 10 mL of bloody fluid. Most likely condition?
questions.explanation: Bloody (hemorrhagic) pericardial effusion in a middle-aged man with constitutional symptoms = metastatic carcinoma invading the pericardium. Tuberculosis is the other classic cause.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man has untreated BP of 175/110 mmHg. If he remains untreated, what cardiac abnormality is he at greatest risk of developing?
questions.explanation: Chronic pressure overload from hypertension always produces left ventricular hypertrophy (concentric LVH) as the heart compensates for the increased afterload. This is the earliest and most universal cardiac consequence.

options: Tear in the ascending aortic intima
questions.question: A 48-year-old man with a brain anaplastic astrocytoma later develops splenic/renal pain, hematuria, and massive bilateral pulmonary emboli. Most likely cardiovascular lesion?
questions.explanation: High-grade glioma + arterial and venous thromboembolic events = Trousseau syndrome (paraneoplastic hypercoagulability). Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis produces sterile mitral vegetations that embolize systemically.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man has bilateral leg swelling, dyspnea, basal crackles, and a prominent widened split S2. CXR shows enlarged right heart. Troponin normal. Most likely condition?
questions.explanation: Right heart failure + loud prominent P2 (widened split S2) + normal troponin = cor pulmonale from pulmonary hypertension. Pulmonary interstitial fibrosis is a leading cause of secondary pulmonary hypertension.

mcq_sets.title: Congenital Heart Disease — MCQ Bank

questions.question: At what stage of gestation does the heart and vasculature become the first fully functional organ system?
questions.explanation: The heart and vasculature become the first fully functional organ system at approximately 4 weeks of gestation.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common genetic cause of congenital heart disease?
questions.explanation: Trisomy 21, or Down syndrome, is the most common genetic cause associated with congenital heart disease.

questions.question: What percentage of patients with Down syndrome have one or more heart defects?
questions.explanation: Approximately 40% of patients with Down syndrome have one or more heart defects.

options: A thickening of the ventricular wall
A complete obstruction of a valve
An abnormal communication between chambers or vessels
A failure of the heart to beat
questions.question: A "shunt" in congenital heart disease is best defined as
questions.explanation: A shunt refers to an abnormal communication allowing blood to flow between chambers or vessels, bypassing normal circulation.
questions.correct_answer_text: An abnormal communication between chambers or vessels

questions.question: Which condition is characterized by a "machinery-like" murmur?
questions.explanation: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is classically associated with a continuous, 'machinery-like' murmur.

questions.question: Cyanosis is a primary clinical feature of which group of disorders?
questions.explanation: Cyanosis, a bluish discoloration of the skin, results from deoxygenated blood bypassing the lungs, which occurs in right-to-left shunts.

options: A left-to-right shunt reverses to right-to-left due to pulmonary hypertension
questions.question: Eisenmenger syndrome occurs when
questions.explanation: Eisenmenger syndrome is characterized by the reversal of a left-to-right shunt to a right-to-left shunt, caused by severe pulmonary hypertension.
questions.correct_answer_text: A left-to-right shunt reverses to right-to-left due to pulmonary hypertension

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four cardinal features of Tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.explanation: The four cardinal features of Tetralogy of Fallot are overriding aorta, ventricular septal defect, right ventricular hypertrophy, and pulmonary stenosis (subpulmonic stenosis). Left atrial dilation is not a primary feature.

questions.question: What is the most common form of congenital heart disease (excluding bicuspid aortic valve)?
questions.explanation: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common form of congenital heart disease, excluding bicuspid aortic valve.

options: Outflow tract, right ventricle, and most of the atria
questions.question: The "second heart field" in fetal development primarily populates which structures?
questions.explanation: The second heart field contributes significantly to the formation of the outflow tract, right ventricle, and much of the atria.
questions.correct_answer_text: Outflow tract, right ventricle, and most of the atria

questions.question: Which transcription factor mutation is specifically linked to DiGeorge syndrome and neural crest migration?
questions.explanation: TBX1 mutation is specifically linked to DiGeorge syndrome, which involves defective neural crest migration.

options: Right-to-left shunts (or transient reversal of left-to-right shunts)
questions.question: Paradoxical embolism is a potential complication of
questions.explanation: Paradoxical embolism occurs when an embolus from the venous system crosses to the arterial system through a right-to-left shunt, such as a patent foramen ovale or an ASD/VSD with reversed flow.
questions.correct_answer_text: Right-to-left shunts (or transient reversal of left-to-right shunts)

questions.question: Which of these is a typical "obstructive" congenital lesion?
questions.explanation: Coarctation of the aorta is an obstructive lesion characterized by a narrowing of the aorta.

questions.question: Secundum ASDs (90% of all ASDs) result from a deficiency in the
questions.explanation: Secundum atrial septal defects, the most common type, are due to a deficiency in the septum secundum.

options: Decreased pulmonary vascular pressure and increased left atrial pressure
questions.question: At birth, the closure of the foramen ovale is triggered by
questions.explanation: At birth, lung expansion leads to decreased pulmonary vascular resistance, increasing pulmonary blood flow and left atrial pressure, which functionally closes the foramen ovale.
questions.correct_answer_text: Decreased pulmonary vascular pressure and increased left atrial pressure

questions.question: "Clubbing" of the fingers is a clinical sign associated with
questions.explanation: Clubbing of the fingers is a sign of chronic severe hypoxia or cyanosis, often seen in cyanotic congenital heart diseases.

questions.question: Most ventricular septal defects (VSDs) occur in which part of the septum?
questions.explanation: The membranous part of the ventricular septum is the most common site for VSDs.

options: Obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract
questions.question: In Tetralogy of Fallot, "subpulmonic stenosis" refers to
questions.explanation: Subpulmonic stenosis in Tetralogy of Fallot refers to the obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract, leading to reduced pulmonary blood flow.
questions.correct_answer_text: Obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract

questions.question: Which medication is used to maintain ductal patency in certain life-threatening CHDs?
questions.explanation: Prostaglandin E1 is administered to maintain the patency of the ductus arteriosus in infants with ductal-dependent congenital heart defects.

questions.question: Which syndrome involves a deletion on chromosome 22q11.2?
questions.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome is characterized by a microdeletion on chromosome 22q11.2, leading to various developmental abnormalities including heart defects.

mcq_sets.title: 50 Multiple Choice Questions — MCQ Bank

questions.question: Barrett esophagus is an example of
questions.explanation: Barrett esophagus represents metaplasia where normal stratified squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells in response to chronic acid reflux. This is an adaptive response to chronic injury.

questions.question: Which cellular adaptation is reversible upon removal of the stimulus?
questions.explanation: All three are potentially reversible if the causative stimulus is removed before irreversible damage occurs. However, dysplasia has a higher risk of progression to cancer if the stimulus persists. ---

options: This leads to increased proliferation of endometrial glands and can be a precursor to endometrial carcinom
questions.question: Endometrial hyperplasia is primarily caused by
questions.explanation: Endometrial hyperplasia results from unopposed estrogen stimulation without adequate progesterone. This leads to increased proliferation of endometrial glands and can be a precursor to endometrial carcinoma. ---

questions.question: Which is the most common cause of cell injury in clinical medicine?
questions.explanation: Hypoxia and ischemia are the most common causes of cell injury, underlying conditions like myocardial infarction, stroke, and tissue infarcts throughout the body. ---

questions.question: The earliest ultrastructural change in reversible cell injury is
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial swelling and formation of amorphous densities in the mitochondrial matrix are among the earliest ultrastructural changes in reversible cell injury, reflecting impaired oxidative phosphorylation. ---

options: They also damage proteins and DNA, but lipid peroxidation is the most significant mechanism.
questions.question: Free radical injury is most commonly caused by
questions.explanation: Free radicals cause cellular injury primarily through lipid peroxidation of membrane lipids, leading to membrane damage. They also damage proteins and DNA, but lipid peroxidation is the most significant mechanism. ---

options: converts superoxide radicals (O2-) to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Catalase and glutathione peroxidase then convert H2O2 to water.
questions.question: Which enzyme protects cells against free radical injury by converting superoxide to hydrogen peroxide?
questions.explanation: Superoxide dismutase (SOD) converts superoxide radicals (O2-) to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Catalase and glutathione peroxidase then convert H2O2 to water. ---

questions.question: The hallmark of irreversible cell injury is
questions.explanation: The point of no return in cell injury is marked by the inability to restore mitochondrial function even after resolution of the original injury. This leads to progressive loss of membrane integrity and cell death. ---

options: Failure of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump
questions.question: Cellular swelling results from
questions.explanation: Failure of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump due to ATP depletion leads to sodium and water influx into the cell, causing cellular swelling (oncosis). This is a characteristic feature of reversible injury. ---
questions.correct_answer_text: Failure of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump

questions.question: Fatty change (steatosis) is most commonly seen in
questions.explanation: The liver is most commonly affected by fatty change due to its central role in fat metabolism. Causes include alcohol, toxins, diabetes, obesity, and protein malnutrition. ---

questions.question: Which microscopic change indicates irreversible injury?
questions.explanation: Nuclear changes (pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis) are hallmarks of irreversible injury and cell death. Cytoplasmic eosinophilia can occur in reversible injury due to ribosomal detachment. ---

questions.question: Hydropic degeneration is characterized by
questions.explanation: Hydropic degeneration (vacuolar degeneration) refers to the accumulation of water in the cytoplasm causing cellular swelling. It represents an early manifestation of reversible cell injury.

questions.question: Coagulative necrosis is characterized by
questions.explanation: Coagulative necrosis maintains the basic tissue architecture for several days due to denaturation of structural proteins and enzymes. It is the most common type of necrosis and typical of ischemic injury in solid organs. ---

questions.question: Liquefactive necrosis is typical of
questions.explanation: Liquefactive necrosis occurs in brain infarctions due to the high lipid content and abundance of hydrolytic enzymes. It also occurs in bacterial infections due to release of lysosomal enzymes from neutrophils. ---

questions.question: Caseous necrosis is most characteristically seen in
questions.explanation: Caseous necrosis is characteristic of tuberculosis and some fungal infections. It has a cheese-like (caseous) appearance, combining features of coagulative and liquefactive necrosis. ---

questions.question: Fat necrosis typically occurs in
questions.explanation: Fat necrosis occurs when pancreatic enzymes (lipases) are released into the peritoneum in acute pancreatitis, breaking down fat cells. It also occurs in traumatic injury to adipose tissue such as breast tissue. ---

questions.question: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in
questions.explanation: Fibrinoid necrosis occurs in blood vessel walls in immune-mediated conditions like vasculitis, malignant hypertension, and autoimmune diseases. It appears as bright pink amorphous material on H&E staining. ---

questions.question: Gangrenous necrosis refers to
questions.explanation: Gangrene is not a specific type of necrosis but refers to coagulative necrosis of a large area (usually an extremity) with superimposed bacterial infection. Wet gangrene has a liquefactive component. ## SECTION 5: APOPTOSIS

questions.question: Apoptosis differs from necrosis in that
questions.explanation: Apoptosis is an ATP-dependent active process of programmed cell death affecting single cells without inflammation. Necrosis is passive, affects groups of cells, and causes inflammation. ---

questions.question: The morphologic hallmark of apoptosis is
questions.explanation: Apoptotic cells show cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation (pyknosis), nuclear fragmentation, and formation of apoptotic bodies. The cell membrane remains intact initially. ---

questions.question: Which pathway initiates apoptosis through death receptors?
questions.explanation: The extrinsic pathway is initiated by binding of death ligands (like FasL, TNF) to death receptors (like Fas, TNFR1) on the cell surface, leading to caspase activation. ---

questions.question: The intrinsic pathway of apoptosis is regulated by
questions.explanation: The intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway is regulated by the Bcl-2 family of proteins. Pro-apoptotic members (Bax, Bak) promote apoptosis, while anti-apoptotic members (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL) inhibit it. ---

questions.question: Cytochrome c is released from mitochondria during apoptosis and activates
questions.explanation: Cytochrome c released from mitochondria binds to Apaf-1 (apoptotic protease activating factor-1) forming the apoptosome, which activates caspase-9, the initiator caspase of the intrinsic pathway. ---

questions.question: Apoptotic bodies are removed by
questions.explanation: Apoptotic bodies are rapidly recognized and phagocytosed by macrophages and neighboring cells without eliciting inflammation. This is due to externalization of phosphatidylserine on the outer membrane. ---

questions.question: Physiologic apoptosis occurs in
questions.explanation: Physiologic apoptosis is essential in embryonic development (digit formation, neural development), normal tissue turnover, elimination of immune cells after immune response, and hormone-dependent involution. ---

options: It acts as the "guardian of the genome" and induces pro-apoptotic proteins like Bax.
questions.question: Which tumor suppressor gene can trigger apoptosis in response to DNA damage?
questions.explanation: p53 is activated by DNA damage and can induce cell cycle arrest for repair or trigger apoptosis if damage is irreparable. It acts as the "guardian of the genome" and induces pro-apoptotic proteins like Bax. ---

questions.question: Caspases are
questions.explanation: Caspases are cysteine proteases that cleave proteins at aspartic acid residues. They exist as inactive pro-caspases and are activated during apoptosis to execute cell death by cleaving key cellular proteins.

questions.question: Lipofuscin is
questions.explanation: Lipofuscin is a yellow-brown "wear and tear" pigment that accumulates in aging or atrophic cells. It represents indigestible material from lipid peroxidation and is considered a marker of aging but is harmless. ---

questions.question: Hemosiderin accumulation is seen in
questions.explanation: Hemosiderin is an iron-containing pigment formed from breakdown of hemoglobin. It accumulates locally (bruises) or systemically (hemochromatosis, multiple transfusions). It appears golden-yellow to brown and stains blue with Prussian blue. ---

options: It leads to iron deposition in liver, pancreas, heart, and skin.
questions.question: Primary hemochromatosis is caused by
questions.explanation: Primary (hereditary) hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder causing excessive iron absorption from the gut due to mutations in the HFE gene. It leads to iron deposition in liver, pancreas, heart, and skin. ---

questions.question: Anthracosis refers to
questions.explanation: Anthracosis is the accumulation of carbon particles (from air pollution or smoking) in the lungs and lymph nodes. It is extremely common in urban dwellers and smokers but usually asymptomatic. ---

options: It appears as clear vacuoles that are PAS-positiv
questions.question: Glycogen accumulation is seen in
questions.explanation: Glycogen can accumulate in glycogen storage diseases (genetic enzyme defects), diabetes mellitus (especially in renal tubular cells and hepatocytes), and with corticosteroid use. It appears as clear vacuoles that are PAS-positive. ---

questions.question: Cholesterol accumulation in macrophages creates
questions.explanation: When macrophages accumulate cholesterol, they develop foamy cytoplasm and are called foam cells. These are characteristic of atherosclerotic plaques and xanthomas.

options: Normal serum calcium with tissue injury
questions.question: Dystrophic calcification occurs in
questions.explanation: Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged or necrotic tissues despite normal serum calcium levels. It is seen in atherosclerotic plaques, damaged heart valves, old tuberculous lesions, and areas of fat necrosis. ---
questions.correct_answer_text: Normal serum calcium with tissue injury

options: . Causes include hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D toxicity, renal failure, and extensive bone destruction from malignancy or…
questions.question: Metastatic calcification occurs in
questions.explanation: Metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues when serum calcium levels are elevated (hypercalcemia). Causes include hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D toxicity, renal failure, and extensive bone destruction from malignancy or Paget disease. ---

options: because alkaline pH favors calcium phosphate precipitation. Blood vessels and pulmonary alveolar septa are commonly affecte
questions.question: Metastatic calcification preferentially affects
questions.explanation: Metastatic calcification preferentially affects tissues that excrete acid (lungs, kidneys, gastric mucosa) because alkaline pH favors calcium phosphate precipitation. Blood vessels and pulmonary alveolar septa are commonly affected. ---

options: Binding of calcium to phospholipids in damaged membranes
questions.question: The mechanism of dystrophic calcification involves
questions.explanation: In dystrophic calcification, calcium binds to phospholipids in damaged cell membranes and forms calcium-phospholipid complexes, which then nucleate further calcium deposition forming hydroxyapatite crystals.
questions.correct_answer_text: Binding of calcium to phospholipids in damaged membranes

questions.question: Cellular aging is associated with
questions.explanation: Aging is associated with accumulation of damaged proteins, lipids, and DNA due to decreased repair capacity, increased oxidative stress, and impaired protein degradation. Telomeres shorten with each division. ---

options: Replicative senescence after limited cell divisions
questions.question: The Hayflick limit refers to
questions.explanation: The Hayflick limit is the finite number of times normal human cells can divide before entering replicative senescence (approximately 50-60 divisions). This is due to progressive telomere shortening with each cell division. ---
questions.correct_answer_text: Replicative senescence after limited cell divisions

options: . Affected individuals show early onset of age-related diseases including atherosclerosis, cataracts, and malignancies.
questions.question: Werner syndrome is characterized by
questions.explanation: Werner syndrome is a premature aging syndrome caused by mutations in the WRN gene (DNA helicase). Affected individuals show early onset of age-related diseases including atherosclerosis, cataracts, and malignancies. ---

questions.question: Oxidative stress in aging results from
questions.explanation: Aging is associated with accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) from mitochondrial respiration and other sources, combined with decreased antioxidant defenses. This causes cumulative damage to cellular components. ---

questions.question: Autophagy in aging
questions.explanation: Autophagy (self-eating of cellular components) declines with aging, leading to accumulation of damaged organelles and proteins. Enhancing autophagy has been shown to extend lifespan in experimental models.

questions.question: Ischemia-reperfusion injury is primarily mediated by
questions.explanation: Paradoxically, restoration of blood flow after ischemia can cause additional injury through production of free radicals (reactive oxygen species), calcium overload, inflammation, and complement activation. This is called reperfusion injury. ---

questions.question: Heat shock proteins function to
questions.explanation: Heat shock proteins (HSPs) are molecular chaperones induced by stress (heat, hypoxia, toxins) that help refold damaged proteins, prevent protein aggregation, and assist in protein degradation, protecting cells from injury. ---

questions.question: Which change distinguishes necroptosis from apoptosis?
questions.explanation: Necroptosis is a programmed form of necrosis that is caspase-independent, mediated by RIP1 and RIP3 kinases. Unlike apoptosis, it results in membrane rupture and inflammation, but unlike necrosis, it is regulated. ---

questions.question: Autophagy can protect cells by
questions.explanation: Autophagy is a survival mechanism where cells degrade and recycle damaged organelles and proteins through lysosomes. It provides nutrients during starvation and removes damaged components, but excessive autophagy can lead to cell death. ---

options: Attempts to restore normal function or triggers apoptosis
Has no role in cell injury
questions.question: The unfolded protein response (UPR) in the endoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation: The UPR is activated when misfolded proteins accumulate in the ER. Initially, it attempts to restore homeostasis by decreasing protein synthesis, increasing chaperone production, and enhancing protein degradation. If unsuccessful, it triggers apoptosis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Attempts to restore normal function or triggers apoptosis

mcq_sets.title: ACID-BASE DISORDERS - CLINICAL CASE MCQs

options: Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic acidosis
questions.question: A 62-year-old man with COPD is brought in with confusion. ABG: pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 64 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 28 mmol/L. Which is the most likely primary disorder?
questions.explanation: ** pH is low (acidosis), PaCO₂ is markedly elevated (respiratory acidosis), and HCO₃⁻ is elevated above normal (24-26), indicating metabolic compensation. The presence of elevated bicarbonate suggests chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation, typical in COPD patients.
questions.correct_answer_text: Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation

options: Mixed metabolic alkalosis and acute respiratory acidosis
Primary respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
Primary metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
Primary metabolic acidosis with compensatory hypoventilation
Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis
questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with vomiting presents with cramps. ABG: pH 7.54, PaCO₂ 48 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 38 mmol/L. Which is the best interpretation?
questions.explanation: ** pH is high (alkalosis), HCO₃⁻ is markedly elevated (primary metabolic alkalosis from vomiting and loss of gastric acid), and PaCO₂ is appropriately elevated (respiratory compensation through hypoventilation to retain CO₂).
questions.correct_answer_text: Primary metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation

options: High anion gap metabolic acidosis only
Mixed metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis only
High anion gap metabolic acidosis + respiratory alkalosis
questions.question: A 45-year-old diabetic in DKA: ABG: pH 7.18, PaCO₂ 24 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 9 mmol/L; Na⁺ 138, Cl⁻ 100, HCO₃⁻ 9. What is the most likely acid-base disorder?
questions.explanation: ** AG = 138 - (100 + 9) = 29 (high). pH is low with low HCO₃⁻ (metabolic acidosis). Expected PaCO₂ by Winter's = 1.5(9) + 8 = 21.5 ± 2 (19.5-23.5). Actual PaCO₂ is 24, which is slightly higher than expected but close, suggesting possible mixed disorder with mild respiratory alkalosis component from Kussmaul breathing.
questions.correct_answer_text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis + respiratory alkalosis

options: Metabolic alkalosis with expected respiratory compensation
Mixed metabolic alkalosis and primary respiratory acidosis
Primary metabolic alkalosis with inadequate compensation
questions.question: A 70-year-old man with vomiting and nasogastric suction: ABG: pH 7.50, PaCO₂ 54 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 40 mmol/L. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: ** pH is high (alkalosis), HCO₃⁻ is markedly elevated (metabolic alkalosis from vomiting/NG suction), and PaCO₂ is appropriately elevated as respiratory compensation (hypoventilation to retain CO₂ and normalize pH).
questions.correct_answer_text: Metabolic alkalosis with expected respiratory compensation

questions.question: A trauma patient: ABG: pH 7.10, PaCO₂ 35 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L. Using Winter's formula, expected PaCO₂ for this HCO₃⁻ is approximately? (choose closest)
questions.explanation: ** Winter's formula: Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5(10) + 8 = 23 ± 2 (21-25 mmHg). The actual PaCO₂ of 35 is higher than expected, suggesting inadequate respiratory compensation or a mixed disorder with respiratory acidosis component.

questions.question: A patient's electrolytes: Na⁺ 140, K⁺ 4.2, Cl⁻ 102, HCO₃⁻ 8. Calculate anion gap (AG = Na - (Cl + HCO₃)). Which is the AG?
questions.explanation: ** AG = 140 - (102 + 8) = 140 - 110 = 30 mmol/L. This is a markedly elevated anion gap (normal 8-12), indicating high anion gap metabolic acidosis from unmeasured anions like ketones, lactate, or toxins.

options: Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
questions.question: A 50-year-old with chronic COPD: ABG: pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 56 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 32 mmol/L. Best interpretation?
questions.explanation: ** pH is near normal (compensated), PaCO₂ is elevated (respiratory acidosis), and HCO₃⁻ is elevated (metabolic compensation). This represents chronic respiratory acidosis with complete renal compensation, typical in chronic COPD.
questions.correct_answer_text: Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation

questions.question: A septic patient: ABG: pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 28 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 12 mmol/L; electrolytes: Na 140, Cl 100, HCO₃ 12. AG = 28. Delta ratio: ΔAG = (28-12) = 16, ΔHCO₃ = (24-12) = 12. What is ΔAG/ΔHCO₃ and its interpretation?
questions.explanation: ** Delta ratio = 16/12 = 1.33. A ratio between 1-2 suggests pure high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA). The rise in anion gap equals the fall in bicarbonate, consistent with lactic acidosis in sepsis.

options: Primary metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
Primary respiratory alkalosis with early metabolic acidosis developing → mixed disorder
questions.question: A patient with salicylate overdose: early ABG: pH 7.55, PaCO₂ 26 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 22 mmol/L. Which best describes this?
questions.explanation: ** Salicylates initially stimulate the respiratory center causing respiratory alkalosis (low PaCO₂, high pH). HCO₃⁻ is starting to drop (22, slightly below 24) indicating developing metabolic acidosis. This represents the early mixed disorder typical of salicylate toxicity.
questions.correct_answer_text: Primary respiratory alkalosis with early metabolic acidosis developing → mixed disorder

options: Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic acidosis
Pure respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
Pure metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
questions.question: ABG: pH 7.10, PaCO₂ 70 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 22 mmol/L. What is the best interpretation?
questions.explanation: ** pH is severely low (acidosis), PaCO₂ is markedly elevated (respiratory acidosis), but HCO₃⁻ is normal/slightly low. The severe acidemia with inadequate bicarbonate elevation suggests mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis rather than chronic respiratory acidosis with compensation.
questions.correct_answer_text: Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic acidosis

options: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA) with respiratory compensation
questions.question: Patient with severe diarrhea: ABG: pH 7.32, PaCO₂ 34 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 17 mmol/L. Which is most likely?
questions.explanation: ** Diarrhea causes loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid, leading to normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA). pH is low, HCO₃⁻ is low, and PaCO₂ is appropriately reduced as respiratory compensation.
questions.correct_answer_text: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA) with respiratory compensation

options: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis due to hyperchloremia (dilutional)
questions.question: Post-operative patient receiving large IV normal saline: ABG: pH 7.32, HCO₃⁻ 18 mmol/L, Na 140, Cl 108. What acid-base disturbance is likely?
questions.explanation: ** Large volumes of normal saline (0.9% NaCl) contain high chloride (154 mmol/L), causing hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. The elevated Cl⁻ (108) and low HCO₃⁻ with normal anion gap confirms NAGMA from dilutional hyperchloremia.
questions.correct_answer_text: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis due to hyperchloremia (dilutional)

options: Acute on chronic respiratory acidosis (acute rise on chronic)
questions.question: A patient with known COPD presents with acute worsening and fever. ABG: pH 7.22, PaCO₂ 81 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 34 mmol/L. Which is the best interpretation?
questions.explanation: ** Elevated baseline HCO₃⁻ (34) suggests chronic respiratory acidosis with compensation. However, pH is significantly acidotic (7.22) with very high PaCO₂ (81), indicating an acute exacerbation on top of chronic disease - acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Acute on chronic respiratory acidosis (acute rise on chronic)

options: Primary metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
Primary respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
questions.question: ABG: pH 7.43, PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 20 mmol/L. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: ** pH is slightly alkalotic, PaCO₂ is low (respiratory alkalosis), and HCO₃⁻ is appropriately reduced as renal compensation. The pH being on the alkalotic side suggests the primary disorder is respiratory alkalosis with compensation.
questions.correct_answer_text: Primary respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation

options: Pure respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
Primary respiratory acidosis with some metabolic acidosis → mixed disorder
Primary metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
questions.question: A 65-year-old with acute pulmonary edema: ABG: pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 52 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 22 mmol/L. Most likely?
questions.explanation: ** Pulmonary edema impairs ventilation causing respiratory acidosis (high PaCO₂). The HCO₃⁻ is normal/low, which doesn't show appropriate elevation for pure respiratory acidosis. The severe acidemia suggests coexisting metabolic acidosis (possibly from hypoperfusion/lactic acidosis) - a mixed disorder.
questions.correct_answer_text: Primary respiratory acidosis with some metabolic acidosis → mixed disorder

options: Metabolic alkalosis with appropriate respiratory compensation (hypoventilation)
questions.question: ABG after vomiting & diuretic use: pH 7.56, PaCO₂ 54 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 45 mmol/L. Which is the best statement?
questions.explanation: ** pH is high (alkalosis), HCO₃⁻ is markedly elevated (metabolic alkalosis from vomiting and diuretics causing H⁺ and Cl⁻ loss), and PaCO₂ is appropriately elevated as respiratory compensation through hypoventilation.
questions.correct_answer_text: Metabolic alkalosis with appropriate respiratory compensation (hypoventilation)

options: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation (likely pure metabolic acidosis)
questions.question: An intoxicated patient: ABG pH 7.20, PaCO₂ 18 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 7 mmol/L. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: ** pH is very low (severe acidosis), HCO₃⁻ is very low (metabolic acidosis), and PaCO₂ is appropriately low (respiratory compensation via hyperventilation). Using Winter's: expected PaCO₂ = 1.5(7) + 8 = 18.5, which matches actual. This is appropriate compensation for severe metabolic acidosis, likely from toxic alcohol ingestion.
questions.correct_answer_text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation (likely pure metabolic acidosis)

options: Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation (compensated)
questions.question: ABG: pH 7.39, PaCO₂ 48 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 29 mmol/L. Patient asymptomatic. Interpretation?
questions.explanation: ** pH is normal (compensated), PaCO₂ is elevated (respiratory acidosis), and HCO₃⁻ is elevated (metabolic compensation). This represents fully compensated chronic respiratory acidosis, typical in asymptomatic chronic lung disease patients.
questions.correct_answer_text: Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation (compensated)

options: 1.75 → HAGMA + metabolic alkalosis or chronic respiratory acidosis
questions.question: A patient: Na 138, Cl 90, HCO₃ 8, AG = 40. ΔAG = 28 (40-12), ΔHCO₃ = 16 (24-8). ΔAG/ΔHCO₃ = ? (select closest) and interpretation.
questions.explanation: ** Delta ratio = 28/16 = 1.75. A ratio >1.6-2.0 suggests HAGMA with concurrent metabolic alkalosis or chronic respiratory acidosis. The rise in anion gap exceeds the fall in bicarbonate, indicating another process is maintaining bicarbonate levels.
questions.correct_answer_text: 1.75 → HAGMA + metabolic alkalosis or chronic respiratory acidosis

options: Expected PaCO₂ ≈ 35 mmHg → coexisting respiratory acidosis
Expected PaCO₂ ≈ 26 mmHg → appropriate respiratory compensation (pure metabolic acidosis)
Expected PaCO₂ ≈ 17 mmHg → respiratory alkalosis present
Expected PaCO₂ ≈ 41 mmHg → chronic respiratory acidosis present
questions.question: ABG: pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 26 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 12 mmol/L. Which best describes respiratory compensation? (expected PaCO₂ using Winter's formula for HCO₃ 12)
questions.explanation: ** Winter's formula: Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5(12) + 8 = 26 ± 2 (24-28 mmHg). The actual PaCO₂ of 26 matches expected, indicating appropriate respiratory compensation for pure metabolic acidosis without mixed disorder.
questions.correct_answer_text: Expected PaCO₂ ≈ 26 mmHg → appropriate respiratory compensation (pure metabolic acidosis)

options: Metabolic alkalosis with appropriate respiratory compensation (hypoventilation)
questions.question: A 30-year-old with repeated vomiting: ABG pH 7.58, PaCO₂ 60 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 48 mmol/L. Which is most likely among choices?
questions.explanation: ** pH is high (alkalosis), HCO₃⁻ is markedly elevated (metabolic alkalosis from vomiting with loss of gastric HCl), and PaCO₂ is appropriately elevated (respiratory compensation through hypoventilation to retain CO₂ and normalize pH).
questions.correct_answer_text: Metabolic alkalosis with appropriate respiratory compensation (hypoventilation)

options: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis from hyperchloremia
Mild metabolic acidosis; consider lactic acidosis (HAGMA) in sepsis/hypoperfusion
questions.question: Post-op patient given large amount of lactated Ringer's now with hypotension: ABG pH 7.34, HCO₃⁻ 20 mmol/L, Na 135, Cl 100. Likely disturbance?
questions.explanation: ** AG = 135 - (100 + 20) = 15 (mildly elevated). With hypotension suggesting hypoperfusion, lactic acidosis (HAGMA) is most likely. The mild metabolic acidosis with elevated AG in the setting of shock points to tissue hypoperfusion and lactate accumulation.
questions.correct_answer_text: Mild metabolic acidosis; consider lactic acidosis (HAGMA) in sepsis/hypoperfusion

options: Severe metabolic acidosis (e.g., DKA, toxins) with respiratory compensation
questions.question: ABG: pH 7.15, PaCO₂ 20 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 6 mmol/L. Which is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: ** pH is very low (severe acidosis), HCO₃⁻ is critically low (severe metabolic acidosis), and PaCO₂ is appropriately very low (respiratory compensation). Using Winter's: expected = 1.5(6) + 8 = 17 ± 2, actual is 20 (close). This represents severe metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation, likely DKA, lactic acidosis, or toxic alcohol.
questions.correct_answer_text: Severe metabolic acidosis (e.g., DKA, toxins) with respiratory compensation

options: High AG metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis
questions.question: A patient's labs: Na 142, Cl 108, HCO₃ 22, AG = 12. ABG pH 7.41, PaCO₂ 38, HCO₃ 24. What does this ABG suggest?
questions.explanation: ** AG = 142 - (108 + 22) = 12 (normal). All ABG values are within normal ranges: pH 7.35-7.45, PaCO₂ 35-45, HCO₃⁻ 22-26. This represents normal acid-base status.

questions.question: A 55-year-old with liver failure: ABG pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 28 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 12 mmol/L; Na 138, Cl 96. AG = ? (choose closest) and likely disorder.
questions.explanation: ** AG = 138 - (96 + 12) = 30 (markedly elevated). Liver failure patients can develop lactic acidosis from impaired lactate clearance and tissue hypoperfusion. The HAGMA with appropriate respiratory compensation (low PaCO₂) is consistent with lactic acidosis.

options: Mild primary respiratory alkalosis with near-normal pH (compensation)
questions.question: ABG: pH 7.44, PaCO₂ 32 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 22 mmol/L. Which is best?
questions.explanation: ** pH is at upper limit of normal (7.44), PaCO₂ is mildly reduced (mild respiratory alkalosis), and HCO₃⁻ is at lower limit of normal (renal compensation beginning). This represents mild compensated respiratory alkalosis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Mild primary respiratory alkalosis with near-normal pH (compensation)

options: Metabolic alkalosis due to diuretics with respiratory compensation
questions.question: A patient with CHF on loop diuretics: ABG pH 7.50, PaCO₂ 46 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 37 mmol/L. Most likely?
questions.explanation: ** Loop diuretics cause loss of H⁺, Cl⁻, and K⁺, leading to metabolic alkalosis (contraction alkalosis). pH is high, HCO₃⁻ is elevated (metabolic alkalosis), and PaCO₂ is appropriately elevated (respiratory compensation through hypoventilation).
questions.correct_answer_text: Metabolic alkalosis due to diuretics with respiratory compensation

options: Severe metabolic acidosis with inadequate respiratory compensation (or mixed respiratory acidosis)
questions.question: ABG: pH 7.02, PaCO₂ 40 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 9 mmol/L. Interpretation?
questions.explanation: ** pH is severely low (severe acidosis), HCO₃⁻ is very low (metabolic acidosis). Expected PaCO₂ by Winter's = 1.5(9) + 8 = 21.5 ± 2. Actual is 40 mmHg, which is much higher than expected, indicating inadequate respiratory compensation or coexisting respiratory acidosis - a life-threatening situation.
questions.correct_answer_text: Severe metabolic acidosis with inadequate respiratory compensation (or mixed respiratory acidosis)

options: Primary metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation (acute)
questions.question: A patient: ABG pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 17 mmol/L. Which is most plausible?
questions.explanation: ** pH is at lower limit of normal, HCO₃⁻ is low (metabolic acidosis), and PaCO₂ is appropriately low (respiratory compensation). The near-normal pH suggests good compensation. This represents compensated metabolic acidosis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Primary metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation (acute)

options: AG = 27 → high AG metabolic acidosis (likely combined with respiratory compensation)
questions.question: ABG: pH 7.22, PaCO₂ 24 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 9 mmol/L; electrolytes: Na 140, Cl 104. Calculate AG and pick the most likely scenario (normal AG assumed 12).
questions.explanation: ** AG = 140 - (104 + 9) = 27 (markedly elevated). This is HAGMA with appropriate respiratory compensation (PaCO₂ 24, expected by Winter's = 1.5(9) + 8 = 21.5 ± 2). The high AG suggests unmeasured anions like ketones, lactate, or toxins.
questions.correct_answer_text: AG = 27 → high AG metabolic acidosis (likely combined with respiratory compensation)

mcq_sets.title: Respiratory Pathology 2 — MCQ Bank

options: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia with respiratory failure
questions.question: A patient presents with transient pulmonary infiltrates, blood eosinophilia, and a completely benign self-limiting clinical course. No cause is identified. This is best described as
questions.explanation: Löffler syndrome = simple pulmonary eosinophilia + transient lesions + benign clinical course. It is self-limiting. Acute eosinophilic pneumonia is more severe with rapid onset hypoxia and BAL >25% eosinophils.

questions.question: BAL fluid in acute eosinophilic pneumonia shows what threshold of eosinophils to support the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia requires BAL eosinophils >25%. It presents with rapid onset fever, dyspnea, and hypoxia, and responds promptly and dramatically to corticosteroids.

options: Presence of noncaseating granulomas on biopsy
Exclusion of all other causes of pulmonary eosinophilia
questions.question: A patient with idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonia presents with high fever, night sweats, and dyspnea. CXR shows peripheral infiltrates. This diagnosis requires
questions.explanation: Idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonia is a diagnosis of exclusion. All other causes (asthma, drug allergies, parasites, vasculitis) must be ruled out first. It characteristically affects the peripheral lung fields.
questions.correct_answer_text: Exclusion of all other causes of pulmonary eosinophilia

options: IL-8 drives eosinophil chemotaxis into alveoli
IL-4 activates eosinophils in alveolar spaces
IL-5 drives eosinophil infiltration and activation
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the eosinophil-activating cytokine central to pulmonary eosinophilia?
questions.explanation: Elevated alveolar IL-5 is the key driver of eosinophil activation in pulmonary eosinophilia. IL-5 is produced by TH2 cells and is also the cytokine responsible for eosinophil activation in asthma.
questions.correct_answer_text: IL-5 drives eosinophil infiltration and activation

options: Bronchiolocentric pigmented macrophages with peribronchiolar fibrosis
Polypoid organizing connective tissue plugs in alveolar ducts
Noncaseating granulomas in a peribronchiolar distribution
Diffuse air space accumulation of smoker's macrophages with mild septal thickening
questions.question: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP) is best characterized by
questions.explanation: DIP shows diffuse accumulation of smoker's macrophages (dusty-brown pigment) in air spaces throughout the lung, with mild alveolar septal thickening. The macrophage distribution is diffuse, unlike RB-ILD which is bronchiolocentric.
questions.correct_answer_text: Diffuse air space accumulation of smoker's macrophages with mild septal thickening

options: Diffuse throughout all alveolar air spaces
Concentrated around first and second order respiratory bronchioles
Predominantly subpleural and along interlobular septa
Confined to alveolar ducts and terminal bronchioles only
questions.question: Respiratory bronchiolitis-ILD differs from DIP in that the macrophage distribution is
questions.explanation: RB-ILD shares the same smoker's macrophages as DIP but in a bronchiolocentric distribution — first and second order respiratory bronchioles. DIP has diffuse air space distribution. Both improve with smoking cessation.
questions.correct_answer_text: Concentrated around first and second order respiratory bronchioles

questions.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis develops progressive bilateral interstitial lung disease. Biopsy shows diffuse uniform interstitial fibrosis without temporal heterogeneity and no honeycombing. The pattern is
questions.explanation: NSIP is the most common pattern in collagen vascular disease lung involvement. It lacks the temporal heterogeneity of UIP and typically has no honeycombing or fibroblastic foci. Prognosis is better than IPF.

options: Collagen vascular diseases and asbestosis among others
questions.question: When a UIP pattern is found on lung biopsy, which of the following must be excluded before diagnosing IPF?
questions.explanation: UIP pattern can be seen in asbestosis, collagen vascular diseases, drug reactions, and other conditions. These known causes must be excluded before the diagnosis of IPF (idiopathic) can be made.
questions.correct_answer_text: Collagen vascular diseases and asbestosis among others

options: Direct drug toxicity and inflammatory cell influx into alveoli
Immune complex deposition in alveolar capillary walls
Inhibition of surfactant production by type II pneumocytes
questions.question: Bleomycin causes pulmonary toxicity through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Bleomycin causes pneumonitis and interstitial fibrosis through direct drug toxicity combined with stimulation of inflammatory cell influx into the alveoli. Amiodarone similarly causes pneumonitis and fibrosis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Direct drug toxicity and inflammatory cell influx into alveoli

options: Within the first 2 weeks of radiation
More than 1 year after completion of treatment
questions.question: Acute radiation pneumonitis characteristically occurs at what time interval after therapy?
questions.explanation: Acute radiation pneumonitis occurs 1–6 months after therapy in up to 20% of patients. The infiltrates precisely correspond to the radiation field. It may progress to chronic radiation pneumonitis with fibrosis.

questions.question: Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis most commonly affects which age group?
questions.explanation: Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis predominantly affects children, though it also occurs in adults who have a better prognosis. Historical mean survival was only 2.5 years, now improved with steroids and immunosuppression.

options: Absence of renal disease and anti-GBM antibody in IPH
Presence of hemoptysis and anemia in Goodpasture only
Linear IgG deposition found only in IPH on biopsy
Diffuse pulmonary infiltrates seen only in Goodpasture
questions.question: The key feature distinguishing idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis from Goodpasture syndrome is
questions.explanation: Both conditions share hemoptysis, anemia, and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates. IPH lacks renal disease and anti-GBM antibody — the two defining features of Goodpasture syndrome.
questions.correct_answer_text: Absence of renal disease and anti-GBM antibody in IPH

options: Recurrent nosebleeds leading to pressure necrosis
Vasculitis causing ischemic necrosis of nasal cartilage
Granulomatous inflammation eroding the nasal septum
Direct bacterial invasion from chronic sinusitis
questions.question: Wegener granulomatosis causes nasal perforation because of
questions.explanation: The necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of Wegener granulomatosis in the upper respiratory tract can erode and perforate the nasal septum. Nasal perforation is a classic pathognomonic clinical feature.
questions.correct_answer_text: Granulomatous inflammation eroding the nasal septum

options: Noncaseating granulomas with lymphocytic infiltrate only
Necrotizing vasculitis combined with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation
Eosinophilic infiltration with bronchospasm and mucus plugs
Organizing pneumonia with polypoid connective tissue plugs
questions.question: Lung lesions in Wegener granulomatosis are characterized by which combination?
questions.explanation: Wegener granulomatosis lung lesions have two components: necrotizing vasculitis (angiitis) AND parenchymal necrotizing granulomatous inflammation. Both features together are characteristic of WG.
questions.correct_answer_text: Necrotizing vasculitis combined with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation

options: More than 4 weeks after the initial trauma
questions.question: Fat embolism syndrome typically develops within what time frame after long bone fracture?
questions.explanation: Fat embolism syndrome (petechiae, neurologic symptoms, respiratory failure) typically develops 24–72 hours after massive trauma or long bone fracture. The mechanism involves mechanical obstruction plus toxic fatty acid release causing endothelial damage.

options: Massive pulmonary infarction from large vessel occlusion
Granulomatous pneumonitis from fetal squamous cells
Right heart failure from chronic pulmonary hypertension
Sudden dyspnea, hypotension, hypoxia, and DIC
questions.question: Amniotic fluid embolism is a catastrophic obstetric emergency primarily because it causes
questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid embolism presents with sudden dyspnea, hypoxia, hypotension, and DIC. It carries high maternal mortality. The mechanism involves fetal squamous cells and debris triggering inflammatory response and coagulopathy in pulmonary microvasculature.
questions.correct_answer_text: Sudden dyspnea, hypotension, hypoxia, and DIC

options: Blocking right heart outflow with a large air bolus
Obstructing multiple small pulmonary arterioles diffusely
Triggering massive release of pulmonary vasoconstrictors
Causing acute left ventricular failure from hypoxia
questions.question: Air embolism causes cardiovascular collapse primarily by
questions.explanation: A large air bolus causes right heart outflow obstruction leading to cardiovascular collapse. The characteristic auscultatory finding is a "mill wheel" murmur. Common causes are iatrogenic (IV lines, surgery, barotrauma).
questions.correct_answer_text: Blocking right heart outflow with a large air bolus

options: Small yeast forms within alveolar macrophages
Non-septate hyphae branching at right angles
questions.question: Blastomyces dermatitidis is pathognomonic for which morphologic finding in tissue?
questions.explanation: Blastomyces dermatitidis forms thick-walled yeast with broad-based budding — this is pathognomonic. Blastomycosis causes mixed suppurative and granulomatous inflammation and is most likely to cause symptomatic disease.

questions.question: The most common extrapulmonary site of dissemination in blastomycosis is
questions.explanation: Skin is the most common extrapulmonary site of blastomycosis dissemination. Contrast with coccidioidomycosis where meningeal involvement is the most serious complication, and histoplasmosis where liver, spleen, and adrenals are affected.

questions.question: In coccidioidomycosis, the most serious complication of dissemination involves
questions.explanation: Meningeal involvement is the most serious and life-threatening complication of disseminated coccidioidomycosis. It causes chronic meningitis that is difficult to treat. Dissemination is rare but more likely in immunocompromised patients.

options: Halo sign — ground-glass opacity surrounding a nodule
Eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes
questions.question: Invasive aspergillosis in a neutropenic patient is angioinvasive. The characteristic CT finding in early disease is
questions.explanation: The "halo sign" on CT (ground-glass opacity surrounding a pulmonary nodule) is characteristic of early invasive aspergillosis. The "air-crescent sign" appears later. Aspergillus shows septate hyphae branching at 45 degrees.
questions.correct_answer_text: Halo sign — ground-glass opacity surrounding a nodule

questions.question: Which antifungal is first-line treatment for invasive aspergillosis?
questions.explanation: Voriconazole is the first-line treatment for invasive aspergillosis. Diagnosis is supported by galactomannan antigen and beta-D-glucan in serum or BAL. Aspergillus shows septate hyphae branching at 45-degree angles.

questions.question: Which immune defect primarily predisposes to infections with encapsulated bacteria like S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae in the lung?
questions.explanation: Humoral immunodeficiency (antibody/B cell deficiency) primarily predisposes to infections with encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae) that require opsonization by antibody for effective clearance.

questions.question: A transplant recipient develops interstitial pneumonitis. Biopsy shows enlarged cells with large basophilic intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo. Treatment is
questions.explanation: CMV pneumonia shows "owl-eye" intranuclear inclusions (large, basophilic, with clear halo) plus cytoplasmic inclusions in enlarged cells. It is the most common viral pneumonia in immunocompromised/transplant patients. Treatment is ganciclovir.

options: Typical carcinoid has 2–10 mitoses per 10 HPF
Typical carcinoid shows necrosis and vascular invasion
Typical carcinoid has fewer than 2 mitoses per 10 HPF and no necrosis
Typical carcinoid arises peripherally rather than centrally
questions.question: A typical carcinoid tumor of the lung differs from atypical carcinoid by
questions.explanation: Typical carcinoid: <2 mitoses/10 HPF, no necrosis, better prognosis (>90% 5-year survival). Atypical carcinoid: 2–10 mitoses/10 HPF, may have necrosis, worse prognosis (50–70% 5-year survival).

Bronchial carcinoids have direct access to systemic lymphatics
questions.question: Carcinoid syndrome from a pulmonary carcinoid can occur without liver metastases because
questions.explanation: Pulmonary carcinoids drain into pulmonary veins directly into systemic circulation, bypassing the liver. This means serotonin is not metabolized by the liver before reaching systemic circulation, enabling carcinoid syndrome without liver metastases.
questions.correct_answer_text: Pulmonary carcinoids drain into pulmonary veins bypassing the liver

questions.explanation: Mesothelioma begins as small nodules on the pleural surface, then progresses to sheets of tumor that encircle and encase the lung in a "rind-like" fashion. It presents with chest pain and recurrent hemorrhagic pleural effusion.
questions.correct_answer_text: Small pleural nodules progressing to rind-like lung encasement

questions.question: Which histologic subtype of mesothelioma has the worst prognosis?
questions.explanation: Sarcomatoid mesothelioma has the worst prognosis among the three types. Epithelioid (most common) has the best prognosis. Biphasic/mixed is intermediate. Overall median survival is 12–18 months regardless of type.

questions.explanation: Restrictive lung disease reduces FVC (reduced lung expansion) while FEV1 is proportionately reduced, keeping the FEV1/FVC ratio near normal. This contrasts with obstruction where FEV1 falls disproportionately, lowering the ratio.
questions.correct_answer_text: Restrictive lung disease from reduced compliance

questions.question: Secondary eosinophilia in the lung is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Secondary pulmonary eosinophilia is associated with asthma, drug allergies, and certain vasculitides. It is distinguished from primary/idiopathic causes by having an identifiable underlying condition driving the eosinophilic response.
questions.correct_answer_text: Asthma, drug allergies, and certain vasculitides

questions.question: What neurotransmitter is associated with runner's high?
questions.explanation: Endorphins are the body's natural opioids that create feelings of euphoria and pain relief. During intense exercise like running, the body releases endorphins, which bind to opioid receptors and produce the characteristic "runner's high" - a feeling of well-being and reduced pain perception. ---

questions.question: What neurotransmitter is associated with anxiety disorders?
questions.explanation: GABA (Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid) is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. Low GABA activity is associated with increased anxiety, as GABA normally helps calm neural activity. Many anti-anxiety medications work by enhancing GABA function. ---

questions.question: Where do neurons store the genetic information they use to code and build all the proteins required for their functions?
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains the cell's DNA, which stores all genetic information. This DNA is transcribed into mRNA, which then travels to ribosomes for protein synthesis. The nucleus is the central control center for all cellular functions. ---

questions.question: Which of the following are major inhibitory neurotransmitters, causing inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs)?
questions.explanation: GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, while glycine is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord. Both cause hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic membrane, making it less likely to fire an action potential. ---

options: The role of potassium channels in hyperpolarization
The role of chloride channels in hyperpolarization
The role of potassium channels in depolarization
The role of sodium channels in depolarization
The role of sodium channels in hyperpolarization
questions.question: The effect of tetrodotoxin (puffer fish poison) on axons demonstrates
questions.explanation: Tetrodotoxin specifically blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing action potentials from occurring. This demonstrates that sodium influx through these channels is essential for depolarization and action potential generation. ---
questions.correct_answer_text: The role of sodium channels in depolarization

questions.question: What neurotransmitter is associated with mood disorders?
questions.explanation: Serotonin is strongly associated with mood regulation. Low serotonin levels are linked to depression, anxiety, and other mood disorders. SSRIs (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors) are commonly prescribed antidepressants that increase serotonin availability. ---

options: Neuron membranes have sodium/potassium ion pumps that take out potassium ions
The semi-permeable membrane keeps sodium ions outside and potassium inside neurons
The cell membrane is impermeable to large charged protein molecules
The summed charges of the unequally distributed ions leave the inside of the membrane at approximately -65 mV relative to the…
questions.question: Which of the following is not true?
questions.explanation: This statement is incorrect. The sodium-potassium pump actually pumps potassium ions INTO the cell and sodium ions OUT of the cell (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in). This maintains the concentration gradients necessary for the resting potential. ---
questions.correct_answer_text: Neuron membranes have sodium/potassium ion pumps that take out potassium ions

questions.question: What neurotransmitter is associated with insomnia?
questions.explanation: Serotonin plays a crucial role in sleep regulation. It's a precursor to melatonin and helps regulate sleep-wake cycles. Imbalances in serotonin can lead to sleep disorders including insomnia. ---

questions.question: What neurotransmitter is associated with seizures?
questions.explanation: Glutamate is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain. Excessive glutamate activity or insufficient GABA inhibition can lead to seizures, as the brain becomes hyperexcitable with uncontrolled neuronal firing. ---

questions.question: What is one of the functions of Dopamine?
questions.explanation: Dopamine is central to the brain's reward system and pleasure pathways. It's released in response to rewarding experiences and motivates behavior toward pleasurable activities. This is why dopamine is often called the "feel-good" neurotransmitter. ---

questions.question: What is one of the functions of Endorphins?
questions.explanation: Endorphins are the body's natural opioids that produce feelings of pleasure and well-being. They're released during exercise, stress, pain, and other activities, binding to opioid receptors to create euphoric feelings and reduce pain perception. ---

questions.question: What neurotransmitter is associated with Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease is characterized by the death of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra. This leads to decreased dopamine levels, causing the characteristic motor symptoms like tremors, rigidity, and bradykinesia (slowness of movement). ---

questions.question: What neurotransmitter is associated with Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease involves significant loss of acetylcholine-producing neurons, particularly affecting memory and cognitive function. Cholinesterase inhibitors, which increase acetylcholine availability, are used as treatments for Alzheimer's. ---

options: Small-molecule neurotransmitters are stored in large dense-core vesicles
Peptide neurotransmitter precursors and their enzymes are axonally transported in vesicles
Small-molecule neurotransmitters are synthesized in the soma
Peptide neurotransmitters are synthesized at the synaptic terminals
Peptide neurotransmitters are synthesized in the nucleus of the neuron
questions.question: Which of the following best discriminates between small-molecule neurotransmitters and peptide neurotransmitters?
questions.explanation: Peptide neurotransmitters are synthesized in the cell body and transported down the axon in vesicles, while small-molecule neurotransmitters are typically synthesized locally at nerve terminals. This is a key distinguishing feature between these two types of neurotransmitters. ---
questions.correct_answer_text: Peptide neurotransmitter precursors and their enzymes are axonally transported in vesicles

questions.question: Which neurotransmitter is released by the postganglionic neurons of the sympathetic nervous system?
questions.explanation: Most postganglionic sympathetic neurons release norepinephrine (noradrenaline) as their neurotransmitter. This activates adrenergic receptors on target organs, producing the "fight or flight" response characteristic of sympathetic activation. ---

questions.question: Enkephalins are peptide neurotransmitters that function in the perception of pain. This is because
questions.explanation: Enkephalins are endogenous opioid peptides that bind to opioid receptors (mu, delta, and kappa) to reduce pain perception. They work similarly to morphine and other opioid drugs by activating these same receptor systems. ---
questions.correct_answer_text: They interact with specific opioid receptor proteins to produce their effects

questions.question: What determines the effect of neurotransmitter release on the post-synaptic neurons?
questions.explanation: The type of postsynaptic receptors determines whether the effect will be excitatory or inhibitory, and the magnitude of the response. The same neurotransmitter can have different effects depending on which receptors are present on the postsynaptic cell. ---
