mcq_sets.title: Chemical Pathology MCQs

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT measured in a basic metabolic panel (BMP)?
questions.explanation: A BMP typically includes glucose, electrolytes (Na+, K+, Cl-, CO2), BUN, and creatinine. Bilirubin is part of liver function tests, not the BMP.

questions.question: Which test is the most specific for liver function?
questions.explanation: ALT (Alanine aminotransferase) is more specific for hepatocellular injury as it's primarily found in the liver, while AST is found in multiple organs including heart and muscle.

questions.question: Which electrolyte is the most abundant cation in extracellular fluid?
questions.explanation: Sodium (Na+) is the predominant cation in extracellular fluid (normal: 135-145 mEq/L), while potassium is the main intracellular cation.

questions.question: An increased anion gap metabolic acidosis can be caused by
questions.explanation: Lactic acidosis causes increased anion gap metabolic acidosis due to organic acid accumulation. Diarrhea and RTA typically cause normal anion gap acidosis.

questions.question: Which analyte is most useful in the diagnosis of multiple myeloma?
questions.explanation: SPEP detects monoclonal proteins (M-proteins) characteristic of multiple myeloma, showing abnormal immunoglobulin bands. ## Section 2: Endocrine Disorders & Hormone Assays

questions.question: Which of the following is an adrenal hormone?
questions.explanation: Cortisol is produced by the adrenal cortex. T3 is thyroid hormone, prolactin is pituitary hormone, and ADH is produced by the hypothalamus.

questions.question: In primary hypothyroidism, TSH levels are typically
questions.explanation: Primary hypothyroidism involves thyroid gland failure, so TSH is elevated due to loss of negative feedback from low thyroid hormones.

questions.question: Which hormone is most useful for diagnosing acromegaly?
questions.explanation: IGF-1 is more stable than GH and better reflects long-term GH secretion, making it the preferred screening test for acromegaly.

questions.question: Which test is used to confirm Cushing's syndrome?
questions.explanation: This test differentiates normal individuals (who suppress cortisol) from those with Cushing's syndrome (who fail to suppress).

questions.question: Which enzyme deficiency is most common in congenital adrenal hyperplasia?
questions.explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for ~95% of CAH cases, leading to cortisol deficiency and androgen excess. ## Section 3: Kidney Function & Electrolytes

questions.question: The best marker for glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is
questions.explanation: Cystatin C is less affected by muscle mass, age, and diet compared to creatinine, providing a more accurate GFR assessment.

questions.question: A low fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) suggests
questions.explanation: FENa <1% indicates intact tubular function with appropriate sodium retention, typical of prerenal causes of AKI.

questions.question: Which electrolyte abnormality is associated with ECG changes such as peaked T waves?
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia causes characteristic ECG changes: peaked T waves, widened QRS, and can progress to sine waves and cardiac arrest.

questions.question: Which acid-base disorder is commonly seen in patients with chronic kidney disease?
questions.explanation: CKD causes metabolic acidosis due to decreased acid excretion, reduced ammonia production, and bicarbonate loss.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions leads to an increased BUN-to-creatinine ratio?
questions.explanation: Prerenal azotemia increases BUN more than creatinine due to enhanced urea reabsorption, raising the BUN:Cr ratio >20:1. ## Section 4: Liver Function & Lipid Metabolism

questions.question: Which liver enzyme is most specific for hepatocellular injury?
questions.explanation: ALT is predominantly found in hepatocytes, making it more specific for liver injury than AST, which is also found in cardiac and skeletal muscle.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best marker of cholestasis?
questions.explanation: Alkaline phosphatase is elevated in cholestatic conditions due to increased synthesis and release from bile duct epithelium.

questions.question: Which lipoprotein is primarily responsible for transporting cholesterol to tissues?
questions.explanation: LDL carries cholesterol from liver to peripheral tissues and is the major atherogenic lipoprotein.

questions.question: Familial hypercholesterolemia is caused by a defect in which receptor?
questions.explanation: FH is caused by mutations in the LDL receptor gene, leading to impaired cholesterol uptake and very high LDL levels.

questions.question: A fasting glucose level of 8.0 mmol/L (144 mg/dL) suggests
questions.explanation: Fasting glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) indicates diabetes mellitus. 144 mg/dL clearly meets this criterion. ## Section 5: Tumor Markers & Cancer Screening

questions.question: Which tumor marker is most commonly used for ovarian cancer screening?
questions.explanation: CA 125 is the most widely used tumor marker for ovarian cancer, though it's not specific and can be elevated in benign conditions.

questions.question: A patient with suspected pancreatic cancer is likely to have elevated levels of
questions.explanation: CA 19-9 is the most useful tumor marker for pancreatic adenocarcinoma, though it's also elevated in biliary obstruction.

questions.question: Which tumor marker is most specific for hepatocellular carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is the most specific tumor marker for hepatocellular carcinoma, though it can also be elevated in other liver diseases.

questions.question: A patient with an enlarged prostate and elevated PSA should undergo
questions.explanation: Elevated PSA with enlarged prostate requires tissue diagnosis via biopsy to rule out prostate cancer.

questions.question: The presence of high levels of CEA is most suggestive of
questions.explanation: CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) is most commonly associated with colorectal cancer, though it's not specific. ## Section 6: Acid-Base Disorders & Blood Gases

questions.question: Which of the following is a primary metabolic alkalosis?
questions.explanation: Vomiting causes loss of gastric acid (HCl), leading to metabolic alkalosis. COPD causes respiratory acidosis.

questions.question: A patient with a pH of 7.25, PaCO₂ of 60 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ of 24 mEq/L has
questions.explanation: pH <7.35 with elevated PaCO₂ (>45 mmHg) indicates respiratory acidosis. Normal bicarbonate suggests acute condition.

questions.question: Which of the following causes a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis?
questions.explanation: RTA causes normal anion gap acidosis due to impaired renal acid excretion. Other options cause high anion gap acidosis.

questions.question: A patient with metabolic acidosis and an increased anion gap likely has
questions.explanation: DKA produces ketoacids, causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis. RTA causes normal anion gap acidosis.

questions.question: Which compensatory response occurs in metabolic acidosis?
questions.explanation: Metabolic acidosis triggers hyperventilation to blow off CO₂ and partially compensate for the acidosis. ## Case-Based MCQs Section 1: Electrolytes & Acid-Base Disorders

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with chronic kidney disease presents with weakness and palpitations. ECG shows peaked T waves. Lab results: K⁺ 6.5 mmol/L, Na⁺ 140 mmol/L, BUN 55 mg/dL, Creatinine 4.2 mg/dL. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation: Severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes (peaked T waves) is a cardiac emergency. IV calcium stabilizes cardiac membrane first.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman with severe vomiting for three days presents with muscle cramps and weakness. Lab results: Na⁺ 138 mmol/L, K⁺ 2.8 mmol/L, Cl⁻ 85 mmol/L, HCO₃⁻ 34 mmol/L. What is the acid-base disorder?
questions.explanation: High bicarbonate (34 mmol/L) with hypokalemia and hypochloremia from vomiting indicates metabolic alkalosis.

questions.question: A 35-year-old diabetic man presents with confusion and deep rapid breathing. Blood gas: pH 7.1, PaCO₂ 22 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L, glucose 550 mg/dL. What is the primary acid-base disorder?
questions.explanation: Low pH (7.1) with low bicarbonate (10) and compensatory hyperventilation (low CO₂) indicates metabolic acidosis from DKA.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with COPD presents with confusion. Blood gas: pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 60 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 28 mmol/L. What is the most likely acid-base disorder?
questions.explanation: Low pH with high CO₂ indicates respiratory acidosis. Elevated bicarbonate suggests chronic compensation.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with chronic diarrhea presents with weakness. Labs: Na⁺ 138 mmol/L, K⁺ 3.0 mmol/L, Cl⁻ 105 mmol/L, HCO₃⁻ 15 mmol/L. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Anion gap = 138 - (105 + 15) = 18 (normal range). Diarrhea causes bicarbonate loss leading to normal anion gap acidosis. ## Case-Based MCQs Section 2: Kidney Function & Renal Pathology

questions.question: A 55-year-old hypertensive patient presents with swelling and decreased urine output. Labs: BUN 45 mg/dL, Creatinine 3.8 mg/dL, Na⁺ 134 mmol/L, K⁺ 5.2 mmol/L. Urine Na⁺ 500 mOsm/kg. What is the likely cause?
questions.explanation: Low urine sodium (<20) and high urine osmolality (>500) indicate intact tubular function trying to conserve sodium and water.

questions.question: A 70-year-old diabetic patient presents with chronic kidney disease. Labs: BUN 55 mg/dL, Creatinine 5.5 mg/dL, eGFR 15 mL/min. What stage of CKD is this?
questions.explanation: eGFR <15 mL/min indicates Stage 5 CKD (kidney failure), requiring renal replacement therapy consideration.

questions.question: A patient with nephrotic syndrome has edema and proteinuria >3.5 g/day. What is the most likely biochemical abnormality?
questions.explanation: Massive proteinuria in nephrotic syndrome leads to hypoalbuminemia, causing decreased oncotic pressure and edema.

questions.question: A patient with acute tubular necrosis (ATN) will have
questions.explanation: Muddy brown casts are pathognomonic for ATN, indicating tubular epithelial cell sloughing.

questions.question: A patient with SIADH will most likely have which lab finding?
questions.explanation: SIADH causes excessive water retention, leading to dilutional hyponatremia with concentrated urine. ## Case-Based MCQs Section 3: Endocrine Disorders

questions.question: A 60-year-old man presents with weight gain, moon facies, and hypertension. Labs: Cortisol remains high after low-dose dexamethasone suppression test. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Failure to suppress cortisol with low-dose dexamethasone confirms Cushing's syndrome. Clinical features support this diagnosis.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with palpitations, weight loss, and sweating. Labs: TSH <0.1 mIU/L, Free T4 high. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Suppressed TSH with elevated T4 and classic hyperthyroid symptoms confirms hyperthyroidism.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presents with fatigue, hypotension, and hyperpigmentation. Labs: Na⁺ 129 mmol/L, K⁺ 5.8 mmol/L, Cortisol low. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Low cortisol with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hyperpigmentation are classic for primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease).

questions.question: A patient with secondary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic kidney disease will have
questions.explanation: CKD causes phosphate retention and vitamin D deficiency, leading to low/normal calcium and compensatory PTH elevation.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is most commonly associated with hypercalcemia?
questions.explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in outpatients, followed by malignancy in hospitalized patients. ## Case-Based MCQs Section 4: Diabetes & Glucose Disorders

questions.question: A 40-year-old man with polyuria and polydipsia has fasting glucose of 150 mg/dL and HbA1c of 8.5%. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL and HbA1c ≥6.5% both meet criteria for diabetes mellitus diagnosis.

questions.question: A patient presents with altered mental status and blood glucose of 35 mg/dL. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Severe hypoglycemia (35 mg/dL) with altered mental status suggests insulin excess, most likely from an insulinoma.

questions.question: A 65-year-old diabetic patient with non-healing ulcers likely has
questions.explanation: Chronic hyperglycemia causes microvascular and macrovascular complications, leading to poor wound healing.

questions.question: Which test is most useful for long-term diabetes monitoring?
questions.explanation: HbA1c reflects average glucose over 2-3 months, making it ideal for long-term diabetes monitoring and management.

questions.question: A diabetic patient with nausea, abdominal pain, and high blood glucose should be evaluated for
questions.explanation: Nausea, abdominal pain with hyperglycemia in a diabetic patient suggests DKA, especially with ketosis and acidosis. ## Chemical Pathology Calculations Section

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents with confusion and deep rapid breathing. Blood gas shows: pH 7.15, PaCO₂ 25 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L, Na⁺ 140 mmol/L, Cl⁻ 100 mmol/L. What is the anion gap?
questions.explanation: Anion gap = Na⁺ - (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) = 140 - (100 + 10) = 30. High anion gap suggests organic acidosis.

questions.question: A patient with an anion gap of 25 has which likely cause?
questions.explanation: High anion gap (>12) suggests organic acid accumulation. DKA produces ketoacids causing elevated anion gap.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis?
questions.explanation: Diarrhea causes bicarbonate loss without organic acid accumulation, resulting in normal anion gap acidosis.

questions.question: A patient presents with metabolic acidosis. Labs: Na⁺ 138 mmol/L, Cl⁻ 114 mmol/L, HCO₃⁻ 14 mmol/L. What is the anion gap?
questions.explanation: Anion gap = 138 - (114 + 14) = 10. Normal anion gap (8-12) suggests hyperchloremic acidosis.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is associated with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis?
questions.explanation: Ethylene glycol metabolism produces organic acids (oxalic acid), causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis. ## Corrected Calcium & Parathyroid Disorders

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman with multiple myeloma has total calcium of 7.5 mg/dL and albumin of 2.5 g/dL. What is her corrected calcium level? (Use: Corrected Ca = Measured Ca + 0.8 × (4 - Albumin))
questions.explanation: Corrected Ca = 7.5 + 0.8 × (4 - 2.5) = 7.5 + 1.2 = 8.7 ≈ 8.2 mg/dL. Corrects for low albumin.

questions.question: A patient with hypercalcemia due to primary hyperparathyroidism will have which lab result?
questions.explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism involves autonomous PTH secretion causing hypercalcemia with inappropriately normal/high PTH.

questions.question: A patient with hypercalcemia, suppressed PTH, and high vitamin D likely has
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH suggests non-parathyroid cause. High vitamin D indicates vitamin D intoxication or granulomatous disease.

questions.question: A patient with tetany, muscle cramps, and a corrected calcium of 6.5 mg/dL likely has
questions.explanation: Severe hypocalcemia (6.5 mg/dL, normal 8.5-10.5) with neuromuscular symptoms indicates hypoparathyroidism.

questions.question: In chronic kidney disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs due to
questions.explanation: CKD causes phosphate retention and decreased vitamin D activation, leading to hypocalcemia and compensatory PTH elevation. ## Osmolar Gap & Fluid Disorders

questions.question: A 50-year-old man presents with altered mental status after alcohol ingestion. Labs: Na⁺ 140 mmol/L, glucose 90 mg/dL, BUN 14 mg/dL, measured serum osmolality 320 mOsm/kg. What is the calculated osmolality? (Use: 2 × Na⁺ + (Glucose/18) + (BUN/2.8))
What is the osmolar gap in the previous case? (Osmolar gap = Measured osmolality - Calculated osmolality)
questions.explanation: Osmolar gap = 320 - 295 = 25 mOsm/kg. Gap >10 suggests presence of unmeasured osmoles (methanol, ethylene glycol).

questions.question: A high osmolar gap suggests
questions.explanation: High osmolar gap (>10) indicates presence of unmeasured osmotically active substances like toxic alcohols.

options: High serum sodium and low serum osmolality
questions.question: A patient with severe dehydration will have
questions.explanation: Dehydration triggers ADH release, causing maximal urine concentration (>800 mOsm/kg) to conserve water.

questions.question: In SIADH, the expected serum sodium and osmolality are
questions.explanation: SIADH causes excessive water retention, diluting both sodium and overall serum osmolality. ## Glucose & Diabetes Calculations

questions.question: A patient has a fasting glucose of 130 mg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL meets criteria for diabetes mellitus. 130 mg/dL exceeds this threshold.

questions.question: A diabetic patient's HbA1c is 10%. What is the estimated average glucose? (Use: eAG = (HbA1c × 28.7) - 46.7)
questions.explanation: eAG = (10 × 28.7) - 46.7 = 287 - 46.7 = 240.3 ≈ 240 mg/dL. Very poor glycemic control.

questions.question: Which test is best for long-term glucose monitoring in diabetes?
questions.explanation: HbA1c reflects 2-3 month average glucose levels, providing the best assessment of long-term glycemic control.

questions.question: A patient with diabetes presents with nausea, high glucose, and pH 7.1. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acidosis (pH 7.1) with hyperglycemia and GI symptoms indicates DKA. HHS typically lacks acidosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) but NOT diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?
questions.explanation: HHS has more severe dehydration due to gradual onset, while DKA has acidosis and ketosis that HHS lacks. ## Lipid Profile & Cardiovascular Risk

questions.question: A patient with LDL of 180 mg/dL and HDL of 35 mg/dL is at risk for
questions.explanation: High LDL (>160) and low HDL (<40 men, <50 women) significantly increase cardiovascular disease risk.

questions.question: Which lipid is most closely associated with pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Severe hypertriglyceridemia (>1000 mg/dL) can cause acute pancreatitis through pancreatic lipase activation.

questions.question: A patient with a total cholesterol of 240 mg/dL has
questions.explanation: Total cholesterol >200 mg/dL is considered elevated; 240 mg/dL represents significant hypercholesterolemia.

questions.question: A patient with low HDL and high triglycerides likely has
questions.explanation: Low HDL (<40/50) and high triglycerides (>150) are key components of metabolic syndrome.

questions.question: The most effective therapy for lowering LDL is
questions.explanation: Statins are first-line therapy for LDL reduction, typically lowering LDL by 30-50% through HMG-CoA reductase inhibition. ## Acid-Base Disorders & Acidosis

options: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis Correct
questions.question: A 60-year-old diabetic presents with confusion, Kussmaul breathing, and fruity breath odor. Blood gas: pH 7.15, PaCO₂ 22 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Classic DKA presentation: acidosis (pH 7.15), compensatory hyperventilation (low CO₂), ketotic breath, and altered mental status.

options: High anion gap metabolic acidosis Correct
questions.question: A patient with chronic diarrhea has a pH of 7.25, PaCO₂ 38 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ 17 mmol/L. What is the acid-base disturbance?
questions.explanation: Diarrhea causes bicarbonate loss without organic acid accumulation, resulting in normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.

questions.question: A 70-year-old COPD patient presents with confusion. Blood gas: pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 60 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 32 mmol/L. What is the acid-base disorder?
questions.explanation: Low pH with high CO₂ indicates respiratory acidosis. Elevated bicarbonate shows chronic renal compensation.

questions.question: A patient with septic shock has lactic acid of 7.0 mmol/L. What is the most likely acid-base disorder?
questions.explanation: Lactic acidosis produces organic acids, causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis in shock states.

questions.question: A young patient with aspirin overdose has the following blood gas: pH 7.45, PaCO₂ 24 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 18 mmol/L. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Salicylates cause both direct respiratory stimulation (alkalosis) and metabolic acidosis, creating a mixed disorder. ## Cardiovascular Pathology & Biomarkers

questions.question: A patient with substernal chest pain and ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF likely has
questions.explanation: ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF indicates inferior wall MI, typically involving the right coronary artery.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most specific marker for myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation: Troponin I is highly specific for cardiac muscle and remains elevated longer than other markers, making it gold standard for MI diagnosis.

questions.question: A 65-year-old diabetic man with chest pain has normal ECG but elevated troponin. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Elevated troponin with normal ECG indicates non-ST elevation MI (NSTEMI), common in diabetic patients with atypical presentations.

mcq_sets.title: Male Reproductive System — Clinical MCQs

questions.question: An epidemiologic study is performed to determine potential risk factors for development of penile squamous intraepithelial neoplasia. It is observed that persons who develop this disease are elderly men. Which of the following diseases is most likely to be found to precede development of penile neoplasia in these men?
questions.explanation: The chronic irritation from accumulation of secretions and smegma under the prepuce is the likely risk. Circumcision reduces the risk for development of penile carcinoma, and can reduce transmission of infections as well.

questions.question: A 20-year-old man has noted a penile discharge with some pain on urination for the last 2 days. A small amount of whitish exudate can be expressed from the urethral meatus. Culture of the penile discharge reveals Neisseria gonorrheae. If untreated, which of the following complications is he most likely to develop?
questions.explanation: When the testis is involved by gonorrhea, it is typically the epididymis. Many male gonorrheal infections are asymptomatic and not followed by significant complications. Urethritis with stricture is a possible complication.

questions.question: A 77-year-old man has a routine check-up. The only finding is slight nodularity of his prostate on digital rectal examination. Serum PSA is 6 ng/mL. A prostate biopsy shows prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN). Which of the following is the best medical care option to offer this man?
questions.explanation: PIN is a potential precursor of prostatic adenocarcinoma, but by itself does not warrant therapy.

questions.question: A 27-year-old man has complained of continuing 'jock itch' for the past year. On physical examination there are small whitish scaling patches on the skin of his perineum. A scraping shows Trichophyton rubrum organisms. Which of the following lesions is he most likely to develop?
questions.explanation: The chronic rubbing and scratching from this dermatophyte infection can result in epidermal hyperplasia and chronic inflammation.

questions.question: A subset of sexually active 30–45-year-old men are found to have a history of pelvic pain with enlarged, tender prostates on digital rectal examination. However, routine microbiologic cultures from prostatic secretions show no growth. Which of the following infectious agents is most likely to produce this condition?
questions.explanation: C. trachomatis, the leading cause of non-gonococcal urethritis, is the most frequent form of prostatitis in young adult men. There is typically no history of chronic urinary tract infection.

questions.question: A 30-year-old sexually active man has experienced burning pain with urination for the past 5 days. There is a profuse yellowish urethral discharge. He is afebrile and is treated with ceftriaxone. He is most likely to be infected with which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation: Gonorrhea is a common cause of urethritis in males. Culture of the purulent discharge is possible, but microbial culture of this fastidious organism is challenging, so molecular methods such as a DNA probe or PCR can be used for diagnosis.

questions.question: A term male infant is born with incomplete development of the dorsal aspect of the penile urethra, with the defect extending to the bladder, which is open onto the lower abdominal wall. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Epispadias is a rare congenital anomaly that may be mild or, as in this case, severe with a large open defect that must be repaired. The failure to close the bladder is termed exstrophy.

questions.question: A 35-year-old healthy man desires a permanent form of contraception and has a vasectomy performed with no complications. Which of the following is most likely to result from prior vasectomy?
questions.explanation: Also called vasitis nodosa, a sperm granuloma results from a foreign body granulomatous reaction to extravasated sperm at the vasectomy site. The granulomatous reaction is typically not florid.

questions.question: A study documents testicular abnormalities in adult males with infertility, some having a patchy pattern of atrophy of testicular tubules. Which of the following infections is most likely to produce these findings?
questions.explanation: This is a very common childhood infection (when vaccinations are not done) resulting in orchitis as well as parotitis. The inflammation rarely causes enough damage to produce a significantly reduced sperm count if acquired in childhood. The virus tends to produce more testicular damage when adults are infected.

questions.question: A 21-year-old sexually active man is notified that his last sexual contact 3 weeks prior has a positive serologic test for syphilis. Which of the following findings is most likely to be indicative of his acquisition of this infection?
questions.explanation: This would be the typical finding for primary syphilis from recent infection by Treponema pallidum.

questions.question: A healthy 17-year-old circumcised adolescent has pearly penile papules noted at the edge of the glans penis. There is no erythema or urethral discharge. He is not sexually active. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is really a normal variation, but some patients may be concerned when they notice that other men do not have them.

questions.question: A 95-year-old man has had difficulty with urination for the past 15 years. His prostate is diffusely enlarged. A transurethral resection shows glandular hyperplasia and a focus of grade 1,2 adenocarcinoma. Which of the following is the next most appropriate treatment plan?
questions.explanation: A Gleason 1,2 adenocarcinoma is so low grade that it is unlikely to progress. At least half of men his age probably have a focus of prostatic adenocarcinoma.

options: Darkfield microscopic examination of exudate or secretions
questions.question: A group of subjects is found to have Chlamydia trachomatis infection. Which of the following laboratory methods is most likely to be useful in diagnosis of C. trachomatis?
questions.explanation: This is the easiest and most cost-effective method, since C. trachomatis cannot be easily cultured by routine methods.

questions.question: A term male infant has an abnormal opening of the urethra onto the ventral surface of the penis for a distance of 0.3 cm. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is a congenital anomaly. Infection is a common complication, and partial urethral stricture may lead to urinary tract obstruction.

questions.question: A 45-year-old uncircumcised man complains of dysuria for the past week. On physical examination he has erythema and edema of the glans penis, with inability to retract the foreskin. Which of the following infectious agents is most likely to be associated with these findings?
questions.explanation: He has balanitis with paraphimosis, and staphylococcal or streptococcal infections are most likely to be present.

questions.question: A pathologic study is performed in men aged 50–100 years with PSA levels above 15 ng/mL who underwent prostatectomy. The sites of adenocarcinomas are mapped within the prostate. In which of the following regions are these adenocarcinomas most likely to arise?
questions.explanation: Most prostatic adenocarcinomas arise in the peripheral zone posteriorly where they can potentially be palpated by digital rectal examination.

questions.question: A clinical study is conducted to determine survival following treatment for testicular neoplasms. Treatments included surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy. Which of the following types of testicular neoplasm is most likely to have responded best to radiation therapy?
questions.explanation: Seminomas are the most radiosensitive of testicular carcinomas.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man has a routine check of his health status. On physical examination the prepuce cannot be fully retracted from the glans of his penis. No other abnormalities are noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Inflammation with scarring may prevent full retraction. There is an increased risk for phimosis and for balanitis in uncircumcised males.

questions.question: A 2-year-old boy has enlargement of the left testis. An ultrasound scan shows a 2 cm solid mass within the body of the testis. Serum AFP is 226 ng/mL. Which of the following neoplasms is this child most likely to have?
questions.explanation: The most common testicular tumor under the age of 3 is a yolk sac tumor (infantile embryonal carcinoma). However, finding any testicular tumor in children is uncommon. The prognosis is good in most cases.

questions.question: A 43-year-old uncircumcised man has noted a lesion on his penis for the past year. On physical examination there is a 0.9 cm diameter rough, tan, firm, slightly raised area at the right lateral base of the glans, with difficulty in retracting the foreskin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is squamous cell carcinoma in situ. If excised at this stage, it is curable. If not treated, it can progress to an invasive carcinoma.

mcq_sets.title: Medical Physiology IV (CNS) — MCQ Bank

questions.question: The following neurotransmitter is used by the substantia nigra neurons that project to the caudate and putamen
questions.explanation: The substantia nigra contains dopaminergic neurons that project to the caudate nucleus and putamen (collectively called the striatum) via the nigrostriatal pathway. This dopaminergic pathway is crucial for motor control and is affected in Parkinson's disease. The other neurotransmitters listed are not the primary neurotransmitters used by substantia nigra neurons in this pathway.

questions.question: Which of the following items correctly describes the relationship of cerebrospinal fluid pressure to the venous pressure in the superior sagittal sinus?
questions.explanation: CSF pressure is normally maintained at a few millimeters of mercury higher than venous pressure in the superior sagittal sinus. This pressure gradient is essential for CSF drainage through the arachnoid granulations into the venous system. If CSF pressure were lower or equal to venous pressure, proper drainage would not occur.

questions.question: Output signals from Golgi tendon organs are transmitted to which of the following higher centers?
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organs send proprioceptive information about muscle tension to the cerebellum via spinocerebellar tracts. The cerebellum uses this information for motor coordination and balance. The other structures listed are not primary targets for Golgi tendon organ afferents.

questions.question: Which type of cholinergic receptor is found at synapses between preganglionic and postganglionic neurons of the sympathetic system?
questions.explanation: All autonomic ganglia (both sympathetic and parasympathetic) use nicotinic cholinergic receptors at the synapse between preganglionic and postganglionic neurons. Muscarinic receptors are found at parasympathetic postganglionic terminals, while alpha and beta receptors are adrenergic receptors found at sympathetic postganglionic terminals.

questions.question: The term limbic cortex includes the orbitofrontal cortex, subcallosal gyrus, cingulate gyrus, and which one of the following areas?
questions.explanation: The limbic cortex includes the parahippocampal gyrus along with the orbitofrontal cortex, subcallosal gyrus, and cingulate gyrus. These areas are involved in emotion, memory, and behavior. The other options are not considered part of the limbic cortex.

questions.question: Occlusion of which of the following structures would lead to communicating hydrocephalus?
questions.explanation: Communicating hydrocephalus occurs when CSF can flow through the ventricular system but cannot be absorbed properly. Obstruction of arachnoid villi (granulations) prevents CSF absorption into the venous system, leading to communicating hydrocephalus. Obstruction of the other structures would cause non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus.

questions.question: The withdrawal reflex is initiated by stimulation delivered to which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation: The withdrawal reflex is a protective reflex triggered by noxious stimuli detected by cutaneous free nerve endings (nociceptors). These receptors detect potentially harmful stimuli and initiate rapid withdrawal from the stimulus. The other receptors listed detect different types of stimuli but are not primarily involved in withdrawal reflexes.

questions.question: Which substance activates adrenergic alpha and beta receptors equally well?
questions.explanation: Epinephrine (adrenaline) has equal affinity for both alpha and beta adrenergic receptors. Norepinephrine has higher affinity for alpha receptors than beta receptors. Acetylcholine, serotonin, and dopamine are not adrenergic receptor agonists.

options: Cardiovascular functions involving blood pressure and heart rate
Signaling that food intake is sufficient (satiety)
Stimulation of uterine contractility and milk ejection from the breast
Regulation of thirst and water intake
Secretion of hormones from the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland
questions.question: The posterior and lateral hypothalamus, in combination with the preoptic area, are involved in the control of which of the following functions?
questions.explanation: The posterior and lateral hypothalamus, along with the preoptic area, are key regions involved in osmoregulation and thirst control. These areas contain osmoreceptors that detect changes in blood osmolality and initiate appropriate responses including thirst and ADH release. The other functions are controlled by different hypothalamic regions.
questions.correct_answer_text: Regulation of thirst and water intake

options: Reticulospinal neurons do not receive input from motor areas of the cerebral cortex
Pontine reticulospinal fibers excite spinal cord motor neurons that activate limb extensor muscles
Pontine reticulospinal fibers course in the spinal cord posterior funiculus
Medullary reticulospinal fibers course in the medial part of the ventral funiculus of the spinal cord
Medullary reticulospinal fibers excite motor neurons that activate extensor muscles
questions.question: Which statement concerning the reticulospinal system is correct?
questions.explanation: Pontine reticulospinal fibers facilitate extensor muscle tone and activity, while medullary reticulospinal fibers generally inhibit extensor muscles and facilitate flexor muscles. The other statements are incorrect: reticulospinal neurons do receive cortical input, medullary fibers inhibit rather than excite extensors, and pontine fibers course in the ventral funiculus, not posterior funiculus.
questions.correct_answer_text: Pontine reticulospinal fibers excite spinal cord motor neurons that activate limb extensor muscles

questions.question: The neurons located in the locus ceruleus release which of the following neurotransmitters at their synaptic terminals?
questions.explanation: The locus ceruleus is the major noradrenergic nucleus in the brain, containing norepinephrine-producing neurons that project widely throughout the CNS. These neurons are involved in arousal, attention, and stress responses. The other neurotransmitters are produced by different neural populations.

options: Tight junctions between the ependymal cells forming the ventricular walls
Tight junctions between adjacent endothelial cells of brain capillaries
questions.question: Which of the following items represents the structural basis of the blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier?
questions.explanation: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by tight junctions between choroid plexus epithelial cells. This barrier controls the movement of substances from blood into CSF. Option E describes the blood-brain barrier, while the other options are not correct structural bases for the blood-CSF barrier.

options: Junction of the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes
Insular cortex on the dominant side of the brain
Medial portion of the precentral gyrus
Most anterior portion of the temporal lobe
questions.question: Damage to which of the following brain areas leads to the inability to comprehend the written or the spoken word?
questions.explanation: Wernicke's area, located at the junction of the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes in the dominant hemisphere, is responsible for language comprehension. Damage to this area results in Wernicke's aphasia, characterized by inability to comprehend written or spoken language. The other areas are not primarily involved in language comprehension.
questions.correct_answer_text: Junction of the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes

questions.question: In an otherwise normal individual, dysfunction of which brain area will lead to behavior which is not appropriate for the given social occasion?
questions.explanation: The amygdala is crucial for processing emotions and social behavior, including the ability to recognize social cues and respond appropriately to social situations. Dysfunction of the amygdala can lead to inappropriate social behavior and difficulty reading social situations. The other structures, while important for various functions, are not primarily responsible for social appropriateness.

questions.question: Which of the following reflexes best describes incoming pain signals that elicit movements performed by antagonistic muscle groups on either side of the body?
questions.explanation: The crossed extensor reflex occurs when a painful stimulus causes withdrawal of the affected limb (flexion) while simultaneously causing extension of the opposite limb to maintain balance and support. This involves antagonistic muscle groups on both sides of the body. The withdrawal reflex only involves the affected side, while reciprocal and autogenic inhibition are different mechanisms.

options: An imbalance in the activity of medullary and pontine reticulospinal systems such that excitation of extensor motor neurons is…
Overactivity in the medullary reticulospinal system leads to hyperactivity in limb extensor muscles
Damage to the brainstem systems that control flexor motor neurons
Interruption of the medullary reticulospinal axons
Interruption of the pontine reticulospinal axons
questions.question: Decerebrate rigidity results from which of the following situations?
questions.explanation: Decerebrate rigidity results from damage above the level of the vestibular nuclei, leading to an imbalance where pontine reticulospinal activity (which facilitates extensors) predominates over medullary reticulospinal activity (which inhibits extensors). This results in excessive extensor muscle tone and rigidity.
questions.correct_answer_text: An imbalance in the activity of medullary and pontine reticulospinal systems such that excitation of extensor motor neurons is…

questions.question: Which portion of the cerebellum functions in the planning of sequential movement?
questions.explanation: The cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) and dentate nucleus are involved in motor planning and coordination of complex, sequential movements. They receive input from cerebral cortex and are important for cognitive aspects of motor control. The other cerebellar regions have different functions related to balance, posture, and limb coordination.

options: Excessive eating, rage and aggression, hyperactivity
questions.question: Bilateral lesions involving the ventromedial hypothalamus will lead to which of the following deficits?
questions.explanation: The ventromedial hypothalamus contains the satiety center. Bilateral lesions of this area result in hyperphagia (excessive eating), leading to obesity, along with increased aggression and hyperactivity. This is opposite to what would occur with lateral hypothalamic lesions, which would cause decreased eating.
questions.correct_answer_text: Excessive eating, rage and aggression, hyperactivity

questions.question: Which structure is an important pathway for communication between the limbic system and the brainstem?
questions.explanation: The medial forebrain bundle is a major pathway connecting limbic structures to the brainstem, particularly the hypothalamus. It carries both ascending and descending fibers and is important for emotional and motivational behaviors. The other structures have different functions and connections within the limbic system.

questions.question: The function of which of the following organs or systems is dominated by the sympathetic nervous system?
questions.explanation: Systemic blood vessels receive predominantly sympathetic innervation and have minimal parasympathetic innervation. Sympathetic stimulation causes vasoconstriction of most systemic vessels. The other organs listed receive dual innervation from both sympathetic and parasympathetic systems, with varying degrees of dominance.

questions.question: Which of the following structures in the vestibular apparatus is responsible for the detection of angular acceleration?
questions.explanation: The semicircular canals detect angular acceleration (rotational head movements). They contain the ampullae with hair cells that respond to endolymph movement during rotation. The macula, saccule, and statoconia are involved in detecting linear acceleration and gravity, not angular acceleration.

questions.question: A person who has had a traumatic brain injury seems to be able to understand the written and spoken word but cannot create the correct sounds to be able to speak a word that is recognizable. This person most likely has damage to which area of the brain?
questions.explanation: Broca's area is responsible for speech production and motor aspects of language. Damage to this area results in Broca's aphasia, where comprehension is intact but speech production is severely impaired. Wernicke's area damage would affect comprehension, while the other areas are not primarily involved in speech production.

questions.question: Schizophrenia is thought to be caused in part by excessive production and release of which of the following neurotransmitter agents?
questions.explanation: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia suggests that excessive dopaminergic activity, particularly in the mesolimbic pathway, contributes to the positive symptoms of schizophrenia. Antipsychotic medications work by blocking dopamine receptors. The other neurotransmitters are not primarily implicated in schizophrenia pathophysiology.

questions.question: Which of the following structures is not considered to be part of the basal ganglia?
questions.explanation: The dentate nucleus is part of the cerebellum, not the basal ganglia. The basal ganglia includes the caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, and subthalamic nucleus. The dentate nucleus is the largest of the deep cerebellar nuclei and is involved in motor planning and coordination.

questions.question: Stimulation of which of the following subcortical areas can lead to contraction of a single muscle or small groups of muscles?
questions.explanation: The red nucleus, particularly the magnocellular part, can produce discrete muscle contractions when stimulated. It has somatotopic organization and gives rise to the rubrospinal tract. The other structures listed do not have this capability for producing discrete muscle contractions upon stimulation.

questions.question: Which structures in the cerebellum have a topographical representation of the body?
questions.explanation: The vermis and intermediate hemisphere (spinocerebellum) have somatotopic organization with topographical representation of the body. The vermis represents axial muscles and the intermediate hemisphere represents limb muscles. The lateral hemispheres are involved in motor planning rather than direct body representation.

options: Crista ampullaris of the horizontal semicircular duct
Crista ampullaris of the anterior semicircular duct
questions.question: Which of the following structures is maximally sensitive to linear head movement in the vertical plane?
questions.explanation: The macula of the saccule is oriented vertically and is maximally sensitive to linear acceleration in the vertical plane (up-down movements). The macula of the utricle is oriented horizontally and detects horizontal linear movements. The cristae ampullaris detect angular acceleration, not linear acceleration.

questions.question: Retrograde amnesia is the inability to recall long-term memories from the past. When damaged, which of the following brain regions leads to retrograde amnesia?
questions.explanation: The hippocampus is crucial for memory consolidation and retrieval. Damage to the hippocampus can cause retrograde amnesia, affecting the ability to recall memories formed before the injury. The other structures, while involved in memory circuits, are not the primary cause of retrograde amnesia when damaged.

questions.question: Which structure connects the hippocampus to the limbic system?
questions.explanation: The fornix is the major output pathway from the hippocampus, connecting it to other limbic structures including the mammillary bodies, septal nuclei, and hypothalamus. It is crucial for hippocampal communication within the limbic system. The other tracts have different functions and connections.

options: Ventral anterior complex of the thalamus
Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum
questions.question: The condition of athetosis results when which area of the brain is dysfunctional?
questions.explanation: Athetosis, characterized by slow, writhing movements, typically results from dysfunction of the globus pallidus. This structure is part of the basal ganglia and is important for controlling movement. Dysfunction of other basal ganglia structures causes different movement disorders.

questions.question: Which component of the basal ganglia plays the major role in the control of cognitive (memory-guided) motor activity?
questions.explanation: The caudate nucleus is part of the associative circuit of the basal ganglia and plays a major role in cognitive aspects of motor control, including memory-guided movements and executive motor functions. The putamen is more involved in automatic motor patterns, while the other structures have different roles in basal ganglia function.

questions.question: A wide variety of neurotransmitters have been identified in the cell bodies and afferent synaptic terminals in the basal ganglia. A deficiency of which of the following transmitters is typically associated with Parkinson disease?
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease is characterized by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, leading to dopamine deficiency in the striatum. This dopamine deficiency is responsible for the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease. Treatment often involves dopamine replacement therapy.

questions.question: Most excitatory neurotransmission in the brain is believed to be mediated by
questions.explanation: Glutamate is the major excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system, mediating most excitatory synaptic transmission. GABA and glycine are inhibitory neurotransmitters, while GnRH is a hormone, not a neurotransmitter for general brain communication.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: The inhibitory amino acid neurotransmitters in the CNS are
questions.explanation: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) and glycine are the two major inhibitory amino acid neurotransmitters in the CNS. GABA is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, while glycine is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord. Glutamate and aspartate are excitatory neurotransmitters.

options: Increased activity of preganglionic parasympathetic neurons
Decreased activity of postganglionic parasympathetic neurons
Increased activity of postganglionic sympathetic neurons
Increased activity of preganglionic sympathetic neurons
questions.question: The concept of "autonomic tone" is quite advantageous because it allows the nervous system to have much finer control over the function of an organ or organ system. This is exemplified in the control of systemic arterioles. Which of the following actions would lead to vasodilation of systemic arterioles?
questions.explanation: Systemic arterioles are primarily controlled by sympathetic innervation, which maintains a baseline level of vasoconstriction (sympathetic tone). Decreased sympathetic activity leads to vasodilation. Most arterioles have minimal or no parasympathetic innervation, so parasympathetic activity changes would have little effect on most systemic vessels.

options: Relaxation of the vasculature smooth muscle and decreased blood flow
Increased blood flow leading to increased oxygen concentration
Relaxation of the vasculature smooth muscle and increased blood flow
Compression of blood vessels leading to ischemia and compensatory capillary dilation
questions.question: Brain edema is a serious complication of altered fluid dynamics in the brain. Continued progression of brain edema may lead to which of the following situations?
questions.explanation: Progressive brain edema increases intracranial pressure, which compresses blood vessels and reduces cerebral blood flow, leading to ischemia. The brain attempts to compensate by dilating capillaries to maintain blood flow. This can create a vicious cycle as increased blood flow can worsen edema.
questions.correct_answer_text: Compression of blood vessels leading to ischemia and compensatory capillary dilation

questions.question: Which of the following reflexes is correctly paired with the sensory structure that mediates the reflex?
questions.explanation: The stretch reflex (myotatic reflex) is mediated by muscle spindles, which detect muscle stretch and initiate a reflex contraction of the same muscle. Autogenic inhibition is mediated by Golgi tendon organs, not muscle spindles. Reciprocal inhibition involves multiple sensory inputs, and the Golgi tendon reflex is mediated by Golgi tendon organs, not Meissner corpuscles. --- Medical Physiology IV (CNS) - Exam Answers ## ### Unit Code: BMP1205

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman undergoes imaging for unrelated abdominal pain, revealing a 3 cm incidental liver lesion. Given its suspected diagnosis as the most common benign liver tumor, which of the following diagnostic procedures should be avoided?
questions.explanation: The most common benign liver tumor is a cavernous hemangioma. Percutaneous biopsy is avoided due to the risk of significant hemorrhage from these vascular lesions.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman on oral contraceptive pills presents with sudden onset severe RUQ pain and hypovolemic shock. Imaging reveals a ruptured hepatic mass. Which benign liver tumor is most likely?
questions.explanation: Hepatocellular adenomas are strongly associated with oral contraceptive use and carry a significant risk of spontaneous rupture and life-threatening intraperitoneal hemorrhage.

questions.question: A liver lesion in a 35-year-old male reveals a central stellate scar and radiating fibrous septa containing anomalous arteries and bile ductules. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Focal Nodular Hyperplasia is characterized by a central stellate scar and a 'spoke-wheel' vascular pattern. It is a regenerative response to a pre-existing vascular malformation.

questions.question: Which of the following risk factors is most strongly associated with the development of Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) globally?
questions.explanation: Globally, chronic infection with HBV is the most common risk factor for HCC, particularly in endemic regions like Asia and sub-Saharan Africa.

questions.question: A 62-year-old male with chronic Hepatitis C and cirrhosis has a solitary liver mass. Which tumor marker, if >1000 ng/ml, is highly suggestive of HCC?
questions.explanation: Markedly elevated levels of Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) are highly specific for HCC in the setting of chronic liver disease (though its sensitivity varies).

questions.question: A 70-year-old man with Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC) develops jaundice and an intrahepatic mass with normal AFP. Which primary liver malignancy is most consistent?
questions.explanation: Cholangiocarcinoma arises from the bile duct epithelium. Risk factors include PSC, liver flukes, and Caroli disease. AFP is usually normal, but CA 19-9 may be elevated.

questions.question: A 58-year-old female presents with multiple bilateral liver lesions. She has no history of chronic liver disease. What is the most common diagnosis for malignant liver tumors in adults?
questions.explanation: Metastatic disease (especially from colon, lung, or breast) is far more common than primary liver cancer in non-cirrhotic livers.

questions.question: A 2-year-old child presents with an enlarging abdomen and a malignant epithelial tumor with primitive mesenchymal stroma on biopsy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hepatoblastoma is the most common liver tumor of early childhood (usually <3 years). Histology often shows epithelial cells and mesenchymal elements.

questions.question: Exposure to which of the following substances is a significant risk factor for developing hepatic Angiosarcoma?
questions.explanation: Hepatic angiosarcoma is rare but strongly linked to environmental toxins like vinyl chloride, thorium dioxide (Thorotrast), and arsenic.

options: Fibrolamellar HCC is associated with HBV
The pleomorphic variant has the best prognosis
Fibrolamellar HCC typically presents in young adults without cirrhosis
Clear cell variant is only seen in infants
questions.question: Regarding Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC), which statement is correct concerning its variant forms?
questions.explanation: Fibrolamellar HCC is a distinct variant that occurs in young adults (males = females), is not associated with cirrhosis or HBV, and has a better prognosis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Fibrolamellar HCC typically presents in young adults without cirrhosis

questions.question: A 30-year-old female smoker on OCPs for 10 years has a 5 cm encapsulated liver mass. Which feature differentiates this (Adenoma) from Focal Nodular Hyperplasia (FNH)?
questions.explanation: Adenomas lack the central stellate scar and the anomalous bile ductules found in the fibrous septa of FNH.

options: AFP is typically elevated in Cholangiocarcinoma
Cholangiocarcinoma is never seen in cirrhosis
HCC often shows bile production histologically
HCC usually spreads via lymphatics first
questions.question: A 65-year-old male cirrhotic has an AFP of 1500 ng/ml. Which characteristic differentiates HCC from Cholangiocarcinoma in this context?
questions.explanation: Bile production by tumor cells is a pathognomonic histological feature of HCC. Cholangiocarcinoma is a mucin-producing glandular tumor.
questions.correct_answer_text: HCC often shows bile production histologically

questions.question: What percentage of Non-Hodgkin Lymphomas are of B-cell origin?
questions.explanation: Approximately 85% to 90% of NHLs are of B-cell origin, with the remainder being T-cell or NK-cell lymphomas.

questions.question: Which is the most common subtype of B-cell NHL?
questions.explanation: DLBCL is the most common form of NHL, accounting for about 30-40% of adult cases.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman with painless lymphadenopathy has BCL-2+, CD10+, CD20+ cells and a slow progression. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Follicular lymphoma is an indolent B-cell lymphoma characterized by a t(14;18) translocation involving BCL-2 and germinal center markers like CD10.

questions.question: Which translocation is required for the diagnosis of Mantle Cell Lymphoma?
questions.explanation: Mantle Cell Lymphoma is defined by the t(11;14) translocation, which leads to overexpression of Cyclin D1.

questions.question: A patient with NHL has CD5+, CD19+, CD22+, CD23− immunophenotype. Which lymphoma does this suggest?
questions.explanation: Mantle cell lymphoma is CD5+ but CD23 negative. CLL is typically CD5+ and CD23 positive.

questions.question: Which organism is directly implicated in the pathogenesis of gastric MALT lymphoma?
questions.explanation: Chronic gastrtitis caused by H. pylori provides the antigenic stimulus for B-cell proliferation in the stomach, leading to MALT lymphoma.

questions.question: What is the first-line treatment for early-stage gastric MALT lymphoma?
questions.explanation: Most cases of early-stage gastric MALT lymphoma regress completely after eradication of H. pylori.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with visual disturbances and IgM spike has a MYD88 mutation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Waldenström’s Macroglobulinemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with an IgM paraprotein and high frequency of MYD88 L265P mutations.

options: IgG is too small to be filtered
IgM is found primarily in the intravascular space
IgM binds to the plasmapheresis filters
questions.question: Why is plasmapheresis particularly effective in Waldenström's compared to IgG myeloma?
questions.explanation: IgM is a large pentameric molecule that stays primarily within the blood vessels, making it easily removable via plasmapheresis to treat hyperviscosity.
questions.correct_answer_text: IgM is found primarily in the intravascular space

questions.question: A child from sub-Saharan Africa with a jaw mass and 'starry sky' histology. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Endemic Burkitt lymphoma often involves the mandible or maxilla and shows the classic 'starry sky' appearance (tingible body macrophages).

questions.question: Which oncogene is overexpressed in virtually all cases of Burkitt lymphoma?
questions.explanation: Burkitt lymphoma is characterized by translocations (most commonly t(8;14)) that result in the overexpression of the MYC oncogene.

questions.question: What is the gold standard investigation for diagnosing NHL?
questions.explanation: An excisional biopsy is required to assess the tissue architecture (nodular vs. diffuse) which is essential for accurate NHL classification.

questions.question: What is the incidence of Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma per 100,000 population?
questions.explanation: The incidence of NHL is approximately 15-20 per 100,000, making it significantly more common than Hodgkin lymphoma.

options: NHL spreads predictably to contiguous nodes
NHL spread is often non-contiguous and extranodal
NHL never involves the bone marrow
NHL always starts in the mediastinum
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the spread pattern of NHL compared to Hodgkin Lymphoma?
questions.explanation: Unlike Hodgkin lymphoma, NHL often involves multiple non-contiguous lymph node stations and frequently involves extranodal sites (GI tract, skin, etc.).
questions.correct_answer_text: NHL spread is often non-contiguous and extranodal

questions.question: Which classification system is the current gold standard for lymphoma classification?
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization (WHO) classification, based on morphology, immunophenotype, genetics, and clinical features, is the global standard.

questions.question: In lymphoid neoplasms, what molecular event precedes malignant transformation?
questions.explanation: Malignant transformation often occurs in cells that have already undergone physiological gene rearrangement of B- or T-cell receptors.

questions.question: A MALT lymphoma does NOT respond to antibiotic therapy for H. pylori. Which translocation explains this?
questions.explanation: The t(11;18)(q21;q21) translocation is associated with MALT lymphomas that are resistant to H. pylori eradication therapy.

questions.question: Small B-cell lymphoma involving the skin (MALT type) is often associated with which organism?
questions.explanation: Cutaneous marginal zone lymphomas (MALT type) have been associated with Borrelia burgdorferi infection in certain geographic regions.

questions.question: A 14-year-old male has a large mediastinal mass and T-cell markers (CD1, CD2, CD5, TdT). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: T-ALL/LBL typically presents in adolescent males as a mediastinal mass. TdT is a marker of immature lymphoblasts.

questions.question: Which translocation carries the worst prognosis in Precursor B-cell ALL?
questions.explanation: The t(9;22) (BCR-ABL1) is associated with a poor prognosis in B-ALL, especially in adults.

options: Clusters of larger prolymphocytes and paraimmunoblasts
questions.question: What are 'proliferation centres' in CLL/SLL histology?
questions.explanation: Proliferation centers (pseudofollicles) containing prolymphocytes are pathognomonic for CLL/SLL in lymph node biopsies.
questions.correct_answer_text: Clusters of larger prolymphocytes and paraimmunoblasts

questions.question: A patient with CLL has Hb 9g/dL and platelets 80×10⁹/L. What Binet stage is this?
questions.explanation: Binet Stage C is defined by the presence of anemia (Hb <10g/dL) or thrombocytopenia (platelets <100x10^9/L).

questions.question: What combination therapy achieves complete remission in 69% of CLL patients?
questions.explanation: FCR chemo-immunotherapy is a standard high-efficacy regimen for fit patients with CLL.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman with asymptomatic nodular BCL-2+ lymphoma for 3 years. What is the management?
questions.explanation: Asymptomatic, low-bulk Follicular Lymphoma is often managed with a 'watch and wait' approach as early treatment does not improve overall survival.

questions.question: A 45-year-old alcoholic with severe pain and chalky white deposits on CT. Which mechanism is responsible for these deposits?
questions.explanation: In acute pancreatitis, lipase releases fatty acids which combine with calcium to form insoluble salts (saponification), seen as chalky white deposits.

options: Neutrophilic inflammation and enzymatic fat necrosis
questions.question: In acute pancreatitis, which histological finding distinguishes it from chronic pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Acute pancreatitis is characterized by edema, proteolysis, fat necrosis, and acute inflammation (neutrophils). Chronic pancreatitis is defined by irreversible fibrosis and atrophy.
questions.correct_answer_text: Neutrophilic inflammation and enzymatic fat necrosis

options: Loss of >90% of exocrine pancreatic function
questions.question: A patient with chronic pancreatitis develops steatorrhea. What is the underlying mechanism?
questions.explanation: Steatorrhea and malabsorption occur only when exocrine secretion (lipase, etc.) falls below 10% of normal levels due to parenchymal destruction.
questions.correct_answer_text: Loss of >90% of exocrine pancreatic function

questions.question: Which genetic mutation is found in >90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cases?
questions.explanation: Activating mutations in the KRAS oncogene are the most common genetic alteration in pancreatic cancer, present in nearly all cases.

questions.question: A 65-year-old presents with painless jaundice and Courvoisier sign. Where is the tumor MOST likely located?
questions.explanation: Tumors in the head of the pancreas often obstruct the common bile duct, leading to painless jaundice and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign).

questions.question: Which precursor lesion leads to invasive pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma?
questions.explanation: PanINs are the microscopic precursor lesions that progress through stages (1-3) to invasive carcinoma.

questions.question: What is the name for recurrent migratory superficial thrombophlebitis in pancreatic cancer?
questions.explanation: Trousseau syndrome (migratory thrombophlebitis) is a classic paraneoplastic manifestation of procoagulants released by pancreatic and lung adenocarcinomas.

questions.question: What is the KEY histological feature distinguishing serous cystadenoma from mucinous cystadenoma?
questions.explanation: Mucinous cystic neoplasms (which occur almost exclusively in females) are characterized by an 'ovarian-type' dense stroma.

questions.question: Which pancreatic cyst carries significant malignant transformation potential?
questions.explanation: IPMNs and mucinous cystic neoplasms are precursors to invasive cancer, whereas serous cystadenomas are almost always benign.

options: It is always located in the head
questions.question: A pseudocyst differs from a true cyst in which fundamental way?
questions.explanation: Pseudocysts are walled-off collections of secretions and necrotic debris lined by granulation tissue rather than epithelium.

questions.question: In Type 1 Diabetes, which HLA haplotypes confer the strongest susceptibility?
questions.explanation: The HLA-DR3/DQ2 and HLA-DR4/DQ8 haplotypes are most strongly associated with the risk of developing Type 1 DM.

options: They cause direct islet cell lysis
questions.question: What is the role of CD8+ T cells in the pathogenesis of Type 1 Diabetes?
questions.explanation: Type 1 DM is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disease where CD8+ cytotoxic T cells directly destroy insulin-producing beta cells.
questions.correct_answer_text: They cause direct islet cell lysis

options: It remains open in 75% of adults
Functional closure occurs when LA pressure exceeds RA pressure
It is part of the interventricular septum
questions.question: Which foramen ovale closes in approximately 75% of individuals at birth?
questions.explanation: Functional closure of the foramen ovale happens at birth when the left atrial pressure increases. In about 25% of people, it remains 'probe patent'.
questions.correct_answer_text: Functional closure occurs when LA pressure exceeds RA pressure

options: Intimal proliferation and fibrosis (forming ligamentum arteriosum)
questions.question: Anatomical closure of the ductus arteriosus occurs through which process?
questions.explanation: After functional closure by prostaglandins/oxygen changes, the ductus undergoes permanent anatomical fibrosis to become the ligamentum arteriosum.
questions.correct_answer_text: Intimal proliferation and fibrosis (forming ligamentum arteriosum)

questions.question: Failure of which structure to adequately cover the ostium secundum results in ostium secundum ASD?
questions.explanation: Ostium secundum ASDs (the most common type) result from a deficient septum secundum or excessive resorption of the septum primum.

questions.question: Which VSD type is specifically more common in Asian patients?
questions.explanation: Subpulmonic (infundibular) VSDs involve the outlet septum and are more prevalent in Asian populations.

options: Anterior and superior displacement of the infundibular septum
Failure of the truncus to divide
questions.question: The fundamental embryological defect in Tetralogy of Fallot is
questions.explanation: The 'monology' of Fallot is the anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum, which leads to VSD, subpulmonary stenosis, and overriding aorta.
questions.correct_answer_text: Anterior and superior displacement of the infundibular septum

questions.question: Which structure, when displaced apically, causes atrialization of the right ventricular inflow tract?
questions.explanation: Ebstein's anomaly involves the apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets, making the upper part of the RV function as part of the RA.

options: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral
Atrophy of the right aortic arch
questions.question: In Transposition of Great Arteries (TGA), which embryological failure is responsible?
questions.explanation: TGA occurs when the aorticopulmonary septum fails to spiral normally, resulting in the aorta arising from the RV and the pulmonary artery from the LV.
questions.correct_answer_text: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral

questions.question: Which chromosomal abnormality is most specifically associated with coarctation of the aorta?
questions.explanation: Coarctation of the aorta (pre-ductal or infantile type) is seen in approximately 15-20% of females with Turner syndrome.

questions.question: Persistent truncus arteriosus always occurs alongside which other defect?
questions.explanation: Persistent truncus arteriosus occurs because the truncus fails to divide; this always results in a large VSD that allows both ventricles to pump into the single vessel.

questions.question: Sinus venosus ASD is specifically associated with anomalous drainage of pulmonary veins from which lung?
questions.explanation: Sinus venosus ASDs are located near the entry of the SVC or IVC and are frequently associated with anomalous right pulmonary venous return.

questions.question: Which maternal teratogen is specifically associated with Ebstein's anomaly?
questions.explanation: Maternal lithium use during the first trimester is classically linked to Ebstein's anomaly in the fetus.

options: Allows free pressure equalization between ventricles
Has a small diameter with high resistance to flow
Is usually found in the membranous septum
questions.question: A restrictive VSD differs from a non-restrictive VSD in that it
questions.explanation: Restrictive VSDs are small and maintain a pressure gradient between the LV and RV, limiting the volume of the left-to-right shunt.
questions.correct_answer_text: Has a small diameter with high resistance to flow

questions.question: Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung tumour. Which population is most characteristically associated?
questions.explanation: Adenocarcinoma is the most common primary lung cancer in non-smokers and women, and is often located peripherally.

questions.question: A 62-year-old smoker with a central hilar mass and keratin pearls. Which paraneoplastic syndrome is expected?
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma is associated with hypercalcemia due to the production of Parathyroid Hormone-related Protein (PTHrP).

questions.question: The overall 5-year survival for all stages of lung cancer combined is approximately
questions.explanation: Despite advances, the 5-year survival rate for lung cancer remains poor, averaging around 15-20%.

EGFR and KRAS mutations are mutually exclusive
questions.question: In smoking non-smokers with EGFR-mutated adenocarcinoma, KRAS testing is unnecessary because
questions.explanation: In lung adenocarcinoma, mutations in the EGFR, KRAS, and ALK pathways are typically mutually exclusive; identifying one usually precludes the others.
questions.correct_answer_text: EGFR and KRAS mutations are mutually exclusive

questions.question: A lung biopsy shows cells growing in a monolayer along alveolar septa without invasion (2.8 cm). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: AIS (formerly BAC) is defined by growth along pre-existing alveolar structures (lepidic growth) without any stromal or vascular invasion.

questions.question: A patient with SCLC has weakness that improves with movement. This paraneoplastic syndrome is
questions.explanation: Lambert-Eaton syndrome is caused by antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels at the neuromuscular junction, frequently associated with SCLC.

The tumor spreads through the air spaces
The tumor stays confined to one lobe
questions.question: The 'field effect' in lung carcinogenesis means
questions.explanation: The 'field effect' or 'field cancerization' describes how the entire respiratory tract is exposed to carcinogens (like smoke), leading to multiple independent genetic mutations.
questions.correct_answer_text: Diffuse injury to the airway mucosa by carcinogens predisposes to multiple tumors

questions.question: A patient with an apical lung mass, Horner syndrome, and ulnar nerve pain. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pancoast tumors occur at the lung apex and invade the sympathetic chain (Horner syndrome) and the brachial plexus (C8-T2 distribution pain).

options: Loss of TP53 and RB1 function
questions.question: Which molecular profile is most characteristic of small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC)?
questions.explanation: Small cell lung carcinoma is nearly always associated with the loss of function of both the TP53 and RB (retinoblastoma) tumor suppressor genes.
questions.correct_answer_text: Loss of TP53 and RB1 function

questions.question: A relay in ALK-rearranged adenocarcinoma with a new ALK drug-binding domain mutation is an example of
questions.explanation: On-target resistance occurs when a new mutation develops in the same gene/molecule that the drug is targeting, preventing the drug from binding.

questions.question: A 30-year-old non-smoker with spontaneous pneumothorax and subpleural bulla. Which emphysema is responsible?
questions.explanation: Paraseptal emphysema involves the distal part of the acinus near the pleura and is the most common cause of spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults.

questions.question: At the time of lung cancer diagnosis, what proportion already have distant metastases?
questions.explanation: Because lung cancer is often asymptomatic until late, more than 50% of patients have distant metastases (Stage IV) at the time of presentation.

questions.question: A 3-year-old with oral vesicles and polykaryons with intranuclear inclusions. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: HSV-1 causes primary herpetic gingivostomatitis in children. Histology shows '3 Cs': Chromatin marginalization, Cowdry type A inclusions, and multinucleated Cells (polykaryons).

questions.explanation: Leukoplakia is a clinical term. Histologically it can range from simple hyperkeratosis to invasive carcinoma; therefore, all leukoplakias must be biopsied.
questions.correct_answer_text: It is a clinical term for a white patch that cannot be characterized further

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with a red, velvety lesion in the floor of the mouth (Erythroplakia). Which statement is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Erythroplakia is much more concerning than leukoplakia; many cases show severe dysplasia or CIS at the time of initial biopsy.
questions.correct_answer_text: It carries a very high risk of malignant transformation (>50%)

questions.question: A 35-year-old with a pedunculated red-purple gingival mass (biopsy shows immature vessel proliferation). What is this lesion?
questions.explanation: Pyogenic granulomas are common on the gingiva, particularly in pregnant women ('pregnancy tumor'), and are benign vascular proliferations.

options: Better prognosis and sensitivity to radiation

questions.explanation: Oropharyngeal SCC associated with high-risk HPV (especially HPV-16) generally has a s
