questions.question: Barrett esophagus is an example of
questions.explanation: Barrett esophagus represents metaplasia where normal stratified squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells in response to chronic acid reflux. This is an adaptive response to chronic injury.

questions.question: Which cellular adaptation is reversible upon removal of the stimulus?
questions.explanation: All three are potentially reversible if the causative stimulus is removed before irreversible damage occurs. However, dysplasia has a higher risk of progression to cancer if the stimulus persists. ---

options: This leads to increased proliferation of endometrial glands and can be a precursor to endometrial carcinom
questions.question: Endometrial hyperplasia is primarily caused by
questions.explanation: Endometrial hyperplasia results from unopposed estrogen stimulation without adequate progesterone. This leads to increased proliferation of endometrial glands and can be a precursor to endometrial carcinoma. ---

questions.question: Which is the most common cause of cell injury in clinical medicine?
questions.explanation: Hypoxia and ischemia are the most common causes of cell injury, underlying conditions like myocardial infarction, stroke, and tissue infarcts throughout the body. ---

questions.question: The earliest ultrastructural change in reversible cell injury is
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial swelling and formation of amorphous densities in the mitochondrial matrix are among the earliest ultrastructural changes in reversible cell injury, reflecting impaired oxidative phosphorylation. ---

options: They also damage proteins and DNA, but lipid peroxidation is the most significant mechanism.
questions.question: Free radical injury is most commonly caused by
questions.explanation: Free radicals cause cellular injury primarily through lipid peroxidation of membrane lipids, leading to membrane damage. They also damage proteins and DNA, but lipid peroxidation is the most significant mechanism. ---

options: converts superoxide radicals (O2-) to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Catalase and glutathione peroxidase then convert H2O2 to water.
questions.question: Which enzyme protects cells against free radical injury by converting superoxide to hydrogen peroxide?
questions.explanation: Superoxide dismutase (SOD) converts superoxide radicals (O2-) to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Catalase and glutathione peroxidase then convert H2O2 to water. ---

questions.question: The hallmark of irreversible cell injury is
questions.explanation: The point of no return in cell injury is marked by the inability to restore mitochondrial function even after resolution of the original injury. This leads to progressive loss of membrane integrity and cell death. ---

options: Failure of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump
questions.question: Cellular swelling results from
questions.explanation: Failure of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump due to ATP depletion leads to sodium and water influx into the cell, causing cellular swelling (oncosis). This is a characteristic feature of reversible injury. ---
questions.correct_answer_text: Failure of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump

questions.question: Fatty change (steatosis) is most commonly seen in
questions.explanation: The liver is most commonly affected by fatty change due to its central role in fat metabolism. Causes include alcohol, toxins, diabetes, obesity, and protein malnutrition. ---

questions.question: Which microscopic change indicates irreversible injury?
questions.explanation: Nuclear changes (pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis) are hallmarks of irreversible injury and cell death. Cytoplasmic eosinophilia can occur in reversible injury due to ribosomal detachment. ---

questions.question: Hydropic degeneration is characterized by
questions.explanation: Hydropic degeneration (vacuolar degeneration) refers to the accumulation of water in the cytoplasm causing cellular swelling. It represents an early manifestation of reversible cell injury.

questions.question: Coagulative necrosis is characterized by
questions.explanation: Coagulative necrosis maintains the basic tissue architecture for several days due to denaturation of structural proteins and enzymes. It is the most common type of necrosis and typical of ischemic injury in solid organs. ---

questions.question: Liquefactive necrosis is typical of
questions.explanation: Liquefactive necrosis occurs in brain infarctions due to the high lipid content and abundance of hydrolytic enzymes. It also occurs in bacterial infections due to release of lysosomal enzymes from neutrophils. ---

questions.question: Caseous necrosis is most characteristically seen in
questions.explanation: Caseous necrosis is characteristic of tuberculosis and some fungal infections. It has a cheese-like (caseous) appearance, combining features of coagulative and liquefactive necrosis. ---

questions.question: Fat necrosis typically occurs in
questions.explanation: Fat necrosis occurs when pancreatic enzymes (lipases) are released into the peritoneum in acute pancreatitis, breaking down fat cells. It also occurs in traumatic injury to adipose tissue such as breast tissue. ---

questions.question: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in
questions.explanation: Fibrinoid necrosis occurs in blood vessel walls in immune-mediated conditions like vasculitis, malignant hypertension, and autoimmune diseases. It appears as bright pink amorphous material on H&E staining. ---

questions.question: Gangrenous necrosis refers to
questions.explanation: Gangrene is not a specific type of necrosis but refers to coagulative necrosis of a large area (usually an extremity) with superimposed bacterial infection. Wet gangrene has a liquefactive component. ## SECTION 5: APOPTOSIS

questions.question: Apoptosis differs from necrosis in that
questions.explanation: Apoptosis is an ATP-dependent active process of programmed cell death affecting single cells without inflammation. Necrosis is passive, affects groups of cells, and causes inflammation. ---

questions.question: The morphologic hallmark of apoptosis is
questions.explanation: Apoptotic cells show cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation (pyknosis), nuclear fragmentation, and formation of apoptotic bodies. The cell membrane remains intact initially. ---

questions.question: Which pathway initiates apoptosis through death receptors?
questions.explanation: The extrinsic pathway is initiated by binding of death ligands (like FasL, TNF) to death receptors (like Fas, TNFR1) on the cell surface, leading to caspase activation. ---

questions.question: The intrinsic pathway of apoptosis is regulated by
questions.explanation: The intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway is regulated by the Bcl-2 family of proteins. Pro-apoptotic members (Bax, Bak) promote apoptosis, while anti-apoptotic members (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL) inhibit it. ---

questions.question: Cytochrome c is released from mitochondria during apoptosis and activates
questions.explanation: Cytochrome c released from mitochondria binds to Apaf-1 (apoptotic protease activating factor-1) forming the apoptosome, which activates caspase-9, the initiator caspase of the intrinsic pathway. ---

questions.question: Apoptotic bodies are removed by
questions.explanation: Apoptotic bodies are rapidly recognized and phagocytosed by macrophages and neighboring cells without eliciting inflammation. This is due to externalization of phosphatidylserine on the outer membrane. ---

questions.question: Physiologic apoptosis occurs in
questions.explanation: Physiologic apoptosis is essential in embryonic development (digit formation, neural development), normal tissue turnover, elimination of immune cells after immune response, and hormone-dependent involution. ---

options: It acts as the "guardian of the genome" and induces pro-apoptotic proteins like Bax.
questions.question: Which tumor suppressor gene can trigger apoptosis in response to DNA damage?
questions.explanation: p53 is activated by DNA damage and can induce cell cycle arrest for repair or trigger apoptosis if damage is irreparable. It acts as the "guardian of the genome" and induces pro-apoptotic proteins like Bax. ---

questions.question: Caspases are
questions.explanation: Caspases are cysteine proteases that cleave proteins at aspartic acid residues. They exist as inactive pro-caspases and are activated during apoptosis to execute cell death by cleaving key cellular proteins.

questions.question: Lipofuscin is
questions.explanation: Lipofuscin is a yellow-brown "wear and tear" pigment that accumulates in aging or atrophic cells. It represents indigestible material from lipid peroxidation and is considered a marker of aging but is harmless. ---

questions.question: Hemosiderin accumulation is seen in
questions.explanation: Hemosiderin is an iron-containing pigment formed from breakdown of hemoglobin. It accumulates locally (bruises) or systemically (hemochromatosis, multiple transfusions). It appears golden-yellow to brown and stains blue with Prussian blue. ---

options: It leads to iron deposition in liver, pancreas, heart, and skin.
questions.question: Primary hemochromatosis is caused by
questions.explanation: Primary (hereditary) hemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder causing excessive iron absorption from the gut due to mutations in the HFE gene. It leads to iron deposition in liver, pancreas, heart, and skin. ---

questions.question: Anthracosis refers to
questions.explanation: Anthracosis is the accumulation of carbon particles (from air pollution or smoking) in the lungs and lymph nodes. It is extremely common in urban dwellers and smokers but usually asymptomatic. ---

options: It appears as clear vacuoles that are PAS-positiv
questions.question: Glycogen accumulation is seen in
questions.explanation: Glycogen can accumulate in glycogen storage diseases (genetic enzyme defects), diabetes mellitus (especially in renal tubular cells and hepatocytes), and with corticosteroid use. It appears as clear vacuoles that are PAS-positive. ---

questions.question: Cholesterol accumulation in macrophages creates
questions.explanation: When macrophages accumulate cholesterol, they develop foamy cytoplasm and are called foam cells. These are characteristic of atherosclerotic plaques and xanthomas.

options: Normal serum calcium with tissue injury
questions.question: Dystrophic calcification occurs in
questions.explanation: Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged or necrotic tissues despite normal serum calcium levels. It is seen in atherosclerotic plaques, damaged heart valves, old tuberculous lesions, and areas of fat necrosis. ---
questions.correct_answer_text: Normal serum calcium with tissue injury

options: . Causes include hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D toxicity, renal failure, and extensive bone destruction from malignancy or…
questions.question: Metastatic calcification occurs in
questions.explanation: Metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues when serum calcium levels are elevated (hypercalcemia). Causes include hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D toxicity, renal failure, and extensive bone destruction from malignancy or Paget disease. ---

options: because alkaline pH favors calcium phosphate precipitation. Blood vessels and pulmonary alveolar septa are commonly affecte
questions.question: Metastatic calcification preferentially affects
questions.explanation: Metastatic calcification preferentially affects tissues that excrete acid (lungs, kidneys, gastric mucosa) because alkaline pH favors calcium phosphate precipitation. Blood vessels and pulmonary alveolar septa are commonly affected. ---

options: Binding of calcium to phospholipids in damaged membranes
questions.question: The mechanism of dystrophic calcification involves
questions.explanation: In dystrophic calcification, calcium binds to phospholipids in damaged cell membranes and forms calcium-phospholipid complexes, which then nucleate further calcium deposition forming hydroxyapatite crystals.
questions.correct_answer_text: Binding of calcium to phospholipids in damaged membranes

questions.question: Cellular aging is associated with
questions.explanation: Aging is associated with accumulation of damaged proteins, lipids, and DNA due to decreased repair capacity, increased oxidative stress, and impaired protein degradation. Telomeres shorten with each division. ---

options: Replicative senescence after limited cell divisions
questions.question: The Hayflick limit refers to
questions.explanation: The Hayflick limit is the finite number of times normal human cells can divide before entering replicative senescence (approximately 50-60 divisions). This is due to progressive telomere shortening with each cell division. ---
questions.correct_answer_text: Replicative senescence after limited cell divisions

options: . Affected individuals show early onset of age-related diseases including atherosclerosis, cataracts, and malignancies.
questions.question: Werner syndrome is characterized by
questions.explanation: Werner syndrome is a premature aging syndrome caused by mutations in the WRN gene (DNA helicase). Affected individuals show early onset of age-related diseases including atherosclerosis, cataracts, and malignancies. ---

questions.question: Oxidative stress in aging results from
questions.explanation: Aging is associated with accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) from mitochondrial respiration and other sources, combined with decreased antioxidant defenses. This causes cumulative damage to cellular components. ---

questions.question: Autophagy in aging
questions.explanation: Autophagy (self-eating of cellular components) declines with aging, leading to accumulation of damaged organelles and proteins. Enhancing autophagy has been shown to extend lifespan in experimental models.

questions.question: Ischemia-reperfusion injury is primarily mediated by
questions.explanation: Paradoxically, restoration of blood flow after ischemia can cause additional injury through production of free radicals (reactive oxygen species), calcium overload, inflammation, and complement activation. This is called reperfusion injury. ---

questions.question: Heat shock proteins function to
questions.explanation: Heat shock proteins (HSPs) are molecular chaperones induced by stress (heat, hypoxia, toxins) that help refold damaged proteins, prevent protein aggregation, and assist in protein degradation, protecting cells from injury. ---

questions.question: Which change distinguishes necroptosis from apoptosis?
questions.explanation: Necroptosis is a programmed form of necrosis that is caspase-independent, mediated by RIP1 and RIP3 kinases. Unlike apoptosis, it results in membrane rupture and inflammation, but unlike necrosis, it is regulated. ---

questions.question: Autophagy can protect cells by
questions.explanation: Autophagy is a survival mechanism where cells degrade and recycle damaged organelles and proteins through lysosomes. It provides nutrients during starvation and removes damaged components, but excessive autophagy can lead to cell death. ---

options: Has no role in cell injury
Attempts to restore normal function or triggers apoptosis
questions.question: The unfolded protein response (UPR) in the endoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation: The UPR is activated when misfolded proteins accumulate in the ER. Initially, it attempts to restore homeostasis by decreasing protein synthesis, increasing chaperone production, and enhancing protein degradation. If unsuccessful, it triggers apoptosis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Attempts to restore normal function or triggers apoptosis

options: Perform an elution on the patient's pre-transfusion sample.
Provide crossmatch-compatible units regardless of Jk(a) status.
Provide Jk(a) negative units even if the crossmatch is compatible.
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) prior to transfusion.
questions.question: A patient with a known anti-Jk(a) antibody requires an urgent transfusion. The current antibody screen is negative. What is the most appropriate next step to ensure a safe transfusion?
questions.explanation: Kidd antibodies can become undetectable over time, but the patient remains sensitized. A historic antibody must always be respected — always provide antigen-negative units regardless of current screen results.
questions.correct_answer_text: Provide Jk(a) negative units even if the crossmatch is compatible.

questions.question: In a patient with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA) and a pan-reactive antibody screen, which method is used to detect underlying alloantibodies if the patient has been transfused in the last 3 months?
questions.explanation: Autologous adsorption can't be used in recently transfused patients (donor cells would adsorb the alloantibody too). Allogeneic adsorption with phenotype-matched cells removes the autoantibody while preserving detectable alloantibodies.

questions.question: Which blood group system is most frequently associated with delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions that present with a rapid drop in hemoglobin but negative initial antibody screens?
questions.explanation: The Kidd system is the classic cause of delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions. Antibodies fade quickly, screen negative, then surge after re-exposure causing rapid intravascular hemolysis.

questions.question: A 32-year-old female experiences severe hypotension and bronchospasm within minutes of starting a red cell transfusion. She has a history of recurrent respiratory infections. What is the most likely underlying deficiency?
questions.explanation: IgA-deficient patients can develop anti-IgA antibodies. Transfusion of blood products containing IgA triggers a severe anaphylactic reaction. Recurrent infections are a clue to the underlying immunodeficiency.

questions.question: Which specific modification to blood products is required to prevent Transfusion-Associated Graft-versus-Host Disease (TA-GvHD) in an immunocompromised bone marrow transplant recipient?
questions.explanation: Irradiation inactivates donor T-lymphocytes, which are responsible for TA-GvHD. Leukoreduction reduces but does not eliminate T-cells — only gamma or X-ray irradiation reliably prevents TA-GvHD.

questions.question: During a massive transfusion protocol, a patient develops ionized hypocalcemia. This is most likely a direct metabolic consequence of which preservative/anticoagulant used in blood storage?
questions.explanation: Sodium citrate is used as an anticoagulant in blood storage. It chelates (binds) free ionized calcium, causing hypocalcemia during massive transfusion when large volumes are infused rapidly.

questions.question: A neonate requires an exchange transfusion for HDFN caused by anti-c. The mother is O positive, R1R1 (CDe/CDe). The infant is A positive, R1r (CDe/ce). What is the most appropriate blood type for the exchange?
questions.explanation: Blood must be c-negative to avoid destruction by maternal anti-c still circulating in the neonate. O type is chosen over A to be compatible with any residual maternal ABO antibodies. c-negative (R1R1) is essential.

questions.question: TRALI is most commonly caused by antibodies in the donor plasma directed against which of the following in the recipient?
questions.explanation: Donor anti-HLA or anti-HNA antibodies bind to recipient neutrophils, activating them in the pulmonary vasculature and causing the capillary leak that defines TRALI (acute lung injury within 6 hours of transfusion).

questions.question: What is the shelf life of a unit of Red Blood Cells that has been 'opened' by entering the system for washing or aliquoting in an open system, if stored at 1-6°C?
questions.explanation: Once the sterile seal of a blood unit is broken (open system), the risk of bacterial contamination requires discarding the unit within 24 hours when stored at 1–6°C.

options: They can safely receive Type O negative blood.
They can receive any Rh-negative blood.
They can only receive blood from another Bombay phenotype donor.
questions.question: A patient is found to have the 'Bombay' phenotype (Oh). Which of the following statements regarding their transfusion needs is correct?
questions.explanation: Bombay phenotype patients lack H antigen entirely and have anti-H, anti-A, and anti-B antibodies. They will hemolyze all standard blood including O negative. Only another Bombay phenotype donor is compatible.
questions.correct_answer_text: They can only receive blood from another Bombay phenotype donor.

questions.question: The main site of haematopoiesis in a healthy adult is
questions.explanation: Red bone marrow in flat bones (sternum, vertebrae, pelvis) is the primary haematopoietic site in adults; liver and spleen are fetal sites.

questions.question: Which cytokine is the primary stimulator of megakaryocyte and platelet production?
questions.explanation: Thrombopoietin (TPO) is produced mainly by the liver and acts on megakaryocytes to drive platelet production.

questions.question: On a peripheral blood film, which cell has a bilobed nucleus connected by a thin strand and prominent pink granules?
questions.explanation: Eosinophils have characteristically bilobed nuclei and large orange-pink granules; they are elevated in allergies and parasitic infections.

questions.question: Target cells on a peripheral blood film are seen in all of the following EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis produces spherocytes, not target cells; target cells reflect excess membrane relative to cell content.

questions.question: A peripheral blood film shows hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes). The most likely underlying deficiency is
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12/folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis, causing nuclear maturation delay and hypersegmentation of neutrophils.

options: Peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney
questions.question: Erythropoietin is produced mainly by
questions.explanation: Peritubular interstitial cells in the renal cortex sense hypoxia via HIF-1α and release EPO to stimulate red cell production.
questions.correct_answer_text: Peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney

questions.question: The normal lifespan of a red blood cell is approximately
questions.explanation: 120 days is the normal RBC lifespan; senescent RBCs are phagocytosed by splenic and hepatic macrophages.

questions.question: Which haemoglobin is predominant in a normal adult?
questions.explanation: HbA (α2β2) constitutes approximately 96–98% of adult haemoglobin; HbA2 is ~2.5% and HbF <1%.

options: Increased O₂ affinity with rising pH

questions.question: In intravascular haemolysis, which urine finding is most specific?
questions.explanation: Haemosiderinuria occurs when free haemoglobin is filtered and reabsorbed by tubular cells; iron deposits detected by Prussian blue stain are specific for intravascular haemolysis.

questions.question: The MCV in iron deficiency anaemia is
questions.explanation: Low MCV (microcytic anaemia) occurs because insufficient iron limits haemoglobin synthesis, reducing RBC size.

questions.question: Which iron study pattern is seen in anaemia of chronic disease?
questions.explanation: Inflammation sequesters iron in macrophages (high ferritin as acute phase reactant), reduces serum iron, and decreases TIBC — distinguishing it from iron deficiency.
questions.correct_answer_text: High ferritin, low serum iron, low TIBC

questions.question: A patient has MCV 110 fL, hypersegmented neutrophils, and serum B12 of 80 pg/mL. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic anaemia from B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils due to impaired DNA synthesis.

questions.question: The most common cause of macrocytic anaemia in the developed world is
questions.explanation: Alcohol causes macrocytosis through direct toxic effects on the bone marrow and poor nutrition; it is the most common cause overall in many populations.

questions.question: Schilling test was used to diagnose
questions.explanation: Pernicious anaemia involves lack of intrinsic factor; the Schilling test showed B12 malabsorption corrected by intrinsic factor supplementation.

options: Mutations causing absent or reduced beta-globin chains
questions.question: Beta-thalassaemia major is caused by
questions.explanation: Mutations in the beta-globin gene reduce (β+) or abolish (β0) beta-chain production, causing excess unpaired alpha chains that damage RBCs.
questions.correct_answer_text: Mutations causing absent or reduced beta-globin chains

questions.question: HbA2 > 3.5% on HPLC is diagnostic of
questions.explanation: Beta thalassaemia trait causes compensatory upregulation of delta-globin chains, raising HbA2 above 3.5%.

questions.question: In sickle cell disease, sickling is promoted by all of the following EXCEPT
questions.explanation: HbF inhibits HbS polymerization by disrupting the deoxygenated HbS polymer structure; high HbF is protective, not a trigger.

options: Antibodies or complement on the RBC surface
questions.question: The direct antiglobulin test (DAT/Coombs) detects
questions.explanation: DAT detects IgG or complement (C3d) already bound to red cells, confirming immune-mediated haemolysis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Antibodies or complement on the RBC surface

questions.question: Hereditary spherocytosis is most commonly due to deficiency of
questions.explanation: Spectrin/ankyrin deficiency destabilizes the RBC membrane skeleton, causing membrane loss and spherocyte formation with reduced osmotic resistance.

questions.question: G6PD deficiency causes haemolytic episodes triggered by
questions.explanation: Oxidative stress depletes glutathione in G6PD-deficient cells (cannot regenerate NADPH), causing Heinz body formation and haemolysis.

questions.question: The Philadelphia chromosome results from translocation
questions.explanation: t(9;22) creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene encoding a constitutively active tyrosine kinase, the hallmark of CML.

questions.question: A 45-year-old presents with fatigue, splenomegaly, WBC 120×10⁹/L with full myeloid spectrum on film. BCR-ABL is positive. Diagnosis
questions.explanation: CML presents with very high WBC, full myeloid spectrum (including basophilia), splenomegaly, and positive BCR-ABL/Philadelphia chromosome.

questions.question: Blast crisis in CML is defined as blasts exceeding what percentage in bone marrow?
questions.explanation: ≥20% blasts in blood or bone marrow defines blast crisis (transformation to acute leukaemia) per WHO criteria.

questions.question: The first-line treatment for CML that targets BCR-ABL is
questions.explanation: Imatinib revolutionized CML treatment by selectively inhibiting the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase, achieving molecular remission in most patients.

questions.question: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is characterized by accumulation of
questions.explanation: CLL is a clonal proliferation of functionally incompetent mature B cells (CD5+, CD23+, CD19+) that accumulate in blood, marrow, and lymph nodes.

questions.question: Smudge (smear) cells on peripheral blood film are characteristic of
questions.explanation: CLL cells are fragile and rupture during film preparation, creating characteristic smudge/smear cells.

questions.question: Reed-Sternberg cells are pathognomonic of
questions.explanation: Reed-Sternberg cells (large binucleated cells with prominent "owl-eye" nucleoli) are the hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.question: The most common chromosomal translocation in follicular lymphoma is
questions.explanation: t(14;18) juxtaposes BCL2 with the IGH locus, causing BCL2 overexpression and resistance to apoptosis in follicular lymphoma.

questions.question: Burkitt lymphoma is associated with which translocation causing MYC overexpression?
questions.explanation: t(8;14) places the MYC oncogene under control of the IGH enhancer, driving rapid B-cell proliferation in Burkitt lymphoma.

options: Clonal plasma cells >10% in bone marrow
questions.question: Multiple myeloma is diagnosed by the presence of all of the following EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Reed-Sternberg cells are seen in Hodgkin lymphoma, not myeloma. Myeloma diagnosis requires plasma cell proliferation with end-organ damage.

options: Free monoclonal light chains (kappa or lambda)
questions.question: Bence Jones proteins in urine represent
questions.explanation: Free light chains filtered by the kidney form Bence Jones proteins; they cause tubular damage and cast nephropathy in myeloma.
questions.correct_answer_text: Free monoclonal light chains (kappa or lambda)

options: Pathognomonic crystalline azurophilic inclusions in myeloblasts
questions.question: In acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), Auer rods are
questions.explanation: Auer rods are fused lysosomal granules forming needle-like inclusions specific to myeloid blasts; their presence confirms AML over ALL.
questions.correct_answer_text: Pathognomonic crystalline azurophilic inclusions in myeloblasts

questions.question: AML M3 (acute promyelocytic leukaemia) is associated with
questions.explanation: t(15;17) creates PML-RARA fusion, blocking myeloid differentiation; ATRA (all-trans retinoic acid) induces differentiation and is curative.

questions.question: The most feared complication of AML-M3 at presentation is
questions.explanation: DIC occurs because promyelocytic granules release procoagulants; it must be treated urgently with ATRA before chemotherapy.

options: Lymphoblasts positive for TdT (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase)
questions.question: The hallmark laboratory finding in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is
questions.explanation: TdT positivity marks immature lymphoid cells; it distinguishes ALL blasts from mature lymphocytes and myeloid blasts.
questions.correct_answer_text: Lymphoblasts positive for TdT (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase)

questions.question: The coagulation cascade's final common pathway begins with activation of
questions.explanation: Factor Xa combines with Factor Va (prothrombinase complex) to convert prothrombin to thrombin — the start of the common pathway.

options: Extrinsic and common pathway (VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen)
questions.question: Prothrombin time (PT) primarily measures
questions.explanation: PT/INR tests the extrinsic pathway via tissue factor/Factor VII; it is used to monitor warfarin therapy.
questions.correct_answer_text: Extrinsic and common pathway (VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen)

questions.question: APTT is prolonged in deficiency of all EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Factor VII is part of the extrinsic pathway only; its deficiency prolongs PT but not APTT.

questions.question: A patient has prolonged APTT, normal PT, normal platelet count, and recurrent haemarthroses. Diagnosis
questions.explanation: Haemophilia A causes isolated APTT prolongation and deep bleeding (haemarthroses, muscle haematomas) due to Factor VIII deficiency.

options: Platelet adhesion to subendothelium and Factor VIII carrier
Factor X activation and fibrinogen binding
questions.question: Von Willebrand factor (vWF) has two main functions
questions.explanation: vWF bridges platelet GPIb receptors to exposed collagen and protects Factor VIII from degradation in plasma.
questions.correct_answer_text: Platelet adhesion to subendothelium and Factor VIII carrier

options: Normal PT, prolonged APTT, reduced vWF antigen and activity
questions.question: In type 1 Von Willebrand disease, laboratory findings show
questions.explanation: Reduced vWF quantity causes mildly prolonged APTT (low Factor VIII), prolonged bleeding time, and reduced ristocetin cofactor activity.
questions.correct_answer_text: Normal PT, prolonged APTT, reduced vWF antigen and activity

options: High fibrinogen, low D-dimer, prolonged PT
Low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, prolonged PT and APTT, thrombocytopaenia
Normal PT, elevated fibrinogen, high platelets
questions.question: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) laboratory profile includes
questions.explanation: Systemic clotting consumes fibrinogen, factors, and platelets while fibrinolysis elevates D-dimers; both PT and APTT are prolonged.
questions.correct_answer_text: Low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, prolonged PT and APTT, thrombocytopaenia

questions.question: D-dimer is a degradation product of
questions.explanation: D-dimer is released when plasmin cleaves crosslinked fibrin; it is elevated in DIC, DVT, PE, and any thrombotic state.

options: Activating antithrombin III to inhibit thrombin and Factor Xa
questions.question: Heparin works primarily by
questions.explanation: Heparin binds antithrombin III, accelerating its inhibition of thrombin (IIa) and Factor Xa by ~1000-fold.
questions.correct_answer_text: Activating antithrombin III to inhibit thrombin and Factor Xa

questions.question: Warfarin anticoagulation is monitored using
questions.explanation: INR standardizes PT measurement across laboratories; therapeutic range is 2.0–3.0 for most indications.

options: Anti-platelet IgG antibodies causing splenic destruction
questions.question: Immune thrombocytopaenic purpura (ITP) is caused by
questions.explanation: ITP involves autoantibodies (usually anti-GPIIb/IIIa) that coat platelets, leading to premature splenic macrophage destruction.
questions.correct_answer_text: Anti-platelet IgG antibodies causing splenic destruction

questions.question: A patient develops thrombocytopaenia 5–10 days after starting heparin with new thrombosis. The diagnosis is
questions.explanation: HIT is caused by IgG antibodies against heparin-PF4 complex, activating platelets and causing paradoxical thrombosis despite low platelet count.

options: ADAMTS13 deficiency causing large vWF multimers
questions.question: Thrombotic thrombocytopaenic purpura (TTP) is caused by
questions.explanation: ADAMTS13 deficiency prevents cleavage of ultra-large vWF multimers, causing platelet aggregation in microvasculature and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia.
questions.correct_answer_text: ADAMTS13 deficiency causing large vWF multimers

questions.question: The pentad of TTP includes all EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Lymphadenopathy is not part of TTP. The pentad is: MAHA, thrombocytopaenia, fever, renal impairment, and neurological symptoms.

questions.question: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is caused by deficiency of
questions.explanation: GPIb-IX-V is the platelet receptor for vWF; its absence prevents platelet adhesion to subendothelium, causing bleeding with giant platelets on film.

questions.question: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is caused by deficiency of
questions.explanation: GPIIb/IIIa deficiency prevents platelet aggregation (no fibrinogen bridging); platelets are normal in number and size but fail to aggregate.

options: Resistance to activated protein C degradation
questions.question: Factor V Leiden mutation causes thrombophilia by
questions.explanation: Factor V Leiden (R506Q) cannot be cleaved by activated protein C, allowing persistent thrombin generation and hypercoagulability.
questions.correct_answer_text: Resistance to activated protein C degradation

questions.question: The most common inherited thrombophilia is
questions.explanation: Factor V Leiden affects approximately 5% of the Caucasian population, making it the most prevalent inherited thrombophilic condition.

questions.question: Aplastic anaemia is characterized by
questions.explanation: Aplastic anaemia involves destruction or suppression of haematopoietic stem cells, leading to empty fatty marrow and pancytopaenia with low reticulocytes.

questions.question: Polycythaemia vera is associated with which mutation in >95% of cases?
questions.explanation: JAK2 V617F causes constitutive activation of the JAK-STAT signalling pathway, driving erythroid (and myeloid) proliferation independent of EPO.

options: Neither, as it is asymptomatic always
questions.question: Essential thrombocythaemia presenting with platelet count >1000×10⁹/L paradoxically causes
questions.explanation: Very high platelet counts consume vWF large multimers (acquired vWD), causing bleeding, while platelet activation causes thrombosis simultaneously.

options: Reticulin/collagen fibrosis with leukoerythroblastic blood film
questions.question: Myelofibrosis on bone marrow biopsy shows
questions.explanation: Reticulin fibrosis replaces normal marrow; the film shows teardrop cells (dacrocytes), nucleated RBCs, and immature myeloid cells (leukoerythroblastic picture).
questions.correct_answer_text: Reticulin/collagen fibrosis with leukoerythroblastic blood film

questions.question: Teardrop cells (dacrocytes) on peripheral film are most characteristic of
questions.explanation: Myelofibrosis forces extramedullary haematopoiesis and squeezes RBCs through fibrotic marrow, deforming them into teardrop shapes.

questions.question: Which finding on peripheral blood film suggests hyposplenism?
questions.explanation: Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants) are normally removed by the spleen; their presence indicates absent or non-functional spleen.

options: Multiple myeloma or elevated ESR states
questions.question: Rouleaux formation on blood film is associated with
questions.explanation: Rouleaux (RBC stacking like coins) occurs when paraproteins or fibrinogen reduce RBC surface charge, seen in myeloma and inflammatory states.
questions.correct_answer_text: Multiple myeloma or elevated ESR states

questions.question: The reticulocyte count helps distinguish
questions.explanation: High reticulocytes indicate the marrow is responding (haemolysis, bleeding); low reticulocytes indicate marrow failure or nutrient deficiency.

questions.question: Serum ferritin is the best marker of
questions.explanation: Ferritin reflects stored iron in macrophages and hepatocytes; it is low in true iron deficiency but elevated as an acute phase reactant in inflammation.

options: Low bilirubin, high haptoglobin, low LDH
High conjugated bilirubin, normal haptoglobin, normal LDH
High unconjugated bilirubin, low haptoglobin, high LDH, high reticulocytes
Low reticulocytes, high haptoglobin, high bilirubin
questions.question: In haemolytic anaemia, which combination of findings is expected?
questions.explanation: RBC destruction releases haemoglobin (consuming haptoglobin), LDH, and unconjugated bilirubin; marrow compensates with reticulocytosis.
questions.correct_answer_text: High unconjugated bilirubin, low haptoglobin, high LDH, high reticulocytes

questions.question: The osmotic fragility test is used to diagnose
questions.explanation: Spherocytes have reduced surface-area-to-volume ratio and lyse at higher NaCl concentrations than normal RBCs — increased osmotic fragility.

options: Rh(D) incompatibility — maternal anti-D IgG crossing the placenta
questions.question: Haemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) most commonly involves
questions.explanation: Rh incompatibility causes severe HDN in subsequent pregnancies; maternal IgG anti-D crosses the placenta and destroys fetal RBCs.
questions.correct_answer_text: Rh(D) incompatibility — maternal anti-D IgG crossing the placenta

questions.question: Which white blood cell is the primary mediator in parasitic infections and allergic reactions?
questions.explanation: Eosinophils degranulate against parasites and release mediators in allergic responses; eosinophilia is a hallmark of both conditions.

questions.question: Pelger-Huët anomaly is characterized by
questions.explanation: Pelger-Huët shows hyposegmented neutrophils (bilobed "pince-nez" or unilobed); it is hereditary or acquired (pseudo-Pelger in MDS/CML).

options: Giant lysosomal granules in leucocytes causing immune deficiency
questions.question: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is characterized by
questions.explanation: Defective LYST gene causes failure of lysosomal trafficking, producing giant granules in neutrophils and NK cells; patients suffer recurrent infections and partial albinism.
questions.correct_answer_text: Giant lysosomal granules in leucocytes causing immune deficiency

options: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
questions.question: The most important initial investigation in a patient presenting with pancytopaenia is
questions.explanation: Bone marrow biopsy is essential to distinguish aplastic anaemia, infiltration (leukaemia, lymphoma, myeloma), myelodysplasia, and megaloblastic causes of pancytopaenia.
questions.correct_answer_text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy

mcq_sets.title: Weekly Year 1: Enzymes, Vitamins and Minerals Exam - June 19, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

options: A. Its dependence on oxygen availability.
C. The rapid accumulation of lactate, leading to muscle fatigue.
B. The relatively low ATP yield per glucose molecule.
D. Its slow rate of ATP production compared to aerobic pathways.
questions.question: The primary disadvantage of anaerobic glycolysis during high-intensity muscle contractions is:
questions.explanation: Anaerobic glycolysis produces ATP rapidly but inefficiently, yielding only 2 ATP per glucose. A major disadvantage in high-intensity contractions is the production of lactic acid (lactate) as pyruvate is converted to regenerate NAD+, which lowers muscle pH and contributes to fatigue.
questions.correct_answer_text: C. The rapid accumulation of lactate, leading to muscle fatigue.

options: A. Endogenous triglycerides from the liver to peripheral tissues.
B. Cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver.
C. Dietary lipids (triglycerides and cholesterol) from the intestine to peripheral tissues.
D. Free fatty acids bound to albumin in the bloodstream.
questions.question: Chylomicrons are lipoprotein particles primarily responsible for the transport of:
questions.explanation: Chylomicrons are synthesized in the intestinal cells and are specifically designed to transport dietary triglycerides and cholesterol absorbed from the gut to various tissues in the body, including adipose tissue and muscle.
questions.correct_answer_text: C. Dietary lipids (triglycerides and cholesterol) from the intestine to peripheral tissues.

questions.question: Phosphocreatine is used to store high-energy phosphate bonds primarily in which type of tissue?
questions.explanation: Phosphocreatine (creatine phosphate) acts as a readily available energy reserve, especially in tissues with high and fluctuating energy demands like skeletal muscle and the brain. It rapidly donates its phosphate to ADP to form ATP during sudden bursts of activity.

options: A. Pyruvate, which is then oxidized.
B. Glucose, which can be returned to the muscles.
C. Acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis.
questions.question: In the Cori cycle, lactate produced in muscles during anaerobic metabolism is transported to the liver and converted into:
questions.explanation: The Cori cycle (lactic acid cycle) involves the transport of lactate from the muscles to the liver. In the liver, lactate is converted back to pyruvate, which is then used in gluconeogenesis to synthesize glucose. This glucose can then be released back into the bloodstream for use by muscles or other tissues.
questions.correct_answer_text: B. Glucose, which can be returned to the muscles.

questions.question: Long-term heavy alcohol consumption can cause a range of detrimental effects. Which of the following is a direct consequence of alcohol's impact on liver metabolism?
questions.explanation: Alcohol metabolism in the liver leads to an increase in NADH/NAD+ ratio, inhibiting fatty acid oxidation and promoting fatty acid synthesis, resulting in the accumulation of triglycerides in hepatocytes, known as alcoholic fatty liver or steatosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common symptom associated with alcohol withdrawal syndrome?
questions.explanation: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome results from the central nervous system's adaptation to chronic alcohol exposure. Symptoms often include tremors, anxiety, hallucinations, tachycardia, hypertension, and potentially life-threatening seizures and delirium tremens.

questions.question: There are many types of alcohol. Intoxication as we know it from alcoholic beverages is caused by:
questions.explanation: Ethanol is the specific type of alcohol found in alcoholic beverages that causes the psychoactive and intoxicating effects. Methanol, isopropanol, and ethylene glycol are other types of alcohol that are highly toxic and not consumed for recreational purposes.

questions.question: Enzymes primarily involved in the transfer of methyl groups from one molecule to another are collectively classified as:
questions.explanation: Transferases are a class of enzymes that catalyze the transfer of functional groups (such as methyl, acyl, or glycosyl groups) from one molecule (the donor) to another (the acceptor). Methyltransferases are a specific type of transferase.

options: A. Regulation of mood and emotions.
C. Direct signaling for skeletal muscle contraction.
questions.question: All of the following are generally associated with the diverse functions of serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine), EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Serotonin is a widely acting neurotransmitter and hormone involved in many physiological processes including mood, appetite, sleep, and gut motility. Skeletal muscle contraction is primarily mediated by acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, not serotonin.
questions.correct_answer_text: C. Direct signaling for skeletal muscle contraction.

questions.question: Under aerobic conditions, the complete degradation of one molecule of glucose ultimately yields a net maximum of approximately how many ATP molecules?
questions.explanation: The complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule, through glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation, yields approximately 30-32 ATP molecules. The exact number can vary slightly depending on the shuttle system used to transport cytoplasmic NADH into the mitochondria.

questions.question: Synthesis of glutamine, a crucial amino acid for nitrogen transport and detoxification, usually occurs primarily in:
questions.explanation: Glutamine is synthesized from glutamate and ammonia by the enzyme glutamine synthetase. This enzyme is highly active in skeletal muscle and the brain, where glutamine serves as a non-toxic carrier of ammonia to the liver and kidneys.

questions.question: The body's central metabolic clearinghouse, responsible for detoxifying various substances, synthesizing plasma proteins, and regulating nutrient levels in the blood, is known to be the:
questions.explanation: The liver plays a central role in metabolism, processing nutrients absorbed from the gut, synthesizing numerous essential molecules, and detoxifying harmful substances, thus acting as the body's primary metabolic clearinghouse.

questions.question: Which enzyme class catalyzes reactions that break chemical bonds by adding water (hydrolysis)?
questions.explanation: Hydrolases are enzymes that catalyze the hydrolysis of a chemical bond, involving the addition of a water molecule. Examples include peptidases, lipases, and nucleases.

options: C. Half of the maximal rate (1/2 Vmax)
questions.question: In Michaelis-Menten kinetics, the Km (Michaelis constant) represents the substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is:
questions.explanation: Km is a measure of the enzyme's affinity for its substrate. A lower Km indicates a higher affinity. By definition, Km is the substrate concentration at which the enzyme achieves half of its maximum reaction velocity (Vmax).
questions.correct_answer_text: C. Half of the maximal rate (1/2 Vmax)

options: A. Binds irreversibly to the active site.
C. Increases the apparent Km without affecting Vmax.
B. Lowers the Vmax without affecting Km.
D. Binds to a site other than the active site.
questions.question: A competitive inhibitor of an enzyme typically:
questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate and bind reversibly to the enzyme's active site, competing with the substrate. This increases the apparent Km (more substrate is needed to reach 1/2 Vmax) but does not change Vmax, as high substrate concentrations can outcompete the inhibitor.
questions.correct_answer_text: C. Increases the apparent Km without affecting Vmax.

options: C. A molecule binding to a site distinct from the active site, causing a conformational change.
B. Covalent modification of the enzyme, such as phosphorylation.
A. A molecule binding to the active site, blocking substrate binding.
D. The synthesis or degradation of the enzyme protein.
questions.question: Allosteric regulation of an enzyme typically involves:
questions.explanation: Allosteric regulation involves the binding of an effector molecule to an allosteric site (a site distinct from the active site) on the enzyme. This binding induces a conformational change that affects the enzyme's activity, either activating or inhibiting it.
questions.correct_answer_text: C. A molecule binding to a site distinct from the active site, causing a conformational change.

options: A. To allow for tighter binding to their substrates.
D. To reduce the energy cost of enzyme synthesis.
C. To increase their stability at high temperatures.
B. To prevent premature or inappropriate enzyme activity.
questions.question: Many proteolytic enzymes are synthesized as inactive precursors called zymogens (proenzymes). The advantage of synthesizing enzymes as zymogens is:
questions.explanation: Zymogens are inactive precursors of enzymes, particularly proteases, that must be cleaved to become active. This mechanism prevents the enzyme from digesting cellular components where it's synthesized and ensures that its activity is confined to specific locations or triggered by specific signals.
questions.correct_answer_text: B. To prevent premature or inappropriate enzyme activity.

questions.question: Which of the following serves as a common coenzyme for dehydrogenases, accepting electrons during metabolic redox reactions?
questions.explanation: NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is a crucial coenzyme that acts as an electron acceptor in many oxidative reactions (catalyzed by dehydrogenases) during metabolism, becoming reduced to NADH.

questions.question: Salivary amylase, an enzyme found in saliva, initiates the digestion of which macronutrient?
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase (also known as ptyalin) begins the breakdown of complex carbohydrates (starches) into smaller oligosaccharides like maltose and dextrins in the mouth.

options: A. Increasing the activation energy of the reaction.
B. Shifting the equilibrium of the reaction towards products.
D. Providing additional energy to the reactants.
C. Decreasing the activation energy of the reaction.
questions.question: Enzymes increase the rate of biochemical reactions by:
questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts. They speed up reactions by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, making it easier for the reactants to reach the transition state. They do not change the overall Gibbs free energy change or the equilibrium of a reaction.
questions.correct_answer_text: C. Decreasing the activation energy of the reaction.

questions.question: A deficiency in Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) is associated with which neurological condition?
questions.explanation: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) is a crucial cofactor for several enzymes involved in carbohydrate metabolism. Its deficiency leads to Beriberi, characterized by neurological (dry beriberi) and cardiovascular (wet beriberi) symptoms.

questions.question: Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin) serves as a precursor for which important coenzymes involved in redox reactions?
questions.explanation: Riboflavin is a component of the coenzymes Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide (FAD) and Flavin Mononucleotide (FMN), which are essential electron carriers in various metabolic pathways, including the electron transport chain.

questions.question: Pellagra, a disease characterized by dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia, is caused by a deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.explanation: Pellagra is caused by a severe deficiency of Niacin (Vitamin B3) or its precursor, tryptophan. Niacin is a component of NAD+ and NADP+, critical coenzymes in many metabolic reactions.

questions.question: Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) in its active form (pyridoxal phosphate) is a coenzyme primarily involved in which type of metabolic reactions?
questions.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active form of Vitamin B6, is a versatile coenzyme for numerous enzymes involved in amino acid metabolism, including transamination, decarboxylation, and racemization reactions.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is a characteristic symptom of Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) deficiency?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 is essential for DNA synthesis and the proper functioning of the nervous system. Its deficiency impairs red blood cell maturation, leading to megaloblastic anemia, and can also cause neurological damage.

questions.question: A patient presents with bleeding gums, impaired wound healing, and petechiae. These symptoms are most consistent with a deficiency in which vitamin?
questions.explanation: These symptoms are classic signs of scurvy, caused by a deficiency of Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid). Vitamin C is crucial for collagen synthesis, acting as a cofactor for hydroxylase enzymes involved in forming stable collagen helices.

options: D. Antioxidant protection of cell membranes
C. Vision, immune function, and epithelial cell maintenance
questions.question: Vitamin A (Retinol) is essential for:
questions.explanation: Vitamin A is critical for several physiological processes, including the formation of rhodopsin (a photopigment in the retina) for vision, maintaining healthy epithelial tissues, and supporting immune function.
questions.correct_answer_text: C. Vision, immune function, and epithelial cell maintenance

questions.question: A deficiency in Vitamin D can lead to which condition in children?
questions.explanation: Vitamin D is essential for calcium and phosphate homeostasis and bone mineralization. In children, Vitamin D deficiency leads to rickets, characterized by defective bone growth and skeletal deformities. In adults, it leads to osteomalacia.

questions.question: Vitamin K is primarily known for its essential role in:
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin crucial for the synthesis of several blood clotting factors (e.g., factors II, VII, IX, X) in the liver, by acting as a cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase.

options: A. Are excreted rapidly in urine.
B. Are required in larger daily amounts.
D. Act primarily as coenzymes in metabolic reactions.
C. Are stored in the body, increasing the risk of toxicity.
questions.question: Compared to water-soluble vitamins, fat-soluble vitamins generally:
questions.explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are absorbed with dietary fats, stored in the body's fatty tissues and liver, and are not easily excreted. This storage capacity means they can accumulate to toxic levels with excessive intake, unlike water-soluble vitamins which are generally excreted if consumed in excess.
questions.correct_answer_text: C. Are stored in the body, increasing the risk of toxicity.

questions.question: Which major mineral is crucial for bone and tooth structure, muscle contraction, nerve transmission, and blood clotting?
questions.explanation: Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body, primarily forming bones and teeth. It also plays vital roles as an intracellular messenger, in muscle contraction, nerve impulse transmission, and blood coagulation.

questions.question: Microcytic, hypochromic anemia is a classic manifestation of a deficiency in which trace mineral?
questions.explanation: Iron is an essential component of hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells. Iron deficiency leads to a reduction in hemoglobin synthesis, resulting in microcytic (small) and hypochromic (pale) red blood cells, a characteristic of iron-deficiency anemia.

options: A. Maintaining fluid balance and blood pressure.
D. Constituting the backbone of DNA and RNA.
questions.question: Sodium (Na+) is a primary electrolyte that plays a critical role in all of the following, EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Sodium is vital for extracellular fluid volume, blood pressure regulation, nerve impulse conduction, and muscle contraction. Phosphate and deoxyribose/ribose form the backbone of DNA and RNA, not sodium.
questions.correct_answer_text: D. Constituting the backbone of DNA and RNA.

questions.question: Iodine is an essential trace mineral primarily required for the synthesis of:
questions.explanation: Iodine is a key component of thyroid hormones (thyroxine, T4, and triiodothyronine, T3), which are vital for regulating metabolism, growth, and development. Iodine deficiency can lead to goiter and hypothyroidism.

questions.question: Which trace mineral functions as a cofactor for numerous enzymes, supports immune function, and is involved in wound healing?
questions.explanation: Zinc is an essential trace mineral that acts as a cofactor for over 300 enzymes involved in diverse metabolic processes. It plays crucial roles in immune function, wound healing, DNA synthesis, and cell division.

{"type":"weekly_exam","unit":"Year 1: Enzymes, Vitamins and Minerals","saqs":[{"question":"Describe the concept of enzyme specificity, differentiate between absolute and group specificity, and provide a brief example for each.","answer":"Enzyme specificity refers to the ability of an enzyme to catalyze a reaction with a particular substrate or a limited range of substrates. This is due to the unique shape and chemical properties of the enzyme's active site, which complement the substrate's shape.

1.  **Absolute specificity**: The enzyme acts on only one specific substrate. For example, urease acts exclusively on urea, catalyzing its hydrolysis into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
2.  **Group specificity**: The enzyme acts on a specific functional group or type of chemical bond, regardless of the rest of the molecular structure. For example, trypsin cleaves peptide bonds specifically where the carboxyl group is contributed by the basic amino acids arginine or lysine.","marks":5},{"question":"List and briefly explain two major factors that can influence the rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction.","answer":"Enzyme activity, and thus the rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction, can be influenced by several factors. Two major factors include:

1.  **Temperature**: Each enzyme has an optimal temperature at which its activity is maximal. Initially, increasing temperature increases kinetic energy and collision frequency between enzyme and substrate, enhancing reaction rate. However, exceeding the optimal temperature leads to denaturation of the enzyme's three-dimensional structure, particularly its active site, causing a significant and irreversible loss of activity.
2.  **pH**: Similar to temperature, enzymes exhibit optimal activity within a narrow pH range. Deviations from this optimal pH can alter the ionization state of amino acid residues in the enzyme's active site or crucial for its structure, affecting substrate binding or catalytic efficiency. Extreme pH values can lead to irreversible denaturation of the enzyme.","marks":5},{"question":"Classify vitamins based on their solubility. For each class, provide one specific vitamin example and briefly state a key physiological function of that example.","answer":"Vitamins are classified into two main groups based on their solubility:

1.  **Fat-soluble vitamins**: These vitamins are absorbed along with dietary fats and are stored in the body's fatty tissues and liver. They are not readily excreted.
    *   **Example**: Vitamin D (Cholecalciferol).
    *   **Key Function**: Essential for calcium and phosphate homeostasis, promoting their absorption in the intestine and regulating bone mineralization.

2.  **Water-soluble vitamins**: These vitamins dissolve in water, are generally not stored in significant amounts, and any excess is typically excreted in the urine.
    *   **Example**: Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid).
    *   **Key Function**: Acts as a crucial antioxidant, is essential for collagen synthesis (e.g., in connective tissue, skin, bones), and enhances the absorption of non-heme iron.","marks":5},{"question":"Outline the primary physiological roles of calcium in the human body and list one common clinical manifestation of chronic calcium deficiency.","answer":"Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body and performs several critical physiological roles:

1.  **Structural Component**: It is the primary mineral component of bones and teeth, providing structural rigidity and support.
2.  **Muscle Contraction**: Calcium ions (Ca2+) are essential for initiating and regulating muscle contraction in skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscles.
3.  **Nerve Impulse Transmission**: Ca2+ plays a crucial role in neurotransmitter release at synapses, facilitating communication between nerve cells.
4.  **Blood Coagulation**: It is an essential cofactor (Factor IV) in the coagulation cascade, necessary for the activation of several clotting factors.
5.  **Hormone Secretion**: Involved in the release of various hormones and enzymes.

One common clinical manifestation of chronic calcium deficiency is **osteoporosis** (in adults), characterized by reduced bone mineral density, leading to increased bone fragility and fracture risk. In children, it can lead to **rickets**, affecting bone development.","marks":5}],"laqs":[{"question":"Discuss the critical role of B vitamins as coenzymes in central metabolic pathways. Choose one specific B vitamin, explain its coenzyme form(s), identify a major metabolic pathway where it functions, and describe the biochemical and clinical consequences of its severe deficiency.","answer":"B vitamins are a group of water-soluble vitamins that play a critical role as coenzymes in numerous metabolic pathways, particularly those involved in energy production and biosynthesis. They are not used as energy sources themselves but are essential for enzymes to function correctly. A coenzyme is a non-protein organic molecule that binds to an enzyme (apoenzyme) to form an active enzyme complex (holoenzyme), facilitating specific biochemical reactions.

Let's consider **Thiamine (Vitamin B1)**:

**1. Coenzyme Form(s)**:
Thiamine is converted in the body, primarily in the liver, into its active coenzyme form: **Thiamine Pyrophosphate (TPP)**, also known as Thiamine Diphosphate (TDP). This conversion is catalyzed by the enzyme thiamine pyrophosphokinase, which phosphorylates thiamine using ATP.

**2. Major Metabolic Pathways where it Functions**:
TPP acts as a crucial coenzyme for several key enzymes involved in carbohydrate metabolism:
    *   **Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex (PDC)**: TPP is an essential coenzyme for the E1 (pyruvate decarboxylase) component of the PDC. This complex catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, which is a critical link between glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle (Krebs cycle). This step is central to aerobic glucose metabolism and ATP production.
    *   **Alpha-Ketoglutarate Dehydrogenase Complex**: TPP is also a coenzyme for this complex in the TCA cycle, catalyzing the oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA. This is another vital step in energy generation.
    *   **Transketolase**: TPP is required by transketolase, an enzyme in the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). The PPP generates NADPH (essential for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense) and ribose-5-phosphate (a precursor for nucleotide synthesis).

**3. Biochemical Consequences of Severe Deficiency**:
Severe thiamine deficiency (Beriberi) primarily impacts tissues with high energy demand, such as the brain, nerves, and heart, due to impaired carbohydrate metabolism:
    *   **Impaired Glucose Metabolism**: Reduced activity of PDC and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase leads to an accumulation of their substrates (pyruvate, lactate, and alpha-ketoglutarate). This can result in lactic acidosis due to increased anaerobic metabolism.
    *   **Reduced Acetyl-CoA Production**: The bottleneck at PDC significantly reduces the supply of acetyl-CoA to the TCA cycle, severely impairing aerobic ATP production.
    *   **Impaired NADPH and Nucleotide Synthesis**: Decreased transketolase activity affects the PPP, reducing NADPH levels and hindering biosynthesis of fatty acids, steroids, and nucleotides.

**4. Clinical Consequences of Severe Deficiency**:
The biochemical impairments lead to distinct clinical syndromes:
    *   **Dry Beriberi**: Primarily affects the nervous system. Symptoms include peripheral neuropathy (muscle weakness, paresthesia, foot drop), Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (acute neurological disorder characterized by confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, and chronic memory impairment).
    *   **Wet Beriberi**: Primarily affects the cardiovascular system. Symptoms include high-output cardiac failure, tachycardia, cardiomegaly, and edema, often due to the heart's inability to meet its high energy demands.
    *   **Infantile Beriberi**: Occurs in breastfed infants of thiamine-deficient mothers, often presenting with cardiac symptoms, aphonia, and acute heart failure.

In summary, thiamine, as TPP, is indispensable for the enzymes that drive central pathways of carbohydrate metabolism. Its severe deficiency leads to a profound disruption of energy production and critical biosynthetic pathways, manifesting in severe neurological and cardiovascular dysfunction.","marks":20}],"generated_at":"2026-06-19T00:00:40.214Z"}

questions.question: An organism without a known sexual stage of reproduction would be classified in which of the following fungal groups?
questions.explanation: Fungi with no known teleomorph (sexual stage) are classified as Deuteromycota (Fungi Imperfecti or Mitosporic fungi).

questions.question: An antifungal drug such as Miconazole inhibits proper formation of which cellular component?
questions.explanation: Azoles like miconazole block ergosterol synthesis, disrupting plasma membrane formation in fungi.

questions.question: Which of the following fungi would you most likely find growing in pigeon droppings?
questions.explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans is commonly found in soil contaminated with pigeon droppings.

questions.question: Which fungal condition causes more than 200 million cases per year worldwide, with symptoms including an itching sensation and burning internal pain?
questions.explanation: Vulvovaginal candidiasis is extremely common worldwide, causing itching and internal burning.

questions.question: The formation of arthrospores and spherules in infected tissue is characteristic of which fungal disease?
questions.explanation: Coccidioides forms arthroconidia in soil/mold form and spherules in tissue.

questions.question: Aflatoxin is produced by which organism, and what type of substance is it?
questions.explanation: Aspergillus flavus produces aflatoxin, a potent hepatocarcinogen.

questions.question: A girl who pricked her finger while pruning rose bushes develops a local pustule that progresses to an ulcer. Several nodules then develop along the local lymphatic drainage. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: This describes the classic 'rose gardener's disease' – lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis caused by Sporothrix schenckii.

questions.question: Fungal cells that reproduce by budding are seen in the infected tissues of patients with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Candida, Cryptococcus, and Sporothrix all appear as budding yeasts in tissue.

options: It is caused by Paracoccidioides brasiliensis.
It is endemic to Latin America.
It typically presents as a chronic granulomatous disease.
Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is resistant to amphotericin B.
questions.question: Which statement regarding paracoccidiomycosis is NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is susceptible to amphotericin B, not resistant.
questions.correct_answer_text: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is resistant to amphotericin B.

questions.question: A kidney transplant patient develops a nosocomial systemic candidiasis. The isolated Candida glabrata is resistant to fluconazole. Which of the following would be a reasonable oral alternative for treatment?
questions.explanation: Posaconazole often retains activity against fluconazole-resistant Candida species.

options: They can originate from inhalation of spores.
They are always restricted to the skin and hair.
questions.question: All of the following are characteristics of systemic/deep mycoses EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Not all systemic fungal infections start in the lungs (e.g., candidiasis can be catheter/GI-related), and they are not always restricted to the skin and hair.
questions.correct_answer_text: They are always restricted to the skin and hair.

questions.question: Thousands of people in the western USA experienced a flu-like illness in 1992 following inhalation of soil fungal spores. This illness is known as 'valley fever.' What is the pathogen?
questions.explanation: Coccidioidomycosis is commonly known as Valley Fever and is endemic to the southwestern US.

questions.question: Amphotericin B would be used to treat all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Amphotericin B is a potent antifungal used for systemic infections; superficial dermatophytoses are typically treated with topical or oral antifungals.

questions.question: All of the following are superficial mycoses EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Candidiasis of the esophagus is a mucosal or deep-seated infection, not a superficial mycosis of the skin or hair.

options: It causes hyperpigmented macules on the palms and soles.
It is caused by a fungus that exists as a yeast in tissue.
It is a superficial fungal infection.
It is treated with oral antifungal medications.
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding Tinea nigra is NOT correct?
questions.explanation: Tinea nigra is typically treated with topical antifungal agents; oral medications are generally reserved for more extensive or recalcitrant cases.
questions.correct_answer_text: It is treated with oral antifungal medications.

questions.question: Which of the following is the common cause of Athlete's foot?
questions.explanation: Dermatophytes, particularly species of Trichophyton, are the most common cause of Tinea pedis (Athlete's foot).

options: They involve the epidermis, hair, and nails.
They are typically caused by dermatophytes.
They are spread by direct contact with infected individuals or contaminated objects.
They often present with pustules and abscesses.
questions.question: All of the following are characteristics of cutaneous mycoses EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: While pustules and abscesses can occur in some cutaneous infections, this is not a universal characteristic, and some cutaneous mycoses present with scaling or discoloration.
questions.correct_answer_text: They often present with pustules and abscesses.

questions.question: All of the following dermatophytes are responsible for nail infections EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Microsporum species typically infect hair and skin but not nails, whereas Trichophyton and Epidermophyton are common causes of onychomycosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is an opportunistic pathogenic fungus in humans?
questions.explanation: While all can cause disease, Candida albicans is a common commensal that becomes opportunistic in immunocompromised individuals or when normal flora is disrupted.

options: Hyphae with septations and dichotomous branching
Large, thick-walled yeast cells with multiple budding
questions.question: Aspergillosis is recognized in tissue by the presence of:
questions.explanation: Aspergillus species are characterized by septate hyphae with dichotomous (45-degree) branching, often forming characteristic conidiophores.
questions.correct_answer_text: Hyphae with septations and dichotomous branching

questions.question: Fungi often colonize lesions caused by other agents. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be present as a colonizer?
questions.explanation: While Staphylococcus aureus can colonize wounds, it's a bacterium and less commonly considered a fungal colonizer in the context of fungal opportunistic infections. Candida, Aspergillus, and dermatophytes are common fungal colonizers.

options: It is primarily caused by yeasts.
It is caused by fungi that utilize keratin for growth.
It is treated with intravenous amphotericin B.
questions.question: Which statement regarding dermatophytosis is correct?
questions.explanation: Dermatophytosis, also known as ringworm, is caused by fungi called dermatophytes that have the ability to digest keratin, found in skin, hair, and nails.
questions.correct_answer_text: It is caused by fungi that utilize keratin for growth.

options: Molecular methods are increasingly used for accurate and rapid identification.
Fungal cultures typically yield results within 24 hours.
India ink staining is the primary method for identifying dermatophytes.
Direct microscopy of KOH mounts primarily identifies fungal species.
questions.question: Which statement regarding laboratory identification of fungi is correct?
questions.explanation: While KOH mounts can reveal fungal elements, definitive species identification often requires culture. Fungal cultures can take days to weeks. India ink is for encapsulated yeasts like Cryptococcus. Molecular methods offer speed and accuracy.
questions.correct_answer_text: Molecular methods are increasingly used for accurate and rapid identification.

questions.question: All of the following are examples of superficial mycoses EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Systemic candidiasis is a deep-seated or disseminated fungal infection, not a superficial mycosis.

questions.question: Amphotericin B would be used to treat all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Cutaneous candidiasis is typically treated with topical or oral antifungals. Amphotericin B is reserved for more severe or systemic infections.

questions.question: A component of the cell membrane of most fungi is:
questions.explanation: Ergosterol is the primary sterol found in fungal cell membranes, analogous to cholesterol in animal cell membranes, and is a target for many antifungal drugs.

options: It is caused by fungi that metabolize keratin.
It is resistant to heat and humidity.
It always requires systemic antifungal treatment.
questions.question: Which statement regarding dermatophytosis is correct?
questions.explanation: Dermatophytes are fungi that can break down keratin, allowing them to infect skin, hair, and nails. Many cases can be treated with topical agents.
questions.correct_answer_text: It is caused by fungi that metabolize keratin.

options: Direct microscopic examination is sufficient for all fungal identification.
Fungal culture media are typically selective for bacteria.
Serological tests are the primary method for diagnosing dermatophytosis.
Special stains like Gomori methenamine silver can highlight fungal elements.
questions.question: Which statement regarding laboratory identification of fungi is correct?
questions.explanation: Special stains like Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) or periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) are valuable for visualizing fungal structures in tissue samples.
questions.correct_answer_text: Special stains like Gomori methenamine silver can highlight fungal elements.

questions.question: Which of the following is an opportunistic pathogenic fungus in humans?
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii is an obligate opportunistic pathogen that causes Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), primarily in immunocompromised individuals.

options: Septate hyphae with acute angle branching
Hyphae with yeast cells in a 'Christmas tree' pattern
questions.question: Aspergillosis is recognized in tissue by the presence of:
questions.explanation: Aspergillus species are characterized by septate hyphae that branch dichotomously at acute angles (around 45 degrees).
questions.correct_answer_text: Septate hyphae with acute angle branching

questions.question: Fungi often colonize lesions caused by other agents. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be present as a colonizer?
questions.explanation: While Staphylococcus aureus can colonize wounds, it is a bacterium. Candida, Aspergillus, and dermatophytes are common fungal colonizers of various lesions.

options: It is a common cause of pneumonia in immunocompetent individuals.
It is commonly found in bird droppings.
questions.question: Each of the following statements concerning Cryptococcus neoformans is correct EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: While Cryptococcus neoformans can cause pneumonia, it is a significant opportunistic pathogen that primarily causes severe disease (like meningitis) in immunocompromised individuals.
questions.correct_answer_text: It is a common cause of pneumonia in immunocompetent individuals.

options: It is a common cause of nosocomial infections.
It can form pseudohyphae and true hyphae.
It is a part of the normal human microbiota.
questions.question: Each of the following statements concerning Candida albicans is correct EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Candida albicans is dimorphic in that it can exist as a yeast or filament (pseudohyphae/hyphae), but it does not typically have a distinct mold phase like some dimorphic pathogens.

options: The respiratory tract of healthy individuals
Soil and decaying vegetation in endemic areas
questions.question: Natural habitat for Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is:
questions.explanation: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is found in soil and on vegetation, particularly in rural areas of Latin America.
questions.correct_answer_text: Soil and decaying vegetation in endemic areas

questions.question: Coccidioidomycosis is also called:
questions.explanation: Coccidioidomycosis is commonly known as Valley Fever. San Joaquin Fever is also used, especially in California. Desert Rheumatism is an older term for associated arthralgias.

questions.question: One of the most common mycotoxins that infects nuts and grains and causes severe reactions is:
questions.explanation: Aflatoxins, produced by Aspergillus species, are potent carcinogens and are commonly found in contaminated nuts and grains.
