# Year 3: Chemical Pathology & Clinical Biochemistry
## 50 MCQs

---

**Q1.** Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is most useful as a tumor marker for

- A. Hepatocellular carcinoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumors
- B. Prostate carcinoma
- C. Breast carcinoma
- D. Colorectal carcinoma

**Answer: A** — AFP produced by yolk sac and fetal liver. Elevated in HCC (>400ng/mL highly suggestive), hepatoblastoma, yolk sac tumors. Pure seminoma does NOT produce AFP. Mildly elevated in cirrhosis/hepatitis but not diagnostic alone.

---

**Q2.** PSA is best described as

- A. Cancer-specific and organ-specific for prostate carcinoma
- B. A marker specific to seminoma cells
- C. Used primarily to diagnose bladder cancer
- D. Organ-specific but NOT cancer-specific — elevated in BPH, prostatitis, and carcinoma

**Answer: D** — PSA is prostate-specific but NOT cancer-specific. Elevated in BPH, prostatitis, post-DRE, and carcinoma. Low free:total PSA ratio (<10%) favors carcinoma. High ratio (>25%) favors BPH. Used for screening, staging, and monitoring.

---

**Q3.** CA 19-9 is most useful as a tumor marker for

- A. Ovarian carcinoma
- B. Prostate carcinoma
- C. Pancreatic carcinoma
- D. Hepatocellular carcinoma

**Answer: C** — CA 19-9 elevated in pancreatic carcinoma (~80% sensitivity). Also elevated in cholangiocarcinoma, gastric, colorectal cancer. NOT useful for screening. Most valuable for monitoring treatment response and recurrence. Cannot be produced by Lewis antigen-negative individuals (5–10% of population).

---

**Q4.** Ectopic ACTH production causing Cushing's syndrome is most commonly associated with

- A. Renal cell carcinoma
- B. Small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC)
- C. Colon carcinoma
- D. Hepatocellular carcinoma

**Answer: B** — SCLC most common cause of ectopic ACTH. Features: rapidly progressive, severe hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperpigmentation, muscle wasting — often WITHOUT classic cushingoid appearance. ACTH very high, NOT suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone. Other causes: bronchial carcinoid, medullary thyroid Ca, pancreatic NETs.

---

**Q5.** The most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalized cancer patients is

- A. Excess vitamin D production by tumor
- B. Ectopic PTH secretion by tumor
- C. Bony metastases causing local osteolytic hypercalcemia only
- D. PTHrP secretion causing humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy

**Answer: D** — PTHrP mimics PTH at PTH1R → hypercalcemia + hypophosphatemia. PTH itself SUPPRESSED — key distinguishing feature from primary HPT. Most common tumors: SCC lung/head/neck, renal cell, breast, bladder carcinoma.

---

**Q6.** SIADH as a paraneoplastic syndrome is most commonly caused by

- A. Renal cell carcinoma
- B. Colorectal carcinoma
- C. Small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC)
- D. Pancreatic carcinoma

**Answer: C** — SCLC produces ectopic ADH → SIADH → dilutional hyponatremia + inappropriately concentrated urine. Features: hyponatremia + low serum osmolality + urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg + euvolemia. Treatment: fluid restriction ± tolvaptan/demeclocycline.

---

**Q7.** CEA is most useful for

- A. Primary diagnosis of colorectal carcinoma
- B. Screening for colorectal carcinoma in the general population
- C. Diagnosing hepatocellular carcinoma
- D. Monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence of colorectal carcinoma

**Answer: D** — CEA NOT useful for screening (low specificity — elevated in smokers, pancreatitis, IBD, cirrhosis). Most valuable post-surgery for detecting colorectal cancer recurrence. Also elevated in breast, lung, gastric, pancreatic cancers. Normal <5 ng/mL.

---

**Q8.** Beta-hCG as a tumor marker is elevated in

- A. Hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma
- B. Ovarian mucinous carcinoma only
- C. Choriocarcinoma, gestational trophoblastic disease, and non-seminomatous germ cell tumors
- D. Prostate carcinoma only

**Answer: C** — Beta-hCG is the marker for gestational trophoblastic disease and non-seminomatous GCTs. Pure seminomas may have mildly elevated hCG (~10%) but AFP is normal. Extremely sensitive — detects tiny tumor burden. Used for diagnosis, staging, monitoring, and recurrence detection.

---

## SECTION 2: GONADAL DYSFUNCTION

**Q9.** Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP) is best described as

- A. Caused by GnRH deficiency requiring lifelong replacement
- B. A pathological condition always requiring hormonal treatment
- C. A normal variant — delayed but eventual spontaneous puberty, normal final height
- D. Associated with anosmia indicating Kallmann syndrome

**Answer: C** — Most common cause of delayed puberty in boys. Family history of late puberty typical. Bone age delayed. GnRH stimulation test shows normal LH/FSH response. Reassurance is key. Short course of low-dose testosterone can be used if causing psychological distress.

---

**Q10.** Gonadotropin-dependent (central) precocious puberty is caused by

- A. McCune-Albright syndrome with GNAS mutations
- B. Adrenal tumors secreting androgens
- C. Exogenous sex steroid exposure
- D. Premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis with elevated LH/FSH

**Answer: D** — Central precocious puberty: premature GnRH activation → elevated LH, FSH → gonadal sex steroid production → puberty before age 8 girls, age 9 boys. Girls = mostly idiopathic. Boys more often have CNS cause (tumor, hamartoma). Treatment: GnRH agonist (leuprolide) to suppress axis.

---

**Q11.** McCune-Albright syndrome causes gonadotropin-INDEPENDENT precocious puberty through

- A. Hypothalamic hamartoma activating GnRH secretion
- B. Exogenous estrogen administration
- C. Adrenal tumor secreting androgens autonomously
- D. Gain-of-function GNAS mutations → constitutively active Gsα → autonomous sex steroid production without LH/FSH

**Answer: D** — Classic triad: precocious puberty + polyostotic fibrous dysplasia + café-au-lait spots (irregular "coast of Maine" borders). GnRH agonists do NOT work (axis not driving it). Treatment: aromatase inhibitors (girls) or testolactone.

---

**Q12.** Kallmann syndrome is characterized by

- A. Precocious puberty with elevated LH/FSH
- B. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism combined with anosmia due to failed GnRH neuron migration
- C. Primary gonadal failure with elevated FSH/LH
- D. Premature ovarian insufficiency in females only

**Answer: B** — Kallmann syndrome: KAL1 (X-linked) or FGFR1 (autosomal dominant) mutations → GnRH neurons fail to migrate from olfactory placode to hypothalamus → absent GnRH + absent olfactory bulbs → anosmia + hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Low LH, FSH, testosterone/estrogen. Treatment: GnRH pulsatile therapy or gonadotropin replacement for fertility.

---

**Q13.** The most common cause of hirsutism in women is

- A. Adrenal carcinoma
- B. Cushing's syndrome
- C. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
- D. Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)

**Answer: D** — PCOS causes ~70–80% of hirsutism cases. Mechanism: insulin resistance → hyperinsulinemia → increased androgen production from theca cells + decreased SHBG → elevated free testosterone → hirsutism, acne, androgenic alopecia. Rotterdam criteria (2 of 3): oligo/anovulation, clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound.

---

**Q14.** Virilism in women differs from hirsutism in that it includes

- A. Only excess facial hair growth
- B. Clitoromegaly, deepening of voice, temporal balding, and muscle development — suggesting androgen-secreting tumor
- C. Mild excess hair responding to OCP
- D. Elevated SHBG levels

**Answer: B** — Hirsutism = excess terminal hair in male-pattern distribution (mild-moderate androgen excess). Virilism = full masculinization including clitoromegaly, voice deepening, temporal balding, breast atrophy, increased muscle mass — suggests severe androgen excess from adrenal or ovarian androgen-secreting tumor. Requires urgent investigation with testosterone, DHEAS, 17-OHP.

---

**Q15.** In semen analysis, the normal sperm count (WHO 2021 criteria) is

- A. >5 million/mL
- B. >50 million/mL
- C. >16 million/mL (lower reference limit)
- D. >100 million/mL

**Answer: C** — WHO 2021 lower reference limits: sperm concentration ≥16 million/mL, total motility ≥42%, progressive motility ≥30%, normal morphology ≥4% (Kruger strict criteria). Azoospermia = no sperm. Oligozoospermia = <16 million/mL. Asthenozoospermia = poor motility. Teratozoospermia = abnormal morphology.

---

**Q16.** Turner syndrome (45,X) causes infertility because of

- A. Androgen insensitivity at target organs
- B. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with low LH/FSH
- C. Premature ovarian failure — streak gonads → primary amenorrhea + elevated FSH/LH
- D. Uterine abnormalities preventing implantation

**Answer: C** — Turner syndrome: 45,X (or mosaic). Streak gonads (fibrous tissue replacing ovaries) → no estrogen/progesterone → no negative feedback → elevated FSH and LH (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism). Features: short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, coarctation of aorta, horseshoe kidney. Requires estrogen replacement for puberty induction and bone protection.

---

---

## SECTION 3: CLINICAL TOXICOLOGY & THERAPEUTIC DRUG MONITORING

**Q17.** Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) is most important for drugs with

- A. Wide therapeutic index and predictable pharmacokinetics
- B. Narrow therapeutic index where small dose changes cause toxicity or treatment failure
- C. No renal excretion and stable metabolism
- D. Short half-lives only requiring single dose monitoring

**Answer: B** — TDM is indicated for: narrow therapeutic index drugs (digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, gentamicin, vancomycin, cyclosporine, theophylline), drugs with unpredictable pharmacokinetics, drugs where toxicity mimics the disease being treated, monitoring compliance, and dose adjustment in renal/hepatic failure.

---

**Q18.** Digoxin toxicity is characterized by

- A. Hypokalemia protecting against toxicity
- B. Tachycardia and hypertension as early signs
- C. Xanthopsia (yellow vision), nausea, bradycardia, heart block, and ventricular arrhythmias
- D. Nephrotoxicity as the primary concern

**Answer: C** — Digoxin toxicity features: GI (nausea, vomiting, anorexia), CNS (xanthopsia — yellow-green visual disturbance, confusion), cardiac (bradycardia, AV block, ventricular arrhythmias — PAT with block is classic). Hypokalemia WORSENS toxicity (K+ and digoxin compete for same Na/K ATPase binding site). Therapeutic range: 0.5–2.0 ng/mL.

---

**Q19.** Lithium toxicity is precipitated by

- A. Hypernatremia and high fluid intake
- B. Dehydration, sodium depletion, NSAIDs, and thiazide diuretics — all increase lithium reabsorption
- C. High renal clearance states
- D. Alkalosis reducing lithium absorption

**Answer: B** — Lithium is reabsorbed in proximal tubule alongside sodium. Anything that depletes sodium → kidney conserves sodium AND lithium → toxicity. Precipitants: dehydration, low-salt diet, NSAIDs (reduce GFR), thiazides (increase proximal reabsorption), ACE inhibitors. Therapeutic range: 0.6–1.2 mmol/L. Toxicity: tremor, ataxia, confusion, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias.

---

**Q20.** Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose causes hepatotoxicity through

- A. Direct inhibition of hepatic protein synthesis
- B. Saturation of glucuronidation/sulfation → excess NAPQI production → glutathione depletion → hepatocyte necrosis
- C. Renal tubular toxicity as the primary mechanism
- D. Mitochondrial uncoupling causing lactic acidosis

**Answer: B** — Normal: paracetamol metabolized by glucuronidation/sulfation (safe). Small amount via CYP2E1 → NAPQI (toxic) → immediately detoxified by glutathione. Overdose: glucuronidation saturated → more NAPQI → glutathione depleted → NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins → centrilobular necrosis. Treatment: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) replenishes glutathione. Nomogram used to guide treatment.

---

**Q21.** Salicylate (aspirin) overdose characteristically causes

- A. Metabolic alkalosis only
- B. Respiratory acidosis followed by metabolic alkalosis
- C. Early respiratory alkalosis followed by high anion gap metabolic acidosis
- D. Pure metabolic acidosis from the start

**Answer: C** — Salicylates: directly stimulate respiratory center → hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis (early). Then: uncouple oxidative phosphorylation → lactic acidosis + ketoacidosis → HAGMA (late). In children: metabolic acidosis often predominates. Features: tinnitus, hyperventilation, hyperthermia, confusion. Treatment: urinary alkalinization (sodium bicarbonate) → increases ionized salicylate in urine → traps it → enhances excretion.

---

**Q22.** Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning causes toxicity by

- A. Direct lung destruction causing ARDS
- B. Binding hemoglobin with 240× greater affinity than O2 → carboxyhemoglobin → functional anemia + tissue hypoxia
- C. Causing methemoglobinemia
- D. Inhibiting carbonic anhydrase

**Answer: B** — CO binds Hb → carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) → reduces O2-carrying capacity + shifts O2 dissociation curve LEFT (Hb holds O2 more tightly → less O2 delivered to tissues). Also inhibits cytochrome oxidase directly. Pulse oximetry FALSELY NORMAL (cannot distinguish COHb from oxyHb). Diagnosis: co-oximetry. Treatment: 100% O2 (shortens COHb half-life from 5hrs to 60–90min) ± hyperbaric O2.

---

**Q23.** The antidote for organophosphate poisoning is

- A. N-acetylcysteine + methionine
- B. Desferrioxamine (deferoxamine)
- C. Atropine + pralidoxime (2-PAM)
- D. Sodium bicarbonate + activated charcoal

**Answer: C** — Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase → ACh accumulates → cholinergic toxidrome: SLUDGE (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI cramps, Emesis) + bradycardia, miosis, bronchospasm, muscle fasciculations → paralysis. Atropine: blocks muscarinic effects. Pralidoxime (2-PAM): reactivates acetylcholinesterase if given EARLY (before aging). Must give before enzyme "ages."

---

## SECTION 4: INHERITED METABOLIC DISORDERS

**Q24.** Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase leading to

- A. Homocysteine accumulation causing vascular thrombosis
- B. Branched-chain amino acid accumulation causing maple syrup odor
- C. Phenylalanine accumulation → phenylketones in urine → intellectual disability, seizures, musty odor, fair skin/hair
- D. Tyrosine accumulation causing liver failure

**Answer: C** — Autosomal recessive. Phenylalanine → normally converted to tyrosine (requires phenylalanine hydroxylase + BH4 cofactor). Blocked → phenylalanine accumulates → phenylpyruvate/phenylacetate in urine (musty/mousy odor). Decreased melanin → fair skin/hair/eyes. Detected on newborn screening (Guthrie test). Treatment: phenylalanine-restricted diet + sapropterin (BH4 analogue) in responsive cases. Start IMMEDIATELY to prevent intellectual disability.

---

**Q25.** Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is caused by

- A. Deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase → accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, valine
- B. Deficiency of homocysteine methyltransferase
- C. Deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase
- D. Deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase

**Answer: A** — Autosomal recessive. Branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) accumulate → maple syrup odor of urine/cerumen. Leucine is most neurotoxic. Presents neonatally: poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy → cerebral edema → death if untreated. Treatment: BCAA-restricted diet + thiamine supplementation (some responsive). Leucine levels monitored closely.

---

**Q26.** Homocystinuria (classical) is caused by deficiency of

- A. Phenylalanine hydroxylase
- B. Cystathionine beta-synthase → homocysteine accumulates
- C. Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase
- D. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase

**Answer: B** — CBS deficiency → homocysteine + methionine accumulate. Features resemble Marfan syndrome (tall, long limbs, lens subluxation — but DOWNWARD in homocystinuria vs UPWARD in Marfan). Plus: intellectual disability, osteoporosis, THROMBOEMBOLISM (homocysteine damages endothelium). Treatment: B6 (pyridoxine) in responsive cases + low-methionine diet + betaine + B12/folate.

---

**Q27.** Alkaptonuria (ochronosis) is caused by deficiency of

- A. Tyrosinase causing albinism
- B. Homogentisate oxidase → homogentisic acid accumulates → deposits in connective tissue
- C. Phenylalanine hydroxylase causing PKU
- D. Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase causing tyrosinemia

**Answer: B** — Autosomal recessive. Homogentisic acid (HGA) accumulates → oxidizes and polymerizes → ochronosis (blue-black pigmentation of connective tissue: ear cartilage, sclerae, tendons). Urine turns dark on standing (oxidation of HGA). Complications: ochronotic arthropathy (spine, large joints), cardiac valve involvement. Benign in childhood, symptomatic in adulthood. Treatment: low protein diet + nitisinone (blocks HGA production).

---

**Q28.** Galactosemia (classical) is caused by deficiency of

- A. Galactokinase → galactose-1-phosphate accumulates damaging liver, brain, kidneys
- B. Lactase → lactose malabsorption only
- C. Glucose-6-phosphatase → glycogen storage
- D. Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) → galactose-1-phosphate accumulation → liver, brain, kidney damage

**Answer: D** — GALT deficiency → galactose-1-phosphate accumulates (toxic). Presents in neonates after milk feeding: jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts (galactitol in lens), intellectual disability, E. coli sepsis (particularly susceptible). Newborn screening: positive Beutler test. Treatment: immediate galactose/lactose-free diet. Note: galactokinase deficiency (milder) causes cataracts only.

---

## SECTION 5: METABOLIC BONE DISORDERS, HYPERURICEMIA & GOUT

**Q29.** Osteoporosis is defined as

- A. T-score between −1.0 and −2.5 (osteopenia)
- B. Elevated bone turnover markers only
- C. Bone mineral density T-score ≤ −2.5 at hip or lumbar spine (WHO definition)
- D. Any fracture occurring after age 50

**Answer: C** — WHO definition: T-score compares BMD to young adult mean. Normal: T ≥ −1.0. Osteopenia: −1.0 to −2.5. Osteoporosis: ≤ −2.5. Severe osteoporosis: ≤ −2.5 + fragility fracture. DEXA scan is gold standard. FRAX tool calculates 10-year fracture probability. Treatment: bisphosphonates (alendronate), denosumab, teriparatide (severe cases).

---

**Q30.** Osteomalacia in adults (rickets in children) is caused by

- A. Excess vitamin D causing hypercalcemia and soft bones
- B. Fluoride toxicity causing dense brittle bones
- C. Vitamin D deficiency or phosphate wasting → defective bone mineralization → soft bones
- D. Excess PTH causing bone resorption

**Answer: C** — Osteomalacia: inadequate mineralization of osteoid (bone matrix laid down but not calcified). Causes: vitamin D deficiency (most common), malabsorption, renal disease (impaired 1-alpha hydroxylation), phenytoin (accelerates vitamin D catabolism), X-linked hypophosphatemia (FGF23 excess). Features: bone pain, muscle weakness, waddling gait, Looser's zones (pseudofractures) on X-ray. Biochem: low Ca, low PO4, high ALP, high PTH, low 25-OH-vitamin D.

---

**Q31.** Paget's disease of bone is characterized by

- A. Decreased bone turnover with dense uniform sclerosis
- B. Defective osteoblasts producing weak unmineralized matrix
- C. Disordered bone remodeling — excessive osteoclast activity followed by disorganized osteoblast activity → enlarged, deformed, structurally weak bone
- D. Autoimmune destruction of osteocytes

**Answer: C** — Paget's: paramyxovirus implicated. Phases: osteolytic (osteoclast excess) → mixed → osteosclerotic. Characteristic histology: mosaic/jigsaw pattern of lamellar bone. Markedly elevated ALP (bone formation marker). Features: bone pain, skull enlargement (hat size increase), bowing of tibia (saber shin), deafness (CN VIII compression), high-output cardiac failure (increased vascularity). Complications: osteosarcoma (<1%). Treatment: bisphosphonates.

---

**Q32.** In gout, monosodium urate crystals under polarized light appear as

- A. Rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent (blue when parallel to slow axis)
- B. Round, non-birefringent crystals
- C. Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel to slow axis)
- D. Rectangular, strongly positively birefringent

**Answer: C** — MSU crystals: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent. Remember: "gout = yellow needles." First MTP joint (podagra) classically affected. Tophi = deposits in soft tissues (ears, tendons). Causes of hyperuricemia: overproduction (Lesch-Nyhan, myeloproliferative disease, chemotherapy) or underexcretion (renal disease, thiazides, low-dose aspirin, alcohol, cyclosporine).

---

**Q33.** Allopurinol prevents gout attacks by

- A. Increasing renal urate excretion (uricosuric effect)
- B. Blocking urate reabsorption in renal tubule
- C. Inhibiting xanthine oxidase → reducing uric acid synthesis from hypoxanthine and xanthine
- D. Chelating uric acid in the bloodstream

**Answer: C** — Xanthine oxidase inhibitor → blocks conversion of hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid. Used for PREVENTION not acute attacks. Acute attack: NSAIDs (first-line), colchicine, or steroids. Never start allopurinol during acute attack (can worsen/prolong it). Febuxostat is an alternative XO inhibitor. Probenecid = uricosuric agent (increases renal excretion).

---

## SECTION 6: RENAL FUNCTION TESTS

**Q34.** The best single measure of glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in clinical practice is

- A. Serum urea concentration
- B. Urine specific gravity
- C. Serum creatinine alone
- D. eGFR calculated from serum creatinine using CKD-EPI or MDRD equation

**Answer: D** — eGFR (CKD-EPI equation) accounts for creatinine, age, sex, and race → more accurate than creatinine alone. Serum creatinine affected by muscle mass, diet, drugs. Cystatin C-based eGFR is more accurate in extremes of muscle mass. True GFR measured by inulin clearance (gold standard) or iohexol clearance — impractical for routine use.

---

**Q35.** In acute kidney injury (AKI), which finding best distinguishes PRE-RENAL from INTRINSIC RENAL cause?

- A. Elevated serum creatinine in both equally
- B. Urine sodium >40 mmol/L and FENa >2% indicating intrinsic renal injury (ATN)
- C. Oliguria occurring in pre-renal only
- D. Elevated urea in pre-renal only

**Answer: B** — Pre-renal AKI: kidneys intact → avidly reabsorb Na and water → urine Na LOW (<20 mmol/L), FENa <1%, urine osmolality HIGH (>500 mOsm/kg), urea:creatinine ratio HIGH (>100:1). Intrinsic renal (ATN): tubules damaged → cannot reabsorb Na → urine Na HIGH (>40), FENa >2%, urine osmolality LOW (<350). FENa = (urine Na × plasma Cr)/(plasma Na × urine Cr) × 100.

---

**Q36.** Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by the tetrad of

- A. Haematuria, hypertension, oliguria, and elevated creatinine
- B. Proteinuria >3.5g/day, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia/lipiduria
- C. Low urine output, high urea, high creatinine, and hyperkalemia
- D. Polyuria, low urine osmolality, low urine sodium, and high serum sodium

**Answer: B** — Nephrotic syndrome: massive proteinuria (>3.5g/24hr) → hypoalbuminaemia → decreased oncotic pressure → oedema. Liver compensates by making more proteins including lipoproteins → hyperlipidaemia. Lipiduria (oval fat bodies, fatty casts). Causes: minimal change disease (children), membranous nephropathy (adults), FSGS, diabetic nephropathy, amyloidosis.

---

**Q37.** Renal calculi (kidney stones) — the most common type is

- A. Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones
- B. Uric acid stones
- C. Cystine stones
- D. Calcium oxalate stones (accounting for ~80% of all renal stones)

**Answer: D** — Calcium oxalate most common (~80%). Appear as envelope or dumbbell-shaped crystals on urine microscopy. Radio-opaque on X-ray. Risk factors: hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, hypocitraturia, low fluid intake. Struvite = infection stones (urease-producing organisms, e.g. Proteus) → staghorn calculi, radio-opaque. Uric acid = radiolucent (NOT visible on plain X-ray). Cystine = hexagonal crystals, cystinuria (autosomal recessive).

---

**Q38.** The urinalysis finding most specific for glomerulonephritis is

- A. Leucocyte esterase positivity
- B. Proteinuria >300mg/day alone
- C. Red cell casts in urine
- D. Elevated specific gravity

**Answer: C** — Red cell (RBC) casts = pathognomonic of glomerulonephritis. RBCs enter tubules through damaged glomerular basement membrane → become trapped in Tamm-Horsfall protein matrix → form casts. Also seen in nephritic syndrome: haematuria, hypertension, oliguria, elevated creatinine, mild-moderate proteinuria. Granular casts = ATN. Waxy/broad casts = advanced CKD.

---

**Q39.** Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is defined as

- A. Any acute elevation of creatinine lasting >48 hours
- B. Single eGFR <60 mL/min on one occasion
- C. Kidney abnormality or eGFR <60 mL/min persisting for >3 months
- D. Proteinuria detected on a single urine dipstick test

**Answer: C** — CKD requires persistence >3 months (distinguishes from AKI). Classified by GFR (G1-G5) AND albuminuria category (A1-A3). CKD G5 = eGFR <15 (kidney failure). Complications: anaemia (decreased EPO), renal osteodystrophy (decreased vitamin D + secondary HPT), hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, hypertension, cardiovascular disease. Commonest causes: diabetes, hypertension, glomerulonephritis.

---

## SECTION 7: CARBOHYDRATE METABOLISM & DIABETES

**Q40.** The diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus include all EXCEPT

- A. Fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L on two occasions
- B. HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (≥6.5%) on two occasions
- C. Random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms
- D. Fasting plasma glucose of 6.2 mmol/L on one occasion (impaired fasting glucose — NOT diagnostic of DM)

**Answer: D** — IFG (impaired fasting glucose): fasting glucose 6.1–6.9 mmol/L = prediabetes, NOT diabetes. DM diagnostic criteria (any one confirmed on repeat unless symptomatic): FPG ≥7.0, 2hr OGTT glucose ≥11.1, random glucose ≥11.1 + symptoms, HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (≥6.5%). Single abnormal result without symptoms must be repeated.

---

**Q41.** The Somogyi effect differs from the dawn phenomenon in that

- A. Both are caused by the same mechanism — overnight GH surges
- B. The Somogyi effect = nocturnal hypoglycemia → counter-regulatory hormone rebound → morning hyperglycemia (manage by reducing evening insulin)
- C. The dawn phenomenon involves nocturnal hypoglycemia as the trigger
- D. The Somogyi effect is caused by GH and cortisol surges without prior hypoglycemia

**Answer: B** — Somogyi effect: excess insulin → nocturnal hypoglycemia → counter-regulatory response (glucagon, adrenaline, GH, cortisol) → rebound morning hyperglycemia. Management: reduce evening insulin dose. Dawn phenomenon: overnight GH/cortisol surges → hepatic glucose output → morning hyperglycemia WITHOUT prior nocturnal hypoglycemia. Management: increase evening insulin or use longer-acting insulin. Distinguish by continuous glucose monitoring or 3am blood glucose check.

---

**Q42.** The polyol pathway in diabetic complications involves

- A. Activation of protein kinase C causing vascular dysfunction
- B. Non-enzymatic glycation of proteins forming AGEs
- C. Aldose reductase converting excess glucose to sorbitol → osmotic damage to cells (lens, nerves, kidneys)
- D. Hexosamine pathway activation causing endothelial dysfunction

**Answer: C** — Four key mechanisms of diabetic microvascular complications: (1) Polyol pathway — sorbitol accumulation (lens → cataracts, nerves → neuropathy). (2) AGEs — glycation of proteins/vessels. (3) PKC activation — vascular permeability, angiogenesis. (4) Hexosamine pathway. Aldose reductase inhibitors (e.g. epalrestat) target the polyol pathway. Know all four mechanisms for exams.

---

## SECTION 8: ADRENAL CORTEX HYPERFUNCTION

**Q43.** The dexamethasone suppression test distinguishes causes of Cushing's syndrome. Which result pattern confirms ectopic ACTH syndrome?

- A. Cortisol suppressed by low-dose but not high-dose dexamethasone
- B. Cortisol suppressed by both low-dose and high-dose dexamethasone
- C. ACTH undetectable with elevated cortisol
- D. Cortisol NOT suppressed by either low-dose or high-dose dexamethasone, with very high ACTH

**Answer: D** — Ectopic ACTH: very high ACTH (often >200 pg/mL) + cortisol not suppressed by any dose of dexamethasone. Primary adrenal tumor: ACTH undetectable (suppressed by high cortisol) + cortisol not suppressed. Cushing's disease (pituitary adenoma): not suppressed by low-dose but suppressed by high-dose. Normal: suppressed by low-dose.

---

**Q44.** The biochemical hallmark of primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) is

- A. Elevated plasma renin activity with high aldosterone
- B. Low renin, high aldosterone, and elevated aldosterone:renin ratio (ARR >30)
- C. Low aldosterone with high renin
- D. High renin and low aldosterone indicating secondary hyperaldosteronism

**Answer: B** — ARR (aldosterone:renin ratio) is the best screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism. ARR >30 (with aldosterone >15 ng/dL) = positive screen → confirm with salt loading test or fludrocortisone suppression test → adrenal CT → adrenal vein sampling (to distinguish unilateral adenoma from bilateral hyperplasia). Unilateral adenoma → surgery. Bilateral hyperplasia → spironolactone/eplerenone.

---

**Q45.** 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency (CAH variant) differs from 21-hydroxylase deficiency in that

- A. It causes salt wasting due to aldosterone deficiency
- B. It causes hypertension due to accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone (a mineralocorticoid)
- C. It does not cause virilization in females
- D. It is more common than 21-hydroxylase deficiency

**Answer: B** — 11β-hydroxylase deficiency (~5% of CAH): blocks conversion of 11-deoxycortisol → cortisol AND 11-deoxycorticosterone → corticosterone. DOC (11-deoxycorticosterone) accumulates → potent mineralocorticoid effect → HYPERTENSION + hypokalemia (unlike 21-hydroxylase which causes salt wasting). Both: elevated androgens → virilization in females, elevated 17-OHP (11-beta) or 17-OHP + DOC.

---

## SECTION 9: PORPHYRIAS

**Q46.** Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) presents with the classic triad of

- A. Blistering photosensitive rash, hepatosplenomegaly, and hemolytic anemia
- B. Abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and dark urine — WITHOUT skin involvement
- C. Peripheral neuropathy, renal failure, and hypertension
- D. Photosensitivity, skin fragility, and hypertrichosis

**Answer: B** — AIP: porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency → ALA and PBG accumulate. No photosensitivity (porphyrins don't accumulate in skin). Precipitants: alcohol, OCP, barbiturates, sulfonamides, fasting, infection. Urine turns dark/port-wine on standing. Diagnosis: elevated urine PBG during attack. Treatment: IV hemin (heme arginate) + IV glucose (suppresses ALA synthase) + avoid triggers.

---

**Q47.** Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) differs from AIP in that it presents with

- A. Severe colicky abdominal pain and psychiatric features
- B. Motor neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction
- C. Elevated urinary PBG during attacks
- D. Blistering photosensitive skin lesions, skin fragility, and hypertrichosis on sun-exposed areas — NO neurological features

**Answer: D** — PCT: uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency → uroporphyrin accumulates in skin → photosensitivity, blistering, skin fragility, hypertrichosis, hyperpigmentation. Associated with: alcohol, hepatitis C, HIV, hemochromatosis (HFE mutations), estrogens. Urine fluoresces pink/red under Wood's lamp. Treatment: phlebotomy (removes iron which inhibits enzyme) + chloroquine (chelates porphyrins).

---

**Q48.** Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) presents with

- A. Abdominal pain and dark urine without skin involvement
- B. Immediate painful photosensitivity (burning, stinging) without blistering — unlike PCT
- C. Blistering rash identical to PCT
- D. Neuropsychiatric features and autonomic dysfunction

**Answer: B** — EPP: ferrochelatase deficiency → protoporphyrin accumulates in RBCs and skin. Immediate painful photosensitivity (within minutes of sun exposure) — burning, stinging, erythema. Characteristically NO blistering (unlike PCT). Can cause liver disease from protoporphyrin accumulation. Treatment: afamelanotide (alpha-MSH analogue → increases skin melanin), beta-carotene, sun avoidance.

---

**Q49.** The enzyme deficient in all acute porphyrias that leads to ALA accumulation when induced is

- A. Ferrochelatase
- B. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase
- C. ALA synthase 1 (ALAS1) — which is actually UPREGULATED, driving excess ALA production
- D. Coproporphyrinogen oxidase

**Answer: C** — In acute porphyrias, the specific enzyme block causes heme deficiency → derepresses ALAS1 (the rate-limiting enzyme) → ALAS1 upregulated → excess ALA (delta-aminolevulinic acid) produced → accumulates proximal to block → neurotoxicity. Drugs/hormones that induce CYP450 also induce ALAS1 → precipitate attacks. Hemin and glucose SUPPRESS ALAS1 → treat/prevent attacks.

---

**Q50.** Lead poisoning causes a porphyria-like syndrome by inhibiting

- A. Only ferrochelatase, causing protoporphyrin accumulation in RBCs
- B. ALA dehydratase AND ferrochelatase → ALA accumulates + zinc protoporphyrin (ZPP) accumulates in RBCs
- C. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase only
- D. Porphobilinogen deaminase causing AIP-like picture

**Answer: B** — Lead inhibits two enzymes: ALA dehydratase (early in pathway) → ALA accumulates (similar to AIP — can cause abdominal pain + neurological features) AND ferrochelatase (late) → zinc incorporated instead of iron → elevated ZPP in RBCs (useful screening test). Also causes: microcytic anaemia (basophilic stippling), encephalopathy, peripheral neuropathy (wrist/foot drop), renal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome). Treatment: chelation with DMSA or EDTA.

---
