mcq_sets.title: Respiratory Pathology — MCQ Bank

questions.question: A 45-year-old male smoker presents with chronic productive cough for 4 months every year for the past 3 years. What is the histologic hallmark in the large airways?
questions.explanation: Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically (3 months/year × 2 years). The histologic hallmark is enlarged submucosal mucous glands, quantified by the Reid index (>0.4 = abnormal).

questions.question: A child presents with inspiratory stridor and harsh barking cough. The most common causative agent is
questions.explanation: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is most commonly caused by parainfluenza virus in children. RSV can also cause it but is less common.

questions.question: A 30-year-old presents with spontaneous pneumothorax. The most likely underlying emphysema type is
questions.explanation: Paraseptal emphysema affects the distal acinus adjacent to the pleura, forming bullae. Rupture of subpleural bullae causes spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults.

questions.question: Which cytokine is released within 30 minutes of acute lung injury and drives neutrophil chemotaxis?
questions.explanation: IL-8 is released by pulmonary macrophages within 30 minutes of an acute insult. It is a potent neutrophil chemotactic and activating agent central to ARDS pathogenesis.

questions.question: The FEV1/FVC ratio is characteristically decreased in which condition?
questions.explanation: COPD (obstructive disease) reduces FEV1 significantly while FVC is near normal, giving a decreased FEV1/FVC ratio. Restrictive diseases maintain a near-normal ratio.

questions.question: A patient with α1-antitrypsin deficiency develops emphysema. Which type and distribution is expected?
questions.explanation: α1-antitrypsin deficiency leads to panacinar emphysema affecting the entire acinus, with lower lobe predominance. Over 80% of patients with this deficiency develop symptomatic emphysema.

questions.question: Which morphologic finding is the HALLMARK of ARDS on microscopy?
questions.explanation: Hyaline membranes (fibrin-rich edema fluid mixed with necrotic epithelial cells) lining distended alveolar ducts are the pathologic hallmark of ARDS/diffuse alveolar damage.

questions.question: Streptococcal tonsillitis is important to recognize early because it can lead to all EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Infectious mononucleosis is caused by EBV, not streptococcal infection. The three important complications of streptococcal tonsillitis are quinsy, glomerulonephritis, and rheumatic fever.

questions.question: A biopsy shows polypoid plugs of organizing connective tissue within alveolar ducts, all of the same age, with normal underlying lung architecture. The diagnosis is
questions.explanation: COP (formerly BOOP) is characterized by polypoid plugs of loose organizing connective tissue within alveolar ducts and bronchioles. All connective tissue is the same age (no temporal heterogeneity) and underlying architecture is preserved.

options: Undifferentiated type is most common and most linked to EBV
Keratinizing type is the most common variant
It is poorly radiosensitive with less than 10% survival
EBV genome is found only in Asian patients
questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE about nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Undifferentiated carcinoma is the most common variant and most closely associated with EBV. EBV genome is found in virtually ALL nasopharyngeal carcinomas regardless of geography.
questions.correct_answer_text: Undifferentiated type is most common and most linked to EBV

questions.question: A farmer presents with fever, cough, and dyspnea 6 hours after entering a barn with moldy hay. Serum shows precipitating antibodies. BAL shows increased CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Farmer's Lung) presents 4–8 hours after antigen exposure. Both Type III and Type IV hypersensitivity are involved. BAL shows increased CD4+ AND CD8+ T cells, distinguishing it from sarcoidosis (CD4+ only).

questions.question: A patient with asthma dies during status asthmaticus. Whorls of shed epithelium found within mucous plugs are called
questions.explanation: Curschmann spirals are whorls of shed epithelium found in the mucous plugs of asthma. Charcot-Leyden crystals are eosinophil protein crystalloids — both are found in asthma plugs.

options: Ratio of alveolar wall thickness to capillary diameter
Ratio of goblet cells to ciliated cells in epithelium
Ratio of FEV1 to FVC on spirometry
Ratio of submucosal gland thickness to bronchial wall thickness
questions.question: The Reid index in chronic bronchitis is
questions.explanation: The Reid index measures submucosal gland layer thickness divided by bronchial wall thickness. Normal is ≤0.4; chronic bronchitis exceeds 0.4 due to gland hypertrophy.
questions.correct_answer_text: Ratio of submucosal gland thickness to bronchial wall thickness

questions.question: Which lung cancer subtype is almost always metastatic at presentation and should NOT be treated surgically?
questions.explanation: SCLC is almost always metastatic at presentation. It is treated with chemotherapy, not surgery. Despite initial sensitivity to chemotherapy, it invariably recurs with a median survival of 1 year.

questions.question: Silicosis is associated with increased susceptibility to which infection?
questions.explanation: Silicosis depresses cell-mediated immunity and impairs macrophage killing of mycobacteria. The combination of silicosis and TB is called silicotuberculosis, with nodules showing central caseation.

questions.question: A 35-year-old presents with hemoptysis, anemia, diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Lung biopsy shows linear IgG deposition. The target antigen is
questions.explanation: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by antibodies targeting the noncollagenous domain of the α3 chain of collagen IV, affecting both pulmonary and glomerular basement membranes.

questions.question: A child develops multiple laryngeal papillomas that recur after excision. The causative HPV types are
questions.explanation: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis in children is caused by HPV types 6 and 11, transmitted vertically during delivery. These do not become malignant and often regress at puberty.

questions.question: Which emphysema type is 20 times more common than panacinar emphysema and is most associated with cigarette smoking?
questions.explanation: Centriacinar (centrilobular) emphysema affects the central/proximal acinus (respiratory bronchioles), sparing distal alveoli. It is strongly associated with cigarette smoking and affects the upper lobes predominantly.

options: Active vitamin D production by granuloma macrophages
questions.question: In sarcoidosis, hypercalcemia occurs due to
questions.explanation: In sarcoidosis, mononuclear phagocytes within granulomas produce active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), increasing intestinal calcium absorption and causing hypercalcemia.
questions.correct_answer_text: Active vitamin D production by granuloma macrophages

options: Asbestos fibers coated with iron-containing protein
Silica particles coated with calcium salts
questions.question: A 60-year-old asbestos worker develops progressive lower lobe fibrosis. Microscopy reveals interstitial fibrosis with golden-brown beaded rods. These structures consist of
questions.explanation: Asbestos bodies are asbestos fibers coated with iron-containing proteinaceous material derived from phagocyte ferritin. They appear as golden-brown, fusiform or beaded rods with a translucent center.
questions.correct_answer_text: Asbestos fibers coated with iron-containing protein

options: Poor hygiene increases bacterial colonization reducing asthma
Viral infections in childhood always prevent asthma development
Eradication of infections alters immune homeostasis promoting allergic responses
Helminth infections directly trigger bronchial hyperreactivity
questions.question: The "hygiene hypothesis" in asthma suggests that
questions.explanation: The hygiene hypothesis proposes that eradication of infections alters immune homeostasis and promotes allergic and other harmful immune responses, explaining the increased asthma incidence in Western countries.
questions.correct_answer_text: Eradication of infections alters immune homeostasis promoting allergic responses

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common manifestation of asbestos exposure?
questions.explanation: Pleural plaques are the most common manifestation of asbestos exposure. They are well-circumscribed plaques of dense collagen, often calcified, on the parietal pleura. They are usually asymptomatic.

questions.question: In Wegener granulomatosis, which ANCA subtype is positive in approximately 95% of cases?
questions.explanation: Wegener granulomatosis is associated with c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA — proteinase 3 antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody) in approximately 95% of cases. The classic triad includes upper respiratory, lower respiratory, and renal involvement.

options: Vascular congestion with protein-rich fluid and neutrophils
Lysis of red cells with persistent fibrinosuppurative exudate
Alveoli packed with neutrophils, red cells, and fibrin
Enzymatic digestion of exudate with macrophage clearance
questions.question: Lobar pneumonia evolves through four stages. What characterizes the "red hepatization" stage?
questions.explanation: Red hepatization follows congestion and is characterized by liver-like consistency of the lung. Alveolar spaces are packed with neutrophils, red blood cells, and fibrin — giving the red, firm appearance.
questions.correct_answer_text: Alveoli packed with neutrophils, red cells, and fibrin

questions.question: A patient with HIV and CD4 count of 150 cells/µL develops bilateral ground-glass perihilar infiltrates. BAL shows foamy alveolar exudate on H&E. GMS stain confirms the diagnosis. The organism is
questions.explanation: PCP (Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia) is the most common opportunistic infection in AIDS when CD4 <200. CXR shows bilateral ground-glass perihilar infiltrates. GMS stain shows cysts; H&E shows foamy exudate.

options: It is X-linked recessive with bronchiectasis
It involves structural ciliary abnormalities causing bronchiectasis and male sterility
It causes cystic fibrosis-like viscid mucus production
It results from immunoglobulin deficiency with recurrent infections
questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE about kartagener syndrome?
questions.explanation: Kartagener syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Structural ciliary abnormalities impair mucociliary clearance leading to bronchiectasis and recurrent infections, and reduce spermatozoa motility causing male sterility.
questions.correct_answer_text: It involves structural ciliary abnormalities causing bronchiectasis and male sterility

options: Distal acinar emphysema with bulla formation
questions.question: A 25-year-old non-smoker develops sudden chest pain and dyspnea. CXR shows a collapsed right lung. He is found to have multiple contiguous enlarged air spaces near the right pleural surface. This is
questions.explanation: Distal acinar (paraseptal) emphysema is most often seen in young adults with spontaneous pneumothorax. It affects the distal acinus adjacent to the pleura, forming characteristic bullae that can rupture.
questions.correct_answer_text: Distal acinar emphysema with bulla formation

questions.question: Eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes on CXR is characteristic of
questions.explanation: Eggshell calcification (calcium surrounding a zone lacking calcification in lymph nodes) is characteristic of silicosis. This represents calcium deposition around the periphery of the fibrotic lymph node.

options: Patchy interstitial fibrosis with temporal heterogeneity
Polypoid plugs of organizing connective tissue
questions.question: In IPF, the histologic pattern is called UIP. The hallmark of UIP is
questions.explanation: The hallmark of UIP (and thus IPF) is patchy interstitial fibrosis with temporal heterogeneity — early fibroblastic foci and late collagenous scars coexist in the same biopsy specimen.
questions.correct_answer_text: Patchy interstitial fibrosis with temporal heterogeneity

options: Obese patient with cyanosis, CO2 retention, and cor pulmonale
Patient with productive cough, hypercapnia, and frequent infections
Patient with barrel chest, dyspnea, prolonged expiration, adequate oxygenation
Thin patient with hemoptysis, night sweats, and upper lobe cavitation
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the "Pink Puffer" in emphysema?
questions.explanation: "Pink Puffer" describes pure emphysema: barrel chest, dyspnea, prolonged expiration (sitting hunched forward), but adequate oxygenation until late in disease. They hyperventilate to maintain oxygen levels.
questions.correct_answer_text: Patient with barrel chest, dyspnea, prolonged expiration, adequate oxygenation

options: Deep veins of the lower legs
Pelvic veins and inferior vena cava
questions.question: More than 95% of pulmonary emboli arise from thrombi in
questions.explanation: Over 95% of pulmonary emboli originate from thrombi in the deep veins of the lower legs, typically in the popliteal vein and larger veins above it.
questions.correct_answer_text: Deep veins of the lower legs

questions.question: A 50-year-old male develops progressive dyspnea over 2 years. Lung biopsy shows honeycomb fibrosis, fibroblastic foci, and temporal heterogeneity. Mean survival from diagnosis is approximately
questions.explanation: IPF has a mean survival of 3 years or less from diagnosis, with relentless progression despite medical therapy. Lung transplantation is the only definitive treatment.

questions.question: Which cell type is central to the pathogenesis of atopic asthma?
questions.explanation: TH2 cells are central to atopic asthma. They produce IL-4 (IgE production), IL-5 (eosinophil activation), and IL-13 (mucus production), orchestrating the allergic inflammatory response.

questions.question: A lung carcinoma secretes PTHrP causing hypercalcemia. Which histologic type is most commonly responsible?
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia from PTHrP secretion (paraneoplastic) is most commonly associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. This is distinct from hypercalcemia caused by osteolytic metastases.

options: Caseous lymph node plus pleural effusion
Subpleural nodule plus hilar/lymph node involvement
questions.question: The Ghon complex in primary tuberculosis consists of
questions.explanation: The Ghon complex = Ghon focus (subpleural nodule, often upper part of lower lobe) + lymphatic drainage + hilar lymph node involvement. When calcified, it becomes the Ranke complex.
questions.correct_answer_text: Subpleural nodule plus hilar/lymph node involvement

options: Respiratory distress out of proportion to radiologic signs
Alveolar spaces filled with neutrophilic exudate
High fever with productive purulent sputum
questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of atypical pneumonia that distinguishes it from typical bacterial pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Atypical pneumonia is characterized by respiratory distress disproportionate to clinical/radiologic findings. Inflammation is predominantly interstitial (alveolar septa), with alveolar spaces generally clear.
questions.correct_answer_text: Respiratory distress out of proportion to radiologic signs

options: PH secondary to recurrent pulmonary embolism
PH secondary to chronic lung disease
questions.question: In pulmonary hypertension, plexiform lesions are characteristic of which type?
questions.explanation: Plexiform lesions — endothelial proliferation forming multiple lumina within small arteries — are characteristic of idiopathic (primary) pulmonary arterial hypertension, not secondary forms.

questions.question: A patient with systemic sclerosis develops bilateral interstitial lung disease. The most common histologic pattern in systemic sclerosis lung involvement is
questions.explanation: NSIP is the most common histologic pattern of lung involvement in collagen vascular diseases, particularly systemic sclerosis. UIP pattern can also occur but NSIP predominates.

questions.question: A 70-year-old male with a 50-pack-year smoking history develops progressive dyspnea. Spirometry shows FEV1 40% predicted, FVC 75% predicted. What is the FEV1/FVC pattern?
questions.explanation: FEV1/FVC = 40/75 = 0.53, which is significantly decreased (normal >0.70). This decreased ratio is the characteristic finding in obstructive lung disease such as COPD.

options: Inhibits COX → shifts arachidonic acid toward leukotriene production
Directly stimulates IgE production against salicylate
Activates mast cell degranulation via IgE-independent mechanism
questions.question: Aspirin-induced asthma occurs because aspirin
questions.explanation: Aspirin inhibits the cyclooxygenase (COX) pathway without affecting lipoxygenase, shifting arachidonic acid metabolism toward leukotriene production. Leukotrienes are potent bronchoconstrictors.
questions.correct_answer_text: Inhibits COX → shifts arachidonic acid toward leukotriene production

questions.question: A coal miner develops multiple intensely black scars >2 cm in diameter in the lungs. This represents
questions.explanation: Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF/complicated CWP) is characterized by multiple intensely black scars >2 cm (up to 10 cm). It develops from coalescence of coal nodules and causes significant pulmonary dysfunction.

options: Broad-based budding yeast with thick walls
Small yeast forms within alveolar macrophages
Non-septate ribbon-like hyphae at right angles
questions.question: Coccidioidomycosis is pathognomonic for which histologic finding?
questions.explanation: Coccidioides immitis forms characteristic spherules — large round structures containing endospores — in tissue. This is pathognomonic for coccidioidomycosis and distinguishes it from other fungal infections.

options: Lymph nodes are matted and may ulcerate like in TB
Peripheral lymphadenopathy occurs but nodes are nonadherent
Lymph node involvement occurs in less than 25% of cases
Lymph nodes always show caseating granulomas
questions.question: Which of the following regarding sarcoidosis lymph node involvement is CORRECT?
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis lymph nodes are characteristically "nonmatted" (nonadherent) and do not ulcerate — unlike tuberculosis where nodes are matted. Hilar/paratracheal nodes are enlarged in 75–90% of patients.
questions.correct_answer_text: Peripheral lymphadenopathy occurs but nodes are nonadherent

options: It is caused by mucous plugs blocking airways
It is caused by pleural fluid compressing the lung
It is irreversible due to fibrotic changes
It is the most common type postoperatively
questions.question: Contraction (cicatrization) atelectasis differs from the other types because
questions.explanation: Contraction atelectasis occurs when local or generalized fibrosis hampers lung expansion and increases elastic recoil. Unlike resorption and compression atelectasis, it is irreversible.
questions.correct_answer_text: It is irreversible due to fibrotic changes

questions.question: In malignant mesothelioma, which immunohistochemical marker is positive (distinguishing it from adenocarcinoma)?
questions.explanation: Calretinin is positive in mesothelioma and negative in adenocarcinoma. Conversely, CEA, TTF-1, and MOC-31 are positive in adenocarcinoma and negative in mesothelioma.

questions.question: A patient develops fever, dyspnea, and pulmonary infiltrates exactly matching the radiation field 4 months after thoracic radiotherapy. This is
questions.explanation: Acute radiation pneumonitis occurs 1–6 months after therapy in up to 20% of patients. Infiltrates precisely corresponding to the radiation field is the diagnostic clue. It may resolve with corticosteroids.

questions.question: A 10-year-old child presents with hemoptysis and anemia. Investigation shows no renal disease and no anti-GBM antibody. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis has the same pulmonary features as Goodpasture (hemoptysis, anemia, diffuse infiltrates) but with NO renal disease and NO anti-GBM antibody. It predominantly affects children.

options: Abnormal chloride transport causing viscid mucus
Structural ciliary abnormalities impairing mucociliary clearance
Chronic aspiration causing repeated necrotizing pneumonia
questions.question: Bronchiectasis in Kartagener syndrome results from
questions.explanation: Kartagener syndrome involves structural ciliary abnormalities (autosomal recessive). Impaired mucociliary clearance leads to persistent infections, bronchial wall destruction, and bronchiectasis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Structural ciliary abnormalities impairing mucociliary clearance

options: Increased vasodilator production by endothelial cells
Abnormal endothelial and smooth muscle cell proliferation
Increased serotonin transporter expression on smooth muscle
Enhanced prostacyclin synthesis in pulmonary arteries
questions.question: The BMPR-2 gene mutation in primary pulmonary hypertension leads to
questions.explanation: BMPR-2 normally inhibits cell proliferation. Loss-of-function mutations found in 50% of familial primary pulmonary hypertension cases result in abnormal vascular endothelial and smooth muscle proliferation.
questions.correct_answer_text: Abnormal endothelial and smooth muscle cell proliferation

questions.question: Which organism most commonly causes community-acquired lobar pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) causes more than 90% of lobar pneumonias and is the most common cause of community-acquired acute pneumonia overall.

options: Type II pneumocytes proliferating in response to injury
Alveolar macrophages accumulating due to smoking
Neutrophils in response to chronic infection
questions.question: DIP (desquamative interstitial pneumonia) gets its name because early pathologists thought the cells filling alveoli were desquamated epithelial cells. They are actually
questions.explanation: The cells filling alveoli in DIP are alveolar macrophages (smoker's macrophages) containing dusty-brown pigment. The name is a misnomer — early pathologists incorrectly identified them as desquamated epithelial cells.
questions.correct_answer_text: Alveolar macrophages accumulating due to smoking

options: Immune complex deposition in bronchial walls
Viscid mucus causing obstruction followed by infection
questions.question: A patient with cystic fibrosis develops severe irreversible airway dilation. The pathogenesis of bronchiectasis in this setting involves
questions.explanation: In cystic fibrosis, abnormally viscid mucus causes bronchial obstruction, predisposing to recurrent infections. The combination of obstruction and chronic necrotizing infection leads to irreversible bronchiectasis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Viscid mucus causing obstruction followed by infection

options: Type II pneumocytes in alveolar walls
Kulchitsky neuroendocrine cells in bronchial epithelium
Mucous gland cells in large bronchi
Mesothelial cells of the visceral pleura
questions.question: Carcinoid tumors of the lung arise from which cells?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary carcinoid tumors arise from Kulchitsky cells (neuroendocrine cells) of the bronchial epithelium. They represent 1–5% of lung tumors and are less aggressive than SCLC.
questions.correct_answer_text: Kulchitsky neuroendocrine cells in bronchial epithelium

options: Irregular cavitary lesion with necrotic center
Diffuse bilateral consolidation of lower lobes
Wedge-shaped, base at pleura, apex toward hilum
questions.question: A pulmonary infarct after embolism has which morphologic shape?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary infarcts are characteristically wedge-shaped with the base at the pleural surface and apex pointing toward the hilum. About 3/4 affect the lower lobes and more than half are multiple.
questions.correct_answer_text: Wedge-shaped, base at pleura, apex toward hilum

options: Magnesium trisilicate (talc) from IV drug mixture
questions.question: A young man uses intravenous drugs and develops pulmonary hypertension. Lung biopsy shows granulomas with birefringent crystals under polarized light. The likely substance is
questions.explanation: IV drug abuse introduces magnesium trisilicate (talc) as a filler in drug mixtures into the pulmonary microvasculature. Talc elicits a granulomatous response; vascular involvement leads to pulmonary hypertension. Talc crystals are visible by polarized light.
questions.correct_answer_text: Magnesium trisilicate (talc) from IV drug mixture

options: Presence of fibroblastic foci and honeycombing in NSIP
Noncaseating granulomas present only in NSIP
Lower lobe predominance only seen in NSIP
Absence of temporal heterogeneity in NSIP
questions.question: Which of the following differentiates NSIP from IPF on lung biopsy?
questions.explanation: NSIP lacks the temporal heterogeneity of UIP/IPF. In NSIP, fibrosis is uniform (all the same age). Fibroblastic foci and honeycombing are typically absent in NSIP but present in IPF.
questions.correct_answer_text: Absence of temporal heterogeneity in NSIP

options: Dry arid soil of the southwestern United States
Forest soil of the Great Lakes region of North America
Soil enriched with bird and bat droppings (Mississippi/Ohio valleys)
Tropical soil with decaying vegetation in Southeast Asia
questions.question: Histoplasma capsulatum infection is associated with which geographic reservoir?
questions.explanation: Histoplasma capsulatum is endemic in the Mississippi/Ohio River valleys. Its reservoir is soil enriched with bird and bat droppings. Infection occurs by inhalation of microconidia.
questions.correct_answer_text: Soil enriched with bird and bat droppings (Mississippi/Ohio valleys)

options: The lung has dual blood supply from pulmonary and bronchial arteries
Most emboli are too small to cause significant obstruction
Fibrinolysis rapidly resolves most emboli before infarction
Collateral circulation from adjacent lung segments prevents necrosis
questions.question: In pulmonary embolism, infarction occurs in only about 10% of cases because
questions.explanation: The lung is protected from infarction by its dual blood supply: pulmonary arteries, bronchial arteries, and direct oxygenation from alveolar air. Infarction only occurs when this is compromised.
questions.correct_answer_text: The lung has dual blood supply from pulmonary and bronchial arteries

options: Cutaneous sarcoid granulomas on the legs
Chronic skin infiltration by noncaseating granulomas
Hallmark of acute sarcoidosis — raised tender nodules on anterior legs
Subcutaneous sarcoid nodules with abundant granulomas
questions.question: Erythema nodosum in sarcoidosis represents
questions.explanation: Erythema nodosum is the hallmark of acute sarcoidosis. It consists of rais
questions.correct_answer_text: Hallmark of acute sarcoidosis — raised tender nodules on anterior legs

{"type":"weekly_exam","unit":"Year 2: GIT Physiology","saqs":[{"question":"Describe the mechanism and clinical significance of the enterogastric reflex.","answer":"The enterogastric reflex is a neuro-humoral response triggered by the presence of chyme (acid, distension, hypertonicity, or fats) in the duodenum. Mechanism: It inhibits gastric motility and secretion via the enteric nervous system, sympathetic nerves, and the vagus nerve. Humoral components involve secretin and CCK. Significance: It prevents the overfilling of the duodenum and ensures the acidity of gastric contents is neutralized before further digestion.","marks":5},{"question":"Outline the role and ionic composition of primary versus modified saliva.","answer":"Primary saliva is produced by acinar cells and is isotonic to plasma (rich in Na+, Cl-, and water). As it passes through the salivary ducts, it is modified: Na+ and Cl- are reabsorbed, while K+ and HCO3- are secreted. Because the ductal epithelium is relatively impermeable to water, the final saliva is hypotonic. This allows for optimal taste bud function and oral hygiene.","marks":5},{"question":"Explain the cellular mechanism of hydrochloric acid (HCl) secretion by parietal cells.","answer":"Parietal cells use H+/K+ ATPase (proton pumps) on the apical membrane to pump H+ into the lumen in exchange for K+. H+ is generated by the action of carbonic anhydrase on CO2 and H2O. Cl- follows H+ into the lumen through chloride channels to maintain electroneutrality. On the basolateral side, HCO3- is exchanged for Cl- (alkaline tide). This process is stimulated by Gastrin, Histamine (H2), and Acetylcholine (M3).","marks":5},{"question":"Describe the Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) and its physiological importance.","answer":"The MMC is a distinct pattern of electromechanical activity observed in the GI smooth muscle during fasting. It consists of four phases, with Phase III being the most active (intense contractions). It is mediated primarily by the hormone Motilin. Its physiological importance is to act as a 'housekeeper' to sweep undigested debris, excess mucus, and bacteria from the stomach and small intestine into the colon.","marks":5},{"question":"Summarize the absorption process of Vitamin B12 in the gastrointestinal tract.","answer":"Vitamin B12 is released from food protein in the stomach and binds to R-binders (haptocorrin). In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases digest R-binders, and B12 binds to Intrinsic Factor (IF) secreted by gastric parietal cells. The B12-IF complex travels to the terminal ileum, where it binds to specific cubilin receptors and is internalized via endocytosis for transport into the blood.","marks":5},{"question":"Explain the role of Bile Salts in lipid digestion and the Enterohepatic Circulation.","answer":"Bile salts act as detergents, emulsifying large fat droplets into smaller micelles to increase the surface area for lipase action. They are amphipathic molecules. 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum via active transport and returned to the liver via the portal vein (enterohepatic circulation). This recycling minimizes the need for new bile acid synthesis by the liver.","marks":5}],"laqs":[{"question":"Discuss the three phases of gastric secretion control. In your answer, include the stimuli for each phase, the neural/hormonal pathways involved, and how the pancreas coordinates its exocrine secretions with these phases.","answer":"1. Cephalic Phase (30% secretion): Stimulated by the sight, smell, or thought of food. Mediated via the Vagus nerve (Vagal-vagal reflex), releasing Acetylcholine to stimulate parietal cells and G-cells (via Gastrin Releasing Peptide). 
2. Gastric Phase (60% secretion): Triggered by food entering the stomach causing distension and chemical stimuli (amino acids/peptides). Distension activates long and short reflexes. Peptides stimulate G-cells to release Gastrin. 
3. Intestinal Phase (10% secretion): Initially excitatory (brief gastrin release from duodenum) then primarily inhibitory. When chyme enters the duodenum, secretin and CCK are released. Secretin inhibits gastrin and stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion. CCK stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion. 
Pancreatic Coordination: During the cephalic and gastric phases, vagal stimulation prepares the pancreas. During the intestinal phase, the hormone secretin responds to low pH to trigger HCO3- (neutralization), while CCK responds to fats/proteins to trigger digestive enzymes (lipase, amylase, proteases). Together they ensure optimal pH and enzymatic conditions for nutrient absorption.","marks":20}],"generated_at":"2026-04-03T00:00:24.125Z"}

{"type":"weekly_exam","unit":"Year 2: GIT Physiology","saqs":[{"question":"Describe the mechanism of gastric acid secretion by the parietal cell, including the specific transporters involved and the role of the 'alkaline tide'.","answer":"Parietal cells use H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) to secret H+ into the lumen against a gradient. Carbonic anhydrase converts CO2 and H2O into H2CO3, which dissociates into H+ and HCO3-. H+ is pumped out, while K+ recycles through channels. HCO3- is transported out of the basolateral membrane into the blood via a Cl-/HCO3- exchanger (causing the 'alkaline tide' post-prandially), and Cl- follows H+ into the lumen via chloride channels to form HCl.","marks":5},{"question":"Outline the components and physiological significance of the Migrating Motor Complex (MMC).","answer":"The MMC is a series of strong electrical and mechanical waves that occur during fasting. It consists of four phases: Phase I (quiescence), Phase II (irregular activity), Phase III (intense contractions/climax), and Phase IV (transition). It is regulated by the hormone motilin. Its primary function is to 'sweep' residual undigested food and bacteria from the stomach and small intestine into the colon, preventing bacterial overgrowth.","marks":5},{"question":"Explain the 'Enterohepatic Circulation' of bile salts and its importance in lipid digestion.","answer":"Bile salts are synthesized in the liver from cholesterol, secreted into the duodenum to emulsify fats, and move to the ileum. 95% of bile salts are actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver via the portal vein. This recycling (6-10 times/day) is essential because the liver's rate of bile acid synthesis cannot meet the daily demand for lipid digestion and absorption.","marks":5},{"question":"Compare and contrast the role of Secretin and Cholecystokinin (CCK) in the regulation of pancreatic secretion.","answer":"Secretin is released from S-cells in response to acid in the duodenum; it primarily stimulates the pancreatic ductal cells to secrete a bicarbonate-rich aqueous fluid to neutralize acid. CCK is released from I-cells in response to fatty acids and amino acids; it primarily stimulates pancreatic acinar cells to secrete digestive enzymes (lipase, amylase, proteases). Both hormones act synergistically for optimal digestion.","marks":5},{"question":"Describe the physiological mechanisms that protect the gastric mucosa from autodigestion.","answer":"The gastric mucosal barrier consists of: 1) A thick layer of bicarbonate-rich mucus that neutralizes acid at the cell surface. 2) Tight junctions between epithelial cells preventing H+ back-diffusion. 3) High regenerative capacity of the epithelium. 4) Prostaglandins (E2/I2) which inhibit acid secretion, stimulate mucus/bicarbonate production, and maintain high mucosal blood flow to remove any diffusing H+.","marks":5},{"question":"Explain the cellular mechanism of water and sodium absorption in the small intestine.","answer":"Sodium absorption occurs via three main pathways: 1) Co-transport with glucose (SGLT1) or amino acids. 2) Na+/H+ exchange. 3) Parallel Na+/H+ and Cl-/HCO3- exchange. Sodium is then pumped into the lateral intercellular spaces by the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase. This creates an osmotic gradient that pulls water through the paracellular (tight junctions) and transcellular (aquaporins) pathways into the blood.","marks":5}],"laqs":[{"question":"Discuss the phases of gastric secretion regulation (Cephalic, Gastric, and Intestinal) and describe the physiological basis of fat malabsorption (steatorrhea).","answer":"1. Gastric Secretion Phases (12 marks): 
- Cephalic: Triggered by sight/smell/taste of food. Mediated by the Vagus nerve (ACh) stimulating parietal cells and G-cells (Gastrin). Accounts for ~30% of secretion. 
- Gastric: Triggered by stomach distension (vagovagal and local enteric reflexes) and presence of peptides/amino acids (G-cell stimulation). Accounts for ~60% of secretion. 
- Intestinal: Triggered by chyme entering the duodenum. Initially stimulatory (gastrin release), then inhibitory via the enterogastric reflex and 'enterogastrones' (Secretin, CCK, GIP) as pH drops and fats/osmolality increase. 

2. Fat Malabsorption/Steatorrhea (8 marks): 
- Physiological causes: Pancreatic insufficiency (lack of lipase/colipase), Bile acid deficiency (obstruction or ileal resection preventing emulsification), Mucosal damage (Celiac disease reducing surface area), or Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison; low pH inactivates lipase). 
- Result: Presence of undigested fat in stool, leading to bulky, foul-smelling, oily stools and deficiency in fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).","marks":20}],"generated_at":"2026-03-13T00:00:21.603Z"}

Is application of simple tests across healthy population before symptoms develop
questions.question: Screening of cancers
questions.explanation: Screening involves applying simple tests to a healthy population before symptoms develop to detect cancer early.

Is currently only possible for pancreatic and ovarian cancers
questions.question: Early detection of cancers
questions.explanation: Early detection encompasses timely diagnosis, including early diagnosis in symptomatic patients and screening in asymptomatic individuals.
questions.correct_answer_text: Is a concept of timely diagnosis including early diagnosis and screening

options: About 33% of cancer cases linked to tobacco smoke
About 10 million deaths in 2020 attributed to cancer
The four mentioned account for more than 40% of all cancers diagnosed
Four most common cancers are breast, lung, bowel and prostate
questions.question: Which is NOT true regarding global cancer statistics?
questions.explanation: The incidence of cancer is increasing globally, not in sharp decline.
questions.correct_answer_text: About 10 million deaths in 2020 attributed to cancer

options: Breast cancer has highest mortality among all cancers
Cancer is the leading cause of death
Risk of death from cancer before age 75 is 20.6%
Risk of developing cancer before age 75 is 14.3% among men and 18% among women
questions.question: In Kenya
questions.explanation: In Kenya, cancer is not the leading cause of death; infectious diseases still lead. The stated risks are correct.

options: Squamous dysplasia of bronchial mucosa in smokers is a risk factor for lung cancer
Removal of precursor lesions does not prevent development of cancer
Squamous metaplasia of bronchial mucosa in smokers is NOT a risk factor
Endometrial hyperplasia and dysplasia with unopposed oestrogen is risk for endometrial carcinoma
questions.question: One of the following is NOT true regarding precursor lesions
questions.explanation: Removal of precursor lesions DOES prevent cancer development. That is the purpose of screening and early intervention.
questions.correct_answer_text: Removal of precursor lesions does not prevent development of cancer

options: Are associated with high risk of transformation to colorectal carcinoma
Develop cancerous change in about 5% of cases
questions.question: Villous adenomas of the colon
questions.explanation: Villous adenomas have the highest malignant potential among colorectal polyps, with a significant risk of transformation.
questions.correct_answer_text: Are associated with high risk of transformation to colorectal carcinoma

questions.question: The following are responsible for alveolar damage in ARDS EXCEPT
questions.explanation: IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that suppresses inflammation, while the others actively damage alveoli in ARDS.

questions.question: Which is NOT a diffuse obstructive pulmonary disease?
questions.explanation: Atelectasis is lung collapse, not an obstructive disease characterized by difficulty exhaling.

questions.question: Which is NOT a typical finding in COPD?
questions.explanation: In COPD, the FEV1 to FVC ratio is DECREASED below 0.70, indicating airflow obstruction.

options: Has a weak epidemiologic link to EBV
Tends to be accompanied with atypical lymphocytosis
questions.question: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma has a strong link to EBV and is notably radiosensitive, making radiotherapy a primary treatment.

questions.question: Which tumour suppressor gene abnormality is most common in BOTH SCLC and NSCLC?
questions.explanation: 3p deletions occur in virtually all lung cancers, regardless of histological type, and involve multiple tumour suppressor genes.

questions.question: Fluid cytopathology specimens include the following EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Lump aspirate is obtained by Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA), which is aspiration cytology, not fluid cytopathology.

questions.question: Which are the most frequent sites of venous thrombosis?
questions.explanation: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) most commonly occurs in the deep veins of the lower extremities.

options: Decreased hydrostatic pressure and increased osmotic pressure
Active process leading to increased volume of blood
questions.question: In a state of shock there is
questions.explanation: Shock is defined as the failure of the cardiovascular system to maintain adequate tissue perfusion, leading to cardiovascular collapse.

questions.question: Which disorder most likely associated with EXUDATE rather than transudate?
questions.explanation: Suppurative inflammation, characterized by pus formation, results in exudate, which is protein-rich and inflammatory.

questions.question: Heart failure cells in lungs are actually
questions.explanation: Heart failure cells are macrophages that have phagocytosed red blood cells that have leaked into the alveoli due to increased pulmonary venous pressure in left heart failure.

questions.question: Hallmark of ACUTE inflammation
questions.explanation: The key hallmark of acute inflammation is increased vascular permeability, allowing plasma proteins and leukocytes to enter tissues.

options: Migration of macrophages at site of injury
questions.question: Hallmark of CHRONIC inflammation
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation is characterized by infiltration of mononuclear cells like lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages.

questions.question: Granulomatous inflammation is characterized by all the following EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Central caseous necrosis is typical of tuberculosis and some fungal infections, but not all granulomatous inflammation features it.

questions.question: The hallmark of acute inflammation
questions.explanation: Increased vascular permeability is the defining hallmark of acute inflammation, leading to the cardinal signs.

questions.question: Which of the following is the hallmark of acute inflammation?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are the characteristic cellular hallmark of acute inflammation, acting as the first responders.

questions.question: Which is a reversible change?
questions.explanation: Swelling of organelles, such as the endoplasmic reticulum, is an early reversible change in cell injury.

questions.question: Which mediates systemic effects of inflammation, chemotaxis and stimulates adhesion molecules?
questions.explanation: IL-1 and TNF are key mediators of systemic inflammatory effects, including fever and induction of adhesion molecules.

questions.question: Which of the following is a 38 year old man's wound — 4cm circumscribed mass with peripheral brightness on x-ray that gradually resolves — best described as?
questions.explanation: The description of a mass with peripheral brightness on X-ray that resolves and is attributed to heterotopic bone formation after trauma is consistent with myositis ossificans, a form of metaplasia.

questions.question: Growth factor elaborated by macrophages recruiting macrophages and fibroblasts and inducing ALL steps of angiogenesis
questions.explanation: Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) is the primary mediator of angiogenesis, inducing all its steps.

questions.question: A 20-year-old with lacerated wound stitched. One week later prominent raised irregular nodular scar develops. Best describes
questions.explanation: A prominent, raised, irregular nodular scar extending beyond wound margins is characteristic of a keloid.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a malignant tumour?
questions.explanation: Leiomyoma is a benign smooth muscle tumor. Its malignant counterpart is leiomyosarcoma.

questions.question: Burkitt lymphoma in Kenya — which lymphoproliferative disorder is common in children?
questions.explanation: Burkitt Lymphoma is the most common childhood cancer in equatorial Africa, strongly associated with EBV and endemic in the malaria belt.

questions.question: Which tumour marker for ovarian cancer?
questions.explanation: CA 125 is the primary tumor marker used for ovarian cancer detection and monitoring.

options: Germ cell tumours are most common testicular neoplasms
Cryptorchidism and infertility are risk factors
Nonseminomatous tumors spread early via lymphatic and hematogenous routes
questions.question: True of testicular tumours EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Seminomas are highly sensitive to radiotherapy, making it an effective treatment modality.

options: Cellular monomorphism and lack of reticulin network
questions.question: Which is a characteristic feature of pituitary adenomas?
questions.explanation: Pituitary adenomas are typically characterized by uniform, monomorphic cells and a loss of the normal reticulin network.
questions.correct_answer_text: Cellular monomorphism and lack of reticulin network

options: Within superficial mucus overlying epithelial cells
Within cytoplasm of glandular epithelial cells
questions.question: H. pylori organisms predominantly demonstrated
questions.explanation: H. pylori colonizes the superficial mucus layer overlying gastric epithelial cells.
questions.correct_answer_text: Within superficial mucus overlying epithelial cells

questions.question: Defects in celiac disease include
questions.explanation: Celiac disease affects all stages of nutrient absorption, including intraluminal digestion, terminal digestion, and transport via blood and lymphatics.

options: Release of chloride ions into lumen after opening of CFTR
questions.question: Features of Vibrio cholerae infection include
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin causes excessive chloride ion release into the lumen via CFTR, leading to massive fluid loss.
questions.correct_answer_text: Release of chloride ions into lumen after opening of CFTR

questions.question: NOT a feature of Crohn's disease
questions.explanation: Toxic megacolon is a characteristic complication of Ulcerative Colitis, not typically Crohn's disease.

questions.question: Features of C. difficile infection EXCEPT
questions.explanation: C. difficile infection leads to damage and sloughing of the epithelium, not hyperplasia.

questions.question: 43-year-old with burning substernal pain. Biopsies show columnar epithelium with goblet cells above GEJ. This represents
questions.explanation: The presence of columnar epithelium with goblet cells above the gastroesophageal junction is known as Barrett's esophagus, a form of intestinal metaplasia.

options: Peaks in incidence at age 20 years
Always manifested by cytological atypia and dysplasia
Is slow but inevitable progression to cervical cancer
questions.question: Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia
questions.explanation: By definition, CIN represents cytological atypia and dysplasia, which are the cellular changes seen in this precancerous condition.
questions.correct_answer_text: Always manifested by cytological atypia and dysplasia

questions.question: Aetiological theories for endometriosis EXCEPT
questions.explanation: The neoplastic theory is not a recognized etiological theory for endometriosis. Theories include regurgitation, metaplasia, and dissemination.

options: It is the most common type
TP53 mutations in nearly all cases
Exposure to unopposed oestrogen is a risk factor
questions.question: True of serous endometrial cancer
questions.explanation: TP53 mutations are found in nearly all cases of serous endometrial cancer, which is an aggressive, non-estrogen-dependent subtype.
questions.correct_answer_text: TP53 mutations in nearly all cases

options: Occur most frequently in cervix uteri
questions.question: Leiomyomata
questions.explanation: Leiomyomas (fibroids) are often asymptomatic, multiple, and found in women of reproductive age. They are estrogen-dependent and shrink after menopause.

questions.question: Most frequent tumours of the ovary
questions.explanation: Surface epithelial-stromal cell tumors are the most common type of ovarian neoplasms, accounting for 65-70% of cases.

questions.question: Fixative used on cervical smear samples
questions.explanation: Cervical smear samples (Pap smears) are typically fixed immediately with 95% ethanol to preserve cellular morphology.

questions.question: What condition does cervical smear test screen for
questions.explanation: Cervical smear tests (Pap smears) are used to screen for Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia (CIN) and cervical cancer.

questions.question: Which is the most common subtype of malignant renal neoplasms?
questions.explanation: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma is the most common subtype of renal cell carcinoma, accounting for 70-80% of cases.

mcq_sets.title: Haematopathology MCQs: Blood Disorders, Lymphoma & Anemia

questions.question: Leukemoid reactions are almost always a sign of?
questions.explanation: Leukemoid reactions — very high WBC counts with immature cells — are most commonly a reactive response to severe infection/sepsis.

options: Stage I & II confined above diaphragm
questions.question: True statement about staging of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma?
questions.explanation: CT scanning is standard for staging NHL; Burkitt's is a B-cell lymphoma, and stages have very different prognoses.

questions.question: Which increases dietary iron uptake by the alimentary canal?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺, the absorbable form, enhancing non-haem iron absorption.

questions.question: Abnormality of nuclear segmentation in neutrophils?
questions.explanation: Pelger-Huet anomaly is characterized by hyposegmented (bilobed "pince-nez") neutrophil nuclei.

questions.question: Burkitt's lymphoma chromosomal translocations involve?
questions.explanation: Burkitt's lymphoma involves t(8;14) placing c-myc under IGH control, causing uncontrolled cell proliferation.

questions.question: Elderly woman with corkscrew hair follicles, perifollicular hemorrhages, gum bleeding — deficiency of?
questions.explanation: Perifollicular hemorrhage and corkscrew hairs are classic signs of scurvy (Vitamin C deficiency), as collagen synthesis is impaired.

questions.question: Which red cell abnormality is most indicative of haemolysis?
questions.explanation: Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs) are the hallmark of mechanical hemolysis, seen in microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and TTP/HUS.

questions.question: Markedly decreased blood level most characteristic of intravascular haemolysis?
questions.explanation: Free haemoglobin released in intravascular haemolysis binds and depletes haptoglobin rapidly.

questions.question: Dashed curve on osmotic fragility test represents?
questions.explanation: Spherocytes have less surface area relative to volume, making them lyse at higher NaCl concentrations — a right-shifted curve.

questions.question: Patient on primaquine develops bite cells and Heinz bodies — diagnosis?
questions.explanation: G6PD-deficient RBCs cannot neutralize oxidative stress from primaquine; denatured Hb forms Heinz bodies and macrophages bite them out.

questions.question: Test to detect haemoglobin S (sickle cell trait)?
questions.explanation: Sodium metabisulfite deoxygenates blood, inducing sickling of HbS-containing cells — a simple screening test.

questions.question: Valine replacing glutamic acid at position 6 of beta chain is associated with?
questions.explanation: This single amino acid substitution (Glu→Val) causes HbS polymerization under deoxygenation, the basis of sickle cell disease.

questions.question: 67-year-old with elevated PSA, myelocytes on blood film, nucleated RBCs, no teardrop cells — best diagnosis for anaemia?
questions.explanation: Metastatic prostate cancer to bone marrow displaces normal haematopoiesis, releasing immature cells (leukoerythroblastic picture).

questions.question: Megaloblasts result from impaired synthesis of?
questions.explanation: B12 and folate are required for thymidine synthesis; without them, DNA replication is impaired, causing nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony.

questions.question: TIBC is inversely proportional to serum levels of?
questions.explanation: When iron stores (ferritin) are high, TIBC decreases; when stores are low, TIBC increases.

questions.question: MCV 70 fL, MCH 22 pg, MCHC 34% — most consistent diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Low MCV + low MCH = microcytic hypochromic anaemia, classic for iron deficiency.

questions.question: Patient on sulphonamide with isolated neutropenia due to antineutrophil antibodies — expected bone marrow finding?
questions.explanation: The marrow compensates by ramping up production of neutrophils in response to their peripheral destruction.

questions.question: Parasitic infections (trichinosis, schistosomiasis, strongyloidiasis) cause elevated numbers of?
questions.explanation: Tissue-invasive parasites trigger Th2 immune responses and IgE production, driving eosinophilia.

questions.question: Reactive T immunoblasts in enlarged lymph nodes during viral infection are found in which region?
questions.explanation: The paracortex is the T-cell zone of the lymph node; it expands during viral infections.

questions.question: Low-grade NHL with cells similar to CLL?
questions.explanation: SLL and CLL are essentially the same disease — SLL is the tissue/lymph node form, CLL is the blood/marrow form.

questions.question: Lacunar cells are variants of Reed-Sternberg cells found specifically in?
questions.explanation: Lacunar cells are RS cell variants pathognomonic of the nodular sclerosis subtype.

questions.question: 28-year-old male with Auer rods in blast cells making up 38% of marrow — diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Auer rods in granular blasts + DIC is classic for APL with t(15;17).

questions.question: 4-year-old with TdT+, PAS+, MPO− blasts — cells originated from?
questions.explanation: TdT is a marker of immature lymphoid cells; MPO negativity rules out myeloid origin.

questions.question: Hairy cell leukemia suspected — which stain is useful?
questions.explanation: Hairy cells are TRAP-positive (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase) — a classic diagnostic marker.

questions.question: 72-year-old with nontender lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, leukocyte count 72,000 — diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Elderly patient, massive lymphocytosis, nontender nodes, splenomegaly = classic CLL presentation.

questions.question: Morphological classification of anaemias is based on?
questions.explanation: Morphological classification uses MCV: microcytic (<80 fL), normocytic (80–100 fL), or macrocytic (>100 fL).

questions.question: Which factor may NOT cause an increase in RBC production?
questions.explanation: Low altitude means higher oxygen availability, reducing EPO stimulus — no need to increase RBC production.

questions.question: What is affected in HbS?
questions.explanation: HbS polymerizes (becomes insoluble) when deoxygenated due to the hydrophobic valine substitution.

questions.question: Anisocytosis means?
questions.explanation: Aniso = unequal; cytosis = cells. Poikilocytosis refers to variation in shape.

questions.question: Peak age of onset of acute lymphoblastic leukemia in childhood?
questions.explanation: ALL has a peak incidence between ages 2–5, making it the most common childhood malignancy.

mcq_sets.title: Haematology Exam 2025: MCQs on Anaemia, Leukaemia & Clotting

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with fatigue and pallor. Complete blood count shows low haemoglobin level and peripheral blood film shows microcytic hypochromic red blood cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Microcytic hypochromic red cells are the classic morphological pattern of iron deficiency anaemia, reflecting impaired haemoglobin synthesis.

questions.question: The primary site of haematopoiesis in adults is
questions.explanation: After birth, the bone marrow (particularly axial skeleton) becomes the main site of blood cell production, replacing the fetal liver and spleen.

questions.question: Which blood cell type is primarily responsible for defence against parasitic infections?
questions.explanation: Eosinophils release cytotoxic granule proteins effective against helminths and other parasites, and are typically elevated in parasitic infection.

questions.question: Which clotting factor is deficient in Haemophilia A?
questions.explanation: Haemophilia A is an X-linked deficiency of Factor VIII, causing prolonged APTT with normal PT.

questions.question: A patient presents with recurrent infections, petechiae, and anaemia. A bone marrow biopsy shows reduced cellularity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow reflects failure of haematopoietic stem cells, defining aplastic anaemia.

questions.question: Haemopoiesis is the process of
questions.explanation: Haemopoiesis refers to the formation of all cellular blood components from haematopoietic stem cells.

options: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents with fatigue, fever and bruising. His full blood count shows WCC 40 × 10⁹/L with 25% circulating blasts, Hb 90 g/L and platelets 50 × 10⁹/L. Which investigation is required to definitively diagnose acute myeloid leukaemia?
questions.explanation: Marrow examination with immunophenotyping and cytogenetics is required for definitive diagnosis and classification of AML.
questions.correct_answer_text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy

questions.question: Which cytochemical stain is most useful to confirm lymphoblasts in suspected ALL?
questions.explanation: TdT is a nuclear enzyme expressed in immature lymphoid precursors, positive in the vast majority of ALL cases.

questions.question: A patient receiving chemotherapy shows a drop in neutrophil count. This condition is termed
questions.explanation: Neutropenia is defined as an abnormally low absolute neutrophil count, a common chemotherapy toxicity.

questions.question: Which chromosomal translocation is pathognomonic of chronic myeloid leukaemia?
questions.explanation: This translocation creates the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL1 fusion gene, the molecular hallmark of CML.

questions.question: Thrombopoietin primarily regulates the production of
questions.explanation: Thrombopoietin stimulates megakaryocyte proliferation and maturation, driving platelet production.

questions.question: Which of the following is a stem cell marker used to identify haematopoietic stem cells?
questions.explanation: CD34 is expressed on haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and is used clinically to enumerate and select stem cells for transplant.

questions.question: In a bone marrow biopsy of a patient with aplastic anaemia, you would expect to find
questions.explanation: Aplastic anaemia is characterised by marrow hypocellularity with replacement by fat, reflecting stem cell failure.

questions.question: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) is used clinically to
questions.explanation: G-CSF stimulates neutrophil precursor proliferation and maturation, shortening chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.

questions.question: A patient with Chronic Lymphoid Leukaemia develops a warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Which test is essential to confirm this complication?
questions.explanation: The DAT detects antibody or complement bound directly to the patient's red cells, confirming autoimmune haemolysis.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and night sweats. Excisional lymph node biopsy shows large binucleated cells expressing CD15 and CD30. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Binucleated Reed-Sternberg cells expressing CD15 and CD30 are the diagnostic hallmark of classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man on warfarin therapy for atrial fibrillation attends clinic for monitoring. His prothrombin time is 30 seconds (normal 11–15s) and his APTT is within normal limits. Which test is used to standardise his anticoagulant dose?
questions.explanation: Warfarin affects the extrinsic pathway; the INR standardises PT results across laboratories for dose monitoring.

questions.question: Which of the following laboratory findings is typically associated with haemolytic anaemia?
questions.explanation: Red cell destruction releases intracellular LDH; haemolysis also raises reticulocytes and unconjugated bilirubin while haptoglobin falls.

questions.question: A patient with HIV has an absolute neutrophil count of 0.4 × 10⁹/L. Which pathogen poses the greatest risk with this degree of neutropenia?
questions.explanation: Severe neutropenia primarily predisposes to bacterial and fungal infections from endogenous flora, with S. aureus being a leading cause of neutropenic sepsis.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man of Mediterranean descent presents with mild anaemia and target cells on a blood film. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Target cells with mild anaemia in a person of Mediterranean origin are classic for thalassaemia trait.

questions.question: A patient with chronic atrophic gastritis is at risk of which type of anaemia?
questions.explanation: Atrophic gastritis destroys parietal cells that produce intrinsic factor, impairing B12 absorption and causing pernicious anaemia.

questions.question: In thalassaemia major, anaemia is primarily caused by
questions.explanation: Imbalanced globin chain production causes ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis of defective red cells.

options: Decreased due to reduced erythrocyte aggregation
Low in the first and second trimesters, rising in the third
Markedly elevated due to increased fibrinogen
questions.question: The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) in normal pregnancy is typically
questions.explanation: Pregnancy increases plasma fibrinogen and other acute phase proteins, promoting red cell rouleaux and raising ESR.
questions.correct_answer_text: Markedly elevated due to increased fibrinogen

questions.question: What is the universal donor blood group for red blood cell transfusion?
questions.explanation: O negative red cells lack A, B, and D (Rh) antigens, making them compatible with recipients of any ABO/Rh type in emergencies.

questions.question: A patient presents with a blood transfusion reaction within 30 minutes, showing fever, chills, and hypotension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rapid onset fever, chills, and hypotension during transfusion suggest ABO incompatibility causing acute intravascular haemolysis, a medical emergency.

questions.question: Which of the following is used to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease in immunocompromised patients?
questions.explanation: Irradiation inactivates donor T-lymphocytes, preventing them from engrafting and attacking immunocompromised recipient tissue.

questions.question: Which of the following blood components is indicated in a patient with thrombocytopenia and active bleeding?
questions.explanation: Platelet concentrate directly replaces the deficient platelets responsible for bleeding in thrombocytopenia.

questions.question: Which infection is most commonly screened for in donated blood?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B is a mandatory transfusion-transmissible infection screened for in all blood donations, alongside HIV and Hepatitis C.

questions.question: A peripheral blood film from a patient with suspected AML shows numerous blasts. Which cytochemical stain is most specific for confirming a myeloid lineage?
questions.explanation: MPO positivity, often seen as Auer rods, is the most specific stain confirming myeloid differentiation in blasts.

questions.question: Which of the following transfusion reactions is associated with hypotension and respiratory distress due to donor antibodies against recipient leukocytes?
questions.explanation: Donor anti-leukocyte antibodies activate recipient neutrophils in the pulmonary vasculature, causing acute lung injury with hypotension and respiratory distress.

options: It contains anti-A and anti-B antibodies
questions.question: Why is group O blood not suitable for plasma transfusion in emergencies?
questions.explanation: Group O plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, which would haemolyse A or B red cells in most recipients.
questions.correct_answer_text: It contains anti-A and anti-B antibodies

questions.question: A patient with liver failure is coagulopathic and actively bleeding. Which blood product is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: FFP replaces the full range of clotting factors that are deficient due to impaired hepatic synthesis in liver failure.

questions.question: How long after collection can CPDA-1 packed red blood cells typically be stored before transfusion?
questions.explanation: CPDA-1 anticoagulant-preservative extends red cell storage to a maximum of 42 days under standard refrigeration.

questions.question: Which sample type is preferred for cytogenetic and molecular analysis in suspected ALL?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow aspirate provides an adequate, representative sample of leukaemic blasts for karyotyping and molecular testing.

questions.question: Which of the following is a known cause of aplastic anaemia?
questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol is a classic drug cause of idiosyncratic bone marrow aplasia through direct toxicity to haematopoietic stem cells.

questions.question: Which diagnostic method is used to detect the Philadelphia chromosome in interphase cells?
questions.explanation: FISH can detect the BCR-ABL1 fusion in non-dividing (interphase) cells, unlike conventional cytogenetics which requires metaphase cells.

options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid cytology
questions.question: A 60-year-old with established CLL complains of headaches and blurred vision. Which diagnostic procedure is indicated to assess for central nervous system involvement?
questions.explanation: CSF cytology directly detects leukaemic cell infiltration of the central nervous system.
questions.correct_answer_text: Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid cytology

questions.question: Which procedure is the gold standard to obtain diagnostic tissue in suspected lymphoma?
questions.explanation: Complete node removal preserves architecture, essential for accurate lymphoma subtyping, unlike FNA which yields insufficient tissue.

questions.question: Which immunophenotypic marker is typically positive in follicular lymphoma?
questions.explanation: CD10 positivity reflects the germinal centre B-cell origin characteristic of follicular lymphoma.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man presents with bone pain, anaemia, and elevated total protein. Serum electrophoresis reveals a monoclonal spike. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bone pain, anaemia, and a monoclonal (M) protein spike are the classic triad pointing to multiple myeloma.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common clinical finding in multiple myeloma?
questions.explanation: Osteoclast-activating factors from myeloma cells cause characteristic punched-out lytic lesions, unlike lymphomas/leukaemias which more often cause organomegaly.

questions.question: Bence Jones proteins in the urine are composed of
questions.explanation: Bence Jones proteins are free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains filtered into the urine in myeloma.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman receives an unfractionated heparin infusion for a deep-vein thrombosis. Which test is most appropriate to monitor her anticoagulant effect?
questions.explanation: Unfractionated heparin prolongs the intrinsic pathway, so APTT is the standard monitoring test for dose titration.

questions.question: In HIV-associated thrombocytopenia, autoantibodies are often directed against which platelet antigen?
questions.explanation: As in classic immune thrombocytopenia, autoantibodies most commonly target the GPIIb/IIIa complex on the platelet surface.

questions.question: Which coagulation factor is most markedly increased during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Fibrinogen rises substantially in pregnancy as part of the physiological hypercoagulable state that protects against peripartum haemorrhage.

options: Elevated M protein without end-organ damage
questions.question: Which of the following features distinguishes monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) from multiple myeloma?
questions.explanation: MGUS is defined by a monoclonal protein below myeloma-defining levels with no CRAB (calcium, renal, anaemia, bone) end-organ damage.
questions.correct_answer_text: Elevated M protein without end-organ damage

questions.question: In patients with AML, marked gingival hypertrophy and infiltration is most commonly associated with which FAB subtype?
questions.explanation: Monocytic subtypes infiltrate soft tissue and gums, making gum hypertrophy a classic finding in M5.

questions.question: Which immunophenotypic marker is most characteristic of T-cell ALL?
questions.explanation: CD3 is the pan T-cell marker used to identify T-lymphoblasts in T-cell ALL, in contrast to CD19/CD20 which mark B-cell lineage.

options: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy with cytogenetic analysis
questions.question: A 55-year-old man presents with fatigue, weight loss and splenomegaly. His full blood count shows WCC 140 × 10⁹/L with marked neutrophilia, left shift and basophilia. Which investigation is required to confirm the diagnosis of chronic myeloid leukaemia?
questions.explanation: Marrow examination with cytogenetics confirms the Philadelphia chromosome, establishing the definitive CML diagnosis alongside molecular BCR-ABL testing.
questions.correct_answer_text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy with cytogenetic analysis

questions.question: Which laboratory test is most widely used as a prognostic tumour marker in lymphoma?
questions.explanation: Serum LDH reflects tumour burden and turnover and is incorporated into prognostic indices such as the International Prognostic Index for lymphoma.

questions.question: Which chromosomal translocation is diagnostic of Burkitt lymphoma?
questions.explanation: This translocation juxtaposes the MYC oncogene with the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer, driving the characteristic Burkitt lymphoma phenotype.

options: Low erythropoietin levels with increased haematocrit
questions.question: Which of the following is a hallmark feature of polycythaemia vera?
questions.explanation: In primary polycythaemia vera, autonomous marrow proliferation (driven by JAK2 mutation) raises red cell mass while suppressing EPO via negative feedback.
questions.correct_answer_text: Low erythropoietin levels with increased haematocrit

questions.question: Which cytokine mutation is most commonly associated with essential thrombocythaemia?
questions.explanation: JAK2 V617F is the most common driver mutation in essential thrombocythaemia, found in roughly half of cases.

options: Fibrotic bone marrow with tear-drop red blood cells
Hypercellular bone marrow with increased blasts
questions.question: Which of the following is most likely seen in myelofibrosis?
questions.explanation: Marrow fibrosis causes extramedullary haematopoiesis and characteristic dacrocytes (tear-drop cells) on the peripheral film.
questions.correct_answer_text: Fibrotic bone marrow with tear-drop red blood cells

questions.question: In the context of the reticuloendothelial system, what is a key histological feature of reactive lymphadenopathy?
questions.explanation: Benign reactive nodes show expanded germinal centres but retain overall nodal architecture, unlike malignant infiltration which effaces it.

questions.question: Mycosis fungoides, a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, characteristically expresses
questions.explanation: As a T-cell lymphoma, mycosis fungoides expresses the pan T-cell marker CD3 rather than B-cell or Hodgkin-associated markers.

questions.question: A 20-year-old man presents with recurrent joint bleeds. His prothrombin time is normal, activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) is prolonged, thrombin time (TT) is normal. Which coagulation factor abnormality is most likely?
questions.explanation: An isolated prolonged APTT with normal PT and TT, plus haemarthroses, is classic for haemophilia A.

questions.question: Which change is characteristic of early HIV infection before CD4 counts fall markedly?
questions.explanation: Early HIV infection can cause transient lymphopenia even before significant CD4 decline becomes established.

questions.question: Which natural anticoagulant is physiologically reduced in pregnancy, contributing to a hypercoagulable state?
questions.explanation: Free Protein S levels fall in pregnancy due to increased binding protein, reducing its anticoagulant activity and contributing to venous thromboembolism risk.

questions.question: In acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL), which coagulation abnormality is most characteristic of disseminated intravascular coagulation?
questions.explanation: APL blasts release procoagulant material that triggers consumptive coagulopathy, consuming fibrinogen and clotting factors while raising D-dimer.
