mcq_sets.title: SINGLE-GENE DISORDERS WITH ATYPICAL INHERITANCE MCQs

questions.question: What is the second most common genetic cause of mental retardation after Down syndrome?
questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome is the second most common genetic cause of mental retardation after Down syndrome, with a frequency of 1 in 1550 for affected males and 1 in 8000 for affected females.

questions.question: What is the normal number of CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene?
questions.explanation: In the normal population, the number of CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene averages around 29, whereas affected persons have 200 to 4000 repeats (full mutations).

questions.question: What defines a premutation in fragile X syndrome?
questions.explanation: Premutations are characterized by 52 to 200 CGG repeats. Carrier males and females have premutations that can be converted to full mutations (200-4000 repeats) during oogenesis.

questions.question: During which process can premutations be converted to full mutations in fragile X syndrome?
questions.explanation: During oogenesis (but not spermatogenesis), premutations can be converted to full mutations by further amplification of CGG repeats, which can then be transmitted to both sons and daughters.

questions.question: What is the only distinctive physical abnormality detected in at least 90% of postpubertal males with fragile X syndrome?
questions.explanation: The only distinctive physical abnormality that can be detected in at least 90% of postpubertal males with fragile X syndrome is macroorchidism (large testicles).

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: What phenomenon describes the worsening of clinical features with each successive generation in fragile X syndrome?
questions.explanation: Anticipation refers to the phenomenon whereby clinical features worsen with each successive generation, as the mutation becomes increasingly deleterious as it is transmitted through generations.

questions.question: What percentage of carrier females with fragile X are affected (mentally retarded)?
questions.explanation: From 30% to 50% of carrier females are affected (mentally retarded), a number much higher than that for other X-linked recessive disorders, explained by inheritance of full mutations.

options: Silencing of FMRP due to methylation
questions.question: What is the molecular basis for fragile X syndrome?
questions.explanation: When CGG repeats exceed 230, the DNA of the FMR1 gene becomes abnormally methylated, extending to the promoter region, resulting in transcriptional suppression and absence of FMRP.
questions.correct_answer_text: Silencing of FMRP due to methylation

questions.question: What is the function of FMRP (Familial Mental Retardation Protein)?
questions.explanation: FMRP is an RNA-binding protein transported from cytoplasm to nucleus, where it binds specific mRNAs and transports them to axons and dendrites, regulating translation at synapses.

questions.question: What condition affects approximately 30% of females carrying the fragile X premutation?
questions.explanation: Approximately 30% of females carrying the premutation have premature ovarian failure (before age 40), indicating that premutations are not benign though abnormalities are milder.

questions.question: What syndrome develops in approximately one-third of premutation-carrying males in their sixth decade?
questions.explanation: About one-third of premutation-carrying males exhibit fragile X-associated tremor-ataxia starting in their sixth decade, characterized by intention tremors and cerebellar ataxia, potentially progressing to parkinsonism.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: In Huntington disease, when does conversion from premutation to full mutation occur?
questions.explanation: Unlike fragile X syndrome where expansion occurs during oogenesis, in Huntington disease and some other trinucleotide repeat disorders, premutations are converted to full mutations during spermatogenesis.

questions.question: What type of mutation occurs when trinucleotide repeats affect coding regions?
questions.explanation: When mutations affect coding regions (like in Huntington disease), they give rise to misfolded proteins that interfere with normal protein function, called toxic gain-of-function mutations.

questions.question: What are diseases involving CAG repeat expansions in coding regions commonly called?
questions.explanation: Diseases involving CAG repeats that encode polyglutamine tracts are referred to as "polyglutamine diseases," which primarily affect the nervous system and feature accumulation of misfolded protein aggregates.

options: Ova contain mitochondria while spermatozoa contain few or none
questions.question: Why does maternal inheritance occur in mitochondrial diseases?
questions.explanation: Ova contain mitochondria within their abundant cytoplasm, whereas spermatozoa contain few if any mitochondria. The mitochondrial DNA of the zygote is therefore derived entirely from the ovum.
questions.correct_answer_text: Ova contain mitochondria while spermatozoa contain few or none

questions.question: Which organs are most affected by mitochondrial diseases?
questions.explanation: Because mitochondrial DNA encodes enzymes for oxidative phosphorylation, diseases from mitochondrial mutations affect organs most dependent on oxidative phosphorylation: skeletal muscle, heart, and brain.

questions.question: What is the prototypical mitochondrial disease?
questions.explanation: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is the prototypical mitochondrial disorder, manifesting as progressive bilateral loss of central vision leading to blindness.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: What is genomic imprinting?
questions.explanation: Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic process whereby certain genes are differentially inactivated during paternal and maternal gametogenesis, creating functional differences between maternal and paternal gene copies.

questions.question: What molecular mechanism is associated with genomic imprinting?
questions.explanation: At the molecular level, imprinting is associated with methylation of the gene promoter, as well as histone protein modifications, which silence the gene.

questions.question: What chromosomal region is deleted in both Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes?
questions.explanation: Both Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes involve deletion of band q12 in the long arm of chromosome 15 (15q11-q13), but the parent of origin differs.

questions.question: In Prader-Willi syndrome, which parental chromosome is deleted?
questions.explanation: In Prader-Willi syndrome, the deletion affects the paternally derived chromosome 15 in all cases, demonstrating parent-of-origin effects on gene function.

questions.question: What clinical features characterize Prader-Willi syndrome?
questions.explanation: Prader-Willi syndrome is characterized by mental retardation, short stature, hypotonia, obesity, small hands and feet, and hypogonadism.

questions.question: In Angelman syndrome, which parental chromosome is deleted?
questions.explanation: In Angelman syndrome, the deletion affects the maternally derived chromosome 15, in contrast to Prader-Willi syndrome where the paternal chromosome is deleted.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: What clinical features characterize Angelman syndrome?
questions.explanation: Angelman syndrome patients are mentally retarded and present with ataxic gait, seizures, and inappropriate laughter, giving rise to the name "happy puppet syndrome."

options: Having three copies of a chromosome
Inheritance of both chromosomes of a pair from one parent
questions.question: What is uniparental disomy?
questions.explanation: Uniparental disomy is the inheritance of both chromosomes of a pair from one parent. In Prader-Willi syndrome, this can occur when both copies of chromosome 15 are from the mother.
questions.correct_answer_text: Inheritance of both chromosomes of a pair from one parent

questions.question: What gene is responsible for Angelman syndrome?
questions.explanation: The Angelman syndrome gene is UBE3A, which encodes a ligase in the ubiquitin-proteasome proteolytic pathway and is expressed primarily from the maternal allele in specific brain regions.

questions.question: What does maternal imprinting mean?
questions.explanation: Maternal imprinting refers to transcriptional silencing of the maternal allele, whereas paternal imprinting means the paternal allele is inactivated.

questions.question: How many CGG repeats define a full mutation in fragile X syndrome?
questions.explanation: Full mutations in fragile X syndrome are characterized by 200 to 4000 CGG repeats, which arise through expansion of premutations (52-200 repeats).

options: Patient lacks functional genes from nonimprinted paternal chromosome
questions.question: Why can Prader-Willi syndrome result from maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15?
questions.explanation: Maternal uniparental disomy means the patient has both copies from the mother and lacks functional genes from the nonimprinted paternal chromosome 15, resulting in the same effect as paternal deletion.
questions.correct_answer_text: Patient lacks functional genes from nonimprinted paternal chromosome

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: Approximately how many diseases are now known to be caused by trinucleotide repeat mutations?
questions.explanation: About 40 diseases are now known to be caused by trinucleotide repeat mutations, and all disorders discovered so far are associated with neurodegenerative changes.

questions.question: What percentage of Prader-Willi syndrome cases show an interstitial deletion detectable by standard cytogenetics?
questions.explanation: In 60% to 75% of Prader-Willi syndrome cases, an interstitial deletion of band q12 in chromosome 15—del(15)(q11;q13)—can be detected. Many others have smaller deletions detectable by FISH.

questions.question: Which technique can detect smaller deletions in Prader-Willi syndrome not visible by standard cytogenetics?
questions.explanation: In patients without detectable cytogenetic abnormality, FISH (Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization) analysis can reveal smaller deletions within the same chromosomal region.

questions.question: Where is FMRP most highly expressed in normal tissues?
questions.explanation: FMRP is widely expressed in normal tissues, but higher levels are found in the brain and the testis, which correlates with the clinical manifestations of fragile X syndrome.

options: Culturing cells in folate-deficient medium showing X chromosome discontinuity
questions.question: What is the original diagnostic method that gave fragile X syndrome its name?
questions.explanation: The syndrome gets its name from culturing patient cells in folate-deficient medium, which revealed a discontinuity of staining or constriction in the long arm of the X chromosome. This method is now replaced by DNA-based analysis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Culturing cells in folate-deficient medium showing X chromosome discontinuity

questions.question: What is the chromosomal location of the FMR1 gene?
questions.explanation: The FMR1 gene maps to Xq27.3 on the long arm of the X chromosome, and mutations in this gene result in fragile X syndrome.

options: Yes, but only sons can transmit further
Yes, to both sons and daughters
No, mitochondrial DNA is not inherited
Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: Can mothers transmit mitochondrial DNA to their sons?
questions.explanation: Mothers transmit mitochondrial genes to all their offspring, both male and female; however, only daughters (not sons) transmit the DNA further to their progeny.
questions.correct_answer_text: Yes, to both sons and daughters

options: No functional genes available since maternal copies are imprinted
questions.question: What is the net effect of having genes from the nonimprinted paternal chromosome 15 in Prader-Willi syndrome?
questions.explanation: Genes on the maternal chromosome 15 are imprinted (silenced), so the only functional alleles come from the paternal chromosome. Loss of these leads to Prader-Willi syndrome.
questions.correct_answer_text: No functional genes available since maternal copies are imprinted

questions.question: What happens when the number of trinucleotide repeats exceeds approximately 230 in the FMR1 gene?
questions.explanation: When CGG repeats exceed approximately 230, the DNA of the entire 5' region becomes abnormally methylated, extending to the promoter region, resulting in transcriptional suppression.

options: Loss of function due to suppressed protein synthesis
questions.question: In trinucleotide repeat disorders affecting noncoding regions, what is the typical outcome?
questions.explanation: When mutations affect noncoding regions (like in fragile X syndrome), there is loss of function since protein synthesis is suppressed, in contrast to coding region mutations that cause toxic gain of function.

options: Accumulation of misfolded proteins in cytoplasmic aggregates
questions.question: What common feature is seen in polyglutamine diseases?
questions.explanation: Accumulation of misfolded proteins in aggregates within the cytoplasm is a common feature of polyglutamine diseases resulting from CAG repeat expansions in coding regions.
questions.correct_answer_text: Accumulation of misfolded proteins in cytoplasmic aggregates

options: It is not a genetic disorder
Several genes in the region are lost, unlike Angelman which involves one gene
questions.question: Why is Prader-Willi syndrome thought to result from loss of multiple genes rather than a single gene?
questions.explanation: Prader-Willi syndrome, unlike Angelman syndrome, probably is caused by loss of function of several genes located on chromosome 15 between q11 and q13, which are still being fully characterized.
questions.correct_answer_text: Several genes in the region are lost, unlike Angelman which involves one gene

options: In ovum or sperm and then stably transmitted to all somatic cells
Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: When is imprinting established?
questions.explanation: Imprinting occurs in ovum or sperm (during gametogenesis) and is then stably transmitted to all somatic cells derived from the zygote.
questions.correct_answer_text: In ovum or sperm and then stably transmitted to all somatic cells

questions.question: What type of disorders are predominantly associated with trinucleotide repeat mutations?
questions.explanation: All trinucleotide repeat disorders discovered so far are associated with neurodegenerative changes, affecting primarily the nervous system.

questions.question: In normal individuals, which regions of the brain primarily express UBE3A from the maternal allele?
questions.explanation: UBE3A is expressed primarily from the maternal allele in specific regions of the normal brain. In Angelman syndrome, UBE3A is not expressed in these areas, causing neurologic manifestations.

questions.question: What is the threshold number of CGG repeats above which abnormal methylation occurs in fragile X syndrome?
questions.explanation: When the number of trinucleotide repeats in the FMR1 gene exceeds approximately 230, the DNA of the entire 5' region becomes abnormally methylated, leading to gene silencing.

questions.question: What is the role of FMRP-mRNA complexes in synapses?
questions.explanation: In synapses, FMRP-mRNA complexes perform critical roles in regulating the translation of specific mRNAs. The absence of this finely coordinated shuttle function underlies fragile X syndrome.

options: Males have moderate to severe mental retardation; 30-50% of carrier females are affected
questions.question: What distinguishes the clinical presentation of males versus females with fragile X syndrome?
questions.explanation: Clinically affected males have moderate to severe mental retardation, while 30-50% of carrier females are affected (mentally retarded), much higher than typical X-linked recessive disorders.
questions.correct_answer_text: Males have moderate to severe mental retardation; 30-50% of carrier females are affected

options: Further amplification of CGG repeats occurs
Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: What happens during the conversion of premutation to full mutation in fragile X syndrome?
questions.explanation: During oogenesis, premutations (52-200 repeats) can be converted to full mutations (200-4000 repeats) by further amplification of the CGG repeats.
questions.correct_answer_text: Further amplification of CGG repeats occurs

options: Different genes are imprinted on maternal versus paternal chromosomes
questions.question: Why do Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes demonstrate "parent-of-origin" effects?
questions.explanation: These syndromes demonstrate parent-of-origin effects because different genes within the same region are imprinted on maternal versus paternal chromosomes, so deletion of maternal or paternal chromosome 15 produces distinct clinical syndromes.
questions.correct_answer_text: Different genes are imprinted on maternal versus paternal chromosomes

mcq_sets.title: Medical Bacteriology & Entomology 2021/2022 Q&A

questions.question: Which one of the following is a complication of streptococcus pharyngitis?
questions.explanation: Rheumatic fever is a post-infectious autoimmune complication of Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) pharyngitis. It occurs 2-4 weeks after untreated strep throat due to molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and cardiac myosin, leading to carditis, arthritis, and other manifestations.

questions.question: The presence of a pseudomembrane is a result of
questions.explanation: Diphtheria toxin produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae causes local tissue necrosis and inflammation, leading to formation of a characteristic gray-white pseudomembrane in the throat that can obstruct airways. This fibrinous exudate is pathognomonic for diphtheria.

questions.question: A paroxysm is a associated with
questions.explanation: Paroxysmal cough is the hallmark of pertussis (whooping cough) caused by Bordetella pertussis. The characteristic paroxysm consists of rapid-fire coughing fits followed by a high-pitched "whoop" during inspiration, often accompanied by vomiting.

questions.question: The Mantoux test is used to identify
questions.explanation: The Mantoux test (tuberculin skin test) uses purified protein derivative (PPD) injected intradermally to detect delayed-type hypersensitivity response indicating previous exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis or BCG vaccination. Induration ≥10mm in normal individuals suggests TB exposure.

questions.question: To treat patients who have ingested botulism toxin, large doses of must be administered
questions.explanation: Botulism antitoxin (equine-derived antiserum) neutralizes circulating botulinum toxin and prevents progression of paralysis. It must be administered early as it cannot reverse existing nerve damage but prevents further toxin binding to nerve terminals.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: The organism Clostridium perfringens multiplies in foods only under conditions
questions.explanation: Clostridium perfringens is an obligate anaerobe that multiplies rapidly in foods under anaerobic conditions. Its spores survive cooking and germinate when oxygen is excluded, leading to rapid multiplication in improperly stored cooked foods.

questions.question: A spore-forming, motile rod that can cause foodborne illness in a diarrheal or emetic form is Bacillus
questions.explanation: Bacillus cereus causes two forms of food poisoning: diarrheal syndrome (8-16 hours after ingestion, watery diarrhea) and emetic syndrome (1-6 hours, nausea and vomiting). It's commonly associated with rice dishes and forms heat-resistant spores.

questions.question: Woolsorter disease applies to the form of
questions.explanation: Woolsorter disease is pulmonary (inhalation) anthrax historically seen in workers processing contaminated wool, hair, or hides. Bacillus anthracis spores are inhaled, germinate in alveolar macrophages, and cause severe pneumonia with high mortality if untreated.

questions.question: Which one of the following describes the mode of action of tetanospasmin?
questions.explanation: Tetanospasmin cleaves synaptobrevin proteins in inhibitory neurons, preventing release of GABA and glycine neurotransmitters. This blocks muscle relaxation signals, resulting in sustained muscle contractions and spastic paralysis characteristic of tetanus.

questions.question: Salpingitis is associated with and can lead to
questions.explanation: Salpingitis (fallopian tube inflammation) is commonly caused by ascending Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. Chronic inflammation leads to scarring and tubal occlusion, resulting in infertility or increased risk of ectopic pregnancy.

questions.question: Ophthalmia is associated with what two STDs?
questions.explanation: Neonatal ophthalmia (conjunctivitis) is primarily caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis transmitted from infected mothers during delivery. Both can cause severe purulent conjunctivitis that may lead to blindness if untreated.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: Toxin-generated S. aureus diseases resulting from contact include
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus produces exfoliative toxins causing staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) and toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) causing toxic shock syndrome. Both are toxin-mediated diseases that can result from skin contact or colonization.

options: Contaminated hand rails on public transportation
Breathing aerosolized droplets containing the microorganism
questions.question: A 22-year-old woman who works in a plant nursery presents with fever and cough for 2 months, 5 kg weight loss, bilateral upper lobe infiltrates with cavities, and acid-fast bacilli in sputum. The likely means of infection acquisition is
questions.explanation: This presentation is classic for pulmonary tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. TB is transmitted via airborne droplet nuclei containing viable bacteria. The patient's occupation and clinical findings suggest respiratory transmission, not soil contact.

options: Complex molecular interactions make antimicrobial therapy difficult, likely requiring catheter removal
S. epidermidis in biofilm are more susceptible to antimicrobials due to decreased metabolism
Extracellular polysaccharide production inhibits S. epidermidis growth
questions.question: A 65-year-old woman with a central venous catheter develops fever and multiple blood cultures positive for Staphylococcus epidermidis with biofilm formation. Which statement about this infection is correct?
questions.explanation: S. epidermidis biofilms on catheters are highly resistant to antimicrobials due to decreased metabolic activity, altered gene expression, and physical barrier effects of the extracellular matrix. Catheter removal is often necessary for cure.
questions.correct_answer_text: Extracellular polysaccharide production inhibits S. epidermidis growth

questions.question: The first microorganism to satisfy Koch's postulates (in the late 19th century) was
questions.explanation: Robert Koch first demonstrated his postulates using Bacillus anthracis in 1876, proving it was the causative agent of anthrax. This established the germ theory of disease and the scientific method for linking specific pathogens to specific diseases.

options: The toxic component is the O side chain
It forms holes in red blood cell membranes yielding hemolysis
questions.question: Which of the following statements about lipopolysaccharide is correct?
questions.explanation: Lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) binds to CD14/TLR4 receptors on macrophages and monocytes, triggering release of inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) that cause fever, hypotension, and other septic shock symptoms. The toxic component is lipid A, not the O antigen.
questions.correct_answer_text: The toxic component is the O side chain

options: Causes release of tumor necrosis factor
Degrades lecithin in eukaryotic cell membranes
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of diphtheria toxin?
questions.explanation: Diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 (eEF2), permanently inactivating it and halting protein synthesis in eukaryotic cells. This leads to cell death and the characteristic local tissue necrosis and systemic toxicity of diphtheria.
questions.correct_answer_text: Degrades lecithin in eukaryotic cell membranes

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: Certain microorganisms are never considered members of normal flora and are always considered pathogens. Which organism fits this category?
questions.explanation: M. tuberculosis is a true (obligate) pathogen that always causes disease when it infects humans and is never part of normal flora. The other organisms can be found as normal flora in certain body sites and cause opportunistic infections.

questions.question: Which one of the following genera is the ODD one out in terms of pathogen transmission?
questions.explanation: Bulinus is a freshwater snail that serves as an intermediate host for Schistosoma haematobium (biological vector), while Fannia, Musca, and Blatta are arthropods that primarily serve as mechanical vectors of pathogens through contamination.

questions.question: Which of the following diseases can be effectively controlled by the use of acaricides?
questions.explanation: Q-fever is transmitted by ticks (Ixodes species), which are arachnids (mites and ticks) controlled by acaricides. Leishmaniasis is transmitted by sandflies, Katayama fever by snails, sleeping sickness by tsetse flies (all insects), and amoebiasis is not vector-borne.

questions.question: Which one of the following genera is a biological vector of scrub typhus pathogens?
questions.explanation: Leptotrombidium mites (chiggers) are the biological vectors of Orientia tsutsugamushi, the causative agent of scrub typhus. The mites serve as both vector and reservoir, with transovarial transmission maintaining the pathogen in mite populations.

questions.question: Which of the following pathogens can be transovarially transmitted by its biological vector?
questions.explanation: Orientia tsutsugamushi (scrub typhus) is maintained in Leptotrombidium mite populations through transovarial transmission from infected female mites to their offspring, making the mites both vector and reservoir host.

questions.question: Which of the following is the BEST treatment for scabies?
questions.explanation: Benzyl benzoate is a topical scabicide effective against Sarcoptes scabiei mites causing scabies. It kills adult mites and eggs when applied to the entire body. Other options treat different parasites: metronidazole for protozoa, amphotericin B for fungi, sodium stibogluconate for leishmaniasis, praziquantel for helminths.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: Which of the following reagents can be used in the diagnosis of mites infection?
questions.explanation: Liquid iodine can be applied to skin suspected of scabies infection to visualize burrows created by Sarcoptes scabiei mites. The iodine stains the burrows dark brown, making them more visible for diagnosis. This is a simple diagnostic technique for scabies.

questions.question: Indoor residual spraying is BEST effective against insect vectors of pathogens
questions.explanation: Indoor residual spraying (IRS) is most effective against endophilic vectors that rest indoors after blood feeding, where they contact insecticide-treated surfaces. Exophilic vectors rest outdoors and have minimal contact with indoor-applied insecticides.

questions.question: Which one of the following genera belongs to the family Argasidae?
questions.explanation: Ornithodoros belongs to the family Argasidae (soft ticks), characterized by lack of a hard scutum and mouthparts not visible from above. The other genera belong to Ixodidae (hard ticks) with visible scutum and prominent mouthparts.

questions.question: Which one of the following vectors utilizes one host in its life cycle and pathogen transmission?
questions.explanation: Boophilus ticks are one-host ticks that complete their entire life cycle (larva, nymph, adult) on a single host animal. The other genera are either two-host or three-host ticks that drop off between life stages to molt before finding new hosts.

questions.question: Which one of the following vectors of pathogens is BEST controlled by using boric acid powder (e.g., borax)?
questions.explanation: Periplaneta species (cockroaches) are effectively controlled using boric acid powder, which acts as a stomach poison when ingested during grooming. Boric acid damages the insect's digestive system and is a common cockroach control method in integrated pest management programs.

questions.question: Which tumor marker is most specific for hepatocellular carcinoma?
questions.explanation: AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) is produced by malignant hepatocytes and is the hallmark marker for HCC monitoring and diagnosis.

questions.question: A patient with small cell lung cancer develops hyponatremia with concentrated urine. The ectopic hormone responsible is
questions.explanation: ADH secreted ectopically causes water retention and dilutional hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine (SIADH).

questions.question: CA 125 is the tumor marker of choice for monitoring treatment response in
questions.explanation: Ovarian cancer is the primary indication for CA 125; it reflects tumor burden and treatment response.

options: Very high ACTH with failed high-dose dexamethasone suppression
questions.question: Which lab finding best distinguishes ectopic ACTH syndrome from pituitary Cushing disease?
questions.explanation: Ectopic tumors produce ACTH autonomously and do not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone, unlike pituitary adenomas which partially suppress.
questions.correct_answer_text: Very high ACTH with failed high-dose dexamethasone suppression

questions.question: A man with bronchogenic carcinoma has calcium 13.2 mg/dL with suppressed PTH. The mediator is
questions.explanation: PTHrP (PTH-related peptide) mimics PTH action on bone and kidney, causing hypercalcemia of malignancy with suppressed true PTH.

options: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
questions.question: The most common cause of delayed puberty in boys is
questions.explanation: Constitutional delay is a normal variant and the most common cause; family history is often positive and pubertal development eventually occurs spontaneously.
questions.correct_answer_text: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

questions.question: A 16-year-old girl has no breast development, primary amenorrhea, and elevated FSH/LH. Karyotype is 45,X. Diagnosis
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes gonadal dysgenesis; elevated gonadotropins reflect absent negative feedback from failed ovaries.

questions.question: Precocious puberty in girls is defined as secondary sexual development before age
questions.explanation: Before age 8 in girls (before age 9 in boys) is the accepted cutoff for precocious puberty.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy has pubic hair, enlarged testes, and pubertal LH response to GnRH. Diagnosis
questions.explanation: Central precocious puberty is GnRH-dependent; enlarged testes confirm gonadal activation, distinguishing it from adrenal causes where testes remain prepubertal.

questions.question: The most common cause of hirsutism in reproductive-age women is
questions.explanation: PCOS accounts for approximately 70–80% of hirsutism cases through excess androgen production from the ovary.

questions.question: Best biochemical marker of adrenal androgen excess in hirsutism
questions.explanation: DHEA-S is produced almost exclusively by the adrenal cortex, making it a specific marker of adrenal androgen overproduction.

questions.question: Which feature is NOT part of virilism in women?
questions.explanation: Galactorrhea is caused by excess prolactin, not androgens, and is not a feature of virilism.

questions.question: Semen analysis: count 10 million/mL, motility 20%, morphology 2%. This is
questions.explanation: OAT syndrome (oligoasthenoteratozoospermia) refers to combined defects in count, motility, and morphology — the most common finding in male infertility.

questions.question: WHO lower reference limit for normal sperm concentration is
questions.explanation: 15 million/mL is the WHO 2010 fifth percentile reference limit for sperm concentration.

questions.question: Elevated FSH with azoospermia in a male infertility workup suggests
questions.explanation: Primary testicular failure destroys seminiferous tubules; loss of inhibin B feedback causes FSH to rise. Obstruction shows normal FSH.

questions.question: Aminoglycoside trough level sample should be collected
questions.explanation: Trough is collected just before the next dose to ensure drug levels fall below toxic threshold, preventing nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

questions.question: Which drug has the narrowest therapeutic index requiring routine TDM?
questions.explanation: Digoxin has a very narrow therapeutic window (0.5–2 ng/mL); small concentration changes cause toxicity or therapeutic failure.

questions.question: In acetaminophen toxicity, N-acetylcysteine works by replenishing
questions.explanation: Glutathione is depleted by the toxic metabolite NAPQI; NAC restores it, preventing hepatocellular necrosis.

questions.question: Carbon monoxide poisoning is confirmed by measuring
questions.explanation: Carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) directly measures CO bound to hemoglobin; PO₂ may be falsely normal on standard ABG.

questions.question: In salicylate toxicity, the earliest acid-base disturbance is
questions.explanation: Respiratory alkalosis occurs first as salicylates directly stimulate the medullary respiratory center, increasing ventilation.

questions.question: Phenylketonuria results from deficiency of
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase converts phenylalanine to tyrosine; its deficiency leads to toxic phenylalanine accumulation causing intellectual disability.

questions.question: The newborn screening test for PKU measures
questions.explanation: Elevated serum phenylalanine on the Guthrie test or tandem mass spectrometry is the basis of newborn PKU screening.

questions.question: A patient with dark urine on standing, ochronosis, and arthritis has
questions.explanation: Alkaptonuria results from homogentisate oxidase deficiency; homogentisic acid accumulates, darkens urine, and deposits in connective tissue causing ochronosis.

questions.question: Maple syrup urine disease involves accumulation of
questions.explanation: Leucine, isoleucine, and valine accumulate due to deficient branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase, giving urine its characteristic sweet odor.

questions.question: Classic galactosemia is due to deficiency of
questions.explanation: GALT deficiency causes galactose-1-phosphate accumulation, leading to liver damage, cataracts, and intellectual disability in neonates.

questions.question: The gold standard for diagnosing osteoporosis is
questions.explanation: DEXA scan measures bone mineral density; T-score ≤ −2.5 defines osteoporosis per WHO criteria.

questions.question: In Paget's disease of bone, which marker is most characteristically elevated?
questions.explanation: Alkaline phosphatase reflects intense osteoblastic activity; calcium and phosphate remain normal in uncomplicated Paget's disease.

options: Low calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
Low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH
High calcium, high phosphate, low PTH
High calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
questions.question: Primary hyperparathyroidism characteristically shows
questions.explanation: Excess PTH mobilizes calcium from bone, increases renal phosphate excretion (causing hypophosphatemia), and elevates serum calcium.
questions.correct_answer_text: High calcium, low phosphate, high PTH

questions.question: The enzyme deficient in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome causing severe hyperuricemia is
questions.explanation: HGPRT deficiency prevents purine salvage, forcing excess purines toward uric acid production; presents with gout, self-mutilation, and neurological symptoms.

questions.question: Allopurinol treats gout by inhibiting
questions.explanation: Xanthine oxidase catalyzes the final steps of uric acid synthesis; its inhibition reduces urate production.

questions.question: The hypothalamic hormone that stimulates both FSH and LH release is
questions.explanation: GnRH is released in pulses from the hypothalamus, stimulating pituitary gonadotrophs to secrete both FSH and LH.

questions.question: Growth hormone excess before epiphyseal fusion causes
questions.explanation: Gigantism results from GH excess before growth plate closure; after fusion, the same excess causes acromegaly.

questions.question: The best screening test for acromegaly is
questions.explanation: IGF-1 is stable throughout the day (unlike pulsatile GH) and reflects integrated GH secretion, making it the best screening test.

options: Low urine osmolality, high serum osmolality
High urine osmolality, low serum osmolality
Low urine osmolality, low serum osmolality
High urine osmolality, high serum osmolality
questions.question: Diabetes insipidus is characterized by
questions.explanation: ADH deficiency or resistance produces dilute urine (low osmolality) while serum becomes hyperosmolar from free water loss.
questions.correct_answer_text: Low urine osmolality, high serum osmolality

questions.question: A patient has low TSH and high free T4. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Primary hyperthyroidism causes excess T4 which negatively feeds back to suppress TSH at the pituitary level.

questions.question: The best initial test to evaluate thyroid function is
questions.explanation: TSH is the most sensitive indicator of thyroid status; it changes before T4 levels become abnormal.

questions.question: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is associated with antibodies against
questions.explanation: Anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are the hallmarks of Hashimoto's autoimmune thyroiditis leading to hypothyroidism.

questions.question: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over the preceding
questions.explanation: 2–3 months (approximately 120 days = RBC lifespan); HbA1c is used to assess long-term glycemic control.

questions.question: Diagnostic criterion for diabetes mellitus using fasting plasma glucose is
questions.explanation: ≥ 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) on two occasions confirms diabetes; 6.1–6.9 mmol/L is impaired fasting glucose.

questions.question: In DKA, the predominant ketone body measured by nitroprusside test is
questions.explanation: Acetoacetate reacts with nitroprusside; beta-hydroxybutyrate (the predominant ketone in DKA) is NOT detected, potentially underestimating ketosis.

options: It is elevated in type 1 DM
It is unaffected by insulin therapy
questions.question: C-peptide measurement differentiates type 1 DM from factitious hypoglycemia because
questions.explanation: Endogenous insulin secretion produces C-peptide; exogenous insulin injection suppresses it while raising insulin levels — the diagnostic pattern of factitious hypoglycemia.

questions.question: The classic triad of Cushing syndrome includes all EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Hypoglycemia does NOT occur; cortisol causes hyperglycemia by stimulating gluconeogenesis and inducing insulin resistance.

questions.question: The best outpatient screening test for Cushing syndrome is
questions.explanation: Overnight DST is simple, cheap, and highly sensitive; failure to suppress cortisol below 50 nmol/L is abnormal.

questions.question: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) characteristically presents with
questions.explanation: Excess aldosterone causes sodium retention (hypertension), potassium wasting, and suppresses renin through negative feedback.

questions.question: In CAH due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which metabolite is most elevated?
questions.explanation: 17-OHP accumulates proximal to the enzyme block and is the diagnostic marker; it is diverted to androgen synthesis causing virilization.

questions.question: The earliest marker of glomerular damage in diabetic nephropathy is
questions.explanation: Microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/day) precedes overt proteinuria and GFR decline; it represents early, potentially reversible glomerular injury.

questions.question: Which formula is used to estimate GFR in clinical practice?
questions.explanation: CKD-EPI is currently preferred for adults; Cockcroft-Gault is also widely used especially for drug dosing.

questions.question: In nephrotic syndrome, the urine dipstick finding is
questions.explanation: Heavy proteinuria (≥3.5 g/day) is the hallmark; massive protein loss drives hypoalbuminemia and edema.

questions.question: The most sensitive early indicator of tubular dysfunction is
questions.explanation: Beta-2 microglobulin is freely filtered and fully reabsorbed by healthy tubules; its appearance in urine indicates proximal tubular damage before creatinine rises.

questions.question: In pre-renal AKI, urine sodium is typically
questions.explanation: < 20 mmol/L reflects avid tubular sodium reabsorption as the kidney tries to restore circulating volume — tubular function is intact.

questions.question: The BUN/creatinine ratio in pre-renal AKI is typically
questions.explanation: > 20:1 occurs because urea is passively reabsorbed with water in dehydration, while creatinine is not, disproportionately raising BUN.

questions.question: Calcium oxalate crystals in urine are most associated with
questions.explanation: Envelope-shaped (dihydrate) or dumbbell-shaped (monohydrate) oxalate crystals are the most common finding in calcium stone formers.

questions.question: Struvite renal stones are associated with
questions.explanation: Urease-producing organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella) hydrolyze urea to ammonia, alkalinizing urine and precipitating magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite).

questions.question: In chronic kidney disease, the most immediately life-threatening electrolyte abnormality is
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia can cause fatal ventricular arrhythmias; impaired renal potassium excretion in CKD makes this the most urgent electrolyte emergency.

questions.question: The enzyme deficient in acute intermittent porphyria is
questions.explanation: PBG deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase) deficiency causes PBG and ALA accumulation, triggering neurovisceral attacks.

questions.question: The most reliable urine marker during an acute AIP attack is
questions.explanation: Urinary PBG is markedly elevated during acute attacks and is the most sensitive and specific diagnostic marker for AIP.

questions.question: Porphyria cutanea tarda presents with
questions.explanation: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency causes porphyrins to accumulate in skin; UV light generates reactive oxygen species causing blistering on sun-exposed areas.

questions.question: Which porphyria involves ferrochelatase deficiency and photosensitivity without blistering?
questions.explanation: EPP causes painful burning photosensitivity without vesicles; protoporphyrin IX accumulates due to deficient ferrochelatase.

questions.question: The rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis is
questions.explanation: ALA synthase is the first and rate-limiting enzyme; it is feedback-inhibited by heme and induced by drugs, fasting, and hormones — explaining porphyria triggers.

questions.question: Prolactinoma causes infertility in women primarily by
questions.explanation: Hyperprolactinemia suppresses hypothalamic GnRH pulses, reducing LH/FSH, causing anovulation and amenorrhea.

questions.question: Which pituitary hormone deficiency occurs last in progressive hypopituitarism?
questions.explanation: GH is typically the first hormone lost; however, ACTH deficiency is most life-threatening. The order is GH → LH/FSH → TSH → ACTH. This question tests awareness of the sequence. GH is lost first, making it the answer to 'which deficiency occurs first,' not last. The last to be lost is typically ACTH.

questions.question: A patient on lithium develops polyuria and polydipsia. The most likely mechanism is
questions.explanation: Lithium causes nephrogenic DI by downregulating aquaporin-2 channels in collecting duct cells, rendering them resistant to ADH.

questions.question: SIADH is characterized by
questions.explanation: Excess ADH causes water retention (dilutional hyponatremia) while urine remains concentrated (>100 mOsm/kg) — inappropriate given the low serum osmolality.

questions.question: In Addison's disease, the expected electrolyte pattern is
questions.explanation: Aldosterone deficiency causes sodium loss and potassium retention; cortisol deficiency causes hypoglycemia and impairs gluconeogenesis.

questions.question: The confirmatory test for primary adrenal insufficiency is
questions.explanation: Short Synacthen test: failure of cortisol to rise above 550 nmol/L after synthetic ACTH injection confirms adrenal insufficiency.

questions.question: Calcitonin is used as a tumor marker for
questions.explanation: Medullary thyroid cancer arises from calcitonin-secreting C-cells; calcitonin serves as both a diagnostic and surveillance marker.

questions.question: A patient has low calcium, high phosphate, and elevated PTH. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs when hypocalcemia (from CKD or vitamin D deficiency) drives compensatory PTH elevation; phosphate rises in CKD.

questions.question: The OGTT uses a glucose load of
questions.explanation: 75 g oral glucose dissolved in water; 2-hour plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L confirms diabetes.

questions.question: Homocystinuria is due to deficiency of
questions.explanation: CBS deficiency blocks homocysteine conversion to cystathionine; homocysteine accumulates causing lens dislocation, Marfanoid habitus, thrombosis, and intellectual disability.

questions.question: In von Gierke disease (GSD type I), fasting hypoglycemia occurs because of inability to
questions.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency prevents both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis from releasing free glucose into the blood, causing severe fasting hypoglycemia with hepatomegaly and lactic acidosis.

questions.question: A gram-positive coccus isolated from a wound shows golden-yellow colonies on blood agar but is coagulase negative. The most likely organism is
questions.explanation: S. saprophyticus can produce yellow pigment but is coagulase negative, unlike S. aureus which is coagulase positive. This organism is commonly associated with urinary tract infections in young women.

questions.question: A patient with "rice water" stool most likely has infection with
questions.explanation: Rice water stool (watery with flecks of mucus resembling water in which rice has been washed) is characteristic of cholera caused by V. cholerae.

questions.question: Which organism can grow at refrigeration temperature (4°C)?
questions.explanation: Listeria is psychrophilic and can multiply at refrigeration temperatures (4°C), making it a significant food safety concern.

questions.question: A 25-year-old sexually active female presents with urinary tract infection. The organism that is coagulase-negative and novobiocin resistant is
questions.explanation: S. saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant and causes UTI in young sexually active women. S. epidermidis is novobiocin sensitive.

questions.question: The "string of pearls" appearance on Loeffler serum medium is characteristic of
questions.explanation: B. anthracis shows string of pearls appearance when grown in the presence of penicillin on Loeffler medium due to the formation of round bodies along the bacilli chain.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: A neonate develops meningitis. CSF culture grows gram-negative bacilli with K1 capsular antigen. The organism is
questions.explanation: E. coli with K1 capsular antigen is the most common cause of neonatal meningitis.

questions.question: "Medusa head" colonies on blood agar are produced by
questions.explanation: B. anthracis produces characteristic medusa head colonies due to chaining of bacilli with irregular edges and comma-shaped projections.

questions.question: Which test differentiates Staphylococcus from Streptococcus?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus is catalase positive while Streptococcus is catalase negative.

questions.question: A patient develops pseudomembranous colitis after prolonged antibiotic therapy. The causative organism is
questions.explanation: C. difficile produces toxins A and B causing antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis when normal gut flora is disrupted.

questions.question: "Chinese letter" or "V and L shaped" arrangement is seen in
questions.explanation: C. diphtheriae shows characteristic angular arrangement resembling Chinese letters due to snapping division.

questions.question: A burn patient develops green-blue pus with a fruity odor. The organism is
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas produces pyocyanin (blue-green pigment) and has a characteristic grape-like or fruity odor.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: The CAMP test is positive for
questions.explanation: Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae) shows enhanced hemolysis (arrowhead-shaped zone) when grown near S. aureus on blood agar.

questions.question: Which organism produces black colonies on bismuth sulfite agar?
questions.explanation: S. typhi produces hydrogen sulfide (H2S) which reacts with bismuth sulfite to form black colonies.

questions.question: A patient presents with flaccid paralysis and descending weakness. The organism that causes this by blocking acetylcholine release is
questions.explanation: C. botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions causing flaccid paralysis.

questions.question: "Swarming" motility on blood agar is characteristic of
questions.explanation: Proteus shows swarming motility creating concentric waves on agar due to highly active flagella.

questions.question: A gram-negative coccus that ferments maltose but not glucose is
questions.explanation: Neisseria species ferment glucose first. N. gonorrhoeae ferments only glucose; N. meningitidis ferments both glucose and maltose.

questions.question: "Elek test" is used to detect toxigenicity of
questions.explanation: Elek immunoprecipitation test detects diphtheria toxin production.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: Which organism produces "boxcar" shaped gram-positive rods?
questions.explanation: C. perfringens appears as large, rectangular, boxcar-shaped gram-positive rods.

questions.question: A patient develops hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) after eating undercooked hamburger. The organism is
questions.explanation: EHEC O157:H7 produces Shiga toxin causing hemorrhagic colitis and HUS.

questions.question: "Drumstick" or "tennis racket" appearance of spores is seen in
questions.explanation: C. tetani has terminal round spores giving a drumstick appearance.

questions.question: The most common cause of acute bacterial meningitis in adults is
questions.explanation: S. pneumoniae is the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in adults.

questions.question: A stool sample shows gram-negative curved rods with "gull wing" or "S" shape. The organism is
questions.explanation: Campylobacter has characteristic S-shaped or gull wing morphology and darting motility.

questions.question: Which organism is urease positive and causes "alkaline tide" in urine?
questions.explanation: Proteus produces urease which splits urea to ammonia, raising urine pH and promoting struvite stone formation.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: "Nagler reaction" is positive for
questions.explanation: Nagler test detects lecithinase (alpha toxin) production by C. perfringens.

questions.question: A patient with infective endocarditis has blood culture showing catalase negative, gram-positive cocci resistant to optochin and not lysed by bile. The organism is
questions.explanation: Enterococcus is optochin resistant and bile insoluble, distinguishing it from S. pneumoniae.

questions.question: "Quellung reaction" is used to identify capsule of
questions.explanation: Quellung reaction (capsular swelling test) can identify capsules of any encapsulated bacteria using specific antisera.

questions.question: Which organism causes "woolsorter's disease"?
questions.explanation: Woolsorter's disease is inhalational anthrax from B. anthracis spores.

questions.question: A comma-shaped gram-negative rod showing "shooting star" motility in hanging drop is
questions.explanation: V. cholerae shows rapid darting or shooting star motility due to its single polar flagellum.

questions.question: "Widal test" detects antibodies against
questions.explanation: Widal test detects antibodies against O and H antigens of S. typhi in typhoid fever.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: Which organism produces "currant jelly" sputum?
questions.explanation: Klebsiella pneumonia produces thick, bloody, mucoid sputum resembling currant jelly.

questions.question: "McFadyean reaction" showing pink-staining capsule is diagnostic for
questions.explanation: McFadyean staining shows a pink/purple capsule around blue B. anthracis bacilli.

questions.question: A patient develops gas gangrene after a crushing injury. The organism most likely responsible is
questions.explanation: C. perfringens produces alpha toxin causing myonecrosis with gas production.

questions.question: Which organism shows "tumbling motility" at 25°C but not at 37°C?
questions.explanation: Listeria exhibits tumbling motility at room temperature (20-25°C) but motility is reduced at 37°C.

options: Staphylococcus aureus providing factors for Haemophilus
questions.question: "Satellite phenomenon" on blood agar indicates
questions.explanation: H. influenzae grows as satellite colonies around S. aureus, which provides V factor (NAD).
questions.correct_answer_text: Staphylococcus aureus providing factors for Haemophilus

questions.question: A patient with facial nerve palsy, meningitis, and rash has CSF showing gram-negative diplococci. The organism is
questions.explanation: N. meningitidis causes meningitis with petechial rash and appears as gram-negative kidney bean-shaped diplococci.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: "Double zone hemolysis" on blood agar is characteristic of
questions.explanation: C. perfringens shows an inner zone of complete beta-hemolysis and an outer zone of incomplete hemolysis.

questions.question: A diabetic patient develops malignant external otitis. The organism is
questions.explanation: P. aeruginosa causes invasive external otitis in diabetic patients, which can extend to the temporal bone.

questions.question: Which organism is both oxidase and catalase positive?
questions.explanation: P. aeruginosa is both oxidase and catalase positive. Enterobacteriaceae are typically oxidase negative.

questions.question: The term "Staphylococcus" is derived from Greek meaning
questions.explanation: The name Staphylococcus comes from Greek "staphyle" meaning "bunch of grapes" because under microscopic examination, these bacteria appear arranged in irregular clusters resembling bunches of grapes.

questions.question: Which test is most useful for distinguishing staphylococci from streptococci?
questions.explanation: The catalase test is the key differentiating test. Staphylococci are catalase-positive (produce bubbles when H₂O₂ is added), while streptococci and enterococci are catalase-negative. This is the first test performed to distinguish these gram-positive cocci.

questions.question: Staphylococci can grow in salt concentrations up to
questions.explanation: Staphylococci are facultative halophiles and can tolerate high salt concentrations of 7.5-10% NaCl. This property is exploited in selective media like Mannitol Salt Agar to isolate staphylococci from mixed cultures.

questions.question: The primary test used to clinically classify staphylococci is
questions.explanation: The coagulase test divides staphylococci into two clinically important groups: coagulase-positive (mainly S. aureus) and coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS). This classification has major therapeutic implications.

questions.question: Which staphylococcal species is coagulase-positive?
questions.explanation: S. aureus is the primary coagulase-positive staphylococcus of clinical importance. Coagulase enzyme helps S. aureus clot plasma, which interferes with phagocytosis and facilitates tissue spread.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: Protein A in S. aureus cell wall has affinity for
questions.explanation: Protein A binds to the Fc portion of IgG antibodies, which inhibits opsonization and phagocytosis. This is an important virulence mechanism that helps S. aureus evade the immune system.

questions.question: Which toxin is responsible for Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS)?
questions.explanation: Epidermolytic (exfoliative) toxins A and B act as proteases that cleave desmoglein protein, which holds epidermal cells together. This results in separation and peeling of the epidermal layer, causing the scalded skin appearance.

questions.question: Staphylococcal food poisoning is caused by
questions.explanation: S. aureus produces heat-stable enterotoxins in contaminated food. Even if bacteria are killed by cooking, the preformed toxin remains active and causes rapid-onset food poisoning when ingested.

questions.question: The characteristic feature of Toxic Shock Syndrome occurring 1-2 weeks after acute illness is
questions.explanation: While fever, hypotension, and rash occur during the acute phase, the pathognomonic (characteristic) late sign is desquamation (skin peeling) of palms and soles occurring 1-2 weeks later.

questions.question: On Mannitol Salt Agar, S. aureus colonies appear
questions.explanation: S. aureus ferments mannitol, producing acid that turns the phenol red indicator yellow. S. epidermidis doesn't ferment mannitol, so colonies remain pink/red.

questions.question: Which enzyme helps S. aureus spread through tissues by destroying connective tissue?
questions.explanation: Hyaluronidase is called the "spreading factor" because it breaks down hyaluronic acid in connective tissues, facilitating bacterial spread through tissues.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: MRSA is resistant to methicillin due to
questions.explanation: MRSA produces an additional penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with low affinity for β-lactam antibiotics, allowing cell wall synthesis to continue despite antibiotic presence.

questions.question: The drug of choice for MRSA infections is
questions.explanation: Vancomycin remains the first-line treatment for MRSA infections as it has a different mechanism of action (inhibiting cell wall synthesis at a different step) that bypasses β-lactam resistance.

questions.question: S. epidermidis is particularly associated with infections of
questions.explanation: S. epidermidis produces glycocalyx (biofilm) that allows it to adhere strongly to medical devices like catheters, shunts, and prosthetic materials, making it a major cause of device-related infections.

questions.question: Which test distinguishes S. epidermidis from S. saprophyticus?
questions.explanation: Both are coagulase-negative, but S. epidermidis is novobiocin-sensitive while S. saprophyticus is novobiocin-resistant. This is the key differentiating test between these two species.

questions.question: S. saprophyticus is most commonly associated with
questions.explanation: S. saprophyticus is the second most common cause of UTIs in young, sexually active women (after E. coli). It inhabits the skin around the genitourinary tract.

questions.question: Which staphylococcal species is vancomycin-resistant?
questions.explanation: S. haemolyticus is naturally resistant to vancomycin and is highly multi-drug resistant, making it a challenging pathogen to treat.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: The most important virulence factor that distinguishes S. aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci is
questions.explanation: Coagulase is the key virulence factor that defines S. aureus. It helps the bacteria clot plasma, creating a protective barrier against phagocytosis and facilitating tissue invasion.

questions.question: Staphylococcal enterotoxin causes food poisoning by
questions.explanation: Enterotoxin stimulates release of IL-1 and IL-2, which activate the enteric nervous system and stimulate the vomiting center in the brain, causing the rapid onset of nausea and vomiting.

options: Children and patients with renal failure
questions.question: SSSS (Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome) is most common in
questions.explanation: SSSS occurs mainly in children (due to immature kidney function) and adults with renal failure because they cannot effectively clear the epidermolytic toxin from their system.
questions.correct_answer_text: Children and patients with renal failure

questions.question: The key test to differentiate Micrococcus from Staphylococcus is
questions.explanation: Micrococcus species are oxidase-positive while Staphylococcus species (except S. sciuri, S. lentus, S. vutulus) are oxidase-negative. This is the most reliable test to differentiate these genera.

questions.question: Micrococcus colonies on blood agar typically appear
questions.explanation: Micrococcus species characteristically produce yellow or red pigments on blood agar, which helps distinguish them from staphylococci that typically produce golden-yellow (S. aureus) or white colonies.

questions.question: Which of the following is characteristic of all staphylococci?
questions.explanation: All staphylococci are catalase-positive. This is a defining characteristic of the genus, while other properties like coagulase production, mannitol fermentation, and hemolysis vary among species.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: The primary reservoir of S. aureus in healthy individuals is
questions.explanation: S. aureus is part of the normal flora of skin and nasal passages in about 20-30% of healthy individuals. The anterior nares (nostrils) are the primary carriage site.

questions.question: Which antibiotic is commonly used topically for staphylococcal skin infections?
questions.explanation: Mupirocin is a topical antibiotic highly effective against staphylococci, including MRSA. It's commonly used for localized skin infections and nasal decolonization.

options: Pumping antibiotics out of the cell
questions.question: The mechanism by which β-lactamase confers antibiotic resistance is
questions.explanation: β-lactamase enzymes cleave the β-lactam ring in penicillins and cephalosporins, inactivating these antibiotics before they can inhibit cell wall synthesis.

questions.question: Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1 (TSST-1) causes disease by
questions.explanation: TSST-1 is a superantigen that causes massive, non-specific T-cell activation and cytokine release (IL-1, IL-2, TNF), leading to the systemic inflammatory response seen in toxic shock syndrome.

questions.question: S. aureus appears as colonies on blood agar with hemolysis
questions.explanation: S. aureus characteristically produces golden-yellow, fairly large colonies that are beta-hemolytic (complete clearing around colonies) on blood agar. This appearance helps in preliminary identification.

questions.question: The DNAase test is positive in
questions.explanation: The DNAase test is strongly positive in S. aureus and weakly positive in S. epidermidis, but negative in S. saprophyticus. This helps differentiate between these species.

options: Limited to a single tissue compartment
questions.question: Prevention of staphylococcal hospital-acquired infections is best achieved by
questions.explanation: The most effective prevention methods are proper hand hygiene, aseptic handling of medical devices and catheters, and proper wound care. These basic infection control measures are more important than antibiotic prophylaxis or screening. ## Score Interpretation: - 26-30 correct: Excellent understanding - 21-25 correct: Good understanding, review weak areas - 16-20 correct: Fair understanding, needs more study - Below 16: Poor understanding, comprehensive review needed

mcq_sets.title: MCQ: Cardiovascular System Pathology

questions.question: Which foramen ovale closes in approximately 75% of individuals at birth?
questions.explanation: Closes by fusion of septum primum and secundum. Persists in 25% of adults as PFO.

questions.question: Anatomical closure of the ductus arteriosus occurs through which process?
questions.explanation: Functional closure via vasoconstriction occurs first. Anatomical closure takes several weeks through intimal proliferation and fibrosis.

questions.question: Failure of which structure to adequately cover the ostium secundum results in ostium secundum ASD?
questions.explanation: Ostium secundum ASD occurs when the septum secundum does not enlarge sufficiently to cover the ostium secundum.

questions.question: Which VSD type is specifically more common in Asian patients?
questions.explanation: Situated in the outlet septum, bordered by fibrous continuity of aortic and pulmonary valves.

options: Anterior cephalad deviation of the outlet septum
Failure of truncus arteriosus to divide
Apical displacement of the tricuspid valve
Failure of endocardial cushions to fuse
questions.question: The fundamental embryological defect in Tetralogy of Fallot is
questions.explanation: This single defect produces all four features of TOF — outlet VSD, pulmonary outflow obstruction, overriding aorta and RVH.
questions.correct_answer_text: Anterior cephalad deviation of the outlet septum

questions.question: Which structure, when displaced apically, causes atrialization of the right ventricular inflow tract?
questions.explanation: This is Ebstein's anomaly. Apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet causes the RV inflow to function as an atrial chamber.

options: Resorption of subpulmonary instead of subaortic conus
Failure of subaortic conus to elongate
Failure of truncus arteriosus to partition
Malalignment of the outlet septum anteriorly
questions.question: In Transposition of Great Arteries, which embryological failure is directly responsible?
questions.explanation: Normally the subaortic conus resorbs, moving the aorta posteriorly to connect with the LV. In TGA the wrong conus resorbs, keeping the aorta anterior and connected to the RV.
questions.correct_answer_text: Resorption of subpulmonary instead of subaortic conus

questions.question: Which chromosomal abnormality is most specifically associated with coarctation of the aorta?
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome is specifically associated with coarctation of aorta and bicuspid aortic valve. Trisomy 21 is associated with AV canal defects.

questions.question: Persistent truncus arteriosus always occurs alongside which other defect?
questions.explanation: The single great vessel overrides both ventricles, so a VSD is always present in persistent truncus arteriosus.

questions.question: Sinus venosus ASD is specifically associated with anomalous drainage of pulmonary veins from which lung?
questions.explanation: Right pulmonary veins drain anomalously into the SVC or right atrium due to the proximity of the sinus venosus defect to the SVC entry.

questions.question: Which maternal teratogen is specifically associated with Ebstein's anomaly?
questions.explanation: Maternal lithium use in first trimester is the specific teratogen classically associated with Ebstein's anomaly.

questions.question: A restrictive VSD differs from a non-restrictive VSD in that it
questions.explanation: Restrictive VSDs cause no significant haemodynamic derangement and may close spontaneously, unlike large non-restrictive VSDs which cause progressive pulmonary hypertension.

questions.question: Which congenital defect results from failure of both subpulmonary AND subaortic conus to resorb?
questions.explanation: Failure of either conus to resorb produces double outlet anomalies of the RV. TGA results from resorption of the wrong conus. TOF results from malalignment, not failure of resorption.

options: Septum primum downward from the roof
Sinus venosus from the posterior wall
questions.question: The ostium primum is created during atrial septation by growth of which structure toward the AV canal?
questions.explanation: The septum primum grows downward creating the ostium primum inferiorly. As it grows, perforations form superiorly creating the ostium secundum.
questions.correct_answer_text: Septum primum downward from the roof

questions.question: VSD accounts for what percentage of all congenital heart disease?
questions.explanation: VSD is the most common congenital heart defect overall, accounting for 25% of all CHD.

questions.question: Which component of the ventricular septum lies directly beneath the aortic valve?
questions.explanation: The small membranous septum lies just underneath the aortic valve. Membranous VSDs often have inlet, outlet or trabecular extension.

questions.question: In which CHD does the right ventricle inflow tract function haemodynamically as an atrial chamber?
questions.explanation: Apical displacement of the septal tricuspid leaflet causes atrialization of the RV inflow tract — it receives atrial pressure and contracts out of synchrony with the functional RV.

options: Septum secundum → ostium primum → ostium secundum → fossa ovalis
Ostium primum → ostium secundum → septum secundum → fossa ovalis
Septum primum → ostium primum → ostium secundum → septum secundum
Fossa ovalis → septum primum → ostium primum → septum secundum
questions.question: Which of the following is the correct sequence of atrial septal development?
questions.explanation: Septum primum grows down creating ostium primum. Perforations coalesce into ostium secundum. Then septum secundum develops to the right, leaving the fossa ovalis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Septum primum → ostium primum → ostium secundum → septum secundum

questions.question: Which of the following maternal infections is a recognised cause of congenital heart disease?
questions.explanation: Maternal rubella is a recognised environmental cause of CHD, particularly PDA and pulmonary stenosis. It is specifically listed among the environmental teratogenic causes of CHD.

questions.question: In Tetralogy of Fallot, which level is the dominant site of right ventricular outflow obstruction?
questions.explanation: The dominant obstruction in TOF is at the subvalvular/infundibular level due to hypertrophied infundibular myocardium from the malaligned outlet septum — not at the valve itself.

options: Juxtaductal — at the ductus arteriosus insertion
questions.question: Coarctation of the aorta occurs most commonly at which location?
questions.explanation: Narrowing occurs just distal to the left subclavian artery at the site of ductus arteriosus insertion.
questions.correct_answer_text: Juxtaductal — at the ductus arteriosus insertion

questions.question: Which radiological finding is specifically associated with coarctation of the aorta?
questions.explanation: Caused by dilated intercostal collateral vessels eroding the inferior rib margins, developing to bypass the coarctation.

questions.question: A patient with an untreated large VSD develops reversed cyanosis. Which term describes this end-stage complication?
questions.explanation: Chronic L→R shunting → pulmonary hypertension → pulmonary pressure exceeds systemic → shunt reverses to R→L → cyanosis. This is irreversible.

questions.question: Patent foramen ovale in adults is specifically associated with which cerebrovascular complication?
questions.explanation: Venous thrombus crosses from right to left atrium through the PFO entering systemic circulation, causing stroke without an obvious arterial source.

questions.question: Ostium primum ASD is associated with a cleft in which specific valve leaflet?
questions.explanation: Both the ostium primum ASD and the cleft mitral leaflet result from the same endocardial cushion maldevelopment. Commonly seen in Down syndrome.

questions.question: Which congenital heart defect is characterised by absence of a direct connection between the right atrium and right ventricle?
questions.explanation: There is no tricuspid valve orifice connecting RA to RV. Survival depends on an ASD for right-sided drainage and a VSD or PDA for pulmonary blood flow.

questions.question: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome is more common in which sex?
questions.explanation: Hypoplastic left heart is among the CHDs more common in males, alongside aortic stenosis, coarctation, pulmonary atresia, tricuspid atresia and TGA.
