mcq_sets.title: MCQ: Here are all 40 questions rewritten with even A/B/C/D spread and no consecutive same-let

options: Prolonged increased intraluminal pressure causing venous wall weakening and valve incompetence
Inflammatory destruction of venous wall smooth muscle from chronic venous stasis
Deep vein thrombosis propagating retrogradely into the superficial venous system
Arteriovenous fistula formation from repeated superficial vein trauma
questions.question: A 55-year-old obese woman develops painful, dilated, tortuous veins in her lower legs after three pregnancies. What is the primary mechanism of their development?
questions.explanation: Varicose veins result from prolonged elevated intraluminal pressure causing progressive venous wall dilation and valve incompetence — worsened by obesity and pregnancy compressing the IVC.
questions.correct_answer_text: Prolonged increased intraluminal pressure causing venous wall weakening and valve incompetence

options: Erythema nodosum from immune complex deposition in venous endothelium
Lipodermatosclerosis from fat necrosis caused by venous hypertension
Chronic contact dermatitis from repeated venous compression bandaging
Stasis dermatitis (brawny induration) from haemolysis of extravasated RBCs releasing haemosiderin
questions.question: A patient with longstanding varicose veins develops brownish discolouration and a non-healing ulcer above the medial malleolus. What is the correct term and mechanism for the skin discolouration?
questions.explanation: Stasis dermatitis (brawny induration) results from chronic venous congestion → extravasation of RBCs → haemolysis → haemosiderin deposition → brawny discolouration and fibrosis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Stasis dermatitis (brawny induration) from haemolysis of extravasated RBCs releasing haemosiderin

options: Trousseau syndrome — migratory thrombophlebitis from occult visceral malignancy secreting procoagulant factors
Buerger disease — thromboangiitis obliterans in a young smoker
Virchow's triad — hypercoagulability, stasis, and endothelial injury occurring simultaneously
Mondor disease — superficial thrombophlebitis of chest wall veins
questions.question: A 45-year-old male with pancreatic cancer develops painful superficial thrombophlebitis in his right leg, which resolves, then recurs in his left arm two weeks later. What eponym describes this phenomenon and its mechanism?
questions.explanation: Trousseau syndrome is migratory thrombophlebitis classically associated with occult visceral malignancy. Tumours (especially pancreatic and GI) secrete tissue factor and mucins that activate coagulation.
questions.correct_answer_text: Trousseau syndrome — migratory thrombophlebitis from occult visceral malignancy secreting procoagulant factors

options: Both carry equal PE risk as thrombus can propagate freely between the systems
DVT is the major source of PE; embolism from superficial varicose veins is very rare
Varicose veins carry higher embolism risk due to greater peripheral venous pressure
Neither causes PE without a concurrent cardiac septal defect
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes superficial varicose veins from deep vein thrombosis regarding pulmonary embolism risk?
questions.explanation: Embolism from superficial varicose veins is very rare. DVT — particularly in popliteal, femoral, and iliac veins — is the major source of potentially fatal pulmonary embolism.
questions.correct_answer_text: DVT is the major source of PE; embolism from superficial varicose veins is very rare

options: Milroy disease unmasked by acute lymphatic inflammation
Lymphoedema from permanent lymphatic fibrosis after the episode
Bacteraemia and sepsis if bacteria escape the draining lymph nodes into the venous circulation
Chylous ascites from lymphatic hypertension spreading to abdominal lymphatics
questions.question: A 30-year-old woman has painful red streaks running from a wound on her finger toward her axilla with tender enlarged nodes. Which outcome is most feared if she is not treated urgently?
questions.explanation: Lymphangitis (most commonly Group A Streptococcus) tracks bacteria through lymphatics. If not contained within draining nodes, bacteria enter the venous circulation causing bacteraemia and potentially fatal sepsis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Bacteraemia and sepsis if bacteria escape the draining lymph nodes into the venous circulation

options: Recurrent breast carcinoma with direct lymphatic invasion causing arm swelling
Superior vena cava syndrome from mediastinal nodal recurrence compressing the SVC
Post-thrombotic syndrome from axillary vein thrombosis from prolonged immobility
Secondary lymphoedema from surgical lymphatic disruption; associated with lymphangiosarcoma
questions.question: A 40-year-old woman who had a left radical mastectomy 8 years ago has a massively swollen, firm, fibrotic left arm with peau d'orange skin changes. Which condition explains this and what long-term complication is associated?
questions.explanation: Surgical severing of axillary lymphatics causes secondary lymphoedema. Chronic post-mastectomy lymphoedema carries a risk of lymphangiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome) developing in the affected arm.
questions.correct_answer_text: Secondary lymphoedema from surgical lymphatic disruption; associated with lymphangiosarcoma

options: GNAQ somatic missense mutation causing constitutive G-protein signalling
ENG (endoglin) or ACVRL1/ALK1 genes — components of the TGF-β signalling pathway in endothelial cells
NF1 and NF2 mutations disrupting neurofibromin in endothelial cells
VHL germline mutation causing haemangioblastoma and AVM formation
questions.question: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease) is autosomal dominant. What genes are mutated and what pathway do they affect?
questions.explanation: Osler-Weber-Rendu disease is caused by mutations in ENG or ACVRL1/ALK1 genes, both encoding components of the TGF-β signalling pathway in endothelial cells, leading to widespread telangiectasias present from birth.
questions.correct_answer_text: ENG (endoglin) or ACVRL1/ALK1 genes — components of the TGF-β signalling pathway in endothelial cells

options: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma — grows rapidly then completely regresses by age 7 in most cases
Cavernous hemangioma — large infiltrative lesion that does not regress spontaneously
Pyogenic granuloma — rapidly growing pedunculated lesion that either regresses or fibroses
Port wine stain — grows with age, thickens the skin, and never regresses
questions.question: A child has a bright red raised patch on the forehead that grows rapidly in the first 3 months, then fades progressively. By age 7 the lesion is gone. What is this lesion?
questions.explanation: Juvenile hemangiomas occur in 1 in 200 births, grow rapidly for a few months, then fade and completely regress by age 7 in most cases — parents should be reassured.
questions.correct_answer_text: Juvenile (strawberry) hemangioma — grows rapidly then completely regresses by age 7 in most cases

options: Germline VHL mutation causing haemangioblastomas and AV malformations
TSC1/TSC2 mutation causing tuberous sclerosis complex with cortical tubers
Somatic GNAQ missense mutation in the Gα subunit causing constitutive signalling
NF1 mutation causing neurofibromas and café-au-lait macules
questions.question: A port wine stain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve is found in a child with seizures, intellectual disability, and skull "tram-track" calcifications. What underlying mutation causes this syndrome?
questions.explanation: Sturge-Weber syndrome (port wine stain + leptomeningeal angiomas + seizures + intellectual disability) is caused by a somatic GNAQ missense mutation occurring early in development — not inherited.
questions.correct_answer_text: Somatic GNAQ missense mutation in the Gα subunit causing constitutive signalling

options: It requires immediate resection as it represents well-differentiated angiosarcoma
It is a capillary hemangioma — the most common vascular tumour of infancy
It represents a glomus tumour of the liver arising from modified smooth muscle cells
It is a cavernous hemangioma — infiltrative, does not regress, and should never be biopsied percutaneously
questions.question: A 35-year-old male has a 2 cm vascular lesion in his liver found incidentally. Biopsy shows large dilated cavernous blood-filled spaces with intravascular thrombi and dystrophic calcification. What is most accurate about this lesion?
questions.explanation: Cavernous hemangiomas are infiltrative, do not regress, and can be difficult to distinguish from malignancy on imaging. Percutaneous biopsy risks fatal haemorrhage — diagnosis is usually made radiologically.
questions.correct_answer_text: It is a cavernous hemangioma — infiltrative, does not regress, and should never be biopsied percutaneously

options: Branchial cleft cyst — lined by squamous epithelium; no chromosomal associations
Capillary lymphangioma — small, pedunculated, well-circumscribed; no syndromic associations
Cavernous lymphangioma (cystic hygroma) — strongly associated with Turner syndrome (45,X)
Cavernous hemangioma — blood-filled spaces with dystrophic calcification
questions.question: A child has a soft fluctuant 8 cm mass in the left neck at birth. Histology shows massively dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelium with indistinct margins. What is the diagnosis and its key association?
questions.explanation: Cystic hygromas are cavernous lymphangiomas with indistinct unencapsulated margins in the neck/axilla. They are strongly associated with Turner syndrome and difficult to resect completely due to poor margins.
questions.correct_answer_text: Cavernous lymphangioma (cystic hygroma) — strongly associated with Turner syndrome (45,X)

options: Endothelial cells confirmed by CD31 and von Willebrand factor — capillary hemangioma
Glomus tumour — modified smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies; NOT endothelial; excision curative
Malignant endothelial cells with high mitotic rate — subungual angiosarcoma
Myoepithelial cells from eccrine sweat glands — syringoma of the nail bed
questions.question: A patient presents with an exquisitely painful small lesion under his thumbnail. Excision reveals a tumour composed of modified smooth muscle cells surrounding arteriovenous channels. What is the cell of origin and key distinguishing feature?
questions.explanation: Glomus tumours arise from modified smooth muscle cells (NOT endothelial) of glomus bodies. They are exquisitely painful, found under fingernails, and are completely cured by excision.
questions.correct_answer_text: Glomus tumour — modified smooth muscle cells of glomus bodies; NOT endothelial; excision curative

options: Kaposi sarcoma — HHV8 causing spindle cell proliferation with slitlike vascular spaces
Pyogenic granuloma — reactive vascular proliferation from a local skin infection
Angiosarcoma — malignant endothelial proliferation confirmed by CD31 immunostaining
Bacillary angiomatosis — Bartonella species causing vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts
questions.question: A 32-year-old HIV-positive male with CD4 count of 45 develops red papules on his skin. Biopsy shows capillary proliferation with epithelioid endothelial cells, scattered neutrophils, and granular eosinophilic material. Warthin-Starry silver stain reveals bacilli. What is the diagnosis and the causative organism?
questions.explanation: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by Bartonella species (B. henselae or B. quintana) in immunocompromised patients. Warthin-Starry stain reveals the causative bacteria — distinguishing it critically from Kaposi sarcoma.
questions.correct_answer_text: Bacillary angiomatosis — Bartonella species causing vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts

options: HHV8 — viral cyclin D homologue disrupts cell cycle controls and viral proteins inhibit p53
EBV — latent membrane protein LMP1 activates NF-κB promoting endothelial proliferation
CMV — UL16 protein activates VEGF receptor signalling in infected endothelial cells
HIV — reverse transcriptase integrates into endothelial genome activating proto-oncogenes directly
questions.question: Which virus causes Kaposi sarcoma and through what molecular mechanism does latent infection promote tumour growth?
questions.explanation: HHV8 (KSHV) causes KS. During latent infection, a viral cyclin D homologue disrupts cell cycle checkpoints and viral proteins inhibit p53, providing infected cells with growth and survival advantages.
questions.correct_answer_text: HHV8 — viral cyclin D homologue disrupts cell cycle controls and viral proteins inhibit p53

options: Excellent — paediatric KS responds better to chemotherapy than adult forms
Intermediate — 50% 5-year survival with aggressive multiagent chemotherapy
Poor — nearly 100% mortality within 3 years for this severe endemic African form in children
Good — visceral KS in children regresses spontaneously as immune maturation occurs
questions.question: A prepubertal child in sub-Saharan Africa has Kaposi sarcoma with extensive lymph node and visceral involvement. What is the expected prognosis?
questions.explanation: The severe endemic African KS in prepubertal children with lymph node and visceral involvement carries nearly 100% mortality within 3 years — one of the most aggressive forms of KS.
questions.correct_answer_text: Poor — nearly 100% mortality within 3 years for this severe endemic African form in children

options: Initiate HAART therapy targeting HHV8 replication in the transplant setting
Start full-dose systemic chemotherapy with liposomal doxorubicin immediately
Administer interferon-γ monotherapy targeting viral replication in infected cells
Reduce or withdraw immunosuppression, accepting the risk of allograft rejection
questions.question: A renal transplant patient on tacrolimus develops Kaposi sarcoma with mucosal and visceral involvement. What is the most appropriate first management step?
questions.explanation: Transplant-associated KS is driven by T-cell immunosuppression. The first step is reducing or withdrawing immunosuppression — lesions may regress spontaneously, though organ rejection is a risk.
questions.correct_answer_text: Reduce or withdraw immunosuppression, accepting the risk of allograft rejection

options: Transformation to frank angiosarcoma requiring different chemotherapy regimens
Regression through immune surveillance in Classic KS as HHV8 viral load decreases
Lymph node and visceral involvement signalling progression from localised to systemic disease
Development of HHV8 drug resistance mutations reducing antiviral therapy response
questions.question: The three progressive morphologic stages of Kaposi sarcoma are patch, plaque, and nodule. What does the nodular stage specifically herald?
questions.explanation: The nodular stage — sheets of plump spindle cells with slitlike vascular spaces — heralds lymph node and visceral involvement, marking progression to systemic disease.
questions.correct_answer_text: Lymph node and visceral involvement signalling progression from localised to systemic disease

options: Angiosarcoma — malignant endothelial neoplasm; 5-year survival approximately 30%
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma — borderline tumour with 15% mortality
Bacillary angiomatosis — infectious; responds completely to antibiotics
Cavernous hemangioma — benign; requires observation not excision
questions.question: A 62-year-old woman develops a rapidly growing fleshy scalp mass with blurring margins. Biopsy shows atypical endothelial cells forming poorly organised vascular channels. CD31 is positive. What is the diagnosis and prognosis?
questions.explanation: Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial neoplasm confirmed by CD31 positivity. It is locally invasive, readily metastasises, and carries an approximately 30% 5-year survival.
questions.correct_answer_text: Angiosarcoma — malignant endothelial neoplasm; 5-year survival approximately 30%

options: Aflatoxin, hepatitis B virus, and vinyl chloride
Arsenic, Thorotrast (radioactive contrast agent), and polyvinyl chloride
Nitrosamines, asbestos fibres, and thorium dioxide
Alcohol, hepatitis C virus, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons
questions.question: Hepatic angiosarcoma is specifically associated with three carcinogenic exposures with long latency periods. Which combination is correct?
questions.explanation: Hepatic angiosarcoma is specifically linked to arsenic (pesticides), Thorotrast (formerly used radioactive contrast agent, now banned), and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) — all with characteristically long latency periods of 15–40 years.
questions.correct_answer_text: Arsenic, Thorotrast (radioactive contrast agent), and polyvinyl chloride

options: Classic Kaposi sarcoma — HHV8 reactivation in a lymphoedematous limb
Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma — borderline tumour associated with venous trauma
Lymphangiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome) arising in chronic post-mastectomy lymphoedema
Recurrent breast carcinoma with direct lymphatic infiltration of subcutaneous tissues
questions.question: A 55-year-old woman develops a new lesion in her right arm 6 years after right mastectomy and axillary clearance. Her arm has been massively swollen since surgery. Biopsy reveals malignant endothelial cells (CD31 positive). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Post-mastectomy lymphangiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome) arises in the chronically lymphoedematous arm years after radical mastectomy — a well-recognised complication of secondary lymphoedema.
questions.correct_answer_text: Lymphangiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves syndrome) arising in chronic post-mastectomy lymphoedema

options: Hypertension and diabetes; they are non-pulsatile and do not blanch with pressure
Hyperestrogenic states (pregnancy, cirrhosis); they are pulsatile and blanch with direct pressure
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia; present from birth and bleed spontaneously
Lymphoedema and venous insufficiency; they are non-pulsatile and do not blanch
questions.question: Spider telangiectasias are most commonly associated with which clinical states and what is their distinguishing physical examination feature?
questions.explanation: Spider telangiectasias are associated with hyperestrogenic states. Composed of dilated subcutaneous arterioles, they are characteristically pulsatile and blanch completely with direct pressure.
questions.correct_answer_text: Hyperestrogenic states (pregnancy, cirrhosis); they are pulsatile and blanch with direct pressure

options: Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) — high-flow shunting causing cardiac strain
Cavernous lymphangioma — lymphatic malformation often in the neck
Sacrococcygeal teratoma with dominant vascular component
Infantile hemangioma — benign lesion that eventually regresses
questions.question: A 3-year-old boy has a large vascular mass overlying his sacrum, associated with high-output cardiac failure. Biopsy shows mature vascular channels of arterial and venous type bypassing the capillary bed. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) are direct connections between arteries and veins bypassing the capillary bed. Large AVMs (e.g., in sacrum, brain) cause significant high-output cardiac failure due to shunting.
questions.correct_answer_text: Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) — high-flow shunting causing cardiac strain

questions.question: What is the most common cause of sustained hypertension?
questions.explanation: Essential (idiopathic) hypertension, without an identifiable secondary cause, accounts for 90-95% of all cases of hypertension.

options: Increased sympathetic nervous system activity directly affecting vascular tone
Reduced glomerular filtration rate leading to volume overload
Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) due to reduced renal perfusion
Endothelial dysfunction and impaired nitric oxide production
questions.question: Renal artery stenosis causes hypertension primarily through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Renal artery stenosis reduces blood flow to the juxtaglomerular apparatus, which stimulates renin release, activating the RAAS and causing hypertension. This is secondary hypertension.
questions.correct_answer_text: Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) due to reduced renal perfusion

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT typically considered a potential complication of hypertension?
questions.explanation: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a primary genetic myocardial disorder, distinct from the left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) that can result from chronic hypertension. LVH is a common complication of hypertension.

options: Haemoperitoneum from intraoperative injury to mesenteric vessels during surgery
Cirrhotic ascites with elevated triglyceride content from hepatic lipid metabolism dysfunction
Rupture of dilated lymphatics from obstruction allowing lymph to accumulate in the abdomen
Bowel perforation with leakage of chyme and fat into the peritoneal cavity
questions.question: A woman develops chylous ascites after surgery for ovarian cancer. What does the presence of chylous (milky) fluid specifically indicate?
questions.explanation: Chylous ascites results from rupture of dilated lymphatics caused by obstruction (tumour, surgery) — allowing lymph to accumulate in the peritoneal cavity. The milky appearance reflects its high lipid content.
questions.correct_answer_text: Rupture of dilated lymphatics from obstruction allowing lymph to accumulate in the abdomen

options: CD3 and CD20 — T and B lymphocyte markers used in lymphoproliferative disease
Desmin and smooth muscle actin — mesenchymal/smooth muscle differentiation markers
S100 protein and HMB-45 — melanocytic differentiation markers used for melanoma
CD31 and von Willebrand factor — endothelial cell-specific markers confirming vascular origin
questions.question: Malignant vascular tumours require immunohistochemistry to confirm their endothelial cell origin. Which markers confirm endothelial derivation?
questions.explanation: CD31 (PECAM-1) and von Willebrand factor (Factor VIII-related antigen) are endothelial cell-specific markers used to confirm endothelial origin of malignant vascular tumours, including angiosarcoma.
questions.correct_answer_text: CD31 and von Willebrand factor — endothelial cell-specific markers confirming vascular origin

options: Uniformly malignant — immediate chemotherapy required as most metastasise early at presentation
Variable — most cured by excision, but up to 40% recur and 20–30% eventually metastasise
Uniformly benign — complete excision is curative with essentially no recurrence risk
Indolent — always follows a benign course unless HHV8-infected tissue is also present
questions.question: An intermediate-grade vascular neoplasm — epithelioid hemangioendothelioma — is found around a medium-sized vein. What is its expected clinical behaviour?
questions.explanation: EHE has variable, intermediate behaviour: most are cured by excision, but up to 40% recur, 20–30% eventually metastasise, and ~15% of patients die of their disease.
questions.correct_answer_text: Variable — most cured by excision, but up to 40% recur and 20–30% eventually metastasise

options: 30-year history of cigarette smoking — tobacco carcinogens directly inducing vascular malignancy
Germline TP53 mutation causing Li-Fraumeni syndrome with predisposition to sarcomas
Prolonged occupational PVC exposure — a known hepatic but not soft tissue carcinogen
Lymphangiosarcoma from chronic post-mastectomy lymphoedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome)
questions.question: A 60-year-old male develops an enlarging right upper arm mass with CD31-positive malignant cells on biopsy, arising in an arm that has been chronically swollen since right mastectomy 10 years ago. Which aetiology does this represent?
questions.explanation: Angiosarcoma (lymphangiosarcoma/Stewart-Treves) arising in the ipsilateral arm after mastectomy and chronic lymphoedema is a classic, well-recognised aetiology — both radiation and lymphatic obstruction contribute.
questions.correct_answer_text: Lymphangiosarcoma from chronic post-mastectomy lymphoedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome)

options: Small grafts are too rigid causing mechanical fatigue and fragmentation over time
Small-bore grafts fail primarily from early thrombosis and late anastomotic intimal hyperplasia
The synthetic material provokes a more intense inflammatory reaction in smaller vessels
Small grafts develop calcification more rapidly than large-bore conduits
questions.question: Large-bore synthetic vascular grafts (≥12 mm) function well in high-flow aortic positions. Why do small-diameter synthetic grafts (≤8 mm) generally fail?
questions.explanation: Small-diameter synthetic grafts fail due to early thrombosis and late intimal hyperplasia developing at the anastomotic junction — the reason autologous vessels (saphenous vein, IMA) are preferred for small-bore bypass.
questions.correct_answer_text: Small-bore grafts fail primarily from early thrombosis and late anastomotic intimal hyperplasia

options: Early thrombosis, intimal thickening (months–years), and accelerated vein graft atherosclerosis
Acute rejection, chronic rejection, and transplant vasculopathy
Calcification, graft infection, and suture-line pseudoaneurysm formation
Progressive graft fibrosis, kinking, and mechanical valve incompetence
questions.question: The mechanisms by which saphenous vein grafts fail over 10 years include three distinct sequential processes. Which combination correctly identifies all three?
questions.explanation: Saphenous vein graft failure occurs through three sequential mechanisms: early thrombosis, later SMC-driven intimal thickening (months–years post-op), and eventual accelerated atherosclerosis — sometimes with plaque rupture.
questions.correct_answer_text: Early thrombosis, intimal thickening (months–years), and accelerated vein graft atherosclerosis

questions.question: An outbreak of sepsis caused by Staphylococcus aureus has occurred in the newborn nursery. What is the most likely source of the organism?
questions.explanation: S. aureus is commonly carried asymptomatically in the anterior nares (nose) of 20-40% of healthy individuals. Healthcare workers' nasal carriage is often the source of nosocomial outbreaks in nurseries.

questions.question: Which Pasteurella species has been associated with female genital tract and newborn infections?
questions.explanation: P. bettyae is associated with human genital tract infections and can cause neonatal infections. P. multocida typically causes wound infections after animal bites.

options: Pneumococci are alpha-hemolytic and can be serotyped based on polysaccharide capsule
Enterococci are group D streptococci and grow in 6.5% NaCl
Pneumococci and viridans streptococci can be differentiated by bile solubility and optochin susceptibility
Viridans streptococci are identified by Lancefield grouping based on C carbohydrate
questions.question: Each statement about streptococci classification is correct except
questions.explanation: Viridans streptococci typically lack the C carbohydrate antigen and are not classified by Lancefield grouping. They are identified by biochemical tests and alpha-hemolysis pattern.
questions.correct_answer_text: Viridans streptococci are identified by Lancefield grouping based on C carbohydrate

questions.question: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is caused by exotoxin produced by
questions.explanation: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is caused by exfoliative toxins (exfoliatins A and B) produced by certain strains of S. aureus. These toxins cause separation of the epidermis.

options: The baby is at risk for congenital syphilis
The mother needs lumbar puncture and CSF VDRL for neurosyphilis
The mother's previous treatment for syphilis was effective
questions.question: A pregnant woman with previous syphilis treatment shows: RPR non-reactive, TP-PA reactive. Which statement is most correct?
questions.explanation: Non-reactive RPR with reactive treponemal test indicates past treated syphilis. The treponemal test remains positive for life, while non-treponemal tests become negative after successful treatment.
questions.correct_answer_text: The mother's previous treatment for syphilis was effective

questions.question: Which bacteria has the lowest 50% infective dose (ID50)?
questions.explanation: Shigella species have extremely low infectious doses (10-100 organisms), making them highly contagious. Salmonella and V. cholerae require much higher doses (10⁴-10⁶ organisms).

questions.question: Which disease is best diagnosed by serologic means?
questions.explanation: Typhoid fever is often diagnosed serologically using the Widal test (though blood culture is gold standard). The others are better diagnosed by direct methods: TB (sputum AFB), gonorrhea (culture/PCR), actinomycosis (direct examination).

questions.question: A woman develops gonococcal PID. What is the most common sequela?
questions.explanation: Gonococcal PID commonly causes fallopian tube scarring and adhesions, leading to infertility and increased risk of ectopic pregnancy.

options: Poor immunogenicity of cell wall glycolipids
Inhibition of phagosome formation and endosomal acidification
Resistance to oxygen radicals in phagolysosome
Rapid escape from endosome to cytoplasm
questions.question: Mycobacterial survival after macrophage ingestion is attributed to
questions.explanation: Mycobacteria prevent phagosome-lysosome fusion and inhibit acidification of the phagosome, allowing survival within macrophages.
questions.correct_answer_text: Inhibition of phagosome formation and endosomal acidification

questions.question: The molecular basis for cholera toxin's effect on duodenal cells is
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gs protein, preventing GTPase activity and leading to continuous adenylyl cyclase activation and cAMP production.

questions.question: Bacterial capsules function as virulence factors by interfering with
questions.explanation: Bacterial capsules are antiphagocytic, making it difficult for neutrophils and macrophages to engulf and destroy encapsulated bacteria.

questions.question: A woman with UTI has gram-negative, lactose-fermenting, indole-positive bacilli. The organism's effectiveness in causing UTI is associated with
questions.explanation: This describes E. coli. P fimbriae allow adherence to uroepithelial cells with P blood group antigens, facilitating ascending UTI and pyelonephritis.

questions.question: Snails are both first and second intermediate hosts of
questions.explanation: E. ilocanum uses the same snail species as both first and second intermediate hosts, unlike other flukes that use different intermediate hosts.

questions.question: How can millipedes cause medical problems?
questions.explanation: Millipedes secrete defensive chemicals (hydrogen cyanide, quinones, phenols) that can cause skin burns, eye irritation, and respiratory problems.

questions.question: Holometabolous insects have
questions.explanation: Holometabolous insects undergo complete metamorphosis with four stages: egg → larva → pupa → adult. Examples include flies, beetles, and butterflies.

questions.question: Rift Valley fever is mainly transmitted by
questions.explanation: Rift Valley fever is primarily transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, especially flood-water Aedes species in endemic areas of Africa.

options: Mate but do not lay eggs
questions.question: Autogenous insects
questions.explanation: Autogenous insects can produce their first batch of eggs without taking a blood meal, using stored nutrients from their larval development.

options: Sexual reproduction with offspring from unfertilized eggs
Asexual reproduction with offspring from fertilized eggs
Sexual reproduction with offspring from fertilized eggs
questions.question: Parthenogenesis is a type of
questions.explanation: Parthenogenesis is asexual reproduction where embryos develop from unfertilized eggs, producing genetic clones of the parent.

questions.question: The best mode of malaria control is
questions.explanation: IVM combines multiple approaches (bed nets, treatment, environmental management, surveillance) for sustainable malaria control, more effective than single interventions.

questions.question: Which insects are included in order Blattaria?
questions.explanation: Order Blattaria (now Blattodea) includes cockroaches and termites. Lice belong to Phthiraptera, flies to Diptera, and beetles to Coleoptera.

questions.question: Which insects are included in order Diptera?
questions.explanation: Order Diptera includes all true flies (two wings). Cockroaches are Blattodea, lice are Phthiraptera, and fleas are Siphonaptera.

questions.question: Which insects transmit cholera pathogens?
questions.explanation: House flies and other true flies mechanically transmit Vibrio cholerae by contaminating food and water after contact with infected feces.

questions.question: Arboviruses are mainly transmitted by
questions.explanation: Different arboviruses are transmitted by various arthropods: Aedes (dengue, yellow fever), Culex (West Nile), and Culicoides (bluetongue). Cimex can potentially transmit some viruses.

questions.question: Anthropophilic insects prefer
questions.explanation: Anthropophilic means "human-loving." These insects preferentially feed on humans rather than other animals (e.g., Aedes aegypti).

questions.question: Exophagic insects prefer
questions.explanation: Exophagic insects prefer to feed outdoors, as opposed to endophagic insects that feed indoors. This affects vector control strategies.

questions.question: Presence of Chrysops in the environment could lead to
questions.explanation: Chrysops species (deer flies) transmit Loa loa (African eye worm), which can cause transient conjunctivitis and the characteristic migration of adult worms across the conjunctiva.

questions.question: Which stage of filarial nematodes is found in the chest muscles of vectors?
questions.explanation: In filarial development within vectors, L3 larvae (infective stage) develop in the flight muscles and then migrate to the mouthparts for transmission during the next blood meal.

questions.question: Which one of the following is a complication of streptococcus pharyngitis?
questions.explanation: Rheumatic fever is a nonsuppurative complication of Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) pharyngitis. It occurs 2-4 weeks after untreated strep throat due to molecular mimicry, where antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac tissue, causing carditis, arthritis, and chorea.

questions.question: The presence of a pseudomembrane is a result of
questions.explanation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces diphtheria toxin that causes local tissue necrosis in the pharynx, forming a characteristic gray-white pseudomembrane composed of fibrin, dead cells, bacteria, and inflammatory exudate. This membrane adheres firmly to underlying tissue and can cause airway obstruction.

questions.question: A paroxysm is a and is characteristic of
questions.explanation: A paroxysm is a sudden, uncontrollable series of coughs characteristic of pertussis (whooping cough) caused by Bordetella pertussis. The paroxysmal stage features severe coughing fits followed by an inspiratory "whoop" sound, often accompanied by post-tussive vomiting.

questions.question: The Mantoux test is used to identify
questions.explanation: The Mantoux test (tuberculin skin test) detects delayed-type hypersensitivity to tuberculin purified protein derivative (PPD), indicating prior exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A positive result shows induration at the injection site 48-72 hours after intradermal injection.

questions.question: This bacterial species is the most common cause of "typical" pneumonia.
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is the most common cause of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia. It presents with typical features: acute onset, high fever, productive cough with rusty sputum, pleuritic chest pain, and lobar consolidation on chest X-ray.

questions.question: To treat patients who have ingested botulism toxin, large doses of must be administered.
questions.explanation: Botulism requires administration of botulinum antitoxin (trivalent or heptavalent). The antitoxin neutralizes circulating toxin but cannot reverse already bound toxin. Early administration is critical. Antibiotics are ineffective against the preformed toxin.

questions.question: The organism Clostridium perfringens multiplies in foods only under conditions.
questions.explanation: Clostridium perfringens is an obligate anaerobe that multiplies only in oxygen-free environments. Improper food storage (inadequate cooling or reheating) creates anaerobic conditions that allow spore germination and toxin production, leading to food poisoning.

questions.question: A spore-forming, motile rod that can cause foodborne illness in a diarrheal or emetic form is Bacillus
questions.explanation: Bacillus cereus causes two forms of food poisoning: the emetic form (1-6 hours, associated with fried rice) caused by cereulide toxin, and the diarrheal form (8-16 hours, associated with meats and vegetables) caused by enterotoxins.

questions.question: Woolsorter disease applies to the form of
questions.explanation: Woolsorter's disease is pulmonary anthrax caused by inhaling Bacillus anthracis spores from contaminated animal products (wool, hides). It causes severe hemorrhagic mediastinitis, septic shock, and high mortality. The name comes from textile workers who processed contaminated wool.

options: It damages and lyses red blood cells
questions.question: Which one of the following describes the mode of action of tetanospasmin?
questions.explanation: Tetanospasmin (tetanus toxin) blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA and glycine) from Renshaw cells in the spinal cord by cleaving synaptobrevin. This prevents muscle relaxation, causing sustained muscle contraction (spastic paralysis) and characteristic lockjaw.

questions.question: Salpingitis is associated with and can lead to
questions.explanation: Salpingitis (fallopian tube inflammation) is commonly caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae as part of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Chronic inflammation causes scarring and tubal obstruction, leading to infertility and increased ectopic pregnancy risk.

questions.question: Ophthalmia is associated with what two STDs?
questions.explanation: Ophthalmia neonatorum (neonatal conjunctivitis) is caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis acquired during passage through an infected birth canal. Both can cause severe conjunctivitis and, if untreated, corneal scarring and blindness.

options: Both B and C are correct
questions.question: Toxin-generated S. aureus diseases resulting from contact include
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus produces exfoliative toxins causing scalded skin syndrome (bullous impetigo, Ritter's disease) and toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) causing toxic shock syndrome. Both are toxin-mediated diseases that can result from skin colonization or infection.

questions.question: The first microorganism to satisfy Koch's postulates (in the late 19th century) was
questions.explanation: Robert Koch first proved Bacillus anthracis as the causative agent of anthrax in 1876, establishing Koch's postulates. He isolated the organism from diseased animals, cultured it in pure form, reproduced the disease in healthy animals, and re-isolated the same organism.

options: The toxic component is the O side chain
It forms holes in red blood cell membranes yielding hemolysis
It interacts with macrophages and monocytes yielding release of cytokines
questions.question: Which of the following statements about lipopolysaccharide is correct?
questions.explanation: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS/endotoxin) binds to TLR4 on macrophages and monocytes via LPS-binding protein and CD14, triggering massive cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6). This causes fever, shock, and DIC. The toxic component is Lipid A, not the O antigen.
questions.correct_answer_text: It interacts with macrophages and monocytes yielding release of cytokines

questions.explanation: E. coli is a gram-negative bacterium with LPS in its outer membrane. Cholera toxin is secreted (not on flagella), lecithinase causes tissue necrosis (not diarrhea), and TSST-1 is produced by S. aureus (not S. epidermidis).

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of diphtheria toxin?
questions.explanation: Diphtheria toxin is an A-B toxin. The A subunit catalyzes ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2 (EF-2), irreversibly inactivating it and blocking protein synthesis. One toxin molecule can kill a cell by halting translation.

questions.question: Certain microorganisms are never considered to be members of the normal flora. They are always considered to be pathogens. Which one of the following organisms fits into that category?
questions.explanation: M. tuberculosis is always pathogenic and never part of normal flora. The others can be normal flora: S. pneumoniae (nasopharynx), E. coli (intestine), S. aureus (skin/nose), N. meningitidis (nasopharynx up to 10% of population).

questions.question: An outbreak of sepsis caused by Staphylococcus aureus has occurred in the newborn nursery. You are called upon to investigate. According to your knowledge of the normal flora, what is the most likely source of the organism?
questions.explanation: The anterior nares (nose) is the primary reservoir for S. aureus colonization, occurring in 20-40% of healthy adults. Healthcare workers can transmit the organism from their nose to patients via hands, making nasal carriage the most likely source in nosocomial outbreaks.

questions.question: Each of the following agent is a recognized cause of diarrhea except?
questions.explanation: Enterococcus faecalis is normal intestinal flora and causes urinary tract infections, endocarditis, and intra-abdominal infections, but not diarrhea. C. perfringens, V. cholerae, and E. coli are all well-recognized diarrheal pathogens.

questions.question: The identification of bacteria by serological test is based on the presence of specific antigens. Which of the following bacterial components is least likely to contain useful antigens?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are internal structures with highly conserved proteins across species, making them poor serological markers. Capsule (K antigens), cell wall (O antigens for LPS), and flagella (H antigens) are surface-exposed and variable, making them excellent for serotyping.

questions.question: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by exotoxin (exfoliatins) produced by
questions.explanation: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins (ETA and ETB) produced by certain S. aureus strains. These serine proteases cleave desmoglein-1 in the epidermis, causing superficial skin separation and blistering resembling scalding.

questions.explanation: Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) is best diagnosed serologically by detecting antibodies to phase I and II antigens. The organism is difficult to culture due to obligate intracellular nature. TB, gonorrhea, and actinomycosis are diagnosed by culture/microscopy.

questions.explanation: S. pyogenes causes pharyngitis, skin infections, and toxic shock syndrome, but not gastroenteritis. C. difficile, Shigella, and Salmonella are all common causes of diarrhea. Note: Shigella typically causes bloody diarrhea but can present with watery diarrhea initially.

The diagnosis is gonococcal pelvic inflammatory disease. What is the common sequela of this infection?
questions.explanation: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) from N. gonorrhoeae causes tubal scarring and adhesions, leading to infertility (10-20% after one episode, higher with recurrent infections) and increased ectopic pregnancy risk. Chronic pelvic pain is also common.

questions.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis prevents phagosome-lysosome fusion and blocks phagosome acidification through various mechanisms including production of ammonia and inhibition of vacuolar ATPase. This allows intracellular survival within macrophages.

questions.explanation: Bacterial capsules (e.g., S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis) are antiphagocytic. The hydrophilic polysaccharide layer prevents complement C3b deposition and blocks phagocyte receptors from binding bacterial surface, inhibiting opsonization and phagocytosis until specific anticapsular antibodies develop.

questions.question: Which of the following is not most important cause of acute bacterial meningitis?
questions.explanation: S. pyogenes (Group A Strep) rarely causes meningitis. The three most common causes of bacterial meningitis are S. pneumoniae (most common overall), N. meningitidis (especially in young adults), and H. influenzae type b (reduced since Hib vaccine).

questions.explanation: S. aureus producing TSST-1 causes toxic shock syndrome. Nasal packing creates ideal conditions for bacterial growth and toxin production. The clinical picture (fever, rash, hypotension, multi-organ involvement) is classic for staphylococcal TSS.

questions.explanation: Mucoid P. aeruginosa produces alginate exopolysaccharide that forms thick biofilms in CF patient airways. These biofilms protect bacteria from antibiotics and immune clearance, causing chronic infection. Biofilm formation is a hallmark of CF pulmonary infection.

questions.question: A 15-year-old girl develops severe watery diarrhea. The stool looks like "rice water." It is voluminous—more than 1 L in the last 90 minutes. She has no fever and seems otherwise normal except for the effects of loss of fluid and electrolytes. The most likely cause of her illness is
questions.explanation: This is cholera caused by V. cholerae producing cholera toxin ( an A-B toxin). The "rice-water" appearance, massive volume (>1L/hour possible), absence of fever, and secretory nature are pathognomonic for cholera. The A subunit ADP-ribosylates Gs protein, causing massive fluid secretion.

questions.question: The most important thing that can be done to treat the patient (Question 43) is
questions.explanation: Immediate oral rehydration therapy (ORT) or IV fluids is life-saving in cholera. Fluid replacement addresses the primary pathology (dehydration and electrolyte loss). Antibiotics (doxycycline or azithromycin) shorten duration but are secondary. Most deaths from cholera are due to inadequate rehydration.

options: Failure of HIF-1α ubiquitination in normoxic conditions
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with VHL syndrome develops multiple tumors. Which molecular mechanism explains the angiogenic phenotype in her renal cell carcinomas?
questions.explanation: ** In VHL syndrome, mutated VHL protein cannot bind and ubiquitinate HIF-1α even in normoxic conditions, leading to constitutive HIF-1α stabilization and VEGF transcription, promoting angiogenesis.
questions.correct_answer_text: Failure of HIF-1α ubiquitination in normoxic conditions

questions.question: What is the maximum diameter a tumor can reach without developing its own vascular supply?
questions.explanation: ** Tumors cannot enlarge beyond 1-2 mm in diameter without angiogenesis due to the maximal diffusion distance for oxygen, nutrients, and waste from blood vessels.

questions.question: A researcher studying tumor angiogenesis finds that proteolytic cleavage of plasminogen produces a potent angiogenesis inhibitor. Which molecule is formed?
questions.explanation: ** Angiostatin is produced by proteolytic cleavage of plasminogen. Endostatin comes from collagen cleavage, and vasculostatin from transthyretin cleavage.

questions.question: Which cell adhesion molecule acts as both an intercellular glue and transmits antigrowth signals by sequestering β-catenin?
questions.explanation: ** E-cadherin functions as an intercellular adhesion molecule and transmits antigrowth signals by sequestering β-catenin. Its function is lost in almost all epithelial cancers.

options: Mismatch repair defects with microsatellite instability
questions.question: A patient with hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer (HNPCC) develops multiple colonic carcinomas. Which genetic finding characterizes this syndrome?
questions.explanation: ** HNPCC is caused by defects in mismatch repair genes, leading to microsatellite instability (MSI) characterized by changes in length of short tandem repeating sequences throughout the genome.
questions.correct_answer_text: Mismatch repair defects with microsatellite instability

questions.question: Normal p53 induces synthesis of which angiogenesis inhibitor?
questions.explanation: ** Normal p53 induces synthesis of TSP-1, the prototypical angiogenesis inhibitor, maintaining vascular quiescence in early tumor growth.

questions.question: Which enzyme is responsible for cleaving type IV collagen in basement membranes and releasing VEGF from ECM-sequestered pools?
questions.explanation: ** MMP-9 is a gelatinase that cleaves type IV collagen of epithelial and vascular basement membranes and stimulates release of VEGF from ECM-sequestered pools.

questions.question: A patient with xeroderma pigmentosum develops multiple skin cancers after minimal sun exposure. Which DNA repair pathway is defective?
questions.explanation: ** Xeroderma pigmentosum involves defects in nucleotide excision repair, leading to inability to repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers and increased risk of skin cancers.

questions.question: Which transcription factors suppress E-cadherin expression, promoting tumor cell invasion?
questions.explanation: ** SNAIL and TWIST transcription factors suppress E-cadherin expression, leading to loss of intercellular adhesion and promoting tumor cell invasion and metastasis.

questions.question: In the Warburg effect, how many ATP molecules are produced per glucose molecule through aerobic glycolysis?
questions.explanation: ** Aerobic glycolysis produces only 2 ATP molecules per glucose molecule, compared to 36 ATP from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, yet supports rapid tumor growth.

questions.question: Which imaging modality exploits the Warburg effect to visualize tumors using 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose?
questions.explanation: ** PET scanning uses 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose, a nonmetabolizable glucose derivative, to visualize the increased glucose uptake characteristic of tumors exhibiting the Warburg effect.

options: Increases oxygen delivery AND removes immune cells
Perfusion supplies nutrients AND newly formed endothelial cells secrete growth factors
Enhances drug delivery AND reduces hypoxia
questions.question: What is the dual effect of neovascularization on tumor growth?
questions.explanation: ** Neovascularization has a dual effect: perfusion supplies oxygen and nutrients, while newly formed endothelial cells stimulate tumor growth by secreting growth factors like IGF, PDGF, and GM-CSF.
questions.correct_answer_text: Perfusion supplies nutrients AND newly formed endothelial cells secrete growth factors

questions.question: A breast cancer patient's tumor shows high expression of CXCR4 and CCR7 receptors. To which organs is this tumor most likely to metastasize based on chemokine ligand expression?
questions.explanation: ** Breast cancer cells expressing CXCR4 and CCR7 metastasize to organs highly expressing their ligands (CXCL12 and CCL21), demonstrating organ tropism through chemokine receptor-ligand interactions.

questions.question: Which DNA repair genes are mutated in familial breast cancers and are involved in homologous recombination?
questions.explanation: ** BRCA1 and BRCA2 are involved in DNA repair through homologous recombination and are mutated in familial breast cancers, increasing cancer susceptibility.

options: Lack of oxygen prevents VHL recognition of HIF-1α
questions.question: In hypoxic conditions within a tumor, what prevents HIF-1α degradation?
questions.explanation: ** In hypoxia, lack of oxygen prevents VHL from recognizing and binding HIF-1α, preventing its ubiquitination and degradation, allowing HIF-1α to translocate to the nucleus and activate VEGF transcription.
questions.correct_answer_text: Lack of oxygen prevents VHL recognition of HIF-1α

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the first step in ECM invasion by tumor cells?
questions.explanation: ** The first step in the metastatic cascade is loosening of tumor cell-to-cell contacts, primarily through loss of E-cadherin function, before cells can invade the ECM.

questions.question: What happens to normal epithelial cells when they lose adhesion to the ECM?
questions.explanation: ** Loss of adhesion in normal cells leads to induction of apoptosis, while tumor cells are resistant to this form of cell death, allowing them to survive during metastasis.

questions.question: Which syndrome is characterized by hypersensitivity to ionizing radiation due to defects in homologous recombination DNA repair?
questions.explanation: ** Ataxia-telangiectasia involves defects in homologous recombination DNA repair and is characterized by hypersensitivity to DNA-damaging agents like ionizing radiation.

questions.question: In the multistep carcinogenesis model of colon cancer, which genetic alteration typically occurs FIRST?
questions.explanation: ** In colon carcinogenesis, inactivation of the APC tumor suppressor gene typically occurs first, followed by RAS activation, then loss of chromosome 18q, and finally loss of TP53.

questions.question: What is the primary reason skeletal muscles are rarely sites of metastasis despite being well vascularized?
questions.explanation: ** Although well vascularized, skeletal muscles provide a nonpermissive microenvironment for tumor cell growth, demonstrating that vascularization alone is insufficient for metastasis.

questions.question: Which growth factor/cytokine is secreted by tumor cells to promote their own locomotion in an autocrine manner?
questions.explanation: ** Tumor cells secrete autocrine motility factors that act on themselves to potentiate and direct migration through degraded basement membranes and matrix zones during invasion.

options: They only present a static barrier to tumor cells
They exhibit altered gene expression that can promote tumorigenesis
They have no interaction with tumor cells
questions.question: What is the role of tumor-associated fibroblasts in the tumor microenvironment?
questions.explanation: ** Tumor-associated fibroblasts exhibit altered expression of genes encoding ECM molecules, proteases, protease inhibitors, and growth factors, actively participating in creating a microenvironment that can promote tumorigenesis.
questions.correct_answer_text: They exhibit altered gene expression that can promote tumorigenesis

options: It is bound by VHL, ubiquitinated, and destroyed
questions.question: In normoxic conditions, what happens to HIF-1α?
questions.explanation: ** In normoxic settings, VHL protein binds to HIF-1α, leading to its ubiquitination and subsequent destruction, preventing inappropriate angiogenesis activation.
questions.correct_answer_text: It is bound by VHL, ubiquitinated, and destroyed

questions.question: Which enzyme cleaves collagen to produce endostatin, a potent angiogenesis inhibitor?
questions.explanation: ** Endostatin is produced by proteolytic cleavage of collagen by various proteases, serving as one of the potent angiogenesis inhibitors that balance pro-angiogenic signals.

questions.question: What characterizes tumor vasculature compared to normal vessels?
questions.explanation: ** Tumor vasculature is abnormal, characterized by leaky, dilated vessels with haphazard patterns of connection, unlike the organized structure of normal blood vessels.

options: Expression of MHC class I molecules
Adhesion to leukocytes and platelets forming emboli
questions.question: Which mechanism do aggregated tumor cells in the bloodstream use to avoid immune destruction?
questions.explanation: ** Tumor cells form emboli by aggregating and adhering to circulating leukocytes and platelets, affording them protection from antitumor host effector cells during circulation.
questions.correct_answer_text: Adhesion to leukocytes and platelets forming emboli

options: It only occurs in malignant tumors
It terminates the stage of vascular quiescence allowing tumor progression
questions.question: What is the significance of the "angiogenic switch" in tumor development?
questions.explanation: ** The angiogenic switch terminates the stage of vascular quiescence, allowing tumors that were small or in situ for years to progress by acquiring blood supply through increased angiogenic factors and/or loss of inhibitors.
questions.correct_answer_text: It terminates the stage of vascular quiescence allowing tumor progression

questions.question: Which chronic inflammatory condition of the gastrointestinal tract increases cancer risk through persistent cell proliferation and DNA damage?
questions.explanation: ** Ulcerative colitis increases cancer risk through chronic inflammation causing compensatory proliferation and DNA damage.

options: By secreting reactive oxygen species causing DNA damage
questions.question: How do inflammatory cells like neutrophils contribute to carcinogenesis?
questions.explanation: ** Neutrophils and other inflammatory cells contribute to carcinogenesis by secreting reactive oxygen species (ROS), which inflict DNA damage in rapidly dividing cells during chronic inflammation.
questions.correct_answer_text: By secreting reactive oxygen species causing DNA damage

questions.question: Which enzyme's increased expression in colon cancers has led to research on its inhibitors for cancer prevention?
questions.explanation: ** COX-2 expression is increased in colon cancers and other tumors. It converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandins and is induced by inflammatory stimuli, making COX-2 inhibitors a target for cancer prevention research.

options: Some primary tumors have gene expression signatures similar to metastases before clinical metastasis
Metastasis only occurs in large tumors
questions.question: What finding challenges the traditional theory that metastasis results from random mutation accumulation in tumor subclones?
questions.explanation: ** Gene profiling studies show some breast cancers have metastasis-like gene expression signatures in primary tumors before clinical metastasis, suggesting metastatic potential may be an early intrinsic property.
questions.correct_answer_text: Some primary tumors have gene expression signatures similar to metastases before clinical metastasis

questions.question: Which paracrine factor produced by stromal cells binds to receptors on tumor cells to promote motility?
questions.explanation: ** HGF/SCF is a paracrine effector of cell motility produced by stromal cells. It binds to receptors on tumor cells and is elevated at advancing edges of invasive tumors.

questions.question: Benign tumors of the breast show little activity of which enzyme compared to their malignant counterparts?
questions.explanation: ** Benign tumors show little type IV collagenase activity, whereas their malignant counterparts overexpress this enzyme, which is crucial for basement membrane degradation.

options: Generation of novel binding sites that stimulate tumor cell migration
questions.question: What is the consequence of MMP-mediated cleavage of basement membrane proteins like collagen IV and laminin?
questions.explanation: ** MMP-2 and MMP-9 cleavage of collagen IV and laminin generates novel sites that bind to receptors on tumor cells and stimulate migration.
questions.correct_answer_text: Generation of novel binding sites that stimulate tumor cell migration

questions.question: Which oncogenes and tumor suppressors stimulate glucose uptake and favor aerobic glycolysis in cancer cells?
questions.explanation: ** TP53, PTEN, and Akt stimulate glucose uptake by affecting glucose transporter proteins and favor aerobic glycolysis (the Warburg effect).

questions.question: In the invasion-metastasis cascade, which step must occur before intravasation?
questions.explanation: ** The invasion-metastasis cascade follows a specific sequence: local invasion must occur before tumor cells can intravasate into blood and lymph vessels.

options: Act as polarized receptors maintaining cells in resting, differentiated state
questions.question: What is the primary function of integrins on normal epithelial cells in relation to the basement membrane?
questions.explanation: ** Normal epithelial cells have integrins at their basal surface for basement membrane components that help maintain cells in a resting, differentiated state.
questions.correct_answer_text: Act as polarized receptors maintaining cells in resting, differentiated state

questions.question: Which cleavage products of matrix components have chemotactic activity for tumor cells?
questions.explanation: ** Cleavage products of collagen and laminin, along with certain growth factors like IGF-I and IGF-II, have chemotactic activity that directs tumor cell migration.

options: They are reduced, tilting balance toward tissue degradation
questions.question: What typically happens to the levels of metalloproteinase inhibitors in malignant tumors?
questions.explanation: ** In malignant tumors, levels of metalloproteinase inhibitors are typically reduced, tilting the balance toward tissue degradation and facilitating invasion.
questions.correct_answer_text: They are reduced, tilting balance toward tissue degradation
